units.la: VIRIBUS TE nominibus saluto & adoro, ea Numini Majestatique Tuæ priva sunt ac propria. Etenim Dominus es, hoc est nomen tuum: gloriam tuam alteri non dabis, nec laudem tuam sculptilibus, ait in Oraculo Esaiæ Vatis, Deus Deorum & Dominus Dominantium, Cœlestis ille Imperator, qui tibi vices suas in mari & terra concessit: Sculptilibus, inquam, id est, tyrannis & pseudo-patribus, cujusmodi sunt ficti, simulati & imaginarii Præstites, qui sese super omnia, quæ Dei, id est, tua Imperatoris sunt, arroganter & superbè extollunt. Nihil impiè, nihil profane dico: recte & vere, id est, pro homine Catholico & Orthodoxo facio, qui sic de Majestate Tua sentiam. Enimvero Divus es, & hoc pacto Te cum prisci illis Christianis Imperatoribus appellare nefas esse nec beati illi veteris Ecclesiæ Patres arbitrantur: sive mavis cum Sacrosancta Scriptura Deus indigetari, Exod. 22. & Psalm. 82. Si quidem talem Te Romanis Jova Optimus maximus constituit, Exod. 7. Cujus Spiritus dixit; Denses & filius Altissimi, Psalm. 6. Et iterum; Quis similis Deo in filiis Dei? Psalm. 89. ubi Divos Imperatores vocat filios Dei, innuens indubiò eos Imperium a solo Deo immediatim tenere, ceu beneficium aliquod & secundum fidei commissarium, Daniel. 9. Proverb. 21. Deuteron. 2. in quo vices ejus visibiles (ut cum vulgo loquar) administrent, Deuteron. 17. & 1. Samuel. 17. Per quem regnare seu imperare dicuntur, Proverb. 8. & a quo cuncta illis potestas & virtus, Sapient. 6. Unde etiam Imperator dicitur Dei & Christi Vicarius in terra, Sapient 6 ubi Lyra in gloss. & Conradus II. cognomento Salicus Imp. infra sol. 230. hujus nostræ Collectionis. quin, quod magis est, Imperator a ipso Cœlesti Oraculo nuncupatur Christus Dei, ac Dominus, ut de Saule Rege 1. Reg. 24. & 26. & 2. Reg. 1. & 23. de Davide Rege, 2. Reg. 19. & 23. Psalm. 20. & 132. Denique de Cyro Imperatore Persarum, Esaiæ 45. scriptum esse legimus.
units.tr: I greet and adore Your Majesty with these titles, which are peculiar and proper to the divine majesty. For you are Lord; this is your name: you will not give your glory to another, nor your praise to graven images, says the prophet Isaiah in his oracle, the God of gods and Lord of lords, that heavenly Emperor who granted you his place on sea and land. Graven images, I say, that is, tyrants and pseudo-fathers, such as the fictitious, feigned and imaginary princes who arrogantly and haughtily raise themselves above all things that belong to God, that is, to you as Emperor. I say nothing impious or profane: I speak rightly and truly, as a Catholic and Orthodox man who thinks thus of Your Majesty. Indeed, you are divine, and the blessed Fathers of the early Church do not think it wrong to address you in this way together with those ancient Christian Emperors. Or if you prefer, Sacred Scripture calls you God, Exod. 22. and Psalm 82. For Jove, the best and greatest, has appointed you such in Rome, Exod. 7. whose Spirit said: You are gods and sons of the Most High, Psalm 6. And again: Who is like God among the sons of God? Psalm 89, where he calls the deified Emperors sons of God, clearly indicating that they hold their empire immediately from God alone, as a benefice and in the manner of a trust, Daniel 9, Proverbs 21, Deuteronomy 2, in which they administer his visible vicariate (to speak as the common people do), Deuteronomy 17 and 1 Samuel 17. Through him they are said to reign or rule, Proverbs 8, and from him all their power and strength come, Wisdom 6. Hence also the Emperor is called Vicar of God and of Christ on earth, Wisdom 6, where Lyra in the gloss, and Conrad II, surnamed the Salian Emperor, below at p. 230 of this our Collection. Indeed, what is more, the Emperor is named by the heavenly oracle itself Christ of God and Lord, as concerning King Saul, 1 Kings 24 and 26, and 2 Kings 1 and 23; concerning King David, 2 Kings 19 and 23, Psalms 20 and 132. Finally, we read that concerning Cyrus, Emperor of the Persians, it is written in Isaiah 45.

units.la: Hinc ergo est, quod Sacratissimum Te homines appellent, quasi unctum & consecratum
units.tr: Hence it is that men call you most sacred, as if anointed and consecrated

units.la: (*) 2 fecratum à Domino. Imò ipsum etiam Sanctitatis nomen in jus ac potestatem tuam tranluvit, ut Sanctus, interim etiam Sanctissimus, in tractatibus sanctorum Patrum & veterum Scriptorum passim vocitareris. Quid? Annon Tibi Imperium Sacrum, Sacra & Divalis Majestas, Coeleste Oraculum, Leges sacra & divina, sacra & divina jussiones, &c. in Jure utroque tribuuntur? Ut mihi nec sacrilegè, nec superbè fecisse prisci illi Catholici & Orthodoxi Imperatores videantur, qui titulis suis honorem Pontificis Maximi præscripserunt, quo indicarent, datam sibi potestatem à Deo Supremo Imperatore & Cœlico Monarcha, in omne hominum genus, sacrum profanum, sub Imperio suo degentium.
units.tr: (*) 2 consecrated by the Lord. Indeed the very name of holiness has passed into your right and power, so that you are called holy, and sometimes even most holy, throughout the treatises of the holy Fathers and the ancient writers. What then? Are not Sacred Empire, sacred and divine Majesty, heavenly oracle, sacred and divine laws, sacred and divine commands, etc., attributed to you in both laws? So it seems to me that those ancient Catholic and Orthodox Emperors did not act impiously or arrogantly when they put the honour of Pontifex Maximus among their titles, to indicate that the power given to them by God, the Supreme Emperor and heavenly Monarch, extends over every kind of men, sacred and profane, who live under their rule.

units.la: Quæ cùm ita sint, IMPERATOR AUGUSTE, monitu sapientissimi Israelitarum Regis Salomonis, per cujus labia Spiritus S. est profatus; Ne des alienis honorem tuum: sed vindica S. Majest. Tuæ jura ac privilegia in eos, qui usurpare & incubare conatu sacrilego ausi sunt; quemadmodum ad id impetrandum & efficiendum sacramento nexus & vadatus es. Non est mens animi nostri, nec cujusquâm (quomodo mihi persuadeo) sanimer in Imperio sapientis, ut in Pontificem Romanum grasseris, cui, ut Imperialis Tuæ Sedis & Capitalis Urbis Romanæ Archimetropolitano, & eā re summo Imperii Tui Occidentalis Antistiti atque Archipatriarchæ, eam reverentiam ac observantiā debes, quam jura legesque ἀμαθαίως ab utroque vestrum exigunt: nec ut in Ordinis Ecclesiastici libertatem, quam illibatam & intemeratam præstare verbis conceptis promisisti, violenter invehãris; multò minus ut confinium Regum, aliorumque in Sacro Imperio Principum & Statuum, justas possessiones miscendo & turbando invadas: verum ut Magnum illum Romanorum Imperatorem Pompejum imiteris, de quo Plutarchus in hunc modum scribit; Phraates Parthorum Regi per Legatos postulantis, ut Euphratem Romanæ ditionis terminum esse vellet: immò, inquit, illud magis postulandum, ut Romanorum fines à Parthorum Regno justitiâ dirimat, significans, Romanis non esse præscribendum, quousque & beant proferre Imperium, à quo propagando nô montes aut flumina debeant arcere: sed ibi demum fore fines Romanæ ditionis, ubi jus non esset ulterius procedere. Quæ igitur nullo jure aut titulo S. Majestati Tuæ, ô Imperator, sive Regio seu Imperatorio, debentur, ea non meo (quis enim ego sum, ut Christo Domini, & Domino meo consilium pethibeam?) sed Magni Pompeij judicio, nec tangere aggrediris, nec infestare, si longum Imperium & fortunam felicem à Jova Opt. Max. successibus Tuis optas. Ea verò, quæ ab sanctissimis majoribus & antecessoribus Tuis optimè constitura, & ab omnibus Imperii Ordinibus, aut majori eorum parte, consentiterque comprobata sunt, & ab aliis injustè turbata, ut jure quodâ Tuo Imperatorio iterum afferas, atque in pristinû vigorem restituas, Augustum S. Majest. Tuæ officium requirere, quod ab augendo & in majorem statū evehendo nomē possidet, videtur.
units.tr: Since these things are so, AUGUSTUS EMPEROR, following the admonition of the wisest king of the Israelites, Solomon, through whose lips the Holy Spirit spoke: Do not give your honour to others; but defend the rights and privileges of Your Sacred Majesty against those who have dared to usurp them and encroach upon them with sacrilegious attempts, as you have bound yourself by oath and pledge to secure and accomplish this. It is not the intention of our mind, nor (as I persuade myself) of anyone's in the empire of a wise man, that you should attack the Roman Pontiff, to whom, as Archmetropolitan of your Imperial See and of the Capital City of Rome, and therefore the highest bishop and Archpatriarch of your Western Empire, you owe that reverence and observance which the laws and rights require reciprocally [ἀμοιβαίως] from both of you; nor that you should violently assail the freedom of the ecclesiastical order, which you promised in your sworn words to preserve inviolate and untouched; much less that you should invade and disturb the just possessions of the neighbouring kings and of the other princes and estates in the Holy Empire. Rather, you should imitate that great Roman Emperor Pompey, of whom Plutarch writes in this manner: When Phraates, King of the Parthians, through his envoys asked that the Euphrates should be the boundary of Roman dominion, he replied: "Nay, rather, it should be asked that justice should divide the Roman frontiers from the kingdom of the Parthians," signifying that the Romans should not be told how far they must extend their empire, since they ought not to keep back mountains or rivers from its expansion; rather, the limits of Roman dominion would be found only where right could go no further. Therefore, whatever is owed to Your Sacred Majesty, O Emperor, by no right or title, whether royal or imperial, you neither touch nor attack, not by my judgement (for who am I, that I should offer counsel to the Lord's Anointed and to my Lord?) but by the judgement of Pompey the Great; and if you desire a long rule and a happy fortune, you should ask it of Jove, the best and greatest, for your successes. Yet those things which were well established by your most holy elders and predecessors, and approved by all the orders of the Empire, or by the greater part of them, and are unjustly disturbed by others, it seems to be the august duty of Your Sacred Majesty, which holds a name derived from increasing and raising the state to greater heights, to reclaim again by some imperial right of yours and restore to their former vigour.

units.la: Quod officium quibus in rebus præcipuè consistat, nemo Consiliarius S. Majestati Tuæ melius exponet, quàm muti illi Magistri, quas LEGES & CONSTITUTIONES IMPERII vocamus. Quum enim ab iis profectæ sint, qui S. Majestatem Tuam in pari eodemq; jure & gradu Augustali præcesserunt, nec corruptæ præmiis esse, nec gratiam aucuparî in assentando, nec veritatem supprimere ex timore, quem æqualis libertas & parrhsia ignorat, æstimandæ sunt. Vel eò etiam magis, quoniam Tuæ S. Majestati enitendum est profectò, ut omnes illæ Leges & Constitutiones Imperii quàm rectissimè sese habeant: in primis autem hæ, per quas (ut ait Demosthenes) parvum aut magnum licet esse Imperium tuum. Magnū licebit esse, si Principibus fortiter facientibus, aut bene præclareq; de communi salute merentibus, præmia decernas, eorumque consilio & consuetudine in Republica reformanda & gubernanda, præsertim avito Hungariæ Regno & Imperio Constantinopolitano ab infidelibus Turcis vindicando, in posterum uteris. Parvum erit, si æqualitatem inter Ordines Imperii ac Regnorum sustuleris, & sive in exteri alicujus seu Principis intestini favorem, hos non modò gratia & quotidiana conversatione, sed etiã ossiciorum ac munium publicorum diributione fovebis; illos contrà non tantùm invidia atque odio prosequeris, quæ Imperator procul habere debet, verùm etiã averfaberis, & longè ab Aula Tua semovebis atq; spernes. Hæc sunt fundamenta Constitutionum Imperialium, IMPERATOR AUGUSTE, & per eas ipsiusmet Imperii, cujus gubernationem felicissimo Tuo regimini supremus illein cœlis Imperator commisit. Unde etiam non inelegantèr & vere a peritis ac prudentibus solent Leges fundamentales Imperii Tui appellari, quibus illud ajunt ab initio institutum, auctum & stabilitum fuisse.
units.tr: In what things this duty chiefly consists, no councillor will explain to Your Sacred Majesty better than those silent masters which we call the LAWS and CONSTITUTIONS OF THE EMPIRE. For since they have come from those who preceded Your Sacred Majesty in the same equal right and Augustan rank, they must be judged neither corrupted by rewards, nor as seeking favour by flattery, nor as suppressing the truth out of fear, which equal liberty and frankness do not know. All the more so because it is certainly incumbent on Your Sacred Majesty to strive that all those laws and constitutions of the Empire be in the best possible condition; and above all those through which (as Demosthenes says) your empire may be small or great. It will be great if, when princes act bravely, or deserve well and nobly of the common welfare, you decree rewards for them, and in the future you use their counsel and advice in reforming and governing the Republic, especially in defending the ancestral Kingdom of Hungary and the Empire of Constantinople from the infidel Turks. It will be small if you abolish the equality among the orders of the Empire and the kingdoms, and if, for the favour of some foreigner or internal prince, you nourish these not only with grace and daily intimacy, but also with the distribution of offices and public duties; while you pursue those others not merely with envy and hatred, which an Emperor ought to keep far away, but also turn away from them and remove them far from your court and despise them. These are the foundations of the Imperial Constitutions, AUGUSTUS EMPEROR, and through them of the Empire itself, whose government the supreme Emperor in heaven has entrusted to your most happy rule. Hence too, not inelegantly and truly, skilled and prudent men are accustomed to call the laws of your Empire fundamental, by which they say it was instituted, increased and established from the beginning.

units.la: Earum Constitutionum præcipua capita S. Majestati Tuæ, quam paucissimis potero, non Jurisconsultorum aut explicantium more, sed relativè, brevitèr, strictim & quasi per satyram enarrabo, ut quid S. Majest. Tuæ ego nunc adoleturus venerim, etiu in speculo quodam contemplari queat. Et primum quidem caput est de Tua ac Imperii majestate, honore, dignitate, præcellentia, & auctoritate. Quæ omnia ac singula per universum hoc Constitutionum corpus sparsim & dilucidè trabitata sunt: quibusve servatis ac stantibus, felix faustumque semper fuit Imperium Tuum: & iterum neglectis ac labentibus, simul ipsum Imperium ruere, in contemptumque abire cœpit est. Vide Majores & antecessores Tuos Imperatores Augustos, Theodoricum, Clodovæum, Carolum Magnum, Arnulphum, Ottonem Magnum, Henricum I II. Fridericum I. Henricum V I. Fridericum I I. & (ut cæteros silentio præteream) propatruum tuum Carolum V. Imp. qui rebelles in Italia Ordines cum ipsa Roma in jus ac ditionem Imperii redegerunt: Turcas & Saracenos Hispaniâ, Italiâ, Siciliâ, & ipsâ adeò Syriâ expulerunt: subacta Regna Imperio Germanico conjungentes, eorum provincias & agros inter Principes ac Milites distribuerunt. Hinc illi vetè Augusti, ab augendo dicti, qui Imperium, quod lateritium acceperant, aureum posteris suis reliquerunt. Quin eo pietas quorundam processit, ut Regna hæreditariò ad se devoluta cum Imperio universo, & Reipub. Germanæ (ut plebeio verbo utar) incorporaverint, eorumque Ordines in numero Liberorum Imperii Statuum reposuerint. Quod de Ottone Primo, qui Longobardiam; de Henrico I I I. qui Burgundiam, & Regnum Arelatense; de Henrico V I. qui Siciliam & Apuliam; de Friderico I I. qui Syriam; de Carolo I V. qui Silesiam & Poloniam; de Sigismundo, qui Hungariam; de Carolo V. qui Belgium, jure uxorio conquisita, Germanico, id est, Fratertio corpori, propter antiquas Imperii prærensiones, iterum intulerunt. Quorum comitatu & beneficio tam larum & amplum Imperium factum est, ut ejus vires subinde auctæ, universo terrarum orbi tremorem incuterent. Nunc autem pudet dicere, & dicendum est tamen, ut olim Samnium in Samnio, ita & Imperium est in Imperio quærendum. In promptu causa est, quia leges, quæ de excellentia ejus latæ fuerant, sunt everst: quibus sublatis & amissis, ipsa quoque Respubl. profligetur & pereat necesse est, ut tradit Aristoteles optimus prudentiæ civilis magister, & Alexandri M. in Macedonica sive Græca Monarchia institucda auctor & cofomator.
units.tr: I will set out the chief heads of those Constitutions for Your Majesty in as few words as I can, not in the manner of jurists or commentators, but in a summary, brief, concise and almost satirical way, so that what I have now come to press upon Your Majesty may be viewed as in a mirror. The first head concerns the majesty, honour, dignity, pre-eminence and authority of Your Majesty and of the Empire. All of these, singly and together, are treated in scattered but clear passages throughout this whole body of Constitutions. While they are kept and upheld, Your Empire has always been happy and prosperous; but when they are neglected and fall, the Empire itself has begun to collapse and to fall into contempt. Look at your greater predecessors, the August Emperors Theodoric, Clovis, Charlemagne, Arnulf, Otto the Great, Henry I, II, and V, Frederick I and II, and (to pass over the rest in silence) your great-uncle Emperor Charles V, who brought the rebellious orders in Italy, together with Rome itself, back under the law and authority of the Empire; who drove the Turks and Saracens out of Spain, Italy, Sicily and even Syria; who joined the conquered kingdoms to the German Empire and distributed their provinces and lands among princes and soldiers. Hence those ancient Augusti, so named from increasing, left to their descendants an empire that they had received as one of brick, as a golden one. Indeed, the piety of some went so far that they incorporated into the whole Empire and the German commonwealth (to use a common word) the kingdoms that had fallen to them by inheritance, and placed their orders among the free estates of the Empire. This was done by Otto I with Lombardy, by Henry III with Burgundy and the kingdom of Arles, by Henry VI with Sicily and Apulia, by Frederick II with Syria, by Charles IV with Silesia and Poland, by Sigismund with Hungary, and by Charles V with Belgium, won by right of marriage, which they again brought into the German body, that is, the Fraternal body, on account of the old claims of the Empire. By their company and benefit the Empire became so wide and so great that its strength, increased from time to time, struck terror into the whole world. But now it is shameful to say, and yet it must be said, that, as once Samnium was sought in Samnium, so now the Empire must be sought within the Empire. The cause is at hand: the laws that had been passed concerning its excellence have been overturned; once these are removed and lost, the commonwealth itself must necessarily be ruined and perish, as Aristotle, the best teacher of civil wisdom, and the founder and creator of Alexander the Great's monarchy among the Macedonians or Greeks, teaches.

units.la: Alterum Constitutionum caput est, ne Jus in avulsas ab Imperio provincias neglegatur, aut temerè in usurpatores earum & incubatores privativè (ut loquuntur) & absolutè, pacto quocunque, transferatur in præjudicium Imperii. Hoc enim formulæ Legum istarum publicarū præcisè interdicunt. Ecce enim S. Majest. Tuæ ternus est in Imperio Archicancellarius; unus per Germaniam; alter per Gallias; tertius denique per Italias. Quamobrem recte atque ordine à nobis factum est, ut moreprisco dicaris Moderator Germanorum, Gallorum & Italorum. Talis namque revera habitus es jam inde à prima Imperii Germanici origine; & eos ritulos Tibi Tuisque successoribus proprios atque perpetuos esse Leges nostræ sanciverunt. Addere debebam, Pannonum quoque & Sarmatarum, nisi eos populos majoribus Tuis & antecessoribus placuisset in Germanicum jus & civitatem, officiumque Archi cancellarii Moguntiani adscribere, quemadmodum Siciliam & cæteras insulas marinas in Colonienlis, & partes Hispanicas in Trevirensis. Quod si per fatum necdū pores esse, quod dicentis, patieris æquo animo, ut exspectes occasionem temporis, quæ perturbatissimas sæpe, & afflictissimas atque desperatissimas res minimè opinantibus reconcinnavit. Et quod hodie non es, etas erit: sic Imperium tuditur. Aliorum novissima omnium merito ger-minat. Crumen paris inter primas, sita quit tempus idoneum opperiuntur rei conficiendæ, etiamsi ferint caperint, sed maturius tolficiunt. Et si nulla in re verum est dictum Græcorum illius Comici:
units.tr: The second chapter of the Constitutions concerns the need to ensure that the right over provinces torn away from the Empire is not neglected, and that they are not rashly transferred by any agreement, in a private and absolute manner (as they put it), to usurpers and squatters, to the prejudice of the Empire. The public formulas of these laws expressly forbid this. For behold, Your Sacred Majesty has three Archchancellors in the Empire: one for Germany, another for Gaul, and a third for Italy. Therefore it was rightly and properly done by us that, in the ancient manner, you should be called Ruler of the Germans, Gauls and Italians. For you have indeed been regarded as such from the very beginning of the German Empire, and our laws have sanctioned that these titles belong to you and your successors in perpetuity. I ought to add that the Pannonians and Sarmatians too would be included, had it not pleased your ancestors and predecessors to assign those peoples to German right and citizenship and to the office of the Archchancellor of Mainz, just as Sicily and the other maritime islands were assigned to Cologne, and the Spanish parts to Trier. But if by fate you are not yet able to do this, which I say, bear it with an even mind, and wait for the opportunity of time, which has often restored the most troubled, afflicted and desperate affairs to those who least expected it. And what you are not today, the age will make you. Thus the Empire is extended. The latest of all to sprout deservedly sprout. They await a suitable time to complete the business, even if they began later, but they finish more quickly. And if in no matter is the saying of that Greek comic poet true:

units.la: μεγάλῳ· ὁδὸς τα βίᾳ ζείνο
units.tr: Great is time; by time all things are done by force. [megalō· hodos ta bia zeino]

units.la: Nullus tempore melior conjunctio.
units.tr: No conjunction is better than the right time.

units.la: in re certè publica verissimum esse comperietur.
units.tr: In matters of state, certainly, it will be found most true.

units.la: Καιρὸι δὲ κατεπλύωσι τὴς τυραννίδος.
units.tr: Καιροὶ δὲ κατέλυσαν τὴν τυραννίδα. [But opportunities dissolved tyranny.]

units.la: Occasiones enim dissolvunt tot remedia,
units.tr: For opportunities dissolve so many remedies,

units.la: ut habet sententia ejusdem longè optimi Sophi, qua Imperatorem monere voluit, ut sibi notaret statum praesentis Reipubl. ejusdemque difficultatem, donec occasio rei bene gerendæ & redintegrandæ opportunam aliquam & praestabilem commoditatem obiecerit. At dicet fortasse aliquis; {a}pulchrum esse inimicos ulcisci. idneg. majus, neq; pulchrius cuiquam, atq; mihi, esse videtur: sed si liceat Respublica salva eos persequi; sed quatenus idfieri non potest, multo tempore, multisq; partibus inimici nostri non peribunt, atque uti nunc sunt, erunt potius, quàm Respublica profligetur atque pereat.
units.tr: as stated in the saying of that far best sage, by which he wished to advise the Emperor to note for himself the condition of the present commonwealth and its difficulty, until an opportunity of doing and restoring the business offers some fitting and excellent advantage. But perhaps someone will say: it is a fine thing to take vengeance on enemies. Nothing seems greater or finer to anyone, or to me, than that; but if the commonwealth can be saved while pursuing them; but since this cannot be done, our enemies will not perish in a long time and by many parts, and they will be as they now are, rather than the commonwealth be ruined and perish.

units.la: Tertia est, libertas Imperii & omnium atq; singulorum ejusdem Ordinum. {b}Agathonis Apophthegma esse memorant, Principem oportere trium meminisse; primum, quod imperet hominibus, deinde, quod secundum leges, tertiò, quod non semper imperet. Prorsus ad conditionem Imperii Germanici; cujus libertas primum cōstitit in patriæ legibus: quibus qui utitur, cum demum optimum esse Principem, sapientissimus Græcorum Bias autumabat. {c}Et Germani hoc ingenio comparati sunt, ut de Heraclitimi sententia putent, se nō minus oportere pugnare pro legibus, quàm pro mœnibus. {d}Et profecto hic fieri solet in Imperio tuo plurimis exemplis observavi, ut illis Imperatoribus & Regibus Ordines semper promptissimam obœdientiam præstiterint, qui & ipsi legibus, ad quas obstricti sunt, parere voluerunt. Et senserunt prudentissimi majores nostri, {e}sine Republica conservari nequaquam posse, ubi ex utraque parte legum fiat neglectus. Quare deliberatis consiliis statuerunt, ut partiri Imperator operas cum Ordinibus, & ex eorum usu, consulto & cōsuetudine res gerendas instituere haberet. Per mihi semper juc indum & volupe fuit legere illud, acre & mansuetum Theopompi judicium super libertate regnicolarum, quod Plutarchus, qui civilis disciplinæ palmam inter Græcos obtinet, hisce verbis refert pariter & exornat; Theopompus interrogatus, quo pacto quis Regnum tuto possit tueri? Si, inquit, amicis concedas justam libertatem, pro viribus mihi interim advigilans, ne subditi afficiantur injuria. Multis Principibus exitio fuit, quod amicis non permitterent, cives injuria affectos negligerent. Hic temperantia adhibenda est, ut Princeps nec amicos alienet tyrannica servitia, nec patiatur illos Regia familiaritate abuti ad quidvis audacium praeter jus adversus plebeios, qui nimium irritati sape reges suos excusserunt. hæc ille cordatissimus scriptor: nec inepte ad honorem ac dignitatem Cæsaris quæ longè præstantior censeri solet in libertate, quàm in servitute eorum qui parent. Hinc B. Gregorius Magnus Pontifex Romanus, in Epist. ad Phocam imperatorem noviter electum; Reformetur jam fragilis sub jugo Imperii publicas sua. Hoc namq; inter Reges gentium & Reipublicæ Imperatores differt, quod Reges gentium, domini servorum sunt; Imperatores verò Reipublicæ, demum liberorum. Procejus sanctissimi Papæ verbis, verissimè olim D. Maximilianus I. Aug. Sacræ Majest. Tuæ abavus, Princeps optimus & fortissimus, dicere solitus erat, se tanto digniorem esse Rege Franciæ, quàto digniorib. imperaret. Sc enim liberis imperare, hùc servis. Quin potestas etiā non modo amplior & augustior, verùm etiam constantior & durabilior est in libertate. Quo enim minor potestas est eorum, qui imperant, tò diuturnius stabile sive omne fiat Imperium, fait Politicorum princeps Plato Nec desunt S. Majest. Tuæ exempla Divorum antecessorum, quæ Cæsarem Celsitudini longe potius erit æmulari, quàm odiosa nescio quorum novorum hominum præcepta Namq; {f}{g}Trajanus Imper. quio PT IM I cognomen a Senatu Populoq; Romano ex mansuetudine communicavit, quum gladio præcedum Prætorio, cui nunc Electores æquiparantur, pro ritu & more solemni accingeret, ad eum dixit; Accipe hunc ensem; quo si recte gesserit, in mos leges imperare, pro me uteris, sin minus, contra me vertes. Et Hadrianum Imperatorem h̄ ferunt in Senatu Romano frequenter dicere solitum; sic gesturum Principatum, ut sciret rem populi, non suam privatam. Et Theodosius Imper. ac Valentiniamus Cæsar, revera majus Imperio esse, subiiciere legibus Principatum rescripserunt. Accedat his Pericles Atheniensium Princeps, qui quoties cunq; belli dux creatus esset, chlamydem indutus apud se dicere consuevit; Attende, Pericles, quod gesturus es Imperium in liberos, in Græcos & in Atheniensis. Hic dein se vestigia seu cordatissimus hortabatur, ut moderate gereret Principatum. Magnus inger. Ieil, addit Plutarch. imperare liberis, at Græci (ut nunc Germani) plusquam liberi tumuerunt; postremo inter Græcos oblivium Atheniensis. Et post eos Spartani, de quibus Agidis Regis dictum refert idem Plutarch. non incongruum, quod hoc loco.
units.tr: The third head is the liberty of the Empire and of all and each of its orders. They report it to be the saying of Agathon, that a prince ought to remember three things: first, that he rules over men; second, that he rules according to the laws; third, that he does not always rule. This is exactly suited to the condition of the German Empire, whose liberty rests first on the laws of the fatherland; the wisest of the Greeks, Bias, used to say that the one who uses these is at last the best prince. And the Germans are by temperament such that, following the opinion of Heraclitus, they think they ought to fight for the laws no less than for the walls. And indeed, this has been observed in your Empire, by very many examples, that those Emperors and Kings have always been given the readiest obedience by the orders who themselves wished to obey the laws by which they were bound. Our most prudent ancestors also perceived that the commonwealth can by no means be preserved where the laws are neglected on either side. Therefore, by deliberate counsel, they decided that the Emperor should share his labours with the orders, and should arrange to conduct affairs by their advice, deliberation and custom. It has always been pleasant and delightful for me to read that keen and gentle judgment of Theopompus on the liberty of subjects, which Plutarch, who holds the palm of civil learning among the Greeks, reports and adorns in these words: Theopompus, being asked how one could keep a kingdom safe, said: "If you grant your friends just liberty, watching over me as far as I can, lest the subjects be wronged." It has been the ruin of many princes that they did not permit their friends, and neglected citizens wronged. Here moderation must be applied, so that the prince neither alienates his friends by tyrannical servitude, nor allows them to abuse royal familiarity for any daring deed beyond right against the common people, who, too much provoked, have often cast out their kings. So wrote that most judicious author; nor is it inappropriate to the honour and dignity of Caesar, which is generally thought far more excellent in the liberty of those who rule than in the servitude of those who obey. Hence Blessed Gregory the Great, Roman Pontiff, in his letter to Phocas, newly elected emperor: Let the fragile public affairs be reformed under the yoke of the Empire. For this is the difference between the kings of the nations and the Emperors of the commonwealth: the kings of the nations are lords of slaves; but the Emperors of the commonwealth, of free men. In the words of that most holy Pope, Maximilian I, Augustus, your great-grandfather, a most excellent and most brave prince, used once truly to say that he was as much more worthy than the King of France as he ruled over freer men: for he ruled over free men, the other over slaves. Indeed, power is not only greater and more august but also more steady and lasting in liberty. For the less power those who rule have, the longer and more stable the whole Empire will be, says Plato, the prince of political philosophers. Nor are there lacking examples of your divine predecessors to Your Majesty, which it will be far better for Caesar's dignity to imitate than the hateful precepts of I know not what new men. For the Emperor Trajan, who received the surname Optimus from the Senate and Roman people for his mildness, when he girded on the Praetorian sword, which now is equated with the Electors, according to the usual solemn rite, said to him: Take this sword; if you act rightly with it, use it for me; if not, turn it against me. And they report that the Emperor Hadrian often used to say in the Roman Senate that he would so conduct the principate as to know that it was the affair of the people, not his private affair. And the Emperor Theodosius and Valentinian Caesar wrote in a rescript that it is truly greater for the Empire to subject the principate to the laws. To these may be added Pericles, prince of the Athenians, who, whenever he had been made commander in war, used to say to himself, clad in his cloak: Consider, Pericles, that you are going to rule over free men, over Greeks, and over Athenians. Thus that most judicious man urged himself to conduct the principate with moderation. Plutarch adds that it is a great thing to rule over free men, but the Greeks (as the Germans now do) felt more than free men; finally, among the Greeks, the Athenians were forgotten. And after them the Spartans, of whom Plutarch also reports a saying of King Agis, not unfitting for this place.

units.la: {a} Verba sunt sapientissima fuerint, Cornelia Gracchorum matris ad filium. co repetatur. Is enim à quodam interrogatus, quod disciplinæ genus post illum exercitatæ Reges Lacedæmoniorum scire, inquit, imperare, & scire imperium. O divinos Principes, & vere patriæ patres! Quos ille demum Imperator luhens merito imirabitur, qui cum animo suo reputaverit, se non modò liberis hominibus, ut Periclen, sed liberrimis Regibus ut S. Majestatis Tuæ abavus dicitare solebat, id est, Principibus atq; Ordinibus imperare, quorum famæ utilitate una in magnis negotiis tractandis & concilio ad summum Imperii decus, & excellens generositas magnanimitatis Cæsareæ culmen convenire, primum videtur.
units.tr: {a} These are very wise words of Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi, to her son. Let them be repeated. When someone asked her what kind of training the kings of Lacedaemon practised after him, she said: "to know how to command, and to know the rule." O divine princes, and true fathers of your country! The emperor who reflects on this in his own mind will rightly admire them. He will see that he rules not only free men, as Pericles did, but also the freest kings, namely the princes and estates of the Empire, as your Majesty's ancestor used to say. In handling great affairs and in counsel, the highest honour of the Empire and the excellent nobility of Caesarean magnanimity seem to meet in this one thing.

units.la: Atfine huic capuit est, pax publica. In hac enim gratia Regis extollitur & servatur, (non hæc mea sunt, sed Theodosii Imperatoris verba) si in æquitate pacis populi dirigat, & injustitia vigore conservet. Hæc enim est honoris artium mater decora; hæc mortalium genus reparabili successione multiplicans, facultates protegit, mores extollit, & tantarum rerum ignarus cognoscitur, quæ sicut munus quæsisse sentiunt. Et iterum pro causa litigantium Imperii Principum componenda sic scribit ad pares & æquales eorum Principes, quibus causam illa judicandam committit. Décet Regalis apicis Curiæ, generalitatis custodire concordiam, quæ ad laudem Regnantis trahitur, si ab omnibus pax ametur. Quid est, quod Principe melius prædicet, quam quietus populus, concors Senatus, & tota Respublica mora honestate vestitat? Et in fine Sacri mandati ad eosdem Principes: Debet enim de talibus viris (sc. Imperii Principibus, Comitibus, &c.) esse cura præcipua, qui dare possunt minoribus evidenter exempla. Nam qui inter pares summos viros lité negligit, aholendo, hoc imitari reliquos sine dubitatione permittit. O aureum dictum & Germano Imperatore dignissimum! Ille, qui absolutissima in Imperio Romano Germano habebat potestatem & omnia poterat, quæcunque volebat, non tamen licere sibi soli putabat judicium in Principes discordantes sumere, sed eorum cognitione Viris Illustribus commendat, quos consuevimus nostris moribus Pares Curiæ appellare. Ratione facto suo ipsemet Imperator assignat, nimirum hanc, quò & illis sua libertas, & pax atque concordia in Imperio conservetur. Multo plurima in care à Divis Imperatoribus & Regibus, tuis in Imperio & Regno prædecessoribus, feliciter decreta atq; sancita fuerunt, quæ ordine atq; per exempla commemorare nimis longum foret. Exinde enim tot præclarae & æternum deprædicandæ Constitutiones de Pace publica, de Pace servanda, de Manutentione Pacis, de pœna si adv. Pacem, de Pace Religiosa, & id genus aliæ cósimiles non paucæ emanarunt. Et iane, si verum dicere velimus, tota legis vis in hoc uno versatur & constitit, ut pax in Imperio conservetur ac custodiatur. Nam nec privatos foro (verbis utor Ciceronis eloquentissimi & potentissimi Romanorum Consulis) nec publicas leges, nec libertatis jura chara habere potest, quæ discordia, quæ a les erectum, quem bellum civile delectat: cuncto, ex numero hominum eucundum, ex finibus humanæ naturæ exterminandis puto. Iste, sive Sylla, sive Marius, & sive quis alius civile bellum optavit, eü detestabile civi Reipubl. natu judicat. Multi igitur hoc cive, ni hil hoc homine utrius, si aut civis aut homo habendus est, qui belli civilis corruptus. Hoc quū maximè præsenti rā afflictio & exacerbato Reipubl. Itatu, In quo dissitæ civium animi ob diversitate religionis facilè ad suspiciones, ad indignationes, denique ad arma commoveri possent. Cui malo cavere, aut mederi, nemo melius, nemo confidatius, nemo justius, quam Imperator, debeat ac potest. Diotogenes Pythagoricus fecit Philosophus, lyræ suis nervis deceter ac omnifariâ instructæ cópa-rat legibus bene constituta Rempubl. candeq; mundi pulchrâ illa harmonia imitari dicit, si Dei officiū inter homines administras Rex, aut Princeps bonus, rationis & æquitatis arte moduletur in cade, rite scilicet, ut in concentu dulce varias hominū dissentiētiū voluntates, ac discrepantes opinionū tonos cōgruceter aptet, inq; cōsensum suavissimum salutis publicæ & cōmunis utilitatis redigat. Atqui, oggi et fortean aliquis, hoc fieri nequit, stare religionū discrepātia, quartū altera prius erit eliminanda & è medio tolleda, quàm cocentus ille nervorū Reip. cógruceter aptari & cocordari possit. Errat toto cœlo (pace ipsius dixerim) quisquis hac opinione fceptus ita sentit. Præcū illud Rom. Imperiū, quo nec majus umquam nec sanctius Solillure alterū, æquis oculis intuearur. Videbit Christianos cū Gentib, & hos cū iis otiosè degere, pacifice vivere, cōveniêtes cōfuescere, côcorditer militare sub unius Principis imperio, nūc Pagano, nūc Christiano; nūc Catholico, nūc Hæretico, sine ulla injuria publica. Est enim Imperator nō Dominus animorū & cordiū, in quibus sedes resident, sed membrorū & corporū, quorū ope auxilio eget. Hortū convenientiā &c. & concordiam mutuam insti tuere habet & debet, si amare esse, quod dicitur, id est, Imperator. Potestas autem illustrandi & conciliandi animos in fide & religione, est summum Imperii Cœlestis regale, quod sibi supremus ille Imperator Jovᴀ soli reservavit, nec ejus vices Imperatori, quamquam Christo & Vicario suo immediato, in terra delegavit. Vocare, allicere, suadere, verbis, edictis, cœcionibus, præmiis potest per ministros suos Episcopos & Sacerdotes, sine cæde & sanguine, & salva interim Republica: cogere fas non est, neq; tenetur; quia res nec motu & turba publica caret, & sine periculo ac dispendio communis salutis non tentari, nedum peragi umquam potuit. Est siquidem Imperium Politia mundana & sæcularis Monarchica, ad hoc naturalem instituta, regimine aristocratico, quod omnium optimum & naturæ convenientissimum est, temperata, & Imperatori cum Electoribus cæterisq; Ordinibus Maximis, Medioximis, Minimis commendata à summo eius auctore & rectore Domino nostro Jesu Christo. Cujus hoc est divinum mandatum, Spiritus sancti ope Apostolo dictatum; Subjecti essote omni humanæ creaturæ, propter Deum; sive Regi(i.e. Imperatori Ethnico, cui tunc orbis parebat) quasi præcellenti, sive Ducibus(olim Præfectis prætorio & Prælidibus Ethnicis, nunc Electoribus ac cæteris Principibus, cujuscumque sint Religionis) tanquam ab eo missis: quia sic est voluntas Dei, ut bene(i.e. rectè) facientes obmutescere faciatis imprudentiam hominum ignorantiam, quasi liberi, & non quasi velamen habentes malitiæ libertatem, sed sicut servi Dei, &c. 1.Reg.2. Ut quietam & tranquillam vitam agamus in omni pietate & castitate, h.e. innocentia, puritate vitæ & integritate, 1.Timoth.2. Quo verbo omnia comprehendit Spiritus Sanctus, ob quæ cœlestis ille Imperator S. Majest. Tuæ vices terreni Imperii desuper concessit. Quare, qui hoc facit, quod Spiritus S. hoc loco præcipit, is me Deus, & verus civis haberi debet, & nervus concinnus in lyra Reipublicæ. Quemadmodum igitur moderatus nō occidit bestias, si absit mor-sus periculum; sic nullus Legislator (ne quidem Imperator) panam decernet contra injustos (sa-ciamus ita esse Protestantes) quiescentes, sed quoties moventur & exercent injusta opera.
units.tr: Next to this head is public peace. For in this the king's grace is exalted and preserved (these are not my words, but those of the Emperor Theodosius), if he governs the people in the fairness of peace, and preserves them by the vigour of justice. For this is the fair mother of the arts of honour; this, multiplying the human race by a repairable succession, protects the resources, raises up morals, and is known to be ignorant of such great evils as they feel to be the gift of seeking. And again, in deciding a dispute among the princes of the Empire, he writes thus to their peers and equals, to whom he entrusts the judging of the case: "It befits the court of the royal crown to keep the concord of the whole, which is drawn to the praise of the ruler, if peace is loved by all. What is there that can commend a prince better than a quiet people, a harmonious Senate, and a whole commonwealth clothed in honesty?" And at the end of the sacred mandate to the same princes: For special care ought to be taken of such men (namely the princes, counts, etc. of the Empire), who can give clear examples to their inferiors. For he who neglects a lawsuit among the leading men of equal rank, by letting it lie, without doubt allows the rest to imitate this. O golden saying, most worthy of a German emperor! He who had the most absolute power in the Roman-German Empire, and could do whatever he wished, nevertheless thought it was not lawful for him alone to take judgment against discordant princes, but commits their examination to illustrious men, whom by our custom we are accustomed to call peers of the court. By his own deed the emperor himself gives the reason: namely, that both their liberty and peace and concord in the Empire may be preserved. Very many things were happily decreed and sanctioned in matters of this kind by the divine emperors and kings, your predecessors in Empire and kingdom, which it would be too long to recall in order and by examples. From these came so many illustrious constitutions, to be proclaimed for ever, concerning public peace, the keeping of peace, the maintenance of peace, the penalty for those who act against the peace, religious peace, and not a few others of this kind. Indeed, if we are to speak the truth, the whole force of the law turns on and rests on this one point, that peace be preserved and guarded in the Empire. For neither private persons (I use the words of Cicero, the most eloquent and most powerful consul of the Romans) nor public laws nor the rights of liberty can hold dear one who delights in discord, in strife, in quarrels, in civil war; I judge him to be cast out from the number of men, and banished from the bounds of human nature. Whoever, whether Sulla or Marius or anyone else, desired civil war, that man judges to be detestable and naturally harmful to the citizen of the commonwealth. Many, therefore, in this citizen, and in nothing of this man, if he is to be counted either a citizen or a man, is corrupted by civil war. This especially, in the present affliction and exasperated state of the commonwealth, in which the minds of citizens, divided by diversity of religion, could easily be moved to suspicions, to indignations, and at last to arms. No one can guard against or cure this evil better, more faithfully, or more justly than the Emperor, who ought and is able to do so. Diotogenes the Pythagorean philosopher, comparing a well-ordered commonwealth to a lyre fitted with its strings, suitably and in every way, says that it imitates the beautiful harmony of the world, if a good king or prince, administering the office of God among men, tunes it by the art of reason and fairness, namely so that, in the concert, he fittingly adapts the sweet varied wills of the men who differ and the discordant tones of opinion, and brings them to the most pleasant agreement of public welfare and common advantage. Yet someone may say: this cannot be done while there is a difference of religions, since the one must first be removed and taken out of the way before that concert of the strings of the commonwealth can be suitably fitted and brought into harmony. Whoever thinks so in this opinion is wrong by the whole heaven (with his leave, I say it). Let him look with even eyes on that Roman Empire, than which none was ever greater or holier. He will see Christians living at leisure with Gentiles, and these with them, living peaceably, meeting together, living in harmony, serving concordantly under the rule of one prince, now a pagan, now a Christian; now a Catholic, now a heretic, without any public injury. For the Emperor is not the lord of minds and hearts, in which the seats of the soul reside, but of the limbs and bodies, whose help and aid he needs. He has and ought to establish harmony and mutual concord, if he is to be, as the word says, an emperor. But the power of enlightening and reconciling minds in faith and religion is the highest royal office of the heavenly Empire, which that supreme Emperor Jehovah reserved for himself alone, and did not delegate its exercise on earth to the Emperor, although he is the immediate vicar of Christ. He can call, attract, persuade, by words, edicts, sermons, and rewards, through his ministers the bishops and priests, without slaughter and blood, and meanwhile with the commonwealth safe; to compel is not lawful, nor is he bound to do so, because such a matter is not free from movement and public tumult, and it could never be attempted, let alone accomplished, without danger and loss to the common welfare. For the Empire is indeed a worldly and secular polity, a monarchy instituted by nature for this purpose, tempered by an aristocratic government, which is the best of all and most suited to nature, and it is entrusted to the Emperor together with the Electors and the other estates, the greater, middling and lesser, by its supreme author and ruler, our Lord Jesus Christ. This is his divine command, dictated by the apostle through the help of the Holy Spirit: Be subject to every human creature for God's sake; whether to the king (that is, the heathen emperor, to whom the world then submitted) as the one who excels, or to the governors (formerly the praetorian prefects and heathen provincial governors, now the Electors and other princes, of whatever religion they are) as sent by him: for so is the will of God, that by doing well (that is, rightly) you should silence the ignorance of foolish men, as free, and not as having liberty for a cover of malice, but as servants of God, etc. 1 Peter 2. That we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity, that is, innocence, purity of life and integrity, 1 Timothy 2. In this word the Holy Spirit comprehends all those things for which that heavenly Emperor granted from above the office of earthly empire to your Majesty. Therefore, he who does what the Holy Spirit commands in this passage ought to be regarded by me as a God-fearing and true citizen, and a well-tuned string in the lyre of the commonwealth. As a moderate man does not kill beasts if there is no danger from their bite, so no lawgiver (not even the emperor) will decree punishment against the unjust (let us suppose the Protestants to be so) who are quiet, but whenever they stir and carry on unjust works.

units.la: Postremum caput est, gravaminum Imperii blanda acceptatio, matura cogni-tio, & quoad ejus potest festina medicatio, id est, aut moderata manifestorum relaxatio, aut æqua intolerabilium abrogatio, aut saltem quorundā ninis durorum relevamen. Nam & hæc ad libertatem Imperii Germani cum primis spectare conseduntur. Inde scil. fontem esse & scaturiginem omnium publicorum malorum, quæ hactenus Sacrum Imperium quassarunt & collabefecerunt. Quibus in posterum persanandis repertum est à S. Majest. Tua promptum remedium & parabile pharmacum, nempe facilitas in audientia caussarum reorum; incunctanter largienda, pari-tas in personis acceptandis, æquabilitas in justitia, ratio qualitatis & idoneitatis in muneribus & officiis publicis distribuendis, ut S. Majestas Tua possit summos cum infimis, Catholicos & Protestantes pari jure retinere, & simul cavere, ne legibus antiquis fundatum Imperium, novis legibus evertatur.
units.tr: The last head is the gracious reception of the Empire's grievances, their careful examination, and, as far as possible, their speedy remedy: that is, either the moderate relaxation of the manifest burdens, or the fair abolition of those that are intolerable, or at least the relief of certain ones that are too harsh. For these matters are also held to concern chiefly the liberty of the German Empire. From them, namely, comes the source and wellspring of all the public evils that have hitherto shaken and overthrown the Holy Empire. For healing these in future, Your Sacred Majesty has found a ready remedy and an available medicine: namely, readiness to hear the causes of the accused, to be granted without delay; equality in admitting persons; evenness in justice; a principle of quality and fitness in distributing offices and public duties. Thus Your Sacred Majesty may hold the highest and the lowest, Catholics and Protestants, under equal law, and at the same time take care that the Empire, founded on ancient laws, is not overturned by new ones.

units.la: Hæc est summa, Imperator Auguste, si jus publicum spectes, harum Constitutionum Imperialium, quas nō Græculi leves, non alienigenæ Reges, non Protestantes Principes, multo minus inferiorum subsellium & minorum gentium Ordines, tulerunt; sed Germani illi Monarchæ Indigetes & Autochthones, gentiumque nostrarum satores & auctores, illi (inquam) majorum nostrorum m Dii majores, Reges item & Imperatores, quibus partim avito jure, (nā duodecim Romanorum Imperatores ac Reges ex Majoribus Tuis Habspurgiæ Comitibus electos suisse commemorat; quorum tametsi Rudolphum Rheinfeldium, Berchtholdum Zæringium, & Fridericum Austriacum, Ludovici Bavari æmulum, nonnulli nō re-ponat in Catalogo Romanorum Principum, tamen absque historiarū monumentis foret, latis diplomata & instrumenta eorum typaris signata fidem abundè præstarent, quibus nunc S. Majestas Tua decimus tertius accedit, partim succedaneæ electionis auctoritate in Imperio & Regno substitutus es, condiderunt. Quanto stu-dio hæc inquisita, quam diligenti indagatione investigata, quam incredibili sumptu comparata, quàm denique æruminabili labore descripta & in ordinem redacta sint, ut Imperio Tuo prodessem, norunt ii, qui me non perfunctorie noverunt. Et tamen extiterunt quidam maleteriati & facetissimi in hoc ipso tuo Imperio, cui me, meaque studia jam pridem olim devovi, vitilitigatores, qui quæ optimè optimè & sanctissimè à majoribus Tuis constituta & sancita sunt, in contumeliam atque injuriam S. Majestatis Tuæ perducere conantur. O Sacrilegos! sed præstat contemnere. Scit Tua Sacra Majestas, scimus nos omnes, quotquot sunt Tui & Sacri Imperii fideles atque obedientes, majorum Tuorum leges minimè esse contemnendas, quarum latores usque adeò sancti & pii inter mortales habiti fuerunt, ut commercium cum Diis immortalibus habuisse crediti sint, eorumque nonnulli Deorum nomen ac cultum vivendo quoque sibi comparaverint. Nam Tuisto, unde adhuc Theutones, Teutschen; Hermino, unde Chermani seu Germani; Francus, unde Franci (refero inveteratas vulgi nostratis opiniones) nuncupamur, Dei à majoribus nostris etiamtum Gentili errore infectis appellati sunt; & Clodovæus Primus, Carolomannus II. Carolus Magnus, Ludovicus Pius, Lotharius Primus, Carolus III. cognomento Crassus, Otto Magnus, Henricus II. ab iisdem majoribus nostris jam tum Christianis in Sanctorum Cœlitum numero repositi. Quod si tantum & legibus & earum latoribus à veteribus illis tributum est, nonne & nos majorum nostrorum vestigia sequentes, eas & observare & venerari debemus, illisque semper parere? Namque ad Sacri Imperii & Ordinum ejus atque Civium commune emolumentum conditæ ac perlatæ sunt.
units.tr: This is the sum, Emperor Augustus, if you look at public law, of these Imperial Constitutions, which were enacted not by flighty little Greeks, not by foreign kings, not by Protestant princes, and much less by the orders of lesser courts and minor nations, but by those German monarchs, native and autochthonous, the begetters and founders of our peoples: those (I say) greater gods of our ancestors, and likewise kings and emperors. Some of them, partly by hereditary right (for he records that twelve Roman emperors and kings were chosen from your ancestors, the Counts of Habsburg; and although some do not place Rudolf of Rheinfelden, Berthold of Zähringen, and Frederick of Austria, the rival of Louis of Bavaria, in the catalogue of Roman princes, nevertheless, even without the monuments of history, their diplomas and documents sealed with their seals would amply attest it), and partly by the authority of a later election, to whom Your Sacred Majesty, the thirteenth, now succeeds, you were installed in Empire and Kingdom. Those who have not merely glanced at me know with what zeal these things were sought out, with what diligent inquiry they were investigated, with what incredible expense they were procured, and finally with what laborious effort they were written up and put in order, so that I might serve your Empire. And yet there have been some malicious and most witty quibblers within this very Empire of yours, to which I long ago devoted myself and my studies, who try to bring into contempt and injury Your Sacred Majesty the things that were most excellently, most holily, and most sanctly established and sanctioned by your ancestors. O sacrilegious men! But it is better to despise them. Your Sacred Majesty knows, and we all know, all who are yours and faithful and obedient to the Holy Empire, that the laws of your ancestors are by no means to be despised. Their makers were thought among mortals to be so holy and pious that they are believed to have had dealings with the immortal gods, and some of them even won for themselves, while still living, the name and worship of gods. For Tuisto, from whom we are still called Theutones, Teutsche; Hermino, from whom Chermani or Germani; Francus, from whom Franci (I repeat the long-standing opinions of our common people), were called gods by our ancestors, who were then still infected with pagan error. And Clovis the First, Carloman II, Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, Lothair the First, Charles III surnamed the Fat, Otto the Great, and Henry II were already placed among the saints of heaven by those same ancestors, who were by then Christians. If such honour has been paid both to the laws and to their makers by those men of old, should not we too, following the footsteps of our ancestors, observe and venerate these laws and always obey them? For they were composed and enacted for the common advantage of the Holy Empire, its orders, and its citizens.

units.la: Verum enimvero, inquiet forte unus aliquis eorum vitilitigatorum, quos modò tetigi, vetera hæc esse, & à moribus nostris remota. Ego vero Sacræ Majestati Tuæ audacter confirmo, longè vetustiora & à moribus nostris multò esse remotiora, quæ in Corpore Juris Justiniani, quàm quæ in hac Collectione, comprehendunrur. Nam mutato Reipubl. Romanæ statu per Populum Germanum, Leges illæ Romanæ, quæ de jure publico loquuntur, pariter mutatæ fuerunt: At hæ Constitutiones fundamentales sunt Imperii Tui, quibus totus Reipubl. Germanæ status tamquam solidis quibusdam basibus firmiter innititur ac fulcitur.
units.tr: But indeed, someone among those quibblers I have just touched upon may perhaps object that these are old things, remote from our customs. I, however, boldly assure Your Sacred Majesty that those contained in the Corpus Juris of Justinian are far older and much more remote from our customs than those contained in this Collection. For when the state of the Roman Republic was changed by the German people, those Roman laws which speak of public law were likewise changed. But these Constitutions are the fundamental constitutions of your Empire, on which the whole state of the German Commonwealth rests and is supported, firmly as on certain solid foundations.

units.la: Erunt itidem alii, qui S. Majestati Tuæ persuasuri sint, obsoleta hæc jam & antiquata esse, pridemque olim in desuetudinem abivisse, nec ullum amplius usum in Imperio Tuo obtinere. Parcat mihi genius S. Majest. Tuæ, ô IMPERATOR, non patieris tibi ab infrunitis & infensatis hominibus id imaginari, quod illi frustrà sunt, dum niituntur ostentare. Dicant enim, si volunt, quibus temporibus, à quibus Imperatoribus, in quibus Comitiis vel Curiis, queis contrariis Decretis, aut receptis consuetudinibus (de communibus & generalibus loquor, non de iis, quæ à Pseudoregibus aut seductis quibusdam Ordinibus in particularibus conventiculis & conciliabulis statuta fuerunt, & à nobis quoque, ne quid eorum prætermitteremus, quæ ad statum Reip. illustrandum pertinent, in his Tomis repositæ) hæ Constitutiones, quæ generales sunt, & de quarum veritate, promulgatione ac universitate certò constat, aut sublatæ, aut abrogatæ, aut saltem derogatæ fuerint. Quod dum nullis rerum argumentis possunt evincere, sinant quæso suam Divorum majorum Tuorum & antecessorum legibus sanctitatem esse intemeratam, quarum vigorem apparet esse ex usu, commodo, honore, dignitate, atque adeò conservatione Imperii tui, sinéque quibus nec stare illud sartum tectum umquàm, nec diu poterit in suæ magnitudinis robore atque splendore perdurare.
units.tr: There will also be others who will try to persuade Your Sacred Majesty that these are now obsolete and out of date, and that they long ago fell into disuse and no longer hold any force in your Empire. May the genius of Your Sacred Majesty spare me, O Emperor. You will not allow yourself to imagine, at the suggestion of unlearned and ill-disposed men, what they are trying in vain to make appear. Let them say, if they wish, at what times, by which emperors, in which diets or courts, by what contrary decrees or accepted customs (I speak of general and common ones, not of those which were enacted by pseudo-kings or by certain seditious orders in private conventicles and conciliabula, and which I have also placed in these volumes, lest I omit anything pertaining to the illustration of the state of the Commonwealth), these Constitutions, which are general, and whose truth, promulgation and universal application are certain, were repealed, abrogated, or at least derogated. Since they cannot prove this by any evidence of the facts, let them, I beg, allow that the sanctity of the laws of your divine ancestors and predecessors remains inviolate. Their force is evident from use, from advantage, from honour, from dignity, and indeed from the preservation of your Empire, without which it could never stand whole and intact, nor for long endure in the strength and splendour of its greatness.

units.la: Confugient rursus alii ad Novellas Imperii, atque ex Recessibus & Ordinationibus novissimis tentabunt priscas illas Constitutiones eludere, in quibus ajunt diversas prorsus Sanctiones, & cum illis veteribus è diametro pugnantes reperiri. Verùm ne horum quidem ratio satis locuples & idonea fidis tuis beneficiariis censetur, quæ debeat ullo modo à S. Tua Majestate attendi; quum vanè & inaniter inventum verba fundant, & quid dicant ignorent, in tantum ut cum aëre pugnare Juris Imperialis peritis videantur. Et sanè erubescere debent, quicunque id sine legum auctoritatibus audent affirmare, juxta regulam ipsius Justinian Imperatoris traditam in Novella 18. cap. 5. Quòd enim expressè non mutatur, cur stare prohibeatur, causam non esse Divi antecessores Tui statuerunt. Itaque cum istæ Constitutiones tam veteres quàm recentes, quæ verbi gratia de potestate Imperii & Ecclesiæ, de libertate Ordinum, de Pace publica, de Comitiorum auctoritate, denique de Processu judicii Cæsarei, per Novellas in Corpus Recessuum Imperii relatas, exfertim abrogatæ aut mutatæ non legantur, sed è contrario non obscurè haud uno loco confirmari videantur, inter utrasque interpositâ interpretationem Augustæ Tuæ Majestati soli & oportet & licet inspicere, ex recepto & approbato decreto Constantini Imp. in l. 1. C. de legib. non autem judicio Cameræ, non Curiæ Rotuillanæ, non Pallantiæ Magdenburgensi, non Judicio Vehmico, non Judiciis Provincialibus, nec Curiis Principum atque Ordinum, multò minus uni alicui ex plebe Legulejorum, quamvis de jure respondendi potestatem acceperint. Nihil ergò dubito, quin Illustrissimi, Illustres ac Prudentissimi S. Majestatis Tuæ Domestici, atque Ordines Imperii, tanquam Ejusdem Majestatis perpetui Consiliarii, Novellas nostras, ut leges posteriores, ad priores illas & antiquiores Constitutiones, juxta Pauli & Tertulliani veterum Consultorum præcepta, per interpretationem tracturi sint. Etenim sic præceperunt etiam Divi prædecessores tui, Imppp. Leo, Alexander & Constantinus, Auggg. quorum hæc sunt verba; Antiquiores leges etiam ad posteriores trahi solent: scilicet ubi de interpretatione earum, non correctione agitur, ut eleganter notant Interpretes ad l. 28. D. de legibus. Et Matthæus de Afflictis, præstantissimus Italiæ suæ Consultus, & Ferdinandi Regis Catholici, abavi tui materni, Consiliarius, in facto vere & perite respondit ad hunc modum; Super isto dubio emanavit c. Imperator Lotharius, quod decidit hoc dubium in favorem patrui. ergo standum est huic decisioni. Et si dicatur, quod ista Constitutio (scil. Friderici II. Imp. per.) est posterior dicto c. Imperator Lotharius; respondeo, quod lex generaliter & simpliciter loquens recipit distinctionem & limitationem per leges veteres, ut est Glossa communiter approbata in l. sciendum, ff. qui satisfd. cogant ubi dicunt Angel. & Paul. de Castro, quod statuta nova imdistincte loquentia, non corrigant jura antiqua cum distinctione loquentia, etiamsi in talibus novis legibus dicatur; Non obstantibus quibuscunque aliis, quia debet intelligi de illis, quæ non possunt cum ipsis fe compati. Glossa est singularis in Auth. de hared. quæ ab inteft. impr. volunt Bart. in Extravag. adreprimendam, in verf. non obstantibus. Cui consentaneè scripsit Jacobus à Saa J.C. Lusitanus, & Regis Portugalliæ Consiliarius, in hæc verba; Accedat Regula posita per Paulum Consultum, quòd leges posteriores per priores recipiant declarationem & interpretationem; & priores per posteriores, quando sunt ambiguæ aut dubiæ.
units.tr: Others will again take refuge in the newer ordinances of the Empire, and from the latest recesses and regulations they will try to elude those ancient Constitutions, in which, they say, quite different sanctions are found, clashing diametrically with those old ones. But even this argument is not considered sufficiently rich and suitable to be heeded in any way by Your Sacred Majesty, your faithful servants: since they found their words in vain and empty, and do not know what they are saying, to such an extent that those skilled in Imperial law seem to be fighting with the air. Indeed, all who dare to affirm this without the authority of laws ought to blush, according to the rule laid down by the Emperor Justinian himself in Novella 18, cap. 5: "For where a thing is not expressly changed, your predecessors, divine emperors, have determined that there is no cause why it should be prevented from standing." Therefore, since these Constitutions, both old and recent, which concern, for example, the power of the Empire and the Church, the liberty of the orders, the public peace, the authority of the Diets, and finally the procedure of the Imperial court, which have been brought into the body of the Recesses of the Empire through newer ordinances, are not read as having been specifically abrogated or changed, but on the contrary seem to be confirmed in more than one place with no obscurity, the interpretation between the two must be examined by Your August Majesty alone, and it is right that you do so, from the accepted and approved decree of the Emperor Constantine in l. 1. C. de legib., and not by the judgment of the Chamber, nor the Rota court, nor the Magdeburg Pallantia, nor the Vehmic court, nor the provincial courts, nor the courts of princes and orders, much less by any one of the common crowd of legal scribblers, even though they have received the power to give legal opinions. I therefore have no doubt that the most illustrious, distinguished and most prudent members of your household and the orders of the Empire, as the perpetual counsellors of the same Majesty, will draw our newer ordinances, as later laws, toward those earlier and more ancient Constitutions by interpretation, according to the precepts of the old jurists Paul and Tertullian. For your divine predecessors, the emperors Leo, Alexander and Constantine, Augusti, likewise prescribed this, in these words: Older laws are usually drawn also to later ones: that is, where the question concerns their interpretation and not their correction, as the commentators elegantly note on l. 28. D. de legibus. And Matthaeus de Afflictis, the most distinguished jurist of his Italy and counsellor of King Ferdinand the Catholic, your maternal great-grandfather, responded in a case, truly and skilfully, in this manner: On this doubt the chapter "Emperor Lothair" was issued, which decided this doubt in favour of the uncle; therefore one must stand by that decision. And if it is said that that Constitution (namely of Emperor Frederick II) is later than the said chapter "Emperor Lothair," I reply that a law speaking generally and simply admits distinction and limitation by older laws, as the commonly approved gloss on l. sciendum, ff. qui satisfd. cogant holds, where Angelus and Paulus de Castro say that new statutes speaking indistinctly do not correct old laws speaking with distinction, even if it is said in such new laws: "Notwithstanding anything else," because it must be understood of those which cannot be reconciled with them. The gloss is singular in the Authentic de haered. quae ab intest., which Bartolus wishes to be repressed in the Extravagant, in the verse non obstantibus. Jacobus à Saa, a jurist of Lusitania and counsellor of the King of Portugal, wrote in agreement with this, in these words: Let the rule laid down by the jurist Paul be added, that later laws receive declaration and interpretation from earlier ones, and earlier ones from later ones, when they are ambiguous or doubtful.

units.la: Hæc habui, Imperator Cæsar, quibus S. T. Majestati, cui post Deum soli pecco, si quid pecco, aliquam instituti mei rationem explicarem. Tanti enim res est, ut hæc scire S. Majestatem Tuam, cui omnium actionum mearum caussas reddere, ut Domino meo, teneor, magno interfit opere. Quid namque majus aut pulchrius cuiquam, atque S. Tuæ Majestati, esse debet amplitudine, auctoritate, communitate, splendore, dignitate & integritate Imperii tui? quorum omnium aut vehementer falsi sunt omnes Sapientes, aut fundamenta sunt hæ majorum tuorum & in Imperio antecessorum divinæ sanctiones, quibus Imperium Germanum firmissimè fundatum, robustè stabilitum, longissimè prolatatum, & feliciter conservatum fuit. Nec ulli umquam Imperatores (fidem omnium Historicorum appello) aut infausiores & miseriores, aut contemptiores cùm apud subditos, tum vicinos suos Principes fuerunt, quàm qui jura Imperii sui neglexerunt. Quæ jura cujusmodi sint, ubertim hæc Collectio docet, cui pleraque omnia, quæ de jure publico à Divis antecessoribus tuis laudabiliter instituta sunt, à me fideliter inseruntur. Quæ ubi sanctissimæ memoriæ patri tuo D. Maximiliano II. & D. Ferdinando avo, & D. Carolo V. propatruo, si denique (ut alios compendiaciam) D. Maximiliano Primo abavo, Imperatoribus Augustissimis, videre contigisset, numquid non auro contrà chariora habituri fuerant? quum certum sit, constetque ex domesticis eorum Historiographis, abavum D. Maximilianum tanti æstimasse antiquitates Imperii Romani, earumque peritos interpretes, ut undiquaque perquirere, & præmiis honestissimis alere atque remunerari solitus sit. Nec minori studio D. Carolus V. propatruus bellum in Italia gesturus incubuit in jura Imperii & regalia, & eorum gnaros ac studiosos passim invitavit ingentibus promissis, quorum consilio in rebus maximè arduis, & perplexissimis uteretur. Et super D. Ferdinando avo relatum à fidedignis commemini, Constitutionem Ludovici Bavari Imp. de Juribus & Excellentia Imperii editam, & S. Majestati ejus à Seldio Cancellario prælectam, tanta cum reverentia rentia suscepisse, ut osculo admotam adoraverit. De S. Majestatis Tuæ patre, D. Maximiliano Aug.sanctissimæ & desideratissimæ memoriæ Principe, unico Imperatoriæ mansuetudinis exemplo, cujus nunc anima placidissima feliciter regnat in æterno Imperio, notior res est, quàm ut à me prolixius explicari debeat.
units.tr: I have set these things out, Emperor Caesar, so that I might give Your Sacred Majesty, to whom I owe an account of all my actions after God alone (if I owe one to anyone), some explanation of my purpose in this undertaking. The matter is of such importance that Your Majesty, to whom I am bound to give the reasons for my actions as to my own lord, has a great interest in knowing these things. For what can be greater or more splendid for anyone, and above all for Your Imperial Majesty, than the greatness, authority, unity, splendour, dignity and integrity of your Empire? All wise men would either be gravely mistaken about these, or their foundations are the divine sanctions of your ancestors who ruled in the Empire, by which the German Empire was most firmly founded, sturdily established, very widely extended and happily preserved. No emperors have ever been (I appeal to the testimony of all historians) more unlucky and wretched, or more despised both by their subjects and by neighbouring princes, than those who neglected the rights of their Empire. What those rights are, this Collection teaches at length, and into it I have faithfully inserted most of what your divine predecessors laudably established concerning public law. If your most holy father of memory, Maximilian II, your grandfather Ferdinand, your great-uncle Charles V, or finally (to pass over others) your great-grandfather Maximilian I, the most august emperors, had been able to see these, would they not have held them dearer than gold? For it is certain, and established by their household historians, that Maximilian, your great-grandfather, so valued the antiquities of the Roman Empire and its skilled interpreters that he was accustomed to seek them out everywhere and to support and reward them with most honourable prizes. With no less zeal your great-uncle Charles V, about to wage war in Italy, applied himself to the rights of the Empire and the regalian rights, and everywhere invited those who knew and studied them with great promises, so that he might use their counsel in the most difficult and perplexing matters. And I recall from trustworthy reports that concerning your grandfather Ferdinand: when the Constitution of Emperor Louis of Bavaria on the Rights and Excellence of the Empire, published and read to His Majesty by Chancellor Seld, was presented to him, he received it with such reverence that he raised it to his lips and kissed it in adoration. Concerning the father of Your Majesty, Maximilian Augustus, a prince of most holy and most longed-for memory, the unique example of imperial gentleness, whose most placid soul now reigns happily in eternal empire, the matter is too well known for me to need to explain it at greater length.

units.la: Quorum Divorum Majorum tuorum exemplo, SACRATISSIME IMPERATOR AUGUSTE, ubi S.Majest. Tuæ Sublimitas imitata, hancce meam Collectionem Imperialem placidè acceperit, & collaudandam annuerit, jam obtinuero, quod affectabam, nimirum ut S. Majestati Tuæ, Sacrove Imperio, studia mea qualiacumque comprobarem. Sin autem quid, quod ne Deus sineret, id cum ardentissimis precibus rogavi) sive S.Tua Majestas, cujus omnimodæ voluntati acjussioni cuncta mea studia venerabundus subjicio, aut ejus Illustres & Excellentissimi Consiliarii, in quorum censura & arbitrio lubens meritoque acquiescā, in hac Collectione offenderint, quod aut injurium, aut positum esse minus cōsiderate pro cōditione horum temporū videatur, illud ego nuncià pro nō dicto, nec scripto, neque posito haberi volo. Nam si quisquam est, qui sese studeat prodesse Reipub. & quàm minimè multos lædere, in eorum numero ego nomen meum primo loco profiteor. Ideoque cum salus Reipublicæ, & cunctorum ejus Ordinum, cūm in columnitate S. Majestatis Tuæ conjuncta sit, à sacro oris tui oraculo totus pendere cupio, ut quidquid Divalis tua jussio mihi super hoc negotio mandaverit, illud ego factum putarivelim. Tuus siquidem sum, ô IMPERATOR, non meus: & qui es Dominus Reipublicæ, idem etiam es corporis mei, tamquam membri cujusmodicumque, si qua fides antecessorum tuorum placitis est habenda: quibus ego quum sponte voluntatis meæ & naturali quadam in Dominum ac Imperatorem meum inclinatione, tum Spiritus sancti doctu & ductu, æquo animo assentior. Etenim data est à Domino potentia tibi, & potestas ab Altissimo, Sapient. 6. Et, ubicunque verbum (id est, mandatum, præceptum) Regis est, ibi dominatio: ecquis dicat ei, quid facis? Ecclesiast. 8. Et alibi monet B. Paulus Apostolus, tuis mandatis parēre, non solum propter iram, seu formidine pœnæ, sed etiam propter conscientiam, sive amore virtutis; Rom.13.
units.tr: Following the example of these divine ancestors of yours, most sacred Emperor Augustus, since Your Majesty's Sublimity has imitated them by receiving my Imperial Collection kindly and by consenting to commend it, I have already obtained what I was aiming at: that my studies, whatever their worth, should be approved by Your Majesty and the Holy Empire. But if anything in this Collection (which God forbid, as I have prayed with most ardent entreaties) has offended Your Majesty, to whose every will and command I humbly submit all my studies, or your Illustrious and most Excellent Counsellors, in whose judgement I gladly and rightly acquiesce, and if it appears either unjust, or stated less carefully than the conditions of these times require, I wish it to be held now as unsaid, unwritten and unpublished. For if there is anyone who strives to benefit the Commonwealth and to injure as few people as possible, I profess my own name first among them. Therefore, since the safety of the Commonwealth and of all its orders is bound up with the majesty of Your Majesty, I wish to depend entirely on the sacred oracle of your mouth, so that whatever your Divine command may have entrusted to me in this matter, I would regard as done. For I am yours, O EMPEROR, not my own; and you who are Lord of the Commonwealth are also lord of my body, as of any member whatever, if the decisions of your predecessors are to be trusted. To these I assent with an equable mind, both from my own willing inclination and natural disposition toward my Lord and Emperor, and by the teaching and guidance of the Holy Spirit. For power has been given you by the Lord, and authority by the Most High, Wisdom 6. And where the word (that is, the command, the precept) of the King is, there is authority: who may say to him, what are you doing? Ecclesiastes 8. And elsewhere the blessed Apostle Paul bids us obey your commands, not only because of wrath, that is, from fear of punishment, but also for conscience, that is, from love of virtue; Romans 13.

units.la: TE igitur huic cœpro, penes quem Dei hominumque consensus, maris ac ter-ræ regimen esse voluit, certissima salus patriæ nostræ, IMPERATOR AUGUSTE, invoco; cujus sollicitâ providētiâ Constitutiones, quas offero, benignissimè toven-tur; transgressiones earum severissimè vindicantur. Nam si prisci illi Scriptores ab Jove Cretensium Monarcha, si alii à numine suorum Principum principia traxerunt: mea parvitas cò justiùs ad favorem S. Majestatis Tuæ decurrerit, quòd illorum divinitas opinione tantùm collecta fuit; Tua verò Divalis Majestas præsenti fide paterno avitoque syderi par videtur: quorum eximio fulgore multum Imperio nostro inclytæ claritatis accessit. Deum enim verum invisibilem credimus & confidimus: Tibi ejus Vicario conspicuo adhæremus, Tibi ministeria nostra devovemus, Tibi fortunas nostras sacrificamus, qui pro S. Majestatis Tuæ Patriæque Reipubl. sospitate vitam & sanguinem fundere, si opus siet, parati sumus. Cujus mei animitestem esse volo hanc Divalium Constitutionum Collectionem; quam uti ea mansuetudine, comitate, benignitate, clementia, placiditate & moderatione accipias, qua me nomine Illustrissimorum meorum Principum solus solum differentem, in arcano tuo conclavi, supra integram horam, non modò audire, verùm etiam sacris assatibus colloqui dignatus es, id S.Majestatem tuam adorabundus ve-neror.
units.tr: To you therefore, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS, I appeal for this undertaking, you to whom the consent of God and men has willed the government of sea and land, the most certain safety of our fatherland. By your watchful providence the Constitutions I offer are most kindly protected, and transgressions of them are most severely punished. For if those ancient writers derived the origins of their princes from Jove, the Cretan monarch, and others from the divinity of their rulers, my littleness has all the more justly sought the favour of Your Majesty, because their divinity was gathered only from opinion; whereas Your Divine Majesty, by present faith, is equal to the paternal and ancestral star, by whose outstanding brilliance much illustrious glory has accrued to our Empire. For we believe in and trust the true, invisible God; in you, His visible Vicar, we cling fast, to you we devote our services, to you we sacrifice our fortunes, we who are ready, if need be, to pour out life and blood for the safety of Your Majesty and of the fatherland's Commonwealth. Of this my mind I wish this Collection of Divine Constitutions to be the witness; which I humbly pray Your Majesty to receive with the same gentleness, courtesy, kindness, clemency, calm and moderation with which you deigned, when I alone, differing from my most illustrious princes, was received in your secret chamber for more than a full hour, not only to hear me but even to converse with me with sacred words.
