units.la: ORDINES SACRI IMPERII ROMANO- GERMANI, SIVE STATUS LIBERI, QUI INTRA ANNOS CIRCITER QUADRINGENTOS CIVITATI GERMANAE ADSCRIPTI, ius suffragiorum ferendorum in Comitiis, legum condendarum generalium, tam civilium quam canonicarum, & Magistratuum adipiscendorum in Imperio, obtinuerunt. Desumpti ex Tabulis publicis, quas FRIDERICUS III. Imp Aug. in Comitiis Ratisponensibus A. C. 1471. conscribi, & in Acta Imperialia referri mandavit; nec non ex Recessibus & Matriculis (quas vocant) Imperii variis, tam veteribus quam novis.
units.tr: The Sacred Orders of the Holy Roman-German Empire, or the Free States which, from about four hundred years ago, joined the German commonwealth and obtained the right to vote in the Diets, to enact general laws, both civil and canonical, and to hold offices in the Empire. Taken from the public records which the Emperor Frederick III, August, ordered to be drawn up at the Diet of Regensburg in 1471 and entered among the Imperial Acts, and also from the various Recesses and so-called Matricula of the Empire, both old and new.

units.la: Sigismundus Imperator allaborabat, ut Ordines Hungariae cum Germanis reuniret. Itaque in Recessibus sub eo factis subscripsisse inter Ordines Imperii leguntur: Archiepiscopus Strigoniensis, qui Granensis. Archiepiscopus Colocensis. Episcopus Tragurien sis. Episcopus Agriensis.
units.tr: The Emperor Sigismund laboured to unite the Orders of Hungary with the Germans. Accordingly, in the Recesses made under him, they are read as subscribing among the Orders of the Empire: The Archbishop of Esztergom, called Granensis. The Archbishop of Kalocsa. The Bishop of Trogir. The Bishop of Eger.

units.la: Et hi quidem tanquam origine Germani, & in provincia Germanica residentes, ad decernendas gravissimas Imperii controversias adhibiti fuerunt, in quarum decisionibus atque decretis variis expresse asseritur, eas nullibi quam apud Germanos Principes, jure & stylo Germanico esse judicandas & determinandas. Hinc etiam Archiepiscopus Strigoniensis, tanquam Germanici Imperii Princeps, receptus est in Archiepiscopum finitimum Salisburgensem. Et Praepositus Strigoniensis fuit Aulae Caesareae Vicecancellarius in Imperio simul & Regno. Sed & Agriensis Episcopus Recessui Nurembergensi, Anno 1431. inter Germaniae Episcopos subscripsit.
units.tr: And these indeed, being Germans by origin and residing in a German province, were called upon to decide the most serious controversies of the Empire; and in the decisions and decrees on these matters it is expressly asserted in various places that such matters are to be judged and determined nowhere else than before German princes, under German law and procedure. Hence also the Archbishop of Esztergom, as a Prince of the German Empire, was received as a neighbouring archbishop of Salzburg. And the Provost of Esztergom was Vice-Chancellor of the Imperial Court, in the Empire and the Kingdom at once. Moreover, the Bishop of Eger subscribed the Recess of Nuremberg in 1431 among the bishops of Germany.

units.la: Episcopi Angliae numquam proprio suo nomine in Comitiis Imperii comparuerunt, sed Regis sui locum & personam semper repraesentarunt, tanquam Legati & Mandatarii.
units.tr: The bishops of England never appeared at the Diets of the Empire in their own name, but always represented the place and person of their King, as legates and proxies.

units.tr: The Abbess of Säckingen, who is of Seckingen, in Rheinfelden on the Rhine.

units.la: Duces.
units.tr: Dukes.

units.la: Bavariæ Inferioris Dux.

units.la: Britanniæ Dux in Gallia.

units.la: Carinthiæ Dux.

units.la: Falckenbergensis Dux in Silesia.
units.tr: The Duke of Falkenberg in Silesia.

units.la: Holsatiæ Dux.

units.la: Lovvenburgiæ Dux in Saxonia. Lucenburgiæ Dux. Lunenburgiæ Dux. Mafovia Dux in Polonia. Maffæ Dux, qui Matriculis est, von Maffa / Politicographis von der Moß. units.tr: The Duke of Löwenburg in Saxony. The Duke of Luxemburg. The Duke of Lüneburg. The Duke of Masovia in Poland. The Duke of Massa, who is in the matrices, von Massa, but in the political writers von der Moß. The Duke of Mecklenburg, or Megalopolis. The Duke of Meran. The Duke of Münsterberg in Silesia. The Duke of Ratibor in Silesia. The Duke of Ratzenil in Lithuania: who nevertheless is not summoned to the Diets, because apart from a bare title he holds nothing from the Empire as a fief. The Duke of Steinau in Silesia. The Duke of Styria. The Duke of Stormarn. The Duke of Strehlen in Silesia. The Duke of Swabia. The Duke of Teck in Swabia. The Duke of Teschen in Silesia. The Duke of Troppau in Silesia. The Duke of Valdemont in Lorraine. The Duke of the Wends, or of the Vinidi. The Duke of Breslau in Silesia. The Duke of Westphalia. The Duke of Württemberg. The Duke of Wolgast in Pomerania. The Duke of Zbarazh in Russia: about whom, however, I have noted nothing in the Imperial Acts, except that the Emperor writes to him: To the illustrious Prince, our faithful and beloved of the Holy Empire. The Duke of Zeringen. The Duke of Znaim in Moravia, von Znaim.

units.la: Landgravii, qui sunt Principes.
units.tr: Landgraves who are Princes.

units.tr: The Landgrave of Alsace. The Landgrave of Thuringia. The Landgrave of Hesse. The Landgrave of Leuchtenberg. The Landgrave of Franconia.

units.tr: The Margrave of Meissen. The Margrave of Ostland, that is, of Eastern Meissen. The Margrave of Landsberg. The Margrave of Moravia. The Margrave of Lusatia. The Margrave of Bautzen. The Margrave of Görlitz. The Margrave of Baden. The Margrave of Hachberg. The Margrave of Rötteln.

units.tr: The Margrave of Cham, who is also of Vohburg, in Bavaria.

units.la: Marchio Hiflria.
units.tr: The Margrave of Istria.

units.la: Marchio Burgovia.
units.tr: The Margrave of Burgau.

units.la: Marchio Segufianus, qui nunc Suzenfis, ad pedes montium Italiæ.
units.tr: The Margrave of Segusia, now called Saluzzo, at the foot of the Italian mountains.

units.la: Marchio Stadenfis in Saxonia.
units.tr: The Margrave of Stade in Saxony.

units.tr: The Margrave of Antwerp, who is commonly called of the Holy Roman Empire.

units.la: Marchio Nummeniæ in Lotharingia.
units.tr: The Margrave of Nomeny in Lorraine.

units.la: Marchio Franchimontii in Belgio.

units.la: Marchio Pontamuffoni in Lotharingia.
units.tr: The Margrave of Pont-à-Mousson in Lorraine.

units.la: Marchio Salutarum, inter Germaniæ Senatores receptus fuit, sub Ludovico Bavaro Imperatore.
units.tr: The Margrave of Saluzzo was received among the Senators of Germany under the Emperor Louis of Bavaria.

units.la: Principes, simpliciter sic dicti.
units.tr: Princes, so called simply.

units.la: Princeps Delphinatus, vel Delphinus Viennensis, qui est Primogenitus Franciæ.
units.tr: The Dauphin of Viennois, or Dauphin of Vienne, who is the eldest son of France.

units.la: Princeps Anhaltinus.
units.tr: The Prince of Anhalt.

units.la: Princeps Hennenbergia.
units.tr: The Prince of Henneberg.

units.la: Princeps Rugiæ.
units.tr: The Prince of Rügen.

units.la: Princeps Cabillonensis in Burgundia, vulgò, de Chalon vel Schalon.
units.tr: The Prince of Chalon in Burgundy, commonly called de Chalon or Schalon.

units.la: Princeps Aureatensis, qui nunc Vraniæ vel Orangia, in Aquitania, inter Germaniæ Senatores cooptatus fuit, sub Ludovico Bavaro Imperatore.
units.tr: The Prince of Orange, who is now called Vraniæ or Orange, in Aquitaine, was admitted among the Senators of Germany under the Emperor Louis the Bavarian.

units.la: Princeps Sedani vel Effedani in Gallia.
units.tr: The Prince of Sedan or Effiat in France.

units.la: Princeps Pedemontii, ad pedes montium Italiæ.
units.tr: The Prince of Piedmont, at the foot of the mountains of Italy.

units.la: Princeps Veronæ & Vincentiæ.
units.tr: The Prince of Verona and Vicenza.

units.la: Princeps Sueviæ.
units.tr: The Prince of Swabia.

units.la: Princeps de Chinay in Belgio, qui tamen nunquam suo nomine Comitiis interfuit.
units.tr: The Prince of Chimay in Belgium, who nevertheless never attended the Diet in his own name.

units.la: Princeps Arenbergiæ in Belgio.
units.tr: The Prince of Arenberg in Belgium.

units.la: Princeps Rofenbergiæ in Bohemia.
units.tr: The Prince of Rosenberg in Bohemia.

units.la: Princeps Transfylvaniæ in Hungaria; quem appono, quia Serenissimus Sigismundus Princeps nuper mihi confirmavit, fe ab Imperatore omnia jura sedendi & suffragandi in Comitiis nactum esse, quæ cæteri Imperii Principes habent.
units.tr: The Prince of Transylvania in Hungary; I add him because His Serene Highness Sigismund, Prince, lately confirmed to me that he has obtained from the Emperor all the rights of sitting and voting in the Diets that the other Princes of the Empire have.

units.la: Waivvoda Valachia | sunt inter Principes Imperii allecti, sed sub patronio Principis Transylvaniæ, à quo eximuntur. Waivvoda Moldavia | Quanquam id in præsentia ipsius supradicti Principis, me rogante, illustrissimi Dominus Caspar Waivvoda Valachiæ negaverit, asserens Principatui Valachico esse eadem jura ab Imperatore concessa, quoad suffragia & dignitates consequendas, quæ ipsi Serenissimo Transylvano.
units.tr: The Voivodes of Wallachia | are admitted among the Princes of the Empire, but under the patronage of the Prince of Transylvania, from whom they are exempt. The Voivode of Moldavia | Although the most illustrious Lord Caspar, Voivode of Wallachia, denied this in the presence of the aforementioned Prince, at my request, asserting that the Wallachian principality has been granted by the Emperor the same rights as to votes and the attainment of dignities as the Serene Prince of Transylvania himself has.

units.la: Princeps Mansfeldia: qui tamen morte præventus nihil principaliter in civilibus Imperii negotiis gessit, dignitate cum persona extincta.
units.tr: The Prince of Mansfeld: who, however, anticipated by death, did nothing as a prince in the civil affairs of the Empire, the dignity having become extinct with the person.

units.la: Princeps Liechtensteini, qui putatur ab Ordinibus recipiendus.
units.tr: The Prince of Liechtenstein, who is thought to be one the Estates ought to receive.

units.la: Burggravius Magdenburgensis.

units.la: Burggravius Misnensis.
units.tr: The Burgrave of Meissen.

units.la: Hannoniæ Comes & Princeps.

Schinensis Comes. †
units.tr: Count of Ortenburg in Bavaria, now called the Older Counts of Ortenburg, in respect of those created by Emperor Charles V, who live under the Austrians; but they are not counted among the free and imperial orders. units.la: CORPUS SACRI IMPERII ROMANO--GERMANI, IN SUA MEMBRA ET OFFICIA QUADRIPERTITUM, quorum Status ex cunctis totius Imperii Occidentalis Gradibus & Ordinibus, cùm in eum modum auæti essent, ut difficilè & nimis impendiosum foret in unum omnes convocari, rerum publicarum deliberandarum, & legum generalium sanciendarum causa, delecti fuerunt, ut vice cæterorum omnium consultarent.
units.tr: THE BODY OF THE HOLY ROMAN-GERMAN EMPIRE, DIVIDED INTO ITS MEMBERS AND OFFICES INTO FOUR PARTS. Since the Estates of all the degrees and orders of the whole Western Empire had grown so numerous that it was difficult and too expensive to convene them all together for deliberating public affairs and enacting general laws, some were chosen to deliberate in place of all the rest.

units.la: IV. Electores Ecclesiastici, {Papa Romanus, S.Rom. Imperii Archipatriarcha Oecumenicus seu Vniversalis. Archiepiscopus Moguntinus, S. Rom. Comes Palatinus Rheni, S. Rom. Imperii Archidapifer. Dux Saxoniae, S. Rom. Imperii Archimarescalcus. Marchio Brandenburgiae, S. Rom. Imperii Archicamerarius.} IV. Reges: Die vier Hohen Königreich: Romanorum. Francia. Polonia. Hungaria. IV. Patriarchae: Romanus. Constantinopolitanus. Aquilegiensis. Ravennas. hi duo successe-runt in vicem Orientalium: Alexandrini. Antiocheni. IV. Primates: Magdeburgensis. Lugaunensis. Strigoniensis. Gnesnensis. V. Cancellarii: Toletanus per Hispaniam. Cantuariensis per Britanniam. Strigoniensis per Pannoniam. Gnesnensis per Sarmatiam. IV. Archiepiscopi: Salisburgensis. Rhemensis. Mediolanensis. .........
units.tr: IV. Ecclesiastical Electors: {The Roman Pope, Oecumenical or Universal Archpatriarch of the Holy Roman Empire. The Archbishop of Mainz, Archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire through Germany and the Slavic lands. The Archbishop of Trier, Archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire through the Gauls and the Kingdom of Arles. The Archbishop of Cologne, Archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire through Italy and the islands of the sea.} IV. Lay Electors, who by decree of Emperor Sigismund are Archprinces: {The King of Bohemia, Archcupbearer of the Holy Roman Empire. The Count Palatine of the Rhine, Archsteward of the Holy Roman Empire. The Duke of Saxony, Archmarshal of the Holy Roman Empire. The Margrave of Brandenburg, Archchamberlain of the Holy Roman Empire.} IV. Kings: the Four High Kingdoms: of the Romans, France, Poland, Hungary. IV. Patriarchs: Rome, Constantinople, Aquileia, Ravenna. These two succeeded in place of the Eastern ones: Alexandria, Antioch. IV. Primates: Magdeburg, Lyon, Esztergom, Gniezno. V. Chancellors: Toledo for Spain, Canterbury for Britain, Esztergom for Pannonia, Gniezno for Sarmatia. IV. Archbishops: Salzburg, Reims, Milan. .........

units.tr: c These four are confirmed by the authority of the Saxon Mirror and the Magdeburg Wichbild. IV. Valiant Counts, which some also call Heregraves: Flanders, Tyrol, Altenburg, Ferrara; perhaps Ferreti, that is, Pfirdt. IV. Provincial Lords: Mirandola, Ocala, that is, Verona, Padua or Padua, Milan. IV. Abbots: Fulda, Kempten, Weissenburg, Murbach. IV. Houses: Austria, Saxony, Brunswick, Bavaria. IV. Islands: Sicily, England, Sweden, Cyprus. IV. Soldiers or Knights, the Four Knights, by others Hereditary Knights: Angers, Meldingen, Strundeck, Frauenberg; in whose places were substituted Weissbach in Meissen and Karlwitz in Meissen. IV. Marshals, the Four Chief Marshals: Bappenheim, Jülich, Meissen, Finstingen; by others, Freising. IV. Ambacts or Ministerials, the Four Servants or Officials: Meissen, according to Albinus in the Chronicle of Meissen, folio 321; Rheinfelden, according to Stumpf in the Chronicle of Helvetia, book 12, chapter 12 at the beginning. IV. Advocates, the Four Land-Advocates or Land-Vogts: Meissen, according to Albinus, loc. cit. IV. Hunters, the Four Chief Huntsmen: Carinthia, according to Münster in the Cosmography, folio 690, at the beginning. IV. Lower Hunters: Forni or Hurni, Frachi, Schomburg, Metsch in Rhaetia Curiensis. IV. Hereditary Officials, the Four Hereditary Offices: Waldburg, Steward; Radach, Cupbearer; Markdorf, Marshal; Kemnat, Chamberlain. IV. Servants or Ministerials, the Four Servants: Waldeck; Hirten of Fulch, by others Herren of Filchen; Arnsberg or Arensberg; Rabnau or Rabenau. IV. Hereditary Stewards, the Four Hereditary Seats: Wellerswalde, according to Albinus, folio 321; ......; ......; ...... IV. Cooks, that is, Masters of the Kitchen, the Four Hereditary Kitchen-Masters: Seldeneck; ......; ......; ...... IV. Inaugural Cities, the Four Coronation Cities: Aachen; Arles; Milan; Rome. IV. Imperial Cities, the Four Principal Cities: Augsburg; Aachen; Metz; Lübeck. IV. Royal Cities, the Four Royal Cities: Naples; Paris; Kraków; Buda, by others Copenhagen. IV. Electoral Cities, the Four Electoral Cities: Prague; Heidelberg, by others Amberg; Wittenberg; Küstrin. IV. Trading Cities, the Four Trade Emporia: Marseille; Mainz, now Frankfurt; Venice; ...... now Antwerp, or Amsterdam. IV. Burgi, that is, Fortified Towns: Altenburg; Magdeburg; Rothenburg on the Tauber; Mecklenburg, by others Luxembourg. IV. Villages, the Four Country Villages: Bamberg; Ulm; Hagenau; Selestadt. IV. Hamlets, the Four Small Towns: Ingelheim; Altdorf, by others Altrip; Liechtenau; Dinkelsbühl, by others Deckendorf. IV. Villae, the Four Hamlets: Orlamünde, according to Albinus folio 321; ......; ......; ...... IV. Mountain Towns, that is, Mountains, the Four Mountains: Münsterberg; Friedberg; Heidelberg; Nuremberg. units.la: LECTORI CANDIDO ET BENEVOLO.
units.tr: To the Candid and Kindly Reader.

units.la: On dubito fore plerosq; , Lector Candide & Benevole, qui hoc genus Collectionis leve, & non satis dignum Constitutionum Imperialium nominibus judicent, quum relata legent Tuistonis instituta, & Herminonis, & Franci, & ejusmodi consimilia, de quorum fide & auctoritate parum constans & incerta fides est. Sed hi erunt fere, qui expertes rerum publicarum, ne dicam bonae mentis, nihil rectum, nisi quod ipsorum distorto judicio conveniat, putabunt. Hi, si didicerint, Leges non demonstrationibus constare, sed opinionibus, atq; ad usum & commodum hominum singulorum esse inventas, easq, solis majorum initiatis judicati, non admirabuntur, nos in Monarcharum nostrorum constitutionibus colligendis opiniones vulgares esse secutos. Nam ad Tuistonem (sic enim apud Tacitum est legendum) & Herminonem, &c. auctores, constantissimo omnium Historicorum consensu referuntur, quae nos ex Aventino & Trithemio Abbate verbatim excripsimus: no quod ita esse at bitraremur, sed quia summis illis viris sic visum fuisse videbam, ut primam legum nostrarum originem ad Deos referrent, more caeterarum nationum. Etenim apud Aegyptios quoque Minos legum Mercurium auctorem finxit, Minos apud Cretenses Jovem, Lycurgus apud Lacedaemonios Apollinem, Zamolxis apud Getas Vestam, Numa Pompilius Romanorum Rex a Dea Aegeria, vel (utali volunt) ab una ex Musis leges accepisse dicitur. Et semper persuasio seu Divinitatis vel Sanctitatis visa fuit habere singularem & prope unicam energiam in obedientia hominum, qui nulla re magis quam religiositate moveri possunt. Si quid autem in veris Imperatorum & Regum nostrorum Constitutionibus dubietatis occurrerit, de qua certior fieri cupias, facies (mi Lector) ut ex te refescam; & dabo operam, ut tibi omnem objectum scrupulum ex animo expectorem ruo, tibi; fidem & integritatem meam ita comprobem, quo ex incerto fias certissimus. Interim vale, & opera mea (si placet) utere.
units.tr: I do not doubt, kind and gentle reader, that many people will judge this sort of collection to be slight and not sufficiently worthy of the name of Imperial Constitutions, when they read the reported institutions of Tuiston, Hermino, Franco and similar things, whose trustworthiness and authority are little established and uncertain. But those who will do so are mostly people who, having no experience of public affairs, not to say sound judgment, think nothing is right except what agrees with their own distorted opinion. If they have learned that laws rest not on demonstrations but on opinions, and that they were devised for the use and advantage of individual men, and are judged only by those initiated into the greater mysteries, they will not be surprised that in gathering the constitutions of our Monarchs I have followed common opinions. For Tuiston (for so it must be read in Tacitus), Hermino and others are cited as authors by the most constant agreement of all historians; these things I have copied word for word from Aventinus and Trithemius the Abbot. I did not do so because I thought them true, but because I saw that those very great men judged it fitting to trace the first origin of our laws back to the gods, in the manner of other nations. For among the Egyptians too, Mercury was imagined as the author of laws; among the Cretans, Jupiter was imagined as the author of Minos's laws; among the Lacedaemonians, Apollo of Lycurgus's; among the Getae, Vesta of Zamolxis's; and Numa Pompilius, king of the Romans, is said to have received his laws from the goddess Egeria, or, as some prefer, from one of the Muses. And the conviction that a thing is divine or holy has always seemed to have a singular and almost unique force in winning men's obedience, since nothing moves men more than religious feeling. If, however, any doubt arises about the true Constitutions of our Emperors and Kings, and you wish to be more fully informed, please (my reader) ask me, and I will take care to clear from your mind every scruple that troubles you, and I will so vouch for my good faith and integrity that you may pass from uncertainty to full certainty. Meanwhile, farewell, and make use of my labour (if you wish).
