units.tr: MARQUARDUS FREHERUS, COUNSELLOR OF THE ARCHPALATINE ELECTORATE, IN his Commentary on the Constitution of Emperor Adolf.

units.la: Curiis Caesarum, quae rogante Caesare, & pro tribunali sedente, liberrimo ordine suffragiis in commune ferebantur Leges, aut super quaestionibus ex facto ortis sententiae accebantur, legis vim & ipsae habituraa, & similium deinceps cansarum fata composita: u: Imp. Theodosius loquitur l. 3. C. de legib.) eas non inepte Curiatas indigitare possumus; non eo quidem sensu, quo olim Curiata apud Romanos Comitia dicebantur, sed tamen a Curiis nihilominus nomen trahentia. Atque utinam hoc genus Curiata, quarum in tot Curiis per alias saecula magnum numerum natum esse credibile est, plures emergerent. non dulcis remus eas eodem loco habere, quo Neapolis illas Caesarum Orientalium, de quibus recuperatis habet res litterarias, juncta gratulentur; & quo Extravagantes pauculas Friderici & Henrici, quas Corpori juris adjicere, & illustris commentariis, amplissimus illustrare dignata est superior aetas. Mallem usque certe etiam dubiis & controversis quaestionibus in foro obortis, decisionem e talibus petere, quam e nefas quibus Consultoribus & rhapsodis.
units.tr: The courts of the Caesars, in which laws were passed by free vote in common, the Caesar presiding from the tribunal and requesting it, or in which judgments were given on questions arising from facts, and which themselves came to have the force of law, so that the fates of similar cases were afterwards settled by them (as the Emperor Theodosius says in l. 3 C. de legibus), may not unfitly be called Curiatae. Not, indeed, in the sense in which the Curiate assemblies were once called such among the Romans, but still deriving their name from the Curiae all the same. And would that more of this kind of Curiatae had come forth, of which, as is credible, a large number was produced in so many curiae over other ages! I would not be unwilling to place them in the same position as those of the Eastern Caesars, which the recovered literature of Naples rejoices to possess, and which the Neapolitan writers have joined together; and in the same position as the few Extravagantes of Frederick and Henry, which the later age deigned to add to the body of law and to illustrate with learned commentaries. Yet I would certainly prefer to seek decisions from such Curiatae even in doubtful and controversial questions arising in the courts, rather than from those wicked consultants and rhapsodists.

units.la: TUISCONIS MONARCHÆ GERMANORUM ET SARMATARUM
units.tr: Tuisco, Monarch of the Germans and Sarmatians

units.la: LEGES ET INSTITVTA.
units.tr: Laws and Institutions.

units.la: ACERDOTIBVS duntaxat animadvertere, vincire, verberare permisit : non quasi in pœnam, aut Ducis iussu, sed velut Deo imperante.
units.tr: He allowed only the priests to admonish, bind and beat, not as a punishment or by the Duke's order, but as if God himself commanded it.

units.la: 1. Virorum fortium facta, quæ exemplum posteris essent, carminibus celebrare instituit.
units.tr: 1. He arranged that the deeds of brave men, which were to serve as examples for posterity, should be celebrated in songs.

units.la: 3. Lucos & nemora, in quibus res divina perpetraretur, consecravit. Arbitrabatur, cœleste numen pro magnitudine sua, nec parietibus cohiberi, nec in ullam humani oris vultusque fluxæque rei speciem adsimulari debere : cùm secretum illud ab omni contagione secis terrenæ sola reverentia videatur, cuius effigiem formamque quærere, imbecillitatis sit humanæ.
units.tr: 3. He consecrated groves and woods in which the divine rites were performed. He held that the heavenly power, because of its greatness, ought neither to be confined within walls nor made to resemble any human face or form, or any perishable thing; for that secret being, free from all earthly contamination, seemed to be honoured only by reverence, and to seek its image and shape belonged to human weakness.

units.la: 4. Auspiciorum fortiumque disciplinam edocuit, ex quorum observatione Sacerdos publicè priùs Deum precatus, cœlum suspiciens, futuros eventus interpretetur.
units.tr: 4. He taught the discipline of auspices and omens, by whose observation the priest, having first prayed to God publicly and looking up to the sky, would interpret the future events.

units.la: 5. Iussit & ædificia magis necessaria pro cœli iniuria vitanda, quam ambitiosa, extruere ; oppida condere parva, attamen munitis natura locis.
units.tr: 5. He also ordered them to build dwellings, more necessary for avoiding the harshness of the sky than showy, and to found small towns, yet in places fortified by nature.

units.la: 6. Qui inter suos ius dicerent, Principes regionum atque pagorum constituit ; controversiasque minuere præcepit.
units.tr: 6. He appointed princes of regions and of districts to give judgment among their own people, and he commanded that disputes be reduced.

units.la: 7. Nulli certum modum agri, aut fines proprios habere permisit : sed Magistratus ac Principes in annos singulos gentibus cognationibusque hominum, qui unà coierunt, quantum eis, & quo loco visum erat, attribuebant agri : atque anno post, alio transfire cogebant, ne latos fines parare studerent, potentioresque humiliores possessionibus expellerent : neve accuratius ad frigora atque æstus vitandos ædificarent, ne qua oriretur pecuniæ cupiditas. qua ex re factiones, dissensiones nascerentur, ut animi æquitate plebem continerent, cum suas quisque opes cum potentissimis æquari videret.
units.tr: 7. He did not allow anyone to have a fixed measure of land or his own boundaries. Instead, the magistrates and princes assigned each year to the tribes and families of men who had come together as much land as seemed fit to them and in whatever place; and a year later they compelled them to move to another, so that they would not strive to acquire wide boundaries and drive the poorer from their holdings by the more powerful, nor build more carefully to ward off cold and heat, lest a greed for money should arise. By this means factions and dissensions would be born, whereas he wished to keep the common people contented by equality of spirit, since each saw his own resources made equal to those of the most powerful.

units.la: 8. Victum & amictum parabilem comparari iussit, ut quæ in lacte, caseo, carne, pellibus, & parvis rhenorum tegumentis consisterent.
units.tr: 8. He ordered that food and clothing be provided that could be easily obtained, consisting of milk, cheese, meat, skins, and the small hides of reindeer.

units.la: 9. Adulteria præsenti pœna cohibuit : nulla publicatæ pudicitiæ venia.
units.tr: 9. He restrained adultery with immediate punishment; there was no pardon for a publicly exposed chastity.

units.la: 10. Ab parvulis duriciæ ac labori studere sobolem præcepit, ut qui diutissimè impuberes permanerent, maximam inter suos ferrent laudem. hoc ali staturam, ali hoc vires, nervosque confirmari putabat.
units.tr: 10. He taught that the offspring from childhood should strive for hardship and toil, so that those who remained unmarried for the longest time would bear the greatest praise among their people. He thought this made the stature grow, this gave strength, and this strengthened the sinews.

units.la: 11. Intra annum vicesimum fœminæ noticiam habuisse, in turpissimis haberi iussit rebus, quò fera iuvenum ætas, eoque inexhausta pubertas foret : nec virgines festinarentur, sed eadem iuventus, similis procueritas, pares validiqúe miscerentur, ut robora parentum liberi referrent.
units.tr: 11. He ordered that a woman who had known a man before the twentieth year be held in the most shameful disgrace, so that the youth of the young men would remain wild and their puberty unexhausted; and the virgins were not to be hurried into marriage, but the same youth, of similar height, equal and strong, were to be joined together, so that the children would bring back the strength of their parents.

units.la: HERMINONIS MONA- RCHÆ GERMANORUM
units.tr: Of Hermin, Monarch of the Germans

units.la: LEGES ET INSTITVTA.
units.tr: The Laws and Institutions.

units.la: DISCIPLINAM militarem instituit, remque militarem ita colere docuit. Quotannis aliquot millia armatorum bellandi causa suis ex finibus educebantur. reliqui, qui domi remanserant, se atque illos alebant. Hi rursus invicem anno post in armis erant : illi domi remanebant. Sicque neque agricultura, neque usus belli intermittebatur.
units.tr: He established military discipline and taught them to cultivate the art of war. Each year several thousand armed men were led out of their own territories to wage war. Those who had stayed at home supported themselves and those men. The following year these in turn were under arms, while the others remained at home. In this way neither farming nor the practice of war was ever interrupted.

units.la: 1. Mercatoribus dabat ad subditos aditum magis eò, ut quæ bello ceperant, quibus venderent, haberent, quàm quò ullam rem ad se importari desiderarent.
units.tr: 1. He gave merchants access to his subjects chiefly so that they would have buyers for the goods they had taken in war, rather than because he wanted any goods imported to him.

units.la: 3. Vinum ad eos omninò importari non sinebat, quòd care ad laborem ferendum remollescere homines atque effœminati arbitrabatur.
units.tr: 3. He did not allow wine to be imported to them at all, since he judged that it made men soft and effeminate and less able to endure labour.

units.la: MARCOMIRI. I. REGIS FRANCORUM
units.tr: MARCOMIRUS I, KING OF THE FRANKS

units.la: INSTITVTVM DE MONARCHIA IMPERII FRANCICI.
units.tr: THE INSTITUTION CONCERNING THE MONARCHY OF THE FRANKISH EMPIRE.

units.la: ANNO Regni sui xx. Marcomirus Rhenum transgressus, cum Gallis Cisrhenanis bellum habuit, plures occidit, terram occupavit, quam fratri Sunnoni tuendam, ut Duci vel Subregulo, commendavit.
units.tr: In the twentieth year of his reign, Marcomirus crossed the Rhine and waged war against the Cisrhenane Gauls; he killed many, occupied the land, and entrusted it to his brother Sunno to hold, as a duke or sub-king.

units.la: ANTHENORIS. I. REGIS FRANCORUM
units.tr: ANTHENOR, FIRST KING OF THE FRANKS

units.la: CONFIRMATIO INSTITVTI MARCOMIRIANI.
units.tr: THE CONFIRMATION OF THE MARCOMIRIAN INSTITUTION

units.la: ANNO Anthenoris xii. Sunno patruus eius obiit, qui reliquit duos filios, Marcomirum & Hectorem; quorum primus in Rheno obiit, secundus loco patris sub Rege Anthenore Comitatum administravit trans flumen Rheni. Primus a fratre Anthenore Rege constitutus est Princeps terrae Septentrionalis, quam noviter acquisierant, id est, circa mare Germanicum. Ex his multi Principes sunt nati, per successum temporis, quorum Hunibald plures commemorat, alii Duces, alii Comites, sed omnes sub nutu permanebant unius Regis.
units.tr: In the twelfth year of Anthenor, his uncle Sunno died, leaving two sons, Marcomir and Hector. The first died on the Rhine; the second, in his father's place and under King Anthenor, administered the county across the River Rhine. The first was appointed by his brother, King Anthenor, as prince of the northern land, which they had newly acquired, that is, the region around the German Sea. Many princes were born from these in the course of time. Hunibald records several of them: some were dukes, others counts, but all remained under the nod of one king.

units.la: 1. Reliquit Sunno & alios quatuor filios, ex quatuor aliis concubinis procreatos, qui non computantur inter Duces, lege Sicambrorum vetante, quae interdixit liberis de prima uxore superstitibus, filios sequentium Principes vel esse vel nominari, quam legem b Cambra ludit Regina, ne Regnum confunderetur.
units.tr: 1. Sunno also left four other sons, born of four other concubines. These were not counted among the dukes, because the law of the Sicambri forbade that the sons of later unions be, or be called, princes while those of the first wife survived. Queen Cambra eludes this law, so that the kingdom would not be thrown into confusion.

units.la: BASANI REGIS FRAN- CORUM
units.tr: King Basanus of the Franks

units.la: LEGES ET INSTITVTA.
units.tr: Laws and Institutions

units.la: REGIS imperio nemini contradicere etiam in minimo licebat sub poena mortis indubitata.
units.tr: By the king's command, no one was allowed to contradict him, even in the smallest matter, on pain of certain death.

units.la: 2. Reltem seu funem, ubicunque pergebat, sibi anreferri iussit, & gladium, in signum iustitiae, quam adeo tenaciter servabat, ut nec filio, nec fratri, nec Principibus, nec Ducibus, imo nulli parceret, qui vel modicum contra legem aequitatis, quam posuerat, commisisset.
units.tr: 2. Wherever he went, he had a halter or rope carried before him, and a sword, as a sign of justice. He kept justice so strictly that he spared neither son, nor brother, nor princes, nor dukes, nor indeed anyone who had committed even a slight offence against the law of equity he had laid down.

units.la: 3. Rapinam, furtum, adulterium, dolum, fraudem, & omnem iniuriam sive contumeliam in ter Sicambros fieri sub poena mortis lege notavit, omnesque vel parum in his contra legales sanctiones peccantes, sine aliqua misericordia punivit.
units.tr: 3. He decreed by law that robbery, theft, adultery, deceit, fraud, and every injury or insult among the Sicambrians should be punished by death. He punished without any mercy all who sinned even slightly against these legal sanctions.

units.la: 4. Filium habuit iuvenem nomine Sedanum. Hic cum iuvenili concupiscentia abstractus, cum uxore cuiusdam viri humilis conditionis perpetrasset, quod lege patris novit prohibitum, accusatus a marito foeminae iudicatur ad mortem. Et cum Proceres rogarent pro filio, pater respondit; Non ego te fili occido, sed lex, quam sciens praevaricatus es. apprehensumque filium propria manu truncavit.
units.tr: 4. He had a young son named Sedanus. Carried away by youthful desire, he committed adultery with the wife of a man of low condition, which he knew his father's law forbade. Accused by the woman's husband, he was judged to die. When the nobles begged for the son, the father replied: "It is not I, son, who kill you, but the law which you knowingly broke." Then, seizing his son, he beheaded him with his own hand.

units.la: 5. Accurrens mater truncati adolescentis lachrymans & furens contra Regem intemperantia muliebri exagitata clamavit: O crudelis tyranne, non Rex, qui crudelitatem sub legis titulo exercet, quomodo parces aliis, qui proprium filium interemisti? Cui Rex coram omni populo dixit: Mulier tuum est obedire marito, Regi non exprobrare. Juro tibi per Deum meum Saturnium Jovem, quoniam nisi essem ira commotus, & te hac ipsa interficerem hora, quae mihi semper fuisti charissima. Post dies octo Rex iudicio Principum & Procerum Regni mulierem repudiavit, & ad patrem Regem Orchadarum remisit.
units.tr: 5. The mother of the beheaded young man ran up, weeping and raging against the king, and, goaded by womanly intemperance, cried out: "O cruel tyrant, not a king, who exercises cruelty under the name of law! How will you spare others, you who have slain your own son?" The king answered her before the whole people: "It is a wife's duty to obey her husband, not to reproach the king. I swear to you by my god Saturn Jove that, were I not moved by anger, I would kill you this very hour, you who have always been most dear to me." Eight days later, by the judgment of the princes and nobles of the realm, the king repudiated the woman and sent her back to her father, the king of the Orkneys.

units.la: 6. Sacra renovavit, Sacerdotes in templo Jovis constituit, viros Graece & Germanice doctissimos in vaticinio, in somnis, in iudicio stellarum, in ethicis, in physicis, & in metaphysicis, qui consilium sanum & rectum Diis inferentibus, dare possent cunctis interrogantibus eos in quacunque necessitate.
units.tr: 6. He restored the sacred rites and appointed priests in the temple of Jove, men most learned in Greek and German lore: in prophecy, dreams, the judgment of the stars, ethics, physics and metaphysics. They were to give sound and right counsel, with the gods inspiring them, to all who consulted them in any necessity.

units.la: 7. Rege, qui summus erat Pontifex, absente, penes Sacerdotes summa decretorum erat potestas, persona Regis excepta, in quam non iudicabant.
units.tr: 7. When the king, who was the chief pontiff, was absent, the highest power in decrees rested with the priests, except for the person of the king, whom they could not judge.

units.la: 8. Ad templum Palladis Veneris&que; Tritoniae Deae solas virgines constituit Sacerdotes, ad quas certis temporibus ingredi viris passim cunctis licebat, uxoribus non copulatis, & agere in templo Veneris, quod ipsum nomen eius sonat. Quæcunque sacerdos tali concubitu concepisset, fœtum Palladi offerebat non occidendum, sed perpetuò ad serviendum. Qui ex his talibus Tritonicæ sacerdotibus consecutus fuisset uxorem, post puerperium sanctus & Diis proximus laudabatur. Post primum partum unaquæque templum deferre cogebatur, quia iam Veneri suam pudicitiam sacerdos mater obtulit, & cui voluisset nubere potuit.
units.tr: 8. He appointed only virgins as priestesses in the temple of Pallas, of Venus and of the goddess Tritonia. At certain times men of every sort were freely admitted to them, though they were not joined in marriage, and they were to act in the temple of Venus, as the very name of the place implies. Whatever priestess conceived by such intercourse offered the child to Pallas, not to be killed but to serve for life. Any of these Tritonian priestesses who afterwards obtained a husband was praised, after childbirth, as holy and near to the gods. After her first delivery, each was compelled to bring her child to the temple, since the priestess-mother had already offered her chastity to Venus, and she could marry whomever she wished.

units.la: CLODOMERI. I. REGIS FRANCORUM
units.tr: CLODOMER I, KING OF THE FRANKS

units.la: RESCRIPTVM AD GALLOS TERRAM occupatam repetentes.
units.tr: A RESCRIPT TO THE GAULS WHO DEMAND BACK THE LAND THAT HAS BEEN OCCUPIED

units.la: CLODOMER Rex Magnus, Sarrapis & populis Gallicanis. Miramur de vestra temeritate, quòd terram à nobis quæsitis recipere, quam progenitores nostri olim à vestris iure belli, sicut ab inimicis suis, à quibus multas acceperunt iniurias, iusta vicissitudine obtinuerunt. Cogitate vires vestras nostris impares, & eessate ab hac temeritate vestra. Quòd si contra nos venire vultis, statuimus vobis non fructi animis occurrere, & defensare gladio, quod gladio maiores nostri acquisiverunt.
units.tr: Clodomer, great king, to Sarrapis and the Gallic peoples. We marvel at your recklessness, in that you seek to recover the land which our forefathers long ago obtained from your people by the right of war, as from their enemies, from whom they had suffered many wrongs, by a just turn of fortune. Consider that your strength is unequal to ours, and cease from this recklessness of yours. But if you wish to come against us, we determine to meet you not in vain, and to defend with the sword what our ancestors won by the sword.

units.la: ANTHENORIS. II. REGIS FRANCORUM
units.tr: Anthenor, the Second King of the Franks

units.la: LEX DE NON IMMOLANDIS HOMINIBVS.
units.tr: A LAW ON NOT SACRIFICING MEN

units.la: PROHIBUIT homines & filios hostium, Diis immolari. Quæ constitutio, quia Sacerdotum consilio & assensu decreta fuit, inviolabilis permansit.
units.tr: He forbade that men and the sons of enemies be sacrificed to the gods. This enactment, because it was decreed by the counsel and assent of the priests, remained inviolable.

units.la: FRANCI REGIS FRANCORUM
units.tr: FRANCIS, KING OF THE FRANKS

units.la: EDICTVM DE NOMINE FRANCORVM.
units.tr: EDICT CONCERNING THE NAME OF THE FRANKS.

units.la: POPULUS Regem postulavit & Principes, quatenus perpetuo sancirent edicto, se non amplius Sicambros vocari, sed Francos. Placuit hæc postulatio Regi, utpote qui nominis sui cupieret immortalitatem consequi, & suo gentem vocabulo insigniri.
units.tr: The people asked the king and the princes that they would by a lasting edict decree that they should no longer be called Sicambri, but Franks. This request pleased the king, since he desired to gain immortality for his name and to have his people distinguished by his own title.

units.la: CLOGIONIS. I. REGIS FRANCORUM
units.tr: Clogio, King of the Franks, I.

units.la: REPETITIO INSTITVTI DE MONARCHIA Francica.
units.tr: A repeated account of the institution concerning the monarchy of the Franks.

units.la: ANNO Regni sui X. Clogio Rex filium suum secundogenitum, nomine Phrisum, ad instantiam matris & Principum, Ducem constituit illius regionis, quæ postea ex nomine eius dicta est Phrisia usque in præsentem diem contra Cimbrorum & Orchadum incursiones.
units.tr: In the tenth year of his reign, King Clogio, at the urging of his mother and the leading men, appointed his second-born son, named Phrisus, as duke of that region, which afterwards took its name from him and is called Phrisia to this day, against the incursions of the Cimbri and the Orkneymen.

units.la: 2. Post annos X. permittente CLOGIONE Rege cunctisque Francorum Proceribus, Phrisus in Regem fuit sublimatus, ea tamen conditione, ut Reges Phrisiæ omnes, sicut & reliqui Duces, Regi Francorum perpetuò manerent subiecti, & ut tributum Francis penderent annis singulis boves CCLX. butyri pure talenta x x. & caseorum Regalium tria milia; & cum Francis more caeterorum amicorum, contra hostes quoscunque dimicarent.
units.tr: 2. Ten years later, with King Clogio and all the nobles of the Franks permitting it, Phrisus was raised to the kingship, on this condition: that all the kings of Phrisia, like the other dukes, should remain forever subject to the king of the Franks; that they should pay the Franks each year as tribute 260 oxen, ten talents of pure butter and three thousand royal cheeses; and that, in the manner of the other friends of the Franks, they should fight alongside them against any enemies whatever.

units.la: HERIMERI REGIS FRANCORUM LEX DE NEGLIGENTIA DU- CUM, & eorum pœna.
units.tr: Law of Herimer, King of the Franks, concerning the negligence of dukes, and their punishment.

units.la: IN potestate Ducali constitutus sub Rege Francorum Princeps, diligenter provinciam tueatur sibi commissam. Quod si cuius negligentia hostes terram nostram vastando invaserint & gentem laeserint, aut si rebus spoliaverint incolas terrae, marsupio Regis communi dimidium pendat bonorum suorum, & amplius ne sit Dux Princeps, sed privatus vivat honore. Si velens introitum hostibus permisit, sepeliatur vivus, aut capite plectatur, & uxores cum liberis & bonis rebusque omnibus Regis ministerio cedant.
units.tr: Let a prince who has been placed in ducal authority under the King of the Franks guard diligently the province committed to him. But if, through anyone's negligence, enemies invade our land, laying it waste and harming the people, or plunder the inhabitants of the land of their goods, let him pay half of his possessions into the common treasury of the King, and let him no longer be a duke or prince, but live as a private man without honour. If he knowingly allowed the enemy entry, let him be buried alive or be punished by beheading, and his wives with their children, together with all his goods and property, shall pass into the King's service.

units.la: CLOGIONIS. II. REGIS FRANCORUM
units.tr: Of Clogio, the second King of the Franks

units.la: FILIIS HELENO ET RICHIMERO MIN- ORENNIBUS, in Regno fuit pralatus patruus eorum CLODOMER, quia
units.tr: To the sons Helenus and Richimer, who were still minors, their uncle Clodomer was preferred in the kingdom, because

units.la: LEge Francorum erat interdictum, ne quis promovetetur in Regem, priusquam quartum atque vicesimum complevisset annum aetatis.
units.tr: By the law of the Franks it was forbidden that anyone should be promoted to king before he had completed his twenty-fourth year of age.

units.la: CLODOMERI. II. REGIS FRANCORUM & Procerum Regni
units.tr: Clodomer II, King of the Franks, and the Nobles of the Kingdom

units.la: RESCRIPTVM AD PETITA TVRIN- GORUM auxilia contra Su- evos.
units.tr: A Rescript in Reply to the Request of the Thuringians for Aid against the Suevi.

units.la: DUce a Genebaldo fratre nostro charissimo referente, dudum intelleximus, quae fuerit inter vos, amici Doringi, & Suevos causa dissidii, & earum, quae hodie foribus instant, occasio turbationum. Vobis nos ex multo fatemur tempore confoederatos, & ius contracti violare foederis nec volumus quidem ullatenus, nec debemus. Sed vos ipsi luce iam clarius, optime Doringi, cernitis, in quantis Regnum Francorum versetur periculis, quoniam nobis Romani cum Gallis quotidie praesoribus imminent, diligentissime observantes introitum nostrum, simul exitum, si quaelibet occasione Regnum queant subvertere nostrum, quod progenitores nostri, multa sanguinis effusione vix tandem acquisitum stabilire potuerunt. Propterea cautum Francorum nequaquam est visum consilio, his praesertim periculosis temporibus, populum dividere, neglectisque propriis alienia defensare, cum ad alterum Duis propinquantibus forsan possimus sufficere; utrumque autem, hoc est, nostrum Regnum & vestrum his diebus ab hostium incursione tueri nostra non sit in potestate. Nimia denique locorum distantia nos plurimum impedit, ne vobis contra Suevos tam crebro possimus conferre suffragium, cum illi principium Rheni fluminis teneant & ortum, nos vero ultima ostia & occasum. Veruntamen ne vobis omnino videamur defuisse amicis, nostro consilio placuit, ut Nuncios ad Suevos dirigamus nostros atque Legatos, per quos triennales rursum vobis indutias obtinearmus & treugas. Interea consilium habeant Doringi, ut cum Suevis vel pacem consequi valeant aeternam, vel alio quocunque medio necessarium defensionis murum interponant, hoc est, vel ex suis vel ex alienis gentibus amicis.
units.tr: Having learned from our dearest brother Genebald, who was leading the embassy, what cause of quarrel lay between you, friend Doringus, and the Suevi, and what occasion of disturbance now presses upon our doors, we have been informed. We confess that we have been bound to you in alliance for a long time, and we neither wish nor ought in any way to violate the terms of the agreement we have made. But you yourselves, most excellent Doringus, see more clearly than light what dangers the kingdom of the Franks is in, since the Romans and the Gauls, our governors, hang over us daily, watching most carefully our every entrance and exit, so that by any chance they might overthrow our kingdom, which our forefathers, after much effusion of blood, could scarcely acquire and at last manage to establish. For this reason it has not seemed prudent to the Franks, least of all in these perilous times, to divide the people and, neglecting what is our own, to defend what belongs to others, since we may perhaps be able to suffice for the one while the enemy is approaching; yet to guard both, that is, our kingdom and yours, against the incursions of the enemy in these days is not within our power. Finally, the great distance between our lands greatly hinders us, so that we cannot so often bring you aid against the Suevi, since they hold the source and beginning of the river Rhine, while we hold its last mouths and its setting. Nevertheless, lest we should seem to have utterly failed you as friends, it has pleased us by our counsel to send to the Suevi our messengers and envoys, through whom we may obtain for you a renewed truce and armistice for three years. Meanwhile let the Doringi take counsel, so that they may either secure a lasting peace with the Suevi, or by whatever other means interpose a necessary wall of defence, that is, either from their own peoples or from friendly foreign nations.

units.la: DAGOBERTI. I. REGIS FRANC- ORUM, DUCUM POPULIQUE REGNI
units.tr: Dagobert I, King of the Franks, Dukes and People of the Kingdom

units.la: RESCRIPTVM AD VALENTINIANVM IMPER. RO- MANORUM, tributa exigentem, pro libertate Francorum.
units.tr: Reply to Valentinian, Emperor of the Romans, who demanded tribute, on behalf of the liberty of the Franks.

units.la: FRancorum sempiterna libertas tributum imponere nationibus caeteris consuevit, non solvere. Tu autem, qui robore Francorum absente, cum paucitate inermi pugnasti, & dolo non fortitudine vicisti, si te à Francis exigendi tributum ius habere confidis, veni cum volueris, & gladio nos liberrimos & esse semperque fuisse, & te servum ostendemus. Histe facimus certiorem, ne super hac re quenquam ad nos mittas inermem, quippe qui vitam potius dare contendimus, quàm perdere libertatem.
units.tr: The everlasting liberty of the Franks is accustomed to impose tribute on other nations, not to pay it. But you, who, when the strength of the Franks was absent, fought with a small and unarmed force and conquered by trickery rather than by courage: if you trust that you have the right to exact tribute from the Franks, come when you wish, and we will show with the sword both that we are most free and have always been so, and that you are a slave. We make this known to you so that you do not send anyone to us on this matter unarmed, since we are determined to give up our lives rather than lose our liberty.

units.la: GENSERICI REGIS ET IMPERA- TORIS CARTHAGINENSIS
units.tr: Genseric, King and Emperor of Carthage

units.la: CONSTITVTIO DE PRIMOGENITVRA REGNI.
units.tr: Constitution on the Primogeniture of the Kingdom

units.la: GIzericus iam senex decedens testamentum condidit, in quo quum alia multa Vandilis mandaret, tum ut per manus eius Regni successores illi propinquiori ex genere virili prolis traderentur, & ex his qui aetate praecederent.
units.tr: Genseric, already old, made his will when dying, in which, while he charged Vandil with many other things, he also directed that the kingdom's successors should be handed over by his hand to the nearer male descendant of his line, and from among those who were older in age.

units.la: THEODORICI REGIS AV- GUSTI ROM. LEGES.
units.tr: The Laws of Theodoric the King, Augustus of the Romans.

units.la: IUBEMUS milites cum Romanis civiliter vivere: Provincias ab incursione hostili defendere.
units.tr: We command the soldiers to live together with the Romans in a civil manner, and to defend the provinces from hostile incursion.

units.la: 2. Ducibus imperamus, ut armis creditos populos tutentur: abstinentiam iusticiamque sectentur, aemulenturque veterum Romanorum prudentiam, uti Provinciales plane intelligant atque sentiant, eos à Principe Romano datos esse Rectores.
units.tr: 2. We instruct the dukes to protect the peoples entrusted to them by arms, to pursue abstinence and justice, and to emulate the prudence of the ancient Romans, so that the provincials may plainly understand and feel that they have been given rulers by the Roman Prince.

units.la: THEODORICI REGIS AVGU- STI ROM. SACRA
units.tr: Letter of King Theoderic, Augustus of the Romans

units.la: AD BURGUNDINORUM, HERCULORUM, VARINORUM, & Turogorum Reges; pro pace & mutua auxilii unitate adversus aemulum Imperii Francorum Regem.
units.tr: To the kings of the Burgundians, Heruli, Varini and Thuringians, for peace and a mutual union of aid against the rival king of the Franks of the Empire.

units.la: PRINCEPS absque iustitia nil aliud profecto est, quàm gentium latro publicus. Quippe ubi leges regi, non regere solet, pro iure libido & licentia invadit, maliciosus, fallax, versutus, sapiens nominatur: calliditas & astutia, prudentia appellantur; pro aequitate superbia, pro abstinentia avaritia, pestilia vitia sub specie virtutum dominantur. Ambae pestes invident, rapiunt, opprimunt, aliorum opibus inhiant, omnes pro hoste ducunt, cuncta sibi servire adpetunt.
units.tr: A prince without justice is truly nothing other than a public robber of nations. Where the law is ruled not by rule but by lust, and licence takes the place of right, the man is called malicious, deceitful, crafty, and clever; cunning and astuteness are called prudence; pride passes for fairness, avarice for self-restraint, and these pestilent vices hold sway under the appearance of virtues. Both plagues envy, seize, oppress, covet the wealth of others, count everyone an enemy, and seek to make everything their slave.

units.la: 1. Hac via nuper ATTILA gradiatus, etsi Visigotarum robore fractus, furoris tamen sui heredem & successorem reliquit Ludovicum Regem Francorum, qui iam pridem (ut est natura mortalium avida imperii, & praeceps ad explendam animi cupiditatem) animo Imperium orbis invasit, & tantos sibi spiritus, tantam sibi arrogantiam sumpsit, ut neminem secum dignitate exaequari velit. Alarico Visigotarum Regi, cura affinitatis affectum, vinculo societatis, fidei sacramento violato, nefandum & impium indixit bellum. Nemini dubium esse potest, quin superatis Gothis, signa victricia in vos convertat.
units.tr: 1. Lately Attila walked this path, and although he was broken by the strength of the Visigoths, he nevertheless left as heir and successor to his fury Louis, King of the Franks. Long ago Louis, as the nature of mortals is greedy for empire and headlong in satisfying the desire of the mind, had already invaded in spirit the empire of the world, and had taken to himself such spirit and such arrogance that he wishes no one to be his equal in dignity. Alaric, King of the Visigoths, though bound to him by the tie of kinship, he has attacked with an unspeakable and impious war, violating the bond of alliance and the sacred oath of faith. No one can doubt that, once the Goths are overcome, he will turn his victorious standards against you.

units.la: 3. Enricus genitor Alarici non solùm opibus, pecunia, stipendiis vos adiuvit, verùm etiam ab hostium imperio & oppugnatione defendit: vires Romanas à cervicibus vestris avertit. Obsecro itaque atque obtestor per ea beneficia, ut cum amicis meis, vestri quoque ad Francos, Ludovicum Q. legentur, qui verbis omnium nostrum, ut pote maximorum, & opulentissimorum Regum, nuncient, velle & censere, eos ab armis discedere, ita seque illisque dignum esse.
units.tr: 3. Enricus, the father of Alaric, not only helped you with resources, money and pay, but also defended you from the power and assault of enemies; he turned the Roman forces away from your necks. I therefore beg and entreat you, by those benefits, that along with my friends, envoys from you also be sent to the Franks, to Louis, who shall declare in the words of all of us, as the greatest and most wealthy kings, that they wish and judge that the Franks should lay down their arms, and that this is fitting for themselves and for those kings.

units.la: ANASTASII IMP. AUG. ET THEODORICI REGIS AUG. ROM. LEGATIO
units.tr: The Embassy of Anastasius, Augustus Emperor, and Theodoric, Augustus King, of Rome

units.la: AD THEODONEM DUCEM ET CAETEROS Bavarie Proceres; ut se Imperio Romano subiciant.
units.tr: To Duke Theodo and the other nobles of Bavaria, urging them to submit to the Roman Empire.

units.la: ETSI Imperatores Romani, rerum praesides, rectoresque mundi, iniuriae contumeliaeque haud temere oblivisci antur, & his duntaxat, qui promeruerint, amicitiam dare consuevere, sanctissimus atque felicissimus Imperator ANASTASIUS Caesar Augustus, memor rerum humanarum, nec ignarus ludi fortunae, & quod illi, qui aliena iniuste invaserunt, Deo optimo maximo poenas reddiderunt, gratiam facit, pacem & societatem ultro vobis, ô Boii Proceres, offert: provinciam, quam occupaftis, licet armis & ferro recuperare facile esset, ut humano parcatur sanguini condonat. Vos in clientulos accipit, Reipublicæ Romanæ socios asciscit, quos omnibus viribus defendere ac rutabitur, atque ab iniuriis Barbarorum adseret. Pro his beneficiis, sicuti certæ pignus amicitiæ, sane exiguum est, quod postulat, annuum nimirum munusculum. Quid stolidius est, quàm quæ citra periculum comparare possis, malle sanguine vestrorum tentare, & incerta pro certis ample Cti: Consuevit Deus summus & immortalis, quò gravius ex commutatione rerum homines doleant, his secundiores interdum res concedere. Nemo igitur compos mentis victoriâ insolenter gloriari solet. Quàm fragiles, quàm incertæ sint res humanæ, quotidie videmus: ipsæ sæpius in adversa commutantur, & tum maximè, ubi quæ ultrò offertur secunda fortuna fordescit.
units.tr: Although the Roman emperors, the governors of affairs and rulers of the world, are accustomed not to forget injuries and insults lightly, and are wont to grant friendship only to those who have earned it, the most holy and most fortunate Emperor Anastasius Caesar Augustus, mindful of human affairs and not ignorant of the game of fortune, and of how those who unjustly seized what belonged to others have paid the penalty to God, best and greatest, grants you his favour and freely offers you peace and alliance, O nobles of the Boii. He pardons the province you have occupied, though it would be easy to recover it by arms and steel, so that human blood may be spared. He takes you on as clients and enlists you as allies of the Roman commonwealth, and he will defend you with all his strength, take care of you, and protect you from the wrongs of the barbarians. In return for these benefits, as a sure pledge of friendship, what he asks is indeed small: merely an annual little gift. What could be more foolish than to risk your people's blood, and to grasp at uncertain things instead of certain ones, when you could obtain the latter without danger? God, the supreme and immortal, is accustomed to grant more favourable circumstances to some men at times, so that they may grieve all the more deeply when the situation changes. Therefore no one of sound mind is wont to boast insolently of victory. We see every day how fragile and uncertain human affairs are: they are often changed into adversity, and especially when a favourable fortune that is freely offered comes to be held cheap.

units.la: 1. Proinde ne quid temerè committatur, Dux vester Theodo cum paucis ad Theodericum in Italiam proficiscatur; ibi de communibus negociis consultabitur. Nihil esse æquius ac utilius, nemo vestrum est, qui inficias ibit aut ambiget. Haud credo vos tam supinos esse, qui hanc benignitatem atque clementiam ultrò oblatam flocci faciatis: quæ omnibus modis, si negaretur, ambienda fore. Diuturniorem impunitatem haud unquam suprema & æterna illa cœli maiestas hostibus Imperii Romani concessit. Sacrosancta est Roma, & curia superum; Princeps Romanus Deus & Dominus est orbis terrarum. ALARICUS & ATTILA, qui lædere Romanam maiestatem ausi fuerunt, subitò interierunt, raptati ad inferos æternis suppliciis mactantur.
units.tr: 1. Therefore, lest anything be rashly undertaken, your duke Theodo should set out with a few men to Theodoric in Italy; there the common business will be deliberated. None of you will deny or doubt that nothing is fairer or more useful. I do not believe you are so careless as to make light of this kindness and clemency freely offered, which, if it were refused, would have to be sought by every means. That supreme and eternal majesty of heaven has never granted enemies of the Roman Empire a longer impunity. Rome is sacrosanct, and the senate of the gods; the Roman Prince is God and Lord of the world. Alaric and Attila, who dared to injure Roman majesty, suddenly perished, and, seized and carried off to the underworld, are being punished with eternal torments.

units.la: GILIMERIS REGIS ET IMPE- RATORIS CARTHAGINENSIS
units.tr: GILIMER, KING AND EMPEROR OF CARTHAGE

units.la: RESCRIPTVM AD IVSTINIANVM IMP. de depositione Regis, & primogenitura Regni.
units.tr: RESCRIPT TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN concerning the deposition of the king and the right of primogeniture to the kingdom.

units.la: IMP. CÆS. FL. JUSTINIANUS AUG. Gilimeri Regi salutem. Impiè facis minimeque dignum Gizerichi testamento, quod Ilderichum legitimum Regem in custodia teneas, quum brevi post tempore tibi liceret ex lege omnino succedere: nunc verò ut modicum prævenias tempus, iuta prodis, & regni nomen in tyrannidem convertis. Hunc igitur hominem sine donec vivat regni salutem imaginem habere, ageque tantum quod regem decet, & avi tui Gizerichi mandatum circa regni successionem expostulat, ut quod nunc iniuste possides, ex æquo retineas. Hoc si in animum induxeris, & res tibi felicius & nostra simul amicitia provenerit.
units.tr: The Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian Augustus to Gilimer the King, greetings. You act impiously and in no way worthily of Gizeric's testament, in holding Hilderic, the lawful king, in custody, when after a short time it would have been entirely yours to succeed by law. Now, by anticipating the time a little, you betray the right and turn the name of king into tyranny. Let this man therefore keep the image of the kingdom's safety for as long as he lives, and do only what befits a king. The command of your grandfather Gizeric concerning the succession to the kingdom demands this, so that what you now possess unjustly you may keep on fair terms. If you take this to heart, both your affairs will prosper more happily and our friendship will prosper with them.

units.la: IMP. CÆS. FL. JUSTINIANUS AUG. Gilimeri Regi salutem. Nos cùm te minime nostris monitis adversaturum putaremus, priorem tibi Epistolam scripsimus: quando verò tibi placet regnum hoc pacto habere, tibi habe quod fortuna ex ipso tributeris. Tu autem Ilderichum & Amerem luminibus cassum eiusque fratrem ad nos mitte, solatium habituros quale poterunt, qui regno aut oculis sunt privati: quod si n immè fecerit, nos profecto coges amicitia iclicta, fœdereque, quod cum Gzericho eiusque successoribus gessimus, soluto, te non solum armis petere, sed pœna quali possumus persequi.
units.tr: The Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian Augustus to Gilimer the King, greetings. We thought you would in no way oppose our admonitions, and so we wrote our earlier letter to you. But since you are pleased to hold the kingdom in this way, keep for yourself what fortune has given you. Now send Hilderic and Amarus, deprived of their eyesight, and his brother to us, so that they may have such consolation as those who have been deprived of kingdom or sight can have. But if you do not do this, we will certainly compel you, our friendship broken and the treaty we made with Gizeric and his successors dissolved, to seek you not only with arms but to pursue you with whatever punishment we can.

units.la: GILIMER REX JUSTINIANO IMPERATORI salutem. Neque Ego per vim regnum accepi, neque contra meos propinquos quicquam iniustum perpetravi. Ilderichum enim nova quaerentem in familiam nostram, Vandilorum Gens magistratu deiecit, mecum tempus & ex lege ætatis honor in regnum vocavit. Talem enim quendam vitam bonum regnum expostulat, qui necalienas res cuias persequatur. Tu verò item rex curiosè facis ac iniustè, aliena curare: quod autem fœdera solves nobis bellum inferendo, respondere iam paratus, quibus potero viribus obtestans atque hidem expostulans, simul & iuniorandum Zenonis cuius tu succedis exilis.
units.tr: Gilimer the King to the Emperor Justinian, greetings. I did not receive the kingdom by force, nor have I committed any injustice against my own kin. For Hilderic, seeking new things against our family, was removed from office by the Vandal people, and together with me, the time and the honour of his age called him to the kingdom according to law. For a good kingdom demands such a man, one who does not pursue other people's affairs. But you, king, act both meddlesomely and unjustly, in caring for what is not yours. As for your breaking the treaties by bringing war upon us, I am already prepared to answer, calling upon God with whatever strength I have and demanding good faith; at the same time I demand the oath of Zeno, whose exile you are succeeding to.

units.la: EIVSDEM RESCRIPTVM, QVOD IM- PERATORE GERM. ANO INDIGNUM SIT, UT SE GRÆCORUM REGIS PO- TESTATI & IMPERIO SUBICIAT.
units.tr: THE SAME RESCRIPT, SHOWING THAT IT IS UNWORTHY FOR THE EMPEROR OF THE GERMANS TO SUBJECT HIMSELF TO THE POWER AND RULE OF THE KING OF THE GREEKS.

units.la: GILIMER REX PHARÆ DUCI SALUTEM. Quod mihi das consilium multas habeo tibi gratias: Servire tamen a inimico, qui magnopere me læsit, nequaquam exitimo rolerandum, à quo potius optaverim sumere, si Deus propitius fuisset, qui nunquam neq; ingratum aliquid ab nec mali quicquam passus, belli adversus me occasionem omni culpa vacantem iumplit. Neque ad hoc fortunæ compulit. Belisarium non video cur etiam feram, quamquam & ipsi, paupereque & imperatori quum sint homines, non absurdum aliquid accidere posse, quod fortasse nolunt. Ego verò tibi plura scribere non habeo, præsens enim fortuna omnem mihi eripuit cogitationem. Sed vale mi care Phara. Datum in Pappua apud Maurusios.
units.tr: Gilimer the King to Pharas the Duke, greetings. I thank you greatly for the advice you give me. Yet I think I must by no means endure being a slave to an enemy who has greatly wronged me, from whom I would rather have wished to take ... if God had been favourable, who has never done anything ungracious to him nor suffered any evil, and who has brought about an occasion of war against me, free of all blame. Nor has fortune compelled me to this. I do not see why I should even bear Belisarius, although he and the emperor are men and poor, and it is not absurd that something may happen which perhaps they do not want. For my part I have no more to write to you, for present fortune has snatched away all my thought. But farewell, my dear Pharas. Given at Pappua among the Mauri.

units.la: ATHALARICI REGIS AVG. ROMAN. RESCRIPTVM.
units.tr: Rescript of Athalaric, King and Augustus of the Romans.

units.la: PRO GOTHIS AD BELISARIVM, SVPER provinciis legitimo iure belli quæsitis.
units.tr: To Belisarius on behalf of the Goths, concerning the provinces won by the lawful right of war.

units.la: LITERAS quas nuper optime Belisarie scripsisti, monitionem quidem veram ad alios fortasse quosdam homines, non aure ad nos Gothos præ se ferre videntur. Nos enim nihil ex Imperatore Iustiniano possidemus, neque ita infami fumus. Siciliam namque omnem nostram existentem belliiure acquisivimus, cuius promontorium unum Lilybei est arx. Sed autem Theoderichi permissu fororcius Vandilorum regi locata hanc cuidam in Siciliæ mercatu tributi utendam, nihil ad rem, neque hoc quodcunque huiusmodi vobis conquerendi occasionem præbere debet. Tu igitur Dux ex æquo nobis cum age, si non ut hostis, sed amicus esse cupis his qui nobis fœderis solutionem dissuadent. Refert enim quum amici quidem in pace aut inimici in pugna decernere sunt apti. Nos Iustiniano Imperatori de his cognoscendis curam permisimus, ut quæ sint legitima & iusta iudicet. Cupimus ut tua consilia salutaria atque optima sint, ac Imperatoris tui celeritet expectare sententiam.
units.tr: The letter you lately wrote, most excellent Belisarius, seems to offer a warning that may fit certain other men, but not us Goths. We hold nothing from the Emperor Justinian, nor are we so ill-reputed. For we acquired all of Sicily, which was ours, by the right of war, and Lilybaeum, its headland, is its citadel. But by the permission of Theodoric, his sister's son let it out to the king of the Vandals, to be used by a certain person in the Sicilian market for a tribute. That is beside the point, and neither this nor anything of the kind ought to give you a reason for complaint. So deal with us as an equal, Commander, if you wish to be a friend rather than an enemy to those who advise us against breaking the covenant. For it matters that friends are fit to decide in peace and enemies in battle. We have left to the Emperor Justinian the task of examining these matters, so that he may judge what is lawful and just. We want your counsels to be wholesome and the best, and we expect your Emperor's decision with all speed.

units.la: THEODAHATI REGIS AVG. ROMANOR.
units.tr: Theodahatus, King of the Romans, Augustus.

units.la: PACTVM CVM IVSTINIANO IMPERATORE, de tradendis ei Imperij Occidentalis habenis.
units.tr: Agreement with the Emperor Justinian, concerning the handing over to him of the reins of the Western Empire.

units.la: NON equidem ipse ad id regium culmen, ut advenitiis & peregrinus perveni, quippe qui ex avunculo rege tim genus sortitus, & pro eius nutritus hic dignitate, bellorum vero ac bellicæ turbulentiæ tum equidem non omnino peritus. Cum n. in audiendis literarum optimis disciplinis exercitus sim, & in eas studium meum omne contulerim, contigit sane, ut à bellicis hisce perturbationibus quam longe semotus, ad id demum venerim, ut haud quaquam decere me ducam, pro terrestris Imperii & bonorum præsentium cupiditate, vitam ut in discrimine agam, sed ab his potius ut procul absint: nimirum cui neutrum sit voluptati, tum quia alterum satietate metimur, nam & suavitudinum omnium sarietas est: tum quia insolentia ipsa desuetudoque in anxietates plerunque & turbas indu-cunt. Ipse igitur, si modo mihi prædia sint, quæ aureos ducentos & mille quotannis ferant, parviquidem tum regnum facturus, tibique statim Gothorum & Italorum permissurus Imperium, ut qui longe malim terræ cultor sine negotio esse, quam in imperatoriis cuius vitam hanc ducere, vicissim in pericula transmittentibus. Remittes ergo quam celerrime hunc ad nos virum, cui cum Italiam ipsam, tum & res cæteras tuo sim nomine traditurus.
units.tr: I did not reach that royal summit as a newcomer and outsider. I am of royal blood, having descended from my uncle, King Theodoric, and was reared here in keeping with my rank. But I was then not at all experienced in war and its turmoil. Since I was trained in the study of the best literary disciplines and devoted all my effort to them, it so happened that I was kept far from those warlike disturbances, and I have come to think that it is by no means fitting for me to put my life at risk for the sake of earthly empire and present wealth. Rather, I should keep well away from them. Indeed, neither gives me pleasure: first, because we measure the one by satiety, and there is satiety of all pleasures; second, because the very unfamiliarity and disuse of such things usually bring anxieties and tumults. So, if I merely had estates bringing in two hundred gold pieces and a thousand a year, I would gladly give up the kingdom and at once hand over to you the rule of the Goths and Italians. I would much rather be a tiller of the soil, free from business, than lead this life in imperial office, exposing myself in turn to dangers. Send this man back to us as quickly as possible, to whom I shall hand over Italy itself and the rest of the affairs in your name.

units.la: IUSTINIANUS IMPERATOR THEODAHATO Regi. Sapientem te esse ante hac audiu & fama perceperam, nunc vero experientia doctus intelligo, quandoquidem animo destinaveristuo, belli eventum non opperiri: quod utique plerique perpetii, cluti demum in rebus maximis sint, & te quidem haud quaquam de cetero pœnitebit, ex hostibus nos tibi amicos fecisse: à nobis vero quæ postulas, impetrabis, & ad hæc quidem accedet, quod honoris causa, Romanorum omnium primus describi impositorum potentis. Nunc itaque Athanasium Petrumque misimus, ut confessione inter utrosque nostrum res confirmentur. Venturus & statim est ad te Belisarius, omnibus inter nos rebus convenientis finem interpositurus.
units.tr: The Emperor Justinian to King Theodahatus. I had heard and learned by report before that you are wise. Now, taught by experience, I understand that, since you have resolved in your mind not to await the outcome of war (which most people do suffer, since such is the way in the greatest matters), you will never regret having made us friends instead of enemies. From us you will obtain what you ask, and in addition there will come this honour: you will be enrolled first of all Romans among the powerful office-holders. Now, therefore, we have sent Athanasius and Peter, so that the matters may be confirmed by agreement between us both. Belisarius too is about to come to you at once, to set an end to all the matters agreed between us.

units.la: VITTIGIS REGIS AVG. ROMANOR.
units.tr: VITIGES, KING, AUGUSTUS OF THE ROMANS.

units.la: ORATIO AD PROCERES DE PROVINCIIS Imperij remotoribus in infantia periculo dedendis.
units.tr: ADDRESS TO THE NOBLES ON THE REMOTE PROVINCES OF THE EMPIRE, WHICH MUST BE GIVEN UP TO DANGER.

units.la: NON equidem, o viri sanguine mihi propinquiores, quæ grata potius sint quàm utilia commonefacturus, vos huc convocavi: Sed ut benigne auscultando præsentibus de rebus pro vestra nunc dignitate in medium consulatis: His namque quibus facta iccirco non ex voto procedunt, quia necessitati haud quaquam, cum opus est, parent, profecto ut moderari eundem in modum præsentia velle, nil prorsus conduxerit. Cætera quidem ad bellum parata nobis egregie sunt. Sed Franci obstant, quibus iampridem nobis hostiliter adversantibus, etsi cum magna nostra ut corporum, ita & terum iactura ad resistendum tunc vires fuere, cum aliunde nobis nil occurrerat hostile; nunc tamen cum in alios ire omnino cogimur hostes, cum Francisi ficeprum necessario fokvendum est bellum, & ea primum de causa, quia si hostes nobis sint hi permanserunt, cum Belisario contra nos arma sine mora consociabunt: Nam quit unum eundemque habent hostem, ut invicem & benevolentiam concilient & fœdera inter se iungant, rerum natura ipsa induxerit. Proinde si inhostiles utrosque exercitus seorsum & ipsi partitis copiis bellum his intulerimus, id procul dubio relinquetur, ut ab utisque trisque vincamur. Satius itaque erit ut paulo imminuti, maiorem nostri Imperii partem firmius tuc amur,quàm omnia possidere dum cupimus,cum totius Imperii viribus, hostium insultibus pereamus. Censeo igitur Francis ut Gallias sibi finitimas ultrò dedamus,& pecunias insuper omnes, quas Theodatus his se daturum promiserat, non solum ut concepta in nos odia Franci deponant, sed nobiscum unà id bellum suscipiant. Quemadmodum verò succedentibus rebus recuperaturi Gallias simus, nemo vestrum nunc animo agitet: vetus nimirum me subit dictum, quod utique præsentibus rebus, ut consulatur, iniungit.
units.tr: I have not called you here, my kinsmen by blood, to remind you of things that are pleasing rather than useful. I have called you so that, by listening attentively, you may deliberate on the present business in a manner worthy of your rank. For things do not turn out as we wish when they do not yield to necessity when it is needed, and to wish to govern present affairs in that way would profit us nothing at all. Our other preparations for war are excellent. But the Franks stand in our way. They have long been hostile to us, and although we had the strength to resist them then, it cost us heavy losses of men and of money, and that was when nothing hostile threatened us from elsewhere. Now, however, we are forced to go against other enemies altogether, and so we must necessarily keep the war with the Franks in check. The first reason is this: if they remain our enemies, they will at once join arms with Belisarius against us. For since they have one and the same enemy, nature itself leads them to win each other's goodwill and to join their covenants together. Therefore, if we attack both armies separately, dividing our own forces, it will undoubtedly come about that we are conquered by each of them. It will be better, then, to give up a little and hold more firmly the greater part of our Empire, than to wish to possess everything and perish by the assaults of enemies with the strength of the whole Empire. I advise, therefore, that we freely give the Franks the Gauls that border them, and also all the money which Theodatus had promised them. This will make the Franks lay aside the hatred they have conceived against us, and they will undertake the war together with us. As for how we shall recover the Gauls when circumstances turn favourable, let none of you think about that now: an old saying comes to my mind, which bids us deliberate only on present matters.

units.la: EIVSDEM RESCRIPTVM AD GOTHOS Auximi obsessos, ne fidem deserant.
units.tr: THE SAME, RESCRIPT TO THE GOTHS BESIEGED AT AUXIMUM, THAT THEY NOT DESERT THEIR FAITH.

units.la: NEmo vestrum, o omniū amantissimi viri,existimet ita me animo concidisse, neque co venisse malignitatis,ut præignavia atq; socordia res ipsas Gothorum neglexerim. Mihi siquidem su- per ad exercitū apparatu quàm maximo educendum summū studiū fuit,Uitiaias deinde quem Mediolanum antea miseram,perme revocatus iam venit. Francorum tamen insultus ex insperato incidens omnem nobis conatum intercurbavit,cuius rei haud quaquam ipse sum incusandus:nam quæcunque supra humanas sunt vires, vel his, qui spe nonnunquam sua fallantur, veniam præbent, & aut crimine vacent,ellieiunt, fortuna semper ad seipsam trahente rerum gestarum delicta: nunc vero ubi & Theodiberum à nobis procul abscessisse compertum habemus,si Deo id placitum sit,cum universo Gothorum exercitu paulo post affuturi vobis auxilio sumus. Oportet igitur ut præsentem stre- nue fortunam feratis: & vos ipsos necessitati accommodetis, vestræ imprimis habita ratione virtutis, cuius ob gratiam Auximi vobis, ut planè delectis custodiam demandavi: & Gothorum de vobis expectationem ut vereamini, qui vestram salutem suæ Ravennæque anteponunt.
units.tr: Let none of you, O most loving of men, think that I have lost heart, or have come to such ill will as to neglect the affairs of the Goths through cowardice and sloth. My greatest concern has been to lead out the army with the greatest possible preparation. Uraias, whom I had earlier sent to Milan, has now come back, recalled by me. Yet an attack by the Franks, falling upon us unexpectedly, has disrupted every effort we made. I am not to be blamed for this at all: for whatever lies beyond human power, both those who are sometimes deceived in their hopes are pardoned, and they are free of blame, since fortune always draws the faults of deeds onto herself. Now, since we have learned that Theodibert has withdrawn far from us, we shall, God willing, come to your aid shortly with the whole Gothic army. You must therefore bear the present fortune bravely and accommodate yourselves to necessity, keeping above all in mind your own courage, for whose sake I have entrusted the guard of Auximum to you as men chosen with special care. Do not fear the expectation the Goths have of you, who put your safety before their own and before Ravenna's.

units.la: VITIGIS REGIS AVG. ROMAN.
units.tr: VITIGIS REGIS AVG. ROMAN.

units.la: ORDINATIO DE OBEDIENTIA PAPAE
units.tr: The ordinance concerning obedience to the Pope

units.la: Senatus Populiq. Romani Imperatori Germanico debita.
units.tr: The obedience owed by the Senate and People of Rome to the German Emperor.

units.la: POST electionem Vitigis Romam venit, Senatumque & Populum alloquutus, beneficia Theoderici memoravit, eosque hortatus est,ne quid novi moliantur, magnas Gothorum vires per Italiam esse docuit,nec ea quæ accidissent incómoda propter imbecillitatē gentis accidisse, sed propter discordes erga Theodatum animos. Nunc autem conspirantibus in unam eandemque voluntarem Gothis,contrarios effectus esse sequuturos. Itaque nem inem sine sua permicie per Italiam res novas moliturum esse. Hæc autem cum Liberio Romanæ urbis præsule egit. Et quoniam novum erat eius regnum ,iureiurando sibi populum & Pontificem obligavit. Ex senatu verò & ex populo Romano permultos delegit, quos obsidum loco constituit: Ubi autem Romæ quendam ex proceribus suis Luderim præfecit, eique delectorum militum quatuor millia reliquit, quibus Romam custodiret.
units.tr: After his election, Vitiges came to Rome, addressed the Senate and People, recalled the benefits of Theoderic, and urged them not to attempt anything new. He showed that the Gothic forces were great throughout Italy, and that the misfortunes which had happened did not arise from the weakness of the nation but from the discordant feelings toward Theodatus. Now, with the Goths united in one and the same will, the opposite results would follow. Therefore no one would undertake new measures anywhere in Italy without his own ruin. He conducted these matters with Liberius, the presiding bishop of the city of Rome. And since his kingdom was new, he bound the people and the Pontiff to himself by oath. From the Senate and the Roman people he chose very many, whom he appointed as hostages. Then, at Rome, he placed one of his leading men, Luderis, in charge as prefect, and left him four thousand chosen soldiers with which to guard Rome.

units.la: HILDOVALDI REGIS AVG. ROMANOR.
units.tr: Of King Hildovaldus, Augustus of the Romans

units.la: ORATIO AD PROCERES DE BELLO NON TE- merè suscipiendo: habita Ravennæ post electionem suam.
units.tr: Speech to the Nobles on Not Undertaking War Rashly, Delivered at Ravenna After His Election

units.la: CUM satis intelligam ô viri commilitones ex diuturna iam belli experientia multorū certamnum vos esse peritos, haud quaquam opportunum nunc duxerim detepente ac temere ut in bella ruamus, cū satis cōstet hæsitabunda & fermidolosam peritiam egregium aliquid audere nequaquam consuevisse. Æquum itaque fuerit pristinos casus omnes vos meminisse,& de præsentib. ut postmodum consulatis: nam plerique vestrum præteritorum obliti,non suo & decenti in tempore præ insolentia forsan extulerint animos, ita ut maximis in rebus falli sit queant. Uuiges itaque nec vobis quidem invitis nec repugnantibus in hostium manus pervenit. Sed tunc sanè desperatis adversis fortunæ casibus, utilius fore existimastis Belisario ad vos domū accito parēre , quàm de summa rerum periclitari. Nunc igitur cum ex Italia decessurum hunc acceperitis, & navigaturum Byzantium, profecto & alia quædam de integro esse hunc aggressurum non ignoratis. Sed illud est vestrum singulis advertendum , non omnia mortalibus ad vota succedere ,sed alteri sæpius evenire ac visum sit: nam ex insperato nonnunquam & temerè fiunt nonnulla: id ferme si Belisario sit occursurum quandoque haud quaquam videri absurdum debet. Consultius itaque fore existimavetim , ut prius quid sibi is velit rogemus, tentemusque uttum ad priores huc placeat redite conventiones: hoc deinde pacto ad ea progrediemur, quæ secundo suat loco gerenda.
units.tr: Since I understand, my fellow soldiers, from your long experience of war, that many of you are already skilled through many struggles, I do not think it at all opportune now to rush headlong into war suddenly and rashly, since it is well established that hesitant and fearful skill has never been accustomed to dare anything outstanding. It would therefore be fair for you all to remember all the earlier mishaps, and to deliberate on the present so that you may consult afterwards. For many of you, forgetting the past, may perhaps have raised your spirits out of insolence at a time that was neither fitting nor opportune, so that one can be deceived in the greatest matters. Thus Witiges came into the hands of the enemy, not against your will nor without your opposition. But then, with the adverse chances of fortune despaired of, you judged it more useful to obey Belisarius, who had summoned you home, than to risk the whole state. Now, therefore, since you have heard that this man is leaving Italy and sailing to Byzantium, you surely know that he will also undertake certain other things afresh. But each of you must note this: not everything turns out for mortals according to their wishes, but often happens otherwise than seemed likely; for some things happen unexpectedly and by chance. It ought by no means to seem absurd if this should sometimes happen to meet Belisarius. It seems more prudent to me, therefore, that we first ask what he wants, and try whether he is pleased to return to the former agreements; after this we shall proceed to those things that must be done in the second place.

units.la: TOTILÆ REGIS AVG. ROMAN.
units.tr: TOTILA, KING, AUG. ROMAN.

units.la: ORATIO AD NEAPOLITANOS, DE PAR- cendis & recipiendis in gratiam civibus per vim ab Imperio abalienatis.
units.tr: SPEECH TO THE NEAPOLITANS, ON SPARING AND RECEIVING BACK INTO FAVOUR THE CITIZENS WHO HAVE BEEN FORCIBLY ESTRANGED FROM THE EMPIRE.

units.la: NIHIL ipsi vel criminationis vel causæ in vobis nacti, viri Neapolitani, ad urbem hanc obsidendam concessimus, sed ut ab infensissimis omnium dominis, vos denique in libertatem vindicaremus, & cuique vestrûm gratias quandoque possemus & pro arbitrio reddere pro vestris erga nos in bello hoc beneficiis, proque his quæ à Romano ante hac hoste perpessi fuistis. Soli nanque Italicensium omnium maximè erga Gothorum hanc gentem benevolentiam præstitistis, & compertum sat habeo, in hostium vos ditionem vel invitos quidem venisse: unde quia cum illis unà & vos obsidere nunc cogor, vestræ erga nos fidei pudet, tametsi non Neapolitanorum malo urbem nunc obsidemus: non igitur quia obsidionis mala ægrè nunc fertis, odio Gothos habendos esse in præsentia censea== ...
units.tr: Nothing in you, men of Naples, gave us any ground for accusation or any cause against you when we undertook the siege of this city. We meant, rather, to deliver you at last into liberty from the most hostile masters of all, and so that one day we might repay each of you, as we see fit, for your kindnesses to us in this war and for what you suffered before at the hands of the Romans. For you alone of all the Italians have shown the greatest goodwill toward the Gothic people, and I am well assured that you came under the enemy's rule even against your will. Therefore, since I am now forced to besiege this city together with them, I am ashamed of your loyalty toward us, although we are not besieging the city to the harm of the Neapolitans. So do not think that, because you now bear the hardships of the siege with discontent, the Goths are to be hated at present ...

units.tr: The text is partly illegible in the scan; the transcription above is approximate for the opening paragraph.

units.la: EIVSDEM RESCRIPTVM AD ROMANOS, de iniurys hostiliter illatis emendandis.
units.tr: THE SAME RESCRIPT TO THE ROMANS, on making amends for injuries inflicted by the enemy.

units.la: Quicunque finitimis iniuriam inferunt, sive id ignorantiâ egerint, sive oblivione, merito debent in eos se clementiores præstare, qui ab se sint mala perpessi: nam peccandi quæ incidérit fortuito causa, maximam delicti his admit partem & depiecarur. Si quis verò præmeditatus iniuriam infert, huic certè nil reliquum fiet, quo eius facta excusct: quippe quem non solum rei patratæ crimen, sed voluntatis etiam culpam ut ferat, par erit.
units.tr: Those who do injury to their neighbours, whether they have done so through ignorance or forgetfulness, ought rightly to show themselves more merciful toward those who have suffered evil at their hands. For when a sin comes about by chance, its cause takes away the greater part of the fault and makes it pardonable. But if anyone inflicts injury on purpose, nothing will remain by which he can excuse his deed, for he will rightly bear not only the guilt of the act done but also the blame of his intention.

units.la: EIVSDEM RESCRIPTVM AD IVSTINIANVM Imp. de Societate Imperij post captam Romam.
units.tr: THE SAME RESCRIPT TO JUSTINIAN, EMPEROR, on sharing the Empire after the capture of Rome.

units.la: Quæ in urbe Roma ad hunc diem contigerint, cum te fuisse edoctum iam putem, silentio prætereunda videntur. Ea verò quorum de causa ad te Oratores hos miserim, statim intelligės bona pacis ture ut deligas, vobisque rradas in primis depositimus.
units.tr: What has happened in the city of Rome up to this day, since I think you have already been informed of it, seems best passed over in silence. But the reasons for which I have sent these envoys to you, you will understand at once: that you should choose the good things of peace, and that you should first of all hand yourselves over to us ...

units.la: EIVSDEM EDICTVM DE NON LAEDENDIS CIVIBVS DEDITIS & imbellibus: de iustitiæ correctione ad Gothos: & de pœna in Roman- os ob perfidiam in captam iterum urbe.
units.tr: THE SAME EDICT, ON NOT HARMING CITIZENS WHO HAVE SURRENDERED, AND THE UNARMED; on correcting injustice among the Goths; and on the punishment of the Romans for their treachery in the city taken a second time.

units.la: Totilas, capta urbe, à Laterano ubi per noctem cōsisterat, movens ad beati Petri ecclesiam profectus est, quasi votū exoluturus. Iter faciebat per urbē stipatus catervis ferocissimorū hominū, qui nudis gladiis ac sanguine distillantibus quoscunq; obvios sine ulla distinctione occidebant.
units.tr: Totila, after taking the city, set out from the Lateran, where he had stayed the night, and moved toward the church of blessed Peter, as one about to fulfil a vow. He made his way through the city surrounded by troops of the fiercest men, who, with naked swords dripping with blood, killed whomever they met without any distinction.

units.la: Ex Aretini lib. de bello Gothico. debant. Emenso totius urbis spatio, quum in Vaticanum ad beati Petri limina pervenissει, præsentiam ejus formidans, soléni religionis habitu indutus Evangelia Christi tenens in manibus ac genua submittens: Parce, inquit, rex supplicibus tuis. Totilas autem super bo nimium aspectu quasi dedignans, Nunc inquit Pelagi mihi supplicaturus venis? Ad quem Pelagius, Nunc inquit, quando Deus te mihi dominum esse voluit. Miserere igitur Domine servorum tuorum. Ex hoc Totilas quasi lenita ira præcepit, ut nemo posthac feriretur, sed finis esset licentiæ gladiorum & cædibus. Præcepit etiam ut nulla ingenua fœmina, seu mulier, seu virgo, seu nupta, seu vidua foret, violaretur, idq; severe cum omni diligentia custodivit. Bona duntaxat Romanorum civium in prædam militibus concessit, corpora libera esse jussit.
units.tr: From Aretinus' book on the Gothic war. Having traversed the whole extent of the city, when he had come to the Vatican, to the threshold of blessed Peter, Pelagius, fearing his presence, dressed in the solemn garb of religion, holding the Gospels of Christ in his hands and bending his knees, said: "Spare, king, your suppliants." Totila, however, looking upon him with a certain disdain, as if scornful, said: "Have you now come to beg of me, Pelagius?" To him Pelagius replied: "Now, since God has willed you to be my lord. Have mercy, therefore, Lord, on your servants." Thereupon Totila, as if his anger had been softened, ordered that no one should be struck from then on, and that the licence of swords and slaughter should end. He also ordered that no free woman, whether maiden, wife or widow, should be violated, and he guarded this strictly and with all diligence. He gave to the soldiers as plunder only the goods of the Roman citizens, and ordered that their free persons be left free.

units.la: Volens ante Gothorum mentes victoria elatas deprimere, in concione postridie vocatos in hunc modum alloquutus est, an quisquam vestrum, commilitones, tantas mutationes intuens, quantas per hos annos contigerunt, non formidet rerum humanarum fragilitatem? & unde mutationes illæ pervenerint, nō facilè deprehendat? Omitto Romam dominatricem quondam orbis terrarum in vestras manus nunc devenisse, hac enim antiquiora sunt, ruinaq; hujus urbis non nunc primum incœpit. Ego nostra commemorare malo. Quid potentius ante hoc bellum fuit, quam Gothorum gens per Italiam? ducenta milia bellatorum ponebat in campo, armis, equis, opibus, auro & argento affatim structa, Italiam universam cum Sicilia, Corsica, Sardinia, & Dalmatia possidebat. Hanc tantam potentiam quis unquam putasset ab septem militibus Græcorum, nec enim plures ab initio in Italiam venerunt, sunt se subversam? Quid autem postea tenentibus omnia Græcis ac plane dominantibus, quisquam ne putasset vos admodum paucos & inopes adversus viginti milia Græcorum Italiam recuperasse, quum ab initio quatuor equitum milia conficeretis, ac præter Papiam, Veronam & Tarvisium nihil per Italiam tenuretis, Romam nunc tandem capur rerum cepisse, quam Vitigis ducentorum milium exercitu, & annua obsidione subigere nequivit? Maxima sunt hæc commilitones, ac digna admiratione non parva. Atqui mutationum istarum causas, si attendere velimus, manifestissimæ sunt. Quamdiu enim Gothi æquitatem ac justiciam inter se colere voluerunt, res eorum ac potentia floruit: quum vero plus habendi cupiditas transversos egit, tunc seditiones domesticæ, cædesq; intestinæ & proditiones clandestinæ inter se ipsos coortæ, ruinam peperetunt. Rursus vero quum in justiciam ducis hæ ipsæ labes transiverunt, vos jam emendati facile eos superastis. Hæc igitur considerantes in hac victoria vestra minime superbire debetis, sed Deum vereri, ac mutabilitatem fortunæ expavescere: Illud intelligere, Imperia ac potentias omnes perfacile amitti, nisi per justiciam, & providentiam, & industriam conservantur. Maximam igitur adhuc vobis commilitones laboris partem restat scitote. Nam tueri quæsita difficilius est quam acquirere. Quoniam in acquirendo ignavia possidentis sæpè plus confert quam propria virtus. Tueri autem quæsita sine propria virtute nemo potest. Hæc tum a Totila dicta sunt, Gothi autem sapientiam regis sui laudaverunt.
units.tr: Wishing to humble the minds of the Goths, who were elated by victory, he addressed the men called to an assembly the next day in this manner: "Does any of you, comrades, when he looks at the great changes that have come about in these years, not fear the frailty of human affairs? And does he not readily perceive whence those changes have arisen? I pass over the fact that Rome, once the mistress of the lands of the world, has now fallen into your hands; for those events are older, and the ruin of this city did not begin only now. I prefer to recall our own times. What was more powerful before this war than the Gothic people throughout Italy? They put two hundred thousand fighting men in the field, abounding in arms, horses, wealth, gold and silver. They held all Italy together with Sicily, Corsica, Sardinia and Dalmatia. Who would ever have thought that this so great power would be overthrown by seven soldiers of the Greeks, for not more than that came into Italy at the start? And again, when the Greeks held everything and were plainly masters, who would have thought that you, very few and poor, would recover Italy against twenty thousand Greeks, when at the beginning you had only four thousand horsemen and held nothing in Italy except Pavia, Verona and Treviso? Who would have thought that Rome, which Vitiges with an army of two hundred thousand and a year-long siege could not subdue, would at last be taken by you as the capital of affairs? These things are very great, comrades, and worthy of no small admiration. Yet the causes of those changes, if we wish to consider them, are most plain. For as long as the Goths wished to cultivate equity and justice among themselves, their affairs and power flourished. But when the desire for more had turned them aside, then domestic sedition, internal slaughter and secret betrayals arose among themselves and brought about their ruin. Again, when these same faults passed over into justice under a leader, you, now reformed, easily overcame them. Considering these things, therefore, you ought not to be proud in this victory of yours, but to fear God and to dread the changeableness of fortune. Understand that all empires and powers are very easily lost unless they are kept by justice, foresight and industry. Know, therefore, comrades, that the greater part of the labour still remains for you. For it is harder to keep what has been won than to win it, since in winning, the idleness of the possessor often contributes more than one's own virtue, but no one can keep what has been won without his own virtue." These things were said by Totila, and the Goths praised the wisdom of their king.

units.la: Post hæc Romanis ad se vocatis, illorum ingratitudinem erroresq; redarguit. Quod cum prius fuissent in manibus Odoacri, opera Theoderici & Gothorum liberati ab illius tyrannide, tanta susceperunt beneficia, quanta vix servissent optare, propter quæ divites atq, beati multos annos vixerunt. Demum vero nulla injuria, nullaq; contumelia accepta, contra fidem ac jusjurandum ad Græcos defecissent, homines levissimos & ne ulla virtute. Qui statim obsessi a Vitige nunquam prodire in aciem auli fuerunt, sed intra mœnia inclusi ac fame macerati omne dedecus tolerraverunt. Qui postquam non armis, sed proditionibus & fallacis facti sunt domini civitatum, publicanis exactoribusq;, & delatoribus omnia retulerunt. Qui civitates populosq; Italiæ mirabili acerbitate ad solutionem eorum tributorum compulerunt, quæ jam multis annis a Theoderico cæterisque regibus fuerant eis condonata atq; remissa. Qui rationes administratorum sub eisdem regibus a populis privatisq; hominibus repopoicerunt, ut Imperatoris fiscus inexplebilis avaritia impleretur. Dicite inquit, Romani, si quid unquam mali a Gothorum Regibus passi fueritis, dicite rursus, si quid boni a Græculis istis accepistis unquam? Qui vobis amicis plura mala, quam hostibus intulerunt, genus vitiosum ac maleficum, & nullare magis quam mentiendo efficax. Atqui Gothi in Italia nati, & unà vobiscum educati sunt. Vobis autem peregrini & ignoti magis placuerunt quam vestrates & noti, usq; adeo quos amare debebatis, odistis nova optantes, & quietem fastidientes, quemadmodum equi ocio & affluentia calcitroli fiunt. Vos igitur his contra rectam fidem contraq; utilitatem vestram patratis, pœnas merito luistis hactenus & luetis.
units.tr: After this he summoned the Romans to himself and rebuked their ingratitude and their errors. When they had been in the hands of Odoacer, they were freed from that tyrant's rule through the work of Theodoric and the Goths, and they received such benefits as they could scarcely have wished for, by which they lived rich and happy for many years. Then, with no injury and no insult received, they went over to the Greeks against faith and oath, men most fickle and devoid of any virtue. Once they were besieged by Vitiges, they never came out to battle, but, shut within their walls and worn down by hunger, they endured every disgrace. And after they became masters of the cities not by arms but by treachery and deceit, they handed everything over to tax-collectors, exactors and informers. They drove the cities and peoples of Italy, with remarkable harshness, to pay those taxes which had been remitted and forgiven them many years before by Theodoric and the other kings. They exacted from the peoples and private persons the accounts of administrators under those same kings, so that the insatiable avarice of the Emperor's treasury might be filled. Say, Romans, if you have ever suffered any evil at the hands of the Gothic kings, say again: have you ever received anything good from these little Greeks? They have inflicted more evils on you, their friends, than on enemies; they are a vicious and wicked race, and effective in nothing so much as in lying. Yet the Goths were born in Italy and were brought up together with you. But you have preferred foreigners and strangers to your own countrymen and acquaintances, so that you hate those whom you ought to love, longing for novelties and despising quiet, just as horses become restive through idleness and plenty. You, therefore, who commit these acts against right faith and against your own interest, have justly paid, and will continue to pay, the penalties.

units.la: CLOTHARII I. REGIS AUG. EDICTUM
units.tr: The Edict of Clotharius I, King and Augustus

units.la: De tributo à bonis Ecclesiasticis exigendo.
