Qui tertius modus non minus quam præcedentes duo, cum nobis simul regnare videtur: cum nullatenus natura nostra & ejus quadam substantiæ unitate conjuncta dinoscatur, & quadam specie discernatur: qui dum per potentiam divinitatis ubiq; sit, tamen non alicui coregnare dici recte potest. Aliud est enim ubiq; esse, aliud cum quoquà simul esse aliud inextabiliter regnare, aliquam coregnare. Coregnare igitur & consedere & plurima hujusmodi fi absolute profertur, nec quisquam cuiquam consedere vel coregnare dicatur, simul duos vel plures coregnare vel consedere designat: Si vero quis cuiquam coregnare vel consedere dicatur, significat cum præcedere cui coregnatur vel confeditur: illum vero ejus participem fieri, qui coregnat & consedet, de tale vase electionis Paulo, Consepulti ejus Christo: & iterum, si consurrexistis Christo, quæ sursum sunt quærite. Unde datur intellegi eum præcedere, qui sepelitur & surgit: eos vero participare ei cui consepeliuntur & consurguntur. Nisi enim redemptor humani generis pro nobis sepultus fuisset & resurrexisset, nos ei consepelirt & conresuscitare minimè poteramus. Quo documento colligitur, à cuncta remoti esse, Deum nobis dicere coregnare: qui non nobis in regnando participat, sed sicut omnium auctor est, ita omnes in esse, vivere & regnare præcedit. Quod si forte contentionis quis hujus verbi astruere tentans errorem, ea quæ secundum formam servi de unigenito Dei filio dicta sunt in testimonium trahat, dicens, Quur non coregnet nobis cui, secundum Apostolum, compatimur, consepelimur, conviviscamus, coresurgimus: cujus promissionis cohæredes & cócorporales & conparticipes sumus in eodem Jesu Christo per Evangelium, in quo Deus coexcitavit nos simul; fecit sedere in cœlestibus: de quo & Evangelista dicit, Convescens elevatus est: & iterum, Illi autem profecti prædicaverunt ubiq;, Domino cooperante: Perpendat abstinetia nebulosæ mœus caligine, nō hoc ex sua divinitate. Sed ex nostra humanitate esse in quo nos ei compatimur, consepelimur, conviviscamus. Sicut n. pati, sepelire, vesci, in quo nos ei consepelimur. Coparticipatur, & ille nobis convescens dictus est, proprie humanum est: ita & regnare proprie divinum est, psalmista adsentante, qui ait, Exaltatus est nomen eius solus, & iterum, Domini est regnum & ipse dominabitur gentis: & idem, Regnum tuum Domine regnum omnium seculorum, & dominatio tua in omni generatione & progenie. Dicimur n. & nos regnare sed abusive nō proprie. Nam regnare, immortale & veracem esse illi est naturale: cæteris vero qui hæc consequuntur, illius largitione est adtributum, qui vere regnat, solus immortalis & verax est, doctore gentium prædicante, qui ait, Est enim Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax: & rursus, Qui solus habet immortalitatem: non quo, ut ait beatus Hieronymus, & angeli & cæteræ rationales creaturæ immortales habent. habeant, & veritatis sint amatores: sed quo ille solus naturaliter sit & inmortalis & verax, caeteri vero inmortalitatem & veritatem ex largitione illius consequantur: & aliud sit habere per semet, aliud in potestate donantis esse quod habeas. Si ergo recte dici possumus Deo commori & conpati, qui immortalis & impassibilis est: ita & recte dici potest Deus nobis conregnare. Etsi illud manifesta ratione lucet, conitemnitur, & illud prudenti indagatione repudiatur. Conpatimur enim Christo qui pro nobis crucis passionem perpessus est, carnem nostram crucifigimus, secundum cum vitiis & concupiscentiis, & morimur mundo, & conmorimur Christo, & sicut corpus crucifigimus, ut desideria ejus calcemus. Consepulti enim sumus cum illo per baptismum in mortem, ut quemadmodum Christus resurrexit a mortuis per virtutem patris: ita & nos in novitate vitae ambulemus: & sic baptizati consepulti sumus ei, ut decetero hanc vitam sequamur, quia Christus resurrexit. baptismus resurrectionis pignus est & imago, ut jam in praeteritis ad praeterita denuo non revolvamur. Convivificamur autem & consurgimus ei, si simulacrum mortis ejus sumus conplantati, id est, si in baptismo omnia vitia deponentes in novam vitam ambulati decetero non peccemus. Similitudo enim mortis similem praestavit resurrectionem. Coharedes autem & coperticipes ejus sumus, non quo aliqua inter nos possessio dividatur, sed quo ipse sit Dominus, haereditas nostra atque possessio. Dominus quippe, ait, hereditas vestra est: & alibi, Dominus pars mea & haereditas mea. Concorporales enim, quia quamquam diversas habeant gratias, hi qui in Christo crediderunt, in uno tamen sunt Ecclesiae corpore conglobati. Si- mul ergo cum Christo in caelestibus, non quo ei sancti consedeant, quamdiu in hoc mundo sunt & peregrinantur ab eo, sed quo juxta praefati doctoris sententiam, mos ite sit Scripturarum, eorum fututa tempore praeterito declinentur per schema, quod dicitur prolepsis: verba ad crucem Domini, Foderunt manus meas & pedes: & alibi de passione ejus, Quasi ovis ad victimam ductus est: vel certe secundum spiritalem sensum, quo modo nequaquam in carne sancti sint, cum vivant in carne, & habeant conversationem in caelestibus, cum graduantur in terra, caro esse desinent, toti vertantur in spiritum: ita eos in caelestibus sedere cum Christo. regnum quippe Dei intus non est, & ubi fuerit thesaurus noster, ibi erit & cor noistrum: firmique & stabiles sedemus cum Christo, sapientia, verbo, justitia, veritate. Praedicabant autem Apostoli Domino cooperante, id est, ad bona opera exercenda eis administrationem praebentes: & idcirco tantam vim illorum operatio habuit, ut eorum praedicationem tot milia hominum crederent, & naturae viribus fractis & mortui vitam, & caeci oculos, & surdi aures acciperent. Cooperatur enim Dominus omnibus sanctis, secundum Apostolum, qui dicit, Factus sum minister secundum donum gratiae, quae data est mihi juxta operationem virtutis. Peccatoribus autem inquantum peccant, neque cooperari, neque conregnare ullo modo dicendus est. Si ergo & illud quod Apostolus dicit, Si sustinuerimus & conregnabimus, putat sibi aliquod adminiculum in hac parte praestare, sentiat hoc ab eo quod ille dicit, tripertita ratione distare, id est, persona, tempore, merito: persona, quia non ille sanctis, sed illi sancti conregnaturi dicuntur. Tempore, quia non conregnalle, nec conregnare, sed conregnaturi dicuntur. Merito, quia numquam libet, sed solummodo sanctici conregnabunt. Ait enim, Si sustinuerimus & conregnabimus, id est, si in hoc saeculo sustinuerimus, in futuro conregnabimus: vel certe post judicium, cum jam erunt in speculum & in aenigmate, sed facie ad faciem contuebimur. Nam si adhuc in hoc mundo sumus, adhuc sustinemus: Si adhuc sustinemus, necdum conregnamus. Si igitur adhuc in hoc mundo sumus, necdum conregnamus. Deinde si conregnamus ei, jam venit quod perfectum est, jam evacuatum est, quod ex parte est. Non autem evacuatum est, quod ex parte est, non igitur conregnamus ei. Si ergo sancti quamdiu in hoc mundo conregnant ei: multo minus ille conregnat eis, cujus est regnum & imperium, & cujus regnum hujus: & si sanctis non conregnat, nullo modo peccatoribus conregnare dicendus est. Quando sanctis conregnabunt, Apostolo Joanne docente didicimus. Ait enim; Charissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quod erimus: scimus quoniam cum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quoniam videbimus eum sicut est. Ut dum apparuerit quod erimus, id est, inmortales & gloriosi, in quo similes ei erimus. Similes videlicet non in corporis similitudine, sed in interiore homine, dicente beato Augustino in epistola ad Italicam virginem; Quis autem dementissimus dixerit corpore nos vel esse vel futuros esse similes Deo: in interiore igitur homine ista similitudo est. Videbimus ergo eum sicut est, cuius secundum suam pollicitationem diligentibus se manifestaverit se ipsum sine fine exsistentem: in quo Deum videbimus infinite, celebrantes perpetui Sabbati solennitatem, dicente nobis Domino; Vacate & videte, quoniam ego sum Dominus, quae omnia non antea conplebuntur in sanctis, nisi juxta Apostolum cum mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, & corruptibile hoc vestiet incorruptionem. Nam si conregnamus ei, jam adparuit quod erimus: si jam adparuit quod erimus, jam similes ei sumus: si jam similes ei sumus, jam videmus eum sicut est: Non autem videmus eum sicut est, nondum igitur conregnamus ei. Regnat ergo ille in nobis, non conregnat nobis: regnat videlicet secundum beati Augustini sententiam, in credentibus, quia in ipsum ad crucem & mortem infirmatus est: hoc autem modo filius proprie regnat in fide credentium. Non enim pater dei aut credit vel ipse natus, vel judicatus, vel crucifixus, per speciem autem quae aequalis est patri, regit contemplantibus vel tantum, non conregnat nobis: quia lucet non participat nobis in regno. Ipsius enim proprie regnum est, sicut superius diximus. Nondum enim conregnamus ei, quamdiu hujus mortalitatis tunica induti sumus: quod tunc nos facturos esse, per ejus mille recordiam
units.tr: Simul Now, according to those who probe the secrets of very keen logic, things are said to be simultaneous in three ways: in time, in nature, and in kind. In time, where two things appear to have arisen together, so that neither is before the other and neither follows from the other, but both seem to have a common origin. In this sense, it must be said that God does not reign together with us, since he is eternal and we are temporal, he without beginning and we with a beginning. In nature, where some things are naturally simultaneous and yet none of them precedes the other: for example, if we set down the single and the double, they must naturally exist together, yet the double does not make the single to be, nor does the single produce the double. But neither can it be said that God reigns together with us in this sense, since his nature is prior to our nature by so many distinctions, and the Creator precedes the created in so many ways. In kind, where things flowing from the same kind seem to be simultaneous in nature but are distinguished by species, as with animal: for both a land animal and a water animal are called animals, and they are distinguished by species; none of them is prior to another, but all are known to arise together from the animal, that is, from one kind. This third way seems no less than the two preceding ones to make God reign together with us; yet our nature is in no way known to be joined with his substance by a certain unity, and distinguished by a certain species; and although he is everywhere through the power of his divinity, he cannot rightly be said to reign together with anyone. For it is one thing to be everywhere, and another to be together with someone, and another to reign inextricably, and another to reign together with someone. Therefore, when coreign, sit together, and many such words are used absolutely, and no one is said to sit or reign together with another, they signify several or many reigning or sitting at the same time. But if someone is said to reign or sit together with another, it signifies that the one with whom he reigns or sits together goes first, and that the one who reigns and sits together becomes his partner. Thus Paul, a vessel of election, says: buried together with him in Christ; and again, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above. Hence it is understood that he who is buried and rises goes first, and that those who are buried together with him and raised together share in him. For unless the Redeemer of the human race had been buried and had risen for us, we could by no means have been buried and raised together with him. From this proof it is gathered that God is very far removed from our being said to reign together with us; for he does not share with us in reigning, but as he is the author of all things, so he precedes all in being, living and reigning. But if anyone, striving to defend this error in an argument, should bring forward in evidence the things said of the only-begotten Son of God according to the form of a servant, saying, "Why should he not reign together with us, with whom, according to the Apostle, we suffer, are buried, live together, and rise together; whose heirs, co-bodies and co-partners we are in the same Jesus Christ through the Gospel, in whom God raised us up together and made us sit in the heavenly places"; and of whom the Evangelist also says, eating together, he was taken up; and again, they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them: let him consider, lest the mist of a cloudy abstinence obscure him, that this is not from his divinity, but from our humanity, in which we suffer, are buried and live together with him. For just as to suffer, to be buried and to eat are properly human, so that in which we are buried together with him, that he too is said to eat with us, is properly human; so also to reign is properly divine, the psalmist agreeing, who says: His name alone is exalted; and again, the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations; and likewise, Your kingdom, O Lord, is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion is in every generation and progeny. For we too are said to reign, but abusively, not properly. For to reign, to be immortal and true, is natural to him; but to the others who attain these things, they are granted by his bounty, who truly reigns; he alone is immortal and true, as the teacher of the Gentiles proclaims, who says: For God is true, but every man is a liar; and again, who alone has immortality; not in the sense, as blessed Jerome says, that angels and other rational creatures have no immortality, and are lovers of truth; but in the sense that he alone is naturally both immortal and true, while the others obtain immortality and truth from his bounty; and it is one thing to have something of oneself, another to be, by the power of the giver, what you have. If, therefore, we can rightly be said to die together with God and suffer together with him, who is immortal and impassible, then it can likewise rightly be said that God reigns together with us. Although that is shining by manifest reason, it is despised, and it is rejected by prudent inquiry. For we suffer together with Christ, who underwent the suffering of the cross for us; we crucify our flesh with its vices and lusts, and we die to the world, and die together with Christ, and as we crucify the body, so we trample its desires. For we are buried together with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the power of the Father, so also we may walk in newness of life; and thus, being baptized, we are buried together with him, so that henceforth we follow this life, because Christ has risen. Baptism is the pledge and image of resurrection, so that we are not turned back again to past things already past. We are made alive together with him and rise together with him if we are planted together in the likeness of his death, that is, if in baptism, laying aside all vices, we walk in a new life and sin no more henceforth. For the likeness of death brings a like resurrection. We are also co-heirs and co-partners with him, not because any possession is divided among us, but because he himself is the Lord, our inheritance and possession. For the Lord, he says, is your inheritance; and elsewhere, the Lord is my portion and my inheritance. And they are co-bodies, because, although they have diverse graces, those who believed in Christ are nevertheless gathered together into one body of the Church. Therefore, to be together with Christ in the heavens does not mean that the saints sit with him while they are in this world and sojourn away from him, but that, according to the sentence of the aforesaid teacher, it is the custom of the Scriptures that their future things are spoken of in the past tense, by a figure called prolepsis: the words about the cross of the Lord, they pierced my hands and feet; and elsewhere about his passion, he was led like a sheep to the slaughter; or certainly, according to the spiritual sense, in which the saints are by no means in the flesh, though they live in the flesh, and have their conversation in heaven while they walk on earth, since they cease to be flesh and are wholly turned into spirit; thus they sit in the heavens with Christ. For the kingdom of God is not within; and where our treasure is, there our heart will be also; and we sit firm and stable with Christ in wisdom, word, justice and truth. The Apostles preached, the Lord working with them, that is, supplying them with help to exercise good works; and therefore their working had such power that many thousands of men believed their preaching, and, with natural powers broken, the dead received life, the blind their eyes, and the deaf their ears. For the Lord works with all the saints, according to the Apostle, who says: I was made a minister according to the gift of grace which was given to me according to the working of his power. But to sinners, insofar as they sin, it must in no way be said that God works with them or reigns together with them. If, therefore, the Apostle's words, If we endure, we shall also reign together, suppose that he is providing some help to them in this respect, let him understand that this differs from what that man says in three respects: in person, in time, and in merit. In person, because it is not said that he reigns together with the saints, but that the saints are to reign together with him. In time, because they are not said to have reigned together, nor to reign together, but to be going to reign together. In merit, because it is never given to the wicked, but only the saints shall reign together. For he says, If we endure, we shall also reign together, that is, if we endure in this age, we shall reign together in the future; or certainly after judgment, when we shall now see in a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face. For if we are still in this world, we still endure; if we still endure, we do not yet reign together. Therefore, if we are still in this world, we do not yet reign together. Then, if we reign together with him, what is perfect has already come, and what is in part has already been done away with. But what is in part has not been done away with; therefore we do not reign together with him. If, then, the saints, as long as they are in this world, reign together with him, much less does he reign together with them, whose is the kingdom and the empire, and whose kingdom this is; and if he does not reign together with the saints, it must in no way be said that he reigns together with the wicked. When they shall reign together with the saints, we have learned from the Apostle John. For he says: Beloved, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when it appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. So that when it appears what we shall be, that is, immortal and glorious, we shall then be like him. Like him, to be sure, not in bodily likeness, but in the inner man, as blessed Augustine says in his letter to the virgin Italica: But who, most senseless, would say that we are or shall be like God in body? This likeness is therefore in the inner man. We shall see him therefore as he is, who, according to his promise, has shown himself without end to those who love him; in whom we shall see God infinitely, celebrating the solemnity of a perpetual Sabbath, the Lord saying to us: Be still and see, for I am the Lord; all of which will not be fulfilled in the saints before, unless, according to the Apostle, this mortal puts on immortality, and this corruptible puts on incorruption. For if we reign together with him, what we shall be has already appeared; if what we shall be has already appeared, we are already like him; if we are already like him, we already see him as he is. But we do not see him as he is; therefore we do not yet reign together with him. He reigns, then, in us; he does not reign together with us. He reigns, that is, according to the sentence of blessed Augustine, in believers, because he was made weak for them unto the cross and death; and in this way the Son truly reigns in the faith of believers. For the Father neither believes, nor is born, nor is judged, nor is crucified; through that appearance which is equal to the Father, he rules contemplators alone, and does not reign together with us, since he does not share the kingdom with us in the light. For it is his kingdom properly, as we said above. For we do not yet reign together with him, as long as we are clothed in the tunic of this mortality; which we hope will be ours then, through his thousandfold remembrance.

units.la: C diam lperamus, cum fecundum contemplationem supernæ veritatis ad obtinendam beatitudinem nullo motu animi,nulla parte corporis reliftente, neminemamante propriam potestatem, erit Deus omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: ...which, according to the contemplation of supernal truth, in order to obtain blessedness, with no motion of the mind, no part of the body resisting, no one loving his own power, God will be all in all.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De eo quod Constantinus & Herena in epistola ad venerabilem Papam Apostolicæ fedis Adrianum directa scripserunt, Elegit nos Deus, qui in veritate qu- ærimus gloriam ejus.
units.tr: Concerning what Constantine and Irene wrote in their letter addressed to the venerable Pope Adrian of the Apostolic See: "God has chosen us, who in truth seek His glory."

units.la: SECUNDUM veritatis sententiam,qui à semetipso loquitur,gloriâ propriam quærit. Quam proffus hi,qui in adorandis imaginibus exarserunt, adeo videtur quærere & amplecti, ut prodeceffores suos vel parentes cum actibus eorum non vereantur aspernari. Despectis enim illis atq; fpretis,jactant fe in veritate gloriam Dei quærere, quos utriq; recte spernunt fi ab ea veritate quæ dixit, Ego sum via,veritas & vita,ullatenus deviaverunt.qui ideo via dicitur,quia per incarnationem bonis præbet vivendi exemplum.Dicitur etenim veritas Christus propter judicium quod in veritate exercet,five quod in eo falsitas ulla penitus invenirí non possit. Vita propter deitatem, per quam est vitæ origo atq; eiomnia vivunt. Eftenim recte ambulantium via ad vitam ducens æternam: à qua via nos deviare Propheta dissuadet cum dicit, Adprehendite disciplinam ne quando irascatur Dominus & pereatis à via justa. Cui viæ de qua idem sanctus dicit, Quoniam novit Dominus viam justorum,auctor mortis cótrarius est, de quo subjungitur,Et iter impiorum peribit.Nam it à veritate recesserunt,mendacio adhæserunt: mendaces effecti sunt. Sigitur à veritate receflerunt,mendaces effecti sunt. Ergo fecudum denominativorum regulam ut à veritate verax,à justitia justus, à pietate pius, à bonitate bonus: ita è contrario à mendacio mendax dicitur.Nam cum mendaces veritatem docere aut vix aut numquam possint, mirandum est unde hi tam veraces ramq; veritatis fectatores effecti sunt: qui videlicet fecundum suam opinionem à mendacibus doch & genti sunt. Non ergo gratiam Dei in ea veritate quærunt, de qua pia veritas & vera pietas dixit,Si permanseritis in verbo meo,cognoscetis veritatem, & veritas liberabit vos. Sed in imaginibus artificum industria formatis,quæ spectatores suos plerumq; obterum gestarum memoriam inducunt in admirationem,adoratores vero semper in errorem.Non enim mediocris est error cum aliud adoratur religionis cultu,quam is qui dixit,Dominum Deum tuum adorabis & illi foli servies. Veritas semper intemerata & inviolata perseverans unius modi est. Istæ vero pro voluntate artificis plura fe demonstrant agere cum nihil agant. Nam cum videntur homines efle cum non sint,pugnare cum non pugnent,loqui cum non loquantur, audire cum non audiant, cernere cum non cernant,innuere cum non innuant,palpare cum non palpent, &c. hujufcemodi, constat figmenta artificum esse,non eam veritatem dequa dictum est,Et veritas liberabit vos.Imagines namq; eas fine sensu & ratione esse,verum est: hominesautem eas efle falsum est.quas & fiquis fecundum æquivocorum rationem homines dici posse adfirmet, ut Augustinus fuit fummus philosophus,& Augustinus legendus est, & Augustinus pictus in Ecclefiaftar,& Augultinus illo loco sepultus est,animadvertat hæc omnia quamquam ab uno fonte,ad est Augultino processerint ,hunc solum fuffe verum Augustinum, de quo dictum est sanctus philosophus.certa vero aliud esse codicem : aliud imaginem,aliud corpus sepultum. Inter hominé autem vt cum verum,hoc principaliter interest,quod unus illorum est verus, alter falsus: necuefpiam nisi in nomine societate junguntur.nam cum hic verus fit,qui hac definitione definiri potest ut dicatur,animalis, rationalis,mortalis,pafus fenfusq; capax, neceflario ille falsus habendus est, qui horum nihil habet: & in ille,qui iis omnibus caret saltus non est,neque verus est,qui iis omnibus regulis subjacet. Ecce cernitur plures stare imagines,quarum quædam sunt colorum lucis conpagináta,quædam auro argento conflatæ,quædam in ligno cælatæ,scalpello ligurata,quædam in marmore incifæ,quædam in gypso vel testa formatæ, in quibus quidem quantum in illis est, & imaginis similitudo , & fuperfcriptio nominis una est: verbi gratia & imago Pauli est,& inperfcriptio,sanctus Paulus.Scilicet undum ab eis est, qui tanto errore laborant,ut cas pro arbitrio suo & veritatem & sanctas & veras, & non potius fecundum venerabilium patrum traditionem sanctorum imagines dicunt,quæ cunctis conparata sanctiores vel verior,quæ omnium sanctissima aut verifllima esse credenda est, quasdum eos æquales dicere pro materiarum & magnitudinum vel operum discretione ratio non permittit, & quasdam quibusdam sanctiores, & quarundam sanctissimas fateri conpescuerit, profitetur conpelluntur fecundum veritatis indagatricem rationem, nec veritatis capaces nec sanctas ilhi debere: quoniam quidem & precio sunt mæquales, quo libuerit per conparationis gradus preferitur, & fanctiratis & veritatis merito æquales, qua omnes omnino valent. Sicut enim pretiosa imago pretiosiorem & pretiosissimam admittit, ita sancta & vera sanctiorem & veraciorem, sanctissimam & veracissimam in posterum admittere, fi tamen effet positivus gradus à quo comparativus & fuperlativus valeret emergere. Esto meft depictæ imagini sanctitas: ubi antequam fieret sunt in ligno quod ex silvis usus famiculæ, cujus refulgentis ignibus manciparatur: an in coloribus, qui plerumque rebus inpuris conficiantur an in ære aut & colorum & sordium capax est: Si in ligno, cur id quod fecundum tundentes, aflomemorie, runcina radente abitrahitur, rogo consumptum, in favillas redactum, aut de coloribus manu artifex sin diverta dilapsum, aut de cera nimio calore igni irquefactum guttatim destillatum pene, cum sanctitas prius necefit: Aut in his quæ exsecuti lumus sanctissimæ non est, & revera non est, quarendum undecumque poltquam ex plurimis materiis conpeginata est, cedat. cedat: quæ dum neq; per manus impositionē, neq; per aliquam canonicam consecrationē ei accedere inveniatur, nec inesse credenda est. Quæ si inesset, quæri poterat, utrum ea vetustate fatiscente cum ea fatiscerer: an ad alia quæ ex rudimentis cōficeretur transfiret? Nā si ei inesset, aliunde veniret: si aliunde veniret, ad alia trāhiret. Non autē ad alia transfiit. Non igitur ei inesse credēda est. Quę dum ita se habeant, quisquis eas veritate dicit, & in eis se gloriam Dei quærere asserit, longe à veritate discessit. Non autem in imaginibus manufactis gloriam Dei David senserat cum dicebat, Super cælos gloria ejus, neque cælestis ille exceptus cum psallebat, Gloria in excelsis Deo; sed neque in vastissima eremo populo Dei in quadam imagine gloria Domini apparebat cum dicitur, Apparuit gloria Domini: & illud, Operuit tabernaculum gloria Domini. Multa enim contra hujus capituli non mediocre delinamentum secundum sanctarum Scripturarum auctoritatem & secundum veritatis indagationem dici poterant: sed hæc breviter pro tempore dicta sufficiant, nec ad alia properantibus hæc obstaculo sint.
units.tr: According to the saying of truth, he who speaks from himself seeks his own glory. Those who have blazed up in the adoration of images seem to seek and embrace glory so eagerly that they do not hesitate to scorn their predecessors and parents along with their deeds. For, despising and rejecting them, they boast that they seek the glory of God in truth, yet they have certainly not strayed from that truth which said, "I am the way, the truth and the life." Christ is called the way because by His incarnation He offers good men an example of living. Christ is called the truth because of the judgement He exercises in truth, or because no falsehood at all can be found in Him. He is called life because of His deity, through which there is the origin of life, and through which all things live. For He is the way of those who walk aright, leading to eternal life. From this way the Prophet warns us not to stray when he says, "Take hold of instruction, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the just way." Opposed to that way, of which the same saint says, "For the Lord knows the way of the righteous," is the author of death, of whom it is added, "and the way of the wicked shall perish." For they have withdrawn from the truth and clung to a lie, and so they have become liars. Therefore, since they have withdrawn from the truth, they have become liars. Thus, according to the rule of denominatives, as from truth one is called truthful, from justice just, from piety pious, from goodness good, so by contrast from a lie one is called a liar. For since liars can scarcely or never teach the truth, it is a wonder whence these men have become so truthful and such pursuers of the truth, who, by their own opinion, are indeed both taught and gathered by liars. They therefore do not seek the grace of God in that truth of which the faithful Truth and true piety said, "If you continue in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." Instead they seek it in images formed by the skill of artists, which, while they often bring their viewers to admire the memory of deeds performed, lead their worshippers always into error. For it is no small error when something is adored with the worship of religion which He who said, "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve Him alone," did not command. Truth, unharmed and unviolated, perseveres always of one kind; but these images, according to the will of the artist, show themselves to do many things when they do nothing. For when they seem to be men when they are not, to fight when they do not fight, to speak when they do not speak, to hear when they do not hear, to see when they do not see, to nod when they do not nod, to touch when they do not touch, and so on of this kind, it is plain that they are the fictions of artists, and not that truth of which it was said, "And the truth shall make you free." It is true that these images have no sense or reason; but it is false that they are men. Even if someone, by the reasoning of equivocals, should maintain that they can be called men, as Augustine was a great philosopher, and Augustine is to be read, and Augustine is painted in the church, and Augustine is buried in that place, let him notice that all these things, although they proceeded from one source, relate to Augustine: only the one of whom it was said was the true Augustine, the holy philosopher. Certainly the codex is one thing, the image another, the buried body another. Moreover, between real men, the principal difference is this: one of them is real, the other false; nor are they joined by anything except a name. For since he is real who can be defined by this definition, that he is an animal, rational, mortal, capable of feeling and suffering, it is necessary that he who has none of these be considered false; and he who lacks all of them is not a living being, nor is he real who is subject to none of these rules. Behold, there are many images standing, some of which are put together from colours, some cast of gold or silver, some carved in wood, sculpted with a chisel, some cut in marble, some formed in plaster or clay; in all of which, so far as they are concerned, there is one likeness of the image and one inscription of the name: for example, there is the image of Paul, and the inscription, "Saint Paul." Plainly, those who labour under so great an error that they call these images, at their own discretion, both truthful and holy and true, and not rather, according to the tradition of the venerable holy Fathers, holy images; these must be judged to be compelled, by a reasoning that searches out the truth, neither capable of truth nor deserving to be called holy. For they are not equal in price: by degrees of comparison, one is preferred as one pleases; and they are not equal in the merit of holiness and truth, which all of them altogether possess. For just as a precious image admits a more precious and a most precious one, so a holy and true image admits a holier and truer one, and in the future a most holy and most true one, if there were a positive degree from which the comparative and superlative might arise. Let it be granted that holiness belongs to the painted image: where, before it was made, was it? In wood, which is used from the forest for the fuel of the hearth, by whose glowing fires it is consumed? Or in colours, which are usually made from impure substances? Or in bronze, which is capable of both colours and filth? If in wood, why is that which is removed by the striking of the chisel and the scraping of the plane, which is consumed, reduced to ashes, or, dropped away from the colours by the hand of the artist, or, melted from the wax by excessive heat in the fire and dripping drop by drop, almost... since holiness must first exist? Or in those things which we have described, holiness is not and truly is not; and it must be sought wherever it may go once the image has been compounded from many materials. It is not believed to be present in it, since it is not found to have come to it either by the laying on of hands or by any canonical consecration. If it were present, one might ask whether it would perish with it when that image perished through the decay of age, or whether it would pass over to other things made from the same materials. For if it were in it, it would come from elsewhere; if it came from elsewhere, it would draw itself to other things. But it has not passed to other things. Therefore it is not to be believed to be in it. While these things stand thus, whoever says that they are true and asserts that he seeks the glory of God in them has departed far from the truth. But David did not perceive the glory of God in man-made images when he said, Above the heavens is His glory; nor did that heavenly host, when it sang, Glory to God in the highest; but neither in the vast desert did the glory of the Lord appear to the people of God in some image, when it is said, The glory of the Lord appeared, and that, The glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. For many things could have been said against this chapter, which is no small blot, according to the authority of the holy Scriptures and according to the investigation of the truth; but let these brief remarks, made for the occasion, suffice, and let them not be an obstacle to those who hasten on to other matters.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De eo quod Constantinus & Herena gesta vel scripta sua Divalia nuncupant.
units.tr: On the fact that Constantine and Irene call their deeds and writings "Divalia."

units.la: PRisc æ gentilitatis obsoletus error Christi adventu repulsus quoddam cernitur in his reliquiis vestigium, qui se fidei & religionis Christianæ jactant retinere fastigiū, qui & intra Ecclesiam novas & ineptas constitutiones audacter statuere affectant: & se Divos suaq; gesta Divalia gentiliter nuncupare non formidant. Unde fit ut quod protoplasti perperravere florigera in fede virosa serpentis promissione inlecti, hoc isti perpetrent in Ecclesia antiqui hostis fraude decepti: cum videlicet & isti per inanem gloriæ cellitudinem se divos nominare non renuant, & per avaritiæ rapacitatē per quam vanæ laudis culmen adire tentant, Ecclesię novū aliquod inferre cōtendant. Quicunq; ergo alta plusquam ordo exposcit appetit, & extraordinarie plus esse cupit quàm est, ab eo qui humilia respicit & alta longe cognoscit dejectus, minus incipit esse, quàm est. Quod illorū exemplo adprobari potest, quorū dum alter fedè suam ab aquilone ponere disponens, angelico honore & consortio privatus tenebris caliginis hujus est deputatus: alter inobediens divinis præceptis & esse cupiens sicut Deus, deliciosissima fede ejectus in mortalitate amissā ad hujus mortalitatis labores & ærumnas est destinarus. Quorū si vitandi sunt casus, fugiendi sunt actus: si fugiēdi sunt actus, humilitatis amplectendus est usus. Sicut vitandi sunt casus, humilitatis amplectendus est usus, per quem cum cæteris bonorū operum instrumentis & di possumus fieri, sicut ille cui dictum est, Ecce constitui te Deum Pharaonis; & filii Dei, juxta illud quod scriptū est, Quotquot autem receperunt eum dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri his, qui credunt in nomine ejus. Nam cum essentialiter Deus dicatur creator omnium, juxta illud, Quoniam Deus magnus Dominus & Rex magnus super omnes terras: est alius modus quo abusive di & supera potestates & homines di vocantur, dicente Apostolo, Et si sunt qui dicuntur di, sive in cælo, sive in terra, nobis tamen unus est Deus pater: & Psalmista, Ego dixi di estis: tertio namq; modo secundū sacrilegam superstitionē aerię potestates di nuncupantur, juxta illud, Quoniam omnes di gentium dæmonia. Nam primo modo nullus esse meliuter Deus dicitur, nisi ille qui est ineffabilis, inconmutabilis, sempiternus, omnipotens, qui est summum bonum, singularis apex, trinus in personis, unus in natura, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in secula. Secundo modo & angeli & homines di dici possunt: ad quod dignitatis nomen non nisi Deo obaedientes, & humilitate amplectendo, & arrogantiam spernendo, & ei per bonum opus inhærēdo pervenire. Tertius modus plures habet species: nam & dæmonia diā gentibus, & lidera sive plura de creaturis mundi di putabantur & dicebantur; & mundanarum quarundam artium inventores, & ubium conditores, vel sceptra imperialia retinentes, post mortē in Deos credebantur transferri, & divi vocabantur, & simulacra illorū di nuncupabantur. Quæ nomina a spernato vero Deo, contempta humilitate, dæmonica vel humana sibi arrogantia usurpavit: quæ ita Christianus odiłe debet, sicut odirauctor, quisquis enim auctorem mendacii sprevit, mendacium spernit, & qui mendacium spernit, mendax quoq; nomen spernere debet. Qui igitur auctorem mendacii sprevit, mendax quoq; nomen spernere debet: auctor autē mendacii ille est de quo dictum est, Ab initio mendax fuit & in veritate non stetit. Mendax nomen Divale non inmerito est, quod peccatores pro suis meritis æternis supplicus mancipatos divinitatē afferre nitiur esse adeptos. Si ergo huius nominis amatores hoc ad divinitatē minime pertinere fatentur, audiant ipsos gentiles, qui hoc nomine familiarius in suis literis utebantur, & divos pro dis, & Deos pro divis pene indifferenter ponere consuevisse: divos pro dis, ut est illud, Tu das epulis accumbere divum: & iterum, Quæ sint ea numina divum Flagitat. — id est, Deorum. Deos autem pro Divis, ut est illud, An Deus immensi venias maris, ac tua nauta Numina sola colant.
units.tr: Of old, the stale error of the heathen, driven out by the coming of Christ, can be seen still lingering in certain remnants among those who boast that they hold to the summit of the Christian faith and religion, and who even dare to set up new and foolish laws within the Church, and do not hesitate to call themselves "divine" in the heathen manner and their deeds "divalia." Hence it comes about that what our first parents, enticed by the flowery promise of the serpent's poisonous lie, committed in Paradise, these men now commit in the Church, deceived by the fraud of the ancient enemy: for they too do not refuse to name themselves gods through empty pride of glory, and by the greed of plunder, through which they seek to reach the height of empty praise, they strive to bring some novelty into the Church. Whoever therefore seeks to rise higher than his order demands, and wishes to be more than he is in an extraordinary way, is cast down by Him who regards the lowly and knows the high from afar, and begins to be less than he is. This can be proved from the example of those two, of whom the one, planning to set his throne in the north, deprived of angelic honour and fellowship, was consigned to the darkness of this gloom; the other, disobedient to the divine precepts and wishing to be like God, was cast out of the most delightful Paradise and, having lost immortality, was destined for the toils and miseries of this mortal life. If the falls of these two are to be avoided, their deeds are to be shunned; and if their deeds are to be shunned, the practice of humility is to be embraced. Just as falls are to be avoided, the practice of humility is to be embraced, through which, together with the other instruments of good works, we too can be made gods, like him to whom it was said, Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh; and sons of God, according to what is written, But as many as received him, to them he gave the power to become the sons of God, to those who believe in his name. For although God is properly called the Creator of all, according to the words, For the Lord your God is a great God and a great King above all the earth, there is another way in which angelic powers and men are called gods in a figurative sense, as the Apostle says, And even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, yet for us there is one God, the Father; and the Psalmist, I said, you are gods. For in a third way, according to sacrilegious superstition, the powers of the air are called gods, according to the words, For all the gods of the nations are demons. In the first sense, no one is rightly called God except him who is ineffable, unchangeable, eternal, almighty, who is the highest good, the unique summit, three in persons, one in nature, who is God over all, blessed for ever. In the second sense, both angels and men can be called gods; but this title of dignity can be reached only by those who obey God, who embrace humility, who spurn arrogance, and who cleave to him through good works. The third sense has many kinds: for demons were thought and called gods by the heathen, and the heavenly bodies, or several of the creatures of the world, were regarded as gods; and the inventors of certain worldly arts, and the founders of cities, or those who held imperial sceptres, after death were believed to be transferred among the gods, and were called divine, and their images were named gods. These names, usurped from the despised true God, by contempt of humility, were claimed by demonic or human arrogance for themselves; and a Christian ought to hate them just as he hates their author. For whoever has spurned the author of lies, must also spurn the lie, and whoever spurns the lie must also reject the name of liar. Therefore, whoever has spurned the author of lies must also reject the name of liar; and the author of lies is he of whom it was said, He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth. The name "Divale" is not undeservedly a lie, since it strives to bring to divinity those sinners who, for their merits, have been bound to eternal punishments, as though they had obtained it. If therefore the lovers of this name confess that it has nothing to do with divinity, let them listen to the heathen themselves, who used this name more familiarly in their writings, and who were accustomed to put divos almost indifferently for gods, and gods for divi: divos for gods, as in that line, You grant the divine to recline at the feast; and again, What are those divine powers she demands, that is, of the gods. And Deos for divi, as in that line, Whether the god of the vast sea comes, and your sailors worship your divinity alone.

units.la: Octaviano enim dictum est, quem post mortem in Divum transferri putabant. Cesset igitur, cesset falsi nominis ambitio, desistuatur antiqui erroris vestigium, faciscat cæcæ superstitionis vocabulum, abdicetur procacis nominis supercilium, pellatur à fidelibus in divos transferendorum hominum gentile mendacium. Jam veritas de terra orta est, jam ortus est fidelibus sol justitiæ: iam qui sedebat in tenebris vidit lucem magnam, jam habitantibus in regione umbræ mortis lux orta est. Omnia falsa, veritate veniente, cassata sunt. Nam si falsorum Deorum gentilis opinio falsa est, post mortem in divos transferendorum hominum fabula falsa est. At si post mortem in divos transferendorum hominum fabula falsa est, divalis nominis nuncupatio vana est. Si igitur falsorum deorum deorū gentilis opinio falsa est, diuialis queq; nominis appellatio vana est. Liquido ergo patet, ré falsam falsum nomé habere, & falso nomine eos, qui veritatis discipuli sunt nuncupari nō debere. Nā etsi qui forte Catholici defunctos quosq; diva memoria nuncupasse uspiam reperiantur, manifestū est eos usum fuisse secutos gentilitatis, sicut nomina diérum & mensiū gentiliū vanitatibus plerunq; nominantur. Sed hæc & his similia Romana potius ambitio quā Apostolica admisit traditio. Nos deniq;, qui & veritatis sectatores, & ab ipsa veritate redempti sumus, sicut sprevimus gentiliū deorum inendaciū, spernere debemus gentilia vocabula. Apostolo docēte, quiait, Quæ sociētas luci ad tenebras? quæ autē conventio Christi ad Belial? A qua cōventione ipso annuēte liberemur, qui nos ereptos de tenebris & umbra mortis, transtulit in regnū filii dilectionis suæ, in quo habemus redemptionem in remissionē peccatorum.
units.tr: For it was said of Octavian, whom they believed to be transferred among the divi after death. Let it therefore cease, let the ambition of a false name cease; let the vestige of ancient error be wiped out, let the word of blind superstition be abolished, let the arrogance of a shameless name be cast down, let the heathen lie of transferring men among the divi be driven away from the faithful. Now truth has sprung up from the earth, now the Sun of righteousness has risen for the faithful; now the people that walked in darkness has seen a great light, now light has dawned on those who dwell in the land of the shadow of death. All falsehoods, with the coming of truth, have been annulled. For if the heathen opinion of false gods is false, the fable of men being transferred among the divi after death is false. But if the fable of men being transferred among the divi after death is false, the naming of the divine title is empty. If therefore the heathen opinion of false gods is false, the designation of the divine title is also empty. It is therefore clear that a false thing has a false name, and that those who are disciples of the truth ought not to be called by a false name. For even if some Catholics are found anywhere to have called the departed "of divine memory," it is plain that they followed the custom of heathenism, just as the names of days and months are very often named after heathen vanities. But such things, and things like them, were admitted by Roman ambition rather than by Apostolic tradition. Finally, we, who are followers of the truth and redeemed by the truth itself, just as we have spurned the lie of the heathen gods, ought to spurn heathen names. The Apostle teaching, who says, What fellowship has light with darkness? And what agreement has Christ with Belial? May we be freed from this agreement by Him who, at His own will, has delivered us from the darkness and the shadow of death and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of His love, in whom we have redemption through the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: CAP. IV. De eo quod Constantinus & Harena in epistola sua venerabili Papa Adriano urbis Romæ scri-pserunt, Rogamus tuam paternitatem & maxime Deus rogat, qui nullum hominem vult perire.
units.tr: Chapter 4: On what Constantine and Harena wrote in their letter to the venerable Pope Adrian of the city of Rome: "We ask your paternity, and above all God asks, who wills that no man perish."

units.la: Ui Deum sibi conregnare procaciter, & sua gesta Divalia superbe & gentiliter dicere audet, indubitanter & Deum, cuius est regnū & imperium, quempiā rogare dicere audebit: ut dum sibi temerariam celsitudinem prorogat, divinæ maiestatis imperio quiddam derogare contendat. Nec mirandum est cur sua præsumar adtollere, cum divina verbis indoctis nitatur submittere. Deus enim imperando lucē condidisse legitur, & aquas ab aquis discreuisse, & limitem his, ne denuo cōfunderentur, firmamentum posuisse, & terram multigenis feminibus fœcundasse, & cælum splendidus siderum fulgoribus perornasse, & aquas natatilibus, aëra volatilibus complevisse, & hominem sive omnium rerum creationem patrasse: & isti dicunt, Rogamus tuam paternitatem, & maximè Deus rogat, qui nullam hominē vult perire. De Moyse legitur eo quòd fecerit quod Dominus imperarat: & idem scribit, Ad imperium Domini movebant castra filii Israhel. & ad imperium Domini ponebant ea: & iste dicit, maximè quidem Deus rogatz utpote qui inconmutabilis, ineffabilis, sempiternus est, & omnium visibilium & invisibilium naturam impetio creavit, imperioq; gubernat, rogare incipiat. Quod quidem verbū non potestatis, sed deprecationis est, non auctoritatis, sed necessitatis, non imperantis, sed obsecrantis. Nam cum in Deo indigentia nulla sit, & rogare obsecrantis sit, & obsecrare indigentis, quisquis igitur Deum rogare quid dicit, ei proculdubio indigentiam adscribit. Cuisi indigentia inest, & necessitas. Si necessitas inest, omnipotentia deest. Omnipotentia autē illi est, igitur indigentia deest. De eo enim scriptum est, Excelsus super omnes gentes Dominus, & supra cælos gloria ejus. Quòd si forte ei cōvenire posse dicunt rogare, praeter personam filii, qui secūdum Apostolum semetipsum exinanivit, formam servi accipiens, in similitudinem hominum factus, & habitu inventus ut homo: audiant eum dicentem, Lazare veni foras: & iterum, Tolle grabatum tuum & vade: & iterum, Talita cumi: & rursus, Adulescens tibi dico surge, & cætera huiusmodi, quæ non rogantis, sed imperantis; non postulantis, sed jubentis verba sunt: cujus imperii potestatem in ejus nomine etiam Apostolos legimus habuisse. Aut enim Pastor Ecclesiæ cum Æneam curasset, In nomine Jesu Nazareni surge & ambula. Ecce in nomine Jesu Petrus imperat, & illi Jesum rogare debere dicunt: servus imperio in Domini nomine dat languido sanitatem, & illi dicunt eum rogare debere sacerdotem. non hoc prudentiæ, sed summæ amentiæ depoꝛtandum est. Qui si ad sui erroris munimen illud surpare velint, quod ipsa veritas dicit, Ego rogabo patrem & alium paracletum dabit vobis: & illud, Pater clarifica tuum nomen: perpendant non eum hoc dixisse secundum divinitatem, in qua unius cum patre substantiæ æqualis patri permanet: de qua dicit, Ego & pater unum sumus: sed secundum humanitatem, qua Verbum caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis, & de qua dicit, Pater maior me est. Quidam in forma servi minor fit patre, in forma Dei æqualis ei proculdubio creditur: unde & Apostolus ait, Non rapinam arbitratus est esse se æqualem Deo, id est, non est suit tanquam rapina, quasi alienū appeteret: quisicut coexternus, ita coæqualis est patri: quē idem Apostolus verū homine & verū Deum confitetur cum dicit, Quorū patres, & ex quibus Christus, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in secula. Cui si secundū illorum socordiā quēpiam rogare necesse est, alicui subest: & si alicui subest, non est super omnia. Super omnia autē est: non igitur ei quēpiam rogare necesse est. Audiant ergo, audiāt hujusce dictā auctores, quid beatus Ambrosius contra quosdā fidei hostes de hoc verbo dixerit: Sed lectū est, quia rogavit, disce distantiā, rogat quasi filius hominis, imperat quasi Dei filius. An nō desertis hoc Dei filio, quod eriam Diabolus dixerat, & vos maiore sacrilegio derogatis? Ille dicit, Si filius Dei es, dic lapidi huic ut fiat panis. Ille dicit, impera: vos dicitis, obsecra. Ille credit quod subente Dei filio elementorū verumq;, maxime sum natura vertatur: vos creditis quod nisi roget Dei filius, nec voluntas ipsius impleatur. Hoc quidem pugione lorica fidei munitus ecclesiæ præliator contra hostes fidei dimicavit. Inter quos quisquis numerari formidat, talis dictū infamiam fugiat. Dicat interea sanctus Evangelista quid Dominus discipulis formidantibus, cū jam navicula operiretur fluctibus, fecerit. Tunc surgens, inquit, imperavit ventu & mari, & facta est tranquillitas magna. Dicat etiam quid Centurio Domino ad domū suam pergere & puerū curare disponenti dixerit, Domine non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum: sed tantum dic verbo, & sanabitur puer meus. O msaufta locutio! O exsecrabilis error! O superbia tumoré potius q; fortitudinē ingeres, inflationem potius q; vires augmentans! Centurio inludendū, flagellandū, patisurum, morte gustaturū, ad inferna descensurū verbo tantū imperii puetū sanare credit, & ru eū sedente ad dexterā patris in cælestibus super omnē principatum, & potestatē, & virtutem & dominationē & omne nomen quod nominatur non solum in hoc seculo, sed etiam in futuro quempiam rogare dicis. non igitur ei necesse est sogare qui cælestium terrestrium & infernorum creditur potestatem habere.
units.tr: Whoever dares to say that he co-reigns with God, and boasts of his imperial exploits in a proud and heathen manner, will undoubtedly also dare to say that God, whose kingdom and empire it is, asks someone for something, so that, while he extends his rash loftiness for himself, he tries to take something away from the authority of the divine majesty. Nor is it surprising that he presumes to exalt himself, when he strives to humble the divine words with his unlearned speech. For we read that God created light by commanding it, separated the waters from the waters, set a firmament as a boundary so that they would not be mixed together again, made the earth fruitful with many kinds of seed, adorned the heavens with the bright gleam of the stars, filled the waters with swimming creatures and the air with flying ones, and accomplished the creation of man and of all things. And these men say: "We ask your paternity, and above all God asks, who wills that no man perish." We read of Moses that he did what the Lord had commanded, and the same author writes: "At the command of the Lord the children of Israel moved their camps," and "at the command of the Lord they pitched them." Yet this man, who says that God, who is unchangeable, ineffable and eternal, and who created the nature of all things visible and invisible by his command and governs them by his command, begins to ask. This word indeed belongs not to power but to entreaty, not to authority but to necessity, not to one who commands but to one who beseeches. For since there is no want in God, and to ask belongs to one who beseeches, and to beseech belongs to one who is in need, whoever therefore says that God asks anything ascribes to him beyond doubt a want. Where there is want, there is also necessity. Where there is necessity, omnipotence is lacking. But omnipotence belongs to him; therefore want is lacking. For it is written of him: "The Lord is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens." But if they perhaps say that asking can belong to him apart from the person of the Son, who, according to the Apostle, "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man," let them hear him saying: "Lazarus, come forth," and again: "Take up your bed and go," and again: "Talitha cumi," and once more: "Young man, I say to you, arise," and the other words of this kind, which are the words not of one asking but of one commanding, not of one petitioning but of one ordering. We read that the apostles too had the power of such command in his name. For when the minister of the Church had healed Aeneas, he said: "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and walk." Behold, Peter commands in the name of Jesus, and they say that Jesus ought to be asked! A servant gives health to the sick man by command in the name of the Lord, and they say that the priest ought to ask him. This is to be rejected not as wisdom but as the greatest folly. But if to fortify their error they wish to seize upon what the truth itself says, "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter," and that other saying, "Father, glorify your name," let them consider that he said this not according to his divinity, in which he remains of one substance with the Father and equal to the Father, of whom he says: "I and the Father are one"; but according to his humanity, by which "the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us," and of which he says: "The Father is greater than I." In the form of a servant he is less than the Father; in the form of God he is undoubtedly believed to be equal to him. Hence the Apostle also says: "He did not think it robbery to be equal with God," that is, it was not as a robbery, as if he were grasping at what belonged to another; for as he is co-eternal, so he is co-equal with the Father. The same Apostle confesses him to be both true man and true God when he says: "Of whom are the fathers, and of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever." If, according to their folly, it is necessary for him to ask anyone, he is subject to someone; and if he is subject to someone, he is not over all. But he is over all; therefore it is not necessary for him to ask anyone. Let them hear, then, let them hear the authors of this assertion, what the blessed Ambrose said about this word against certain enemies of the faith: "But it is read that he asked; learn the difference. He asks as the Son of man, he commands as the Son of God. Do you not, by denying this, detract from the Son of God, something even the devil had said, and with greater sacrilege? He says, 'If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.' He says, 'Command'; you say, 'Beseech.' He believes that at the bidding of the Son of God the elements and the very nature of things are changed; you believe that unless the Son of God asks, his will is not fulfilled." Armed with this dagger and the breastplate of faith, the Church's champion fought against the enemies of the faith. Whoever fears to be numbered among them should flee the infamy of such a saying. Meanwhile let the holy Evangelist tell what the Lord did when the disciples were afraid and the little boat was already covered by the waves. "Then he arose," he says, "and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm." Let him also tell what the centurion said to the Lord when he was intending to go to his house and cure his servant: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." O mad speech! O accursed error! O pride that brings swelling rather than strength, increasing inflation rather than power! The centurion believes that one about to be mocked, scourged, to suffer, to taste death, and to descend into hell, could be healed by a mere word of command; and you say that he who sits at the right hand of the Father in the heavens, above every principality, power, virtue and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this world but also in the world to come, asks someone. Therefore it is not necessary for him to ask who is believed to have power over the heavenly, the earthly and the infernal.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quod non parvi sit periculi scripturas sanctas aliter intellegere quam intellegenda sunt, & ad hos sensus usurpatas ad commodare quos ille non continent: sicut in erronea synodo quae in Bithynis, regnante Constantino, mediante Helena matre ejus, residente Tharasio Constantinopolitano episcopo gesta est.
units.tr: That it is no small danger to understand the Holy Scriptures otherwise than they are to be understood, and to apply them to senses which they do not contain: as happened in the erroneous synod held in Bithynia, under the reign of Constantine, with his mother Helena mediating, and with Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, presiding.

units.la: Sicut legis docente didicimus oraculo, quòd percussa petra, latices fluxerunt populo, & eandem petram Christum sentire debere documento instituimur Apostolico. Qui dum sit petra, cujus fluentis arentia corda irrigantur, & flumen, cujus impetus laetificat civitatem dei; & fons vitae, à quo credentibus perpetua vita manat; & panis caelestis, qui aeternae famis inediam à fidelium cordibus eradicat: quisquis ejus spirituales potus, & spirituales escas aliter quàm ille dat, percipit, divinas videlicet scripturas alio sensu, & non eo quo à sancto spiritu traditae sunt interpretari nititur, ab ejus pascuis alienus esse convincitur. Eloquia namque domini ait Prophera, eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum: quorum caititatem ille procul dubio adulterina labe vitiare appetit, qui ea ad extranei sensus commixtionem sociare contendit. Qui enim propter arrogantiae et vanae laudis appetitum ad sui erroris munimen aestruendum, divinarum scripturarum adtrahit testimonium, quid aliud facit nisi captivatem divini eloquii probrose captivat in adulterium? & argentum igne divini spiritus examinatum ad aliorum metallorum, id est, extraneorum sensuum, protrahit inquinamentum. De talibus dominus ita queritur per prophetam, Dedis eis argentum & aurum, & illi fecerunt Baal: id est, spiritalis intelligentiae dignitatem & eloquii venustatem ad pravorum sensuum & inanis gloriae verterunt inmanitatem. Nam cum legislator dicat, In dextera domini ignea lex, mirandum est quantae sint haberudinis, qui nec cendum mulceantur candore, nec ejus terrentur ardore.
units.tr: As we learn from the teaching of the Law, that when the rock was struck the waters flowed out for the people, and by apostolic instruction we are taught that this rock is to be understood as Christ. Since he is the rock by whose streams the parched hearts are watered, and the river whose flow gladdens the city of God, and the fountain of life from which everlasting life flows to believers, and the heavenly bread that removes the hunger of eternal famine from the hearts of the faithful: whoever takes his spiritual drink and spiritual food in any other way than he gives them, that is, tries to interpret the divine Scriptures in a sense other than that in which they were delivered by the Holy Spirit, is shown to be a stranger to his pastures. For the Prophet says, The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tried in the fire: and whoever seeks to join them to a mixture of foreign sense undoubtedly seeks to defile their purity with an adulterous stain. For he who, from desire for arrogance and empty glory, draws the testimony of the divine Scriptures to buttress the defence of his error, what else does he do but shamefully lead the captive of the divine utterance into adultery? And the silver tried by the fire of the divine Spirit he drags into the pollution of other metals, that is, of foreign senses. Of such people the Lord complains through the prophet: You have given them silver and gold, and they have made Baal: that is, they have turned the dignity of spiritual understanding and the beauty of the utterance into the savagery of depraved senses and empty glory. For when the lawgiver says, In his right hand a fiery law, it is to be wondered at how great the hardness is of those who are neither softened by its brightness nor terrified by its heat.

units.la: Sicut enim eos qui ad eam intellegendam puro sensu & devota mente accedunt, perlustrat sui splendore candoris, ita à contrario qui ad eam sibi temere usurpandam adpropinquant, perurit sui magnitudine ardoris. Sicque qui ei inhaerent humili mente & sacratis sensibus, gressus habent munitos in praesentis vitae stadio illius lampadis inluminatione: illi vero qui eam petunt cum extraneis & temerariis sensibus, aeterni ignis cremantur adustione: quod figuratum est in quatuor filiis Aaron. Nam cum Eleazar & Itamar juxta institutionem Moysi ignem sanctuarii domino offerentes lacerdotalis infulae dignitatem indepti sunt: Nadab vero & Abiu ignem alienum domino offerre nitentes, formidolosissime atrocissimo mortis genere multati sunt. quorum quisquis vult vitare periculum, debet fugere exemplum. Quem ergo, quem in hoc facto qui bene dicta male interpretari arripiunt, imitantur? nisi eum qui quod de simplici viro justo dictum est, in mediatore dei & hominum interpretari conatur, cum dicit. Scriptum est enim, Quoniam angelis suis mandavit de te ut in manibus tollant te, ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum. Ut enim validius esset sui tentamenti argumentum, divinorum apicum traxit exemplum, quo libentius abhauriretur suae tentationis poculam, si sanctarum scripturarum haberet condimentum. Nam nisi interpretandis scripturis imitandus est, & in facilibus tentamentis sequendus: Et si in fallacibus tentamentis sequendus est, & in caeteris moribus amplectendus: non autem in ceteris moribus amplectendus est: non igitur in interpretandis scripturis imitandus. Ait enim beatus Hieronymus, Male diabolus scripturas interpretatur: Siquidem & haeretici & scismatici, qui ejus utique sequaces sunt, male divinas scripturas intellegunt, pejus interpretantur, pessime vero obscervant. Catholici autem veritatis eruditi exemplis & antiqui hostis resistunt tentamentis, & haereseorum obsistunt machinamentis, & divini verbi manna puro & sano sensu sufcipientes, ejus dulcibus alunturalimentis: quibus non inportune collectum manna vermes ebullit, id est, non ejus conscientiae archana, & sensuum intima, superbiae stimulis confodit. Discussis itaque quae vel arroganter vel indocte à Constantino & Haerena ad venerabilem Papam urbis Romae Adrianum scripta sunt, sive quam brevissime digestis qualiter scripturae sanctae non aliter intellegendae, vel interpretandae, vel pro suo cuique arbitrio proprio sensu adcommodandae sint, sed secundum sanam sobriam doctrinam intellegi debeant: nunc resti monitorum ordinem qui à sanctis scripturis sive à sanctorum patrum tractatibus digestus est, & inordinate sive non proprie ab his qui in praefata synodo sedificare nolcuntur, usurpatus, ordine competenti domino favente exlequamur: ponentes duntaxat summam quid sanctorum patrum de his definierit sententia, vel quomodo à venerabilibus viris prolata sint, quasi quum erroremque struendum illorum adglomeravit amentia: quibus pro tempore in praesentib. duobus primis volumnibus. enumeratis, quid proprio sensu minus docte & contra sanctorum patrum institutionem ob adorandarum imaginum superfluam protulerint constitutionem, sequentium duorum librorum series domino annuente discutiet, praemittentes in sequenti capitulo, qualiter sancta Romana ecclesia inter caeteras ecclesias maxime veneratione habita, pro causis fidei sit consulenda.
units.tr: Just as it illuminates with the splendour of its brightness those who approach it with a pure sense and a devout mind to understand it, so on the contrary it burns with the greatness of its heat those who draw near to seize it rashly. Thus those who cling to it with a humble mind and holy senses have their steps secured on the course of the present life by the light of that lamp; but those who seek it with foreign and rash senses are consumed by the burning of eternal fire, as was foreshadowed in the four sons of Aaron. For when Eleazar and Ithamar, offering fire of the sanctuary to the Lord according to the institution of Moses, obtained the dignity of the priestly mitre, while Nadab and Abihu, striving to offer strange fire to the Lord, were punished with a most dreadful and atrocious kind of death. Whoever wishes to avoid that danger must flee the example. Whom, then, do those imitate who snatch up good words and interpret them badly in this matter, unless him who tries to apply to the Mediator between God and men what was said of a simple just man, when he says: For it is written, He will give his angels charge over you, that they may bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone. For, to make the argument of his temptation more forceful, he drew on the example of divine letters, so that the cup of his temptation might be drunk more willingly if it had the seasoning of the holy Scriptures. For if he is to be imitated in interpreting the Scriptures, and followed in easy temptations, and followed in deceitful temptations and embraced in other morals, but he is not to be embraced in other morals, therefore he is not to be imitated in interpreting the Scriptures. For blessed Jerome says, The devil interprets the Scriptures badly. Indeed heretics and schismatics, who are surely his followers, understand the divine Scriptures badly, interpret them worse, and observe them worst of all. But Catholics, instructed by the examples of truth, resist the temptations of the ancient enemy and withstand the machinations of heresies, and receiving the manna of the divine word in a pure and sound sense, are nourished by its sweet food; on which the worm does not breed, as it does on manna gathered unseasonably, that is, it does not pierce the secrets of their conscience and the inmost parts of their senses with the goads of pride. Therefore, having examined what has been written, whether arrogantly or ignorantly, by Constantine and Helena to the venerable Pope Hadrian of the city of Rome, and having briefly set out how the Holy Scriptures are not to be understood or interpreted otherwise, nor adapted to each one's own sense at his pleasure, but must be understood according to sound and sober doctrine: now, with the Lord favouring, we shall pursue in fitting order the arrangement of the testimonies drawn from the Holy Scriptures or from the treatises of the holy Fathers, which those who are unwilling to be edified in the aforesaid synod have used in a disordered or improper way, setting forth only in summary what the holy Fathers have determined about these matters, and how the venerable men have put them forward, when the madness of those who gathered them built up their error. The two first volumes having been set out in their time, the series of the two following books will, by the Lord's will, examine what they have improperly and ignorantly put forward in their own sense, against the institution of the holy Fathers, in the superfluous constitution concerning the adoration of images, first premising in the following chapter how the holy Roman Church, held in greater veneration than the other churches, is to be consulted in matters of faith.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Quod sancta Romana, Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia caeteris ecclesiis praelata, pro causis f- idei, cum quaestio surgit, omnino fit consulenda.
units.tr: That the holy Roman, Catholic and Apostolic Church, set above the other churches, is by all means to be consulted when questions of faith arise.

units.la: Nequam discutiendorum testimoniorum, quod absurde orientales in sua synodo taxaverunt, sylvá grediamur, dignum duximus, ut qualiter sancta Romana ecclesia caeteris ecclesiis à Domino plata, & a fidelibus consulenda fit, prosequamur: praesertim cum non ab aliis scripturis, nisi ab his, quae illa inter canonicas recipit, testimonia sint sumeda: nec aliorum doctorum, nisi eorum qui à Gelasio, vel caeteris illius sanctae sedis pontificibus suscepti sunt, dogmata sint amplectenda: nec aliter atq; aliter pro cujusibet arbitrio, sed sane sobrieque, quae ab illis dicta fuerint, sint intellegenda. Ait enim B. Augustin. cum ineum institueret, quae scriptura esset recipienda vel qualiter intellegenda: Erit igitur divinarum scripturarum solertissimus indagator, qui primo totas legerit nonnullas, habuerit scripturas, etsi nondum intellectu, iam tamen lectione, duntaxat eas, quae appellantur canonicae. Nam caeteras securius leget, fide veritatis instructus, ne praeoccupent imbecillum animum, et periculosis mendaciis atque phantasmatis eludentes praeiudicent aliquid contra sanam intellegentiam. In canonicis autem scripturis ecclesiarum catholicarum quamplurimum auctoritatem sequatur: inter quas sane illae sunt quae apostolicas sedes habere et epistolas accipere meruerunt. Nam cum hic cunctis per orbem constitutis sedibus apostolicas generaliter praeferat sedes, multo magis illa omnibus praeferenda est, quae etiam caeteris apostolicis sedibus praelata est. Sicut igitur caeteris discipulis apostoli, et apostolis omnibus Petrus eminet: ita nimirum caeteris sedibus apostolicae, et apostolicis Romana eminere dinoscitur. Haec enim nullis synodicis constitutis caeteris ecclesiis praelata est, sed ipsius domini auctoritate primatum tenet, dicentis, Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam, et portae inferni non praevalebunt adversus eam. Et tibi dabo claves regni caelorum, et quodcunque ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum et in caelis: et quodcunque solveris super terram, erit solutum et in caelo. Cui non incongrue B. Pauli doctoris gentium est adtributa societas, ut illius sanctae ecclesiae omnino firmaretur auctoritas: quatenus altero ad piscandas animas electo ex piscatore, altero ad muniendam ecclesiam ex persecutore: ut in altero Dei filii vera confessio, in altero appareret divini verbi sacra praedicatio: cum alteri concesserit idem dei filius claves regni caelorum, alteri clavem aperiendorum legalium verborum: utrique tamen virtutem signorum, quo alter ad eum cruce, alter gladio pergens, fidelibus arrabonem corporalis sarcinae relinquentes, et exempli fulgore, et verbi decore, et sancto cruore supradictam ecclesiam Romanam eidicarent, quam supra solidissimam petram fundatam nec defecedens pluvia, nec veniential flumina, nec flantes venti ruere conpellerent. Hacc ergo sanctae fidei spiritalib. munita armis, et a fonte lucis et origine bonitatis, salutarib. satiata fluentis, et horrendis atrocibusque haeresum obsistit monstris, et mellifluia praedicationis pocula catholicis per orbem ministrat ecclesiis. Nam beatissimus Hieronymus vir divinis legib. et multarum linguarum peritia eruditus, dum Bethleemitis moraretur in arvis, et a B. Papa Damaso Romae posito de difficilib. consulerentur quaestionibus, eum pro causis fidei versa vice consuluisse dinoscitur, et sive tacendarum sive dicendarum hypostaseon, vel quibus in orientalibus partibus communicare debeat humillimis apicibus ut apices accipiat deprecatur. Mira res et magnis praedicanda praeconiis. Interrogat a quo interrogatur: consulitur a quo consulitur, qui magistrum se in interpretandis divinis scripturis sentit, in causis fidei venerandi pontificis le discipulum minime erubescit: et cui sacrae legis quaestionum nexus enodat, utrum hypostasis dicere debeat, quibus sive in oriente communicare, efflagitat. Unde datur intellegi, sanctos et enditos viros per diversas mundi partes praedicationis et sciëtiae lampade coruscantes, non solum a S. Romana ecclesia non recessisse, sed etiam tempore necessitatis ob fidei corroborationem ab ea adjutorium implorasse. Quod regulariter, ut praefati sumus et exemplis docuimus, omnes catholicae debent observare ecclesiae, ut ab ea post Christum ad muniendam fidem adjutorium petant, quae non habens maculam nec rugam et portentuosa haeresum capita calcat, et fideliū mentes in fide corroborat. A cujus sancta et veneranda communione multis recedentib. nostrae tamen partis nunquam recessit ecclesia, sed ea apostolica eruditione instruente, et eo a quo est omne donum optimum et omne datum perfectum, tribuente, semper suscepit reverenda charismata. Quae dum a primis fidei temporib. cum ea perlaret in sacrae religionis unione, et ab ea paulo distaret, quamvis contra fidem non est, in officiorum celebratione, venerandae memoriae genitoris nostri illustrissimi atque excellentissimi viri, Pipini regis cura, et inductria sive adventu in Gallias reverentissimi et sanctissimi viri Stephani Romanae urbis antestitis, est et etiam in psallendi ordine copulata: ut non esset dispar ordo psallendi, quib. erat compar ardor credendi: et quae unitae erant unius sanctae legis sacra lectione, ellent etiam unitae unius modulationis veneranda traditione: nec sejunngeret officiorum varia celebratio, quas conjunxerat unitas fidei pia devotio. Quod quidem et nos, conlato nobis a deo Italiae regno fecimus, S. Romanae ecclesiae fastigium sublimare cupientes, et reverentissimi papae Adriani salutaribus exhortationibus parere nitentes: scilicet ut plures illius partis ecclesiae, quae quondam apostolicae sedis traditionem in psallendo suscipere recusabant, nunc eam cum omni diligentia amplectantur: et cui adhaerant fidei munere, adhaerent quoque psallendi ordine: non solum omnium Galliarum provinciae, et Germaniae, sive Italiae, sed etiam Saxones et quaedam Aquilonaris plagae gentes per nos. Deo annuente ad veram fidei rudimenta converse, facere noscuntur, et ita B. Petri Sedem in omnibus sequi curant, sicut illo pervenire, quo illic clavicularius exstat, deliderant. Ad quam beatitudinem nos pervenire, et in sanctae ecclesiae consortio et unione ille nos faciat perseverare, qui ecclesiam suam in Petro dignatus est fundare: et ipso interveniente, cujus cathedrae sumus sequaces, regni caelorum, cujus ille claviger factus est, mereamur effici compotes.
units.tr: Having resolved not to linger in the examination of the testimonies, which the Easterners in their synod absurdly found fault with, we have thought it right to proceed to show how the holy Roman Church, set above the other churches by the Lord, is to be consulted by the faithful; especially since testimonies are to be taken not from other writings but only from those which she receives among the canonical books, and the doctrines of the teachers are to be embraced only if they have been received by Gelasius or the other pontiffs of that holy see; and what has been said by them is to be understood not in one way or another at each person's pleasure, but soberly and properly. For blessed Augustine, when he was setting out which Scripture was to be received and how it was to be understood, says: "The most skilful investigator of the divine Scriptures will therefore be one who has first read through, if not yet understood, at least by reading, all those scriptures which are called canonical. For he will read the others more safely, instructed in the faith of truth, lest they take hold of a weak mind and, by deceiving it with dangerous lies and phantasms, prejudice it against sound understanding." Moreover, in the canonical Scriptures he should follow the authority of the catholic churches most of all; and among these, surely, are those which have deserved to have apostolic sees and to receive epistles. For since this one [the Roman see] is generally set before all the apostolic sees established throughout the world, much more is she to be preferred to all, she who is also set above the other apostolic sees. Just as, therefore, Peter stands out among the other disciples and all the apostles, so the Roman see is recognised to stand out among the other apostolic sees and among the apostolic ones. For she was set above the other churches by no synodal decrees, but holds the primacy by the authority of the Lord himself, who says: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven."
