Not unfittingly was the fellowship of blessed Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, added to him, so that the authority of that holy church might be wholly confirmed: the one chosen from a fisherman to fish for souls, the other from a persecutor to fortify the church; so that in the one appeared the true confession of the Son of God, in the other the sacred preaching of the divine word. For the same Son of God granted to the one the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and to the other the key of opening the legal words; yet to both the power of signs, by which each, going to it, the one by the cross, the other by the sword, leaving to the faithful a pledge of bodily sustenance, and by the brilliance of example, the grace of the word and the holy blood, proclaimed the aforesaid Roman church, which, founded on the most solid rock, neither the falling rain, nor the coming floods, nor the blowing winds could force to fall. This church, therefore, fortified with the spiritual arms of holy faith, and nourished by the saving streams from the fountain of light and the origin of goodness, withstands the horrible and savage monsters of heresies, and supplies the honeyed cups of preaching to the catholic churches throughout the world. For the most blessed Jerome, a man learned in the divine laws and skilled in many languages, while he was staying in the fields of Bethlehem, and when questions of difficulty were put to him by blessed Pope Damasus at Rome, is known to have in turn consulted him on matters of faith, and with the most humble entreaties asked him whether he should keep silent about or speak of the hypostases, and with which people in the eastern parts he ought to communicate, so that he might receive instruction. A wonderful thing, and worthy of great praise! He who is asked asks in turn; he who is consulted consults; he who feels himself a teacher in interpreting the divine Scriptures is not at all ashamed to be the disciple of a venerable pontiff in matters of faith; and he who unravels the knots of the questions of the sacred law asks whether he ought to say hypostasis, and whether he should communicate with those in the East. From this it is to be understood that holy and learned men, shining through the various parts of the world with the lamp of preaching and learning, not only did not withdraw from the holy Roman Church, but also, in a time of need, sought help from her for the strengthening of the faith. This, as we have said before and shown by examples, all catholics ought to observe as a rule: that after Christ they seek help from her to fortify the faith, she who, having no spot or wrinkle, tramples on the monstrous heads of heresies and strengthens the minds of the faithful in the faith. Although many have withdrawn from her holy and venerable communion, our part of the church has never withdrawn from her; but, taught by apostolic learning, and receiving from him from whom comes every best gift and every perfect gift, she has always received her venerable graces. These, while from the first times of the faith they were brought to her in the unity of the sacred religion, and while they differed somewhat from her in the celebration of the offices (not against the faith), were joined also in the order of psalmody, through the care and industry, or the coming into the Gauls, of our most illustrious and excellent father of venerable memory, King Pepin, and of the most reverend and holy man Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome: so that the order of psalmody should not be unlike that in which the zeal for believing was equal, and those who were united by the sacred reading of one holy law should also be united by the venerable tradition of one mode of chanting; and the varied celebration of the offices should not divide those whom the unity of faith and pious devotion had joined. This indeed we too have done, after the kingdom of Italy was granted to us by God, desiring to raise up the dignity of the holy Roman Church, and striving to obey the salutary exhortations of the most reverend Pope Adrian: namely, that the many parts of that church which once refused to receive the tradition of the apostolic see in psalmody now embrace it with all diligence; and those who adhered to her in the gift of faith now adhere also in the order of psalmody. It is known that not only the provinces of all the Gauls and Germany, or Italy, but also the Saxons and certain peoples of the northern region, through us, God consenting, have been converted to the true rudiments of the faith; and they take care to follow the See of blessed Peter in all things, desiring to come to that place where he stands as keeper of the keys. May he who deigned to found his church upon Peter enable us to reach that blessedness and to persevere in the fellowship and unity of the holy church; and through the intercession of him whose chair we follow, may we deserve to be made partakers of the kingdom of heaven, of which he was made the bearer of the keys.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Quod non ad adorandas imagines pertineat quod scriptum est, Creavit deus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam.
units.tr: That the words, "God created man in his own image and likeness," do not pertain to the worship of images.

units.la: IN hoc testimonio inconsequenter, et ultra quam inconsequenter, ab illis in sua synodo ob adorandarum imaginum astruendum errorem posito, non nostro ingenio plurimum est sudandum, cum tot indiciis ab eorum sit adsertione alienum: quoniam ubi nulla est verisimilitudo, non magna in discernendo oritur disputatio. Quia ergo a nullo, in quo sanae mentis viget acumen, illi rei credditur pertinere, cui illi hoc nituntur adcommodare, sed spiritale dictum spiritali differendum est indagatione retione: restat ut quid de eo sanctorum patrum protulerit stylus, sententiali brevitate notemus: quatenus quod ab illis est neglegenter usurpatum, & à viris venerabilibus & spiritu sancto repletis spirituali[?] proratum, lectoris industria sit diligenter acceptum. ait enim B. Ambrosius, In principio ipsius mundi patrem & filium esse audio, & unum opus cerno audio loquentem, agnosco facientem, sed & patris & filii unam imaginem, unam similitudinem lego: similitudo hæc non diversitatis, sed unitatis est. Non enim homo ad imaginem dei nisi per imaginem dei, sed imago ergo dei ex interioris hominis nobilitate est consideranda: primo quidem, ut sicuti deus unus, totum est omnia vivificans, movens & gubernans, sicut Apostolus confirmat, quod in eo vivimus, movemur & sumus, sic animam in suo corpore ubique tota viget vivificans illud, movens & gubernans. Nec enim in majoribus corpus est major, & in minoribus minor, sed in minimis tota, & in maximis tota: & hæc est imago unitatis omnipotentis dei quæ anima habet in se: quæ quandam sanctæ trinitatis habet imaginem: primo in eo, quia sicut deus est unus & trinus, ita & anima secundum suum modum est, vivit & sapit. Est quoque & alia trinitas in ea, quæ ad imaginem perfectam quidem & summæ trinitatis quæ est in patre, filio & spiritu sancto condita: & licet unus sit, habet tamen in se dignitates habet, ad est, intellectum, voluntatem & memoriam, quod idem licet alius verbum & alio differatur dum dicitur: Diliges dominum deum tuum ex toto corde tuo & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota mente tua, id est, ex toto intellectu, & ex tota voluntate, & ex tota memoria.
units.tr: In this testimony, they have gone wrong, and far more wrong than one might expect, in the error they set out in their synod to establish the adoration of images. We need not sweat much over our own wits, since so many signs show that it is foreign to their assertion. Where there is no likelihood, there is no great dispute in distinguishing. Since no one of sound mind, with a sharp understanding, will believe that this text bears on the matter to which they try to apply it, and since a spiritual saying must be examined by spiritual reasoning, it remains for us to note briefly what the pen of the holy Fathers has said about it, so that what has been carelessly seized upon by them, and set forth by venerable men filled with the Holy Spirit, may be received diligently by the reader's care. For blessed Ambrose says: "I hear that the Father and the Son are at the beginning of the world itself; I see one work, I hear one speaking, I recognise one making. But I read that there is one image and one likeness of the Father and of the Son. This likeness is not of difference but of unity. For man is not made in the image of God except through the image of God. The image of God, then, must be considered from the nobility of the inner man. First, indeed, just as God is one, he is wholly giving life to all things, moving and governing them, as the Apostle affirms: in him we live, move and have our being. So the soul flourishes wholly in its body everywhere, giving it life, moving and governing it. For the body is not greater in the greater parts and smaller in the smaller, but is whole in the least parts and whole in the greatest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God which the soul has in itself. It has in itself a certain image of the holy Trinity. First, in this, that as God is one and three, so the soul too, in its own way, is one and three: it lives, and it understands. There is also another trinity in it, formed indeed as a perfect image of the highest Trinity, which is in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Although it is one, it has in itself powers, namely the mind, the intellect, the will and the memory; and although these are called by different words, they are the same. So it is said: 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,' that is, with all your intellect, and with all your will, and with all your memory."

units.la: Iam sicut ex patre generatur filius, ex patre procedit Spiritus sanctus, ita ex intellectu generatur voluntas, & ex his utem ambobus procedit memoria, sicut ... quolibet intelligi potest.
units.tr: Now, just as the Son is begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, so will is begotten of understanding, and memory proceeds from both of these, as can be understood in any case.

units.la: Deut. 6. Gen. 1. 1. Cor. 2. hoc modo; Scito quoniam dominus corda hominum novit, & qui finxit spiritum omnibus ipse fecit omnia. Ergo ipse spiritus ad imaginem dei nullo dubitante facile accipitur, in quo est intelligentia veritatis. haec enim veritas nulla interposita creatura, catera hominum ad similitudinem facta videri volunt; quia omnis quidem imago similis est: non autem omne quod simile est etiam imago proprie, sed forte abusive dici poterit. Sed cavendum in talibus, ne quid nimis adseverandum putetur illa re sane salubriter custodita, ne quoniam corpus quodlibet per localid spatia porrectum est, aliquid tale credatur esse substantia Dei. Nam res quae in parte minor est quam in toto, nec dignitati animae convenit, quanto minus majestati Dei? Ecce quam subtiliter quamque salubriter sancti viri hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei factum esse, imaginem videlicet in anima, in qua est intellectus, voluntas & memoria: similitudinem in moribus, id est, in charitate, justitia, bonitate & sanctitate, quae omnia incorporea sunt, intellegentes distinguere a quorum sensu & doctrina quantum distent qui hoc testimonium imaginibus artificum manu formatis adcommodant, non nostro est differendum eloquio, sed lectoris relinquendum judicio: ut quantae in hac parte sint vecordiae non nostrum eum stylus, sed suus permoneat sensus. Quisquis igitur ita hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem dei factum, sicut ad imaginem hominis imaginem ab artifice formatam esse credit, aliquid in deo corporeum, quod credere nefas est, credere se offendit. Nam quid quod homo ad imaginem & similitudinem dei factus est, manufactis imaginibus convenit, secundum corpoream speciem homo ad imaginem dei factus est: & si homo secundum corpoream speciem ad imaginem dei factus est, corporeus est deus: incorporeus autem deus est: non igitur id, quod homo ad imaginem & similitudinem dei factus est, manufactis imaginibus convenit.
units.tr: Deut. 6. Gen. 1. 1. Cor. 2. In this way: "Know that the Lord knows the hearts of men, and he who formed the spirit, he himself made all things." Therefore the spirit itself is readily received, without any doubt, as the image of God, in which is the understanding of truth. For this truth, with no creature interposed, wishes the other things made in the likeness of man to be seen; because every image is indeed like, but not everything that is like is properly an image, though it may perhaps be called so loosely. But in such matters one must take care lest anything be thought to be asserted too far, while that point is wholesomely guarded, lest, because any body is extended through local spaces, something of that kind be believed to be the substance of God. For a thing which is smaller in part than in the whole does not even suit the dignity of the soul, how much less the majesty of God? See how subtly and how wholesomely the holy men have taught that man was made in the image and likeness of God: the image, namely, in the soul, in which are understanding, will and memory; the likeness in morals, that is, in charity, justice, goodness and holiness, all of which are incorporeal. To distinguish these things from the sense and teaching of those who apply this testimony to images formed by the hand of craftsmen, and to see how far apart they stand, is not for our words to argue, but must be left to the reader's judgement; so that the pen does not admonish us how great their folly is in this matter, but their own sense does. Whoever therefore believes that man was made in the image and likeness of God in the same way as an image made by a craftsman is an image of man, offends by believing something corporeal in God, which it is wrong to believe. For what is it that man made in the image and likeness of God is not fitting for manufactured images? If man was made in the image of God according to bodily form, then God is corporeal; but God is incorporeal. Therefore what man was made in the image and likeness of God is not fitting for manufactured images.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Quae sit differentia imaginis & similitudinis sive aequalitatis.
units.tr: What the difference is between image and likeness, or equality.

units.la: QUONIAM opinulante deo secundum sanam sobriamque doctrinam sanctorum patrum tentantiis inbuti, qualiter intellegendum sit, quod deus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem fecit creavit, exequi sumus: nunc operaepretium est, ut quae sit differentia imaginis & similitudinis seu etiam aequalitatis breviter exe quamur: quatenus & illi qui ob adorandas imagines per patentes inanium adsertionum campos effrenes feruntur, horum trium, quae illi omnia pene unum putant, differentiam cognoscentes, in quanto sint errore perpendant: & studiosi quique hoc legentes ad quasdam intelligentiae utilitates accedant. Haec ergo tria distinguenda sunt, quia omne quod imago est similitudo est, non tamen omne quod similitudo, imago est: & cum imago nunquam similitudine careat, similitudo vero multories imagine careat, plerunque & similitudo & imago aequalitate carere nescuntur, quae etiam aequalitas nonnunquam & imagini & similitudini copulari potest, quae tria quamquam unius sint categoriae quae relatio dicitur, habent tamen inter se quasdam proprietates, quibus aliae catent. Nam imagini proprium est, ut semper ab altero expressa sit: similitudini vero & aequalitati proprium est, ut in sua substantia permanentes, non ab altero expressae, sed aliis rebus, adsimilatae vel coaequatae hoc nomine censeantur: & imago magis vel minus non sibi admittat, similitudo vero & aequalitas admittant. Sicut enim dicitur magis similis vel minus similis, magis aequalis vel minus aequalis, non sic dici potest, magis imago vel minus imago. Nam & in conversione carum quae Graece antistrophe dicitur, subtilis quaedam repugnantia est: quae omnia permanent longum est, verumtamen ut horum trium nominum differentia lucidius pateat, beati Augustini verba ad medium deducenda sunt. Ait enim: Ubi imago, non continuo similitudo, nec continuo aequalitas, continuo similitudo, non continuo imago. Ubi similitudo, non continuo imago, non continuo aequalitas, ut in speculo est imago, quia de illo expressa est, est etiam necessario similitudo, non tamen aequalitas, quia nulla de imagine, quae insumit illi res de qua expressa est. Ubi aequalitas, continuo & similitudo, non continuo imago: velut in duobus ovis paribus quia mest aequalitas, nec est similitudo. Quicumque enim adsunt una, adsunt & alteri: imago tamen non est, quia nec utrum de altero expressum est: ubi similitudo, non continuo imago, non continuo aequalitas. Omne quippe ovum omni ovo in quantum ovum est, simile est: sed ovum perdicis quantum est, in quantum est ovum, simile est ovo gallinae, nec imago tamen ejus est: quia non de illo expressum est: nec aequale, quia brevius est: est & alterius generis animantium. Sed ubi dicitur, non continuo, utique intelligitur, quia esse aliquando potest: potest ergo esse aliqua imago in qua sit etiam aequalitas: ut in parentibus & filiis invenietur imago, & aequalitas, & similitudo, si intervallum temporis defuisset. Nam & de parente expressa est filii similitudo: ut recte imago dicatur, & potest esse tanta, ut recte etiam dicatur aequalitas, nisi quod parens tempore praecedit, ex quo intellegitur & aequalitatem aliquando non solum similitudinem habere, sed etiam imaginem: quod in superiore exemplo manifestum est. Potest etiam aliquando similitudo & aequalitas, quamvis non sit imago, ut de ovis paribus diximus: potest similitudo & imago, quamvis non sit aequalitas: ut in speculo oslendimus: potest & similitudo esse, ubi & aequalitas & imago sit, sicut de filiis commemoravimus, excepto tempore quo praecedunt parentes. His igitur huius differentiae regulis breviter prolatis ad ea quae incoepta sunt ordine conperenti eranseamus, & divinae legis testimonia ab illis non ita ut urfurpata, a nobis venerabilium patrum documentis recte sint promulgata: quatenus & illorum volatus, his alis fractis quas sibi arroganter adcommodaverunt, tatescat, & studiosorum lectorum, qui his bene uti desiderant, sensus ad alta conscendat.
units.tr: Since we have set out, with God's help and in keeping with the sound and sober teaching of the holy Fathers, how it is to be understood that God made and created man in his image and likeness, it is now worth while to explain briefly what the difference is between image and likeness, or equality too. The purpose is that those who are carried headlong across the wide fields of empty assertions in their zeal for adoring images may know the difference between these three things, which they almost all take to be one, and may weigh how far they have gone astray; and that eager readers of this may arrive at some useful understanding. These three must therefore be distinguished. Everything that is an image is a likeness, but not everything that is a likeness is an image. An image never lacks likeness, but a likeness often lacks image; and for the most part neither likeness nor image is known to lack equality, although equality can sometimes be joined both to image and to likeness. Although these three belong to one category, which is called relation, they still have certain properties by which they differ from one another. For it is proper to an image that it is always expressed from something else. It is proper to likeness and equality that they remain in their own substance, are not expressed from another, but are called by this name when they are made like or equal to other things. An image does not admit of more or less, but likeness and equality do. For just as we say more similar or less similar, more equal or less equal, so we cannot say more image or less image. There is also a certain subtle inconsistency in the converse of these, which in Greek is called conversion [ἀντιστροφή]; to go through all of these at length would take too long. Yet so that the difference of these three names may appear more clearly, the words of blessed Augustine must be brought forward. For he says: Where there is an image, there is not always likeness, nor always equality; where there is likeness, there is not always image. Where there is likeness but not image, and not equality, as there is an image in a mirror, because it is expressed from that which it shows, there is necessarily likeness, but not equality, because no equality of the image arises with the thing from which it is expressed. Where there is equality, there is always likeness, but not always image, as in two equal eggs: since there is equality there, there is no likeness, and there is no image, because neither was expressed from the other. Where there is likeness, there is not always image, nor always equality: for every egg is like every egg insofar as it is an egg, but the egg of a partridge, insofar as it is an egg, is like a hen's egg, and yet it is not its image, because it was not expressed from it; nor is it equal, because it is smaller; and it is of another kind of living creature. But where it is said "not always," it is understood that it can sometimes be so; therefore there can be some image in which there is also equality, as one finds image, equality and likeness in parents and children, if the interval of time were absent. For the likeness of the son is also expressed from the parent, so that it may rightly be called an image; and it can be of such a kind that it may rightly be called equality too, except that the parent comes first in time. From this it is understood that equality sometimes has not only likeness but also image, as is clear in the earlier example. Likeness and equality may sometimes exist without image, as we said of equal eggs; likeness and image may exist without equality, as we showed in the mirror; and likeness may exist where equality and image are also present, as we mentioned of sons, except for the time in which the parents precede. Having briefly set out these rules of difference, let us pass on in order to what was begun, and let us make known the testimonies of the divine law, not as they have been seized upon by those men, but as they have been rightly proclaimed by us through the teaching of the venerable Fathers; so that the flight of those men may be checked, now that the wings they arrogantly fitted to themselves are broken, and so that the minds of studious readers who desire to make good use of these things may rise to lofty heights.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Quomodo intelligendum sit quod scriptum est, Abraham adoravit populum terræ, filios Heth, sive quod Moyses Jetro legitur adorasse: quibus exemplis hi qui propter adorandas imagines synodos faciunt, suum errorem fulcire affectant: & quia nec Jacob Pharaonem, nec Danihel Nabuchodonosor regem, ut illi dicunt, uspiam legantur adorasse.
units.tr: How it is to be understood that it is written that Abraham worshipped the people of the land, the sons of Heth, and that Moses is read to have worshipped Jethro. Those who hold synods about the worship of images try to prop up their error with these examples, and yet nowhere is it read that Jacob worshipped Pharaoh, or Daniel worshipped King Nebuchadnezzar, as they say.

units.la: ILLI qui in adorandis imaginibus æstuant, hoc peculiariter atque familiariter exemplo utuntur, quod Abraham filios Heth, & Moyses Jetro sacerdotem Madian adorasse legunt. Quorum quidem adoratio tantum distat à pictæ imaginis adoratione, quantum pictus ipse homo à vero homine ratione. quantum enim verus homo à picto, rationalis ab irrationali, sensibilis ab insensibili, animatus ab inanimato in sui definitione secernitur, tantum procul dubio & huius adoratio ab illius adoratione discernitur. Aliud namque est hominem salutationis officio & humanitatis obsequio adorando salutare, aliud pictúram diversorum colorum fucis conpaginatam, sine gressu, sine voce vel cæteris sensibus careo quo cultu adorare. Fraternitatem autem diligendam, & dilectionem erga proximos exhibendam, & humilitatis gradum amplectendum, perquæ nos mutuo salutantes adoramus, pene sanctarum scripturarum perdocemur exemplis: imagines vero adorare, vel salutare, vel insensatas naenias colere inhibemur potius, quàm instituimur, pene in cunctis divinæ scripturæ locis. Nam, ut cæteros taceam, sacratissimus pastor, super quem solidissimam petram ecclesia fundata est, non ait imagines, sed fraternitatem diligite: nec subditi estote picturis, sed omni humanæ creaturæ & Dominum Christum sanctificare non imaginibus, sed in cordibus nostris instituit. Denique sane & ab omni ratione seclusum est, hoc ad astruendam imaginum adorationem in exemplum trahere, quod Abraham populum terræ, & Moyses Jetro sacerdotem Madian legantur adorasse, cum videlicet plerumque sancti viri per humilitatem, qua Deo placuerunt homines salutationis gratia adoraverint, plerumque ne ab aliis adorarentur humiliter refugerint, plerumque rigore suæ sanctitatis erecti superbos quosque adorare contempserint. Imagines vero nusquam nec tenuiter quidem adorati sunt. Nam in eo, quod Abraham sive Moyses homines humiles suis utilitatibus necessarias adorasse legantur, & Mardocheus Aman hominem arrogantem, & in populi Dei interitum inhiantem adorare contempsisse reperitur, hoc evidenter ostendirur, quòd sancti viri erga humiles sive utrumque melius hortentur, sive ut ejusdem summæ virtutis munera non amittant, per eandem humilitatem fuerunt socii: contra pravorum vero nequitias sive ut malorum societates declinent, sive ut eos religere conpellant, fortiter fuerunt erecti. In eo igitur, quòd Iohannes in Apocalypsi ab angelo colligendus adoret, dicente eodem angelo, Vide ne feceris: conservus tuus sum: & Pastor ecclesiæ Petrus blandiens Cornelium adorationem vitaverit, dicens, Surge frater, & ego homo sum; sed & tu: & vas electionis Paulus cum Barnaba Lycaonum adorationem valida reluctatione prohibuerunt, procul dubio omni creatura, quæ solum deum decet, qui solus adorandus, solus colendus est, in pendenda esse veritatis.
units.tr: Those who are zealous for the worship of images use this example particularly and familiarly: they read that Abraham worshipped the sons of Heth, and that Moses worshipped Jethro, priest of Midian. But the worship of these is as far removed from the worship of a painted image as a painted man is from a real man in nature. For just as a real man is distinguished in his definition from a painted one, a rational being from an irrational one, a sensible being from an insensible one, and a living being from a lifeless one, so without doubt the worship of the one is distinguished from the worship of the other. For it is one thing to greet a man with the courtesy of a salutation and the deference of humanity, and another to worship a picture put together from coloured pigments, which has no movement, no voice, and none of the other senses. Moreover, that we should love our brothers, show love to our neighbours, and embrace the grade of humility by which we greet and worship one another, we are taught almost throughout the examples of the holy Scriptures. But that we should worship or greet images, or honour senseless trifles, we are warned against rather than instructed, in almost every passage of divine Scripture. For, to pass over the rest, the most holy minister, upon whom the Church has been founded as on a most solid rock, does not say "Images," but "Love the brotherhood"; nor does he say "Be subject to pictures," but "to every human creature"; and he taught us to sanctify the Lord Christ not with images but in our hearts. Finally, it is altogether unreasonable to draw into the argument for the worship of images the fact that Abraham and Moses are read to have worshipped the people of the land and Jethro, priest of Midian. For clearly holy men, through that humility by which they pleased God, often greeted people with a salutation, and often humbly shrank from being worshipped by others, and often, raised up by the rigour of their holiness, scorned to worship even the proud. But images were never worshipped, not even slightly. For in that Abraham or Moses are read to have worshipped humble men who were necessary for their own advantage, and Mordecai is found to have scorned to worship Haman, an arrogant man panting for the destruction of the people of God, this is clearly shown: holy men were companions of the humble, either to urge them towards something better, or so that they might not lose the gifts of the same high virtue, by that same humility; but against the wickedness of the depraved they were firmly upright, either so that they might avoid the company of the wicked or compel them to repent. Therefore, in that John in the Apocalypse wished to worship the angel who was to be gathered to him, and the angel said, "See that you do not do so, for I am your fellow servant," and Peter, the minister of the Church, gently refusing Cornelius's worship, said, "Rise, brother, for I too am a man"; and Paul, the chosen vessel, with Barnabas, prevented the worship of the Lycaonians by a strong resistance, it is beyond doubt that the worship which befits God alone, who alone is to be worshipped and alone honoured, is to be weighed against every creature in the balance of truth.

units.la: Dicat igitur nobis, dicat Augustinus quid de hac adoratione Abrahæ vel Moysi senserit. ait enim; Insinuatur hic alius exemplum, quod Moyses cum quo deus loquebatur, non fastidivit neque contemp sit alienigenæ socerī suo, quamquam & ipse Jetro, cum Israelita non fuisset, utrum inter viros deum verum colentes religiosæque fuit, quemadmodum & Iob cum ex ipso populo non fuisset, merito quaeritur, imo credibilius habeatur quippe posita sunt verba) vel utrum sacrificaverit deo vero in populo ejus quando vidit generum suum, utrum eum adoraverit ipse Moyses. Quamquam de adoratione etiamsi expressè positum esset, honor videretur facto reddidisse eo modo quo solet hominibus honorificentiæ causa exhiberi a patribus: sicut de Abraham scriptum est, quod adoraverit filios Heth. Sed nec illud silentio prætereundum est, quod dicunt Jacob Pharaonem adorasse, sive Danihel Nabuchodonosor regem, quod quidem nec in Hebræo habetur, nec in nostris Latinis codicibus, quia à beato Hieronymo ex Hebraica veritate translati sunt, uspiam reperitur. Non enim Jacob in conspectu Pharaonis fuisse legitur: quod quidem hoc modo scriptum narrat, Post hæc introduxit Ioseph patrem suum ad regem, & statuit eum coram eo, qui benedicens illi, & interrogavit eum, quot sunt dies annorum vitæ tuæ: respondit Iacob, Dies peregrinationis & vitæ meæ, centum triginta annorum parvi & mali, & non pervenerunt usque ad dies patrum meorum quibus peregrinati sunt, & benedictio regis foras. In quibus verbis non eum adorasse, sed benedixisse monstratur. Quod quidem & si ita fecisset, non ideo faceret ut inde adorandarum imaginum exemplum sumeretur: sed ut humilitas patrarcharum deum timentis, regem honorificantis monstraretur. Quæ dum ita se habeant, reor illi arbitrentur divinam scripturam illo familiarissimo illorum loquendi genere, quod quidam ... ita benedicere pro adorare, qui loquendi modo tanto eis peculiaris ... hunc loquendi modum abnuit, sed putæ, pprius, suis sive prudentibus semper verbis, sive sententiis utitur, Propheta adtestante, quia it: Lex domini ımreprehensibilis: quæ si benedicere possunt pro adorare, impropriis dictionibus utitur. Si in propriis dictionibus utitur, reprehensibilis est: est autem ımreprehensibilis: non igitur benedicere posuit pro adorare. Dic ergo tu, dic sancte Daniel, dic vir desideriorum, dic scrutator archanorum, dic indagator scripturarum, dic propheta qui redemptorem mundi in eo apertius cæteris dixisse probaris, quia non solum scribis eum esse verum, quod est tibi commune cum cæteris: sed quo tempore venturus sit doces, & reges perdendum digeris, & annos enumeras ac manifestissima signa prænuntias: dic utrum Nabuchodonosor, ut illi garrunt, adoraverit. Non in meo volumine hoc, inquam, fecisse me legis: quod quidem & si fecissem, nulla ex parte inde illorum adsertio fulciretur: ego proposui in corde meo ne polluerer de mensa eius, neque de vino potu eius, & illi me dicunt eum adorâsse. Cadentem ergo in faciem suam, & me adorantem, & hostias & incensum sacrificare mihi præcipientem, & deum deorum & dominum regum & revelatorem mysteriorum, qui potest aperire sacramenta confitentem, & eum in quo potius ob ignorum magnitudinem, cuius ego habitaculum sum, quam me adorantem blandis alloquiis affatus sum, & ab eo vt misericordia semper exerceret in genere Israhel, sive ut concap tivos meos, Ananiam, Azariam, & Misaelem constitueret super opera provinciæ Babylonis postulavi, non adulatorie adoravi. Quem quidem & si adorassem, non reni quandam infensatam adorarem, sed per humilitatis officium sublimiori potestati subditus manens, sciens non esse potestatem nisi à Deo, rationalem hominem salutando adorarem. Nam cùm tam felicem quondam habuerim conuersationem, ut quæsitis occasionibus ex latere regis quibus accusari possem ab invidis, & non in alio nisi in legitimis Dei mei accusatus fuerim, & in lacum leonum projectus, & nunc accuser adorasse quem non adoraverim, & à falsis testibus dicar egisse quod non egi, restat ut cum David clamem, In surrexerunt in me testes falsi, & mentita est iniquitas sibi. Cùm ergo ob imaginum amorem & Iacob patriarcham & Danihelem prophetam criminentur, & scripturarum divinarum sensus ad peregrinas intelligentias convertere nitantur, & suos prodecessores sive parentes contra legis imperium alpernentur, superest ut his tantum contenti sint, & earum patrocinio, si errorem suum corrigere nolunt, sicut & ipsi credunt, muniantur. Atque illi glorientur in imaginibus: nos autem gloriemur in cruce domini nostri Iesu Christi, per quem nobis mundus crucifixus est, nosque mundo.
units.tr: Let Augustine tell us, then, what he thought of this worship of Abraham or Moses. For he says: "Here another example is hinted at: that Moses, with whom God was speaking, did not disdain or despise his foreign father-in-law, although Jethro himself, not being an Israelite, was (as the words are written) properly asked whether he was among the men who worshipped the true God and were religious, just as Job, though he was not of that people, is rightly thought to have been so, indeed more credibly so; or whether he sacrificed to the true God among his people when he saw his son-in-law; and whether Moses himself worshipped him. Yet even if worship had been expressly stated, it would seem that the act paid honour in the manner in which fathers commonly show honour to men for the sake of respect, as it is written of Abraham that he worshipped the sons of Heth." But nor must we pass over in silence what they say, that Jacob worshipped Pharaoh, or Daniel worshipped King Nebuchadnezzar: this is nowhere found, neither in the Hebrew nor in our Latin codices, which were translated by the blessed Jerome from the Hebrew truth. For it is not read that Jacob was in the presence of Pharaoh; the text narrates it in this way: "After these things Joseph brought in his father to the king, and set him before him; and he blessed him, and asked him, 'How many are the days of the years of your life?' Jacob answered, 'The days of my pilgrimage and life are a hundred and thirty years, few and evil, and they have not reached the days of my fathers in which they were pilgrims'; and the king's blessing went forth." In these words he is shown to have blessed, not to have worshipped. And even if he had so done, it would not follow that an example for worshipping images could be taken from it; it would rather show the humility of the patriarchs who feared God and the honour they paid to a king. Since these things stand thus, I think they should consider that Scripture, in that most familiar manner of speaking of theirs, in which they say "to bless" for "to worship"... Yet he refuses this manner of speaking, but uses his own proper words, always prudent, or sentences, as the Prophet bears witness, when he says, "The law of the Lord is unblameable." If they can take "to bless" for "to worship," he uses improper words. If he uses proper words, it is blameable; but it is unblameable; therefore he did not put "to bless" for "to worship." Speak then, you, speak, holy Daniel; speak, man of desires; speak, searcher of hidden things; speak, interpreter of the Scriptures; speak, prophet who are proved to have spoken more plainly than the others of the Redeemer of the world, for you not only write that he is true, which you share with the others, but you teach at what time he is to come, you arrange the kings to be destroyed, you count the years and foretell the most manifest signs. Tell us whether Nebuchadnezzar, as they babble, worshipped. I say that in my book I read no such thing; and even if I had, their assertion would not be supported in any way. I purposed in my heart that I should not be defiled by his table, nor by his wine to drink; and they say that I worshipped him. But falling on his face and worshipping me, and ordering me to offer victims and incense, he addressed me with flattering speech as God of gods, Lord of kings, and revealer of mysteries, who can open secrets to one who confesses, and he to whom, rather than worship him, I, the dwelling of the Most High, spoke—I did not worship him with flattery. And I asked of him that he would always show mercy to the race of Israel, and appoint my captive companions Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael over the affairs of the province of Babylon. Even if I had worshipped him, I would not have worshipped some unformed thing, but, remaining subject to a higher power through the duty of humility, knowing that there is no power except from God, I would have worshipped by greeting a rational man. For when I had once had so happy a conduct that, when occasions were sought, I might have been accused by the envious from the king's side, and I was accused in nothing except the lawful things of my God, and was cast into the lions' den, and now I am accused of having worshipped one whom I did not worship, and I am said by false witnesses to have done what I did not do, it remains for me to cry with David, 'False witnesses have risen up against me, and iniquity has lied to itself.' Since, therefore, Jacob the patriarch and Daniel the prophet are accused on account of their love of images, and men strive to turn the senses of the divine Scriptures to foreign meanings, and to disparage their predecessors or parents against the command of the law, it remains that they should be content with these alone, and be defended by their patronage, if they are unwilling to correct their error, as they themselves believe. And let them glory in images; but we will glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to us, and we to the world.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De eo quod Iohannes presbyter & legatus Orientalium incautè imagi- num adorationem stabilire nitens, dixisse legitur. Erexit Iacob titulum Deo, quatinus & benedixit eum.
units.tr: On how John the presbyter and legate of the Orientals, rashly striving to establish the adoration of images, is reported to have said: Jacob set up a title to God, so that he also blessed him.

units.la: NON mediocris socordiæ est hoc etiam ad imaginum adorationem adstruendam exemplum proferte, quod Iacob lapidem erexit in titulum, sicut Iohannes presbyter & legatus Orientalium protulisse in eadem synodo, quæ pro adorandis imaginibus agitata est, legitur: quoniam ille lapis non alicuius præteritæ rei im gø vel similitudo fuisse creditur. Qui si ob aliquius præteritæ rei memoriam ab eiusdem rei similitudine expressus, & à sancto patriarcha ad adorandum futurus eret- ctus, quoddam fortassis posset illis ferre adminiculum, qui ranti erroris subire non formidavere periculum. Sed dum aliud sit quædam per patriarcham fieri ad præfigurationem futurorum, aliud à pictore pingi quædam ob memoriam præteritorum gestorum: aliud sit spiritu sancto esse repletum, aliud pictoria arte imbutum: aliud iste gerat cælesti munere fretus, aliud ille operandi usu expertus: aliud lit Iacob in titulum erigere lapidem, aliud quendam pictorem in parietem statuere imaginem: aliud secundum typicam figuram desuper oleum fundere, aliud secundum vaniloquam adiectionem adorare iubere: inutile & ultra quàm inutile est hoc ad adstruendam aliquam rem in exemplum proponere, quod ab illa re omnium argumentationum diverticulis videtur distare. Numquid nam Iacob illum lapidem ut adoretur erexit, aut alicuius rei in eo imaginem depinxit? Nam dum imagines pene nullum officium aliud, nisi mentibus per sui intuitum memoriam inferendi habeant, lapis qui à patriarcha erectus est tria insignia & summo honore digna creditur officia habuisse. Primum, quod cervicem Israhelitieam fulcierit, & pulvillis carenti patriarchæ pulvilli visem præstiterit, & ejus capite fuerit onerarus, qui non solum scalam à terra usque ad cælum pertingetem, & angelos per eam ascendentes & descendentes, sed etiam ipsum dominum bona sibi pollicentem cernebat. Secundum, quod in insigne & titulo, quo sanctus patriarcha illius sancti loci reminisceretur, erectus est, quo rediens prolis & coniugum affectu exhilararus, & magna rerum opulentia ditatus. Hia domino vota qui hæc sibi cuncta concesserat redderet. Tertiū, quod typum gerebar nostri mediatoris, qui factus est in caput angeli, & est mirabilis in oculis nostris: qui unctus est à patre oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus suis: quem & Danihel lapidem abscisum dicit de monte sine manibus præcidentium, absque coitu & humano videlicet semine ex utero virginali genitum. Quem & David petram nuncupat dicens, Dominus petra mea & robur meum & salvator meus. De quo etiam in Esaia propheta scribitur; Ecce ponro in fundamentis Sion lapidem summum, angularem, probatum, electum, pretiosum, & qui crediderit in eum non confundetur. Qui idcirco angularis dicitur, eo quod duos parietes ex adverso venientes, excircumcutione vel delicet & præputio, vel etiam duo testamenta in se summo, probato, electo & pretioso lapide cohjungit, & in uno sanctæ ecclesiæ cœtu, cuius ille caput est, connectit. De quo & per prophetam Zachariæ paterna voce dicitur, Ecce ego adducam filium meum orientem : quia lapis quem dedi coram Iesu septem in eo oculi sunt. In quibus septem oculis septiformis gratiæ spiritus, qui à patre filioque procedit, evidenter ostenditur: & per Esaiam prophetam, Spiritus Domini spiritus sapientiæ & intellectus, spiritus consilii & fortitudinis, spiritus scientiæ & pietatis, spiritus timoris Domini nominatur. De quo etiam angulari lapide petra ecclesiæ ait; Sicut modo geniti infantes, rationabiles, sine dolo lac concupiscite, ut in eo crescatis in salutem : si tamen gustastis quam dulcis est Dominus, ad quem accedentes lapidem vivum, ab hominibus quidem reprobatum, à Deo autem electum & honorificatum: & post pauca, Vobis igitur honor credentibus, non credentibus autem: lapis, quem reprobaverunt ædificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli, & lapis offensionis & petra scandali his qui offendunt verbo nec credunt in quo & positi sunt. Quo documento monstratur illum & honorem fortitudinis credentibus, & scandalum duritiæ incredulis esse. Quod etiam per iustum Simeonem hoc sensu prædictum est. Ait enim, Positus est hic in ruinam & in resurrectionem multorum in Israel: in ruinam scilicet incredulorum, in resurrectionem vero credentium: qui etiam ignis nuncupatur, sive quod in se credentes æterni luminis fulgore perlustrat, sive quod incredulos æterni ignis ardore torrebit. De unctione vero huius lapidis & paulo superius David oraculis prolatum est, & nunc præfati pastoris ecclesiæ testimonio proferendum est, qui ait, Iesum Nazarenum quem unxit Deus spiritu sancto & virtute. Quia ergo spiritus sanctus plerumque in divinis scripturis olei nomine innuitur, Iohannes Apostolus testis est qui dicit, Sicut unctio eius docet nos de omnibus. Cujus si inenarrabilis nectaris unctione delibuti sunt ob imaginum adorationem stabiliendam, synodos agitare & scripturas sanctas ad extraneos sensus usurpare nequaquam debent.
units.tr: It is no small folly to bring forward this example too, to establish the adoration of images: that Jacob set up a stone as a title, as John the presbyter and legate of the Orientals is reported to have put forward in the same council that was held to debate the adoration of images. For that stone is not believed to have been an image or likeness of some past event. If it had been raised by the holy patriarch to be adored, having been shaped as a likeness of some past event for the memory of it, it might perhaps offer some support to those who did not shrink from the danger of so great an error. But it is one thing for certain things to be done by a patriarch as a foreshadowing of things to come, another for things to be painted by a painter for the memory of past deeds; one thing to be filled with the Holy Spirit, another to be steeped in the art of painting; one thing for this man to act relying on a heavenly gift, another for that man to act from experience of his craft; one thing for Jacob to set up a stone as a title, another for some painter to set up an image on a wall; one thing to pour oil from above according to a typical figure, another to command adoration according to a babbling addition. It is useless, and more than useless, to bring this forward as an example to establish any matter, since it seems to be far removed from that matter by all the windings of argument. For did Jacob set up that stone so that it might be adored, or did he paint an image of something on it? For since images have almost no office other than to bring memory to minds through being looked at, the stone which was set up by the patriarch is believed to have had three distinguished offices, worthy of the highest honour. First, that it supported the Israelite's neck and gave a pillow to the patriarch lacking a pillow, and was burdened with his head; he who saw not only a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, and angels ascending and descending by it, but also the Lord himself promising him good things. Second, that it was set up as a sign and title by which the holy patriarch would remember that holy place, returning to which he was gladdened by the affection of children and wife, and enriched by great abundance of goods; and so he might render vows to the Lord who had granted him all these things. Third, that it bore the type of our Mediator, who was made the head of the corner, and is wonderful in our eyes; who was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his fellows; whom Daniel also calls the stone cut out of the mountain without hands cutting it, that is, born of a virginal womb without intercourse and human seed. David also calls him a rock, saying, The Lord is my rock and my strength and my saviour. Of him also it is written in the prophet Isaiah: Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a chief stone, the corner, tried, elect, precious, and he who believes in him shall not be confounded. He is called the corner stone for this reason, that he joins together the two walls coming from opposite sides, circumcision and uncircumcision, or indeed the two covenants, in himself as the chief, tried, elect and precious stone, and binds them into one assembly of the holy Church, of which he is the head. Of him also the Father speaks through the prophet Zechariah: Behold, I will bring forth my son, the Orient; for the stone which I have laid before Jesus, upon that one stone are seven eyes. In these seven eyes the sevenfold Spirit of grace, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, is clearly shown; and through the prophet Isaiah he is named the Spirit of the Lord, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord. Of this same corner stone the rock of the Church also says: As newborn infants, rational, desire without guile the milk, that you may grow thereby unto salvation; if indeed you have tasted how sweet the Lord is; coming to him, a living stone, indeed rejected by men but chosen and honoured by God: and after a few words, To you therefore who believe, honour; but to those who do not believe: the stone which the builders rejected, this has been made the head of the corner, and a stone of offence and a rock of scandal to those who stumble at the word and do not believe, in which they were also set. By this testimony it is shown that he is an honour of strength to believers, and a scandal of hardness to unbelievers. This was also foretold in this sense by the righteous Simeon. For he says, This child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel: for the fall of unbelievers, but the rising again of believers; he is also called fire, either because he illumines believers with the brightness of eternal light, or because he will scorch unbelievers with the heat of eternal fire. Concerning the anointing of this stone, something has been brought forward in David's oracles a little above, and now it is to be brought forward by the testimony of the aforesaid minister of the Church, who says, Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power. Since therefore the Holy Spirit is in the divine Scriptures often signified by the name of oil, the apostle John is a witness who says, The anointing teaches you concerning all things. If men have been steeped in the anointing of his ineffable nectar, they must by no means convene councils to establish the adoration of images, nor seize upon the holy Scriptures for foreign senses.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De eo quod præfatus Iohannes dixit, In hominis forma luctatus est cum ipso, & vocavit cum Israhel, quod est interpretatum, mens videns Deum.
units.tr: Concerning what the aforesaid John said: "In the form of a man he wrestled with him, and called him Israel, which is interpreted, a mind seeing God."

units.la: SED necillud quidem à reprehensione vacat quod idem Iohannes presbyter & legatus Orientalium inter cætera deliramenta de Iacob dixisse fertur, In hominis forma luctatus est cum ipso, & vocavit cum Israhel, quod est interpretatum, mens videns Deum: cum hoc dictum & à re propolita longe distet, & in nominis interpretatione usitatorem quandam omittens, pene inusitatum quid persequit. Nam dum quidam id nomen interpretentur, vir videns Deum, quidam vero, fortis cum Deo, nonnulli: etiam veracius, princeps cum Deo: nescio tamen an ullus eorum qui in canone recipiuntur, reperiatur hoc, mens videns Deum, interpretatus fuisse: unde non solum ille reprehendendus est qui usitationibus interpretationibus prætermissis pene inusitatum quid protulit, sed & omnis illa synodus, quæ in pluribus sommianti adsensum præbuit, quæ non solum dicenti non restitit, sed etiam dicta in volumine taxavit. Cum ergo sancta ecclesia secundum sanctorum patrum institutionem omne quod inreprehensibile est recipiat: omne vero quod reprehensibile abiciat, hanc quoque eorum synodum, quæ utique reprehensibilis est, abicit: & si hanc quæ reprehensibilis est non abicit, neque eas quæ inreprehensibiles sunt suscipit: suscipit autem eas quæ inreprehensibiles sunt: hanc igitur quia reprehensioni patet, penitus suscipere non debet. Illas enim synodos sancta & universalis recipit ecclesia, quæ pro diversis fidei, sive religionis causis diversis locis, seu temporibus, à doctis & catholicis viris celebratæ, à sana sobriaque doctrina nullatenus deviare perhibentur. Præterea tanti patriarchæ cum angelo luctatio non quandam imaginum adorationem, sed dominicam præfiguraffe dicitur in eodem populo passionem: qui populus & ei luctando prævaluit, quia crucifixit: & ab eo benedictionem in his qui in eum crediderunt accepit: & in his claudus qui in eum credere contempserunt, remansit, dicente beato Augustino, Quod ab illo angelo desiderat benedici Iacob cui luctando prævaluit, magna est de CHRISTO prophetia. Nam eo ipso ammonet mysticum aliquid sapere, quia omnis homo à majore vult benedici. Quomodo ergo ab eo ipse voluit quem luctando superavit? prævaluit enim Iacob Christo, vel potius prævalere visum est per eos Israhelitas à quibus crucifixus est Christus: & ab eo tamen benedicitur in eis Israhelitis qui crediderunt in Christum, ex quibus erat qui dicebat, Nam & ego Israhelita sum ex genere Abrahæ & tribu Benjamin. Unus ergo atq; idem Iacob & claudus & benedictus. Claudus in latitudine femoris tanquam in multitudine generis, de quibus dictum est, Et claudicaverunt à femitu suis: benedictus autem in eis de quibus dictum est. Reliquiæ per electionem gratia salvæ factæ sunt.
units.tr: BUT that statement is not free from criticism, which John the presbyter, legate of the Easterners, is said to have made about Jacob among his other nonsense: "In the form of a man he wrestled with him, and called him Israel, which is interpreted, a mind seeing God." This saying is far removed from the matter in hand, and by omitting the usual interpretation of the name it pursues something almost unheard of. For while some interpret that name as "a man seeing God," others as "strong with God," and some, more truthfully, as "a prince with God," I do not know whether any of those received in the canon is found to have rendered it "a mind seeing God." Hence not only is he to be blamed who, passing over the usual interpretations, brought forth something almost unheard of, but also that whole synod which gave assent to the dreamer in many matters, which not only did not resist him when he spoke but even censured the sayings in the volume. Since therefore the holy Church, following the teaching of the holy Fathers, receives everything that is irreproachable and rejects everything that is reprehensible, it rejects also that synod of theirs, which is certainly reprehensible; and if it does not reject what is reprehensible, neither does it take up what is irreproachable; yet it does take up what is irreproachable; therefore, since this synod lies open to reproach, it ought not to receive it at all. For the holy and universal Church receives those synods which learned and catholic men celebrated in various places or times, for various causes of faith or religion, and which are said in no way to have departed from sound and sober doctrine. Moreover, the wrestling of so great a patriarch with the angel is said to have prefigured, not some adoration of images, but the Lord's passion among the same people: that people prevailed over him in wrestling because they crucified him, and received a blessing from him in those who believed in him, while in those who scorned to believe in him he remained lame. The blessed Augustine says: "That Jacob, whom he overcame in wrestling, desires to be blessed by that angel, is a great prophecy about Christ. For by this very fact it warns that something mystical is meant, since every man wishes to be blessed by one greater. How then does he wish to be blessed by him whom he overcame in wrestling? For Jacob prevailed over Christ, or rather it seemed that he prevailed through those Israelites by whom Christ was crucified; yet he is blessed by him in those Israelites who believed in Christ, from among whom was the one who said, 'For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.' One and the same Jacob is therefore both lame and blessed. Lame in the breadth of the thigh, as in the multitude of the race, of whom it is said, 'And they limped from their paths'; blessed, however, in those of whom it is said, 'A remnant has been saved by the election of grace.'

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Quod non ad adorationem imaginum pertineat, nec in nostris codicibus qui ex Hebraica veri- tate translati sunt, inveniatur, quod illi in sua synodo dicunt, Iacob suscipiens à filiis suis vestem talarem tabefactam Ioseph osculatus est cum lachrymis, & propriis oculis inposuit.
units.tr: That this does not pertain to the adoration of images, and is not found in our codices, which were translated from the Hebrew truth, as those men claim in their synod: that Jacob, receiving from his sons the stained tunic reaching to the feet, kissed Joseph's garment with tears and laid it upon his own eyes.

units.la: NON mirandum est si Iacob accusetur ab illis tunicam Ioseph osculatus fuisse, & oculis inposuisse, à quibus etiam Pharaonem accusatur adorasse. Accidere etenim plerumque solet, ut qui semel falli cœperit, crebro fallatur: & qui semel à via recesserit, & tramitem sui itinetis ducem sequi neglexerit, per abrupta & invia affatim errore duce feratur. Tunica enim Ioseph nec in Hebraeis Hebrĕis codicibus, nec in Latinis qui ex Hebraica veritate translati sunt, à patre oculata vel oculis inpolita fuisse narratur. Quod quidem & si factum fuisse narraretur, nullo modo in hoc facto vel tenuiter imaginum adoratio innueretur: cum tamen aliud sit adorare, aliud oculari, quod illi acyrologice unum putant: atque aliud pictam imaginem adorare, aliud à paterno affectu vestis filii qui extinctus credebatur dolore compellente madefscentibus fletu oculis inponi: aliud cuidam similitudini colla submittere, aliud præ ceteris dilecti filii vesti interna pietate oculum dare. Adeo itaque sanctus patriarcha angebatur animi procella turbati, ut non solum vestem filii quem inclementia mortis raptum credebar, oculararetur, vel oculis inponeret: sed etiam consolatione postposita funereis vocibus lugubi rer mala sua exaggerans, se etiam fore post hunc ad infernum descensurum ediceret. Qualiter ergo beatus Iacob tunicam filii non oculatus fuisse, aut oculis inposuisse, sed vidisse tantum & cognovisse credatur, hoc ordine sancta scriptura commemorat. Ait enim; Tulerunt autem tunicam ejus, & in sanguine hœdi quem occiderant tinxerunt, mittentes qui ferrent ad patrem, & dicerent, Hanc invenimus, vide utrum tunica filii tui, an non. Quam cum agnovisset pater, ait, Tunica filii mei est: fera pessima comedit eum, bestia devoravit Ioseph. Denique quid hæc illius sancti viri tunica, per quam illi imaginum adorationem adstruere nihil sunt, typicis præfiguraverit sacramentis & ractitis innuerit mysteriis, oportet ut breviter exequamur: quo & illorum vana adsertio destituatur, & lectoris animus mulceatur. Ioseph namque, qui augmentum interpretatur, & ab Ægyptiis salvator mundi est nuncupatus, illius typum gessit, qui & genus humanum sua morte salvavit, & mundum spiritali frumento refecit, & in tantum augmentum sue fidei semen crescere fecit, ut & totum mundum impleret, & per eandem fidem tenena ce etibus copularet. Ejus vestis hœdi sanguine tincta est, quia in similitudine carnis peccati secundum Apostolum apparuit, & de peccato damnavit peccatum: vel etiam hostia pro peccatis effectus, peccata nostra portavit in corpore suo super lignum, ut a malis liberati cum justitia vivamus: cujus vulnere sanati sumus, qui velut oves errabamus. Est etiam & vestis eius sancta ecclesia, quæ est corpus Christi, Paulo adtestante qui ait; Gaudeo in passionibus meis, quia expleo ea quæ desunt passionum Christi in carne mea propter corpus ejus, quod est ecclesia: quæ vestis polymira sive varia est: quia videlicet sancta ecclesia de diversarum gentium sive linguarum varietate colligitur, Psalmographo docente qui ait: Adstitit regina à dextris tuis in vestitu deaurato circumamicta varietate. Solereteiam eadem vestis quæ talaris fuisse describitur, sanctorum virorum qui utique membra Christi sunt, perfectionem designare, qui perceptum boni operis indumentum ad talos, id est, ad finem usque perducunt.
units.tr: It is no wonder that Jacob is accused by those men of having kissed Joseph's tunic and laid it upon his eyes, the same men who also accuse Pharaoh of having worshipped. For it usually happens that one who has once begun to err is often deceived again, and one who has once left the road and neglected to follow the guide of his path is carried on, with error as his guide, through precipices and trackless places. For Joseph's tunic is not narrated, either in the Hebrew codices or in the Latin ones translated from the Hebrew truth, as having been kissed by the father or laid upon his eyes. Yet even if it were narrated that this was done, the worship of images would in no way, not even faintly, be hinted at in such a deed: for it is one thing to worship, another to kiss, which those men, by an abuse of language, think to be one and the same; and it is one thing to worship a painted image, another for a father, compelled by grief, with eyes wet with tears, to lay them upon the garment of a son who was believed dead; and another to bow the neck before some likeness, and another, out of inner devotion, to give a look to the garment of a son beloved above all others. So much was the holy patriarch tormented, troubled by the storm of his mind, that he not only kissed the garment of the son whom he believed snatched away by the cruelty of death, or laid his eyes upon it, but also, setting consolation aside, lamenting with funereal cries and magnifying his woes, he declared that after this son he too would go down to hell. How the blessed Jacob is believed to have not kissed his son's tunic or laid his eyes upon it, but only to have seen and recognized it, holy Scripture relates in this order. For it says: "They took his tunic, and dipped it in the blood of the kid which they had killed, and sent men to carry it to the father and say, 'We have found this; see whether it is your son's tunic or not.' When the father recognized it, he said, 'It is my son's tunic; a most evil beast has eaten him, a wild beast has devoured Joseph.'" Finally, what this tunic of that holy man prefigured by typical sacraments, and what hidden mysteries it signified, through which those men's assertion is in no way supported, we must set out briefly, so that their empty claim may be refuted and the reader's mind soothed. Joseph, indeed, who is interpreted increase, and was called by the Egyptians saviour of the world, bore the type of him who by his death saved the human race, refreshed the world with spiritual grain, and caused the seed of his faith to grow to such an increase that it filled the whole world and joined the faithful together through the same faith. His garment is stained with the blood of a kid, because, according to the Apostle, he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh and condemned sin in the flesh; or also, made a sacrifice for sins, he bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that we, freed from evils, might live in righteousness, by whose wound we were healed, who like sheep were going astray. His garment is also the holy Church, which is the body of Christ, as Paul bears witness, who says: "I rejoice in my sufferings, because I fill up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for his body, which is the Church." That garment is many-coloured or varied, because the holy Church is clearly gathered from the variety of diverse nations and tongues, as the psalmist teaches, who says: "The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety." The same garment, which is described as reaching to the feet, is also wont to signify the perfection of holy men, who are indeed members of Christ, and who bring the garment of good work, once received, down to the ankles, that is, right to the end.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: De eo quod indocte & inordinate dicunt, Si calumniaris me, quoniam ut Deum ad- oro lignum crucis, quur non calumniaris Jacob adorantem summita- tem virgæ Joseph? Sed manifestum est, quoniam non lignum vi- dens adoravit, sed per lignum Ioseph, sicut & nos per crucem Christum.
units.tr: On what they say foolishly and carelessly: "If you accuse me because I adore the wood of the cross as God, why do you not accuse Jacob, who adored the top of Joseph's staff?" But it is plain that he did not worship the wood as he saw it, but worshipped God through Joseph's staff, just as we worship Christ through the cross.

units.la: ILLUD fare quod dicunt: Iacob etiam summitatem virgæ Ioseph adorasse, non est omittendum quoniam quidem magnum eo ob adorandas imagines in hac re gratulantur habere exemplum: cum videlicet, in Lari in codicibus non legatur, Adoravit summitatem virgæ Iosephi: sed in quibusdam, Adoravit super caput virgæ, & in Hebrea veritate, cui potissimum fides adhibenda est, nullam penitus vel tenuiter mentionem virgæ faciat, sed dicat tantum, Adoravit Israel Deum conversus ad lectulum caput. in quo utique, ut ait beatus Augustinus, senex jacebat, & sic positum habebat ut in eo sine labore quando vellet oraret. Quia ergo, ut prædicti sumus, quidam Latinorum codicum habent, Adoravit super summitatem virgæ, necesse est ut memorari doctoris documentis qualiter intelligendum sit explicemus. ait enim; Quod habent Latini codices, Et adoravit super caput virgæ ejus, nonnulli emendantes habent. Adoravit super caput virgæ suæ, vel in capite virgæ suæ, sive in cacumen, vel super cacumen. Fallit enim eos Græcum verbum, quod eisdem litteris scribitur sive ejus sive suæ: sed accentus differes sunt, & ab eis qui ista noverunt in codicibus non contemnuntur. Valent enim ad magnam discretionem, quamvis & unam plus litteram habere posset: si esset sive aut non esset ὧν τοῦ, sed ἐὰν τοῦ, ac per hoc merito quæritur, quid sit quod dictum est. Nam facile intelligeretur, senem qui virgam ferebat eo more quo illa atas baculum solet, ut se inclinavit ad Deum adorandum, id utique fecerit super cacumen virgæ suæ, quam sic ferebat ut super eam caput inclinando adoraret Deum. Quid est ergo, Adoravit super cacumen virgæ ejus, id est, filii sui Ioseph: an forte tulerat ab eo virgam quando ei jurabat idem filius, & dum eam tenet post verba jurantis, nondum illa reddita, mox adoravit Deum? Non enim pudebat eum ferre tantisper insigne potestatis filii sui, ubi figuræ magnæ rei futuræ præsignabantur. Dicant ergo, dicant, quid contra hæc dicturi sunt, qui ob adorandas imagines tantum patriarcham criminari non formidant, & scripturas sanctas velana mente permutare affectant. Ecce Hebraica veritas eundem patriarcham Deum adorasse ad caput lectuli clamat: ecce Latinorum bibliotheca eum aut super caput virgæ, aut in capite, aut in cacumine, vel super cacumen adorasse denuntiat: ecce vir eruditissimus Augustinus, & divini muneris flamine afflatus, solerti indagatione cum aut in sua, aut in filii virgæ summitate Deum, non eandem virgam, nec eundem filium adorasse personat. Dicant, quis sanctæ legis translator eum summitatem virgæ filii, &in eadem virga filium adorasse transtulerit: quis sanctæ legis studiosissimus indagator eum virgam filii vel filium potius quàm Deum adorasse tractaverit: & cum hunc invenire nequiverint, depravatricem, sive refragatricem potius, quàm indagatricem suam intellegentiam divinarum scripturarum esse persentiant. Iam verò quia pene omnis divinæ legis series ab illis ob imaginum adoratio-nem aut mutilarur aut permutatur, nova necesse est post Moysen legis tradatur scriptio: nova post Esdram ... gis reperiatur restauratio: nova post septuaginta interpretes, Theodotionem & Symmachum & Aquilam, sive etiam beatum Hieronymum legis quæratur translatio: nova post Apostolos & Apostolicos viros Spiritu sancto repletos scrutentur tractatio, quæ adeo divinis scripturis refragari queat, ut omnes imaginum adorationem spernentes anathematis vinculo nectat. Quæ sit præterea differentia crucis Christi & imaginum pictorum arte pictarum, vel quanto mysterio crux imaginibus eminet, sive quomodo humanum genus non per imagines, sed per crucem Christi redemptum sit, quæ duo illi vel patria vel æqualia purant, in sequentibus loco suo Domino favente explicabimus.
units.tr: As for what they say, that Jacob also worshipped the top of Joseph's staff, it must not be passed over that they rejoice to have here a great precedent for adoring images. For in the Latin codices one does not read "He worshipped the top of Joseph's staff"; in some it reads "He worshipped upon the head of the staff," while the Hebrew truth, to which above all faith must be given, makes no mention at all, not even a faint one, of a staff, but says only, "Israel worshipped God, turned toward the head of the bed," and in that bed, as the blessed Augustine says, the old man was lying, and he had it so placed that he could pray in it without effort whenever he wished. Since, then, as we have said, some Latin codices read "He worshipped upon the top of the staff," we must explain how the teacher's instruction requires it to be understood. For he says: "What the Latin codices have, 'and he worshipped upon the head of his staff,' some emending read as 'he worshipped upon the head of his own staff,' or 'in the head of his staff,' or 'upon the top,' or 'upon the summit.'" For the Greek word, which is written with the same letters whether it is his or his own, deceives them; but the accents differ, and they are not to be disregarded by those who know these things in the codices. For they make a great difference, although one letter more could be present, if it were ὧν τοῦ rather than ἐὰν τοῦ. Hence it is rightly asked what is meant by what is said. For it would easily be understood that the old man, carrying the staff in the way that age usually carries a stick, bowed himself to worship God, and did so upon the top of his own staff, which he held in such a way that he could bow his head over it and worship God. What then is the meaning of "he worshipped upon the top of his staff," that is, of his son Joseph? Or had he perhaps taken the staff from him when the same son swore to him, and while he still held it after the words of the one swearing, not yet returned, did he at once worship God? For he was not ashamed to hold for a while the emblem of his son's power, where great future things were foreshadowed by figures. Let them say, then, let them say what they will answer to these things, those who do not hesitate to accuse the patriarch of this for the sake of adoring images, and who strive to alter the holy Scriptures with a perverse mind. Behold, the Hebrew truth cries out that this same patriarch worshipped God at the head of the bed; behold, the Latin library proclaims that he worshipped either upon the head of the staff, or in the head, or in the top, or upon the summit; behold, the most learned Augustine, inspired by the breath of divine grace, by careful investigation declares that God was worshipped neither upon the same staff nor upon the same son, but upon the top of his own staff. Let them say who among the translators of the holy law has rendered it as "he worshipped the top of his son's staff, and in the same staff the son"; who among the most diligent investigators of the holy law has treated it as meaning that he worshipped the son's staff, or rather the son, rather than God; and when they cannot find such a person, let them feel that their understanding of the divine Scriptures is corrupting, or rather opposing, rather than examining. Indeed, since almost the entire series of the divine law is either mutilated or altered by them for the sake of the adoration of images, a new writing of the law must be handed down after Moses; a new restoration after Ezra must be sought; a new translation after the Seventy, Theodotion, Symmachus and Aquila, or even after blessed Jerome, must be looked for; a new treatment must be examined after the Apostles and apostolic men filled with the Holy Spirit, one which could so oppose the divine Scriptures that it binds with the chain of anathema all who scorn the adoration of images. What the difference is, moreover, between the cross of Christ and images painted by the art of painters, or with how great a mystery the cross stands out above images, or how the human race was redeemed not through images but through the cross of Christ, which two things are either passed over or treated as equal, we shall explain in the following chapters in their proper place, the Lord favouring us.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XIV.

units.la: Non pertinere ad imaginum adorationem, ut illi dicunt, quod scriptum est, Iacob Pharaonem benedixit.
units.tr: That what is written, that Jacob blessed Pharaoh, does not pertain to the adoration of images, as they claim.

units.la: Quoniam sæpe memoratus patriarcha Iacob Pharaonem non adorasse, sed benedixisse legatur, superius dictum est. Nunc vero quia in alia ejusdem vanissima synodi lectione benedictio quodammodo posita est pro adoratione, breviter exsequendum est. Quoniam quidem tantis est illius vanitatis scriptura ignorantiæ obsita caliginibus, ut nec sequentia præcedentibus, nec præcedentia convenire videantur sequentibus, & ut se habet vanitas mendacium, semper fugitiva, semperque caduca, semperque labenti sequi ur, dicente Salomone; Qui mumbit mendacia, hic pascit ventos, ipse autem sequitur aves volantes. Ut ergo imaginum adorationem, in quarum amore eorum mens pendet, & totius sanctitatis propositum est, stabiliant, plurima verba vel sensus quæ ad aliud pertinent, in adorationem mutare affectant. Nam & hæc, quod idem sanctus vir Phataonem benedixit, non ad eandem benedictionem pertinere putant, quam solent ple-rumque exsules civibus, sibiditi præsatis, pauperiores ditioribus, & quam maxime senes, qui sibi quædam commoda impendunt exhibere, sed ad nescio quam adorandarum imaginum pictūram: quæ nimirum tanto inutilior est, quanto minus suæ utilitatis efficaciam potest loquendo edicere. Ajunt enim, Benedixit Iacob Pharaonem, sed non ut Deum benedixit: adoramus nos imaginem, sed non ut Deum adoramus. O inconveniens conparatio! O hebes conjectura! O stolidissima dictio! Similem dicis benedictionem, quam sanctus patriarcha regi exhibuit, qui pie cæteris ailecti ssimo filio insigne contulit potestatis: qui sibi cum universa prole uberem ad inhabitandum glebam concessit: qui sibi non cuiuscunque provinciæ portionem, sed totius sui imperii terræ donavit optionem, adorationi quam imaginibus exhibes? quæ adorantibus nihil præter rei memoriam cujus sunt, exhibere valent. Benedixitque Iacob Pharaonem, non ut Deum quem omnis creatura benedicit & laudat, neque ut pictūram quam manus artificis aprat, sed ut hominem cui propter sublimitatem concessæ à Deo potestatis honor est exhibendus. Benedixit, inquam, eum, non ut imaginem infensatam, sed ut rationem hominem: non ut industria pictoris conpaginatum, sed ut ad Dei imaginem & similitudinem conditum: non ut in parietibus innumerabiliter stantem, sed ut sibi vel proli pro pera commodi & cur ita dixerim, benedixit Israhel regem qui ejusdem spiritus nectare delibutus erat: qui per Apostolum dicturus esset, Benedicite & nolite maledicere: qui non solum pro eo qui se opuientia terrarum dirabat, sed pro calumniantibus & persequentibus orare debebat. Non ergo hæc modi benedictio, quæ profecto bonæ retributionis causa extitit celebrata, imaginum adorationi congruit: quæ neque se adorantibus, neque adorare spernentibus quandam pro qualitate meritorum possunt inferre retributionem.
units.tr: Since it has been said above that the patriarch Jacob is often recorded as having not worshipped Pharaoh but blessed him, it must now be explained briefly, because in another reading of that most vain synod the blessing has been somehow put in place of adoration. Scripture is so clouded by the darkness of their ignorance that the following does not seem to agree with what precedes, nor what precedes with what follows. And since falsehood is always fleeting, always falling and always pursuing what slips away, as Solomon says: He who feeds on lies feeds on the wind, and he himself pursues flying birds. So, in order to establish the adoration of images, on whose love their minds hang and which is the whole aim of their holiness, they strive to turn many words or senses that belong to something else into adoration. For they also do not think that this statement, that the same holy man blessed Pharaoh, refers to the same kind of blessing that exiles commonly give to citizens, the poor to the rich, and the old especially, who are wont to offer some benefit to themselves. Rather, they think it refers to I know not what painting of images to be adored. This is surely all the more useless, the less it can state the effectiveness of its usefulness. For they say: Jacob blessed Pharaoh, but not as he blessed God; we adore the image, but not as we adore God. O unfitting comparison! O dull conjecture! O most stupid expression! Do you call it a blessing like that which the holy patriarch showed to the king, who, out of piety, conferred the emblem of power on his most beloved son, who granted him with all his offspring a fertile land to dwell in, who gave him not a portion of some province but the choice of land in his whole empire? Is that the adoration that you show to images, which can offer nothing to those who adore them except the memory of the thing whose images they are? Jacob blessed Pharaoh not as God, whom every creature blesses and praises, nor as a painted picture that the hand of an artist has produced, but as a man, to whom honour is to be shown because of the high power granted him by God. He blessed him, I say, not as a lifeless image but as a rational man; not as something put together by the skill of a painter, but as one made in the image and likeness of God; not as something standing countless times on walls, but as one to be blessed for himself or for his offspring, and, if I may so put it, for the sake of his profit. Likewise, he blessed the king of Israel, who was anointed with the nectar of the same Spirit, who would later say through the Apostle: Bless and do not curse, who ought to pray not only for those who cursed him of the world's lands, but also for those who slandered and persecuted him. Therefore this kind of blessing, which indeed was celebrated as the cause of a good recompense, does not fit the adoration of images, which cannot bring any recompense, by way of the quality of merits, either to those who adore them or to those who scorn to adore them.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Quam absurde agant qui ad confirmandas imagines exemplum divinæ legis proferunt dicentes, propitiatorium & duos cherubim aureos & archam testamenti præ- cipiente Domino Moysen fecifle.
units.tr: How absurdly those act who, to confirm images, bring forward the example of the divine law, saying that the Lord commanded Moses to make the mercy seat, the two golden cherubim and the ark of the covenant.

units.la: Fecisse sanctus Moyses, præcipiente Domino, propitiatorium & archam testamenti. & duos cherubim aureos, necnon & excidisse tabulas lapideas legitur: non tamen adorare jussisse, nec ea ob præteritarum quarundam rerum memoriam, sed ob futurorum mysteriorum sacratissimorum figuram credidit condidisse. Quæ dum ita se habeant, quantæ sint absurditatis quantitatis demenriæ illi qui his sacratissimis & summo honore dignis rebus, præcipiente Domino, à leguc conditor, imagines æquiperare conantes, illarum adorationem his exemplis stabilire moliuntur, nec ferrea vox explicare, nec nostri sensus existimatio poterit indagare: præsertim cum illa sacratissimorum sensuum exuberent archanis, hæc parum utilitatis habeant, excepta recordatione rei cujus
units.tr: Holy Moses is read to have made the mercy seat, the ark of the covenant and the two golden cherubim at the Lord's command, and also to have broken the stone tablets.
