Yet he was not ordered to worship them, nor did he believe that he had made them to remind people of some past event, but as a figure of the most sacred mysteries to come. Since this is so, how great is the absurdity, how great the folly, of those who try to set images on a level with these most sacred things, which were made at the Lord's command by the lawgiver himself. They strive to establish the worship of images by these examples. No human voice can explain this, and no estimate of our understanding can search it out. This is especially so because the former abound in the hidden secrets of the most sacred meanings, while the latter have little use, except to recall the thing whose

units.la: Rom.13. deorũ gentilis opinio falsa est, divalis quoq; nominis appellatio vana est. Liquido ergo patet, ré falsam falsum nomé habere, & falso nomine eos, qui veritatis discipuli sunt nuncupari nõ debere. Nā etsi qui forte Catholici defunctos quosq; dira memoria nuncupasse uspiam reperiantur, manifestū est eos usum fuisse secutos gentilitatis, sicut nomina dierum & mensiū gentiliū vanitatibus plerunq; nominantur. Sed hæc & his similia Romana potius ambitio quā Apostolica admisit traditio. Nos deniq, qui & veritatis sectatores, & ab ipsa veritate redempti sumus, sicut spernere debemus gentilia vocabula, Apostolo docēte, qui air, Quæ societas luci ad tenebras? quæ autē conventio Christi ad Belial? A qua conventione ipso annuēte liberemur, qui nos ereptos de tenebris & umbra mortis, translatulit in regnū filii dilectionis suæ, in quo habemus redemptionem in remissione peccatorum.
units.tr: Rom. 13. The belief of the heathen in gods is false, and the title of "divine" given to rulers is empty. It is therefore plain that a false thing has a false name, and that those who are disciples of the truth ought not to be called by a false name. For even if some Catholics are found anywhere to have called the dead by the name of dira memoria, it is clear that they followed the custom of the heathen, just as the names of days and months are often named after heathen vanities. But this and similar practices were admitted by Roman ambition rather than by Apostolic tradition. We, finally, who are followers of the truth and have been redeemed by the truth itself, ought to shun heathen terms, as the Apostle teaches, who says: What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? May we be freed from that agreement by his own consent, who has rescued us from the powers of darkness and the shadow of death, and has transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De eo quod Constantinus & Herena in epistola sua venerabili Papa Adriano urbis Romæ scripserunt, Rogamus tuam paternitatem & maximè Deus rogat, qui nullum hominem vult perire.
units.tr: Concerning what Constantine and Irene wrote in their letter to the venerable Pope Hadrian of the city of Rome: "We ask your fatherhood, and especially God asks, who wills that no man perish."

units.la: Qui Deum sibi consregnare procaciter, & sua gesta Divalia superbe & gentiliter dicere audet, indubitanter & Deum, cujus est regnū & imperium, quempiā rogare dicere audebit: ut dum sibi temerariam celsitudinem prorogat, divinæ majestatis imperio quiddam derogare contendat. Nec mirandum est cur sua præsumar adtollere, cum divina verbis indoctis nitatur subuiictere. Deus enim imperando lucē condidisse legitur; & aquas ab aquis discreuisse, & limitem his, ne denuo cōfunderentur, firmamentum posuisse, & terram multigenis feminibus fœcundasse, & cælum splendifluis sidera m fulgoribus perornasse, & aquas natatilibus, aëra volatilibus complevisse, & hominem sive omnium rerum creationem patrasse: & isti dicunt, Roganus tuam paternitatem, & maximè Deus rogat, qui nullum hominem vult perire. De Moyse legitur eo quòd fecerit quod Dominus imperarat: & idem scribit, Ad imperium Domini movebant castra filii Israhel, & ad imperium Domini ponebant ea: & iste dicit, maximè quidem Deus rogat: utpote qui inconmutabilis, ineffabilis, sempiternusque est, & omnium visibilium & invisibilium naturam imperio creavit, imperioq; gubernat, rogare incipiat. Quod quidem verbū non potestatis, sed depreccationis est, non auctoritatis, sed necessitatis, non imperantis, sed obsecrantis. Nam cum in Deo indigentia nulla sit, & rogare obsecrantis sit, & obsecrare indigentis, quisquis igitur Deum rogare quid dicit, ei proculdubio indigentiam adscribit. Cui si indigentia inest, & necessitas. Si necessitas inest, omnipotentia deest. Omnipotentia autē illi est, igitur indigentia deest. De eo enim scriptum est, Excelsus super omnes gentes Dominus, & supra cælos gloria ejus. Quòd si forte ei convenire posse dicunt rogare, propter personam filii, qui secundum Apostolum semetipsum exinanivit, formam servi accipiens, in similitudinem hominum factus, & habitu inventus ut homo: audiant eum dicentem, Lazare veni foras: & iterum, Tolle grabatum tuum & vade: & iterum, Talita cumi: & rursus, Adulescens tibi dico surge, & cætera hujusmodi, quæ non rogantis, sed imperantis; non postulantis, sed jubentis verba sunt: cujus imperii potestatem in ejus nomine etiam Apostolos legimus habuisse. Aut enim Pastor Ecclesiæ cum Æneam curasset, In nomine Jesu Nazareni surge & ambula. Ecce in nomine Jesu Petrus imperat, & illi Jesum rogare debere dicunt: servus imperio in Domini nomine dat languido sanitatem, & illi dicunt eum rogare debere sacerdotem. non hoc prudentiæ, sed summæ ametiæ deputandum est. Qui si ad sui erroris munimen illud fortè usurpare velint, quod ipsa veritas dicit, Ego rogabo patrem & alium paraclitum dabit vobis: & illud, Pater clarifica tuum nomen: perpendant non eum hoc dixisse secundum divinitatem, in qua unius cum patre substantiæ æqualis patri permanet: de qua dicit, Ego & pater unum sumus: sed secundum humanitatem, qua Verbum caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis, & de qua dicit, Pater major me est. Qui dum in forma servi minor sit patre, in forma Dei æqualis ei proculdubio creditur: unde & Apostolus ait, Non rapinam arbitratus est esse se æqualem Deo, id est, non ei fuit tanquam rapina, quasi alienū appeteret: qui sicut coæternus, ita coæqualis est patri: quē idem Apostolus verum hominē & verū Deum confitetur cum dicit, Quorū patres, & ex quibus Christus, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in sęcula. Cui si secundū illorum socordiā quæpiam rogare necesse est, alicui subest: & si alicui subest, non est super omnia. Super omnia autē est: non igitur ei quæpiam rogare necesse est. Audiant ergo, audiat hujusce dicti auctores, quid beatus Ambrosius contra quoslibet fidei hostes de hoc verbo dixerit: Sed lectū est, quia rogavit, discē distantia, rogat quasi filius hominis, imperat quasi Dei filius. An nō defertū hoc Dei filio, quod etiam Diabolus ætulit, & vos majore sacrilegio derogatis? Ille dicit, Si filius Dei es, dic lapidi huic ut fiat panus. Ille dicit, impera: vos dicitis, obsecra. Ille credit quod jubente Dei filio elementorū rerum, m adversum naturā vertatur: vos creditis quod nisi roget Dei filius, nec voluntas ipsius impleatur. Hoc quidem pugione lorica fidei munitus ecclesiæ præliator contra hostes fidei dimicavit. Inter quos quisquis numerari formidat, talis dicti insaniam fugiat. Dicat interea sanctus Evangelista quid Dominus discipulis formidantibus, cū jam navicula operiretur fluctibus, fecerit. Tunc surgens, inquit, imperavit ventu & mari, & facta est tranquillitas magna. Dicat etiam quid Centurio Domino ad domū suam pergere & puerū curare disponenti dixerit, Domine non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum: sed tantū dic verbo, & sanabitur puer meus. O infausta locutio! O exsecrabilis error! O superbia tumore potius q fortitudine ingeres, inflationem potius q vires augmentans! Centurio inludendū, flagellandū, pa-
units.tr: Whoever dares insolently to make God his co-ruler, and to speak of his own deeds as divine in a proud and heathen manner, will undoubtedly also dare to say that someone asks God, whose kingdom and empire it is. By doing so, while he claims for himself a rash eminence, he strives to take something away from the authority of the divine majesty. Nor is it to be wondered at that he presumes to exalt his own power, since he tries to subject the divine to unlearned words. For God is read to have created light by command; to have separated the waters from the waters, and set a boundary and a firmament so that they would not be mixed again; to have made the earth fruitful with many kinds of seed; to have adorned the heaven with stars of gleaming brightness; to have filled the waters with swimming creatures and the air with flying ones; and to have accomplished the creation of man and of all things. Yet these people say, "We ask your fatherhood, and especially God asks, who wills that no man perish." Of Moses it is read that he did what the Lord had commanded, and the same text says, "At the command of the Lord the children of Israel moved their camps, and at the command of the Lord they pitched them." But this man says, "especially God asks," although he who is unchangeable, ineffable and eternal created the nature of all visible and invisible things by command, and governs them by command, and begins to "ask." This word belongs not to power but to entreaty, not to authority but to necessity, not to one who commands but to one who beseeches. For since there is no lack in God, and "to ask" belongs to one who entreats, and "to beseech" to one who is in need, whoever says that God asks something ascribes to him, without doubt, need. If need is in him, then necessity is in him; if necessity is in him, then omnipotence is lacking. But omnipotence is his; therefore need is not in him. For it is written of him, "The Lord is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens." But if they perhaps wish to say that asking may belong to him on account of the person of the Son, who, according to the Apostle, "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man," let them hear him saying, "Lazarus, come forth," and again, "Take up your bed and go," and again, "Talitha cumi," and once more, "Young man, I say to you, arise," and other words of this kind, which are not the words of one asking but of one commanding, not of one requesting but of one ordering. We read that the Apostles too had the power of such command in his name. For when the minister of the Church, Peter, had cared for Aeneas, he said, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and walk." Behold, in the name of Jesus Peter commands, and yet they say that Jesus must ask him; a servant gives health to the sick man by command in the name of the Lord, and yet they say that the priest must ask him. This is to be ascribed not to prudence but to the highest folly. If they wish, perhaps, to use for the defence of their error what the truth itself says, "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter," and that, "Father, glorify your name," let them consider that he said this not according to the divinity, in which he remains of one substance with the Father and equal to the Father, of which he says, "I and the Father are one," but according to the humanity, by which "the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us," and of which he says, "The Father is greater than I." Since in the form of a servant he is less than the Father, in the form of God he is without doubt believed to be equal to him. Whence the Apostle also says, "He did not think it robbery to be equal to God," that is, it was not a robbery for him, as if he were seeking what belonged to another: he who, being co-eternal, is also co-equal with the Father. The same Apostle confesses him to be true man and true God when he says, "Of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever." If, according to their folly, he must ask something of someone, then he is subject to someone; and if he is subject to someone, he is not over all. But he is over all; therefore it is not necessary for him to ask anything. Let them hear, then, let the authors of this saying hear, what the blessed Ambrose said about this word against all enemies of the faith: "But it is read that he asked; learn the distinction: he asks as the Son of man, he commands as the Son of God." Do you not detract from the Son of God what even the Devil put forward, and do you derogate from him with greater sacrilege? That one says, "If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread." That one says, "Command"; you say, "Beseech." That one believes that at the command of the Son of God the elements of nature are turned against their nature; you believe that unless the Son of God asks, his will is not even fulfilled. Armed with this shield and breastplate of faith, the champion of the Church fought against the enemies of the faith. Whoever fears to be numbered among them, let him flee the madness of such a saying. Meanwhile let the holy Evangelist say what the Lord did when the disciples, in fear, saw the little boat already covered by waves: "Then rising," he says, "he commanded the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm." Let him say also what the centurion said to the Lord when the Lord was intending to go to his house and cure the boy: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my boy will be healed." O unhappy speech! O accursed error! O pride that brings swelling rather than strength, inflation rather than increased power! The centurion believes that the boy can be healed by a mere word of command, though the Lord was to be mocked and scourged,

units.la: surum, morte gustaturū, ad inferna descensurū verbo tantū imperii puerū sanare credit, & tu eū sedente ad dexteram patris in cælestibus super omne principarum, & potestate, & virtutem & dominatione & omne nomen quod nominatur non solum in hoc seculo, sed etiam in futuro quempiam rogare dicis. non igitur ei necesse est rogare qui cælestium terrestrium & infernorum creditur potestatem habere.
units.tr: to suffer, to taste death, and to descend into hell; and you say that he who sits at the right hand of the Father in the heavens, above every principality, power, virtue and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come, must be asked by someone. Therefore he has no need to ask, who is believed to have power over things in heaven, on earth and under the earth.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quod non parvi fit piaculi scripturas sanctas aliter intellegere quam intellegenda sunt, & ad hos sensus usurpatas adcommodare quos ille non continent: sicut in erronea synodo quae in Bithinia, regnante Constantino, mediante Helena matre ejus, residente Tharasio Constantinopolitano episcopo gesta est.
units.tr: That it is no small wrong to understand the holy Scriptures otherwise than they are to be understood, and to apply them to senses which they do not contain, as happened in the erroneous synod held in Bithynia under the reign of Constantine, with his mother Helena, and with Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, presiding.

units.la: Acerx legis docente didicimus oraculo, quòd percussa petra, latices fudienti profluxerint populo, & eandem petram Christum fenisse debere documento instituimur Apostolico. Qui dum fit petra, cujus fluentis attentia corda intigantur, & flumen, cujus impetus laetificat civitatem dei; & fons vitae, à quo credentibus perpetua vita manat; & panis caelestis, qui aeternae famis inediam à fidelium cordibus eradicat: quisquis ejus spiritales potus, & spiritales escas aliter quàm ille dat, percipit, divinas videlicet scripturas alio sensu, & non eo quo à sancto spiritu traditae sunt interpretari nititur, ab ejus pascuis alienus esse convincitur. Eloquia namque domini ait Propheta, eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum: quorum caistatem ille proculdubio adulterina labe vitiare appetit, qui ea ad exctanei sensus conmixtionem sociare contendit. Qui enim propter arrogantiae et vanae laudis appetitum ad sui erroris muniment astruendum, divinarum scripturarum adtrahit testimonium, quid aliud facit nisi castitatem divini eloquii probrose captivat in adulterium: & argentum igne divini spiritus examinatum ad aliorum metallorum, id est, extraneorum sensuum, protrahit inquinamentum. De talibus dominus ita queritur per prophetam, Dedi eis argentum & aurum, & illi fecerunt Baal: id est, spiritalis intelligentiae dignitatem & eloquii venustatem ad pravorum sensuum & inanis gloriae verterunt inmanitatem. Nam cum legislator dicat, In dextera domini ignea lex, mirandum est quantae sint hebetudinis, qui nece-jus inulcentur candore, nec ejus terrentur ardore. Sicut enim eos qui ad eam intellegendam puro sensu & devota mente accedunt, perlustrat fui splendore candoris, ita e contrario qui ad eam sibi temere usurpandam adpropinquant, perurit sui magnitudine ardoris. Sicque qui ei inhaerent humili mente & sacratis sensibus, gressus habent munitos in praesentis vitae stadio illius lampadis inluminatione: illi vero qui eam petunt cum extraneis & temerariis sensibus, aeterni ignis cremantur adustione: quod figurarum est in quatuor filiis Aaron. Nam cum Eleazar & Itamar juxta institutionem Moysi iguem sanctuarii domino offerentes sacerdotalis infulae dignitatem indepti sunt: Nadab vero & Abiu ignem alienum domino offerre nitentes, formidolosissime atroeissimo mortis genere multati sunt. quorum quisquis vult vitare periculum, debet fugere exemplum. Quem ergo, quem in hoc facto qui bene dicta male interpretari arripiunt, imitantur? nisi eum qui quod de simplici viro justo dictum est, in meditatione dei & hominum interpretari conatur, cum dicit. Scriptum est enim, Quoniam angelis suis mandavit de te ut in manibus tollant te, ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum. Ut enim validius esset sui tentamenti argumentum, divinorum apicum traxit exemplum, quo libentius abhauriretur suae tentationis poculum, si sanctarum scripturarum haberet condimentum. Nam nisi interpretandis scripturis imitandus est, & in facilibus tentamentis sequendus: Et si in fallacibus tentamentis sequendus est, & in caeteris moribus amplectendus: non autem in ceteris moribus amplectendus est: non igitur in interpretandis scripturis imitandus. Ait enim beatus Hieronymus, Male diabolus scripturas interpretatur: Siquidem & heretici & sciismatici, qui ejus utique sequaces sunt, male divinas scripturas intellegunt, pejus interpretantur, pessime vero obser vant. Catholici autem veritatis studii exemplis & antiqui hostis resistunt tentamentis, & haereticorum oblistunt machinamentis, & divini verbi manna puro & sano sensu suscipientes, ejus dulcibus alluntur alimentis: quibus non inportune collectum manna vermes ebullit, id est, non ejus conscientiae archana, & sensuum intima, superbia stimulis confodit. Discussis itaque quae arrogantur vel indocte à Constantino & Harena ad venerabilem Papam urbis Romae Adrianum scripta sunt, sive quam brevissime digestis qualiter scripturae sanctae non aliter intellegendae, vel interpretandae, vel pro suo cuiq; arbitrio proprio sensui adcommodandae sint, sed secundum sanam fobriamque doctrinam intellegi debeant: nunc testimoniorum ordinem qui à sanctis scripturis sive à sanctorum patrum tractatibus digestus est, & inordinate sive non proprie ab his qui in praefata synodo sedisse noscuntur, usurpatus, ordine competenti domino favente exequamur: ponentes duntaxat summarum quid sanctorum patrum de his definierit sententia, vel quomodo à venerabilibus viris prolata sint, ut ad illum errorem astruendum illorum adglomeravit amentia: quibus pro tempore in praesentib. duobus primis volumimb. enumeratis, quid proprio sensu minus docte & contra sanctorum patrum institutionem ob adorandarum imaginum superfluam protulerint constitutionem, sequentium duorum librorum feries domino annuente discutiet, praemittentes in sequenti capitulo, qualiter sancta Romana ecclesia inter caeteras ecclesias maxime venerationi habira, pro causis fidei sit consulenda.
units.tr: We have learned from the Law's teaching that when the rock was struck, waters flowed out for the people, and we are taught by the apostolic testimony that this rock was Christ. He is the rock whose streams refresh the hearts that attend to them, the river whose rush gladdens the city of God, the fountain of life from which everlasting life flows to believers, and the heavenly bread which drives away the hunger of eternal famine from the hearts of the faithful. Whoever takes his spiritual drink and spiritual food otherwise than he gives them, that is, who tries to interpret the divine Scriptures in a sense other than that in which they were delivered by the Holy Spirit, is shown to be a stranger to his pastures. The prophet says, The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in the fire. The one who seeks to defile their purity with an adulterous stain is plainly the one who tries to join them to a foreign sense. For whoever, out of arrogance and a desire for empty praise, draws the testimony of the divine Scriptures in order to support the defence of his own error, what else does he do but hand over the chastity of the divine word to adultery, and drag the silver tried in the fire of the divine Spirit into the pollution of other metals, that is, of alien senses? The Lord complains of such people through the prophet: I gave them silver and gold, and they made Baal. That is, they have turned the dignity of spiritual understanding and the beauty of the word into the monstrosity of perverse senses and empty glory. Since the lawgiver says, From his right hand went a fiery law, it is astonishing how dull they are: they are neither kindled by its brightness nor terrified by its heat. For just as it illumines with the splendour of its brightness those who approach it with a pure sense and a devout mind, so, on the contrary, it burns with the greatness of its heat those who draw near to it rashly to appropriate it for themselves. Thus those who cling to it with a humble mind and a holy sense have their steps made secure in the course of this present life by the light of that lamp; but those who seek it with alien and reckless senses are consumed by the burning of eternal fire. This is prefigured in the four sons of Aaron. When Eleazar and Ithamar, according to the institution of Moses, offered fire to the Lord in the sanctuary, they obtained the dignity of the priestly mitre; but Nadab and Abihu, who tried to offer strange fire to the Lord, were punished by the most dreadful and cruel kind of death. Whoever wishes to avoid the danger should flee the example. Whom, then, do those imitate who seize upon good words and interpret them badly in this matter, unless it is the one who tries to apply to God and to men what was said of a simple, righteous man, when he says: For it is written, that he has given his angels charge over you, to bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone. In order to give greater force to his temptation, he drew on the example of the divine letters, so that the cup of his temptation might be drunk more willingly if it had the seasoning of holy Scripture. For if he is to be imitated in interpreting Scripture and followed in the easier temptations, and if he is to be followed in the deceitful temptations and embraced in his other ways, yet he is not to be embraced in his other ways; therefore he is not to be imitated in interpreting Scripture. Blessed Jerome says, The devil interprets the Scriptures badly. Indeed, heretics and schismatics, who are certainly his followers, understand the divine Scriptures badly, interpret them worse, and observe them worst of all. Catholics, however, by the examples of their zeal for truth, resist the temptations of the ancient enemy and withstand the machinations of heretics; receiving the manna of the divine word in a pure and sound sense, they are nourished by its sweet food. Worms do not breed in the manna gathered for them, that is, pride does not pierce with its goads the secret recesses of their conscience and the inner parts of their understanding. Therefore, having examined what Constantine and Helena, in their arrogance or ignorance, wrote to the venerable Pope Hadrian of the city of Rome, and having briefly set out how the holy Scriptures are not to be understood or interpreted otherwise than they should be, nor adapted to each man's private sense at his own pleasure, but must be understood according to sound and sober doctrine, we shall now, with the Lord's favour, set out in fitting order the series of testimonies, which were drawn from the holy Scriptures or from the treatises of the holy Fathers, and which were used without order or not properly by those known to have sat in the aforesaid synod. We will set down only the summary of what the holy Fathers have decided about these matters, or how the venerable men who put them forward (so that the madness of those men might bring together these testimonies to support that error) have expressed them. In the two first volumes already published we have listed what they have put forward in their own sense, less learnedly and contrary to the institution of the holy Fathers, in their superfluous decree concerning the adoration of images. In the two following books, with the Lord's permission, we shall examine the sequence of these matters. In the next chapter we shall first set out how the holy Roman Church, held in the highest veneration among the other churches, is to be consulted in matters of faith.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Quod sancta Romana, Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia caeteris ecclesiis praelata, pro causis fidei, cum quaestio surgit, omnino sit consulenda.
units.tr: That the holy Roman, Catholic and Apostolic Church, set above the other churches, is to be consulted in all matters of faith whenever a question arises.

units.la: Arequam discutiendorum testimoniorum, quàbsurde orientales in sua synodo taxaverunt, sylvà gredi amur, dignum duximus, ut qualiter sancta Romana ecclesia caeteris ecclesiis à Domino plata, & à fidelibus consulenda sit, prosequamur: praesertim cum non ab aliis scripturis, nisi ab his, quae inter canonicas recipit, testimonia sint sumenda: nec aliorum doctorum, nisi eorum qui à Gelasio, vel caeteris illius sanctae sedis pontificibus susceptis sunt, dogmata sint amplectenda: nec aliter atq; aliter pro cujusibet arbitrio, sed sane sobrieque, quae ab illis dicta sunt, sint intellegenda. Ait enim B. Augustin. erum institueret, quæ scripturæ esserent recipiendæ vel qualiter intellegendæ: Erit igitur diuinarum scripturarum folertissimus indagator, qui primò totas legerit non vsq; habuerit scripturas, etsi nondum intellectu jam tamen lectione, duntaxat eas, quas appellantur canonicæ. Nam cæteras securius leget, fide veritatis instructus, ne præoccupent imbecillum animum, & periculosis mendaciis atq; phantasmatis eludentes prajudicent aliquid contra sanam intellegentiam. In canonicis autem scripturis ecclesiarum catholicarum quamplurimum auctoritatem sequatur: inter quas sane illæ sunt quæ apostolicas sedes habere & epistolas accipere meruerunt. Nam cum hic cunctis per orbem constitutis sedib. apostolicas generaliter præferat sedes, multo magis illa omnib. præferenda est, quæ etiam cæteras apostolicis sedib. prælata est. Sicut igitur cæteris discipulis apostoli, & apostolis omnib. Petrus eminet: ita nimirum cæteris sedib. apostolicæ, & apostolicis Romana eminere dinoscitur. Hæc enim nullis synodicis constitutis cæteris ecclesiis prælata est, sed ipsius domini auctoritate primatum tenet, dicentis, Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferni non prævalebunt adversus eam. & tibi dabo claves regni cælorum, & quodcunq; ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum & in cælis: & quodcunq; solveris super terram, erit solutum & in cælo. Cui non incongrue B. Pauli doctoris gentium est attributa societas, ut illius sanctæ ecclesiæ omnino firmaretur auctoritas: quatinus altero ad piscandas animas electo ex piscatore, altero ad muniedam ecclesiam ex persecutore: ut in altero Dei filii vera confessio, in altero appareret divini verbi sacra prædicatio: cum alteri concesserit idem dei filius claves regni cælorum, alteri clavem aperiedorum legalium verborum: utriq; tamen virtutem lignorum, quo alter ad eum cruce, alter gladio pergens, fidelibus arrabonem corporalis farinæ relinquentes, & exempli fulgore, & verbi decore, & sancto cruore supradictam ecclesiam Romanam eradicarent, quam supra solidissimam petram fundatam nec defecdens pluvia, nec venientia flumina, nec flantes venti ruere conpellerent. Hæc ergo sanctæ fidei spiritalib. munita armis, & à fonte lucis & origine bonitatis, salutarib. satiata fluentis, & horrendis atrocibusq; hæresum obsistit monstris, & mellifiua prædicationis pocula catholicis per orbem ministrat ecclesias. Nam beatissimus Hieronymus vir divinis legib. & multarum linguarum peritia eruditus, dum Bethleemiticis moraretur in arvis, & à B. Papa Damaso Romæ posito de difficilib. consulteretur quæstionibus, eum pro causis fidei versa vice consuluisse dinoscitur, & five tacendarum sive dicendarum hypostaseon, vel quibus in orientalibus partibus communicare debeat humillimis apicibus ut apices accipiat deprecatur. Mira res & magnis prædicanda præconiis. Interrogat à quo interrogatur: consulit à quo consulitur: qui magistrum se in interpretandis divinis scripturis sentit, in causis fidei venerandi pontificis se discipulum minime erubescit: & cui sacræ legis quæstionum nexus enodat, utrum hypostasis dicere debeat, quibusve in oriente communicare, eliagitat. Unde datur intellegi, sanctos & eruditos viros per diversas mundi partes prædicationis & scientiæ lampade coruscantes, non solum à S. Romana ecclesia non recessisse, sed etiam tempore necessitatis ob fidei corroborationem ab ea adjutorium inplorasse. Quod regulariter, ut præfati sumus & exemplis docuimus, omnes catholicæ debent observare ecclesiæ, ut ab ea post Christum ad muniendam fidem adjutorium petant, quæ non habens maculam nec rugam & portentuosa hæresum capita calcat, & fideliū mentes in fide corroborat. A cujus sancta & veneranda communione multis recedentib. nostræ tamen partis nunquam recessit ecclesia, sed ea apostolica eruditione instruente, & eo à quo est omne donum optimum & omne datum perfectum, tribuente, semper susceptit reverenda charissimata. Quæ dum à primis fidei temporib. cum ea perstaret in sacræ religionis unione, & ab ea paulo distaret, quamvis contra fidem non est, in officiorum celebratione, venerandæ memoriæ gentiis nostri inlustrissimi atq; excellentissimi viri, Pipini regis curia, & inductia sive adventu in Gallias reverentissimi & sanctissimi viri Stephani Romanæ urbis antistitis, eiusdem etiam in psallendi ordine copulata: ut non esset dispar ordo psallendi, quib. erat comparardor credendi: & quæ unitatem erant unius sanctæ legis sacra lectione, essent etiam unitas unius *modulationis veneranda traditione: nec sejungeret officiorum varia celebratio, quas cõjunxerat unica fidei pia devotio. Quod quidē & nos, conlato nobis à deo Italiæ regno fecimus, S. Romanæ ecclesiæ fastigium sublimare cupientes, & reverentissimi papæ Adriani salutatib. exhortationibus parere nitentes: scilicet ut plures illius partis ecclesiæ, quæ quondam apostolicæ sedis traditionem in psallendo suscipere recusabant, nunc eam cum omni diligentia amplectantur: & cui adhærerant fidei munere, adhærent quoq; psallendi ordine: non solum omnium Galliarum provinciæ, & Germaniæ, sive Italia, sed etiam Saxones & quædam Aquilonaris plagæ gentes per nos, Deo annuente ad veræ fidei rudimenta converti, facere noscuntur, & ira B. Petri Sedem in omnibus sequi curant, sicut illo pervenire, quò ille clavicularius exstat, deliderant. Ad quam beatitudinem nos pervenire, & in sanctæ ecclesiæ consortio & unione ille nos faciat perseverare, qui ecclesiam suam in Petro dignatus est fundare: & ipso interveniente, cujus cathedræ sumus sequaces, regni cælorum, cujus ille claviger factus est, mereamur effici compotes.
units.tr: Before entering the thicket of examining the testimonies which the Easterners in their synod foolishly found fault with, we have thought it right to set out how the holy Roman Church, exalted above the other churches by the Lord, is to be consulted by the faithful. This is especially so because testimonies are to be drawn only from those Scriptures which are received among the canonical books, and only the doctrines of those teachers are to be embraced who have been received by Gelasius or the other bishops of that holy see. Nor are these things to be understood in any way at the pleasure of anyone, but soberly and sensibly. For Blessed Augustine says, when he sets out which Scriptures are to be received and how they are to be understood: The most diligent investigator of the divine Scriptures will therefore be one who first reads through all those books which are called canonical, and does not stop until he has at least read them, even if he does not yet understand them. For he will read the others more safely, instructed in the faith of truth, lest they preoccupy his weak mind and, deceiving him with dangerous lies and fantasies, prejudice him against sound understanding. In the canonical Scriptures, moreover, he should follow the authority of the Catholic churches very closely, and among these especially those which have deserved to have apostolic sees and to receive epistles. For since the apostolic see is generally placed before all the sees established throughout the world, much more is that see to be placed before all others which is also set above the other apostolic sees. Just as Peter stands out among the other disciples and among all the apostles, so the Roman see is recognised as standing out among the other apostolic sees and the apostolic ones. For it was set above the other churches not by any synodical decrees, but holds its primacy by the authority of the Lord himself, who says: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven. To this, not inappropriately, is joined the companionship of Blessed Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, so that the authority of that holy Church might be fully established: one having been chosen from a fisherman to catch souls, the other from a persecutor to fortify the Church, so that in the one there might appear the true confession of the Son of God, and in the other the holy preaching of the divine Word. For the same Son of God granted the keys of the kingdom of heaven to the one, and the key of opening the legal words to the other; yet both had the same power, since each went forth, the one to the cross and the other to the sword, leaving to the faithful a pledge of bodily bread, and with the brilliance of example, the beauty of word and holy blood they uprooted the aforesaid Roman Church, which, founded upon the most solid rock, neither falling rain, nor rising rivers, nor blowing winds could cause to collapse. This Church, therefore, fortified with the spiritual arms of holy faith, and satisfied with saving streams from the fountain of light and the origin of goodness, withstands the horrible and savage monsters of heresies, and supplies the honeyed cups of preaching to the Catholic churches throughout the world. For the most blessed Jerome, a man learned in the divine laws and skilled in many languages, while he dwelt in the fields of Bethlehem and was consulted at Rome by Blessed Pope Damasus about difficult questions, is known in turn to have consulted him on matters of faith. He begs with the most humble letters that he receive an answer on whether he should say or refrain from saying "hypostasis," and with whom in the eastern regions he ought to communicate. A remarkable thing, worthy of great praise! He who is questioned questions in turn; he who is consulted consults; he who feels himself a teacher in interpreting the divine Scriptures is not at all ashamed to be a disciple of the venerable bishop in matters of faith; and he who unties the knots of questions of sacred law begs to be told whether to say "hypostasis," and with whom to communicate in the East. From this it may be understood that holy and learned men, shining like lamps of preaching and knowledge in different parts of the world, did not only not depart from the holy Roman Church, but also, in a time of necessity, sought help from her for the strengthening of the faith. As we have said before and shown by examples, all Catholic churches ought to observe this as a rule: that after Christ they seek help to fortify the faith from that Church which, having no spot or wrinkle, tramples on the monstrous heads of heresies and strengthens the minds of the faithful in the faith. Although many have withdrawn from her holy and venerable communion, our church of this party has never withdrawn from her; rather, while she instructs with apostolic learning and bestows what comes from him from whom every best gift and every perfect gift comes, she has always received her revered gifts. From the first times of the faith, while she remained in the union of the sacred religion with that Church, and differed from her somewhat, though not against the faith, in the celebration of the offices, the court of King Pippin, of most illustrious and excellent memory, our forefather, and the coming and arrival into Gaul of the most reverend and most holy Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, joined her also in the order of psalmody, so that the order of psalmody should not be unequal to that to which the order of belief was matched; and so that those who were united in one holy law by the sacred reading should also be united in the venerable tradition of one melody, and the varied celebration of offices should not separate those whom the single pious devotion of faith had joined. This indeed we too have done, since the kingdom of Italy was granted to us by God, desiring to raise the dignity of the holy Roman Church and striving to obey the salutary exhortations of the most reverend Pope Adrian: namely, that many of that part of the Church which once refused to receive the tradition of the apostolic see in psalmody, now embrace it with all diligence, and that those who adhered to it in the matter of faith now also adhere to it in the order of psalmody. Not only the provinces of all Gaul and Germany and Italy, but also the Saxons and certain peoples of the northern region, are known to have been converted through us, by God's grace, to the first principles of the true faith; and they take care to follow the See of Blessed Peter in all things, desiring to come to that place where he stands as the keeper of the keys. May he who deigned to found his Church upon Peter grant that we come to that blessedness, and that he make us persevere in the fellowship and unity of the holy Church; and through the intercession of him whose chair we follow, may we deserve to be made partakers of the kingdom of heaven, of which he was made the keybearer.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Quod non ad adorandas imagines pertineat quod scriptum est, Creavit deus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem suam.
units.tr: That the words "God created man in his own image and likeness" do not pertain to the adoration of images.

units.la: IN hoc testimonio inconsequenter, & ultra quā inconsequenter, ab illis in sua synodo ob adorandarum imaginum astruendum errorem posito, non nostro ingenio plurimum est fundandum, cum tot indiciis ab eorum sit adsertione alienum: quoniam ubi nulla est verisimilitudo, non magnam discernendo oritur disputatio. Quia ergo à nullo, in quo sanæ mentis viget acumen, illi rei credditur pertinere, cui illi hoc nituntur adcommodare, sed spiritale dictum spiritali differendum est indagaritione: restat ut quid de eo sanctorum patrum protulerit stylus, sententiali brevitate notemus: quatenus quod abiit est negotiatum, et a viris venerabilibus et spiritu sancto repletis spirituali lite prolatum, lectoris industria sit diligenter acceptum. Ait enim B. Ambrosius, In principio ipsius mundi patrem et filium esse audio, et unum opus cerno: audio loquentem, aguosco facientem, sed et patris et filii unam imaginem. Unam simil-itudinem lego: similitudo haec non diversitatis, sed unitatis est. Non enim homo ad imaginem dei nisi per imaginem est. Imago ergo dei ex interioris hominis nobilitate est considerauda: primo quidem, ut sicut deus unus, trinus, totus est, omnia vivificans, movens et gubernans, sicut Apostolus confirmat, quod in eo vivimus, movemur et sumus, ita anima in suo corpore ubique tota viget vivificans illud, movens et gubernans. Nec enim in maioribus corporum sui membris major, et in minoribus minor, sed in minimo tota, et in maximis tota: et hac est imago unitatis omnipotentis, quam anima habet in se, quae quandam sanctae trinitatis habet imaginem: primo in eo, quia sicut deus est totus et sapiens et anima secundum suum modum est, vivit et sapit. Ipse quoque et alia trinitas in ea, quae ad trinam gloriam totam perfectam quidem et summam trinitatis quae est in patre, filio et spiritu sancto condita: et licet unus sit trinitas, tamen in se dignitates habet, id est, intellectum, voluntatem et memoriam, quod idem licet aliis verbis appellatur, dum dicitur: Diliges dominum deum tuum ex toto corde tuo et ex tota anima tua, et ex toto intellectu, et ex tota voluntate, et ex tota memoria. Iam sicut ex patre generatur filius, ex patre procedit spiritus sanctus, ita ex intellectu generatur voluntas, et ex his nam ambobus procedit memoria, sicut sapientia dicitur quaelibet intellegi potest. Nec enim anima perfecta esse potest sine his tribus, nec horum trium unum sine alio quam pertinet beatitudinem, sine aliis duobus integrum constat: et sicut deus pater, deus filius, deus spiritus sanctus, non tamen tres di sunt, sed unus deus tres habens personas, ita et anima intellectus, anima voluntas, anima memoria, non tamen anima tres in uno corpore, sed una anima tres habens dignitates. Atque in his tribus ...
units.tr: In this testimony, carelessly, and more than carelessly, the Papists have put forward in their synod, to establish their error about adoring images. We should not base much on our own wit, since by so many signs it is foreign to their assertion. Where there is no likelihood, a dispute arises that is not easily settled. Since therefore no one of sound mind, who has keenness of judgment, believes that this passage pertains to the thing they strive to fit it to, but a spiritual saying must be explained by spiritual inquiry, it remains that we briefly note in a few sentences what the pen of the holy Fathers has said about it, so that what was handled in that business, and was brought forward in a spiritual contest by venerable men filled with the Holy Spirit, may be received with the diligence of the reader. For St. Ambrose says: "I hear that at the beginning of the world there were the Father and the Son, and I see one work. I hear the speaker, I recognise the maker, but one image of the Father and the Son. I read one likeness: this likeness is not of difference but of unity." For man is not made in the image of God except through an image. The image of God is therefore to be considered from the nobility of the inner man. First, indeed, as God is one, three, and whole, quickening, moving and governing all things, as the Apostle affirms, that in him we live, move and have our being, so the soul in its body lives everywhere whole, quickening, moving and governing it. For it is not greater in the larger members of its body and less in the smaller, but whole in the smallest and whole in the greatest. This is the image of the almighty unity which the soul has in itself, and which has a certain image of the holy Trinity: first in this, that as God is whole and wise, so the soul, according to its own measure, lives and is wise. Also there is another trinity in it, which is founded for the threefold glory, wholly perfect and supreme, of the Trinity which is in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. And although the soul is one, yet it has in itself three powers, that is, understanding, will and memory, which are also called by other words when it is said: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your understanding, and with all your will, and with all your memory." Now as the Son is begotten of the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, so the will is begotten of the understanding, and from both together proceeds the memory, as whatever is understood may be called wisdom. For the soul cannot be perfect without these three, nor can any one of these three, which pertains to blessedness, subsist entire without the other two. And as God the Father, God the Son and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one God having three persons, so the understanding soul, the willing soul and the remembering soul are not three souls in one body, but one soul having three powers. And in these three…

units.la: Similitudo vero in moribus cernenda est: ut sicut deus fecit ad similitudinem suam creavit, est charitas, est bonitas, et iustus, patiens atque mitis, mundus et verax virtutum sanctorum insignia quae de eo leguntur, ita homo creatus est, ut charitatem haberet, bonitatem, patientiam atque mitem, mundum et misericordem fore: quas virtutes quanto plus quisque in semetipso habet, tanto magis deo et magis ...
units.tr: But the likeness is to be seen in morals: as God, who made man in his own likeness, is love, is goodness, and just, patient and gentle, pure and true, and as the notable virtues of the saints are read of him, so man was created to have love, goodness, patience and gentleness, to be pure and merciful. The more each one has these virtues in himself, the more he is made like God and more…

units.la: Beatus quoque Augustinus ita hominem ad imaginem dei factum esse dilecta: Cum exteriorem et interiorem hominem divina scriptura et animam eos discernat, et ab Apostolo dictum est: Et si exterior homo noster corrumpitur, sed interior renovatur. Quaeri potest, utrum unus horum factus ad imaginem et similitudinem dei nam illud quod ...
units.tr: Blessed Augustine also declared that man was made in the image of God in this way: "Since divine Scripture distinguishes the outer and inner man and the soul, and the Apostle said: 'Though our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed.'" It may be asked whether one of these was made in the image and likeness of God…

units.la: Ergo primitus bonus. Multa enim modis dicitur possunt simul deo, alia secundum virtutem et sapientiam ...
units.tr: Therefore first good. For many things can be said of God in many ways at once, others according to virtue and wisdom…

units.la: Nam et ita dicitur se ex: quia creatura nihil est melior exterior homo, vita illa accipitur quae per corpus sentimus, quam nec notissimus sensibus, quos cum pecoribus habemus. Non immerito partes dicitur similitudinem dei non solum quia vivit, quod etiam in bestiis apparet, sed amplius, quod ad rationem ...
units.tr: For it is also said thus, because no creature is better than the outward man. That life is understood which we perceive through the body, which even the most familiar senses, which we have in common with the beasts, do not reach. Not undeservedly is it said to be the likeness of God, not only because it lives, which also appears in the beasts, but more, because it reaches reason…

units.la: Iam ... quia homo ... Nemo potest quod agatur in deo nisi spiritus dei. Ite de spiritu hominis dicit: Salvi facta est ...
units.tr: Now… because man… No one knows what is done in God except the Spirit of God. Of the spirit of man he says: The…

units.la: ... hoc modo ...
units.tr: … in this way …

units.la: Deut. 6. Diliges dominum deum tuum ex toto corde tuo.
units.tr: Deut. 6. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.

units.la: Gen. 1. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram.
units.tr: Gen. 1. Let us make man in our image.

units.la: 1 Cor. 2. Quis enim cognovit mentem domini? hoc modo; Scito quoniam dominus corda hominum novit, & qui finxit spiritum omnibus ipse fecit omnia. Ergo iste spiritus ad imaginem dei nullo dubitante factus accipitur, in quo est intelligentia veritatis. haec enim veritas nulla interposita creatura, catera hominus ad similitudinem facta videri volunt, quia omnis quidem imago similis est: non autem omne quod simile est etiam imago propria, sed forte abusive dici potest. Sed cavendum in talibus, ne quid nimis adseverandum putetur illa res sane falsa, ne quoniam corpus quodliber per localia spatia porrectum est, aliquid tale credatur esse substantia Dei. Nam res quae in parte minor est quia in toto, nec dignitati animae convenit, quanto minus majestati Dei? Ecce quam subtiliter quamque salubriter sancti viri hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei factum esse, imaginem videlicet in anima, in qua est intellectus, voluntas & memoria: similitudinem in moribus, id est, in charitate, iustitia, bonitate & sanctitate, quae omnia incorporea sunt, intellegentes disseruere a quorum sensu & doctrina quantum distent qui hoc testimonium imaginibus artificum manu formatis adcommodant, non nostro est differendum eloquio, sed lectoris relervandum iudicio: ut quantae in hac parte sint vecordiae non nosterum stylus, sed suus permoneat sensus. Quisquis igitur ita hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem dei factum, sicut ad imaginem hominis imaginem ab artifice formatam esse credit, aliquid in deo corporeum, quod credere nefas est, credere se offendit. Nam si id quod homo ad imaginem & similitudinem dei factus est, manufactis imaginibus convenit, secundum corpoream speciem homo ad imaginem dei factus est: & si homo secundum corpoream speciem ad imaginem dei factus est, corporeus est deus: incorporeus autem deus est: non igitur id, quod homo ad imaginem & similitudinem dei factus est, manu factis imaginibus convenit.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2. For who has known the mind of the Lord? In this way: Know that the Lord knows the hearts of men, and he who formed the spirit of all men, he himself made all things. Therefore that spirit, without any doubt, is understood to have been made in the image of God, in which is the understanding of truth. For this truth, with no creature interposed, the other men wish to be seen as made in the likeness; for every image is indeed like, but not everything that is like is also a proper image, though it may perhaps be called so loosely. But in such matters one must take care lest anything be asserted too much, which is a plainly false matter, lest, because any body is extended through local spaces, one should believe that something of that kind is the substance of God. For a thing which is smaller in part because it is in the whole does not even suit the dignity of the soul, how much less the majesty of God! See how subtly and how wholesomely the holy men, understanding it, have taught that man was made in the image and likeness of God: the image, namely, in the soul, in which is understanding, will and memory; the likeness in morals, that is, in love, justice, goodness and holiness, all of which are incorporeal. How far from their sense and teaching are those who fit this testimony to images formed by the hand of craftsmen, we must not argue in our own words, but leave to the judgment of the reader, so that their own meaning, not our pen, may show how great is the folly in this part. Whoever therefore believes that man was made in the image and likeness of God in the same way as an image formed by a craftsman is made in the likeness of a man, he is offended by believing that something corporeal is in God, which it is wicked to believe. For if what man is, being made in the image and likeness of God, fits manufactured images, then man was made in the image of God according to bodily form; and if man was made in the image of God according to bodily form, then God is corporeal; but God is incorporeal; therefore what man is, being made in the image and likeness of God, does not fit images made by hand.

units.la: C·A·P. VIII.
units.tr: Chapter VIII.

units.la: Quae sit differentia imaginis & similitudinis sive aequalitatis.
units.tr: What the difference is between image and likeness, or equality.

units.la: Quoniam opitulante deo secundum sanam sobriamque doctrinam sanctorum patrum sententius inbuti, qualiter intellegendum sit, quod deus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem suam creaverit, exequi fiumus: nunc operae pretium est, ut quae sit differentia imaginis & similitudinis seu etiam aequalitatis breviter exiesquamur: quatenus & illi qui ob adorandas imagines per patentes manium ad sertionum campos et firmes feruntur, horum trium, quae illi omnia pene unum putant, differentiam cognoscentes, in quanto sint errore perpendant: & studiosi quique hoc legentes ad quasdam intelligentiae utilitates accedant.
units.tr: Since, by the help of God, we have been instructed in the sound and sober teaching of the holy Fathers' opinions, we shall now set out how it is to be understood that God created man in his own image and likeness. Now it is worth while to explain briefly what the difference is between image, likeness, and also equality, so that those who are carried by open paths onto the fields of disputation about venerating images may recognise the difference between these three, which they almost all regard as one, and weigh how far they are in error; and so that all diligent readers who take up this book may come to some useful understanding.
Gen. 1.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Quomodo intelligendum sit quod scriptum est, Abraham adoravit populum terræ, filios Heth, sive quod Moyses Jetro legitur adorasse: quibus exemplis hi qui propter adorandas imagines synodos faciunt, suum errorem fulcire assectant: & quia nec Jacob Pharaonem, nec Danihel Nabuchodonosor regem, ut illi dicunt, ublam legantur adorasse.
units.tr: How what is written should be understood, that Abraham worshipped the people of the land, the sons of Heth, or that Moses is read to have worshipped Jethro; by which examples those who hold synods to enforce the worship of images strive to bolster their error; and because it is not read that Jacob worshipped Pharaoh, nor Daniel King Nebuchadnezzar, as they claim, at any time.

units.la: LXX qui in adorandis imaginibus æstuant, hoc peculiariter atque familiariter exemplo utuntur, quod Abraham filios Heth, & Moyses Jetro sacerdotem Madian adorasse legunt. Quorum quidem adoratio tantum distat à pictæ imaginis adoratione, quantum pictus ipse homo à veri hominis ratione. quantum enim verus homo à pícto, rationalis ab irrationali, sensibilis ab insensibili, animatus ab inanimato in sui definitione secernitur, tantum procul dubio & huius adoratio ab illius adoratione discernitur. Aliud namque est hominem salutationis officio & humanitatis obsequio adorando, aliud picturam diversorum colorum fucis conpaginatam, sine gressu, sine voce vel ceteris sensibus, nec ullo quo cultu adorare.
units.tr: The Seventy, who are heated about the adoration of images, use this example in a special and familiar way: they read that Abraham adored the sons of Heth, and Moses adored Jethro the priest of Midian. Indeed, the adoration of those men differs from the adoration of a painted image as much as the painted man himself differs from the true man in nature. For just as a true man is distinguished from a painted one in his definition, rational from irrational, sensible from insensible, animate from inanimate, so without doubt is the adoration of the one distinguished from the adoration of the other. For it is one thing to adore a man by the duty of greeting and the courtesy of respect, and another to adore a picture put together from dyes of various colours, which has no step, no voice, no other senses, and deserves no worship at all.

units.la: Fraternitatem autem diligendam, & dilectionem erga proximos, benignam, & humilitatis gradum amplectendum, perquæ nos mutuo salutantes adoramus, pene omnium sanctarum scripturarum perdocemur exemplis: imagines vero adorare, vel salutare, vel quasi reverentia inseri potius, quàm institui debemur, pene in cunctis divinæ scripturæ locis. Nam, ut cæteros taceam, sacratissimus pastor, super quem solidissimam petram ecclesiam fundata est, non ait imagines, sed fraternitatem diligite: nec subditi efflote picturis, sed omni humanae, & Dominum Christum sanctificare non imaginibus, sed in cordibus nostris instituit.
units.tr: Moreover, that brotherly love should be cherished, and affection toward our neighbours kind, and the degree of humility embraced, by which we greet and adore one another, we are taught by almost all the examples of the holy Scriptures. But that images should be adored, or saluted, or that we should be drawn into reverence for them rather than taught it, is almost nowhere in the places of divine Scripture. For, to pass over the others, the most holy pastor, upon whom the Church is founded on a most solid rock, does not say "love images" but "love the brotherhood"; nor do his subjects bow down before pictures, but before every human being; and he ordained that the Lord Christ be sanctified not by images but in our hearts.

units.la: Denique sane & ab omni ratione seclusum est, hoc ad afferendam imaginum adorationem in exemplum videlicet plerumque sancti viri per humilitatem qua Deo placuerunt homines salutationis gratia adoraverint, plerumque ne ab aliis adorarentur humiliter refugerint, plerumque rigore suæ sanctitatis superbos quoque adorare contempserint.
units.tr: Finally, it is also altogether excluded by all reason that this is brought forward as an example in support of the adoration of images: namely that holy men, through the humility by which they pleased God, have often adored men out of courtesy, often humbly refused to be adored by others, and often, by the rigour of their holiness, have scorned to adore even the proud.

units.la: Imagines vero nilsquam nec teneriter quidè adorati sunt. Nam in eo, quod Abraham sive Moyses homines humiles suis utilitatibus necessarie adorasse leguntur, & Mardocheus Aman hominem arrogantem, & in populi Dei interitum insurgentem adorare contempsisse reperitur, hoc evidenter ostenditur, quòd sancti viri erga humiles sive mitiores hortentur, sive ut ejusdem summæ virtutis munera non amittant, percandem humanitatem sunt socii: contra pravorum vero nequitias sive ut malorum societates declinent, sive ut eos compellant, fortiter sint erecti. In eo igitur, quòd Iohannes in Apocalypsi ab angelo cohibere adoret, dicente eodem angelo, Vide ne fecerit: conservus tuus sum: & Pastor ecclesiæ Petrus blandiens adorationem vitaverit, dicens, Surge frater, & ego homo sum sicut & tu: & vas electionis Paulus, & Barnabas Lycaonum adorationem valida reluctatione sprevent, procul dubio omni creaturæ ...
units.tr: Images, however, were never adored, not even tenderly. For in that Abraham or Moses are read to have adored humble men out of necessity for their own advantage, and Mordecai is found to have scorned to adore Haman, an arrogant man rising up to destroy the people of God, this is clearly shown: holy men, toward the humble or the gentler, either exhort them so that they do not lose the gifts of the same highest virtue, or they are companions of the same humanity; but against the wickedness of the depraved, either to avoid the fellowship of the wicked or to compel them, they stand firm and strong. Therefore, in that John in the Apocalypse is restrained by the angel from adoring him, the same angel saying, "See that you do not; I am your fellow servant," and the minister of the Church, Peter, avoiding adoration with flattering words, saying, "Rise, brother, I too am a man, as you are," and the chosen vessel, Paul, and Barnabas, rejected the adoration of the Lycaonians with strong resistance, undoubtedly to every creature ...

units.la: Augustinus quid de hac adoratione Abrahæ vel Moysi senserit, ait enim: Insinuatur hic civium ... exemplum, quod Moyses cum quo deus loquebatur, non fastidivit neque contempsit alienigenæ socerī sui Ietro, cum Israelita non suffecit, utrum inter viros deum verum colentes religiosique sint, quamadmodum & Iob cum ex ipso populo non fuisset, merito quæritur, imo credibilius habetur ambigi quippe posita sunt verba) vel utrum sacrificaverit deo vero in populo ejus quando vidit generum suum, vel utrum cum adoraverit ipse Moyses.
units.tr: What Augustine thought about this adoration of Abraham or Moses he sets out, for he says: "Here is inserted the example of the citizens ... that Moses, with whom God spoke, did not disdain or scorn his foreign father-in-law Jethro, though an Israelite was not enough for him; whether they were among men who worship the true God and are religious, just as Job, though he was not of that people, is rightly asked about, nay rather it is held more credible that it is in doubt (since the words are placed thus), or whether he sacrificed to the true God among his people when he saw his son-in-law, or whether Moses himself adored."

units.la: Quanquam de adoratione etiamsi expresse positum esset, honor videretur ferre redditus commodo quo solet hominibus honorificentiæ causa exhiberi a patribus: sicut de Abraham scriptum est, quod adoraverit filios Heth. Sed nec illud silentio prætereundum est, quod dicunt Jacob Pharaonem adorasse, & Danihel Nabuchodonosor regem, quod quidem nec in Hebræo habetur, nec in nostris Latinis codicibus, qui à beato Hieronymo ex Hebraica veritate translati sunt, ut supra reperitur. Non enim quam semel Jacob in conspectu Pharaonis fuisse legitur: quod quidem hoc modo scribitur narrat: Pofl hæc introduxit Ioseph patrem suum ad regem, & statuit eum coram eo, qui benedicens illi, & interrogatus ab eo quot sunt dies annorum vitæ tuæ? respondit Iacob, Dies peregrinationis & vitæ meæ, centum triginta annorum sunt parvi & mali, & non pervenerunt usque ad dies patrum meorum quibus peregrinati sunt & benedictio redditur.
units.tr: Although, even if adoration had been expressly stated, it would seem to carry the meaning of the honour which is usually shown to men by fathers for the sake of honour, just as it is written of Abraham that he adored the sons of Heth. But this too must not be passed over in silence, that they say Jacob adored Pharaoh, and Daniel Nebuchadnezzar the king. This is not found in the Hebrew, nor in our Latin codices, which were translated by the blessed Jerome from the Hebrew truth, as is found above. For Jacob is read to have been before Pharaoh only once, and the Scripture relates it in this way: "After these things Joseph brought his father in to the king, and set him before him; and he blessed him, and being asked by him, 'How many are the days of the years of your life?' Jacob answered, 'The days of my pilgrimage and life are a hundred and thirty years, few and evil, and they have not reached the days of my fathers, in which they were pilgrims,' and a blessing is given."

units.la: In quibus verbis non enim adorasse, sed benedixisse monstratur. Quod quidem & si fecisset, non ideo faceretur inde adorandarum imaginum exemplum sumeretur: sed ut humiliras patrorum, & deum timentis, regem honorificantis monstraretur. Quæ dum ita se habeant, reor arbitrentur divinam scripturam illo familiarissimo illorum loquendi genere, quod quidam ... benedicere ponerent pro adorare, qui loquendi modus tanto eis peculiaris ... habere & adorare & oculari & venerari pro adorare & ipsi ponant, & ab aliis positi acceperunt, pene omnes ... eis huiusmodi verba in adorare conversa sunt. Sancta vero scriptura ... errores, ita etiam hunc loquendi modum abnuit, sed purus, prius, sive prudentibus semper verbis. vel sententiis utitur, Propheta adtestante, qui ait: Lex domini irreprehensibilis quae si benedicere potuit pro adorare, inpropriis dictionibus utitur. Si inpropriis dictionibus utitur, reprehensibilis est: est autem irreprehensibilis: non igitur benedicere posuit pro adorare. Dic ergo tu, dic sancte Danihel, dic vir desideriorum, dic scrutator archanorum, dic indagator scripturarum, dic propheta qui redemptorem mundi in eo apertius caeteris dixisse probaris, quia non solum scribis eum esse veritatem, quod est tibi commune cum caeteris: sed quo tempore venturus sit doces, & reges per ordinem degeris, & annos enumeras ac manifestissima signa praenuntias: dic utrum Nabuchodonosor, ut illi garriant, adoraveris. Non in meo volumine hoc, inquam, fecisse me legis: quod quidem & si fecissem, nulla ex parte inde illorum adsertio fulciretur: ego propositum in corde meo ne polluerem de mensa eius, neque de vino potus eius, & illi me dicunt eum adoralle. Cadentem ergo in faciem suam, & me adorantem, & hostias & incensum sacrificare mihi praecipientem, & deum deorum & dominum regum & revelatorem mysteriorum, qui potest aperire sacramenta confitentem, & eum in quo potius ob signorum magnitudinem, cuius ego habiraculum sum, quam me adorantem blandis alloquiis affatus sum, & ab eo ut misericordia semper exerceret in genete Israhel, sive ut concaptivos meos, Ananiam, Azariam, & Misaelem constituerit super opera provinciae Babylonis postulavi, non adulatorie adoravi. Quem quidem & si adorasset, non rem quandam insensatam adorarem, sed per humilitatis officium sublimiori potestati subditus manens, sciens non esse potestatem nisi a Deo, rationalem hominem salutando adorarem. Nam cum tam felicem quondam habuerim conversationem, ut quaesitis occasionibus ex latere regis quibus accusari posset ab invidis, & non in alio nisi in legitimis Dei mei accusatus fuerim, & in lacum leonum projectus, & nunc accuser adorasse quem non adoraverim, & a falsis testibus dicar egisse quod non egi, restat ut cum David clamem, Insurrexerunt in me testes falsi, & mentita est iniquitas sibi. Cum ergo ob imaginum amorem & Iacob patriarcham & Danihelem prophetam criminentur, & scripturarum divinarum sensus ad peregrinas intelligentias convertere nitantur, & suos prodecessores sive parentes contra legis imperium alpernentur, superest ut histantum contenti sint, & earum patrocinio, si errorem suum corrigere noluerint, licut & ipsi credunt, muniantur. Atque illi glorientur in imaginibus: nos autem gloriemur in cruce domini nostri Iesu Christi, per quem nobis mundus crucifixus est, nosque mundo.
units.tr: In these words it is shown that he did not adore but blessed. Even if he had done so, an example of adoring images would not be drawn from it; rather it would be shown as the humility of the fathers, and of one who feared God and honoured the king. Since these things stand thus, I suppose they consider that divine Scripture, in that most familiar manner of speaking of theirs, which some ... put "bless" for "adore", a way of speaking so peculiar to them ... have and adore, and look upon, and venerate for "adore", and they themselves put these, and those set by others have received, nearly all ... such words have been turned into "adore". But holy Scripture ... errors, thus also rejects this manner of speaking, but uses pure, prior, or always prudent words or sentiments, the Prophet bearing witness, who says: "The law of the Lord is unblemished." If it could put "bless" for "adore", it would use improper terms. If it uses improper terms, it is blameworthy; but it is unblemished; therefore it did not put "bless" for "adore". Say then, you, say, holy Daniel; say, man of desires; say, searcher of mysteries; say, investigator of the Scriptures; say, prophet who are proved to have spoken of the Redeemer of the world more plainly than the others, for you not only write that he is the truth, which is common to you with the others, but you teach at what time he is to come, and you set out the kings in order, and you enumerate the years and foretell the most manifest signs: say whether you adored Nebuchadnezzar, as they chatter. I say, you read that I did not do this in my volume. Even if I had done it, their assertion would not be supported in any part by it. I purposed in my heart not to defile myself with his food or with the wine of his drink, and they say that I adored him. Falling on his face, and I adoring him, and he commanding me to offer victims and incense, and to God of gods and Lord of kings and revealer of mysteries, who can open secrets to one confessing, and in whom, rather because of the greatness of the signs, of whom I am the dwelling place, than adoring him, I spoke to him with gentle address, and asked that he might always show mercy to the race of Israel, or that he appoint my fellow captives Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael over the affairs of the province of Babylon, I did not adore him with flattery. Even if I had adored him, I would not have been adoring some senseless thing, but, remaining subject to a higher power through the duty of humility, knowing there is no power but from God, I would have adored a rational man by greeting him. For since I once had such a happy conduct that, seeking occasions from the king's side by which I might be accused by the envious, and I was accused in nothing but the laws of my God, and I was cast into the lions' den, and now I am accused of having adored one whom I did not adore, and I am said by false witnesses to have done what I did not do, it remains for me to cry with David: False witnesses have risen against me, and iniquity has lied to itself. Since, then, for the love of images they accuse both the patriarch Jacob and the prophet Daniel, and strive to turn the senses of the divine Scriptures to foreign meanings, and defend their predecessors or parents against the command of the law, it remains that they should be content with these alone, and if they refuse to correct their error, be fortified by their patronage, as they themselves believe. And let them glory in images; but we will glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to us, and we to the world.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De eo quod Iohannes presbyter & legatus Orientalium incaute imagi- num adorationem stabilire nitens, dixisse legitur. Erexit Iacob titulum Deo, quatinus & benedixit eum.
units.tr: Concerning what John the presbyter and legate of the East is read to have said when he rashly tried to establish the adoration of images: Jacob erected a title to God, so that he also blessed him.

units.la: NON mediocris socordiae est hoc etiam ad imaginum adorationem adstruendam exemplum proferre, quod Iacob lapidem erexit in titulum, sicut Iohannes presbyter & legarus Orientalium protulisse in eadem synodo, quae pro adorandis imaginibus agitata est, legitur: quoniam ille lapis non alicuius praeteritae rei memoriam ... go vel similitudo fuisse creditur. Qui si ob aliquius praeteritae rei memoriam ab eiusdem rei similitudine expressus, & a sancto patriarcha ad adorandum fuisset erectus, quoddam fortassis posset illis ferre adminiculum, qui ranri erroris subire non formidavere periculum. Sed dum aliud sit quaedam per parriarcham fieri ad praefigurationem futurorum, aliud a pictore pingi quaedam ob memoriam praeteritorum gestorum: aliud sit spiritu sancto esse repletum, aliud pictoria arte inbutum: aliud iste gerat caelesti munere fretus, aliud ille operandi usu expertus: aliud sit Iacob in titulum erigere lapidem, aliud quendam pictorem in pariete statuere imaginem, aliud secundum typicam figuram desuper oleum fundere, aliud secundum vaniloquam adsertionem adorare iubere: inutile & ultra quam inutile est hoc ad adstruendam aliquam rem in exemplum proponere, quod ab illa re omnium argumentationum diverticulis viderur distare. Numquid nam Iacob illum lapidem ut adoretur erexit, aut alicuius rei in eo imaginem depinxit? Nam dum imagines pene nullum officium aliud, nisi mentibus per sui intuitum memoriam inferendi habeant, lapis qui a patriarcha erectus est tria insignia & summo honore digna creditur officia habuisse. Primum, quod cervicem Israheliticam fulcierit, & pulvillis carenti patriarchae pulvillii visem praestiterit, & ejus caput fuerit oneratus, qui non solum scalam a terra usque ad caelum pertingerem, & angelos per eam ascendentes & descendentes, sed etiam ipsum dominum bona sibi polliccentem cernebat. Secundum, quod in insigne & titulum, quo sanctus patriarcha illius sancti loci reminiscerretur, erectus est, quo rediens prolis & coniugum affectu exhilaratus, & magna rerum opulentia ditatus, sina domino vota qui haec sibi cuncta concesserat redderer. Tertium, quod typum gerebar nostri mediatoris, qui factus est in caput angeli, & est mirabilis in oculis nostris: qui unctus est a patre oleo laeritiae praeconsortibus suis: quem & Danihel lapidem abscisum dicit de monte sine manibus praecidentium, absque coitu & humano videlicet femine ex utero virginali genirum. Quem & David petram nuncupat dicens, Dominus petra mea & robur meum & salvator meus. De quo etiam in Esaia propheta scribitur; Ecce ponam in fundamentu Sion lapidem summum, angularem, probatum, electum, pretiosum, & qui crediderit in eum non confundetur. Qui idcirco angularis dicitur, eo quod duos parietes ex adverso venientes, ex circumcisione videlicet & praeputio, vel etiam duo testamenta in se summo, probaro, electo & pretioso lapide conjungit, & in uno sanctae ecclesiae coetu, cuius ille caput est, connectit. De quo & per prophetam Zachariam paterna
units.tr: It shows no small dullness to bring forward, in support of the adoration of images, the example that Jacob erected a stone as a title. John the presbyter and legate of the East is read to have put this forward at the same synod that was held to debate the adoration of images. For that stone is not believed to have been a memorial or likeness of any past event. If it had been set up by the holy patriarch for adoration, as an image expressing the memory of some past event, it might perhaps give some support to those who did not fear to run the risk of that vain error. But one thing is for a patriarch to do something to prefigure future things, and another for a painter to paint something to remember past deeds; one thing is to be filled with the Holy Spirit, another to be trained in the art of painting; one thing is for this man to carry something relying on a heavenly gift, another for that man to be skilled through practice in the work; one thing is for Jacob to erect a stone as a title, another for some painter to set up an image on a wall; one thing is to pour oil from above according to a typical figure, another to command adoration according to an empty assertion. It is useless, and more than useless, to propose this as an example to establish any matter, since it seems to be far removed from that matter by all the twists of argument. Did Jacob then erect that stone so that it might be adored, or paint an image of something on it? For since images have almost no office other than to bring memory to the mind through the sight of them, the stone that the patriarch erected is believed to have had three distinguished offices, worthy of the highest honour. First, it supported the Israelite's neck, and gave the patriarch, who lacked a pillow, the service of a pillow, and it bore the head of him who saw not only a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending on it, but also the Lord himself promising good things to him. Second, it was set up as a sign and title by which the holy patriarch would remember that holy place, to which, returning, he would render vows to the Lord who had granted him all these things, rejoicing in the affection of offspring and wife and enriched with great abundance of possessions. Third, it bore the type of our mediator, who was made the head of the corner and is wonderful in our eyes, who was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions; whom Daniel also calls the stone cut out of the mountain without the hands of those who cut it, that is, born without intercourse and from a human seed, from a virginal womb. David also names him a rock, saying, The Lord is my rock and my strength and my saviour. Of him it is also written in the prophet Isaiah: Behold, I will lay in the foundation of Zion a stone, a chief corner stone, tried, chosen, precious, and he who believes in him shall not be confounded. He is therefore called the corner stone, because he joins together the two walls coming from opposite sides, namely circumcision and uncircumcision, or indeed the two covenants, in himself, the highest, tried, chosen and precious stone, and binds them together in the one assembly of the holy Church, of which he is the head. Of him also, through the prophet Zechariah, the

units.la: Psalm. 27. Gen. 33. Psal. 37. Esa. 24. paterna voce dicitur, Ecce ego adducam filium meum orientem: quia lapis quem dedi coram Iesu septem in eo oculi sunt. In quibus septem oculis septiformis gratiæ spiritus, qui à patre filioque procedit, evidenter ostenditur: & per Esaiam prophetam, Spiritus Domini spiritus sapientiæ & intellectus, spiritus consilii & sortitu-dinis, spiritus scientiæ & pietatis, spiritus timoris Domini nominatur. De quo etiam angulari lapide petra ecclesiæ air; Sicut modo geniti infantes, rationabiles, sine dolo lac concupiscite, ut in eo crescatis in salutem: si tamen gu- stastis quàm dulcis est Dominus, ad quem accedentes lapidem vivum, ab hominibus quidem reprobatum, à Deo autem electum & honorificatum: & post pauca, Vobis igitur honor credentibus, non credentibus autem lapis, quem reprobaverunt ædificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli, & lapis offensionis & petra scandali his qui offendunt verbo nec credunt in quo & positi sunt. Quo documento monstratur illum & honorem fortitudinis credentibus, & scandalum duritiæ incredulis esse. Quod etiam per iustum Simeonem hoc sensu prædictum est. Ait enim, Positus est hic in ruinam & in resurrectionem multorum in Israhel: in ruinam scilicet incredulorum, in resurrectionem vero credentium: qui etiam ignis nuncupatur, sive quod in se credentes æterni luminis fulgore perlustrat, sive quod incredulos æterni ignis ardore torrebit. De unctione vero hujus lapidis & paulo superius David oraculis prolatum est, & nunc prælati pastoris ecclesiæ testimonio proferendum est, qui ait, Iesum Nazarenum quem unxit Deus spiritu sancto & virtute. Quia ergo spiritus sanctus plerumque in divinis scripturis olei nomine innuitur, Iohannes Apostolus testis est qui dicit, Sicut unctio eius docet nos de omnibus. Cujus si inenarrabilis nectaris unctione delibuti sunt ob imaginum adorationem stabiliendam, synodos agitare & scripturas sanctas ad extraneos sensus usurpare nequaquam debent.
units.tr: Psalm 27. Gen. 33. Psal. 37. Esa. 24. Father's voice says: Behold, I will bring forth my son the Branch, for the stone that I have laid before Jesus has seven eyes upon it. In these seven eyes the sevenfold spirit of grace, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, is plainly shown; and through the prophet Isaiah he is named: The Spirit of the Lord, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, the spirit of the fear of the Lord. Of this same corner stone the Rock of the Church also says: As newborn babes, desire the reasonable milk without guile, that you may grow up unto salvation through it, if indeed you have tasted how sweet the Lord is.
