Habet & pontificem summum de quo Paulus Apostolus dicit, Christus autem sanctus pontifex, in maiori & perfectiori tabernaculo non manufactum, id est, non hujus creationis, neque per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum, sed per proprium sanguinem introivit semel in sanctuarium redemptione inventa: sive cui per Psalmistam dicitur, Tu es sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech: qui est vestitus podere byssino, cum sancti ejus qui utique ei adhærent castitatis lampades luntur. Habet & humerale gemmatum, quia electi ejus operum fulgoribus coruscant, quorum opera videntes homines glorificant patrem eorum qui in cælis est: qui habet in pectore logium rationale dicitur, quaterno lapidum ordine distinctum, quo sermo evangelicus significat quadruplicato ordine veritatem fidei nobis & manifestationem trinitatis exponit. Habet frontem ... aureum laminam in fronte resplendentem, quod petalum appellatur, id est, divinitatem qua unitatis cum patre subsistentiæ est: quoniam sicut in metallis nil conparatur auro, ita & in creaturis nihil est creatori. Qui etiam pontifex habet in interioribus partibus operimenta sua, quia in incarnationis ejus investigari difficile est, Johanne adtestante qui ait, Cujus ego non sum dignus solvere corrigiam calciamenti. Habet etiam per indumenti circuitum tintinabula quæ in extremo ejusdem vestimenti posita sunt, ut semper sonitum dent: quia videlicet sancti prædicatores, qui ejus utique indumentum sunt, de extremis temporibus & hinc mundi reticere nesciunt, sed semper nos ad futuris admonent, adtendentes illud quod per quendam sapientem dicitur, In omnibus operibus tuis memorare novissima tua, & in æternum non peccabis. Habet etiam hæc domus Dei, id est, ecclesia cujus decorem breviter enumeramus, sancta sanctorum: quia videlicet in præsenti sæculo pro sanctis habet sanctam conversationem: pro sanctis vero sanctorum, in quæ semel tantum modo intrat-tur, sed in sublimitate ad cælum, quando vilibilibus contemptis ad invisibilia transit. De quibus Apostolus dicit, Charissimi nondum apparuit quod erimus: scimus quoniam cum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est. Hunc excellentissimum ergo & cælestis patriæ decorem dilexerat vir ille sanctissimus, non in ginum & colorum fucos, non materialium picturarum similitudines. ob hunc decorem, non in materiales figuras quali quodam intolerabili desiderio resolutus erat, cum dicebat: Hæc memoriam vestram & meam effudi in me animam meam, quoniam ingredior locum tabernaculi admirabilis usque ad domum Dei. De hac domo, non de his visibilibus parietibus Apostolus dixit; Scimus quoniam si terrestris domus nostra tabernaculi habitationis dissolvatur, quod ædificationem ex Deo habemus, domum non manufactam, æternam in cælis. Hunc decorem Esaias, non pictorum opera respiciendo considerabat, cum dicebat, Respice Sion civitatem solemnitatis tuæ: oculi tui videbunt Hierusalem, habitationem opulentam tabernaculum quod nequaquam transferri poterit. De hac domo per David dicitur, Beati qui habitant in domo tua, in seculorum laudabunt te. Num quidnam sancti Patres, ut cæteros taceam, Paulus, Antonius, Hilarion, vel omnis Anachoritarum sive Eremitarum cateva, qui de coram basilicarum sive imaginum depictarum non habuerunt, sed in quibuscunque tuguriolis suis Deo animas dedicaverunt, idcirco sanctæ non sunt? & ideo aut non diligebant decorem domus Domini, aut locum habitationis gloriæ Dei fragranti pectore contemplari non desiderabant, quia imagines non habebant nec adorabant? Interea etenim sicut & cæteræ sanctæ animæ templum Dei & locum habitationis gloriæ ejus habebant, dicente vale electionis, Templum enim Dei sanctum est quod estis vos. Plurimi præterea ex divinarum scripturarum amœnis pratis colligi ambrosiei flores poterunt, quibus & secundum tropologiam, & secundum allegoriam, & secundum anagogen sanctæ ecclesiæ decor monstraretur, sibi brevitatis causa studemus, non præpediremur habenis. Hi ergo pauci pro pluribus prolati sufficiant, quibus diligens lector cetera quæ hic prolata non sunt indagare curabit, & domus Dei decorem, non in imaginibus materialibus, sed in virtutibus spiritalibus refulgentem esse videbit.
units.tr: The house of God is the Church, according to allegory; according to anagoge it is the heavenly house; according to tropology it is the soul of the man. For this reason, in many places of Holy Scripture the house of God is read of, not walls nor some material building, but a spiritual and unshakeable dwelling of God must be understood. Minds that are wholly ignorant of these senses think that the beauty of the house of the Lord is not the virtues of the Church but material images. For that outstanding prophet had certainly seen certain images, or indeed the beauty of pictures, or the costly furnishings of the ministries, when he said: Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells. Is the place where the glory of the Lord dwells to be believed to be in any man-made thing? The holy Church therefore has the beauty that the Prophet loved, that is, spiritual virtues. She has silver, that is, faith or the inner sense; she has silver plate, that is, confession or the truth of speech; she has silver pillars, that is, holy men gained by reasonable patience and the beauty of the sayings. These pillars have silver bases, since they are set upon the firmness of the Word of God that is handed down to us through the prophets and apostles. They also have a golden head, because the golden head is the faith of Christ, as the Apostle testifies, who says: For the head of every man is Christ. She also has, in place of imperishable wood, knowledge that comes through the wood, or the incorruption of chastity that knows no decay. She has, in place of fine linen, virginity; in place of scarlet, the glory of confession; in place of purple, the brightness of charity; in place of hyacinth, the hope of the kingdom of heaven. Her priests are clothed with these materials, according to the voice of David, who says: Let your priests be clothed with righteousness. Paul also exhorts them with these words when he says: Put on the bowels of mercy. Her priests also have other, nobler garments, which the same chosen vessel names when he says: Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its lusts. She also has a library, that is, holy men instructed in the teachings of the divine law, of whom the Prophet says: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek them with the whole heart. And again he calls blessed those who keep his commandments in memory so as to do them. She has ten other things stretched out, since the spiritual sense of the law is enlarged not only in one word of the law, nor in two or three, but throughout the whole decalogue; or when, adding the fruit of the Spirit, that is, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, faith, self-control, she brings forth charity, which is greater than all. She also has an altar, that is, the firmness of faith, on which she offers to God the sacrifices of prayers and the victims of mercy; on which, with the knife of self-control, she slays pride as a bullock, cuts the throat of joy as a ram, and separates luxury and every lust like goats and kids, whose right arm, cheeks and breast she gives to the priests, that is, good works, right works, in which nothing of the left-handed kind is found at all. She also has a lampstand of light, either because the Lord is its light, or because the holy men, whose lamps are burning and shining, await the coming of their Lord, who waits to return from the wedding, and pour forth the doctrines of preaching as light-bringing torches. This lampstand of lamps is placed toward the south so that it looks toward the north, that is, so that the holy men may always watch carefully and attentively the cunning of the devil, and with a fearful mind look to where the temptation is to come from. For the Prophet also says that he saw a seething pot, with its face turned away from the face of the north; and in another place it is said: For from the north evil will be spread over the whole earth. And the Apostle Peter says: Because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. She also has a table of showbread, with twelve loaves set in the northern part, which looks toward the south, that is, the twelve Apostles, whom she is commanded to set out daily without ceasing, facing the south, because, of course, she daily awaits the coming of the Lord. For the Lord, says the Prophet, will come from the south. She has an altar of incense, because from the firmness of her building the smoke of holy prayers rises in the sight of the Lord, and daily with David she cries out: Let my prayer be set forth as incense in your sight. Or because, according to the Apostle, we are to God the fragrance of Christ. She has the mercy seat, the ark and the two cherubim, about which was discussed above in a certain chapter. She also has the high priest, of whom the Apostle Paul says: But Christ, the holy high priest, entered once for all into the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, nor through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. Or he to whom it is said by the Psalmist: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, who is clothed in the fine linen ephod, while the lamps of chastity of his holy ones, who indeed cling to him, are lit. She also has the jewelled shoulder-piece, because her chosen ones shine with the brightness of their works; seeing their works, men glorify their Father who is in heaven. She has on her breast the breastplate of judgment, set with four rows of stones, by which the Gospel message signifies that the truth of faith is set forth in a fourfold order and reveals to us the manifestation of the Trinity. She has a forehead ... a golden plate shining on the forehead, which is called the plate, that is, the divinity which belongs to the unity of substance with the Father, since, as nothing is compared to gold among metals, so nothing in creatures is to the Creator. This high priest also has his hidden parts within, because his incarnation is hard to investigate, John bearing witness, who says: I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. She also has, around the hem of the garment, little bells placed at the edge of the same robe, so that they always give a sound; for, of course, the holy preachers, who are indeed his garment, do not know how to keep silent about the last times and about this world, but always warn us about the future, attending to what a certain wise man says: In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin. This house of God, that is, the Church, whose beauty we briefly list, also has the Holy of Holies: for in the present age she has holy conversation in place of holy things, but the Holy of Holies in place of holy things, into which one enters only once, is in the heights of heaven, when, the visible things being despised, she passes to the invisible. Of these the Apostle says: Beloved, it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when it appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. Therefore that most holy man had loved this most excellent beauty of the heavenly fatherland, not the colourful dyes of gold and hues, not the likenesses of material paintings. For the sake of this beauty, not for material figures, he was dissolved with a kind of unbearable longing when he said: I have poured out my soul in me, remembering your presence and mine, because I enter the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. The Apostle spoke of this house, not of these visible walls: We know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Isaiah was considering this beauty, not looking at the works of painters, when he said: Look upon Zion, the city of your solemnity; your eyes shall see Jerusalem, a rich habitation, a tabernacle which can never be moved. Of this house it is said through David: Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ages. Did the holy Fathers, to pass over the rest, Paul, Antony, Hilarion, or the whole company of anchorites or hermits, who had no churches of this kind or painted images, but dedicated their souls to God in whatever little huts they had, therefore not become holy? And did they therefore either not love the beauty of the house of the Lord, or not desire to contemplate with a fragrant heart the place of the glory of God, because they had no images and did not adore them? Meanwhile, indeed, like the other holy souls they had the temple of God and the place of his glory, the chosen vessel saying: For the temple of God is holy, which you are. Moreover, many flowers of ambrosia could be gathered from the pleasant meadows of the divine Scriptures, by which the beauty of the holy Church would be shown according to tropology, according to allegory, and according to anagoge; but for the sake of brevity we take care not to be drawn further by the reins. Let these few, brought forward for many, suffice; the diligent reader will take care to search out the rest which are not set forth here, and he will see that the beauty of the house of God shines not in material images but in spiritual virtues.

units.la: CAP. XXX. Quod non pro manufactis imaginibus per Psalmistam, ut illi ajunt, dictum est, Sicut audivimus ita & vidimus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX. That the verse "As we have heard, so have we seen" was not said by the Psalmist, as they claim, concerning handmade images.

units.la: QUONIAM igitur manufactas imagines se vidisse gratulati sunt, Psalmistæ sibi versiculum accommodavimus dicentes, Sicut audivimus ita & vidimus, dicant quæso, dicant ubi hoc audierunt quod modo in imaginibus vident: dicant quis Patriarcharum Prophetarumve aut Apostolorum hoc illorum auditu intulerit, quod modo illorum visibus patet: dicant quis hoc privilegium prædixerit, quod imagines non solum visuri, sed adoraturi forent, cujus pollicitationis conpotes effecti merito dicant, Sicut audivimus ita & vidimus. Nos autem qui opitulante Deo Psalmorum prophetiam spiritaliter pro viribus intellegimus, non hoc comma de manufactis imaginibus dictum, sed de insignioribus & eminentioribus mysteriis prophetatum fuisse censemus: qui videlicet in lege de Christi adventu audivimus, in evangelio videmus: sicut in Prophetis de ejus incarnatione competimus, in novo testamento nunc serie cernimus: sicut in hagiographis & in cunctis fideris de ejus nativitate, passione, resurrectione, ad cælum ascensione typicis videbamus praefigurarum fuisse mysterium, nunc peracta cuncta fuisse in sanctis videmus evangelis: qui etiam conscii ad æternam patriam venerunt, & in ea visuri sumus quæ in hujus mortalitatis ærumna de ejus felicitate audivimus, dicturique sumus, Sicut audivimus ita & vidimus, id est, Sicut audivimus mortales, videmus nunc immortales; sicut audivimus corruptibiles, videmus nunc incorruptibiles; sicut audivimus in ærumnosa peregrinatione, videmus nunc in vivorum felicissima regione: quod audivimus cum patiebamur procellosissimas tempestates sæculi, videmus nunc quum potimur suavissima securitate paradisi; quodque audivimus cum timebamus periculosissimum naufragium, videmus cum pervenimus ad cautissimum & nobis longe ante desideratissimum portum. In hoc sane arti lo hunc primum librum claudendum esse putavimus, ut quoniam de portu mentionem fecimus, illum quoque in hoc loco, ad portum deducamus, ut remoratæ navigatione fatigati aliquanti per portu spatiantes, resumptisque viribus, ad secundi libri navigationem Domino auxiliante velarum damus.
units.tr: Since, therefore, they boast that they have seen images made by hand, we have applied to them the verse of the Psalmist, saying: "As we have heard, so have we seen." Let them tell us, I beg, let them tell us where they heard what they now see in images. Let them tell us who among the Patriarchs, Prophets or Apostles foretold by their hearing what is now plain to their eyes. Let them tell us who predicted this privilege, that images would not only be seen but adored, and, having been made partakers of this promise, let them rightly say, "As we have heard, so have we seen." But we, who by God's help try to understand the prophecy of the Psalms spiritually, judge that this verse was not said concerning handmade images, but was prophesied concerning the more notable and eminent mysteries. Namely, we heard in the Law of the coming of Christ and see it in the Gospel; as we gather in the Prophets his incarnation, so now we discern it in the order of the New Testament; as in the Hagiographa and in all the lights we saw the mystery of his nativity, passion, resurrection and ascension into heaven foreshadowed by types and figures, so now we see all these things accomplished in the holy Gospels. Having also come, as witnesses, to our eternal fatherland, we shall see in it what we heard in the troubles of this mortal life concerning his happiness, and we shall say, "As we have heard, so have we seen": that is, as we heard that we were mortal, we now see that we are immortal; as we heard that we were corruptible, we now see that we are incorruptible; as we heard in our sorrowful pilgrimage, we now see in the most blessed region of the living; what we heard when we were suffering the most stormy tempests of the age, we now see when we enjoy the sweetest security of paradise; and what we heard when we feared the most dangerous shipwreck, we see when we arrive at the safest harbour, long desired by us. Indeed, we have thought it right to close this first book in this way: since we have mentioned a harbour, we bring the book also into port at this point, so that, wearied by the long voyage, we may walk about a little in the harbour, recover our strength, and with the Lord's help set our sails again for the voyage of the second book.

units.tr: THE FIRST BOOK ENDS.

units.la: PRÆFATIO LIBRI SECUNDI.
units.tr: Preface to the Second Book

units.la: TRACTATIS in superiore libro quam brevissime divinæ legis quibusdam commatibus, quæ, ut crebro memoravimus, illi contra quos huic nostro stilo conflictus est, ob suæ vanitatis mate-riam fulciendam protulisse noscuntur, vel etiam quibusdam in eodem libro prolatis capitulis, quæ de eorum reprehensione non inconsequenter proferenda erant, necesse est ut in præsenti, secundo videlicet libro, & divinæ legis sanæ sobrieque resídua comminata tractaturi, & quorundam sanctorum Patrum male mihi nominus sententias ab illis usurpatas propriis sensibus redditum, Domino favente, adgrediamur. In quo etiam libro quædam capitula inserentur quæ eorum errori ad mentes fidelium transfeundi adiutum inrecipiant, quo res sanctitate sive auctoritate carentes sacratissimæ rebus & ab ipso Domino institutis æquiperare nituntur: ut in his duobus voluminibus per duorum testamentorum salutaria arma eorum vanissimis nænis obnitentes, ad tertium in cujus principio nostræ fidei fundamentum erit, liberius accedamus, ut quoniam sanctæ in eo & unicæ trinitatis confessio continebitur, tertio quoque libri numerus habeatur exornaturque sacratissimo numero qui exornandus est sanctæ fidei mysterio: omnem siquidem nostræ disputationis sive cæterorum actuum spem non in mundanarum artium argumentosis allegationibus, sed in eo conloquentes, qui & per præsentiam corporalem ait, Non enim vos estis qui loquimini, sed Spiritus patris vestri qui loquitur in vobis: & quondam per Prophetam dixerat, Dilatavi tuum & ego admiplebo illud. Ideo igitur per quendam prodicendi diendi ordinem hujus nostræ disputationis quibusdam librorum intercapedinibus distinximus grefsim, ne ordinata ut menti tramite inordinata prolixitas efficeret fastidiosum, nec libuis nobis quoddam affert inconpositum vel indigestum, ne operis inordinata congenes lectori perturbata vociferatione istiusmodi quendam præberet tumultum: quia & iter carpentes congruis quibusdam temporibus pacem non renuunt, & agrorum, vinearum vel etiam hortorum cultores per quasdam camporum inter capedines, vel etiam per agrorum dimensiones limites statuere constituerunt.
units.tr: In the previous book I touched, as briefly as I could, on certain sayings of the divine law which, as I have often noted, those against whom this work is directed are known to have put forward to bolster their vanity, and on certain chapters in that book that had to be brought forward, not without reason, in refuting them. Now, in this present second book, with the Lord's favour, we must take up the remaining sound and sober threats of the divine law, and also the opinions of certain holy Fathers, which have been wrongly attributed to me and which those men have seized on and twisted to their own meaning. In this book certain chapters will also be inserted, which they admit to help spread their error into the minds of the faithful, and by which they strive to set things lacking holiness or authority on a level with the most sacred matters instituted by the Lord himself. So, in these two volumes, I will resist their most empty trifles with the saving arms of the two testaments, and then approach the third more freely. At the beginning of that book will lie the foundation of our faith, since it will contain the confession of the holy and only Trinity, so that the third book too may be numbered and adorned with the most sacred number that befits the mystery of holy faith. For the hope of this discussion, and of our other undertakings, rests not on the sophistical arguments of worldly arts but on him who speaks through those who converse with him, who also said in his bodily presence, "For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you" [Matth. 10.20], and who once said through the prophet, "Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it" [Psal. 80.11]. Therefore, by a certain order of publishing and dividing this discussion, I have marked its progress with intervals between books, so that unordered prolixity should not make the reader weary, and so that I should not offer anything disjointed or undigested, which would present the reader with a disorderly mass and a confused tumult of such noise. For travellers on a journey do not refuse rest at suitable times, and cultivators of fields, vineyards or even gardens have chosen to mark out boundaries by certain intervals between their plots, or even by measuring out their fields.

units.la: LIBER SECUNDUS.
units.tr: BOOK II.

units.la: CAP. I. Quod non propter eos scriptum sit qui imagines adorare contemnunt, sicut illi dicunt qui eas adorant, quod in Psalmo legitur, Quanta malignatus est inimi- cus in sanctis tuis.
units.tr: CHAP. I. That it was not written for those who scorn to adore images, as those who do adore them argue from what is read in the Psalm: "How much the enemy has wrought evil in your saints."

units.la: Est quoque & illud non mediocris insaniæ quod ea, quæ de his longe ante prædicata sunt qui urbem Hierusalem everterunt, & templum Domini incenderunt, isti de illis intellegunt qui nec ne adorare contemnunt: præsertim cum aliud & longe aliud sit, de templo mare æneum & duos columnas & vasa cæteraque ornamenta tollere, & aliud manufactas imagines non adorare: aliud urbicium signibus templi pulchritudinem mancipare, aliud imaginum adorationem vitare: aliud sanctaque sanctorum diruere, aliud prudenter picturis colla deflectere inhibere. Denique quis nosse cupit de quo Psalmista dixerit; Quanta malignatus est inimicus in sanctis tuis, non solum libri Regum historiis, & Romanorum gestis perdocetur, quæ præteritum urbis Hierusalem & templi excidium narrant, sed etiam ipsius David egregii Prophetæ varicinio instruitur, qui futuras urbis & eversionem sacratissimi illius templi per schema, quod prolepsis dicitur, sutura quasi præterita modulavit dicens, Deus, venerunt gentes in hereditatem tuam, polluerunt templum sanctum tuum, posuerunt Hierusalem velut pomorum custodias, & cætera.
units.tr: It is also no small madness to take those things which were foretold long before of those who overthrew the city of Jerusalem and burned the temple of the Lord as applying to those who scorn to adore. This is especially so, since it is one thing to remove from the temple the bronze sea, the two pillars and the other vessels and ornaments, and quite another not to adore hand-made images; one thing to hand over the beauty of the temple to a city's standards, another to avoid the adoration of images; one thing to destroy the holy of holies, another to refrain prudently from bowing the neck before pictures. Finally, whoever wishes to know of whom the Psalmist spoke, "How much the enemy has wrought evil in your saints," is taught not only by the histories in the books of Kings and by the Roman deeds, which relate the past destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the temple, but is also instructed by the prophecy of David, that excellent prophet, who, by a figure called prolepsis, described the future overthrow of the city and of that most sacred temple as if they were already past, saying: "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a heap of ruins," and the rest.

units.la: Et in Psalmo, cujus hic versiculus est, de quo nunc agimus, dicit; Quanta malignatus est inimicus in sanctis tuis, & gloriati sunt omnes qui te oderunt, in medio atrio tuo posuerunt signa sua signa, & non cognoverunt tanquam in via super summum, tanquam in silva lignorum securibus excideunt januas ejus, bipenne & asia dejecerunt eas incenderunt igni sanctuarium tuum, in terra polluerunt tabernaculum nominis tui. quod etiam in alio Psalmo expressius dicto dicit; Exterminavit eam aper de silva, & singularis ferus depastus est eam. Sed ne quem moveat quod non dixit, Quanta malignatus est, sed, Quanta malignatus est, advertat hoc per figuram locutionis disiunctæ, quæ syllepsis nuncupatur, per quam & pro uno multi ponuntur, ut in evangelio, Et latrones eodem crucifixerant improperabant ei: sive, Defuncti sunt enim qui quærebant animam pueri: & pro uno ut in Exodo legitur, Ora ad Dominum ut auferat a nobis serpentem: & in Psalmo, Misit in eos canes in caninam & comedit eos, & rana exterminavit eos. Quod & si quis secundum mysticam intellectum alibi scrutetur, non incongrue sanctam ecclesiam advertet & malignanter in ea hæreticos intelleget, qui eam semper pravis dogmatibus infestare nituntur: verumtamen a nullo eorum quibus non obtrunqué intellectum habent de imaginum adorationem contemnentibus intellegentibus. Quanto ergo illi sani sensus expertes sunt, qui hunc versiculum de eis dictum fuisse autumant, tanquam hi in sui sensus vigore permanent qui imagines non adorant.
units.tr: And in the Psalm from which this verse comes, the one we are now discussing, he says: "How much the enemy has wrought evil in your saints! And all who hate you have boasted. In the midst of your court they have set up their standards as signs, and they did not know, as men who lift up axes in a thicket of trees. They have broken down its gates with axe and hatchet, they have set fire to your sanctuary, and in the earth they have defiled the tabernacle of your name." He says the same more plainly in another Psalm: "The boar out of the wood has laid it waste, and the wild beast of the field has devoured it." But lest anyone be troubled that he did not say "How much he has wrought evil," but "How much the enemy has wrought evil," let him note that this is by a figure of speech called syllepsis, in which many things are put for one. Thus in the Gospel: "The thieves who were crucified with him also reproached him"; or "For those who sought the child's life are dead"; and one for many, as in Exodus: "Pray to the Lord that he take away the serpent from us"; and in the Psalm: "He sent among them dogs of flies, which devoured them, and frogs, which destroyed them." And if anyone elsewhere searches out the mystical sense of this, he will rightly see the holy Church and understand that heretics maliciously attack her, since they always strive to trouble her with wicked doctrines. Yet this in no way applies to those who scorn the adoration of images. How far, then, are they destitute of sound sense who maintain that this verse was said of them, as if those who do not adore images were remaining in the strength of their own meaning.

units.la: CAP. II. Hæc illud ad hanc rem pertineat, sicut illi dicunt, quod scriptum est, Quoniam non est jam Propheta & nos non cognoscet amplius.
units.tr: CHAP. II. That this pertains to the matter, as they say, from what is written: "For there is no longer a prophet, and he will know us no more."

units.la: Hæc quoque versiculus in ejusdem synodi lectione inconpetenter positus est: quoniam nec nostra vox est qui Patrem in Spiritu & veritate adoramus: nec illorum qui Deum in sanctos in imaginibus adorare conantur: quia Propheram magnum habemus Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum de quo per Moysen dicitur, Suscitabit Dominus Deus Prophetam vobis, ipsum audite. Quem etiam secundum Apostolum, advocatum habemus apud patrem, quem cotidie spiritalibus oculis intuemur, & cujus vaticinia sedulo perdocemur: sed Judæorum excidium & dispersiones & cladem & mortes gentis suæ, nec non etiam diruptionem templi, cæremoniarum abolitionem, a prophetis & a Dei cognitione recessionem deflentium & dicentium, Quoniam non est jam Propheta & nos non cognoscet amplius: quod etiam per Osee Prophetam prædictum est qui ait, Quia diebus multis sedebunt filii Israel sine rege & sine principe, sine sacrificio & sine altari, & sine Ephod, & sine Seraphim. qui etiam coram ad fidem conversionem quam circa finem mundi fore credimus, subsequenter adjunxit, Et post hæc revertentur filii Israel & quærent Dominum Deum suum, & David regem suum, & pavebunt ad Dominum, & ad bonum ejus in novissimo dierum.
units.tr: This verse too is placed inappropriately in the reading of the same synod. For it is neither our voice, we who worship the Father in spirit and truth, nor the voice of those who try to worship God in the saints through images. We have a great Prophet, Jesus Christ our Lord, of whom it is said through Moses: "The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you; hear him." We have him also, according to the Apostle, as our advocate with the Father; we daily behold him with spiritual eyes, and we are diligently taught his prophecies. But the lament of the Jews, over the ruin and dispersions and destruction and deaths of their nation, and also over the breaking down of the temple, the abolition of the ceremonies, and their withdrawal from the prophets and from the knowledge of God, is what is expressed in those who say: "For there is no longer a prophet, and he will know us no more." This was also foretold through the prophet Hosea, who said: "For many days the children of Israel shall sit without king and without prince, without sacrifice and without altar, and without ephod and without teraphim." Afterwards, he also added the conversion to faith, which we believe will come near the end of the world: "And afterwards the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God, and David their king; and they shall tremble before the Lord and before his goodness in the latter days."

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Quomodo intelligendum est, Domine in civitate tua imaginem illorum ad nihilum rediges : quod quidam capitulum sicut & cætera, illi aliter quam dictum est intelligunt.
units.tr: How the words "Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing" are to be understood; some people understand this chapter, as well as the rest, otherwise than has been said.

units.la: CIVITAS Dei figuraliter in sacris literis interdum anima hominis, quæ à Deo inhabitatur, dicente scriptura: Habitabo in eis: & iterum, Anima justi sedes sapientiæ, accipitur: interdum præsentis temporis ecclesia, quam fluminis impetus lætificat, & cui per Prophetam dicitur, Sicut laetus suo tui Hierusalem, obliviscatur me dextera mea: plerumque cælestis Hierusalem, quæ Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, Apostolorum, martyrum, confessorum vel cæterorum fidelium agminibus constructa intelligitur: de qua per Apostolum dicitur, quæ autem sursum est Hierusalem, libera est, quæ est mater omnium nostrum: cui etiam per Esaiam Prophetam à Domino pollicetur, Non enim in occasum tertium veniet sol, & luna tibi non deficiet in æternum tempus: quam etiam Johannes in Apocalypsi vidisse se dicit descendentem de cælo, ornatam monilibus suis: de cujus beatitudine peue innumerabiliter poterant dici, quæ hujus brevitatis stilo non valent digeri. In hac civitate imagines impiorum ad nihilum redigentur: quia illorum aspectus divinis non poterit adparere conspectibus: sed sicut pollicentur in se imaginem Domini in præsentis vitæ curriculo, ita in cælesti Hierusalem illorum non adparebit imago, qui æterno quidem mancipabuntur incendio: de quibus alias per Psalmistam dicitur, Et homo cum in honore esset non intellexit, comparatus est jumentis insipientibus & similis factus est illis: quia videlicet cum in tanto honore esset quod ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei conditus erat, non intelligendo, ad tantam labem vitiorum est devolutus, ut non inmetito jumentis irrationalibus esset comparatus. Ad nihilum ergo impiorum imagines rediguntur, quando se eis ipsa veritas subtrahens ab ejus luce alienantur, nec similitudinem valent retinere, cujus beatitudinis expertes noscuntur ut quecunque manere. Propter dolositatis itaque eorum adposita eis in superioribus dixerat, Dominus judex justus reddit unicuique secundum opera sua. Dixerat etiam eos dejecille cum allevarentur, quia Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Dixerat eos subito desectos & perilleb propter iniquitatem suam, velut somnium exsurgentis: quia sicut quibusdam præstigiis mortalium pectora in somnis eluduntur, & optata quæque subito se nanctos suisse gratulantur, cum aut desideraro quis potitur regno, aut cupito sublimatur aliquis ministerio: aut paupertate fugato liquis subito ditatur, aut optato aliquis fruitur conjugio, aut debilis aliquis amissos artus se recepisse gratulatur, aut criminosus aliquis honorabilem se gaudet, aut aliquis ignobilis nobilem, nūt insipiens sapientem se putat: & subito amittit evigilans quod adquisierat dormiens, & patesactis se oculis non videre oculis quæ gaudebat videre clausis: hic felicitas impiorum quasi per somnium quodammodo videtur, quia post modicum tempus non videbitur: & sicut evigilantes ea quæ subito præ somnum adquisierant perdunt, sic morientes ea quæ habere videbantur amittunt: quoniam & illi præstigiosa lætitia quam sternentes nansti sunt, in momento carent, & isti vana, & ut ita dixerim, sumea mundi gaudia diu tenere non valent. Ob quorum impietates quasi quasdam severitate accensus Propheta subjunxit, Domine, in civitate tua imaginem illorum ad nihilum rediges: ut videlicet qui in se cui characteris decus malis operibus inquinaverunt, illorum facies in tua civitate non videantur, quæ est æterna felicitas, summa beatitudo, perpetuum gaudium: in cujus palatiis regnat rex, cujus regni non erit finis, cujus subsellia Patriarcharum senatu resplendent, cujus curia Prophetarum rutilat cuneis, cujus mœnia martyrum numerosa militia exornantur, cujus portæ Apostolicis decorantur cœtibus, cujus plateæ redundant virgineis choris, cujus domicilia confessorum plena sunt legionibus: quæ non indiget sole, quia Dominus lux ejus est, per cujus omnes vicos Alleluja cantatur.
units.tr: The city of God is figuratively taken in Holy Scripture sometimes for the soul of a man, which is inhabited by God, as Scripture says: I will dwell in them; and again, The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. Sometimes it is taken for the Church of the present time, which the rush of the river gladdens, and to which it is said through the Prophet, If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill. Most often it is taken for the heavenly Jerusalem, understood to be built from the companies of the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, martyrs, confessors and the other faithful. Of her the Apostle says: But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all. To her also the Lord promises through the Prophet Isaiah: The sun shall no more go down, and your moon shall not wane for ever. John also says in the Apocalypse that he saw her coming down from heaven, adorned with her jewels. Of her blessedness countless things could almost be said, which cannot be set out in the compass of this brief style. In this city the images of the wicked will be reduced to nothing, because their appearance cannot be seen by the divine eyes. Just as they promise in themselves the image of the Lord during the course of the present life, so in the heavenly Jerusalem the image of those will not appear who are indeed to be given over to eternal fire. Of these, elsewhere the Psalmist says: And man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he is compared to the senseless beasts and made like them. For clearly, since he was in such honour that he was made in the image and likeness of God, by not understanding he fell down into such a ruin of vices that he was rightly compared to irrational beasts. The images of the wicked, therefore, are reduced to nothing when, the truth itself withdrawing from them, they are alienated from its light, and cannot keep the likeness of that blessedness of which they are known to be deprived, as if they had never been. Because of their deceit, therefore, he had said above, to the things set before them: The Lord, the just judge, renders to each according to his works. He had also said that they were cast down when they were lifted up, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. He had said that they were suddenly cut off and perished through their iniquity, like the dream of one who rises: for just as the hearts of mortals are mocked in sleep by certain illusions, and they rejoice that they have suddenly got whatever they wished for, when someone gains a kingdom he desired, or someone is raised to a ministry he longed for, or someone, poverty being put to flight, is suddenly enriched, or someone enjoys the marriage he wished for, or a crippled man rejoices that he has recovered his lost limbs, or a criminal rejoices that he is honoured, or a man of low birth that he is noble, or a fool thinks himself wise; and on waking he suddenly loses what he had acquired in his sleep, and with his eyes open he does not see what, with his eyes closed, he rejoiced to see. So the happiness of the wicked is seen in some way as if in a dream, because after a short time it will not be seen; and just as those who wake lose what they suddenly acquired in sleep, so the dying lose what they seemed to possess. For those illusory joys which they seized while sleeping vanish in a moment, and those empty and, so to speak, smoky joys of the world cannot be held for long. Kindled, as it were, with severity against their impieties, the Prophet added: Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing: that is, that those who have defiled in themselves the honour of the character of God by evil works may not be seen in your city, which is eternal happiness, supreme blessedness, perpetual joy; in whose palaces the King reigns, whose kingdom will have no end; whose seats shine with the senate of the Patriarchs; whose court glows with the ranks of the Prophets; whose walls are adorned with the numerous army of martyrs; whose gates are graced with the companies of the Apostles; whose squares overflow with choirs of virgins; whose dwellings are full of the legions of confessors; which has no need of the sun, because the Lord is its light, and through all whose streets Alleluia is sung.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: Quomodo intelligendum est quod Psalmographus cecinit, Misericordia & veritas obviaverunt sibi, justitia & pax se conplexæ sunt: quod temere & adulatorie à Johanne presbytero & legato orientalium in participatione venerabilis Papæ Adria- ni & Tarafii Patriarchæ dicitur esse completum.
units.tr: How the words of the Psalmist are to be understood, Mercy and truth have met each other, righteousness and peace have kissed: which John the presbyter, legate of the East, rashly and flatteringly says were fulfilled in the presence of the venerable Pope Adrian and Patriarch Tarasius.

units.la: MISERICORDIAM & veritatem sibi mutuo obviasse, justitiam & pacem invicem se conplexas fuisse David vatum luculentissimus elegantèr decantat: quod tandem constat esse conpletum, cum post incarnationem Domini duo testamenta in unius conpagem copulationem sunt adduista. Quoniam quanquam inter se diversa quodammodo cernuntur, ad unum tamen bi in Christo qui est pax nostra, qui fecit utraq; unū, convenire noscuntur. In novo n. misericordia est, in qua per gratiam genus humanū liberatur: in veteri veritas, ubi legis & Prophetarū adnunciatio cōtinetur. Hæc autem duo sibi mutuo obviasse dicuntur, non ad contrarietatem exercendā, sed ad gratiam promisse perfectionis implendā: unum quippe cōstat factū quod tēporibus probabatur esse divisum; & ut genus ipsum fœderis hymnidicus David evidenter exprimeret, hoc ipsum varia nominum iteratione geminavit, amplexu scilicet quodam dilectionis duas res, id est, justitiam & pacem, in mutuam protinus venisse concordiam: quem quidem versiculum, & secundum somatopœian, id est, corporis attributionem, per quem loquutionis modum tebus incorporeis corpora tribuuntur, dictum esse constat: & per metaphoram, id est, rerum verborumque translationem, per quam plerunque à rebus animalibus ad animales, ab inanimalibus ad inanimales, ab inanimali ad animales translata sit, quæ duæ locutionum figuræ inter se differunt, quòd una rebus incorporeis corpora, altera & rebus corporeis membra & motus, & incorporeis & membra & motus & formas tribuit. Hunc denique versiculum temerarie & adulatorie Johannes presbyter in participatione venerabilis Papæ Adriani, & Tarasii Constantinopolitani Episcopi protulit, qui tamen presbyter quamquam Episcopis in eadem synodo residentibus minor fuerit honore, non tamen legitur minor fuisse errore, qui & si præcedebant eum gradus sublimitate, superabantur tamen ab eo multiloqua procacitate: nec superari potuit à prælatis subjectus intemeratis loquacitatibus, qui subjectus à prælatis superabatur pontificalibus dignitatibus. Qui præsertim duplex in hac parte creditur patrasse delinquium: sive quia verba mysteriorum archanis plena ab Spiritu sancto prolata ad res humanas intellectere nisus sit superstitiosa intentione adorandarum imaginum: sive quia eadem perversa intentione excæcatus in adulationis miserabile corruerit vitium: quod vitium adulationis expavit Propheratum ille nobilissimus, qui dixit, Corripiet me justus in misericordia & increpabit me, oleum autem peccatorum non impinguet caput meum. Unde bene etiam & alia Scriptura dicit, Melius est autem objurgari à justo quàm a peccatore laudari: & iterum, Qui vos felices felices dicunt, iterrorem vos mittunt: quoniam adulatores ut inlicitant laudant, non ut ad æternam felicitatem provocent, quæ quidem felicitas nullo bono indiget.
units.tr: David, the most brilliant of the prophets, sings elegantly that mercy and truth met each other, and that righteousness and peace embraced one another. This is at last shown to be fulfilled, since after the incarnation of the Lord the two covenants were joined together into one structure. For although they appear in some way different from each other, they are known to come together into one in Christ, who is our peace, who made both one. In the New there is mercy, by which the human race is set free through grace; in the Old there is truth, where the proclamation of the Law and the Prophets is contained. These two are said to have met each other not to carry on opposition, but to fulfil the grace of the promised perfection. For it is clear that one thing was made which in earlier times was seen to be divided; and so that the hymnist David might plainly express the very nature of the covenant, he doubled this same thing by a varied repetition of names, namely, that by a certain embrace of love two things, that is, righteousness and peace, came straightway into mutual concord. It is agreed that this verse is spoken by somatopoeia, that is, the attribution of bodies, a mode of speech by which bodies are ascribed to incorporeal things, and by metaphor, that is, the transfer of things and words, by which very often things are transferred from animate to animate, from inanimate to inanimate, and from inanimate to animate. These two figures of speech differ from each other, in that the one ascribes bodies to incorporeal things, while the other ascribes both members and motions to corporeal things, and to incorporeal things members, motions and forms. Finally, John the presbyter rashly and flatteringly brought forward this verse in the presence of the venerable Pope Adrian and of Tarasius, Bishop of Constantinople. Yet this presbyter, although he was lower in honour than the bishops sitting in the same synod, is not read to have been lower in error. Although the bishops preceded him in the height of their rank, he was nonetheless surpassed by him in long-winded impudence. Nor could he, a man subject to the prelates, be overcome by the prelates in unbroken loquacity; he who, being subject to the prelates, was surpassed by them in pontifical dignities. He is believed to have committed a double offence in this matter: either because, with a superstitious intent to adore images, he tried to make the words full of mysteries, uttered by the Holy Spirit, fit human affairs; or because, blinded by the same perverse intent, he fell into the wretched vice of flattery. That most noble prophet dreaded this vice of flattery, who said, The righteous shall reprove me in mercy and rebuke me, but the oil of sinners shall not anoint my head. Hence another Scripture also rightly says, It is better to be rebuked by the righteous than to be praised by the sinner; and again, Those who call you happy, happy, they put terror into you; since flatterers praise in order to entice, not in order to summon to eternal happiness, which happiness needs no good thing.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quod non ad adorationem imaginum pertineat, ut illi dicunt, quod scriptum est, Exaltate Dominum Deum nostrum, & adorate scabellum pedum ejus, quoniam sanctus est.
units.tr: That it does not pertain to the worship of images, as they claim, what is written: Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at his footstool, for he is holy.

units.la: HOc Psalmistæ versiculo error qui ob adorandas imagines adeo in quorundam pectoribus inolevit, ut ad eum statuendum synodos faciant, & ad eum muniendum scripturarum sanctarum sibi testimonia usurpare contendant, tueri se posse credit: cum scabellum pedum Dominiado randum audit: hac casside apicem corporis munitam habere arbitratur, ne cornisci ensis inlimnes perfentiat: hac lorica cæterum corpus munitum habere se putat, ne pilorum ictibus suæ statuæ jacturam incurrat: hoc clypeo tutelam se nanctum esse credit, per quam spiculorum missilium olatus vulnificos non pertimescat: sed ita aut obcumbendo fatescet, aut delitescendo ausugiet his nauniminibus expoliatus, sicut his est incassum & inutiliter abusus, & tantum sentiet spiritu ad ii per sanctos viros inlati rigorem, ut nec tenuem quidem sibi credat inesse vigorem. Numquid quia scabellum pedum Domini adorari præcipitur à Propheta, ideo erit imaginum adoratio ... da? quæ est ergo similitudo scabelli pedum Domini & materialium imaginum: aut quæ commercia inenarrabilibus Dei operibus & imaginibus à quibuslibet conditis artificibus? aut quæ sociatam excellenti tamque præclaro mysterio & figuris insensatis humano patratis ingenio? aut ubi intum est ut imagines adorentur, sicut institutum ut scabellum pedum Domini adoretur? Nam David ait, Adorate imagines quorundam sanctorum: sicut ait, Adorate scabellum pedum Domini: sed Dominus ait, Opera manuum hominum sedes mea sunt, imagines autem scabellum pedum eorum. Cœlum mihi sedes est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum. Audi igitur dementissime vel potius error, audi inconparabilis dementia, audi ridiculosa segnities, audi beatum Ambrosium quid sit scabellum pedum Domini, aut quomodo adorandum sit. Ait enim, Adoraverunt Apostoli Dominum, quia detulerunt fidei testimonium, acceperunt fidei magisterium: adoraverunt & angeli de quibus scriptum est; Et adorent eum omnes angeli ejus. Adorant autem non solum divinitatem ejus, sed etiam scabellum pedum ejus quoniam sanctus est. & post pauca; Sed ne forte propositum aliquos præterfugere videatur ex- ... quia ratione ad incarnationis Dominicæ sacramentum spectare videatur, quod ait propheta; Et adorate scabellum pedum ejus, consideremus. Non enim ex usu hominum æstimare debemus scabellum: neque enim corporalis Deus aut non immensus, ut tamquam fulcrum pedibus ejus scabellum subjectum putemus: neque adorandum quicquam præter Deum legimus, quia scriptum est, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ipsi soli servies: quomodo ergo advirtus legem Prophetæ præcieperet, sub lege nutritus, & eruditus in lege? Non mediocris igitur quæstio: & ideo diligentius consideremus quod sit scabellum. Legimus enim alibi, Cœlum mihi thronus, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum: sed nec terra adoranda nobis, quia creatura est Dei. Videamus tamen an terram illam dicat adorandam Propheta, quam Dominus Jesus in carnis adsumptione suscepit. Itaque per scabellum terra intelligitur, per terram autem Christi, quam hodieque in mysteriis adoramus, & quam Apostoli in Domino Jesu, ut supra diximus, adorant. Neque enim divisus Christus, sed unus: neque cum adoretur tamquam Dei filius, natus ex virgine negabatur. Cum igitur incarnationis adorandum sit sacramentum, incarnatio autem opus Spiritus sancti sit, sicut scriptum est, Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi: & quod nascetur ex te sanctum vocabitur Filius Dei. Hoc etiam scabellum pedum Domini sanctus Augustinus diligentissimus exquisitor, corpus Domini,quod de Maria virgine sumpsit, scabellum divinitatis ejus asseruit sentiri debere, propter naturam humanitatis quam est dignatus adsumere: quod utique illi virtuti sicut subjectum atque unitum,ut constet idomnibus creaturis esse excelsius, sicut dicit Apostolus, Quod infirmum est Dei, fortius est hominibus. & alibi de eodem mediatore Dei & hominum homine Christo Jesu Apostolus dicit; Propter quod Deus exaltavit illum & donavit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, caelestium, terrestrium & infernorum. Per pedum igitur Domini magnificentiam in hoc versiculo stabilitas divinitatis, quae semper in naturae suae omnipotenti gloria, tamquam pedum indefessa firmitas perseverat, intelligitur. Possunt etiam tropologice pedes Domini extrematem-
units.tr: This verse of the Psalmist is the error which has taken such deep root in the minds of some people that they think they can defend it. They convene synods to establish it and strive to use the testimonies of Holy Scripture to fortify it, because they hear that the footstool of the Lord is to be worshipped. They think that by this helmet the top of their body is protected, so that the point of a sword cannot pierce it. They believe their body is further guarded by this breastplate, so that under the blows of javelins it will not suffer the loss of its statue. They think they have found protection in this shield, through which they need not fear the wounding whistle of missiles. But they will either grow weary by lying down or flee by hiding, stripped of these defences, since they have misused them in vain and to no purpose. They will feel only so much of the rigour brought against them by the holy men as to think that not even a slight strength remains in them. Does it follow, because the Prophet commands the footstool of the Lord to be worshipped, that the worship of images will be ... ? What, then, is the likeness between the footstool of the Lord and material images? Or what fellowship is there between the ineffable works of God and images made by any craftsmen? Or what connection is there with that excellent and so illustrious mystery, and with lifeless figures wrought by human ingenuity? Or where is it found that images are to be worshipped, as it is ordained that the footstool of the Lord is to be worshipped? For David says, Worship the images of certain saints, as he says, Worship the footstool of the Lord: but the Lord says, The works of men's hands are my seat, and their images are their footstool. Heaven is my seat, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. Hear then, most senseless, or rather error; hear, incomparable folly; hear, ridiculous sluggishness: hear what blessed Ambrose says the footstool of the Lord is, and how it is to be worshipped. For he says: The Apostles worshipped the Lord, because they brought the testimony of faith and received the teaching of faith; the angels also worshipped, of whom it is written: And let all his angels worship him. Moreover, they worship not only his divinity but also his footstool, because he is holy. And a little later: But lest perhaps we seem to flee the proposed matter, let us consider whether the words of the Prophet, And worship his footstool, seem to pertain to the sacrament of the Lord's incarnation. We ought not to judge the footstool by human custom; for God is not corporeal, nor is he so limited that we should think a footstool is placed under his feet as a support. Nor do we read that anything is to be worshipped besides God, since it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone. How then could the Prophet, nourished under the law and taught in the law, command against the law? This is therefore no small question, and so let us consider more carefully what the footstool is. For we read elsewhere: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet; but the earth is not to be worshipped by us, because it is a creature of God. Let us see, however, whether the Prophet means that earth which the Lord Jesus took up in the assumption of flesh. Thus the footstool is understood as the earth, and the earth of Christ is what we still worship today in the mysteries, and what the Apostles, as we said above, worship in the Lord Jesus. For Christ is not divided but one, and when he is worshipped as the Son of God, it is not denied that he was born of the virgin. Since therefore the sacrament of the incarnation is to be worshipped, and the incarnation is the work of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and that which is born of you will be called the Holy Son of God. Likewise the most diligent inquirer, holy Augustine, asserted that the body of the Lord, which he took from the virgin Mary, must be perceived as the footstool of his divinity, on account of the nature of humanity which he deigned to assume; which indeed is subject to and united with that power, so that it is clear that it is higher than all creatures, as the Apostle says: That which is weak in God is stronger than men. And elsewhere the Apostle says of the same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus: For this reason God exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of heavenly, earthly and infernal beings. Therefore through the greatness of the Lord's footstool in this verse is understood the stability of the divinity, which always remains in the glory of its own omnipotent nature, like the untiring firmness of the feet. The feet of the Lord can also be tropologically understood as designating the lowest parts, when the Lord deigned to be made flesh.

units.la: porum, quando Dominus incarnari dignatus est, designari. unde & Iohannes evangelista dicit; Filio- in novissima hora est. Paulus quoque Apostolus dicit; Cum venisset plenitudo temporum misit Deus filium suum natum ex muliere, factum sub lege. Notandum sane quia non dixit; Quoniam sanctum est, sed quae-
units.tr: Hence also the evangelist John says: My son, it is the last hour. The Apostle Paul also says: When the fullness of time had come, God sent his son, born of a woman, made under the law. It must certainly be noted that he did not say: Because it is holy, but because he is holy.

units.la: niam sanctus est: scilicet ut corpus Domini a divinitate non discernatur, salva utriusque naturae proprietate, sed ad unam personam referatur. Unde dicit Evangelium, Verbum caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis. Haec de scabello pedum Domini breviter promulgata sufficiant: nunc ad cetera transeamus.
units.tr: That is: so that the body of the Lord is not distinguished from the divinity, the properties of each nature being preserved, but is referred to one person. Hence the Gospel says: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. Let these things briefly set forth about the footstool of the Lord suffice: now let us pass on to the rest.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Quod nec de eo imaginum adoratio adstrui possit, ut illi putant, quod scriptum est, Adorate in monte sancto ejus.
units.tr: That the worship of images cannot be founded on the words, as they suppose, "Worship at his holy mountain."

units.la: Sed necin eo quoque imaginum adoratio adstrui potest, ut illi fatentur, quod per eundem sanctum Prophetam, Adorate in monte sancto ejus, cantatur: cum scilicet non montem, sed in monte sancto adorandum Dominum, idem sanctus vir harmonica modulatione decantet. Quasi montem adorandum praeciperet, non idcirco imaginum adoratio, sed Domini Jesu Christi mentibus intelligeretur, qui est mons cunctis montibus sublimior: cujus videlicet altitudo & virtus omnium sanctorum altitudinibus & virtutibus eminet: de quo per Esaiam prophetam dicitur, Et erit in novissimis diebus praeparatus mons domus Domini in vertice montium, & elevabitur super colles, & fluent ad eum omnes gentes, & ibunt populi multi. Dicatur ergo, Adorate in monte sancto ejus, quia videlicet non hic montem, sed in monte sancto Dominum, Propheta praecipit adorare, quod ad montem Sion quae est ecclesia, referri posse non dubium est, quae est mons montium, & sancta sanctorum: cujus habitator est Christus. Unde bene sanctum Dominum in sancto monte praecipit adorandum. Quoniam sicut laus ejus non convenit ori pravo, ita nec ejus culturae loci potest congruere turpitudo. Adoramus igitur in monte sancto ejus, non imagines vel quasdam simperstitiosas res, sed cunc-
units.tr: But neither can the worship of images be established from this either, as they admit, by the words the same holy prophet sings, "Worship at his holy mountain." For the same holy man, in harmonious measure, sings that the Lord is to be worshipped not on a mountain but in a holy mountain. As if he were commanding the worship of a mountain, the meaning would be not the worship of images but of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mountain above all mountains. His height and power surpass the heights and powers of all the saints, and of him the prophet Isaiah says, "And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it, and many people shall go." Therefore it is said, "Worship at his holy mountain," because the prophet bids us worship the Lord not on this mountain but in a holy mountain. There can be no doubt that this may be referred to Mount Zion, which is the Church, the mountain of mountains and the holy of holies, whose inhabitant is Christ. Hence he rightly commands that the holy Lord be worshipped in the holy mountain. For just as his praise does not befit a wicked mouth, so no baseness can suit the place of his worship. We therefore worship in his holy mountain, not images or certain superstitious things, but all...

units.la: Dominum, qui illius montis caput est, & ut eundem montem adquireret, non solum nasci, sed mori dignatus est. de quo per Propheten dicitur; Adduxit eos in montem sanctificationis suae, montum hunc quem adquisivit dextera ejus: & de quo per Legislatorem dicitur; Introduces & planta eos in monte haereditatis tuae in praeparata habitatione tua quam praeparasti tibi Domine: sanctuarium tuum Domine quod praeparaverunt manus tuae Domine, qui regnas in aeternum & in saeculum saeculi & adhuc.
units.tr: ...the Lord, who is the head of that mountain, and who deigned not only to be born but to die, in order to acquire the same mountain. Of this it is said through the prophet, "Thou hast brought them in and planted them in the mountain of thine inheritance, in the place which thou hast made for thy dwelling, the sanctuary, O Lord, which thy hands have established; the Lord shall reign for ever and ever." And of it the Lawgiver says, "Thou shalt bring them in, and plant them in the mountain of thine inheritance, in the place prepared for thy habitation, which thou, O Lord, hast prepared; the sanctuary, O Lord, which thy hands have established. The Lord reigneth for ever and ever, and to all eternity."

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: Chapter VII.

units.la: Quod non, ut illi gloriantur, propter illos dictum est qui imagines adorant, Quoniam non derelinquet Dominus virgam peccatorum super sortem justo- rum, ut non extendant justi ad iniquitatem manus suas.
units.tr: That it was not said, as they boast, with reference to those who worship images: "The Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity."

units.la: Non mirandum est, si fallantur in minimis, qui fallluntur in magnis: nec in eo amplius illorum error admirandus est, quod ideo se justos, quia imagines adorant, esse gloriantur, nos autem qui eas adorare contemnimus, peccatores fareantur: cum ob illarum amorem & scripturum divinarum puritatem violare conentur, & potissimum sua fidei emolumentum in hiscesse arbitrentur: & eos qui spretis his sive caeteris hujusmodi vanitatibus soli Deo serviunt, cumque colentes adorant, anathematizare obstinata mente nitantur. Quomodo ergo hujus verisimilitextus, non ad eandem rem pertineat, ob quam ab illis prolatus est, qualiterve eorum sensui reluctari credatur, quantisve ab eorum opinatione differt indiciis, non solum simplicibus lectoribus, sed etiam idiotis patet: quippe qui postpositis aenigmaticis sive allegoricis involucris aperte demonstret, quod non diu permittat Dominus flagellari justos ab impiis, ne in desperationis labem corruant diutinis addicti flagellis, sed si ad tempus ad probationem quibusdam eos adversis macerat, secundis eos denuo diuturnitate temporis interrupta sublevat, qualiter eorum innocentia inconvulsa permaneat.
units.tr: It is no wonder if those who are deceived in great matters are also deceived in small ones. Nor is their error to be marvelled at further in this, that they boast of being righteous because they worship images, while they declare us, who scorn to worship them, to be sinners. They strive to violate the purity of the divine Scriptures out of love for those images, and chiefly they think their faith gains advantage from them. With obstinate minds they struggle to anathematize those who, scorning these and other such vanities, serve God alone and worship him alone. How this text, which seems to be genuine, does not pertain to the same matter for which they brought it forward, how it is believed to resist their own sense, and how far it differs from their opinion by its indications, is clear not only to simple readers but also to the unlearned. For, setting aside enigmatic or allegorical wrappings, it plainly shows that the Lord does not allow the righteous to be scourged by the impious for long, lest they fall into the ruin of despair, being given over to prolonged scourges. Rather, if for a time he afflicts them with adversities to test them, he then raises them up again with prosperity after an interval of time, so that their innocence remains unshaken.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Quod non propter illos qui imaginum adorationem spernunt, ut illi delirant, per Prophetam dicatur, Declinantes ad obligationem adducet Dominus cum operantibus iniquitatem.
units.tr: That this is not said by the Prophet about those who reject the adoration of images, as those people rave: "The Lord will lead those who turn aside to the bond with the workers of iniquity."

units.la: Deo quoque hunc versiculum singillatim nobis in nostro opere ponere libuit, quia etsi est cum superiore in unius Psalmi textu, distat tamen ab eo in sensu & quamquam ad unum errorem adstruendum ab illis sit prolatus, diversoque tamen loco in saepe memoratae synodi lectione hunc constitute positum. Declinantes igitur ad obligationem non illi credendi sunt, qui imaginum superstitionem contemnunt adorationem, sed qui antiquo hostis retinaculis inretiti proni sunt ad iniquitatem, quantoque amplius peccare noscuntur, tanto nimirum strictius diabolicis spiritus nectuntur. Unde profecto per quendam sapientem dicitur, Funibus peccatorum suorum unusquisque constringitur: de qua etiam obligatione sanctus Propheta Esaias dicit, Vae qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis & quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum. Eos itaque qui ad hanc obligationem declinant, adducet dominus cum operantibus iniquitatem: quia videlicet cum quibus in hoc peccant saeculo, cum his damnabuntur in futuro: & ad eum ignem qui auctori criminum & angelis ejus praeparatus est, ibunt, cujus in hoc saeculo retinaculorum obligationem rumpere neglexerunt. A cujus obligatione ille nos liberos efficiat, qui nos in libertatem redemit, & nobis sedentibus in tenebris suae claritatis lucem magnam ostendit, live habitantibus in regione umbrae mortis ipse lux vera exortus est: atque idem ejus severissimae damnationis nos reddat expertes, qui suae clarissimae fidei spiritusque & charitatis fecit esse sequaces.
units.tr: I have also wished to set this verse out separately in our work, because although it is joined with the preceding verse in the text of one Psalm, it differs from it in sense. And although it has been brought forward by them to support one error, it has nonetheless been placed in this position in a different passage of the synod often mentioned. So those who turn aside to the bond are not to be understood as those who despise the superstition of image adoration, but as those who, caught in the old snares of the enemy, are prone to iniquity; and the more they are known to sin, the more tightly are they bound by the devil's spirits. Hence indeed a certain wise man says, "Each one is held fast by the cords of his own sins", and of this same bond the holy Prophet Isaiah says, "Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with the rope of a cart." The Lord will therefore lead those who turn aside to this bond along with the workers of iniquity: that is, they will be condemned in the future with those with whom they sin in this age, and they will go to that fire which has been prepared for the author of crimes and his angels, the bonds of which they neglected to break in this age. May he who redeemed us into liberty free us from this bond, he who, when we sat in the darkness of his brightness, showed us a great light, since the true Light has risen for us who dwelt in the land of the shadow of death; and may he who has made us followers of his most clear faith, Spirit and charity, keep us free of the most severe damnation.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Quod non ab eo quod Salomon dicitur in templo fecisse boves & leones, imaginum adoratio firmari posset, ut illi somniant, qui in earum adorationem anhelant.
units.tr: That the adoration of images cannot be confirmed from what is said of Solomon making oxen and lions in the temple, as those dream who pant after their worship.

units.la: Salomon in templo boves & leones legitur condidisse: quorum conditione nos qui secuti sumus Apostolum legem spiritalem esse scimus, quibusdam mysteriorum archanis instruimur: illi vero qui imaginum adorationem diligunt suae vecordiae vanitatem firmare moliuntur: nos sensibus perdocemur, illi in sui erroris magnitudine firmantur: nos admoniti per umbram veritatem, illi decepti per rem bene gestam ad rem non gerendam sumunt auctoritatem. Quid ergo eos Davidica proles, quod Israelitice rex, quod sapientium sapientissime fecisti? Feci, inquam, eos, non ut adorari deberent, sed ut quaedam mystica significarent: non ut errori favercnt, sed ut mysteriorum archana monstrarent: non ut offendiculum caecis mentibus esset, sed ut magnum quoddam subtilia subtiliter scrutantibus innuerent. Cui si ideo succensceri debet, quia per ea quae a bene gesta sunt, a pravis pravum exemplum sumitur, legislatori nihilominus succensendum est, quidem multorum vilibus necessariam, in cremo exaltavit, qua prava hominum voluntas postmodum utebatur. Non igitur nos effigies ob memoriam rerum gestarum & venustatem basilicarum quodammodo abdicamus, cum per Moysen & Salomonem, quamquam in typis figuris, eas factas fuisse sciamus, sed earum insolentissimam vel potius superstitiosissimam adorationem cohibemus, quam neque per Patriarchas, neque per Prophetas, neque per Apostolos, neque per Apostolicos viros usquam instituram esse repererimus. Sed ut ad propositam redeamus, Salomon templo boves & leones fecit, quia & Christus in ecclesia Apostolos eorumque successores ... sicut beati Gregorii sententiam, bene agentibus per humilitatem sunt socii contra delinquentium vitia, per zelum justitiae erecti, quatenus & istos manusuetudo bovis sustentet, & illos feritas leonis stimulet. quod utrumque patris ecclesiae exemplo colligi potest, qui & Cornelium humilitate utentem blandis allocutionibus delinivit, & contra Ananiam & Sapphiram fraudulenter agentes se vehementer erexit. Sanctitas aliquando manuetudinem boum, aliquando ferocitatem habent leonum: quia & virgam tenent qua fortes fortiter regant, & baculum quo infirmorum debilitates sustentent.
units.tr: It is read that Solomon made oxen and lions in the temple. We who have followed the Apostle, knowing that the law is spiritual, are instructed in certain secret mysteries by their making; but those who love the adoration of images labour to confirm the vanity of their own madness. We are taught by the senses, they are confirmed in the greatness of their error. We are warned by the shadow towards the truth, they, deceived by a deed well done, take up authority for a deed that should not be done. What then, you Davidic offspring, King of Israel, most wise of the wise, did you do with them? I made them, I say, not to be adored, but to signify certain mystical things; not to favour error, but to show the secrets of mysteries; not to be a stumbling block to blinded minds, but to hint at something great to those who subtly search out subtle things. If Solomon ought therefore to be blamed for this, because from things well done by good men bad men take a bad example, then the lawgiver likewise ought to be blamed, who lifted up in the wilderness the bronze serpent, necessary for the healing of the wounds of many, which the perverse will of men afterwards made use of. Therefore we do not in some way reject images for the memory of deeds done and the beauty of churches, since we know that through Moses and Solomon, although as types and figures, they were made; but we restrain their most insolent, or rather most superstitious, adoration, which we find was never instituted anywhere, neither by the Patriarchs, nor by the Prophets, nor by the Apostles, nor by apostolic men. But to return to the matter proposed: Solomon made oxen and lions in the temple, because Christ too in the Church [made] the Apostles and their successors ... as the saying of blessed Gregory goes: those who act well through humility are companions against the vices of offenders, raised up through zeal for justice, so that the gentleness of the ox sustains the one and the ferocity of the lion goads the other. Both of these can be gathered from the example of the Fathers of the Church, who both soothed Cornelius, who was using humility, with gentle addresses, and vehemently rose up against Ananias and Sapphira, who acted fraudulently. Holiness sometimes has the gentleness of oxen, sometimes the ferocity of lions: because they hold a rod, by which they rule the strong with strength, and a staff, by which they support the weaknesses of the infirm.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Quomodo intelligendum est, quod in Canticis Canticorum scribitur, Ostende mihi faciem tuam, & audiram fac mihi vocem tuam: quoniam vox tua suavis est mihi, & facies tua speciosa: quod quidem capitulum illi impudentissime ad imaginum visionem protulerunt.
units.tr: How is what is written in the Song of Songs to be understood: "Show me your face, and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet to me, and your face is comely"? This passage they most shamelessly brought forward in support of the vision of images.

units.la: Faciens ecclesiae quam Christus blandis nominum varietatibus alloquitur, modo eam columbam, modo formosam, modo amicam vocans: quam surgere, id est, credere, properare, in operibus bonis excrescere, venire, ad aeternam remunerationem accedere jubet, non corporalis, sed spiritalis
units.tr: Speaking of the church, whom Christ addresses with varied tender names, now calling her dove, now fair one, now friend, he bids her rise, that is, believe, hasten, grow in good works, come, and draw near to eternal reward. This is spiritual, not bodily.

units.la: Psal. 125. Prov. 5. Esai. 5. Cant. 2. spiritalis est: quia & cætera quæ de ea in iisdem Canticis Canticorum scribuntur, non carnaliter, sed spiritaliter intelligenda sunt. Nam si hic versiculus cuidam corporaliter adcommodari potest, similiter quoque ... Christi ecclesiæ membris scribuntur, corporalia credenda sunt: & si haec omnia non membris visibilibus, sed virtutibus conveniunt invisibilibus: ergo & facies ejus, virtus potius invisibilis quàm cujusdam corporis intelligi visus imaginis. Facies itaque ecclesiæ cognitio virtutum ejus est, cujus pulchritudo venustate ab sponso diligitur: cui bene per Prophetam dicitur, Quoniam concupivit rex speciem tuam.
units.tr: Psal. 125. Prov. 5. Esai. 5. Cant. 2. It is spiritual, because the other things written of her in the same Song of Songs must also be understood not carnally but spiritually. For if this little verse can be applied bodily to someone, then likewise, if the things written of the members of Christ's church are to be believed bodily, and if all these things belong not to visible members but to invisible virtues, then his face too must be understood as invisible virtue rather than the sight of some bodily image. The face of the church, therefore, is the knowledge of her virtues, whose beauty is loved by the bridegroom for its loveliness. To her it is well said through the Prophet: For the king has desired your beauty.

units.la: Hortatur ergo Christus ecclesiam, ut faciem suam ei ostendat, id est, ut semper cum contemplentur de & operibus, ut cum Elia dicere possit, Vivit Dominus in cujus conspectu sto: ne fit de illis quos per Prophetam denotar dicens, Verterunt terga ad me & non faciem. Hortatur etiam ut vox ejus sonet in ausibus illius, quia paratus est ad exaudiendum sanctos suos Psalmista adtestante quiait, Clamaverunt justi & Dominus exaudivit eos, & ex omnibus tribulationibus eorum liberavit eos. Vocem ejus dulcem & faciem dicit esse decoram, quia orationes sanctorum semper Deo acceptæ sunt, eorumque grata præsentia qui de Christi lumine acceperunt, ut in decore justitiæ permanerent. Esto, convenit ut ad similitudinem visionem aptari possit hic versiculus, Ostende mihi faciem tuam, sive facies tua speciosa, quid de voce dici poterit, quam & suavem Propheta decantat, & auditam sibi fieri hortatur: Quæ utique [...] non vegetantur, multo minus vocem fruuntur: & si voce non fruuntur, multo minus vocis suavitate potiuntur: si igitur anima non vegetantur, nec vocis dulcedine potiuntur.
units.tr: Christ therefore urges the church to show him her face, that is, to contemplate him always in his works, so that she may say with Elijah: As the Lord lives, before whom I stand. Let her not be among those whom the Prophet denotes, saying: They have turned their back to me and not their face. He also urges that his voice sound in her ears, since he is ready to hear his saints, as the Psalmist bears witness, who says: The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their troubles. He calls his voice sweet and his face comely, because the prayers of the saints are always acceptable to God, and the pleasing presence of those who have received the light of Christ, so that they remain in the comeliness of righteousness. Granted that this verse, Show me your face, or your face is comely, can be fitted to a vision in the manner of a likeness, what can be said of the voice, which the Prophet too praises as sweet and urges to be heard by him? Those who [...] are not enlivened, much less do they enjoy the voice; and if they do not enjoy the voice, much less do they possess its sweetness. So if souls are not quickened, they do not possess the sweetness of the voice.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Quomodo intellegendum est quod per Esaiam Prophetam scribitur, Erit altare Domini in medio terræ Ægypti: quod capitulum illi stolidè & minus dicte admi- rationem adorationem referre nituntur.
units.tr: How the passage written by the Prophet Isaiah should be understood, "There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt"; a chapter which they strive, foolishly and without due consideration, to refer to wonder and adoration.

units.la: HANC prophetiam Iosephus in Onia sacerdote qui profugus in Ægyptum plurimis Iudæorum vallatus catervis descendit, altaréque ibi & templum construxit, impleriam fuisse narratur: verò qui ea quæ de Christi adventu & vocatione gentium prophetata sunt, non ut fuerunt, ut præ oculis devota mente tenemus, & credimus, non hanc prophetiam completam fuisse sententiam per Oniam sacerdotem, sed per Christum Dominum, Dei & hominum mediatorem. Qui videlicet fidem in hoc mundo, qui plerumque Ægypti nomine designatur, constituit, in cujus iniquitate à fidelibus orationum sacrificia & sanctorum meritorum libamina Domino liantur: cujus terminum titulum potest, id est, evangelium sive Apostolicam doctrinam, quibus in entes hujus ad peragenda bona opera informari. Quod verò subjungit; Erit in signum & in testimonium Domino exercituum in terra Ægypti, signum ... estimonium Dominicæ voluit passionis mysterium intellegi. Tunc hi qui crediderint contra Ægyptios, contra Ægyptios, & pugnante viro contra suum, & civitate contra civitatem dimicante, cum persecutionis scilicet tempus ingruerit, implorabunt misericordiam, salvator adveniet, id est, Iesus. (hoc enim in lingua nostra sonat) & cognoscent Dominum ab Ægyptiis, & cognoscent eum sive perseguentes qui fuerunt superati, sive credentes sancti auxilio liberati.
units.tr: This prophecy is said to have been fulfilled by Onias the priest, who fled into Egypt, went down there surrounded by a host of Jews, and built an altar and a temple there, as Josephus relates.
