But we hold, as we keep before our eyes with a devout mind and believe, that the prophecies about the coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles were not fulfilled as they were spoken; and that this prophecy was fulfilled not by Onias the priest but by Christ the Lord, the mediator between God and men. He, indeed, establishes faith in this world, which is usually designated by the name of Egypt, and in whose midst the sacrifices of prayers and the offerings of holy merits are offered to the Lord by the faithful. His title is the gospel, that is, the evangelical or apostolic teaching, by which the inhabitants of this world are instructed to perform good works. As for what he adds, "It shall be for a sign and for a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt," he meant the sign and testimony to be understood as the mystery of the Lord's passion. Then those who have believed, when the time of persecution comes upon them, will cry out for mercy, as Egyptians fight against Egyptians, a man against his neighbour, and city against city; a Saviour will come, that is, Jesus (for this in our language means "Saviour"). And they will know the Lord, the Egyptians will know him, both the persecutors who were overcome and the faithful saints who were freed by his help.

units.la: Cant. 2. Esa. 19.
units.tr: Cant. 2. Esa. 19.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Absurdissime & incaute contra eos qui imagines adorare contemnunt, ab his qui eas adorant, prolatum testimonium sancti Evangelii, Nemo accendit lucernam & ponit eam sub modio.
units.tr: Absurdly and carelessly, by those who worship images, a testimony of the holy Gospel is brought against those who scorn the worship of images: "No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel."

units.la: {*}ONes inconsequens & risu digna, quòd quædam nescio quo sensu in ejusdem vanitatis lectione de nobis qui imaginum adorationem spernimus, scribuntur, ex his quæ dominus discipulos ad prædicandum mittens, instituit ut magnam haberent fiduciam prædicandi, & ne persequentium terrore exerciti delitescerent & similes essent lucernæ sub modio, sed omni metu postposito totis libertatis insignibus se proderent, & quod audierant in cubiculis in tectis prædicarent. Illi ergo lucernam suam, id est, imaginum culturam adorando in suæ fidei fastigio ponant: nos vero si quis nobis scientiæ splendor est, in Christo, qui est lucis origo conlocemus: quatenus nobiscum in sanctæ ecclesiæ domo manentibus, & verbi & exempli splendorem exhibere valeamus.
units.tr: It is an inconsequent thing, and worthy of laughter, that certain things are written in that same vanity-filled reading, in some sense I know not what, about us who despise the worship of images, drawing on those words by which the Lord, sending his disciples to preach, instructed them to have great confidence in preaching, and not, troubled by the terror of persecutors, to hide themselves and be like a lamp under a bushel, but, with all fear laid aside, to reveal themselves with the full badges of liberty, and to preach in the house-tops what they had heard in the chambers. Let them, then, set their lamp, that is, the cult of images, by worshipping it, on the summit of their faith; but as for us, if there is any brightness of knowledge in us, let us place it in Christ, who is the source of light, so that, remaining with us in the house of the holy Church, we may be able to show forth the brightness both of word and of example.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Deo quod ad summ errorem confirmandum dicunt beatum Silvestrem Romanæ urbis antistitem Apostolorum imagines Constantino Imperatori detulisse, cum tamen eas non legatur adorare jussisse.
units.tr: That the blessed Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, brought images of the Apostles to Emperor Constantine, which they cite to confirm their greatest error, although it is not read that he ordered them to be adored.

units.la: SÆPE in hoc nostro speciali de imaginibus opere fateri cogimur, quod illæ non haberi sed adorari a nobis inhibeantur: nec illarum in ornamentis basilicarum & memoria rerum gestarum constituturarum fugienda sit visio, sed insolentissima vel potius superstitiosissima execranda sit adoratio. Unde sicut in cæteris ita & in hoc exemplo adsertio frustrabitur, qui suum errorem in adoratione imaginum enitentem in eo fulcire conentur, quòd Silvester Romanæ ecclesiæ præsul Constantino Imperatori, Apostolorum imagines detulisse legitur. Detulit ergo eas illi ad videndum, non ad adorandum: detulit non ut adorare, quem à simulacrorum cultu abstrahere & ad solius dei adorationem convolare hortabatur, compelleret: sed ut idem Imperator quos in somnis viderat, eorum vultus in pictura fucis cognosceret. Detulit, non ut ab idolorum cultura fugientem imaginum adorationi cederet informaret, & ab hostili gladio liberatum intestini ensis rigore perimeret, sed ut per res notas ad res ignotas ejus mentem extolleret: ut quos non poterat mentis oculo cernere, nec dum spiritalitatis maculis exutus, spiritalibus miraculis cerneret, nimirum eorum imagines corporalibus conditas instrumentis. Has igitur ei & si adorare jussisset, cum tamen non jusserit, ideo fortasis jubet, ut eum qui visibilium cultor erat, per visibilia ad invisibilia provocaret, non ut nos de invisibilibus ad visibilia revocaret: nec ideo nobis qui ad percipiendum solidum cibum vires accepimus, ad lacteam escam lactentium more infantium redeundum esset: si illi cum necdum per fidei teneritudinem solidus cibus inpertiri poterat, sine dolo lac concupiscendum darerur in quo crescceret. Unde & Apostolus novellæ ecclesiæ ex circumcisione & gentilitate venienti, spiritalis lactis & olerum cibum dabat, id est, faciliora ad intellegendum documenta, & leviora ad explendum præcepta, quibus carnalis mentes quasi in quadam infantiæ teneritudine enutritæ ad percipiendum spiritalium archanorum capaces efficerentur. Libro igitur actuum beati Silvestri, ubi de imaginibus Constantino Imperatori delatis scribitur, ideo obniti poterat, quia quamquam à pluribus catholicis legatur, non tamen ad quæstionem veniunt adfirmanda plene idoneus perhibetur: quod in libro beati Gelasii Romanæ urbis antistitis qui inscribitur, Decretalis de recipiendis sive de non recipiendis codicibus, apertius demonstratur.
units.tr: Often in this our special work on images we are obliged to confess that they are not forbidden to be kept, but are forbidden to be adored by us. The sight of them is not to be shunned in the decoration of churches and in the commemoration of deeds done, but the most insolent, or rather most superstitious, adoration is to be condemned. Hence, as in other cases, so also in this example, the assertion will fail those who try to prop up their error of adoring images by the claim that Silvester, bishop of the Roman Church, is read to have brought images of the Apostles to Emperor Constantine. He brought them, therefore, for the Emperor to see, not to adore. He did not bring them to compel a man whom he was urging to turn away from the worship of idols and hasten to the adoration of the one God alone to adore images. He brought them so that the same Emperor could recognise, in the painted colours, the faces of those he had seen in dreams. He did not bring them to instruct a man fleeing the worship of idols to yield to the adoration of images, and so to be destroyed by the stiff blade of an inner sword after being freed from the hostile sword. He brought them so that through known things he might raise the Emperor's mind to unknown things, so that he might see with spiritual wonders those whom he could not discern with the eye of the mind, since he was not yet stripped of the stains of the flesh. Those were their images, made from bodily materials. If Silvester had ordered him to adore these, though he did not order it, perhaps he would order it so that one who was a worshipper of visible things might be led through visible things to invisible things, and not so that we might be called back from invisible things to visible things. Nor, on that account, should we who have received strength to take solid food return to milk, like infants. If, when solid food could not yet be given to him because his faith was still tender, milk was rightly to be desired in which he might grow, that does not mean we must go back to it. The Apostle also gave the young church, coming from circumcision and from the Gentiles, the food of spiritual milk and of herbs, that is, teachings easier to understand and precepts lighter to fulfil, by which carnal minds, nourished as if in the tenderness of infancy, might be made capable of receiving the spiritual mysteries. So, in the Acts of the blessed Silvester, where it is written that images were brought to Emperor Constantine, one could object, since although many Catholics read it, it does not come to the point of affirming that it is fully reliable. This is shown more plainly in the Decretal of the blessed Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, which is entitled On the receiving or not receiving of books.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Quod non ita intellegenda sit sententia beati Athanasii Alexandrinæ urbis episcopi, ut illi eam intellegendam putant, qui hanc ad adorationem imaginum adcommodare nituntur.
units.tr: That the saying of blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, is not to be understood as those understand it who strive to apply it to the adoration of images.

units.la: SENTENTIA nempe beati Athanasii Alexandrinæ urbis Episcopi, quam illi inconsequenter, sicut & cætera divinarum scripturarum testimonia, ad suum errorem adstruendum protulerunt, prorsus huic rei extranea esse deprehenditur: cum non in ea quædam cujuslibet imaginum adorationis vel tenuiter mentio fiat, sed ad comparationem rei de qua sermo fiebat fassus sit imagines in eadem materia atque elemento recuperari posse, dicens: Sicut ea quæ scribitur in lignis forma abolita exterioribus sordibus, iterum necesse est in idipsum recuperari atque uniri his cujus est forma, ut innovari possit imago, in eadem materia atque elemento. Per ejus enim formam & ipsa materia ubi & conscribitur, non deperit, sed in ipsa configuratur. Dicant ergo quod eis adminiculum hæc sententia præbeat: dicant ubi imagines adorare percenseat: & cum hoc adseverare nequiverint, restat ut ita à sanis mentibus intellegatur sicut à venerabili viro prolata est.
units.tr: The saying of blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, which they have brought forward without good reason, as they did the other testimonies of the divine Scriptures, to support their error, is plainly found to be foreign to this matter. For no mention at all, not even a slight one, is made in it of the adoration of any images. Rather, comparing it with the thing under discussion, he states that images can be recovered in the same matter and element, saying: Just as that which is written on wood, its form destroyed by outward filth, must again be recovered and united to that of which it is the form, so that the image may be renewed in the same matter and element. For through its form the matter itself, where it is written, does not perish but is shaped within it. Let them therefore say what support this saying gives them; let them say where it counts the adoration of images. And when they cannot assert this, it remains that it be understood by sound minds just as it was uttered by that venerable man.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Quòd male ad suum errorem adstruendum sententiam beati Ambrosii Mediolanensis urbis episcopi quam ex libro tertio capitulo nono esse mentiuntur, usurpent, qui per eam imaginum adorationem firmare cupiunt.
units.tr: That those who wish to confirm image-worship misuse the opinion of blessed Ambrose, bishop of the city of Milan, which they falsely claim to be from the third book, ninth chapter, in order to establish their error.

units.la: FAcillime namque sanctorum praedicatorum sententias criminari audebunt, qui divinae legis & prophetarum oracula criminari non metuunt, nec formidabunt, ob sui erroris materiam stabiliendam, iuniorum documentis quandam inferre violentiam, qui seniorum doctrinis immo seniotibus non formidant inferre injuriam. Beati igitur Ambrosii Mediolanensis ecclesiae sacerdotis sententiam ut illorum errori faveret, ordine, sensu verbisque turbasse perhibentur. Ordine scilicet, quia non in libro tertio capitulo nono, ut illi somniant, sed in libro nono exarata reperitur: Sensu, quia cum ille dixerit, Nunquid cum & divinitatem ejus adoramus & carnem, Christum dividimus? Illi dixerunt, Nunquid nec cum & deitatem & carnem ejus adoramus dividimus Christum? Quae quidem particula subjunctivae coniunctionis, ne, tantam huic sententiae permutati sensus ingerit iacturam, ut eam profsus confiteri compellat quod illa negare contendit. Verbis, quod in sequenti commate, ubi ille posuit, veneramur, illi, adoramus, posuisse deteguntur: & ut apertius nostrae disputationis sensus pateat, qualiter haec sententia ab inlustri viro & eloquentiae coturnis cum spiritali sensu compto prolata, qualiterve ab illis falsata sit singillatim ponamus. Ille enim ut in duarum naturarum proprietatibus unam domini veriqueque hominis personam adseveraret, ait, Nunquid cum & divinitatem ejus adoramus & carnem, Christum dividimus? Nunquid cum in eo imaginem dei crucemque veneramur dividimus eum? Isti vero ex hac sententia imaginum adorationem adstruere nitentes dixerunt, Nunquid ne quando deitatem & carnem ejus adoramus, dividimus Christum? aut quando in ipso & dei imaginem & crucem adoramus dividimus eum? per imaginem scilicet dei quae Christus est, & per crucem ejus, quae in hoc loco propter mortalitatem carnis ejus posita est, imaginum introducere cupientes obstinata mente adorationem.
units.tr: It will be very easy for those men to slander the sayings of holy preachers, who do not fear to slander the oracles of the divine law and the prophets, and who, in order to establish the foundation of their error, do not hesitate to do violence to the teachings of the holy fathers by introducing the documents of younger men, and who do not hesitate to do injury to their elders' doctrines, or rather to their elders themselves. They are said to have so twisted the saying of blessed Ambrose, bishop of the church of Milan, as to favour their error, in its order, its sense and its words. In its order, because it is not found in book three, chapter nine, as they dream, but is written in book nine. In its sense, because he said, Do we not divide Christ when we adore both his divinity and his flesh? whereas they said, Do we not divide Christ when we adore neither his divinity nor his flesh? This little particle of the subjunctive conjunction, ne, so changes the meaning of the sentence that it compels us to confess altogether what it strives to deny. In its words, it is revealed that in the following clause, where he wrote we venerate, they wrote we adore. So that the sense of our argument may appear more plainly, let us set out one by one how this saying was uttered by that distinguished man, who was a master of eloquence, with its spiritual sense adorned, and how it was falsified by them. For he, in order to assert that there is one person of the Lord and of true man in the properties of the two natures, says, Do we not divide Christ when we adore both his divinity and his flesh? Do we not divide him when in him we venerate the image of God and the cross? But those men, striving to establish the worship of images from this saying, said, Do we not ever divide Christ when we adore his divinity and his flesh? Or do we divide him when in him we adore the image of God and the cross? Meaning by the image of God, which is Christ, and by his cross, which is placed in this passage on account of the mortality of his flesh, they wished with obstinate mind to introduce the adoration of images.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Quòd non pro materialibus imaginibus, ut illi aiunt, beatus Augustinus dixerit, Quid est imago Dei nisi vultus Dei in quo signatus est populus Dei?
units.tr: That blessed Augustine did not say, as they claim with respect to material images, "What is the image of God but the face of God in which the people of God is signed?"

units.la: DEum nemo vidit unquam, ait Iohannes Apostolus, nisi unigenitus filius, qui est in sinu patris: & Moysi eadem summa maiestas, dixit; Non enim videbit me homo & vivere poterit: qui si invisibilis est, immo quia invisibilis est, necesse est ut incorporeus sit: & si incorporeus est, necesse est ut corporaliter pingi non possit: igitur si invisibilis est, & incorporeus prorsus corporalibus materiis pingi non poterit. Unde solicitius nobis quaerendum est, quid sit imago dei: quidve vultus eius, in quo signatus est populus dei. Interrogemus ergo egregium praedicatorem, forsitan ab eo docti nosse valehimus quid sit imago dei. Dic vas electionis, dic doctor gentium quid sit imago dei. Gratias, inquam, agentes deo patri, qui dignos fecit nos in partem sortis sanctorum in lumine, qui eripuit nos de potestate tenebrarum, & transtulit in regnum filii dilectionis suae, in quo habemus redemptionem in remissionem peccatorum, qui est imago dei invisibilis. Dixi de imagine, dico etiam de figura. Novissimis diebus istis loquutus est nobis deus in filio quem constituit heredem universorum, per quem fecit & saecula, qui est splendor gloriae & figura substantiae ejus, portansque omnia verbo veritatis suae. Ecce, Paulo Apostolo docente, didicimus Christum esse imaginem dei: & illi hortantur materiales imagines hanc intelligere debere. Iste dicit eundem filium qui est unius cum patre substantiae imaginem esse dei & splendorem gloriae & figuram substantiae ejus: & illi dicunt opificum industria praeparatas figuras imaginem esse dei. O execrabilis error, o impudens dementia, o inprovida vecordia, tanto imaginum amore exaestuans ut ea quae de unigenito Dei filio dicta sunt, materialibus figuris conferte non erubescas.
units.tr: No one has ever seen God, says the Apostle John, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; and to Moses the same supreme majesty said, For no man shall see me and live. If he is invisible, or rather because he is invisible, it is necessary that he be incorporeal; and if he is incorporeal, it is necessary that he cannot be painted corporeally. Therefore, if he is invisible and wholly incorporeal, he cannot be depicted in corporeal materials. Hence we must inquire more carefully what the image of God is, or what the face of God is, in which the people of God is signed. Let us therefore question the distinguished preacher; perhaps, taught by him, we may come to know what the image of God is. Tell me, chosen vessel, tell me, teacher of the Gentiles, what the image of God is. Giving thanks, I say, to God the Father, who has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption and forgiveness of sins; who is the invisible image of God. I have spoken of the image; I now speak also of the figure. In these last days God has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the worlds; who is the brightness of his glory and the express image of his substance, and upholds all things by the word of his power. Behold, with the Apostle Paul teaching, we have learned that Christ is the image of God; and they urge that material images are to be understood in this sense. The one says that the same Son, who is of one substance with the Father, is the image of God and the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance; and they say that figures prepared by the skill of craftsmen are the image of God. O execrable error, O shameless madness, O heedless folly, burning with such love of images that you are not ashamed to compare with material shapes the things that have been said of the only-begotten Son of God!

units.la: Dicat etiam sanctissimus Augustinus, quid sit imago dei, qui ab illis hanc materialem exsistere dixisse criminatur. Ait enim, In deo conditio temporis vacat. non enim potest recte videri deus in tempore generasse filium per quem condidit tempora: consequens autem est ut non solum imago ejus sit, quia de illo est, & similitudo, quia imago est, sed etiam aequalitas tanta ut nec temporis intervallum impedimento sit. Dicitaque etiam tu sanctissime Ambrosii, quid de hac imagine sentire te constet. defende beatum Augustinum per te favente deo ad fidei rudimenta conversum, quem vides nunc ab imaginum adoratoribus infauste criminatum. Praebe ei adminiculum, ut exuatur tanti criminis mole, qui quondam per te exutus est haeresici dogmatis errore. Prophetae, inquam, dicunt Christum qui est imago patris invisibilis & figura substantiae ejus, quod ipse sit splendor lucis aeternae, & speculum sine macula dei majestatis, & imago bonitatis illius. Hoc ergo modo cum prophetis & apostolis Augustino meo, immo deo cultori tutelam conferre curabo. Vide quanta dicantur: splendor, & claritas paternae lucis in filio sit: Speculum sine macula, & pater in filio: imago bonitatis, & non corpus in corpore, sed virtus in filio tota cernatur. Imago docet non esse dissimilem, characterem expicitum. expressum esse significat, splendor signat aeternum. Imago itaque non vultus est corporalis, non sucis conpostia, non ceris, sed simplex de deo, egressa de patre, expressa de fonte: per hanc imaginem Philippo patrem dominus monstravit, dicens, Philippe, qui me videt, videt & patrem: & quomodo tu dicis ostende nobis patrem? Non credis quia ego in patre, & pater in me est. Vult enim in imagine patrem qui vidit in filio. Vide quam imaginem dicat: imago veritas est, imago ista justitia est, imago ista dei virtus est: non muta, quia verbum est: non insensibilis, quia sapientia est: non inanis, quia virtus est: non vacua, quia vita est: non mortua, quia resurrectio est. Vides ergo quia dum imago dicitur, patrem significat esse, cujus imago sit filius, quia nemo potest ipse sibi imago sua esse. Quoniam igitur imaginem dei non materiales imagines, ut illi garriunt, sed dei filium sanctorum patrum sententiis adprobavimus, restat ut qualiter in eo signati simus breviter explicemus. Signati itaque sumus in eo, quando secundum Apostolum in morte ejus baptizati sacrosancti unguinis liquore delibuti sumus, & accepimus Christiani nominis praerogativam, juxta illud quod ei in canticis canticorum dicitur, Oleum effusum est nomen tuum: impleturque divinum per Esaiam prophetam quondam promulgatum oraculum, quo ait, Servientibus vero mihi vocabitur nomen novum. Signamur ergo in eo qui secundum Apostolum signavit nos, & dedit pignus spiritus in cordibus nostris, in quo etiam spiritus pignore signati sumus in die redemptionis: signati autem sumus spiritu dei sancto, ut & spiritus noster & anima inprimantur signaculo dei, & illam recipiamus imaginem ad quam in exordio conditi sumus, quam peccando nec in totum amisimus, nec in totum in nobis intemerata remansit: quia si hanc in totum amisissemus, nequaquam diceretur, Quamquam in imagine ambulet homo, tamen vane conturbatur: & si hanc in totum intemeratam conservassemus, nequaquam Apostolus diceret, Reformamini in novitate mentis vestrae: & illud, In eandem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem.
units.tr: Let the most holy Augustine himself also say what the image of God is, he who is accused by them of having said that it is material. For he says: In God the condition of time is empty. For it cannot rightly be thought that God begot in time the Son through whom he made time; and it follows that he is not only his image, because he is from him, and his likeness, because he is the image, but also such equality that not even an interval of time can be a hindrance. Tell us then, most holy Ambrose, what you yourself are known to think of this image. Defend the blessed Augustine, who, by your favour and God's, was converted to the rudiments of the faith, and whom you now see unhappily accused by the worshippers of images. Give him help, that he may be freed from the weight of so great a charge, he who was once freed by you from the error of heretical doctrine. The prophets, I say, declare that Christ, who is the image of the invisible Father and the figure of his substance, is the splendour of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of his goodness. Thus, with the prophets and apostles, I will take care to bring protection to my Augustine, or rather to the worshipper of God. See how great the things said are: the splendour and brightness of the Father's light is in the Son; the spotless mirror shows the Father in the Son; the image of goodness, and not body in body, but the whole power is seen in the Son. The word image teaches that it is not unlike; the word character signifies that it is expressed and impressed; splendour denotes the eternal. An image, therefore, is not a bodily face, not a thing composed of juices or wax, but a simple thing from God, issuing from the Father, expressed from the fountain. Through this image the Lord showed the Father to Philip, saying: Philip, he who sees me sees the Father also; and how do you say, Show us the Father? Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? For in the image he wills that the Father be seen who is seen in the Son. See what kind of image he means: the image is truth, this image is righteousness, this image is the power of God; not mute, because it is the Word; not insensible, because it is wisdom; not empty, because it is power; not lifeless, because it is life; not dead, because it is resurrection. You see, then, that while it is called an image, it signifies that the Father is, whose image the Son is, since no one can be his own image. Since, therefore, we have established by the sentences of the holy Fathers that the image of God is not material images, as those babblers say, but the Son of God, it remains that we briefly explain how we are signed in him. We are signed in him when, according to the Apostle, we are baptized into his death and anointed with the liquid of the holy chrism, and receive the privilege of the Christian name, according to what is said of him in the Song of Songs: Your name is oil poured out. And the oracle once proclaimed by the prophet Isaiah is fulfilled, where he says: But to those who serve me the name shall be called new. We are signed, therefore, in him who, according to the Apostle, signed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts, and in whom we are also sealed with the pledge of the Spirit unto the day of redemption; and we are sealed by the Holy Spirit of God, so that both our spirit and soul may be stamped with the seal of God, and receive that image to which we were made at the beginning, which by sinning we did not wholly lose, nor did it remain wholly unharmed in us. For if we had wholly lost it, it would never be said: Although man walks in the image, yet he is vainly disturbed; and if we had kept it wholly unharmed, the Apostle would never say: Be renewed in the newness of your mind; and that other: We are transformed into the same image from glory to glory.

units.la: C- AP. XVII.
units.tr: Chapter XVII.

units.la: Quod Gregorii Nysseni episcopi, ex quo illi ad suum errorem adstruendum testimonia trahunt, & vita nobis & praedicatio sit incognita.
units.tr: That the life and preaching of Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, from whose writings they draw testimonies to support their error, are unknown to us.

units.la: Quid in hac parte nobis observandum sit, Apostoli * Pauli monitis perdocemur, qui ait, Probate spiritus an ex deo sint: & iterum, Noli credere omni spiritui, sed proba mentem: nam dum, ut praefati sumus, Gregorii Nysseni Episcopi & vita nobis & praedicatio sit ignota, testimonia quae de eius opusculis proferuntur ad res dubias confirmandas, minus cernuntur esse idonea: unde ejus doctrina nec a nobis est insigni laude praeferenda nec admodum reprehendenda, sed illius dogmate cum caeterorum dogmatibus quos ignoramus postposito, restat ut post propheticas & evangelicas sive Apostolicas scripturas inlustrium etiam Latinorum doctorum, quorum nobis & vita & praedicatio innotuit, sive Graecorum qui & catholici fuerunt, & a catholicis aeque in nostram linguam translati sunt, tantum in dogmatibus contenti simus.
units.tr: What we ought to observe in this matter we are taught by the admonitions of the Apostle Paul, who says: Test the spirits whether they are of God; and again: Do not believe every spirit, but test the mind. For since, as we have said above, both the life and the preaching of Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, are unknown to us, the testimonies which are brought forward from his little works to confirm doubtful matters are seen to be of little fitness. Hence his teaching is neither to be placed before us with great praise nor to be greatly censured; rather, with his doctrine set aside along with the doctrines of others whom we do not know, it remains that we should be content in matters of doctrine only with the prophetic and evangelical or apostolic Scriptures, and with the illustrious Latin teachers whose life and preaching are known to us, and with the Greeks who were also catholic and have likewise been translated into our language by catholic writers.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Quod non ad adorationem imaginum pertineat testimonium, quod de sexta synodo protulerunt.
units.tr: That the testimony which they cite from the sixth synod does not pertain to the adoration of images.

units.la: Textus sane testimonii quod de sexta synodo in eadem nugarum adglomeratione, quae pro adorandis imaginibus scripta est, taxasse perhibentur, talis est: In quibusdam venerabilium imaginum picturae agnus digito praecursoris monstratus designatur, quod in signum relictus est gratiae, verum nobis per legem praemonstrati agnum, Christum dominum nostrum. Qui tamen quamquam non ita ab illis prolatus sit, sicut in eadem synodo habetur, nec sic quidem, ut ab illis usurpatus est, cujusdam imaginum adorationis quandam fecisse dinoscitur mentionem: sed cum pene nullum habeat Latinae integritatis vigorem, sensuque sit tepidus, verbisque inlepidus, & quadam ex parte ratione nudatus, nullum tamen eorum errori adminiculum praebere monstratur.
units.tr: The text, indeed, of the testimony which they are said to have cited from the sixth synod, in the same heap of trifles written in favour of adoring images, is as follows: In some pictures of the venerable images the Lamb is designated, shown by the finger of the forerunner, which is left as a sign of grace, but for us the Lamb was foreshadowed through the law, Christ our Lord. Yet although it is not cited by them as it stands in the same synod, nor even as they have used it, it is clear that it makes no mention of any adoration of images; but since it has almost no vigour of Latin correctness, is weak in sense, clumsy in words, and in some respects bare of reason, it is nevertheless shown to offer no support whatever to their error.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Quod sententia Johannis Constantinopolitani Episcopi, quam illi in testimonium adoranda- rum imaginum trahunt, non ad id quod illi putant, pertinere dinoscitur.
units.tr: That the opinion of John, Bishop of Constantinople, which they bring forward as testimony for the veneration of images, is shown not to bear on what they suppose.

units.la: Sed neque sententia Johannis Constantinopolitani Episcopi, quamquam ab illis mutilata sit, sicut & caeterae sanctorum patrum sententiae, quas in ejusdem synodi scriptura depravatas ab illis reperimus, quoddam illorum errori deferre creditur adjutorium: quippe cum in eadem non illarum imaginum quaedam mentio sit, quae in basilicis esse consueverunt, sed illarum quas gentili & superstitioso ritu Romanorum Imperatores oftentabiliter ob sui favoris arrogantiam adorare censuerunt. Quam quidem sacrilegam impietatem ita nullos antiquorum regum reperimus habuisse, sicut & pene nullam gentem tantae crudelitatis tantorumque idolorum servitiis subditam, ut illam, ut quam legimus extitisse. Magnae ergo crudelitatis & revera magnae crudelitatis & fortitudinis quondam fuit, quae a propheta Daniele in expositione quae dicitur statuae, quae quatuor fortissimorum mundi regnorum praesagium fuit, post caput aureum, quod Assyriorum sive Chaldaeorum regnum significavit: pectus vero argenteum, quod Medorum Persarumque regnum figuravit: femora vero aerea, per quae Macedonum regnum monstratum est: in cruribus ferreis designata est: & quomodo ferrum conterit & domat omnia, ita hæc pene omnia regna edomuit. quæ etiam à præfato propheta in quatuor bestiarum visione post lexnam, per quam Babyloniorum regnum monstratum est, & ursum per quem Medorum & Persarum regni successio designata est, sive pardum per quem Macedonum regnum figuratum est, quarto nimirum loco sicut in statua in cruribus ferreis, ita etiam in bestiis quædam terribilis ac formidolosissima bestia dentes ferreos habere describitur, de qua nunc dicere longum est: in qua non sint, sicut in cæteris bestiis, singula, sed omnia quæ in superioribus fuere crudelitatis indicia, quæ gentes quas delevit, devorasse, quas verò tribus addixit, pedibus conculcasse dicitur, & interim dæmonum culturis inservivit, ut quarundam gentium quas subegerat idola suis nihilominus idolis socians infeliciter adoraret. Unde vanissimum & ab omni ratione seclusum est, ab ea re intra sanctam ecclesiam sumere exempla quæ propter gentilitatis maculam prorsus à catholicis creditur abdicata: nisi forte illud in hac parte concedatur, ut ab errore error fulciatur, & res vana rem nihilominus vanam habeat in exemplum, resque obliqua à re non recta putetur accipere posse munimen.
units.tr: But the opinion of John, Bishop of Constantinople, is not believed to lend any support to their error, even though they have mutilated it, as they have the other sayings of the holy Fathers, which we find corrupted by them in the record of the same synod. For in that passage there is no mention of those images which are customarily found in the basilicas, but of those which the Roman Emperors, out of the arrogance of their favour, thought fit to display and worship in the manner of the Gentiles and the superstitious. We find that no ancient kings had this sacrilegious impiety, nor did almost any nation submit to such cruelty and servitude to such great idols as the one we read of as having existed. So there was once a great cruelty, and truly a great cruelty and strength, which the prophet Daniel described in his interpretation of the statue, which was a foreshadowing of the four most mighty kingdoms of the world. After the golden head, which signified the kingdom of the Assyrians or Chaldeans, came the silver breast, which figured the kingdom of the Medes and Persians; the bronze thighs showed the kingdom of the Macedonians; and the iron legs designated the fourth, and just as iron grinds down and subdues all things, so this kingdom subdued almost all the others. The same prophet, in his vision of the four beasts, describes the fourth, in the same place as the iron legs of the statue, as a certain terrible and most dreadful beast with iron teeth. To speak of it now would take long. Unlike the other beasts, it did not have single features, but all the marks of cruelty found in the earlier kingdoms. It is said to have devoured the nations it destroyed, and to have trampled underfoot those it gave over to the tribes, and meanwhile it served the worship of demons, so that, joining the idols of the nations it had subdued to its own idols, it worshipped them to its own misfortune. Hence it is most vain and utterly alien to reason to take examples from that quarter into the holy Church, examples which, on account of their Gentile stain, are believed by Catholics to have been wholly renounced. Unless, perhaps, it is conceded in this matter that error is propped up by error, and a vain thing may take a vain thing as its example, and an oblique thing, not a straight one, may be thought to receive support.

units.la: Textus igitur sententiæ Iohannis (si tamen ejusdem Iohannis est) hoc modo in eadem dementissima synodi lectione taxatus habetur, Nonne eum qui inducitur injurias? nescit quia si quis imaginem imperatoris injuriat, ad eum ipsum imperatorem principaliter dignitati ejus affert injuriam? Nescu, quia si quis imaginem ex ligno aut ex colore detrahet, non sicut ad elementum sine anima ausus judicatur, sed sicut adversus imperatorem diffegregata imaginem totidem imperatoris gestant ei, injuriam ad imperatorem deducit? Et iterum idem de code patie, sermone in quinta feria paschæ, Omnia facta sunt propter gloriam dei: usu vero nostro nubes ad imbrium ministerium, terram ad fructuum abundantiam, mare navigantium, absque invidia omnia famulantur homini, nosgis autem imagini dei. neque enim quando imperialis vultus & imagines in civitates introducuntur, & obviant judices & plebes cum laudibus non tabulam honorantes, neque effusæ ceræ scripturas, sed figuram imperatoris, sic & creaturam non terrenam speciem honorat, sed eadem ipsam calestem figura revererentur. Quæ sententia quanquam loquutionum phaleris & verborum eruditione careat, & procul a negocio cui inpolita est, evagari credatur, necillorum adsertioni eam præbere solatium, nec nostræ constat quoddam conferre dispendium: nec aliquod Christianæ religionis sensibus inculcare difficile: præsertim quæ ne divinæ imaginis characterem in nobis malis operibus inquinemus, neve ei ad cujus imaginem & similitudinem conditi fumus peccando ejusque imaginem & similitudinem polluendo injuriam intrographus, hoc dicere videatur: ut quisquis imperatoris imagini injuriam inrogat, non imagini, sed eidem imperatori injuriam inrogare credatur. Quod autem dixit, Nubes, terram sive mare famulari imagini domini, non hoc pro manufacta & inrationabili imagine dixit, si tamen idem quem illi dicunt aut quislibet catholicus dixit, sed aut pro Christo qui est imago dei, cui flectitur omne genu cœlestium, terrestrium & infernorum, aut pro homine, qui utique ad dei imaginem conditus pene omnibus visibilibus creaturis prælatus est. Quod si quis contentiosus pro insensatis dictum fuisse arbitretur imaginibus, adseveret, quo pacto quove modo, quâve familiaritate nubes, terra, mare imaginibus famulentur, & mox adtectionem suâ magna ex parte fultam habere dinoscetur. Si ergo vulgus partim lætitiæ bacchatu effrenis, partim sæcularis pompæ novitate arcessitus, partim ventosi honoris inflatione cupidus, partim adulationis vitio famulatus, partim publicæ fluctus metu perterritus, imperatorum imagines vanis & perniciosis laudibus honorat, quid ad nos qui gloriamur in cruce domini nostri Iesu Christi, per quem nobis mundus crucifixus est, nosque mundo? quorum conversatio in cœlis est, qui cum Apostolo dicimus, Nobis quibus Christus crucifixus est, quid nobis cum foro? qui tanto errori obniti potius quam adiensum præbere debemus, qui non solum ab eo exemplum ad adorandas imagines minime sumere, sed etiam eum cum suis sequacibus prorsus exsecrari debemus.
units.tr: The text of John's opinion (if indeed it is John's) is therefore censured in that most insane reading of the synod in this way: Does he not know that he who is injured in the image of the emperor, that the injury is principally done to the emperor himself, to his dignity? Does he not know that if anyone tears down an image made of wood or colour, he is judged to have dared not against an insensate element but against the emperor, and that the injury is carried to the emperor by those who bear the emperor's images? And again the same man, in his sermon on Good Friday: All things were made for the glory of God. Yet for our use the clouds serve for the ministry of rains, the earth for abundance of fruits, the sea for sailors; all things serve man without envy, and indeed the image of God. For when the imperial countenance and images are brought into the cities, and the judges and the common people go to meet them with praises, they honour not the board, nor the wax poured out in writing, but the figure of the emperor. So also the rational creature honours not the earthly appearance, but reverences that same heavenly figure. Although this saying lacks the ornaments of rhetoric and the learning of words, and is thought to wander far from the matter to which it is unpolished, it neither offers comfort to their assertion nor is it known to bring any loss to ours, nor is it difficult to impress on the minds of the Christian religion. Especially since it seems to say, lest we stain the character of the divine image in us by evil works, and lest by sinning and polluting the image and likeness of him to whose image and likeness we were made, we do injury to him: that whoever does injury to the image of the emperor is believed to do injury not to the image but to the emperor himself. As for what he said, that the clouds, earth or sea serve the image of the Lord, he did not say this of a handmade and irrational image, if indeed the man they name, or any Catholic, said it; but he meant either Christ, who is the image of God, to whom every knee of the heavenly, earthly and infernal bows, or man, who indeed, made to the image of God, has been set above almost all visible creatures. But if some contentious person thinks that this was said of images, which have no sense, let him assert by what manner, in what way, and by what familiarity the clouds, earth and sea serve images; and he will soon be seen to have a claim propped up in large part by a mere addition. If therefore the common people, partly unbridled in the frenzy of joy, partly drawn by the novelty of worldly pomp, partly eager through the inflation of empty honour, partly serving through the vice of flattery, partly terrified by fear of public upheaval, honour the images of the emperors with vain and pernicious praises, what is that to us who glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to us and we to the world? Our conversation is in heaven; we who say with the Apostle, For us, to whom Christ is crucified, what have we to do with the forum? We ought rather to resist such great error, and not to give it any assent. We ought not only to take no example from it for adoring images, but also utterly to execrate it, together with its followers.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Quod non ad adorationem imaginum pertineat, ut illi asserunt, sententia B. Cyrilli in expositione evangelii secundum Matth.
units.tr: That the saying of St Cyril in his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew does not pertain to the adoration of images, as they claim.

units.la: IN eo etiam quod dicunt B. Cyrillum Alexandrinæ urbis antestitem dixisse, Depingitur enim fides quod in forma dei exsistit verbum, sicut & nostra vita redemptione oblatus est deo, secundum nos similitudine & factus homo, quanquam aut interpretis impetitia, aut scriptoris vitio semiplenum sensum habere videatur, non tamen ibi quodammodo imaginum adoratio innuitur: sed neque in eo quædam hujus erroris, non dicam adfirmatio, sed nec etiam mentio fit, quod dicunt cum post pauca dixisse, Imaginum nobis explent opus parabole significantium virtute, cui quomodo & oculorum adhibeat & palpatu manus afferri in vestigiis mentibus madparabiliter habens visionem. Quoniam ergo hic liber apud nos non habetur, qui utique Græco sermone editus esse à prælato doctore perhibetur, hujus capituli sensus in inconpositis & in impropriis dictionibus ita nobis per conjecturam sensus quærendus est, veluti quis in pulvereis vel in cujuslibet materiæ sordidis involucris nummos quærat. Hoc enim ut conjicimus, hujus capituli textus significare videtur, Quod dum Christus in forma dei existens verbum, nostræ carnis similitudine indutus & factus est homo, & pro nostræ vitæ redemptione oblatus deo in se vera patris imagine ejusdem patris visionem nobis ostendit: juxta illud, Qui videt me, videt & patrem: & in parabolarum imaginationibus, ita nostris sensibus mysteriorum significavit archana, sicut in imaginibus earum rerum, cujus sunt imaginatio quodammodo monstratur: hoc quidem juxta conjecturæ ambiguitatem. cæterum exclusis dubietatis ambagibus nullam hic imaginum adorationem designari manifestum est.
units.tr: As for what they say, that St Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, said, "For the faith is portrayed: that the Word, existing in the form of God, was offered to God for the redemption of our life, and was made man in our likeness," although either the translator's incompetence or a fault of the writer makes it seem to have an incomplete sense, nevertheless no adoration of images is in any way hinted at there. Nor is there any mention, let alone assertion, of this error in it. And as for what they say, that after a few words he said, "Parables that signify by their power fulfil for us the work of images, to which both the eyes are applied and the hand is brought to touch, having in the footprints of the mind a wonderfully [obscure] vision," since this book is not available to us, though it is said to have been published in Greek by that distinguished teacher, the sense of this chapter, in its disordered and improper words, must be sought by conjecture, as one might search for coins in dusty or filthy wrappings of some material. For, as we conjecture, the text of this chapter seems to mean this: "When Christ, existing in the form of God, the Word, clothed in the likeness of our flesh, became man, and was offered to God for the redemption of our life, he showed us in himself the true image of the Father and a vision of the same Father, according to that saying, 'He who sees me sees the Father also'; and in the imaginings of parables he signified the secrets of mysteries to our senses, just as in images the thing of which they are the images is in some way shown. This, indeed, is according to the ambiguity of conjecture. But, with the ambiguities of doubt set aside, it is clear that no adoration of images is designated here."

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXI.

units.la: Quod non fit contra religionem Christianam, ut illi dicunt, non colere & non adorare imagines.
units.tr: That it is not contrary to the Christian religion, as they say, not to cultivate or adore images.

units.la: MAgna quidem sunt Christianæ religionis instrumenta, quæ quanquam ex fidei soliditate & ex dilectione dei & proximi pendeant, singillatim enumerare longissimum est: inter quæ nullum penitus locum imaginum cultus & adoratio tenent, quoniam quidem nullo antiquitatis institiuntur documento, vel sulciuntur exemplo, sed penè cunctarum divinarum scripturarum abdicantur eloquio. solum namque Deum colere, ipsum adorare, ipsum glorificare debere, totius divinæ scripturæ tuba terribilis intonat. Unde cavendum illis est, & modis omnibus pertimescendum, ne dum imaginum cultum & adorationem Christianæ religioni ingerere niteruntur, singularem unius dei cultum & adorationem frustrari videantur. Quæ duo ita inter se mutuo reluctantur, ut si unum steterit, aliud stare non possit. Si enim singularis cultus soli & uni deo debitus inconvulsus erit, & revera inconvulsus erit, imaginum cultus modis omnibus cassabitur: & si imaginum cultus non convellatur, soli & uni deo cultus debitus non erit singularis. Ac per hoc fidei religionis Christianæ arx sive munimen, & gloriosum insigne unius dei cultus & adoratio est, immo quia est hanc imaginibus vel quibuslibet rebus exhibere contra religionem Christianam est: & si has non adorare seu colere contra religionem Christianam est, ut illi delirant, solum deum adorare seu colere, eusque cultus & adorationis arcem singularem esse fateri contra religionem Christianam erit. Solus igitur deus colendus, solus adorandus, solus glorificandus est, de quo per Prophetam dicitur, Exaltatum est nomen ejus solius: cujus etiam sanctis qui triumphato diabolo cum eo regnant, sive quia virilitec certaverunt, ut ad nos incolumis status ecclesiæ perveniret, sive quia eadem ecclesiam assiduis suffragiis & intercessionibus adjuvare noscuntur, veneratio exhibenda est: imagines vero omni sui cultura & adoratione seclusa, utrum in basilicis propter memoriam rerum gestarum & ornamentum sint, an etiam non sint nullum fidei catholicæ adferre poterunt præjudicium: quippe cum ad peragenda nostræ salutis mysteria nullum penitus officium habere noscantur.
units.tr: The instruments of the Christian religion are great indeed. Although they depend on the firmness of faith and on the love of God and neighbour, it would be too long to list them one by one. Among them the cult and adoration of images holds no place at all, since it is founded on no witness of antiquity and supported by no example, but is almost entirely disowned by the testimony of all divine Scripture. The terrible trumpet of the whole of divine Scripture thunders that God alone is to be worshipped, adored and glorified. Hence they must take care, and must dread in every way, lest, while they strive to force the cult and adoration of images upon the Christian religion, they seem to frustrate the singular cult and adoration of the one God. These two things so struggle against each other that if the one stands, the other cannot stand. For if the singular cult owed to God alone and to the one God remains unshaken, and truly it will remain unshaken, the cult of images will be quashed in every way; and if the cult of images is not overthrown, the cult owed to God alone and to the one God will not be singular. Thus the citadel and bulwark of the faith of the Christian religion, and its glorious badge, is the singular cult and adoration of the one God. Indeed, to offer this to images or to any things whatever is against the Christian religion; and if not to adore or cultivate these is against the Christian religion, as they rave, then to adore or cultivate God alone, and to confess that the citadel of this cult and adoration is singular, will be against the Christian religion. God alone, therefore, is to be cultivated, God alone adored, God alone glorified, of whom it is said through the Prophet, The name of him alone is exalted. Veneration is also to be shown to his saints, who reign with him having triumphed over the devil, whether because they fought manfully so that the safe condition of the Church might come to us, or because they are known to aid the same Church by constant prayers and intercessions. But images, with all cult and adoration set aside, whether they are in the churches for the memory of deeds done and for ornament, or whether they are not, can bring no prejudice to the Catholic faith, since they are known to have no office at all in accomplishing the mysteries of our salvation.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Quod non bonam habeant memoriam, qui ut non oblivisçantur sanctorum vel certe ipsius domini, idcirco imagines erigunt.
units.tr: That those who set up images so as not to forget the saints, or certainly the Lord himself, do not have a good memory.

units.la: MIhi autem, ait Propheta, adhærere deo bonum est: qui cum sit spiritus, juxta illud, Dominus deus spiritus est, & in spiritu & veritate adorari debeat, non ei carnaliter, sed spiritaliter quis adhærere potest, nec corporalibus ei sensibus sed rationali animæ intuitu jungi valet. Quamobrem, ut ait sanctissimus Augustinus, saluberrime admonemur averti ab hoc mundo qui profecto corporeus est & sensibilis, & ad deum, id est, veritatem quæ intellectu & interiore mente capitur, quæ semper manet, & ejusdem moli est quæ non habet imaginem falsi, à quo discerni non possit, tota alacritate converti. Ad contemplandum itaque Christum, quiest dei virtus & dei sapientia sive ad intruendas virtutes quæ ab eo in sanctis ejus derivatæ sunt, non corporeus nobis visus, quem communem cum irrationalibus animantibus habemus, sed spiritalis est necessarius, quem sibi impertiendum Propheta à domino postulabat cum dicebat, Revela oculos meos, & considerabo mirabilia de lege tua. Hunc ergo spiritalem auditum non carnales aures Dominus quærebat cum dicebat, Qui habet aures audiendi audiat. His sensibus privari pro culpa perfidiæ populum Ieahel, non membris debilitari jubet, cum Esaiæ prophetæ dicit, Excæca cor populi hujus, & aures ejus adgrava, & oculos ejus claude, ne forte videant oculis suis, & auribus suis audiant, & corde suo intelligant. Quæ dum ita se habent, magna se cæcitate obrutos esse fatentur, qui vim illam animæ, quæ memoria nuncupatur, ita se viiatam habere demonstrant, cui nisi imaginum adminiculum suffragar, ab intentione servitutis dei & veneratione sanctorum ejus recedere compellatur: necse idoneos arbitrantur mentis oculum supra creaturam corporeum levare ad hauriendum æternum lumen nisi creaturæ corporeæ adjutorio fulciantur. Sed ne forte sui erroris murum his tentent tueri munitionibus eo quod & nos ob memoriam rerum gestarum imagines quibuslibet habendas esse concedimus, his à nobis eorum firmitas arcubus, tantis veritatis quatietur impulsibus quod aliud est eas habere oblivionis timore, aliud ornamenti amore: aliud voluntate, aliud indigentia: aliud idcirco videre, ne dei & sanctorum ejus valeat cuis oblivisci, aliud ideo spectare, ut gestarum rerum possit reminisci: aliud est eas res videre, quod nisi videantur, non obsunt: aliud eas quod nisi videatur officiunt, cum videlicet sine imaginum intuitu homo salvari possit, sine dei vero notitia omnino non possit. Cum ergo mens hominis ita ei inhærere debeat, ad cujus imaginem condita est, ut nulla creatura interposita ab ipsa veritate quæ Christus est, formetur, demetissimum est ea inter positis materialib. imaginib. ne ejus oblivione patiatur admoneri debere, cum videlicet hoc infirmitatis sit vitium, non libertatis indicium. Quia vero descensio Christi ad inferos, sive ascensio ejus ad cælos, sive spei nostræ fructus non in rebus visibilibus sed in corde tantum quærendus sit, Paulus Apostolus testatur cum dicit, Spes quæ videtur non est spes: quod enim videt quis, quid sperat? Si autem quod non videmus, speramus, per patientiam expectamus: & iterum, Ne dixeris in corde tuo, Quis ascendit in cælum? id est Christum deducere: vel quis descendit in abyssum? hoc est Christum ex mortuis revocare. Sed quid dicit scriptura? Prope est verbum in ore tuo, & in corde tuo, hoc est, verbum fidei quod prædicamus, quia si confitearis in ore tuo dominum Iesum, & in corde tuo credideris, quod deus illum suscitavit à mortuis, salvus eris: corde enim creditur ad justitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Multa quidem ad rem pertinentia & huic negocio necessaria in hoc capitulo dici poterant, si brevitas cui studemus permitteret.
units.tr: But for me, says the Prophet, it is good to cling to God. Since God is spirit, according to that saying, The Lord God is a Spirit, and ought to be worshipped in spirit and truth, one can cling to him not carnally but spiritually, and one can be joined to him not by bodily senses but by the gaze of the rational soul. Therefore, as the most holy Augustine says, we are most wholesomely admonished to turn away from this world, which is certainly corporeal and sensible, and with our whole eagerness to turn to God, that is, to truth, which is grasped by the understanding and the inner mind, which always remains, and is of the same substance, which has no image of falsehood, and from which it cannot be distinguished. Therefore, to contemplate Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, or to implant the virtues that have flowed from him into his saints, we need not a bodily sight, which we share with irrational animals, but a spiritual sight. The Prophet asked the Lord to grant him this when he said, Reveal my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law. It was this spiritual hearing the Lord sought, not carnal ears, when he said, He who has ears to hear, let him hear. The Lord did not command the people of Israel to be deprived of these senses as punishment for their faithlessness, by weakening their limbs, when he says to the prophet Isaiah, Make the heart of this people dull, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart. Since these things stand so, those who show that the power of the soul called memory is so damaged in them that, unless it is propped up by the aid of images, they are compelled to withdraw from attention to the service of God and the veneration of his saints, confess that they are overwhelmed by great blindness. Nor do they think themselves fit to lift the eye of the mind above corporeal creation to drink in the eternal light, unless they are supported by the help of a corporeal creature. But lest they try to defend the wall of their error with these fortifications, on the ground that we too allow images of any kind to be kept for the sake of remembering deeds done, let their firmness be shaken from us by such strong blows of truth: it is one thing to have them out of fear of forgetting, another out of love of ornament; one thing by choice, another by need; one thing to look at them therefore so as not to be able to forget God and his saints, another to gaze at them so as to be able to recall the deeds done; one thing to see those things, which do no harm unless they are seen; another to see them, which do harm if they are seen, since a man can be saved without looking at images, but cannot possibly be saved without knowledge of God. Therefore, since the mind of man ought so to cling to him after whose image it was made, that it is formed by no creature interposed between it and the very truth which is Christ, it is most shameful that it should need to be reminded, by material images placed between, lest it suffer forgetfulness of him; for this is a vice of weakness, not a sign of freedom. And because the descent of Christ into hell, or his ascent into heaven, and the fruit of our hope are to be sought not in visible things but in the heart alone, the Apostle Paul bears witness when he says, Hope that is seen is not hope; for why does a man hope for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience; and again, Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven?, that is, to bring Christ down; or who will descend into the abyss?, that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. But what does Scripture say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart, that is, the word of faith which we preach; for if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved; for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Many things pertinent to this matter, and necessary for this business, could have been said in this chapter, if the brevity to which we are committed allowed it.
F

units.la: C A P. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIII.

units.la: Quod contra beati Gregorii Romanæ urbis antestitis sententiam insti- tutum sit imagines adorare seu frangere.
units.tr: That, contrary to the opinion of blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, it was established to adore or to break images.

units.la: IMAGINES sane quarum insolentissimæ adorationis amor Constantino & matri ejus Hærenæ necnon & Tarasio Constantinopolitano Episcopo exercendæ synodi causa extitit, quorum difcutiendus error præsentis nobis disputationis materiam præbuit, à beato Gregorio Romanæ urbis antestite & adorari prohibentur, & frangi, qui non longe, à causa vagantibus verbis nullisque dubietatis ambagibus involutis sermonibus, sed proprie ac pure quid in hac parte observandum quidve tenendum sit Sereno Massiliensi Episcopo suis mandavit apicibus. Nam dum isti prædecessores sive parentes suos qui eas fregere, exsecrabiliter damnare perhibeantur, & illi istos qui eas adoraturi erant abominabiliter damnasse credantur, inter has diversi erroris acies ad unius socordiæ bivium tenentes medium, se præfatus interponit antestis, & utrique parti inter se mutuo conligenti arma præbet, cum & istos qui eas adorant cum illis qui eas fregere: & illos qui eas fregere cum iltis qui eas adorant pontificalis teli exspide ferit. Et iltis hinc adorantibus, illisinde frangentibus spretis, nostræ partis sibi ecclesiam adficit, quæ mediocritatis callem recti itineris carpens, & in ornamentis ob memoriam habere concedit, & istos hinc adorantes, illos illinc frangentes despiciendo postponit: siquidem præfatum Serenum & laudasse quia adorare prohibuerit, & reprehendisse quia fregerit idem venerabilis Papa perhibetur. Perlatum, inquit, ad nos fuerat quòd inconsiderato zelo succensiu sanctorum imagines sub hac quasi excusatione ne adorari debuissent, confringeres: & quidem qui eas adorare vetuissetomnino laudavimus, fregisse vero reprehendimus: & post pauca, Frangi ergo non debuit quod non ad adorandum in ecclesiis, sed ad instruendas sollummodo mentes fuit nescientium conlocatum. Et quia in locis venerabilibus sanctorum depingi historias non sine ratione ne vetustas admisit, si zelum discretione condiffes, & ea quæ intendebas salubriter obtinere & collectum gregem non dispergere, sed potius poteras congregare. Putabat enim idem venerabilis præsul in imaginum commutione populares animos perturbatos, & ideo pusillorum scandalum pertimescens hæc inferebat. Unde & in subsequentibus eum instruit qualiter eas & habere in ecclesiis quibuslibet permittat, & adorare modis omnibus devitet. Aut enim, Convocandi sunt diversi ecclesiæ filii eisque scriptura sacra est testimonium offendendum, quia omne manu factum adorari non liceat: quoniam scriptum est, Dominum deum tuum adorabis & illi soli servies: ac deinde subjungendum, Quia pictura imaginum quæ ad ædificationem imperiti populi facta fuerant, ut nescientes literas ipsam historiam intendentes quod dictum sit discerent, transfiffe in adorationem viderat, idcirco commotus esut eas imagines frangi præciperes: atque eis dicendum, Si ad hanc instructionem ad quas imagines antiquitus factæ sunt habere vultis, in ecclesiis eas modis omnibus & offerri & haberi permittas, atque indica quod non tibi ipsa visio historiæ, quæ pictura tegte pandebatur displicuerit, sed illa adoratio quæ pictura fuerat incompetenter exhibita. Atque in his verbis eorum mentes demulcens eos ad concordiam tuam revoca: & si quis imagines facere voluerit, minime prohibe, adorare verò imagines omnibus modis devita. Ecce quo magisterio quòve documento venerandi pontificis imbuti imagines in ecclesiis habere non renuimus, sed earum adorationem prorsus abdicamus, cujus institutis contraire se, quisquis eas vel frangit vel adorat, modis omnibus recognoscat.
units.tr: IMAGES indeed, whose excessive love of adoration gave occasion to the holding of a synod under Constantine, his mother Irene, and Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, and whose error, to be examined, has supplied the matter of our present dispute, are forbidden both to be adored and to be broken by blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome. He did not say this in wandering words or in discourse wrapped in ambiguous doubts, but plainly and purely told Serenus, bishop of Marseilles, in his letters what must be observed or held in this matter. For while those predecessors or parents of theirs who broke the images are said to be cursed and condemned, and those who were about to adore them are believed to have been abominably condemned by the others, the aforesaid bishop places himself between these battle lines of opposite error, holding the middle ground at the crossroads of a single folly. He offers arms to each side, which join together against each other: he strikes both those who adore images along with those who break them, and those who break them along with those who adore, with the spear of the pontifical weapon. Rejecting those adoring on this side and those breaking on that side, he claims for himself the Church of our party, which, following the path of moderation as the way of right travel, allows the images to be kept as ornaments for remembrance, and by despising and setting aside those who adore from this side and those who break from that side, puts them behind. For the same venerable Pope is reported to have both praised the aforesaid Serenus because he forbade adoration, and rebuked him because he broke the images. It was reported to us, he says, that you, kindled with inconsiderate zeal, broke the images of the saints under this pretext, that they ought not to be adored: we indeed wholly praised you for forbidding them to be adored, but we rebuke you for breaking them. And a little after: What was not placed in churches for adoration, but only to instruct the minds of the unlearned, ought not to have been broken. And since antiquity, not without reason, did not allow the stories of the saints to be painted in venerable places, if you had tempered your zeal with discretion, you could have healthfully obtained what you intended, and not scattered the gathered flock, but rather could have gathered it. For the same venerable prelate thought that the minds of the people were disturbed by the change of images, and therefore, fearing a scandal to the little ones, he made these remarks. Hence, in what follows, he instructs him how he may permit the images to be kept in churches in any way, and avoid their adoration in every way. For: The sons of the Church are to be called together, and Holy Scripture is to be set against them as testimony, that it is not lawful to adore anything made by hand, since it is written: You shall adore the Lord your God and serve him alone. And then it is to be added: Because the painting of images, which had been made for the edification of the unlearned people, so that those who do not know letters might learn by attending to the history itself what had been said, he had seen passed over into adoration; therefore, moved by this, he ordered the images to be broken. And it is to be said to them: If you wish to have the images made in antiquity for that instruction, you should in every way permit them to be both offered and kept in churches, and show that it was not the sight of the history, which was revealed through the painting, that displeased you, but that adoration which had been improperly paid to the painting. And soothing their minds with these words, call them back to your harmony; and if anyone wishes to make images, do not forbid it at all, but avoid adoring images in every way. Behold by what teaching or what instruction, imbued with the venerable pontiff's words, we do not refuse to have images in churches, but utterly renounce their adoration; let whoever either breaks or adores them acknowledge in every way that he sets himself against his decrees.

units.la: C A P. XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24.

units.la: Cum præter deum solum nihil aliud debeat adorari, aliud est hominem adorare charitatis & salutationis officio, aliud imagi- nes manufactas.
units.tr: Since nothing else ought to be adored besides God alone, it is one thing to adore a man out of the duty of love and greeting, and another to adore images made by hand.

units.la: ADEO genus humanum deus dilexisse credendum est, ut in ipso conditionis ejus exordio nos utcumque, sed ad suam imaginem & similitudinem id condiderit, & creaturis cæteris præstulerit, & à florigeræ sedis felicitate per peccata ad hujus mortalitatis ærumnas transmissum studiis miraculis & luculentis vatum oraculis erudire per momenta temporum non desierit: & angelis qui utique ab eo peccando discesserant, perpetua damnatione multatis, ut id denuo civib. æthereis pro quorum societate condiderat, sociaret, hominem adsumere non despexerit, dicente Apostolo; Nusquam enim angelos adprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ adprehendit. Unde datur intellegi aliud & longe aliud esse hominem adorare salutationis gratia, qui tot meritorum prærogativis pollet, aliud imagines quæ his omnibus carent. aliud est hoc homini humilitatis gratia exhibere qui opus dei est, quam imagini quæ opus artificis est. aliud est illam naturam humilitatis officio adorare quæ in cæli rege ab angelis & archangelis adoratur: aliud illam quæ nisibus non solum hominum, sed & cæterorum animalium adhibita famulatur. Quantum ergo opera dei eminent humanis operibus, efficientia effectis, rationabilia inrationabilibus, sensibilia insensibilibus, viventia non viventibus, tantum adoratio, quæ, ut prædixit, humilitatis & salutationis officio erga homines agitur, adoratione quæ imaginibus superstitiose & superflue exhibetur.
units.tr: God must be believed to have loved the human race, so that at the very beginning of its creation he made it, in whatever way, to his own image and likeness, and set it above the other creatures. After it was sent down from the happiness of the flowery seat, through sin, into the hardships of this mortal life, he has never ceased to instruct it, from moment to moment, by studies, miracles and clear oracles of the prophets. And since the angels, who had indeed fallen away from him by sinning, were punished with perpetual damnation, he did not disdain to take on man, so that he might join man to those heavenly citizens for whose fellowship he had created him, as the Apostle says: For surely he does not take hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Hence it is understood that it is one thing, and a very different thing, to adore a man for the sake of greeting, a man who excels in so many privileges of merit, and another to adore images, which lack all these things. It is one thing to show this humility to a man, who is the work of God, and another to show it to an image, which is the work of a craftsman. It is one thing to adore with the service of humility that nature which in the King of heaven is adored by angels and archangels, and another to adore that nature which, applied by the labours of men and of other animals too, is made to serve. Therefore, just as the works of God surpass human works, the effective the effects, the rational the irrational, the sensible the insensible, and the living the non-living, so much does the adoration which, as he has said, is offered to men in the duty of humility and greeting, exceed the adoration which is offered superstitiously and superfluously to images.

units.la: Quoniam quidem homines deus non imagines diligere jussit: propter homines filium suum in mundum, non propter imagines misit. ab hominibus pater vocari, non ab imaginibus voluit: & dominus in evangelio non ait, Nolite scandalizare unam de imaginibus istis, sed, unum de pusillis istis: quoniam angeli eorum semper vident faciem patris mei qui in cælis est: & Apostolus invicem nos honore prævenire. nire, non imagines honorare hortatur. Quia ergo melior sit opifex opere & efficiens effectis, liber Sapientiæ testatur.ait enim,Nemo enim sibi similem homo poterit Deum fingere: cum sit enim mortalis mortuum fingit manibus iniquis. Melior est enim ipse his quos colit,quia ipse quidem vixit,cum esset mortalis,illi autem nunquam. & beatus Augustinus ait,Fateor tamen altius demersos esse, qui opera hominum deos putant, quàm qui opera Dei. Hoc quidem de idolis eorumq; cultoribus. Cæterum illi qui intra sanctam Ecclesiam in sacro eloquio solum Deum adorandum solumq; colendum prædicant, & ut imagines adorentur synodos adgregant,videant ne forte domesticam pacem intestino bello perturbent & prosperitatem rerum nostrarum,isto errore,quasi quodam civili bello conmaculent. Quod facillimè vitare poterunt si intra metas Propheticæ & Evangelicæ,sive Apostolicæ prædicationis continentur, & exclusis vocum novitatibus sanctorum patrum soluinmodo institutis contenti sint.
units.tr: Since God commanded men, not images, to be loved; for the sake of men, not of images, he sent his Son into the world. He wished to be called Father by men, not by images. And the Lord in the gospel does not say, Do not offend one of these images, but one of these little ones, for their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven; and the Apostle urges us to go before one another in honour, not to honour images. That the maker is better than the work, and the one who effects better than the effects, the Book of Wisdom bears witness. For it says: For a man cannot fashion a god like himself; since he is mortal, he fashions a dead thing with wicked hands. For he himself is better than those whom he worships, since he himself has lived, though mortal, whereas they have never lived. And blessed Augustine says: I confess, however, that those are sunk more deeply who think the works of men to be gods than those who think the works of God to be gods. This indeed concerns idols and their worshippers. But as for those who, within the holy Church, proclaim in sacred speech that God alone is to be adored and alone worshipped, and yet gather synods so that images may be adored, let them see to it that they do not disturb domestic peace with internal war, and stain the prosperity of our affairs with this error as with a kind of civil war. They will be able to avoid this very easily if they keep within the bounds of Prophetic, Evangelical and Apostolic preaching, and, with novelties of words excluded, are content with the institutions of the holy Fathers alone.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Quod nusquam ab Apostolis exemplis aut verbis,ut illi garriunt,imagines ad- orare institutum sit.
units.tr: That the Apostles never instituted, by example or by word, the adoration of images, as the Papists babble.

units.la: ECclesiasticæ norma institutionis Prophetarum & Apostolorum vel ipsius Domini aliquando nobis commendatur verbis, aliquando exemplis, aliquando obumbratis, aliquando patefactis monstratut oraculis,nonnunquam etiam figuratis;nonnunquam simplicibus perdocetureloquiis: inter quæ omnia omnium rerum adoratione inhibita, salva adoratione quæ nos mutuo salutantes adoramus, solius Dei adoratio instituitur. Nam dum hanc imaginibus hi, qui illarum cremantur amore exhibendam ab Apostolis fateantur esse traditam, dicant necesse est quibus ab illis exemplis sit institutum, quibusve documentis constet esse promulgatum. An forte Petrus hanc imaginibus exhibendam instituit, qui Cornelium ne se adoraret blande conpescuit? An Johannes, qui angelum adorare cupiens,ne id tacetet, sed ut Deum adoraret audivit? An Paulus, qui hanc superstitiose Lycaonibus sibi inferre cupientibus expavit? An Barnabas, qui hanc pariter cum Paulo refugiit? Cum ergo angelus & Apostoli se adorari prohibeant, quis tam vecors tamq; vesanus est, qui dicere audeat eos imagines adorari instituisse? præsertim qui etli se adorari deberent: cum videlicet alterius meriti alteriusve definitionis sint angeli sive homines, & alterius imagines. Si igitur Angeli sive homines,ut præsentis exempli ratio docet, minime adorandi sunt salva adoratione quæ charitatis & salutationis officio exhibetur: multo minus imagines quæ rationis expertes sunt, nec salutatione necadora tione dignæ eo quod insensatæ sint,adorandæ sunt: quæ si adorandæ non sunt, immo quia non sunt, duplex illi in hac parte deliquium patrare perhibentur, sive quia eas adorant, sive quia ut hoc facerent ab Apostolis sibi traditum esse mentiuntur. Apostolus deniq; Paulus, Evangelicus ille stabularius, qui à visione patriæ cœlestis genus humanū digressum, & ad hujus defectionis ærumnas dilapsum, & à malignis spiritibus vulneratum, à custode omnium ad sanandum prædicationis verbis lenibus & austeris accepit, cui redemptor duplicis scientiæ sive duorum testamentorum pecuniam concedit,& si quid ad erudiendum redemptum populum consilium dans supererogaverit, redditurum se ei esse promittit, nec in his de quibus libere præcepta dat, nec in his de quibus supererogans consilium dat,sicut de virginibus fecisse perhibetur,nihil tale de imaginum adoratione, ut illi somniant, usquam instituisse vel præcepisse reperitur. Nam & idem doctor gentium cum discipulis Timotheo & Tito scriberet, instruens eos & docens de ordinatione episcopatus, presbyterii & diaconii & omnis Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ, sive de spirituali conversatione & hæreticis vitandis, ideo imaginum adorationem minime instituit, quia hanc à religione Christiana alienam esse cognovit: qui & in cæteris epistolis quas universo orbi scripsit, quæ vitanda essent quæve sequenda edocens, hanc penitus tem parvipendit, quam nec abnuere quendam errorem, nec statuere quandam credidit esse virtutem. Qui ergo has non adorare scelus, has autem adorare inter prima hdei sacramenta ab Apostolis institutum esse delirant, perpendant quoniam idem vas electionis nec eas spernere inter scelera enumerat,cum dicit; Manifesta sunt autem opera carnis quæ sunt fornicatio,immunditia, impudicia, luxuria, idolorum servitus,veneficia,mimicitiæ,contentiones,æmulationes,ira, rixæ, dissensiones, sectæ,hæreses,invidia, homicidia, ebrietates,comessationes,& his similia quæ prædico vobis sicut prædixi,quoniam qui talia agunt regnum Dei non consequentur. Neceas adorare inter spiritales fructus enumerat, cum dicit, Fructus autem spiritus est, charitas,gaudium,pax,patientia,longanimitas,bonitas,benignitas,fides,modestia,continentia: adversus huiusmodi non est lex: qui autem sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis & concupiscentiis. Sed neque in eadem eloquentiæ venustate, qua sensus suos quibusdam rivulis per membra & cæsa & decentes circuitus rhetorico de flumine derivans ab anaphora incipit, & per ἀντίθεσις ὀνομάτων decurrit,& contraria contrariis per topicorum argumentationem quam philosophi à contrariis nominant opponens, pulcherrimis antithetis orationem suam honestat: ubi hujus vitæ tempus acceptabile, pœnitentiæ videlicet aptum & dies salutis,id est,ad bene agendum aptos denuntiat,inter cæteras quas enumerat virtutes hujusce adorationis quandam vel levem fecisse noscitur mentionem.Ait enim, Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis: nemini dantes ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum, sed in omnibus exhibeamus nosmetipsos sicut Dei ministros,in multa patientia,in tribulationibus,in necessitatibus,in angustiis, in plagis,in carceribus,in seditionibus,in laboribus,in vigiliis,in jejuniis,in castitate,in scientia, in longanimitate,in suavitate, in Spiritu sancto,in charitate non ficta,in verbo veritatis, in virtute Dei, per arma justitiæ à dextris & à sinistris, per gloriam & ignoignobilitatem, per infamiam & bonam famam, ut seductores, & veraces: sicut ignoti, & cogniti: quasi morientes, & ecce vivimus: ut caeligati, & non mortificati: quasi tristes, semper autem gaudentes: sicut egentes, multos autem locupletantes: tamquam nihil habentes, & omnia possidentes. In quo virtutum catalogo, ut praefati sumus, idem egregius praedicator imaginum adorationem inserere, si hanc harum sociam Ecclesiaeq; proficuam esse decerneret, quam dinumerare ideo distulit, quia hanc utilem minime esse persensit.
units.tr: The rule of the Church's teaching, from the Prophets and Apostles and from the Lord himself, is commended to us sometimes by words, sometimes by examples, sometimes by hidden meanings, sometimes by plainly revealed oracles, sometimes by figures, and sometimes by simple sayings. In all of these, the adoration of every created thing is forbidden, and the adoration of God alone is taught, while the greeting by which we honour one another remains untouched. For if those who burn with love for images admit that the Apostles handed down that images are to be adored, they must necessarily say by what examples it was instituted for them and by what teachings it is known to have been proclaimed.
