Did Peter perhaps institute that images be adored, when he gently checked Cornelius from worshipping him? Did John, who wanted to adore the angel, not keep silent about it but heard that he should worship God? Did Paul, who shrank in horror when the Lycaonians wished to offer this superstition to him? Did Barnabas, who likewise shrank from it together with Paul? Since, therefore, the angel and the Apostles forbid themselves to be adored, who is so mad and so frenzied as to dare to say that they instituted the adoration of images? All the more so, since they ought to be adored, if they were such men; for angels and men are clearly of a different worth and definition, and so are their images. If, then, angels or men, as the reasoning of the present example teaches, are by no means to be adored (apart from the honour that is shown in the duty of love and greeting), much less are images to be adored, which lack reason and are not worthy of greeting or of worship, because they are insensible. If these are not to be adored, or rather, because they are not, those people are charged with committing a double offence in this matter: either because they adore them, or because they lie that it was handed down to them by the Apostles to do so. Finally, the Apostle Paul, that evangelical innkeeper, who, having fallen away from the vision of the heavenly fatherland and sunk into the miseries of this defection, and wounded by evil spirits, received from the custodian of all things the words of preaching, gentle and stern, for his healing, to whom the Redeemer entrusts the money of the twofold knowledge, or of the two covenants, and who promises that, if he gives any advice for the instruction of the redeemed people beyond what is required, he will repay him, is nowhere found to have instituted or prescribed anything of the sort concerning the adoration of images, as those men dream, neither in the matters on which he gives commands freely, nor in those on which he gives advice beyond what is required, as he is said to have done concerning virgins. For when this teacher of the Gentiles wrote to his disciples Timothy and Titus, instructing and teaching them about the ordination of bishops, elders and deacons, and all church discipline, and about spiritual conduct and the avoiding of heretics, he did not institute the adoration of images at all, because he knew that it was foreign to the Christian religion. And in the other epistles which he wrote to the whole world, teaching what was to be avoided and what was to be followed, he so completely disregarded this matter that he believed it was neither a sin to renounce nor a virtue to establish. Therefore, those who rave that not to adore these things is a crime, while to adore them was instituted by the Apostles among the first sacraments of faith, should consider that the same chosen vessel does not count even the scorning of them among the crimes, when he says: Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Nor does he count the adoration of images among the spiritual fruits, when he says: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. Nor does he, in the same elegance of eloquence, by which he pours out his thoughts in a rhetorical stream through clauses, members and balanced periods, beginning with anaphora and running on through antithesis of words, setting contraries against contraries by the argument of the topics, which the philosophers call arguments from contraries, adorning his speech with most beautiful antitheses, when he proclaims that this time of life is acceptable, that is, fit for repentance, and that these are the days of salvation, that is, fit for doing good, among the other virtues he enumerates, he is known to have made even a slight mention of this adoration. For he says: Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation: giving no offence in anything, that our ministry be not blamed; but in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings; by pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned, by the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, by honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report: as deceivers, and yet true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things. In this catalogue of virtues, as we have said above, that same distinguished preacher would have included the adoration of images, if he had judged it to be a companion of these virtues and profitable to the Church; but he postponed counting it precisely because he perceived that it was in no way useful.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: Quod non parvi sit erroris manufactas imagines archae testamenti Domini coaequare conari, ut illi in sua synodo facere conati sunt.
units.tr: That it is no small error to try to equate man-made images with the ark of the covenant of the Lord, as those at their synod attempted to do.

units.la: MAGNAE absurditatis immo temeritatis est, archae testamenti Domini imagines coaequare conari: cum tot mysteriorum indiciis ab illa noscantur differre; & rei quae condita est Domini nicae vocis imperio res adsimilafe quae cujuslibet artificis conduntur arbitrio. Siquidem illa condita est Domino imperante, istae conduntur artis industria juvante: illa a sancto viro Moyse, istae a quolibet opifice: illa a legislatore, istae a pictore: illa redundet mysteriis, istae colorum tantummodo fucis: illa & praesentibus fuerit in miraculorum stuporem, & e futuris mystica quaedam & archana significarit: istae & praesentibus miraculis, & futurorum significationibus nudae rei cujus sunt, tantum memoriam ingerant. De cujus typicis praefigurationibus sive horum quae intra eam sunt, in superiore libro monstratum est: nunc vero quantum a manufactis imaginibus differat, brevirer exsequendum est. Qui igitur materiales imagines a quibuslibet opificibus conditas, archae testamenti Domini, quae Domino imperante, Moyse obaedience, condita est, aequiperare contendunt, inveniant, si queunt, opificem qui Moysi meritis aequiperari queat, qui flumineis sit fluctibus expositus, cujus salus inter lymphaticos cursus Deo soli relinquatur, a quibus excepetus & matri restituatur, & ab his quibus perimi jussus fuerat, deliciosissime ali jubeatur: qui omni sapientia Aegyptiorum eruditus sit, qui videat arboreos ramos incendia pati & non uti, qui miretur fragilem materiam admirabili igne nec modicum nulla ei dando alimenta pati dispendium, vel potius inde voce emissa se ex nomine vocari, & mystica sibi praecepta & spem liberandae gentis, & adipiscendae paternae promissionis dari: qui obstupescat suae virgae rigorem in sinuosum conversum esse draconem, cujus administratione Nilicolae decem prodigiolis feriantur plagis, qui Aegyptiis opibus diratis cuneis, & aequoreos fluctus pede sicco transmeantibus, dux fieri valeat: qui amaras aquas in dulcem convertat saporem, & jejunam silicem ictu virgae undifluum cogat evomere liquorem: qui extensione manuum hostiles tumultus vinci compellat, & suos victoria potiti concedat: qui inter terrificos tubarum strepitus, & fulminum coruscationes, & nubis densissimae obumbrationem, & crepitantium ignium rogos exterritus & tremebundus montem conscendat, legem accipiat, & inter DEUM & homines verus interpres a Domino promulgata praecepta populis observanda demonstret: qui secundum exemplar quod ei in monte monstratum fuerit, tabernaculum faciat, quod cum ingressus fuerit gloria Domini operiat: qui sit mitissimus super omnes, qui morantur in terra, ad quem loquatur Deus facie ad faciem, sicut loqui solet homo ad amicum suum: qui dones sol quater decies ortum occasumque perficiat, omni cibo penitus potuque careat, cujus facies nimio splendore vix intueri queat, qui de duobus regibus mirabiliter triumphet, qui quater tricenis annorum cursibus exemptis nec oculorum caliginem, nec dentium motionem patiatur: qui faciat ex qualibet materia imaginem, quae tot redundet mysteriis & exuberet sacramentis, ut in ejus superficie tremenda audiantur oracula: ante cujus conspectum hostica terrore quatiantur agmina, & per medium sui arentem praestent transeuntibus flumina, & antiquae urbis in momento funditus eversa pugnacibus legionibus ingressum undique praebeant moenia, quae vocetur scabellum pedum Dei nostri: ad cujus introitum pavendis hostium regio feriatur flagellis, quam indomitae contra naturam vaccae vitulis post terga relictis ad Israheliticam terram plaustri novi gestamine trahant, ad cujus regressum stupendis indigenae terreantur miraculis, ante quam egregius propheta & rex infulatus magna cum exultatione ludere non erubescat, & eam ad locum destinatum in musicis concentibus hymnorumque suavisonis modulaminibus introducat: quae dum & suis & opificis tot signorum emicuerit praerogativis, non inmerito archae testamenti Domini poterit coaequari. Cum ergo nec tanti meriti opifex, nec tantae gloriae opificium reperire valuerint, restat utlegislatorem nostrae aetatis hominibus, & archam testamenti Domini manufactis imaginibus modis omnibus anteponant: nec res tam viles tamque mysteriis nudas rei tam sublimi totque mysteriorum insignibus exuberanti aequiperare conentur. Nam si, ut illi delirant, imagines archae testamenti Domini adsimilari queunt, necesse est ut quiddam sit circa eas quod propitiatorio adsimilari queat: necesse est ut metuenda inde oracula dentur. Non autem inde quaedam oraculo dantur: non igitur, ut illi desipiunt, imagines archae testamenti Domini adsimilari queunt.
units.tr: It is a great absurdity, indeed a rashness, to try to equate images of the ark of the covenant of the Lord with it, since they are known to differ from it by so many indications of mysteries; and to liken a thing made at the command of the Lord's own word to things made at the discretion of any craftsman. For the one was made at the Lord's command, the others are made with the help of artistic skill; the one by the holy man Moses, the others by any workman; the one by the lawgiver, the others by a painter; the one abounds in mysteries, the others only in the pigments of colours; the one, both by its presence, was a cause of astonishment at miracles, and signified certain mystical and hidden things about the future; the others, even with miracles present and with signs of future things, merely bring to mind the bare thing of which they are images. Concerning its typical prefigurations, or those things which are within it, it was shown in the earlier book; but now it must be set forth briefly how much it differs from man-made images. Let those, then, who strive to equal material images made by any craftsmen with the ark of the covenant of the Lord, which was made at the Lord's command and by Moses' obedience, let them find, if they can, a craftsman who can be equalled to Moses' merits: one who was exposed on the river waters, whose safety among the watery currents was left to God alone; who was taken up by them and restored to his mother, and ordered to be most delicately nursed by those by whom he had been commanded to be killed; who was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; who saw a bush suffer fire and not be consumed; who wondered that a fragile material could endure a wonderful fire without loss, and, with no nourishment given to it, suffer no diminution; or rather, who, when a voice was uttered from it, was called by his own name, and was given mystical precepts and the hope of freeing his people and of obtaining the promise made to his fathers; who was astonished that the rigid rod in his hand was turned into a writhing serpent, by whose agency the Nile dwellers were struck with ten plagues; who, with the Egyptians' wealth stripped away, and the sea waves crossed on dry foot, was able to become a leader; who turned bitter waters into sweet taste, and by a blow of his rod compelled the barren flint to pour out a flowing liquid; who by the extension of his hands compelled hostile uproars to be conquered, and granted victory to his own people; who, amid terrifying blasts of trumpets, flashes of lightning, the shadow of a very dense cloud, and the blazing pyres of crackling fires, frightened and trembling, climbed the mountain, received the law, and, as a true interpreter between God and men, set forth to the peoples the precepts promulgated by the Lord to be observed; who made the tabernacle according to the pattern shown him on the mountain, which the glory of the Lord covered when it entered; who was the meekest of all who dwell on the earth, with whom God spoke face to face, as a man is wont to speak with his friend; who, for forty days and forty nights, carried through without any food or drink at all, whose face could scarcely be looked upon for excessive brightness; who triumphed wonderfully over two kings; who, after four times forty years, suffered neither dimness of eyes nor loosening of teeth; who could make an image of any material which would abound in so many mysteries and overflow with sacraments, so that fearful oracles were heard from its surface; before whose presence hostile armies were shaken with terror, and who made dry rivers to pass through its midst for those crossing, and whose walls, when the ancient city was overthrown from its foundations in a moment, offered entry on every side to warlike legions, and which was called the footstool of our God; at whose coming the region of enemies was struck with dreadful scourges, and whom untamed cows, contrary to nature, with their calves left behind, drew to the land of Israel on the carriage of a new cart; at whose return the native inhabitants were terrified by stupendous miracles; before which the eminent prophet and anointed king was not ashamed to dance with great exultation, and led it to the appointed place amid musical harmonies and sweet-sounding modulations of hymns: since such a thing shines with so many tokens of signs both from its own privileges and from its maker, it could not without reason be equated with the ark of the covenant of the Lord. Since, therefore, they have been able to find neither a maker of such merit nor a work of such glory, it remains that they set the lawgiver of our age and the man-made images, in every way, before the ark of the covenant of the Lord; nor let them attempt to equate things so cheap, and so bare of mysteries, with a thing so sublime and abounding in so many mysteries. For if, as they rave, images of the ark of the covenant of the Lord can be made like it, it is necessary that there be something about them which could be likened to the mercy seat: it is necessary that fearful oracles be given from them. But no oracles are given from them; therefore, as they are foolish to suppose, images of the ark of the covenant of the Lord cannot be made like it.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Quòd magna sit temeritatis ingentiúq; absurditatis, sæpe memoratas imagines corpori & sanguini Dominico æquiperare velle, sicut in eadem vanitate quæ pro illis scripta est legitur.
units.tr: That it is a great rashness and a huge absurdity to wish to equate the images so often mentioned with the body and blood of the Lord, as is read in the same vanity written in their favour.

units.la: QUUM Dominus in Evangelio dicat, Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in Spiritu & veritate, mirantur eorum vesaniam, qui in adorandarum imaginum tantam exarsere socordiam, ut cum eas nec Spiritum nec veritatem esse constet, non solum adorare, sed etiá corpori & sanguini dominico æquiperare eas præsumant dicentes, Sicut corpus dominicum & sanguis à fructibus terræ ad insigne mysterium traiecit, ita & imagines artificum industria conpaginata ad earum personarum, in quarum similitudinem conpaginantur, transeant veneration em. Cum scilicet corporis & sanguinis dominici sacramentum ad commemorationem suæ passionis & nostræ salutis nobis concessum ab eodem mediatore Dei & hominum, per manum sacerdotis & invocationem divini nominis conficiatur: imagines verò nullius manus inpolitionis vel consecrationis mysterio indigentes, non ab aliis nisi ab his, qui pictoriæ artis experientia imbuti sunt, & coniiciendorum colorum peritiam habent, vel ab his, qui fabrilis vel cælaturæ vel certæ alicujus artis conperta institutione, & cognita vi materiæ vultus conponunt, formati & conpaginati noscantur. Et numirum ad horum consecrationem sacerdos infulatus, circumstantis populi deprecationes suis precibus miscens, cum interno rugitu memoriam faciat dominicæ passionis, & ab inferis resurrectionis, necnon & in cælos gloriosissimæ ascensionis, & hæc perferri per manus angeli in sublime altare Dei, & in conspectum majestatis depositat: pictor verò patrandi operis loca congrua appetens, in hanc formationem colorum tantum venustatem, & operis supplementum quærat. Nimium igitur nimiumque à veritatis, rationis & discretionis trainite distat, qui corpori & sanguini dominico imagines æquiperare conatur. Nam Melchisedech rex Salem, sacerdos Dei summi, in typo dominici corporis & sanguinis, non imaginem quandam, sed panè & vinum legitur obtulisse. Nam & Moysaico ore in præfiguratione nostri redemptoris, cujus carnem in remissionem peccatorum sumimus, & sanguinis tinctione percutientis angeli impetum evadimus, Agnus per familias comedi jubetur, & colendarum vel adorandarum imaginum usus omnino abdicatur. Psalmographus quoque & panem angelorum, Christum videlicet, ab hominibus manducandum, & imaginum conditores similes his quæ conduntur imaginibus fieri, suavisona modulatione cantavit.
units.tr: Since the Lord says in the Gospel, "The true worshippers will worship the Father in Spirit and in truth" (John 4:23), we marvel at the madness of those who have burned with such foolish zeal for adoring images that, although it is plain that images are neither Spirit nor truth, they presume not only to adore them but even to equate them with the body and blood of the Lord, saying: "Just as the body and blood of the Lord were brought from the fruits of the earth into a remarkable mystery, so too images, put together by the skill of craftsmen, pass over into the veneration of the persons in whose likeness they are fashioned." For the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, given to us by the same Mediator between God and men in remembrance of his passion and our salvation, is consecrated by the hand of a priest and by the invocation of the divine name. Images, on the other hand, need no mystery of anointing or consecration; they are known to be formed and put together not by just anyone, but by those trained in the art of painting and skilled in mixing colours, or by those who, through a known training in carving, engraving or some other definite craft, and through knowledge of the properties of their material, shape and compose the face. And indeed, for the consecration of these images, a priest in his vestments, mingling his prayers with the supplications of the people standing around, makes with inward groaning a memorial of the Lord's passion, of his resurrection from the dead, and of his most glorious ascension into heaven, and sets these things, carried by the hands of an angel, upon the high altar of God and in the sight of his majesty. The painter, however, seeking suitable places to carry out his work, looks for beauty and completion in the mixing of these colours. Therefore he is far, far removed from the truth, from reason and from sound judgement, who tries to equate images with the body and blood of the Lord. For Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, is read to have offered, as a type of the Lord's body and blood, not some image, but bread and wine. Also, through the mouth of Moses, in the prefiguring of our Redeemer, whose flesh we take for the remission of sins and by whose blood we escape the attack of the destroying angel, the lamb is commanded to be eaten by each household, and the use of venerating or adoring images is utterly forbidden. The psalmist too, in sweet-sounding melody, sang that the bread of angels, namely Christ, is to be eaten by men, and that the makers of images are made like the images they fashion.

units.la: Ipse namque auctor humani generis, qui pro salute nostra carnem nostri causa non est dedignatus accipere, cum & veteris Testamenti terminum & novi, adpropinquante suæ sacratissimæ passionis die salutiferum constitueret initium, & in se lapide angulari duos ex adverso parietes connectens, & secundum Apostolum faciens utraq; unum, accepto pane, benedicto ac fracto, hoc salutare discipulis dedit præceptum: Accipite, inquit, & manducate, hoc est corpus meum: similiter & calicem postquam cœnavit accipiens, dedit discipulis suis, Accipite & bibite: hic est enim calix sanguinis mei novi & æterni testamenti, qui pro vobis & pro multis effundetur in remissionem peccatorum. Hæc quotiescunque feceritis, in mei memoriam facietis. Cum ergo illius evidentissimi & sacrosancti mysterii & per veteris Testamenti mysticas figuras, & per novi institutionem salutiferam & luce clarius teneat ecclesia documentum, adorandarum imaginum huic non est coæquandus insolentissimus usus, qui videlicet non solum fieri non jubetur, verum etiam & per paginam veteris instrumenti interdicitur: & in novi sexte Testamenti non solum non conceditur, verum etiam reprehenditur. Qui enim dixit, Caro mea vere est cibus & sanguis meus vere est potus: &; qui manducat meam carnem & bibit meum sanguinem, in me manet & ego in illo, non dixit; Imago mea vere est vita, & pictura nomini meo adscripta vere est salus, & qui pingit meam similitudinem, & adorat meam imaginem manufactam, in me manet & ego in illo, & qui dixit, Nisi manducaveritis carnem filii hominis, & biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis: non dixit, Nisi depinxeritis meam imaginem, & adoraveritis meam pictoria arte constructam similitudinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Qui igitur dixit, Ego sum panis vivus, qui de cælo descendi, si quis ex ipso manducaverit non morietur, sed habebit vitam æternam, & ego suscitabo eum in novissimo die: & iterum, Sicut misit me vivens pater, & ego vivo propter patrem, & qui manducat me, ipse vivit propter me: & iterum, Hic est verus panis Dei, qui de cælo descendit, & vitam tribuit mundo: qui manducaverit ex eo permanet in æternum, & panis quem ego dabo et caro mea est pro mundi vita. qui credit in me non sitiet neq; esuriet unquam, nihil tale usquam de imagine legitur dixisse: cum videlicet, ut præfati sumus, commemorationem suæ sacratissimæ passionis non in artificium, non in mundanarum artium opificiis, sed in consecratione sui corporis & sanguinis constituerit, nec fidem & confessionem suam in picturis, sed in ore & corde heri decreverit, dicente Scriptura, Corde creditur ad justitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Cum enim dicit, Si manseritis in me & verba mea in vobis manserint, evidentissime ostendit, non imagines in nobis & nos in imaginibus permanere debere, sed nos in se per fidem, & verba sua in nobis per lectionis studium & operis conplementum necessario mansura designat, Paulus quippe Apostolus, vas electionis, corporis & sanguinis Dominici sacramentum non omni sacramento æquiperandum, sed pene omnibus præferendum esse conspicieris dicit, Probet autem se homo, & sic de pane illo manducet, & de calice bibat. Qui autem manducat & bibit indigne, judicium sibi manducat & bibit. Cum ergo tantæ solicitudinis studio probandos eos, qui ad hæc sumenda accedunt, ostendat, & qui neglegenter & indigne ad hæc percipienda conveniunt, tantæ animadversionis telo feriat, nihil huic simile de his, qui imaginum adorationem refugiunt profert, sed è contrario de his, qui male imaginibus utuntur dicit, Et mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis, & cætera. Multum igitur & ultra quam mentis oculo perstringi queat, distat sacramentum dominici corporis & sanguinis ab imaginibus pictorum arte depictis: cum videlicet illud efficiatur operante invisibiliter Spiritu Dei, hæc visibiliter manu artificis: illud consecretur à sacerdote divini nominis invocatione, hæc pingantur à pictore humanæ artis eruditione: illud angelicis manibus in sublime Dei deferatur altare, hæ humanis manibus per artem structæ ad mirantium intuitus ponantur in pariete: per illud peccata remittuntur, per has si incaute abutantur adiciuntur: illud in virtute nec quo crescat habet, nec ullo modo minuitur, hæ pro artificis ingenio in pulchritudine & crescunt & quodammodo minuuntur: illud confirmat nova antiquitas & antiqua novitas, has plerumque corrumpit cariosa vetustas: illud est vita & refectio animarum, hæ cibus tantummodo oculorum: illud ducit per esum ad cælestis regni introitum, hæ rerum gestarum deferunt memoriam per intuitum: illud aboleri ab ecclesia nec in persecutionibus potuit, harum interdum colorem guttarum inluvies abluit: & cum sine illius perceptione nemo salvetur, sine istarum vero observatione omnes qui recta fidei sunt salventur, constat eas à nullo eorum, qui sanæ mentis intellegentiam habent, tanto mysterio æquiperandas. Qui ergo absolute omnes imaginum adorationem carentes anathematis vinculo nituntur obligare, quæriendum ab eis est, quid de Apostolis sentiant, quos nulla docet Catholicæ Scripturæ series imagines usquam adorasse? & tamen nullus fidelium ambigit, non solum eos, sed etiam eorum sequipedas cælestia regna penetrasse: quidve de martyribus, qui à fonte baptismatis confestim per lictorum manus sine adoratione imaginum ad cælestia regna migrabant? quidve de infantibus, qui originali noxa per lavacrum regenerationis abluti, & necdum per corporales sensus aliquid hujusce modi agere valentes, pene ante cælestia regna quàm terrenorum gressuum efficaciam apperere meruerunt? Si omnes imaginum adoratione carentes secundum illorum salsissimam opinionem pereunt, infantes baptismatis unda loti, & corporis dominici edulio & sanguinis haustu satiati, qui necdum imagines adorare valuerunt, & sic è seculo migraverunt, pereunt: & si pereunt, veritatis verbum cassatur dicentis, Sinite parvulos venire ad me: talium est enim regnum cælorum. non autem veritatis verbum infantibus regnum cælorum promittentis cassatur: non igitur pereunt omnes imaginum adoratione carentes.
units.tr: For the very author of the human race, who did not disdain to take on our flesh for our sake, when he was drawing near the day of his most holy passion, and was making the saving beginning of the new covenant as the end of the old, joining the two walls from opposite sides in himself as the cornerstone, and, as the Apostle says, making both one, took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave this saving precept to his disciples: "Take, eat; this is my body." Likewise, after supper, taking the cup, he gave it to his disciples, saying: "Take and drink; for this is the cup of my blood of the new and eternal covenant, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins. As often as you do this, you will do it in remembrance of me." Since, therefore, the Church holds this most evident and sacred mystery with a teaching clearer than light, both through the mystical figures of the Old Testament and through the saving institution of the New, the most outrageous custom of adoring images must not be equated with it. This custom is not only not commanded, but is even forbidden in the pages of the Old Testament; and in the New, the sixth Testament, it is not only not permitted, but is even condemned. For he who said, "My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink; he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him," did not say, "My image is truly life, and a picture inscribed with my name is truly salvation, and he who paints my likeness and adores my image made by hand abides in me and I in him." And he who said, "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you," did not say, "Unless you paint my image and adore my likeness constructed by the art of painting, you will not have life in you." Therefore he who said, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven; if anyone eats of it he will not die, but will have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day," and again, "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me will live because of me," and again, "This is the true bread of God, which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world; whoever eats of it abides for ever, and the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world; he who believes in me will never thirst or hunger," has nowhere said anything like this about an image. For, as we have said, he established the remembrance of his most holy passion not in craftsmanship or in the products of worldly arts, but in the consecration of his body and blood; and he decreed that our faith and confession be fixed not in pictures but in mouth and heart, since Scripture says, "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." When he says, "If you abide in me and my words abide in you," he most clearly shows that we ought not to abide in images, nor images in us, but that he designates us as abiding in him through faith, and his words as necessarily abiding in us through the study of reading and the fulfilment of work. Indeed, the Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, says that the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord is not to be equated with every sacrament, but is to be preferred almost to all: "Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgement on himself." Since he shows that those who come to receive these things must be tested with such earnest care, and strikes with the arrow of such severe rebuke those who come to receive them carelessly and unworthily, he says nothing like this about those who refuse the adoration of images. On the contrary, he speaks of those who misuse images: "They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man," and so on. Therefore the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord differs by far, and more than the mind's eye can grasp, from images painted by the art of painters: the one is effected by the invisible working of the Spirit of God, the other by the visible hand of the artist; the one is consecrated by a priest through the invocation of the divine name, the other is painted by a painter through human skill; the one is carried by angelic hands to the high altar of God, the others are built by human hands and placed on a wall for the gaze of onlookers; through the one sins are forgiven, through the others, if they are carelessly abused, sins are added; the one has no capacity to grow, nor is it at all diminished in its power, whereas the others grow in beauty and in some way diminish according to the skill of the artist; the one is strengthened by a new antiquity and an ancient newness, while the others are for the most part corrupted by decaying age; the one is life and refreshment of souls, the others merely food for the eyes; the one leads through eating into entrance to the heavenly kingdom, the others only bring the memory of past deeds through sight; the one could not be abolished by the Church even in persecutions, whereas the colour of these is sometimes washed away by a stain of water. And since no one is saved without receiving the one, while all who hold the right faith are saved without observing the others, it is evident that none of those who have sound understanding ought to be equated with so great a mystery. Therefore, those who strive absolutely to bind all who lack the adoration of images with the chain of an anathema, must be asked what they think of the Apostles, whom the whole series of Catholic Scripture nowhere teaches to have adored images. And yet no believer doubts that they, and also their followers, entered the heavenly kingdoms. Or what of the martyrs, who passed straight from the font of baptism, through the hands of the executioners, to the heavenly kingdoms without any adoration of images? Or what of infants, who, washed of original guilt through the bath of regeneration, and not yet able to do anything of this kind through their bodily senses, have almost merited to reach the heavenly kingdoms before they could show any effective use of their earthly steps? If all who lack the adoration of images perish, according to their most foolish opinion, then infants who are washed in the water of baptism and fed with the food of the Lord's body and the drink of his blood, who have not yet been able to adore images and have thus departed from this age, perish. And if they perish, the word of truth which says, "Suffer the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven," is made void. But the word of truth promising the kingdom of heaven to infants is not made void. Therefore, not all who lack the adoration of images perish.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXVIII.

units.la: Quanta ratione mysterium dominicæ crucis ab imaginibus distet, quas quidem illi eidem æquiperare contendunt.
units.tr: How far the mystery of the Lord's cross is from the images, which the Papists nevertheless strive to set on a level with it.

units.la: QUot excellentiæ prærogativis, quorve virtutum insignibus mysterium dominicæ crucis manufactis imaginibus, quas illi temere ei æquiperare affectant, emineat, operæ pretium est breviter pandere: quamquam nostra prosecutione prorsus explicari nequeat. Hoc enim vexillo antiquus hostis, non imaginibus, victus est: his armis, non colorum fucis, Diabolus expugnatus est: per hanc, non per picturas, interni claustra destituta sunt: per hanc, non per illas, humanum genus redemptum est. In cruce namque, non in imaginibus, pretium mundi pependit. Illa itaque ad servile supplicium, non quædam imago, ministra extitit: hoc est nostri regis insigne, non quædam pictura quod nostri exercitus indesinenter aspiciunt legiones: hoc est signum nostri imperatoris, non conpagnatio colorum, quod ad prælium nostræ sequuntur cohortes. Non igitur quædam materialis imago, sed dominicæ crucis mysterium est vexillum, quod in campo duelli, ut fortius configamus, sequi debemus: arma, quibus libertatem tueri valeamus: munitio, qua infestantium hostium incursus evitemus. Est enim cassis, qua diabolici ensis impulsio quatitur: est clypeus, qui ad retinendum illius missilibus telis opponitur: est thorax, quo illius spiculorum sive pilorum inlisio ignita fructratur. Hoc est munimen, quo illius flexuosæ fraudis mæandros, & callida machinamenta devincimus, ne vincere valeat tentatos, quos primi hominis tenuit suasione captivos. Per crucis lignum, non per imagines, antiquæ illius sceleris facinus diluitur, quod in protoplasto per ligni esum contractum est. In crucis hamo, non in quadam pictura, criminum auctor captus est, eùm ratione potius quàm dominatione, & justitia potius quàm potentia constrictus prædam conpullus est evomere, quam absorptam jam dudum noscebatur tenere. Non ergo per materiales ab opificibus conditas imagines, sed per crucis mysterium, quæ à Judæis putatur scandalum, à gentibus stultitia, superba seculi & inflata sapientia corruit. Nec per picturam quandam, sed per crucem patuit, quod stultum Dei est quanto sit hominibus sapientius, & quod infirmum Dei est, quanto sit fortius hominibus. Interrogemus igitur doctorem gentium, interrogemus egregium prædicatorem: dicat nobis utrum in imaginibus, an in cruce Christi glorietur. Mihi, inquit, absit gloriari nisi in cruce Domini nostri Jesu Christi, per quem mihi mundus crucifixus est & ego mundo. Dicat etiam utrum ut Deo viveret, imaginibus, an cruci confixus sit. Ego, inquit, per legem legi mortuus sum, ut Deo vivam, Christo confixus sum cruci: vivo autem jam non ego, vivit vero in me Christus. Dicat etiam utrum in intellegendis coloribus fucis, & imaginum formis, aut materiarum qualitatibus, an ad intellegendum quæ sit latitudo crucis & longitudo, sublimitas & profunditum inluminatos cordis oculos habere debeamus. Ut possitis, inquit, comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis quæ sit latitudo & longitudo & sublimitas & profundum. Iex, quendis igitur his tanti prædicatoris verbis nec nostros sensus temere ostentare. care, nec alienos furari debemus, sed hos quos à beato Augustino in libris de doctrina Christiana positos repertimus, nos quoq; ponamus. Latitudo ergo est, transversum lignum quo extenduntur manus: altitudo, quæ à transverso ligno incipiens superius eminet, ubi fuit caput: longitudo verò est, quæ à transverso ligno incipiés usq; ad terram desinit: profundum verò, quod terræ infixum absconditur, ex quo ligno crucis omnis vita sanctorum describitur, qui rollentes crucem suam & mortificantes membra sua quæ sunt super terram, Christum sequuntur: quotum quanto exterior homo corrumpitur, tanto interior renovatur de die in diem, & ipse æternæ requiei gaudentes cum hilaritate bonis operibus insistunt. Hanc hilaritatem significat crucis latitudo in transverso ligno, ubi figuntur manus. per manus enim opus intellegitur: per latitudinem, hilaritas operantis, quia rriftitia facit angustias: porro per altitudinem crucis, cui caput adjungitur, expectatio sempiternæ retributionis de sublimi justitia Dei significatur, ut & ipsa opera bona, non propter beneficia Dei terrena ac temporalia facienda credantur, sed potius propter illud quod desuper sperat fides quæ per dilectionem operatur. Jam vero per longitudinem, qua totum corpus extenditur, ipsa tolerantia significatur, ut longanimes permaneamus: unde longanimes dicuntur, qui tolerant. profundo autem, hoc est, parte illa ligni quæ in terræ abdito adfixa latet, sed inde consurgit omne quod est innet, incorruptibilia indicantur judicia Dei, de quibus occulta ejus voluntate vocatur homo ad partici-pationem rantæ gratiæ, alius sic, alius autem sic. Sed quid tantum in Apostolicis sermonibus inmoramur? quid tantum per ejus sensus latissimos campos evagamur? Veniamus ad Dominum, sedeamus cum Maria ad pedes ejus, audiamus verbum ex ore ejus, audiamus eum in seipso, quem hactenus in Apostolo loquentem audivimus. Audivimus ergo quid de cruce dixerit doctor gentium, audiamus quid dicat creator gentium: audivimus egregium prædicatorem, audiamus rerum omnium conditorem. Siquis, inquit, vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam & sequatur me. O mirum præceptum, ô salutifera exhortatio, ô vitale tonitruum, dixisti ô fons lucis, dixisti ô origo bonitatis, eo quod deponentes vererem hominem cum operibus ejus, denegemus nosmetipsos, tollamusque unusquisque crucem suam, & mundo crucifigamur, mundusque nobis crucifigatur, ut per carnales cruciatus & per mortificationem membrorum nostrorum quæ sunt super terram, vivamus tibi vel potius tu vivas in nobis: & tanto mysterium crucis exrulisti, ut & tu per eam principatus & potestates, & omnem inflationem mundi evacuares, & in crucis nomine, quæ quotidie te secuturis portanda est, ardorem tuæ dilectionis vel cæterarum virtutum emolumenta designares. Dicetjam quod de imaginibus præceptum, quas quidam sacratæ cruci æquiperare niruntur, constituas. Reddite, inquiam, quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, & quæ Dei Deo. Sergo crucem tollere & te, qui per crucem triumphans terrena cœlestibus sociati, sequi, & imaginem Cæsaris Cæsari reddere debemus, non sunt imagines crucis æquiperandæ, non adorandæ, non colendæ, sed huic mundo cum cæteris quæ mundi sunt relinquendæ, & tu solus adorandus, tu solus sequendus, tu solus colendus es qui in unitate subsistantiæ cum patre & Spiritu sancto perpetim regnas.
units.tr: It is worth briefly setting out the many excellences and the distinguished virtues by which the mystery of the Lord's cross stands out above the man-made images, which they rashly strive to equal with it, although it cannot be fully explained in our account. For it was by this banner, not by images, that the ancient enemy was conquered; by these weapons, not by the paint of colours, that the Devil was overcome; through this, not through pictures, were the barred gates of hell broken open; through this, not through those, the human race was redeemed. For it was on the cross, not on images, that the price of the world hung. That, then, was an instrument of servile punishment, not some image; this is the badge of our King, not some painting, which our armies look upon without ceasing; this is the sign of our Emperor, not a patchwork of colours, which our cohorts follow into battle. It is therefore not some material image but the mystery of the Lord's cross that is the banner which we ought to follow into the field of battle, so that we may fight more bravely; it is the arms by which we are able to defend our liberty, and the defence by which we avoid the onslaughts of attacking enemies. For it is the helmet by which the stroke of the devilish sword is turned aside; it is the shield that is set against his missiles to hold them back; it is the breastplate by which the fiery impact of his darts and javelins is rendered vain. This is the fortification by which we overcome the winding labyrinths and crafty devices of his crooked deceit, so that he may not be able to conquer those whom he held captive by the persuasion of the first man. Through the wood of the cross, not through images, the guilt of that ancient wickedness is washed away, which was contracted in the first-formed man by eating of the tree. On the hook of the cross, not on some picture, the author of crimes was caught; for he was constrained, by reason rather than by lordship and by justice rather than by power, to be forced to vomit up the prey which he was known long since to have swallowed and to hold. Therefore it was not through material images fashioned by craftsmen, but through the mystery of the cross, which the Jews think a stumbling-block and the Gentiles foolishness, that the proud and inflated wisdom of this age fell. Nor was it through some picture, but through the cross, that it became plain how much the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and how much the weakness of God is stronger than men. Let us therefore question the teacher of the Gentiles, let us question the eminent preacher: let him tell us whether he glories in images or in the cross of Christ. Far be it from me, he says, to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world. Let him also say whether, that he might live to God, he was crucified to images or to the cross. I, he says, through the law am dead to the law, that I might live to God; I am crucified with Christ on the cross: yet I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Let him also tell us whether, in understanding colours, paints and forms of images, or the qualities of materials, we ought to have our hearts' eyes enlightened, or rather to understand what is the breadth and length of the cross, its height and depth. That you may be able, he says, to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth. Therefore we ought neither rashly to display our own notions from the words of so great a preacher, nor to steal those of others; but let us set down also those which we find laid down by the blessed Augustine in his books On Christian Doctrine. The breadth, then, is the transverse beam to which the hands are stretched; the height is that which rises above from the transverse beam, where the head was; the length is that which begins at the transverse beam and ends at the ground; the depth is that which is hidden, fixed in the earth, and from this wood of the cross the whole life of the saints is described, who take up their cross and mortify their members which are upon the earth and follow Christ, and whose outward man is corrupted the more, the more their inward man is renewed from day to day, and who, rejoicing in the hope of eternal rest, persevere in good works with cheerfulness. This cheerfulness is signified by the breadth of the cross in the transverse beam, where the hands are fixed; for by the hands is understood the work, and by the breadth the cheerfulness of the one who works, since sadness makes for narrowness. Moreover, by the height of the cross, to which the head is joined, is signified the expectation of everlasting recompense from the lofty justice of God, so that the good works themselves are believed to be done not for God's earthly and temporal benefits, but rather for that which faith, which works through love, hopes for from above. Now by the length, by which the whole body is stretched out, is signified endurance itself, so that we may remain long-suffering; whence those are called long-suffering who endure. But by the depth, that is, that part of the wood which lies fixed in the hidden place of the earth, yet from which rises everything that stands, are indicated the incorruptible judgements of God, by which, through his hidden will, one man is called to partake of so great a grace, and another in another way. But why do we dwell so long on the Apostle's sermons? Why do we wander so far over the most broad fields of his meaning? Let us come to the Lord, let us sit with Mary at his feet, let us hear the word from his mouth, let us hear him speaking in himself, whom hitherto we have heard speaking in the Apostle. We have heard then what the teacher of the Gentiles said about the cross; let us hear what the Creator of the Gentiles says: we have heard the eminent preacher, let us hear the Maker of all things. If anyone, he says, wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross and follow me. O wondrous precept, O saving exhortation, O life-giving thunder! You have spoken, O fountain of light, you have spoken, O origin of goodness: so that, laying aside the old man with his deeds, we may deny ourselves, and each of us take up his cross, and be crucified to the world, and the world be crucified to us, so that through fleshly sufferings and through the mortification of our members which are upon the earth, we may live to you, or rather that you may live in us. And you have so exalted the mystery of the cross that through it you might also make void principalities and powers and all the swelling of the world, and by the name of the cross, which must be carried daily by those who follow you, you might signify the fervour of your love and the advantages of the other virtues. Now I will tell you what you command concerning the images, which some strive to set on a level with the holy cross. Render, I say, to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. Since we ought to take up the cross and follow you, who triumph through the cross and join earthly things to heavenly, and to render Caesar's image to Caesar, the images of the cross are not to be set on a level with it, nor worshipped, nor honoured, but are to be left to this world together with the other things that belong to the world; and you alone are to be adored, you alone are to be followed, you alone are to be honoured, who in unity of substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit reign for ever.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: Chapter XXIX.

units.la: Quod præsumptivè & indocte eas Tarasius cum sequacibus suis sacratis vasis æquiperare non formidet.
units.tr: That Tarasius, with his followers, does not hesitate to place images on a level with sacred vessels, rashly and without learning.

units.la: Facile quisque fallitur in minimis qui facillime fallitur in magnis: nec mirandum si brevium & penè invisibilium erroris jaculorum inevitabiliter perferat ictus, qui evitare nequit inmanes & ad evitandum faciles pilorum inpulsus. Quid itaque mirandum est, si factis vasis Tarasius &, cui præfuit, synodus, imagines æquiperare nitatur, cum archæ testamenti Domini, & omnibus quæ intra & quæ circa eam fuisse noscuntur, sive mysterio dominicæ crucis, necnon corporis & sanguinis dominici evidentissimo & nostræ salutis aptissimo sacramento, eas æquiperare conetur. Cujus videlicet in coæquandis his sacris vasis error, cum magno poterat admirari stupore, nisi tanto prævenieretur errore. Quanta ergo excellentia vasa divino cultui mancipata imaginibus eminent, divinæ legis instrumenta demonstrant: cum utique illa præcipiente Domino per Moysen in testimonii tabernaculo condita, & instituente vatuna sanctissimo David per Salomonem in templo Hierosolymis condita atque dicata, & typicorum sensuum archiana significaverint, & in his quæ ad Dei cultum pertinent diuturni ministerii officium gestaverint. Hæ autem salva ratione cherubim, sive boum & leonum, qui non ad adorandum, sed ad rerum futurarum significationem conditi sunt, non solum à quoquam sanctorum non conditæ vel dedicatæ, sed pene cunctorum divinæ legis oraculorum testimoniis usquequaque sunt abdicatæ. Hæcquoque vasa quæ ad peragendā nostræ redemptionis mysteria sancta habet ecclesia, semper sunt fidelibus necessaria, semperque in divino cultu officiosa. In vasis igitur Deo sacrificium, non in imaginibus offertur, in vasis thymiamata, luminaria vel cætera divinis cultibus apta, non in imaginibus dedicantur: in quibus tamen & si quædam imagines sunt, non ideo sunt ut adorentur, aut quasi sine his sacrorum charismatum munus vilescere queat, sed ut pulchrior his imprestis materiatum qualiras fiat: denique in ne imaginibus & lavacri unda, & sacri liquoris unctio percipi, & thymiamata adoleri, & luminanbus loca sancta per ultrari, & corporis & sanguinis dominici consecratio effici potest: sine vasis vero nunquam. Nam & nostræ salutis auctor cum & veteri Testamento terminum, & novo initium poneret, non imaginem, sed calicem accepisse perhibetur, & per prophetam Dominus non ait, Mundamini qui fertis imagines, sed, Mundamini qui fertis vasa Domini. Babylonicus ergo rex non oblicujus injuriam imaginis corripitur, sed quia vasa divinis cultibus officiosa, quae abavus de Judaea adlata in delubris suorum posuerat idolorum, religionis siquidem & reverentiae causa, inter comessationes delubris eximi, & ubibus humanis exhibita peregrinari censuerit, & praesago miraculi stupore attonitus, quae sibi ventura essent audivit, & inter hostiles cuneos vitae pariter regniq; jacturam sentiit. Qui prophetas scit, ea, quae dicimus cognoscit.
units.tr: Anyone who is most easily deceived in great matters is easily deceived in small ones too, and it is no wonder if he inevitably takes the blows of brief and almost invisible errors, since he cannot escape huge missiles and the thrusts of spears, which are easy to avoid. So what is surprising if Tarasius and the synod over which he presided strive to place images on a level with the vessels, when they try to put them on a level with the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and with all the things known to have been in and around it, whether with the mystery of the Lord's cross, or with the body and blood of the Lord, the most evident sacrament and most suited to our salvation? Indeed, the error in equating these sacred vessels would have been cause for great astonishment, had it not been anticipated by a still greater error. How greatly the vessels dedicated to divine worship surpass images is shown by the instruments of the divine law: those vessels were made in the tabernacle of the testimony at the command of the Lord through Moses, and were made and dedicated in the temple at Jerusalem by Solomon, at the instruction of the most holy prophet David. They signified the mysteries of the types and have borne the office of continual ministry in all that pertains to the worship of God. Setting aside the cherubim, or the figures of oxen and lions, which were made not for adoration but to signify things to come, no saint has not only not made or dedicated such things, but almost all the testimonies of the divine oracles have everywhere rejected them. Likewise, the vessels which the Church holds for performing the sacred mysteries of our redemption are always necessary to the faithful and always serviceable in divine worship. So the sacrifice is offered to God in the vessels, not in the images; incense, lamps and the other things fit for divine worship are dedicated in the vessels, not in the images. Yet even if there are some images among them, they are not there to be adored, nor as though the office of the holy gifts could lose its value without them; rather they are there so that the material may be made more beautiful by these adornments. Indeed, without images the washing of baptism and the anointing with holy oil can be received, incense can be burned, holy places can be lit with lamps, and the consecration of the body and blood of the Lord can be effected; but never without vessels. For the author of our salvation, when he set the end to the Old Testament and the beginning to the New, is said to have taken not an image but a cup; and the Lord through the prophet does not say, "Be clean, you who carry images," but "Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord." Therefore the Babylonian king was rebuked not for an injury to an image, but because he thought fit to take out of the temples, during his feasting, the vessels that served divine worship, which his ancestor had brought from Judea and placed in the temples of his idols, and to display them profanely among human uses out of a sense of religion and reverence; and, astonished by the stupor of a foreseen miracle, he heard what was to come upon him, and at the same time he felt the loss of his life and kingdom among the enemy's ranks. Whoever knows the prophets knows what we are saying.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Contra eos qui dicunt, Sicut divinae Scripturae libros, ita imagines ob memoriam ve- nerationis habemus, nostrae fidei puritatem observantes.
units.tr: Against those who say that, just as we have the books of divine Scripture, so we have images as aids to the memory of veneration, while keeping the purity of our faith.

units.la: Sihicerror quo divinae Scripturae libris imagines aequiperare nituntur, caeteris eorum erroribus conparetur, quamquam erga se sit magnae enormitatis, aliis vero conparatus, quibus eas & Domini, & corporis & sanguinis Dominici sacramento, & crucis mysterio aequiperare nisi, minor proculdubio reperitur, praesertim cum necillis, necistis rite aequiperari possint: cum videlicet solius Dei altissimo archaeoque ac praesago judicio sinerante secula praedestinatae, & per momenta seculorum ad humanae salutis emolumenta clementi exhibitione concessit, habeantque auctores sanctos ac venerabiles viros virtutum lampadibus & miraculorum insignibus coruscantes, vel ipsum Dominum, qui corporis & sanguinis sui mysterium sive crucis sacramentum nostrae salutis concessit: illae vero & gentilium auctorum vanitate prolatae sint, & nullam salutis exhibitionem, nullam sacramenti alicujus mortalibus praerogativam adducant, sed oculis tantummodo vivant, per quos quasi per quosdam legatos gestarum rerum memoriam cordibus mandent. Eo tempore quo Moyses cum populo Dei in eremo morabatur, & praecipiente Domino sacrae legis Trinam & caeremoniarum sacratissimos ritus populo tradebat, & genus humanum ad divinum cultum eruditionem informabat, Cecrops quidam rex Atheniensium daemonico inlectus veneno, rudium mentes ad imaginum simulacrorumque & ad vanorum Deorum culturas extavit: & quo pore populus Dei mandata vitae percepit, hocille inliciendis animabus perpetuae mortis pocula diuturni erroris seminaria praeparavit: de quo est illud Sedulii, Quos letale malum quos vanis dedit curis, Attica Cecropei serpit doctrina veneni.
units.tr: If the error of those who strive to set images on a level with the books of divine Scripture is compared with their other errors, it is certainly of great enormity in itself. But when it is compared with the others, by which they try to equate images with the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood and with the mystery of the cross, it is without doubt found to be the lesser, especially since those things cannot be rightly equated with these either. For the books of Scripture alone were predestined by the most high, ancient and prescient judgment of God, who permitted them to exist from the ages and, through the moments of the ages, granted them by a gracious manifestation for the benefit of human salvation. They have as authors holy and venerable men, shining with the lamps of virtues and the marks of miracles, or the Lord himself, who granted the mystery of his body and blood, or the sacrament of the cross, for our salvation. Images, on the other hand, were brought forth by the vanity of pagan authors. They offer no manifestation of salvation and no special privilege of any sacrament to mortals, but only living to the eyes, through which, as through certain messengers, they commit the memory of past deeds to the hearts. At the time when Moses was dwelling in the wilderness with the people of God, and at the Lord's command was delivering the sacred law, the threefold ceremonies and the most holy rites to the people, and was instructing the human race in the knowledge of divine worship, a certain Cecrops, king of the Athenians, enticed by a demonic poison, drew the minds of the untaught to images, likenesses and the worship of vain gods. And at the time when the people of God received the commands of life, he prepared, to entice souls, the cups of perpetual death and the seedbeds of lasting error. Of him is that line of Sedulius: "Those whom deadly evil has given to empty cares, the Attic doctrine of the Cecropian poison creeps on.

units.la: Unde magnum usus, qui a gentilium traditionibus inolevit, sacrae legis libris aequiperare debet nec valet: quia in libris non in imaginibus, doctrinae spiritualis eruditionem discimus. Nam ait Paulus Apostolus, Quaecumque picta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam picta sunt: sed ait, Quaecumque scripta sunt ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum ipsam habeamus Deum. Necait, Omnis pictura, sed Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad erudiendum, ut perfectus sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum instructus. Quinquagesimo denique die agni immolationem, & maris rubri transitum, Dominus in montem Synai descendens, legem picatam, sed scriptam Moysi dedit, & in tabulis lapideis non imagines, sed apices qui indices verum signa verborum esse perhibentur, tradidit. Idem quoq; Moyses originem mundi non pinxit, sed scribendo edocuit, & omnia quae per spiritum propheticae sive de praeteritis cognovit, ut ea quae mundi principio, de creatione hominis, de diluvio, sive de caeteris Patriarcharum per ordinem promulgavit, sive quae praesenti sibi tempore fiebant, ut ea quae per Balaam, sive Balaac, sive pterosque, qui illi absentes erant, agebantur, conperit, sive ea quae de futuris Spiritus sancti flamine intellexit, ut est illud quod de praevaricatione populi Judaeorum, sive de eorum captivitate vel de adventu Christi dixisse legitur: in quinque libris adnotans non pingendo, sed scribendo post futuris Domino imperante mandavit: nec de eo scribitur, Accepit picturas, sed, Accepit libros Moyses & restituit in aures populi verba libri. Unde & Apostolus scribit, Lecto enim omni mandato legis a Moyse universo populo: & post pauca. Ipsum quoq; librum & omnem populum aspersit, ut nolle possimus legislatorem non fucatis picturis, sed saluberrimis Scripturis usum fuisse. Josue etiam tuccessor ejusdem Moysi qui cum populo Dei Jordanen sicco pede transiit, & Cananitidis gentis prostratis regibus reprobatis: terram filiis Israhel forte divisit, typumq; mediatoris Dei & hominum gestit: qui translatis veteris legis ritibus per baptisma populum Dei ad terram repromissionis adducit, & prostratis vitiorum sive aeriarum potestatum tyrannis, patriae caelestis fidelibus praedia infert cuncta, quae tempore sibi vel populo cui praerat, cōtigerunt, scribendo potius quam pingendo memoriae posteritatis mandavit. Samuel quoq; magnae sanctitatis & excellentiae vir, qui matri petenti potest magnam orationem instantiam divino munere colatus est, & ab ipsis cunabulis in Domini tabernaculo militia prophetarum militavit, & in deliniendis regibus exemplar extitit, historias Judicum sive Ruth vel etiam Regum usque ad David non imaginibus, sed apicibus praenotavit. Et post hunc per David res suo tempore gestae conscriptae, sive caeterorum regum historiae, aut per reges, aut per prophetas, qui tunc temporis fuere, conscriptae, usque ad Hieremiam, qui omnes regum historias in unum colligens, Malachim vero tum edidit ad nostram usque memoriam, non per picturam, sed per Scripturam, delatae sunt. Prophetae etiam singuli, qui libros habent, prophetias suas post futuras saeculis profuturas, non in picturis, sed Scripturis constituere. Unde & Daniel non in coloratis figuris, sed in libris intellexit numerum annorum.
units.tr: Hence the great custom that has grown up from pagan traditions ought to be, and cannot be, set equal to the books of the sacred law, because in books, not in images, we learn the instruction of spiritual doctrine. For the Apostle Paul says: "Whatever things have been painted, they have been painted for our teaching"; but he says: "Whatever things have been written, they have been written for our teaching, so that through the patience and comfort of the Scriptures we may have God himself." He does not say "every painting," but "every Scripture divinely inspired is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for instruction, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work." Finally, on the fiftieth day after the sacrifice of the lamb and the crossing of the Red Sea, the Lord, descending onto Mount Sinai, gave Moses the law, not painted but written, and delivered it on tablets of stone, not as images but as letters, which are said to be the true signs of words. Moses also did not paint the origin of the world, but taught it by writing; and all the things he learned through the prophetic Spirit, both about the past, such as the beginning of the world, the creation of man, the flood, and the other patriarchs, which he set forth in order, and about what was happening in his own time, such as what was done through Balaam, or Balak, and the others who were absent from him, and what he understood about the future by the breath of the Holy Spirit, such as what is read to have been said about the transgression of the Jewish people, their captivity, or the coming of Christ, these he recorded in five books, not by painting but by writing, commanded by the Lord, and transmitted them to posterity. Nowhere is it written that Moses "received pictures," but that he "received books and restored the words of the book to the ears of the people." Hence the Apostle also writes: "For when every commandment of the law had been read by Moses to all the people," and a little later: "He sprinkled both the book itself and all the people." So we cannot be willing to say that the lawgiver used not painted embellishments but most wholesome Scriptures. Joshua too, the successor of the same Moses, who crossed the Jordan with the people of God on dry feet, and after the kings of the Canaanite nation were overthrown and rejected, divided the land by lot among the sons of Israel, and bore the type of the Mediator of God and men, who, by transferring the rites of the old law through baptism, leads the people of God into the land of promise, and, when the tyrannies of vices and of the aerial powers are overthrown, brings the faithful into the heavenly fatherland with all their estates, committed to the memory of posterity by writing rather than by painting all that happened in his time or to the people he led. Samuel also, a man of great holiness and eminence, who was obtained by divine gift through the earnest prayer of his mother, who from his cradle served in the Lord's tabernacle as a soldier of the prophets, and who was an example in anointing kings, recorded in writing, not in images, the histories of the Judges, of Ruth, and even of the Kings down to David. After him, the deeds done in David's time were written down, as were the histories of the other kings, whether written by the kings or by the prophets who were then living, down to Jeremiah, who gathered all the histories of the kings into one and then published them; and Malachi too has been handed down to our own memory, not through painting but through Scripture. Each of the prophets who have books set down their prophecies, to profit ages to come, not in pictures but in Scriptures. Hence Daniel too understood the number of years not in coloured figures but in books, the number of years for which the people of God were to remain in Babylonian captivity. For he says: "I, Daniel, understood in the books the number of the years, of which the word of the Lord came."

units.la: notum norum quo populus Dei in captivitate Babylonica detinen deberet. Aitenim, Ego Danihel intellexi in libris numerum annorum, in quo factus est sermo Domini. David quoque sanctissimus prophetarum, qui de Christi incarnatione, nativitate, passione, morte, resurrectione, gloria, regno, sicut cæteris patribus in ejusdem Domini secundum humanitatem genealogia prælatus est, ut videlicet idem Dominus filius David nuncupetur, ita etiam cæteris uberius apertiusque cantavit: ita in persona Christi dixisse legitur, in capite libri scriptum est de me. Non enim ait pictum, sed scriptum: nec in capite parietum sive tabularum, sed in capite libri. In capite itaque libri Geneseos, qui utique cunctorum librorum caput est, ita scribitur, In principio creavit Deus cælum et terram: in principio, id est, in filio. ipse enim Judæis interrogantibus quis esset, respondit, Ego sum principium, quod et loquor vobis. Poteritque et jam & in hoc verso primi Psalmi principium intelligi, qui de Christi incarnatione adoritur, & per o-
units.tr: David also, the most holy of the prophets, who was foremost among the other fathers in prophesying of the incarnation, nativity, passion, death, resurrection, glory and kingdom of Christ, and of the genealogy of the same Lord according to his humanity, so that the same Lord is called son of David, sang of these things more abundantly and more openly than the rest. Thus it is read that he said in the person of Christ: "In the head of the book it is written concerning me." He did not say "painted" but "written," nor "at the head of the walls or of the tablets," but "at the head of the book." So in the head of the book of Genesis, which is certainly the head of all books, it is written: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." In the beginning, that is, in the Son. For when the Jews asked him who he was, he himself answered: "I am the beginning, who also speak to you." Also in this verse of the first Psalm the beginning can already be understood, which speaks of the incarnation of Christ and through

units.la: ctavam speciem definitionis quam Dialectici καθ' ἀφαίρεσιν τῆς ἐναντίας, id est, per privantiam contrarii ejus quod definitur, Christum non abisse in consilio impiorum, id est, detestabiles cogitationes quas sibi genus humanum peculiariter vindicat, non habuisse demonstrat: et in via peccatorum non stetit, id est, actus vitiosæ conversationis penitus evitasse, sed in mundo venientem mundi vitia immaculata conversatione tranfisse prædicat: nec eum in cathedra pestilentiæ sedisse, id est, doctrinas abhominabiles, quæ pestilentis dogmatis venena dissiminant, sed mundi vulnera medicabili prædicatione sanasse declarat: eumque tribus illis modis quibus humanos constat provenire errores, cogitatione, facto videlicet & dicto, modis omnibus caruisse commemorat, declaratque eum nec impium fuisse, qui in Deum peccasset, eo quod nequaquam in Deum peccaverit, qui semper utique voluntatem patris fecerit: nec peccatorem, qui in se deliquerit, qui utique ait, Venit enim princeps mundi hujus, et in me non invenit quicquam: nec pestilentem, qui numquam proximum depopulatus fit atque læserit, quum hoc venit, ut salvum faceret quod perierat. Hæc enim figura apud Grammaticos pro eo, quod singula verba singulis quibusque apte clausulis ibi subjunguntur,
units.tr: the eighth kind of definition, which the dialecticians call by negation of the contrary (kath' aphairesin tēs enantias), that is, by denying the contrary of what is defined [καθ' ἀφαίρεσιν τῆς ἐναντίας], shows that Christ did not "walk in the counsel of the wicked," that is, did not have the detestable thoughts which the human race claims peculiarly for itself; and that he "did not stand in the way of sinners," that is, that he completely avoided the deeds of a sinful life, but proclaims that, coming into the world, he passed through the vices of the world with an unstained conduct; nor that he "sat in the seat of pestilence," that is, taught abominable doctrines which scatter the poisons of a pestilent dogma, but declares that he healed the wounds of the world by a healing preaching. He also recalls that he was free of all those three ways by which, as is well known, human errors arise: namely by thought, by deed and by word. He declares that he was neither impious, as one who had sinned against God, because he never sinned against God, who always did the will of the Father; nor a sinner, as one who had sinned against himself, for he says: "For the prince of this world comes, and finds nothing in me"; nor a pestilent man, who never ravaged or injured his neighbour, since he came "to save what had perished." For this figure, which the grammarians name by the term homoioteleuton, is the one in which single words are attached, each to its own suitable clause,

units.la: & pro eo quod dictiones plures simili modo finiuntur, ut, abiit, fletit, sedit, ὁμοίως λευτον nuncupatur. Merito igitur hic Psalmus, qui est caput libri, & in cujus capite de Christo scriptum est, titulo caret: sive quia capiti nostro quod est Christus, nihil præponi debet, qui est verbum, principium: sive quia hic Psalmus cæterorum Psalmorum tituli & , utrita dixerim, præfationis locum tenet. quoniam quamquam alii Psalmi de Christo multa dicant, nullus tamen de ejus, quæ fuit in terris conversatione tam evidenter loquitur: qui cum eum per octavam speciem definitionis, perea quæ non fecit, beatum definierit, protinusad secundam nihilominus definitionis speciem, quæ ab artigraphia ... id est, notio dicitur, convolavit: & per ea quæ egit quasi per quædam signa in noticiam devocata non quid fit, sed quid egit specialiter indicavit dicens, Sed in lege Domini fuit voluntas ejus, & cætera. Quia vero paulo longius capitis libri dulcedine captiā causa secedentes evagati sumus, reducamur ut ad propositum redeamus. Veniamus nunc ad Evangelia, videamus utrum Evangelistæ, an ipse Dominus imaginum, an scripturarum fecerint mentionem. Ait enim Evangelista, Sicut scriptum est in libro sermonum Esaiæ Prophetæ. Scriptum dixit, non pictum, & in libro, non in quadam ma-
units.tr: And as to the figure whereby several words end in the same way, as in abiit, fletit, sedit, it is called homoeoteleuton [ὁμοιοτέλευτον]. Rightly, therefore, this Psalm, which is the head of the book, and in whose head it is written concerning Christ, has no title: either because nothing should be placed before our Head, who is Christ, the Word, the beginning; or because this Psalm holds the place of the titles of the other Psalms and, as I may say, of a preface. For although other Psalms say much about Christ, none speaks so plainly of his conversation on earth. When it has declared him blessed by the eighth kind of definition, through what he did not do, it nonetheless at once flies to the second kind of definition, which is called notio, that is, notion; and through what he did, as though through certain signs brought to notice, it indicates not what he is but specifically what he did, saying, But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and so on. But since we have been drawn a little too far afield by the sweetness of the head of the book, let us be led back so that we return to our purpose. Let us now come to the Gospels and see whether the Evangelists, or the Lord himself, made mention of images or of Scriptures. For the Evangelist says, As it is written in the book of the words of the prophet Isaiah. He said "written," not "painted," and "in a book," not "in some material

units.la: teria & idem Dominus ac redemptor noster dum antiqui hostis machinamenta destrueret, sive in plurimis præ​dicationis locis, scripturarum, non picturarum exempla protulisse perhibetur: & dum multitudinem in adulterii reatu comprehensam, ejus, stipante caterva ablata fuisset, & Pharisæi illius deceptionis plenus syllogismi, quia secularium literarum magistris ... id est, inevitabilis, nuncupatur, communiter cavitans, qui nec crudelis esset sanguinisque effusionem consentiens, qui per severitatem legis adulteram lapidare jussisset, nec legis transgressor peccatorumque fautor, qui contra vetustatem eandem indemnem dimittere jussisset, sed justus & manuetus gravissimæ eos proponens telo, utpote cœlestis Philosophus perculisset, illis sua quibusque facinora audire timentibus alterpolt alterum abeuntibus, digito in terra non pinxisse, sed scripsisse perhibetur: ut cujus digito in lapide propter significandam duritiam cordis Judæorum lex scripta est, ipsius nihilominus digito in terra cordis gentilium, quæ divini verbi femina accipiens fructus dignos suo conduxit quamdiu affert, Evangelica lex scriberetur, quatenus & per lapideas tabulas rigor veteris Testamenti & duritia Israelitice gentis, & per terram quæ digito Domini scripta est gentilium ad credendum & ad fructus adferendos mollia corda sive suavitas Testamenti novi innueretur. Apostoli denique, de quibus per Prophetam dictum est, Quam pulchri sunt pedes, qui adnunciant pacem, & prædicant salutem, qui euntes ibant & flebant mittentes semina sua, qui per multas videlicet tempestates tribulationes divini verbi semina jaciebant, & cum exultatione venturi sunt ad illud genus examen, portantes manipulos, populos videlicet per suam prædicationem ad fidei documenta conversos, non imagines, sed epistolas ad diversas mundi partes destinasse leguntur: nec per picturas genus humanum ab idolorum cultibus ad veræ fidei puritatem revocavere, sed per Scripturas quibus redemptor sensum aperuit, non ut intellegerent picturas, sed Scripturas. Scriptum est enim, Tunc aperuit illis sensum, ut intelligerent Scripturas. In Evangelio quoque legitur, Multa quidem et alia signa fecit Jesus in conspectu discipulorum suorum, quæ non sunt scripta in libro hoc. Hæc autem scripta sunt, ut credatis quoniam Jesus est Filius Dei, et ut credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ejus. Joannes quoque, qui de archano dominici pectoris necarca hauriens fluenta, cœlestia pocula arrendibus cordibus propinavit, dum Cæsareis jussibus in Patmos insula relegatus dominici calicis gustum
units.tr: And the same Lord and our Redeemer, while he was destroying the devices of the ancient enemy, is said to have brought forward examples of Scripture, not of pictures, in many places of his preaching. And when a multitude caught in the guilt of adultery had been brought before him, with a crowd gathered around her, the Pharisee, full of that deceptive syllogism which the masters of secular letters call inevitabilis, that is, inescapable, sought to trap him with a dilemma: he would be either cruel and consenting to the shedding of blood, if he ordered the adulteress stoned by the severity of the law, or a transgressor of the law and a patron of sinners, if he ordered her to be dismissed unpunished against that same ancient law. But he, just and gentle, proposed to them a most weighty missile, as a heavenly Philosopher, and struck them down. When they, fearing to hear their own crimes, went away one after another, he is said not to have painted with his finger in the earth, but to have written, so that, just as by his finger the law was written on stone to signify the hardness of the heart of the Jews, so by the same finger in the earth of the hearts of the Gentiles, which, receiving the seeds of the divine word, bring forth worthy fruit for as long as they bear it, the Gospel law might be written. Thus through the stone tablets the rigour of the Old Testament and the hardness of the Israelite people were indicated, and through the earth written by the finger of the Lord, the soft hearts of the Gentiles, ready to believe and to bear fruit, or the sweetness of the New Testament. Finally, the Apostles, of whom it was said through the Prophet, How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, and preach salvation, who went forth weeping and casting their seed, who indeed, through many storms and tribulations, sowed the seeds of the divine word, and who came with rejoicing to that harvest, bearing their sheaves, that is, peoples converted through their preaching to the teachings of faith, are read to have sent not images but letters to the various parts of the world. Nor did they call the human race back from the worship of idols to the purity of the true faith through pictures, but through the Scriptures, by which the Redeemer opened their understanding, not that they should understand pictures but Scriptures. For it is written, Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures. It is also read in the Gospel, Many other signs also Jesus did in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. John too, who, drinking the streams of nectar from the secret of the Lord's breast, offered heavenly cups to willing hearts, when he was exiled by Caesar's orders to the island of Patmos and received a taste of the Lord's cup promised to him beforehand, and, full of heavenly mysteries, heard or saw certain secrets as the Lord revealed them, was ordered to write these in a book, not to paint them

units.la: G stum ante sibi promissum acciperet, & cœlestibus plenus mysteriis secreta quædam Domino revelante audiret seu cerneret, scribere ea in libro, non pingere jussus est. Et in septem Ecclesiis unam sanctam Catholicam sive Apostolicam Ecclesiam septiformis gratiæ Spiritu plenam non pingendo, sed scribendo admonuit. Dictum enim illi supernæ voces tonitruo est, Quod vides scribe in libro, & mitte septem Ecclesiis. Unde datur intelligi, non pictúras, sed Scripturas ad nostræ fidei erudition-em esse concessas. Quàm ergo sit incautum, quamque à ratione remotum dicere, Sunt divinæ Scripturæ libros, ita imagines ob memoriam venerationis habemus, facile intellegete potest quisquis divinarum Scripturarum cognitionem habet.
