In illis inveniuntur arma, quibus contra adversa consligatur, quibus vitia reprimantur, quibus virtutes erigantur, quibus gulæ concupiscentia vigiliis & conpunctione cordis reprimatur, quibus fornicatio contritione cordis & corporis aflictione, orationum instantia, laboris exercitio, metuque supplicitorum vel amore æternæ patriæ refrenetur: quibus invidia amore fraternæ dilectionis & cœlestis regni desiderio, quod non nisi concordes adipiscuntur, superetur: quibus ira modestissimæ patientiæ gravitate & acumine rationis & æquanimitatis munere frägatur: quibus avaritia eleemosynis & spe æternæ retributionis calcetur, quibus tristitia fraternis allequiis, assiduis lectionibus vel orationibus pellatur; quibus arrogantia metu amittendarum virtutum, cum qua illæ haberi non possunt, & accessus vanæ gloriæ, qui est virtutum inimicus secluditur: in quibus superbia metu diabolicæ ruinæ & exemplo humilitatis Christi conterntur. In illis inveniuntur strumenta fructus justitiæ, id est, charitas, gaudium, pax, patientia, longanimitas, bonitas, benignitas, fides, modestia, continentia. In illis invenitur medela, qua nec sapientes in sua sapientia gloriantur, nec fortes in sua fortitudine consisi periclitentur, nec simplices sive infirmi sua impossibilitate deieantur: qua nec lætos nimia lætitia extollat, nec tristes nimia animi contritio afflicit: qua nec divi-tes rerum opulentia elatos efficiat, nec pauperes rerum indigentia frangat. In illis invenitur norma perquam instruitur qualiter prælati erga subditos, & subditi erga prælatos agere debeant, qualiter congia diligantur, qualiter secularia consilia prudenti deliberatione tractentur, qualiter patria defendutur, hostes pellantur, extranearum domesticarum; rerum administratio habeatur, & ut cuncta breviter conpleƈtar, in illis & animæ perpetuus cibus, & præsentis vitæ d oƈtrina & sapientia quæ decorent vitæ, & vitæ perpetuæ documenta continentur. Est enim thesaurus nullo bono carens, omnibus bonis redundans: ad quem quisquis devotus accedit, quicquid fideliter quærit, feliciter se adquisisse gaudet. Elto mundanæ sapientiæ & seculares scholæ quemquam amor obleƈtat, accedat ad divinæ legis armaria, quæ sapientes mundi sicut meritorum celsitudine, ita etiam tempore præcedit, & liberalium studiorum profunditates, quas scit cognovisse, & quas nescit invenire se gaudeat. Illic invenietur & ornatus loquutionis decorem, etymologias nominum, schematum varietates, tropicas perplexiones, quibus beatus Augustinus ait, Sciant autem literati modus omnium loquutionum, quos Grammatici Græco nomine tropos vocant, auctores nostros usos fuisse: quos tamen tropos, id est, modos loquutionum, qui noverunt agnoscunt in literis sanctis, eorumque scientia ad eas intellegendas aliquantulum adjuvantur: inveniet etiam historias, metra, quæ omnia proprie artis grammaticæ sunt. Sed dicet fortassis aliquis: Non illic metrorum scansiones & temporum certas dimensiones invenio: cognoscat multa in dominis Scripturis metra, plures rhythmos esse, sed translatio linguæ non eadem sinit habere tempora intervalla in peregrina, quæ habentur in propria: cum tamen eosdem sensus easdemque rerum proprietates habeat, quia & si quis nobis debitor aurum reddat, non multum distat cum non unius sint ne-tæ cum illo quod acceperat, si tamen unius sit ponderis uniusque fulgoris. Nam ut beato Hieronymo Hebraicæ linguæ peritissimo docente didicimus, quædam divinæ Scripturæ Hebræo daƈtylo spondeoque, quædam anapæsto, quædam vero iambo juxta artis rigorem decurunt. Illic etiam inveniet nitorem & copiam eloquentiæ, genera causarum & status: illic exordia quibus benevoli, docili vel adtenti auditores fiunt: illic narrationes aperras & breves, causas etiam & longas, quæ non nisi Spiritu sancto referante panduntur: illic conclusiones quibus proprietas rerum monstratur: argumentationes quibus animi audientium concitantur ad implenda ea quæ dicuntur: illic leges sive sententiæ, illic magna granditer, parva summisse, mediocria temperate promuntur: illic prosopopœiam, ethopœiam vel omnes figuras locutionum quæ à rhetoribus traduntur: invenient, & plures illis angustiores, quæ percepisse se gaudebit ad quas nec grammaticorum nec rhetorum schola pertingere potuit: illic quoque mvenie siagogas quæ ad inquirendas res lectorem utiliter introducunt, categorias quæ prædicamentorum utilitate ad investigandas res excellunt: definitiones vel modos syllogismorum, quæ subtili indagatione ea de quibus dubitatur adfirmant: topica quæ dum sint fontes sensuum & origines distionum, omnibus communitet grammaticis videlicet, poetis, oratoribus vel etiam Philosophis argumenta præstant: quæ non solum scholastico, sed etiam vulgari & tumultuoso sermoni perpetuo cohærent. Nam quamquam tumultuosus, quamquam vulgaris sit sermo, si pro quibus libet vitæ utilitatibus proferatur, ad topica veniet: per ea quasi per quædam magisteria locales regu-lis quibus evagari, aut non possit, aut non debeat, invenier: in illis etiam terminum, qui sine sensus dispendio transgredi difficile sit, se reperisse cognoscet. Et ut cuncta breviter dicam, omnis sermo, nisi ad topica venerit, indefinitus proculdubio remanebit. Illic ἀπὸ ἐρωτήσεως, quarum scrupulosis semitis & laciniosis diverticulis profunditas inveniendorum sensuum dubiorum-que affirmatio invenitur, quibusque syllogismorum vel cæterarum argumentationum silva exoritur: quæ omnia propriæ artis sunt Dialeƈticæ. Illic in numeris per arithmeticam artem archana scientiam profunditatesque reperiet: quoniam, dicente eadem Scriptura, Omnia in mensura & numero & pondere Deus fecit. Illic etiam musicæ non solum consonantias instrumentaque, quibus pleriq; sanctorum patrum usi sunt, sed etiam repertorem inveniet.
units.tr: taste of the cup promised to him, and in the seven Churches he admonished the one holy, Catholic, or Apostolic Church, full of the Spirit of sevenfold grace, not by painting but by writing. For that heavenly voice spoke to him like thunder, What you see, write in a book, and send it to the seven Churches. Hence it is to be understood that not pictures but Scriptures were given for the instruction of our faith. How rash, then, and how far from reason it is to say, As we have the books of the divine Scriptures, so we have images for the memory of veneration, anyone who knows the divine Scriptures can easily understand. In them are found the weapons by which one fights against adversity, by which vices are restrained, by which virtues are raised up; by which the lust of the belly is curbed by vigils and compunction of heart; by which fornication is restrained by contrition of heart and mortification of body, by persistence in prayer, by the exercise of labour, and by fear of punishment or love of the eternal fatherland; by which envy is overcome by love of brotherly affection and desire for the heavenly kingdom, which only the concordant obtain; by which anger is quenched by the gravity of most modest patience, by the keenness of reason, and by the gift of equanimity; by which avarice is trampled down by almsgiving and hope of eternal reward; by which sadness is driven away by brotherly consolations, constant reading, and prayers; by which arrogance is shut out by fear of losing the virtues, without which they cannot be held, and by the approach of vainglory, which is the enemy of the virtues; in which pride is crushed by fear of diabolical ruin and by the example of the humility of Christ. In them are found the instruments of the fruit of righteousness, that is, love, joy, peace, patience, longanimity, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, and self-control. In them is found a remedy by which the wise are not made to glory in their wisdom, nor the strong put at risk by trusting in their strength, nor the simple or weak cast down by their incapacity; by which the joyful are not lifted up by excessive gladness, nor the sad crushed by excessive distress of mind; by which the rich are not made proud by their abundance of goods, nor the poor broken by their want. In them is found the rule by which it is taught how prelates ought to act towards subjects, and subjects towards prelates, how the people are to be loved, how worldly counsels are to be handled with prudent deliberation, how the homeland is to be defended, enemies driven off, and the administration of foreign and domestic affairs carried on; and, to sum up briefly, in them are contained both the perpetual food of the soul, and the teaching and wisdom that adorn the present life, and the lessons of eternal life. For it is a treasure lacking no good and overflowing with all goods; whoever approaches it devoutly rejoices that whatever he faithfully seeks he has happily obtained. Even if love of worldly wisdom and the secular schools should attract anyone, let him approach the armoury of the divine law, which precedes the wise of the world not only in the eminence of its merits but also in time, and let him rejoice in the depths of the liberal studies, which he knows he has learned and which he does not know how to find. There he will find both the adornment and beauty of speech, the etymologies of names, the varieties of figures, and the tropical turns of which the blessed Augustine says, Let the learned know that our authors used the whole manner of speech which the Grammarians call tropes in Greek; and those who know these tropes, that is, the modes of speech, recognise them in the holy letters, and by their knowledge are somewhat helped to understand them. He will also find histories and metres, which all belong properly to the art of grammar. But perhaps someone will say: "I do not find there the scansion of metres and the fixed measures of times." Let him know that there are many metres in the divine Scriptures and several rhythms, but the translation of one language does not permit the same time intervals in a foreign tongue as are found in the original; yet it keeps the same meanings and the same properties of things, just as if someone who owes us gold repays it, it makes little difference whether the coins are not of the same mint as what he received, provided they are of the same weight and the same lustre. For, as we learned from the blessed Jerome, most skilled in the Hebrew tongue, some passages of the divine Scriptures run in the Hebrew dactyl and spondee, some in the anapaest, and some in the iamb, according to the strictness of the art. There too he will find the brilliance and abundance of eloquence, the kinds and states of causes: there the openings by which the hearers are made well-disposed, docile, or attentive; there plain and brief narratives, and also long ones, whose causes are not unfolded except by the Holy Spirit's relating; there the conclusions by which the nature of things is shown; the arguments by which the minds of the hearers are stirred to carry out what is said; there the laws or maxims; there great things are set forth grandly, small things humbly, and middling things moderately. There too are prosopopoeia, ethopoeia, and all the figures of speech that are handed down by the rhetoricians. They will find also, and more narrow ones, which he will rejoice to have perceived, and which the school of neither grammarians nor rhetoricians could reach. There also he will find the isagogues, which usefully lead the reader into the investigation of things; the categories, which excel in the usefulness of the predicaments for investigating things; the definitions and the modes of syllogisms, which by subtle inquiry affirm those things about which there is doubt; the topics, which, while they are the sources of meanings and the origins of words, furnish arguments common to all, namely grammarians, poets, orators, and even philosophers, and which cling perpetually not only to scholarly speech but also to the common and turbulent discourse. For although speech may be turbulent and common, if it is put forth for whatever useful purposes of life, it comes to the topics; by them, as by certain teachers, he will find the limits within which one either cannot or ought not to wander, and he will recognise that he has found a boundary which it is difficult to cross without loss of sense. And, to say everything briefly, every discourse, unless it comes to the topics, will undoubtedly remain indefinite. There, by ἀπὸ ἐρωτήσεως [by questions], in whose scrupulous paths and intricate byways is found the depth of discovering hidden meanings and of affirming doubtful points, and from which a forest of syllogisms and other arguments arises; all these belong properly to the art of Dialectic. There, in numbers, he will discover through the art of arithmetic the hidden knowledge and depths, since, as the same Scripture says, God made all things in measure and number and weight. There too he will find music, not only the consonances and instruments which many of the holy Fathers used, but also its inventor.

units.la: Inveniet quoque rerarum situs dimensionesque, quæ proprie artis sunt geometricæ. Necnon & quorundam sideru cursus, & positiones, & temporum varietates, mensium annorumq; sive horarum curricula, diem etiam & causam conditionis siderum, quæ proprie artis sunt astronomicæ, illic reperisse se studiosus quisq; cognoscet. Sed dicit forte aliquis, Nec nomina principaliter disciplinarum, nec uniuscujusq; disciplinæ lingillatim partes, nec uniuscujusq; partis membra lingillatim in sacris literis inveniuntur. quibus breviter respondendum est, Omnia in scripturarum sanctarum amplissimis pratis per partes inveniri posse, quæ artigraphi in suorum hortorum areolis posuere: inveniuntur, inquam, virtute sensuum, non in promulgatione verborum, in radicum profunditatibus, non in foliorum lapsibus. Sic enim in profunditate divinarum scripturarum liberales artes ab studiosis quibusque cernuntur, sicut vina in vitibus, segetes in seminibus, frondes in radicibus, fructus in ramis, arborumq; magnitudines seu situ cötemplantur in nucleis. Est plane divina Scriptura verax, est fixa, est casta, est cælestis magisterii instrumentum, & æterna prædicatio purissimo nitens eloquio, est lux mortalium, dicente Propheta, Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum Domine, & lumen semitis meis: est vivax & mori nescius, dicente Apostolo, Vivus est Dei sermo & efficax & penetrabilior omni gladio anceps, & pertingens usque ad divisionem animæ ac spiritus: est tenebrarum discussio, Salomone adtestante, quia it, Lucerna est mandatum legis & lux vitæ & increpatio & disciplina: de quo per Esaiam dicitur, De nocte spiritus meus vigilat ad te Deus, quia lux præcepta tua sunt super terram. Semper enim vitalia jubet, noxia prohibet, tenebras removet, cælestia persuadet. Est, inquam, fons æthereo de margine scaturiens, de quo quanto amplius hauritur, tanto minus expenditur, & quanto in plures partes derivatur, tanto amplius in sensibus argumentatur: est pecunia martupium, de quo nec ea quæ dantur amittuntur, nec diminutionem assiduus dandi usus adfert, sed quanto inde amplius dandi devotione eicitur, tanto illud magis magisque completur. Nihil igitur horum quæ perstrinximus, sive his similium, quæ brevitatis studio prætermisimus, in imaginibus, ô imaginum adorator, ô rerum insensatarum cultor invenire posse te constat, quæ dum his omnibus meritorum prærogativis careant, dolendus potius quam mirandus es, quur eas divinæ Scripturæ libris, in quibus tot bona reperiuntur, æquiperare affectes? Tu qui fidei tuæ puritatem in imaginibus conservare te dicis, supplex eis adstare memento cum thymiamatibus: nos præcepta Domini solerti indagatione perquiramus in divinæ legis codicibus. Tu luminaribus perlustra picturas: nos frequentemus divinas Scripturas. Tu fucatorum venerator esto colorum: nos veneratores & capaces sensuum archanorum. Tu depictis demulcere tabulis: nos divinis mulceamus alloquiis. Tu figuris rerum insta, in quibus nec visus, nec auditus, nec gustus, nec odoratus, nec tactus est: nos in sensibus divinæ legi quæ est inreprehensibilis, in qua testimonium Domini, justitiæ sive judicia ejus in veniuntur. Quæ singula pulchrè Psalmographus per septimam definitionis speciem quam dialectici καταμετάφορα, id est, per translationem vocant, eo quod rem aliquam brevi prænomine quæ sit osteudit, sub senarii numeri perfectione, qui juxta arithmeticæ experientiam disciplinæ perfectus habetur, eo quod suis partibus dimensus, & his iterum in unum redactis, ablataque ullo detrimento aut incremento sui in se redit: ita definivit dicens, Lex Domini inreprehensibilis, convertens animas, testimonium Domini fidele, sapientiam præstans parvulis: Justitiæ Domini rectæ lætificantes corda, præceptum Domini lucidum illuminans oculos: Timor Domini sanctus permanens in seculum seculi, judicia Domini vera justificata in semetipsa, desiderabilia super aurum & lapidem pretiosum multum, & dulciora super mel & favum. Quæ omnia ideo senarii numeri perfectione decorantur, quia quamquam quodammodo inter se distare videantur, singulatamen ad perfectionem legis, qua viri sancti perfecti efficiuntur, pertinent. E quibus sicut uno subtracto sextus numerus minime adimpletur, ita si aliquid detrahatur, perfectionis integritas mutilatur. Lex enim inreprehensibilis est, quia perfecta veritate consistit, quæ per Salvatorem non reprehensa, sed potius probatur impleta: Non veni, inquit, legem solvere, sed adimplere. Et ut nolle possemus Evangelium quoque legem Domini esse, & duobus testamentis novo videlicet & veteri legem consistere, adjunxit, Convertens animas: quoniam veteris Testamenti pagina rigorem habet inreprehensibilis severitatis: novi vero convocationem & mansuetudinem, per quam errantes corrigantur, & ad Christi gratiam animarum conversio fiat. Testimonium ergo Domini fidele, quoniam quæcumque pollicetur Deus, plenissima veritate conplentur. Quod testimonium sapientiam præstat parvulis, non utique superbis nec tumida se elatione jactantibus, sed his parvulis de quibus Apostolus dicit, Nolite pueri effici sensibus, sed malitia parvuli esse. Dat itaque testimonium pater, dat filius, dat & Spiritus sanctus: & licet sint unius essentiæ & naturæ, ita etiam in reddendo testimonio sublimes. De patre in Evangelio legitur, quod testimonium de filio perhibuerit: de filio autem Apostolus ad Timotheum scribit, Præcipio tibi coram Deo, qui vivificat omnia, & Christo Jesu, qui testimonium reddidit sub Pontio Pilato: de Spiritu quoque sancto idem Apostolus dicit, Nam & ipse Spiritus testimonium perhibet Spiritui nostro. Justitiæ itaque Domini rectæ ideo dicuntur, quia non aliter cognoscitur tecisse quam docuit, nec aliud illi in ore, aliud in opere est. Lætificantes sunt corda, quia justorum mentes æternorum præmiorum collatione demulcent: quorum præmiorum perceptione confisus erat ille, qui dicebat, De reliquo repositta est mihi corona justitiæ, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illa die justus judex. Nam præceptum Domini recte lucidum dicitur, sive quia à patre luminum procedit, sive metonymicè, quòd lucidos efficiat. Inluminat etiam oculos, non carnales, quos nobiscum animantia communes habere noscuntur, sed interiores, qui divini muneris jubare spiritaliter perlustrantur. Timor autem Domini sanctus permanens in seculum seculi, mixta est cum pavore dilectio, quae usu seculari reverentia nuncupatur. In omni ergo sanctitate versatur, qui suum judicem & timere cognoscitur & amare. Inter timorem namque Domini & formidinem humanam hoc interest, quod formido humana cum tempore commutatur: de ea, ni fallor, dictum est, Perfecta charitas foras mittit timorem. Timor autem Domini a proprio statu nulla temporali conversione mutatur: sed in idipsum sinceritate bonae conscientiae perseverat. Porro judicia Dei, quae & vera & justificata in semetipsa a prophetas describuntur, mandata sunt ejus, quae in veteri & novo Testamento conscripta habentur, quia revera ex judicio sunt prolata. Vera, inquam, metonymice & justificata, quia veraces & justificatos observatores suos efficiunt. Inter judicium tamen Dei & judicia ejus hoc interest, quod judicium numero singulari illud generale examen est; judicia vero ejus numero plurali sacramenta sunt quae in duobus testamentis, non in imaginibus nec in picturis inveniuntur: quae idem Psalmographus per schemata quod Graece αὐξησις, id est, augmentum, eo quod paulatim ad superiora concrescat, ita expressit dicens; Desiderabilia super aurum & lapidem preciosum multum & dulciora super mel & favum. Sicut enim lapides preciosi auro praeferuntur in precio, ita nimirum auro & lapidibus preciosis mel & favum dulcedine praefertur. Per hanc enim figuram idem Psalmista susceptorem suum, gloriam etiam & exaltantem caput suum Dominum esse decantat dicens, Tu autem Domine susceptor meus es, gloria mea & exaltans caput meum: Et Apostolus ait, Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? tribulatio an angustia? an persecutio? an fames? an nuditas? an periculum? an gladius? in qua per augmenta nominum rerum magnitudo sensim crescit. Cui quamquam vicina sit figura, quae Graece κλίμαξ, Latine gradatio dicitur, quando positis quibusdam gradibus, sive in laude, sive in vituperatione semper adcrescit, ab ea tamen plurimum distat: quod αὐξησις sine ulla iteratione nominum, rerum procurat augmenta, κλίμαξ vero posterius verbum, quod est in primo commate positum, in sequenti membro modis omnibus repetit: sic quoque velut catena aliud semper in alio nectitur, ut est illud Apostoli, Scientes quod tribulatio patientiam operatur, patientia probationem, probatio spem. Spes autem non confundit: item illud, Nam quos praescivit & praedestinavit, eos & vocavit; & quos vocavit, illos & justificavit; quos autem justificavit, illos & glorificavit. Nam si forte tu amator vel pomis adorator imaginum interiore pectoris rancore submurmurans dicens, Quid necesse est tantum per schemata evagari? cognoscesca nobis amabiliora imaginibus sive pictis tabulis tuis esse, & ideo tantum in illis evagatos esse. Has etenim dulcedines, has refectiones in Scripturis sive in scripturarum schematibus, nos sive ceteros scripturarum amatores reperire cognoscere, quas tu sive socii tui in figuris, neq; in tabulis, in quibus cordis tui putitatem servare te dicis, penitus non reperies.
units.tr: He will also find there the arrangement and measurements of things, which properly belong to the art of geometry. Likewise, any diligent student will recognise there the courses and positions of certain stars, the variations of times, the cycles of months, years and hours, and even the day and cause of the constitution of the stars, which properly belong to the art of astronomy. But perhaps someone will say: the names of the disciplines as such, the separate parts of each discipline, and the members of each part, are not found by name in the Holy Scriptures. To this we must briefly reply that everything can be found in the broad meadows of the Holy Scriptures, in the parts which the artists placed in the little beds of their gardens. They are found, I say, by the power of the senses, not in the mere utterance of words; in the depths of the roots, not in the falling of the leaves. For in the depth of the divine Scriptures the liberal arts are discerned by all earnest students, just as wines are in the vines, crops in the seeds, leaves in the roots, fruit on the branches, and the size and position of trees are contemplated in the kernels. The divine Scripture is certainly true, it is fixed, it is pure, it is the instrument of heavenly teaching, and an eternal proclamation shining with the purest eloquence. It is the light of mortals, as the Prophet says, Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, O Lord, and a light unto my paths. It is living and knows not death, as the Apostle says, For the word of God is living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, and piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit. It is the dispelling of darkness, as Solomon bears witness, for he says, The commandment is a lamp, and the law is light, and reproofs of instruction are the way of life; of which it is said through Isaiah, With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early, for when thy judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness. For it always commands what is life-giving, forbids what is harmful, removes darkness, and persuades to heavenly things. It is, I say, a fountain springing from the heavenly border, from which the more is drawn, the less is spent, and the more it is channelled into many parts, the more it is multiplied in the senses. It is money of the very best kind: what is given away is not lost, and constant use of giving does not diminish it, but the more it is poured out by the devotion of giving, the more and more it is filled up. Nothing of these things that we have touched upon, nor anything similar which we have passed over for the sake of brevity, is known to be found in images, O worshipper of images, O cultivator of insensible things. Since they lack all these prerogatives of merit, you are to be pitied rather than admired, for why do you wish to equal them with the books of divine Scripture, in which so many goods are found? You who say that you preserve the purity of your faith in images, remember to stand before them as a suppliant with incense; we, with careful inquiry, seek out the precepts of the Lord in the codices of the divine law. You examine pictures with lamps; we frequent the divine Scriptures. You be a venerator of painted colours; we are venerators and receivers of the hidden senses. You soothe yourself with painted panels; we soothe ourselves with divine words. You dwell upon figures of things, in which there is neither sight, nor hearing, nor taste, nor smell, nor touch; we dwell upon the senses of the divine law, which is blameless, in which the testimony of the Lord, his righteousness and his judgments are found. The Psalmist beautifully set forth each of these points through the seventh species of definition, which the dialecticians call katametaphora, that is, translation, because it shows a thing by a short name that is put in place of it. He did so under the perfection of the number six, which according to the experience of arithmetic is held to be a perfect number, because it is measured by its own parts, and when these are again brought together into one, it returns to itself without any loss or increase of itself. He defined it thus, saying, The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring for ever: the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. All these are adorned by the perfection of the number six, because although they seem in some way to differ from one another, each one nevertheless pertains to the perfection of the law, by which holy men are made perfect. As, when one is taken away from these, the sixth number is by no means completed, so if anything is taken away, the integrity of perfection is maimed. For the law is blameless, because it consists in perfect truth, which, far from being found fault with by the Saviour, is rather shown to be fulfilled: I came not, he says, to destroy the law, but to fulfil it. And so that we might not be unwilling to hold that the Gospel too is the law of the Lord, and that the law consists in the two testaments, namely the new and the old, he added, converting the soul: because the page of the Old Testament has the strictness of blameless severity, while the New has the call and gentleness by which the erring are corrected, and the conversion of souls to the grace of Christ takes place. Therefore, the testimony of the Lord is sure, since whatever God promises is completed in the fullest truth. This testimony makes wise the simple, not indeed the proud, nor those who boast with swollen elation, but those simple ones of whom the Apostle says, Brethren, be not children in understanding, but in malice be ye children. Thus the Father gives testimony, the Son gives testimony, and the Holy Spirit also gives testimony; and although they are of one essence and nature, they are equally sublime in giving testimony. In the Gospel it is read of the Father that he bore witness concerning the Son; and of the Son the Apostle writes to Timothy, I charge thee in the sight of God, who quickeneth all things, and of Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession; and of the Holy Spirit too the same Apostle says, The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit. The righteousnesses of the Lord are therefore called right because he is not known to have acted otherwise than he taught, nor is there one thing in his mouth and another in his work. They rejoice the heart, because they soothe the minds of the righteous with the bestowal of eternal rewards; and in confidence of these rewards that man was confident who said, Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day. The commandment of the Lord is rightly called bright, either because it proceeds from the Father of lights, or by metonymy, because it makes people bright. It also enlightens the eyes, not the fleshly eyes, which are known to be shared with the living beasts, but the inner ones, which are spiritually illumined by the radiance of the divine gift. But the fear of the Lord, which is clean and endures for ever, is a love mingled with awe, which in ordinary usage is called reverence. Therefore he who is known both to fear and to love his judge dwells in all holiness. For between the fear of the Lord and human dread there is this difference: human dread changes with time. Of that, I think, it was said, Perfect love casteth out fear. But the fear of the Lord is never changed from its proper state by any temporal alteration; rather it persists in the same sincerity of a good conscience. Further, the judgments of God, which the prophets describe as both true and righteous altogether, are his commandments, which are contained in the Old and New Testaments, because they have truly come forth from judgment. They are true, I say, by metonymy, and righteous, because they make those who observe them true and righteous. Yet between the judgment of God and his judgments there is this difference: judgment in the singular is that general examination; his judgments in the plural are the sacraments which are found in the two testaments, not in images or pictures. These the same Psalmist expressed through a figure which in Greek is called auxesis, that is, augmentation, because it grows gradually toward higher things, saying, More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold, and sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. For as precious stones are preferred to gold in value, so honey and the honeycomb are preferred to gold and precious stones in sweetness. By this figure the same Psalmist sings that the Lord is his upholder, his glory, and the lifter up of his head, saying, But thou, O Lord, art my upholder, my glory, and the lifter up of my head. And the Apostle says, Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? In this figure the magnitude of the things grows gradually through the augmentation of the names. Although a figure that in Greek is called klimax, and in Latin gradatio, is closely related to it, when, with certain steps set in place, the sense always increases, whether in praise or in censure, it nevertheless differs greatly from it: because auxesis brings about the increase of things without any repetition of names, whereas klimax repeats in every way in the following clause the last word that stood in the first clause, and so, like a chain, one thing is always linked to another. Such is the saying of the Apostle, Knowing that tribulation worketh patience, and patience experience, and experience hope; and hope maketh not ashamed; likewise that, For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate, and whom he did predestinate, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified. But if perhaps you, a lover and adorer of images, murmuring with inner rancour of the heart, say, What need is there to wander so far through figures? know that your pictures and painted panels are more lovable to us, and that therefore you have wandered only among them. For we, and other lovers of the Scriptures, find these sweetnesses and these refreshments in the Scriptures, or in the figures of the Scriptures; these you will not at all find in your figures, nor in your panels, in which you say you preserve the purity of your heart.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Quod contra dominicae vocis imperium faciunt hi, qui parentes suos anathematizant: & si secundum eorum opinionem praedecessores eorum haeretici fuere, isti ab haereticis geniti, docti: & consecrati sunt: sive de non judicandis hiis, qui de seculo recesserunt: vel quantum istorum error a parentum errore differentiat, cum videlicet illi imagines frangere, isti adorare censuerint.
units.tr: That those who curse their parents act against the Lord's command. If, by their own reckoning, their predecessors were heretics, and these men were born, taught and consecrated by heretics, then they should not judge those who have departed this life. Also, how far the error of these men differs from the error of their parents, since the parents thought images should be broken and these men think they should be adored.

units.la: DENIQUE illi qui eas corpori & sanguini dominico coexquare praesumunt, tanto illarum instigantur amore, ut etiam parentes suos, qui eas sprevisse noscuntur, anathematizare no dubitent, errorem errori nectentes: cum videlicet & illis incongruam & inordinatam exhibeant adorationem, & his vel a quibus per carnis materiam propagari sunt, vel hos per quorum consecrationem & baptismi sacramentum & cetera charismata sumplere, inopportunam ingerant excecrationem. Nam si secundum illorum vesaniam omnes imaginum adorationem carentes haeretici sunt, constat majores eorum, qui eas non adoravere haereticos fuisse: qui si haeretici fuere, neque consecrationes faciendi, neq; manus imponendi potestatem habuerunt: qui si hanc non habuerunt, hi qui ab eis hanc se accepisse putant, neque consecrationem, neque manus impositionem habent. Item si prodecessores eorum, ut illi ajunt, anathematis colligatione digni fuerunt, ligandi solvendiq; potestatem non habuerunt: quam si non habuerunt omnia quaecunq; ab eis in ecclesia gesta sunt cassanda sunt: si omnia abnuenda sunt, gradus & ordinationes abnuenda sunt: si igitur prodecessores illorum anathematis colligatione digni fuerunt, istorum gradus & ordinationes cassanda sunt. Non enim schismaticis & anathematis vinculo conligatis ligandi solvendiq;, sed idoneis & Catholicis potestatem a Domino lege gimus esse concessam. Parentibus interea honorem impendendum, non solum legalis, Prophetica & Apostolica, verumetiam Evangelica admonitio docet, dicente Domino, Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam. Qui enim & per paginam veteris instrumenti, & per sui corporis praesentiam hoc salutare praeceptum contulit, idem Moisaico ore promulgavit dicens, Benedictus, qui honorat patrem suum & matrem suam; & e contrario, maledictus, qui non honorat patrem suum & matrem suam. Unde perpendendum est & magnopere animadvertendum, quanta sit arrogantia, quantaeque temeritatis & ut ita dicerim, sceleris, parentes anathematizare, si ille maledictioni subjacet, qui eos convincitur non honorare. Nam cum lex dicat, Non reveles turpitudinem patris tui, & Apostolus, Filii obedite parentibus vestris in Domino, isti utrique praecepto reluctari videntur: cum nec turpitudinem celare, nec honorem minuunt impendere.
units.tr: FINALLY, those who presume to place images on a level with the Lord's body and blood are so driven by love of them that they do not hesitate to curse even their parents, who are known to have scorned them, thus tying error to error. They offer an unfitting and disorderly adoration to images, and they inflict an unseasonable curse on those through whom they were propagated by the matter of the flesh, and on those through whose consecration they received the sacrament of baptism and their other gifts. For if, according to their madness, all who lack the adoration of images are heretics, it follows that their elders, who did not adore images, were heretics. And if they were heretics, they had no power to consecrate or to lay on hands; and if they had no such power, then those who think they received it from them have neither consecration nor the laying on of hands. Likewise, if their predecessors, as they say, deserved to be bound by the anathema, then they did not have the power of binding and loosing. And if they did not have that power, everything done by them in the Church must be annulled; and if everything must be renounced, then grades and ordinations must be renounced. So if their predecessors deserved to be bound by the anathema, the grades and ordinations of these men must be annulled. For we hold that the power of binding and loosing was granted by the Lord not to schismatics bound by the chain of anathema, but to the fit and the Catholic. Meanwhile, honour must be paid to parents, as not only the Law, the Prophets and the Apostles teach, but also the Gospel admonition, the Lord saying, Honour your father and your mother. He who conferred this saving precept both through the page of the Old Testament and through his own bodily presence is the same who proclaimed it with the mouth of Moses, saying, Blessed is he who honours his father and his mother; and on the contrary, cursed is he who does not honour his father and his mother. Hence we must weigh carefully and consider how great is the arrogance, how great the rashness and, so to speak, the wickedness, of cursing parents, if he is subject to the curse who is shown not to honour them. For since the Law says, Do not uncover the nakedness of your father, and the Apostle says, Children, obey your parents in the Lord, these men seem to resist both precepts, since they neither hide their shame nor render honour.

units.la: Matth.15. Exod.20. Deut.5. Exod.21. Matth.15. Marc.7. Prov.20. Levit.18. Ephes.6. impedere. Sacri igitur canones de non contemnendis parentibus omni occasione seclusa, hanc viden-tur protulisse sententiam; QUICUNQUE FILII A PARENTIBUS SUB PRÆTEXTU DIVINI CULTUS ABSCEDUNT NEC DEBITAM REVERENTIAM DEPENDUNT ILLIS, ANATHEMA SINT. Si vero hi, qui eis debitam reverentiam non impendunt, anathematizantur, quopuras damnationis vinculo, qui eos anathematizant connectantur? Salubertimus namque à sanctis patribus ecclesiis traditus usus est, pro defunctorum spiritibus Dominum deprecari, quem nos cum sancta omni Catholica & universali ecclesia amplectentes, non solum pro nostrorum parentum, verumetiam pro amicorum fidelium, qui nobis in pace dominica præcesserunt, spiritibus, clementissimam Domini pietatem exposcimus. Cui venerandæ & ecclesiasticæ constitutioni non mediocriter contraire videntur, qui defunctorum parentum Spiritus non orationibus adjuvare, sed anathematis vinculo conligare nituntur: & qui orare etiam pro inimicis Apostolicæ eruditionis documento jubentur, pro suis hoc facere parentibus reluctantur. Nos nostris secundum ecclesiasticum usum pes orationum & eleemosynarum instantiam deposcimus veniam: illi suis per inanium conciliorum conventus exoptant pœnam. Nos nostris quietem exposcimus per missarum solennia: illi suis ingerunt convicia per mordinata concilia. Nos nostrorum memoriam facimus in oratione, illi suis anathemas iaciunt cum quadam abdicatione. Nos nostrorum Spiritus requie potiri oramus in sinu Abrahæ: illi suorum optant damnari animas cum Arrio, Sabellio, Dioscoro, Nestorio, & Eutychete. Nos nostros conlocari postulamus parentes inter agmina beatorum: illi suos inter obstinatas turbas hæreticorum. Quæ cum ita se habeant, constat eos duplex in hac parte patrare deliquium, cum & parentibus honorem derogent contra dominicæ vocis imperium, & contra Apostoli sententiam his, qui à seculo migraverunt, temerarium conentur inferre judicium. Quod non sit ergo temere judicandum de his, qui jam è seculo migraverunt, vel de rebus ad Deum solum pertinentibus, hæc est beati Pauli sententia. Nemo nostrum sibi vivit, & nemo sibi moritur: sive enim vivimus Domino vivimus, sive morimur Domi-no morimur: sive enim vivimus, sive morimur Domini sumus. In hoc enim Christus resurrexit à mortuis, ut & vivorum & mortuorum dominetur. Tu autem quid judicas fratrem tuum, aut quare spernis fratrem tuum? omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Dei. Scriptum est enim, Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, quoniam mihi flectet omne genu, & omnis lingua confitebitur Deo. Itaq; unusquisq; nostrum pro se rationem reddet Deo. Non ergo amplius judicemus: sed hoc judicare magis, ne ponatis offendiculum fratri vel scandalum. De qua re etiam sanctæ ecclesiæ Romanæ antistes Anastasius Imperatori sic perhibetur scripsisse; Ne quod sit in hoc offendiculum in ecclesia, quod facere non possumus, de his qui jam transierunt judicare conemur, observandum esse tranquillitas tua cognoscat. Qua ergo nec à filiis parentes inhonorandi, nec à viventibus mortui temere judicandi sunt, divinatum scripturarum paginis prolatum est. Nunc mentis oculo sollicite intuendum est, quantum in supra memoratarum imaginum abolitione vel veneratione filiorum errorà parentum errore dissentiat: cum utrimq; sibi & illorum & illorum error repugnare non desinat. Illi enim eas convellendas atq; comtemnendas esse censuerunt ab ecclesia perpetua abdicatione: isti eas non solum habendas, verum nicitam venerandas studeant supplici adoratione. Illi eas mancipavere crepitantibus ignibus: isti honorant odoriferis thymiamatibus. Illi eas effugiebant etiam cernere: isti non ce_ssant amplecti. Illi effodere ad ornamentum ecclesiæ ab antiquis constitutas in parietibus: isti nuper conditas oblatas perlustrant luminaribus. Illi eas studebant prorsus abominari: isti sanciunt omnino osculari. Illi anathematizabant habentes: isti è contrario non adorantes. Quæ duo mala cum alterutrum sibi contraria sint, & à recto tramite remota, restat nobis ut viam regiam secundum Apostolum gradientes, neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram declinemus: ut nec cum illis prorsus abolendas dijudicemus, nec cum istis adorandas decernamus: sed solum Deum adorantes, & ejus sanctos venerantes secundum antiquam patrum & ecclesiasticam traditionem eas in ecclesia in ornamento & memoria rerum gestarum, si libet, habeamus, & cum justitia hinc severitatem, illinc adulationem contemnentes: cum prudentia hinc verfitiam, illinc hebitudinem declinantes: cum temperantia hinc libidinem, illinc insensibilitatem spernentes: cum fortitudine, hinc timiditatem, illinc audaciam abicientes; cum sanctis patribus, qui eas in ornamento solummodo esse ecclesiæ siverunt, istis-hinc ado-rantibus, illis hinc abominantibus postpositis, viam mandatorum Domini teneamus, qualiter ad eum qui est via, veritas & vita, ipso opitulante pervenire valeamus.
units.tr: Matth. 15. Exod. 20. Deut. 5. Exod. 21. Matth. 15. Mark 7. Prov. 20. Lev. 18. Eph. 6. Therefore the sacred canons, with every occasion removed, seem to have laid down this sentence on not despising parents: WHOEVER SONS DEPART FROM THEIR PARENTS UNDER THE PRETEXT OF DIVINE WORSHIP AND DO NOT PAY THEM DUE REVERENCE, LET THEM BE ANATHEMA. But if those who do not pay them due reverence are anathematized, with what kind of bond of condemnation are those who anathematize them bound? For the custom handed down by the holy Fathers to the churches is wholesome: to pray to the Lord for the spirits of the dead. We, embracing this together with the whole holy, Catholic and universal Church, ask the most merciful goodness of the Lord not only for the spirits of our parents but also for those of our faithful friends who have gone before us in the Lord's peace. Those who try to bind the spirits of their dead parents with the chain of anathema rather than help them with prayers seem to act in no small measure against this venerable and ecclesiastical constitution; and those who are commanded, by the teaching of the Apostle, to pray even for enemies, resist doing this for their own parents. We, according to ecclesiastical custom, seek pardon for ours by the urgency of prayers and almsgiving; they wish punishment on theirs through the gatherings of empty councils. We seek rest for ours through the solemnities of the Masses; they heap reproaches on theirs through disordered councils. We make mention of ours in prayer; they hurl anathemas at theirs with a certain renunciation. We pray that the spirits of ours may enjoy rest in the bosom of Abraham; they wish the souls of theirs to be damned with Arius, Sabellius, Dioscorus, Nestorius and Eutyches. We ask that ours be placed among the host of the blessed; they place theirs among the obstinate crowds of heretics. Since these things stand thus, it is clear that they commit a double fault in this matter: they both take honour away from parents, against the command of the Lord, and against the Apostle's sentence they attempt to pass rash judgment on those who have departed from the world. That we should not rashly judge those who have already departed this life, or matters that pertain to God alone, is the sentence of the blessed Paul: None of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; or whether we die, we die to the Lord. Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. But you, why do you judge your brother? or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of God. For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God. Therefore let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you put no stumbling block or offence before a brother. Concerning this matter, Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, is said to have written to the Emperor: Let your tranquillity know that, lest there be in this a stumbling block in the Church, we must not try to judge those who have already passed away, which we are not able to do. Thus it has been shown from the pages of the Scriptures that parents are not to be dishonoured by their children, nor the dead rashly judged by the living. Now with the eye of the mind we must carefully look at how far the error of the sons differs from the error of the parents in the abolition or veneration of the images mentioned above, since each side's error never ceases to contradict the other's. For the former thought that they should be torn down and despised, with perpetual abdication by the Church; the latter not only wish them to be kept but eagerly venerate them with suppliant adoration. The former handed them over to crackling fires; the latter honour them with fragrant incense. The former fled even from looking at them; the latter never cease to embrace them. The former dig out of the walls those set up by the ancients for the ornament of the Church; the latter go over newly made offerings with lamps. The former strove utterly to abominate them; the latter insist that they be kissed in every way. The former anathematized those who had them; the latter, on the contrary, those who do not adore them. Since these two evils are contrary to each other and far removed from the straight path, it remains for us, following the royal way according to the Apostle, neither to turn to the right nor to the left: neither to judge that they must be utterly abolished with the former, nor to decree that they must be adored with the latter. Rather, adoring God alone and venerating his saints, let us keep them in the Church, if it pleases, as ornament and as memorial of deeds done, according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers and of the Church; and, rejecting on one side severity without justice and on the other flattery, avoiding on one side rashness and on the other dullness without prudence, despising on one side lust and on the other insensibility without temperance, casting off on one side timidity and on the other audacity without fortitude; and, with the holy Fathers, who allowed them to remain in the Church only as ornament, setting aside on the one hand those who adore and on the other those who abominate, let us keep to the way of the commandments of the Lord, so that, by his help, we may be able to come to him who is the way, the truth and the life.

units.tr: END OF BOOK II. PREFACE TO BOOK III.

units.la: CONSTAT hujus nostri operis stilum sive in superioribus, qui jam Deo annuente digesti sunt libris, sive in præsenti in cujus inceptionis adornmur articulo, sive etiam in eo quem postmodum Domino opitulante digesturi sumus, adversus eorum insaniam vigilare, qui quamquam diversis temporibus diversisq; voluntatib. synodos, aut ut abdicari, aut ut adorari imagines in ecclesia censeant, adiolent adgregari. Et quoniam illius insaniæ Scriptura, quam inani desiderio Septimæ synodi vocabulo censeri ambiunt, proprierum sensuum erroris, quasi membris concreta, & divinæ legis cestimonionum inconpetenter libi adhibitorum comminatibus quasi quibusdam pinnis cernitur esse sufful ta: libuit nobis in præcedentibus libris pinnarum subsidia ei, quibus incassum fulciri arbitratur, demere: in sequentibus vero eam vanorum conpage membrorum, quibus subsistere se posse suspicatur, destituere: ut præcedentes ab ea pinnarum remigia auferant, sequentes ejus artus fiuftratim dirimant: præcedentes cam volatu, sequentes privent gressu: ut videlicet spiritalis intellegentiæ & divini eloquii pinnis, quibus enormiter vehi putabatur, abscissis, & propriis sensibus à quibus violenter in aliis peregrinari compellebatur restitutis, & Catholicæ fidei fortis & inexpugnabilis pugni impulsione, qua satis vacuarum & ratione carentium adsertionum acervis, & congruis sensibus & divinorum apicum testimoniis carens, omnibus appareat enervata, quæ non ab omnibus creditur esse digesta: quoniam quidem dum suorum intetat auctorum in sublime laudis insigne efferre, prosperitatem rerum domesticarum civili non formidat certamine perturbare: dumq; pestiferum ad quamundam rerum interdictam cives adorationè provocat, civium in se domestica arma territat, & spiculorum ictus quibus & libertas debuit tueri & hostili globo obnixi in indigenas, pro dolor, compellit intorqueri. Hanc igitur non versutis cavillationibus, non forensi facundia, non procul à causa vagatibus loquutionum phaleris, non lepore lenocinioso coturni, non callidæ exsequutionis nodosis argumentationibus, pertinenter enervare decrevimus, sed puræ ac simplicis orationis ambitu divinorum eloquiorum tenacibus nervis concreto, & sanæ sobriæque doctrinæ eloquentia colorato, qui elationis ostentatione carens ecclesiæ sanctæ potius profectus amator, quam suæ vel nostræ fit ventosæ laudis sectaror. Quoniam igitur in præsentis libri textu, in quo nunc adoriri nos liquet, illorum sententias discutientes, qui aliter quædam quam à sanctis patribus tradita sunt in sua synodo posuere, de fide quodammodo disputarum sumus, ordo exposcit ut primum nostræ fidei fundamentum jaciamus, hoc videlicet de quo ait Apostolus, Fundamentum enim aliud ponere nemo potest præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Cujus venerandæ fidei sinceritatem, mox ut sicut corde credimus, ore protulerimus, & tanti fundaminis firmitate futuri operis primordia munierimus, liberius nostra fabrica surgens rectius solidiusve struatur, & illorum sicubi minus recte minusve solide surrexerit, facilius deiiciatur. Quia ergo primùm nos munire nostraq; firmare, & post contra adversa confligere, & oppositis resistere debemus, non solum sacrarum literarum perdocemur documentis, sed etiam ipsius Romani auctoris eloquii monemur institutis, qui ait, Argumentandum est ita ut primum nostra firmemus, deinde adversa confringamus.
units.tr: It is agreed that the aim of this work, whether in the books already completed by God's permission, or in the present one at whose beginning we stand, or in the one we shall afterwards, by the Lord's help, complete, is to stand guard against the madness of those who, at various times and with various wills, try to gather synods which judge that images in the Church should either be abolished or be worshipped. And since the Scripture of that madness, which they vainly strive to call by the name of the Seventh Synod, is seen to be propped up, as with certain wings, by the distorted senses of its own authors, and by testimonies of the divine law wrongly applied to itself, we have resolved, in the preceding books, to remove from it the supports of the wings on which it vainly thinks it can be held up, and in the following books to dismantle the framework of empty members on which it supposes it can stand. Thus the earlier books will strip it of the oars of its wings, and the later books will take apart its limbs one by one; the earlier will rob it of flight, the later of its walk. That is, with the wings of spiritual understanding and of the divine utterance, on which it was thought to be carried away beyond measure, cut off, and with its own proper senses, from which it was forced violently into foreign meanings, restored, and by the blow of the strong and unconquerable fist of the Catholic faith, it will be plainly seen to be weakened, since it lacks sound senses and the testimonies of the divine letters, and is buttressed only by heaps of empty assertions that lack reason, and it is not believed by everyone to be well put together. For while it seeks to raise its own authors to the heights of the glory of praise, it does not hesitate to disturb the prosperity of domestic affairs with civil strife; and while it provokes the citizens to the pestilent adoration of certain forbidden things, it frightens the domestic arms of the citizens against itself, and, alas, compels the blows of its spears, which ought to have protected liberty, to be hurled, pressed together in a hostile mass, against its own countrymen. We have therefore decided to overturn this, not with crafty quibbles, not with forensic eloquence, not with the ornaments of speech that wander far from the case, not with the wanton charm of the buskin, not with the knotty arguments of a clever line of reasoning, but with the compass of a pure and simple speech, bound together with the tough sinews of the divine utterances and coloured with the eloquence of sound and sober teaching; a speech which, lacking the display of boasting, is rather a lover of the advancement of the holy Church than a seeker of empty praise for itself or for us. Since, then, in the text of the present book, in which it is clear that we now proceed to attack, we are discussing the opinions of those who, in their synod, have set down some things otherwise than they were handed down by the holy Fathers, and have in some measure disputed about the faith, order requires that we first lay the foundation of our faith, namely that of which the Apostle says: For no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Once we have, with the heart, believed and, with the mouth, professed the sincerity of this venerable faith, and have fortified the beginnings of the work to come by the firmness of so great a foundation, our structure will rise more freely and be built more rightly and solidly, and if any part of theirs has risen less rightly or less solidly, it will be more easily cast down. Because we ought first to fortify ourselves and make our own position firm, and afterwards to contend against the adversary and resist opposing arguments, we are taught this not only by the lessons of the sacred letters but are also admonished by the rules of the Roman author himself, who says: One must argue so that we first strengthen our own position, then break down the opposing one.

units.la: LIBER III.
units.tr: BOOK III.

units.la: CAP. I. Confessio fidei Catholicæ quam à sanctis patribus accepimus, tenemus, & puro corde credimus.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. The Catholic confession of faith, which we have received from the holy Fathers, hold, and believe with a pure heart.

units.la: CREDIMUS in Deum patrem omnipotentem omnium creatorum visibilium & invisibilium conditorem. Credimus & in Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum per quem omnia creata sunt, verum Deum, unigenitum & verum Dei filium, non factum aut adoptivum, sed genitum & unius cum patre substantiæ, atq; ita per omnia æqualem Deo patri, ut nec tempore, nec gradu, nec potestare esse possit inferior: tantumq; esse confitemur illum, qui est genitus, quantus est ille, qui genuit. Non autem quia dicimus genitum à patre filium, divinæ & ineffabili generationi aliquod tempus adscribimus, sed nec patrem aliquando coepisse nec filium. non enim aliter confiteri possumus æternum patrem, nisi confiteamur etiam coæternum filium: ex filio enim pater dicitur, & qui semper pater fuit, semper habuit filium. Credimus & in Spiritum S. Deum verum ex patre & filio procedentem, æqualem per omnia patri & filio, volùtate, potestate, æternitate, substantia: nec est prorsus aliquis in trinitate gradus, nihil quod inferius superiusve dici possit, sed tota Deitas sui perfectione æqualis est, ut exceptis vocabulis quæ proprietatem personarum indicant, quicquid de una persona dicitur, de tribus dignissime possit intellegi: atq; ut confundentes Arrium unam eandemque dicimus trinitatis esse substantiam, & unum in tribus personis fatemur Deum, ita impietatem Sabellii declinantes, tres personas expressas sub proprietate disjungimus, non ipsum sibi patrem, ipsum sibi filium, ipsum Spiritum sanctum esse dicentes, sed aliam patris, aliam filii, aliam Spiritus sancti esse personam. Non enim nomina tantummodo, sed etiam nominum proprietates, id est, personas, vel ut Græci ex primunt, ὑποστάσεις, hoc est, subsistentias, confitemur. Nec paret filii aut sancti Spiritus personam aliquando excludit: necrursus filius aut Spiritus sanctus patris nomen personamq; recipit, sed pater semper pater est, filius semper filius, Spiritus sanctus semper Spiritus sanctus: itaq; substantia unû sunt, personis ac nominibus distinguuntur. Ipsum autem Dei filium, qui abs q; initio æternitate cum patre & Spiritu S. possidet, dicimus in fine seculorum perfectum naturæ nostræ hominem suscepisse ex Maria semper virgine, & verbum carnem esse factum adsumendo hominem, non permutando Deitatem: nec, ut quidam sceleratissime opinantur, Spiritum sanctum dicimus fuisse pro femine, sed potentia ac virtute creatoris operatum. Sic autem confitemur in Christo unam filii esse personam, ut dicamus duas perfectas atq; integras esse substantias, id est, deitatis & humanitatis, quæ ex anima cotinentur & corpore: atq; ut condemnamus Fotinum, qui solum & nudum hominem confitetur in Christo, ita anathematizamus Apollinarè & ejus similes, qui dicunt Dei filium minus aliquid de humana suscepisse natura, & vel in carne, vel in anima, vel infensu adsumptum hominem his propter quos adsumptus est fuisse dissimilem, quem absq; sola peccati macula quæ naturalis non est, nobis confitemur esse consormem. Illorum quoq; similiter exsecramur blasphemiam, qui novo sensu afferere conantur à tempore suscepta
units.tr: We believe in God the Father almighty, maker of all things created, visible and invisible. We also believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created, true God, the only-begotten and true Son of God, not made or adopted but begotten, of one substance with the Father, and so equal to God the Father in all things that he can be inferior to him neither in time, nor in rank, nor in power. We confess that the one who is begotten is as great as the one who begot him. But when we say that the Son was begotten by the Father, we do not ascribe any time to that divine and ineffable generation, nor do we say that the Father ever began or the Son ever began. For we cannot confess the Father to be eternal unless we also confess the Son to be co-eternal. The Father is called Father from the Son, and he who was always Father always had a Son. We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, equal to the Father and the Son in all things: in will, in power, in eternity, and in substance. There is absolutely no degree within the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher. Rather, the whole Deity is equal in its perfection, so that, apart from the terms that indicate the properties of the persons, whatever is said of one person can most fittingly be understood of all three. As we, opposing Arius, say that the substance of the Trinity is one and the same, and confess that there is one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish the three persons by their properties, not saying that the Father is himself his own Son, or that the Son is himself the Holy Spirit, but affirming that the person of the Father is one, the person of the Son another, and the person of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not only the names but also the properties of the names, that is, the persons, or, as the Greeks express it, the hypostases, that is, the subsistences. The person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit never excludes the Father, nor does the Father or the Holy Spirit receive the name or person of the Son. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance and are distinguished by persons and names. We say that the Son of God himself, who from the beginning possesses eternity together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, at the end of the ages took up a perfect man of our nature from Mary, ever virgin, and that the Word was made flesh by assuming a man, without changing the Deity. Nor, as some most wickedly think, do we say that the Holy Spirit was the father of the seed, but that he worked by the power and virtue of the Creator. We confess that there is one person of the Son in Christ in such a way that we say there are two perfect and complete substances, that is, of the Deity and of the humanity, which consists of soul and body. Just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses Christ to be only a bare man, so we anathematize Apollinaris and his like, who say that the Son of God took on something less of human nature, and that the man he assumed was, either in flesh or in soul, or in both, unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. We confess him to be like us in everything except the stain of sin, which is not natural. Likewise we execrate the blasphemy of those who try to assert in a new sense that, from the time the flesh was taken up, all the things that belonged to the Deity passed over into the man, and again that the things that belonged to the humanity were transfused into God, so that, through this confusion, both substances, that of the Deity and that of the humanity, are emptied and changed from their own state into something else. (No heresy has ever dared to say this.) They confess God to be imperfect in the Son, as they do man, so that they are believed to hold neither God truly nor man.

units.la: * Sc. Cicero-nis. susceptæ carnis omnia quæ erant deitatis in hominem demigrasse : & rursum quæ erant humanitatis in deum esse transfusa, ut quod nulla unquam hęresis dicere ausa est videatur hac confusione utraque exinanita substantia scilicet deitatis & humanitatis, & à proprio statu in aliud esse mutatam, qui tam deum inperfectum in filio quàm hominem confitentur, ut nec deum vere nec hominem tenere credantur. Nos autem ita dicimus, susceptum à dei filio passibile nostrum, ut deitas inpassibilis permaneret. Passus enim filius non putative sed vere, omnia quæ scriptura testatur : Id est esuriem, sitim, lassitudinem, dolorem, mortem & cætera hujusmodi secundum illud passus est quod pati poterat, id est, non secundum illam substantiam quæ adsumpsit, sed secundum illam quæ adsumpta est. Ipse enim dei filius secundum deitatem suam inpassibilis est ut pater, inconprehensibilis ut pater, invisibilis ut pater, inconvertibilis ut pater. Et quamvis propria persona filii, id est, dei verbum suscepit passibilem hominem, ita tamen ejus habitatione secundum suam substantiam deitas verbi nihil passa est, ut tota trinitas quam inpassibilem necesse est confiteri. Mortuus est ergo dei filius secundum scripturas, juxta id quod mori poterat, resurrexit tertia die, ascendit in cælum, sedet ad dexteram dei patris, manente ea natura carnis in qua natus & passus est, in qua etiam resurrexit. Non enim exinanita est humanitatis substantia, sed glorificata, in æternum cum deitate mansura. Accepta ergo à patre potestate omnium quæ in cœlo sunt & in terra, venturus est ad judicium vivorum ac mortuorum, ut & justos remuneret, & puniat peccatores. Resurrectionem carnis ita credimus, ut dicamus nos in eadem in qua nunc sumus veritate membrorum esse reparandos, qualesque semel post resurrectionem fuerimus effecti, in perpetuo mansuros : unam esse vitam sanctorum, sed præmia pro labore diversa : è contrario pro modo delictorum peccatorum quoque esse supplicia. Baptisma unum tenemus, quod hisdem sacramentum verbis in infantibus, quibus etiam in majoribus esse celebrandum. Homine si post baptismum lapsus fuerit, per pœnitentiam credimus posse salvari. Novum & vetus testamentum recipimus in eorum librorum numero, quem sanctæ catholicæ ecclesiæ tradidit auctoritas. Animas à deo dari credimus quas ab ipso factas dicimus, anathematizantes eos qui animas quasi partem dei divinæ dicunt esse substantiæ. Eorum quoq; condemnamus errorem, qui eas ante peccasse vel in cœlis conversatas fuisse dicunt quàm in corpora mitterentur. Exsecramur etiam eorum blasphemiam qui dicunt, inpossibile aliquid homini à deo esse præceptum, & mandata dei non à singulis, sed ab omnibus in commune posse servari : vel qui primas nuptias cum Manicheo, aut secundas cum Cataphrygis damnant. Anathematizamus etiam illos qui dei filiũ necessitate carnis mentitum esse dicunt, & eum propter adsumptum hominem non omnia facere potuisse quæ voluit. Joviniani quoque damnamus hæresin, qui dicit, nullam in futuro meritorum esse distantiam : nosque eas ibi habituros virtutes quas hic habere neglexerimus. Liberum sic confitemur arbitrium, ut dicamus nos semper dei indigere auxilio : & tam illos errare qui cum Manicheo dicunt hominem peccatum vitare non posse, quàm illos qui cum Joviniano asserunt hominem non posse peccare : utercque enim tollit arbitrii libertatem. Nos vero dicimus hominem semper & peccare & non peccare posse, ut semper nos liberi consiteamur esse arbitrii. Hæc est catholicæ traditionis fidei vera integritas, quam syncero corde credimus & fatemur, & in hoc opere beati Hieronymi verbis expressam taxavimus. Hæc est vera fides, hanc confessionem conservamus atque tenemus, quam quisque inconvulsè & intemeratè custodierit, perpetuam salutem habebit.
units.tr: * i.e. of Cicero. We, however, say that the Son of God took up our passible nature in such a way that the impassible Deity remained. For the Son suffered, not in appearance but truly, all the things Scripture bears witness to: that is, hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind. He suffered according to what he could suffer, that is, not according to the substance that assumed, but according to the substance that was assumed. For the Son of God himself, according to his Deity, is impassible as the Father is, incomprehensible as the Father is, invisible as the Father is, unchangeable as the Father is. And although the Word himself, in his own person, took up a passible man, yet by that indwelling the Deity of the Word, according to its own substance, suffered nothing, so that the whole Trinity must be confessed to be impassible. Therefore the Son of God died according to the Scriptures, in that he could die; he rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the nature of the flesh in which he was born, suffered, and also rose again remaining. For the substance of the humanity was not emptied but glorified, and it will remain with the Deity for ever. Having therefore received from the Father power over all things in heaven and on earth, he will come to judge the living and the dead, both to reward the righteous and to punish sinners. We believe in the resurrection of the flesh in such a way that we say we shall be restored in the same truth of members in which we now are, and that we shall remain in the condition we have once been made after the resurrection. There is one life of the saints, but their rewards differ according to their labours; and conversely, punishments for sins also differ according to the measure of their offences. We hold one baptism, which is to be celebrated with the same words as a sacrament for infants as for adults. If a man falls after baptism, we believe he can be saved through repentance. We receive the Old and the New Testament among the books which the authority of the holy catholic Church has handed down. We believe that souls are given by God, whom we say made them, and we anathematize those who say that souls are a part of the divine substance of God. We also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned before, or lived in heaven before they were sent into bodies. We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that something impossible has been commanded of man by God, and that God's commandments cannot be kept by each individual but only by all in common; or of those who condemn first marriages with Mani, or second marriages with the Cataphrygians. We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied out of necessity of the flesh, and that because of the man he assumed he could not do all that he willed. We also condemn the heresy of Jovinian, who says that there will be no difference of merits in the future, and that we shall have in that life those virtues which we neglected to have in this one. We so confess free will that we say we always need God's help; and those err as much who with Mani say that man cannot avoid sin, as those who with Jovinian assert that man cannot sin. For each of them takes away the freedom of the will. But we say that man can always both sin and not sin, so that we always confess ourselves to be free in our will. This is the true integrity of the faith of the catholic tradition, which we believe and confess with a sincere heart, and which we have set forth, expressed in the words of the blessed Jerome, in this work. This is the true faith. Whoever keeps and holds this confession, guarding it unshaken and undefiled, will have eternal salvation.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Quod Tarafius ab errore errorem linire conatus sit, & quod ab ægritudine ad ægritudinem dilapsus sit, scilicet videlicet repente ex laico conversus & ad episcopatum promotus nititur hoc emendare in imaginum adoratione, quod admisit in repen- tina consecrationis susceptione.
units.tr: That Tarasius tried to smear one error with another, and that he slipped from one sickness into another: having suddenly passed from layman to bishop, he now strives to correct in the veneration of images what he admitted in the hasty acceptance of consecration.

units.la: Peritorum vetus iste medicorum mos est, sic unius ægritudinis molestiis medicaminibus crepitus curando instare, ut tamen alterius pestis nequitiæ non videatur adminicula præstare : quoniam quædam res sicut unius vires extenuant, ita adhibitæ alterius viribus alimenta ministrant : & spiritalis vitæ cultorum est, sic quorundam convellere vitiorum stirpes, ut tamen aliorum nullis convalescant incrementis radices : quoniam quorundam vitiorum pestifera plantatio aliorum abolitione vitiorum inolescit, sicque alu pesti subsidia præbens agro mentis officit, quæ per se officere non valens suis viribus extirpata fatescit. Quorum utrorumque præstantibus moribus, sive peritorum medicorum, sive spiritalium cultorum, non mediocriter Tarafius perhibetur obniti, qui per rem penitus interdictam & nullatenus proficientem nititur emendare rem penitus interdictam & prorsus officientem. Et veluti si quis lutulentum quid ingesta impuritate eluere cupiens, dum lutulentis nihilominus eluere nititur aquis, quo magis abluere appetit, eo magis eisdem impuritatibus inficit : ita idem ex laico repente ad episcopatum, ut fertur, promotus, dum repentinam tanti gradus susceptionem per infolentem nisus est emendare imaginum adorationem, inlicitum inlicito adposuit : & quanto unum erroremaltero errore linire putavit, tanto se majoribus errorum nexibus præpedivit. Nam si iuoportuna imaginum adoratione inoportuna ordinatio stabilire potest, facile res inlicitæ rebus poterunt firmari inlicitis, & si res inlicitæ rebus poterunt firmari inliciis, facillimè inpura quæque quibusdam inpuris ablui poterunt. Non autem inpura quæque quibusdam inpuris ablui poterunt : nonignur inoportum ordinatio adoratione inoportuna nihilominus imaginum quoquomodo poterit stabiliri. Etsi ecclesiasticæ ordinationis regula à sanctis patribus tradita intemerata servanda est, immo quia servanda est, omnino corrumpi non debet: & si omnino corrumpi non debet, nec pro utili quadam re corrumpi quidem debet: & si pro utili quadam re nullatenus corrumpi debet, multo ergo minus pro inutili corrumpi debet: cum videlicet utrumque & imagines adorare, & sine ordine graduum pontificalem cathedram subire inutile sit. Sed quoniam ista accedamus ad Apostolum, veniamus ad vas electionis, interrogemus egregium prædicatorem, initonet nobis quid de ordinatione episcopi censeat qui proculdubio respondebit, Manus cito nemini imposueris. Et rursus, Non neophytum, ne in superbia elatus in judicium incidat diaboli: ne videlicet dum putat se non tam ministerium humilitatis quam administrationem secularis potestatis adeptum, condemnatione superbiæ sicut diabolus per jactantiam deiciatur. Unde periculosissima est talis ordinatio, in qua diaboli judicium suspicatur: & formidolosissimum est, ejus doctrina, quæ imagines adorare censet, uti, in quo tam atrocis exempli ruina formidatur: cum prohibitum sit popularem hominem sacerdotii magisterium adimplere debere, cujus nec officium tenuisse, nec disciplinam creditur agnovisse: & eum ea docere posse, quæ constat eum nequaquam antea didicisse. De tali itaque ordinatione hæc est beati Gregorii Romanæ urbis sententia, Quidam desiderio honoris inflati defuncto episcopo confurantur, & repente fiunt ex laico sacerdotes, atque inverecunde religiosi propositi ducatum arripiunt, qui nec esse adhuc milites duxerunt. Quid putamus, quod isti subjectis præsulatum sunt? qui antequam discipulatus limen adtingant, tenere locum magisterii non formidant? Quare nec necesse est, ut & si inculpati quisque sit meriti, ante tamen per distinctos ordines ecclesiasticos exercetur officium: videat quod imitetur, discat quod doceat, informetur ad id quod teneat, ut postea non debeat errare, qui eligitur viam erantibus demonstrare. Diu ergo religiosa meditatione poliatur, ut placeat: & sic lucerna super candelabrum posita luceat, ut adversa ventorum vis mrnens conceptam eruditionis flammam non extinguat, sed augeat: nam cum scriptum sit, ut prius quis probetur, & sic ministret, multo amplius ante probandus est, qui populi intercessor adsumitur, ne fiant causa ruina populi sacerdotes mali. Nulla igitur contra hoc excusatio, nulla potest esse defensio, quia cunctis liquido notum est, quæ sit in hujus rei diligentia sancta egregii sollicitudo doctoris, quæ neophytum ad ordines vetat sacros accedere. Sicut autem tunc neophytus ducebatur, qui initio sanctæ fidei erat conversatione plaikatus, sic modo neophytus habendus est, qui repente in religionis habitu plantatus ad ambiendos honores sacros surepserit. Ordine ergo ad ordinem accedendum est. Non gradum sacrum recte appetit, qui ad summa loci fastigia postpositis gradibus per abrupta quærit ascensum: & cum idem apostolus doceat inter alia sacri ordinis instituta discipulum, manus non esse cuiquam citius imponendas, quid hoc celerius, quidve præcipitantius quam ut exoriatur à summitate principium, ut ante esse incipiat episcopus quam magister? Contra quam ecclesiasticæ institutionis normam dum superius memoratus Tarasius sacerdotale culmen, ut ajunt, contendit, turbare potius quam gubernare dinoscitur plebes. Nec mirandum est si non recte prædicet, qui ad prædicationis officium non recte pervenit. De cujus inordinata consecratione multa sanctorum patrum poni testimonia poterant, quæ tamen brevitatis causa omissa sunt. Hæc tantum de hac re potuisse sufficiat.
units.tr: This is the old custom of skilled physicians: when treating the troubles of one disease with remedies, they take care not to supply aid to the wickedness of another plague. For just as some substances weaken the strength of one thing, so when applied they supply nourishment to the strength of another. And it is the practice of those who cultivate the spiritual life to uproot the stems of certain vices in such a way that the roots of others do not grow stronger by their increase. For the pestilent growth of certain vices thrives when other vices are destroyed, and so a weed that gives aid to a pest harms the field of the mind, and when it is uprooted it withers, since by its own strength it cannot harm. Tarasius is reported to strive, not moderately, toward both of these excellent customs, whether of skilled physicians or of spiritual cultivators; yet through a thing wholly forbidden and in no way profitable, he tries to correct a thing wholly forbidden and utterly harmful. It is like someone who, wishing to wash off something muddy and foul, tries to rinse it with muddy water: the more he seeks to cleanse himself, the more he is infected by the same filth. So this man, who was, as is said, suddenly promoted from layman to bishop, while he tried to correct the hasty acceptance of so high a rank by an insolent effort in the veneration of images, has laid an unlawful thing upon an unlawful thing. And the more he thought to smear one error with another, the more he entangled himself in greater knots of error. For if an unseasonable ordination can be confirmed by an unseasonable veneration of images, then unlawful things can easily be confirmed by unlawful things; and if unlawful things can be confirmed by unlawful things, then every impure thing can easily be cleansed by certain impure things. But not every impure thing can be cleansed by certain impure things; therefore an unseasonable ordination cannot in any way be made firm by an unseasonable veneration of images. Even if the rule of ecclesiastical ordination handed down by the holy Fathers must be kept inviolate, indeed because it must be kept, it ought not to be corrupted at all; and if it ought not to be corrupted at all, it ought not be corrupted even for some useful purpose; and if it ought in no way to be corrupted for some useful purpose, much less ought it to be corrupted for a useless one. Clearly it is useless both to venerate images and to ascend the papal throne without the order of the grades. But since we are to come to the Apostle, let us approach the chosen vessel, and ask that outstanding preacher what he thinks about the ordination of a bishop. He will surely answer, Lay hands hastily on no one.
