And again, Not a neophyte, lest being puffed up with pride he fall into the judgment of the devil; that is, lest, thinking he has obtained not so much the ministry of humility as the administration of secular power, he be cast down by the condemnation of pride, as the devil was by his arrogance. Therefore such an ordination is most perilous, in which one suspects the judgment of the devil; and it is most dreadful to use the teaching of a man who holds that images are to be venerated, when the fall of so terrible an example is to be feared; since it is forbidden that a common man should fulfil the office of the priesthood, when it is not believed that he held the office or learned its discipline, and that he could teach those things which it is clear he never learned before. Concerning such an ordination, then, this is the judgment of blessed Gregory of the city of Rome: Some, puffed up with desire for honour, when the bishop has died, press their own candidacies, and suddenly from laymen they become priests, and shamelessly seize the leadership of a religious way of life, though they have not yet thought themselves soldiers. What do we suppose those men will do to their subjects, who do not fear to hold the place of teacher before they have touched the threshold of discipleship? Therefore it is not necessary that, however blameless each one may be, he should not first exercise the office through the distinct ecclesiastical orders: let him see what he is to imitate, learn what he is to teach, be formed for that which he is to hold, so that afterwards he ought not to err, he who is chosen to show the way to those who are wandering. Let him therefore be polished for a long time by religious meditation, so that he may please; and so let him shine like a lamp set upon a lampstand, so that the adverse force of the winds does not extinguish the flame of learning he has received, but increases it. For since it is written that a man must first be proved, and then minister, much more must he be proved beforehand who is taken up as an intercessor for the people, lest evil priests become the cause of the people's ruin. Therefore there is no excuse against this, and no defence can exist, because it is clearly known to all what holy solicitude that outstanding teacher showed in this matter of diligence, who forbids a neophyte to approach the sacred orders. But just as at that time one was called a neophyte who had been newly planted in the faith by his conversion, so now he is to be regarded as a neophyte who, planted suddenly in the habit of religion, creeps in to seek sacred honours. One must therefore approach order by order. He does not rightly seek a sacred grade who, passing over the steps, seeks to climb by sheer precipices to the highest peak of the place; and since the same Apostle teaches his disciple, among other rules of the sacred order, that hands must not be laid on anyone too quickly, what could be quicker or more headlong than for the beginning to arise from the summit, so that one begins to be a bishop before being a teacher? Contrary to the norm of ecclesiastical institution, while the aforementioned Tarasius strives, as they say, for the priestly summit, he is seen to disturb the peoples rather than govern them. Nor is it surprising if he does not preach rightly, who has not rightly come to the office of preaching. Many testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning his disorderly consecration could be cited, but they have been omitted for the sake of brevity. Let so much on this matter suffice.

units.la: CAP. III. Utrum Tarasius recte sentiat qui spiritum sanctum non ex patre & filio secundum veritatem sanctæ fidei regulam, sed ex patre per filium procedentem in sua credulitatis lectione profiteatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. Whether Tarasius rightly holds, when in his confession of faith he professes that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father and the Son, according to the truth of the rule of the holy faith, but from the Father through the Son.

units.la: NOstris memorialibus nequaquam subtraxit oblivio sensibus, quod in primordiis hujus nostri operis polliciti sumus, nihil nos indiscussum relicturos, nihilque silentio praeteritum, quod in eadem synodo quæ pro adorandis imaginibus gesta est, reprehensione dignum inveniretur: nisi forte quod aut difficultas inordinati sermonis nostro intellectui impertire negaret, aut puerilis dicti ineptiam reverentia cohibente nostra disputatio perseqvi despiceret. Ideoque non est consequens ut ab hoc nostra suspendatur disputatio, quod Tarasius spiritum sanctum non ex patre tantum, sicut quidam qui quamquam cum ex filio procedere quodammodo tacuerint, tamen ex patre & filio procedentem omnino crediderunt: neque ex patre & filio, sicut omnis universaliter confitetur & credit ecclesia cum procedere, sed ex patre per filium in suæ fidei professione procedere confessus est. In qua professione nisi puritas & syncer/ tas cordis sit, quæ credat eum non creaturam esse, sed creatorem, nec patre filioque minorem, sed eis æqualem & consubstantialem & ab utroque procedere, perniciosum virus poterit exoriri. Omnium ergo rerum definitio talis esse debet, ut omnibus obscuritatibus seu ambiguitatibus explosis, ad demonstrandæ rei recto tramite tendant indicium, & si aliarum rerum definitio tam perspicua tamque debet esse dilucida, ut ea quæ demonstranda sunt, evidenter demonstret, multo magis fidei definitio dilucida & perspicua & omni ambiguitate sive tortuositate carens esse debet. In qua si aliquid aut tortuosum aut ambiguum, aut quodam nubilo verborum obductum fuerit, magnam affert dicenti vel audienti jacturam. Ex patre enim & filio spiritum sanctum, non ex patre per filium procedere, recte creditur, & utitate conspectur: quia non per filium ut pote creatura quæ per ipsum facta sit, neque quasi posterior tempore aut minor potestate, aut alterius substantiæ procedit, sed ex patre & filio ut coæternus, ut consubstantialis, ut coæqualis, ut unius gloriæ, potestatis atque divinitatis cum eis existens procedere creditur. Alteram namque vim habet, ex, præpositio & alteram, per. Unde & dei filius natus ex homine non per hominem creditur, id est, non per coitum, non per humanam operationem, sed ex virgine carnem adsumendo natus. Et idcirco quæri potest, utrum recte dici queat, spiritus sanctus à patre per filium procedere, ne dum incautè hæc præpolitio, per, in tanti mysterii professione ponitur, Arriani illius erroris virosum cuiquam poculum ministret, qui spiritum sanctum creaturam esse, & per filium sicut & cætera quæ creata sunt, creatum esse blasphemat: qui etiam sui baptismatis tinctionem non juxta fidem evangelicam, in nomine patris & filii & spiritus sancti, sed in nomine patris per filium in spiritu sancto infelicibus quibusq; ad se convertis impertivit. Spiritus namque sanctus non creatura, sed creator esse his testimoniis adprobatur. Ait enim David, Verbo domini cæli firmati sunt, & spiritu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum. & Salomon dicit, Ipse creavit ea per spiritum sanctum. item David, Emitte spiritum tuum & creabuntur, & renovabis faciem terræ. & in libro Iob scribitur, Spiritus divinus est, inquit, qui creavit me. & in libro Judith, Tibi, inquit, serviet omnis creatura tua: quoniam dixisti & facta sunt, misisti spiritum tuum & ædificavit. Tantæ enim potestatis si-ve virtutis spiritus sanctus ostenditur, ut ipso cooperante corpus domini nostri Iesu Christi, quod est nostra redemptio, in utero virginis formaretur, Evangelista dicente, Ne timeas Ioseph accipere Mariam conjugem tuam, quod enim in ea natum est de spiritu sancto est. item, Inventa est in utero habens de spiritu sancto: non quod salvatoris nostri spiritus sanctus pater dicendus est, ut duo patres credantur, sed quod patris & filii idem spiritus sanctus cooperator & unius potestatis cum eisdem esse credatur, domino adfirmante; Ite, inquit discipulis, baptizate omnes gentes in nomine patris & filii & spiritus sancti. Sicut enim dominus Apostolos ad prædicandum destinavit, pariter etiam modo spiritus sanctus facere declaratur. Scribitur enim in Actibus apostolorum, quòd Petro cogitante de visione, dicit ei spiritus sanctus; Ecce viri quærunt te, exurgens vade cum eis nihil dubitans, quia ego eos misi ad te. & item, Segregate mihi Paulum & Barnabam ad opus quod elegi eos. & item; Adtendite vobis & universo gregi in quo vos spiritus sanctus constituit episcopos. Nam & universa cum patre & filio, ut ostensum est, procedavit, & deus esse unus cum iisdem essentiæ his testimoniis adprobatur. David enim ait; Audiam quid loquatur in me dominus deus. Lucecitaque clarius constat, quòd omnes prophetæ non nisi per spiritum sanctum adnunciant vel loquantur, domino adtestante, qui ait; Cùm venerit spiritus ille sanctus quem pater mittet in nomine meo, ipse vos docebit & ventura adnuntiabit vobis. item per Prophetam dominus dicit; Noluerunt audire sermones meos quos mandavi in spiritu meo per os prophetarum priorum, dicit dominus. Paulus quoque Apostolus ad Hebræos scribens ait; Testificatur nobis spiritus sanctus, & hoc est testamentum quod dispono ad eos post dies illos, dicit dominus. In Actibus quoque Apostolorum ad Ananiam dixille pastorem ecclesiæ legimus; Ut quid Satanas implevit cor tuum mentiri te spiritui sancto? & ostendens cum Deum esse, in subsequentibus dicit, Non es mentitus hominibus, sed Deo. Paulus quoque vas electionis ad Corinthios scribit; Divisiones autem donationum sunt, idem verò spiritus: & divisiones ministeriorum sunt, idem ipse dominus: & divisiones operationum sunt, idem verò deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. Quibus apostolicis verbis spiritus sanctus idem deus, idem dominus declaratur. idem verò dominus in evangelio dicit, Spiritus est deus. item ad Corinthios Paulus scribens ait, Dominus autem spiritus est: & ad Ephesios, Nolite, inquit, contristari spiritum sanctum dei: item ad Corinthios, An nescitis, inquit, quia membra vestra templum sunt spiritus sancti quem habetis à deo? & cum deum in humanis corporibus habitantem ostendeus adjungit, & dicit; Glorificate ergo & portate deum in corpore vestro. Qui dum his testimoniis & creator & deus adprobetur, & ex patre & filio ab omni catholica ecclesia procedere credatur, quæreudum est utrum necesse sit eum per filium a patre & non potius ex patre & filio procedere profiteri, cùm hujuscemodi professio nequeim Niceno neque in Chalcidonensi symbolo à sanctis patribus facta inveniatur. Per filium enim super Apostolos in igne apparuit: per filium hominibus datus est, quoniam ab omnibus spiritus sanctus accipi non nisi per filium poterat. Per filium verò eum à patre procedere profiteri, synodicæ confessioni insitatū est: quoniâ Sp.S. ut à patre procedat non eget alterius adjurorio, ut per aliquē procedat: cùm utriq; sit tertia in eadē sanctatriuitate persona & unius cū patre & filio sit potestatis atque essentiæ. Quì cùm à se deus sit, ad nos autem relativè dominū est, distribuens singulis prout vult gratiarū dona. Nam & prophetias quibus vult inpertit, & peccata quibus vult dimittit, quæ huc illo nō donantur. qui inde proprie charitas nuncupatur, vel quia naturaliter eos à quibus procedit conjungit, & se unū cū eis esse ostendit: vel quia in nobis id agit, ut in deo maneamus, & ipse in nobis: unde in & donis dei nihil majus est charitate, & nullum est majus donum dei quàm spiritus sanctus: ipse est & gratia, quæ quia non meritis nostris, sed divina voluntate gratis datur, inde gratia nuncupatur. Sicut autem unicum dei verbum proprie vocamus nomine sapientiæ, cùm sit universaliter & spiritus sanctus & pater ipse sapientia: ita spiritus sanctus proprie nuncupatur vocabulo charitatis, cum sit & pater & filius universaliter charitas. Est enim spiritus patris adtestante domino, qui ait, Non enim vos estis qui loquimini, sed spiritus patris vestri qui loquatur in vobis. Est & spiritus filii, Paulo adtestante qui ait, Quisquis autem spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est ejus, ac per hoc spiritus amborum dicitur, quia ex patre & filio procedens unius probatur esse substantiæ & naturæ: qui ù ingenitus diceretur, duo patres profiterentur: si genitus, duo filii incompetenter diceretur. Sed quia nec pater est nec filius, ideo nec ingenitus nec genitus, sed ex utroq; procedens dicitur. Pater enim solus non est de alio, ideo solus appellatur ingenitus, non quidem in scripturis, sed in consuetudine disputantium & de re tanta sermonem qualem valuerunt ad præsentium sive futurorum prophetarum proferentium: filius solus de patre est natus, ideo solus dicitur genitus: Sp.S. solus de patre & filio procedit, ideo solus amborū nuncupatur spiritus. Procedit enim ex utroq; non nascendo, ut alicujus filius dici possit. Diceretur aūt filius patris & filii, si abhorret ab emnium fidelium sensibus, cum ambo genissent: non igitur ab utroq; est genitus, sed procedit ab utroq; amborum spiritus. A patre illū aūt procedere dominus noster Iesus Christus dixit discipulos docuit dicens, Cùm autem venerit ille spiritus veritatis...
units.tr: Our memory has by no means lost the sense of what we promised at the beginning of this work: that we would leave nothing unexamined and pass over nothing in silence that might be found worthy of censure in the same synod which was held concerning the veneration of images. Unless, perhaps, the difficulty of an unordered speech denies our understanding any access to it, or we think it beneath us to pursue a childish saying in our discussion, out of reverence. Therefore it does not follow that our discussion should be held back by this: that Tarasius confessed that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone, as some have done, who though they were silent in some way about the procession from the Son, nevertheless believed wholly that he proceeds from the Father and the Son; nor from the Father and the Son, as the whole Church universally confesses and believes; but he confessed in his profession of faith that he proceeds from the Father through the Son. In this profession, unless there is purity and sincerity of heart, which believes that he is not a creature but the Creator, and not less than the Father and the Son but equal to them and consubstantial, and proceeding from both, a pernicious poison can arise. Therefore the definition of all things ought to be such that, with all obscurities and ambiguities cast out, it tends by a straight path to the indication of the thing to be shown. And if the definition of other things ought to be so clear and so lucid that it demonstrates evidently what is to be demonstrated, much more must the definition of the faith be lucid, clear, and free of every ambiguity or crookedness. If anything in it is crooked or ambiguous, or wrapped in a certain cloud of words, it brings great loss to the speaker or the hearer. For it is rightly believed, and is plainly seen, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, not from the Father through the Son: not as a creature made through him, nor as later in time or less in power, nor as of another substance, but he is believed to proceed from the Father and the Son as coeternal, consubstantial, coequal, existing with them in one glory, power and divinity. For the preposition ex has one force, and per another. Hence also the Son of God is said to be born of a woman, not through a man, that is, not through intercourse, not through human action, but born of the virgin by taking flesh. And so it may be asked whether it can rightly be said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, lest this preposition through, placed incautiously in the profession of so great a mystery, should offer a deadly cup to anyone of that Arian error, who blasphemes that the Holy Spirit is a creature and was created through the Son as other created things were; who also gave the consecration of his baptism to unhappy converts not according to the evangelical faith, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, but in the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. For that the Holy Spirit is not a creature but the Creator is proved by these testimonies. For David says, By the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth. And Solomon says, He created them by the Holy Spirit. Likewise David: Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth. And in the book of Job it is written, It is the divine Spirit, he says, who created me. And in the book of Judith, Your whole creation, he says, shall serve you; for you spoke and they were made; you sent forth your Spirit and it formed them. For the Holy Spirit is shown to have such power and strength that, by his cooperation, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is our redemption, was formed in the womb of the virgin, the Evangelist saying, Do not fear to take Mary your wife, for what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, She was found with child of the Holy Spirit. Not that the Holy Spirit is to be called the Father of our Saviour, so that two fathers would be believed, but that the same Holy Spirit is believed to be the cooperator of the Father and the Son and to be of one power with them, the Lord affirming it: Go, he says to the disciples, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For as the Lord sent out the Apostles to preach, so in like manner the Holy Spirit is declared to act. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that when Peter was thinking about the vision, the Holy Spirit said to him: Behold, men are seeking you; rise and go with them, doubting nothing, for I have sent them to you. And again, Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them. And again: Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops. For the Spirit also proceeds from the Father and the Son, as has been shown, and is proved by these testimonies to be one God with them in essence. For David says, I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me. Hence it is clearer than light that all the prophets announce or speak only through the Holy Spirit, the Lord bearing witness, who says, When that Spirit of truth comes, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you and declare to you things to come. Likewise, through the prophet the Lord says, They would not hear my words, which I commanded in my Spirit through the former prophets, says the Lord. The Apostle Paul also, writing to the Hebrews, says, The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after those days, says the Lord, this is the covenant that I will make with them. We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that the minister of the Church said to Ananias, Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? and, showing that he is God, he says in what follows, You have not lied to men, but to God. Paul, the chosen vessel, also writes to the Corinthians: There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all. By these apostolic words the Holy Spirit is declared to be the same God, the same Lord. And the same Lord in the Gospel says, God is Spirit. Likewise Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says, Now the Lord is the Spirit. And to the Ephesians: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God. Likewise to the Corinthians: Do you not know, he says, that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit whom you have from God? And when he shows God dwelling in human bodies, he adds and says, So glorify God and bear him in your body. Since by these testimonies he is proved both Creator and God, and is believed by the whole catholic Church to proceed from the Father and the Son, it must be asked whether it is necessary to profess that he proceeds from the Father through the Son rather than from the Father and the Son, since such a profession is not found in the Nicene or the Chalcedonian creed made by the holy Fathers. For he appeared over the Apostles in fire through the Son; he was given to men through the Son, since the Holy Spirit could not be received by all except through the Son. But to profess that he proceeds from the Father through the Son has been inserted into the synodical confession; since the Holy Spirit, in order to proceed from the Father, does not need another's help, so that he should proceed through someone, since he is a third person in the same holy Trinity and of one essence and power with the Father and the Son. He is of himself God, but in relation to us he is Lord, distributing the gifts of grace to each as he wills. For he bestows prophecies on whom he wills and forgives sins on whom he wills, and these are not given here or there. He is properly called charity, either because he naturally joins those from whom he proceeds and shows himself to be one with them, or because he works in us so that we remain in God and he in us. Hence among the gifts of God nothing is greater than charity, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit; he himself is also grace, which, because it is given freely by divine will and not by our merits, is therefore called grace. Just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name of wisdom, since the Holy Spirit and the Father are universally wisdom itself, so the Holy Spirit is properly named by the word charity, since both the Father and the Son are universally charity. For he is the Spirit of the Father, the Lord bearing witness, who says, For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. He is also the Spirit of the Son, Paul bearing witness, who says, Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. And so he is called the Spirit of both, because, proceeding from the Father and the Son, he is proved to be of one substance and nature. If he were called unbegotten, two fathers would be professed; if begotten, two sons would be improperly named. But because he is neither Father nor Son, he is therefore neither unbegotten nor begotten, but is said to proceed from both. For the Father alone is not from another, and therefore he alone is called unbegotten, not indeed in the Scriptures, but in the custom of disputants and in such discourse about so great a matter as the prophets, present or future, were able to utter. The Son alone is born of the Father, and therefore he alone is called begotten. The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son, and therefore he alone is named the Spirit of both. For he proceeds from both not by being born, so that he could be called the son of anyone. He would be called the son of the Father and the Son, if that were not abhorrent to the sense of all the faithful, since both would have begotten him. Therefore he is not begotten of both, but proceeds from both, the Spirit of both. That he proceeds from the Father our Lord Jesus Christ said, teaching the disciples, saying, But when that Spirit of truth comes...

units.la: tein vētem venerit, inquit, paraclitus, quem ego mittam vobis a patre spiritum veritatis, qui a patre procedit, ille testimonium perhibebit de me. & rursum ipse dei & hominum mediator dominus Iesus Christus post resurrectionem suam, ut ostenderet a se procedere spiritum sanctum sicut & a patre, insufflans in discipulos suos ait, Accipite spiritum sanctum: qui nisi ab eo procederet, nequaquam cum insufflans discipulis daret. Unus ergo est spiritus patris & filii, unus, ut supra memoravimus, amborum spiritus. Quòd si quis quaerat, quomodo filius a patre nascendo procedit, spiritus vero sanctus procedendo non nascitur: aut quare non utrumque sint filii, cum utrumque a patre procedant: aut quur non & spiritus sanctus dicatur ingenitus, sicut pater: aut quomodo ab utroque procedat, aut quur filius dicat, Sicut habet pater vitam in semetipso, sic dedit filio vitam habere in semetipso, quasi antea sine vita idem filius exstiterit, & hanc patre dante suscepterit: aut quomodo pater numquam sine filio, & tamen pater genuit filium: aut quomodo filius numquam sine spiritu, & tamen ait, Nisi ego abiero, paraclitus non veniet ad vos: aut quomodo filius non de se, sed de patre est, nec tamen ei est posterior de quo est: aut quomodo spiritus sanctus de patre procedit & filio, nec tamen ab eis praeceditur a quibus procedit: sciat haec & his similia humanae fragilitatis sensibus inscrutabilia & inconprehensibilia esse. Quis enim ista consideret? quis ista comprehendat? si enim humanae nativitatis Christi secreta non capimus, divinae naturae mysteria quomodo capiemus? Verum quia in illa coaeterna & aequali & incorporali & ineffabiliter inmutabili atq; inseparabili trinitate difficillimum est generationem a processione distinguere, sufficiat hoc credere, hoc firmiter tenere, hoc toto corde fateri patrem ingenitum, filium genitum, Spiritum vero sanctum nec creatum nec genitum, sed ex patre & filio procedentem: ita duntaxat ut in confessione fidei omnes opinationes, omnes verborum novitates caveantur: & his verbis, hisque sententiis fidelium confessio roboretur, quae sanctae & universales synodi in symbolo taxaverunt.
units.tr: But when that Comforter comes, he says, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me. And again, the Lord Jesus Christ, mediator between God and men, after his resurrection, to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself just as from the Father, breathed on his disciples and said, Receive the Holy Spirit. He would not have given the Spirit by breathing on the disciples unless the Spirit proceeded from him. One, then, is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, one, as we have mentioned above, the Spirit of both. But if anyone asks how the Son proceeds from the Father by birth while the Holy Spirit does not come by birth but by procession; or why both are not called sons, since both proceed from the Father; or why the Holy Spirit is not called unbegotten, as the Father is; or how he proceeds from both; or why the Son says, As the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself, as though the Son had existed before without life and received it from the Father when it was given; or how the Father is never without the Son, and yet the Father begot the Son; or how the Son is never without the Spirit, and yet says, Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; or how the Son is not from himself but from the Father, and yet is not later than him from whom he is; or how the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and yet is not preceded by those from whom he proceeds: let him know that these and similar matters are inscrutable and incomprehensible to the senses of human frailty. For who can consider these things? Who can grasp them? If we do not grasp the secrets of Christ's human birth, how shall we grasp the mysteries of the divine nature? But since in that co-eternal, equal, incorporeal, ineffably immutable and inseparable Trinity it is most difficult to distinguish generation from procession, it is enough to believe this, to hold this firmly, and to confess with the whole heart that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither created nor begotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. Only let all opinions and all novelties of words be avoided in the confession of faith, and let the confession of the faithful be strengthened by these words and these sentiments which the holy and universal synods set down in the creed.

units.la: CAP. IIII. Utrum Theodorus Episcopus Heraclyomorum recte sentiat, qui cum patrem sine prin- cipio penitus & sempiternum se credere dixerit, filium nescio sub qua am- bage verborum non aliud principium, quam patrem agnoscen- tem & ex ipso substantiam habentem profiteatur.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. Whether Theodore, Bishop of the Heraclyomorites, rightly thinks, who, when he has said that he believes the Father to be altogether without beginning and eternal, professes that the Son, in some ambiguity of words, has no other beginning than the Father, acknowledging him and having his substance from him.

units.la: ET superiore quidem capitulo exsecuti sumus, in sanctae fidei confessione dilucidam & perspicuam definitionem fieri debere, & nunc necessario idipsum exsequimur. Quoniam nisi recto tramite, omnibus ambagibus hinc inde postpositis, ad demonstrandam rei veritatem sermo gradiatur, & de ejus a quo proferatur fidei integritate ab audientibus dubitatur, & haereticae pravitati & si non voto, sono tamen ad propinquare videtur. Unde cavendum est, ne in professione fidei Theodori Episcopi, qui dum patrem dicat sine principio, & filium non aliud principium quam patrem agnoscentem, & ab ipso subsistentiam habentem, pater filium, aut tempore, qui sibi consempiternus est: aut substantia, qui sibi consubstantialis est: aut honore, qui sibi aequalis est, praecedere suspicetur. Quod quidem etsi a praefato viro recte & catholice creditur, ita tamen ambigue positum est, ut legenti de ejus fide possit oriri suspicio, quod plerunque non infirma credulitas, sed sermonis solet esse dificultas. Quoniam igitur in hac professione non elucet evidenter, utrum ejus fides aut probari aut improbari debeat, cum eam probandam potius quam improbandam esse nostra mallet mentio, restat ut quae de hac re a sanctis patribus percepimus, credimus & tenemus, breviter exsequamur. Hoc enim in tali professione expavescendum est, ne dum pater sine principio dicitur, & filius non aliud principium quam patrem agnoscere, antiquior pater filio quia genuerit, & filius posterior patre quia genitus sit suspicetur: cum videlicet nihil sit in sancta trinitate anterius posteriusve, ubi nihil ex tempore inchoatur, ut consequenti perficiatur in tempore. Quoniam sicut tres personae consubstantiales sibi sunt, ita etiam consempiternae. Et sine tempore generatio filii de patre intelligitur, sine tempore etiam processio spiritus sancti de utroque. Est enim pater filio principium non creando, sed gignendo, non tempore procedendo, sed ineffabilis pater ineffabilem filium sine quo numquam fuit, ineffabiliter sibi consempiternum generando. Est & filius principium non patri, sed rebus a se conditis: est & spiritus sanctus principium omnibus quae ab eo creata sunt: quia nullo modo separari potest ab appellatione creatoris. Sunt pater & filius principium spiritui sancto non gignendo, quia non est filius, neque creando, quia non est creatura, sed dando quia ab utroque procedit. Est item pater & filius & spiritus sanctus unum principium, omnibus quae a se solo & uno creatore creata sunt. Et cum sit pater principium, & filius principium, & spiritus sanctus principium, non tamen tria principia, sed unum est principium, una divinitas, una substantia, una omnipotentia. Haec enim quae breviter perstrinximus, praedicatoris egregii Augustini verbis ad probanda sunt. Aut enim, Dicitur ergo relative pater, idemq; relative dicitur principium, & si quid forte aliud ipse pater ad filium dicitur: principium vero ad omnia quae ab ipso sunt. Item dicitur relative filius, relative dicitur & verbum, & imago, & in omnibus his vocabulis ad patrem refertur, nihil autem horum pater dicitur. Et principium filius dicitur: cum enim diceretur ei, Tu quis es? respondit, Principium quia & loquor vobis. Sed nunquid patris principium? creaturae se quippe offendere voluit, cum se dixit esse principium, sicut & pater primum principium est creaturae quod ab ipso sunt omnia. Nam & creator relative dicitur ad creaturam, sicut dominus ad servum. Et ideo cum dicimus & patrem principium, & filium principium, non duo principia creatura dicimus, quia pater & filius simul ad creaturam unum principium est, sicut unus creator, sicut unus deus. Si autem quicquid in se manet & gignit aliquid vel operatur, principium est eis rei quam gignit vel eis quam operatur, non possumus negare etiam Spiritum sanctum recte dici principium,
units.tr: AND in the previous chapter we have set out that in the confession of holy faith a clear and plain definition ought to be given, and now we necessarily carry out the same task. For unless the discourse proceeds by a straight path, with all ambiguities set aside on every side, toward demonstrating the truth of the matter, the hearers doubt the soundness of the faith of the one who speaks, and it seems to come near, if not in intent then at least in sound, to heretical perversity. Hence care must be taken, lest in the profession of faith of Theodore, the Bishop, who, while saying that the Father is without beginning, and that the Son acknowledges no other beginning than the Father, and has his subsistence from him, is suspected of placing the Father before the Son in time, who is co-eternal with him; or in substance, who is consubstantial with him; or in honour, who is equal to him. Although this is indeed rightly and catholically believed by the aforesaid man, it is nonetheless stated so ambiguously that a suspicion about his faith may arise in the reader, which is usually caused not by a weak belief but by a difficulty of expression. Since therefore in this profession it does not clearly appear whether his faith ought to be approved or disapproved, and since our account prefers that it be approved rather than disapproved, it remains for us briefly to set out what we believe and hold concerning this matter from what we have learned from the holy Fathers. For in such a profession this must be feared above all: that while the Father is called without beginning and the Son is said to acknowledge no other beginning than the Father, the Father might be thought earlier than the Son because he begot him, and the Son later than the Father because he was begotten. For in the holy Trinity there is nothing earlier or later, where nothing begins in time so as to be completed afterward in time. Just as the three persons are consubstantial with one another, so they are also co-eternal. The generation of the Son from the Father is understood without time, and the procession of the Holy Spirit from both is likewise without time. The Father is a principle to the Son not by creating but by begetting; not by proceeding in time, but the ineffable Father, by ineffably begetting the ineffable Son, without whom he never was, makes him co-eternal with himself. The Son is also a principle, not to the Father, but to the things created by him; and the Holy Spirit is a principle to all the things that were created by him, because he can in no way be separated from the name of Creator. The Father and the Son are a principle to the Holy Spirit not by begetting, since he is not a son, nor by creating, since he is not a creature, but by giving, since he proceeds from both. Likewise the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one principle to all things that were created by the one Creator, who is alone and one. And although the Father is a principle, and the Son a principle, and the Holy Spirit a principle, they are not three principles, but there is one principle, one divinity, one substance, one omnipotence. For these things which we have briefly touched upon are to be proved in the words of the outstanding preacher Augustine. For: Thus the Father is said relatively, and likewise the Father is said relatively to be the principle, and if anything else is said of the Father in relation to the Son; but the principle is said relatively to all the things that are from him. Likewise the Son is said relatively, and the Word and the Image are also said relatively, and in all these names he is referred to the Father; yet none of these is said of the Father. The Son is also called the principle: for when they said to him, Who are you? he answered, The beginning, because I also speak to you. But is he the principle of the Father? For he wished to show himself to the creature when he called himself the principle, just as the Father too is the first principle of the creature, since all things are from him. For the Creator is also said relatively to the creature, as the Lord is said relatively to the servant. And therefore when we say both that the Father is a principle and that the Son is a principle, we do not say that there are two principles to the creature, since the Father and the Son together are one principle to the creature, as one Creator, as one God. But if whatever remains in itself and begets something or works is a principle to that which it begets or to that which it works, we cannot deny that the Holy Spirit too is rightly called a principle,

units.la: cipium, bipium, quia non cum separamus ab appellatione creatoris: & scriptum est de illo, quod operetur, & utique in se manens operatur. Non enim in aliquid eorum quae operatur, ipse mutatur & vertitur, & quae operatur fide. Unicuique, ait Apostolus, datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem: alii quidem datur per spiritum sermo sapientiae, alii sermo scientiae secundum eundem spiritum, & reliqua. item idem post pauca, Nam & singillatim si interrogemur de spiritu sancto, verissime respondemus, quod deus sit, & cum patre & filio simul unus deus est. Unum ergo principium ad creaturam dicitur deus, non duo vel tria principia, ad se autem invicem in trinitate, si gignens ad id quod gignit principium est, pater ad filium principium est, quia genuit eum. Utrum autem & ad spiritum sanctum principium sit pater, quoniam dictum est, De patre procedit, non parva quaestio est: quia si ita est, non jam principium ei tantum rei erit quam gignit aut facit, seiletiam et quam dat, ubi & illud elucescit, utpote quod solet multos movere, cur non sit filius etiam spiritus sanctus, cum & ipse a patre exeat sicut in evangelio legitur. Exit enim non quomodo natus, sed quomodo datus: & ideo non dicitur filius, quia neque natus est, sicut unigenitus, neque factus, ut per gratiam in adoptionem nascerentur sicut nos. Quod enim de patre natum est ad patrem solum refertur, cum dicitur filius, & ideo filius patris est non & nosler: quod autem datum est & ad eum qui dedit refertur, & ad eos quibus dedit. Itaque spiritus sanctus non tantum patris et filii qui dederunt, sed etiam nostri dicitur qui accepimus: sicut dicitur donum salus quia dat salutem, eadem etiam nostra salus est qui accipimus. item idem post pauca; Si ergo & quod datur principium habet enim a quo datur, quia non aliunde accepit illud quod ab ipso procedit, fatendum est patrem & filium principium esse spiritus sancti, non duo principia, sed sicut pater & filius unus deus: & ad creaturam relative unus creator & unus dominus, sic relative ad spiritum sanctum unum principium, ad creaturam vero pater & filius & spiritus sanctus unum principium, sicut unus creator & unus dominus.
units.tr: principle, principle, because we do not separate it from the name of Creator; and it is written of him that he works, and works assuredly while remaining in himself. For he is not changed or turned into any of the things he works, and he works through faith. To each, says the Apostle, is given the manifestation of the Spirit for profit; to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, and so on. Likewise a little later: For if we are questioned individually about the Holy Spirit, we answer most truly that he is God, and together with the Father and the Son is one God. Therefore God is called one principle with respect to the creature, not two or three principles; but with respect to one another within the Trinity, if the begetter is a principle to what he begets, then the Father is a principle to the Son, because he begot him. Whether the Father is also a principle to the Holy Spirit, since it has been said, He proceeds from the Father, is no small question: for if so, he will be the principle not only of what he begets or makes, but also of what he gives; and here too there becomes clear what commonly moves many: why the Holy Spirit is not also called a son, since he too goes out from the Father, as is read in the Gospel. He goes out not as one born but as one given; and therefore he is not called a son, since he is neither born, as the only-begotten is, nor made, so that we might be born into adoption by grace as we are. For what is born of the Father refers to the Father alone when he is called Son; therefore he is the Son of the Father and not also ours. But what is given refers both to him who gave it and to those to whom it was given. So the Holy Spirit is called not only of the Father and the Son who gave him, but also ours who have received him; just as salvation is called a gift because it gives salvation, and yet salvation is also ours who receive it. Likewise a little later: If then what is given also has a principle (for it has that from which it is given, since it did not receive from elsewhere what proceeds from him), we must confess that the Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit, not two principles, but as the Father and the Son are one God; and as with respect to the creature there is one Creator and one Lord, so with respect to the Holy Spirit there is one principle; but with respect to the creature the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one principle, as one Creator and one Lord.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: Quod Tarasius non recte spiritum sanctum contribulum patri & filio dixerit, cum sufficeret dicere coaeternum, consubstantialem ejusdemque essentiae & naturae.
units.tr: That Tarasius was wrong to call the Holy Spirit a co-tribesman of the Father and the Son, when it would have been enough to say co-eternal, consubstantial, and of the same essence and nature.

units.la: Dixisse quoque in suae fidei professione spiritum sanctum patri & filio contribulum Tarasius perhibetur: quod absurdissimum & dictum & a catholicae fidei confessione penitus convelendum, non solum ab eorum sensibus qui literariae scholae disciplinam non nesciunt, sed etiam ab eorum qui communibus tantum utuntur literis prorsus respuitur, & modis omnibus abdicandum. Est enim in promptu animadvertere, quod sicut consanguinei dicuntur qui sunt unius sanguinis, & consortes qui sunt unius sortis, & coaetanei qui sunt unius aetatis, qui etiam coevi dicuntur, & conformes qui sunt unius formae, ita contribuli dicuntur qui de una tribu sunt.
units.tr: Tarasius is also reported to have said in his profession of faith that the Holy Spirit is a co-tribesman of the Father and the Son. This is a most absurd expression, and it must be wholly torn out of the confession of the Catholic faith. It is rejected outright not only by those who know the discipline of the schools of letters, but also by those who use only ordinary literacy, and it must be renounced in every way. For it is plain to see that as those are called kinsmen who are of one blood, partners who are of one lot, contemporaries who are of one age (also called coevals), and conformed who are of one form, so those are called tribesmen who belong to one tribe.

units.la: Ioan. 3. ftum ante sibi promissum acciperet, & cœlestibus plenus mysteriis secreta quædam Domino revelante audiret seu cerneret, scribere ea in libro, non pingere jussus est. Et in septem Ecclesiis unam sanctam Catholicam sive Apostolicam Ecclesiam septiformis gratiæ Spiritu plenam non pingendo, sed scribendo admonuit. Dictum enim illi superne voci stonitruo est, Quod vides scribe in libro, & mitte septem Ecclesiis. Unde datur intelligi, non picturas, sed Scripturas ad nostræ fidei eruditionem esse conceßas. Quàm ergo sit incautum, quamque à ratione remotum dicere, Sicut divinæ Scripturæ libros, ita imagines ob memoriam venerationis habemus, facile intelligere potest quisquis divinarum Scripturarum cognitionem habet. In illis inveniuntur arma, quibus contra adversa confligatur, quibus vitia reprimantur, quibus virtutes erigantur, quibus gulæ concupiscentia vigilis & compunctione cordis reprimatur, quibus fornicatio contritione cordis & corporis afflictione, orationum instantia, laboris exercitio, metuque supplicorum vel amore æternæ patriæ retinetur: quibus invidia amore fraternæ dilectionis & cœlestis regni desiderio, quod non nisi concordes adipiscuntur, superetur: quibus ira modestissimæ patientiæ gravitate & acumine rationis & æquanimitatis munere frangatur: quibus avaritia eleemosynis & spe æternæ retributionis calcetur, quibus tristitia fraternis alloquiis, assiduis lectionibus vel orationibus pellatur; quibus arrogantia metu amittendarum virtutum, cum qua illæ haberi non possunt, & accessus vanæ gloriæ, qui est virtutum inimicus secluditur: in quibus superbia metu diabolicæ ruinæ & exemplo humiliatis Christi conteritur. In illis inveniuntur instrumenta fructus justitiæ, id est, charitas, gaudium, pax, patientia, longanimitas, bonitas, benignitas, fides, modestia, continentia. In illis invenitur medela, qua nec sapientes in sua sapientia gloriantes, nec fortes in sua fortitudine confisi periclitentur, necque simplices sive infirmi sua impossibilitate deiciantur: qua nec laetos nimia laetitia extollat, nec tristes nimia animi contritio afficiat: qua nec divites rerum opulentia elatos efficiat, nec pauperes rerum indigentia frangat. In illis invenitur norma per quam instruitur qualiter prælati erga subditos, & subditi erga prælatos agere debeant, qualiter conjugia diligantur, qualiter sæcularia contilia prudenti deliberatione tractentur, qualiter patria desendatur, hostes pellantur, extranearum domesticarumque rerum administratio habeatur, & ut cuncta breviter complectar, in illis & animæ perpetuus cibus, & præsentis vitæ doctrina & sapientia quæ decoreft vitæ, & vitæ perpetuæ documenta continentur. Est enim thesaurus nullo bono carens, omnibus bonis redundans: ad quem quisquis devotus accedit, quicquid fideliter quærit, feliciter se adquisisse gaudet. Esto mundanæ sapientiæ & sæcularis scholæ quemquam amor oblectat, accedat ad divinæ legis armaria, quæ sapientes mundi sicut meritorum celsitudine, ita etiam tempore præcedit, & liberalium studiorum profunditates, quas scit cognovisse, & quas nescit invenisse se gaudeat. Illic inveniet & retinet loquutionis decorem, etymologias nominum, schematum varietates, tropicas periplexiones: de quibus beatus Augustinus ait, Sciant autem literati modis omnium loquutionum, quos Grammatici Graeco nomine tropos vocant, auctores nostros usos fuisse: quos tamen tropos, id est, modos loquutionum, qui noverunt, agnoscunt in literis sanctis, eorumque scientia ad eas intellegendas aliquantulum adjuvantur: invenient etiam historias, metra, quæ omnia proprie artis grammaticæ sunt. Sed dicet fortassis aliquis: Non illic metrorum scansiones & temporum certas dimensiones invenio: cognoscat multa in divinis Scripturis metra, plures rhythmos esse, sed translano linguæ non eadem finit habere temporum intervalla in peregrina, quæ habentur in propria: cum tamen eosdem sensus eafdemque rerum proprietates habeat, quia & si quis nobis debitor aurum reddat, non multum distat cum non unius si rmenerae cum illo quod acceperat, si tamen unius sit ponderis uniusque fulgoris. Nam ut beato Hieronymo Hebraicæ linguæ permissimo docente didicimus, quædam divinæ Scripturæ Hebraeo dactylo spondeoque, quædam anapaesto, quædam vero jambo juxta artis rigorem decurrunt. Illic etiam invenient nitorem & copiam eloquentiæ, genera causarum & status: illic exordia quibus benevoli, dociles vel attenti auditores fiunt: illic narrationes apertas & breves, causas etiam & longas, quæ non nisi Spiritu sancto referente panduntur: illic conclusiones quibus proprietas rerum monstratur: argumentationes quibus animi audientium concitantur ad implenda ea quæ dicuntur: illic leges sive sententiæ, illic magna granditer, parva summille, mediocria temperate promuntur: illic prosopopœiam, ethopœiam vel omnes figuras locutionum quæ à rhetoribus traduntur: invenient, & plures illis angustiores, quæ percepisse se gaudebunt ad quas nec grammaticorum nec rhetorum schola pertingere potuit: illic quoque invenient sagogas quæ ad inquirendas res lectorem utiliter introducunt, categorias quæ prædicamentorum utilitate ad investigandas res excellunt: definitiones vel modos syllogismorum, quæ subtili indagatione ea de quibus dubitatur adfirmant: topica quæ dum sint fontes sensuum & origines dictionum, omnibus communiter grammaticis videlicet, poetis, oratoribus vel etiam Philosophis argumenta præstant: quæ non solum scholastico, sed etiam vulgari & tumultuoso sermone perpetuo cohærent. Nam quamquam tumultuosus, quamquam vulgaris sit sermo, si pro quibuslibet vitæ utilitatibus profertur, ad topica veniet: per ea quali per quædam magisteria locales regulas quibus evagari, aut non possit, aut non debeat, invenier: in illis etiam terminum, qui fine sensus distpendio transgredi difficile sit, se reperiffe cognoscet. Erit cuncta breviter dicam, omnis sermo, nisi ad topica venerit, indefinitus proculdubio remanebit. Illic æ ιερμηνείας, quarum scrupulosis sermonis & laciniosis diverticulis profunditas inveniendorum sensuum dubiorumque affirmatio invenitur, quibusque syllogismorum vel cæterarum argumentationum silva exoritur: quæ omnia proprie artis sunt Dialecticæ. Illic in numeris per arithmeticam artem archana sensuum profun-
units.tr: ...that he might receive what had been promised to him beforehand, and, full of heavenly mysteries, hear or perceive certain secrets as the Lord revealed them, he was ordered to write them in a book, not to paint them. And to the one holy, Catholic, or Apostolic Church, full of the Spirit of sevenfold grace, he gave his admonition, not by painting but by writing, among the seven churches. For the voice from heaven, like thunder, said to him: What you see, write in a book, and send it to the seven churches. From this it is clear that it is not pictures but Scriptures that have been granted for the instruction of our faith. How rash, and how far from reason, it is to say: As we have the books of the divine Scriptures, so we have images for the sake of memory and veneration, anyone who knows the divine Scriptures can easily understand. In them are found the weapons by which one fights against adversity, by which vices are restrained, by which virtues are raised up. By them lust of the belly is held in check by vigil and compunction of heart; by them fornication is restrained by contrition of heart, bodily affliction, persistence in prayer, labour and exercise, and by fear of punishments or love of the eternal homeland. By them envy is overcome by love of brotherly affection and desire for the heavenly kingdom, which only those who are of one mind attain. By them anger is broken by the gravity of most modest patience, by the keenness of reason and the duty of equanimity. By them avarice is trampled down by almsgiving and hope of eternal reward. By them sadness is driven away by brotherly exhortations and by constant reading and prayer. By them arrogance is shut out, through fear of losing the virtues, without which they cannot be had, and by the approach of vainglory, which is the enemy of the virtues. In them pride is crushed by fear of diabolical ruin and by the example of the humbled Christ. In them are found the instruments of the fruit of righteousness, that is, love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. In them is found the remedy by which neither the wise, glorying in their wisdom, nor the strong, trusting in their strength, are endangered, nor the simple or the weak are cast down by their inability; by which excessive joy does not puff up the glad, nor excessive distress of mind afflict the sad; by which the abundance of wealth does not make the rich proud, nor the lack of goods break the poor. In them is found the rule by which it is taught how prelates ought to behave toward subjects and subjects toward prelates, how marriages are to be loved, how secular councils are to be conducted with prudent deliberation, how the homeland is to be defended and enemies driven away, and how the administration of foreign and domestic affairs is to be carried on. And, to sum up briefly, in them are contained both the perpetual food of the soul, the teaching and wisdom of the present life which becomes life, and the instructions for eternal life. For it is a treasure lacking no good and overflowing with all goods. Whoever devoutly approaches it, whatever he faithfully seeks, he rejoices to have obtained happily. If anyone is delighted by the love of worldly wisdom and secular learning, let him come to the storehouses of the divine law, which surpass the wise of the world not only in the height of merit but also in time, and let him rejoice in the depths of the liberal studies that he knows he has learned and in those he does not know he has found. There he will find and keep the grace of speech, the etymologies of names, the varieties of figures, and the tropical circumlocutions. Of these the blessed Augustine says: Let the learned know that our authors used all the modes of speech which the grammarians call tropes in Greek. Those who know these tropes, that is, the modes of speech, recognise them in the holy letters, and their knowledge helps them somewhat to understand these. They will also find histories and metres, all of which properly belong to the art of grammar. But perhaps someone will say: "I do not find in them the scansions of metres and the fixed measures of syllables." Let him know that there are many metres in the divine Scriptures and several rhythms, but in translation from one language the same intervals of time do not necessarily remain as in the original; yet it has the same meanings and the same properties of things. For even if someone repays us gold that he owed, it makes little difference whether the coin is of the same mint as what he had received, provided it has the same weight and the same lustre. For, as we learned from the blessed Jerome, who was the most learned teacher of the Hebrew tongue, some parts of the divine Scriptures run in Hebrew dactyls and spondees, some in anapaests, and some in iambs according to the strict rule of the art. There too they will find the brilliance and abundance of eloquence, the kinds of causes and their stages; there the exordia by which listeners are made kindly, teachable, or attentive; there open and brief narratives, and also long ones, which are only unfolded when the Holy Spirit relates them; there the conclusions by which the nature of things is shown; the arguments by which the minds of the hearers are stirred to carry out what is said; there the laws or sentences; there great things are set forth grandly, small things modestly, and middling things moderately; there prosopopoeia, ethopoeia, or all the figures of speech that are handed down by the rhetoricians. They will find also more slender ones, which they will rejoice to have grasped and to which the school of grammarians and of rhetoricians could not attain. There too they will find the Isagoge, which usefully introduces the reader to the investigation of things; the Categories, which excel in the usefulness of predicaments for investigating things; the definitions and the modes of syllogisms, which by subtle inquiry affirm those matters about which there is doubt; and the Topics, which, being the sources of meanings and the origins of words, supply arguments common to all, namely grammarians, poets, orators, and even philosophers. These do not cling only to scholarly speech but also to ordinary and tumultuous speech without end. For although speech may be tumultuous and common, if it is uttered for any useful purpose of life, it will come to the Topics; through them, as through certain teachers, one will find the local rules by which one cannot or ought not to wander. In them one will also recognise a limit, which it is hard to cross without loss of meaning. In short, every discourse that does not come to the Topics will undoubtedly remain undefined. There are the hermeneutics [ἑρμηνεῖαι], in whose scrupulous word-by-word analyses and winding digressions the depth of finding meanings and the affirmation of doubtful points are found, and from which springs a forest of syllogisms and other arguments; all of which properly belong to the art of dialectic. There, through arithmetic, in numbers, he will find the hidden depths of the meanings...

units.la: Apocal 1. profunditatesque reperiet: quoniam, dicente eadem Scriptura, Omnia in mensura & numero & pondere Deus fecit. Illic etiam musicae non solum consonantias instrumentaque, quibus plerique sanctorum patrum usi sunt, sed etiam repertorem inveniet.
units.tr: Apocal 1. ...and he will find the depths: since, as the same Scripture says, God made all things in measure and number and weight. There too he will find not only the consonances and instruments of music, which most of the holy Fathers used, but also the inventor of them.

units.la: Inveniet quoque terrarum situs dimensionesque, quae proprie artis sunt geometricae. Necnon & quorundam siderum cursus, & positiones, & temporum varietates, mensium annorumque; sive horarum curricula, diem etiam & causam conditionis siderum, quae proprie artis sunt astronomicae, illicreperisse se studiosus quisque cognoscet. Sed dicit forte aliquis, Nec nomina principaliter disciplinarum, nec uniuscujusque disciplinae singillatim partes, nec uniuscujusque partis membra singillatim in sacris literis inveniuntur. quibus breviter respondendum est, Omnia in scripturarum sanctarum amplissimis pratis per partes inveniri posse, quae artigraphium suorum hortorum areolis posuere: inveniuntur, inquam, virtute sensuum, non in pronunciatione verborum, in radicum profunditatibus, non in foliorum lapsibus. Sicenim in profunditate divinarum scripturarum liberales artes ab studiosis quibusque cernuntur, sicut vina in vitibus, segetes in seminibus, frondes in radicibus, fructus in ramis, arborumque magnitudines sensu contemplantur in nucleis. Est plane divina Scriptura verax, est fixa, est casta, est caelestis magisterii instrumentum, & aeterna praedicatio purissimo nitens eloquio, est lux mortalium, dicente Propheta, Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum Domine, & lumen semitis meis: est vivax & mori nesciens, dicente Apostolo, Vivus est Dei sermo & efficax & penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti, & pertingens usque ad divisionem animae ac spiritus: est te nebrarum disfusio, Salomone adrestante, qui ait, Lucerna est mandatum legis & lux vitae & increpatio & disciplina: de quo per Esaiam dicitur, De nocte spiritus meus vigilat ad te Deus, quia lux praecepta tua sunt super terram. Semper enim vitalia jubet, noxia prohibet, terrena removet, caelestia persuadet. Est, inquam, fons aethereo de margine scaturiens, de quo quanto amplius hauritur, tanto minus expenditur, & quanto in plures partes derivatur, tanto amplius in sensibus argumentatur: est pecuniae martupium, de quo nec ea quae dantur amittuntur, nec diminutionem assiduus dandi usus adfert, sed quanto inde amplius dandi devotione eicitur, tanto illud magis magisque completur.
units.tr: He will also find the positions and measurements of lands, which properly belong to the art of geometry; likewise the courses and positions of certain stars, the variations of times, of months and years, or the courses of hours; and also the day and the cause of the constitution of the stars, which properly belong to the art of astronomy. Every diligent student will recognise that he has found these there. But perhaps someone says: "Neither the names of the disciplines as such, nor the parts of each discipline singly, nor the members of each part singly, are found in the holy letters." To this we must briefly reply that all things can be found in parts in the very ample meadows of the holy Scriptures, which the artists have placed in the little beds of their gardens. They are found, I say, by the power of the senses, not in the pronunciation of words; in the depths of the roots, not in the falling of the leaves. For just as the liberal arts are discerned in the depth of the divine Scriptures by every studious person, so wines are in vines, crops in seeds, leaves in roots, fruits in branches, and the greatness of trees is contemplated in their kernels, in the sense. The divine Scripture is truly true, it is fixed, it is chaste, it is the instrument of heavenly teaching and the eternal preaching, shining with the purest eloquence; it is the light of mortals, as the Prophet says: Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths. It is living and does not know how to die, as the Apostle says: The word of God is living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, and reaches even to the dividing of soul and spirit. It is the spreading of light into darkness, Solomon agreeing, who says: The commandment is a lamp, and the law is light, and reproof and discipline are the way of life. Of it Isaiah says: My spirit watches for you in the night, O God, for your precepts are light upon the earth. For it always commands what is vital, forbids what is harmful, removes what is earthly, and persuades toward what is heavenly. It is, I say, a fountain springing from the ethereal edge, from which the more it is drawn, the less it is spent, and the more it is channelled into many parts, the more it is strengthened in its meanings. It is a treasure of money, from which what is given is not lost, nor does the constant use of giving bring diminution; but the more it is poured out from it with devotion in giving, the more and more it is filled.

units.la: Nihil igitur horum quae perstrinximus, sive his similium, quae brevitatis studio praeteriminus, in imaginibus, o imaginum adorator, o rerum insensatarum cultor invenire posse te constat, quae dum his omnibus meritorum praerogativis careant, dolendus potius quam mirandus es, quur eas divinae Scripturae libris, in quibus tot bona reperiuntur, aequiperare affectes? Tu qui fidei tuae puritatem in imaginibus conservare te dicis, supplex eis adstare memento cum thymiamatibus: nos praecepta Domini solerti indagatione perquiramus in divinae legis codicibus. Tu luminaribus perluastra picturas: nos frequentemus divinas Scripturas. Tu fucatorum venerator esto colorum: nos veneratores & capaces sinus sensuum archanorum. Tu depictis demulcere tabulis: nos divinis mulceamur alloquiis. Tu figuras rerum insta, in quibus nec visus, nec auditus, nec gustus, nec odoratus, nec tactus est: nos instemus divinae legi quae est inreprehensibilis, in qua testimonium Domini, justitiae sive praecepta, timor sive judicia ejus inveniuntur. Quae singula pulchre Psalmographus per septimam definitionis speciem quam dialectici καταμέτρον, id est, per translationem vocant, eo quod rem aliquam brevi praeconio quae sit ostendit, sub senarii numeri perfectione, qui juxta arithmeticae experientiam disciplinae perfectus habetur, eo quod suis partibus dimensus, & his iterum in unum redactis, absque ullo detrimento aut incremento sui in se redit: ita definivit dicens, Lex Domini inreprehensibilis, convertens animas, testimonium Domini fidele, sapientiam praestans parvulis: Justitia Domini recta laetificantes corda, praeceptum Domini lucidum illuminans oculos: Timor Domini sanctus permanens in saeculum saeculi, judicia Domini vera justificata in semetipsa desiderabilia super aurum & lapidem pretiosum multum, & dulciora super mel & favum. Quae omnia ideo senarii numeri perfectione decorantur, quia quamquam quodammodo inter se distare videantur, singula tamen ad perfectionem legis, qua viri sancti perfecti efficiuntur, pertinent. E quibus sicut uno subtracto sextus numerus minime adimpletur, ita si aliquid detrahatur, perfectionis integritas mutatur. Lex enim inreprehensibilis est, quia perfecta veritate consistit, quae per Salvatorem non reprehensa, sed potius probatur impleta: Non veni, inquit, legem solvere, sed adimplere. Et ut nosse possemus Evangelium quoque legem Domini esse, & duobus testamentis novo videlicet & veteri legem consistere, adjunxit, Convertens animas: quoniam veteris Testamenti pagina rigorem habet inreprehensibilis severitatis: novi vero convocationem & mansuerudinem, per quam errantes corrigantur, & ad Christi gratiam animarum conversio fiat. Testimonium ergo Domini fidele, quoniam quaecumque pollicetur Deus, plenissima veritate conplentur. Quod testimonium sapientiam praestat parvulis, non utique superbis nec tumida se elatione jactantibus, sed his parvulis de quibus Apostolus dicit, Nolite pueri effici sensibus, sed malitia parvuli esfote. Dat itaque testimonium pater, dat filius, dat & Spiritus sanctus: & sicut sunt unius essentiae & naturae, ita etiam in reddendo testimonio sublimes. De patre in Evangelio legitur, quod testimonium de filio perhibuerit: de filio autem Apostolus ad Timotheum scribit, Praecipio tibi coram Deo, qui vivificat omnia, & Christo Jesu, qui testimonium reddidit sub Pontio Pilato: de Spiritu quoque sancto idem Apostolus dicit, Nam & ipse Spiritus testimonium perhibet Spiritui nostro. Justitiae itaque Domini rectae ideo dicuntur, quia non aliter cognoscitur fecisse quam docuit, nec aliud illi in ore, aliud in opere est. Laetificantes sunt corda, quia justorum mentes aeternorum praemiorum coulatione demulcent: quorum praemiorum perceptione confisus erat ille, qui dicebat, De reliquo reposita est mihi corona justitiae, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illa die justus judex. Nam praeceptum Domini recte lucidum dicitur, sive quia a patre luminum procedit, sive metonymice, quod lucidos efficiat. Inluminat etiam oculos, non carnales, quos nobiscum animantia communes habere noscuntur, sed interiores, qui divini muneris jubare spiritaliter perlustrantur. Timor autem Domini sanctus permanens in seculum seculi, mixta est cum pavore dilectio, quæ usu seculari reverentia nuncupatur. In omni ergo sanctitate versatur, qui suum judicem & timere cognoscitur & amare. Inter timorem namque Domini & formidinem humanam hoc interest, quòd formido humana cum tempore commutatur: de ea, ni fallor, dictum est, Perfecta charitas foras mittit timorem. Timor autem Domini à proprio statu nulla temporali conversione mutatur: sed in idipsum sincerita te bonæ conscientiæ perseverat. Porro judicia Dei, quæ & vera & justificata in semetipsa à propheta describuntur, mandata sunt ejus, quæ in veteri & novo Testamento conscripta habentur, quia revera ex judicio sunt prolata. Vera, inquam, metonymice & justificata, quia veraces & justificatos observatores suos efficiunt. Inter judicium tamen Dei & judicia ejus hoc interest, quod judicium numero singulari illud generale examen est; judicia verò ejus numero plurali sacramenta sunt quæ in duobus testamentis, non in imaginibus nec in pictu ris inveniuntur: quæidem Psalmographus per schema quod Græce αὔξησις, id est, augmentum, eo quod paulatim ad superiora concrescat, ita expressit dicens; Desiderabilia super aurum & lapidem preciosum multum & dulciora super mel & favum. Sicut enim lapides preciosi auro præferuntur in precio, ita numirum auro & lapidibus preciosis mel & favum dulcedine præferitur. Per hanc enim figuram idem Psalmista susceptorem suum, gloriam etiam & exaltantem caput suum Dominum esse decantat dicens, Tu autem Domine susceptor meus es, gloria mea & exaltans caput meum: Et Apostolus ait, Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? tribulatio an angustia? an persecutio? an fames? an nuditas? an periculum? an gladius? in qua per augmenta nominum rei magnitudo sensim sucrecrescit. Cui quamquam vicina sit figura, quæ Græce κλῖμαξ, Latine gradatio dicitur, quando positis quibusdam gradibus, sive in laude, sive in vituperatione semper adcrescit, ab ea tamen plurimum distat: quod αὔξησις sine ulla iteratione nominum, rerum procurat augmenta, κλῖμαξ vero postremum verbum, quod est in primo commate positum, in sequenti membro modis omnibus repetit: sicq; velut catena aliud semper in alio nectitur, ut est illud Apostoli, Scientes quod tribulatio patientiam operatur. patientia probationem, probatio spem. spes autem non confundit: item illud, Nam quos præscivit & prædestinavit, eos & vocavit; & quos vocavit, illos & justificavit; quos autem justificavit, illos & glorificavit. Nam si forte tu amator vel potius adorator imaginum interiore pectoris rancore submurmures dicens, Quid necesse est tantum per schemata evagari? cognoscesea nobis amabiliota imaginibus sive pictis rabulis tuis esse, & ideo tantum in illis evagatos esse. Has erenim dulcedines, has refectiones in Scripturis sive in scripturarum schematibus, nos sive ceteros scripturarum amatores reperire cognosce, quas tu sive socii tui in figuris, neq; in tabulis, in quibus cordis tui puritatem servare te dicis, penitus non reperies.
units.tr: Nothing, then, of the things we have touched on, or of things like them that we have passed over for the sake of brevity, can be shown to exist in images, O adorer of images, O worshipper of insensate things. Since they lack all these prerogatives of merit, you are to be pitied rather than admired. Why do you wish to set them level with the books of Holy Scripture, in which so many good things are found? You who say you keep the purity of your faith in images, remember to stand before them as suppliants with incense. Let us seek out the precepts of the Lord with careful inquiry in the codices of the divine law. You brighten pictures with lamps; let us frequent the divine Scriptures. Be a lover of painted colours; let us love and embrace the hidden meanings of the senses. You soothe yourself with painted boards; let us be soothed by divine words. You pursue figures of things in which there is neither sight, hearing, taste, smell nor touch; let us pursue the divine law, which is blameless, in which the testimony of the Lord, his righteousness or precepts, his fear or judgments, are found. Each of these the Psalmist finely expresses by the seventh kind of definition, which the dialecticians call καταμέτρον, that is, translatio, because it shows what a thing is by a brief proclamation. He does so under the perfection of the number six, which by the experience of arithmetic is held to be perfect, since it is measured by its own parts and, when these are brought back together into one, returns to itself without any loss or gain. So he defined it, saying: The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones. The righteousness of the Lord is right, rejoicing the hearts; the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever; the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether, more to be desired than gold and much fine gold, sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. All these are adorned by the perfection of the number six, because, although they may seem in some way to differ from one another, each one nevertheless pertains to the perfection of the law, by which holy men are made perfect. Just as the number six is not made complete if one of its parts is taken away, so the integrity of perfection is altered if anything is removed from these. The law is blameless because it stands in perfect truth, which, through the Saviour, is not found fault with but is rather proved fulfilled: I came not to destroy the law, he says, but to fulfil it. And so that we might know that the Gospel too is the law of the Lord, and that the law consists of both covenants, the new and the old, he added converting souls. For the page of the Old Testament has the rigour of blameless severity, while the New has the calling and gentleness by which those who have gone astray are corrected and souls are converted to the grace of Christ. The testimony of the Lord is therefore faithful, since whatever God promises is fulfilled in fullest truth. This testimony gives wisdom to the little ones, not of course to the proud or to those who boast with swollen arrogance, but to those little ones of whom the Apostle says: Brethren, be not children in understanding; but in malice be ye children. So the Father gives testimony, the Son gives testimony, and the Holy Spirit gives testimony; and just as they are of one essence and nature, so they are also exalted in giving testimony. In the Gospel it is read that the Father bore witness concerning the Son; and the Apostle writes to Timothy concerning the Son: I charge thee before God, who quickeneth all things, and before Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession. Concerning the Holy Spirit too the same Apostle says: For the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit. The righteousnesses of the Lord are called right because he is not known to have acted otherwise than he taught, nor is there one thing in his mouth and another in his work. They rejoice the hearts, because they soothe the minds of the just with the bestowal of eternal rewards: he was confident of these rewards who said: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day. The commandment of the Lord is rightly called clear, either because it proceeds from the Father of lights, or by metonymy, because it makes people bright. It also enlightens the eyes, not the fleshly eyes which we are known to share with the living creatures, but the inner eyes, which are spiritually illumined by the radiance of the divine gift. But the fear of the Lord, holy, enduring for ever and ever, is a love mingled with reverence, which in ordinary usage is called respect. He therefore lives in all holiness who is known both to fear and to love his judge. For between the fear of the Lord and human dread this difference lies: human dread changes with time; of it, unless I am mistaken, it is said: Perfect love casts out fear. But the fear of the Lord is not changed from its proper state by any temporal alteration; rather it persists in the same sincerity of a good conscience. Moreover, the judgments of God, which the prophet describes as both true and righteous altogether, are his commandments, which are contained in the Old and New Testaments, because they have truly been issued from judgment. True, I say, by metonymy, and righteous altogether, because they make their observers truthful and righteous. Yet between the judgment of God and his judgments this difference lies: judgment in the singular is that general examination; but his judgments in the plural are the sacraments which are found in the two Testaments, not in images nor in pictures. These the Psalmist expresses by a figure which in Greek is called αὔξησις, that is, augmentum, because it rises gradually to higher things: More to be desired than gold and much fine gold, sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. For just as precious stones are preferred to gold in value, so honey and the honeycomb are preferred to gold and precious stones in sweetness. Through this figure the same Psalmist sings that the Lord is his supporter, his glory, and the one who lifts up his head: But thou, O Lord, art my supporter, my glory, and the lifter up of my head. And the Apostle says: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? tribulation, or distress? or persecution? or famine? or nakedness? or peril? or sword? In this passage the greatness of the thing grows gradually through the increasing of the nouns. Although the figure called in Greek κλῖμαξ, in Latin gradatio, is closely related to it, since, when certain steps are set in place, whether in praise or in blame, the sense always rises, it is nevertheless very different from it. For αὔξησις produces increases of things without any repetition of nouns, whereas κλῖμαξ in every way repeats in the following clause the last word which was placed in the first clause; and so, like a chain, one thing is always linked to another, as in the Apostle's words: Knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope; and hope maketh not ashamed. Likewise: For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate; and whom he did predestinate, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified. But if perhaps you, a lover or rather an adorer of images, should mutter with inward rancour of the breast, saying: Why is it necessary to wander so far through figures? Know that these things are more lovable to us than your images or painted trifles, and that we have wandered in them for this reason. For these sweetnesses, these refreshments, you will know that we and the other lovers of the Scriptures find in the Scriptures and in the figures of the Scriptures; and you and your companions will by no means find them in figures, nor in the tablets in which you say you keep the purity of your heart.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Quòd contra dominicæ vocis imperium faciunt hi, qui parentes suos anathematizant: & si secundum eorum opinionem prædecessores eorum hæretici fuere, isti ab hæreticis geniti, docti: & consecrati sunt: sive de non judicandis hiis, qui de seculo recesserunt: vel quantum istorum error à parentum errore differentiat, cum videlicet illi imagines frangere, isti adorare censuerint.
units.tr: That those who curse their parents act against the command of the Lord's voice; and that, if by their opinion their predecessors were heretics, these men were born, taught and consecrated by heretics; also concerning not judging those who have departed from this world; and how far the error of these men differs from the error of their parents, since the latter thought images should be broken and the former think they should be adored.

units.la: DE NTQUE illi qui eas corpori & sanguini dominico coæquare præsumunt, tanto illarum instiganrur amore, ut etiâ parentes suos, qui eas sprevisse noscuntur, anathematizare nō dubitent, errorem errori nectentes: cum videlicet & illis incongruam & inordinatam exhibeant adorationem, & his vel à quibus per carnis materiam propagati sunt, vel hos per quorum consecrationem & baptismi sacramentū & cetera charismata sumpsere, inoportunam ingerant exsecrationem. Nam si secundum illorum vesaniam omnes imaginum adoratione carentes hæretici sunt, constat majores eorum, qui eas non adoravere hæreticos fuisse: qui si hæretici fuere, neque consecrationes faciendi, neq; manus inponendi potestatem habuerunt: qui si hanc non habuerunt, hi qui ab eis hanc se accepersse putant, neque con secrationem, neque manus inpositionem habent. Item si prædecessores corum, ut illi ajunt, anathematis colligatione digni fuerunt, ligandi solvendiq; potestatem non habuerunt: quam si non habuerunt omnia quæcunq; ab eis in ecclesia gesta sunt cassanda sunt: si omnia abnuenda sunt, gradus & ordinationes abnuenda sunt: si igitur prædecessores illorum anathematis colligatione digni fuerunt, istorum gradus & ordinationes cassanda sunt. Non enim schismaticis & anathematis vinculo conligaris ligandi solvendiq;, sed idoneis & Catholicis potestatem à Domino legimus esse concellam. Parentibus interea honorem inpendendum, non solum legalis, Prophetica & Apostolica, verumetiam Evangelica admonitio docet, dicente Domino, Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam. Qui enim & pst paginam veteris instrumenti, & per sui corporis præsentiam hoc salutare præceptum contulit, idem Mosaico ore promulgavit dicens, Benedictus, qui honorat patrem suum & matrem suam; & è contrario, maledictus, qui non honorat patrem suum & matrem suam. Unde perpendendum est & magnopere animadvertendum, quanta sit arrogantia, quantæque temeritatis & ut ita dixerim, sceleris, parentes anathematizare, si ille maledictionem subjacet, qui cos convincitur non honorare.
