Nam cum lex dicat, Non reveles turpitudinem patris tui, & Apostolus, Filii obedite parentibus vestris, isti utrique præcepto reluctari videntur: cum nec turpitudinem celare, nec honorem nituntur impe nimpedere. Sacri igitur canones de non contemnendis parentibus omni occasione seclusa, hanc videntur protulisse sententiam; Quicunque Filii a parentibus sub praetextu divini cultus abscedunt nec debitam reverentiam dependunt illis, anathema sint. Si vero hi, qui eis debitam reverentiam non impendunt, anathematizantur, quo putas damnationis vinculo, qui eos anathematizant connectantur? Saluberrimus namque a sanctis patribus ecclesius traditus usus est, pro defunctorum spiritibus Dominum deprecari, quem nos cum sancta omni Catholica & universali ecclesia amplectentes, non solum pro nostrorum parentum, verumetiam pro amicorum fidelium, qui nos in pace dominica praecesserunt, spiritibus, clementissimam Domini pietatem exposcimus. Cui venerandae & ecclesiasticae constitutioni non mediocriter contraire videntur, qui defunctorum parentum Spiritus non orationibus adjuvare, sed anathematis vinculo conligare nituntur: & qui orate etiam pro inimicis Apostolicae erudionis documento jubentur, pro suis hoc facere parentibus reluctantur. Nos nostris secundum ecclesiasticum usum pes orationum & eleemosynarum institutiam deposcimus veniam: illi suis per inanium conciliorum conventus exoptant poenam. Nos nostris quietem exposcimus per missarum solennia: illi suis ingeruut convicia per inordinata concilia. Nos nostrorum memoriam facimus in oratione, illi suis anathemae jaciunt cum quadam abdicatione. Nos nostrorum Spiritus requie potiri oramus in sinu Abrahae: illi suorum optant damnari animas cum Arrio, Sabellio, Dioscoro, Nestorio, & Eutychete. Nos noftros conlocari postulamus parentes inter agmina beatorum: illi suos inter obstinatas turbas haeretico-rum. Quae cum ita se habeant, constat eos duplex in hac parte patrare deliquium, cum & parentibus honorem derogent contra dominicae vocis imperium, & contra Apostoli sententiam his, qui a saeculo migraverunt, temerarium conentur inferre judicium. Quod non sit ergo temere judicandum de his, qui jam e saeculo migraverunt, vel de rebus ad Deum solum pertinentibus, haec est beati Pauli sententia, Nemo nostrum sibi vivit, & nemo sibi moritur: sive enim vivimus Domino vivimus, sive morimur Domino morimur. sive enim vivimus, sive morimur Domini sumus. In hoc enim Christus resurrexit & mortuus, ut & vivorum & mortuorum dominetur. Tu autem quid judicas fratrem tuum, aut quare spernis fratrem tuum? omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Dei. Scriptum est enim, Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, quoniam mihi flectet omne genu, & omnis lingua confitebitur Deo. Itaque unusquisque nostrum pro se rationem reddet Deo. Non ergo amplius judicemus: sed hoc judicate magis, ne ponatis offendiculum fratri vel scandalum. De qua re etiam sanctae ecclesiae Romanae antistitis Anastasius Anastasio Imperatori sic perhibetur scripsisse; Ne quod sit in hoc offendiculum in ecclesia, dum quod facere non possumus, de his qui jam transierunt judicare conemur, observandum esse tranquillitas tua cognoscat. Quia ergo nec a filiis parentes inhonorandi, nec a viventibus mortui temere judicandi sunt, divinarum scripturarum paginis prolatum est. Nunc mentis oculo sollicite intuendum est, quantum in supra memoratarum imaginum abolitione vel veneratione filiorum error a parentum errore differt: cum utrimque, sibi & illorum error repugnare non desinat. Illi enim eas convellendas atque contaminandas esse censuerunt ab ecclesia perpetua abdicatione: isti eas non solum habendas, verumetiam venerandas studeant supplici adorationi. Illi eas manipavere crepitantibus ignibus: isti thure honorant odoriferis thymiamatibus. Illi eas effugiebant etiam cernere: isti non cessant amplecti. Illi effodere ad ornamentum ecclesiae ab antiquis constitutas in parietibus: isti nuper conditas oblatis perlustrant luminaribus. Illi eas studebant prorsus abominari: isti sancunt omnino osculari. Illi anathematizabant habentes: isti e contrario non adorantes. Quae duo mala cum alterutrum sibi contraria sint, & a recto tramite remota, restat nobis ut viam tegiam secundum Apostolum gradientes, neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram declinemus: ut nec cum illis prorsus abolendas judicemus, nec cum istis adorandas decernamus: sed solum Deum adorantes, & ejus sanctos venerantes secundum antiquam patrum & ecclesiasticam traditionem eas in ecclesia in ornamento & memoria rerum gestarum, si libet, habeamus, & cum justitia hinc severitatem, illinc adulationem contemnentes: cum prudentia hinc versutiam, illinc hebitudinem declinantes: cum temperantia hinc libidinem, illinc insensibilitatem pernentes: cum fortitudine, hinc timiditatem, illinc audaciam abicientes; cum sanctis patribus, qui eas in ornamento solummodo esse ecclesiae siverunt, istis hinc adorantibus, illis hinc abominantibus postpositis, viam mandatorum Domini teneamus, qualiter ad eum quae est via, veritas & vita, ipso opitulante pervenire valeamus.
units.tr: And indeed, those who presume to make images equal to the body and blood of the Lord are so driven by love of them that they do not hesitate to anathematize even their parents, who are known to have despised images, thus tying error to error. They offer an unfitting and disorderly adoration to images, and they heap an unseasonable curse upon their parents, either because they were begotten by them through the matter of the flesh, or because through their consecration they received the sacrament of baptism and their other gifts. For if, by their madness, all who lack the adoration of images are heretics, it is clear that their elders, who did not adore images, were heretics. And if they were heretics, they had no power to make consecrations or to lay on hands; and if they did not have this power, those who think they received it from them have neither consecration nor laying on of hands. Likewise, if their predecessors, as they say, deserved to be bound by the anathema, they had no power of binding and loosing. And if they had no such power, everything done by them in the church must be annulled; and if everything must be repudiated, orders and ordinations must be repudiated. So if their predecessors deserved to be bound by the anathema, the orders and ordinations of these men must be annulled. For we read that the power of binding and loosing was granted by the Lord not to schismatics bound by the chain of anathema, but to fit and Catholic men. Meanwhile honor must be paid to parents, as not only the law, the Prophets and the Apostles, but also the Gospel admonition teaches, the Lord saying, Honor your father and your mother. He who both in the pages of the Old Testament and by the presence of his own body gave this saving precept, the same proclaimed it by the mouth of Moses, saying, Blessed is he who honors his father and his mother; and on the contrary, cursed is he who does not honor his father and his mother. Hence one must weigh carefully and mark well how great is the arrogance, how great the rashness, and, so to speak, the crime, of anathematizing parents, if he is subject to that curse who is shown not to honor them. For since the law says, Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father, and the Apostle, Children, obey your parents, these men seem to resist both precepts, since they strive neither to conceal the shame nor to pay honor. Therefore the sacred canons, with every occasion set aside, seem to have issued this sentence concerning not despising parents: whoever children withdraw from their parents under the pretext of divine worship and do not render them due reverence, let them be anathema. But if those who do not pay their parents due reverence are anathematized, by what bond of damnation, do you think, are those bound who anathematize them? For the most wholesome custom handed down by the holy Fathers in the Church is to pray to the Lord for the spirits of the dead. We, embracing this with the whole holy, Catholic and universal Church, ask the most merciful piety of the Lord not only for the spirits of our parents but also for those of faithful friends who have gone before us in the Lord's peace. Those who strive not to help the spirits of dead parents with prayers, but to bind them with the chain of anathema, seem to oppose this venerable and ecclesiastical constitution not a little; and those who are bidden by the teaching of the Apostle to pray even for enemies resist doing this for their own parents. We, according to ecclesiastical custom, seek pardon for ours by prayers and almsgiving; they wish punishment upon theirs through the gatherings of empty councils. We seek rest for ours through the solemnities of the Mass; they heap insults on theirs through disorderly councils. We keep the memory of ours in prayer; they cast anathemas at theirs with a certain renunciation. We pray that the spirits of ours may possess rest in the bosom of Abraham; they wish the souls of their own to be damned with Arius, Sabellius, Dioscorus, Nestorius and Eutyches. We ask that our parents be placed among the ranks of the blessed; they place theirs among the obstinate crowds of heretics. Since these things stand thus, it is clear that they commit a double offence in this matter: they detract from the honor due to parents, against the command of the Lord's voice, and against the sentence of the Apostle they attempt to pass rash judgment on those who have departed this life. That one should not therefore rashly judge those who have already departed this life, or matters that belong to God alone, is the sentence of blessed Paul: None of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; and whether we die, we die to the Lord. Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead. But why do you judge your brother, or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of God. For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. So each of us shall give account of himself to God. Let us therefore judge one another no more; but rather judge this, that you put no stumbling block or occasion of offence before your brother. Concerning this matter, Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, is reported to have written thus to the Emperor Anastasius: Let your tranquillity know that, to avoid any stumbling block in the Church in this matter, we must observe that we should not try to judge those who have already passed away, since we cannot do so. Therefore, that parents are not to be dishonored by their children, nor the dead rashly judged by the living, has been set forth in the pages of the divine Scriptures. Now with the eye of the mind one must attentively consider how far the error of the children differs from the error of the parents in the abolition or the veneration of the aforementioned images, since on each side the one error does not cease to contradict itself and the other. The parents judged that images should be torn down and defiled, and banished from the Church with perpetual renunciation; these men not only want them kept but eagerly study to venerate them with humble adoration. The parents burned them with crackling fires; these men honor them with fragrant incense. The parents shunned even the sight of them; these men never cease to embrace them. The parents dug up those set up on the walls by the ancients for the adornment of the church; these men illuminate with offered lights those recently made. The parents strove utterly to abominate them; these men decree that they must altogether be kissed. The parents anathematized those who possessed them; these men, on the contrary, anathematize those who do not adore them. Since these two evils are contrary to each other and remote from the straight path, it remains for us, walking the royal way according to the Apostle, neither to turn aside to the right nor to the left. So we should judge them neither to be utterly abolished, with the parents, nor decree that they be adored, with these men; but adoring God alone and venerating his saints according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers and the Church, we may keep them in the church, if one wishes, as an ornament and memorial of things done. Thus, with justice, we despise flattery on one side and severity on the other; with prudence we avoid craftiness on one side and dullness on the other; with temperance we shun lust on one side and insensibility on the other; with fortitude we cast off timidity on one side and audacity on the other. Setting aside, with the holy Fathers, who allowed them only as an ornament of the church, the adoration of these men on one side and the abomination of those men on the other, let us keep the way of the commandments of the Lord, that with his help we may come to him who is the way, the truth and the life.

units.tr: HERE ENDS BOOK II.

units.tr: Preface to Book III

units.la: CONSTAT hujus nostri operis stilum sive in superioribus, qui jam Deo annuente digesti sunt libris, sive in praesenti in cujus inceptionis adorumus articulo, sive etiam in eo quem postmodum Domino opitulante digesturi sumus, adversus eorum insaniam vigilare, qui quamquam diversis temporibus diversisque voluntatib. synodos, aut ut abdicari, aut ut adorari imagines in ecclesia censeant, adsolent adgregari. Et quoniam illius insaniae Scriptura, quam inani desiderio Septimae synodi vocabulo censeri ambiunt, propriorum sensuum errorib. quasi membris concreta, & divinae legis testimoniorum inconpetenter sibi adhibitorum comminatibus quasi quibusdam pinnis cernitur esse suffulta: libuit nobis in praecedentibus libris pinnarum subsidia ei, quibus incallum fulciri arbitratur, demere: in sequentibus vero eam vanorum conpage membrorum, quibus subsistere se posse suspicatur, destituere: ut precedentes ab ea pinnarum remigia auferant, sequentes ejus artus fructatim diri-mant: precedentes eam volatu, sequentes privent gressu: ut videlicet spiritalis intellegentiæ & divini eloquii pinnis, quibus enormiter vehi putabatur, abscissis, & propriis sensibus à quibus violenter ab aliis peregrinari compellebatur restitutis, & Catholicæ fidei fortis & inexpugnabilis pugni impulsione, qua satis vacuarum & ratione carentium adfectionum acervis, & congruis sensibus & divinorum apicum testimoniis carens, omnibus appareat enervata, quæ non ab omnibus creditur esse digesta: quoniam quidem dum suorum interdictam civesadorationè provocat, civium in se domestica arma territat, & spiculorum ictus quibus & libertas debuit tueri & hostili globo obniti in indigenas, pro dolor, conpellit intorqueri. Hanc igitur non versutis cavillationibus, non forensi facundia, non procul à causa vagatibus loquutionum phaleris, non lepore lenocinioli coturni, non callidæ exsequurionis nodosis argumentationibus, stantes enervare decrevimus, sed purae ac simplicis orationis ambitu divinotū eloquiorum tenacibus nervis concreto, & sanæ sobriæque doctrinæ eloquentia colorato, qui elarionis ostentatione carens ecclesiæ sanctæ potius profectus amator, quam sua vel nostræ sit ventosæ laudis sectator. Quoniam igitur in præsentis libri textu, in quo nunc adoriri nos sequet, illorum sententias discutientes, qui aliter quædam quam à sanctis patribus tradita sunt in sua synodo posuere, de fide quodammodo disputaturi sumus, ordo exposcit ut primum nostræ fidei fundamentum jaciamus, hoc videlicet de quo aut Apostolus, Fundamentum enim aliud ponere nemo potest præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Jesus. Cujus venerandæ fidei sinceritatem, mox ut sicut corde credimus, ore protulerimus, & tanti fundaminis firmitate futuri operis primordia munierimus, liberius nostra fabrica surgens rectius solidiusve struatur, & illorum sicubi minus recte minusve solide surrexerit, facilius deiciatur. Quia ergo primum nos munire nostraq; firmare, & post contra adversa confligere, & oppositis resistere debemus, non solum sacrarum literarum perdocemur documentis, sed etiam ipsius Romani auctoris eloquii monemur instituti, qui ait, Argumentandum est ita ut primum nostra firmemus, deinde adversa confringamus.
units.tr: It is well known that in this work of ours we keep watch against the madness of those who, at various times and with various wills, are wont to gather synods that decree either that images be abolished in the Church or that they be worshipped. In the books already completed, by God's permission, and in the present one, whose beginning we are now approaching, and in the one we shall later write with the Lord's help, we keep this watch. Since the madness of that party, which vainly longs to have its council counted as the Seventh Synod, is seen to be propped up, as by certain wings, on the errors of its own senses, which are joined to it like limbs, and on the threats of divine testimonies improperly applied to it: we decided in the preceding books to strip from it the wing-supports on which it thinks it stands, and in the following books to dislodge it from the framework of empty limbs on which it suspects it can stand. The earlier books will take away its oars of wings, the later will tear its limbs apart piece by piece; the earlier will rob it of flight, the later of its footing. So that, with the wings of spiritual understanding and of the divine word, by which it was thought to be carried far beyond its means, cut away, and with its own senses, by which it was forced to wander violently away from others, restored, and by the strong and unconquerable blow of the Catholic faith, it may appear to all to be enfeebled, lacking congruent senses and the testimonies of divine letters, among the heaps of empty affections that have no reason in them, and which are not believed by everyone to have been put together. For while it provokes its own citizens with its forbidden worship, it frightens the domestic arms of its citizens against itself; and it forces the blows of its spears, which ought to have defended liberty, and its hostile crowd to press upon its own countrymen, alas. We have therefore decided to weaken this party, not with crafty cavils, not with forensic eloquence, not with the ornaments of speech that wander far from the case, not with the charm of a trifling flourish of the tragic buskin, not with the knotted arguments of a shrewd exposition; but to bind it together with the sinews of the divine words, which hold fast, in the compass of a pure and simple style, and to colour it with the eloquence of a sound and sober doctrine. Lacking any display of brilliance, I am a lover of the holy Church's advancement rather than a pursuer of my own or our empty praise. Therefore, since in the text of the present book, in which we now proceed to attack, we shall discuss the opinions of those who, in their synod, have set forth some things differently from what was handed down by the holy Fathers, and shall in a sense dispute about the faith, the order of the work requires that we first lay the foundation of our faith, namely that of which the Apostle says: For no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. When we have, as soon as we have confessed with the heart, professed with the mouth, the sincerity of this venerable faith, and have fortified the beginnings of the future work by the firmness of so great a foundation, our structure will rise more freely and be built more rightly and more solidly; and if theirs has risen anywhere less rightly or less solidly, it will be more easily thrown down. Because, then, we must first fortify ourselves and make our own position firm, and afterwards contend against adversaries and resist opponents, we are taught this not only by the instructions of the sacred letters, but also we are admonished by the precept of the Roman author himself, who says: One must argue in such a way that we first strengthen our own position, and then break down the adversary's.

units.la: LIBER III. CAP. I.
units.tr: Book III, Chapter I.

units.la: Confessio fidei Catholicæ quam à sanctis patribus accepimus, tenemus, & puro corde credimus.
units.tr: The confession of the Catholic faith, which we have received from the holy Fathers, hold, and believe with a pure heart.

units.la: CREDIMUS in Deum patrem omnipotentem conditorem cunctorum visibilium & invisibilium. Credimus & in Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum per quem omnia creata sunt, verum Deum, unigenitum & verum Dei filium, non factum aut adoptivum, sed genitum & unius cum patre substantiæ, atque ita per omnia æqualem Deo patri, ut nec tempore, nec gradu, nec potestate esse possit inferior: tantumque esse confitemur illum, qui est genitus, quantus est ille, qui genuit. Non autem quia dicimus genitum à patre filium, divinæ & ineffabili generationi aliquod tempus adscribimus, sed nec patrem aliquando cœpisse nec filium. Non enim aliter confiteri possumus æternum patrem, nisi confiteamur etiam coæternum filium: ex filio enim pater dicitur, & qui semper pater fuit, semper habuit filium. Credimus & in Spiritum S. Deum verum ex patre & filio procedentem, æqualem per omnia patri & filio, volutate, potestate, æternitate, substantia: necesse est profusus aliquid sit in trinitate gradus, nihil quod inferius superiusve dici possit, sed tota Deitas sui perfectione æqualis est, ut exceptis vocabulis quæ proprietatem personarum indicant, quicquid de una persona dicitur, de tribus dignissime possit intelligi: atque ut confundentes Arium unam eandemque dicimus trinitatis esse substantiam, & unum in tribus personis fatemur Deum, ita impietatem Sabellii declinantes, tres personas expressas sub proprietate disjungimus, non ipsum sibi patrem, ipsum sibi filium, ipsum Spiritum sanctum esse dicentes, sed aliam patris, aliam filii, aliam Spiritus sancti esse personam. Non enim nomina tantum modo, sed etiam nominum proprietates, id est, personas, vel ut Græci ex primunt, ὑποστάσεις, hoc est, subsistentias, confitemur. Nec pater filii aut sancti Spiritus personam aliquando excludit: nec rursus filius aut Spiritus sanctus patris nomen personamque recipit, sed pater semper pater est, filius semper filius, Spiritus sanctus semper Spiritus sanctus: itaque substantia unum sunt, personis ac nominibus distinguuntur. Ipsum autem Dei filium, qui abs; initio æternitate cum patre & Spiritu S. possidet, dicimus in fine seculorum perfectum naturæ nostræ hominem suscepisse ex Maria semper virgine, & verbum carnem esse factum adsumendo hominem, non permutando Deitatem: nec, ut quidam sceleratissime opinantur, Spiritum sanctum dicimus fuisse pro femine, sed potentia ac virtute creatoris operatum. Sic autem confitemur in Christo unam filii esse personam, ut dicamus duas perfectas atque integras esse substantias, id est, deitatis & humanitatis, quæ ex anima continentur & corpore: atque ut condemnamus Fotinum, qui solum & nudum hominem confitetur in Christo, ita anathematizamus Apollinare & ejus similes, qui dicunt Dei filium minus aliquid de humana suscepisse natura, & vel in carne, vel in anima, vel infensu adsumptum hominem his propter quos adsumptus est fuisse dissimilem, quem absq; sola peccati macula quæ naturalis non est, nobis confitemur esse conformem. Illorum quoq; similiter exsecramur blasphemiam, qui novo sensu afferre conantur a tempore susceptæ
units.tr: We believe in God the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. We also believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created, the true God, the only-begotten and true Son of God, not made or adopted, but begotten, and of one substance with the Father, and so equal to God the Father in all things that he can be inferior neither in time, nor in rank, nor in power. We confess that he who is begotten is as great as he who begot him. Yet when we say that the Son was begotten by the Father, we do not assign any time to the divine and ineffable generation; nor did the Father ever begin to be, nor the Son. For we cannot confess the Father as eternal unless we also confess the Son as co-eternal: the Father is called Father from the Son, and he who was always Father always had a Son. We also believe in the Holy Spirit, the true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, equal to the Father and the Son in all things, in will, power, eternity, and substance. There must be no gradation of any kind in the Trinity, nothing that can be called inferior or superior; the whole Deity is equal in its perfection, so that, apart from the terms which indicate the property of the persons, whatever is said of one person can most fittingly be understood of all three. Thus, while we confront Arius, we say that the substance of the Trinity is one and the same, and we confess one God in three persons; and while we avoid the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish the three persons by their properties, not saying that the Father is himself his own Son, or that the Son is himself the Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not only the names but also the properties of the names, that is, the persons, or, as the Greeks express it, subsistences [ὑποστάσεις], that is, subsistences. The Father never excludes the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor does the Son or the Holy Spirit ever receive the name and person of the Father; but the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance and are distinguished by persons and names. We say that the Son of God himself, who from the beginning possesses eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in the fullness of time assumed a perfect human nature from Mary, ever a virgin, and that the Word was made flesh by taking on a man, not by changing his Deity. Nor, as some most wickedly think, do we say that the Holy Spirit was the father of the seed, but that it was wrought by the power and virtue of the Creator. We confess that in Christ there is one person of the Son, yet we say that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely of Deity and of humanity, which consists of soul and body. And just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses in Christ only a bare man, so we anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less of human nature, either in flesh or in soul, or that the man he assumed was unlike those for whose sake he assumed him, whom, apart from the stain of sin, which is not natural, we confess to be like us. Likewise we curse the blasphemy of those who strive to maintain, in a new sense, that from the time the flesh was assumed, all that belonged to the Deity passed over into the man, and again that what belonged to the humanity was transfused into God, so that, what no heresy has ever dared to say, both substances, of Deity and of humanity, seem to be emptied by this confusion and changed from their proper state into something else; they who confess God in the Son as imperfect, as they confess man, are believed to hold neither God truly nor man. But we say that the passible nature of ours, which the Son of God assumed, remained impassible in its Deity. For the Son suffered not in appearance but truly, all the things which Scripture attests: that is, hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and the like, and he suffered according to what could suffer, that is, not according to that substance which assumed, but according to that which was assumed. For the Son of God himself, according to his Deity, is impassible as the Father is, incomprehensible as the Father is, invisible as the Father is, unchangeable as the Father is. And although the Word, in his own person, took up a passible man, yet by his indwelling the Deity of the Word itself suffered nothing in its own substance, so that the whole Trinity must be confessed as impassible. Therefore the Son of God died according to the Scriptures, in that he could die; he rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the nature of the flesh in which he was born and suffered, and in which he also rose again, remaining. For the substance of the humanity was not emptied but glorified, to remain for ever with the Deity. Having therefore received from the Father power over all things in heaven and on earth, he will come to judge the living and the dead, both to reward the righteous and to punish sinners. We believe in the resurrection of the flesh in such a way that we say we shall be restored in the same truth of members as we now have, and that we shall remain for ever in such condition as we shall have been made once after the resurrection: there is one life of the saints, but the rewards are different according to their labours; on the contrary, there are also punishments for sins according to the measure of the offences. We hold one baptism, which is celebrated in the same words of the sacrament for infants, and which is also to be celebrated for adults. If a man falls after baptism, we believe that he can be saved through repentance. We receive the New and the Old Testament among the books which the authority of the holy catholic Church has handed down. We believe that souls are given by God, whom we say were made by him, and we anathematize those who say that souls are of the divine substance, as if they were a part of God. We also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned before, or lived in heaven before they were sent into bodies. We also curse the blasphemy of those who say that something impossible has been commanded of man by God, and that the commandments of God cannot be kept by all in common, but only by individuals; or who condemn first marriages with the Manichaeans, or second marriages with the Cataphrygians. We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied out of necessity of the flesh, and that he could not do all that he wished because of the man he assumed. We also condemn the heresy of Jovinian, who says that there will be no difference of merits in the future, and that we shall there have the virtues which we have neglected to have here. We so confess free will that we say we always need the help of God; and those err who, with Manichaeus, say that man cannot avoid sin, as much as those who, with Jovinian, assert that man cannot sin; for both destroy the liberty of the will. But we say that man can always both sin and not sin, so that we always confess ourselves free in choice. This is the true integrity of the faith of the catholic tradition, which we believe and profess with a sincere heart, and which we have set forth and marked in this work in the words of the blessed Jerome. This is the true faith; let us keep and hold this confession, and whoever shall guard it unshaken and undefiled will have eternal salvation.

units.la: * Sc. Cicero-nis. suscepta carnis omnia quæ erant deitatis in hominem demigrasse: & rursum quæ erant humanitatis in deum esse transfusa, ut quod nulla unquam hæresis dicere ausa est videatur hac confusione utraque exinanita substantia scilicet deitatis & humanitatis, & à proprio statu in aliud esse mutata: qui tam deum imperfectum in filio quàm hominem confitentur, ut nec deum vere nec hominem tenere credantur. Nos autem ita dicimus, susceptum à dei filio passibile nostrum, ut deitas inpassibilis permaneret. Passus enim filius non putative sed vere, omnia quæ scriptura testatur: Id est esuriem, sitim, lassitudinem, dolorem, mortem & cætera hujusmodi secundum illud passus est quod pati poterat, id est, non secundum illam substantiam quæ adsumpsit, sed secundum illam quæ adsumpta est. Ipse enim dei filius secundum deitatem suam inpassibilis est ut pater, inconprehensibilis ut pater, invisibilis ut pater, inconvertibilis ut pater. Et quamvis propria persona filii, id est, dei verbum suscepit passibilem hominem, ita tamen ejus habitatione secundum suam substantiam deitas verbi nihil passa est, ut tota trinitas quam inpassibilem necesse est confiteri. Mortuus est ergo dei filius secundum scripturas, juxta id quod mori poterat, resurrexit tertia die, ascendit in cælum, sedet ad dexteram dei patris, manente ea natura carnis in qua natus & passus est, in qua etiam resurrexit. Non enim exinanita est humanitatis substantia, sed glorificata, in æternum cum deitate manśura. Accepta ergo à patre potestate omnium quæ in cælo sunt & in terra, venturus est ad judicium vivorum ac mortuorum, ut & justos remuneret, & punirat peccatores. Resurrectionem carnis ita credimus, ut dicamus nos in eadem in qua nunc sumus veritate membrorum esse reparandos, qualesque semel post resurrectionem fuerimus effecti, in perpetuo manśuros: unam esse vitam sanctorum, sed præmia pro labore diversa: e contrario pro modo delictorum peccatorum quoque esse supplicia. Baptisma unum tenemus, quod hidem sacramenti verbis in infantibus, quibus etiam in majoribus esse celebrandum. Homine si post baptisma lapsus fuerit, per pœnitentiam credimus posse salvari. Novum & vetus testamentum recipimus in eorum librorum numero, quem sanctæ catholicæ ecclesiæ tradidit auctoritas. Animas à deo dari credimus quas ab ipso factas dicimus, anathematizátes eos qui animas quali partem dei divinæ dicunt esse substantiæ. Eorum quoq; condemnamus errorem, qui eas ante peccasse vel in cælis conversatas suisse dicunt quàm in corpora mitterentur. Exsecramur etiam eorum blasphemiam qui dicunt, inpossibile aliquid hominì à deo esse præceptum, & mandata dei non à singulis, sed ab omnibus in commune posse servari: vel qui primas nuptias cum Manicheo, aut secundas cum Cataphrygis damnant. Anathematizamus etiam illos qui dei filiũ necessitate carnis mentitum esse dicunt, & eum propter adsumptum hominem non omnia facere potuisse quæ voluit. Joviniani quoque damnamus hæresin, qui dicit, nullam in futuro meritorum esse distantiam: nosque eas ibi habituros virtutes quas hic habere neglexerimus. Liberum sic confitemur arbitrium, ut dicamus nos semper dei indigere auxilio: & tam illos errare qui cum Manicheo dicunt hominem peccatum vitare non posse, quàm illos qui cum Joviniano asserunt hominem non posse peccare: utrumque enim tollit arbitrii libertatem. Nos vero dicimus hominem semper & peccare & non peccare posse, ut semper nos liberi confiteamur esse arbitrii. Hæc est catholicæ traditionis fidei vera integritas, quam syncero corde credimus & fatemur, & in hoc opere beati Hieronymi verbis expressam taxavimus. Hæc est vera fides, hanc confessionem consérvamus atque tenemus, quam quisque inconvulsè & intemeratè custodierit, perpetuam salutem habebit.
units.tr: * That is, Cicero-nis. Nor, after the flesh was taken up, did all the things that belonged to the deity pass over into man, nor were the things that belonged to the humanity transfused into God, so that what no heresy has ever dared to say would seem to follow: that both substances, of deity and of humanity, are emptied by this confusion and changed from their own state into something else. They confess a God imperfect in the Son, as they confess a man, so that they are believed to hold neither God truly nor man. We, however, speak thus: that the passible nature which the Son of God took up is so taken up that the deity remains impassible. For the Son suffered, not in appearance but truly, all the things that Scripture attests: that is, hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and the other things of this kind. He suffered according to what could suffer, that is, not according to the substance that took up, but according to the substance that was taken up. For the Son of God himself, according to his deity, is impassible as the Father is, incomprehensible as the Father is, invisible as the Father is, unchangeable as the Father is. And although the Word of God, in his own person, took up passible man, yet by that indwelling the deity of the Word, according to its own substance, suffered nothing, so that the whole Trinity must be confessed as impassible. The Son of God therefore died according to the Scriptures, according to what could die; he rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the nature of the flesh in which he was born and suffered remaining, and in which he also rose again. For the substance of the humanity was not emptied but glorified, to remain for ever with the deity. Having therefore received from the Father power over all things in heaven and on earth, he will come to judge the living and the dead, both to reward the righteous and to punish sinners. We believe in the resurrection of the flesh in such a way that we say we are to be restored in the same truth of members in which we now are, and that we shall remain in perpetuity in the condition we have once been made after the resurrection: that there is one life of the saints, but the rewards differ according to their labours; and, on the contrary, that punishments also correspond to the measure of sins and offences. We hold one baptism, which is to be celebrated with the same words of the sacrament in infants, as also in adults. If a man falls after baptism, we believe he can be saved through repentance. We receive the New and the Old Testament in the number of those books which the authority of the holy catholic Church has handed down. We believe that souls are given by God, since we say they are made by him, anathematizing those who say that souls are some part of the divine substance. We also condemn the error of those who say that they sinned before, or lived in heaven before they were sent into bodies. We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that something impossible has been commanded to a man by God, and that the commandments of God can be kept not by individuals but by all in common; or who condemn first marriages with the Manichaean, or second marriages with the Cataphrygians. We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied out of necessity of the flesh, and that because of the man he had taken up he could not do all that he willed. We also condemn the heresy of Jovinian, who says that there will be no difference of merits in the future, and that we shall there have those virtues which we have neglected to have here. We so confess free will that we say we always need the help of God; and that those are wrong who, with the Manichaean, say that man cannot avoid sin, as well as those who, with Jovinian, assert that man cannot sin: for both take away the liberty of the will. But we say that man can always both sin and not sin, so that we always confess ourselves to be free in our will. This is the true integrity of the faith of the catholic tradition, which we believe and profess with a sincere heart, and which we have set forth, expressed in the words of blessed Jerome, in this work. This is the true faith; let us keep and hold this confession, and whoever shall guard it unshaken and undefiled will have perpetual salvation.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: Quod Tarasius aberrore errorem tinire conatus sit, & quod ab ægritudine ad ægritudinem dilapsus sit, cum videlicet repente ex laico conversus & ad episcopatum promotus nititur hoc emendare in imaginum adoratione, quod admisit in repen- tina consecrationis susceptione.
units.tr: That Tarasius, trying to cure one error by another error, passed from one sickness to another, since he, having been suddenly converted from a layman and promoted to the episcopate, strives to correct in the adoration of images what he committed in the sudden acceptance of consecration.

units.la: PERITORUM vetus iste medicorum mos est, sic unius ægritudinis molestiis medicaminibus crebris curando inštare, ut tamen alterius pestis nequitiæ non videatur adminicula præstare: quoniam quædam res sicut unius vires extenuant, ita adhibitæ alterius viribus alimenta ministrant: & spiritalis vineæ cultorum est, sic quorundam convellere vitiorum stirpes, ut tamen aliorum nullis convalescant incrementis radices: quoniam quorundam vitiorum pestifera plantatio aliorum abolitione vitiorum moleseit, siveque alii pesti subsidia præbens agro mentis officit, quæ per se officere non valens suis viribus exinpata fatescit. Quorum utrorumque præstantibus moribus, sive peritorum medicorum, sive spiritualium cultorum, non mediocriter Tarasius perhibetur obniti, qui per rem penitus interdictam & nullatenus proficientem nititur emendare rem penitus interdictam & prorsus officientem. Et veluti si quis lutulentum quid ingesta inpuritate eluere cupiens, dum lutulentis nihilominus eluere utitur aquis, quo magis abluere appetit, eo magis eisdem inpuritatibus inficit: ita idem ex laico repente ad episcopatum, ut fertur, promotus, dum repentinam tanti gradus susceptionem per insolentem nisus est emendare imaginum adorationem, inlicitum inlicito adposuit: & quanto unum erroremum altero errore linire putavit, tanto le majoribus errorum nexibus præpedivit. Nam si inopportuna imaginum adoratione inopportuna ordinatio stabiliri potest, facile res inlicitæ rebus poterunt firmari inlicitis, & si res inlicitæ rebus poterunt firmari inliciis, facillime inpura quæque quibusdam impuris ablui poterunt. Non autem impura quæque quibusdam impuris ablui poterunt: non igitur inoportuna ordinatio adoratione inopportuna nihilominus imaginum quoquomodo poterit stabiliri. Etsi ecclesiasticae ordinationis regula à sanctis patribus tradita intemerata servanda est, immo quia servanda est, omnino corrumpi non debet: & si omnino corrumpi non debet, nec pro utili quadam re corrumpi quidem debet: & si pro utili quadam re nullatenus corrumpi debet, multo ergo minus pro inutili corrumpi debet: cum videlicet utrumque & imagines adorare, & sine ordine graduum pontificalem cathedram subire inutile sit. Sed quoniam ista accedamus ad Apostolum, veniamus ad vas electionis, interrogemus egregium praedicatorem, intonet nobis quid de ordinatione episcopi censeat, qui proculdubio respondebit, Manus cito nemini imposueris. Et rursus, Non neophytum, ne in superbiam elatus in judicium incidat diaboli: ne videlicet dum putat se non tam ministerium humilitatis quam administrationem saecularis potestatis adeptum, condemnatione superbiae sicut diabolus per jactantiam deiciatur. Unde periculosissima est talis ordinatio, in qua diaboli judicium suspicatur: & formidolosissimum est, ejus doctrina, qua imagines adorare censet, uti, in quo tam atrocis exempli ruina formidatur: cum prohibitum sit popularem hominem sacerdotii magisterium adimplere debere, cuius nec officium tenuisse, nec disciplinam credidit agnovisse: & eum ea docere posse, quae constat eum nequaquam antea didicisse. De tali itaque ordinatione haec est beati Gregorii Romanae urbis antecessoris sententia.
units.tr: This is the old custom of skilled physicians: while treating the troubles of one disease with frequent remedies, they take care not to provide aid to the wickedness of another plague. For certain things weaken the strength of one thing, yet when applied they supply nourishment to the strength of another. And it is the way of those who cultivate the spiritual vineyard to pluck up the roots of certain vices, yet so that the roots of others do not grow strong by their increase. For the pestilent planting of certain vices is harmed by the destruction of other vices, and thus one who gives help to one plague hinders the field of the mind, which, unable to harm by itself, withers when uprooted by its own strength. Tarasius is said to have struggled, not moderately, with both of these practices, whether of skilled physicians or of spiritual cultivators. He tries to correct by a thing wholly forbidden and in no way profitable a thing wholly forbidden and utterly harmful. And just as if someone wishing to wash away some filth, by the infection of which he is soiled, uses muddy waters for washing, and the more he seeks to cleanse himself the more he is stained by the same impurities, so this man, who was suddenly promoted, as it is said, from a layman to the episcopate, while by an insolent effort he tries to correct the sudden acceptance of so great a rank by the adoration of images, has added the unlawful to the unlawful; and the more he thought to smear over one error with another, the more he entangled himself in greater bonds of error. For if an inopportune ordination can be confirmed by an inopportune adoration of images, then unlawful things can easily be confirmed by unlawful things; and if unlawful things can be confirmed by unlawful things, then every impure thing can most easily be cleansed by certain impure things. But not every impure thing can be cleansed by certain impure things. Therefore an inopportune ordination cannot in any way be confirmed by an inopportune adoration of images. Although the rule of ecclesiastical ordination handed down by the holy Fathers must be kept inviolate, indeed because it must be kept, it ought not to be corrupted at all; and if it ought not to be corrupted at all, it ought not to be corrupted even for some useful purpose; and if it ought in no way to be corrupted for some useful purpose, much less ought it to be corrupted for a useless one. For clearly both to adore images and to ascend the episcopal chair without the order of degrees is useless. But since we are to come to the Apostle, let us approach the vessel of election, let us ask that outstanding preacher what he thinks of the ordination of a bishop, and he will undoubtedly answer: Lay hands on no one hastily. And again: not a novice, lest being puffed up with pride he fall into the judgment of the devil; namely, lest, thinking that he has obtained not so much the ministry of humility as the administration of secular power, he be cast down by the condemnation of pride, as the devil was through boasting. Hence such an ordination is most perilous, in which the judgment of the devil is to be feared; and it is most dreadful to use his teaching, by which he judges that images are to be adored, in which the ruin of so terrible an example is to be dreaded; since it has been forbidden that a common man should be made to fill the office of the priesthood, whose duty he has not held and whose discipline he is not believed to have known, and that he should be able to teach those things which it is clear he has in no way learned before. Concerning such an ordination, then, this is the judgment of the blessed Gregory, predecessor in the city of Rome.

units.la: Quidam desiderio honoris inflati defuncti episcopi tonsurantur, & repente fiunt ex laico sacerdotes, atque inverecunde religiosi propositi ducatum arripiunt, qui nec esse adhuc milites didicerunt. Quid putamus, qui isti subjectis praelaturi sunt? qui antequam disciplinatus limen admittant, tenere locum magisterii non formidant? Qua de re necesse est, ut & si inculpati quisque sit meriti, ante tamen per distinctos ordines ecclesiastici exerceatur ossicium: videat quod imitetur, discat quod doceat, informetur ad id quod teneat, ut postea non debeat errare, qui eligitur viam errantibus demonstrare.
units.tr: Some, swollen with desire for honour, are tonsured when bishops have died, and suddenly from laymen they become priests, and without shame they seize the leadership of a religious way of life, though they have not yet learned how to be soldiers. What do we think of those who are to be set over subjects, who do not hesitate to hold the place of teaching before they have been admitted to the threshold of discipline? For this reason it is necessary that, however blameless a man may be, he first exercise the office of the church through its distinct orders: let him see what he is to imitate, let him learn what he is to teach, let him be formed for that which he is to hold, so that afterwards he need not err, he who is chosen to show the way to those who err.

units.la: Diu ergo religiosa meditatione poliatur, ut placeat: & sic lucerna super candelabrum posita luceat, ut adversa ventorum vis inruens conceptam eruditionis flammam non extinguat, sed augeat: tam cum scriptam sit, ut prius quis probetur, & sic munistret, multo amplius ante probandus est, qui populi intercessor ad sumuntur, ne fiant causa ruinae populi sacerdotes mali. Nulla igitur contra hoc excusatio, nulla potest esse defensio, quia cuiuslibet notum est, quae sit in hujus rei diligentia sancta egregii sollicitudo doctoris, qua neophytum ad ordines vetat sacros accedere.
units.tr: Let him therefore be polished for a long time by religious meditation, so that he may be pleasing; and so let him be like a lamp placed upon a candlestick, that it shines, so that the adverse force of the winds rushing in does not extinguish the flame of learning once kindled, but increases it. Since it is written that a man should first be proved, and then minister, much more must those be proved before they are taken up as intercessors for the people, lest evil priests become the cause of the people's ruin. Therefore there is no excuse against this, no defence can exist, because it is known to everyone what holy care is taken in this matter by that outstanding teacher, who forbids a novice to approach the sacred orders.

units.la: Sicut autem tunc neophytus dicebatur, qui initio sanctae fidei erat conversatione plantatus, sic modo neophytus habendus est, qui repente in religionis habitu planatus ad ambiendos honores sacros inrepserit. Ordine ergo ad ordinem accedendum est. Non gradum sacrum recte appetit, qui ad summa loci saltigia post positis gradibus per abrupta quaerit ascensum: & cum idem apostolus doceat inter alia sacri ordinis instituta discipulum, manus nou esse cuquam citius imponendas, quid hoc celerius, quidve praecipitantius quam ut exoriatur a summitate principium, ut esse incipiat episcopus quam magister? Contra quam ecclesiasticae institutionis normam dum superius memoratus Tarasius sacerdotale culmen, ut ajunt, contendit, turbare potius quam gubernare dinoscitur plebes.
units.tr: Just as a novice was then called one who had been planted in the conversation of the holy faith at its beginning, so now he is to be regarded as a novice who, planted suddenly in the habit of religion, has crept in to seek sacred honours. One must therefore advance from order to order. He does not rightly seek a sacred rank who, with the steps set aside, seeks by steep and sudden ways the ascent to the highest places. And since the same Apostle teaches, among other precepts of the sacred order, that hands are not to be laid on anyone too quickly, what could be more hasty or more headlong than for the beginning to arise from the summit, so that one begins to be a bishop before he is a teacher? Contrary to this rule of ecclesiastical institution, the Tarasius mentioned above, as they say, strives for the summit of the priesthood, and he is shown to disturb the peoples rather than to govern them.

units.la: Nec mirandum est si non recte praedicet, qui ad praedicationis officium non recte pervenit. De cujus inordinata consecratione multa sanctorum patrum poni testimonia poterant, quae tamen brevitatis causa omissa sunt. Haec tantum de hac re potuisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Nor is it to be wondered at if he does not preach rightly, who has not rightly come to the office of preaching. Many testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning his disordered consecration could have been set forth, which have nevertheless been omitted for the sake of brevity. Let it suffice to have said this much about the matter.

units.la: CAP. III. Utrum Tarasius recte sentiat qui spiritum sanctum non ex patre & filio secundum veritatem sanctae fidei regulam, sed ex patre per filium procedentem in suae credulitatis lectione proficiatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. Whether Tarasius rightly holds, who does not profess in his creed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, according to the true rule of the holy faith, but from the Father through the Son.

units.la: NOSTRIS memorialibus nequaquam subtraxit oblivio sensibus, quod in primordiis hujus nostri operis polliciti sumus, nihil nos indiscussum relicturos, nihilque silentio praeteriturus, quod in eadem synodo quae pro adorandis imaginibus gesta est, reprehensione dignum inveniretur: nisi forte quod aut difficultas inordinati sermonis nostro intellectui impertire negaret, aut puerilis dicti ineptiam reverentia cohibente nostra disputatio persequi desiceret. Ideoque non est consequens ut ab hoc nostra suspendatur disputatio, quod Tarasius spiritum sanctum non ex patre tantum, sicut quidam qui quamquam eum ex filio procedere quodammodo tacuerint, tamen ex patre & filio procedentem omnino crediderunt: neque ex patre & filio, sicut omnis universaliter confitetur & credit ecclesia eum procedere, sed ex patre per filium in suae fidei professione procedere confessus est. In qua professione nisi puritas & syncerias cordis sit, quae credat eum non creaturam esse, sed creatorem, nec patre filioque minorem, sed eis aequalem & consubstantialem & ab utroque procedere, perniciosum virus poterit exoriri.
units.tr: Our memory has by no means lost the sense of what we promised at the beginning of this work: that we would leave nothing unexamined and pass over nothing in silence that might be found worthy of censure in the same synod which was held concerning the veneration of images, unless perhaps the obscurity of the disordered language denied our understanding any grasp of it, or unless, out of reverence, we failed to pursue a childish remark with our disputation. Therefore it does not follow that our discussion should be held back on this account: that Tarasius confessed the Holy Spirit to proceed not from the Father alone, as some did who, though they were silent about his proceeding from the Son in some sense, nevertheless believed him to proceed wholly from the Father and the Son; nor from the Father and the Son, as the Church universally confesses and believes that he proceeds, but in his profession of faith he confessed that he proceeds from the Father through the Son. In such a profession, unless there is purity and sincerity of heart, which believes that he is not a creature but the Creator, and not less than the Father and the Son but equal to them and consubstantial, and that he proceeds from both, a deadly poison may arise.

units.la: Omnium ergo rerum definitio talis esse debet, ut omnibus obscuritatibus seu ambiguitatibus explosis, ad demonstrandae rei recto tramite tendant indicium, & si alia rerum definitio tam perspicua tamque debet esse dilucida, ut ea quae demonstranda sunt, evidenter demonstret, multo magis fidei definitio dilucida & perspicua & omni ambiguitate sive tortuositate carens esse debet. In qua si aliquid aut tortuosum aut ambiguum, aut quodam nubilo verborum obductum fuerit, magnam affert dicenti vel audienti jacturam.
units.tr: Therefore the definition of all things ought to be such that, with every obscurity or ambiguity cast out, it leads by a straight path to the indication of the thing to be shown. And if the definition of other things ought to be so clear and lucid that it demonstrates plainly what is to be shown, much more must the definition of faith be lucid and clear, free from all ambiguity or crookedness. If anything in it is crooked or ambiguous, or is veiled by a certain cloud of words, it brings great loss to the speaker or the hearer.

units.la: Ex patre enim & filio spiritum sanctum, non ex patre per filium procedere, recte creditur, & ut itaque confiretur: quia non per filium ut potecreatura quae per ipsum facta sit, neque quasi posterior tempore aut minor potestate, aut alterius substantiae procedit, sed ex patre & filio ut coaeternus, ut consubstantialis, ut coaequalis, ut unius gloriae, potestatis atque divinitatis cum eis existens procedere creditur. Alteram namque vim habet, ex, praepositio & alteram, per. Unde & dei filius natus ex homine non per hominem creditur, id est, non per coitum, non per humanam operationem, sed ex virgine carnem adsumendo natus. Et idcirco quæri potest, utrum recte dici queat, spiritus sanctus à patre per filium procedere, ne dum incautè hæc præpositio, per, in tanti mysterii professione ponitur, Arriani illius erroris virosum cuiquam poculum ministret, qui spiritum sanctum creaturam esse, & per filium sicut & cætera quæ creata sunt, creatum esse blasphemat: qui etiam sui baptismatis tinctionem non juxta fidem evangelicam, in nomine patris & filii & spiritus sancti, sed in nomine patris per filium in spiritu sancto infelicibus quibusq; ad se conversis inpertivit. Spiritus namque sanctus non creatura, sed creator esse his testimoniis adprobatur. Ait enim David, Verbo domini cæli firmati sunt, & spiritu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum. & Salomon dicit, Ipse creavit ea per spiritum sanctum. item David, Emitte spiritum tuum & creabuntur, & renovabis faciem terræ. & in libro Iob scribitur, Spiritus divinus est, inquit, qui creavit me. & in libro Judith, Tibi, inquit, serviet omnis creatura tua: quoniam dixisti & facta sunt, nihilsti spiritum tuum & ædificavit. Tantæ enim potestatis sive virtutis spiritus sanctus ostenditur, ut ipso cooperante corpus domini nostri Iesu Christi, quod est nostra redemptio, in utero virginis formaretur, Evangelista dicente, Ne timeas Ioseph accipere Mariam conjugem tuam, quod enim in ea natum est de spiritu sancto est. item, Inventa est in utero habens de spiritu sancto: non quod salvatoris nostri spiritus sanctus pater dicendus est, ut duo patres credantur, sed quod patris & filii idem spiritus sanctus cooperator & unius potestatis cum eisdem esse credatur, domino adfirmante; Ite, inquit discipulis, baptizate omnes gentes in nomine patris & filii & spiritus sancti. Sicut enim domihus Apostolos ad prædicandum destinavit, pari etiam modo spiritus sanctus facere declaratur. Scribitur enim in Actibus apostolorum, quòd Petro cogitante de visione, dicit ei spiritus sanctus; Ecce viri quaerunt te, exurgens vade cum eis nihil dubitans, quia ego eos misi ad te. & item, Segregatemi- hi Paulum & Barnabam ad opus quod elegi eos. & item; Attendite vobis & universo gregi in quo vos spiritus sanctus constituit episcopos. Nam & universa cum patre & filio, ut ostensum est, procreavit, & deus esse unius cum iisdem essentiæ his testimoniis adprobatur. David enim ait; Audiam quid loquatur in me dominus deus. Luceiraque clarius constat, quòd omnes prophetæ non nisi per spiritum sanctum adnuncient vel loquantur, domino adtestante, qui air; Cùm venerit spiritus ille sanctus quem pater mittet in nomine meo, ipse vos docebit & ventura adnuntiabit vobis. item per Prophetam dominus dicit; Noluerunt audire sermones meos quos mandavi in spiritu meo per os prophetarum priorum, dicit dominus. Paulus quoque Apostolus ad Hebræos scribens ait; Testificatur nobis spiritus sanctus, & hoc est testamentum quod dispono ad eos post dies illos, dicit dominus. In Actibus quoque Apostolorum ad Ananiam dixisse pastorem ecclesiæ legimus; Ut quid satanas implevit cor tuum mentiri te spiritui sancto? & ostendens eum Deum esse, in subleguentibus dicit, Non es mentitus hominibus, sed Deo. Paulus quoque vas electionis ad Corinthios scribit; Divisiones autem donationum sunt, idem vero spiritus: & divisiones ministeriorum sunt, idem ipse dominus: & divisiones operationum sunt, idem vero deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. Quibus apostolicis verbis spiritus sanctus idem deus, idem dominus declaratur. idem vero dominus in evangelio dicit, Spiritus est deus. item ad Corinthios Paulus scribens ait, Dominus autem spiritus est: & ad Ephesios, Nolite, inquit, contristare spiritum sanctum dei: item ad Corinthios, An nescitis, inquit, quia membra vestra templum sunt spiritus sancti quem habetis a deo? & cum deum in humanis corporibus habitantem ostendens adjungit, & dicit; Glorificate ergo & portate deum in corpore vestro. Qui dum his testimoniis & creator & deus adprobetur, & ex patre & filio ab omni catholica ecclesia procedere credatur, quærendum est utrum necesse sit eum per filium a patre & non potius ex patre & filio procedere profiteri, cùm hujuscemodi professio neque in Niceno neque in Chalcedonensi symbolo à sanctis patribus facta inveniatur. Per filium enim super Apostolos in igne apparuit: per filium hominibus datus est, quoniam ab omnibus spiritus sanctus accipi non nisi per filium poterat. Per filium verò cum à patre procedere profiteri, Synodicæ confessioni inusitatum est: quoniam Sp.S. ut à patre procedat non eget alterius adjutorio, ut per aliquid procedat: cùm utiq; sittertia in eadem sanctatrinitate pei sona & unius cum patre & filio sit potestatis atque essentiæ. Qui cùm à se deus sit, ad nos autem relative dominum est, distribuens singulis prout vult gratiarum dona. Nam & prophetias quibus vult impertit, & peccata quibus vult dimittit, quæ sine illo nō donantur. qui inde propriè charitas nuncupatur, vel quia naturaliter eos à quibus procedit conjungit, & se unū cū eis esse ostendit: vel quia in nobis id agit, ut in deo maneamus, & ipse in nobis: unde in & donis dei nihil majus est charitate, & nullum est majus donum dei quàm spiritus sanctus: ipse est & gratia, quæ quia non meritis nostris, sed divina voluntate gratis datur, inde gratia nuncupatur. Sicut autem unicum dei verbum proprie vocamus nomine sapientiæ, cùm sit universaliter & spiritus sanctus & pater ipse sapientia: ita spiritus sanctus proprie nuncupatur vocabulo charitatis, cum sit & pater & filius universaliter charitas. Est enim spiritus patris adtestante domino, qui ait, Non enim vos estis qui loquimini, sed spiritus p.s. tris vestri qui loquitur in vobis. Est & spiritus filii, Paulo adtestante qui air, Quisquis autem spiritum Christi n.n habet, hic non est ejus, ac per hoc spiritus amborum dicitur, quia ex patre & filio procedens unius probatur esse substantiæ & naturæ: qui si ingenitus diceretur, duo patres profiterentur: si genitus, duo filii inconpetenter dicerentur. Sed quia nec pater est nec filius, ideo nec ingenitus: nec genitus, sed ex utroq; procedens dicitur. Pater enim solus non est de alio, ideo solus appellatur ingenitus, non quidem in scripturis, sed in consuetudine disputantium & de re tanta sermonem qualem valuerunt ad præsentium live futurorum prolectum proferentium: filius solus de patre est natus, ideo solus dicitur genitus: Sp.S. solus de patre & filio procedit, ideo solus amborum nuncupatur spiritus. Procedit enim ex utroq; non nascendo, ut alicujus filius dici possit. Diceretur aut filius patris & filii, si, quòd abhorrer ab omnium fidelium sensibus, cum ambo genuissent: non igitur ab utroq; est genitus, sed procedit ab utroq; ambo spiritus. A patre illū aut procedere dominus noster Iesus Christus dicit discipulos docuit dicens, Cùm au-
units.tr: For it is rightly believed, and so it ought to be confessed, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and not from the Father through the Son: because he does not proceed through the Son as a creature made through him, nor as one later in time or lesser in power, or of another substance, but is believed to proceed from the Father and the Son as coeternal, consubstantial, co-equal, of one glory, power and divinity, existing with them. For the preposition ex has one force and per another. Hence also the Son of God is believed to be born of a woman, not through a man, that is, not through coition or human activity, but born of the virgin, taking on flesh. And so it may be asked whether it can rightly be said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son; lest, while this preposition through is carelessly placed in the confession of so great a mystery, that Arian heresy should hand a deadly cup to anyone, which blasphemes that the Holy Spirit is a creature, and created through the Son like all other created things. That heresy also gave the baptismal immersion, not according to the evangelical faith, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, but in the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, to unhappy people who turned to it. For that the Holy Spirit is not a creature but the Creator is proved by these testimonies. David says: By the word of the Lord were the heavens made firm, and all their power by the breath of his mouth. And Solomon says: He created them by the Holy Spirit. Likewise David: Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth. And in the book of Job it is written: The Spirit of God is he who made me. And in the book of Judith: All your creatures shall serve you, for you spoke and they were made; you sent forth your Spirit and it built them. For the Holy Spirit is shown to have such power and might that, by his cooperation, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is our redemption, was formed in the virgin's womb, the Evangelist saying: Do not fear to take Mary your wife, for what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit. Likewise: She was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit. Not that the Holy Spirit is to be called the Father of our Savior, so that two fathers would be believed, but that the same Holy Spirit is believed to be the cooperator of the Father and the Son and of one power with them, the Lord affirming it: Go, he said to the disciples, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For just as the Lord sent out the apostles to preach, so the Holy Spirit is shown to act in the same way. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that when Peter was thinking about the vision, the Holy Spirit said to him: Behold, men are seeking you; rise, go with them, doubting nothing, for I have sent them to you. Likewise: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them. And again: Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops. For he also created all things with the Father and the Son, as has been shown, and that he is God of one essence with them is proved by these testimonies. For David says: I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me. And it is quite clear that all the prophets announced or spoke only through the Holy Spirit, the Lord bearing witness, who says: When that Holy Spirit comes, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you and announce to you things to come. Likewise the Lord says through the Prophet: They would not hear my words, which I commanded in my Spirit through the former prophets, says the Lord. The Apostle Paul also, writing to the Hebrews, says: The Holy Spirit bears witness to us, and this is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord. We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that the minister of the Church said to Ananias: Why has Satan filled your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit? and, showing that he is God, he says in what follows: You have not lied to men, but to God. Paul, the vessel of election, also writes to the Corinthians: There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all. By these apostolic words the Holy Spirit is declared to be the same God, the same Lord. And in the Gospel the same one says: God is Spirit. Likewise Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: Now the Lord is the Spirit; and to the Ephesians: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God. Likewise to the Corinthians: Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God? And when he shows God dwelling in human bodies he adds and says: Therefore glorify and bear God in your body. Since he is proved by these testimonies to be both Creator and God, and is believed by the whole catholic Church to proceed from the Father and the Son, it must be asked whether it is necessary to profess that he proceeds through the Son from the Father, rather than from the Father and the Son, since such a profession is not found in the Nicene or the Chalcedonian creed as made by the holy Fathers. For he appeared over the Apostles in fire through the Son; he was given to men through the Son, since the Holy Spirit could not be received by all except through the Son. But to profess that he proceeds from the Father through the Son is unusual in the synodal confession, since the Holy Spirit, in order to proceed from the Father, needs no help from another, to proceed through something, since in the same holy Trinity the third person is of one power and essence with the Father and the Son. Who, since he is God of himself, is related to us as Lord, distributing the gifts of grace to each as he wills. For he bestows prophecies on whom he wills, and forgives sins to whom he wills, which are not granted without him. He is therefore properly called love, either because he naturally joins those from whom he proceeds and shows himself one with them, or because he works in us so that we remain in God and he in us. Hence nothing is greater than love among the gifts of God, and there is no greater gift of God than the Holy Spirit: he is also grace, and because he is given freely by the divine will and not on account of our merits, he is therefore called grace. Just as we properly call the unique Word of God by the name of wisdom, although the Holy Spirit and the Father himself are universally wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly named by the word love, though the Father and the Son are universally love. For he is the Spirit of the Father, the Lord bearing witness, who says: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. He is also the Spirit of the Son, Paul bearing witness, who says: Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. And so he is called the Spirit of both, because, proceeding from the Father and the Son, he is shown to be of one substance and nature. If he were called unbegotten, they would be professing two fathers; if begotten, two sons would be improperly named. But since he is neither Father nor Son, he is therefore neither unbegotten nor begotten, but is said to proceed from both. For the Father alone is not from another, and therefore alone is called unbegotten, not indeed in the Scriptures, but in the custom of disputants, who in so great a matter have spoken as best they could to set forth what is present or future. The Son alone is born of the Father, and therefore alone is called begotten. The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son, and therefore alone is called the Spirit of both. For he proceeds from both not by being born, so that he could be called the son of one. He would be called the son of the Father and the Son, if (which is abhorrent to the senses of all the faithful) both had begotten him. He is therefore not begotten by both, but proceeds from both, and both are the Spirit. That the Lord Jesus Christ taught his disciples that he proceeds from the Father he says, But when the Advocate comes…

units.la: tem vebipium, quia non cum separatus ab appellatione creatoris: & scriptum est de illo, quod operetur, & utique in se manens operatur. Non enim in aliquid eorum quae operatur, ipse mutatur & vertitur, & quae operatur fide. Unicuique, ait Apostolus, datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem: alii quidem datur per spiritum sermo sapientiae, alii sermo scientiae secundum eundem spiritum, & reliqua. item idem post pauca, Nam & singillatim si interrogemur de spiritu sancto, verissime respondemus, quod deus sit, & cum patre & filio simul unus deus est. Unum ergo principium ad creaturam ducitur deus, non duo vel tria principia, ad se autem invicem in trinitate, si gignens ad id quod gignit principium est, pater ad filium principium est, quia genuit eum. Utrum autem & ad spiritum sanctum principium sit pater, quoniam dictum est, De patre procedit, non parva quaestio est; quia si ita est, non jam principium ei tantum rei erit quam gignit aut facit, sed etiam eis quam dat, ubi & illud elucescit, utpote quod solet multos movere, cur non sit filius etiam spiritus sanctus, cum & ipse a patre exeat sicut in evangelio legitur. Exit enim non quomodo natus, sed quomodo datus: & ideo non dicitur filius, quia neque natus est, sicut unigenitus, neque factus, ut per gratiam in adoptionem nascerentur sicut nos. Quod enim de patre natum est ad patrem solum refertur, cum dicitur filius, & adeo filius patris est non & nostrer; quod autem datum est & ad eum qui dedit refertur, & ad eos quibus dedit. Itaque spiritus sanctus non tantum patris & filii qui dederunt, sed etiam nostrer dicitur qui accepimus: sicut dicitur dominus salus quia dat salutem, eadem etiam vestra salus est qui accipimus. item idem post pauca; Si ergo & quod datur principium habet cum a quo datur, quia non aliunde accepit illud quod ab ipso procedit, fatendum est patrem & filium principium esse spiritus sancti, non duo principia, sed sicut pater & filius unus deus: & ad creaturam relative unus creator & unus dominus. sic relatave ad spiritum sanctum unum principium, ad creaturam vero pater & filius & spiritus sanctus unum principium, sicut unus creator & unus dominus.
units.tr: ...not separated from the name of Creator. And it is written of him that he works, and he certainly works while remaining in himself. For he is not changed or turned into any of the things he works, and he works them by faith. To each one, says the Apostle, is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, and so on. Likewise, a little later: For even if we are asked about the Holy Spirit one by one, we answer most truly that he is God, and together with the Father and the Son he is one God. Therefore God is referred to the creature as one principle, not two or three principles; but in relation to one another within the Trinity, if the begetter is the principle of what he begets, the Father is the principle of the Son, because he begot him. Whether the Father is also the principle of the Holy Spirit, since it is said, "proceeds from the Father," is no small question; for if so, he will be the principle not only of what he begets or makes, but also of what he gives. Here it also becomes clear what commonly moves many: why the Holy Spirit is not also called Son, since he too goes out from the Father, as is read in the Gospel. For he goes out not as one born but as one given; and therefore he is not called Son, because he is neither begotten, like the only-begotten, nor made, so that by grace we might be born into adoption as we are. For what is born of the Father is referred to the Father alone when he is called Son, and so he is the Son of the Father and not of ours; but what is given is referred both to the one who gave it and to those to whom it was given. Thus the Holy Spirit is called not only of the Father and the Son who gave him, but also ours who have received him; just as the Lord is called salvation because he gives salvation, and the same is also our salvation, we who receive it. Likewise, a little later: If therefore what is given also has a principle in that from which it is given, since it did not receive from elsewhere that which proceeds from him, it must be confessed that the Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit, not two principles, but as the Father and the Son are one God: and in relation to the creature, one Creator and one Lord. Thus in relation to the Holy Spirit there is one principle; but in relation to the creature, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one principle, just as there is one Creator and one Lord.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Quod Tarasius non recte spiritum sanctum contribulum patri & filio dixerit, cum sufficeret dicere coaeternum, consubstantialem ejusdemque essentia & natura.
units.tr: That Tarasius was wrong to call the Holy Spirit a co-tribesman of the Father and the Son, since it would have been enough to say co-eternal, consubstantial, and of the same essence and nature.

units.la: Dixisse quoque in sua fidei professione spiritum sanctum patri & filio contribulum Tarasius perhibetur: quod absurdissimum & dictum & a catholicae fidei confessione penitus convellendum, non solum ab eorum sensibus qui literariae scolarum disciplinam non nesciunt, sed etiam ab eorum qui communibus tantum utuntur literis prorsus respuitur, & modis omnibus abdicatur. Est enim in promptu animadvertere, quod sicut consanguinei dicuntur qui sunt unius sanguinis, & consortes qui sunt unius sortis, & coaetanei qui sunt unius aetatis, qui etiam coaevi dicuntur, & conformes qui sunt unius formae, ita contribuli dicuntur qui de una tribu sunt.
units.tr: It is also reported that Tarasius, in his profession of faith, called the Holy Spirit a co-tribesman of the Father and the Son. This is a most absurd expression, and it must be utterly rejected and removed from the confession of the catholic faith. It is rejected entirely, and cast off in every way, not only by those who are acquainted with the discipline of the schools of learning, but even by those who use only ordinary literature. For it is easy to see that just as those are called kinsmen (consanguinei) who are of one blood, and comrades (consortes) who share one lot, and coevals (coaetanei) who are of one age, who are also called coeval, and conformed (conformes) who are of one form, so those are called co-tribesmen (contribuli) who are of one tribe.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De eo quod Basilius Anchira episcopus in suae fidei lectione post confessionem patris & filii & spiritus sancti imaginum, & lipsanorum oculationem & adorationem inseruerit, fidem se habere dicens participare ipsis sanctificatione: remissionem vero peccatorum, sive carnis resurrectionem, seu vitam suturam omnino tacuerit.
units.tr: Concerning how Basil, bishop of Ancyra, in the reading of his faith, after the confession of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, inserted the images and the kissing and adoration of relics, saying that he holds the faith that they share in sanctification; but he entirely passed over the remission of sins, or the resurrection of the flesh, or the life to come.

units.la: REMISSIO peccatorum quae à Basilio Anchirae Episcopo in suae fidei confessione est praetermissa, inter summa ecclesiasticae dignitatis est charismata numeranda. Hanc Prophetia insignia laude praefert, cum eos beatos dicit quibus fit; Beati, inquiens, quorum remissae sunt iniquitates & quorum tecta sunt peccata. Hanc vox verbi, vox sapientiae, amicus sponsi inter prima evangelicae tubae tonitrua intonavit, sicut scriptum est; Et venit in omnem regionem circa Iordanem praedicans baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum. Hanc mediator dei & hominum, agnus dei qui tollit peccata mundi, pietate qua mundum redimere venerat dedicavit, cum & quibusdam ante passionem peccata remisit, & ut totius mundi peccata diluaret: se deo patri in sacrificium obtulit: & ut hanc perpetim ecclesia consequi valeret, spiritus ei ineffabile donum & sui characteris insuperabile signum, & sacramenti baptismatis salutiferum sacramentum concessit. Hanc Apostoli in conlatione fidei, quam ab invicem discessum quali quandam credulitatis & praedicationis normam statuerunt, post confessionem patris & filii & spiritus sancti posuisse perhibentur: & in tanti verbi brevitate de quo per Prophetam dictum est, Verbum adbreviatum faciet dominus super terram, hanc ponere minime distulerunt: quia sine hac fidei sinceritatem integram esse minime petierunt. Nec cohibuit eos ab ejus professione illius symboli brevitas quam expositionem factae fidei integritas, tantique doni veneranda sublimitas.
