Fit enim per spiritum sanctum per quem remittuntur peccata, sive sanguinem Christi qui à nobis in sacramento sumitur, & pro nobis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum. Fit & per aquam baptismatis, in qua originalis noxae antiquum & obsoletum vulnus diluitur. Unde & Apostolus tres dicit testimonium perhibere, spiritum, sanguinem, & aquam, & tres unum esse: quia & per spiritum sanctum & per sanguinem Christi & per aquam baptismatis ad unum compitum, id est, ad remissionem peccatorum pervenitur. Hanc quidam doctorum cum quid sit canticum novum luculenter dissereret, inter ceteras novitates, quas in Christi incarnatione dixit esse completas, enumeravit dicens; Novum est filium dei hominem fieri, novum est eundem ab hominibus mortis tradi, novum est die tertia surgere, novum est cum corpore ad coelum ascendere, novum est remissionem peccatorum hominibus dari. Novum itaque dixit remissionem peccatorum hominibus dari, quae licuit in novo testamento datur, in veteri non dabatur. Pagina enim instrumenti veteris peccata non dilnit, sed oltendit. Carnis quoque resurrectio quam credere & fateri Christianorum, non credere vero Sadducaeorum est, quam praefatus Episcopus in suae fidei professione ticuit, & veteris instrumenti lectione monstratur, cum & per Iob virum evangelicum potius quam legalem dicitur, Scio quod redemptor meus vivat, & in novissimo de terra surrecturus sim, & rursus circumdabor pelle mea & in carne mea videbo deum: quem visurus sum ego ipse & oculi mei conspecturi sunt & non alius. & per Daniel virum sanctissimum & archanorum dei scrutatorem monstratur dicentem; Multi de hus qui dormiunt in terra pulvere resurgunt, alii in vitam aeternam, alii in obprobrium ut videant semper. & ipsa veritate ad terras pro salute generis humani descendente, omnino commendatur qui eam & praedicatio sua sacrosanctis oraculis edocuit, & suae resurrectionis salutari exemplo monstravit. Si vero aliquis dicat Iob in hac sententia suam solummodo resurrectionem, non generalem omnium hominum dixisse, audiat eum in alio loco generalem omnium resurrectionem adfirmantem & dicentem, Lignum habet spem, si praecisum fuerit rursum virescit, & rami ejus pullulant: si senuerit in terra radix ejus, & in pulvere mortuus fuerit truncus ejus, ad odorem aquae germinabit, & faciet comam quasi cum primum plantatum est: homo vero cum mortuus fuerit & nudatus atque consumptus, ubi quaeso est? quomodo si recedant aquae de mari, & fluvius vacuefactus arescat, sic homo cum dormierit non resurget, donec adteratur coelum, nec evigilabit, nec consurget de somno suo. Quod totum ita intellegendum est, Nunquid lignum habet spem revirescendi & homo non habet resurgendi? numquid quomodo si recedant aquae de mari & fluvius vacuefactus arescat, sic homo cum dormierit non resurget? numquid donec adteratur coelum non evigilabit, nec consurget de somno suo? quibus verbis non solummodo, sed totius humani generis resurrectionem generalem demonstrat. Sequitur. Hanc etiam Apostolicum diversas quidem nationes non diversa fide, diversis linguis imbuit, non diversas constitutiones traditurus peterent, omnibus gentibus inter cetera mysteriorum spiritualium archana tradiderunt: & ne oblivione diluceretur aut haereticorum pravitate calumnia per tempora rum incrementa fructuaretur, in symbolo posuerunt, & in tam authentico fidei indicio, in quo totius fidei integritas admirabili brevitate conplectitur, locaverunt. Hanc unus illorum qui fera gentium corda sacri stili doctrina perdomuit, inter cetera quae ea profatus est, in momento, in ictu oculi fore praedixit. Vita quoque futuri seculi, quam idem Basilius neglegenter reticuisse dinoscitur, & ab ipso nobis domino pollicetur, & pene in omnibus sanctarum scripturarum oraculis praedicatur: quippe cum sine ea carnis resurrectio nil valeat, & ob eam adipiscendam totius nostrae religionis desudet intentio. Unde datur intellegi non eum mediocriter delirasse, cum in suae fidei confessione res tantis mysteriis plenas, & revera mysteriis plenas, sine quibus Christiana credulitas stare nō potest, silentio praeterierit. teriecit & in earum loco res non necessarias & risu dignas protulerit. Non igitur ei ideo tantummodo succensetur quia eas profiteri distulit, si tamen eas corde credit, cum plerumque quædam aut brevitatis studio, aut quadam occasione in dicendo prætermittuntur quæ in credendo firmiter tenentur: sed quia in earum loco id intulit quod à nullo sanctorum patrum in fidei professione inlatum fuisse perlegit: quia & miles qui quondam pugnavit, aut quandoq; pugnaturus est, non ideo arguitur si ad tempus non pugnet: sed si fuga lapsus & suam nobilitatem ignobilitet, & sociorum vites mutilit exemplo enervet. Dixit enim præfatus Episcopus, postquam imaginum adorationem & osculationem inter prima suæ fidei munimenta fassus est, fidem se habere participare illis sanctificatione. Nec in merito rebus insensatis & non solum sanctificatione, sed etiam vita carentibus participare dignus, qui post confessionem sanctæ & unicæ trinitatis in talibus næniis fidem se habere dixit: & ea quæ inter prima Christianæ religionis charißimata enumeranda sunt, remissionem videlicet peccatorum, carnis resurrectionem & vitam futuri seculi desidiose præteriit. Esto denique, utile quiddam est imagines adorare, quid adimitur Christianæ religioni si inter primas fidei professiones illius quoque rei professio non detur? cum pleraq; sint quæ inter cæteras ecclesiasticæ institutionis traditiones fidelibus tradita sunt, quorum etsi in fide confessione professio tacetur, nihil tamen ideo sanctæ religioni adimitur, aut in quo præjudicat, si earum adoratio taceatur, fidei integritati? cum à sanctis patribus inhibita potius quàm instituta credatur. Non enim eo modo præjudicat præteremissio imaginum adorationis factæ fidei puritati, quæ interdicta potius quàm instituta est, sicut præjudicant remissio peccatorum, carnis resurrectio & vita futuri seculi in confessione præterMittantur, quæ utiq; & in omnium scripturarum sanctarum serie prædicantur, &, ut præfati sumus, ab Apostolis in symbolo laudabili brevitate connexæ tenentur.
units.tr: The remission of sins, which Basil, bishop of Ancyra, left out of his confession of faith, must be counted among the chief gifts of the ecclesiastical dignity. The prophecy praises it with notable commendation, when it calls those blessed to whom it is granted: Blessed, it says, are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. The voice of the Word, the voice of wisdom, the friend of the bridegroom, sounded this among the first thunders of the gospel trumpet, as it is written: And he came into all the region about the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. The Mediator between God and men, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, dedicated this with the kindness by which he came to redeem the world, when before his passion he forgave the sins of some, and to wash away the sins of the whole world he offered himself to God the Father as a sacrifice; and so that the Church might obtain this continually, he gave it the ineffable gift of the Spirit, the unconquerable seal of his own mark, and the saving sacrament of the sacrament of baptism. The Apostles are said to have placed this after the confession of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in the common statement of faith, which they drew up when they parted from one another as a kind of rule of belief and preaching; and in the brevity of that word of which the prophet said, The Lord will make a short work upon the earth, they by no means delayed to set it down, because they did not judge that the sincerity of the faith could be whole without it. Nor did the brevity of that creed, nor the integrity of the confession of faith, nor the venerable sublimity of so great a gift, keep them from professing it. For it comes through the Holy Spirit, by whom sins are remitted, and through the blood of Christ, which is received by us in the sacrament and was poured out for us for the remission of sins. It comes also through the water of baptism, in which the ancient and old wound of original guilt is washed away. Hence the Apostle says that three bear witness, the Spirit, the blood and the water, and that the three are one, because by the Holy Spirit, by the blood of Christ and by the water of baptism we arrive at one goal, namely the remission of sins. One of the teachers, when he clearly discussed what the new song is, listed among the other novelties which he said were fulfilled in the incarnation of Christ, saying: It is new that the Son of God became man; it is new that he was delivered to men to death; it is new that he rose on the third day; it is new that he ascended to heaven with his body; it is new that the remission of sins is given to men. He therefore called it new that the remission of sins is given to men, which is granted under the new testament and was not granted under the old; for the page of the old instrument does not wash away sins but points them out. The resurrection of the flesh, which it is the faith and confession of Christians to believe, and the unbelief of the Sadducees to deny, the aforesaid bishop also passed over in the profession of his faith; and it is shown by reading the old instrument, where through Job, a man more evangelical than legal, it is said: I know that my redeemer lives, and that at the last I shall rise from the earth, and I shall again be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God; whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold him, and not another. And through Daniel, a most holy man and a searcher of God's secrets, it is shown saying: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall rise, some to everlasting life, and some to shame, that they may see it always. And since the truth itself descended to the earth for the salvation of the human race, he is wholly commended who taught it by his own preaching from the most holy oracles, and showed it by the saving example of his own resurrection. But if anyone says that Job in this sentence spoke only of his own resurrection and not of the general resurrection of all men, let him hear him affirming the general resurrection of all in another place, saying: There is hope for a tree: if it is cut down, it sprouts again, and its shoots do not fail. If its root grows old in the earth and its stump dies in the dust, at the scent of water it will bud and make boughs as when it was first planted. But man, when he dies and is stripped and consumed, where, I ask, is he? As if the waters should go from the sea, and the river be emptied and dry up, so man, when he has lain down, will not rise; until the heavens are worn away, he will not awake nor rise from his sleep. All of this must be understood thus: Does a tree have hope of sprouting again, and man have no hope of rising? Does man, when he has lain down, not rise, as when the waters go from the sea and the river is emptied and dries up? Until the heavens are worn away, will he not awake, nor rise from his sleep? By these words he shows not only but the general resurrection of the whole human race. It follows. The Apostles also handed down to all nations, among the other secrets of spiritual mysteries, this same thing, which they had imbued into diverse nations of differing tongues, though not to hand down differing constitutions; and lest it be washed away by forgetfulness, or be made the occasion of slander by the wickedness of heretics as time went on, they placed it in the creed, and set it in that most authentic sign of the faith, in which the whole integrity of the faith is embraced in admirable brevity. One of those who tamed the fierce hearts of the nations by the teaching of the holy pen, among the other things he said, predicted that this would take place in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. The life of the age to come also, which the same Basil is known to have passed over carelessly, is promised to us by the Lord himself and is proclaimed in almost all the oracles of the holy Scriptures; since without it the resurrection of the flesh avails nothing, and for the sake of obtaining it the whole intention of our religion labors. Hence it is to be understood that he did not rave in a small measure, when in the confession of his faith he passed over in silence matters full of such mysteries, and truly full of mysteries, without which Christian belief cannot stand. Nor is he therefore chiefly blamed merely because he put off professing them, if indeed he believes them in his heart, since often certain things are omitted in speaking, either from a desire for brevity or on some occasion, which are nonetheless held firmly in belief; but because in their place he introduced what, as we have read, was introduced into the profession of faith by none of the holy fathers. For a soldier who once fought, or who is about to fight, is not blamed for not fighting for a time; but if he slips away in flight and disgraces his own nobility, and by his example weakens and maims the courage of his comrades. For the aforesaid bishop, after he confessed the adoration and kissing of images among the first defenses of his faith, said that he holds the faith that they share in sanctification. And he is not rightly worthy to share in things devoid of sense, and lacking not only sanctification but life too, who after the confession of the holy and only Trinity said that he held the faith in such trifles; and he negligently passed over those things which must be counted among the first gifts of the Christian religion: namely the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh and the life of the age to come. Grant, finally, that the adoration of images is some useful thing; what is taken from the Christian religion if no profession of that thing is given among the first professions of faith? Since there are many things which have been handed down to the faithful among the other traditions of ecclesiastical institution, of which the profession is passed over in the confession of faith, yet nothing is therefore taken from holy religion, or does it any harm, if their adoration is passed over, for the integrity of the faith? Since they are believed to have been forbidden by the holy fathers rather than instituted. For the omission of the adoration of images from the profession of faith does not harm the purity of the faith in the same way, since it was forbidden rather than instituted; as the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh and the life of the age to come do harm when they are omitted from the confession. These are indeed proclaimed in the whole series of the holy Scriptures, and, as we have said before, are held together by the Apostles in the creed in praiseworthy brevity.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: De eo quod Theodosius Amori Episcopus desidiose fidem sanctæ & unicæ trinitatis tacuerit, de imaginibus vero incaute & extraordinarie dixerit, Confiteor & promitto & suscipio & osculor & adoro imagines: & post pauca, Qui non instruunt diligenter omnem Christo dilectum populum adorare & venerari sacras & honorandas imagines omnium sanctorum qui à sæculo deo placuerunt, anathema.
units.tr: Concerning how Theodosius, Bishop of Amorium, negligently passed over in silence the faith of the holy and only Trinity, but spoke rashly and extravagantly about images: "I confess, I promise, I receive, I kiss and I adore images"; and a little later: "Those who do not diligently instruct every people beloved of Christ to adore and venerate the holy and honourable images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of the world, let them be anathema."

units.la: BASILIUM Anchiræ Episcopum in superiore capitulo arguendum recte ostendimus, eo q; suæ fidei jacto fundamine in ædificio tam excellentis mysterii res valde necessarias superædificare neglexerit, & vice earum res ab omni penitus religionis fabrica abnuendas superædificare nisus est: in præsenti vero Theodosium Amori Episcopum rectius conpetentiusq; arguendum decernimus, qui nullo suæ fidei in præfata synodo posito fundamento, res tantum inanes & ratione seclusas inaniter & irrationabiliter ædificare cœpir. In illius enim ædificio si id quod inaniter surrexit deciatur, salvum quod bene fundatum est remanebit: in istius vero si omne quod inane & frivolum est destituatur, nil quod remaneat erit: si ergo illi recte succensetur qui sanctæ & unicæ trinitatis confessioni imaginum adorationem inserunt, multo rectius huic succensebitur qui illius summi & ineffabilis mysterii confessione postposita, de illarum adoratione friuola nescio quæ tantummodo somniavit. Ita enim est, Confiteor, & promitto, & suscipio, & osculor, & adoro imagines. O mira confessio Episcopi! O pulchra dictio sacerdotis! O laudanda devotio præsulis! Tacet confessionem excellentissimæ majestatis, & insanat confessionem insolentissimæ vanitatis. Ab ejus confessione pedem retrahit qui dixit, Omnis qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor & ego eum coram patre meo qui est in cœlis: & in imaginum consessione totis se gressibus insert. Tacet q & ille fateri, & cæteros ut fatererentur debuit hortari: & fassus est quod nec ille fateri, & ne cæteri fatericetur debuit reluctari: & qui opponere murii pro domo Israhel debuit & stare in prælio in die domini, ipse ad deditionis dedecus, pro dolor, sponte dilabitur: quia videlicet quid debuit à prava confessione & à ridiculoso errore aliorum mentes coercere prædicationis studio, iple primum illis errandi via efficitur pravæ confessionis exemplo. Quod vero anathematizat omnes qui non instruunt omnè Christo dilectum populum adorare & venerari imagines omnium sanctorum quià sæculo deo placuerunt, quàm absurde quamque incaute agat, prudens lector advertat, præsertim qui anathema quod aliis temerarila præsumptione inferre contendit, in se suosque inreverenter intorquet, & telum quo sui erroris extraneam nituur pœsfodere partem, in suam civiumq; destectit necem.
units.tr: We have shown rightly that Basilius, Bishop of Anchira, is to be censured in the previous chapter, since, having laid the foundation of his faith, he neglected to build upon it the things that were most necessary in the edifice of so excellent a mystery, and instead strove to erect upon it things that ought to be rejected altogether from the whole structure of religion. In the present case we judge that Theodosius, Bishop of Amorium, should be censured more justly and more fittingly, for he, having laid no foundation of faith in the aforesaid synod, began to build with empty things and things set apart from reason, vainly and unreasonably. For if in the building of the former what rose up in vain is pulled down, what was well founded will remain; but in the building of the latter, if everything empty and frivolous is removed, nothing will remain. If therefore he is rightly blamed who inserts the adoration of images into the confession of the holy and only Trinity, much more rightly will he be blamed who, setting aside the confession of that highest and ineffable mystery, has dreamed up I know not what trifles about the adoration of those images. For it goes thus: I confess, and I promise, and I receive, and I kiss, and I adore images. O wondrous confession of a bishop! O fine utterance of a priest! O praiseworthy devotion of a prelate! He is silent about the confession of the most excellent majesty, and raves over the confession of the most insolent vanity. He draws back from the confession of him who said, Whoever shall confess me before men, him will I also confess before my Father who is in heaven, and he throws himself with all his steps into the confession of images. He was also silent about confessing, and he ought to have exhorted the others to confess; and he confessed what he ought not to have confessed, and ought to have resisted others from confessing. And he who ought to have stood as a wall for the house of Israel and stood in battle in the day of the Lord, he, alas, slips away of his own accord into the shameful surrender: namely, because he ought to have restrained the minds of others from a perverse confession and a ridiculous error by the zeal of preaching, he himself is first made the way of error for them by the example of a perverse confession. As to his anathematizing all who do not instruct every people beloved of Christ to adore and venerate the images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of the world, let the prudent reader observe how absurdly and how rashly he acts, especially since the anathema which he strives to hurl at others with rash presumption, he turns irreverently back upon himself and his own people, and the weapon with which he strives to pierce the foreign part of his error falls back to the destruction of his own and his fellow citizens.

units.la: Nec liberat imaginum adoratio ab anathematis conligatione suos, quæ nectere tantummodo nitebatur exteros. Anathematizat enim qui non instruunt omnem Christo dilectum populum adorare imagines, nunquid nam, ut cæteros taceam, in sibi commissa plebe omnes instruunt omnem Christo dilectum populum imagines adorare, qui nec instruendi habent officium, nec prædicationis gradum? nunquid & ipse omnem Christo dilectum populum instruit? cum videlicet pene totus mundus Christi populo plenus sit: quoniam desiit tantummodo in Iudæa notus esse deus, sed in omnem terram exiit. Ionus Apostolorum, & repleta est omnis terra gloria domini, & omnes gentes veniunt & adorant in conspectu domini, juxta Malachiæ vaticinium in verbo domini dicentis, Ab ortu solis usque ad occasum magnum est nomen meum in gentibus, & in omni loco sacrificatur & offertur mihi hostia munda: & pastor ecclesiæ, cui in figura disci diversorum animantium generibus pleni totus orbis diversis gentibus pleuus ad dei gratia vocandus ostenditur, dicit, In veritate comperi, quoniam non est personarum acceptor deus, sed in omni gente qui timet cum & operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi. Nam si secundum ejus deliramentum quicunq; non instruunt struunt omnem Christo dilectum populum, anathemate digni sunt, neq; ipse idem, neque coepiscopi qui in eadem synodo fuisse perhibentur, neq; illis subditæ plebes anathematis vinculo carere quibut, quia etsi instruunt duarum aut trium vel certe plurimarum provinciarum gentes, non tamen omne Christo dilectum populum instruunt, cum per tam prolixas tamq; vastas mundi partes sit catholica ecclesia, quæ utiq; Christi dilectus populus est, diffusa, & tam per inaccelsas & ignotas nationes sit domino largiente dilatata. Aut ergo omne Christi ecclesiam ab oriente usq; ad occidentem, à septentrione usq; ad meridiem, se suosq; in imaginum adoratione instruete perdocebit, aut secundum suæ vanitatis sententiam cum sociis sive subditis anathemati subjacebit: quoniam etsi omnem populum instruere possent, non igitur omnium sanctorum qui à seculo deo placuerunt, imagines in quarum adoratione universitatem populi instruerêt, habere poterant: quorum multitudo tanta est, ut de his per Prophetam expersona filii ad patrem dicatur, Nimis honorati sunt amici tui, deus, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum: dimi-nuetur eos & super arenam multiplicabuntur. Quod etsi hyperbolice dictum sit, tanta eorum qui ab initio deo placuerunt sunt agmina, ut nec pingi nec dinumerari possint ab alio, nisi ab eo in cujus libro eorum scripta habentur nomina. Nam si à se prolati idem Episcopus anathematis jactura vitare cupit, necesse est uromnium sanctorum qui per diversas mundi partes ab initio deo placuerunt, imagines & habeat & adoret: & si eas præ multitudine sui habere nequiverit, immo quia nequibit, à se ergo prolato anathemati colla submittat.
units.tr: Nor does the adoration of images free his own people from the bond of the anathema, which he strove to bind only on outsiders. For he anathematizes those who do not instruct every people beloved of Christ to adore images. Do then, to say nothing of others, all those who have no office of instruction and no rank of preaching instruct in the people committed to them every people beloved of Christ to adore images? Does he himself instruct every people beloved of Christ? Since, to be sure, almost the whole world is full of Christ's people, for God has ceased to be known only in Judea but has gone out into all the earth. The sound of the Apostles has gone out, and the whole earth is filled with the glory of the Lord, and all nations come and adore in the sight of the Lord, according to the prophecy of Malachi, the word of the Lord saying: From the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a pure offering is sacrificed and offered to me. And the minister of the Church, in whose figure the whole world, full of the various kinds of living creatures, is shown to be filled with diverse nations to be called to the grace of God, says: I have found in truth that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. For if, according to his delirium, all who do not instruct every people beloved of Christ are worthy of anathema, then neither he himself nor his fellow bishops, who are said to have been in the same synod, nor the peoples subject to them, can be free from the bond of the anathema; for even if they instruct the nations of two or three or certainly very many provinces, they do not instruct every people beloved of Christ, since the Catholic Church, which is indeed the people beloved of Christ, is spread through such long and vast parts of the world, and by the Lord's bounty has been extended even among the remote and unknown nations. Either, therefore, he will teach that the Church of Christ from east to west and from north to south is to instruct itself and its own in the adoration of images, or according to the judgment of his vanity he, with his associates or subjects, will be subject to the anathema. For even if they could instruct every people, they could not therefore have images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of the world, in whose adoration they might instruct the whole body of the people; their multitude is so great that of them it is said through the Prophet, in the person of the Son to the Father: Your friends, O God, are greatly honoured; their dominion is exceedingly strengthened; I will diminish them and they shall be multiplied above the sand. And even if this is said hyperbolically, the throngs of those who have pleased God from the beginning are so great that they cannot be painted or numbered by anyone other than him in whose book their names are written. For if the aforesaid bishop wishes to avoid the loss of the anathema he has pronounced, he must have and adore images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning in the various parts of the world; and if he cannot have them because of their multitude, indeed because he cannot, let him then submit his neck to the anathema he has pronounced.

units.la: CAP. VIII. Quod pene de omnium fide ambigitur, cum spiritum sanctum quidam à patre tantum, quidam vero neque à patre neque à filio procedentem confessi sint.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. That almost everyone is uncertain about the faith, since some have confessed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and others from neither the Father nor the Son.

units.la: EX patre & filio spiritum sanctum procedere, quantum attinet ad brevitatem hujus stili cui stu-demus, domino annuente in superioribus monstratum est. Nam cum pene omnes in præfata synodo hocaut penitus tacuerint, aut ambigue protulerint, nos quasi homines humana inbecillitate cogitationum, & eorum quæ necaudimus nec legimus ignari, nec eorum fidei testimonium perhibenius qui hoc silentio præterierunt, nec eorum qui ambigue protulerunt, nec ideo eorum credu-latem abnuimus, quia hoc tacuerunt vel ambigue protulerunt. Quoniam qualiter teneant nescimus, sed hanc rem & indiscussam præterite, ne eis tacendo adsensum præbere videamur, & quia non patetter elucet quid velit, inprobare timentes, illius examini reservamus quem occulta non fallunt. Scimus sdenique eos haud procul ab errore esse, qui ii ab eo ideo elongantur, quia bene de hac re sentiunt, ideo tamen ei adpropinquant, quia quod recte sentiunt recte fateri neglexerunt, quod autem recte corde creditur ad justitiam, recte ore debet profiteri ad salutem.
units.tr: That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son has, so far as the brevity of this treatise, which we are labouring to finish, permits, been shown above by the Lord's permission. For since almost all in the aforesaid synod either kept entirely silent on this point or expressed themselves ambiguously, we, as men of human weakness in our thinking, and ignorant of those things which we neither hear nor read, neither bear witness to the faith of those who passed over it in silence, nor of those who spoke ambiguously; nor on that account do we deny their belief, because they were silent or spoke ambiguously. For we do not know how they hold it, but we pass over this matter undiscussed, lest by our silence we seem to give them assent; and since it is not clearly evident what they mean, we fear to condemn it, and reserve it for the judgment of him from whom hidden things are not concealed. Finally, we know that those are not far from error who are removed from that truth because they think rightly about this matter, and yet they draw near to it because they have neglected to confess rightly what they rightly think; for what is believed rightly in the heart unto righteousness ought to be confessed rightly with the mouth unto salvation.

units.la: CAP. IX. De eo quod si forte aliquis error in præsatorum Episcoporum sententiis de fide prolatis indiscussus re- manserit, propter difficultatem & enormitatem sermonis illarum remanebit, qui ple- rumque tanta ignavia obscuritas est, ut quid signifi-are velit quive sensus in eo intellegendum sit, minime pateat.
units.tr: ## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the possibility that some error may have remained undiscussed in the statements of the aforesaid bishops concerning the faith, because of the difficulty and obscurity of their language, which is so often so obscure through sheer ineptitude that it is not at all clear what they mean or what sense is to be understood in it.

units.la: CUM multa eloquutionum sint genera, quæ à grammaticis sive à rhetoribus copiose ac variè traduntur, omnium tamen sermonum sive dictionum senes quadripertita ratione dividitur. Omnis aut sermo aut sapiens est & dissertus, aut sapiens & non dissertus, aut dissertus & non sapiens, aut nec sapiens nec dissertus. Sapiens ergo est & dissertus, sicut plurimi divinarum scripturarum libri, & ut ce-teros taceam, ut est liber Esaiæ prophetæ: cujus sermo & sapiens est, ut post quem Spiritus S. dictaverit dissertus, quia alvinlustri & urbano viro prolatus est. Sapiens autem & non dissertus, ut quidam in ipsis etiam divinis scripturis habetur. Sapiens videlicet in sententiarum cessitudinibus divini flaminis necte promulgatis, indissertus vero aut simplicitate sanctorum virorum, à quibus prolatus est, qui sensuum potius quàm verborum venustatibus uti maluerunt, aut indigenarum loquendi usu, inter quos sancti viri divini verbi latores nati aut conversati fuisse noscuntur: sicut de B. Hieremia & Hieronymus dicit, quod simplicitas sermonis de loco ei Anathoth in quo natus est accesserit. Dissertus ergo & non sapiens, sicut gentilium scriptorum est, qui etsi venustus est humanarum artium eruditione, insipiens tamen est, quia & veri dei notitia & salutifera caret exhortatione. Est & quorundam hæreticorum sermo dissertus, nec tamen sapiens, qui si memorabiliter sententiarum speciebus est aliena, & diabus sequentibus omnino conserta: quia nec sermonum cultu aut eloquentiæ cothurno adtollitur, nec puritate aptæ loquutionis texitur, quin altero ob sui puritatem ad intellegendum promoveat: nec culta est & nō aperta, quia non longis periodis involvitur, non varis topicorum perplexitatibus exornatur, nec lubricis syllogismorum conclusionibus ex industria dialecticæ armis venientibus catenatur: quæ omnia & culta sunt, utpote quæ sophistico poliuntur cylindro: & non aperta, quia a simplicium lectorum sensu procul remota eruditissimorum tantummodo se inferunt ingenio: sed aut aperta est, quæ eruditione carens omnibus legentibus sive audientibus patet: aut inordinate & incompte digesta, & solæcissimis mutilata, barbarissimis corrupta, cæteris vitiorum nubilis obducta, & luculenta oratione carens, & ordine texendorum sensuum explosso, nec culta est nec aperta. Ideoque si forte aliquis error in sententiis de fide prolatis indiscussus remanserit, his a nobis se tuebitur armis, quia se talibus inconpositarum dictionum abdidit involucris: & a nobis ideo deprehendi nequivit, quia ad nos difficultate sermonis quasi quodam pallio obsitus advenit.
units.tr: Although there are many kinds of expression, which the grammarians and rhetoricians set out at length and in varied ways, all speech or discourse may nonetheless be divided on a fourfold principle. Every discourse is either wise and eloquent, or wise and not eloquent, or eloquent and not wise, or neither wise nor eloquent. Discourse that is wise and eloquent is found in very many books of divine Scripture, and, to pass over the rest, it is found in the book of the prophet Isaiah: his speech is wise, since the Holy Spirit dictated it, and eloquent, since it was delivered by a cultivated and urbane man. Discourse that is wise but not eloquent is found in some passages even of the divine Scriptures: wise, certainly, in the close connection of the sentences, which were promulgated by the divine breath, but unpolished, either through the simplicity of the holy men by whom it was delivered, who preferred the graces of meaning to those of words, or through the everyday speech of the natives among whom the holy men, the bearers of the divine word, are known to have been born or to have lived; as Jerome says of the blessed Jeremiah, that the simplicity of his speech came from the place Anathoth where he was born. Discourse that is eloquent but not wise is that of the Gentile writers, who, though elegant through the learning of the human arts, are nonetheless foolish, because they lack both the knowledge of the true God and saving exhortation. The speech of some heretics is also eloquent but not wise: it is indeed remarkably alien to the forms of sound sentences, and wholly woven together with the most shameless (?) and disconnected [?] periods; for it is not raised by any polish of style or the buskin of eloquence, nor is it woven with the purity of fitting expression, but it is rather so that it may be advanced to understanding by its own lack of purity. Nor is it refined and yet not clear, since it is not wrapped in long periods, nor adorned with the intricate variety of commonplaces, nor linked together by the slippery conclusions of syllogisms, brought in by design as the weapons of dialectic; all these things are refined, being polished, as they are, with the sophist's roller, and not clear, since they lie far from the understanding of simple readers and present themselves only to the genius of the most learned. Yet, if it is clear, it is so only in that it lacks learning and lies open to all who read or hear; or else it is arranged in disorder and without polish, mutilated by solecisms, corrupted by barbarisms, and clouded over by the mists of other faults, lacking lucid expression and with the order of the matters to be woven together loosened; such speech is neither refined nor clear. Therefore, if some error should perhaps remain undiscussed in statements set forth concerning the faith, it will defend itself with these weapons of ours, since it has concealed itself in such wrappings of disordered words, and it could not be detected by us for this reason: that it came to us covered, as if with a kind of cloak, by the difficulty of its speech.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: Ridiculose & pueriliter dictum in sententia fidei Theodori Episcopi, Mirabilis deus in sanctis suis, & continuo, sanctis qui in terra sunt ejus mirificavit omnes volunta- tes meas inter illos, tamquam hic versiculus illum priorem subsequatur.
units.tr: Ridiculously and childishly put in the statement of faith of Theodore the Bishop: "Wonderful is God in his saints," and immediately, "to the saints who are on earth, he has made all my desires wonderful among them," as if this little verse followed the former one.

units.la: ID vero quod Theodorus Episcopus hos duos psalmistæ versiculos ita interjecta particula advertit continuo, in unum protulit, quasi alter alterum nulla intercapedine aliorum vel suum interposita subsequatur, cum videlicet hic versiculus quem illum continuo subsequi dicit, non solum confestim non subsequatur, sed etiam ferme ante quinquaginta psalmos, cui postponitur præcedere noscatur: non ideo nobis reprehendere libuit quod fidei quoddam præjudicium afferat, sed quia ridiculo sui reprehensioni subjaceat & reprehendentibus deridendi materiam conferat, pateatque talem scripturam non esse idoneam, ut magna absque errore instruat, quæ in parvis absque vigore titubat: nec habere eam vim res dubias adfirmandi & incognitas docendi, quæ non habet ingenium res non dubias narrandi & notas proferendi. Quomodo ergo illius synodi poterit recipi doctrina, cujus in tot locis reprehenditur scriptura? aut quomodo cum cæteris synodalibus a sanctis patribus digestis vel susceptis scriptis societatis poterit adipisci dignitatem, quæ earum sensuum & verborum fugit societatem? Illæ enim in nullo reprehenduntur, & ideo in omnibus suscipiuntur: hæc vero quia in multis reprehenditur, non immerito pene in omnibus repudiatur.
units.tr: But as for the fact that Theodore the Bishop, separating these two verses of the Psalmist by the particle "immediately," brought them together into one, as if the one followed the other without any interval of other verses or of its own, when in fact the verse which he says follows the other "immediately" not only does not follow it at once, but is also found to come almost fifty psalms before the one it is placed after: this I did not choose to censure because it brings some prejudice to the faith, but because it is ridiculous in its own censure and gives those who censure it material for mockery, and it shows that such a writing is not fit to teach great matters without error when it stumbles in small ones; nor has it the power to affirm doubtful things and teach unknown ones, when it lacks the ability to narrate things that are not doubtful and to set forth things that are known. How, then, can the teaching of that synod be received, when Scripture is censured in so many places? Or how can it obtain the dignity of a place among the other synodal writings digested or accepted by the holy Fathers, when it shuns the company of their senses and words? For those are censured in nothing, and therefore are accepted in everything; but this one, because it is censured in many things, is not undeservedly rejected in almost everything.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAP. XI.

units.la: Quid inter iliter & incaute Græci ecclesiam catholicam anathematizare conati sint in eorum synodo, eo quod imagines non adoret: cum utique prius debuerint omnino scrutari quid unius- cujusque partis ecclesia de hac causa sentire vellet.
units.tr: How the Greeks, both unadvisedly and rashly, tried in their synod to anathematize the catholic Church because it does not adore images, when they should first have thoroughly inquired what the Church of each part thought about this question.

units.la: ECCLESIASTICÆ tubæ prædicatio intonat, peccantem fratrem primo clam corripiendum: qui si audire noluerit, seorsum adhibitis fratribus vel corrigendi studio, vel conveniendi restimonio admonendus est: qui si & illos audire contempserit, tunc multis res notescenda est, ut detestatio-ni eum habeant, & qui nequivit salvari pudore, saltim obprobriis salvetur: qui si neque multorum admonitioni adsensum præbuerit, ethnicorum sive publicanorum more detestandus est. Cui prædicationi non mediocriter illorum ecclesia contraire videtur quæ totius mundi ecclesias puusquam more ecclesiastico per epistolare eloquium consulendo sive scrutando alloquatur, præsumptive sive incaute anathematizare conatur. Debuerat enim ad circumjacentium provinciarum ecclesias legationem scisscitativam facere, utrum imagines adorari aut non adorari deberent: ut juxta cujusdam sapientis vocem, per consilium & sequenda sequens & vitanda vitans, non eam postmodum pœnitere constaret, sed quicquid de hac re plures secundum apostolicam institutionem tenere vellent ecclesiæ, ipsa quoque teneret: & quæ pluribus consentientibus antiquis institutionibus obniti tentaret & obstinata mente ab universitate ecclesiastici corporis se dirimere vellet, hanc detestationi multaret.
units.tr: The preaching of the ecclesiastical trumpet sounds out that a sinning brother must first be rebuked privately. If he will not listen, he must be admonished with brethren taken aside, either for the purpose of correction or to serve as witnesses to the meeting. If he also scorns to listen to them, the matter must then be made known to many, so that they may hold him in detestation, and so that he who could not be saved by shame may at least be saved by reproach. If he does not yield even to the admonition of many, he must be detested in the manner of heathens and tax collectors. The church of the Greeks seems to be quite at odds with this preaching, since, contrary to the Church's custom, it does not address the churches of the whole world by letter to consult and inquire, but presumptuously and rashly tries to anathematize them. For they ought to have sent a delegation to the churches of the neighboring provinces to ask whether images ought to be adored or not. Then, according to the word of a certain wise man, by counsel, following what is to be followed and avoiding what is to be avoided, they would not afterwards have reason to repent. Whatever the many churches, according to the apostolic institution, wished to hold on this matter, that church itself would also hold. And whoever tried to resist what the majority held by the ancient institutions, and with an obstinate mind wished to separate himself from the whole body of the Church, that man it should punish with detestation.

units.la: Nam quis furor est, quæve dementia ut unius partis ecclesia rem q neque ab Apostolis, neq; ab eorum successoribus statuere, totius mundi ecclesias conetur anathematizare, & conpellantur aut apostolicis institutis contraire, aut ab illis protelaro vanissimo anathemati subjacere: sed cum illorum dementissimum anathema illis potius quam nobis jacturam inpertiat, dicente Apostolo, Neque mu-ledici regnum dei possidebunt, etiam si quodammodo lædere posset, tolerabilius nobis esset illud perpeti quam Apostolorum sive cæterorum sanctorum patiu moniiis obniti, quippe qui cum Susanna dicimus, Meliusest incidere in manus hominum, quam derelinquere legem dei nostri: & pastoris ecclesiæ verbis perdocemur, obedire oportere deo magis quam hominib. Sicut enim cuiliber civium sive principis societate suentia seditiosis quibusdam qui contra principem & cives agunt, tolerabilius est ab illis inlata convicia sustinere, quam cum eis in seditione conspirare, ita utique tolerabilius nobis est, ab illis exsecrari qui etiam suos parentes exsecrati non formidant, qui cum illis res insensatas contra divinarum scripturarum instituta adorare. Exsecratio namque sine ratione, & ita sine potestate, & damnatio sine auctoritate, quantum eos contra quos inhiant minime lædunt, tanto auctores suos majoribus tardiis afficiunt, & magis delides & inpatientes esse produnt. Nisi ergo eos vetusta pernicies & antiqua lues, dux mortis, radix malorum, quæ & angelos ab æthereorum civium societate, & homines a Horigeræ sedis dignitate expulit, stimulis suæ nequitiæ inflammaret, nec synodū ob adorandas imagines sine conhibentia plurimarū catholicarum & deo fidelium ecclesiarū, adgregatam universale nominare curarent, nec tot tantasque ecclesias quæ utique corpus Christi sunt, tā insolenter anathematizare auderent, nec rerū insensatarum culturam & adorationem
units.tr: For what madness or what insanity is this, that the church of one part should try to anathematize the churches of the whole world over a question settled neither by the Apostles nor by their successors, and that they should be compelled either to act against the apostolic institutions or, by that most empty anathema, to be made subject to those who curse them? But since their most insane anathema brings loss upon them rather than upon us, as the Apostle says, Neither revilers shall possess the kingdom of God, even if it could somehow harm us, it would be more tolerable for us to suffer it than to resist the teaching of the Apostles and of the other holy men. For we say with Susanna, It is better for me to fall into the hands of men than to forsake the law of our God, and we are taught by the words of the Church's pastor, We ought to obey God rather than men. Just as, for any citizen who lives in fellowship with a prince, it is more tolerable to bear the insults hurled by certain seditious men who act against the prince and the citizens than to conspire with them in sedition, so surely it is more tolerable for us to be cursed by those who do not fear to curse even their own parents, and who, with them, adore insensate things against the institutions of the divine Scriptures. For a curse without reason, and so without power, and a condemnation without authority, as much as they scarcely harm those against whom they gape, so much more do they burden their authors with greater ruin, and show them to be foolish and impotent. Unless that ancient pestilence and old plague, the leader of death and root of evils, which expelled the angels from the fellowship of the heavenly citizens and men from the dignity of the heavenly seat, had inflamed them with the goads of its wickedness, they would not have taken care to call a synod, gathered over the adoration of images without the agreement of many catholic churches faithful to God, a universal synod. Nor would they have dared so insolently to anathematize so many and such great churches, which are indeed the body of Christ; nor would they have attempted to establish the worship and adoration of insensate things

units.la: contra divinarum apicū institutionem statuere tentarent. Nemo enim, ait Apostolus, in spiritu dei loquens dicit, Anathema Jesu. Unde cavendū est, ne dum ecclesiā quæ est corpus Christi inconsulte & incaute anathematizare nituntur, illi qui ejus caput est injuriam inferre videantur. Tanta itaque dilectione sibi Christus ecclesiā adscivit, ut inseparabiliter ei, utpote caput corpori, præmineat, & illa ei perpetim, utpote corpus capiti cohæreat, ut nequaquā corpori aut injuria aut honorificentia exhibeatur & non ad caput referatur. Ecclesiæ etenim persecutione à Judæis inlatam suā Christus referebat, cum rapaci lupo Saulo, nec dū Paulo, mane prædam in vastatione ecclesiæ comedenti, vespere spolia in saluberrima prædicatione sive epistolarū missione divisuro, dicebat, Saule Saule, quid me persequeris? Non & ille Christum persequeretur in ætheriis arcibus regnantem, sed ecclesiam jam tunc pullulantem & in hujus sæculi horrisonis fluctibus natantem. Christus ergo in corpore suo quod est ecclesia, etiam nunc persecutione sustinet, non quidem corporaliter, ut dudum pro mundi salute, sed quadam pietatis miseratione, qua suorū membrorum, id est, fidelium in unitate sanctæ ecclesiæ commanentium semper miseretur, de quibus erat ille qui dicebat, Gaudeo in passionibus meis, quia expleo ea quæ desunt passionum Christi in carne mea propter corpus ejus quod est ecclesia. Hanc passione quam Christus in sanctis suis sustinet, David præfigurabat cum dicebat, Adhuc ludam & vilior apparebo: quia dum se humilians usq; ad mortem ad crucis perveniret mysterium, & a synagoga, quæ sterilis extunc remansit, despiceretur, in sudore sanguineo membrorum suorum passiones ostendebat esse futuras, ac contra ecclesiæ exhibitam honorificentiam suam esse testatus cum dicit, Qui vos recipit, me recipit. Et, quandiu fecistis uni de minimis istis, mihi fecistis. Si ergo illi de quibus sermo est, custodem virtutum, magistram bonorum humilitatem amplecterentur, nec corpus Christi quod est ecclesia, inpudentissime anathematizare tentarent, nec ob suæ immò vanæ laudis appetitum pro re tam inutili tamque inofficiosa synodum adgregarent.
units.tr: against the institution of the divine writings. For, says the Apostle, no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, Anathema Jesus. Therefore we must take care that, while they strive unadvisedly and rashly to anathematize the Church, which is the body of Christ, they do not seem to inflict injury upon him who is its head. Christ so loved the Church and took her to himself that he rules over her inseparably, as the head over the body, and she clings to him perpetually, as the body to the head, so that neither injury nor honor is shown to the body that is not referred to the head. Christ himself reckoned the persecution inflicted on the Church by the Jews as done to himself, when he said to the rapacious wolf Saul, not yet Paul, who in the morning devoured the prey in the ravaging of the Church and in the evening would divide the spoils in the most wholesome preaching and the sending of letters: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? Not that he who reigns in the heavenly citadels could be persecuted by him, but the Church, already then sprouting and swimming amid the dreadful waves of this age. Christ therefore still suffers persecution in his body, which is the Church, not indeed bodily, as once for the salvation of the world, but by a certain merciful pity of piety, by which he always has compassion on his members, that is, on the faithful who remain in the unity of the holy Church. Of these was he who said, I rejoice in my sufferings, because I fill up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh for his body, which is the Church. David foreshadowed this suffering, which Christ endures in his saints, when he said, I will yet play and appear more vile. For while humbling himself even to the death of the cross, he was despised by the synagogue, which thereafter remained barren. In the bloody sweat of his members he showed that their sufferings were to come, and by testifying that his own honor stands against the honor shown to the Church, he says, He who receives you receives me, and as long as you did it to one of these least, you did it to me. If, therefore, those of whom we speak embraced humility, the guardian of virtues and teacher of good things, they would not impudently attempt to anathematize the body of Christ, which is the Church, nor, for the appetite of their own, indeed vain, praise, would they gather a synod for a matter so useless and so unbecoming.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Quod magna ex parte mansuetudinem & patientiam abjecerint in non continen- do os suum & inordinate loquendo.
units.tr: That for the most part they cast aside gentleness and patience, by failing to restrain their mouths and by speaking without order.

units.la: ADGREGATA igitur synodo si in ea ecclesiastico more egissent, res necessarias & fidelibus profuturas pertractantes, omnes vocum novitates & inordinatas loquutionum nænias evitarent, & mediocritatis callem tenentes neque ab apostolicis doctrinis, neque ab antiquarum synodorum institutionibus dissentirent, sed patientiæ & mansuetudinis ornamentis ornati, nequaquam dicentes bonum malum, & malum bonum, ponentes amarum dulce, & dulce amarum, prophetico sermoni contrairent: & ea quæ necessario statuenda erant prudenter statuerent, & quæ dicenda diligenter dicerent, & spreto supervacuo & extraordinario anathemate, res utiles perdocerent, res vero ambiguas aut certe inutiles silentio multarent, & nostræ partis sive cæterarum mundi partium ecclesiæ eorum statutis parerent: sed quoniam impossibile est & eorum statutis adlensum præbere, & antiquis patrum institutionibus parere, cum videlicet inter se diversa sint, & quantum lux tenebris, vita morte, visio cæcitate, probitas inprobitate, puritas impuritate, sanitas ægritudine, tantum eorum institutā à sanctorum patrum institutis distent, idcirco detestioribus spretis, potioribus contenti simus, & contemtis fallacibus diverticulis certum ac regum tramitem tenere desideramus. Ubi quæso præstantissima virtus mansuetudo? vel tu fortissima surus sive cunctis levibus incitantibus inimica patientia? quo abieratis? quo discedetaris, cum tam incautas tamq; perversas constitutiones à tot sacerdotib. patrari videretis? cum ecclesiæ tot anathematum vincula inferre cerneretis? quur nō saltim in duobus vel tribus hospitiū habuistis? quur omnes sprevistis? quur cunctis vestræ ablentiam præsentastis? quur non eos à tot nugis vestri moderaminis compescuistis fraenis? quur non à rot delirantium vestræ industriæ coercuistis habenis? stimulante namq; jactantia sive ventosæ laudis appetitu, & ministram suam, oris videlicet incontinentiā, contra nos pugnaturā inpellente, quæ omnia ut cætera malorum fomenta non incongrue nostræ legiones recipiunt, ab eis abscesserimus, & apud eos tandem hospitari nequivimus, quos taliū errorū tumultibus invalos esse conperimus. Nulla enim est societas luci & tenebris, nec quidam communicatio Christi & Belial: quoniam juxta cujusdam sapientis sententiam, spiritus dei, qui utiq; nostri exercitus dux est, effugiet fictū, non habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis. Non enim nos in medio ejus, nec ille in medio nostrū habitavit qui facit superbiā. Quoniam juxta verba Jesu filii Sirach, odibilis coram deo & hominibus superbia, & synagoge superborū non erit sanitas: frutex enim peccati radicabitur in illis. Tanto enim in coetū synodo discipula superbiæ, oris scilicet incontinentia, viguit, quanto modestia sive prudentia vigere debuit, & cujus nec extrema quidē manus in tali actu duci debuit, principatū, pro dolor, tenuit: & q principatū tenere debuit, nec extremā quidē ejus manus illorū coetibus interfuit. Tuo itaq; instinctu, ô incontinentia oris, q gressus hominū in terra viventium dirigi prohibes, dicente Propheta, Vir linguosus non dirigetur super terrā: & cujus anni sui peccatū non deest, juxta illud, Ex multiloquio non effugies peccatū. parcens autem labiis sapiens eris: & per q anima lætatur, juxta sapientis vocē dicentis, Qui multis utitur verbis, ledit animā suā: & q non solū respondere æquā audias, verūtia sancta ecclesia anathematizare, antequam adloquatur tuos sequaces, compellis, juxta illud; Qui respondet verbū prufquā audiat stultitia est illi & obprobrium: te urgente ita penitus nostrum abnuere consortium, ut nostra societas in eorum metibus nec leve quidem posset inprimere vestigium. Nos enim sequi, decor vitæ est, & nos spernere, error insaniæ, & secundum magistræ nostræ sapientiæ vocem; Exitus nostri exitus vitæ sunt. Nisi enim legislator nostrorum monitorum sequax fuisset, & nostri moderaminis retinaculis grellus suæ mentis connexos habuisset, dicente scriptura; Et erat Moyses mansuetus pra omnibus hominibus qui sunt super terram, nequaquam tantoties divinis alloquiis fruerētur: neq; tot mysteriorū archanis domino insinuante inbuerc buperetur, nec de eo ab eodem rerum omnium domino diceretur; At non sicut servus meus Moyses ad quem loquor facie ad faciem, sicut loqui solet homo ad amicum suum. Patientiae itaque & mansuetudinis virtus & ab illis prorsus abjecta esse perhibetur, qui pessum & extraordinarie ad catholicam ecclesiam anathematizandam synodum adgregare nisi sunt: & eam quae benedictione perpetua benedicta est, maledicere insanis auspibus conati sunt, & a nobis fidei brachio & dilectionis manu & cordis amplexu modis omnibus est adeunda & perpetim retinenda. Ait enim Psalmista; Dulcis & mansuetus dominus, propter hoc legem statuit delinquentibus in via: dirigit mites in judicio, docebit mansuetos vias suas. Unde datur intellegi, quod qui mansueti domini sequax esse desiderat, mansuetudinem non debet spernere, sed ut de viis domini doceatur, eam ei conveniet amplectiin Proverbiis quoque scribitur; Mansuetus vir cordis medicus est: tinea autem ossibus cor intelligens. item ibi; Melior est mansuetus cum humilitate, quam qui dividit praedam cum contumeliosis. In Ecclesiastico quoque legitur; Filii in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, & ab omni homine dilige. item ubi supra, Esto mansuetus ad audiendum verbum, ut intellegas, & cum sapientia loquere responsum verum. Nam & praefectus Jesus filius Sirach ita intonat, Fili in mansuetudine serva animam tuam, & da illi honorem secundum dignitatem suam. Doctor itaque gentium ita ad Ephesios scribit, Obsecro vos ego vinctus in domino, ut digne ambuletis vocatione, qua vocati estis, cum omni humilitate & mansuetudine, cum magnanimitate, subportantes invicem in charitate, solliciti servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis. & Jacobus Apostolus dicit, Quis prudens & sciens vestrum, monstret de bono opere conversationem suam in mansuetudine & prudentia. quibus omnibus praeceptis illi proculdubio renisi sunt qui propter imaginum adorationem ecclesiae aulis sunt anathema infere, quae utique tanto est immunis ab eorum maledictione quae injusta est, quanto a Christo qui eam redemit delinitur unctione laetitiae, quae inmarcescibilis & perpetua est. De prudentia quoq; & patientia & continentia oris scriptum est, Qui parcit verbum proferre durum, prodest ei: patiens autem vir sapiens est. Quod enim verbum poterit esse durius anathemate? quod si proferre incaute parcerent, non longe a via discederent. Aut quae patientia aut prudentia in hoc negotio illis utilior esset, quam ut ecclesiam per diversas mundi partes constitutam suis apicibus consulerent, & quod omnium adsensus decrevisset, prudenter & patienter sancirent? Dicitur enim per quendam sapientem, Palpebrae tuae praecedant gressus tuos. In quo dicto dum metonymice per palpebras providens ante acta consilium, & per gressus ipsas actiones significeet, nobis perspicaciter innuit, ut semper nostrarum actionum exercitia providas & prudentia praeveniant consilia, ut antea mentis oculus praevideat in quibus se postmodum actus extendat. A multiloquio igitur quo illi in sua synodo usi sunt, his verbis Psalmista se coercitum esse decantat, Dixi custodiam vias meas ut non delinquam in lingua mea, posui ori meo custodiam: & ut coerceri tute valeat, his precibus dominum inplorare contendit, Pone domine custodiam ori meo, & ostium circumstantiae labiis meis: ut non declines cor meum in verba malitiae. Si ergo omnia quae per patientiam & mansuetudinem a sanctis patribus sive in veteri, sive in novo testamento gesta sunt innumeremus, & e contrario quae per superbiam sive oris incontinentiam a perditis quibusque perpetrata sunt, edicere curemus, & quibus testimoniis hoc vitium perhibeatur, non dicam unius capituli, sed nec quidem unius libri textus cuncta poterit continere. Nunc autem monstratis ex parte quae egerint, quaeve agere debuerint, & illorum nugis ex parte discussis ad alia quae huic operi necessaria sunt, domino accedamus.
units.tr: If, then, after the synod had been convened, they had conducted themselves in it in the manner of the Church, treating matters that were necessary and profitable to the faithful, they would have avoided all novelties of expression and all disorderly trifles of speech. Keeping to the middle path, they would not have departed from the apostolic teachings or from the institutions of the ancient synods. Adorned with the graces of patience and gentleness, they would never have called good evil and evil good, nor put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter, which runs against the prophetic word. They would have decided prudently what had to be decided, said carefully what had to be said, and, rejecting superfluous and extraordinary anathemas, taught useful matters thoroughly, while passing over in silence matters that were doubtful or at least useless. They would also have submitted to the decrees of the churches of our part of the world and of the other parts of the world. But since it is impossible both to give assent to their decrees and to obey the ancient institutions of the Fathers, given that the two are mutually at odds, and since their institutions differ from the institutions of the holy Fathers as far as light differs from darkness, life from death, sight from blindness, honesty from dishonesty, purity from impurity, and health from sickness, therefore we have rejected the more detestable and chosen the better, and, having spurned deceitful byways, we desire to keep to the sure and royal road. Where, I ask, is that most excellent virtue, gentleness? Where is patience, the strongest guardian and enemy of all light provocations? Where have you gone? Whither have you withdrawn, when you saw such rash and perverse decrees being carried through by so many bishops? When you saw so many chains of anathemas being laid upon the Church, why did you not at least lodge in two or three of them? Why did you spurn them all? Why did you present your absence to all of them? Why did you not restrain them from so many trifles with the bridle of your moderation? Why did you not check with the reins of your diligence so many of their ravings? For vainglory, and the desire for empty praise, stirred up their pride, and urged on its servant, namely incontinence of the mouth, to fight against us. Our forces rightly receive all these, like other fomenters of evil; we have withdrawn from them, and at last we could not lodge among those whom we found to be weakened by the uproar of such errors. For there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor any agreement between Christ and Belial. As a certain wise man says, the Spirit of God, who is surely the leader of our army, will flee from deceit and will not dwell in a body subject to sins. For he who does pride has not dwelt in the midst of us, nor has he dwelt in the midst of us. As the words of Jesus the son of Sirach put it: "Pride is hateful before God and before men, and the synagogue of the proud shall have no health, for the root of sin will take hold upon them." For in proportion as the disciple of pride, that is, incontinence of the mouth, flourished in their synod, so far as modesty and prudence ought to have flourished there, and as the hand that ought not to have been led in such an action, to say nothing of the chief hand, alas, held the leadership, so the one who ought to have held the leadership did not even take part in those assemblies with the least of his hands. By your prompting, O incontinence of the mouth, you forbid the steps of men living on the earth to be directed, as the Prophet says: "A man full of words shall not be established upon the earth." Sin is not lacking from your years, according to that saying, "In the multitude of words there lacks not sin; but he that refraineth his lips is wise." Through you the soul is not gladdened, according to the voice of the wise man who says, "He that uses many words hurts his own soul." You compel them not only to answer hastily but also to anathematize the holy Church before they have addressed your followers, according to that saying: "He that answers a matter before he hears it, it is folly and shame to him." Under your urging they so utterly refused our fellowship that our society could not leave even a slight footprint in their minds. For to follow us is the beauty of life, and to despise us is the error of madness; and, in the words of the wisdom of our teacher, "The outcomes of our lives are the outcomes of life." For if the lawgiver had not followed our admonitions, and had not kept his mind bound to the reins of our moderation, as Scripture says, "Now Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth," he would never have enjoyed so many divine addresses, nor been instructed by the Lord in so many mysteries of hidden things, nor would the Lord of all things have said of him: "My servant Moses is not so; he is faithful in all mine house. With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches." Thus the virtue of patience and gentleness is said to have been utterly cast aside by those who dared to convene a synod, most wickedly and extraordinarily, to anathematize the Catholic Church, and who, with mad omens, tried to curse her who has been blessed with a perpetual blessing. By us she must be approached in every way, and always kept, with the arm of faith, the hand of love, and the embrace of the heart. For the Psalmist says: "Good and upright is the LORD: therefore will he teach sinners in the way. The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way." Hence it is understood that whoever desires to be a follower of the gentle Lord ought not to despise gentleness, but should embrace it, so that he may be taught the ways of the Lord. It is also written in the Proverbs: "A wholesome tongue is a tree of life; but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit." Likewise there: "Better is it to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud." In Ecclesiasticus too we read: "My son, perform thy works in meekness; so shalt thou be beloved above the praise of men." Likewise in the same place: "Be swift to hear, and answer with understanding." For Jesus the son of Sirach also thunders thus: "My son, keep thy soul in meekness, and give it honour according to its dignity." Accordingly the teacher of the Gentiles writes to the Ephesians: "I beseech you, therefore, that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness, with long-suffering, forbearing one another in love, endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." And the Apostle James says: "Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? let him show out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom." Undoubtedly those who cast anathema upon the Church because of the adoration of images have resisted all these precepts. The Church is free from their curse, which is unjust, to the same degree that she has been anointed with the oil of gladness by Christ, who redeemed her, and that anointing is unfading and perpetual. Concerning prudence, patience, and restraint of the mouth it is also written: "He that spareth his words is a man of knowledge; and he that is of a cool spirit is a man of understanding." For what word could be harder than anathema? If only they had refrained from uttering it rashly, they would not have strayed far from the right way. Or what patience or prudence would have been more useful to them in this business than to consult by their letters the Church established in the various parts of the world, and prudently and patiently to ratify what the assent of all had decided? For a certain wise man says, "Let thine eyelids look straight before thee." In this saying, while by a metonymy the eyelids signify foresight and counsel beforehand, and the steps signify the actions themselves, he subtly hints to us that we should always foresee the exercises of our actions, and that prudence should go before counsel, so that the eye of the mind may see beforehand where the action afterwards will extend itself. Therefore, from the wordiness with which they used their synod, the Psalmist sings that he restrained himself with these words: "I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a bridle." And, so that he might be able to be restrained safely, he strives to implore the Lord with these prayers: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. Incline not my heart to any evil thing." If, therefore, we were to count up all the deeds of patience and gentleness performed by the holy Fathers, whether in the Old or the New Testament, and, on the other hand, were to set out what was done by the ruined through pride or incontinence of the mouth, and by what testimonies this vice is attested, the texts not of one chapter, nor even of one book, could contain them all. But now that we have shown in part what they have done, and what they ought to have done, and have in part dispelled their trifles, let us go on to the other matters which are necessary for this work, with the Lord's help.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XIII.

units.la: Quia mulier in synodo docere non debet, sicut Haerena in eorum synodo fecisse legitur.
units.tr: Because a woman ought not to teach in a synod, as is read of Haerena in their synod.

units.la: CUM pene in omnibus illa synodus quae pro adorandis imaginibus adgregata est, divinarum scripturarum salubertimis institutis refragetur, in hac quoque parte oppido refragari illis videtur, quod mulierem institutricem sive doctricem habuisse perhibetur: quod quidem non solum divinae legis documentis, sed ipsius naturae lege inhibetur. Non enim eam sexus fragilitas sive animi nobilitas doctrinae sive praelationis super viros apicem tenere permittit, sed tamquam infirmius vas & ad decipiendum facilius subditam & virili auctoritate repressam esse compellit. Unde & divinis legibus sancitum est, quaedam foeminarum vota virili deliberatione cassari posse, & humanis constitutum est, foeminas innuptas, quamvis provectae sint aetatis, propter ipsam animi levitatem in tutela consistere debere. Novimus enim foeminam causa prolis, causa adjutorii, causa incontinentiae viro concedi solere: causa vero docendi nusquam penitus legimus. Causa inquam prolis, ut in Genesi legitur; Et benedixit eos dicens, Crescite & multiplicamini. Hoc est enim matrimonium quod neque secundum Pelagium peccatum esse putandum est, neque secundum Jovinianum virginitati coaequandum: sed virginitas illi praeferenda est propter mundiriae sanctitatem & corporis integritatem, dicente Apostolo; Nupta cogitat quae sunt mundi, quomodo placeat viro: virgo autem cogitat quae sunt domini, quomodo placeat domino, ut sit sancta corpore & spiritu. Illud vero quamquam altero tibi praelato non est abiciendum, neque omnino postponendum, sed cum gratia his quibus conpetit adpetendum, quoniam est & erga se non extraordinarium & erga virginitatem secundum. est enim virginitatis seminarium, quia sicut uva non aliunde nisi ex vite nascitur, ita & virginitas non aliunde nisi ex matrimonio gignitur: & quamquam sit virginitas centesimus fructus, habet tamen infra se tricesimum, id est, matrimonium, inter quos medius sexagesimus est, qui in viduis non inconpetenter accipitur. Causa itaque adjutorii foemina viro concessa est, dicente domino; Non est bonum hominem solum esse, faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi. Causa vero incontinentiae, juxta illud Apostoli; Qui incontinens est, nubat: & iterum, Melius est nubere quam uri. Interrogemus ergo Apostolum, dicat egregius praedicator, dicat vas electionis, utrum foeminas docere permittat, au in viros dominari. Ait enim ad Timotheū; Mulier in silentio discat cum omni subjectione: docere autem mulieri non permitto, neque dominari in virum, sed esse in silentio. Qui quasi interrogaretur, quur eā & docere & dominari in virum prohibuerit, Adam, inquit, primus formatus est, inde Eva: & Adam non est seductus, mulier autem seducta in prævaricatione fuit: ut nosse possemus idcirco ei & doctrinæ & dominationis dignitatem ab Apostolo in virum minimè esse concessam, quia non ut doceret, sed ut adjuvaret virum, nec ut ei præesset, sed subesset, condita esse perhibetur: sive quia animo est infirmior & ad tentandum facilior. Non enim, ut ait Apostolus, vir propter fœminam, sed fœmina propter virum creata est. Nam si quis forte tanti erroris præsumptionem hoc ancilli tueri nitatur, quòd idem Apostolus, cùm de habitu & continentia anuum ageret, ait; Bene docentes, sed prudentiam doceant, perpendant quod non eas docere quandam insaniam vel quandam traditionem sacrosanctis patrum institutionibus resistentem, vel certè cujusdam insensatæ rei adorationem, sed prudentiam & bene vivendi exempla permiserit: nec eas id facere in ecclesia, neq; in conventu, neq; in synodo, sed privatim longævæ ætatis experientia & explosis propter ævi maturitatem vitiorum incentivis, inter domesticos permiserit: nec omnes, sed eas quæ in operibus bonis testimonium habent, quæ hospites recipiunt, quæ sanctorum pedes lavant, quæ tribulationem patientibus submi-nistrant, quæ omne opus bonum subsecutæ sunt, quarum & ipse inceßus, motus, vultus, sermo, silentium, quandam sacræ continentiæ gestet honestatem. Aliud est enim matremfamilias domesticos verbis & exemplis erudire, aliud antestitibus sive omni ecclesiastico ordini vel etiam publicæ synodo quædam inutilia docentem interesse: cùm videlicet ista quæ domesticos exhortatur, eorum & suum in commune adipisci cupiat profectum: illa verò in conventu ventosæ tantum laudis & solius arrogantiæ ambiat appetitum. Sicut igitur caput viri Christus est, ita nimirum caput mulieris vir: ac per hoc si mulier viris præesse debet, jam eorum caput est: & si illa eorum caput est, illi necessario caput Christi erunt. Non autem ullus caput Christi præter patrem esse poteßt, secundum Apostolum qui ait, Caput Christi deus: & de quo in Canticis canticorum dicitur, Caput ejus aurum optimum. non igitur mulier viris se præferendo eorum caput esse debet, nedum sexus inferior ultra se quam ordo exposcit, adtollit, & superiori sexui præfert, caput quod præeminere cæteris membris debet, infima petat, & pedes qui cæteris membris præeminentibus infima loca tenent, cæteris præeminentes ad superiora tollantur, sicque naturæ ordo permutatis ac potius perversis legibus fœdetur. Nam si forte aliquis his sacrosanctis apostolicis institutionibus obniti tentans, mulieres viros docere, virisq; præesse, & synodos instituere debere, ideo adhirmare nisus fuerit, quod secundum evangelicæ tubæ præconium mulieres crebro mediatori dei & hominum ministraverint, ad pedes scilicet ejus sedentes, & verbum ex ore ejus audientes, ac circa frequens ministerium satagentes, & lachrimis pedes ejus rigantes, & capillis tergentes, & corpus ejus miro unguentorum liquore linientes, eumq; ad passionem pergentem sequi non distulerint, & post resurrectionem ejus ad ejus monumentum recurrentes ejus sacratissimæ resurrectionis gloriosum mysterium & primæ cognoverint & discipulis nunciaverint: animadvertat quòd aliud sit ad pedes domini sedere, & cætera quæ præmisimus agere, aliud synodos statuere, in conventibus viros docere: perversas constitutiones tradere, & viris præferri appetere. Illæ etenim typum sanctæ ecclesiæ gestantes domino ministravere, & sacratissimis ejus alloquiis inhæsere: illæ verò si quæ sunt, Athaliæ nimirum exempla sequuntur, quæ dum viris præesse inconpetenti desiderio appetit, pene omne semen regium extinxit, & sui nefandissimi capitis interitu ad ultimum indignam vitam digna morte finivit. Fœmina verò idcirco domini & salvatoris nostri resurrectionis nunciatrix esse existimatur, ut quia fuerat ei fœmina de cælis ad terras venienti iter, fieret etiam ei à terris ad cælos redeunti index: & quem venientem Maria virgo mundo edidit, redeuntem nimirum Maria à domino sanata discipulis nunciaret. Qui mediator dei & hominum non idcirco de fœmina natus esse perhibetur, ut fœmineum sexum vitis præferret, sed ut utrumq; sexum in culpâ lapsum suæ incarnationis mysterio redimeret: virum videlicet, quia vir fieri pro nostra salute dignatus est, juxta illud propheticum, Ecce venit vir, oriens est nomen ejus: de quo scribitur. Jesum Nazarenum virum adprobatum à deo virtutibus & signis, quæ fecit per illum dominus: fœminam verò, quia de fœmina sine ullo masculino sexus contagio nasci dignatus est, & utriusque sexus sicut verus conditor, ita etiam verus permanet restaurator.
units.tr: Although that synod which was gathered in favour of adoring images opposes the most salutary institutions of the divine Scriptures almost throughout, it seems to oppose them outright in this respect too, in that it is said to have had a woman as its teacher and instructor. This is forbidden not only by the precepts of the divine law but by the law of nature itself. For the frailty of her sex, the nobility of her mind notwithstanding, does not allow her to hold the summit of teaching or of authority over men; rather it compels her to be treated as a weaker vessel, more easily deceived, and to be held in check by male authority. Hence the divine laws have also decreed that certain vows of women may be annulled by a man's judgement, and human law has ruled that unmarried women, however advanced in years, must remain under guardianship because of their own lightness of mind. For we know that a woman is customarily granted to a man for the sake of offspring, for the sake of help, and for the sake of restraining incontinence; but we nowhere at all read of her being granted for the sake of teaching. For the sake of offspring, as is read in Genesis: And he blessed them, saying, Increase and multiply. This is indeed the matrimony which is not to be thought sinful, as Pelagius held, nor to be made equal to virginity, as Jovinian held; but virginity is to be preferred to it on account of the holiness of purity and the integrity of the body, the Apostle saying: The married woman thinks of the things of the world, how she may please her husband; but the virgin thinks of the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit. Yet that other state, although it is not to be cast aside when the first is preferred, nor altogether held in low regard, is to be sought with grace by those to whom it is granted; for it is not extraordinary in comparison with itself, and it is second to virginity. For it is the seed-plot of virginity: just as the grape is born from nothing but the vine, so virginity is begotten from nothing but matrimony; and although virginity is the hundredfold fruit, it nevertheless has beneath it the thirtyfold, that is, matrimony, and between them lies the sixtyfold, which is not unfittingly understood as widowhood. Woman was therefore granted to man for the sake of help, the Lord saying: It is not good that man should be alone; let us make him a help like unto himself. But for the sake of incontinence, according to that saying of the Apostle: He who is incontinent, let him marry; and again, It is better to marry than to burn. Let us therefore ask the Apostle; let the outstanding preacher say, let the vessel of election say, whether he permits women to teach or to rule over men. For he says to Timothy: Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection; but I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to have dominion over the man, but to be in silence. As if he were asked why he forbade her both to teach and to rule over the man, he says: Adam was first formed, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, being deceived, fell into transgression. So that we may know that for this reason the dignity neither of teaching nor of dominion over the man was by the Apostle granted to her at all, because she was made not to teach but to help the man, nor to preside over him but to be subject to him; or because she is weaker in mind and more easily tempted. For, as the Apostle says, man was not created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man.
