But if anyone perhaps should try to defend so great a presumption of error by this, that the same Apostle, when he was speaking of the dress and self-restraint of older women, said: Let them teach what is good, that they may teach prudence, let them weigh this, that he did not permit them to teach some madness, or some tradition opposed to the holy institutions of the Fathers, or certainly the adoration of some senseless thing, but prudence and examples of living well; nor did he permit them to do this in the church, nor in the assembly, nor in a synod, but privately, among the members of their household, by the experience of advanced age and with the incentives to vice cast out by the maturity of their years; and not all women, but those who have a testimony for good works, who receive strangers, who wash the feet of the saints, who minister to those suffering affliction, who have followed every good work, and whose very bearing, movement, countenance, speech and silence display a certain dignity of holy self-restraint. For it is one thing for a mother of a household to instruct her household by word and example; it is another to take part among the bishops, or in every ecclesiastical order, or even in a public synod, teaching certain useless things: since she who exhorts her household desires to attain profit for them and for herself in common, whereas the other, in an assembly, seeks only the empty applause and the appetite of mere arrogance. Therefore, just as Christ is the head of man, so assuredly man is the head of woman; and thus if woman ought to rule over men, she is already their head; and if she is their head, they will of necessity be the head of Christ. But no one can be the head of Christ except the Father, according to the Apostle who says, The head of Christ is God; and of whom it is said in the Song of Songs, His head is most fine gold. Therefore woman, by setting herself before men, ought not to be their head; much less should the inferior sex raise itself beyond what its order requires and prefer itself to the superior sex, seeking the lowest place as head, which ought to stand out above the other members, while the feet, which hold the lowest places beneath the other members, should be lifted up above them; and so the order of nature would be defiled, its laws overturned and rather perverted. For if anyone, trying to resist these holy apostolic institutions, should attempt to maintain that women ought to teach men, to preside over men, and to found synods, on the ground that, according to the proclamation of the gospel trumpet, women often ministered to the Mediator of God and men, namely sitting at his feet and hearing the word from his mouth, busying themselves with frequent service, watering his feet with tears, wiping them with their hair, anointing his body with a wondrous liquid of ointments, and not hesitating to follow him as he went to the passion, and after his resurrection, returning to his tomb, they both recognised the glorious mystery of his most holy resurrection first and announced it to the disciples: let him observe that it is one thing to sit at the feet of the Lord and to do the other things we have mentioned, and another to establish synods, to teach men in assemblies, to hand down perverse constitutions, and to desire to be placed above men. For those women, bearing the figure of the holy church, served the Lord and clung to his most holy words; but those women, if there are any such, follow the examples of Athaliah, who, while she desired with unfitting ambition to rule over men, nearly extinguished all the royal seed, and at last, by the destruction of her own most wicked head, ended an unworthy life with a worthy death. Moreover, a woman is thought to have been made the announcer of the resurrection of our Lord and Saviour so that, since a woman had been the way for him in coming down from heaven to earth, she might also be the guide for him in returning from earth to heaven; and as the Virgin Mary brought forth the one who came into the world, so Mary, healed by the Lord, was to announce the one who returned to the disciples. Nor is it said that the Mediator of God and men was born of a woman so that he might place the female sex above the male, but so that by the mystery of his incarnation he might redeem both sexes, fallen in sin: the male, namely, because he deigned to become a man for our salvation, according to that prophetic saying, Behold a man comes, whose name is the Rising; of whom it is written: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God through the virtues and signs which the Lord did through him; and the female, because he deigned to be born of a woman without any contagion of the male sex, and as he is the true Creator of both sexes, so he also remains their true Restorer.

units.la: CAP. XIIII. Contra eos qui diount, Dei cooperantes nos direximus congregare vos, sive congregavit vos deus consilium proprium statuere volens.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. Against those who say, "We, cooperating with God, have directed you to gather," or "God gathered you, wishing to establish his own counsel."

units.la: IN primo hujus operis libro in prima parte libri, cum eorū error discuteretur, qui dicunt deum sibi conregnare, aliquantulum disputatum est, unde hic quoq; error quo se dei cooperantes superciliosè jactant, cassari potest: quoniam & deum sibi conregnare, & dei cooperantes esse, non humiliter, nō sanctorum regum exemplis contenti, non sanctarum scripturarum institutionibus instructi, sed perperam & fastu arrogantiæ elati delirant: & dum appetunt id sibi usurpare quod non competit, timendum est ne id amittant quod conpetit: quia quisquis ambit inlicita, amittete solet adquisita. Sed quoniam, ut præfati sumus, in superioribus hic error ex parte discussus est, nunc ad id quod ideo illos qui in eadem synodo fuisse noscuntur congregatos dicunt, ut per eos deus consilium suum statueret, nostræ disputationis vertamus articulum. Dicunt enim, Congregavit vos deus consilium proprium statuere volens, quasi non scriptum sit, Qui vivit in æternum creavit omnia simul: & quasi deo quædam nova voluntas quæ antea non accesserat, accedat: de quo per Prophetam scribitur, Statuit ea in æternum & in seculum seculi, præceptum possint, & non præteribit: aut quasi ullius adminiculo indiguus idcirco alios congreget, ut plurium deliberatione quid agere debeat statuat. Est enim consilium à consulendo dictum, quo aliquid aut faciendi, aut non faciendi assidua consideratione decernitur. Est enim genus causæ quod oratores deliberativum dicunt, in quo genere de quibusliber vitæ utilitatibus quid aut debeat aut non debeat fieri tractatur. Sunt enim in eo suasio & dissuasio, id est, de expetendo & fugiendo, de faciendo & non faciendo. In suasione autem duo sunt fortiora, spes & metus. Quia igitur Deus omnipotens est, ideo nullius est indiguus: ideoque nec alterius suasione ad ea, quæ non vult peragenda promovetur, nec ab his quæ agere vult ullius dissuasione removetur: nec quodam metu ab aliquibus quæ agere vult agenda hortatur, nec cum alio consilii sui deliberationem statuit. Quibus omnibus si indigeret, necessitatem pateretur, omnipotens non esset: est autem omnipotens, nullam igitur indigentiam habet: ac per hoc incautum est dicere, Congregavit vos Deus consilium proprium statuere volens. Consilium namque Dei filius est, qui non statutus est à patre quadam deliberatione, sed genitus ante sæcula inefabili nativitate: quem pater genuisse, & sine quo numquam fuisse à fidelibus creditur. Est enim sapientia Dei patris quæ ei consempiterna est, & quæ dicit, Ante colles ego parturiebar, adhuc terram non fecerat, quando parabat cælos aderam illi: dum vallaret mari terminum, & legem poneret aquis, ego cum illo eram. Quæ etiam cœlitudinem suam his verbis demonstrat dicens, Ego in altissimis habitavi & thronus meus in columna nubis: & iterum, Gyrum cœli circuivi sola, & in fluctibus maris ambulavi, in omnem gentem & in omnem populi primatum tenui: & iterum, Ego quasi terebinthus expandi ramos meos. ego feci ut oriretur lucifer in cælo. ego omnes qui me amat diligo. exitus enim mei exitus vitæ sunt. De hoc enim consilio Psalmographus dixit, Consilium Domini manet in æternum, cogitationes cordis ejus in sæculum sæculi. Qui ideo consilium dicitur, eo quod incarnationis ejus archanum ad consulendum humano generi sit concessum, quod consilium nulla ætate dissolvitur, sed in æternum manet: quia triumphalis mors domini diabolicum perenniter extinxit exitium. Cogitationes namque cordis ejus prædestinationem interni ejus judicii innuunt, in quibus cuncta repolita sunt, quæ vel fuerunt vel sequentibus sæculis futura succedunt. Hominum etenim consilia plerumque frustrantur: domini autem consilium permanet in æternum. Homo enim mortalis caduca sapit, æternus dominus numquam reprehendenda constituit. Unde & hoc consilium quod illi dicunt quod per eos dominus statuisset, ideo à domino statutum esse minime creditur, quia dominicis præceptis contraire dinoscitur: cum videlicet & per veteris & per novi Testamenti paginam Deus se solum adorari seu coli instituerit: isti autem quasdam res insensatas adorandas sive colendas esse absurdissima deliberatione percenseant. Non enim Deus commutabilis est, ut quæ antea inhibuerat modo peragenda concedat: sed quod ante sæcula in consilio suo, hoc est, in filio, constituit, semper stabilia esse permittit, Esaias adtestante, qui ex persona Dei patris ait, Omne consilium meum stabile erit, & omnia quæcunque cogitavi efficiam. Hoc etenim consilium, id est, filius, & testamentum dicitur: unde & Hieremias ait, Si non esset testamentum meum in custodia die ac nocte, præcepta cæli & terræ non dedissem. De quo testamento dicitur, Et testamentum pacis erit in Hierusalem. Quomodo ergo Deus illos ideo congregaret, ut per eos cōsilium proprium statueret, ut illi somniant? in quo tanta est scientia ut nec præterita ei quædam, nec futura, sed omnia præsentia sint: cujus substantiam sicuti est, nulla poterit adtingere opinio, nulla conplectidefinitio: quoniam plus est quam quicquid dici aut cogitari potest. Est enim spiritus natura simplex, lux inaccessibilis, invisibilis, inæstimabilis, infinitus, perfectus, nullius egens, æternus, immortalis, cui omnia vivunt, à quo omnia initium consequuta sunt, venerandus, diligendus, metuendus, extra quem nihil est, immo in quo sunt omnia quæque; sunt sursum, deorsumve, summa & ima, omnipotens, omnia tenens, vere in omnibus dives, quia nihil est, ubi non sit, nec aliquis ei locus absens est, exceptis impiorum cordibus, ubi quamvis sit per potentiam, non est tamen per gratiam, qui ubique esse his divinæ legis testimoniis conprobatur. Aut enim Psalmista, Quo ibo ab spiritu tuo, & à facie tua quo fugiam? Si ascendero in cælum tu illic es. & si descendero in infernum, ades: si sumpsero pennas meas ante lucem, & habitavero in extremu maris, etenim illuc manus tua deducet me, & tenebit me dextera tua. In Esaia quoque legitur, Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus Sabaoth, plena est terra gloria majestatis tuæ. per Hieremiam quoque dicit, Deus adpropinquans, ego sum, dicit Dominus, & non Deus de longinquo: quod si abscondit se fuerit homo in abditis, ego eum videbo. Nonne cælum & terram ego impleo? dicit Dominus. Liber quoque Sapientiæ dicit, Sanctus enim Spiritus sapientiæ, & non liberavit maledictum à labiis suis: quoniam renum illius testis est Deus, & cordis illius speculator est verus, & linguæ auditor, quia Spiritus Domini replebit orbem terrarum. In Ecclesiastico quoque scribitur, Quoniam multa sapientia Dei, fortis in potentia, videns omnes sine intermissione: qui bonitate sua eum, qui non erat creavit, justitia eum, qui peccaverat condemnavit, misericordia immo magna misericordia eum, qui perierat restauravit. De quo per Prophetam dicitur, Magna opera Domini exquisita in omnes voluntates ejus: confessio & magnificentia opus ejus, & justitia ejus manet in sæculum sæculi. & iterum, Universa via Domini misericordia & veritas: & cui per eundem Prophetam dicitur, Et tu Domine Deus miserator & misericors, patiens & multæ misericordiæ & verax. Nam quid cum quem dominationes adorant, tremunt potestates, & cælestibus hymnis lætabunda angelorum conlaudat militia, quem cherubim & seraphim, sublimes virtutes ejus scientia repletæ, ejus amore ardentes, sensu minime conprehendere valent, quem nemo novit nisi filius, qui utiq; unius est cum eo substantiæ, credere oportunum est ut alterius consilio egeat? & ideo alios convocet ut per alios cōsilium suum statuat? O dementissimum dictum, ô insulsa loquutio, ô verba cunctis divinis verbis obnitentia! quæ si ab his quibus dicta sunt defendantur, insaniæ vicina sunt: si non defendantur, ignorantiæ & ignaviæ deputanda sunt. Adhærere enim Deo quis poterit bonis actibus insistendo, sicut ille cupiebat qui dixit, Mihi autem adhærere Deo bonum est: cōlilium autē illi dare nemo poterit, est enim auctor & fons omnium bonorum,&,ut crebro diximus,nullius indiguus,Magnus, ait Propheta,Dominus noster,& magna virtus ejus,& sapientia ejus non est numerus. Dic quaeso,sancte Esaias, dic nobilissime vatum,dic dominicae incarnationis & gentium vocationis Evangelice potius quam Prophetice narrator,dic utrum aliquis sensum Domini cognoscere potest,aut ei consiliarius effici valet? Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit? cum quo iniit consilium,& erudivit eum scientia, & viam prudentiae ostendit illi? item,idem Propheta dicit, Numquid nescis & non audisti? Deus sempiternus Dominus, qui creavit terminos terrae, non est deficiens, neque laborans, nec est investigatio sapientiae ejus. Dicat etiam magister gentium quid de hac re sentiat. Aut enim, O altitudo divitiarum sapientiae & scientiae Dei: quam inconprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus & investigabiles viae ejus! Cujus enim judicia inconprehensibilia & viae investigabiles sunt, nullo modo credendus est alterius consilio ad res deliberandas egere: quia sicut natura, ita & sapientia super omnes est, & sicut coaequari ei quis nequit per naturam, ita nec ejus scientiae potest aliquid conferri per consilium. Consilium enim ab eo quaeritur, qui aut per naturam, aut per intellegentiam socius est. Deo enim nullus aequalis, nullus socius est, dicente Moyse, Quis similis tibi in diis Domine? quis similis tibi, honorificus, sanctus, mirabilis, in majestatibus faciens prodigia? De quo etiam per Psalmistam dicitur, Quoniam quis in nubibus aequabitur Domino, aut quis similis erit Deo inter Filios Dei? Deus qui glorificatur in consilio sanctorum, magnus & metuendus super omnes, qui in circuitu ejus sunt. Domine Deus virtutum, quis similis tibi? potens es Domine & veritas tua in circuitu tuo.
units.tr: In the first book of this work, in the first part of the book, when the error of those who say that they reign with God was being examined, we disputed at some length. So this error too, by which they proudly boast that they are cooperators with God, can be overthrown. For to reign with God and to be cooperators with God is not a humble aim. Men who are not content with the examples of holy kings, nor instructed by the teaching of the holy Scriptures, but are carried away perversely and by the pride of arrogance, go mad. And while they seek to claim for themselves what does not belong to them, they must fear lest they lose what does belong to them, since whoever pursues unlawful things usually loses what he has already gained. But since, as we said above, this error has already been partly examined in the earlier passages, we now turn the point of our argument to that claim which they make, that those who are known to have been gathered together at the same synod were gathered so that God might establish his counsel through them. For they say, God gathered you, wishing to establish his own counsel, as if it were not written, He who lives forever created all things at once, and as if some new will, which had not previously arisen in God, now arose. Of this it is written through the Prophet, He has established them forever and ever, a precept that cannot pass away. Or they say it as if God, who needs no help from anyone, therefore gathers others so that he may decide what he ought to do by the deliberation of many. For counsel is named from consulting, by which something is decided by careful consideration either to be done or not to be done. There is a kind of case that the orators call deliberative, in which it is considered, concerning any of the advantages of life, what ought or ought not to be done. In it there is persuasion and dissuasion, that is, concerning what to seek and what to avoid, what to do and what not to do. In persuasion there are two stronger forces, hope and fear. Therefore, because God is almighty, he is in need of nothing. Consequently he is neither moved by another's persuasion to bring about what he does not will, nor turned away by anyone's dissuasion from what he wills to do; nor does he urge with any fear the things that he wills to be done, nor does he establish the deliberation of his counsel together with another. If he needed any of these things, he would be subject to necessity, and would not be almighty; but he is almighty, and therefore has no need at all. Hence it is rash to say, God gathered you, wishing to establish his own counsel. For the Counsel of God is the Son, who was not established by the Father through some deliberation, but was begotten before the ages by an ineffable birth, whom the Father begot and without whom, the faithful believe, he never was. For he is the Wisdom of God the Father, which is coeternal with him, and which says, Before the hills I was brought forth; while as yet he had not made the earth, when he prepared the heavens I was there with him; when he enclosed the sea within its bounds and set a law for the waters, I was with him. She also shows her loftiness in these words, saying, I dwelt in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud. And again, I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the depths of the sea; over every people and over every nation I have held the first place. And again, I have spread out my branches like the terebinth. I caused the morning star to rise in heaven. I love all who love me. For my goings forth are the goings forth of life. Of this Counsel the Psalmist said, The counsel of the Lord stands forever; the thoughts of his heart to all generations. He is called the Counsel because the secret of his incarnation was given to mankind as counsel; this counsel is dissolved in no age, but remains forever, because the triumphal death of the Lord has destroyed the devil's ruin forever. For the thoughts of his heart point to the predestination of his inner judgment, in which all things are stored up, whether they have been or will come in the ages that follow. Indeed, the counsels of men are often frustrated, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever. For mortal man thinks of perishable things, but the eternal Lord decrees things that are never to be reproved. Hence also this counsel, which they say the Lord established through them, is by no means believed to have been established by the Lord, because it is known to be contrary to the precepts of the Lord, since, as is clear from both the Old and the New Testament, God has ordained that he alone be adored or worshipped; but these men, by a most absurd decision, assert that certain senseless things are to be adored or worshipped. For God is not changeable, so as to grant now what he had previously forbidden. But what he has established before the ages in his counsel, that is, in his Son, he allows to remain always stable, Isaiah bearing witness, who says in the person of God the Father, All my counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure. This counsel, that is, the Son, is also called the covenant. Hence Jeremiah says, If my covenant were not kept day and night, I would not have appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth. Of this covenant it is said, And there shall be a covenant of peace in Jerusalem. How, then, would God gather those men so that through them he might establish his own counsel, as they dream? In him there is such knowledge that for him nothing is past or future, but all things are present. His substance, as it is, no opinion can reach, and no definition can grasp, since it is more than whatever can be said or thought. For the Spirit is by nature simple, light inaccessible, invisible, inestimable, infinite, perfect, needing nothing, eternal, immortal; by whom all things live, from whom all things have received their beginning; to be venerated, to be loved, to be feared; outside whom nothing is, indeed in whom all things are; they are above or below, highest and lowest; almighty, holding all things, truly rich in all things, since there is no place where he is not, and no place is absent from him, except the hearts of the wicked, where, although he is present by his power, he is not present by his grace. That he is everywhere is proved by these testimonies of the divine law. For the Psalmist says, Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I make my bed in hell, behold, you are there. If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. It is also read in Isaiah, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of Hosts; the whole earth is full of the glory of your majesty. Through Jeremiah also he says, I am a God near at hand, says the Lord, and not a God from afar. If a man hides himself in secret places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord. The Book of Wisdom also says, For the holy Spirit of wisdom will not acquit a man who speaks evil with his lips; for God is witness of his inmost thoughts, and a true observer of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue; for the Spirit of the Lord fills the whole world. In Ecclesiasticus also it is written, For the wisdom of God is great and strong in power, and sees all things without ceasing. In his goodness he created him who did not exist; in his justice he condemned him who had sinned; in his mercy, yes, in his great mercy, he restored him who had perished. Of him it is said through the Prophet, The great works of the Lord are sought out for all his pleasures; his work is confession and majesty, and his justice endures forever and ever. And again, All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. And to him it is said through the same Prophet, And you, O Lord God, are merciful and gracious, patient, abundant in mercy and true. For what must one believe, whom the dominions adore, the powers tremble before, and the host of angels praises with heavenly hymns in joyful song; whom the cherubim and seraphim, lofty powers filled with knowledge, burning with his love, can scarcely comprehend by their understanding; whom no one knows except the Son, who is indeed of one substance with him: that he needs the counsel of another, and therefore calls others together so that he may establish his counsel through them? O most senseless statement, O foolish speech, O words that fight against all divine words! If those who uttered them defend them, they border on madness; if they are not defended, they must be ascribed to ignorance and sloth. For who can cleave to God by persevering in good deeds, as he desired who said, But it is good for me to cleave to God? Yet no one can give him counsel, for he is the author and fountain of all good things, and, as we have often said, he needs nothing. Great, says the Prophet, is our Lord, and great is his power, and his wisdom is beyond number. Tell me, I beg you, holy Isaiah, tell me, most noble of the prophets, tell me, a narrator of the Lord's incarnation and of the calling of the Gentiles more than of prophecy: tell me whether anyone can know the mind of the Lord, or can become his counsellor? For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? With whom did he take counsel, and who taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of prudence? Likewise the same Prophet says, Do you not know, have you not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord, who created the ends of the earth, does not faint or grow weary; there is no searching of his wisdom. Let the teacher of the Gentiles also say what he thinks about this matter. For he says, O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! Since his judgments are unsearchable and his ways past finding out, he is by no means to be believed to need another's counsel in deciding matters. For as he is above all in nature, so he is also above all in wisdom; and as no one can be made equal to him in nature, so nothing can be added to his knowledge by counsel. For counsel is sought from one who is a companion either by nature or by understanding. There is no one equal to God, no one is his companion, as Moses says, Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you, glorious in holiness, wonderful in praises, doing wonders? Of him the Psalmist also says, For who in the heavens can be compared to the Lord? Or who among the sons of God is like God? God is glorified in the counsel of the saints, great and to be feared above all who are around him. O Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth surrounds you.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Contra eos, qui dicunt, Si enim imperialis effigies & imagines emissas in civitates & provincias obviabunt populi cum cereis & thymiamatibus, non cera perfusam tabulam honorantes, sed imperatorem: quanto magis oportet in Ecclesiis Christi depingi, imagines Salvatoris nostri Dei & intemeratae matris ejus & sanctorum omnium?
units.tr: Against those who say: If indeed the imperial effigy and images sent into cities and provinces are met by the people with candles and incense, honouring not the wax-smeared board but the emperor, how much more ought the images of our Saviour God, and of his inviolate mother, and of all the saints, to be painted in the churches of Christ?

units.la: QUisquis alicujus artis sedula meditatione cupit habere peritiam, non inperitorum, sed peritorum artificum monitis adhaerendo discendae arti praebet instantiam, nec affectat eorum sibi magisterium usurpare, quos videt in propria arte minus doctos & despicabiles esse: ne dum desiderat instanti opere ex adepta arte adipisci laudem, incassum & suum deperdat opus, & ceteris sit in subsannationem. Hoc a liberalium artium sectatoribus, hoc a medicis, hoc a metallorum conflatoribus sive sculptoribus, hoc a lignorum lapidumque caesoribus, hoc ab agrorum cultoribus fixa ratione observatur: solum ab his observare neglegitur, qui ut imagines adorare instituant a pravis rebus exempla sumere affectant, & rem tam inutilem, tamque perversam nonnunquam bonis rebus inconpetenter, plerumque perversis afferre niti untur impudenter: & in modum temulenti, qui nimio madefactus mero trementibus membris, titubantibus gressibus, nudatis sensibus, modo barbaris, modo Latinis utitur verbis, modo ignium caloribus, modo pruinarum delectatur algoribus, modo insensate jacere, modo enerviter delectatur ludere & in nulla parte fixam habens intentionem, huc illucque nutabundam & rationes egenam efferre non definit mentem: ita isti modo divinarum scripturarum testimoniis inconpetenter adhibitis, modo suarum adlertionum deliramentis, modo mala, modo malarum quarundam rerum malorum, actuum exemplis suum nituntur usquequaque firmare errorem. Nam quis furor est quaeve dementia, ut hoc in exemplum adorandarum imaginum ridiculum adducatur, quod imperatorum imagines in civitatibus & in plateis adorantur, & a re inlicita res inlicita stabiliri paretur? Doctor enim gentium non vos imperatorum imitatores, sed suos, immo Christi fieri hortatur dicens, Imitatores mei estote sicut & ego Christi: & ut imperatorum fasces sive vulgi bacchatus a Christicolarum mentibus dirimeret, ait, Nobis quidem Christus crucifixus est, quid nobis cum foro? jam vero quia de forensibus sive publicis actionibus exempla sumere intra sanctam Ecclesiam affectant, quur non scenicas mimicasque nugas, vel etiam crudelitates quae in theatris sive in orchestris de ludis gladiatoriis infeliciter fiunt sibi usurpant? Quur non clerus cum antestite more sequutoris populum velut retiarium insectatur? Quur non tota circi gentilia vel potius infelicia exempla sectatur, qui Christi custodit ecclesiam? Sed absit Catholica religione, ut actiones perversas quas pridem proterva gerebat gentilitas, nunc Christiana imitetur & fervet gravitas. Nostra enim conversatio, ait Apostolus, in caelis est. Ideoq; quisquis illo tendere desiderat quo caput nostrum Christus praecessit, non debet fieri sectator forensium vel publicarum actionum, sed ipsius capitis nostri Christi, aut ejus membrorum, Apostolorum videlicet sive Apostolicorum virorum. Exempla enim prava ita Catholicis vitanda sunt, sicut & seductio malorum hominum sive societas injustorum, dicente Domino, Non audies auditum vanum, non consenties cum injusto fieri testis injustus, non eris cum pluribus in malitia. Odisse enim debet Christianus exemplo Psalmistae eos, qui oderunt Dominum & super inimicos ejus tabescere. Neq; enim Tobias vir probabilis & Deo charus filium suum exempla perversa sectari hortabatur, cum dicebat, Vide fili ne sequaris iter iniquorum, & multitudo peccantium non suadeat te, quoniam stipendia eorum mors est: tu autem si operatus fueris veritatem, erit respectus Dei in operibus tuis, & cum omnibus qui faciunt justitiam hereditabis vitam aeternam. Quisquis ergo videns imagines imperatorum adorari a populorum frequentius, hoc exemplo munitus imagines adorare percensetur in basilicis, huic sancti viri praecepto non mediocriter reluctari convincitur: nec cum David dicere poterit, Non sedi in concilio vanitatis, & cum iniqua gerentibus non introibo: odio habui congregationem malignorum, & cum impiis non sedebo: lavabo inter innocentes manus meas & circumdabo altare tuum Domine. Sed si fortasse hujusce erroris defensor dicet, Imperatorum imagines adorare peccatum non est, perpendat quanta gloria tribus pueris id facere nolentibus in flagrante camino angelo caelitus emisso, edacis rogi flammam excutiente & salutiferum rorem illis impertiente conlata sit, quantoque miraculo Babylonicus princeps inter eos se vidisse simile m filio Dei testetur, non ad suam, sed ad illorum gloriam vel etiam ad suam pertinaciam refutandam. Audiant etiam beatum Hieronymum in commentario quem in libro Danielis edidit taliter dicentem, Ecce enim, inquit, Deus noster quem colimus, potest eripere nos de camino ignis ardentis, & de manibus tuis, rex, liberare. Unde putaverat se terrere pueros, inde cernit in eis materiam fortitudinis. Nec in longum differunt, sed praesens sibi pollicentur auxilium dicentes, Ecce enim Deus noster quem colimus, ipse nos & de eo quod minaris incendio, & de tuis potest manibus liberare. Quod si noluerit: pulchre ad id quod dixerat, Potest eripere nos, non iutulit contrarium. Si non poterit, sed, Si voluerit: ut non impossibilitatis Dei, sed voluntatis sit si perierint; Notum tibi sit rex, quod Deos tuos non colimus. & statuam auream quam erexisti non adoramus, sive statuam ut Symmachus, sive imaginem auream ut ceteri transtulerunt, volueri mus legere, cultores Dei eam adorare non debent. Ergo judices & principes saeculi, qui imperatorum statuas adorant & imagines, hoc se facere intelligant quod tres pueri facere noluerunt placuerunt Deo. Et votanda proprietas, Deos coli, imaginem adorari dicunt: quod utrum q, servis Dei non convenit. Ecce sancti viri documentis instruimur, imperatorum imagines adorari minime debere: & quis tam perversus eas non solum adorare decernat, sed ab earum adoratione exempla perversitatis ad alianum nihil dominus imaginum adorationem adsumat? Et si homines mortales protervia vanitatis inflati, pompa saeculari elati, honorum ambitione cupidi, jactantia pleni, loco circumscripti, situ contenti, quia non ubique esse poterant, ideo imagines suas hominibus adorandas mandavere, quia in ipsis non ubique poterant adorari, quid necesse est Deum in imagine adorare, qui incircumscriptus est? qui ubique totus est? ubique mirabilis? qui loco non continetur, situ non circumscribitur? quem, sicut ait Salomon, caelum & caeli caelorum non capiunt, quem non capit mundus, sed ille capit mundum. Cum enim tanta sit ejus virtus, tanta gloria, tanta potentia, non est quaerendus in imaginibus, sed in mundis & sanctis pectoribus: non est adorandus in depicta tabula, sed in aula sancta, dicente Propheta, Adorate Dominum in aula sancta ejus, qui non invenitur per picturam statutis locis, sed per opera à mentibus piis, quem non in loco, non in pictura, non tabulis Helias quaerebat, sed ubique eum praesentem sciebat ei, qui se instantia bonorum operum praesentem exhibuerat cum dicebat, Vivit Dominus in cujus conspectu sto. In tabulis ergo Deum, qui in localis & omnipotens est, adorare velle, sicut gentiles reges suos locales sive mortales adorabant, profanum est, & incredulitati vicinum. Nullam enim hoc seculus fecisse legimus gentem, nisi Babylonios & Romanos, vel eas gentes quae ab his aut subactae, aut finitimae fuere, aut ab his exemplasumpsere: ut sicut in ferocitate, sive in fortitudine haec duo regna ceteris mundi regnis eminuisse noscuntur, ita etiam in colendis idolis & adorandis proniora fuisse credantur. Fuit itaque inter haec duo fortissima regna magna concordantia, magna similitudo, magna crudelitas, magna etiam sortitudo, & revera fortitudo quae ceteris mundi regnis suo tempore imperaverit. Nam ut illud ab oriente, ita nimirum istud eminuit ab occidente: illud mundo pubescente, istud jam mundo senescente. Nam omnem, ut ajunt historiae, Babylonii regni haereditatem & apicis cumulum Romanum suscepit imperium. Et inter haec duo regna quasi inter patrem senem, qui jam posse deficere, & filium pubem, quae necdum dominandi vires acceperit, duo regna vice tutoris Persarum videlicet sive Macedonum suisse traduntur: at dum haeres, id est, Romanum Imperium, atlolevit, hoc quod tutoris locum tenebat abcesset, & suscepit haereditatem filius adolescens quam pater amiserat veteranus: quorum duorum regnorum consonantias sive concordias persequi longum est. Nam, ut cetera taceamus, in hac parte non minima eorundem regnorum consonantia est, quod utraque reges suos in statuis sive imaginibus per campos, sive plateas adorare censuerint, & haec facere nolentibus diversa supplicia multerint. Nam hoc malum cum ceteris malis quae Christi adventu fructrata sunt, fructrari omnino debet, & non solum ab eo ad alia peragenda exempla sunt sumenda, sed idipsum à Christicolis radicitus est extirpandum: ne qua, secundum Apostolum, radix amaritudinis rursum pullulet & inquinet multos. Nam cum Apostolicis instruamur documentis, nullam nos dare debere occasionem maligno, quur talem gentilibus occasionem demus mortalium regum imagines adorando, & ab his exempla sumendo? ut nobis ingerere possint dicentes, Nos eorum simulachra vel imagines adoramus quos vel vera religione Deos credimus, vel antiquorum traditionibus docti Deos non esse nescimus: vos vero quibus istud abominatio est, quur imagines hominum vel ceris pictas vel metallis conflatas sub regum reverentia etiam publica adoratione veneramini, & ut ipsi praedicatis, Deo tantum honorem debitum etiam hominibus datis? quod si inlicitum legique contrarium est, quur hoc facitis, Christiani? aut quur vestri non prohibent sacerdotes? ne id quod id ignorantibus nobis pro sacrilegio adscribitis, scientes sub officii excusatione subeatis. Quaedam & his similia primis fidei temporibus à Philosophis gentium nostris inlata fuisse, nostri taliter respondisse feruntur; Hoc nam que quod dicitis, nec debemus probare, nec possumus: quia evidentibus Dei dictis, non elementa, non angelos, nec quoslibet caeli ac terrae vel aeris principatus adorare permittimur. Divini enim [speciale hoc nomen est officii, & altius omni terrena veneratione vel reverentia, sed sicut in hujusmodi malum primum adulatio homines inpulit, sic nunc ab errore cōsuetudo vix revocat. In quo tamen incauto oblequio quamquam divinus non deprehendatur cultus, sed propter similitudinem amabilium vultuum gaudia interna plus tacent, quam aut hi forte exigant quibus defertur, aut perfungi oporteat deferentes: reverentiores tamen
units.tr: Whoever wishes to gain skill in any art through diligent study should attach himself to the instructions of skilled craftsmen, not of the unskilled, and should not presume to take as his teachers those whom he sees to be ignorant and contemptible in their own art. Otherwise, while he hopes by his finished work to win praise from the art he has acquired, he will waste his labour in vain and become a laughingstock to others. This rule is kept firmly by students of the liberal arts, by physicians, by metalworkers and sculptors, by those who cut wood and stone, and by farmers. Only those who undertake to worship images neglect it. They seek their examples from bad things, and they shamelessly try to defend this useless and perverse practice, sometimes by applying good things inappropriately, but mostly by applying perverse things. They are like a drunkard who, soaked in too much wine, has trembling limbs, staggering steps and dulled senses. Now he speaks barbarous words, now Latin; now he delights in the heat of fires, now in the chill of frost; now he lies senseless, now he plays feebly. Having no fixed purpose anywhere, his mind keeps wavering this way and that, and he never ceases to bring forth arguments that are empty. So these men, now applying the testimonies of divine Scripture inappropriately, now the ravings of their own assertions, now bad examples of bad deeds, strive everywhere to support their error. For what madness or folly is this, that they cite as an example for worshipping images the fact that images of emperors are worshipped in cities and in squares, and that they try to establish an unlawful thing by an unlawful thing? The teacher of the Gentiles does not urge you to be imitators of emperors, but of himself, or rather of Christ, saying: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. And so that the fasces of emperors or the frenzy of the crowd might not divert the minds of Christians, he says: Christ was crucified for us; what have we to do with the forum? But if they seek examples within the holy Church from public and civic affairs, why do they not also adopt the theatrical and mimic trifles, or even the cruelties that are wretchedly carried out in the theatres and the orchestras at gladiatorial games? Why does the clergy not hunt the people, along with the bishop, like a net-man, after the manner of a pursuer? Why does the whole of the circus, that is, the Gentile or rather wretched examples, not follow those who guard the Church of Christ? But far be it from the Catholic religion that Christian seriousness should imitate the perverse actions which Gentile wantonness formerly performed and now burns with. For our conversation, says the Apostle, is in heaven. Therefore whoever desires to go where Christ our head has gone before must become a follower not of forensic or public actions, but of Christ our head himself, or of his members, namely the Apostles and apostolic men. For perverse examples must be avoided by Catholics, just as the seduction of evil men and the company of the unjust must be avoided, the Lord saying: You shall not listen to a vain report; you shall not join with the unjust to be an unjust witness; you shall not be with the many in wickedness. For the Christian ought to hate, after the example of the Psalmist, those who hate the Lord and waste away over his enemies. Nor did Tobias, a upright man and dear to God, urge his son to follow perverse examples when he said: See, son, that you do not follow the way of the wicked, and let not the multitude of sinners persuade you; for their wages are death. But if you do what is true, there will be regard for God in your works, and with all who do justice you shall inherit eternal life. Therefore, whoever sees that the images of emperors are more frequently worshipped by the peoples, and, fortified by this example, is counted among those who worship images in the churches, is shown to resist no small part of this holy man's precept. Nor will he be able to say with David: I have not sat in the council of vanity, nor will I go in with those who do iniquity; I have hated the assembly of the malignant, and I will not sit with the impious; I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord. But if perhaps a defender of this error says, "To worship the images of emperors is not a sin," let him consider what great glory was brought to the three boys, who refused to do this, when an angel sent from heaven drove back the flame of the devouring fire and bestowed on them a saving dew; and with what great miracle the Babylonian prince testified that he had seen among them one like the Son of God, not to refute their glory, but even his own obstinacy. Let them also hear blessed Jerome in the commentary which he published on the Book of Daniel, saying thus: Behold, says he, our God whom we worship is able to rescue us from the furnace of burning fire, and to deliver us from your hands, O king. Whence he had thought to terrify the boys, there he perceives in them the material of fortitude. Nor do they put off the help, but they promise present aid, saying: Behold, our God whom we worship is able to rescue us both from the fire with which you threaten and from your hands. But if he should be unwilling, then, as to what he had said, is able to rescue us, he did not carry the contrary; he did not say, If he will not be able, but if he will, so that if they should perish, it would be a matter of his will and not of God's inability. Let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, nor do we adore the golden statue which you have erected. Whether we read "statue," as Symmachus does, or "golden image," as the others have translated, the worshippers of God ought not to adore it. Therefore let the judges and princes of the world, who adore the statues and images of emperors, understand that they do what the three boys refused to do, and what has not pleased God. And they say that the property of God is to be worshipped, and that the image is to be adored; whether this is one or the other, it does not agree with the servants of God. Behold, we are taught by the instructions of holy men that the images of emperors ought by no means to be adored. And who is so perverse as to decree not only that they be adored, but to take from the adoration of these images an example of perversity to be applied to other things? And if mortal men, puffed up by the arrogance of vanity, exalted by worldly pomp, eager for the ambition of honours, full of boasting, confined to a place and content with their position, because they could not be everywhere, therefore commanded their images to be worshipped by men, since they could not be worshipped everywhere in their own persons, why is it necessary to worship God in an image, who is uncircumscribed? who is wholly everywhere? who is wonderful everywhere? who is not contained by place, nor limited by position? Whom, as Solomon says, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain; whom the world does not contain, but who contains the world. For since his power is so great, his glory so great, and his might so great, he is not to be sought in images, but in pure and holy hearts. He is not to be adored in a painted panel, but in his holy court, as the Prophet says: Worship the Lord in his holy court. He is not found through a picture in set places, but through works, by pious minds. Elijah did not seek him in a place or in a picture or on tablets, but knew that he was present everywhere, to him who had shown himself present by the diligence of good works, when he said: The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand. Therefore to wish to worship God, who is present in place and almighty, on tablets, as the Gentile kings worshipped their local or mortal kings, is profane and akin to unbelief. For we read that no nation has done this in this age except the Babylonians and the Romans, or those nations which were subdued by them, or were neighbours to them, or took examples from them. Thus, just as these two kingdoms are known to have excelled the other kingdoms of the world in ferocity and in strength, so too they are believed to have been more prone to worship and adore idols. Therefore between these two most powerful kingdoms there was great agreement, great similarity, great cruelty, and also great strength, and indeed a strength which in its time ruled over the other kingdoms of the world. For as the one rose from the East, so surely the other rose from the West: the one when the world was in its youth, the other when the world was already growing old. For, as the histories say, the Roman empire received the whole inheritance of the Babylonian kingdom and the summit of its power. And between these two kingdoms, as between an old father who is now unable to rule and a son in his prime who has not yet received the strength to govern, the two kingdoms are said to have stood in the place of guardian, namely the Persians and the Macedonians. But when the heir, that is the Roman Empire, grew up, that which had held the place of guardian withdrew, and the young son received the inheritance which the aged father had lost. It would be long to pursue the agreements or harmonies of these two kingdoms. For, to pass over other things, in this part there is no small agreement between them, namely that both kingdoms decreed that their kings should be worshipped in statues or images in the fields or squares, and both punished with various torments those who refused to do this. Now this evil, along with the other evils which were brought to nothing by the coming of Christ, ought altogether to be brought to nothing, and not only should examples be taken from it for carrying out other things, but this very thing must be uprooted from the roots by Christians, lest, according to the Apostle, some root of bitterness spring up again and defile many. For since we are instructed by apostolic teachings that we ought to give no occasion to the evil one, why should we give the Gentiles such an occasion, by worshipping the images of mortal kings and taking examples from them? So that they might say to us: "We worship the images of those whom you believe to be gods by true religion, or whom, taught by the traditions of the ancients, we know are not gods. But you, to whom this is an abomination, why do you venerate, under the reverence of kings and even by public adoration, images of men painted in wax or cast in metal, and, as you yourselves preach, give to men the honour due to God alone? But if this is unlawful and contrary to the law, why do you do it, Christians? Or why do your priests not forbid it? Lest you, knowing it, excuse yourselves under the pretext of your office, while we, who are ignorant of it, are charged by you with sacrilege." Some things like these, and similar to these, are said to have been brought in by the philosophers of the Gentiles in the first times of the faith; and our people are reported to have answered in this way: "What you say we neither ought to approve nor can, since by the plain words of God we are not permitted to worship the elements, nor angels, nor any principalities of heaven, earth, or air. For this is the special name of divine office, and it is higher than any earthly veneration or reverence. But just as flattery first drove men into this evil, so now custom scarcely recalls them from error. Yet in this unwary compliance, although no divine worship is detected, because of the similarity of lovable faces the inner joys are more pleasing than either those to whom it is paid perhaps require, or those who pay it ought to enjoy. Nevertheless, Christians who are more reverent and stricter abhor this custom, to whom, when such things are introduced, it does not appear that the kings of that time had wished their images to be worshipped, although the minds of men converted from Gentilism were still rude and not yet solid enough to receive solid food.

units.la: mcn men & districtiores hanc consuetudinem perhorrent Christiani, quibus taliter inlatis non apparent eos tunc regum imagines adorare censuisse, quamquam rudes adhuc & necdum solidae ad percipiendum solidum cibum mentes hominum fuerint de gentilitate conversae. Jam vero, quia dicunt exemplo imperialium imaginum imaginem Dei, vel sanctae Dei genetricis Mariae, vel omnium sanctorum adorari debere, quam sit absurdum quamve inutile in promptu est, etiam sive in hoc capitulo, sive in aliis ex parte monstratum est. Nullus enim praeter Deum omnipotentem omnium sanctorum imagines, vel nomina habere vel retinere potest, dicente Propheta; Nimis honorati sunt amici tui, Deus, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum: dinumerabo eos & super arenam multiplicabuntur. Et Dominus Abrahae dixerit, Si possunt stellae caeli numerari prae multitudine, semen quoq; tuum numerari poterit: semen autem Abrahae omnes credentes esse, omnibus manifestum est. Ipse enim est pater gentium, in cujus semine, id est, in Christo, benedicentur omnes gentes: qui, secundum Apostolum, non ex circumcisione, sed ex credulitate amicus Dei vocatus est: nec ei observatio legis, sed credulitas fidei ad justiciam reputata est.
units.tr: Men and the stricter Christians shrink from this custom, for when such things are brought forward it does not appear that they judged the images of kings to be worshipped, although the minds of men converted from heathenism were still rude and not yet solid enough to take in solid food. Now, as for their claim that by the example of imperial images the image of God, or of the holy Mother of God Mary, or of all the saints ought to be worshipped, how absurd and how useless this is lies ready to hand, as has been shown both in this chapter and in others. For no one but almighty God can have or retain the images or names of all the saints, as the Prophet says: Too honoured are your friends, O God; their principality is exceedingly strengthened. I will number them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand. And the Lord said to Abraham: If the stars of heaven can be numbered for their multitude, your seed also can be numbered. That the seed of Abraham is all believers is plain to everyone. For he is the father of the nations, in whose seed, that is in Christ, all the nations shall be blessed; who, according to the Apostle, was called the friend of God not from circumcision but from faith, and to whom the observance of the law was not reckoned for righteousness, but his faith was.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: Contra eos, qui dicunt quod imaginis honor in primam formam transfit.
units.tr: Against those who say that the honour paid to an image passes to its prototype.

units.la: VSITATISSIMUM & oppido familiarissimum illis, qui in adorandis imaginibus aestuant, hoc est, ut credant & asserant imaginis honorem in eandem formam posse transire cujus imago est. Quod quidem quomodo fieri valeat, & utrum fieri valeat, nulla ratione percipitur, nec divinorum eloquiorum testimonio adprobatur. Numquidnam sancti, qui pro meritis suis caelestia regna conscendere valuerunt, quorum illi inofficioso obsequio imagines adorare percensent, superstitiosos aut supervacuos honores ambierunt? Numquid adorari se permiserunt? quidam enim ex illis abjecti esse cupiebant, ut Domini gratiam merterentur: de quibus erat ille, qui dicebat, Elegi abjectus esse in domo Dei magis quam habitare in tabernaculis peccatorum: quidam vero flagellari potius quam venerari maluerunt: testis est ille, qui dixit, Ego autem non solum alligari, verumetiam mori pro Christo paratus sum.
units.tr: It is most common and very familiar to those who are fervent in adoring images, namely that they believe and assert that the honour of an image can pass over into the very form of which it is the image. How this could happen, and whether it could happen at all, is grasped by no reasoning, and it is not confirmed by the testimony of the divine oracles. Did the saints, who by their merits were able to climb into the heavenly kingdoms, and whom those men think they honour by their dutiful homage in adoring images, ever seek superstitious or superfluous honours? Did they ever allow themselves to be adored? For some of them wished to be cast down, that they might earn the Lord's favour; of these was he who said, I have chosen to be cast down in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners. Others preferred to be scourged rather than venerated; the witness is he who said, I am ready not only to be bound but even to die for Christ.

units.la: Non enim eos honorum appetitores, sed spiritali vigore flagrantes & contra adversa munitos atque igne tribulationis decoctos & mundanis adversitatibus fortiores effectos, doctor gentium fuisse commemorat: cum quosdam ex illis dicit tentatos, ut Achiam: quosdam lapidatos, ut Zachariam & Stephanum: quosdam illorum sectos, ut Esaiam, qui per figuram syllepsis pluraliter ponitur: quosdam in occisione gladii mortuos, sicut plures prophetarum fuisse noscuntur: quosdam circuisse in melotibus, in pellibus caprinis, sicut Heliam & Johannem: quosdam angustatos sive egentes fuisse illisque dignum non fuisse mundum, sicut de pene omnibus sanctis passim credendum est, commemorat, quibus exemplis monstratur non eos honorum, sed virtutum desiderio aestuasse. Nam si ambitione honorum dum mortaliter viverent, uterentur, non hodie in caelestibus tanta gloria fruerentur. Cum ergo sit illis a Domino honor perpetuus adtributus, non sunt transitoriorum honorum indigni. Honor itaque digne sanctorum corporibus, reliquiis sive basilicis exhibitus, & omnipotenti Deo & sanctis ejus manet acceptus: inconpetens vero & indecens, nec Deo, nec sanctis ejus manet acceptus.
units.tr: For the teacher of the Gentiles recalls that they were not seekers of honours, but men burning with spiritual vigour, armed against adversity, tempered in the fire of tribulation, and made stronger than worldly hardships. He mentions that some of them were tested, like Ahiam; some stoned, like Zechariah and Stephen; some of them sawn asunder, like Isaiah, who is put in the plural by the figure of syllepsis; some died by the sword, as many of the prophets are known to have done; some wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, like Elijah and John; and some were straitened or needy, and the world was not worthy of them, as is to be believed of almost all the saints everywhere. By these examples it is shown that they did not burn with a desire for honours, but for virtues. For if they had used ambition for honours while they lived as mortals, they would not now enjoy such great glory in heaven. Since therefore everlasting honour has been bestowed on them by the Lord, they are not unworthy of passing honours. Therefore the honour fittingly paid to the bodies, relics or basilicas of the saints remains acceptable both to almighty God and to his saints; but honour that is unfitting and indecent remains acceptable neither to God nor to his saints.

units.la: Hinc est quod beatus Joseph post prophetiam ossa sua cum adjuratione filiis Israel ad terram repromissionis venturis secum deferendi percensent: nedum Aegypti memores essent illius, sive administrationis qua in magna egestate Aegyptum gubernaverat, ejus ossibus inutilem exhiberent venerationem: & qui erat in Dei creatoris devotione firmatus, & a vana superstitione Aegyptiorum omnino alienus, eo propensius suam ostenderet sanctitatem, quo & vivens humiliter & recte Deo servierit, & post obitum cineribus suis inconpetens obsequium exhiberi recusaverit. Cum ergo sancti viri & Deo per omnia accepti vana obsequia hominum devitaverint, sicut Paulus & Barnabas Lycaonum superstitiosa obsequia devitasse noscuntur, & Petrus Cornelii devotam venerationem praeverit, angelus etiam in apocalypsi Johannem ne se adoraret prohibuerit, quis eos credat imaginum adorarione delectari? aut picturarum obsequiis demulceri? aut qualiter ad eos honor picturis exhibitus quae nec de illorum corpore, seu vestibus, sunt, sed pro captu ingenii cujusque ab artificibus praeparantur, poterit pervenire? Non enim deliniuntur pictorum operibus, qui cum Christo regnant in caelestibus, nec ambiunt ab opificibus in tabulis sive in parietibus pingi, qui a Christo in libro vitae meruerunt adscribi. Dicant igitur quibus hoc tam peculiare est dicere, quod imaginis honor in primam formam transit: dicant ubi hoc legerint aut quibus valeant testimoniis adprobare. Dominus namque & Salvator noster non ait, Quamdiu fecistis imaginibus, sed, Quamdiu fecistis unum de minimis istis, mihi fecistis: nec ait, Qui imagines, sed, Qui vos recipit me recipit: nec Apostolus ait, Diligamus imagines, sed, Diligamus nos invicem, quia charitas ex Deo est: nec imaginum onera, sed nostra alterutrum mutuo vehenda percensuit dicens, Alter alterius onera vestra portate, & sic adimplebitis legem Christi. Nam cum imagines plerumque secundum ingenium artificum fiant, ut modo sint formosae, modo deformes, nonnunquam pulchrae, aliquando etiam foedae, quaedam illis quorum sunt similimae, quaedam vero dissimiles, quaedam novitate fulgentes, quaedam etiam vetustate fatiscentes, quaerendum est quae earum sint honorabiliores. Utrum ea quae preciosiores, an ea quae viliores esse noscuntur: quoniam si preciosiores plus habent honoris, operis in eis causa vel materiarum qualitas habet venerationem, non fervor devotionis: si vero viliores ea quae minus similes sunt illorum quibus aptari parantur, injustum ftum est, cum hæ quæ nec opere, nec materia præcellunt, nec personis similes esse noscuntur, auctius propensiusq; venerantur. Nam dum nos nihil in imaginibus spernamus præter adorationem, quippe qui in basilicis sanctorum imagines non ad adorandum, sed ad memoriam rerum gestarum & venustatem parietum habere permittimus: illi vero pene omnium suæ credulitatis spem in imaginibus conlocent, reliquias ut nos sanctos in eorum corporibus vel potius reliquiis corporum, seu etiam vestimentis veneremur, juxta antiquorum patrum traditionem: illi vero parietes & tabulas adorantes in eo se arbitrentur magnum fidei habere emolumentum, eo quòd operibus sint subjecti pictorum. Nam etsi a doctis quibusq; vitari posset hoc quod illi in adorandis imaginibus exercet, qui videlicet nō qui sint, sed quid innuant venerantur, indoctis tamen quibusque scandalum generant, qui nihil aliud in his præterid quod vident venerantur & adorant. Unde cavendum est ne Evangelicam sententiam subeant, qui tot pusillos ad scandalizandum impellunt, quoniam si is, qui unum de pusillis scandalizaverit, formidolosissimæ sententiæ subjacet, multo magis exitiabili ille ferietur severitate, qui pene omnem Christi ecclesiam aut ad imagines adorandas impellit, aut imaginum adorationem spernentes anathemati submittit. Quod utrumq; cum magna cautela vitare necessarium est, nedum in utramlibet partem plus se quis quam ordo exposcit, impegerit, jacturam suæ salutis evitare non possit.
units.tr: Hence it is that blessed Joseph, after his prophecy, charged the sons of Israel, with an oath, to carry his bones with them when they went to the land of promise. Lest, mindful of Egypt and of the administration by which he had governed Egypt in great want, they should show veneration to his bones, which would be useless; and since he, who was firm in devotion to God the Creator and wholly estranged from the vain superstition of the Egyptians, would show his holiness all the more eagerly, in that he had served God humbly and rightly while living, and after death refused that unfitting homage be paid to his ashes. Therefore, since holy men, and men wholly acceptable to God, have avoided the vain homage of men, just as Paul and Barnabas are known to have avoided the superstitious homage of the Lycaonians, and Peter forestalled the devout veneration of Cornelius, and the angel in the Apocalypse forbade John to adore him, who would believe that they delight in the adoration of images? Or are soothed by the homage of pictures? Or how could the honour paid to pictures, which are not made of their body or clothing, but are prepared by craftsmen according to the capacity of each one's talent, reach them? For those who reign with Christ in heaven are not gratified by the works of painters, nor do they desire to be painted by craftsmen on boards or walls, they who have deserved to be enrolled by Christ in the book of life. Let those, then, to whom it is so peculiar to say that the honour of an image passes to its prototype, say it; let them say where they have read this, or by what testimonies they can prove it. For our Lord and Saviour does not say, As often as you have done it to images, but, As often as you have done it to one of these least, you have done it to me; nor does he say, He who receives images, but, He who receives you receives me; nor does the Apostle say, Let us love images, but, Let us love one another, for love is of God; and he counts not the burdens of images but our own, to be borne mutually one by another, saying, Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ. For since images are for the most part made according to the talent of the artists, so that some are now beautiful, now deformed, sometimes fair, and at other times even foul, some like those whom they resemble, others unlike, some shining with newness, others crumbling with age, the question is which of them are more honourable: whether those that are known to be more precious, or those that are known to be cheaper. For if the more precious have more honour, the veneration rests on the workmanship or the quality of the materials, not on the fervour of devotion; but if the cheaper, which are less like those whom they are prepared to represent, are venerated more readily and more eagerly, that is unjust, since those which excel neither in workmanship nor in material, nor are known to be like the persons, are venerated more abundantly. For while we reject nothing in images except adoration, since in the basilicas of the saints we allow images to be kept not for adoration, but for the memory of deeds done and for the beauty of the walls; they, on the other hand, place almost all the hope of their faith in images. We venerate the saints in their bodies, or rather in the relics of their bodies, or also in their garments, according to the tradition of the ancient Fathers; but they, adoring walls and boards, think they gain a great advantage for their faith in this, that they are subject to the works of painters. For although by learned men what they do in adoring images could be avoided—they venerate not what the images are but what they signify—yet they cause a stumbling-block to the unlearned, who venerate and adore nothing in these things beyond what they see. Hence care must be taken lest they fall under the sentence of the Gospel, who drive so many little ones to offence; for if he who offends one of the little ones is subject to a most dreadful sentence, much more will he be struck by the most deadly severity who either drives almost the whole Church of Christ to adore images, or subjects to anathema those who despise the adoration of images. Both of these things must be avoided with great caution; for unless one is restrained from pressing too far into either side beyond what the order requires, he cannot escape the loss of his salvation.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Quod infauste & præcipitanter sive insipienter Constantinus Constantiæ Cypri Episcopus dixit, Suscipio & amplector honorabiliter sanctas & venerandas imagines secundum servitium adorationis, quod consubstantiali & vivificatrici trinitati emitto, & qui sic non sentiunt neq; glorificant, a sancta Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia segrego, & anathemati submitto, & parti qui abnegaverunt incarnatam & salvabilem dispensationem Christi veri Dei nostri emitto.
units.tr: That Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, spoke ill-advisedly and rashly, or foolishly: "I receive and embrace with honour the holy and venerable images, with the service of adoration which I offer to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity; and those who do not think and glorify thus I separate from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church and submit to anathema, and I offer them to the party that denies the incarnate and saving dispensation of Christ our true God."

units.la: Quiam præcipitanter, & ut ita dixerim, insipienter Constantinus Constantiæ Cypri Episcopus cæteris consentientibus se suscepturum & amplexurum honorabiliter imagines dixerit, & servitium adorationis quod consubstantiali & vivificatrici trinitati debetur, ei si redditurum gaudierit, non est plurimum nostra disputatione discutiendum: quoniam omnibus qui hoc vel legunt vel audiunt liquido patet, illum non modici erroris voraginibus immersum: quippe qui servitium soli debitum creatori exhibere se fatetur creaturis, & dum cupit favere picturis reluctatur cunctis sacris Scripturis. Quis ergo unquam sani capitis talem absurditatem, vel dixerit, vel dicenti consenserit, ut in tanto honore habeatur picturarum varietas, quanto sancta, vivificatrix & omnium creatrix trinitas? & tale impendatur servitium picturæ, quale exhibetur Domino totius creaturæ? aut quis illum talia naufragantem potius quàm loquentem audire pateretur? aut quæ aures tanti facinoris noxam non abdicare potius quàm percipere niterentur? quoniam quidem perversum est, ut omnibus hoc rebus insensatis tale impendatur servitium adorationis, quale Deo omnipotenti cui non est simulis, cui per Salomonem dicitur, Domine non est tibi similis in cælo sursum nec in terra deorsum. Cum ergo fronte, ut de cæteris taceam, hoc unum comma divinæ legis, audit, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis & illi soli servies, qui hoc spreto non solum creaturis servit, sed earum servitium servitio Deo deberet æquiperare contendit? Stet namq; Episcopus in Ecclesia & legat, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis & illi soli servies, & mox ut in conventu tederit dicat, Suscipio & amplector honorabiliter sanctas & venerandas imagines, & illis servitium adorationis quod consubstantiali & vivificatrici trinitati debetur impendo, ideoque se in divinis verbis instabilem, se aliud ore profitentem, aliud corde credentem, aliud divinis paginis legentem, aliud in antro pectoris sui tenentem, & divinis verbis obnitentem, & suas nugas dominicis præceptis præferentem demonstret. Nam cum tibi suisque dinoscatur in sua perversa professione obesse, nobis e contrario, qui illorum nugis reniti cupimus, dinoscitur prodesse: cum videlicet errorem detegit infaustum, quem illi videntur plebibus ingerere palliatum. Ajunt enim, Non adoramus imagines ut Deum, nec illis divini servitii cultum impendimus, sed dum illas aspicimus & adoramus, illå mentis nostræ acumen designimus, ubi eos quorum ille sunt, esse non ignoramus: at contra ille illorum detegens errorem & suam pandens absque ulla obumbratione cogitationem, fatetur se quale sanctæ Trinitati, tale illis exhibere servitium, talemque adorationem: ideoque absurditatem quam illi introrsus retinent latenter, hanc ille egerit patenter. Nec latere quemquam potest illorum ignavia, cum hanc pandat hujusce professionis furentia. Quia ergo omnes, qui suo errore dissentiunt a sancta Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia segregare & anathemati submittere, & illis qui Domini Jesu Christi incarnationem salutiferam credere recusaverunt, admittere nititur, quantæ hic fatuitatis cuncti legentibus liquet agnoscere: quippe qui suæ ignaviæ demersus barathro, dum cæteros ad se ieiunium talia pallidos protrahur, si quos tanti periculi voraginem vitare conspicit, eos convitiis, & communicatis affatibus objurgare contendit. Nam quæ infamia, vel quæ amentia est, ideo Christi plebem ab Ecclesiæ matris ubertibus conari convellere, eo quod servitium soli Deo debitum rebus sensu carentibus obnitur exhibere? aut quæ perversitas est æquales judicare illos, qui mediatoris Dei & hominum Christi Jesu vivificatricem incarnationem obstinata mente credere recusant, illis qui spreto secundum divinæ legis imperium creaturas omnium servitio soli Deo cum omnia famulantur, servire desiderant. aliud est enim mundi redemptionem non credere, aliud soli Deo velle servire: aliud est salutem mundi spernere, aliud imaginum adorationem contemnere: aliud est salutiferis monitis refragari, aliud vanis & superstitiosis observationibus reniti. Idem namque Dominus & Salvator cum & per paginam veteris Testamenti imagines adorare inhibuerit, & per corporalem præsentiam imaginem Cæsaris Cæsari potius reddendam quam adorandam censuerit, talia in se credendi præcepta contulit dicens, Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam. & iterum, Ego sum ostium & vita, si quis per me introierit salvabitur, & ingredietur & regredietur & pascua inveniet. & iterum, Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu sancto, non intrabit in regnum cælorum. Veritas hoc dicit, salus mundi hoc testatur, redemptor generis humani hoc profatur: & quis tam hebes tamque segnis parem illum judicet, qui his tam authenticis monitis contradicit, illi qui contemptus divinis eloquiis res sine sensu adorare contemnit? Esto, imagines adorare virtus & bonum opus est: nunquidnam fidei æquari potest? cum tamen cunctis bonis operibus insistendum sit. Nullum opus bonum ad perfectam salutem quemquam adducere valet, nisi fidei fundamento superponatur & ejus munimine fulciatur. Abraham denique non ex operibus, sed ex fide justificatus est: Moyses fide grandis factus est: Sancti per fidem vicerunt regna, & sancti omnes juxta fidem defuncti sunt. & Propheta dicit, Omnia opera ejus in fide. & Dominus in Evangelio, Fides tua te, inquit, salvum fecit. tem, idem, Amen dico vobis, si habueritis fidem & non hæsitaveritis, non solum de ficulnea facietis, sed & si huic monti dixeritis, Tolle & jacta te in mare, fiet: & omnia quæcunque petieritis in oratione credentes accipietis. Unde datur intelligi cæteris virtutibus fidem præeminere: & quamquam ei spes & charitas connectantur, tamen per fidem ad eas pervenitur: nec pari damnatione judicandus est, qui in cæteris operibus quam qui in fide delinquit: quoniam quidem cum nullus absque fide imagines adorando salvari possit, innumerabiles in cælesti patria sunt legiones, quæ sive per martyria, sive per innocentiam, sive per solitudinum conversationes, cum imagines penitus nec habuerint, nec adoraverint, per fidei tamen observantiam cælicolis cœtibus societati perpetuis gaudiis perfruuntur. CAP. XVIII. Quod Eutimius Sardensis Episcopus à præfati Constantini errore, non multum dissentit in eo quod ait, Ex toto corde suscipio venerandas imagines cum condecenti honore & amplectibili adoratione. Illos enim qui aliter aut contrarie sentiunt, aut dogmatizant contra sanctas imagines alienos Catholicæ Ecclesiæ deputans & prædico & hæreticos adnuntio. CUm Eutimius Sardensis Episcopus Constantino Constantiæ Cypri Episcopo pene par confessione, non est ambiguum parem eos habere fidem paremque adepturos retributionem, nisi emendatio in utro illorum præcesserit. Ex toto enim corde uterque se confitetur suscipere imagines cum summo honore, & amplectibili adoratione. O demens Episcoporum confessio! o nap præsulum prædicatio. Ecclesia Catholica voce præsulum incarnationis Christi mysterium cepisse congratulans Domino dicit, Suscepimus Deus misericordiam tuam in medio templi tui: & isti dicunt, Suscipimus & adoramus imagines. Caterva credentium Christum, qui est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum, Apostolos sive Apostolicos viros suscipere precatur dicens, Suscipiant montes pacem populi tui. isti dicunt, Suscipimus imagines adorationi amplectibili. Cum ergo isti pene omnem auxilium sui spem imaginibus defigant, non mediocriter à sancta & universali dissentiunt ecclesia, quæ spem auxilii non in pictura fucis, non in manufactis artificum operibus, sed in Deo omnium creatore defigit, quæ habet adjutores Apostolos & Apostolicos viros, qui pro ea cotidie Dominum interpellant, & susceptum dono sancti Spiritus de supernis sedibus imbrem sanctæ prædicationis, utpote altiora in Ecclesia loca fidelibus plebibus sive rectoribus diffundunt, secundum Joel vaticinium dicentis, Erunt in illa die, distillabunt montes dulcedinem, & colles fluent lac: quod etiam his verbis Ezechiel intonat dicens, Vestri autem montes Israel facient uvam, & fructum vestrum quem vos manducabitis populus meus. Quæ uva, & qui fructus, quamquam Christus Dominus intellegatur, qui de montibus Israel processit, à Patriarchis videlicet hominem adsumens, poteritque etiam dulcedo prædicationis veteri & novo Testamento conpaginata intellegi, quæ diffunditur per humilium fidelium mentes, & incredulorum cordas credendum & ad fructum afferendum mollificat, & rectorum sensus æternæ spei retributione latificat, eosque justitia indui & cum subjectis plebibus Deo hymnum canere exhortatur, inplerunque illud Propheticum, Campi tui replebuntur ubertate, pinguescent fines deserti & exultatione colles accingentur, indunt sunt arietes ovium & convallies abundabunt frumento: etenim clamabunt, & hymnum dicent. Levat enim oculos suos ad eos, cum dicit, Levavi oculos meos ad montes, unde veniet auxilium mihi. Non enim ait, Levavi oculos meos ad res insensatas, ut ab his adjutorium adipisceretur, sed, Levavi oculos meos ad montes ad eos videlicet montes super quos Ecclesia Christi fundata est, dicente Propheta, Fundamenta ejus in montibus sanctis: qui etiam videntes liberari populum Dei à servitute Ægyptia, & ad terram repromissionis conscendere, id est, mundi hujus ærumnosam servitutem, fideles quosque spernere, ad æternam patriam convolare exultant, dicente eodem sanctissimo Prophetarum, Montes exultaverunt ut arietes, & colles sicut agni ovium. Quisquis ergo ad hos montes spreta cum cæteris vanitatibus creaturarum adoratione, soli Deo servitium exhibens, mentis oculos somno infidelitatis depulso, levat, cumaeriæ potestates sive earum sequaces superbi quique ad eximiabiles Erebi densitates detenderint, non timebit, & cum cæteris hujusmodi hominibus cum summa jubilatione cantabit; Propterea non timebimus dum conturbabitur terra, & transferentur montes in cor maris. Sonuerunt & turbatae sunt aquae ejus, conturbati sunt montes in fortitudine ejus. Quia igitur antiquus hostis, cujus satellites in factis literis plerumque montium nomine designantur, illorum indubitanter montium, malignorum videlicet, de quibus per Naum prophetam dicitur, Montes commoti sunt ab illo, & colles tremuerunt: & de quibus Apostolus dicit, Si habuerit omnem fidem ita ut montes transferam, omnium malorum suasor, & è contrario omnium bonorum diffusor, idcirco hominibus perluasit creaturas colere, ut eos à creatore averteret, illius per suasiones pessimis actum est, ut creaturarum adoratio inoleseceret, quæ sub praetextu quodammodo religionis & reverentiæ sanctorum, magnum in his locum tenet, qui imagines te ce tota corde de suscipere & adorare fatentur. Nam dum amborum error pene par, ut praefati sumus, sit in eo namque quodam modo dispar esse dinoscitur, quod Constantinus eos, qui servitium soli Deo debitum creaturis impendere recusant, infidelies & incredulos, judicat; Eutimius vero non eos ut incredulos, sed ut haereticos damnat, qui tamen sunt, ut ait Sedulius de quibusdam,
units.tr: Whether Constantine, Bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, rashly and, so to speak, foolishly said that, with the others agreeing, he would receive and honourably embrace images, and that he rejoiced to render to them the worship of adoration which is due to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity, need not be debated at length by us. It is plain to everyone who reads or hears this that he is plunged into the whirlpools of no small error. For he confesses that he offers to creatures the worship owed to the Creator alone, and while he desires to favour pictures, he fights against all the holy Scriptures. Who, then, of sound mind has ever said such an absurdity, or agreed with one who said it, that the variety of pictures should be held in as great honour as the holy, life-giving and all-creating Trinity, and that such service should be paid to a picture as is shown to the Lord of all creation? Or who would allow such a shipwrecked man to speak rather than be silenced? Or what ears would strive to turn away from the harm of so great a crime rather than to hear it? For it is surely perverse that such worship of adoration should be given to all these insensate things as is due to almighty God, of whom there is none like, of whom it is said through Solomon, Lord, there is none like thee in heaven above, nor on earth beneath. Since he hears with his own forehead, not to mention the rest, this one clause of the divine law, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and serve him only, who, despising this, not only serves creatures but strives to make their service equal to the service of God? Let the Bishop stand in the Church and read, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and serve him only, and presently, when he is in the assembly, let him say, I receive and honourably embrace holy and venerable images, and to them I offer the worship of adoration which is due to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity, and so he shows himself unstable in the divine words, professing one thing with his mouth, believing another in his heart, reading one thing in the divine pages, holding another in the cave of his breast, resisting the divine words, and preferring his own trifles to the Lord's commands. For while he is seen to harm himself and his own by his perverse profession, on the contrary he is seen to benefit us, who desire to resist their trifles, since he uncovers the unhappy error which they seem to force upon the people under a cloak. For they say, We do not adore images as God, nor do we offer them the worship of divine service, but when we look at them and adore them, we direct the keenness of our mind through them to those whose images they are, knowing well who these are. But he, on the contrary, uncovering their error and laying open his thought without any shadow, confesses that he offers to them the same service and adoration as to the holy Trinity. Therefore the absurdity which they keep hidden within, he has openly brought forth. Nor can the folly of these men remain hidden from anyone, since he lays bare the madness of this profession. Therefore, since he strives to separate from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church all who dissent from it in their error, and to hand them over to anathema, and to admit to himself those who have refused to believe in the saving incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ, everyone who reads can see how great a folly this is. He, sunk in the pit of his own sloth, while he drags others pale with fasting to himself in such a way, if he sees any whom he observes to avoid the whirlpool of so great a danger, he strives to rebuke them with reproaches and with common conversation. For what infamy or madness is it to try to tear the people of Christ from the breasts of the mother Church, on the ground that the worship owed to God alone is offered to things devoid of sense? Or what perversity is it to judge equal those who obstinately refuse to believe in the life-giving incarnation of Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and men, with those who, despising the command of the divine law, desire to serve creatures, the service of all things, while all things are subject to the one God alone?
