For it is one thing not to believe in the redemption of the world, another to wish to serve God alone; one thing to spurn the salvation of the world, another to despise the adoration of images; one thing to resist saving warnings, another to resist vain and superstitious observances. For the same Lord and Saviour, when he forbade through the page of the Old Testament the adoration of images, and when by his bodily presence he judged that the image of Caesar was to be rendered to Caesar rather than adored, has laid upon himself such precepts of belief, saying, He who believes in me has eternal life. And again, I am the door and the life; if anyone enters through me he will be saved, and he will go in and go out and find pasture. And again, Unless a man is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven. The truth says this, the salvation of the world bears witness to this, the Redeemer of the human race proclaims this. And who is so dull and so slothful as to judge equal to him who contradicts these so authentic warnings, him who, despising the divine oracles, scorns to adore insensate things? Grant that to adore images is a virtue and a good work: can it nevertheless be equated with faith? Yet all good works must be pursued. No good work can bring anyone to perfect salvation unless it is placed upon the foundation of faith and supported by its strength. Abraham, indeed, was justified not by works but by faith; Moses became great by faith; by faith the saints conquered kingdoms, and all the saints died according to faith. And the Prophet says, All his works are in faith. And the Lord in the Gospel, Thy faith, he says, has made thee whole. Again the same: Amen I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but if you say to this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea, it will be done; and whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive. From which it is to be understood that faith surpasses the other virtues; and although hope and love are joined to it, yet it is through faith that we attain to them. Nor is he to be judged with the same condemnation who offends in other works as he who offends in faith; for since no one can be saved by adoring images without faith, there are innumerable legions in the heavenly fatherland who, whether through martyrdom, or through innocence, or through the lives of solitude, never had images at all nor adored them, yet through their observance of faith they enjoy eternal joys in the company of the heavenly assemblies.

units.la: Ambo errore pares quamquam diversa sequentes,
units.tr: Both equal in error, though following different paths,

units.la: Qui videlicet ob unius erroris infamiam sanctam Catholicam partim incredulam, partim haereticam meminerunt Ecclesiam. Nam si nos omnes generaliter Christiani, qui spretis creaturarum cultutis servitium soli Deo debitum illi soli impendere cupimus, cui merito soli debetur, ideo haereticî, quia magis ... non servimus, ab istis judicamur, illi proculdubio, sive ante adventum redemptoris, sive post adventum, qui creaturis inservicebant, omnino Catholici judicabuntur: & si illi increduli, & revera ... quia pro creatore creaturas colebant, modis omnibus judicantur, nos qui uni & soli Dei spretis vanitatibus servimus, & ejus sanctis consequens, & congruum obsequium impertimus, Catholici & fideles habebimur & judicabimur.
units.tr: Who indeed, on account of the infamy of one error, speak of the holy Catholic Church as partly unbelieving and partly heretical. For if we Christians in general, who, having rejected the worship of creatures, desire to render the service owed to God alone to him alone, to whom it is rightly owed, are judged heretics by them because ... we do not serve [him], then those who served creatures, whether before the coming of the Redeemer or after his coming, will without doubt be judged wholly Catholic. And if those are unbelievers, and in truth ... because they worshipped creatures in place of the Creator, they are judged in every way [unbelievers]; but we, who serve the one and only God, having spurned vanities, and render to his saints the fitting and proper obedience, will be held and judged Catholic and faithful.

units.la: CAP. XIX. Inutile & dementia prolatum & risu dignum dictum Agapii Cæsareæ Cappadociæ Episcopi reprehenditur in eo quod dixit, Scriptum est in nostris divi- nis Scripturis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX. The saying of Agapius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is rebuked as useless, mad and worthy of laughter, in that he said, "It is written in our divine Scriptures."

units.la: Eplerumque inperitia fons est, & insons: sed inperitia fons crebro ut officiat laborat, inperitia vero insons officere nulli affectat, sed dum utrumque genus non sit peccato subjectum, utrumque tamen est reprehensioni obnoxium: quoniam inperitia fons & peccato subjacet, ut putae quae probrosa officiendi impellitur voluntate, & reprehensioni, sive quia peccatum non caret reprehensione, sive quia quod vel profatur vel operatur, & insipienter id facit & incrudite: inperitia vero insons etsi in eo peccato caret, eo quod neminem laedit, reprehensione tamen non caret, quia imperitum inerudituem est, & omne ineruditum reprehensioni succumbit: ac per hoc ridiculum dictum Agapii Cæsareae Cappadociae Episcopi, quod dixit, Scriptum est in nostris divinis Scripturis aut eidem reprehensioni quae peccato obnoxia est, aut eidem quae inperitiae subjacet, cedere probatur: quoniam aut eo peccato obnoxia est, quod quo pacto principes eorum dum sint leviores, caeteris mortalitate non dissimiles, Deum sibi conregnare dicunt, & se divos suaque gesta vel dicta nuncupant, eo nimirum pacto suas Scripturas divinas nuncupant: aut in eo reprehensioni succumbit, quod eloquentiae insciius, loquendi venustatis ignarus dum dicere debuerat, in nostris conscribentibus Scripturas continentibus, aut aliquid hujusmodi, id est contrario inconposite & vitiose fertur, in nostris divinis Scripturis: quod quidem, sicut praefati sumus, arrogantiae falsu, quo & Deum contegnare, & se divos nuncupare praesumunt, protulisse creduntur, insania est: si vero aliud dicere cupientes, aliud dixerunt, nec tanta in eis acuminis vis est, ut quae corde concipiunt, vix ac proprius verbis significare queant, ignavia est: ac per hoc in utramvis partem per devia aut superbia ferantur relati, aut ignorantiae caliginosis retinaculis creduntur addicti. Quis ergo unquam sani capitis tale quid dixerit? quis sanae mentis tale quid protulerit? quae vecordia, quaeve sit amentia hominem mortalem, passionibus subjacentem dicere? Scriptum est in nostris divinis Scripturis. Si ergo nostrum quomodo divinis: & si divinis, quomodo nostris? ab homine ergo derivatur humanus, a Deo detinet divinus. Nostrae etenim Scripturae humanae sunt, Dei Scripturae divinae sunt: de codicibus tamen legis dicere nos ratio permittit, nostri codices, de Scripturis vero divinis non aliter nisi divinas Scripturas recte & convenienter secundum rationem dicere valemus. Esto, hoc dictum rationabiliter poterat cum tamen non posset, quo nec de jactantiae fonte scaturisse nosceretur, nec de imperitia hominis sed ei credi retur: in eo denique reprehendi modis omnibus poterat, quod cum ... inutile in rem inutilem, ad imaginum videlicet adorationem adstruendam, prolatum ... Nec tamen agari ei potest quodam modo simplicitas, quae plerumque rectis quibusque inlaudere videtur: sed non pura, non recta, sed pervertit a voluntate prolatum esse constat. Si enim sanctitate sancta quae ibi solum interdum proficit, simpliciter & innocue, & non ad aliquid inlicitum tum adferendum processisse dinosceretur, à Deo, qui scrutator cordis & renum est, qui plerumque voluntates potius quàm actus considerat, ei proculdubio ignosceretur. Sicut enim mala voluntas non aliquid mali opere perpetret, tamen pro actu plerumque tenetur: ita nimirum bona voluntas pro bono opere semper accipitur. Quod ut exemplis inlustremus, & Balaam mala voluntas quae pulum Dei maledicere cupiebat, quamquam ad id quod desideraverat non pervenerit, a culpa fuit indemnis, & David bona voluntas quae templum Domino aedificare cupiebat, quamquam opere non fuerit expleta, divinis tamen est conlaudata oraculis.
units.tr: Ignorance is often a source, and an innocent one; but ignorance often labours to do harm, while innocent ignorance does not aim to harm anyone. Yet although neither kind is subject to sin, both are liable to reproof. For ignorance that is a source of harm is subject to sin, since it is driven by a shameful will to harm, and to reproof, either because sin is never free from reproof, or because whatever it says or does, it does foolishly and crudely. Innocent ignorance, although it is free of that sin because it harms no one, is nonetheless not free of reproof, since it is unlearned and every unlearned thing is open to reproof. Hence the ridiculous saying of Agapius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, that he said, "It is written in our divine Scriptures," is shown to fall under either the reproof that attaches to sin or the reproof that attaches to ignorance. For either it is guilty of that sin, since, in the way their princes, while they are but lesser men, no different in mortality from others, say that God reigns together with them, and call themselves gods and their deeds or words divine, in just that way they call their own divine Scriptures by that name; or else it falls under reproof because, ignorant of eloquence and unacquainted with the grace of speech, when it ought to have said something like "in our Scriptures that contain the writings," it says instead, in a disordered and faulty way, "in our divine Scriptures." This, as we have said above, is believed to have been put forward from a false arrogance, by which they presume both to despise God and to call themselves gods, and it is madness; but if, wishing to say one thing, they said another, and there is not such sharpness in them that they can express in words what they conceive in the heart, this is sloth. Thus, whichever way they are carried, whether away from the path through pride or bound by the dim fetters of ignorance, they are shown to be enslaved. Who of sound mind would ever say such a thing? Who of sane judgement would ever utter such a thing? What madness, what folly, is it for a mortal man, subject to passions, to say, "It is written in our divine Scriptures"? If, then, it is ours, how is it divine; and if divine, how is it ours? The human is derived from man, the divine belongs to God. Our Scriptures are human, God's Scriptures are divine. We may, however, reason that we speak of the codices of the law as our codices, but of the divine Scriptures we can speak rightly and fittingly only as divine Scriptures. Grant that this saying could be defended on reasonable grounds; yet it could not be, since it is not known to have sprung from a fount of boasting, nor from the ignorance of a man, but is believed to be so. Finally, it could be reproved in every way on the ground that it was put forward, uselessly, for a useless purpose, namely to establish the adoration of images. Nor can a certain simplicity be pleaded on his behalf, which often seems to be praised in all upright persons; but it is plain that what he said was not pure or upright, but was put forth from a perverted will. For if it were known to have been said simply and innocently, with a holy simplicity that sometimes profits there alone, and not to introduce anything unlawful, God, who is the searcher of heart and reins, who considers wills rather than deeds, would undoubtedly pardon him. For just as an evil will, though it does not carry out any evil deed, is nonetheless often held answerable for the deed, so likewise a good will is always accepted in place of a good deed. To illustrate this by examples: the evil will of Balaam, who wished to curse the people of God, though he did not attain what he desired, was free from blame; and the good will of David, who wished to build a temple for the Lord, though it was not carried out in deed, was nonetheless commended by the divine oracles.

units.la: CAP. XX. De eo quod Johannes presbyter Theodosio Abbati monasterii sancti Andreae resistante verbal- is Chrysostomi, & dicente, Vidi angelum in imagine persequentem barbarorum mul- titudinem, dixit, Quis est iste angelus, nisi de quo scriptum est? Quoniam angelus Domini percussit centum octoginta quinque milia Assyrio- rum in una nocte in circuitu Hierusalem exercitantium.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. Concerning John the presbyter, who, when Theodosius, abbot of the monastery of St Andrew, resisted the words of Chrysostom and said, "I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians," replied, "Who is that angel, unless it is he of whom it is written: 'For the angel of the Lord slew a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians in one night, when they were encamped round about Jerusalem'?"

units.la: DIXIT Johannem Chrysostomum Theodosius Abbas monasterii sanctae Andreae in scepe morata vanissima synodo, quae pro adorandis imaginibus gesta est, referet, Vidi angelum in imagine persequentem multitudinem barbarorum. Nam dum hi, qui in eadem synodo fuisse memorantur, Patriarcharum, Prophetarum caeterorumque sanctorum & illustrium virorum verba ob ginum adorationem stabiliendam perturbare nitantur, eos denique Patriarchas quosdam egisse non egerint mentiantur, non est mirandum si etiam Johannem Chrysostomum talia dixisse commentur. Numquid enim praefatus vir tam eloquens tamque eruditus diceret, Vidi angelum in imagine persequentem barbarorum multitudinem, cum sciret angelorum immortalem naturam nequaquam hominibus videatur picturarum esse indiguam.
units.tr: Theodosius, abbot of the monastery of St Andrew, said that John Chrysostom, in the frequently mentioned and most vain synod which was held in favour of the adoration of images, reported, "I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians." For since those who are recorded to have been present at that same synod strive to distort the words of the patriarchs, the prophets and the other saints and illustrious men in order to establish the adoration of images, and falsely claim that certain patriarchs did things they did not do, it is no wonder if they also invent that John Chrysostom said such things. For would that eloquent and learned man have said, "I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians," when he knew that the immortal nature of angels does not seem to need pictures of any kind to be seen by men?

units.la: Prov.29. Quis est iste angelus. 4.Reg.18. 2.Paral.32. pallè dinoscitur, tamquam inibi scriptum sit, In circuitu Hierusalem exercitantium, in nullo sanctæ legis authenticorum codicum invenitur. Quod ut lucidius cöprobetur, ipsa sanctæ legis verba, prout in codicibus habentur, per ordinem ponenda sunt. Ita enim in libro Regum legitur; Factum est igitur in nocte illa, venit angelus Domini, & percussit in castris Assyriorum centum octoginta quinque millia: cumque diluculo surrexissent viderunt omnia corpora mortuorum, & recedens abiit, & reversus est Sennacherib rex Assyriorum, & mansit in Ninive. Liber quoque sanctissimi ac disertissimi vatis Esaiæ hoc modo hanc textum historiam; Egressus est autem angelus Domini, & percussit in castris Assyriorum centum octoginta quinque millia, & surrexerunt mane, & ecce omnia cadavera mortuorum, & egressus est, & abiit, & reversus est Sennacherib, &c cætera. Liber quoq; verborum dierum, qui cum sit, ut prædicti sumus, totius divinæ legis chronicon, historias tamen regum e latere libri Regum, quæ in eo prætermissæ sunt, enucleatim edisserit, hoc modo hanc narrat historiam; Et misit Dominus angelum, qui percussit omnem virum robustum & bellatorem & principem exercitus regis Assyriorum, reversusque est cum ignominia in terram suam. In quibus exemplis, hoc quod à Johanne usurpatum est, minime invenitur.
units.tr: Prov. 29. "Who is that angel?" 4 Kings 18; 2 Chron. 32. It is clearly recognised, as if it were written there, "encamped round about Jerusalem," and it is found in no authentic codex of the holy law. To prove this more clearly, the very words of the holy law, as they are found in the codices, must be set out in order. Thus it is read in the book of Kings: "And it came to pass that night that the angel of the Lord went out and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and eighty-five thousand; and when they arose early in the morning, behold, all were dead corpses; and he departed and went away, and Sennacherib king of Assyria returned and dwelt at Nineveh." The book also of the most holy and eloquent prophet Isaiah narrates this history in this way: "Then the angel of the Lord went out and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and eighty-five thousand; and they rose early in the morning, and behold, all were dead corpses; and he went out and departed, and Sennacherib returned," and so on. The book of the Words of the Days, which, as we have said, is a chronicle of the whole divine law, but which supplies in detail the histories of the kings omitted from the book of Kings, narrates this history thus: "And the Lord sent an angel, who slew every mighty man and warrior and leader of the army of the king of Assyria, and he returned in shame to his own land." In these examples, what John is said to have used is by no means found.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Quod nulla auctoritate vigeat, neque in ullo authenticorum librorum reperiatur quod illi dicunt, per imaginem cujusdam Polemonis quendam ab adulterii perpetratione coercitum fuisse: quod quidem æquare nituntur miraculo quod fimbria dominicæ vestis actum est, quam mulier contingens exoptatam recepit sanitatem.
units.tr: That no authority supports it, and that nothing in any of the authentic books is found to match what they say: that a certain Polemon was restrained from committing adultery by an image; which they strive to equate with the miracle of the hem of the Lord's garment, by touching which a woman received the health she desired.

units.la: Inter cætera quæ ob suum errorem adstruendum deliramenta in ejusdem vanissimæ synodi lectione conglomerasse deteguntur, hoc illis est familiarissimum, quòd per imaginem cujusdam Polemonis quendam adseverant ab adulterii perpetratione coercitum, quòd quidem gestum, si tamen gestum esse credatur, quamquam in nullo vel veteris vel novi Testamenti authenticorum codicum repertum, nec ab ullo eorum doctorum, qui à sancta Romana Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia recipiuntur, sit prolatum, tamen id & ad suum errorem fulciendum, quasi quoddam probatissimum miraculum, proferunt: & miraculo quod dominicæ vestis fimbria gestum est, æquiparare non metuunt. Quod quidem si, ut illi adseverant, gestum est, salutaribus dominicis gestis, nec debet, nec potest coæquari: quoniam quanta est distantia inter nescio quem Polemonem, & Dei & hominum mediatorem, tanta nimirum distantia est inter gesta præfati Polemonis ejusque imaginis & sanctissima miracula Domini Salvatoris: nec possunt similes actus habere, qui nimium nimiumque sunt dissimiles in virtute. Quis in nubibus, inquit Propheta, æquabitur Domino? aut quis similis erit Deo inter filios ... de eo etiam dicitur in Canticis canticorum. Caput ejus aurum optimum: quoniam sicut auro nullo potest metalli coæquari natura, ita creatori omnium, qui caput utique Christi est, nulla potest coæquari creatura: de quo etiam in eisdem Canticis canticorum ab sponsa dicitur; Sicut malum inter ligna sylvarum, sic dilectus meus inter filios: quoniam sicut malum cum sit pulchrum aspectu, odorcque suavissimum præeminet lignis sylvarum, ita nimirum redemptor noster, qui est odor vitæ in vitam, quem quondam Ecclesia in odore sequitur unguentorum, cunctis præeminet cœtibus sanctorum: qui idcirco filiorum nomine censentur, quia no mundo cui nati sunt, sed Christo cui renati sunt, adhærere noscuntur. In Apocalypsi quoque viginti quatuor seniores coronas suas ante agnum projecisse legunt, quia videlicet omnes sanctorum virtutes cunctæque illorum victoriæ, quibus ipso opitulante claruerunt, ejus virtutibus & victoriæ comparatæ minores esse cernuntur: quoniam & rivulus a perenni fonte derivatus minor esse perhibetur eidem fonti comparatus, & vilis pampinus vitis vivacibus tabulibus vel etiam fructiferis palmitibus vilior omnino creditur comparatus. Esto, factum est, & credibile est virtus Polemonicæ imaginis ab adulterii scelere quendam conpescerent, num ideo omnes imagines adorandæ sunt? numquid quia pecualis animantis lingua rudis humanas loquelas profundenda ratio ... dam perversam intentionem, qua benedictum populum maledicere nitebatur, conpescuit, angelicosque terrificos ictus irrationale animal rationali homini vitare concessit, ideo animalia sunt pecualia adoranda? aut quia atrocium ferarum vulnifica ferocitate puerilis turba virum Dei vanis insultationibus lacescens est prostrata, ideo est ursorum rabies adoranda? plerumque etenim casualiter eventu res quoquammodo accidentes noxiarum rerum perpetrationem quibusque perpetrare cupientibus inhibent, sed non ideo eadem res per quas hæc fiunt, adorare ratio permittit. Sicut ergo hoc quod de Polemone & imagine ejus dicunt, cujus adminiculo suum errorem fulcire cupiunt, in veritate gestum est, ideo imagines adorandæ non sunt, quia secundum exempla quæ breviter prænimius, non omnes res quibus quædam utilia mortalibus inferuntur adorandæ sunt: si vero in veritate gestum non est, ut & nos arbitramur, nec illi plene rationabili auctoritate proferunt, qui nullis hoc in veritate gestum authenticis adprobant indiciis, nec ideo vanissima sensu carentium rerum est adoratio stabilienda, quia mendacus nec mendaciorum exemplis res quæ rationabiliter & veritate fieri debet, nusquam legitur esse statuta: quoniam sicut veritas numquam mendacio subjungitur, ita nimirum mendacia veritati semper refragari creduntur: quæ duo ita sibi diversis vicissitudine constant, ut sibi mutuo semper credantur reni. Sicut ergo ignis fomitem non potest aquarum fluentis nutrire, vel e contrario aquatum flucuta nemo potest ignem fomentare ibus augere, ita etiam nemo potest veritatem, ut illi facere adpetunt, mendaciis comprobare. Decaelo igitur breviter & ex parte probatis quod gestum imaginis Polemonis, si tamen, ut illi fasi suos istum est, gesto dominicæ fimbriæ coæquari nec debet nec valet, sive, quod prorsus ambigitur, utrum gestum sit, quod illi gestum fuisse dicunt, an non, sive quod etiam si gestum fuerit, non nisi cuiusdam adoratio adstrui valebit, necnon & id quod mendacius adprobari seu constituit veritas utique nunc operæprecium est, ut quid fimbria dominicæ vestis, quam illi imagini Polemonis coæquari contendunt, typicis innuerit archanisque mysteriis, breviter exequamur. Fimbria namque dominicæ vestis hdes est incarnationis, cujus adtactu gentilitas ægritudinem amisit idolatriæ fœdæ. Sicut enim fimbria ad comparationem corporis sive totius indumenti pars minima est, ita et incarnatio redemptoris divinæ & ineffabili generationi qua a patre ante sæcula genitus est, cuius minima esse videtur: de qua generatione per Esaiam dicitur, Generationem ejus quis enarrabit? subauditur, nullus. humanam autem ejus generationem ita Evangelista enarrat, Liber generationis Christi filii David. Mulier ergo post tergum fimbriam dominicæ vestis adtingens exoptatam
units.tr: Among the other nonsense which they are found to have piled together in the reading of that most vain synod to support their error, this is most familiar to them: they assert that a certain Polemon was restrained from committing adultery by an image of him. Even if this was done (if indeed it is to be believed that it was done), it is found in none of the authentic codices of the Old or New Testament, and it has not been brought forward by any of the teachers received by the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church. Yet they put it forward to prop up their error, as if it were some most approved miracle, and they do not fear to set it on a par with the miracle wrought by the hem of the Lord's garment. If indeed it was done, as they assert, it neither ought nor can be equated with the saving deeds of the Lord. For as great as is the distance between I know not what Polemon and the Mediator between God and men, so great without doubt is the distance between the deeds of the said Polemon and his image and the most holy miracles of the Lord and Saviour. Nor can acts have likeness when they are so very unlike in power. Who in the clouds, says the Prophet, will be likened to the Lord? Or who will be like God among the sons... Of him also it is said in the Song of Songs: His head is most fine gold: for just as no nature of metal can be compared with gold, so no creature can be compared with the Creator of all, who is indeed the head of Christ. Of him also the bride says in the same Song of Songs: As an apple among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons: for just as the apple, beautiful to look at and most sweet in smell, excels the trees of the wood, so assuredly our Redeemer, who is the fragrance of life unto life, whom the Church once followed in the odour of ointments, excels all the companies of the saints. These are reckoned by the name of sons for this reason: they are known to cleave not to the world into which they were born, but to Christ by whom they were born again. In the Apocalypse, too, we read that the twenty-four elders cast their crowns before the Lamb, because, clearly, all the virtues of the saints and all their victories, by which they shone with his help, are seen to be less than his virtues and victory. A stream derived from a perennial spring is said to be lesser when compared with that spring, and a worthless vine-shoot is thought altogether worse when compared with the lively tendrils of the vine or the fruitful branches of the palm. Grant that it was done, and that it is credible that the power of the Polemonic image restrained someone from the crime of adultery: are therefore all images to be adored? Or, because the tongue of a dumb beast, ... restrained the perverse intention by which he strove to curse the blessed people, and allowed the irrational animal to escape the terrifying angelic blows against a rational man, are therefore dumb beasts to be adored? Or, because a crowd of boys, provoking the man of God with vain taunts, was struck down by the wounding ferocity of savage beasts, is therefore the rage of bears to be adored? For very often things that happen by chance, through some accident, prevent the commission of harmful acts by those wishing to commit them, but reason does not permit that the very things through which these things happen should be adored. Therefore, just as what they say about Polemon and his image, by whose help they wish to prop up their error, was done in truth, images are not therefore to be adored, since, according to the examples I have briefly set out, not all things through which some benefits come to mortals are to be adored. But if it was not done in truth, as we also believe, and those who bring it forward do not do so with fully reasonable authority, since they prove by no authentic signs that it was done in truth, then the most vain adoration of senseless things is not to be established on that account either. Nowhere is it read that a lie, or an example of lies, has established something that ought reasonably and in truth to be done. For just as truth is never subjected to a lie, so lies are always believed to oppose truth; these two stand in such mutual opposition that they are always held to be contrary to each other. Therefore, just as fire cannot be nourished by the flow of waters, or conversely no one can foment fire by pouring on water, so no one can confirm truth, as they strive to do, by means of lies. Having therefore briefly and in part proved from what has been said that the deed of the image of Polemon, if indeed it was done as they lie, ought not and cannot be equated with the deed of the Lord's hem; or, what is entirely doubtful, whether it was done at all, which they say was done, or not; or that even if it was done, it could establish only the adoration of a certain person; and having shown that what they bring forward is a lie, it is now worth while to explain briefly what the hem of the Lord's garment, which they strive to equate with that image of Polemon, signifies by its types and secret mysteries. The hem of the Lord's garment is a sign of the incarnation, by touching which the Gentile world lost the sickness of foul idolatry. For just as the hem is the smallest part in comparison with the body or the whole garment, so the incarnation of the Redeemer is, in comparison with his divine and ineffable generation, by which he was begotten of the Father before the ages, as it were the least part. Of this generation it is said through Isaiah: Who will declare his generation? understood: no one. His human generation, however, the Evangelist sets forth thus: The book of the generation of Christ the son of David. The woman, therefore, touching from behind the hem of the Lord's garment, obtained the desired

units.la: tatem, quam medicorum industria longa per tempora negaverat, recepit, quia post passionem et resurrectionem sive in cælum ascensionem Domini gentilitas credulitatis sanitatem, quam nec Patris charum, nec Prophetarum ei prædicatio quiverat impertire, dominicæ vestis fimbriam tangendo carnationis videlicet ejus mysterium credendo, percepit: & cum ad ipsius Domini prædicationem vix modica discipulorum turba crediderit, ad prædicationem tamen Apostolorum tanta multitudo celerrimo fidei ardore succensa est, ut una die quinque millia hominum, alia tria ac tria induceantur: quod & ipsa veritas discipulis promisit dicens, Qui credit in me, opera quæ ego facio & ipse faciet, & majora horum faciet. Quod quidem & in miraculo quod per Petrum a Domino gestum est, intelligi posse putant: quoniam dum Dominus imperio verbi sive tactu infirmos sanaverit, Petrus umbræ suæ tantum attactu infirmos legitur sanasse. Dominus ergo ad filiam archisynagogi dam pergens, hæmorrhoissæ attactu fœminam a profluvio languoris liberat: quia videlicet dum ... gam, quæ utique Patriarcharum & Prophetarum de stirpe descendit, somno incredulitatis evigilare tendit, gentilitatem a dæmoniorum insolentissimo cultu suæ fidei cognitione sanavit bonum quod illa perfidiæ culpa meruerat percipere neglexit, illa fidei devotione percipere meruit. Ad synagogam ergo liberandam se Dominus venisse testatur, cum & per præsentiam corporalem cit, Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierant domus Israel: sive cum discipulos in vias gentium abire in civitates Samaritanorum cohibet introire: & quondam allegorice per Salomonem in Canticorum ad Israeliticæ gentis hortum se descensurum promittit dicens, Descendi ad hortum nucum ut viderem poma convallis: quia scilicet dum ad Judaici populi hortum in quo erat lex in cortice pandat, acerrimam austeritatem, in nucleo occultans inconparabilem suavitatem, per carnis suscepionem descendit, gentilicæ convallis abjecta operam invilit, eamque sibi fidei integritate adscivit. Porro lunata in itinere fœminaad domum archisynagogiæ Domino venitur ejus; filia mortis vinculis solutis suscitatur, synagoga quandoque somnum suæ diffidentiæ difficultura, & Christo per hæc resurrectura, & ei perpetuum victura monstratur: quandoquidem miox ut plurimum gentium lectionem apostolum subintraverit, cœcitatem quæ ex parte in non credendo in mediatorem Dei & hominis contigit, a se discutiendo, & in eum credendo, qui sibi per Patriarchas & Prophetas sacrorum lorum tomitruis olim adnunciatus est, credens, sic omnis Israel salvus erit. Cum igitur his mihbus mysteriis, quæ in dominicæ fimbriæ gestio innuitur, Polemonis imago penitus careat, in modo ut dominici indumenti fimbria habenda est: nec debet ei coæquari nomine, quæ æquitur in tot mysteriorum fulgore.
units.tr: health, which the skill of physicians had long denied her. For after the passion and resurrection, or the ascension of the Lord into heaven, the Gentile world, by touching the hem of the Lord's garment, that is, by believing in the mystery of his incarnation, received the health of faith, which neither the dearness of the Father nor the preaching of the Prophets had been able to bestow. When the small crowd of disciples scarcely believed at the preaching of the Lord himself, yet at the preaching of the Apostles so great a multitude was kindled with the swift ardour of faith that five thousand men were brought in one day, and others three and three thousand. The truth itself promised this to the disciples, saying: He who believes in me, the works that I do he also shall do, and greater works than these shall he do. They think this can also be understood of the miracle which the Lord wrought through Peter: for while the Lord healed the sick by the command of his word or by touch, Peter is read to have healed the sick by the mere touch of his shadow. The Lord, then, going to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, frees the woman from the flux of her sickness by touching her; because, while the daughter, who indeed sprang from the stock of the Patriarchs and Prophets, strives to awake from the sleep of unbelief, he has healed the Gentile world from the most insolent worship of demons by the knowledge of its faith, and what the other had neglected to receive through the fault of faithlessness, she merited to receive through the devotion of faith. The Lord bears witness that he came to free the synagogue, both by his bodily presence, saying: I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; and when he restrains the disciples from going into the ways of the Gentiles and from entering the cities of the Samaritans. And once, allegorically, through Solomon in the Song of Songs, he promises that he will come down into the garden of the Israelite people, saying: I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley: because, namely, while he spreads out in the bark of the Jewish people's garden, in which was the law, the most bitter austerity, hiding in the kernel an incomparable sweetness, he descends by taking on flesh, and having cast aside the valley of the Gentiles, he takes it to himself in the integrity of faith. Further, the woman who had been ill in the way is shown to have been brought to the house of the ruler of the synagogue by the Lord's coming; the daughter of death is raised, her chains loosed; the synagogue is shown, at some time, about to awake from the sleep of its distrust, and by these things it will rise again in Christ and live forever in him: since, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, and blindness, which in part came upon Israel through not believing in the Mediator between God and men, has been dispelled by Israel itself, and it believes in him who was of old announced to it through the Patriarchs and Prophets with the thunder of the sacred oracles, then, as the Apostle says, all Israel will be saved. Since, therefore, the image of Polemon is wholly lacking in these holy mysteries, which are shown in the deed of the hem of the Lord's garment, it is to be held in no way equal to the hem of the Lord's garment, and it ought not to be equated with it in name, which is itself equated with so many mysteries in their splendour.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Quod judices qui in prefata synodo fuerunt, insolenter & incongrue artem pictoriam extollere constituunt, dicentes, Pia enim est ars pictoris, & non recte eam quidam insipienter detrahunt. ipse enim pater pictorem pie agentem commendat.
units.tr: That the judges who were at the aforesaid synod insolently and inappropriately resolve to extol the art of painting, saying: "For the art of the painter is pious, and some foolishly disparage it without good reason; for the Father himself commends the painter who acts piously."

units.la: SI pestilens humor arcem corporis, id est, caput obsederit, facile ad cetera membra transfundi: nec mirandum est, si ad pedum ima transfusus eos vehementer lædat, si eum jam caput quod omnibus membris præminet, lædisse constet. Vesania igitur adorandarum imaginum quæ Constantini & Hærenæ matris ejus, sive etiam Tharasii Constantinopolitani Episcopi cæterumque illarum partium sacerdotum mentem inrepsit, non est plurimum magnipendenda, h ad predicum sive plebium usque metas subripiendas descendit: quoniam ut superiori exemplo mutilum est, cum caput infolicia cujusdam ei invaditur, facile cætera invadantur, quæ capiti subesse ii stratur. Omne caput languidum, aut Propheta, & omne cor mœrens, a planta pedis usque ad verticem non est in eo sanitas, quia videlicet dum a regibus & a sacerdotibus, qui exemplar bene vivendi subjectis plebibus debent, rectè vivendi rectè agedi studium prætermittitur, de interna sanitate subjectarum plebium quomodo dubitatur. Cum ergo in eadem synodo tot sacerdotum fuerint oblitæ mentes erroribus quo non poterat error judicium inhærere mentibus? aut quis ab errore reducat oves, si errandi ita teneat pastores? sacerdotes enim quum errore subditas plebes inducere nolcuntur, talibus per Hieremiam ... mizm miam prophetam increpationibus arguuntur; Propterea haec dicit Dominus ad pastores, qui regunt populum meum, Vos dispersistis oves meas, & expulistis eas, & non visitastis eas: ubi protinus quanta sit cura Dei erga populum, qualiterve amotis negligentibus studiosiores populo Dei dentur rectores, protinus subinfertur; Ecce ego vindico in vos secundum malitias studia vestra, & suscitabo illis pastores, qui pascant eas, & ultra non timebunt neque terrebuntur, dicit Dominus. In Ezechiel quoque Propheta de talibus, quod quidem non sine ingenti animi angore prosequimur, qui stipendiis ecclesiasticis utuntur, & exemplis erroneis & incautis populum in errorem inducere creduntur, sicut in fecisse perhibentur, qui in vanam imaginum adorationem exarserunt, & populum subditum praelati sibi in errore professionis sociaverunt, ita scribitur; Et ideo pastores audite verbum Domini, Oves meas devoratis, & lanas earum vos cooperitis, & quod eraf-sum est jugulatis, & oves meas dispersistis: quod infirmum erat non confortastis, & quod male habebat non curastis, & contritum non alligastis, & quod errabat non convertistis, & quod perierat non requisistis, & fortem oppressistis laboré, & dispersae sunt oves meae, eo quod non sint pastores, & factae sunt in devorationem omnibus bestiis agri, & dispersae sunt oves meae super omnem montem & in omnem collem altum, & super faciem totius terrae dispersae sunt, nec erat, qui requireret, neque qui revocaret. Non ergo in hujus negotii vanissima professione tantae est nequitia judicium, quanto perversitas sacerdotum: sed in illis deprehenditur ignavia, in illis ingens redundat insania: praesertim cum illi se imagines adoraturos, eisque servitium quod sanctae trinitati debetur, exhibituros profiteantur: illi pictorum artem piam esse, & non debere subsannari, & pictorem pie agentem a patre commendari profitentur dicentes, Pia enim est ars pictoris & non recte eam quidam mispicientes detrahunt; ipsum enim pater pictorem pie agentem commendat. In quibus utrorumque professionibus evidenter ostenditur, tanto sacerdotes praeminuisse judicibus in errore, quanto minimum praeeminent per gradus sublimitatem in honore, nec coaequari potuisse laicos praesulibus in absurda professione, qui non coaequari possunt in sacerdotali cathedrae sessione: sed dum in neutra parte reperiatur quod recte queat laudari, in utraque tamen parte cernatur quod merito possit vituperari, & praesulum error, qui simulacros adoraturos eisque servitium soli Deo debitum exhibituros falsi sunt, ex parte discussus sit, restatut judicium etiam error quo artem pictoriam piam esse adseverant, nostri stili invectione discutiatur. Dicunt enim artem pictoriam piam esse, quasi non cum ceteris mundanis artibus communionem pietatis aut impietatis sortiatur. Quid enim ars pictorum amplius habet pietatis arte fabrorum, sculptorum, conflatorum, caelatorum, latomorum, lignariorum, terrae cultorum, vel ceterorum opificum? Omnes enim quas praemisimus artes, quae non nisi discendo possunt adtingi, & pie & impie possunt ab his quibus exercentur habere, nec in eas pietas aut impietas cadit, sed in hominibus, qui earum sunt sequaces, qui plerumque aut vitiorum procaciissimis tumultibus coartantur, aut virtutum salutiferis coribus exornantur. Si ergo idcirco ars pictorum pia esse perhibetur, quia per eam pleraque piorum hominum actus & pia quaedam gesta pinguntur, ergo & ideo impia perhibebitur, quia plerumque per eam impietates multae, id est, trucidationes hominum, atrocitates bellorum, crudelitates sceleratorum, inimicitates ferarum, impetus bestiarum vel cetera his similia depinguntur: & ideo impia nullatenus esse creditur, quia haec quae exsecuti sumus adumbrationibus vel etiam lineamentis quibusque humanis vitiis impertiuntur: nec ideo pia erit, quia per eam bonorum hominum nomina signantur. Sicut enim ferrum nec ideo impium dicitur, quia ex eo homines interimuntur: nec ideo pium, quia ex eo quaedam instrumenta fiunt quibus & ensium vibrantium inlisiones quatiantur, & homines tueantur, & a medicis salutis humanae consulitur; ita & ars pictorum nec ideo impia, quia per eam crudelia, nec ideo pia, quia clementia quaedam pinguntur. Quod vero ei non recte, a quibusdam insipientibus detrahi suspirant, a nullo qui sanae mentis est ambigitur eos in hac quoque parte sicut & in ceteris dementiam sequi: quippe cum nullus sani capitis neque imaginibus detrahat, neque artis pictoriae, sed eorum, qui eas adorant eisque servitium inconsequens exhibent, abominetur vehementiam. Non enim vinum quia ebrietatem generat, reprehenditur, cum plerumque Deo in sacrificium libetur: nec sylvae quae furibus hospitium praebent, quia plerumque hominum usibus multa quae expediunt administrant: nec ideo igni imputatur, quia interdum edaciter domos vel cetera humanis stipendiis apta devorat, cum mortalium vitae multis administratis suffragetur. Porro quod dicunt, Ipse enim pater pictorem pie agentem commendat, cur pater, aut ubi scriptum sit, pictorem commendet, nec illorum est adprobare, nec nostrum credere: quippe cum in nullo oraculorum divinorum volumine pictorum laus perhibeatur inesse. Reperiunt ergo illi in quolibet divinarum scripturarum loco, in quo etiam secundum propriam adseverationem pictoris, ideo quod conponedis imaginibus instent conlaudet, & nos reperiemus qualiter eis respondere valeamus: quia omnipotens Deus non opera, sed devotionem operum, nec actus, sed voluntates actuum, nec res, sed causas rerum, nec quisquis faciat, sed qua mente id faciat, plerumque aut probat aut improbat.
units.tr: IF a pestilent humour has beset the citadel of the body, that is, the head, it easily spreads to the other members, and it is no wonder if, having spread down to the soles of the feet, it grievously harms them, since it is established that it has already harmed the head, which stands out above all the members. Therefore the madness of adoring images, which crept into the minds of Constantine and his mother Helena, and also of Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, and of the other priests of those regions, is not to be held in great regard, since it has descended even to the boundaries of the people and the commonalty. For, as in the example above, when the head of a certain body is attacked by disease, the other parts that lie beneath the head are easily attacked as well. Every head is sick, and every heart is faint; from the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no soundness in it (Isa. 1:5–6). For when the zeal for living rightly and acting rightly is neglected by kings and priests, who ought to be the example of good living to the peoples under them, how can anyone doubt the inner health of the peoples under them? Therefore, since in that same synod the minds of so many priests were blinded by errors, how could error fail to take hold of the minds of the judges? Or who will lead the sheep back from error, if the shepherds themselves are held fast in error? For when priests are unwilling to lead the peoples under them into error, they are reproved by the rebukes which the prophet Jeremiah addresses to them: Therefore thus says the Lord to the shepherds who rule my people: You have scattered my sheep, and driven them away, and not visited them (Jer. 23:2). Immediately after this, there follows how great is God's care for the people, and how, once the negligent have been removed, more zealous rulers are given to the people of God: Behold, I will visit upon you according to the wickedness of your doings, and I will raise up for them shepherds who will feed them, and they shall fear no more nor be dismayed, says the Lord (Jer. 23:2, 4). Likewise the prophet Ezekiel, concerning such men (which we pursue not without great anguish of spirit), who enjoy ecclesiastical stipends and are believed to lead the people into error by erroneous and careless examples, as is reported of those who burned with zeal for the vain adoration of images and joined the people under them to themselves in an erroneous profession, is written thus: And therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: You devour my sheep, and clothe yourselves with their wool, and slaughter what is fat, and you have scattered my sheep. The weak you have not strengthened, and the sick you have not healed, and the broken you have not bound up, and the straying you have not brought back, and the lost you have not sought, but you have ruled over them with harshness and violence. And my sheep were scattered because there were no shepherds, and they became food for all the beasts of the field, and my sheep were scattered over every mountain and every high hill, and over the face of the whole earth they were scattered, and there was no one who sought them, nor anyone who brought them back (Ezek. 34:2–6). Therefore the judgment of wickedness is not so great in the vain profession of this matter as the perversity of the priests is; in them is found the sloth, in them the great madness overflows. Especially since they profess that they will adore images and offer to them the service that is owed to the Holy Trinity; and they profess that the art of painters is pious and ought not to be mocked, and that the painter who acts piously is commended by the Father, saying: For the art of the painter is pious, and some foolishly disparage it without good reason; for the Father himself commends the painter who acts piously. In these professions of both groups it is clearly shown that the priests excelled the judges in error by as much as they excel them in the dignity of rank and honour; and that the laity could not be made equal to the prelates in an absurd profession, when they cannot be made equal in the seat of the priestly chair. But since in neither part is anything found that could rightly be praised, yet in both parts something is seen that may justly be blamed, and since the error of the prelates, who falsely profess that they will adore images and offer to them the service due to God alone, has been discussed in part, the error by which they assert that the art of painting is pious remains to be examined by the attack of our pen. For they say that the art of painting is pious, as if it did not share with the other worldly arts a common lot of piety or impiety. For what does the art of painters have more of piety than the art of smiths, sculptors, founders, engravers, stonecutters, carpenters, farmers, or the other craftsmen? For all the arts we have mentioned, which cannot be acquired except by learning, can be possessed by those who practise them either piously or impiously, and piety or impiety does not attach to the arts themselves but to the men who follow them, who are often constrained either by the most violent tumults of vices or adorned by the saving ornaments of virtues. If therefore the art of painters is called pious because through it many deeds of pious men and certain pious events are depicted, then by the same reasoning it will also be called impious, because through it many impieties are often depicted, that is, the slaughter of men, the atrocities of wars, the cruelties of criminals, the hostilities of wild beasts, the attacks of animals, and other things like these. And it is not believed to be impious in any way because the things we have set out are represented by outlines or even by the lineaments of human vices; nor will it be pious because through it the names of good men are marked. For just as iron is not called impious because men are killed with it, nor pious because instruments are made from it by which the blows of brandished swords are warded off, men are protected, and the health of men is cared for by physicians; so the art of painters is not impious because cruel things are depicted through it, nor pious because certain acts of mercy are depicted. But as for their sighing that it is wrongly disparaged by certain foolish men, no one of sound mind doubts that in this respect too, as in the others, they follow folly; for no one of sound mind disparages images, nor the art of painting, but abhors the vehemence of those who adore images and offer them an unbecoming service. For wine is not condemned because it produces drunkenness, although it is often poured out as a sacrifice to God; nor are forests condemned because they offer shelter to thieves, since they often supply many things useful for human needs; nor is fire blamed because at times it greedily devours houses and other things fit for human use, since it helps the life of mortals in many ways. Moreover, as to their saying, For the Father himself commends the painter who acts piously: why it is the Father, or where it is written that he commends the painter, it is neither for them to prove nor for us to believe; for in no volume of the divine oracles is praise of painters found. Let them therefore find in any passage of the divine Scriptures where, according to their own assertion, the painter is praised for pressing on with the making of images, and we shall find how we may answer them. For almighty God does not approve or disapprove of works but of the devotion of the works, nor of acts but of the wills behind the acts, nor of things but of the causes of things, nor of whoever does a thing but of the mind in which he does it.

units.la: CAP. XXIII. Inutile & mendacio plenum dictum Johannis presbyteri & legati orientalium dicentis, Non contraeunt pictores Scripturis, sed quidquid Scriptura dicit haec de- monstrant, quatenus concordes sunt scripturarum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. The saying of John the presbyter and envoy of the Easterners, that "painters do not contradict the Scriptures, but demonstrate whatever Scripture says, insofar as they agree with the Scriptures," is useless and full of falsehood.

units.la: Omnia Johannis presbyteri & legati orientalium deliramenta quae in eadem synodo, in cujus inofficiosae lectionis reprehensionibus nostr stilus versatur, protulit, singillatim a nobis discussa in unum fuissent congesta, magnorum voluminum tantae disputationis sylva esset indigua: sed nos ea partim brevitatis studio, cui prorsus studemus, partim ordinem ipsius lectionis servan-tes, quo non singulorum singula seorsum, sed quorundam passim per ordinem, prout quisque loquutus est, vel etiam in eodem codice posita inveniuntur, discutienda in nostra disputatione ponentes, & brevissimae disputationis cuncta articulo coartare compellimur, & non singula seorsum, sed pene omnia sparsim, prout ordo dictavit, exsequimur: est interea operaeprecium diligenter discutere, qualiter, ut idem profatus est, pictores haudquaquam credantur Scripturis contraire: aut qualiter quicquid Scriptura dicit demonstrent, qualiterve concordes sint scripturarum. Quamvis enim non euceat de quibus Scripturis ille hoc dixerit, credendum est tamen eum de sacris Scripturis dixisse, quas usitate Scripturas solemnis vocare, ut est illud in Evangelio, Tunc aperuit illis sensum ut intellegerent Scripturas. S.R. Pictura interea ars cum ob hoc inolevit, ut rerum in veritate gestarum memoriam male pleientibus defertet, & ex mendacio ad veritatem recolendam metes promoveret, versa vice interdum pro veritate ad mendacia cogiranda sensus promovet, & non solum illa quae aut sunt aut fuerunt aut fieri possunt, sed etiam ea quae nec sunt, nec fuerunt, nec fieri possunt visibus defert. Mendacium enim aut de his est quae non sunt, sed fieri possant, aut de his quae nec sunt, nec fieri possunt, de quibus in per-nerimeneiis a philosophis acutissima sive subtilissima disputatio est, quam huic operi interponere longissimum est. Nam dum dicat non contrarie pictores Scripturis, & multa a pictoribus pinguntur quae Scripturae divinae tacent, & ab hominibus non solum a doctis, sed etiam ab indoctis salsissima esse comprobentur, quis non ejus dictum ridiculosissimum vel potius salsissimum esse fateatur? Nonne divinis Scripturis contraire noscuntur, cum abyssum figuram hominis fingunt habere, & lymphuarum inundationem affarim fundere? Nonne divinis Scripturis eos cotraire haud dubium est, cum tellus in figura humana modo aridam sterilemve, modo fructibus adfluentem depingunt? Nonne divinis Scripturis eos contraire manifestum est, cum flumineos amnes in figuris hominum aut situlis aquas fundere, aut alios in alios confluere depingunt? Nonne cum solem & lunam & caetera caeli ornamenta figuras hominum, & capita radiis succincta habere fingunt, sanctis Scripturis modis omnibus contrariunt? Nonne cum duodecim ventus singulis singulas formas pro qualitate virium adtribuunt, aut menses singulis pro qualitate temporum quid unusquisque; deferat quibusdam nudas quibusdam feminas, quibusdam etiam indutas diversis vestibus figuras dant? aut dum quatuor tempora anni singula diversis figuris depingunt, aut floribus vernante ut ver, aut aestibus exustam, vel etiam segetibus onustam ut aestate, aut vindemiae labris vel botris oneratam ut autumnum, aut modo frigorib. algidam, modo ignibus se calefacientem, modo animantib. pabula praebente, modo nimiis frigorib. marcidas volucres capientes ut hyeme, Scripturis divinis in quib. haec ita minime contineantur contraire noscuntur? quomodo ergo pictoribus, qui poetarum vanissimas fabulas plerumque sequuntur, sanctis Scripturis minime contrariantur? Fin guntur.n. per eos interdum res in veritate gestae in alias atq; alias incredibiles naenias; finguntur etiam quae nec facta sunt, nec fieri poterant, sed aut mystice a philosophis intelliguntur, aut inaniter a gentilibus venerantur, aut veraciter a catholicis respuuntur. quae omnia quamquam gentilium habeantur in hieris, ab ipsis tamen prorsus sunt alienae scripturis. An non divinis literis alienum est ab illis Chymaera tricipit Bellerophonte fingitur interfecta? cum Bellerophon non bestia, ut illi meminerunt, prostraverit, sed more, ut plerique intelligunt, habitabile fecerit. An non divinis scripturis alienum est, quod Vulcani claudi & Terrae filius Erichthonius esse, & in monte Aethna ferri coquere, ejusque fornax Vesuvius mons Campaniae esse fingitur, qui perpetuis ignibus ardere perhibetur? An non divinis scripturis alienum sunt, quod Scyllae capitibus fingitur succincta canibus? & Phyllis ob amore juvenis cujusdam in arbore fingitur esse coversa, & altera Scylla eo quod Nisus patris et nec abscideret purpureum, una cum patre, & Itys ob stupri materni et patre gestu, & homicidium matris sive matertera in ipso patratu, una cum parentibus, sive matertera, volucres finguntur fuisse coversi? aut cum Syrenes ex parte virgines, & ex parte volucres fingunt, aut cum Ixion illusione Junonis, cum Nube coiens Centauros fingitur generasse? aut cum Neptunus tridentem armatus marinis fingitur fluctibus dominari? An non divinis Scripturis alienum est, quod Perseus tres sorores Gorgonas adjutorio Minervae interfecisse, aut cum alatus averso volare fingitur, aut cum de sanguine ejus nasci fertur Pegasus, equus alatus, qui ungula sua fonte rupisse Musis depingitur? An non divinis Scripturis contrarium est, quod Prometheus homines ex luto finxisse inanimatos fingunt, & eunde Prometheus a Minerva in caelum levatus inter oras septemplicis clypei, & dum omnia caelestia videret, fingunt eum ferulam Phoebiacis adplicasse rotis, igneque esse furatum, & pectusculo hominis quae finxerat applicato animatum reddidisse corpus? An non divinis scripturis contrarium est, quod Tantalus fingunt in inferno in quodam lacu depositum, ejus fallace aqua gulosis labia tillamentis adtingere, pomaque, fugitivis cineresciente tactibus delupere faciem tenus pendula apparere, ejusque esse locupletem visum & pauperem effectum? An non divinis scripturis alienum est, cum Phineus caecus fingitur, cujus cibos Harpyiae rapuisse, ejusque prandia stercore fedasse pinguntur, quas Zetus & Calais Aquilonis venti filii fugasse a conspectu ejus medaciter fingunt? An non divinis scripturis contrarium est, cum Admetus rex Graeciae, ut Alcestae conjugio fructetur, lecto dum propositum soceri leone & apro ad currum iunctos, Apollinis & Herculis adjutorium habuisse pingitur? aut cum Hercules Cerberum tricipite canem inferorum interemisse pingitur? An non divinis scripturis contrarium est, quod Acteonem quendam venatorem eo, quod Dianam lavantem viderit, in cervum fingunt esse coversum, & a canibus suis non agnitum, eorumque morsibus devoratum? An non divinis scripturis contrarium est, quod Berecynthia puerum formosissimum Atyn amasse, eumque zelotypiae vi... succensa castrate, & semimasculum fecisse depingitur? An non divinis scripturis contrarium est, quod Orpheus Eurydicen nymphamamasse & sono cythara persuasam uxorem duxisse pingitur, qui etiam dam dum Aristei pastoris persequutione non ferens fugeret, & in serpentem incidens mortua esset, camú maritus insequens ad inferos descenderet, & legem acciperet ne eam conversus aspiceret, hanc conversusaspexisse & denuo perdidisse fingitur? An non divinis scripturis alienum est, quod Venus cum Marte concubuisse & à Sole deprehensa, & à Vulcano prodita, & ab illo adamantinis catenis una cum Marte pingitur fuisse religata? Hæc & his similia, quæ & nobis ad retexendum sunt fastidiosa, & poetis sive philosophis gentium vel ad cantandum suavia, vel ad tractandum mystica, & pictoribus ad formandum familiaria, prorsus sunt, ut præfati sumus, à divinis literis aliena. Nam, ut cætera taceamus, si quis pictor duo capita in uno corpore, aut in duobus corporibus caput unum, aut alterius animantis caput, alterius cæteta membra, ut Hippocentaurum toto corpore equino & capite humano, & Minotaurum semibovem semivirumque affectet pingere, nunquid non scripturis dicitur contraire? ecquid est dicere, Non contraeunt pictores scripturæ? quasi non aliquà à pictoribus possint depingi quæ sacris literis credantur refragari. in sacris etenim literis, nihil vitiosum, nihil inconveniens, nihil impurum, nihil falsum, nisi forte id quod perversos quosque dixisse vel fecisse sancta scriptura commemorat, penitus invenitur: in picturis autem plura falsa, plura vitiosa, plura inconsequentia, plura inconvenientia, &, ut singula taceam, pene omnia sive possibilia, sive impossibilia, ab erudiris pictoribus depinguntur: quibus documentis Johannes presbyter, & legatus orientalium in hacquoque parte, sicut & in cæteris delirasse convincitur. Quod autem presbyter idem ait, pictores quidquid scriptura loquitur demonstrare, quam sit falsum quamque inutile, prudens lector advertat. Nunquidnam divinæ cunctæ legis præcepta quæ à domino per Moysen data sunt, ut est illud, Audi Israhel, domi-nus deus tuus deus unus est, & cætera hujuscemodi, in quibus nihil sonant, quæ pingi possint, à pictoribus demonstrantur? Nunquidnam omnia verba prophetarum, in quibus doctrinæ, exhortationes, redargutiones, contemplationes, minæ, vel cætera his similia continentur, in quibus crebro inveniuntur, Hæc dixit dominus, aut, Iuravit dominus, aut his similia, quæ ab scriptoribus potius quàm à pictoribus exarantur, pictura secundum ejus vanitatem demonstrare valet? Nunquidnam verba ipsius domini & Apostolorum singula à pictoribus possunt demonstrari? Pictores igitur rerum gestarum historias ad memoriam reducere quodammodo valent: res autem quæ sensibus tantummodo percipiuntur & verbis proferuntur, non à pictoribus, sed ab scriptoribus comprehendi, & aliorum relatibus demonstrari valent: ac per hoc absurdum est dicere, Non contraeunt pictores scripturis: sed quicquid scriptura loquitur, hoc demonstrant. Porro quod ait, Concordes sunt scripturarum, quàm sit insulsum, quamque absurdum, multis potest approbari indiciis. Qualem enim concordantiam possunt habere cum scripturis sacris, cum illæ veraces sint, isti plerunque falsa confingant? & de illis dicatur, Eloquia domini eloquia casta, isti interdum fingant inpura & incasta? illæ semper suadeant honesta & salubria, isti multoties inhonesta & ludibria? illæ semper instent humanæ saluti, isti plerumque vanirati? illæ semper hortentur ad cælestia dona, isti crebro depingant terrestria quæque & caduca? Quanta enim concordantia est inter id quod semper veritati innititur, & id quod plerumque veritatem, plerumque falsitatem insequitur, tanta nimirum concordantia est inter scripturas divinas quæ semper puras & six regulas tenent, & pictores qui mortalium more plures permutationes habent.
units.tr: If all the nonsense of John the presbyter and envoy of the Easterners, which he put forward at that same synod, and whose absurd readings occupy our criticisms here, were gathered together and discussed one by one, they would make a forest too large for a work of many volumes. But because we aim at brevity, and because we follow the order of his reading, we are forced to set out the matters for discussion in our argument not one by one separately, but as some of them appear scattered in order, as each man spoke, or as they are found in the same codex. We must confine everything to a brief article, and we deal with almost everything scattered about, as the order dictates, rather than with each item apart. Meanwhile it is worth examining carefully how, as he himself said, painters are by no means believed to contradict the Scriptures, or how they demonstrate whatever Scripture says, or in what way they agree with the Scriptures. For although it is not clear which Scriptures he meant, we must believe that he spoke of the holy Scriptures, which are commonly called "the Scriptures" in the usual way, as in the Gospel: "Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures." (Luke 24.) Painting, moreover, as an art, has grown up for this reason: it conveys to those who are ill-informed the memory of things that really happened, and from falsehood it advances the senses toward recalling the truth. In turn, it sometimes, on the contrary, puts its senses in the service of contriving falsehoods in place of truth, and it presents to the eyes not only those things that are, or were, or can be, but also those that neither are, nor were, nor can be. For a lie concerns either things that are not but could be, or things that neither are nor can be. About these the philosophers have a most acute and subtle debate in the books Peri Hermeneias, and it would be very long to insert that debate into this work. For while he says that painters do not contradict the Scriptures, and many things are painted by painters which the divine Scriptures pass over in silence, and are proved by men, not only learned but also unlearned, to be most absurd, who would not confess that his saying is most ridiculous, or rather most absurd? Are they not known to contradict the divine Scriptures when they depict the abyss as having the figure of a man, and pour out floods of water from it? Is it not beyond doubt that they contradict the divine Scriptures when they paint the earth in human form, now dry and barren, now overflowing with fruits? Is it not manifest that they contradict the divine Scriptures when they paint river-streams in the figures of men, pouring water from pitchers, or flowing one into another? When they imagine the sun, the moon and the other ornaments of heaven as having the figures of men, with heads girded with rays, do they not contradict the holy Scriptures in every way? When they assign to the twelve winds one shape each according to the quality of their strength, or give to each month a figure according to the quality of its season, some bare and some female, some even clothed in various garments; or when they paint the four seasons of the year each with its own figure: spring as blooming with flowers, summer as scorched by heat or laden with crops, autumn as loaded with the vintage vats and grape-clusters, and winter as chilled by frosts, or warming itself at fires, or offering food to animals, or catching birds withered by excessive cold, do they not contradict the divine Scriptures, in which none of these things is contained? How, then, do they by no means contradict the holy Scriptures, these painters who for the most part follow the most empty fables of the poets? For through them things that really happened are sometimes shaped into various incredible tales. They also invent things that neither happened nor could have happened, which are understood allegorically by the philosophers, or vainly venerated by the Gentiles, or truly rejected by the Catholics. Although all these things are counted among the sacred things of the Gentiles, they are nonetheless entirely alien to the Scriptures. Is it not foreign to the sacred letters that the three-headed Chimaera is feigned to have been slain by Bellerophon? Bellerophon did not slay a beast, as some have recalled, but, as most understand, made the land habitable. Is it not foreign to the divine Scriptures that Erichthonius, son of Earth, is feigned to be the son of lame Vulcan and to smelt iron on Mount Etna, and that Vesuvius, a mountain of Campania, which is said to burn with perpetual fires, is pictured as his furnace? Are these not foreign to the divine Scriptures: that Scylla is feigned to be girded with dogs' heads; that Phyllis, for love of a certain young man, is feigned to have been turned into a tree; that the other Scylla, because she cut off the purple lock of her father Nisus, was turned into a bird along with her father; that Itys, for his mother's defilement and the father's deed, and Procne or her sister, in the very act of the murder of the mother, were turned into birds along with their parents? Or when they feign the Sirens partly virgins and partly birds? Or when they feign that Ixion, by a deception of Juno, begot the Centaurs by mating with a cloud? Or when they feign that Neptune, armed with his trident, rules over the sea waves? Is it not foreign to the divine Scriptures that Perseus, with Minerva's help, slew the three sisters, the Gorgons, or when he is feigned to fly with his face turned away, or when Pegasus, a winged horse, is said to have been born from Medusa's blood, and is depicted as striking a spring with his hoof for the Muses? Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that they feign Prometheus to have shaped men from clay without life, and that the same Prometheus, lifted into heaven by Minerva among the rims of her sevenfold shield, and while he gazed upon all the heavenly things, applied a fennel stalk to the wheels of Phoebus, stole fire, and by applying it to the little breast of the man he had shaped, gave the body life? Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that they feign Tantalus placed in hell in a certain lake, whose lips, though greedy, could scarcely touch the deceitful water with their drops, and whose fruits, flying away at his touch, hung before his face, and that he, from being rich, became poor? Is it not foreign to the divine Scriptures that Phineus is feigned to be blind, whose food the Harpies are painted as having snatched away, and whose meals they fouled with dung, and that Zetes and Calais, sons of the north wind, falsely feigned to have driven them from his sight? Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that Admetus, king of Greece, in order to enjoy his marriage with Alcestis, is painted as having had the help of Apollo and Hercules, when a lion and a boar, yoked to his father-in-law's chariot, were set before him? Or that Hercules is painted as having slain Cerberus, the three-headed dog of the underworld? Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that a certain hunter, Actaeon, because he saw Diana bathing, is feigned to have been turned into a stag, not recognized by his own dogs, and devoured by their bites? Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that Berecynthia is painted as having loved the most beautiful boy, Attis, and, inflamed by the force of jealousy, as having castrated him and made him a half-man? Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that Orpheus is painted as having loved the nymph Eurydice, and having won his wife by the sound of his lyre, who, while fleeing the pursuit of the shepherd Aristaeus, was bitten by a serpent and died, and her husband, following her, descended to the underworld and received the law that he must not look back at her, but looking back, he saw her and lost her again? Is it not foreign to the divine Scriptures that Venus is feigned to have lain with Mars, and, caught by the Sun and betrayed by Vulcan, is painted as having been bound together with Mars by him in adamantine chains? These and similar things, which are tedious even for us to unfold, and which are pleasing for the poets or philosophers of the Gentiles, either to sing or to treat as mysteries, and familiar to painters for shaping, are altogether, as we have said before, alien to the divine letters. For, to pass over the rest, if some painter should attempt to paint a creature with two heads on one body, or one head on two bodies, or the head of another animal with the other limbs, as a hippocentaur with a whole horse's body and a human head, or a Minotaur half ox and half man, is he not said to contradict the Scriptures? What is it to say, "Painters do not contradict the Scriptures"? As if painters could not depict some things that are believed to conflict with the sacred letters. For in the sacred letters nothing vicious, nothing unsuitable, nothing impure, nothing false is found at all, except perhaps what the holy Scripture records that wicked men have said or done. But in pictures there are many false things, many vicious things, many inconsistent things, many unsuitable things, and, to pass over single items, almost everything, whether possible or impossible, is painted by unskilled painters. By these proofs John the presbyter and envoy of the Easterners is shown to have raved in this respect too, as in other matters. As for the presbyter's further claim that "painters demonstrate whatever Scripture says," let the prudent reader consider how false and how useless it is. Are all the precepts of the divine law which were given by the Lord through Moses, such as "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God" and others of this kind, in which there is nothing that can be painted, demonstrated by painters? Can painting, according to its own vanity, demonstrate all the words of the prophets, in which teachings, exhortations, rebukes, contemplations, threats, and other things of this kind are contained, in which such phrases as "Thus says the Lord," or "The Lord has sworn," or similar ones, are frequently found, which are written down by writers rather than by painters? Can all the individual words of the Lord himself and of the Apostles be demonstrated by painters? Painters, then, can in some measure bring the histories of things done back to memory. But things which are perceived only by the senses and expressed in words cannot be grasped by painters, but by writers, and can be demonstrated by the accounts of others. And so it is absurd to say, "Painters do not contradict the Scriptures, but they demonstrate whatever Scripture says." Moreover, how silly and how absurd is his statement that they "agree with the Scriptures" can be shown by many proofs. For what kind of agreement can they have with the holy Scriptures, since the latter are true, while these for the most part invent falsehoods? And of the former it is said, "The words of the Lord are pure words" (Ps. 11.), while these sometimes invent impure and unchaste things? The former always urge what is honest and wholesome, while these very often urge the dishonourable and the ridiculous? The former always press upon human salvation, while these for the most part press upon vanity? The former always exhort to heavenly gifts, while these often depict all earthly and fleeting things? For as great as is the agreement between that which always rests upon truth and that which for the most part pursues truth and for the most part falsehood, so great, no doubt, is the agreement between the divine Scriptures, which always keep to pure and unchanging rules, and painters, who, after the manner of mortals, have many changes.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: Quod non sint coæquandæ imagines reliquiis sanctorum martyrum & confessorum, ut illi in sua errore synodo facere niteruntur, eo quod reliquiæ aut de corpore sunt, aut de his quæ in corpore, aut de his quæ circa corpus cujus iam sancti fuerunt: imagines vero nec in corpore, nec circa corpus fuisse vel fore creduntur illis quibus adscribuntur.
units.tr: That images are not to be placed on a level with the relics of the holy martyrs and confessors, as those men in their error at the synod try to do, because relics are either from the body, or from things that were in the body, or from things around the body of those who were later saints; whereas images are believed by those to whom they are ascribed to have been neither in nor around the body.

units.la: Siguti igitur sacratis rebus sive quæ per legislatorem, sive quæ per dei & hominum mediatorem sacratæ sunt, sive etiã quæ cotidie à sacerdotibus divini nominis invocatione sacrantur, & in mysterium nostræ redemptionis sumuntur, imagines nequaquam coæquandæ sunt, ita etiam nec sanctorum martyrum seu confessorum reliquiis, quæ apud fideles ipsorum amore veneratione habentur coæquandæ creduntur. Quas quidem illi qui in earum adorationem exarserunt cum omnibus sacratis rebus & mysteriis plenis æquiperare nitantur, reliquiis etiam sanctorum martyrum insolenter atque absurde æquiperare niteruntur. Cum ergo sanctorum corporibus aut certè corporum reliquiis, necnon & vestibus aut his similibus, quibus sancti dum mortaliter viverent usi sunt, isti picturæ aut sculpturas sive sculptilia vel conflatilia quæque ab artificibus quibusque formata coæquare in honore moliuntur, non modicam sanctis injuriam inferre monstrantur: cum præsertim sanctorum vestes, & his similia ideo veneranda sint, quia aut in corporibus eorundem sanctorum, aut circa corpora fuisse, & ab his sanctificationem ob quam venerentur percepisse credantur, necnon & sanctorum corpora vel etiam corporum reliquiæ, quonsam quanquam nunc in pulverem redacta fatescantur, juxta mundi terminum cum gloria sunt resurrectura & cum Christo perpetim regnaturæ: imagines vero quas illi inani voto his quæ præmisimus coæquare contendunt, ideo his minime coæquari queunt, quæ neq; id sunt ꝙ sanctorum corpora, neq; in eorum corporibus vel circa eosdem sacratissima corpora fuerè, sed pro captu uniuscujusq; ingenii, vel instrumentis artificii, modo formosæ, modo deformes, plerumq; etiã rebus impuris siunt. Unde datur intelligi nõ eos mediocriter errare qui illas sanctorum reliquiis niti untur æquiperare. Sanctorum itaque corpora venerari, corumque reliquiis honorem exhibere non sine causa vetustas admisit. Nam Abraham pater gentium vir fide plenus, devotione summus, obœdientia præcipuus, in præceptis domini strenuus, non in quolibet loco, sed in agro studiose empto, conjugem legitur sepelisse, & ossa sua non in loco quolibet, sed in spelunca pulcherrima, in cujus interiore parte protoplastus sepultus fuit, juxta suum imperium à filiis tumulatus legitur fuisse. Isaac quoque utero senili profusus, atque deo in sacrificium in figura nostri redemptoris ad offerendum ductus, virque sanctitate & caltinionia clarus juxta patrem secundum propriam jussionem creditur à filiis fuisse sepultus. Jacob quoque vir magnæ patientiæ divinis affatim roboratus oraculis, & crebris repromissionibus exhortatus, cum famis iuopiam vitare, & dulcissimum pignus quod extinctum crediderat cernere cupiens, cum clara progenie Niliacas descendisset in oras, non se ibidem sepeliri permisit, sed corpus suum ad terram sibi patribusque suis repromissam, juxta ossa patris avisque sepelicendum advehi lanxit: & quia quartus in eadem spelunca, in cujus interiore parte Adam sepultus fuerat, juxta avum patremque sepultus est, loco nomen Arbee, id est, quatuor dedit. Joseph quoque qui typicis mysteriis à gentilibus salvator mundi appellari meruit, & mita sanctitate inter fratres emituit, ossa sua filius Israel ad terram repromissionis vehenda præcepit: quod quidem legislator idcirco minime agere diltulit, quia id haudquaquam contra fidem esse cognovit. Viri itaque sancti corpus qui de Juda ad arguendam nequitiam Irahelitici regis in Bethel venerat, dum propter inobœdientiam, quia cibos civitatis inhibitos sumpsit, à leone fuisset extinctum, ab eodem nimirum leone legitur custoditum, sed culpa inobœdientiæ mortis acerbitate soluta, non præsumpsit crudelis fera sanctum corpus prophetæ contingere, quem atrociter præsumpserat interimere. Prophetes itaque Bethel, nisi sanctis ossibus venerationem exhibendam sciret, nunquam se juxta ossa viri sancti sepeliri præciperet dicens, Sepelite me juxta ossa Prophetæ. Vir itaque sanctus Josias & antequam nasceretur ex nomine nuncuparus, idolorumque dissipator, & paternarum legum strenuus observator duorum prophetarum ossa, cum plurimorum hominum ossa ob altare profanum pollnendum combureret, nequaquam incontaminata servare præciperet, nisi sanctis ossibus venerationem exhibendam sciret. Ecce quibus exemplis, ut cetera taceamus, monstratum est sanctorum cinteribus venerationem exhiberi debere: dicant illi ubi unquam jubeamur imagines adorare. Sanctis ergo corporibus honorem impendere, magnum est fidei emolumentum: quo præsertim & illi in cœlestibus sedibus cum Christo vivere, & eorum ossa quandoque resurrectura creduntur. Imaginibus ergo quæ nec vixisse ... quam creduntur, nec resurrecturæ, sed aut ignibus aut carie consumendæ perhibentur, adorationem soli deo debitam impertire, aut segnitiæ est si utcumque agitur, aut insaniæ vel potius infidelitatis si pertinaciter defenditur. Nos itaque nec cum Vigilantio ejusque sequacibus reliquias abnuentes, nec cum Simone ejusque conplicibus imagines adorantes, & reliquiis sive sanctorum corporibus oportunum obsequium exhibemus, & basilicas prout libet sanctorum imaginibus, sive etiam auro argentove exornamus, & servitium adorationis sive culturæ soli deo cui soli debetur ipso opitulante impendimus.
units.tr: Therefore, just as sacred things are not to be put on a level with images, whether those consecrated by the Lawgiver, or those consecrated by the Mediator between God and men, or even those which every day are consecrated by priests with the invocation of the divine name and taken up into the mystery of our redemption, so likewise the relics of the holy martyrs or confessors, which the faithful hold in veneration out of love for them, are not to be considered equal to images. Those who have burned to adore images try to match them with all consecrated things and mysteries full of sanctity, and they also insolently and absurdly strive to equate them with the relics of the holy martyrs.
