Therefore, when they set out to honour with paintings, sculptures, or carved or cast figures formed by craftsmen of any kind, by placing them on a level with the bodies of the saints, or at least with the remains of their bodies, and with the garments and similar things which the saints used while they lived as mortals, they are shown to do no small injury to the saints. This is especially so since the garments of the saints and similar things are to be venerated for this reason: that they were either on the bodies of the saints or around their bodies, and are believed to have received from them the sanctification for which they are venerated. Also the bodies of the saints, or even the remains of their bodies, although they are confessed to be now reduced to dust, will rise again in glory at the end of the world and will reign with Christ for ever. But the images which those men, with an empty vow, struggle to equal to the things we have mentioned, cannot for that reason be equated with them, since they are neither the bodies of the saints nor were they in or around those most sacred bodies. Rather, according to the skill of each craftsman or the tools of his art, they are made now beautiful, now misshapen, and mostly of impure materials. From this it can be understood that those who try to equate them with the relics of the saints do not err slightly. Therefore antiquity has not without reason admitted that the bodies of the saints are to be venerated and that honour is to be shown to their relics. For Abraham, the father of nations, a man full of faith, outstanding in devotion, pre-eminent in obedience, and vigorous in the precepts of the Lord, is read to have buried his wife not in just any place but in a field carefully bought; and he is read to have had his own bones laid, not in just any place but in the most beautiful cave, in whose innermost part the first-formed man was buried, and to have been entombed there by his sons according to his own command. Isaac also, born of an aged womb, and led to God as a sacrifice in the figure of our Redeemer, and a man famed for holiness and chastity, is believed to have been buried by his sons beside his father, according to his own instruction. Jacob too, a man of great patience, richly strengthened by divine oracles and encouraged by frequent promises, when he wished to escape the want of famine and to see again the dearest pledge which he had believed lost, went down with his illustrious progeny to the Egyptian shores; but he did not allow himself to be buried there. He ordered his body to be carried to the land promised to him and to his fathers, to be buried beside the bones of his father and grandfather. And because he was the fourth to be buried in that cave, in whose innermost part Adam had been buried, beside his grandfather and father, he gave the place the name Arbee, that is, "four". Joseph too, who by the Gentiles deserved to be called salvator mundi by typical mysteries, and who shone among his brothers with singular holiness, commanded the children of Israel to carry his bones to the land of promise. The lawgiver indeed did not delay to do this, because he knew that it was in no way contrary to faith. Likewise, the body of the holy man from Judah, who had come to Bethel to rebuke the wickedness of the king of Israel, when he had been slain by a lion for disobedience, because he had eaten food forbidden in that city, is read to have been guarded by that same lion; but, the sin of disobedience having been expiated by the bitterness of death, the cruel beast did not presume to touch the sacred body of the prophet, whom it had savagely presumed to kill. Therefore the prophet of Bethel, unless he had known that veneration was to be shown to holy bones, would never have ordered himself to be buried beside the bones of the holy man, saying: Bury me beside the bones of the prophet. Likewise the holy man Josiah, who was named by name before he was born, the destroyer of idols and the vigorous keeper of his fathers' laws, when he burned the bones of many men upon the profane altar to defile it, would not have commanded the bones of two prophets to be kept uncorrupted, unless he had known that veneration was to be shown to holy bones. Behold by what examples, to pass over the rest, it has been shown that veneration must be shown to the ashes of the saints; let them say where we are ever commanded to adore images. Therefore to bestow honour on the holy bodies is a great benefit of faith, especially since by it they are believed to live with Christ in the heavenly abodes, and their bones are believed to rise again at some time. But to bestow the adoration due to God alone upon images, which are not believed to have lived ... nor to rise again, but are said to be consumed either by fire or by decay, is either sloth if it is done in any way, or madness, or rather unbelief, if it is stubbornly defended. Therefore we, neither rejecting relics with Vigilantius and his followers, nor adoring images with Simon and his accomplices, pay due reverence to relics, that is, to the bodies of the saints; we adorn churches with images of the saints as we please, or even with gold and silver; and, with his help, we render the service of adoration or worship to God alone, to whom alone it is owed.

units.la: C A P. XXV. Quod non ideo adorandæ sunt imagines quod per eas, ut illi dicunt, nonnulla signa mon- strata fuisse putentur, cum tamen non omnes res adorentur per quas vel in quibus miracula apparent.
units.tr: CHAP. XXV. That images are not to be adored merely because, as they say, certain signs are thought to have been shown through them, since not all things through which, or in which, miracles appear are to be adored.

units.la: HOc etiam illis ad suum errorem adstruendum familiare est, quod per quasdam imagines nonnulla miracula facta fuisse perhibent: quod tamen nec veteris nec novi testamenti pagina demonstrat, quæ quidem & si ipsam visa vel audita fuisse probarentur, dubitandum erat, ne forte tortuosi serpentis flexuosissimis mirandis viderentur vel audirentur: qui cum sit teterrimus & tenebris suæ nequitiæ obsitus, transfigurat se in angelum lucis, audens se dicere lucem. Multa etenim in gna, multaq; miracula, per angelos refugas, vel etiam per eorum sequaces fiunt, qui dum sint spiritales potentiæ, & ut ita dixerim, spiritales nequitiæ, & prophetias infelicibus quibusque impertiunt, & virtutes multas per suos sacrificios faciunt: de quibus erunt illi qui dicturi sunt, Domine domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus, & in nomine tuo damonia ejecimus, & in nomine tuo virtutes multas fecimus: quibus aeternus arbiter dicturus est, Nescio vos. Quia igitur signa plerumque diabolico instinctu fiunt, ideo beatissimus Gregorius sanctus Romanæ ecclesiæ an: estes dixit, Nolite fratres mei amare signa quæ possunt cum reprobis bonis communia. Sanctissimus quoque Augustinus, à dæmonibus miracula hent, similia miraculis quæ habent per sanctos servos dei his verbis testatur, ait enim, Non oportet moveri cum magicis artibus, miracula sint plerumque, similia miraculis quæ fiunt per sanctos servos dei: sicut scriptum est in Exodo, quod Magi Pharaonis fecerunt nonnulla similiter sicut fecit Moyses Non ergo hæc oportet mirari, quia omnia quæ visibiliter fiunt, etiam per infectores potestates actus hujus non absurde fieri posse creduntur. Sed hoc interest, quod cum sancti talia faciunt in nomine dei domini omnium rerum, de sublimioribus apparatibus jubetur inferiori creaturæ; cum autem mali homines magicis artibus operantur similia in manus suas dantur cum exaudiuntur à dæmonibus. Digni sunt enim qui tali exaudltione decipiantur, ut pœna illis fiat hoc quod volentur impetrare beneficium: cum eis exhibeant quasi privatim inferiores potestates quædam miracula, ut eos habeant subjugatos, permissu tamen divino pro meritis animarum suarum cum tribuuntur. Unde signa & miracula quæ illi dicunt in imaginibus apparuisse, si non apparuerunt, licut &c nullis. dell hoc authentica tradit historia, mendacium est, & mendacio quicumque veritatis sunt servi uti non debent: quoniam ut ipsa veritas ait, Nemo potest duobus dominis servire: quae si apparuerunt, & per phantasticas quasdam obumbrationes ad inliciendas mentes apparuerint, periculosissimum est, ne forte callidi satis furaftu antiquus hostis dum mira quaedam demonstrat, ad inlicita petagenda fraudulenter inducat. Si vero apparuerint veritatis signa, quod tamen fieri nullius certis lectionis probatur, & nec mendacio illorum in hac parte sententia subjacet, nec fraudulentis hostis machinationibus secundum exempla quae superius monstrata sunt, sed dei operatione gesta probantur, sunt possibilia, cui nihil impossibile est, animadvertendum fuminopere est, quod cum multa & frequenda nunc dei per quasdam creaturas, vel etiam in quibusque creaturis peracta facta sint, non omnia in quibus vel per quas facta sint adoranda credantur: quoniam quidem omnipotens deus signa pleraque quae mortalibus ostendit, quae per res quasdam visibiles & tractabiles fiunt, quatenus visibilium & mortalium hominum duritiam rebus visibilibus mollirent, non ideo fecit, ut quarundam rerum celebrandam statueret adorationem: quippe qui se solum adorari, solum praestari & colere. Numquidnam quia dominus de rubo in igne Moysi locutus est, ideo rubi adorandi sunt? non enim ideo in rubo apparuit, ut rubi materiam adorandam percenseret, sed ut peccata pro quibus lex venerat demonstraret. Quia ergo rubus radicem non habet, cum in superioribus spinis densetur, in eo evidenter peccata non esse ex natura nominantur. Quare ideo ab igni non est combusta, ut innueret per legem peccata non esse delenda, sed tantummodo ostenderet: lex enim, peccata tantummodo ostendit: gratia autem quae per Christum peccata quae lex monstraverat curavit. Quia ergo in igne dominus apparuit, non ideo igne adorandum decrevit: sed in ea natura apparere voluit, quae semper ad alta conscendere contendit. Quare igitur in monte dignatus est apparere, non montium adorationem creditur statuisse, sed quia immobiliter factum est ut colorum rex in ea re apparuerit quae semper alta appetit, & non in humili, sed in alto loco: ut & se altissimum demonstraret, & suos sequaces ad alta conscensuros evidenter ostenderet. Numquid quia circumcisione acutissimo lapide facta legislator tremendi judicii & mortis interitum evasit, lapides adorandi sunt? Merito enim legislator angelum in se tamen vidit, quia habitans in terra Madian, filium circumcidere neglexit, & qui dei Abrahae populus erat, signum fidei Abrahae in filio non ferebat, in quo gloriari Judaeos sciebat: qui non ideo circumciditur, ut lapidis ex hoc facto adoratio firmetur, sed ut per Christum qui est lapis angularis peccata amputanda & mortis pericula evadenda ostendantur. Numquid quia virga totiens in serpentem conversa, toties legitur in virgae rigore redacta, quae typicis figuris Christum de vita in morte, de morte in vitam redisse ad vitam, aut quia cade virga quam Christi dixinus gestasse figuram maris rubri, aquae unde divisa ad terram repromissionis, id est, ad caelestia regna populo dei pergenti campum praebuit, ideo virgae adorandae sunt? Numquid quia aquae amarae ligno indulcatae legunt, legem non immerito Christi ligno indulcatam, & spiritali dulcedine populorum mentes innuunt, ideo ligna adoranda sunt? Numquid quia serpentis aenei inspectio, qui Christum praefiguravit in ligno populum a serpentum morsibus, id est, ab spiritualium immundorum perculos vulneribus salvavit, ideo aut aes aut serpentes adorandi credantur? Numquid quia petra ex oxuitis in arvis laticum fluenta produxit, & sitientem populum situs ariditate liberavit, quae minimum Christi figuram gessit, qui est lapis de monte abscisus sine manibus praecidentium, qui evangelicae praedicationis fluentis sitim incredulitatis a fidelium mentibus fugat, qui cotidie iuxta fitque venit ad me & bibat, ideo aut lapides credunturne adorari, aut lacues? Numquid quia Joan. 7. virgae Aaron, quia beatae virginis partus innuitur naturali lege calcata, nulla humanae operationis incundata, floruit & fronduit, & protulit nuces, ideo virgae adorandae credantur? Numquid quia Hierobaal sicca area madido vellere, aut madens area sicco vellere apparuit, quae mundi gentilitatem caelesti rore immunem Israelitici solummodo generis, vellus verbi imbre, ac postmodum pro culpa perfidiae eundem populum suae infidelitatis, mundique gentilitatem sacrae fidei rore perfusam significari manifestum est, ideo aut vellera adoranda sunt? Numquid quia Samson mandibula asini mille viros peremit, ejusteque mandibulae molare evulso aquarum fluentis satiatus est, typum gerens nostri mediatoris, qui potestates devicit, & spiritalibus fluentis fidelium, qui utique membra ejus sunt, dentes ornavit, ideo mandibulae, aut molares adorandi sunt? Numquid quia Helias pallio Jordanis, per quod dominicae incarnationis mysterium figuratum est, per quod Jordanis baptismatis videlicet, invertitur. Jordanem divisisse legitur, ideo pallia adoranda creduntur? Numquid quia Naaman Syrus in flumine lavacro leprae contagio ablutus est, per quem gentilitas Christi baptismate ab idolatria contagione abluta figurata est, ideo flumina adoranda sunt? Numquid quia viro sancto Helisaeo Spir. S. adventus eatenus dilatus est, quatenus psaltes applicaretur, applicato vero psaltes spiritus se profudit praecordiis, per quem Judaicus populus significatur qui spiritus sancti adventum nunc minime recepit, quia & incarnatione redemptoris minime in credendo suscepit, quam cum ut ea rationem in numero percepit Spir. S. flamine, & omnium charismatum donis exornari debebit? Numquid ergo quia fimbria dominicae vestis, cujus attactu foemina sanguinis fluxum vestita est, per dominicae incarnationis credulitatem per quam gentilitas sanata est, superna sunt dicimus, ideo fimbriae adorandae sunt? Aut quia Petri umbra infirmi sanati sunt,
units.tr: This also is a familiar argument with them, to support their error, that they report miracles to have been wrought through certain images. Yet neither the page of the Old nor of the New Testament shows this. Even if it were proved that these things had been seen or heard, we would have to fear that they were the crooked and most winding marvels of the twisting serpent, who, being most foul and wrapped in the shadows of his wickedness, transforms himself into an angel of light, daring to call himself light. For many signs and many miracles are done through angels of Satan, or even through their followers, who, being spiritual powers, and, as I may say, spiritual wickednesses, impart prophecies to whomever are unhappy and work many powers through their sacrifices. Of these there will be those who say, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and cast out devils in your name, and done many mighty works in your name? To whom the eternal judge will say, I never knew you. Therefore, since signs are for the most part done by the devil's prompting, the most blessed Gregory, holy teacher of the Roman Church, said: Do not love signs, my brothers, which may be shared by the good with the reprobate. The most holy Augustine too, testifying that miracles are wrought by demons similar to the miracles that are wrought through the holy servants of God, says in these words: One ought not to be moved by magic arts, since they are often similar to miracles that are done through the holy servants of God, as it is written in Exodus, that the magicians of Pharaoh did some things in the same way as Moses did. Therefore we ought not to wonder at these things, since all things that are done visibly, even through hostile powers, are believed not unreasonably to be possible by the working of this kind. But this is the difference: when the saints do such things in the name of God, the Lord of all things, the lower creature is commanded from the higher appearances; but when wicked men work similar things by magic arts, they are given into their hands when they are heard by demons. For those who are deceived by such a hearing are worthy, so that what they wish to obtain becomes a punishment for them, since the lower powers exhibit certain miracles to them, as if privately, so that they hold them in subjection; yet these are granted by the divine permission in accordance with the merits of their souls. Hence, if the signs and miracles which they say have appeared in images did not appear, as authentic history relates nothing of them, it is a lie, and those who are servants of the truth ought not to use a lie, since the truth itself says, No one can serve two masters. But if they did appear, and appeared through certain phantasmal shadows to entice minds, it is most dangerous, lest the ancient enemy, cunning enough in his deceit, while he displays certain marvels, lead people fraudulently to seek unlawful things. But if signs of the truth have appeared, which however is not proved by any certain reading, and if they are not subject to the falsehood of those men in this respect, nor to the fraudulent machinations of the enemy according to the examples shown above, but are proved to have been done by the working of God, and are possible, for nothing is impossible to Him, we must observe most carefully that, although many and frequent works of God have been done through certain creatures, or even in various creatures, not all those things in which or through which they were done are to be believed to be adored. For almighty God, who shows many signs to mortals, which are done through certain visible and tangible things, did so in order to soften the hardness of visible and mortal men by visible things; He did not therefore establish that the adoration of certain things should be celebrated, since He alone wishes to be adored, alone to be served and worshipped. Surely because the Lord spoke to Moses out of the bush in the fire, are bushes therefore to be adored? For He did not appear in the bush so that the matter of the bush should be counted as worthy of adoration, but to show the sins for which the law had come. Since therefore the bush has no root, and is thickened with thorns above, it is evidently named as showing that sins are not of nature. Hence it was not consumed by the fire, to signify that through the law sins are not to be destroyed, but only shown; for the law only shows sins, but grace, which came through Christ, healed the sins which the law had pointed out. Since therefore the Lord appeared in fire, He did not therefore decree that fire is to be adored; but He willed to appear in that nature which always strives to rise to the heights. Why then He deigned to appear on a mountain, it is not believed that He established the adoration of mountains; but because it was fitting that the King of glory should appear in that thing which always seeks the heights, and not in a low place but in a high one, so that He might both show Himself as the Most High and clearly show that His followers would ascend to the heights. Are stones therefore to be adored because the lawgiver, circumcised with a very sharp stone, escaped the destruction of terrible judgment and death? For the lawgiver rightly saw an angel against himself, because, dwelling in the land of Midian, he had neglected to circumcise his son, and he who was the people of God, the God of Abraham, did not bear the sign of Abraham's faith in his son, in which he knew the Jews would glory. He was not circumcised so that the adoration of the stone might be established by this deed, but so that through Christ, who is the chief cornerstone, sins are shown to be cut away and the dangers of death to be escaped. Is a rod to be adored because, as often as it was turned into a serpent, it is read to have been brought back to the stiffness of the rod, which by typical figures showed Christ returning from life to death and from death to life; or because the rod which we say Christ bore was a figure of the Red Sea, the water whence, when it was divided, it afforded to the people of God, travelling to the land of promise, that is, to the heavenly kingdoms, a plain? Are wood and trees to be believed to be adored because it is read that bitter waters were made sweet by wood, which signified that the law, made sweet by the wood of Christ, and the minds of the peoples, with spiritual sweetness, are signified? Is bronze, or are serpents, to be believed to be adored because the look at the bronze serpent, which prefigured Christ on the wood, saved the people from the bites of serpents, that is, from the wounds of spiritual uncleanness? Are stones or pools to be believed to be adored because the rock, struck in the dry places, brought forth streams of water and freed the thirsty people from the dryness of thirst, a rock which bore the least figure of Christ, who is the stone cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut it, who puts to flight the thirst of unbelief from the minds of the faithful by the streams of evangelical preaching, and who daily comes to me and drinks as he comes? Are rods to be believed to be adored because the rod of Aaron, in which the virgin birth of the blessed Virgin is signified, trodden under the natural law, untouched by any human work, flourished and bore leaves and produced nuts? Num. 17. Are fleeces to be believed to be adored because Gideon's fleece appeared wet while the threshing floor was dry, or the threshing floor wet while the fleece was dry, which evidently signified that the Gentile world, free from the heavenly dew, was of the Israelite race alone, and that the fleece, moistened by the rain of the word, and afterwards, on account of the guilt of faithlessness, the same people, and the Gentile world, drenched with the dew of sacred faith, was signified? Are jawbones or molars to be adored because Samson slew a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass, and, when a molar of that jawbone was torn out, was refreshed by the flow of waters, bearing a type of our Mediator, who conquered the powers, and adorned with spiritual streams the teeth of the faithful, who are indeed His members? Are cloaks believed to be adored because it is read that Elijah divided the Jordan with his cloak, by which the mystery of the Lord's incarnation is figured, through which the Jordan, namely of baptism, is turned back? Are rivers to be adored because Naaman the Syrian was cleansed of the contagion of leprosy in the river's washing, by which the Gentile world, washed from the contagion of idolatry by the baptism of Christ, is figured? Is the coming of the Holy Spirit to the holy man Elisha delayed so far that a psaltery was applied, and when the psaltery was applied the Spirit poured itself into the heart, by which the Jewish people is signified, who now by no means receive the coming of the Holy Spirit, because they did not receive the incarnation of the Redeemer in belief, which, if they had received it, they would have been adorned with the flame of the Holy Spirit and the gifts of all the charisms? Therefore if we say that the hem of the Lord's garment, by whose touch the woman with the flow of blood was healed, is above, because through the belief in the Lord's incarnation, by which the Gentile world was healed, are hems therefore to be adored? Or because the shadow of Peter healed the sick, are shadows therefore to be adored?

units.la: sint. sunt, ideo umbrae adorandae sunt: Non igitur, ut superius praemisimus, omnes res per quas vel in quibus miracula quaedam dei ordinatione monstrata sunt, quodammodo adorandae creduntur. Quae res in quibus miracula apparuere adorandae non sunt, multo minus imagines adorandae creditur, in quibus vel per quas quaedam miracula apparuisse, nulla authentica lectione monstratur.
units.tr: are? Or because the sick were healed by the shadow of Peter, are the shadows therefore to be worshipped? Therefore, as we premised above, it is not the case that all things through which, or in which, certain miracles were displayed by a certain ordering of God are believed in some way to be worshipped. Those things in which miracles have appeared are not to be worshipped, and much less is an image believed to be worshipped in which, or through which, certain miracles are shown to have appeared, when no authentic text demonstrates it.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: Quod Theodorus Mirensis episcopus ridiculose & puerliter egerit, qui ut imaginum adorationem adstrueret somnia archidiaconi sui in eadem synodo retulit.
units.tr: That Theodore, bishop of Mira, acted ridiculously and childishly when, to support the adoration of images, he related in the same synod the dreams of his archdeacon.

units.la: CUm in eadem vanitatis lectione quam illi Septimae synodi nuncupatione conseriastuant, nec omnia somniorum imaginationibus & phantasticis quibusdam obumbrationibus firmata sint, & pene nihil sit ibi quod non aut somnii vanitatem, aut alterius cuiusdam delirantis hebitudinem redoleat, cunctaque interiori palato degustata, insapidum insulsumque quendam lapo-rem referant, speciali tamen deliramento Theodorus Mirensis Episcopus somnia Archidiaconi sui ilidem legitur retulisse: ut errorem, quem nec divinarum scripturarum auctoritatibus nec ullis sanctorum patrum doctrinis vel exemplis valuit fulcire, saltem somniorum delusionibus valeret adstruere, nec immerito ad tam frivolum tamque vecors stabiliendum negotium dignum, & pene par exhibet adminiculum. Quanquam igitur somniorum usus nec in totum sit adprobandus, quia plerunque deinonum fallacis exhibetur: nec in toto improbandus, quia interdum per eum quaedam mysteria celantur: ad astruendas tamen res dubias, & ea quae in conventione veniunt adfirmanda, nunquam ii neus invenitur. Quis enim unquam somnio suo rem dubiam valeat adfirmare: cum utrum ita ut se vidisse profatur viderit, nullius rei testis testimonio valeat adprobare. Ad rem ergo dubiam, & quae in quaestionem venit roborandam, non somniorum ludificatrix vanitas, non apocryphorum acerbissima procacitas, nec levium & inurilium verborum sallitas, sed divinorum librorum sive catholicorum patrum authenticae requirenda auctoritas.
units.tr: Since in that reading of vanity, which they call the proceedings of the Seventh Synod, almost everything is built on the imaginings of dreams and certain phantastic shadows, and there is nearly nothing in it that does not smell of the vanity of a dream or of the dullness of some other raving person, and since everything, when tasted by the inner palate, gives off a flat and insipid flavour, Theodore, bishop of Mira, is read to have related in that same place a dream of his archdeacon, in a particular piece of madness. He did this so that he might be able to establish, by the delusions of dreams, an error which he could not support by the authority of the divine Scriptures or by any doctrine or example of the holy Fathers. And not without reason does he offer, for establishing so frivolous and so senseless a business, an aid that is worthy of it and nearly equal to it. Although the use of dreams is not to be approved altogether, because for the most part it is shown to be the deceit of demons, nor is it to be wholly rejected, because at times certain mysteries are hidden in them, yet it is never found to be the proper means for establishing doubtful matters, or for affirming things that are in dispute. For who could ever confirm a doubtful matter by his own dream, since he cannot prove by the testimony of any witness that he saw what he says he saw? Therefore, to strengthen a doubtful matter which has come into question, one must seek not the mocking vanity of dreams, nor the most bitter impudence of apocryphal books, nor the slippery talk of light and useless words, but the authentic authority of the divine books or of the Catholic Fathers.

units.la: {y} Nam licet res profuturae & mysteriorum archanis comptae, cum per somnia untur, per angelos revelantur: ita econtrario, dum res noxiae & omni utilitate carentes per somnia monstrarur, a daemonibus demonstrari creduntur.
units.tr: {y} For although things that will be advantageous, and that are adorned with the secrets of mysteries, are revealed by angels when they are shown through dreams, so conversely, when harmful things devoid of all usefulness are shown through dreams, they are believed to be demonstrated by demons.

units.la: Unde si somnium, quod in synodo retulit, ad imaginum adorationem stabiliendam ab angelo Archidiacono ejus demonstratum est, imagines adorare proficuum est: & si imagines adorare proficuum est, caeteras res sensu carentes adorare proficuum est, aut res sensu carentes adorare noxium: non igitur Archidiacono ejus somnium quod retulit ad imaginum adorationem stabiliendam ab angelo demonstratum est. Liquido namque patet id ei, cum ab angelo monstratum non sit, ab incentore spiritu qui semper vanitatibus & rebus noxiis instat, inlatu fuisse ut lucidius pateat, rationabili argumento firmandum est: quoniam si incentor spiritus id ei minime tulit, angelus proculdubio intulisse credendus est: & si angelus intulisse credendus est, consensum bus prohibitis angeli exhibet. Non aut angeli rebus prohibitis vel noxis seu divinis monitis obnitentibus consensum exhibent: spiritus igitur incentor id ei intulisse credendus est. Cum ergo probatur id ei ab angelo sancto minime fuisse exhibitum, eo quod cum spiritus in sui conditionis laude continua permanentes, & peccato prorsus carentes, res impuras & delictis obnoxias penitus abnuant, restat ut delusione nequissimi spiritus id sibi fateatur exhibitum, aut se prorsus tectum fuisse mentitum, quod utrum servis dei non convenit.
units.tr: Hence, if the dream which he related in the synod, to establish the adoration of images, was shown to his archdeacon by an angel, then it is profitable to adore images; and if it is profitable to adore images, then it is profitable to adore other things lacking sense; or else to adore things lacking sense is harmful. Therefore the dream which he related to establish the adoration of images was not shown by an angel to his archdeacon. For it is clear that, since it was not shown by an angel, it was brought to him by the inciting spirit, who always presses on vanities and harmful things. That this may appear more clearly, it must be confirmed by a reasoned argument: if the inciting spirit did not bring it to him, then an angel must undoubtedly be believed to have brought it; and if an angel is believed to have brought it, then the angel gives his consent to forbidden things. But the angels do not give consent to forbidden or harmful things, nor do they resist divine admonitions. Therefore the inciting spirit must be believed to have brought it to him. Since, then, it is proved that it was in no way shown to him by a holy angel, because the spirits who remain continually in the praise of their condition, and are wholly free from sin, utterly reject impure things and things liable to offence, it remains that he must confess it was shown to him by the delusion of the most wicked spirit, or else he must falsely claim that he was entirely deceived. Which is not fitting for the servants of God.

units.la: Nam & spiritibus inmundis catholico cuique relinquendum est, dicente Apostolo: Resistite Diabolo, & fugiet a vobis: & mendacio spernendum est, dicente scriptura, Nolite velle mentiri omnino, sed diligite caritatem. Probandi interea, juxta Apostoli sententiam, spiritus iunt, an ex doctrina & juxta veritatis voce a fructibus suis cognoscuntur. Unde ex fructu suo quo imaginum adorationem fectat, id somnium fulcire evidentissime deprehenditur ille spiritus qui id intulit, ex deo non esse. Sed forte nostris solummodo argumentationibus hoc videamur edicere, recurramus ad divinas scripturas interrogemus legislatorem, dicat utrum somnia recipienda sint: dicat qualiter nobis erga somnia agendum est. Dic oro sancte Moyses, dic mitissime virorum, dic vir nobilis & archanorum dei strenue instructor, dic vir clementissime, & ineffabilis dei fidelissime interpres, qui legem in monte peccatis contraria & vitiis inimica accipiens, glorificata facie vultu intolerabilem peccatori populo adduxistis, quam deferebas peccatis contraria erat, ita nimirum vultus tuus spectantibus terribilis esset. Dic vir inclite, qui typum veri redemptoris gerens, mediator inter deum & homines extitisti. Da praeceptum utrum quaelibet somnia credenda sint.
units.tr: For a Catholic must also be on guard against unclean spirits, since the Apostle says: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. And a lie is to be rejected, since Scripture says: Do not wish to lie at all, but love charity. Meanwhile, according to the saying of the Apostle, the spirits must be tested, whether they are known by their fruits according to doctrine and the voice of truth. Hence, from the fruit that it produces, namely the adoration of images, it is most evidently plain that the spirit which brought that dream is not from God. But perhaps we seem to say this only from our own arguments. Let us have recourse to the divine Scriptures and question the lawgiver: let him say whether dreams are to be received, and let him say how we ought to act towards dreams. Tell us, I pray you, holy Moses; tell us, most gentle of men; tell us, noble man and strenuous instructor of the secrets of God; tell us, most merciful man and most faithful interpreter of the ineffable God, who, receiving the law on the mountain, which was contrary to sins and hostile to vices, with your face glorified, you brought an intolerable countenance to the sinful people, for the law you carried was contrary to sins, so that your face would be terrible to those who looked upon it. Tell us, illustrious man, who bore the type of the true Redeemer and became mediator between God and men. Give the precept: whether any dreams whatever are to be believed.

units.la: Fare utrum quibuslibet inlusionibus consensus exhibendum sit: Surrexerit in medio tui propheta, aut somniator qui somnium vidisse se dicat, & praedixerit signum aliquod atque portentum, & evenerit quod locutus est, & dixerit tibi, Veni & sequamur deos alienos quos ignoras, non audiendas verba prophetae illius aut somniatoris, quia tentat vos dominus deus vester, ut palam faciat utrum diligatis eum ex toto corde vestro an non.
units.tr: Say whether consent is to be given to any illusions whatever: If there arise in the midst of you a prophet, or a dreamer who says that he has seen a dream, and he foretells some sign or wonder, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, Come, and let us follow other gods whom you do not know, you shall not hear the words of that prophet or that dreamer, for the LORD your God tests you, to know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul.

units.la: Ecce legislatoris auctoritate perdocemur quod verba somniatorum, quanquam efficaces habeant, non adtendantur. Dicat nunc Sapientia, quid de somniis sentiat. Ait enim: Ubi multa somnia, plurima vanitates, & sermones innumeri: tu vero deum time.
units.tr: Behold, by the authority of the lawgiver we are taught that the words of dreamers, although they may have some efficacy, are not to be attended to. Now let Wisdom say what she thinks of dreams. For she says: For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities; but fear thou God.

units.la: Nam & Aegyptios somnia pertur-bantur, dicentes scriptura, Somnia enim quae illos turbaverunt; haec significabant, ne in fucu ellent quaedam ... pateretur. Manifestum est enim divinae legis auctoritatibus somnia & augurial vana esse: & quanto quis ea amplius timuerit, tanto cor ejus amplius fallit. Unde modis omnibus reprehendendum vimus, quae praefatus Episcopus, cum divinae legis armis contra somniatores vel caeteras nugas confirmare dnm erat, somnia Archidiaconi sui ad rem inutilem roborandam in synodo retulit. Haec enim pendenda non solum divinae legis oraculis, sed & in ipsis gentilium reperitur litteris. Ait enim plius Cato, Somnia ne cures: nam mens humana quod optat,Cum vigilat, sperat, per somnum cernit idipsum.
units.tr: For the Egyptians were also troubled by dreams, as Scripture says: For the dreams which troubled them signified these things, lest they should be deceived by certain ... they should suffer. It is clear, then, from the authority of the divine law, that dreams and auguries are vain; and the more anyone fears them, the more his heart is deceived by them. Hence we have seen that the aforesaid bishop acted in every way reprehensibly, when, having to confirm against dreamers and other trifles with the weapons of the divine law, he related in the synod the dreams of his archdeacon to establish a useless matter. For these things are to be weighed not only by the oracles of the divine law, but they are also found in the writings of the Gentiles. For the poet Cato says: Do not heed dreams: for the human mind, what it desires, while awake, it hopes for; and in sleep it sees the very same thing.

units.la: Nam si quis forte nobis succenfere nitatur, eo quod gentilium verba nostro inseruimus operi, legat primum libros beatissimorum atq; eruditiffimorum virorum, Hieronymi sive Augustini, & mox ut in illorum opusculis, non solu philosophorum, sed etiam poetarum gentilium quaedam verba repererit, nos magistros & auctores, quorum vestigia sequimur, habere cognoscer: cum quibus nec culpari abnuimus, nec reprehendi erubescimus. Nam ut altius repetamus, vas etiam electionis quiddam de gentilium verbis sūs inseruit operibus, ut est illud, Cretenses semper mendaces, mala bestia, ventres pigri. Praeterea cum somniorum observationes, vel potius vanitates discutimus, non penitus illorum usum abdicandum esse testamur: cum & patriarchis & prophetis, quaedam sacratissima mysteria in somnis, vel potius in visionibus monstrata sint: & Magi tres in somnis moniti ne ad truculentum redirent tyrannum, alterius callis transirent terentes proprias repedaverunt ad sedes, & viro sancto Joseph in somnis angelus apparuisse, & eiusmodi mysteriorum archana multis retro seculis a prophetis adnuntiata legitur demonstrasse. Unde ne quisquis, & his similibus exemplis somniorum insolenter appetat usum, & eas sequi vel credere, vel inconvenientibus recitare, aut ab his more Theodori res in contentione venientes adfirmare praesumat, idcirco est ut paulo superius praemiserimus, a sanctis scripturis prohibitum. Legimus etiam infidelibus accepta s quibusq; regibus quaedam archana per somnia demonstrata, quae non illis revelata sunt ullis propter illorum meritorum praerogativas, sed ut vni sancti qui ea illis Spir. S. revelante monstravere, honoribus biblia rentur, & suis valerent prodesse concaptivis. Quamquam ergo & visiones & somnia mixtim dici consuetudo admiserit: inter visiones vero & somnia hoc quidam distare dicunt, q somnia ea sunt quae plerunq; falluntur: veniunt ergo nonnunquam ex revelatione, multoties vero aut ex cogitatione, aut ex tentatione, aut ex aliquibus his similibus. Visiones vero dicunt, quasdam veraciores revelationes: quarum tria sunt genera, corporale videlicet, & spiritale, sive etiam intellectuale. Corporale igitur est, q fit per corpus: spiritale, cum imagines eorum quae videmus, in memoria condimus: intellectuale nempe, cum ea quae corporaliter videmus, & imaginaliter in memoria retinemus, intellectu discernimus. Intellectu igitur discernimus, q illud sit corpus, illud similitudo corporis. Hunc quoque intellectu bestiae & pecora atq; volatilia nullatenus habent. Vident & ipsa per corpus, & eorum q videntimaginaliter spiritus informantur: unde & pecora praesepia recognoscunt, & aves ad nidos suos redeunt: sed nec seipsa intellegunt, nec illa quae oculis cernunt. Postremo corporalis ista visio, sine spiritali esse non potest. Ergo cum a vertimus oculos ab eis quae vidimus, imagines eorum q non videmus, in memoria retinemus. Spiritalis vero visio sine corporali esse non potest: unde absentes homines recordamur, & in tenebris ea q non videmus, imaginaliter cernimus. Intellectualis nempe nec corporaliger, nec spiritali. Intellectu nec corpus videmus, nec imaginem corporis: per hunc quippe videmus iustitia, charitas, ipse deus, ipsa mens hominis quae nullum corpus habet, nullam soliditatem corporis. Hic interponendum de quinq; generibus visionum, juxta Theodosium Macrobium. Cum ergo omniorum ae visionum tot tantaq; sint genera e diversis partibus venientia, solenter intuendum est ne illum quis quid se in somnis vidisse cognoscit, statim ea firmiter teneat, atque ad res dubias deliberandas quasi quandam authenticam authoritatem in synodo proferat: ne dum vanitatem vanitaubus confirmare conatur, ipse, quod absit, in vanitatem labatur.
units.tr: For if anyone should perhaps try to be angry with us because we have inserted words of the Gentiles into our work, let him first read the books of the most blessed and most learned men, Jerome or Augustine. And as soon as he finds in their little works certain words not only of the philosophers but also of the Gentile poets, he will know that we have as masters and authors those whose footsteps we follow, and with whom we neither refuse to be blamed nor are ashamed to be reprehended. For, to go back further, the vessel of election also inserted something from the words of the Gentiles into his works, as in that saying: The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies. Moreover, when we examine the observances of dreams, or rather their vanities, we testify that their use is not to be wholly renounced: since certain most sacred mysteries were shown in dreams, or rather in visions, both to the patriarchs and to the prophets; and the three Magi, warned in dreams not to return to the cruel tyrant, went back to their own homes by another road; and an angel is read to have appeared in a dream to the holy man Joseph; and the secrets of such mysteries are read to have been announced by the prophets many ages earlier. Therefore, lest anyone, following these and similar examples, presume insolently to seek the use of dreams, and either to follow or believe them, or to apply them to unsuitable matters, or to affirm from them, in the manner of Theodore, matters that are in dispute, it is for this reason that, as we set forth a little above, it is forbidden by the holy Scriptures. We also read that certain secrets were shown in dreams to unbelieving kings, which were not revealed to them because of any privilege of their merits, but so that the holy men who revealed them to them by the Holy Spirit might be honoured and might be able to benefit their fellow captives. Although, therefore, common custom has allowed visions and dreams to be spoken of together, some say that between visions and dreams there is this difference: that dreams are those things which are for the most part deceptive; they come sometimes from revelation, but very often from thought, or from temptation, or from some such things. Visions, on the other hand, they call somewhat truer revelations, of which there are three kinds: namely corporeal, spiritual, and also intellectual. The corporeal is that which comes through the body; the spiritual is when we store in memory the images of the things we see; the intellectual is when, by understanding, we discern those things which we see bodily and retain in memory as images. By understanding, then, we discern that one is the body and that other is the likeness of the body. Beasts, cattle and birds have no such understanding at all. They see also through the body, and by what they see their spirits are shaped as images; hence cattle recognise the mangers, and birds return to their nests; but they understand neither themselves nor the things they see with their eyes. Lastly, that corporeal vision cannot exist without the spiritual. Therefore, when we turn our eyes away from the things we have seen, we retain in memory the images of things we do not see. The spiritual vision, however, cannot exist without the corporeal: hence we remember absent men, and in the darkness we picture by imagination the things we do not see. The intellectual, indeed, is neither corporeal nor spiritual. By the understanding we see neither the body nor the image of the body; for through this we see justice, charity, God himself, and the mind of man itself, which has no body and no bodily solidity. Here is to be inserted something about five kinds of visions, according to Theodosius Macrobius. Therefore, since there are so many and such great kinds of dreams and visions coming from different parts, one must take care that, when someone recognises that he has seen something in a dream, he does not immediately hold it firmly and bring it forward in a synod as some authentic authority for deliberating doubtful matters; lest, while he tries to confirm vanity by vanities, he himself, which God forbid, should fall into vanity.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Quod & in deus inlocalis sit, illi minus docte dixerint, Veneramur & adoramus sicut locum dei.
units.tr: That God is also without place; those less learned men said, "We venerate and adore [images] as the place of God."

units.la: Icunt etiam venerandas & adorandas imagines sicut locum dei: q si pro templo dei dicunt, q plerumq; abusive locus dei dicitur, vehementer errant. In templo enim domini sacrificia, non in imaginibus, offerunt; nec in templo, non in picturis, nullarum solennia celebrarentur: in templo ... ...
units.tr: They also say that images are to be venerated and adored as the place of God. If they mean the temple of God, which is often called the place of God in an improper sense, they err greatly. For sacrifices of the Lord are offered in the temple, not in images; and solemn rites of no kind were ever celebrated in the temple by means of pictures: in the temple ... ...

units.la: Quantum enim distat inter templum q multorum hominum capax est, & imaginem quae iter memoriam visionis quam intuentibus infert, nullis est congrua officiis, tantum distare venerationem sive adorationem imaginum, a veneratione, quae templo dei exhibetur, multis patet indiciis.
units.tr: For how greatly the temple, which can hold many people, differs from an image, which brings to those who look at it only the memory of a sight and is fit for no duties, that the veneration or adoration of images is as far from the veneration shown to the temple of God as can be, is plain from many indications.

units.la: Vero locum dei animam justi hominis dicunt, quae familiarius locus dei dici potest, quam dominus sanctificando inhabitat, & inhabitando sanctificat, in hoc quoque vehementissime errant. Pro salute animarum non pro salute imaginum deus legem dedit: ad liberandas animas, non ad imagines tempt ormundi ad terras descendit: propter homines quia animatum nomine plerumq; tropice denantur, non propter imagines quae ab artificibus formantur, patri dixit, Quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi ego, & ipsi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam quam dedisti mihi, quia dilexisti me. Cum igitur deus omnium hominibus naturalem legem dederit, quae ab hominibus corrupta, dederit postea scriptam: etiam violata sese per praesentiam corporalem videndum exhibuerit, & ante legem, & sub lege gratia semper humanae saluti ctedatur constituisse: nunquam ut piam tale aliquid imaginis credidit constituisse. Ac per hoc veneration quae hominibus charitatis causa est exhibenda, imagi-ne venerat ratio nullatenus est coarquanda. Hoc quidem de loco dei, aut de templo quod abutive, aut de animarum de anima hominis justi, quæ convenientius locus dei dicitur, quibus nullatenus imagines secundum illorum vesaniam coæquandæ sunt, breviter dixisse sufficiat. Cæterum de loco dei qui localis non est, qui loco non continetur, qui omnia continet, & locus non est, cui nihil de sex illis partibus loci adest, cui nihil anterius posteriusve, dexterius aut sinistrius, superius vel inferius est, disputare subtile intelligentiæ est. Quamquam igitur decem illorum prædicamentorum, quæ à philosophis pertractantur, ordo de eo videatur adscribi, ut pro οὐσίᾳ ejus, quæ ineffabilis est, dicatur dominus deus, deus numinis, deus fortis, deus potens: pro quantitate ejus quæ immensa est, a magnus dominus & laudabilis valde, pro qualitate ejus quæ inenarrabilis est, dicatur b bonus omnium conditor: pro relatione dicatur c dominus omnium in secredentium pater: pro situ, d qui sedes super cherubim: pro tempore, e & annui tui non defuerunt: pro loco, f dominus in cælo paravit sedem suam: pro habitu, g abyssus sicut pallium amictus ejus: pro aegritudine, h sicut ... à terra inopem & de stercore exaltat pauperem: pro pati, laborare me fecistis in peccatis vestris: tamen haec omnia & his similia humano more de deo, de quo nihil digne dici à mortalibus potest, dicta monstruosa sunt.
units.tr: But they say that the soul of a just man is the place of God, and it can more fittingly be called the place of God, since the Lord dwells in it by sanctifying it and, by dwelling in it, sanctifies it; in this too they err most grievously. God gave the law for the salvation of souls, not for the salvation of images; he came down to earth in the fulness of time for the liberation of souls, not of images, for the sake of men, and the word "animated" is often used figuratively of them, not of images formed by craftsmen. He said to the Father: "Those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which you have given me, because you have loved me." Since God gave the natural law to all men, which men corrupted, and afterwards gave it in writing, and, when that was violated, showed himself to be seen in bodily presence, and before the law and under the law always provided for human salvation by grace, he never thought fit to establish anything of this kind of images as pious. And therefore the veneration which is to be shown to men out of charity must in no way be equated with the veneration of images. It is enough to have said this briefly about the place of God, or the temple, which is so called improperly, or about the soul of the just man, which is more fittingly called the place of God, and to which images by no means are to be equated according to their madness. But to discuss the place of God, who is not local, who is contained by no place, who contains all things and is not a place, to whom nothing belongs of those six parts of place, to whom nothing is before or after, right or left, above or below, is a subtle matter of understanding. Although, then, the order of those ten categories, which the philosophers treat, seems to be applied to him, so that for his substance, which is ineffable, it is said "Lord God, God of might, strong God, powerful God"; for his quantity, which is immense, "great Lord and greatly to be praised"; for his quality, which is inexpressible, it is said "good creator of all"; for relation, "Lord of all, Father of the ages"; for situation, "who sits upon the cherubim"; for time, "and your years shall not fail"; for place, "the Lord has prepared his throne in heaven"; for condition, "the deep is his garment as a mantle"; for affliction, "as ... raises the poor from the dust and the needy from the dunghill"; for suffering, "you have made me labour with your sins"; yet all these things, and things like them, said of God in a human manner, of whom nothing worthy can be said by mortals, are monstrous expressions.

units.la: Est enim substantia nulli ad indagandum facilis, & ideo ineffabilis, quia nulli invesigabilis. Eiusmodi quantitate magnus, sine qualitate bonus, sine relatione omnium dominus, & cætera his similia, quæ uberioris disputationis materiam quærunt. Nam ut de loco dei aliquid dicamus, sancti Augustini vestigia ponenda sunt, qui deum illocalem esse unius tantummodo quinque partium syllogismo perplexum probavit. Ait enim; Deus non alicubi est: quod alicubi est enim continetur loco: quod continetur loco est. Deus autem non est corpus: non igitur alicubi est. Ubi in sequentibus in alio syllogismo probavit cum locum non esse, & omnia in illo esse. Ait enim, Et tamen quia est & in loco non est, in illo sunt potius omnia quam ipse alicubi: nec tamen ita in illo ut ipse sit locus. Locus enim in spacio est quod longitudine, latitudine, altitudine corporis occupatur: nec deus tale aliquid est: & omnia igitur in ipso sunt, & locus non est. Ubi in sequentibus perpendicut vo decentissimo commate, locum dei abusive dici asserunt templum dei, sed animam hominis mente posse dici: Locus tamen dei, inquit, abusive dicitur templum dei, non quod continetur, sed quod ei praesens sit, tamen nihil melius quam anima munda intelligitur. Cum igitur illa ita venerandas dicant imagines, ut cum dei, an pio templo dei, an pro anima justi hominis hoc dicant, utrumque non convenit. Si vero eo verbo aliquid de deo locale sentiunt, multum illorum sensus à veritate dissentit. Nos ergo ut pote cogitationum ignari, cum quo affectu quove sensu hoc dixerint nescimus, ea tantum discutimus quæ apicum indicio percepimus.
units.tr: For the substance is not easy for anyone to investigate, and therefore it is ineffable, because it cannot be searched out by anyone. Of such a kind is the one who is great in quantity, good without quality, Lord of all without relation, and other things like these, which call for a fuller discussion. To say something about the place of God, we must follow the footsteps of St Augustine, who proved by a single syllogism of five parts that God is not in place. For he says: "God is not somewhere; what is somewhere is contained by a place; what is contained by a place is a body. But God is not a body; therefore he is not somewhere." Where in what follows he proved by another syllogism that God is not a place and that all things are in him. For he says: "And yet, because he is and is not in a place, all things are in him rather than he is somewhere; nor is he in him in such a way that he himself is a place." For a place is a space occupied by the length, breadth and height of a body; God is not any such thing; therefore all things are in him, and he is not a place. Where in what follows they argue in a most fitting sentence that the place of God is called the temple of God improperly, but that it can be called the soul of a man: "Yet the place of God," he says, "is called the temple of God improperly, not because it is contained, but because he is present to it"; yet nothing is understood better than a pure soul. Therefore, since they say that images are to be venerated in such a way that they say this either of the temple of God or of the soul of a just man, neither applies. If indeed by that word they mean something local about God, their meaning differs far from the truth. We, therefore, being ignorant of their thoughts, do not know with what feeling or meaning they said this, and we discuss only those things which we have perceived from the marks of the letters.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: Inutile & demens & errore plenum dictum quod dicunt, Qui deum timet hono- rat omnino, adorat & veneratur sicut filium dei Christum deum nostrum, & signum crucis ejus, & figuram sanctorum ejus.
units.tr: The saying they use, that he who fears God honours wholly, adores and venerates as the Son of God, Christ our God, and the sign of his cross and the figure of his saints, is useless, foolish and full of error.

units.la: EST quoque & in hoc insanissimum & ab omni penitus cautela remotum quod dicunt, Qui deum timet, honorat omnino, adorat seu veneratur sicuti filium dei & signum crucis ejus, & figuram sanctorum ejus. Quantum ergo distet mysterium dominicæ crucis, ad quod intelligendum revelatos nos habere oculos Apostolus, ut intellegamus quæ sit altitudo, & longitudo, & latitudo crucis Christi, & profundum, in superioribus hujus operis partibus, domino opitulante monstratum est: & quantum distet adoratio, & cultura soli deo debita ab adoratione & cultura quam illi imaginibus exhibent, asseverant, in hoc tertio libro verba Constantini Constantiæ Cypri Episcopi, seu Eutimii Sardensis Episcopi, discuteremus, prout nobis dominus opem ferre dignatus est, differimus: nunc vero quantum timor domini ab adoratione imaginum distet, breviter domino auxiliante disseramus. Dicunt enim, Qui timet deum, adorat omnino imagines sicut filium dei. Numquidnam omnes patriarchæ & prophetæ, quia imaginum adorationem sprevere, ideo deum credendi sunt non timuisse? aut Apostoli, quia nusquam leguntur celebrasse imaginum adorationem, ideo dei non habuisse dicendi sunt timorem aut sanctorum martyrum, anachoritarum, seu etiam cunctorum generaliter ecclesiasticorum virorum turbæ, quos constat in dei servitio devotissime militasse, ideo timorem domini putandi sunt non habuisse, eo quod imaginum adorationem nusquam leguntur vel probantur celebrasse? Non enim sanctissimus vatum David adorationem imaginum se docturum, sed dei timorem docebat, cum omnes in Christi persona filios nuncupans blandis exhortationibus ad se venire hortabatur dicens; Venite filii, audite me, timorem domini docebo vos. Nec suspiam imaginum cultum, sed timorem domini sanctum testatur dicens; Timor domini sanctus permanens in saeculum saeculi. Nec quempiam qui imagines adorat, sed qui deum timet beatum nuncupat dicens, Beatus vir qui timet dominum, in mandatis ejus cupiet nimis: & iterum, Beati omnes qui timent dominum, qui ambulant in viis ejus. Non enim ait, ut abs furdissime delirant, Qui timet dominum, adorat imagines, sed ait, Qui timet dominum, in mandatis ejus cupiet nimis. Unde liquidissime patet timorem domini non in adoratione imaginum, sed in luntate & instantia mandatorum dei esse. Non enim idem sanctus vir oculos domini super timentes eum, & in eos qui sperant in misericordia ejus, nec ait, Adorate imagines, quoniam nihil deest adorantibus eas, sed ait, Timete dominum omnes sancti ejus, quoniam nihil deest timentibus eum: sed neque initium sapientiae imaginum adorationem, sed domini testatur timorem dicens, Initium sapientiae timor domini.
units.tr: There is also in this the most insane saying, and one wholly lacking any caution, which they say: He who fears God honours wholly, adores or venerates as the Son of God and the sign of his cross and the figure of his saints. How far the mystery of the Lord's cross is removed from this, which the Apostle says we have eyes revealed to understand, that we may grasp what is the height, length, breadth and depth of the cross of Christ, has been shown in the earlier parts of this work, with the Lord's help. How far the adoration and worship owed to God alone is from the adoration and worship which they give to images, they assert; we will discuss the words of Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, or of Eutymius, bishop of Sardis, in this third book, as the Lord deigns to help us, and we defer that. Now, with the Lord's help, we shall briefly argue how far the fear of the Lord is from the adoration of images. For they say: He who fears God adores images wholly, as the Son of God. Are we to think that all the patriarchs and prophets did not fear God, because they rejected the adoration of images? Or that the Apostles had no fear of the Lord, because they are nowhere read to have practised the adoration of images? Or that the multitudes of holy martyrs, anchorites, and indeed all churchmen in general, who are known to have served God most devotedly, lacked the fear of the Lord, because they are nowhere read or shown to have practised the adoration of images? For the most holy of the prophets, David, did not teach the adoration of images, but taught the fear of God, when, calling all the sons in the person of Christ, he exhorted them with gentle words to come to him, saying: Come, sons, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Nor does he bear witness to the worship of images, but to the holy fear of the Lord, saying: The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever. Nor does he call blessed anyone who adores images, but him who fears God, saying: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he shall greatly delight in his commandments; and again: Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. For he does not say, as they rave most absurdly, He who fears the Lord adores images, but he says, He who fears the Lord greatly delights in his commandments. Whence it is most clearly evident that the fear of the Lord lies not in the adoration of images, but in the delight and diligence of God's commandments. For the same holy man does not say: The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy; nor: Adore images, for nothing is lacking to those who adore them; but he says: Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for nothing is lacking to those who fear him. Nor does he testify that the beginning of wisdom is the adoration of images, but the fear of the Lord, saying: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

units.la: Pfal. 34. Quod quidem praeceptum Dominici timoris ita per Moysen legitur institutum; Post Dominum Deum vestrum, inquit, pergite, & ipsum timete, & praecepta ejus custodite, & vocem ejus audite, & adhaerescite ei. Inter quae salutaria praecepta nusquam imaginum adoratio legitur instituta. Cum ergo imaginum adoratio in divinis eloquiis inveniatur prohibita, timori Domini qui tot divinae legis oraculis commendatur, nullatenus est coaequanda. Flores igitur quibus timor Domini haberi jubetur, quos per vastissimos divinae legis campos inpigro ungue decerpsimus, ordo exposcit ut sub brevitate digeramus, quibus & lectoris animus mulceatur, etsi quis illis rerum sensu carentium adorationem aequare conatur, pudore & reverentia indui cogatur. In Proverbiis namque dicitur; Timor Domini adiicit dies: anni autem impiorum minuentur. Item in Proverbiis; b Munitio justi, timor Domini: contritio autem operantibus mala.
units.tr: Ps. 34. This precept concerning the fear of the Lord is thus laid down through Moses: Go after the Lord your God, he says, and fear him, and keep his precepts, and hear his voice, and cleave to him. Among these saving precepts, the adoration of images is nowhere laid down. Since, therefore, the adoration of images is found forbidden in the divine oracles, it must in no way be equated with the fear of the Lord, which is commended by so many oracles of the divine law. The order of our work requires us to set out briefly the flowers by which the fear of the Lord is commanded to be held, which we have plucked with a nimble hand from the vast fields of the divine law, so that the reader's mind may be soothed, and so that, if anyone tries to equate adoration with those things which lack sense, he may be compelled to be clothed in shame and reverence. For in Proverbs it is said: The fear of the Lord adds days, but the years of the wicked shall be shortened. Again in Proverbs: The fortress of the just is the fear of the Lord, but destruction awaits those who work evil.
