units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: Dementissimum & ratione carens dictum Johannis presbyteri orientalium, in eo quod ait, quod non adsistente imperatore imago ejus honoratur: non enim inhonoratur, quatenus & nunc dominatorem omnium Iesum Christum visibiliter nobis non apparentem, invisibilis enim est carnalibus nostris oculis: sicut enim Deus ubique inest honorandam ejus imaginem, sicuti & imperatorem pater sensit.
units.tr: The most senseless and irrational saying of John the presbyter of the Orientals, that when the emperor is not present his image is honoured. For it is not dishonoured, since even now we do not see Jesus Christ, Lord of all, visibly present to us, for he is invisible to our carnal eyes. Just as God is present everywhere, so his image is to be honoured, as the Father also understood with regard to the emperor.

units.la: Deo quod generaliter omnes aut dixisse aut dicentibus consensisse perhibentur, quod exemplo imperialium imaginum, quas in civitates emissas obviant cunei populorum cum cereis & thymiamatibus, imago quoque salvatoris sive sanctorum omnium adoranda sit, in praeceptis jam disputatum est, & quia judicum & imperatorum imagines ex quibus illi exempla sumuntur, adorandae non sint, beati Hieronymi verbis adprobatum est. Nunc autem specialiter Johannis discutienda sunt, qui in hoc negotio reperitur & crebrius caeteris locutus fuisse, & minus delirasse: quoniam quidem quamquam generalem omnium errorem sequatur, speciale tamen aliquid eidem errori augere conatur, & ut reor, generalibus nugis ideo suas magis multiplicare nugas adsociare curavit: quia omnium vanitates huic tanto errori adcumulando sufficere nunquam credidit. Quasi igitur imperatoris modo deus localis sit, & dum uno loco est alio esse nequeat, idcirco ejus imaginem sicut imaginem imperatoris adorandam adstruere affectat: quod penitus omni ratio vetat. Deus enim nusquam absens est: qui si usquam absens est, localis est: si localis est, nec omnia continet, nec omnia implet. Omnia autem & complet, & implet: nusquam igitur absens est, quae dum ita se habeant, non est in materialibus imaginibus adorandus vel quaerendus, sed in corde mundissimo semper habendus. Nam dum imperatoris imaginem adorare perversum, ejusdem quoque imaginem qui localis est, imagini Dei qui inlocalis est adsimilare profanum sit, illum procul dubio profanum & perversum esse constat, qui a re inlicita rem inlicitam corroborare affectat, & errorem passibus quasi quibusdam gradibus dum suae mentis seu linguae moderamen habere neququam enerviter, pro dolor, ad deteriora decurrit. Quod autem ait, Christi imaginem honorandam sicut & imaginem imperatoris pater fecit, quaerendum est, ubi, aut quando, aut quur, aut quemadmodum hoc fecerit, aut quid fit, fecit. Numquidnam cum ab alio jussum esset, aut ab aliis fieret, ita patet sensit? Quia ergo nos non eorum errores qui in verbis sunt discurrimus, quod immensum esset, & peragendum difficile, quippe cum pene nullus ibi verborum ordo sensum legenti adferat: sed earum solummodo sensus seu sententias reprehendendo percurramus: restat ut non quid dicant, sed praesertim ita ut dictum est, nullum pene sensum habeat, sed quid dicere velint perstractemus. Quod ait honorandam ejus imaginem sicut & imperatorem pater fecit, hunc vult habere sensum, ut dicat, Pater jussit imaginem Christi adorare sicuti Imperatorem. Quod quidem ubi, quando, quur, quemadmodum gestum sit, ab omni penitus catholico ignoratur. Non enim pater imaginem ejus, sed ipsum eundemque honorare & audire jussit, cum ad fluenta Jordanis sancta trinitas in unitate substantiae, pater videlicet in voce qua intonuit, Hic est filius meus dilectus in quo mihi bene complacui, ipsum audite, filius in corpore, spiritus vero sanctus in specie columbae mirabiliter claruit. Esto, pater juberet honorandam Christi imaginem sicut imperatorem, numquid non rectius esset imperatorem honorandum decernere, sicuti imaginem Christi, ut imago Christi eminentiorem in tali ratione locum teneret non ergo pater imaginem Christi quoquam legitur aut depingere aut adorare aut honorare jussit, quippe qui se solum adorari sibique soli servire instituit. Quia ergo imperatores & reges sinte divinis honorandi quibusdam divinae Scripturae exemplis potest adprobari. Si enim honorandi nunc essent, nequaquam David, vir sanctus Saulem, postquam Deus ab eo recessserat, Christum Domini vocatet. Non enim erat nescius praefatus vir divinam esse dispensationem in officio ordinis legis: idcirco Saulem in eadem adhuc dignitate positum honorificat, ne Deo injuriam facere videretur, qui his ordinibus inperiendum honorem decrevit. Quam diu ergo in ea dignitate est, honorandus est, si non propter se, vel propter ordinem. Unde & Apostolus, Omnibus, inquit, potestatibus sublimioribus subditi estote. Non est enim potestas nisi a Deo. & in alio loco, Deum timete, regem honorificate. Ulterius non nisi ex hac ratione disputatio oriri poterat, sed quia jam aliquantulum ex ea in superioribus huius peris est partibus disputatum, nobis nunc est his praetermissis ad alia transeundum.
units.tr: As for the view that all, or those who agree with them, are generally said to have held, namely that, by the example of imperial images, which the crowds meet with wedges of people bearing candles and incense when they are sent out into the cities, the image of the Saviour or of all the saints is to be worshipped, this has already been discussed in the earlier sections. And that the images of judges and emperors, from which they take their examples, are not to be worshipped, has been proved by the words of blessed Jerome. But now John's own views must be examined in particular. He is found in this matter, and he spoke more often than the others and raved less. For although he follows the general error of all, he nonetheless tries to add something special to that same error, and, as I suppose, he took care to join his own trifles to the general nonsense, because he never believed that the vanities of everyone else were enough to pile upon so great an error. As if, then, God were local in the way an emperor is, and could not be in one place while he is in another, therefore he is eager to assert that God's image is to be worshipped just as the emperor's image is. Reason utterly forbids this. For God is nowhere absent. And if he is absent anywhere, he is local; if he is local, he neither contains all things nor fills all things. But he both contains and fills all things; therefore he is nowhere absent. Since these things stand so, he is not to be worshipped or sought in material images, but is always to be held in the purest heart. For while it is perverse to worship the emperor's image, it is profane to liken the image of him who is local to the image of him who is not local. It is beyond doubt that he is profane and perverse who seeks to strengthen an unlawful thing by an unlawful thing, and who, as if by certain steps, runs headlong, alas, into worse things, having, to no avail, no restraint over the government of his mind or tongue. As for his saying, the Father made the image of Christ to be honoured just as the image of the emperor, it must be asked where, when, why, or in what manner he did this, or what is meant by "made." Did he perhaps perceive it in this way when it was commanded by another, or when others were doing it? Since, therefore, we do not run through the errors of his words, which would be immense and hard to finish, since there is almost no order of words there that gives the reader any sense, but only run through their meanings and opinions in refuting them, it remains that we set out not what they say, but what they wish to say. Especially so, since, as has been said, the statement has almost no sense at all. What he says, the Father made his image to be honoured just as the emperor, he means in this sense: that the Father commanded the image of Christ to be worshipped as the emperor is. Where, when, why, and in what manner this was done is entirely unknown to every catholic. For the Father did not command his image, but him, and to hear him, when at the waters of the Jordan the holy Trinity, one in substance, shone forth wonderfully: the Father, namely, in the voice with which he thundered, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him; the Son in the body; and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. Granted that the Father commanded Christ's image to be honoured as the emperor, would it not be more right to decree that the emperor be honoured just as Christ's image is, so that the image of Christ might hold a more eminent place in such a rank? Therefore the Father is nowhere read to have commanded the image of Christ to be painted, or adored, or honoured, since he established that he alone is to be adored and that he alone is to be served. Therefore, that emperors and kings are to be honoured, as they are divine, can be proved by certain examples from divine Scripture. For if they were now to be honoured, David, a holy man, would by no means have called Saul the Lord's anointed after God had withdrawn from him. For that man was not ignorant that the arrangement of the office of the order of the law was divine. Therefore he honours Saul, still placed in the same dignity, lest he seem to do injury to God, who decreed that honour be rendered to these orders. So long, then, as he is in that dignity, he is to be honoured, if not for his own sake, then for the sake of the order. Hence also the Apostle: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power but of God. And in another place: Fear God, honour the king. Further discussion could arise only from this line of reasoning. But since something of it has already been discussed in the earlier parts of this book, we must now pass over these matters and move on to others.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: De eo quod apogryphas & derisione dignas naenias suis locutionibus interposuerunt.
units.tr: On the apocryphal and laughable trifles which they inserted into their discourses.

units.la: SI quis ligneam domum aedificans si parietes cupit marmoreis exornare tabulis, aut variare multicoloribus vitri fructulis, dum cernit ligno eadem metalla per naturam minime posse cohaerere, spretis his metallis quae ligno per naturam cohaerere nequaquam possunt, lignis denuo conatur perficere: aut si quis stagneum vas facere cupiens, si ejusdem materiae ei supplementum desit, nonnullorum preciosorum metallorum materias, quae stagno cohaerere nequeunt, sed ide stagnum adsciendum coeptum opus quaerit: ita nimirum illi in sua synodo cum erroris sui instrumentum, scripturam videlicet, quae pro adorandis imaginibus compolita est, amplificare nisi suis, scripturasque divinas ei cohaerere minime posse senserunt, ad apogryphas quasdam & risu dignas naenias dictandi pedem verterunt: & cum viderent divinae legis testimonia inconpetenter eidem operi adhibita nequaquam posse cohaerere, tales eidem sententias aptavere, quae ei sensu verbisque nequaquam possent distare: quoniam sicut ferreo anulo preciosissima smaragdus inserta, aut cilicino regumento textae vestis falcia minime convenit adsuta, ita penitus divinorum eloquiorum testimonia illorum peri nequaquam conveniunt adhibita. Res ergo dubia & in contentionem veniens nó debet adsumi apogryphorum naeniis, sed aut divinae legis oraculis, aut eorum doctorum qui a catholica & apostolica ecclesia recipiuntur, salutaribus monitis, & luculentissimis documentis. Sed fortasse aliquis hujusce erroris scrupulosissimus adseverator dicet, Non illi apogryphorum librorum sententias suo operi inserere ad rem propositam confirmandam, sed insultantes ad quorundam haereticorum vestium subsummandam: cui nostrer stilus facillimam poterit inferre responsione. Numquidnam cum Polemonis imaginem, quod nulla authentica lectio narrat, dicunt quidam ab scelere coercuisse, alicui insultant? Sunt itaque in eadem lectione quaedam, quae illi ad rem propositam adfirmandam posuere: sunt etiam pleraque quae quamquam insultando posuerunt, ita sunt involuta, ita inordinate, ita enormiter prolata, ita permixtim digesta, ut pene vix deprehendi valeat, vixque lectoris mentem adringat, utrum ea quae dicuntur verba sint insultantium, aut his quae dicuntur fidem exhibentium. Quae res & sia doctis quibusque ita ut dicitur, intellegitur, indoctis vero quibusdam scandalum generare perhibetur, nec inmerito, quae ita inperitia tegitur ut vix intellegatur.
units.tr: If someone building a wooden house wants to decorate its walls with marble panels, or to vary them with multicoloured bits of glass, and sees that these metals cannot by nature cohere with wood, and so sets aside those metals that can in no way cohere with wood and tries instead to finish the work with more wood; or if someone who wants to make a tin vessel, lacking enough tin, looks for materials of some precious metals, which cannot cohere with tin, and adds them to the work begun in tin: so, in their synod, when they perceived that the instrument of their error, namely the writing compiled in favour of adoring images, could not be enlarged from their own resources, and that the divine Scriptures could not cohere with it at all, they turned their foot to dictating certain apocryphal and laughable trifles. And when they saw that the testimonies of the divine law, brought inappropriately into the same work, could not cohere with it, they fitted to it such sentences as could by no means differ from it in sense or words. For just as the most precious emerald set into an iron ring, or a patch of Cilician cloth sewn onto a royal garment, fits in not at all, so the testimonies of the divine oracles, when brought into their cause, do not agree in any way. Therefore a doubtful matter that comes into dispute ought not to be settled by the trifles of the apocryphal books, but by the oracles of the divine law, or by the wholesome admonitions and most lucid teachings of those teachers who are received by the catholic and apostolic Church. But perhaps some over-scrupulous defender of this error will say that they did not insert sentences from apocryphal books into their work to confirm the matter proposed, but insultingly to fasten them upon the vestments of certain heretics. To this our style can give a very easy reply. When some men say that the image of Polemon restrained him from crime, a thing no authentic reading relates, do they not insult someone by it? So in the same reading there are some things which they put forward to affirm the matter proposed; and there are also many things which, although they set them down insultingly, are so wrapped up, so disordered, so outrageously expressed, and so mixed together, that they can scarcely be grasped, and it is hard for the reader's mind to tell whether the words being spoken are those of insulters or of those who give faith to what is said. This matter is understood, as is said, by all the learned, but it is reported to cause scandal among certain unlearned people, and not undeservedly, since it is covered by such ignorance that it is scarcely understood.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: Chapter XXXI.

units.la: Deliramentum errore plenum quod de Retrusio quodam dixerunt qui Daemoni jurasse, & idipsum juramentum irritum fecisse perhibetur, cujus Abbas non mediocriter delirasse dinoscitur dicens, ei commodius esse omnia in civitate lupanaria ingredi, quam abnegare adorationem imaginis Domini aut ejus sanctae genetricis.
units.tr: A ridiculous and error-filled tale is told of a certain Retrusius, who is said to have sworn an oath to the devil and to have made that same oath void. Its abbot is clearly quite out of his mind, saying that it would be better for him to go into every brothel in the city than to deny the worship of the image of the Lord or of his holy mother.

units.la: SAEPE in hoc opere cogimur dicere a rebus noxiis exempla minime debere sumere: & hoc ideo tam crebro repetimus, quia eos ob suum errorem adhirmandum id crebro fecisse reperimus. Sicut enim ordine competenti bonis actibus adminiculum praebent bonorum nihilominus actuum exempla, ita nimirum illi erroneis actibus erroneorum actuum quaerunt suffragia. Ad propositum namque errorem stabiliendum Retrusi cujusdam proferunt exemplum: qui si ita gesit ut illi asseverant, tripertitum noscitur in ea parte patrasse deliquium: sive quia daemonico sponte paruerit alloquio, sive quod eo inliciente se jurejurando constrinxerit, sive etiam quia id juramentum irritum fecerit: quae tria non solum in exemplum minime sunt adtrahenda, verum etiam ab omni catholico penitus abdicanda: quoniam multis divinae legis sunt testimoniis interdicta. Societates ergo & seductiones non solum daemonum, sed etiam malorum hominum pluribus divinorum eloquiorum praeceptis inhibentur. Scribitur enim in Exodo, Non audies auditum vanum: & in Proverbiis, Fili, non te seducant viri impii. Si ergo malorum hominum seductiones vitandae sunt, multo magis malignorum spirituum alloquia & adsensus vitanda creduntur: quoniam cum sint humanitatis inimici, & nobis semper infesti, tanto semper debemus de eorum esse deceptione suspecti, & contra eorum nequitias effecti, quanto eos subtilioris esse scimus naturae vel ingenii. In eo quoque quod daemoni juravit, divinis verbis quibus juramenta prohibentur contraiit. In Ecclesiastico namque scribitur, Iurationi non adsuefaciat os tuum: multi enim casus in illa. Sicut enim servus interrogatus assidue a livore non minuetur, sic omnis jurans & nominans in toto a peccato non purgabitur. Vir multum jurans implebitur iniquitate, & non discedet a domo ejus plaga. Ipsa quoque veritas in Evangelio dicit: Ego autem dico vobis, ne omnino juretis, neque per caelum, quia sedes Dei est, neque per terram, quia scabellum est pedum ejus, neque per Hierosolymam, quia civitas est magni regis, neque per caput tuum jurabis, quia non potes unum pilum facere album aut nigrum: sit autem sermo vester, est est, non non: quod autem amplius est, a malo est. Porro quod eidem daemoni se pejerasse perhibetur, & in hoc abuse egisse detegitur. Ait enim Dominus per Moysen, Non jurabis in nomine meo injuste, & non profanabis nomen sanctum meum: ego sum Dominus Deus vester. & in Zacharia Propheta legitur, Et juramentum falsum nolite diligere, quia haec omnia odivi, dicit Dominus omnipotens. Cum ergo idem Retrusus haec tria divinis verbis obnitentia perpetraverit, ejus Abbas nihil in eo correctionis exhibuit, sed ei deteriorem peccandi viam ostendit dicens, Commodius tibi est omnia in civitate lupanaria ingredi, quam abnegare adorationem imaginis Domini, aut ejus sanctae genetricis. O inconparabilis absurditas! O exitiabile malum! O vere iniquis vesaniis praeferenda! Commodius dicit perpetrare rem & per legem, & per evangelium constitutam, quam abstinere se a re quam neque per legem, neque per evangelium constitutam. Commodius dicit facinus perpetrare, quam a facinore abstinere. Commodius dicit in profundum se ultro inmergere, quam viam recti tramitis inoffenso pede tenere. Commodius dicit Dei violare, quam rerum infensatarum adorationem spernere. Commodius dicit Christi & facere membra meretricis, quam contemnere adorationem operis cujuslibet. Dicat ergo, si ulspiam reperire poterit, dixisse Dominum, Non abneges adorationem imaginis, licut dixisse eum manifestissimum est, Non moechaberis. Dicat, si alicubi reperire valet, dixisse Domi-num, Si videris imaginem & non adoraveris eam, peccasti, sicut apertissime dixisse eum constat, Si videris mulierem ad concupiscendum eam, iam moechatus es eam in corde tuo. Quae cum non repererit, vehementer se errasse persentiat qui rem tam probrosam perpetrare ob evitandam rem infructuosam concessit. Nam dum Dominus & per legem accingere lumbos super ubera, in corde videlicet libidines resecare, & per evangelium lumbos accingere, & lucernas tenere, castitati sollicitor bona opera adiociare percenseat, & in divinis eloquii libris castitatis praecepta dentur, nusquam tale aliquid de imaginum adoratione jussum fuisse reperitur. Unde dum Retrusio illi Abbas suus, qui ei utique ducatum salutis praebere debuit, peccandi habenas laxavit: & qui eum ab erroris laqueo quo daemoni juraverat retrahere debuit, ipse quoque cum eo in erroris voraginem, qui ei gravissimum facinus ait esse commodius perpetrandum, corruit: proculdubio evangelicum illud implevit, Si caecus, inquit, caeco ducatum praebeat, ambo in foveam cadent. Quisquis ergo tali exemplo suam vult fulcire assertionem, non suam insaniam mediocrem sed ceteris demonstrat esse validiorem. Quia igitur illorum absurditatis instantia & augurum continuatas sive etiam deliramentorum congeries nullis in eorum volumine, cujus errores dulcuimus, intercapedinibus requiescunt, saltim librorum istorum intercapedine qui inter unius
units.tr: OFTEN in this work we are compelled to say that examples should by no means be taken from harmful things, and we repeat this so frequently because we find that they have often done this to confirm their own error. For just as examples of good deeds lend support to good actions in their proper order, so too those in error seek the support of erroneous deeds for their erroneous actions. To establish their error, they put forward the example of a certain Retrusius. If he acted as they assert, he is known to have committed a threefold offence in this matter: first, that he willingly obeyed a demonic address; second, that under the devil's enticement he bound himself by oath; and third, that he made that oath void. These three things must not only not be drawn into example, but must be utterly renounced by every Catholic, since they are forbidden by many testimonies of the divine law. Alliances with, and seductions by, not only demons but also wicked men are prohibited by many precepts of the divine oracles. For it is written in Exodus: "You shall not listen to a vain report," and in Proverbs: "My son, let not wicked men entice you." If therefore the enticements of wicked men are to be avoided, much more must the addresses and assent of evil spirits be believed to be avoided. Since they are enemies of humanity and always hostile to us, we ought always to be all the more suspicious of their deceit and all the more on guard against their wickedness, in proportion as we know them to be of a more subtle nature or intellect. In the matter of swearing an oath to the devil, he also acted against the divine words by which oaths are forbidden. For in Ecclesiasticus it is written: "Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, for there are many falls in it. As a servant constantly questioned will not be free from bruises, so every man who swears and names God will not be cleansed of sin throughout. A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house." Truth itself also says in the Gospel: "But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is God's throne; nor by the earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be yes, yes; no, no; and whatever is more than these is of evil." Further, that he is said to have perjured himself to the same devil, and is shown to have acted deceitfully in this, is clear. For the Lord says through Moses: "You shall not swear falsely in my name, nor profane my holy name; I am the Lord your God." And in the prophet Zechariah we read: "Do not love a false oath, for I hate all these things, says the Lord Almighty." Since therefore this same Retrusius committed these three things, which are opposed to the divine words, his abbot showed no correction in him, but pointed out to him a worse way of sinning, saying: "It is more convenient for you to enter every brothel in the city than to deny the worship of the image of the Lord or of his holy mother." O incomparable absurdity! O deadly evil! O truly to be preferred to the maddest follies! He says it is more fitting to commit a deed that is forbidden both by law and by the gospel than to abstain from a thing that is forbidden neither by law nor by gospel. He says it is more fitting to commit a crime than to abstain from crime. He says it is more fitting to plunge oneself willingly into the depths than to keep to the path of right with an unstumbling foot. He says it is more fitting to violate God than to spurn the worship of insensible things. He says it is more fitting to make the members of Christ the members of a harlot than to despise the worship of any work whatever. Let him say, if he can find it anywhere, that the Lord said, "Do not deny the worship of the image," just as it is very plain that he said, "You shall not commit adultery." Let him say, if he can find it anywhere, that the Lord said, "If you see an image and do not worship it, you have sinned," just as it is clear that he said most openly, "If you look on a woman to lust after her, you have already committed adultery with her in your heart." Since he will not find such words, he who consented to commit so shameful a deed in order to avoid an unprofitable thing will perceive that he has gone grievously astray. For while the Lord, by the law, bids us gird up our loins, that is, cut off lusts of the heart, and, by the gospel, bids us gird our loins and hold up lamps, and in the books of the divine oracles precepts of chastity are given, nowhere is anything of this kind found to have been commanded concerning the worship of images. Hence, since his abbot, who ought to have offered him the guidance of salvation, loosened the reins of sin for Retrusius, and since he who ought to have drawn him back from the snare of error by which he had sworn to the devil, himself fell with him into the abyss of error, by saying that the most grievous crime was to be preferred and committed: without doubt he fulfilled that gospel saying, "If a blind man lead a blind man, both will fall into the pit." Whoever therefore wishes to support his assertion with such an example shows that his own madness is not moderate but greater than that of others. Since therefore the persistence of their absurdity and the continued heap of their augurs, or even of their follies, rests in no interval of their volume, whose errors we have examined, let at least the interval of these books, which lies between one end and the beginning of another, be a resting place, so that, just as their error is shaken by continual argument, so too the continuity of the books may be somewhat divided by the interval.

units.la: TRibus hujus nostræ disputationis libris Deo auxiliante decussis, in quibus quædam divinæ legis testimonia, & si breviter propriis tamen secundum sanctorum patrum doctrinam sensibus restituta, & nostræ fidei confessio, quamquam pedestri sermone, sincera tamen est apostolicæ traditionis firmitate exarata, & illorum qui novas institutiones ecclesiæ inferre nituntur res sensu carentes adorare percensent, vesania quodammodo est discussa: ad quartum nunc librum peraccedere ratio cogit: in quo si qua de illorum vanitatibus capitula remansere, Domino opitulante sunt discutienda: quoniam quidem tumultuosum inordinatumque dicendi genus evitantes, librorum numerositatem ordinavimus, & brevitati studentes non amplius quam ad quatuor libros huius nostri operis sermonem protendimus: & paucorum prolixitatem pluriumq; diminutionem fugientes in hoc numero nostræ disputationis pedem firmavimus, quæ prorsus divinorum eloquiorum testimoniis sacratum esse comperimus. Quaternarius ergo numerus, & à Physicis in elementorum ac totius mundanæ molis, vel etiam ratione humani corporis laboriosissima indagatione, de quibus nunc scire longum est, usitatus adprobatur, & à divinis literis quæ plura sacrata, & ad mysterium perunentes eodem numero coartata esse testantur, sacratissimus demonstratur. Quatuor etenim flumina de uno Paradisi fonte emanantia, & quatuor evangelia de fonte lucis & originæ bonitatis procedentia, & quatuor virtutes, prudentia videlicet, fortitudo, justitia, seu temperantia, humanam vitam honestè regulis moderantes esse describuntur. Quadratis etiam lignis archa fabricata est, in qua humanæ generis sive omnium animantium vita aquis cuncta vastantibus reservata est: nunc quoque archa & ecclesiæ, quæ in hujus seculi procellosis tentationum innatatundis, quæ electorum reproborumque capax est, quadratis lignis, sanctis scilicet viris patientiæ virtute decoratis, fabricata firmatur: quorum vita quocumque vertitur firmiter stat: quia nec in adversis deiciuntur, nec in prosperis sublevantur. Quorum nos vestigia sequentes, & vocum novitates vitantes, & rerum sensu carentium adorationes spernentes, soliqueque Deo cultum servitutis exhibentes, ejusque sanctis competentem honorem impendentes, in patientia nostra possessuros nos speramus animas nostras.
units.tr: With the three books of this our disputation thoroughly examined, by God's help, in which certain testimonies of the divine law, though briefly, have been restored to their proper sense according to the doctrine of the holy Fathers, and our confession of faith, though set down in plain speech, has been written with the sincere firmness of apostolic tradition, and the folly of those who strive to introduce new institutions into the Church, and who count as worship things that lack sense, has been in some measure refuted: reason now compels us to proceed to the fourth book, in which, if any chapters of their vanities remain, they are to be discussed with the Lord's help. For, avoiding a tumultuous and disorderly style of speaking, we have arranged the number of books, and, aiming at brevity, we have extended our discourse to no more than four books of this work. Shunning both the prolixity of a few and the multiplicity of many, we have fixed our foot in this number for our disputation, which we have found to be wholly hallowed by the testimonies of the divine oracles. Accordingly, the number four is commended in common use by the natural philosophers, in their most laborious investigation of the elements and the whole mundane mass, or even of the structure of the human body, matters it would take too long to know now; and it is shown to be most sacred by the divine Scriptures, which testify that many sacred things, reaching to a mystery, are confined to this same number. For four rivers flowing from the one fountain of Paradise, and four Gospels proceeding from the fountain of light and the origin of goodness, and four virtues, namely prudence, fortitude, justice, or temperance, are described as moderating human life honourably by their rules. The ark was also built of squared timbers, in which the life of the human race, or of all living creatures, was preserved while the waters laid waste everything. Now too the ark of the Church, which in the stormy temptations of this age is capable of bearing up the elect and the reprobate, is made firm, built of squared timbers, that is, holy men adorned with the virtue of patience; whose life stands firm whichever way it turns, because they are neither cast down in adversity nor lifted up in prosperity. Following their footsteps, avoiding novelties of words, spurning the worship of things that lack sense, and offering the worship of service to God alone while paying his saints the honour that is fitting, we hope to possess our souls in our patience.

units.la: LIBER QUARTUS.
units.tr: BOOK FOUR.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Falsissimum & risu dignum dictum Iohannis presbyteri, qui non minus caeteris in imaginum adoratione insanisse dinoscitur. Ait enim, Qui adorat imaginem, & dicit, quoniam hic est Christus filius Dei, non peccat.
units.tr: A most false saying, worthy of laughter, of John the presbyter, who is recognised as having gone mad no less than others in the adoration of images. For he says: "Whoever adores an image and says, 'This is Christ the Son of God,' does not sin."

units.la: MAGNAM nobis in hoc opere disputandi materiam Johannes presbyter & legatus omnium dedit, qui inter cæteras suæ professionis absurditates nec fallit in hoc negotio, quo sermo est vitavit, nec fallere timuit, nec mentiri seu ad mendacium alios hortari cohibuit. Falli etenim non vitavit, cum sanctarum scripturarum calle quæ unius & solius Dei cultum & adorationem censent, postposito, per abrupta & devia errans mentis suæ pedem ad res sensu carentes adorandas divertit. Fallere non timuit, cum callem recti itineris à se prætermissum aliis pertinere, & secum per invia errare multis adsertionibus ac potius vanitatibus persuasit. Mentiri quoque & ad mendacium alios exhortari non erubuit, qui rem inlicitam perpetrare, & mendacium proferre peccatum non esse asseruit. Ait enim, Qui adorat imaginem, & dicit, quia hic est Christus filius Dei, non peccat. Cui vanitati facillima argumentatione hoc modo potest reniti, quoniam id dicere quod non est, mendacium non est, neque id dicere quod est verum esse potest: ac per hoc si mentiri vitium non est, neque veritatem proferre virtus est: etsi veritatem proferre ac sectari vitium est, proculdubio mentiri mendaciumque sequi vitium est. unde cum dicit quis picturam Christum esse Dei filium, mentitur: & cum mentitur, perperam agit: & cum perperam agit, peccat. Igitur picturam dicit esse Christum Dei filium, peccat. non enim pictura quæliber nostræ salutis causa hominem adsumpsit eundemque flagellari & pro nobis cruci adfigi permisit, nec imago quæliber mortis impesio destituto Erebique profundo spoliato de sepulchro surrexit: nec cujuslibet terreni artificis opus Apostoli salutaribus monitis institutus, & per totius mundi compita ad prædicandum destinatus, cum corpore ad cœlum ascendit, & ad Dei patris omnipotentis dexteram sedit. Hic enim omnia non pictura quæliber, sed Christus qui est unicus Dei patris filius ante secula à patre effabiliter genitus, in fine seculorum ad terras humanæ salutis causa missus peregit: qui est unxit oleo lætitiæ præconsortibus suis, qui secundum Apostolum pacificavit omnia per sanguinem crucis suæ, sive quæ in cœlis, sive quæ in terris sunt, cui flectitur omne genu cœlestium, terrestrium, & infernoadorans dicit, Hic est Christus filius Dei, non solum peccat, sed etiam insaniens sceleste agit qui rei tam sublimis excellentissimum nomen (si tamen res dici fas sit, & non potius rerum omnium origo vel causa) tam vili rei tamque abjectae, & non solum mysteriis sed & vita carenti aptare contendit. Sicut enim imago quaelibet Christo in natura coaequari nequit, ita etiam in nomine coaequari minime potest. Quod si quis forte aequivocorum nominum in hanc partem rationem arbitretur posse cadere, sciat hanc quam nunc discutimus sententiam ab aequivocorum nominum ratione longe distare. Aliud est enim dicere, homo pius & verus, leo pictus & verus & caelestis, atque aliud imaginem safren Christum filium Dei esse: cum videlicet illic nominis sit tantum consonantia, hic perspicua prosessionis plena sententia, quoniam aequivocorum ratio in solo tantundem nomine communionem habet, mox vero ut ad definitionem pervenerit, quod nominis communio sono solum modo vocis tegebat, definitio sola certissime pandit. Aliud namque, ut praefati sumus, & longe aliud est, pictura quandam nomine tantummodo illius rei nuncupatae, cujus imago est secundum aequivocorum nominum rationem, atque aliud rem insensatam adorare, & eandem rem plena sententia Christum Dei filium profiteri & dicere, Hic est Christus filius Dei.
units.tr: John the presbyter, the legate of all, has given us a great subject for dispute in this work. Among the other absurdities of his profession, he neither avoided error in this business, of which we are speaking, nor feared to deceive, nor restrained himself from lying or from urging others to lie. He did not avoid error, for he abandoned the path of the Holy Scriptures, which hold that worship and adoration belong to the one and only God, and his wandering mind turned aside, through rough and devious ways, to adore things devoid of sense. He did not fear to deceive, for he persuaded many, by assertions and rather by vanities, that the path of right conduct which he had himself abandoned belongs to others, and that they should wander with him through trackless country. Nor was he ashamed to lie, or to urge others to lie, for he asserted that it is no sin to commit what is forbidden and to utter a falsehood. For he says: "Whoever adores an image and says, 'This is Christ the Son of God,' does not sin." This folly can be resisted by a very simple argument. A man does not lie when he says what is not, and he cannot speak the truth when he says what is true. So if lying is not a vice, neither is telling the truth a virtue; but if telling the truth and pursuing it is a vice, then undoubtedly lying and following falsehood is a vice. Hence when someone says that a picture is Christ the Son of God, he lies; and when he lies, he acts wrongly; and when he acts wrongly, he sins. Therefore whoever says that the picture is Christ the Son of God sins. For no picture whatever took on man for the sake of our salvation, nor allowed itself to be scourged and fastened to the cross for us, nor did any image rise from the tomb, having conquered death and despoiled the depths of hell. Nor did the work of any earthly craftsman, appointed by the apostles with saving admonitions and sent to preach through the crossroads of the whole world, ascend to heaven in the body and sit at the right hand of God the Father Almighty. For all these things were done not by any picture, but by Christ, who is the only Son of God the Father, begotten ineffably from the Father before the ages, and sent in the end of the ages to the earth for the cause of human salvation. He is the one who was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows, and who, according to the Apostle, made peace through the blood of his cross for all things, whether in heaven or on earth, and before whom every knee of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth is bowed. Therefore whoever adores and says, "This is Christ the Son of God," not only sins, but also, acting in madness and wickedness, seeks to apply the most excellent name of so sublime a thing (if indeed it is lawful to call it a thing, and not rather the origin or cause of all things) to a thing so cheap and abject, one that lacks not only mysteries but also life. For just as no image can be made equal to Christ in nature, so it can by no means be made equal in name. But if anyone perhaps thinks that the argument from equivocal names can apply in this case, let him know that the opinion we are now examining is far removed from the reasoning of equivocal names. For it is one thing to say "a pious and true man," "a painted lion, true and heavenly," and quite another to say that an image is Christ the Son of God. In the former case there is only a likeness of the name; in the latter there is a clear and full statement of faith. For the reasoning of equivocal names shares a community only in the name, but as soon as one reaches the definition, the definition alone very certainly reveals what the community of name hid under the mere sound of the word. For, as we have said above, it is one thing, and quite another, to call a picture by the name only of that thing of which it is the image, according to the reasoning of equivocal names, and to adore a senseless thing, and to confess that same thing with a full statement of faith as the Son of God, saying, "This is Christ the Son of God."

units.la: Nam si tale mendacium proferre, ut ille falsus est, peccatum non est, inlicita quaeque perpetrare nullum peccatum est: & si inlicita quaeque perpetrate nullum peccatum est, sanctarum scripturarum vigor, quae utique ab inlicitis abstinere censent, fateri credendus est. Non autem sanctarum scripturarum vigor quae ab inlicitis quibusque abstinere censent, fateri credendus est: est igitur tale mendacium proferre peccatum. Nam dum pene omne mendacium quod fallendi studio profertur peccatum sit, multo magis hoc tale mendacium peccatum esse poterit: cum tam vilem rem tanti nominis confessione nuncupare studet, & confessionem quam pastor ecclesiae eidem redemptori protulit, quamque quotidie ei omnis sancta catholica & universalis profert ecclesia, per quam & salvatur & suae salutis specimen adipiscitur de re insensata quis proferre conetur? Sicut ergo caeteva vitia, ira etiam mendacii vitium divinarum scripturarum documentis est inhibitum. Unde quisquis ejusdem Johannis monitis pareat, ut & imagines adoret & easdem Christum Dei filium appellet, & supervacuatem nequam exercet, & se indisciplinatum esse demonstrat.
units.tr: For if it is no sin to utter such a falsehood as he has uttered, then it is no sin to commit whatever is forbidden. And if it is no sin to commit whatever is forbidden, then we must believe the Scriptures, whose force surely requires abstinence from all that is forbidden, to be saying what is false. But we must not believe that the force of the Scriptures, which requires abstinence from all that is forbidden, is saying what is false. Therefore to utter such a falsehood is a sin. For since almost every lie told with the intent to deceive is a sin, this particular lie can all the more be a sin, since it strives to name a thing so cheap by the confession of a name so great. And how can anyone try to bring out, about a thing without sense, the confession which the minister of the Church has offered to that same Redeemer, and which every holy, catholic and universal Church offers to him every day, through which she is saved and obtains a sign of her salvation? Therefore, just as the other vices, so also the vice of lying is forbidden by the teachings of the divine Scriptures. Hence whoever obeys the admonitions of this same John, so as both to adore images and to call them Christ the Son of God, practises wicked vanity and shows himself to be undisciplined.

units.la: Si ergo hoc fecelus, ut ille protestans est, perpetretur, implebitur illud quod Hieremiae vaticinio voce Domini dicitur; Mendacium & non fides in valut super terram: quia a malis mala exierunt, & me non cognoverunt. Paulus quoque egregius praedicator mendacium deponere & veritatem loqui his verbis persuadet. Aut enim in epistola ad Ephesios, Deponentes mendacium, loquimini veritatem: unusquisque cum proximo suo: quia sumus invicem membra. item idem ad Colossenses; Nolite mentiri invicem, spoliantes vos veterem hominem cum actibus suis. Johannes quoque Apostolus ait; Omne mendacium non est de veritate. Unde liquido patet, si pictura, ut ille fateri hortatur, Christus Dei filius non est, mendacium sit id quod dicitur: & si id quod dicitur mendacium est, juxta Apostoli vocem de veritate non est. Cum igitur talis professio mendacium sit, proculdubio de eadem veritate non est, quae ait; Ego sum via & veritas & vita. Cultus enim adorationis soli Deo, & confessio filii Dei illi soli qui vere ejus filius coessentialis est, non adoptivus, exhiberi debet. Si vero Hic particula in eodem loco pro adverbio loci, non pro pronomine, posita est, utcumque haec sententia stare poterit, quia Deus ubique est.
units.tr: If therefore this crime, as that man urges, is committed, there will be fulfilled what is said by the voice of the Lord in the prophecy of Jeremiah: "There is no truth nor faith upon the earth, for from evil they have gone out to evil, and they have not known me." Paul too, that excellent preacher, persuades us to put away lying and speak the truth, in these words in the Epistle to the Ephesians: "Putting away lying, speak the truth, each one with his neighbour, for we are members one of another." Likewise the same to the Colossians: "Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his deeds." The Apostle John also says: "Every lie is not of the truth." Hence it is clear that if the picture, as that man exhorts us to confess, is not Christ the Son of God, then what is said is a lie; and if what is said is a lie, then according to the voice of the Apostle it is not of the truth. Therefore, since such a profession is a lie, it is undoubtedly not of that truth which says: "I am the way, the truth and the life." For the worship of adoration is due to God alone, and the confession of the Son of God is due to him alone who is truly his Son, co-essential and not adoptive. But if the word Hic in that passage is placed as an adverb of place and not as a pronoun, then this sentence could stand in some way, because God is everywhere.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De eo quodidem Johannes non recte dixit, Per imaginem quae per colores apparet, adoratur fortitudo ejus, & glorificatur, & ad memoriam ve- niemus de ejus in terra praesentia.
units.tr: On what John said wrongly, that through an image which appears through colours the strength of God is adored and glorified, and we come to remember his presence on earth.

units.la: HAnc quoque dementiam saepe memoratus Johannes presbyter suis frivolis addere non dissimulat, ut diceret, Per imaginem quae per colores apparet, Domini fortitudinem adorari, quasi Dominus cujus rei sit indiguus, & per aliquam rem suam fortitudinem quae nullam habet indigentiam. Numquidnam cum caeli sive lucis nomine, primam omnium creaturam, angelicam condiderit, quae ab ipso creationis suae exordio Dei fortitudinem & adorasse creditur & laudasse, quia necdum homines erant, qui de quibusque materiis, nec quaedam materiae erant in quibus imagines pingi possent, ideo Domini fortitudinem nec adorasse credendi sunt, nec laudasse? aiticenum Scriptura; Quando creata sunt omnia sydera, simul laudaverunt me omnes angeli mei. ubi jam evidenter ostenditur, non per imaginem quae per colores apparet, sed per suam ineffabilem potentiam Dei fortitudinem semper fuisse laudatam & adoratam. Nunquidnam post conditionem hominum, cum necdum pictoria ars in mundo inolevisset, fortitudo Domini minime fuit a sanctis quibusque adorata? Denique neque Abel justus, neque Enoch, neque Noe, neque ullus sanctorum qui in illa aetate fuisse leguntur, per imaginem, neque per colores Domini fortitudinem adorasse creduntur: quippe cum in rudi adhuc mundo necdum quarundam mundanarum artium experientiae haberentur. Cum ergo sint plures mundi partes, in quibus homines pictoriae artis sint ignari, numquidnam ibidem sortitudo Domini minime creditur adorari? Adoratur ergo fortitudo Domini non per imaginem quae per colores apparet, ut ille somniat, sed per ejus ineffabilem potentiam qua omnis mundi compago constat esse dinoscitur. Adoratur etiam fortitudo ejus non per quaedam materias, sed per verbum suum, filium videlicet, quem ante saecula ineffabiliter genuit, & per quem & in quo universa creavit, qui est dextera & fortitudo patris, per quam fortitudinem sicut universalis creaturarum constat esse per quam creatio, ita etiam perpetua & ab angelis & ab hominibus et celebratur adoratio: qui nimirum sicut causae est omnis creationis, ita etiam causa est iustissimae & decentissimae adorationis. Sanctus igitur & universalis ecclesia non per imagines, quae ex coloribus fiunt, ut saepe memoratus Johannes naufragus dimoscitur, Deum adorare nos mortales homines, neque aetherias potestates, sed per Christum Dominum confitetur, cum suae redemptionis mysteria celebrans dignum & iustum equumque & salutare dicit esse, ut nos et semper & ubique gratias agamus, per quem ineffabilem patris majestatem angelos laudare, dominationes adorare, potestates tremere, caelos caelorumque milites suppliciter et confessione hymnum gloriae constat suavissima modulatione cantare. Adoratur ergo factus est, ut eius non per coloris figuram imaginem ejus, sed per sacratissimam, & vivificatricem ejus incarnationem. Adoratur ejus potentia non per picturam, sed per sua opera: per haec videlicet, quibus formae servi accipere, de virgine nasci, surdis auditum, mutis eloquium, claudis gressum, leprosis sive caecis lumen reddere, infernales ... mortis imperium destruere, de sepulchro surgere, ad caelos ascendere dignatus est. Haec sunt enim instrumenta quibus a catholicis fortitudo Domini adoratur: haec munimina quibus fides ecclesiastica tuetur: haec confessio a qua, si quis dissentit, periclitatur: quam si quis corde retinet, salutem perpetuam adipiscitur: hoc memoriale perpetuum, quo Christum fidelium mentes interioribus semper intuentur, ad quarum rerum plenam cognitionem non per picturam venitur, sed per fidem, spem & dilectionem.
units.tr: This folly too is one that the oft-mentioned John the presbyter does not hesitate to add to his trifles, saying that through an image which appears by means of colours, the strength of the Lord is adored, as if the Lord lacked something, and as if his strength, which has no need of anything, were served by some thing of his own. Did not the Scripture say, when it mentions heaven or light, that he created first of all creatures the angelic one, which is believed to have adored and praised the strength of God from the very beginning of its creation, although men did not yet exist, nor were there any materials from which or in which images could be painted? Are they therefore to be believed neither to have adored nor praised the Lord's strength? Scripture says: When all the stars were created, all my angels praised me together. Here it is plainly shown that God's strength was always praised and adored, not through an image that appears by colours, but through his ineffable power. Was the strength of the Lord not adored by holy men after the creation of man, when the art of painting had not yet grown up in the world? Indeed, neither Abel the just, nor Enoch, nor Noah, nor any of the saints who are read of in that age, are believed to have adored the Lord's strength through an image or through colours, since in the still rude world they had no experience of certain worldly arts. Since there are therefore many parts of the world where men are ignorant of the art of painting, is the Lord's strength believed not to be adored there at all? The strength of the Lord is therefore adored not through an image which appears by colours, as he dreams, but through his ineffable power, by which the whole fabric of the world is known to stand. His strength is also adored not through certain materials, but through his Word, namely the Son, whom he ineffably begat before the ages, and through whom and in whom he created all things, who is the right hand and strength of the Father. As through this strength all creation is known to stand, so through it too the perpetual adoration is celebrated by angels and men. He who is the cause of all creation is surely also the cause of the most just and most fitting adoration. Therefore the holy and universal Church does not confess that we mortal men, or the heavenly powers, adore God through images made of colours, as the oft-mentioned John, that shipwrecked man, is shown to do, but through Christ the Lord. When she celebrates the mysteries of his redemption, she says it is worthy, just, fitting and salutary that we should always and everywhere give thanks, through whom the angels praise the ineffable majesty of the Father, the dominions adore, the powers tremble, and the heavens and the heavenly hosts, with humble confession, sing the hymn of glory in the sweetest harmony. He is therefore adored, not through the figure of colour or his image, but through his most sacred and life-giving incarnation. His power is adored not through a painting, but through his works: those by which he deigned to take the form of a servant, to be born of a virgin, to give hearing to the deaf, speech to the dumb, walking to the lame, sight to the lepers and the blind, to destroy the dominion of the infernal ... death, to rise from the sepulchre, and to ascend to the heavens. These are the instruments by which the strength of the Lord is adored by Catholics; these are the bulwarks by which the faith of the Church is guarded; this is the confession, and whoever dissents from it is in danger; whoever holds it in his heart attains eternal salvation. This is the perpetual memorial by which the minds of the faithful constantly contemplate Christ inwardly; and the full knowledge of these things is reached not through a picture, but through faith, hope and love.

units.la: Quia igitur idem Johannes imperitiae suae nubilo obsitus, ut reor, dixit, dum tamen aliud dicere vellet, haec contra ea, quae dixit, dicta sufficiant: caeterum ad ea quae cere volunt hujus disputationis pes vertendus est, ut & quid nolens asseveravit, & quid volens dicere studuit, hujus illi pugno rationabilibus armis munito quatiatur, quatenus nos & dicenda quae propriis verbis oblita sunt sensibile, & dicta quae intellegere in promptu sunt, disputando contra lectorem agnoscat. Cum enim ait; Per imaginem quae per colores apparet, adoratur fortitudo Domini, ut communis, dicere volunt, Vita imagine colorum fucis compaginata, fortitudo Domini adoratur: quod idem & in sequentibus pene patefecit, cum ait, Et ad memoriam venimus de ejus in terra praesentia.
units.tr: Since, therefore, this John, clouded over by his own ignorance, as I suppose, has spoken, though he wished to say something else, let what has been said against his words suffice. But let the foot of this discussion now be turned to the matters which they wish to be dealt with, so that what he unwillingly asserted and what he eagerly wished to say may be struck by the fist of reason, armed with rational weapons, so that the reader may recognise, in the disputation, both the things to be said which have been forgotten in his own words, and the things said which are readily understood. For when he says, through an image which appears through colours, the strength of the Lord is adored, they wish to say, as is commonly said, that the strength of the Lord is adored by a life-like image put together from coloured dyes. He very nearly makes this clear as well in what follows, when he says: and we come to remember his presence on earth.

units.la: Cum propositioni hoc facillime possumus obicere, quod nec scripturarum sanctarum lectione, nec patrum exemplis est institutum, Deum in manufactis quibusdam debere quaerere. In corde meo, inquit David, non imaginibus, abscondi eloquia tua: in toto corde meo exquisivi te Deus, ne repellas me a mandatis tuis. Moyses dicit, Ponite verba Domini in cordibus vestris. & Dominus per Propheram, Convertimini ad me ex toto corde vestro. & e contrario de reprobis ait, Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me. Unde datur intelligi, quod non in rebus visibilibus, non in manufactis, sed in corde Deus est quaerendus: nec carnalibus oculis, sed mentis solummodo oculo aspiciendus.
units.tr: Against this proposition we can very easily object that neither the reading of the holy Scriptures nor the examples of the Fathers instruct us to seek God in any handmade things. In my heart, says David, not in images, have I hidden your words; with my whole heart I have sought you, O God; do not drive me away from your commandments. Moses says: Lay up the words of the Lord in your hearts. And the Lord through the Prophet: Turn to me with your whole heart. And on the contrary, he says of the reprobate: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Whence it is given to understand that God is not to be sought in visible things or in handmade things, but in the heart; and he is to be beheld not with carnal eyes, but only with the eye of the mind.

units.la: Nam quae vesania est, Per imaginem quae per colores apparet, adoratur fortitudo ejus, & ad memoriam venimus de ejus in terra praesentia. Infelix memoria, quae ut Christi memoretur, qui numquam a pectore justi hominis recedere debet, imaginariae vilitatis est indigna: nec aliter potest Christi habere in se praesentiam, nisi in parietem aliqua materia ejus videtur imaginem pictam: quoniam talis memoria quae imaginibus foveatur, venit ex cordis amore, sed ex vilitatis necessitate: quia videlicet non hanc internus amor ad memorandum Christum incendit, sed necessitas, qua etiam res exosas mox ut videmus pictas, ut cumque mentem vilitate duce reducimus.
units.tr: For what madness is this: through an image which appears by colours, the strength of God is adored, and we come to remember his presence on earth. Wretched memory, which, in order that Christ be remembered, who ought never to depart from the breast of a righteous man, is unworthy of an imaginary cheapness! Nor can he have Christ's presence in himself otherwise than if an image of him painted in some material is seen on the wall. For such a memory, which is fostered by images, comes not from the love of the heart but from the necessity of cheapness; that is to say, it is not inner love that kindles us to remember Christ, but necessity, by which we also, as soon as we see hateful things painted, call them back to mind, with cheapness as our guide.

units.la: De talibus ergo qui tanta necessitate atcantur, ut nisi picturas derint, Christi difficile memorentur, timendum est, nisi forte aut communem hanc lucem quadam corporis molestia urgente viventes amiserint, aut picturis quodam casu, quae tamen non semper beri possunt, carucrint, Christi prorsus qui semper ante oculos habendus est, oblivisçantur.
units.tr: Concerning those, therefore, who are so beset by such necessity that, unless they have pictures, they can hardly remember Christ, we must fear, unless perhaps, living with that common light lost through some pressing bodily affliction, or having lost the pictures through some accident, which cannot always be had, they forget altogether Christ, who ought always to be kept before the eyes.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De eo quod dicunt, non scandalizandum quendam, eo quod ante imagines sanc- torum luminaria fiant, & odoris thymia- mata.
units.tr: On what they say, that no one should be scandalized because lights are set up and incense burned before images of the saints.

units.la: ENIQVE cum eadem synodus, cujus lectionem inculcandam arripuimus, plura suadeat, quibus nullus sanae mentis adsensum praebere audebit, plura difluadere nitatur, a quibus nullus capitis gressum operis retorquere tentabit, plura vituperet quae prorsus sunt laudanda, & e contrario plura laudet quae penitus sunt vituperanda, admonet etiam ne quis scandalizetur, eo quod ante imagines luminaria concinnantur, & thymiamata adoleantur: quasi non illi scandalizati, qui rebus luce carentibus luminaria incendunt, & odore carentibus odorifera thymiamata osserunt. Illi etenim scandalizantur, qui ea quae Deo digne offerenda sunt, rebus sensu carentibus osserunt, & offerre hortantur: & nos scandalizandos autumant, a quibus suam vesaniam rationabiliter subsannandam formidant: & dum se a nobis reprehendendos exi-stimant, nostram salutem zelantes jactant. Nositaque in hac parte scandalum pati formidant, & se bonis operibus uti putant: sed tanto nobis hujusce partis scandalum valebit obesse, quanto & illis ipsius insolentis obsequii exbitio prodesse: quia nimirum ordo exposcit, ut talem illis praefatae imagines inlati obsequi retributionem impertire cogantur, qualem impertiti honoris sensum, cum sint penitus insensatae, percipere nolcuntur. Sed fortasse hanc nostram assertionem frustrari cupientes dicent, Cur eos... nibus sensu carentibus luminaria conciunantes, & thymiamata adolentes, subsannatis, cum & nos in basilicis aeque sensu carentibus, & luminaria concinnemus, & thymiamata adoleamus? Quibus facilis poterit oboriri objectio; quoniam aliud est loca divinis cultibus mancipata luminaribus perlustrari, & in eisdem locis & orationum & thymiamatum Deo fumum offerri, & aliud, imagini oculos habenti & nihil cernenti lumen offerre, & nares habenti & nihil odoranti thymiamata adolere: aliud est loca divino cultui mancipata venerari, aliud pictoris quibuslibet coloribus comptis luminaria & thymiamata offerre: aliud domum majestatis Domini a fidelibus quibusque aedificatam & a pontifice dedicatam solenniter venerari, atque aliud & longe aliud, imagines a pictoribus quibusque conpositas oblatis muneribus irrationabiliter osculari. Domus enim mea, ait Dominus, domus orationis vocabitur: item alibi, Munera accepta erunt super altare meum, & domus orationis meae honorabitur. Multis namque honoribus locus ille sublimandus est, ubi a fidelibus populis undique convenitur, & eorum supplicationes Deo miserante exaudiuntur, & nostrae salutis mysteria celebrantur, & Deo sacrificium laudis offertur, ubi ad perferenda Deo sacrificia a fidelibus populis per manus sacerdotum inlata, angelicus fit concursus, ubi crebro suavisonus psallentium reboat concentus, ubi divinae lectionis arentia corda inliquantes personant fluctus. Denique in eorum plerisque locis, qui se imaginibus luminaria & thymiamata offerre gloriantur, a quibus nos quid facere contemnimus, scandalum pati putamur, ita loca divino cultui mancipata delpicabilia sunt, ut sicut Legatis nostris sive illis qui tempore reverendae memoriae inlustrissimi viri patris mei, sive eis qui a nobis illas sunt destinati in partes, referentibus conperimus, plerasque basilicae in eorum terris non solum luminaribus & thymiamatibus, sed etiam ipsis carent tegminibus: quippe cum in regno a Deo nobis concesso basilicae ipso opitulante, qui eas conservare dignatur, affluenter auro argentoque, gemmis ac margaritis caeteris venustissimis redundent adparatibus, & qui imaginibus luminaria concinnare & thymiamata adolere respuimus, loca divinis cultibus mancipata rebus pretiosissimis exornamus.
units.tr: Finally, although this same synod, whose reading we have undertaken to press, recommends many things to which no sane person will dare to give assent, and urges many things from which no one will attempt to turn the course of the work aside, and it censures many things that are wholly to be praised, and conversely praises many things that are wholly to be censured, it also warns that no one should be scandalized because lights are arranged before images and incense is burned. As if those were not the ones who are scandalized, who light lamps for things that lack light and offer fragrant incense to things that lack smell! Indeed, those are scandalized who offer to things without sense what is rightly offered to God, and urge others to do so. They think that we ought to be scandalized, and they fear that their own madness will rightly be mocked by us. And while they think they are to be rebuked by us, they boast of zeal for our salvation. They fear to suffer scandal in this matter, and they think they are using good works. But the scandal of this matter will harm us just as much as the ruin of their own unseemly obsequiousness will benefit them. For order itself requires that they be made to repay those images with the same kind of service as the honour they pay, since they are wholly senseless and refuse to perceive the honour given to them. But perhaps those who wish to thwart this assertion of ours will say: "Why do you mock those who light lamps and burn incense before images without sense, since we too in the basilicas likewise light lamps and burn incense, though they lack sense?" To them an easy objection can be raised: it is one thing to walk through places set apart for divine worship, lit with lamps, and to offer the smoke of prayers and incense to God in those same places; and it is another to offer light to an image that has eyes but sees nothing, and to burn incense before one that has nostrils but smells nothing. It is one thing to venerate places dedicated to divine worship; it is another to offer lamps and incense to paintings decked out in any colours by a painter. It is one thing to venerate solemnly a house of the majesty of the Lord, built by the faithful and dedicated by a bishop; and it is another, and far different, to kiss irrationally, with offered gifts, images put together by any painters. For my house, says the Lord, shall be called a house of prayer; and elsewhere: The gifts accepted will be upon my altar, and the house of my prayer shall be honoured. Indeed, that place is to be exalted with many honours, where the faithful peoples gather from every side, and their supplications are heard by God's mercy, and the mysteries of our salvation are celebrated, and a sacrifice of praise is offered to God; where, for the offering of sacrifices to God brought by the faithful peoples through the hands of priests, there is an angelic gathering; where the sweet sound of singing psalms resounds again and again; where the waves of divine reading resound, softening hearts that are dry. Finally, in most of those places where they boast that they offer lamps and incense to images, and where we are thought to suffer scandal because we scorn to do this, places dedicated to divine worship are so despised that, as we have learned from our envoys, both those sent in the time of my father of most illustrious memory and those sent by us to those regions, most of the basilicas in their lands lack not only lamps and incense but even roofs. Yet in the kingdom granted to us by God, with his help who deigns to preserve them, the basilicas abound with gold and silver, with gems, pearls and other most beautiful ornaments; and we, who refuse to light lamps and burn incense before images, adorn the places dedicated to divine worship with the most precious things.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De eo quod dicunt, Ejusdem criminis est, qui imagines spernit, cujus & Nabuchodo- nosor qui ossa regum Juda protulit e sepulchris, & Judaici regis oculos occisis filiis eruit, & Cherubim de templo abstulit.
units.tr: On what they say: that he who despises images is guilty of the same crime as Nebuchadnezzar, who brought the bones of the kings of Judah out of their tombs, who blinded the king of Judah after killing his sons, and who carried off the cherubim from the temple.

units.la: MAGINES namque, ut crebro jam diximus, spernendo frangere, luminaribus & thymiamatibus offerendo adorare, nulla penitus authentica lectione censetur, neque ullius sancti exemplo fieri debere monstratur: cum praesertim frangere eas sive adorare a quibusdam sanctis Patribus sit probitum; & non inmeriro, quia a cautela est omnino remotum, quod utrumque illi perpetrant qui synodos faciunt, aut ob earum non necessariam abolitionem, aut etiam ob earum inopportunam adorationem. Dicunt ergo eos qui eas spernunt ejusdem criminis esse, cujus Nabuchodonosor qui peccatis Israelitica gentis invalescentibus tremendi arbitrii ira urgente Judaeae regnum destruxit, multos sanctae quondam civitatis evertit, & diruta totius templi venustate, cherubim quoque dejecit. Quod quidem si ita esset, non in nos hoc crimen posset cadere, qui eas in ornamentis ecclesiae habere permittentes, modis omnibus spernimus adorare, sed in eorum prodecessores vel parentes qui eas ornamentis basilicarum ab antiquis adhibitas fregere, & penitus abolendas sanxere. Tam anceps hujusce partis in eos sententia pendere cernitur, ut quicquid ex ea molestius exsecrabiliusque proveniat, aut se aut prodecessores suos inevitabiliter damnare videantur. Cum igitur illi majores suos ob earum abolitionem spernant, sequeque ob earum adorationem magnam meritorum praemia habere jactent, nec isti coaequari queunt aedificatoribus illius venerandi templi in laude, nec illorum majores ejusdem eversoribus eo aequabuntur in crimine: quoniam quanta est distantia inter templum summi Dei quod aedificatum est tempore prophetarum a viris inlustribus, & quasdam imagines quae a quibuslibet fiunt artificibus, tanta proculdubio distantia est inter ejusdem templi eversores, & imaginum conteemptores. Sed dum nos & istos vera ratione, qui eas inopportune adorandas decernunt, & illorum majores qui eas incaute prorsus abdicaverunt, reprehendamus, restat ut templi Domini eversores majoris multoque majoris criminis nexibus inretitos fuisse, quam earum pretores perdoceamus. Non enim talium imaginum abolitionem quales illi se adorare gloriantur, Propheta deflebat, sed templum quod necdum fundatum erat, & urbis quae caeteris urbibus eminebat, eversionem prophetico spiritu longe post futuram respiciens, velut praeteritam cantando deplorabat dicens; Ut quid repulisti nos Deus in finem, iratus est furor tuus super oves gregis tui: memento congregationis tuae quam creasti ab initio. Nec imaginum contemptorem, sed ejusdem sacratissimi templi eversorem inimicum vocat, cum subinfert; Quanta malignatus est inimicus in sanctis tuis, & gloriati sunt odientes te, qui oderunt. Nec in picturis, sed in atrio Domini ligna sua, vexilla videlicet hostilia Chaldaeorum sive Romani exercitus posita, deplorat dicens; In medio atrio tuo posuerunt signa sua, & signa non cognoverunt tanquam in via super summum. Nec pictorum januas, sive quorundam artificum vel etiam pictarum tabularum materias, securibus & ascis dejectas fuisse, sed templi Domini, in quo erant
units.tr: For images, as we have often said already, are not supported by any authentic reading of Scripture, nor is it shown that anyone among the saints set an example of making them. This is especially so because breaking them or adoring them has been approved by some holy Fathers, and not without good reason, since caution is wholly absent from the conduct of those who make synods, either for the sake of abolishing images that were not needed, or for the sake of adoring them at an unseasonable time. They say, then, that those who despise images are guilty of the same crime as Nebuchadnezzar, who, when the sins of the Israelite nation had grown strong and the anger of his terrible judgment pressed upon them, destroyed the kingdom of Judea, overthrew many of the once holy city, and, when the beauty of the whole temple was laid waste, also cast down the cherubim. Now if this were so, the crime could not fall upon us, who, while allowing images to be kept as ornaments of the Church, utterly refuse to adore them. It would fall upon their predecessors or parents, who broke the images which the ancients had used as ornaments of the churches and decreed that they be wholly abolished. The judgment against them on this point hangs so precariously that whatever more troublesome and detestable outcome follows from it seems inevitably to condemn either themselves or their predecessors. Since, therefore, those forefathers of theirs despise them for the sake of abolishing images, while these men boast of great rewards of merit for adoring them, neither can these men be compared with the builders of that venerable temple in praise, nor will their forefathers be made equal to its destroyers in guilt. For just as great as is the distance between the temple of the most high God, which was built in the time of the prophets by illustrious men, and certain images made by whatever craftsmen, so undoubtedly great is the distance between the destroyers of that same temple and the despisers of images. But while we rightly reprove both those who decree that images be adored at an unseasonable time, and their forefathers who abolished them with utter carelessness, it remains for us to show that the destroyers of the Lord's temple were entangled in the bonds of a crime far greater, far greater indeed, than that of those who despised images. For it was not the abolition of such images as they boast of adoring that the Prophet lamented. Looking forward in the spirit of prophecy to the overthrow of the temple, which was not yet founded, and of the city which stood out above the other cities, a overthrow that would come long afterwards, he lamented it in song as if it had already happened, saying: O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture? Remember thy congregation, which thou hast purchased of old. He does not call the despiser of images the enemy, but the destroyer of that most holy temple, when he adds: How much hath the enemy done wickedly in the sanctuary! and they that hate thee have roared in the midst of thy congregation. He laments not over pictures but over the standards of the enemy set up in the court of the Lord, that is, the hostile ensigns of the Chaldeans or of the Roman army, saying: Thine enemies roar in the midst of thy congregation; they set up their ensigns for signs. Nor does he lament that the doors of painters, or the materials of certain craftsmen, or even painted tablets, were cast down with axes and adzes, but that the doors of the Lord's temple, in which were the holy of holies, had been cut by enemy wedges, saying: As in the day of the axe amongst the thick trees, so they broke down all the carved work with axes and hammers. Nor does he lament with the anguish of his soul the burning or defiling of certain images, but the sanctuary of the Lord; They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling-place of thy name. Nor in the same Psalm does he sing that the wrath of the Lord is to be poured out upon despisers of images, with similar words, but he prays against the destroyers of the city or temple, or even against the wasters of the whole Israelite people, saying: How long, O Lord, wilt thou be angry for ever? shall thy jealousy burn like fire? Pour out thy wrath upon the nations that have not known thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name, for they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling-place. He does not speak of despisers of pictures, but under the name of the Edomites he speaks of all nations hostile to the Israelite people: Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who said, Raze it, raze it, even to the foundation thereof. He does not threaten those who despise the adoration of images, but under the name of the daughter of Babylon he threatens the nation of the Chaldeans or the Quirites: O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be who rewardeth thee as thou hast served us. Happy shall he be who taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones. Yet nothing of this kind is found anywhere concerning the despisers of images. Many oracles of the prophets similar to these, spoken concerning the destroyers of the Lord's temple or of the city of Jerusalem, are found, which for the sake of brevity we pass over. Our Lord and Redeemer, too, is read to have wept over the coming ruin of that same temple and city. All these things, although they are overshadowed by mystical figures and could be understood of the destroyers of the soul of the Church, who, always attacking, strive to overthrow the virtues of the soul, like walls, against whose defences vice is fought, and the faith placed in the breast, in which pure sacrifices are offered to God, like a certain temple, and who labour to strike down pure thoughts, or the exercises of good works, like a certain people, nevertheless are received as having been spoken historically of the overthrow of the profaned temple. Whence it is clear that their forefathers were by no means incautious in the sport of removing images from the ornaments of the churches, yet they must by no means be compared with the subverters of that most holy and most reverend temple: for in the former there is lightness, in the latter atrocity; in the former ignorance, in the latter wickedness. The former, thinking that they were rendering service to God, removed them from the ornaments of the churches; the latter, provoking to anger in themselves God, who was angry with his people, cruelly overthrew his house. Against both of these, with God's help, we, having set aside those things, adorn places given over to divine worship, and we offer the service of adoration to God alone.

units.tr: Esai. 66.

units.la: Psal. 74.
units.tr: Psal. 74.

units.la: Ibid.
units.tr: Ibid.

units.la: Ibid. erant sanćta sanctorum, sacratissimas januas hostilibus cuneis incisas defleri dicens; Tanquam in ira furoris et indignationis sue exciderunt januas ejus, bipenne & ascia dejecerunt ea. Nec combustionem sive inquinamentum quasi quandam imaginum, sed sanctuarii Domini animi angore prosequitur; Incenderunt igni sanctuarium tuum in terra, polluerunt tabernaculum nominis tui. Nec cum his similia in Psalmo ille ibidem modulatione cantabat, super imaginum contemptores iram Domini effundendam, sed super urbis sive templi eversores, vel etiam totius Israelitici populi vastatores orabat dicens; Usquequo Domine irasceris in finem? an in finem exardescet velut ignis zelus tuus? effunde iram tuam in gentes quae te non noverunt, et in regna quae nomen tuum non invocaverunt, quia comederunt Jacob, et locum ejus desolaverunt. Nec de picturarum contemptoribus, sed sub nomine Idumaeorum de cunctis gentibus Israelitico populo infestis dicit; Memento Domine filiorum Edom in die Hierusalem, qui dicunt, Exinanite, exinanite usque ad fundamentum in ea. Nec imaginum adorationem contemnentibus, sed sub nomine filiae Babylonis Chaldaeorum sive Quiritium genti comminatur; Filia, inquiens, Babylonis misera, beatus qui retribuet tibi retributionem tuam, quam retribuisti nobis: Beatus qui tenebit et allidet parvulos tuos ad petram. De imaginum vero contemptoribus nihil tale usquam reperitur. Multa his similia Prophetarum oracula de templi Domini sive Hierosolymae urbis eversoribus dicta inveniuntur, quae a nobis brevitatis causa praetermittuntur: Dominus quoque & redemptor noster ejusdem templi sive civitatis ruinam post futuram flevisse legitur. Quae omnia quamquam mysticis obumbrata figuris, de ecclesiae animae everioribus possint intelligi, qui virtutes animae velut quosdam muros quarum munimenta contra vitia pugnatur, & fidem in pectore collocatam in qua Deo sacrificia munda litantur, quoddam templum semper insectantes evertere moliuntur, & cogitationes mundas sive quasi bonorum operum exercitia velut quendam populum prostrate niuntur, tamen historialiter de profanati templi eversione dicta fuisse accipiuntur. Unde liquido patet, majores eorum quaquam in ludis a basilicarum ornamentis imaginibus quodammodo fuerint incauti, subversoribus tamen cratissimi ac reverendissimi illius templi nequaquam sunt coexquandi: quoniam in istis quidem levitas, in illis vero atrocitas: in istis imperitia, in illis nequitia: isti Deo se obsequium praestare arbitrantes eas ab ornamentis basilicarum abstulerunt, illi Deum qui populo suo erat iratus in se ad iracundiam provocantes ejus domum crudeliter diruerunt, quibus nos utrimque, Deo opitulante, postpositis locis divino cultui mancipatis exornamus, & soli Deo servitium adorationis impendimus.
units.tr: Ibid. The holy of holies were there; they lament the most sacred doors cut by enemy wedges, saying: As in the anger of his fury and indignation they have cast down his doors, they have thrown them down with axe and adze. He laments not a burning or defiling of certain images, but of the sanctuary of the Lord with anguish of soul: They have set fire to thy sanctuary on the earth; they have defiled the tabernacle of thy name. Nor in the Psalm does he sing in the same manner, with similar words, that the wrath of the Lord is to be poured out upon despisers of images; but he prays against the destroyers of the city or temple, or even against the wasters of the whole Israelite people, saying: How long, O Lord, wilt thou be angry, for ever? Shall thy zeal burn like fire? Pour out thy wrath upon the nations that do not know thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name, for they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place. He speaks not of despisers of pictures, but under the name of the Edomites he speaks of all nations hostile to the Israelite people: Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say, Raze it, raze it even to its foundation.
