He threatens not those who despise the adoration of images, but under the name of the daughter of Babylon he threatens the nation of the Chaldeans or of the Quirites: O daughter of Babylon, miserable one, happy is he who shall repay thee the repayment thou hast paid us. Happy is he who shall take and dash thy little ones against the rock. Of despisers of images nothing of this kind is found anywhere. Many similar oracles of the prophets, spoken concerning the destroyers of the Lord's temple or of the city of Jerusalem, are found, which we pass over for the sake of brevity. Our Lord and Redeemer, too, is read to have wept over the coming ruin of that same temple or city. All these things, although they are overshadowed by mystical figures and could be understood of the destroyers of the soul of the Church, who strive always to overthrow, as certain walls, the virtues of the soul, by whose defences vice is fought against, and the faith placed in the breast, in which pure sacrifices are offered to God, as a certain temple, and who labour to strike down pure thoughts, or the exercises of good works, as a certain people, nevertheless are taken as having been said historically of the overthrow of the profaned temple. Whence it is clear that their forefathers were indeed somewhat careless in removing images from the ornaments of the churches, yet they must by no means be compared with the subverters of that most holy and most reverend temple: for in the former there is lightness, in the latter atrocity; in the former ignorance, in the latter wickedness. The former, thinking that they rendered obedience to God, removed them from the ornaments of the churches; the latter, provoking the anger of God, who was angry with his people, cruelly overthrew his house. Against both of these, with God's help, we, having set aside those things, adorn places given over to divine worship, and we offer the service of adoration to God alone.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quod epistola, quam illi sancti Symeonis fuisse dicunt, missa ad Justinianum Imperatorem, multum distet a divinis scripturis, sive a sanctorum patrum documentis, in eo quod ait praefato imperatori, Pro quibus commemorantes referimus divinis vestris auribus: sive in eo quod eidem imperatori misericordia uti prohibuerit.
units.tr: That the letter which they say was sent by the holy Symeon to the Emperor Justinian differs greatly from the divine Scriptures and from the teachings of the holy Fathers, both in that it says to the said emperor, "Recalling these things, we refer them to your divine ears," and in that it forbids the same emperor to use mercy.

units.la: SOLET plerumque haereticorum versutia probrosa quaedam & errorem suadentia apicibus notare, & sanctorum quorundam probabiliumque virorum nominibus praetitulare, quasi virorum poculum mellis inlitum sapore facilius valeant ad potandum nescientibus quibusque porrigere. Unde timendum est, ne epistola quam illi cujusdam sancti Symeonis dicunt, ex qua monia ad suum errorem stabiliendum adducunt, non verba sint viri sancti, sed cujusdam mentis versuti. Quoniam quidem ideo de ea a nobis sive a caeteris quibusque orthodoxis dubitatur, quia ejus sermo in quibusdam locis sanctarum scripturarum documentis refragatur, nec praetermittenda ejus lectionem in testimonium ad res dubias firmandas sumere, quam novimus divinae legis instituta contraire. Non enim nos ex ejus textu amplius usquam legisse meminimus, nisi id quod ab eorum codice taxatum reperimus. Quod quidem quamvis sensuum verborumque venustate caeca insulsum nescio quid rusticumve redoleat, liber tamen nobis ita id texere, ut constat nos in codice reperisse. Dicunt enim praefatum sanctum Symeonem, cujus vita nobis & praedicatio ignota, pro quibusdam Samaritanis, imaginibus injuriam inferentibus Justiniano Imperatori scripsisse; Pro quibus commemorantes referimus divinis vestris auribus: & iterum; Non habeo quod dicam talia pro mentes ne una in eis facta humanitate quatenus precamur victoriosam vestram fortitudinem, ne faciat misericordiam in eis qui hoc praesumpserunt, neque parcere illis, neque quodlibet rogum aut responsum suscipere pro illis. & post ea; Sed conjuro vos Domine per Emanuel Deum excelsum non morari neque ad modicum fieri ducentem vindictam & iterum; Quos & suscipiet, propinquitates eorum tenebras in condemnationem, qui expectat eos consumere me guibibile & tenebrosum ignem, & anathematizet eos in inferiora abyssi ipse sanctus & omnipotens spiritus Jesu Christi Domini nostri qui ex Patre procedit, ad perdendum illos in infinita perditione. & post pauca; In ipso qui tuae pietati vestrae. In quibus stolidissimis verbis & non solum eloquii venustatem, verumetiam compositionem loquendi sensum fugientibus & barbarissimis ac folicissimis concretum nescio quid relinquens, haec prorsus reprehenduntur, quod Justiniani Imperatoris hominis aeque mortalis atque fragilis, & cunctis humanis permutationibus subjacentis, aures divinas nuncupaverit, cundemque misericordiam uti prohibuerit, & ad reddendum malum pro malo facilis fuerit, & patienter ac manuerit gere in eadem causa neglexerit: & qui debuerat pro damnatorum ereptione laborans iram regis restituere, illius iram magis magisque succenderit, eumque atrociter ad iracundiam impulerit, nec ejus exce plo usus sit qui neminem vult perire: & qui pro lucrandis animabus invigilare debuerat, anathema & maledicta iniecerit, & eidem Imperatori Deum conregnare dixerit. Quæ verba dum in tot locis reprehendantur, ad roborandam adorationem imaginum minus idonea reperiuntur: quoniam difficile potest per præcipitia currere, qui in planis cernitur titubare: nec valet in ambiguis diverticulis dux esse itineris, qui publici tramitis viam tenere nequit in patentibus viis: & a liberalium disciplinarum subtilissimo magistro reprobatur, qui communium literarum usitatissimam notitiam minime habere reperitur. Nam dum de eo quod ille Imperatoris aures divinas dixit, eiq; Deum conregnare profatus est, contra eorum deliramenta qui hactenus talibus adhuc nugis utuntur, plenissime in superioribus hujus operis partibus a nobis affatim disputatum sit: nunc cordo exposcit ut de cæteris, de quibus nunc sermo est, divinorum eloquiorum testimoniis gressus sermonum nostrorum munientes, prout Dominus dederit, disputemus. Cum enim misericordia uti imperatorem prohibuisse reperitur, quid aliud facit, nisi omnibus sanctis scripturis quæ misericordiam habendam percensent, reluctantdinoscitur? Unde periculosissimum est talium literarum præcepta sequi, quæ divinis scripturis videntur obniti. Ait enim Dominus in evangelio, a Estote misericordes sicut & pater vester misericors est. & iterum; b Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. & doctor gentium ait; c Estote autem invicem benigni, miserycordes, donantes vobis sicut & Deus in Christo donavit vobis. & Psalmographus dicit; d Dominum misericordiam diligere, &c, e misericordia Domini plena est omnem terram. & idem Dominus per Prophetam dicit; f Quia misericordiam volo & non sacrificium. Nam dum misericordia tam authenticis habenda censeatur præceptis, & eam se in æternum cantaturum Propheta testetur, Misericordias tuas, inquiens, Domine in æternum cantabo, & ita a Domino dicatur diligi, quisquis ea uti prohibet, eamq; habere contemnit, & Deum convincitur non diligere, & ejus præstantissimis monitis penitus contraire. Unde & ipsi veritas legis perito dicenti, ipsum esse proximum qui fecit misericordiam, respondit, Vade & tu fac similiter. Quo documento monstratur, non solum a nobis homines qui unius nobiscum naturæ sunt diligendos, sed etiam angelos qui quamvis alterius sint naturæ, in eo tamen quod misericordiam erga nos exercent, & proximi esse creduntur, & diligi prorsus ab eo qui Deum & proximum diligere iussit, omnino jubentur, in eo etiam quod tam facilis ad reddendum malum pro malo fuerit, divinis prorsus monitis contradixit. Necille enim ad exercendam vindictam tam severus esse, nec imperatorem ad hanc exercendam impellere debuit: quippe cujus ministerium non fuerit vindictam exercere, aut exercendam jubere, sed opera misericordiæ amare, & amanda cæteris prædicare. Ait enim Dominus in Exod. Si occurreris bovi inimici tui aut asino errantis, reduc ad eum. Cui præcepto nullatenus paruit cum errantes præfatos Samaritanos, si tamen errasse creduntur, ab errore minime revocavit, sed ut in eodem errore perirent, imperatoris meritum postulando concitavit: & quos vidit sub onere peccatorum ceciderere, non solum non erexit, sed sub eodem onere atrociter perire permisit, dicente Domino, Si videris asinum odientis jacere sub onere, nõ pertransibis, sed sublevabis cum eo. in Proverb. quoq; scribitur; Si esurierit inimicus tuus cibam illum, si sitit potum da illi: hoc enim faciendo carbones ignis congeres super caput ejus, Deus autem retribuet tibi: quia videlicet quos peccando inimicos sciebat, & spiritalium ciborum edulis & salutaris poculis nos, si divinorum verborum esca sive potu saturarec, carbones ignis qui & peccatorum rubiginem consumerent, & eos ad dilectionem Dei & proximi accenderent, super capita, mentes scilicet eorum, coreret. Vindictam ergo quaerere & misericordiam spernere iramq; servare, quæ omnia superius posita liter præfatum imperatorem hortatæ fuisse perhibentur, his Ecclesiastici libri documentis cohibentur; qui inquit, non vindicat, a Deo invenient vindictam, & peccata illius servabit. relinque proximo nocenti te, & tunc tibi solventur peccata. Homo homini servat iram, & a Deo quærit medelam: in hominem sibi similem non habet misericordiam, & de peccatis suis deprecatur: ipse retinet iram, & propitiationem petit a Deo, quis deprecabitur pro delictis suis? Item Esaiæ vatis oraculo pro malis mala reddere hoc modo prohibetur; Audite, inquit, verba nostra qui tremetis nomen ejus: dicite, Fratres nostri estis qui vos oderunt & abominantibus vos, ut nomen Domini manifestetur & appareat ipsis in jocunditate eorum, & illi confundentur. Dominus quoq; in evangelio inimicos sive nō ira sitiscitandā, nec vindictā exercendā, necque maledictā cogerenda præcepit, sed diligite exhibendam his factatissimis verbis instituit; Diligite inimicos vestros, & orate pro eis qui vos persecuntur, benefacite eis qui vos oderunt, ut sitis filii patris vestri qui in cælis est, qui solem suum oriri facit super bonos & malos, & pluit super justos & injustos. Nā si illi voce veridica diligēdi potius quam maledicendi & exsecrandi sunt qui nos oderunt & persequuntur, qui utiq; imago Dei sumus, multo minus illi maledicendi seu plectendi sunt, qui pictui is injurias injecisse feruntur. Vas quoq; electionis nulli mali pro malo reddendū esse his verbis admonet. ait enim in Epist. ad Rom. Nolite prudetes fieri a-pud vosmetipsos, nulli malum pro malo reddentes, providentes bona non solum coram Deo, sed etiam coram omnibus hominibus, si fieri potest: quod ex vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habete, non vosmetipsos defendentes, sed date locum irae: scriptum est enim, Mihi vindictam, ego retribuam, dicit Dominus. Si ergo nosmetipsos egregii prædicatoris documento defendere minime debemus, quis furor est, quæve dementia ut rerum insensatum secundum exhortationem earum dem literarum quæ Justiniano missæ sunt, injurias defendere vindicus & pietatis opera quæ nec pro nobis: is quidem calumniis amittere debemus, pro picturarum conflictus, quas illæ minime sentiunt, amittamus: Non igitur in hac parte scriptor ejusdem epistolæ Stephani protomartyris exemplafecutus est, cum videlicet ille dum lapidum grandine unde libi millo atrociter quateretur, flexis poplitibus pro persecutoribus otavit: ille vero imaginū injurias quæ ab illis minime sentiuntur nō ferens, ejusdem injuriæ perpetratores perniciter & absq; misericordia magna sub adtestatione interimēdos esse rogavit, eorūq; animas anathematis vinculo nexas ad perpetua supplicia destinare curavit. neglexit interea earundem literarum scriptor patienter five mansuete in hac parte agere, sprevitque eius prædicationem adimplere, qui ad Theffalonicenses (bit; Patientes estote ad omnes, videte ne quis malum pro malo alicui reddat, sed semper quod bonum est, invicem fequimini, & in omnes: illiusque monitis contempsit parcere, qui ait; Melior est mansuetus cum humilitate, qui dividit prædam cum superbis: & dum debuit in eripiendis miseris irâ regis retrænate, dicente mone; Erue eos qui ducuntur ad mortem, & redime qui interficiuntur, neparcas: fi autem dixeris, Non novi hunc, feto quia Dominus corda hominum novit, & qui finxit spiritum omnibus, ille scit omnia, qui reddet unicuique fecundum opera sua: versa vice ad interfectionem & crudelitatem exercendam impetatoris animum sut teris excitavit. Quia ergo hi qui injuriam patiuntur, liberandi sunt, liber Ecclesiasticus demonfAitenim; Libera eum qui injuriam patitur de manu proterví, & ægre feras in anima tua: in judicando esto pupil misericors ut pater, & pro viro matri illorum: & eris velut filius altifimi obediens, & miserebitur tibi magis quam mater. per Efaiam quoque prophetam ita de hac re dicitur; Inquirite judicium, eripite injuriam accipientem, & judicate pupillo, & justificate viduam, & venite disputemus, dicit Dominus: & si fuerint peccata vestra ut phoenicium, ut nivem dealbabo: fi autem ut coccinum ut lanam albam efficiam: eripite direptum de manu injuriantis. Unde fi quis vult fieri velut filius altissimi Dei, utique operibus bonis instando, & cupit fui a Deo miferere, & peccatorum sordibus ablui, his potius debet saluberrimis monitis uti quam illius epistolae perverfitatem crudelissimam sequi. Porrò quòd ad irascendum imperatoris animum impulit, & hoc quoque crudeliter egit, & sacris literis penitus in hac parte sicut & in cæteris contraiit. Dicit enim per quendam sapientem, Anima benedicta omnis simplex: vir autem animosus vel iracundus non honeft agit: ita & per eundem, Noli esse amicus viro animoso: cum amico autem iracundo nolis commorari, ne forte discas vias ejus, & sumas laqueum animæ tuæ: quæ viæ cum à sapiente disci prohibeantur, multo magis docere & sub adreftatione hortati prohibentur. Liber quoque Ecclesiasticus taliter de hac re intonat, Homo iracundus incendit litem, & vir peccator turbabit amicos, & in medium pacem habentium inmittettlaturam. Nam & Ecclesiastes hæc præcepta dat; Noli festinare in spiritu tuo irasci, quia ira in sinu stultorum requiescit. Doctor itaque gentium ita ad Ephesios scribit; Irascimini & nolite peccare, sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram: item idem, Omnis amaritudo, inquit, & ira, & indignatio & clamor, & blasphemia auferatur a vobis cum omni malitia. idem quoque; Nunc autem, inquit, deponite omnem iram, indignationem, malitiam, blasphemiam, multiloquium: quæ quidem pene omnia, fi liquidius indagentur, in præfatæ epistolæ textu reperientur. Dicat ergo justissimus vir & Deo charus Jacobus Apostolus, utrum juxta epistolæ exhortationem velox quis ad irascendum esse debeat: intonet utrum huic epistolae consentiendum fit, quæ imperatorem citatum ad iracundiam fore sanxit. Ait enim; Scitis fratres dilecti, fit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum, & tardus ad loquendum, tardus quoque ad iram: nam viri justitiam Dei non operatur. Dicat etiam ipsa veritas, quid de hac re ejus membra sequin beant: dic, inquam, sancte Matthææ, quid de paradisi fonte perpetuo hauriens iui fluminis vitalis bus rivulis profudisti. Ait enim fons perennis, fons vitæ, fons luminis; Omnis qui irascitur fratri suo reus erit judicio. Cum vero tot divinæ legis exemplis, tantisque divinorum eloquiorum culis ira, quæ inter principalia vitia enumeratur, dicitur exsecranda, in promptu est intelligere quod hæ literæ ad res in quæstionem venientes roborandas non sunt idoneæ, per quas imperi tori sub magna adtestatione, ac supplici adjuratione committitur habenda & operæ perpetrandæ. Debuerat sane auctor ejusdem epistolæ quos videbat periclitari ad pœnitentiam exhortari: fi forte pœnitentiam contempsissent, poterat imperatorem supplicibus precibus convenire, ut ad convertendum cogeret: fortitan id fui profectus bonum sequerentur coacti, quod conferant spontanei, quoniam Deus omnipotens neminem vult perire, Paulo attestante, qui Hoc enim bonum & acceptum coram salvatore nostro Deo, qui omnes homines vult salvos fieri & in agnitionem veritatis venire. Si enim lucrandis animabus insisteret, illos magis quos errasse videbat ad poenitentiam debuit provocare, quàm principis animum ad effundendum sanguinem incitare: quia pœnitentiæ virtus non est cæteris virtutibus postponenda, sed optimis quibusque æquiparanda: quippe quæ quasi quoddam medicamentum fracta consolidet, languida fanet, perditu restituat, & plerumque post lapsum peccatores ad pristinum statum reducat. Hanc enim Pli amographus commendat, cum dicit; Delictum meum cognitum tibi feci, & injustitias meas non operui: dixi, Pronunciabo adversum me justitias meas Domino, & tu remisisti impietatem cordis mei. Hanc Efaias hortatur, bendam præcepit, dicens; Memores estote horum & ingemiscite, pœnitentiam habete qui erratis, convertimini ex corde. Hæc Hieremiæ variis oraculis censetur dicentis; Convertimini filii revertentes, & fanabo contritiones vestras. in alio quoque loco idem dicit; Avertatur jam nunc unusquisque a via sua mala, & media facite studia vestra. Joel quoque voce Domini intonat, dicens; Convertimini ad me ex toto corde vestro, & ex tota anima vestra in jejunio & fletu & planctu, & disrumpite corda vestra & non vestimenta vestra, & convertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum, quia misericors & patiens est, magnanimis & multum misericors & patiens in benignitatibus. Liber etiam Ecclesiasticus dicit; Si pœnitentiam non egerimus, incidimus in manus Domini secundum magnitudinem ejus, & misericordia ejus cum ipso est. In Actibus hoc Apostolorum scribitur; Pœnitentiam agite & convertimini, ut deleantur peccata vestra. Pastor quoque clefiæ in epistola secunda dicit; Non tardat Dominus sui promissi sicut quidam existimant, sed ex quoque vos, nolens aliquem perdere, sed omnes exspectat in pœnitentia locum reverti. Quanto igitur hæc eminet virtus ad salvandum, quam ille errantibus prædicare neglexit, tanto proculdubio cæteris nequitiis præeminet hæc levitas ad nocendum: quia ille & misericordia uti principem prohibuit, eum eam ad israscendum & ad vindictam exercendam gravibus obtestationibus inpulit. Si ergo juxta Dominicam sententiam grave scelus est unum de pusillis scandalizare, quam grave putas fit non pusillum quendam, sed regem qui caput utique plebium est ad scandalizandum promovere? Nam & in eo quod praefatae epistolae scriptor inter caeteras saevitias, quas erga eos, quos errare conspexit, exercuit, maledictis usus est, non mediocriter erralle & sacris eloquiis contraisse deprehenditur, dicente vale electionis; Benedicite & nolite maledicere. item alibi; Neque maledici regnum Dei possidebunt. Petra etiam ecclesiae maledictis uti his verbis prohibet. Ait enim in epistola prima; Quapropter omnes consentanei esse, unanimes, compatientes, fraternitatis amatores, misericordes, humiles, non reddentes malum pro malo vel maledictum pro maledicto, sed e contrario benedicentes, quia in hoc vocati estis ut benedictionem hereditate possideatis. Sed ne quis nos putet aliquem judicare, aut cuiusdam cujus meriti fumus ignari, detrahere, cognoscat nos non vitam alicujus justi, non meritum discutere, sed verba solummodo ventilabro divinorum eloquiorum studiose ventilare, quae inconpetenter ad errorem nutriendum ad medium sunt deducta, cum sint errorum nervis usquequaque concreta. Nec enim alia ejusdem Symeonis verba discutimus, quae, ut superius diximus, nusquam nos legisse meminimus, sed ea solummodo quae eorum apicibus narrantibus sensu percepimus: & cum nesciamus utrum ejusdem Symeonis, ut illi fatentur, aut alterius cujusdam verba sint in ejus nomine praenotata: novimus tamen ea omni ambiguitate postposita a sanctarum scripturarum sensibus aliena, & merito ab omni ecclesiastico dogmate abdicanda.
units.tr: It is common for the cunning of heretics to mark their shameful and error-promoting writings with titles, and to label them with the names of certain holy and respected men, so that they can more easily offer them to the unwary, as one offers a cup smeared with honey to those who would drink. So we must fear that the letter which they say belonged to a certain St Symeon, and from which they bring forward arguments to establish their error, is not the words of a holy man but the work of some crafty mind. We and other orthodox readers doubt it for this reason: its language in some places contradicts the teachings of the holy Scriptures, and we must not pass over its reading and use it as testimony to confirm doubtful matters, when we know it is opposed to the institutions of divine law. For we do not remember having read anything more from its text than what we found criticised in their manuscript. Although this letter, for all the charm of its thoughts and words, smacks of I know not what blind, insipid and rustic quality, the book nonetheless weaves it together just as we found it in the manuscript. For they say that the aforesaid St Symeon, whose life and preaching are unknown to us, wrote to the Emperor Justinian on behalf of certain Samaritans who were doing injury to images: "Recalling these things on their behalf, we report them to your divine ears"; and again: "I have nothing to say such things on their behalf; therefore, we beg your victorious strength, do not show mercy to those who have dared this, nor spare them, nor receive any request or answer on their behalf." Afterwards: "But I charge you, Lord, by Emmanuel the high God, not to delay nor to make the avenging hand small"; and again: "Those whom their dark kin will receive into condemnation, whom the consuming and gloomy fire awaits, may the holy and almighty Spirit of Jesus Christ our Lord, who proceeds from the Father, curse them into the depths of the abyss, to destroy them in endless perdition." And after a few words: "In him who is to your piety..." In these utterly foolish words, which lack not only the charm of eloquence but also the sense of composition, and which are put together in a barbarous and clumsy way, these things are plainly condemned: that the letter has called the ears of the Emperor Justinian, a man as mortal and frail as anyone, subject to all human change, divine; that it has forbidden him to show mercy to the same people; that it was quick to render evil for evil; that in the same cause it neglected to act patiently and meekly; and that, though he ought to have laboured to rescue the condemned by restraining the king's anger, it rather kindled his anger more and more and drove him savagely to wrath, and did not use the example of him who wills that no one should perish; and that, though he ought to have watched over the winning of souls, it hurled anathemas and curses, and said that the Emperor should reign together with God. Since these words are rebuked in so many places, they are found unfit to uphold the veneration of images, for it is hard to run down precipices for one who stumbles on level ground; nor can a guide of a road be sure in doubtful byways if he cannot keep to the public highway in open roads; and he is rejected by the most subtle master of the liberal disciplines, who is found to have no familiarity at all with common letters. For concerning what he called the Emperor's ears divine, and said that he should reign together with God, we have already disputed at length in the earlier parts of this work against the follies of those who still use such trifles. Now it is fitting that, supporting the steps of our arguments with the testimonies of the divine utterances, we should discuss the other matters now under discussion, as the Lord grants. For when it is found that the emperor was forbidden to show mercy, what else does this do but clearly contradict all the holy Scriptures which command that mercy be shown? Hence it is most dangerous to follow the precepts of such writings, which seem to oppose the divine Scriptures. For the Lord says in the Gospel: "Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful." And again: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy." And the teacher of the Gentiles says: "Be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, as God in Christ also forgave you." And the Psalmist says: "The Lord loves mercy", etc.; "the mercy of the Lord fills the whole earth." And the same Lord says through the Prophet: "For I desire mercy and not sacrifice." For since mercy is held to be commanded by such authoritative precepts, and the Prophet bears witness that he will sing of it for ever, saying, "Your mercies, O Lord, I will sing for ever", and since whoever is said by the Lord to love mercy, but forbids its use and despises having it, is shown not to love God and to be wholly opposed to his most excellent admonitions. Hence also the Truth itself answered the lawyer who said that the one who showed mercy was the neighbour: "Go and do likewise." By this teaching it is shown that not only men of our own nature are to be loved by us, but also the angels, who, though of another nature, are nevertheless believed to be our neighbours in that they show mercy towards us, and are altogether commanded to be loved by him who bade us love God and our neighbour; and in that the emperor was so ready to render evil for evil, he utterly contradicted the divine admonitions. For he ought neither to have been so severe in exacting vengeance, nor to have driven the emperor to exact it; for his ministry was not to exercise vengeance or to command it to be exercised, but to love works of mercy and to preach that they be loved by others. For the Lord says in Exodus: "If you meet the ox of your enemy or his ass going astray, bring it back to him." He did not in any way obey this precept, since he did not at all call back the aforesaid Samaritans from their error, if indeed they are believed to have erred, but rather stirred up the emperor's merit by asking that they should perish in the same error. And those whom he saw fall under the burden of their sins, he not only did not raise up, but allowed to perish savagely under the same burden, though the Lord says: "If you see the ass of one who hates you lying under its burden, you shall not pass by, but you shall help him with it." Also in Proverbs it is written: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head, and God will repay you." For those whom he knew as enemies through sin, if they were fed with the food and drink of spiritual and saving meals, that is, if they were satisfied with the food of the divine words, would heap upon their heads, that is upon their minds, coals of fire which consume the rust of sins and kindle them to the love of God and neighbour. To seek vengeance, therefore, to scorn mercy and to keep wrath, all of which the letter is said to have urged upon the emperor, are condemned by these teachings of the Book of Ecclesiasticus, which says: "He who does not avenge will find vengeance from God, and he will keep his sins. Leave your neighbour who has harmed you, and then your sins will be forgiven. One man keeps wrath against another, and seeks healing from God; he has no mercy on a man like himself, and yet prays about his own sins. He keeps wrath himself, and seeks propitiation from God. Who will pray for his sins?" Likewise, by the oracle of the prophet Isaiah, it is forbidden in this way to render evil for evil: "Hear our words, you who tremble at his name. Say, 'You are our brothers,' to those who hate you and abhor you, so that the name of the Lord may be made manifest and appear to them in their joy, and they will be confounded." The Lord also in the Gospel commanded that enemies should not be provoked to anger, nor vengeance exacted, nor curses forced, but instituted that they be loved, in these most express words: "Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you; do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the just and the unjust." For if, by the true voice, those who hate and persecute us are to be loved rather than cursed and execrated, since we are indeed the image of God, how much less should those be cursed or punished who are said to have done injury to pictures. The chosen vessel also admonishes by these words that evil is to be rendered to no one for evil. For he says in the Epistle to the Romans: "Do not be wise in your own sight, rendering evil to no one for evil, taking thought for good things not only before God but also before all men, if it be possible; as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all men, not defending yourselves, but give place to wrath; for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.'" If, then, we ourselves ought by no means to defend ourselves by the teaching of this excellent preacher, what madness or what folly is it that, according to the exhortation of the same letter sent to Justinian, we should defend, with the zeal of vengeance, injuries done to insensible things, and, since we should not lose the works of piety for our own sake, should lose them for the sake of conflicts about pictures, which those things do not feel at all? Therefore the writer of that letter did not follow the example of Stephen, the first martyr, in this respect, since Stephen, when he was savagely shaken by a hail of stones, fell on his knees and prayed for his persecutors; but the writer of the letter, not enduring the injuries done to images, which those images do not feel at all, asked that the perpetrators of the same injury be destroyed swiftly and without mercy under solemn attestation, and took care to send their souls, bound by the chain of anathema, to eternal punishments. Meanwhile the writer of the same letter neglected to act patiently or meekly in this matter, and despised fulfilling the preaching of him who wrote to the Thessalonians: "Be patient towards all; see that no one renders evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good, both among yourselves and towards all." And he disregarded the admonitions of him who says: "Better is the meek man with humility than he who divides spoil with the proud." And when he ought, in rescuing the wretched, to have restrained the king's anger, the saying was: "Rescue those who are led to death, and redeem those who are being killed; do not spare. But if you say, 'I did not know this man,' does not he who weighs hearts know it? He who keeps your soul knows it, and he will render to each according to his works." In turn, he stirred up the emperor's mind to slaughter and cruelty. Therefore, since those who suffer injury ought to be freed, the Book of Ecclesiasticus shows this: "Rescue him who suffers injury from the hand of the proud, and do not bear it grievously in your soul; in judging, be merciful to the orphan as a father, and for the husband be like a mother to them; and you will be as a son of the Most High, obedient, and he will have mercy on you more than a mother." Through Isaiah the prophet it is also said about this matter: "Seek judgment, rescue him who suffers injury, judge for the orphan, justify the widow, and come, let us dispute, says the Lord; and if your sins are like crimson, I will make them white as snow; if they are like scarlet, I will make them white as white wool; rescue the one plundered from the hand of the one who injures him." Hence, if anyone wishes to become as a son of the Most High God, by diligently doing good works and desiring to obtain mercy from God and to be washed of the filth of sins, he ought rather to use these most wholesome admonitions than to follow the most cruel perversity of that letter. Moreover, that it drove the emperor's mind to anger, and did so cruelly, and that in this respect it has altogether contradicted the sacred letters, as in other respects too, is evident. For a certain wise man says: "Every simple soul is blessed, but the man who is fiery or quick to anger does not act honourably." Likewise through the same: "Do not be a friend to a fiery man, and do not live with an angry friend, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul." And since such ways are forbidden to be learned from the wise, much more are they forbidden to be taught and urged under solemn attestation. The Book of Ecclesiasticus likewise thunders on this matter: "The angry man kindles strife, and the sinful man will trouble friends, and will bring a stumbling block into the midst of those who are at peace." For Ecclesiastes also gives this precept: "Do not hasten in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools." So the teacher of the Gentiles writes to the Ephesians: "Be angry and do not sin; let not the sun go down on your wrath." Again the same: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and indignation, and clamour, and blasphemy be put away from you, with all malice." The same also: "But now, put away all wrath, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and filthy talk." Almost all of which, if they are examined more closely, will be found in the text of the aforesaid letter. Let the most just man, and the apostle dear to God, James, therefore say whether, according to the exhortation of the letter, anyone ought to be quick to anger; let him declare whether this letter, which decreed that the emperor should be provoked to anger, ought to be agreed with. For he says: "You know, beloved brethren: let every man be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow also to anger; for the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God." Let the very Truth also say what its members ought to follow in this matter. Speak, I say, holy Matthew, what you poured out from the perpetual spring of paradise, from the living streams of the river of life. For the everlasting spring, the spring of life, the spring of light says: "Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment." Since, then, by so many examples of the divine law and by so many sayings of the divine utterances, wrath, which is counted among the chief vices, is called to be execrated, it is plain to understand that these letters are not fit to uphold the matters now in question, by which the emperor is committed, under solemn attestation and fearful adjuration, to hold and carry out a work. Indeed, the author of that letter ought to have exhorted to repentance those whom he saw to be in danger; if perhaps they had despised repentance, he could have besought the emperor with humble prayers to compel them to convert; perhaps those who were compelled would have followed the good which the willing would have contributed, since God almighty wills that no one perish, as Paul attests, who says: "For this is good and acceptable before our Saviour God, who wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth." For if he had been intent on winning souls, he ought rather to have urged to repentance those whom he saw to have gone astray than to stir the prince's mind to shed blood; since the virtue of repentance is not to be put below other virtues, but is to be counted equal to the best of them, for it, as a kind of medicine, mends the broken, heals the sick, restores the lost, and often brings sinners back to their former state after their fall. For the Psalmist commends it when he says: "I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my injustices. I said, 'I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord,' and you forgave the wickedness of my heart." Isaiah exhorts to it and commands it, saying: "Remember these things and mourn; you who have gone astray, repent; turn back from the heart." Jeremiah is said to say this in various oracles: "Turn back, you wandering sons, and I will heal your wounds." Elsewhere too he says: "Let each one now turn away from his evil way, and make your endeavours good." Joel also thunders with the voice of the Lord, saying: "Turn to me with all your heart, and with all your soul, in fasting, weeping and mourning; rend your hearts and not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and patient, great in kindness and very merciful and patient in goodness." The Book of Ecclesiasticus also says: "If we do not repent, we fall into the hands of the Lord according to his greatness, and his mercy is with him." In the Acts of the Apostles it is written: "Repent and turn, that your sins may be blotted out." The Shepherd of the Church also says in the second epistle: "The Lord does not delay his promise, as some think, but he is patient with you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." So, then, as much as this virtue of repentance excels in saving, which the writer of that letter neglected to preach to the erring, by just so much, without doubt, does this levity surpass other wickednesses in doing harm; for the one forbade the prince to show mercy, and by grave adjurations drove him to anger and to exacting vengeance. If, then, according to the Lord's sentence, it is a grave crime to scandalise one of the little ones, how grave do you think it is to promote not some little one, but a king, who is indeed the head of the people, to scandalise? For also in that the writer of the aforesaid letter, among his other cruelties which he practised against those whom he saw to be in error, used curses, he is found to have erred no little and to have contradicted the sacred utterances, the chosen vessel saying: "Bless and do not curse." Again elsewhere: "Neither the cursers nor the abusers shall possess the kingdom of God." Peter also, the rock of the Church, forbids the use of curses in these words. For he says in his first epistle: "Finally, be all of one mind, sympathetic, loving the brethren, merciful, humble, not rendering evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary blessing, because you were called to this, that you might inherit a blessing." But lest anyone think that we are judging anyone, or slandering someone of whose merits we are ignorant, let him know that we do not discuss the life or merit of any just man, but only diligently winnow the words with the winnowing-fan of the divine utterances, words which have been wrongly brought forward to nourish error, although they are everywhere bound to the sinews of error. For we are not discussing other words of this same Symeon, which, as we said above, we do not remember having read anywhere, but only those which we have perceived in the sense of their written titles; and although we do not know whether these are words of this same Symeon, as they confess, or of some other man, whose name has been prefixed to them, we nevertheless know that, without any doubt, they are alien to the senses of the holy Scriptures, and rightly to be renounced by every ecclesiastical doctrine.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De eo quod omnibus haereticis Samaritanos deteriores, & Samaritanis deteriores eos dicunt qui ima- gines destruunt, cum parentes eorum secundum illorum opinionem omnibus haereticis deteriores fuerint, qui utique imagines destr- uxere.
units.tr: On the claim that the Samaritans are worse than all heretics, and that those who destroy images are worse than the Samaritans, although their ancestors, by their own opinion, were worse than all heretics, since they are known to have destroyed images.

units.la: NON sufficiebat illis prodecessores sive parentes eorum formidolosis anathematibus abdicare ac diversis conviciis lacerare, nisi eos omnibus haereticis dixissent deteriores fuisse: qui quanto eos atrociorlbus injuriis exsecrari contendunt, tanto amplius divinis monitis contradicunt. Dicunt enim Samaritanos omnibus haereticis deteriores, eisque in crimine praeferunt eos qui imagines destruunt. Constat enim majores eorum imagines destruxisse, & secundum eorum opinionem qui imagines destruunt Samaritanis deteriores sunt, & Samaritani, ut illi ajunt, omnibus haereticis deteriores sunt: omnibus igitur, ut illi fatentur, haereticis majores eorum deteriores fuere, quos constat imagines destruxisse. Nam dum sint, ut ipsi adseverant, ab omnium haereticorum doctrinis aut per carnis materiam propagari, aut in scripturarum dogmatibus educari, aut per manus impositionem ad peragenda Christianae religionis mysteria consecrati, mirandum est qui se caeteris catholicis in constitutionibus exhibendis, & ecclesiae traditionibus statuendis eminentiores exstiment, tantamque se auctoritatis praerogativam habere jactent, cum hanc eos habere nec proprium actuum sive documentorum exercitia, nec majorum suorum exempla probent. Nam si isti imaginum adorationem omnibus catholicis praeferendi sunt, jam non in ecclesia virtutum sectatores, sed imaginum adoratores eminentiorem locum tenebunt: & si imaginum adoratores intra ecclesiam eminentiorem locum tenebunt, jam non virtutibus, sed erroribus est utendum: est autem virtutibus non erroribus utendum: non igitur ilii ob imaginum adorationem omnibus catholicis praeferendi sunt. Samaritani namque, quos illi dicunt omnibus haereticis deteriores, non sunt haeretici Christianorum, sed Judaeorum: nec se novum testamentum, sed vetus tenere fatentur: qui Judaei resurrectionem corporum credant, propheras sive hagiographa recipiant, illi & resurrectionem spernunt, & exceptis quinque legis libris omnes scripturas & veteris & novi testamenti postponunt. Sunt autem reliquiae gentium quas Sennacherib rex Assyriorum decem tribubus Medos translatis, ad custodiendam terram Israel misit. Qui dum leonibus caeterisque pessimis sens vel quibusdam rebus inconmodis in terra Israel vastarentur, & legationem regi facerent, se in eadem regione perdurare minime valere, nisi legitima Dei terrae custodirent, quosdam de Levitis ad eos missi fuisse perhibentur, a quibus legis caerimonias docerentur: quibus ex parte fusceptis & in pluribus haeresoeos partibus usurpatis, adeo eorum barbara gentilitas cordis tumore inflata est, ut postpositis Judaeis, qui utique de Jacob germine processisse creduntur, se solummodo filios Jacob esse gloriantur: atque ira Judaeorum communionem sicut & caeterarum gentium spernere fastu impellente cogantur: de quorum stirpe erat Samaritis foemina, quae ad pureum Dominicis conloquiis communicans, mani jactantia patrem suum Jacob qui sibi puteum dedisset; & redemptorem mundi eo majorem non esse eum magna cervicositate adferebat, majoresque suos non Hierosolymis, sed in monte adorasse dicebat. Quam cervicositatem simul cum hydria & incredulitate depositum, & salutaribus monitis adquievit. Quae quid typicis innuerit mysteriis si breviter exsequamur, non est inconsequens. Gestit ergo typum totius humani generis, quod seneseente jam mundo ad Dominum venit, qui sexta utique aetate mundi ad puteum sedit, qui mundi hujus terrenum laborem & errorem profunditate significat, sedit, inquam, humilitatem carnis pro nobis suscepta fatigatus, insimitem ejusdem carnis significans, quamvis alio intellectu sellio ejus magisterii & doctrinae dignitatem demonstret. Sitivit non tantum aquam, sed fidem gentium haurire cupiens. Unde & disca& discipulis manducare hortantibus cibum se dixit habere quem illi nescirent. Sitiebat ergo fidem gentilium ut faceret in ea voluntatem patris, & perficeret opus ejus. Promisit ergo se illi daturum quam vivam, spiritum videlicet quem accepturi erant credentes in eum. Dixit ergo eam quinque viros habuisse, id est, quinque carnalibus sensibus usam fuisse, & sensum quem tandem haberet Christo crediturā erat, cum quo legitimum posset habere connubium, jam non suum esse: nam post quinque carnales responsiones sexta responsione nominat Christum. Prima namque ejus responsio est, Tu cum sis Judaeus quomodo à me bibere petis? secunda, Domine neque haurilorium habes & puteus altus est: tertia, Domine da mihi hanc aquam ut neque sitiam, neque veniam huc haurire: quarta, Non habeo virum: quinta, Video quia Propheta es: patres nostri in monte hoc adoraverunt: nam ista responsio carnalis est. Carnalibus enim datus fuerat locus terrenus ubi orarent, non ut locum aut rem aliquam in eo potius adorarent, sed in eodem loco adorarent Dominum, spiritales autem in spiritu & veritate, non in imaginibus, non in picturis, non in rebus sensu carentibus oraturos Dominus dixit. quod potius locutus est, sexta mulieris responsio Christum faretur omnium istorum esse doctorem.
units.tr: It was not enough for them to renounce their predecessors or parents with dreadful anathemas and to tear them apart with various insults, unless they had also said that these were worse than all heretics. The more bitterly they strive to curse them with such atrocious slanders, the more they contradict the divine admonitions. For they say that the Samaritans are worse than all heretics, and in crime they set above them those who destroy images. It is established that their ancestors destroyed images, and according to their opinion those who destroy images are worse than the Samaritans, and the Samaritans, as they say, are worse than all heretics. Therefore, as they themselves admit, their ancestors, who are known to have destroyed images, were worse than all heretics. For since, as they themselves assert, they are propagated from the material of the flesh of all heretics, or educated in the doctrines of Scripture, or consecrated by the laying on of hands to perform the mysteries of the Christian religion, it is astonishing that they think themselves more eminent than the other Catholics in drawing up constitutions and establishing the traditions of the Church, and that they boast of so great a prerogative of authority, when neither the practice of their own acts and documents nor the examples of their ancestors prove that they have it. For if those men are to be preferred to all Catholics on account of their adoration of images, then they will hold the more eminent place in the Church not as followers of virtues but as adorers of images. And if adorers of images are to hold the more eminent place within the Church, then we must make use not of virtues but of errors; yet we must make use of virtues, not errors. Therefore those men are not to be preferred to all Catholics on account of the adoration of images. For the Samaritans, whom they call worse than all heretics, are not heretics of the Christians but of the Jews. Nor do they profess to hold the New Testament, but the Old. Unlike the Jews, who believe in the resurrection of bodies and receive the Prophets and the Hagiographa, they reject even the resurrection, and, apart from the five books of the Law, they set aside all the Scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments. They are the remnants of the nations whom Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, sent to guard the land of Israel after he had transferred the ten tribes to the Medes. When these, being laid waste in the land of Israel by lions and other fierce beasts and by certain other troubles, sent an embassy to the king saying that they could not possibly remain in that region unless they kept the lawful worship of the God of the land, it is reported that certain Levites were sent to them, from whom they were taught the ceremonies of the Law. When they had partly received these and adopted them in many parts of the heresy, their barbarous paganism was so inflated with swelling of heart that, setting aside the Jews, who are indeed believed to have come from the seed of Jacob, they boast only that they are sons of Jacob. Thus, with pride driving them on, they are compelled to despise communion with the Jews just as with the other nations. Of their stock was the Samaritan woman who, conversing with the Lord at the well, boasted with empty pride that her father Jacob had given them the well, and with great stubbornness asserted that the Redeemer of the world was not greater than he. She also said that their ancestors worshipped not in Jerusalem but on the mountain. This stubbornness, together with her water jar and her unbelief, she laid down, and she assented to the saving admonitions. If we briefly set out what this signifies in the typical mysteries, it is not out of place. He therefore bears the type of the whole human race, which came to the Lord when the world was already growing old; he who sat by the well in the sixth age of the world, which by its depth signifies the earthly toil and error of this world. He sat, I say, wearied by the humility of the flesh taken up for us, signifying the weakness of that same flesh, although in another sense the seat shows the dignity of his office and teaching. He thirsted not only for water but desired to draw in the faith of the nations. Hence also, when his disciples urged him to eat, he said that he had food which they did not know. He was thirsting, then, for the faith of the Gentiles, so that he might do the Father's will in it and complete his work. He therefore promised to give her living water, namely the Spirit which believers in him were to receive. He said that she had had five husbands, that is, that she had used five carnal senses, and that the sense which she would at last have, believing in Christ, with which she could have lawful marriage, was no longer her own. For after five carnal answers she names Christ in the sixth answer. Her first answer is: How do you, since you are a Jew, ask me for a drink? The second: Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep. The third: Sir, give me this water, that I may neither thirst nor come here to draw. The fourth: I have no husband. The fifth: I see that you are a prophet; our fathers worshipped on this mountain. For that answer is carnal. A earthly place had been given to carnal men where they might pray, not so that they should worship the place or any thing in it, but so that they should worship the Lord in that same place. Spiritual worshippers, however, the Lord said, would pray in spirit and truth, not in images, not in pictures, not in things devoid of sense. What he rather said, the woman's sixth answer, confesses Christ to be the teacher of all these things.

units.la: Ibid. enim, Scio quoniam Messias venit qui dicitur Christus, cum venerit ipse adnuntiabit nobis omnia. Sed adhuc credit, quia eum quem venturum sperat, venisse non videt, qui error misericordia Domini dicentis, Ego sum qui tecum loquor, tanquam adulter expellitur. quo audito nihil respondit, sed relicta hydria, ditate videlicet atque amore laculi hujus, quo sibi homines de tenebrosa profunditate & retrorsum conversatione hauriunt voluptatem, qua percepta denuo in ejus adpetitum inardescunt, sicut et cum est, De aqua illa qui biberit sitiet iterum: iit in civitatem, quia videlicet mundo praedicavit quod credidit, corde credens ad justitiam, ore confitens ad salutem. Quia ergo paulo longius à re propositā digressi sumus, ad propositum denuo revertamur. Samaritani namque cum sint gentiles, & ficte Judaismum tenere videantur, non amplius caeteris incredulis contra ecclesiam saevire noscuntur: quidem isti dum haereticos Christianorum putent, omnibusque haereticis nequiores existimentur, quibus eis clementia favent, cum majores suos in nequitia illis praeferendos esse perdocent. non est omnium deterrimus, cui in culpa alius quilibet invenitur praeferendus.
units.tr: For she says, I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will tell us all things. But she still believes that the one she hopes is coming has not yet come, and this error is cast out like an adulterer by the mercy of the Lord who says, I am he who speaks with you. Hearing this, she answered nothing, but left her water jar, that is, the wealth and love of this pit, from which men draw pleasure out of dark depths and a backward way of life. Once that pleasure has been tasted, they burn again for its desire, as it is said: Whoever drinks of that water will thirst again. She went into the city, because she preached to the world what she believed, believing in her heart unto righteousness and confessing with her mouth unto salvation. Since we have digressed a little far from the matter proposed, let us now return to our proposal. The Samaritans, since they are Gentiles and seem to hold Judaism only in pretence, are no longer known to rage against the Church more than the other unbelievers. Indeed, although they are thought to be heretics of the Christians and are considered more wicked than all heretics, they are favoured by clemency, since they teach that their own ancestors are to be preferred to them in wickedness. He is not the worst of all to whom some other can be preferred in fault.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: De eo quod quanto plura exempla haereticorum & imagines spernentium vel despicientium tra- hunt, tanto parentes suos majoribus convicius & injuriis inhonorant, quos procul dubio eorum sequaces in hac parte fuisse profitentur.
units.tr: Concerning how, the more examples of heretics and of those who scorn or despise images they bring forward, the more they dishonour their parents with reproaches and insults, whom without doubt they profess to have been followers of in this matter.

units.la: VETUSTISSIMUS non solum philosophorum, sed etiam oratorum mos est, cum aliquid probare velint, aut in ipso negotio de quo agitur, aut ex rebus alius, aut certe extrinsecus band rei argumentationem adsumere. Quos illi dum in caeteris inperitia intervenientes, qui contemnunt, in hac nimirum parte sequi omnino contendunt, cum prodecessores sive patentes suos ob imaginum abolitionem, aut ex ipso negotio, aut abunde aut extrinsecus argumentes damnare statuunt, & convitiis lacerare, anathematibus exsecrare, insanissimis verbis norare non metuunt: quantoque plura quorundam haereticorum exempla in testimonium trahuntur, quorum eos sequaces fuisse profitentur, tanto & eos gravioribus exsecrationibus abdicant, & sed nis monitis quae parentibus honorem impendendum sanciunt, contraire demonstrant. Honorabit Dominus, patrem tuum & matrem tuam, ut bene sit tibi. Quod quidem praeceptum tanta auctoritate viget, ut & in tabulis digito Domini scriptum sit, & ab Apostolo primum mandatum nominetur. Ait enim; Honora patrem & matrem, quod est mandatum primum in promissione, in ea videlicet promissio qua statim subjecit, Ut sis longaevus super terram & bene tibi sit. Animadvertendum sane est quantae damnationis, qui parentes conviciis lacerant, aut anathematibus execrantur, cum tanti sint mercedes tantamque repromissionem habeant qui eos juxta Dominicae vocis imperium honorant. Quanto eos qui huic praecepto parent optima demulcet promissio, tanto illos qui eidem Domini imperio reluctantur, formidolosa deterrere debet damnatio. in Levitico quoque scribitur; Unusquisque patrem suum, & matrem suam timeat. in Ecclesiastico quoque de honorandis parentibus scribitur: Qui honorat patrem suum, longiori vita vivet: & qui obaudit patrem, refrigerat matrem, & quasi Dominus fratribus qui se generaverunt, in opere & sermone & omni patientia, & benedictio ejus in novissimo manet. Item in Ecclesiastico; Fili suscipe senectam patris tui, & non contristes eum in vita ipsius: & si deficit sensu, da veniam, & ne spernas eum in tua virtute. Non est tibi gloria, sed confusio: Doctor etiam gentium dicit; Filii, obedite parentibus vestris in omnia, hoc enim placet Domino. Si enim honorem impendere, sive obedire parentibus Deo placet, contrarium eis & execrationes ingerere modis omnibus displicet: & hoc non displicet, neque illud placet, grave ergo & formidolosum est parentes non honorare: gravissimum vero & formidolosissimum eos abominari, aut anathematizare, dicente Domino; Qui maledixerit patri suo, aut matri suae, morte moriatur. & iterum, Maledictus homo, qui non honorificat patrem suum, aut matrem suam, & dicet omnis populus, fiat. In Proverbiis quoque scribitur, Qui maledicit patri suo & matri, extinguetur lucerna ejus in medio tenebris. Item ibi; Qui repellit patrem suum & matrem suam, & aestimat se non peccare, hic particeps est viro impio. Unde sciendum est, non eos esse mediocris insaniae, qui pro rebus sensu carentibus in majores maledicta non pertimescunt congerere, & dum imaginibus volunt favere, nec parentes pertimescunt inhonorare, nec divinis oraculis contraire. Nos quidem haec dicentes, non illorum majoribus favemus, quos in hoc quoque negotio absurde egisse comperimus, sed quanta sit istorum praesumptio, in talibus ausis divinae legis testimoniis demonstramus.
units.tr: It is the most ancient custom not only of philosophers but also of orators, when they wish to prove something, to take their argument either from the matter under discussion itself, or from other things, or certainly from outside the matter altogether. Those who, though ignorant in other matters, despise these things, strive entirely to follow them in this respect, when they decide to condemn their predecessors or parents for the abolition of images, whether from the matter itself, abundantly or from outside arguments, and do not fear to tear them with insults, curse them with anathemas, and brand them with the most insane words. And the more examples of certain heretics they bring forward as testimony, whose followers they profess to have been, the more they renounce them with heavier curses, and show themselves to be opposed to the precepts which command honour to be paid to parents. The Lord will honour your father and your mother, that it may be well with you. This precept is held in such authority that it was written with the finger of the Lord on the tablets, and by the Apostle it is named the first commandment. For he says: Honour your father and mother, which is the first commandment with promise, namely the promise which he immediately added: that you may live long upon the earth and that it may be well with you. It must certainly be noted how great is the damnation of those who tear their parents with insults or curse them with anathemas, since those who honour them according to the command of the Lord have such great rewards and so great a promise. As the best promise soothes those who obey this precept, so the fearful damnation ought to terrify those who resist the command of the Lord. In Leviticus it is also written: Let each one fear his father and his mother. In Ecclesiasticus also, concerning the honouring of parents, it is written: He who honours his father shall live a longer life; and he who obeys his father refreshes his mother, and as the Lord he serves those who begot him, in work and word and all patience, and his blessing remains to the last. Likewise in Ecclesiasticus: My son, receive the old age of your father, and do not grieve him in his life; and if he fails in understanding, pardon him, and do not despise him in your strength. It will not be glory to you but confusion. The teacher of the Gentiles also says: Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is pleasing to the Lord. For if to pay honour, or to obey, parents is pleasing to God, to set oneself against them and to heap curses upon them is displeasing in every way; and this does not please, nor does that please; it is therefore grave and fearful not to honour parents, but most grave and most fearful to abhor them or curse them, the Lord saying: He who curses his father or his mother shall die the death. And again: Cursed is the man who does not honour his father or his mother, and all the people shall say: So be it. In Proverbs also it is written: He who curses his father and his mother, his lamp shall be extinguished in the midst of darkness. Likewise there: He who drives away his father and his mother, and thinks he does not sin, is a partner of the wicked man. Hence it must be understood that those are not of ordinary madness who, against things devoid of sense, do not fear to heap curses upon their ancestors, and while they wish to favour images, neither fear to dishonour parents nor to oppose the divine oracles. Indeed, in saying these things, we do not favour the ancestors of those whom we find to have acted absurdly in this matter too, but by the testimonies of the divine law in such daring deeds we demonstrate how great is the presumption of these men.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: Chapter VIII.

units.la: De eo quod secundum Demetrii Diaconi dictum, incaute & inordinate, parentes eorum egerunt, duos libros inargentatos, eo quod quiddam de imaginibus in his continebatur, combu- rentes, & alterius libri duo folia praciderunt.
units.tr: Concerning what their parents did rashly and disorderly, according to Demetrius the deacon's account: they burned two silver-plated books because something about images was contained in them, and they cut away two leaves of another book.

units.la: Cum in neutra parte moderamen habentes, neque isti rationis coerceatur, neque illorum progenitores coercti fuisse credantur habenis, sed utrique convincantur per abrupta & invia ferri effrenes rerumque prohibitarum & profectu carentium sequaces: dum videlicet, sicut credo jam dictum est, isti imagines supplicirer censeant adorare, illi inpatienter censuerint frangere, ut Demetrius eorum diaconus ait, incaute & inordinate inter cetera egerunt, duos libros inargentatos eo quod quaedam in eis imaginum mentio haberetur, comburentes, & alterius libri duo folia praecidentes, quasi non aliter imaginum possit mentio fieri, nisi protinus censeantur adorari. Nam dum nullus recipiendorum codicum vel tenuiter imagines adorare percenseat, in pluribus tamen illarum mentio quodammodo fit. Qui si omnes in quibus illarum mentio fit, comburendi sunt, multa protinus scripturarum instrumenta peribunt. Primum namque unaquaeque res probanda est, et postea judicanda. quod cum pluribus sive divinarum sive mundanarum legum exemplis possit adprobari, ipsorum quoque rhetorum documentis potest adstrui, qui primum genus posuerunt deliberativum, secundum demonstrativum, tertium judiciale: ut videlicet quicquid deliberatio aut abnuendum, aut sequendum repererint, demonstratio id aut laudabile, aut reprehensibile demonstret, judiciale, aut poenis, aut praemiis sententiam dent: ne si non judiciale haec duo sequentia genera praecedant, versus in contrarium caulis deliberationis examine praepositio, demonstrationis ordine neglecto, aliter res quaelibet quam jutum est judicetur. In omnibus igitur rebus moderatio sive mediocritas habenda est, et memoria retinendum est illud philosophicum; Nequid nimis. quae moderatio probationis semper societate multicenda est. non enim ait Apostolus, Omnia absque moderatione & absque probatione comburite, sed, Omnia, inquit, probate & quod bonum est retinete.
units.tr: Since neither side keeps any measure, neither their reason restrains them, nor are their forebears believed to have been held in check by the reins, but both are shown to be carried headlong through precipices and trackless places, unbridled and pursuing things that are forbidden and bring no benefit. For, as I believe has already been said, these men think images should be adored with supplication, while those men impatiently thought they should be broken. As Demetrius their deacon says, among other things they acted rashly and disorderly: they burned two silver-plated books because some mention of images was found in them, and they cut away two leaves of another book, as if mention of images could not be made without its at once being taken that they are adored. For while none of the books to be received is thought even slightly to adore images, yet in many of them mention of images is in some way made. If all the books in which mention of images is made were to be burned, many instruments of Scripture would at once perish. For first each thing must be proved, and afterwards judged. Since this can be confirmed by many examples both from divine and from secular laws, it can also be supported by the teachings of the rhetoricians themselves, who laid down three kinds: the deliberative first, the demonstrative second, and the judicial third. So, whatever deliberation finds must be rejected or followed, demonstration shows to be either praiseworthy or blameworthy, and judgment passes sentence either of punishment or of reward. Otherwise, if these two following kinds did not precede the judicial, the order would be reversed under the scrutiny of deliberation, the order of demonstration being neglected, and any matter would be judged otherwise than is right. In all things, therefore, moderation or the mean is to be observed, and that saying of the philosophers must be kept in memory: Nothing in excess. This moderation must always be joined with a careful testing of the matter. For the Apostle does not say, Burn all things without moderation and without testing, but, Prove all things, he says, and hold fast what is good.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De eo quod in eodem libro in tabulis argenteis Leontius a Secreta imagines cernens acutissimum & ingeniosissimum sui erroris emolumentum invenisse gloriatus est.
units.tr: Concerning what Leontius of the Secreta, seeing the images on the silver tablets in the same book, boasted that he had found the most acute and ingenious advantage from his error.

units.la: Neco denique libro, in quo duo folia ob quandam imaginum mentionem in eorum priore synodo quae ob abolendas imagines gesta est, praecisa fuerant, habebantur in tabulis argenteis quaedam imagines sicut in vasculis sive in pluribus rebus haberi solent, quas in secunda eorum synodo quae pro adorandis imaginibus adgregata est, mox ut Leontius a Secreta conspexit, magnum se sui erroris emolumentum invenisse putavit, eosque insignis fuisse dementiae judicavit, a quibus in eodem libro ubi imagines erant, ob imaginum mentionem duo folia abscisa fuisse cognovit: sicque idem liber per intervalla temporum variis eventibus disparibusque modis & ab illis est propter imaginum mentionem abscidi judicatus, & ab istis propter imagines quae habebantur in tabulis adorari jussus: ab illis foliorum jacturam injuste perpessus, ab istis adoratione inlicita sublimatus: illis auferentibus quod habebat & habere debuerat, inconpetenter amisit, istis exhibentibus quae nec habebat nec habere debuerat, inconsequenter adquisivit: qui nec pro ullis instantibus culpis folia perdidit, nec pro quibusdam insignibus meritis adorationem invenit: et quanto meruit recte habita amittere, tanto nimirum meruit inhibita adquirere. Numquidnam omnes libri in quibus auro argentoque vel etiam quibuslibet coloribus historiae inter scripturas pictoria arte insertae sunt, quia imagines habent aut ab illis sunt comburendi sive praecidendi, aut ab istis colendi sive adorandi? Numquidnam sericae sive quarumlibet materiarum vestes sive pallia humanis usibus apta, aut divinis cultibus mancipata, figuris quibusdam decorata, variisque coloribus fucata, eo quod imagines habent, aut ab illis sunt concremanda, aut ab istis adoranda? Numquidnam metalla sive ligna quibuslibet utilitatibus formata, eo quod sculptorio vel etiam caelatorio opere quibusdam imaginibus decorantur, ideo aut ab illis conburenda aut frangenda, aut ab istis sunt adoranda? Infelix mens quae semper aut in exscrandis, aut e contrario in adorandis imaginibus aestuat. Infelix sensus, qui semper in abdicandis rebus quae sine offensione haberi queunt, & sine offensione adorari nequeunt, anhelat. Infelix consuetudo quae mediocritatis recto tramite aspernato, fixam tenere regulam nesciens, huc illucque semper nutabunda deflectitur, modo inordinate abdicans quod nequaquam est abdicandum, modo infauste adorans, quod non est penitus adorandum, modo ultra quam ordo exigit rem minime deiciendam deicit, modo ultra quam ordo exposcit rem non nimium extollendam extollit, & rebus necessariis omnibus rebus non necessariis instans, aut ob imaginum abolitionem, aut ob earum adorationem, quod utrumque non convenit, synodos adgregat, quasi Christianae religioni aut in habendo, aut in non adorando quoddam possint afferre praejudicium: cum videlicet imagines nihil si non lu-bentur derogant, nihil si habentur protogant, cum tamen abdicatae quandam incautam levitatem inferant, adoratae vero culpam mutant.
units.tr: Finally, in the same book, in which two leaves had been cut out because of some mention of images in their earlier synod, which was held to abolish images, there were on silver tablets certain images, such as are commonly kept on little vessels or on many other objects. When Leontius of the Secreta saw these in their second synod, which was assembled to adore images, he thought he had found a great advantage from his error, and he judged those men to be of remarkable madness by whom, in that same book where the images were, two leaves had been cut out because of the mention of images. So the same book, over intervals of time and through different events and in different ways, was judged by those men to be cut up because of the mention of images, and by these men was ordered to be adored because of the images that were on the tablets. By the former it unjustly suffered the loss of leaves; by the latter it was raised up by unlawful adoration. The former, taking away what it had and ought to have had, it lost without cause; the latter, granting what it neither had nor ought to have had, it gained without consequence. It lost its leaves for no present faults, and it found adoration for no outstanding merits; and as it deserved to lose what was rightly held, so it deserved to acquire what was forbidden. Surely, then, are all books in which histories are inserted among the writings by the art of painting, with gold or silver or even with any colours, to be burned or cut up by those men because they have images, or to be worshipped and adored by these men? Surely are silken garments, or garments and cloaks of whatever material, fit for human uses or dedicated to divine worship, adorned with certain figures and dyed with various colours, to be burned by those men, or adored by these, because they have images? Surely are metals or wood, shaped for whatever uses, to be burned or broken by those men, or to be adored by these, because they are decorated with certain images by sculpted or even engraved work? Unhappy the mind that always rages either in execrating images or, on the contrary, in adoring them! Unhappy the sense that always gasps after rejecting things which can be kept without offence and cannot be adored without offence! Unhappy the habit which, having spurned the straight path of moderation and not knowing how to keep a fixed rule, is always swaying and turning this way and that: now recklessly rejecting what by no means ought to be rejected, now wrongly adoring what is not at all to be adored, now casting down beyond what order requires a thing not to be cast down, now exalting beyond what order demands a thing not to be greatly exalted, and, pressing on unnecessary things while neglecting all necessary ones, it gathers synods either for the abolition of images or for their adoration, both of which are out of place, as though they could bring some harm to the Christian religion either by keeping them or by not adoring them. For images, if they are not loved, detract nothing, and if they are kept, add nothing; yet when they are rejected they bring a certain rash levity, and when they are adored they change into guilt.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Quod nulla evangelii lectio tradat Jesum ad Abgarum imaginem misisse, ut illi dicunt.
units.tr: That no reading of the Gospel records that Jesus sent an image to Abgarus, as they say.

units.la: EVANGELIUM est bonum nuntium, & revera bonum nuntium, quoniam qui id suscipiunt filii Dei vocantur. Est enim amnis quadrifluus ab uno ineffabili Paradisi fonte progressus, & quatuor amnes insigniter derivatus, & ad arentia corda inriganda salubriter emissus. Est via ducit ad vitam; est lux a tenebris vitiorum reducens & inoffenso calle gressus mortalium ad caelestia dirigens. Est urbis Hierusalem nobilissimae munimentum, in quo firmiter stare praestantissimum vitae emolumentum, a quo recedere periculosissimum detrimentum est. Sunt fluenta veritatis, quae fallere nesciunt, in quorum vastissimis amnibus cum plura dominicorum gestorum insignia habeantur, eundem dominum Abgari cujusdam regis epistolam suscepisse, eique reciprocam destinasse minime putetur. Quae duae epistolae cum a sancti evangelii lectione sint penitus extraneae, & a beato Gelasio Romanae urbis antecessore, vel a ceteris aeque catholicis & orthodoxis viris inter apocryphas scripturas prorsus deputatae, non sunt in testimonium quodammodo producendae, quia ad ea quae in quaestionem veniunt adprobanda vel improbanda sicut & caeterae apocryphae scripturae minus sunt idoneae. Harum ergo textus cum sit ab evangelistis minime in codicibus evangeliorum taxatus, & merito a catholicis inter apocrypha deputatus, & ab iis ob adorandarum imaginum errorem adstruendum in symbolum adlatus, nec iuris quidem vel renuiter favet sequacibus praesertim cum ibidem nequaquam Abgaro domino imaginem quandam adoraturus postulasse legatur, aut idem omnium dominus eidem imaginem adorandam destinasse perhibeatur. Si vero hi qui earum lectione tuentur rursus fulcire moliuntur, eadem epistolas, unam a domino susceptam, alteram missam ad firmare linent, dicentes, Non omnia scripta in evangelio quae a Domino dicta vel facta sunt, & utantur testimonio Johannis dicentis, Multa quoque et alia signa fecit Jesus in conspectu discipulorum suorum quae non sunt scripta in libro hoc, advertant hoc de signis non de epistolis, de signis non de constitutionibus intelligi posse. Quod vero ipsae epistolae a sancta ecclesia ob hanc lectionem remotae & a catholicis inter apocrypha deputatae sint, & in earum lectione adorationis imaginum nulla documenta habeantur, manifestum est. Nos & imaginum adoratione sanctorum, & eas inter apocrypha legentes omnia probamus, quae bona sunt retinemus.
units.tr: The Gospel is a good message, and truly a good message, since those who receive it are called sons of God. For it is a four-branched river, flowing from the one ineffable fountain of Paradise and drawn off into four notable streams, and sent forth healthfully to water hearts that are dry. It is the way that leads to life; it is the light that brings mortals back from the darkness of vices and directs their steps along an unobstructed path to heavenly things. It is the fortress of the most noble city of Jerusalem, where to stand firm is the greatest benefit of life, and to withdraw from which is the most dangerous loss. These are the fountains of truth, which know not how to deceive. In their vast streams many notable deeds of the Lord are found, but it is not thought that the same Lord received a letter from a certain king, Abgar, or sent a reply to him. Since these two letters are entirely foreign to the reading of the holy Gospel, and have been wholly classed among the apocryphal writings by the blessed Gelasius, predecessor at the city of Rome, or by other equally catholic and orthodox men, they are not to be produced as testimony in any way, because, like the other apocryphal writings, they are poorly suited to prove or disprove the matters now in question. Therefore, since this text is nowhere listed by the evangelists among the codices of the Gospels, has rightly been classed by Catholics among the apocrypha, and has been brought into the creed by others to establish the error of adoring images, it favours its followers neither by right nor even reluctantly, especially since there it is nowhere read that Lord Abgar asked for an image to be adored, or that the same Lord of all is said to have sent an image there to be adored. But if those who defend them by reading them try again to prop them up, they labour to daub over the same letters, one received by the Lord and the other sent, to confirm them, saying, "Not all the things written in the Gospel are things said or done by the Lord," and they use the testimony of John, who says, Jesus also did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. Let them consider that this can be understood of signs, not of letters, and of signs, not of constitutions. That the letters themselves were removed from the holy Church on account of this reading, and have been classed by Catholics among the apocrypha, and that in their reading there are no proofs of the adoration of images, is manifest. We, both in the adoration of the images of saints and in reading these letters among the apocrypha, test all things and retain what is good.

units.la: Joan.ult.
units.tr: Joan. ult.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Quod illi libri gestorum patrum, quorum auctores ignorantur, non prorsus idonei sint ad testi- monia danda, & ad haec quae in contentionem veniunt adfirmanda.
units.tr: That those books of the Acts of the Fathers whose authors are unknown are not wholly fit to be used as testimonies, or to confirm those matters which are brought into dispute.

units.la: APOSTOLICA nos admonet praedicatio, omnia probare, & ea quae bona sunt retinere. Quod de doctrinarum diversitatibus quam maxime intelligi poterit. Non enim nos omnium articulorum vel etiam rerum gustum capere permisit, ut quasi praegustantes omnia bona solummodo tenentes mala quaeque abiciamus, quod fieri ablata; quaedam inlicitorum perpetratione nequaquam tenet, sed probare nos jussit, & spiritali palato degustare omnes doctrinas & eas quae a viris probatis inlatae, interna saturitate mentes reficiunt solummodo retinere, ceteras vero omnes cum doctoribus abicere. Unde cum penè in omnibus hujusmodi scripturis haec regula prorsus sit observanda, in libris quoque qui gesta quorundam sanctorum patrum retinent, penitus est custodienda. Quoniam & magna illorum est multitudo, & varia narratio diversaque praedicatio, & tanto plerumque illorum dictis a fidelibus dubitatur, quanto nimirum eorum auctores ignorantur. Atque ideo non omnes sunt ad res dubias adfirmandas in testimonium proferendi, quia nec omnes auctorum suorum praetitulatione muniti, aut virorum fortium & eloquentissimorum stilo digesti. Venerabilis itaque Gelasii Papae caeterorumque Patrum doctrinis instituimur, vitas Patrum, Pauli, Antonii, Hilarionis vel ceterorum quae a beato Hieronymo aut editae sunt, aut de Graeco in Latinum translatae sermone, aut illorum doctorum sunt stilo digestae quorum cetera opuscula a sancta catholica & apostolica ecclesia suscipiuntur, cum omni honore suscipere; ceteras vero quarum auctores ignorantur, inter apocryphas scripturas deputare. Cum ergo illi imaginum adorationem modo divinorum eloquiorum commutationis inconsiderate adhibitus, modo ignotorum quorundam doctorum dictis, modo apocryphorum nactui adprobare adfectent, animadvertere debent rem se impositi bile agendam arripuisse: cum videlicet nec divinorum eloquiorum testimonia ad peregrinos sensus violenter nec valeant nec debeant usurpari, nec ignotorum praedicatio, quorum spiritus necdum probati sunt an ex Deo sint, in testimonium deduci, nec apocryphorum frivolis rebus ambiguis & nec dum deliberatis firmitas valeat exhiberi. Quanto si cujuslibet verba falsitatis fuco nequaquam vitianda sunt, multo minus divina eloquia, quae sunt eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum, quodammodo ad alias res quam ordo se habet sufficere panda sunt: & cum in humanis negotiis viles sive ignotae personae ad ea quae in quaestione veniunt ad probanda, minime admittantur, multominus in tantis rebus quæ cælestis magisterii eruditione indigent, incognitorum doctorum aut apocryphorum scripturarum testimonia sunt adhibenda.
