Probandæ namque sunt scripturæ & subtili examinatione perscrutandæ, & sanctorum Patrum testimonia roborandæ, quæ ad res dubias adfirmandas intra sanctam ecclesiam in testimonium sunt proserendæ: quoniam & servus nequam in evangelio, eo quod pecuniam nummulariis non dederit, à Domino arguitur: unde dare nobis convenit pecuniam nummularis, ne forte cum eodem servo argumur, quasi tunc nummularus impendimus, cum scripturas quaslibet sanctorum Patrum examinandas in certas inpertimus. Pecuniam namque nummularii quadam pertio modo examinant, utrum aurum probatum sit, utrum purum, necne, aliquo fuco falsitatis introductus vitiatum, an regis potius quàm tyranni inscriptione signatum sit, vel etiam plenissimi ponderis æqualiarem gerat: quæ omnia in magni patrisfamilias pecunia, id est, in nostri redemptoris doctrinis à nummulariis, à sanctis videlicet & eloquentissimis viris, superni ignis examine perquirunter. Quæritur ergo in unumquemque quæ scripturæ numinis, utrum aurum probatissimum sit, unde archa Domini valeat exornari, vel etiam totius sanctuarii opus resplendear, ut videlicet in ea spiritalis intelligentiæ rector emineat, quo divina lex intelligatur & totius ecclesiæ pulchritudo consistat. Quæritur utrum purum sit & nullo falsitatis fuco introrsus vitiatum, ne forte alicujus hæreseos perversum dogma nitore eloquentiæ tectum, & quasi spiritalibus sensibus inmixtum internus lateat obumbratum, & dum putat se quis divini verbi percipere nummum, viroli dogmatis percipiat exitiabile malum. Quæritur an regis in eo sit inscriptio, an tyranni, quia scilicet hoc a doctissimis viris in hujusmodi scripturis sollertissima indagatione perscrutatur, utrum ad falurem animæ pertineant, & regis nostri qui salvator vel salutaris dicitur, salutaria monita habeant, ne forte postpositis his antiquis hostis quædam noxia machinamenta habeant, & dum secundus fit is, qui air, Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, qui per humilitatem terrena cælesti Matth. ult. bus sociavit, ille, quod ablit, sequatur qui dum per tyrannidem similis altissimo arrogantèr esse voluit, divino judicio ad inferiora dilapsus infeliciter ruit. Quæritur etiam à rebus nummularus, utrum tanti patrisfamilias nummus plenissimi ponderis æqualitatem gerat, id est, utrum doctrina quælibet Propheticis atque Apostolicis doctrinis concordet, ne forte illis quodammodo dissentiens aut superflua quæque aut minus plena promulgetur: quoniam & donaria auri & argenti quæ in opere tabernaculi à populo offerebantur, à legislatore ad pondus sanctuarii adpensa suscipiebantur. Unde datur intellegi eas scripturas sive doctrinas, vel etiam opera à vero legislatore, mediatore videlicet Dei & hominum, veraciter intra sanctam ecclesiam esse suscipienda, quæ à pondere sanctuarii, id est, ab antiquorum Patrum norma nequaquam sunt sensibus vel operibus dispregata. Hæc ergo omnia dum singillatim sive in libris qui inscribuntur GESTA PATRUM, sive in omnibus passim dogmatibus fuerint prudenti examine quæ litta & summa industria reperta, confidenter sunt eorundem libr orum dogmata vel testimonia ad res dubias confirmandas in medium deducenda; nec potest talis pecunia à quolibet inprobari, quæ per tales trapezitas tanti examinis indagatione valuit adprobari.
units.tr: The apostolic preaching admonishes us to test all things and hold fast what is good. This applies especially to diversities of doctrine. For it has not permitted us to taste every article or even every thing, so that, as tasters, we keep only what is good and cast away whatever is evil, which cannot be done by those who have not tasted it. Rather, it has bidden us to test all doctrines, to taste them with a spiritual palate, and to retain only those which, brought forward by approved men, refresh the minds with inward satisfaction, while casting aside all the others together with their teachers. Therefore, since this rule must be observed almost throughout all writings of this kind, it must also be kept most carefully in those books which record the deeds of certain holy Fathers. For there are many of them, their narratives and teachings are varied and diverse, and the more their authors are unknown, the more often the faithful doubt their sayings. Hence not all of them are to be produced as testimony for affirming doubtful matters, since not all are supported by the title of a known author, nor composed in the style of brave and most eloquent men. Therefore we are instructed by the teachings of the venerable Pope Gelasius and the other Fathers: the Lives of the Fathers, of Paul, Antony, Hilarion and the others, which either were published by blessed Jerome or translated from Greek into Latin, or were written by those learned men whose other little works are received by the holy catholic and apostolic Church, we are to receive with all honour; but the others, whose authors are unknown, we are to count among the apocryphal writings. Therefore, since those who seek to defend the adoration of images now by carelessly twisting the words of the divine oracles, now by the sayings of certain unknown teachers, now by the support of apocryphal writings, ought to notice that they have undertaken a task beyond their strength. For the testimonies of the divine oracles can neither be violently applied to foreign senses, nor ought they to be so applied; nor can the preaching of unknown men, whose spirits have not yet been tested to see whether they are from God, be brought forward as testimony; nor can firmness be given to frivolous and doubtful matters by apocryphal writings that have not yet been weighed. If the words of any man must not be tainted with the gloss of falsehood, much less must the divine oracles, which are chaste words, silver tried by fire, be made to serve in some way for purposes other than their proper order. And since in human affairs, obscure or unknown persons are by no means admitted to prove the matters in question, much less in such great matters, which need the instruction of the heavenly teaching, must the testimonies of unknown teachers or of apocryphal writings be used. For the writings must be tested and searched out by subtle examination, and the testimonies of the holy Fathers must be confirmed, which are to be brought forward within the holy Church as testimony for affirming doubtful matters. For the wicked servant in the Gospel is also rebuked by the Lord because he did not give the money to the bankers; so it becomes us to give the money to the bankers, lest perhaps we be accused along with that servant, as if we then neglected the bankers' task when we deliver any writings of the holy Fathers to be examined and approved. For bankers examine money in a certain manner: whether the gold is proven, whether it is pure or not, whether it has been corrupted by some false gloss, whether it bears the inscription of a king rather than of a tyrant, or whether it has the full weight and equal measure. All these things are examined in the money of the great householder, that is, in the teachings of our Redeemer, by the bankers, that is, by the holy and most eloquent men, in the test of the heavenly fire. Therefore each writing is asked whether its gold is most proven, from which the ark of the Lord may be adorned, or the work of the whole sanctuary may shine, so that in it the guide of spiritual understanding may stand out, by which the divine law is understood and the beauty of the whole Church consists. It is asked whether it is pure and not corrupted inwardly by any false gloss, lest perhaps the perverse dogma of some heresy, covered with the polish of eloquence and mixed with spiritual senses, lie hidden within, shadowed, and while someone thinks he receives a coin of the divine word, he receives the deadly poison of a false doctrine. It is asked whether the inscription is that of the king or of the tyrant, because these things are searched out by the most learned men through the most careful investigation in such writings, namely whether they pertain to the salvation of the soul and whether they carry wholesome warnings from our King, who is called the Saviour and the Giver of salvation; lest perhaps, with these old things set aside, the enemy have some harmful contrivances, and, while he who says, All power is given to me in heaven and in earth (Matth. last chapter), who by humility joined earthly things to heavenly, is made second, that one, which God forbid, follows, who, wishing arrogantly through tyranny to be like the Most High, fell down to lower things by divine judgment and ruined unhappily. It is also asked of the bankers' matters whether the coin of so great a householder has the equality of full weight, that is, whether any doctrine agrees with the Prophetic and Apostolic teachings, lest perhaps something superfluous or less complete be published, differing in some way from them; for the gifts of gold and silver which were offered by the people for the work of the tabernacle were received by the lawgiver and weighed by the standard of the sanctuary. Hence it is to be understood that those writings or doctrines, or also works, which come from the true lawgiver, namely the mediator between God and men, are truly to be received within the holy Church, and those which are by no means rejected in their senses or works by the weight of the sanctuary, that is, by the rule of the ancient Fathers. Therefore, when all these things have been examined singly, whether in the books entitled THE ACTS OF THE FATHERS, or in all doctrines scattered elsewhere, by prudent scrutiny and with diligent care, the doctrines or testimonies of those same books may confidently be brought forward to confirm doubtful matters; nor can such money be disapproved by anyone, which has been proved by such bankers through the investigation of so strict an examination.

units.la: CAP. XII. De eo quod Dionysius presbyter ecclesiæ Ascalonitanæ in eadem Synodo retulisse fertur, quendam monachum coram imagine sanctæ Mariæ semper virginis lucernam inluminasse, & post tertium vel quintum seu etiam sextum mensem redeuntem inextinctam reperisse.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. Concerning what Dionysius, presbyter of the church of Ascalon, is said to have related in the same synod: that a certain monk lit a lamp before the image of holy Mary, ever virgin, and on returning after the third, fifth, or even sixth month found it unextinguished.

units.la: EGITUR denique in ejusdem synodi lectione Dionysius presbyter ecclesiæ Ascalonitanæ in supra memorata synodo retulisse quendam monachum coram imagine beatæ Dei genetricis Mariæ lucernam concinnasse, & post quartum vel quintum necnon & sextum mensem in extinctam perisse. Qui relatus dum, sicut & cætera quæ ibidem relata sunt, non ob aliud fuerit adlatus, nisi ut habilendam adorationem, nec de eo sicut nec de cæteris eadem imaginum adoratio quendam potestatem obtinere vigorem: quippe cum & de ejus fide qui id retulerit, & de facto utrum factum sit, & de tempore, quando factum sit, & de loco ubi factum sit, & de modo quemadmodum factum sit penitus dubitetur. Nam dum prorsus an id quod retulit idem presbyter in veritate gestum significetur, etiam si in veritate gestum fuisse probaretur, sollicitius indagandum esset quoniam modo gestum fuisse perhiberetur: quoniam quidem miracula interdum per reprobos, interdum etiam per aereas potestates, plerumque tamen per sanctos quosque, sive per angelica ministeria fiunt. Quod si quodammodo antiqui hostis flexuosissimo machinamento actum est, non solum ex eo minime potent imaginum adoratio adstrui, sed etiam cum auctore suo cunctisque ejus inlusionibus perpetuo debet abici: si vero per angelicos apparatus gestum est, ut plerasque signa fieri solent, nec ex eo quidem rei cujusdam intentionalis adoratio poterit inolescere: quoniam credibilius quidem est hoc miraculum loci sancti reverentia potius quam alicujus imaginis præsentia gestum fuisse, si tamen gestum est. Venerabilioreverentiam sunt basilicæ imagine, & reverentiora sunt loca cultibus mancipata divinis, quibuslibet piæ, Domino adeistanc, qui majus dixit esse altare quàm munus quod in eo offertur, majusque est templum auro quod in eo est, quia templo & aliari aurum sive munera consecrantur. Legimus namque Gregorium dixisse quod in quadam basilica ingruente insolentissima aquarum alluvione, eundem aquatum incursus usque ad fenestras pervenerint, easque Domini virtute resistere minime intrare potuisse, & luminaria quae à custodibus basilicae dudum fuerant extincta, ab eisdem custodibus postmodum in luminata reperta fuisse: quod quidem miraculum non imaginis cuiusdam, sed sancti loci reverentia factum fuisse prohibetur. Si ergo id miraculum quod Ascalonitanae ecclesiae presbyter erga imaginem apparuisse retulit, ob eandem imaginem apparuisse constaret, non imagines adorandae forent, quoniam non omnia per quae vel in quibus miracula apparuere adoranda creduntur: si ergo omnia in quibus vel per quae miracula quaedam apparuere adoranda sunt, nihil remanebit quod non adoretur: quippe cum tot tantisque modis pene in omnibus creatuns miracula ostensa sint, in quibus huic nostrae disputationi inmorari otiosum est, quoniam in ioribus hujus operis partibus ex hac re aliquantulum Domino annuente disputatum est.
units.tr: Then, in the reading of the same synod, it is recorded that Dionysius, presbyter of the church of Ascalon, related in the synod mentioned above that a certain monk had lit a lamp before the image of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, and that after the fourth or fifth, and even the sixth, month it was found extinguished. This report, like the other things related there, was brought forward for no other purpose than to recommend the adoration of images, and the same adoration of images gains no force of authority from it, either in this case or in the others. For both the faith of the one who reported it, and whether the thing was done, and when it was done, and where it was done, and how it was done, are all entirely in doubt. For even if it were certain that what the same presbyter related signifies something truly done, it would still need to be investigated more carefully how it is said to have been done. Miracles are sometimes performed by the reprobate, sometimes by aerial powers, but most often by saints, or through the ministry of angels. If it was done by some very crooked machination of the ancient enemy, then not only can the adoration of images not be established from it, but it must be cast off forever, together with its author and all his deceptions. If, however, it was done through angelic provision, as many signs usually are, then neither can an adoration of some intended object grow out of it, since it is more credible that this miracle was done through reverence for the holy place rather than through the presence of any image, if indeed it was done at all. Greater reverence is due to the basilica than to the image, and places dedicated to divine worship are more reverend than any pious objects whatever, since the Lord, standing by, said that the altar is greater than the gift offered upon it, and the temple is greater than the gold in it, because gold and gifts are consecrated through the temple and the altar. For we read that Gregory said that in a certain basilica, when a most violent flood of waters came on, the rush of the waters reached the windows, yet by the power of the Lord they could not resist or enter; and the lamps which the guardians of the basilica had earlier extinguished were afterwards found lit by those same guardians. This miracle is said to have been done not through reverence for some image, but through reverence for the holy place. Therefore, if it were established that the miracle which the presbyter of the church of Ascalon reported as having appeared through an image had appeared on account of that very image, images would still not have to be adored, since not everything through which or in which miracles appear is believed to be adored. But if everything in which or through which certain miracles appeared were to be adored, nothing would remain that is not adored, since miracles have been shown in almost all creatures in so many and such great ways. It would be idle to linger on this in our present dispute, since in other parts of this work, with the Lord's permission, something has already been argued on this matter.

units.la: CAP. XIII. Quod haec synodus nullatenus aequiperari posset Nicaenae synodo, quanquam in eodem sit agitata loco, sicut Johannes presbyter a Iolanter dixisse perhibetur, quippe cum ab ea non solum in caeteris, sed & in symbolo discrepare noscatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. That this synod could by no means be equated with the Synod of Nicaea, although it was held in the same place, as John the presbyter of Iolanter is reported to have said, since it is known to differ from that synod not only in other respects but also in its creed.

units.la: QUANQUAM igitur haec synodus in Nicaea Bithyniae urbe sit agitata, nequaquam secundum illorum ostentationem, & secundum Johannis presbyteri adorationem equiperari valet Nicaenae synodo: quoniam cum in pluribus ab ea discordet, nec in symbolo quidem omnino concordat. Habet enim haec in sua fidei professione nova verba quaeque & inusitata sancta Nicaena synodo nequaquam in symbolo sunt adnotata, de quibus in tertii hujus operis exordiis prout valuimus Domino opitulante disputavimus. Habet etiam post confessionem sanctae trinitatis confessionem quoque adorandarum imaginum inditam, quam neque in Prophetarum miraculis, neque in evangeliorum tonitruis, neque in Apostolorum dogmatibus, neque in antiquis sanctarum synodorum relatibus vel quorumlibet orthodoxorum Patrum doctrinis ulpiam inserta mus inseram. Longe quippe & ultra quam dici potest longe ab illa haec distat, praesertim cum illam ecclesiam catholicam ab errore reducat, ista e contrario in errorem inducat: illa a periculosissimo naufragio eam depellat, ista eam in adorandarum imaginum naufragium coactam impellat: Illa patri esse consubstantialem & coaeternum perdoceat, ista res insensatas adorare percenseat: illa divinitatem coaequalem patri filium adfirmet, ista quaslibet picturas archae testumenti Dominicae crucis Dominicae, corporis & sanguinis Dominici sacramento, vel caeteris sacratissimis rebus comparandas esse deliret: illa in tribus coaequalibus, coessentialibus, coaeternis personis unam divinae substantiam adorandam salubrrime sentiat, ista imagines secundum servitium sanctae trinitatis adorandas impudenter dicat: in illa damnentur Arriani dogmatis errores, in ista nihilominus abdicentur haereses majores: in illa exsecrentur eorum blasphemiae qui filium coessentialem patri pertinaciter negant, nec credunt, nec fatentur, in ista abominetur eorum puritas qui spreta picturarum adoratione toti servituros strenua mente & devoto pectore profitentur: in illa post confessionem sanctae trinitatis remissio peccatorum, carnis resurrectio & vita futuri saeculi a pontificibus perdocetur, in ista post confessionem ejusdem sanctae & unicae trinitatis imaginum adoratio inconpetenter statuitur: in caeteris synodis pro defunctis fidelibus Deo sacrificium offerri non prohibetur, in ista defunctis progenitoribus sive parentibus a filiis vel successoribus anathemata ingeruntur: & ut caetera mus quae recensere longum est; in illa cccxviij. fuere pontifices, in ista, ut ipsi adseveraut, cccv. non immerito haec ab illa duodenario numero subtracto distat, sive quia idem numerus dum perfectos numeros habet, sive quia in ternario quem quater habet, & in quaternario quem ter habet mysterium sanctae trinitatis in quatuor evangeliis & quatuor evangeliorum fortem eandem sanctam trinitatem esse demonstrat: sive quia idem duodenarius numerus omnem disciplinam scientem & discernentem creaturam atque creatorem & ad superna ducentem, quae illi synodo tus deest, hoc modo demonstrat. Est autem creator Deus, ex quo omnia, per quem omnia, in omnia, dicente Apostolo, Quoniam ex ipso, & per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia, & ideo trinitas pater & Spiritus sanctus: creatura vero partim est invisibilis, sicut anima, partim visibilis, sicut corpus, invisibili ternarius numerus tribuitur: quare diligere Deum triplicitur jubemur, ex toto corde, ex tota mente & ex tota mente: corpori quaternarius propter evidentissimam naturam ejus, id est, calidam & frigidam, humidam & siccam. Universae ergo creaturae septenarius, cui adjuncta sanctae trinitatis conditione denarius numerus perficitur, in quo est omnis sapientiae disciplina, quae ad homines et ad dos pertinet, creatorem creaturamque dinoscere, & illum colere dominantem, istam subjectam teri. Ac per hoc adjunctis huic disciplinae duobus eminentissimis praeceptis, dilectionis Dei et proximi, duodenarius numerus perficitur. Nam et ii praefato septenario numero, in quo humanam naturam partim visibilem, partim invisibilem demonstrari diximus, quinque legis libri quosad Dei cognitionem & ad dilectionem Dei & proximi venitur addantur, duodenarius numerus minus numerus completur: cum si quatuor evangeliorum libri adjungantur, ad sextumdecimum numerum ordo protenditur: quoniam & idem duodenarius partibus suis multiplicatus ad sextumdecimum numerum pervenit. Adsumpti enim sex quos bis habet, & duo quos sexies habet, & tres quos quater habet, & quatuor quos ter habet, & unus quem duodecies habet, sextumdecimum numerum efficiunt: ut per has quinque partes in quibus quinque librorum figura tenetur: & septem in quo crescit. creatura visibilis & invisibilis demonstratur, & quatuor in quibus sancta evangelia designantur,ad sextum decimum numerum perveniatur: ubi & in decem decalogi praecepta, & in sex totius perfectionis summa quae in novo testamento per mediatorem Dei & hominum data est, ostenditur,ut per duodecim Apostolorum,& per quatuor evangeliorum, & per sedecim nobilissimorum vatum qui libros habent tonitrua,ad unius solummodo Dei culturam & adorationem spretis cunctis vanitatibus mortalium,mentes erigantur. Cum ergo sint duodecim Patriarchae, duodecim minores Prophetae,duodecim etiam Apostoli,& plures hujusmodi qui in divinis literis ab studiosis lectoribus indagari possunt.sunt etiam in eodem numero multa quae ad physicos pertinent conlocata. Sunt namque in zodiaco circulo duodecim signa, quae illum quasi quidam gemmarum ordines ambiunt; sunt duodecim venti mundum in circuitu ternatim per quatuor caeli partes perflantes; sunt duodecim menses, quibus annus perficitur; sunt duodecim horae quibus dies completur, & plura hujusmodi quae ab eruditis viris & secundum saecularium literarum cognitionem indagantur, & spiritaliter secundum ecclesiasticam doctrinam intelleguntur.
units.tr: ALTHOUGH this synod was held in Nicaea, the city of Bithynia, it cannot be equated with the Synod of Nicaea, despite their display and John the presbyter's praise of it, since it disagrees with that synod in many respects and does not wholly agree with it even in the creed. For in its profession of faith it has new and unusual words, which the holy Synod of Nicaea never recorded in its creed, and I have discussed these in the opening chapters of the third part of this work, as far as I could, with the Lord's help. It also has, after the confession of the holy Trinity, an added confession about the adoration of images, which I will not and cannot insert anywhere, neither in the miracles of the Prophets, nor in the thunderings of the Gospels, nor in the teachings of the Apostles, nor in the ancient records of the holy synods, nor in the doctrines of any orthodox Fathers. It is far, and farther than can be said, from that Synod. This is especially so because that Synod leads the Catholic Church away from error, whereas this one, on the contrary, leads it into error; that one drives it away from a most dangerous shipwreck, whereas this one drives it, compelled, into the shipwreck of image-worship. That one teaches that the Son is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father; this one dares to reckon insensate things to be adored. That one affirms that the Son is equal in divinity to the Father; this one raves that any pictures are to be compared with the ark of the covenant, the Lord's cross, the Lord's body and blood in the sacrament, or other most sacred things. That one most wholesomely teaches that the one divine substance is to be adored in three equal, co-essential, coeternal persons; this one shamelessly says that images are to be adored with the worship owed to the holy Trinity. In that one the errors of the Arian doctrine are condemned; in this one, nonetheless, the greater heresies are renounced. In that one the blasphemies of those who obstinately deny, do not believe, and do not confess that the Son is co-essential with the Father are cursed; in this one their purity is abominated, namely of those who, rejecting the adoration of pictures, profess with a resolute mind and devoted heart that they will serve the Lord wholly. In that one, after the confession of the holy Trinity, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the life of the world to come are taught by the bishops; in this one, after the confession of the same holy and single Trinity, the adoration of images is set down out of place. In the other synods it is not forbidden to offer sacrifice to God for the faithful departed; in this one, anathemas are hurled by sons or successors against deceased forefathers or parents. And, to mention other things, which would take long to list: in that one there were 318 bishops, in this one, as they themselves assert, 305. This is not without reason; it differs from that by the subtraction of the number twelve, either because that number is itself perfect, or because the number three, which the number four contains, and the number four, which three contains, show that the mystery of the holy Trinity is in the four Gospels and that the four Gospels proclaim the same holy Trinity; or because the same number twelve, in this way, shows the whole discipline of the creature who knows and discerns, both creator and creature, and leads to the things above, which that synod lacks. Now God is the Creator, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, as the Apostle says: "For of him, and through him, and to him are all things." Hence the Trinity, the Father and the Holy Spirit. The creature, however, is partly invisible, like the soul, and partly visible, like the body. To the invisible is attributed the number three, which is why we are commanded to love God in a threefold way: with the whole heart, with the whole soul, and with the whole mind. To the body is attributed the number four, on account of its most evident nature, namely hot and cold, moist and dry. Thus the seven belongs to the whole creature, and when the condition of the holy Trinity is added to it, the number ten is completed, in which lies all the discipline of wisdom, which pertains to men and angels: to recognise the creator and the creature, to worship the one who rules and to subject the other. Accordingly, when the two most eminent precepts of this discipline, the love of God and of neighbour, are added, the number twelve is completed. For when the five books of the Law, by which we come to the knowledge of God and to the love of God and neighbour, are added to the aforesaid number seven, in which we said the human nature, partly visible and partly invisible, is shown, the number twelve is completed, less one. But if the four books of the Gospels are added, the order extends to the number sixteen, since the same twelve, multiplied by its parts, also reaches sixteen. For six, which is taken twice, and two, which is taken six times, and three, which is taken four times, and four, which is taken three times, and one, which is taken twelve times, make sixteen. Thus through these five parts, in which the figure of the five books is held, and the seven, in which the visible and invisible creature is shown to grow, and the four, in which the holy Gospels are designated, one arrives at the number sixteen. In it both the ten precepts of the Decalogue and the six, the sum of all perfection, which in the New Testament was given through the Mediator of God and men, are shown; so that through the twelve Apostles, the four Gospels, and the sixteen most noble prophets who have books of thunderings, minds are raised, with all the vanities of mortals spurned, to the worship and adoration of the one God alone. Therefore, since there are twelve patriarchs, twelve minor prophets, and likewise twelve apostles, and many more such things can be sought out in the divine letters by diligent readers, there are also in this same number many things that pertain to natural philosophy. For in the zodiac there are twelve signs, which surround it like certain ranks of gems; there are twelve winds blowing through the four quarters of heaven around the world, three at a time; there are twelve months by which the year is completed; there are twelve hours by which the day is filled out, and many other such things which learned men investigate according to the knowledge of secular letters and understand spiritually according to the ecclesiastical doctrine.

units.la: Nam si forte aliquis hujus nostri operis obtrectator nos mordere nitatur,eo quod de physicis, de his videlicet quae in mathematica habentur, exempla posuimus,legat beatum Hieronymum, & nos aur cum eo mordeat,aur ejus doctrinam caeterorumque patrum sequentes literarum non nescios recognoscat.
units.tr: For if perhaps some detractor of this work of ours tries to bite us, because we have set out examples from the natural sciences, namely those found in mathematics, let him read the blessed Jerome, and either bite along with him or recognise that those who follow his teaching and that of the other Fathers are not ignorant of letters.

units.la: Sancta quoque hic numerus multis mysteriis consectatus, quae singula retexere brevitatis studio non valemus, & ut nolle possimus, ideo huic istorum synodo duodecim pontifices minus fuisse quam illi sanctae Nicaenae synodo, quia duodecim Apostolorum sacratissima praedicatione sive auctoritate, quibus illam prorsus constat esse munitam, istam constare in plerisque extraneam.
units.tr: This sacred number, pursued through many mysteries which we cannot unfold one by one for the sake of brevity, and which we would not wish to do even if we could, is the reason why this synod of theirs had twelve bishops fewer than that holy Synod of Nicaea. For it is clear that the latter was fortified by the most sacred preaching and authority of the twelve Apostles, whereas this one consists in many respects of things foreign to them.

units.la: {y} Genesis. his temporibus Bithyniæ urbs in hac parte antiquorum Parrum valebit habere defensionem minum diversissimis huc illucque vergentibus permutationibus loca pro honorum qua & à sanctis posse sanctificari, & à peccatoribus pollui manifestum est. Legimus domum Dei ab Eleazaro & Phinees sacerdotibus archæ testamenti Domini sive tabernaculi conlocatione siciorumque jugibus oblationibus consecrata, & postmodum ab Ophni & Phinees filiis Heli doribus perpetratione nefandorum operum inquinatam. Legimus quoque Salem nobilem quondam urbem, quæ postea Jebus sive Solyma, quæ nunc per derivationem Hierosolyma vocatur, primam post diluvium à sancto viro Sem, qui postea, ut ferunt, Melchisedech vocatus est, ditam & inhabitatam, & postmodum ab exsecrabili gente Jebusæorum subactam, & longo tempore usque ad David possessam. Legimus quoque sacratissimum ac reverentissimum templum Domini à David sanctissimo vatum dispositum, & à Salomone dedicatum, angelorum excubiis frequentatum, divinis oraculis inlustratum, sacratissimarum cæremoniarum perpetuis observationibus paratum, quod ob tot charismatum insignia ab antiquis Patribus fuerat veneratum, à subsequentibus quibusque ejusdem generis pessimis regibus idolorum sordibus cæterisque flagitiis, profanatum, inquinatum, & ubi Dominus sanctuarium suum & locum habitationis gloriæ suæ constituerat, nasses rex duodecim lignis omnique militiæ cæli aras erexit. Post restaurationem quoque sui & sive Zachariæ prophetam eandem quoque domum à Græcorum regibus legimus fuisse profanatam, nec à perpetrandis rebus iniquis illarum ætatum homines loci compescuit reverentia, quorum mentes diabolicarum inlecebrarum infecerat sævitia. Judæorum nempe catervæ quæ merito insignibus carentes templi soluummodo sic munitione tueri arbitrabantur, his per Hieremiam
units.tr: {y} Genesis. In these times it is clear that the city of Bithynia, in this part, will be able to have the defence of the ancient Fathers, since places, through the most diverse changes this way and that, can be sanctified by the holy and polluted by sinners. We read that the house of God was consecrated by the priests Eleazar and Phinehas, through the placing of the ark of the covenant of the Lord or the tabernacle, and by the continual offerings of incense, and afterwards was polluted by the wicked deeds of Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli. We read also of Salem, once a noble city, which afterwards was called Jebus or Solyma, and which now by derivation is called Jerusalem, first founded and inhabited after the flood by the holy man Shem, who afterwards, as they say, was called Melchizedek, and afterwards subdued by the accursed nation of the Jebusites, and held for a long time until David. We read also of the most sacred and reverend temple of the Lord, arranged by David, the most holy of the prophets, dedicated by Solomon, frequented by the watches of angels, illuminated by divine oracles, prepared by the constant observances of the most sacred ceremonies, which on account of so many marks of grace had been venerated by the ancient Fathers, but was afterwards profaned and defiled by the filth of idols and other shameful deeds by the subsequent wicked kings of the same kind; and where the Lord had established his sanctuary and place of the habitation of his glory, King Manasseh set up altars with twelve pieces of wood to all the host of heaven. After its restoration, we read that the same house was profaned by the kings of the Greeks, and that the reverence of the place did not restrain the men of those times from committing unrighteous deeds, since savagery had infected their minds with diabolical enticements. The bands of Jews, who, deservedly lacking distinguished marks, thought that the temple was protected only by such a fortification, were rebuked with these words through Jeremiah

units.la: mino verbis arguuntur; Nolite, inquit, confidere in verbis mendacii, dicentes, Templum Domini, templum Domini, templum Domini est, & cætera. Si ergo ad novi testamenti tempora veniamus, ealdem quoque sanctorum locorum à pravis hominibus profanationes perpetratas fuisse repertemus, cum videlicet in crucis rupe sive in loco resurrectionis vel etiam in specu Bethleem, ubi Dominus parvulus idola posita fuisse à gentilibus pethibeantur. Ait enim beatus Hieronymus; Ab Adriani tempore quæ ad imperium Constantini per annos circiter clxxx in loco resurrectionis simulachrum Jovis, in cruce rupe ex marmore Veneris à gentilibus posita colebatur, exsistentibus perfequutionis auctoribus quod tollerent nomen resurrectionis & crucis, si loca sancta per idola polluissent: Bethleem nunc nostram & angustissimum tumulum, de quo Psalmista canit; Veritas de terra orta est, lucus inumbrabat Tamuz, id est, Adonidis: & in specu Christus quondam parvulus vagiit, Veneris amasius plangebatur. Si ergo nativitatis Christi locum Adonidis potuit inquinare, quid mirum si sanctæ synodi locum perversæ conventionis turba potuit inlicitas statuendas usurpare? Etsi Calvariæ montis locum, quem Christus ad crucis trophæum pergens glorioso calle calcavit, à gentilibus positum Veneris simulachrum fœdavit, quid mirum eum quem quondam sanctorum Patrum insignis caterva ad fidem catholicam roboirandam demens postea sacerdotum multitudo ad novas & ecclesiæ contrarias constitutiones toboappetiit? Et si locum resurrectionis quem Christus resurgendo angelicosque cœtus mortalibus stendendo dicavit, Jovis simulachrum profanavit, quid mirum si imaginum adoratio à demente quibusque in eadem sit statua urbe Birhyniæ, in qua Christus pridem à venerandis præsulibus dicatus est unius eum patre esse subsistentiæ? His itaque documentis potest adprobari quod cundam illorum jactantiam locorum quædam vis unam posse habere semper constantiam, quia homines cum sint mutabiles, unius semper retinentur tenacitatis rigore constricti: præsertim Judas qui quondam fuerat Apostolus, postmodum effectus est Apostata: & Paulus qui quondam fuerat Saulus & persecutor, postea effectus est doctor gentium & prædicator: & loca quæ fuerant divinis cultibus mancipata, postea fuerint à gentibus profanata: & explotis plerumque nationibus loca quæ inpura credebantur, divinis postmodum cultibus mancipentur. Insolentia desiderio tamen isti quam eorum prodeceflores synodum ambiunt agitare, eamque lex venit libus synodis quæ pro quibusdam ecclesiæ utilitatibus diversis temporibus, sed non diversa sanctis viris agitare sunt adsociare, & Septimæ synodi nuncupatione censeri. Nam dum & illi in hac re inportune credantur inhiasse, neque illi neque isti hanc ad suæ ambitionis effectum runt perducere. Cupientes ergo illam quæ ab eorum prodecessionibus incauto & enormiter abolere, & suam quæ inepte & ltolide nihilominus gelia est statuere, paradigma cujusdam rei. Qui sex aureis nummis septimum volens adsociare, dum admittere misus est aureum, æreum loco dicitur admisisse: quo isti expulso aureum aureis se gloriantur adsociasse: qui si diligenter tant dum nisi sunt loco ærei ingerere aureum, intulisse creduntur stanneum, & septimum synodum merum quem prodecessiones eorum æneæ synodo voluerunt complere, stannea isti nihilominus do adplicata moliuntur adimplere, sed repulsio a septimi numeri mysterio numismate ærco, abacto que stanneo, solum tantum modo sex remanebunt: quos & numeri perfectio & fulgor catholicæ tionis inlustratum quibus & in fidei puritate purisimum aurum utilitat, & in numero perfectionem ria regnat: quoniam in senario numero qui utique perfectus est, perfectionem ecclesiastice prinionis habere videntur, ut in tribus, quod est ejus mediæ, sanctæ trinitatis confessio declaretur duobus, quod est ejus tertia pars, duorum talentorum, sive duorum talentorum, uterlectus liceat & operationis munus à sancta & unica trinitate concessum innuatur: porro in uno, quod tæjus pars, sive veteris hominis conditio, qui sexto die formatus est, sive novi adsumptio, qui salute mundi sexta ætate sæculi hiatus persona suscepit, evidentissime demonstratur: sicque in hu- ciau cratissimis synodis & sanctæ trinitatis mysterium prædicatur, & duorum testamentorum consonantia vel intellectus & operationis munus habetur, & Dominicæ incarnationis pro humana salute fides perdocetur: & quia nihil horum illis deest, senatu numeri perfectione muniuntur. Jam vero quia tam ardenti desiderio suam synodum antiquis synodis cupiunt adsociare, adsociari hæc quidem antiquæ cuidam Ariminensium synodo atque adnumerari poterit: quoniam sicut in illa ὁμοουσίων consessio abdicatur, ita in ista solius Dei cultores & veri adoratores exsecrantur: & sicut in illa diversarum rerum comitate subsantiarum perniciosissimum dogma statuitur, ita in ista diversarum retum cultus & adoratio soli Deo debita petcensetur. Sit ergo in hujusce modi numero prima synodus Ariminensium: secunda illa quæ ab istorum prodecessoribus pro basilicarum abolendis ornatibus gesta est: tertia hæc quæ ab istis ob imaginum cultum & adorationem in urbe Nicæa agitata est: ita dumtaxat ut prima sit nummus æreus, secunda stanneus, tertia plumbeus: quoniam cum habeant inter se remporum distantiam magnam, tamen habent quorumdam errorum consonantiam. At si istorum fastu & ostentatione secunda abicitur, nos quoque eis ad eam ex hoc numero abiciendam adminiculum præbeamus, & prima sit, ut prædicti sumus, Ariminensium, secunda vero hæc quæ ab istis gesta est, prima videlicet, ut prædicti sumus, nummus æreus: & quia illa contemnitur, secunda istorum, quæ plumbei nummi locum tenet, computetur: atque his postpositis, sex tantummodo nos sanctis universalibus synodis & localibus conciliis, quæ ab his nec fide nec prædicatione dissentiunt contenti simus, & ad tenendi examinis ultimique diei nos fidei integritate & bonorum operum incrementis omnino terrificum præparemus adventum, qui ejus gloriose reditu celebrabitur, de quo ab angelis, Apostolis dictum est, Viri Galilei quid statis aspicientes in cælum: hic Jesus qui adsumptus est a vobis, sic veniet quemadmodum vidistis eum euntem in cælum.
units.tr: ...are refuted by words: "Do not trust in lying words, saying, The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is here," and so on. If we come to the times of the New Testament, we find that these holy places were likewise profaned by wicked men: on the rock of the cross, at the place of the resurrection, and even in the cave of Bethlehem, where the little Lord was born, idols are said to have been set up by the Gentiles. For blessed Jerome says: "From the time of Hadrian until the reign of Constantine, for about one hundred and eighty years, a statue of Jupiter was worshipped at the place of the resurrection, and a statue of Venus was set up by the Gentiles on the rock of the cross, the persecutors being the authors of this, so that they might remove the name of the resurrection and of the cross by polluting the holy places with idols. Bethlehem, our own now, is a very narrow tomb, of which the Psalmist sings, 'Truth has sprung out of the earth' (Ps. 85:11). A grove shaded Tammuz, that is Adonis; and in the cave Christ once wailed as a little child, while the lover of Venus was mourned." If, then, the place of Christ's nativity could be defiled by the rites of Adonis, why is it surprising that the crowd of a perverse assembly could seize the place of the holy synod for unlawful decrees? And if the Gentiles' statue of Venus defiled the hill of Calvary, which Christ trod on his glorious path to the trophy of the cross, why is it surprising that the same place, once famous for the holy Fathers' gathering to strengthen the Catholic faith, was later so eagerly sought by a senseless multitude of priests for new decrees contrary to the Church? And if a statue of Jupiter profaned the place of the resurrection, which Christ consecrated by rising and by showing the angelic companies to mortals, why is it surprising that the worship of images should be pursued by madmen in that same city of Bithynia, where Christ was once proclaimed by venerable bishops to be of one substance with the Father? By these examples it can be shown that all their boasting about places can have only one constancy, because men, being changeable, are always held fast by the same rigour of one tenacity. Judas, who was once an apostle, afterwards became an apostate; and Paul, who was once Saul and a persecutor, afterwards became a teacher of the Gentiles and a preacher; places once devoted to divine worship were afterwards profaned by the Gentiles; and when nations have often been cast out, places that were thought unclean are afterwards devoted to divine worship. Nevertheless, in their arrogant desire they seek to convene a synod like their predecessors, and this has come to be counted among the synods which, at different times but not by different holy men, were gathered for various benefits of the Church, and is reckoned as the Seventh Synod. For while those others seem to have aspired to this matter without measure, neither they nor these have been able to bring it to the end of their ambition. Wishing therefore to abolish what was rashly and excessively decreed by their predecessors, and to set up their own, which is foolish and senseless, let us offer an illustration. Someone who wished to add a seventh to six gold coins, when he was allowed to admit a gold one, is said to have admitted a bronze one in its place; then, with that bronze one expelled, he boasts of having added gold to gold; but if he is carefully examined, he is believed to have put a tin coin in place of the bronze one and to have introduced a tin coin into the gold. Thus the seventh synod, which their predecessors wished to complete from the bronze synod, these men now strive to complete by attaching tin to it. But, the mystery of the number seven being rejected, the bronze coin removed and the tin coin cast out, only six will remain. These six, illuminated by the perfection of number and the splendour of the Catholic confession, are a true gold in the purity of the faith and reign in the perfection of number. For in the number six, which is indeed perfect, they seem to have the perfection of the ecclesiastical confession: in three, which is its half, the confession of the holy Trinity is declared; in two, which is its third part, the gift of working and of understanding granted by the holy and one Trinity is signified (the two talents, or two talents, by which either reading is allowed); but in one, which is its sixth part, is most evidently shown either the condition of the old man, who was formed on the sixth day, or the taking up of the new man, who in the sixth age of the world took on the person of the Saviour of the world. And so in these most sound synods the mystery of the holy Trinity is proclaimed, the agreement of the two Testaments, or the gift of understanding and working, is held, and faith in the Lord's incarnation for human salvation is taught; and since none of these is lacking to them, they are fortified by the perfection of the number six. Now, since they desire with such fervent longing to join their synod to the ancient synods, this one may indeed be joined and counted with that ancient synod of the men of Rimini: for as in that one the homoousion is rejected, so in this one the worshippers of God alone and the true adorers are cursed; and as in that one a most pernicious dogma was set up, that of a mixture of different substances, so in this one the cult and adoration of different things is ascribed to what is due to God alone. Let therefore the first synod in this series be that of Rimini; the second, that which was held by their predecessors for the removal of ornaments from the basilicas; the third, this one which was debated by them in the city of Nicaea concerning the cult and adoration of images. Let it be so, that the first is a bronze coin, the second a tin one, the third a lead one; for although they are far apart in time, they agree in certain errors. But if the second is cast out by their pride and display, let us also provide them with a help toward casting it out of this number: let the first, as we have said, be that of Rimini, and the second, which was held by them, be the first, as we have said, a bronze coin; and since that one is held in contempt, the second, which holds the place of a lead coin, should be counted as theirs. Setting these aside, let us be content with the six holy universal synods and local councils, which do not differ from these in faith or in preaching, and let us prepare ourselves, with the integrity of faith and the growth of good works, for the most dreadful coming of the last and examining day, which will be celebrated at his glorious return, of which the angels said to the Apostles: "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11).

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: Chapter 14.

units.la: De eo quod Gregorius Neocæsareæ episcopus ait, Lætentur & exultent & præsumant qui veram Christi imaginem benigno animo facientes & diligentes & venerantes ad salutem animæ & corporis offerentes, quam ipse sacrificii persector & Deus noster am ex nobis ex toto suscipiens massam secundum tempus voluntariæ passionis in signum & in memoriam manifestam suis tradidit discipulis.
units.tr: On the statement of Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea: "Let them rejoice, exult and presume, who make, love and venerate the true image of Christ with a kind mind, and offer it for the salvation of soul and body; which the perfecter of the sacrifice and our God, taking from us the whole lump of our nature at the time of his voluntary passion, handed to his disciples as a clear sign and memorial."

units.la: Gregorii igitur Neocæsareæ Episcopi inutile dictum & imperitiæ nubilo tectum acineptiæ involucris oblitum, in eo quoque reprehenditur quod ait, Lætentur & exultent, & præsumantur qui veram Christi imaginem facientes & diligentes & venerantes ad salutem animæ & corporis offerunt, &c etera. Quid namque in hac dictione, Lætari & exultare, sit in promptu est intellegere: quid vero sit quod adjunctum est, Et præsumantur, nullius penitus sensus lectori ingerit indicium, quia & a sensuum regulis est alienum, & a Latinæ locutionis integritate penitus extraneum: quippe cum si de præsumptione dicere voluit, non duobus præcedentibus, hoc tertium valeat infensus sapore cohærere: nisi forte illos dixit lætari & exultare qui rem inlicitam & a sanctis Patribus prohibitam adorare præsumunt, & qui tantæ præsumptionis instigantur stimulis, ut in adoratione rerum sensu carentium cuncta contraire videantur authenticis scripturis. O demens episcopi dictio & risu digna! quæ quam dixit veram Christi imaginem non evidenter ostendit. Qui si hanc dixit veram quæ ab artificibus ex materiis fit, absurdissime & inconpetenter loquutus est: cum præsertim liquido pateat nemini mortalium veram Christi posse formare imaginem. Cum enim vera dicitur, multum ab hac quæ artificibus fingitur elongatur: quoniam quantum veritas a falsitate differt, tantum vera Christi imago quâ artificis docta sive indocta man° pro captu ingenii format: si vero de corporis & sanguinis Domini mysterio, quod quotidie in sacramento a fidelibus sumitur, dicere voluit, quod inter ipsam quidem suarum nugarum conglomerationem pene patefecit, cum ait, Quam ipse sacrificii persector & Deus noster am ex nobis ex toto suscipiens massam secundum tempus voluntariæ passionis in signum & in memoriam manifestam suis tradidit discipulis, & in hoc quoque non mediocriter erravit. Non enim imaginem aut adumbrationem prefigurationem, sed semetipsum Deo patri pro nobis in sacrificium obtulit: & qui quondam umbra legis in magni immolatione, sive in quibusdam rebus imaginarie prefigurabatur offerendus, sicut ea consummans quæ de se vatis oraculis prophetata sunt, Deo patri est victima salutaris oblata: nec nobis legis transeuntibus umbris imaginarium quoddam indicium, sed sui sanguinis & corporis sacramentum. Non enim sanguinis & corporis Dominici mysterium imago jam nunc dicendum est, sed veritas, non umbra sed corpus, non exemplar futurorum sed id quod exemplaribus præfigurabatur. Jam secundum Canticum canticorum adspiraverit dies, & amota sunt umbræ: jam filegis ad justitiam omni credenti, Christus advenit: jam legem adimplevit: jam qui sedebat in regione umbræ mortis, luce magnam vidit: jam velamen faciei Moysi decidit, & velum templi scissum, ut ana nobis & ignota quæque ostendit: jam verus Melchisedech, Christus videlicet, rex justus, rex pacis, non peccatum victimas, sed sui nobis corporis & sanguinis contulit sacramentum. Nec ait, Hæc est corpus meum quod pro vobis tradetur: &, Hic est sanguis meus qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Cum ergo, ut præfati sumus, nec artificum opus vera Christi
units.tr: So the useless saying of Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, veiled in the fog of ignorance and wrapped in the trappings of silliness, is also faulted in this: he says, "Let them rejoice and exult, and let them presume, who make the true image of Christ and love and venerate it, and offer it for the salvation of soul and body," and so on. Now what is meant by "rejoice and exult" is plain enough to understand. But what is added, "and let them presume," gives the reader no sign of any sense at all, since it is foreign to the rules of meaning and wholly alien to the correctness of Latin speech. For if he meant to speak of presumption, this third word cannot cohere with the two preceding ones in any tolerable way, unless perhaps he meant those who rejoice and exult to be those who presume to worship a thing that is forbidden and unlawful and rejected by the holy Fathers, and who are driven by the goads of such presumption that they seem to contradict everything in the authentic Scriptures by worshipping things that have no sense. O foolish saying of the bishop, worthy of laughter! He does not clearly show what he means by "the true image of Christ." If he meant what is true in the sense of what is made by craftsmen from materials, he has spoken most absurdly and inappropriately, since it is quite clear that no mortal can form a true image of Christ. For when something is called true, it is far removed from what craftsmen fashion; for as truth differs from falsehood, so a true image of Christ differs from one that a craftsman, learned or unlearned, forms according to his ability. But if he meant the mystery of the body and blood of the Lord, which is received daily in the sacrament by the faithful, which he almost revealed in the very heap of his trifles when he said, "which the perfecter of the sacrifice and our God, taking from us the whole lump of our nature at the time of his voluntary passion, handed to his disciples as a clear sign and memorial," then in this too he has erred not a little. For he did not offer himself to God the Father for us as a sacrifice as an image or a foreshadowing or a figure. In the great sacrifice, the one who was once foreshadowed under the shadow of the law, and in certain things imaginatively prefigured as to be offered, was offered to God the Father as a saving victim, fulfilling those things that were prophesied about him in the oracles of the prophets. And to us, now that the shadows of the law have passed, he gave not some imaginary sign but the sacrament of his own blood and body. For the mystery of the Lord's body and blood must now be called not an image but the truth; not a shadow but a body; not a pattern of things to come but that which the patterns foreshadowed. Now, according to the Song of Songs, "the day has breathed and the shadows have fled away." Now Christ has come to justice for every believer; now he has fulfilled the law; now he who sat in the region of the shadow of death has seen a great light; now the veil of Moses' face has fallen, and the veil of the temple has been torn, and he has shown us the hidden and unknown things; now the true Melchizedek, namely Christ, the righteous king, the king of peace, has given us not the sacrifices of sins but the sacrament of his own body and blood. Nor did he say, "This is my body which is given for you," and "This is my blood which is poured out for many for the remission of sins." Therefore, since, as we have said above, neither the work of craftsmen can be called a true image of Christ

units.la: Cant. 2. Christi possit imago dici, nec corporis & sanguinis ejus mysterium quod in veritate gestum e[st] constat non in figura, merito aut in quolibet horum aut in utroque Gregorius Neocaesareæ episcopus reprehenditur, qui rot indicijs tantisque documentis talem ineptiam protulisse convincitur. In eo ergo quod idem episcopus ait de Christo, Quam ipse sacrificij perfectior & Deus noster ex nobis ex toto substantiam massam, justa est reprehensio: quoniam cum massa perditionis genus humanum dicatur cum originali peccato, incaute nostram ex nobis ex toto Christum suscepisse massam idem episcopus profert: quia videlicet quamquam Christus totam humanam naturam, carnem videlicet cum sensibus suis, & animam cum ratione sua, non divinitate in humanitatem conversa, neque humanitate in divinitatem mutata, sed permanente utriusque naturæ proprietate, Deus verbum hominem in unitate personæ suscepit, hominis tamen originale peccatum non suscepit: ac per hoc absurdum est dicere nostram ex nobis ex toto eum suscepisse minime sine massam, quia originalis peccati, quo omne hominum genus ante baptismum connexum tenetur, quamquam suscepisse credendus est noxam. Tanta ergo illius antiqui peccati est cum quo nascimur, ut si particulatim diligenti consideratione dividatur, omnia in eo criminalia possint inveniri peccata. Nam & superbia est illic, quia homo in sua potius esse quam in Dei potestate dilexit: & sacrilegium, quia Deo non credidit: & homicidium, quia se præcipitavit in mortem: & fornicatio spiritualis, quoniam integritas mentis humanæ serpentina suasione corrupta est: & furtum, quia cibus proximi usurpatus est: & avaritia, quia plusquam sufficere illi debuit, adpetiit. Quibus omnibus tanto est humanum genus infectum, ut de legitimo etiam matrimonio procreatus dicat, In iniquitatibus conceptus sum, & in peccatis peperit me mater mea. Christus ergo Dei virtus & Dei sapientia naturam hominis non peccati massam suscepit. Sed ut ad id redeamus unde digressi sumus, de ejusdem episcopi prosectione aliquantulum a nobis ambigitur, qui totam ex nobis nostram Christum suscepisse massam dixisse perhibetur: quoniam aut magnam eum hoc profiteri incruditio coegit, aut innatus error id eum proferre impulit. Nam dum nos eum & eruditum & orthodoxum esse volumus, exemplo Domini minem cupientes perire, si utrumvis istorum illi deest, & revera deest, mallemus id quod profanum est imperitiæ potius quam schismati deputare.
units.tr: Cant. 2. Christi possit imago dici, nor the mystery of his body and blood, which is acknowledged to have been done in truth and not in figure, rightly, or in one or both of these respects, Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, is blamed, who is shown to have put forward such folly despite so many indications and such great proofs. So in what the same bishop says of Christ, "which the perfecter of the sacrifice and our God, taking from us the whole lump of our substance," the rebuke is just; for since the human race is called a lump of perdition on account of original sin, the same bishop carelessly puts forward that Christ took from us the whole lump. For although Christ took the whole of human nature, namely the flesh with its senses and the soul with its reason, not by the divinity being changed into the humanity nor the humanity into the divinity, but with the property of each nature remaining, God the Word took man into the unity of his person, yet he did not take man's original sin. And therefore it is absurd to say that he took our whole lump from us, if by that is meant something sinful, since the original sin, by which the whole human race is held bound before baptism, is not to be believed to have been taken up by him, though it is a guilt. So great is that ancient sin with which we are born that, if it is divided part by part with careful consideration, all the criminal sins can be found in it. For there is pride in it, because man loved to be in his own power rather than in God's; and sacrilege, because he did not believe God; and murder, because he cast himself into death; and spiritual fornication, since the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by serpentine persuasion; and theft, because the food of his neighbour was seized; and avarice, because he sought more than he ought to have been satisfied with. By all these the human race is so infected that even one born of a lawful marriage says, "Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sin did my mother bear me." Christ, therefore, the power of God and the wisdom of God, took the nature of man, not a lump of sin. But to return to where we digressed: concerning the same bishop's utterance there is some doubt among us, for he is reported to have said that Christ took our whole lump from us; for either lack of learning compelled him to profess this, or inborn error impelled him to put it forward. For while we wish him to be both learned and orthodox, in the manner of the Lord's ministers who do not wish to perish, if either of these is lacking in him, and indeed it is lacking, we would rather ascribe what is profane to ignorance than to schism.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: De eo quod Epiphanius diaconus imaginum adorationem adstruere volens dixit, Quoniam hic titulum erigens Domini, & seipsa tangens fimbriis tituli sicuti quidem vestimentum sanctum evangelium, quoniam salutem adepta est inter medium illæ & Domini imaginis, herba quædam germinavit quæ adpropinquans pedem tituli omnes infirmitates curat.
units.tr: Concerning what Epiphanius the deacon said, wishing to establish the veneration of images: "Since here, raising up the title of the Lord and touching herself with the fringes of the title, just as the holy Gospel is a garment, since she obtained salvation between those and the image of the Lord, a certain herb sprang up which, drawing near the foot of the title, cures all infirmities."

units.la: Sæpe jam in hoc opere diximus, quod & perspicue apparet, pene omnes eorum sententias ob imaginum adorationem in sua synodo protulerunt, quodammodo tantis esse ignaviæ calumniis interpolatas, ut eloquentia sensuque carentes difficile earum sensus lectorum attingat. Cum ergo illarum ineptissimi rerum compago haud quaquam ea quæ profari cupiunt, evidenter monet exprimat, habet tamen inter eadem verborum nubila quædam perspicua indicia nominum delicet, seu rerum notissimarum mentiones, veluti cum inter densas tenebras quorundam tot igniculi interlucent, ut per rerum vocabula & res notissimas lectoris animus ea quæ exprimere volunt percipiat. Exprimere etenim ni fallor in prolata sententia Epiphanius diaconus nisus est, Mulierem a profluvio sanguinis Dominicæ vestis fimbriæ tactu sanatam, titulum sive imaginem in ejus Domini honorem erexisse, ejusdemque imaginis fimbrias le denuo tetigisse, subter quam imaginem habam quandam ortam fuisse, quæ si paulatim succrescens summitate sua pedem contigerit erecta imaginis, cunctis ægritudinibus medetur. In quo quidem facto, si tamen factum esse credatur, nulla imaginum adoratio comedatur. Si ergo illa mulier fœminei sexus facilitate & quadam animi levitate perceptio sanitatis beneficio, utpote Domini semper præsentia quærens, cumque ubique esse posse ignorans, imagine erexit, quis tamen vecors perceptis sacræ fidei charismatibus, eumque ubique esse non nescens, ut ejus habere queat præsentiam, idcirco imaginem eriget eamque adorabit? Et si illa mundo nec dii ab idolorum cultibus liberato vilis mortuorum quorundam hominum in urbibus statuis ob quandam rerum memoriam sive cultum erectis, similiter, prout valuit, agere studuit, quis sanæ mentis ejus actibus adsensum præbebit, & Dominum non in manu factis, sed in cælo vel potius ubique esse credens talia agere curabit? Aut si forte illa superstitioso ritu habuit zelum Dei, sed non secundum scientiam, quis catholicus in fide roboratus ex ejus actibus in hac parte exempla sumet, hisque similia faciet? Aut si forte illa rudimento conversionis suæ quæ necdum solido cibo vesci poterat, ideo tenero cibo utebatur, ut ad percipiendum solidum cibum paulatim sumptis viribus creceret: scilicet ut per rem visibilem & tractabilem ad invisibilis & ineffabilis Dei cultum accederet, quis ejus in hoc facto imitator effectus, spreta solidi cibi fortitudine, ad infantiæ denuo cibos cupiat esse redactus? In miraculo igitur quod in herba fit, si tamen factum fuisse credatur, quæ, ut ille fallus est, cunctis ægritudinibus medetur, haudquaquam potent illorum assertio quodammodo fulciri: quoniam non ut herbæ aut imagines adorentur id factum fuisse perhibetur, sed ut in fidelium mentes spretus vanitatibus idolorum ad verae fidei rudimenta converterentur: quoniam secundum Apostolum signa non pro fidelibus, sed pro infidelibus data fuisse creduntur. Ecclesia namque catholica, ut ad fidem cresceret, miraculis erat nutrienda, & ut ejus novella plantatio convalesceret, assiduis erat irrigationibus fovenda.
units.tr: We have often said in this work, as is also quite plain, that nearly all their opinions concerning the veneration of images, which they put forward in their synod, have been so corrupted by the calumnies of ignorance that, lacking eloquence and sense, readers can hardly grasp their meaning. Since the disordered structure of their sentences by no means sets out clearly what they wish to express, yet it contains among these verbal clouds certain clear indications, namely the mention of names or of very well-known things, just as among the dense darkness of some men so many little sparks shine through that, through the words for things and the very well-known things, the reader's mind grasps what they want to express. For Epiphanius the deacon, if I am not mistaken, strove in the statement he put forward to express that the woman, healed of her flow of blood by touching the fringe of the Lord's garment, erected a title or image in honour of that same Lord, and again touched the fringes of that same image, beneath which image a certain herb had sprung up, which, if it gradually grew and touched with its top the foot of the erected image, heals all diseases. In this deed, if indeed it is believed to have been done, no veneration of images is established. If, then, that woman, from the feminine frailty and a certain lightness of mind, having received the benefit of health, since she sought the Lord's presence and, not knowing that he can be everywhere, erected an image, who of sound mind, having received the gifts of sacred faith and knowing that he is everywhere, would erect an image and worship it, so as to have his presence? And if she, in a world not yet freed from the worship of idols, and in a city where the statues of certain dead men, erected for some memory or honour, were vile, strove to act in the same way as she was able, who of sound mind will give assent to her actions, and will take care to act thus, believing that the Lord is not in hand-made things but in heaven, or rather everywhere? Or if perhaps she, with a superstitious rite, had zeal for God but not according to knowledge, what Catholic, strengthened in the faith, will take examples from her actions in this respect and do things like them? Or if perhaps she, in the beginning of her conversion, when she could not yet feed on solid food, used tender food so that, by gradually gathering strength, she might grow to take solid food, namely that through a visible and tangible thing she might approach the worship of the invisible and ineffable God, what imitator of hers in this deed, scorning the strength of solid food, will wish to be reduced again to the food of infancy? Therefore, as for the miracle that occurs in the herb, if indeed it is believed to have happened, which, as that fable goes, cures all diseases, their assertion can by no means be supported in any way: since it is not said that this happened so that herbs or images might be worshipped, but so that the minds of the faithful, scorning the vanities of idols, might be turned to the rudiments of the true faith; since, according to the Apostle, signs are believed to have been given not for believers but for unbelievers. For the Catholic Church, in order to grow in faith, had to be nourished by miracles, and to make its new planting grow strong, had to be cherished by constant watering.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Inutile dictum Epiphanii diaconi reprehenditur, in eo quod ait; Multa quae in nobis sacrantur orationem sacrata non suscipiunt: & post pauca, Nec plurimum sicut veneranda & honoramur & amplificamur: ipse enim signum vivificae crucis sine oratione facit a nobis, veneranda est: & sufficiemus signum ejus accipere sanctificationem per quae facta a nobis ad eum adorationem quidam in fronte sanctificatione, & quae in aere per digitum factum signum effugari daemones speramus similiter & imagine per nomen significationis ad primam formam honoris deducimus, & osculantes eam & honorabiliter honorates accipiemus sanctificationem nam & sacra dive sa vasa habentes haosculamur & amplectimur, & sanctificationem quandam speramus.
units.tr: The useless saying of the deacon Epiphanius is rebuked, where he says: "Many things that are consecrated in us do not receive consecration by prayer." And a little later: "Nor are we honoured and magnified as much as things to be venerated. For he himself makes the sign of the life-giving cross without prayer, and it is to be venerated. And we shall be sufficient to receive the sign of his consecration, by which we make an adoration to him, some on the forehead by consecration, and we hope that the sign made by a finger in the air drives away demons. Likewise, with the image, by the name of the signification, we bring it to the first form of honour, and kissing it and honourably honouring it we shall receive consecration. For also, holding the holy and divine vessels, we kiss and embrace them, and we hope for a certain consecration."

units.la: Si videris, inquit Scriptura, virum velocem in verbis suis, sicut quia spem habet insipiens magis quam ille: &, in multiloquio peccatum non deerit. Secundum hanc ergo sacrae scripturae sententiam Epiphanius diaconus, qui in eadem synodo velox in verbis & multiloquio idem ille fuisse perhibetur, & spem habere insipientem magis quam se ostendit, & in multiloquio errata quaeque contraxit. Nam dum in superiori capitulo in ejus nugis a nobis aliquantulum ut putatum sit, in hoc nihilominus aliquantulum disputandum est. Disposuimus quidem in earum profectionibus non verba, sed sententias discutere, nec literaturam sed sensus vestitus quoniam literaturae ordinem in his finitum est quaerere, quippe cum nulla sententia in ejusdem lectionis prolixo textu pari casu possit stare, in raris autem verborum erratibus & eruditionis lima nec dum politis facile inter sensuum errata disputatur. Ubi ergo in prolixa lectionis serie nec sensuum est puritas, nec verborum integritas, difficile de singulis disputatur: quoniam in infinitum disputationis ordo protenditur. Si enim de singulis verborum erratibus disputetur dum debent archana rimari, & ea quae ad ecclesiasticas res pertinent foliorum indagatione scrutari, grammaticae artis multiplices regulae, quae in scholis discuntur, iradi vid buntur. Sed dum in hoc opere nostri itineris gressus plurimum impediatur, sive quia eorum sermonis difficultate nonnulla quid significare velint difficile deprehendantur, sive quia eorum enuntiationes barbarismis ac solecismis caeterisque vitiis infectas nostris disputationibus coacti, quia res exigit, in eiferinus, sive quia cum inter corrupta eorum verba corrupti nihilominus sensus sint, & nos verborum repr&henliones prolixitatis causa omittentes, sensuum solummodo sericem inculcemus & laboriose id, quippe cum unum pendeat ex altero alterum; sic infertum in altero, faciamus, restat ut annuente Domino postpositi reprehensione quae verborum vitiis accidit, sensuum tantum inordinatas coglomerationes spiritalis pugni incrustationes quasi ante iter & magna ex parte peractum pergamus. Ait enim praefatus Epiphanius diaconus, cujus sententiam discutere coeperamus; Multa quae in nobis sacrantur orationem sacrata non suscipiunt. quod quidem cum ita, ut dicitur, nullum plenum sensum habeat, hoc eum conicinnus voluisse significare ut diceret, Multa sunt in nobis sacrata quae per sacerdotis orationem vel manus impositionem sacrantur. quod si ita est, qualiter verum esse possit non satis elucescit: quoniam quaecumque in ecclesia sacrantur, sive ecclesiastici ordines, sive sacerdotum templorum dedicationes, sive caeterae nomina conspiciuntur, constituitur, per sacerdotales ecclesiastico more consecrationes fiunt: quippe cum ad Christianae fidei nobilitatem per quam ad caeteros gradus acceditur, in ipsis infantiae rudimentis per manus impositiones & ad Deum orationes veniatur. Si vero de locis sive vasis vel quibusdam utensilibus divinis culti bus mancipatis dicere voluit, in hoc ejus dictio frustrari potest: quoniam pene nihil est in his quae enumeravimus, quod nō per sacerdotum orationes & consecrationes consecrentur, sed & exorcismis & salis & aquae asperione uti consuevit ecclesia: quorum omnium consecrationes vel institutiones ab ipsis ecclesiae rudimentis ab ecclesiarum praesulibus traditae fuisse noscuntur, & in libris sacerdotalibus exaratae habentur. Cum ergo id ideo diaconus ideo intulerit ut imagines, quam adorationem illi proficuo roborare aestuant, de quarum utique consecratione nulla est ecclesiastica institutio, vasis vel caeteris rebus divinis cultibus mancipatis adiociaret, hoc introducere moliens, ut haec sine orationibus consecrata, ita illas quoque sine orationibus consecratas esse perdoceret, in eo molimen cafflari potest, quod istorum consecrandorum in libris sacerdotalibus scripta habetur, & per sacerdotes solenniter celebratur prisca traditio: illarum vero neque consecrandarum, neque adorandarum vila in his quae ab ecclesia recipiuntur habetur institutio. in eo vero quod ait; Nec plurimum sicut veneranda & honoramur & adplicamur: ipse enim signum vivificae crucis sine oratione sacra fatur a nobis veneranda est, id puro voluisse dicere, quod signum venerandae crucis, quod nos honorifice nobis indimus abiq; amen sacerdotum oratione vel consecratione, est, & tamen sacrarum habetur: in quo minimum dicto, & in caeteris, non mediocre suam demonstrat infamiam, quod signum crucis non alia quaerit consecrationem quam eam quae per Dei & hominum facta est mediatorem. Quod vero subjunxit; Et sufficiemus signum ejus accipere sanctificationem per quae facta a nobis ad eum adorationem quidam in fronte sanctificatione, & qua quae in aere per digitum factum signum effugari daemones speramus, ad id quod superius inlatum est pertinet. Crucis igitur lignum magnum in se habere mysterium, eique imagines non esse æquiperandas sed dentibus est indiciis manifestum, & in superioribus huius operis partibus, prout Dominus donare dignatus est, demonstratum. Nam dum imagines, ut superius diximus, nulla oratione vel manus impositione sacrentur, crucis signum ubicumque ingeritur divini nominis invocatione infertur. Sed illam hæc consecrationem quandam nec habeant nec habere queant nec debeant, illud vero adeo est denique Christi mundi faciatum, ut non solum cuiuscumque consecratione indigeat, sed divini nominis invocatione inlatum alia quaeque consecret & benedicat. Porro quod ait; Similiter & imaginem per mensificationis ad primam formam honoris deducimus, & oculantes eam & honorabiliter honorantes accipiemus sanctificationem, quam sit absurdum quamque a ratione alienum liquido patet. Dixit enim, in nomen significationis ad primæ formæ honorem, id est, ad sancti in cuius nomine praetitulatum venerationem posse deduci: quod fieri posse nullius rationis indiciis evidentibus potest ad probationem nominis tantummodo inscriptio eas ad eorundem sanctorum quorum nomina superscribuntur honorem deducit: ergo quaelibet res, cui sancti cuiusdam nomen superscribitur, ad ejusdem sancti honorem conscendit. Ergo lapides, ligna, vestes, sive animalia quaedam quorundam sanctorum nominibus superscripta, ad eorundem sanctorum honorem transeunt, quorum sunt nominibus praenotata: & si nomina superscripta haec, quae enumeravimus, ad eorum quorum nomina sunt honorem perducere minime queunt, nec illas quoque nominum inscriptiones ad sanctorum honorem quodammodo perducunt: & si istud prudenti consideratione abnuitur, & illud solleriti indagatione abiicitur, offeruntur cuilibet eorum qui imagines adorant, verbi gratia, Duarum feminarum pulcherrimarum imagines superscriptione carentes, quas ille parvipendens abicit, abiectasque quolibet in loco jacere permittit, dicit illi quis, Una illarum sanctae Mariae imago est, abici non debet: altera Veneris, quae omnino abicienda est, vertit se ad pictorem quaerens ab eo, quia in omnibus similimae sunt, quae illarum sanctae Mariae imago sit, vel quae Veneris? Ille huic dat superscriptionem Sanctae Mariae, illi vero superscriptionem Veneris: ista quia superscriptionem Dei genetricis habet, erigitur, honoratur. Ille illa quia inscriptionem Veneris Aeneae cuiusdam profugi genetricis habet, deicitur, exprobratur, sacratum: pari utraque sunt figura, paribus coloribus, paribusque factae materiis, superscriptione tantum distant. Dicat mihi, quaeso, Epiphanius diaconus, qui per nominis inscriptionem imagines ad honorem primae formae deduci posse dixit, ubi haec sanctitas hujus antequam superscriberetur fuit, ubi illius exprobratio prius quam superscriberetur extitit? Superscriptio itaque, quae imaginibus additur, solet, secundum morem literarum, quibus tanta vis est ut tacite loquantur, & nonnumquam absentium, nonnumquam vero praesentium sine voce edisserant, notitiam inferre valet: illis imaginibus quibus inditur, sanctificationem exhibere non potest. Sanctificatio enim rationalibus creaturis bonorum operum exhibitione & meritorum praerogativis conceditur: rebus vero inanimatis & sensu carentibus, utpote sunt vasa divinis cultibus mancipata, & his similia non superscriptione qualibet, sed sacerdotali consecratione & divini nominis invocatione accedit. Ac per hanc videnti ratione monstratur, nullam imaginibus inhaerere posse sanctificationem per quamlibet superscriptionem: quoniam ista quae beatae Dei genetricis Mariae superscriptione sortitur, & quae quondam despicabiliter abiecta jacuit, nunc venerabiliter adornatur, quantum valuit contemptus suis spreta jacens obesse, tantum nihilominus valet cultoribus suis erecta & adorata prodesse: & quantum posset juvare si erigeretur, tantum potest laedere cum spernitur. Quod vero ait; Frustra eam & honorabiliter adorantes accipiemus sanctificationem, tantum valeret quantum si diceret, Ob eam & honorabiliter adoramus sanctificationem ab ea accipere cupientes, quam nec illa habet nobis impertire valet. Quanto ergo potest caeco lumen reddere, cum ipsa non videat; odoris carenti odorem, cum ipsa eodem sensu creat; surdo auditum, cum non audiat; muto loquium, cum ipsa non loquatur; debili manibus tactum, cum ipsa nihil palpare queat; claudo gressum, quo illa pedes nitus caret; mortuo vitam, cum ipsa non vivat, tanto nihilominus nobis sanctificationem impertire valet quae ipsa penitus caret. In parvo vero commate, quod superest, non est diutius immorandum, quoniam pene totum in superioribus commatibus per partes videtur esse connexum. Aut enim, Nam & sacra diversa vasa habentes hasce oculamur & amplectimur & sanctificationem quandam speramus. Non enim ad homines per vasa, sed ad vasa per homines divini nominis invocatione & sacrorum mysteriorum celebratione sanctificatio venit: nec vasis imagines coequandae sunt, quoniam in vasis, non in imaginibus, Deo sacrificium offertur. Nam si a vasis, quae utique sanctificata sunt, hominibus sanctificatur, ut diximus, immune impertitur, multominus ab imaginibus impertietur, quae nec sanctificare nec sanctificari possunt.
units.tr: "If you see a man swift in his words," says Scripture, "there is more hope for a fool than for him"; and "in much speaking sin will not be lacking." According to this sentence of Holy Scripture, the deacon Epiphanius, who is said to have been the same swift-tongued and loquacious man in that synod, and who showed that there is more hope for a fool than for himself, has gathered together all sorts of errors in his many words. For although in the preceding chapter we have, as far as seemed right, dealt with his trifles, in this one we must nonetheless dispute somewhat more.
