Indeed, we have decided in the course of these refutations to examine not words but sentences, and to seek not the literal form but the senses clothed in it, since in these matters the order of the letters is not the point; for in the long text of his reading no sentence can stand in the same case, and in the rare slips of words and in the file of learning, not yet polished, it is easy to dispute among the errors of meaning. Where then in a long series of reading there is neither purity of sense nor integrity of words, it is difficult to dispute each point, since the order of the dispute would stretch to infinity. For if we were to dispute each slip of words, while we ought to search out deep matters and scrutinise by turning over the leaves those things that pertain to ecclesiastical affairs, the manifold rules of the art of grammar, which are learned in the schools, would seem to be thrown in our way. But since in this work the steps of our journey are greatly hindered, partly because some of his statements are hard to understand and it is hard to grasp what they wish to signify, and partly because we are compelled, as the matter requires, to take up his statements infected with barbarisms, solecisms and other faults; and since, though his corrupt words are corrupt, the senses nonetheless are corrupt too, and we, for the sake of brevity, omit the corrections of words and urge only the order of the senses, and do so with labour, since one depends on another and the other is fixed in the one: it remains that, with the Lord's permission, we set aside the rebuke of the faults that affect the words, and proceed, as if before a journey that is for the most part already accomplished, to the disordered clusters of senses, the encrustations of his spiritual dirt. For the aforesaid deacon Epiphanius, whose opinion we have begun to examine, says: "Many things that are consecrated in us do not receive consecration by prayer." Since this, as it stands, has no full sense, let us suppose he wished to signify this, that he would say: "There are many things in us consecrated which are consecrated by the prayer or laying on of hands of a priest." If that is so, it is not sufficiently clear how it could be true; for whatever is consecrated in the Church, whether ecclesiastical orders, or the dedications of temples of priests, or other things that are named, are constituted by consecrations performed by priests according to ecclesiastical custom. Indeed, to the nobility of the Christian faith, by which one advances to the other grades, one comes at the very beginnings of infancy through laying on of hands and prayers to God. But if he meant to speak of places or vessels or certain utensils devoted to divine worship, his word can be defeated here; for there is almost nothing among those we have listed that is not consecrated by the prayers and consecrations of priests, and the Church is accustomed to use exorcisms and the sprinkling of salt and water as well. The consecrations or institutions of all these are known to have been handed down from the very beginnings of the Church by the bishops of the churches, and they are found written in the priestly books. Therefore, since the deacon introduced this in order to add to the vessels and other things devoted to divine worship the adoration of images, which they strive to strengthen with this benefit, though of whose consecration there is certainly no ecclesiastical institution, and since he strives to introduce this, that as these things are consecrated without prayers, so he might teach that those images too are consecrated without prayers, that attempt can be refuted by this: the ancient tradition of their consecration is written in the priestly books and is solemnly celebrated by priests, whereas of those images, neither consecration nor their being worthy of adoration is found among the things the Church receives as instituted. But as for what he says: "Nor are we honoured and magnified as much as things to be venerated. For he himself makes the sign of the life-giving cross without prayer; it is to be venerated," he clearly wished to say this: that the sign of the venerable cross, which we set up with honour for ourselves, is without any prayer or consecration of priests, and yet is held to be holy. In this he says very little, and in the rest he displays no small infamy of his own, in that the sign of the cross seeks no other consecration than that which was made through God and man, the mediator. But as for what he added: "And we shall be sufficient to receive the sign of his consecration, by which we make an adoration to him, some on the forehead by consecration, and we hope that the sign made by a finger in the air drives away demons," this belongs to what was brought in above. Therefore that the wood of the cross has a great mystery in itself, and that images are not to be equated with it but are far below it, is manifest by indications, and has been demonstrated in the earlier parts of this work, as the Lord has deigned to grant. For since images, as we said above, are consecrated by no prayer or laying on of hands, the sign of the cross, wherever it is made, is made with the invocation of the divine name. But those images neither have nor can have nor ought to have such a consecration; whereas the cross is so made by Christ that it not only needs no consecration by anyone, but, being made with the invocation of the divine name, it consecrates and blesses other things. Moreover, as for what he says: "Likewise, with the image, by the name of the signification, we bring it to the first form of honour, and kissing it and honourably honouring it we shall receive consecration," how absurd and how alien to reason this is, is plain. For he said that by the name of the signification the image can be brought to the honour of the first form, that is, to the veneration of the saint in whose name it is inscribed. That this can happen is shown by no evident grounds of reason; for the inscription only brings them, as proof by the name alone, to the honour of those same saints whose names are written over them. Therefore any thing to which the name of some saint is written rises to the honour of that same saint. Therefore stones, wood, garments, or certain animals inscribed with the names of certain saints pass to the honour of those same saints whose names are written on them. And if these inscribed names, which we have listed, cannot bring things to the honour of those whose names they are, neither do those inscriptions of names in some way bring them to the honour of the saints. And if this is denied by prudent consideration, and that is cast aside by careful inquiry, let us offer to anyone of those who adore images the following: for example, the images of two most beautiful women, without any inscription, which he, despising them, casts away, and, having cast them aside, allows them to lie in any place. Someone says to him: "One of these is an image of Saint Mary; it must not be cast away. The other is of Venus, and it must altogether be cast away." He turns to the painter and asks him, since they are all most alike, which of them is the image of Saint Mary, or which of Venus? The painter gives this one the inscription of Saint Mary, and that one the inscription of Venus. This one, because it has the inscription of the Mother of God, is raised up and honoured. That one, because it has the inscription of Venus, the mother of Aeneas, a certain fugitive, is cast down and reviled as accursed. Both are of the same figure, of the same colours, and made of the same materials; they differ only in their inscription. Let me ask, let Epiphanius the deacon tell me, who said that by the inscription of a name images can be brought to the honour of the first form: where was this holiness before it was inscribed, where was that reproach before it was inscribed? The inscription, then, which is added to images, according to the custom of letters, by which there is such power that they speak silently, and sometimes explain to the absent, sometimes to the present, without voice, is able to convey knowledge; but to those images on which it is placed it cannot give sanctification. For sanctification is granted to rational creatures through the display of good works and the prerogatives of merits; whereas to inanimate things without sense, such as vessels devoted to divine worship and things like them, sanctification comes not by any inscription, but by sacerdotal consecration and the invocation of the divine name. And by this plain reasoning it is shown that no sanctification can cling to images through any inscription; for that image which receives the inscription of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, and which once lay cast down and despised, is now venerably adorned. As much as it was harmed by its contempt while lying cast down, so much does it now benefit its worshippers when it is raised up and adored; and as much as it could help if it were raised up, so much can it harm when it is spurned. But as for what he says: "Vainly, adoring it and honourably, we shall receive sanctification," this would mean as much as if he said: "On account of it we honourably adore, desiring to receive sanctification from it, which it neither has nor is able to impart to us." How then can it give light to the blind, when it does not see itself? Smell to one lacking smell, when it has no such sense? Hearing to the deaf, when it does not hear? Speech to the dumb, when it does not speak? Touch to the one weak in hands, when it can feel nothing? Walking to the lame, since it lacks feet? Life to the dead, since it does not live? Just so much does it, which entirely lacks sanctification, nevertheless have the power to impart sanctification to us. But in the short clause that remains, we need not linger long, since almost the whole of it is seen to be connected part by part with the preceding clauses. For: "Also, holding the various holy vessels, we kiss and embrace these and hope for a certain sanctification." For sanctification comes not to men through vessels, but to vessels through men, by the invocation of the divine name and the celebration of the holy mysteries. Nor are images to be equated with vessels, since in vessels, not in images, sacrifice is offered to God. For if sanctification is imparted by men from vessels, which indeed are consecrated, as we have said, it is imparted just as much less from images, which can neither sanctify nor be sanctified.

units.la: CAP. XVII. Ridiculosissimum dictum Epiphanii reprehenditur, in eo quod ait, Ex proprio ven- tre locutus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII. The ridiculous saying of Epiphanius is rebuked, where he says, "Spoke out of his own belly."

units.la: Quod in eadem synodo scribitur eo quod praefatus Epiphanius de quodam dixit, Ex proprio ventre locutus, quamquam rebus ad fidem pertinentibus nullum afferat praejudicium, & hoc negotio de quo sermo est nec quicquam vel inroget vel deroget, ideo tamen a nobis non praeterminatur, quoniam indoctum quid sonat & insulsum: & quia nec debent nec possunt talis conceptura. ptura novæ quæliber constitutiones ecclesiæ prorogari, quæ tot modis potest reprehendi. Omne enim quod inreprehensibile est, hoc recipit sancta catholica ecclesia: quod autem in pluribus reprehenditur, hoc ab ecclesiastico dogmate abdicatur. Nec debet illius lectionis quæ reprehensionibus & talibus nugis est plena, de adorandis imaginibus observari censura. Dixerunt nempe quendam ex proprio ventre locutum. Quod dictum non solum à doctis verum etiam ab indoctis auribus respuitur, & veluti anile quoddam deliramentum abnuitur. Ex corde enim ea, quæ mens concepit, lingua interpretè producuntur: ex ventre ea administrantur quæ in secessum missa egeruntur: & licut non potest cor, quod plerumque & in divinis literis, & in consuetudine loquentium pro mente sive sensu ponitur, ełcas conficere, humorum collectiones habere: ita non potest venter cogitationes concipere, casuque per verba producere. Habent ergo singula membra officia sua, ut quinque sensus quinque membrorum partibus distributi sint, excepto tactu, qui quamvis in manibus sedem habere putetur, per cætera membra diffusus est. Et secundum philosophorum experientiam in corde est timor, in splene lætitia, in jecore voluptas, in tribus ventriculis cerebri, in anteriore qui est ad faciem, sensus, in eo qui posteriot ad cervicem est, motus, in eo verò qui inter utrumque est, memoria vigere demonstratur, in pulmonibus anhelandi, voces modificandi, spiritum ducendi officium habetur: ventrem autem, quem maris constat habere figuram, scatum tantum confectionibus humorumque collectionibus manifestum est inservire. Nam si forte hujusce dicti erroteni his velint adminiculis fulcire, quod plerumque ventris mentio in sacris literis reperiatur, ut est illud, a Venter meus conturbatus est, sive, b Ventrem meum doleo, & cætera hujuscemodi, adveniant numquam hujus membri vocabulum pro loquutione, sed pro aliis atque aliis rebus quæ per ventrem significantur, tropicè positum, de quibus nunc disputare longum est. Illud enim sicubi dictum est, tropologicum est, istud vero acyrologicum: per illud obumbratur allegorice veritas, per istud mutilatur sensus puritas: illud nicet mysteriis, istud squalet ineptiis. Cæterum si de Pythonibus dicere voluerunt, quos septuaginta ventriloquos transtulerunt, de quibus in Deuteronomio legitur; Noninvenietur in te sustrans filium suum aut filiam in igne, & divinans divinationem, augurans & arúspicans & ne- cromantiam suspicans, incantator, ventriloquus, & portenta inspicions, & interrogans mortuos: nec hoc reprehensione caret: quoniam cum illi quendam hominem ex proprio ventre loquutum fuisse dixerint, ut Pythonem, nec ab ipsius quidem Pythonis ventre homo, sed malignus loquitur spiritus: ita dumtaxat ut eodem Pythone, qui ventriloquus dicitur, per os humano more loquente de ventre ejus spiritus immundi voces audiantur, & responsa dentur, quos quidem ventriloquos in Assyriorum sive Ægyptiorum gentibus, apud quos magicæ artes copiosæ sunt, plures esse manifestum est.
units.tr: As for what is written in the same synod, that the aforementioned Epiphanius said of a certain man, Spoke out of his own belly: although this saying does no harm to the matters that pertain to faith, and neither charges nor detracts anything in the business under discussion, we do not pass it over for that reason, because it sounds untaught and foolish, and because no new constitutions of the Church ought or can be extended to such things, since it can be censured in so many ways. For the holy catholic Church accepts whatever cannot be found fault with; whatever is faulted in many respects, however, is rejected from ecclesiastical doctrine. Nor should the censure about the adoration of images be applied to a reading that is full of reproaches and such trifles. They said that a certain man spoke out of his own belly. This saying is rejected not only by learned ears but also by untaught ones, and it is dismissed as a sort of old woman's nonsense. For the things that the mind conceives are produced by the tongue as interpreter, out of the heart (which in divine letters, and in the usage of speakers, is often put for mind or understanding); the things that are passed into the privy and discharged are dealt with out of the belly. And just as the heart cannot make bile or have collections of humours, so the belly cannot conceive thoughts and bring them forth in words. Therefore each member has its own office, just as the five senses are distributed among the parts of the five members, except touch, which, although it is thought to have its seat in the hands, is spread through the other members. And according to the experience of the philosophers, fear is in the heart, gladness in the spleen, pleasure in the liver; in the three ventricles of the brain, sense is shown to flourish in the anterior one, which is toward the face, motion in the posterior one, which is toward the neck, and memory in the one that lies between the two; the office of panting, of modulating the voice, and of drawing breath is assigned to the lungs; but the belly, which, as is well known, has the shape of a sack, is clearly serviceable only for digestion and the collection of humours. For if perhaps they wish to prop up this error of saying with these supports, because mention of the belly is frequent in the sacred letters, as in that passage, a My belly is troubled, or b I am pained in my belly, and others of this kind, they should note that this word for the member is never used for speaking, but figuratively for other things signified by the belly, about which it would be long to dispute now. For where that is said, it is tropological; but this is acyrological. By the former the truth is veiled allegorically; by the latter the purity of the sense is maimed. The former is pleasing with mysteries; the latter is squalid with absurdities. Moreover, if they wished to speak of the Pythons, whom the Seventy rendered ventriloquists, of whom we read in Deuteronomy: There shall not be found among you anyone who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire, or who uses divination, augury, soothsaying, or necromancy, a charmer, a ventriloquist, one who inspects portents, or one who consults the dead; even so this is not free from censure. For although they say that a certain man spoke out of his own belly, as a Python does, the speaking is not done by the man from the belly of the Python itself, but by a malignant spirit; so that, only in this way, through the same Python, who is called a ventriloquist, speaking with the mouth in the human manner, the voices of the unclean spirit are heard from his belly and answers are given. Indeed it is clear that such ventriloquists are many among the nations of the Assyrians or Egyptians, among whom magical arts abound.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Contra eos qui dicunt, Qui imaginem idolorum dixerunt dæmoniorum imaginibus similem, accusent Abel & Noe & Abraham & Moysen & Samuhel & Da- vid, quòd ipsi aliena & pagana sacrificia Deo liba- verunt.
units.tr: Against those who say that the images of idols were like the images of demons, let them accuse Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Samuel and David, because they offered sacrifices to God that were foreign and pagan.

units.la: QUantum in hoc capitulo sonat & nos ex aliis eorum dictis experti sumus, hoc introducere niteruntur, ut quia à paganis quondam occisorum pecudum sacrificia dæmonibus libabantur, nec tamen ob hoc à sanctis viris in veteri lege prætermittebatur, quin & ab illis occisorum pecudum Deo victimæ offerrentur, nec ideo sit prætermittendum quin intra sanctam ecclesiam imagines adorentur, pro eo quòd à gentilibus idola colebantur, sed licet in aliis ex hoc negotio adversus eorum objectiones incassum adhibitæ frustrantur, ita etiam hæc quoque objectio instar radihibita prudentis adsertionis objectu frustrabitur. Manifestum namque est pridem & viris Deo omnipotenti, & à gentilium sacerdotibus occisorum pecudum sacrificia dæmonibus oblata fuisse: & antiquitus nefandorum hominum simulacra dæmonico instinctu posita in delubris, & quorundam sanctorum imagines ob rerum gestarum memoriam & ædificiorum pulchritudines, à catholicis habitas fuisse in basilicis. Sicut ergo occisorum pecudum sacrificii usus & à sanctis ante legem patribus legitur celebratus, & in lege à Domino per Moysen est traditus, dicant ubi adorandarum imaginum usus aut ante legem à Patriarchis, aut in lege per legislatorem, aut in novo testamento à Domino & salvatore, aut ab Apostolis vel ab Apostolicis viris sit institutus, & cum illorum celebratio tam authenticam habeat traditionem, dicant quem istarum adorationum obtineat vigorem. Qui dum hoc dicere nequiverint, rem se inutilem protulisse erubescant, & mater sanctorum sacrificiorum oblationi adorationem imaginum adsociare nisos fuisse resipiscant atque cognoscant. Quomodo ergo potest credi imagines à catholicis ad adorandum conditas, cum recipsa quidem gentilium simulacra primum ad adorandum perhibeantur condita fuisse? Simulacrum itaque usus exortus est, cum ex desiderio mortuorum quorumlibet virorum fortium aut regum aut quarundam urbium conditorum, aut quarumlibet artium inventorum imagines vel effigies his qui eos dilexerant conderentur, ut posterorum vel dilectorum dolor haberet aliquod de imaginum contemplatione remedium: sed paulatim hunc errorem persuadentibus dæmonibus ita in posteros inrepsisse, ut quos illi pro sola nominis memoria pingédos censuerat, successores deos existimarent atque colerent, & in his sibi dæmones sacrificare inlectos quosque miseros perceuserent. Hoc etiam exemplo adeo cernimus imaginum usum inolescere, ut quæ prius ob ornamentum basilicarum & memoriam erant compaginatæ rerum gestarum, inolescente paulatim nefario usu adeo nunc à catholicis quibusque extollantur, ut adorentur, eisq; luminaria, thymiamata, primitiæ vel quædam munuscula offerantur, & quod nequius est, ut in Græciæ partibus factum legimus, pontifices qui solum Deum adorandum, solumq; colendum, illique soli serviendum prædicare debuerant, & ipsi eis se servituros fateantur, easq; colant & adorent, & earum contemptores soliusq; Dei cultores, vel osque adoratores ob earum contemptum & hæreticos judicent, & anathematizare affectent. Uno namque & pene pari modo, ut prefati sumus, adorandorum & colendorum simulachrorum vel potius dæmonum & gentilibus nequissimus usus inolevit, & catholicis, quod nō sine quodam animi mœrore prosequimur, adorandarum imaginum ineptissima consuetudo adcrescit, & res ad aliud conditæ, ad aliud videntur usurpatæ. Non enim nos imagines in basilicis positas idola nuncupamus, sed ne idola nuncupentur, adorare eas & colere eisque servitium impendere recusamus, quoniam plerumque non res, sed causa rei pro scelere reputatur: dum videlicet multa quibus bene potest uti male usa in flagitiū convertuntur, siq; una eademq; res bene utentibus non est causa piaculi, & male utentibus est causa periculi. Sollicitè ergo præcavendum est & summa industria procurandum, ne dum quidam nostrorum quasdam res ultra quàm ordo exposcit sublimare affectant, vetustissimi illius & carnosi erroris redivivi illis cineres convalescant, & victoriam quam in campo adepti sunt, intra urbis mœnia perdant, subigatq; civilis belli insuspicabiliter dolosa inlusio, quos subigere externi hostis aperta nequivit impulsio. Cum ergo illi accusandos garriant sanctos patres, Abel videlicet, Noe & Abraham, Moysen, Samuhelem & David, non eos nobis accusare libet, sed laudare, dicente Ecclesiastico; Laudemus viros gloriosos, & parentes nostros in generatione sua. multam gloriam fecit Dominus magnificentia sua, à sæculo dominantes in potentatibus suis homines magni virtute & prudentia sua praditi in dignitate prophetarum, & imperantes in præsenti populo, & in virtute prudentia populi sanctissima verba, & cætera. Quis ergo tam profanam habeat metem, ut Abel, qui ab ipso Domino justus appellatus est, accusare audeat? cujus sanguis de terra ad Dominum clamasse legitur, qui exemplar & norma est omnium justorum, qui primus persecutionem passuris sanctis prævius extitit, & civitatis Dei quam fluminis impetus lætificat, primus fundamenta jecit. Aut quis Noe virum justum accusare præsumat? quem Dominus gratiam coram se invenisse testatur: qui secundus post Adam humani generis pater orbis extitit reparator, & in typo Christi ecclesiam diversis gentibus plenam inter mundanorum fluctuum innane procellas gubernatur erat, archæ diversis animantibus plenæ, inter horrisonorum fluctuum inlisiones extitit gubernator, qui tot meritorum exornatur insignibus, ut ille tantum cum Danihele & Job in die judicii liberandus dicatur, Ezechiele adtestante, qui ait; Si pestilentiam immisero super terram illam, & effudero indignationem meam super eam in sanguinem, ut auferam ex ea hominem & jumentum, & Noe & Danihel & Job fuerint in medio ejus, vivo ego, dicit dominus Deus, quia filium & filiam non liberabunt, sed ipsi justitia sua liberabunt animas suas. In quibus tribus sanctis omnis sanctorum multitudo signatur, ut per Noe ecclesiæ gubernatores, per Danihelem virgines & continentes, per Job conjugati & pœnitentes innuantur. Aut quis Abraham patriarcham accusare affectet? qui est prima credentium via & beati seminis serus pater, cui non legis observantia, sed fides credulitatis est ad justitiam reputata: qui triniratem in typo videns, & unitatem in mysterio venerans, divini judicii archana, & de conjuge sua suscipiendæ soboli stupendum miraculum audire promeruit: qui fidei cujus ipse specimen tenuit, futuras circa finem mundi angustias figuraliter sensit, cum circa finem diei terror nimius & tenebrosus super eum intrat. Aut quis Moysen legislatorem accusare præsumat? de quo scriptum est, quòd esset mirissimus super omnes qui mirabantur in terra, qui in typo Christi mediator inter Deum & homines constitutus devicto nequissimo hoste populum de servitute Ægyptia signis ac prodigiis terribilibus liberavit. Aut Samuhelem qui ab ipsis cunabulis Domino consecratus usque ad decrepitam senectutem in Domini militia militavit. Aut David? qui vir dicitur secundum cor Domini inventus, & in eo meritis sanctorum prælatus, ut & de Christo apertius cunctis prophetarit, & secundum formam servi ejus pateret fit nunc upatus. Quorum si laudes & mysteria singillatim proferamus, ante dies quàm verba, cessabit. Non enim illi offerebant Deo sacrificia pagana, sed mysteriis plena: quia necdum à pagis Athenien-sium pagans nuncupabantur, quando jam ab illis Deo sacrificium offerebatur, & ut ita dixerim, necdum Athenarum urbs condita erat, nec Cecrops offerendorum sacrificiorum institutiones & ararum erectiones & dæmonum appellationes gentilibus tradiderat, cum jam Abel & Noe & Abraham Deo sacrificia obtulerant. Offerebant, inquam, sancti sive ante legem, sive sub lege, sacrificia typicis mysteriis obumbrata, quæ in novo testamento per mediatorem Dei & hominum expulsis obumbratis præfigurationibus sunt completa, & ecclesiæ tradita, quibus usque in finem ipso auxiliante erit contenta. Quur ergo antiqui Patres visibiliter sacrificaverint & carnalia sacrificia Deo litaverint, beati Augustini verbis lectorem agnoscat. Ait enim, Qua sunt etiam sacra spiritalia, quorum imagines carnalem populum celebrare oportebat, ut præfiguratio novi populi servitute veteris fieret, quorum duorum populorum differentiam etiam in unoquoque nostrum licet advertere, cùm quisque ab utero matris veterem hominem necesse est agat, donec veniat ad juvenilem ætatem, ubi jam non est necesse carnaliter sapere, sed potest ad spiritalia voluntate converti & intrinsecus regenerari. quod ergo in uno homine rectè educato ordine naturæ disciplinaq; contingit, hoc proportione in universo genere humano fieri per divinam providentiam, peragiq; pulcherrimum est.
units.tr: As far as this chapter goes, and as we have learned from their other sayings, they strive to argue the following. Sacrifices of slaughtered cattle were once offered to demons by pagans, yet the holy men of the Old Law did not on that account stop offering slaughtered victims to God. Therefore, they say, one must not refrain from worshipping images within the holy Church merely because the Gentiles worshipped idols. But just as in other matters the futile arguments they have brought against these objections fail, so this objection too, brought forward like a bow, will be defeated by a prudent assertion. For it is clear that long ago sacrifices of slaughtered cattle were offered to demons by the priests of the Gentiles, and that by demonic instinct the images of wicked men were set up in shrines in antiquity, and that Catholics kept images of certain saints in churches as memorials of their deeds and as ornaments of the buildings. Therefore, just as the practice of sacrificing slaughtered cattle is read of as observed by the saints before the Law, and was handed down by the Lord through Moses in the Law, let them say where the practice of worshipping images was instituted, whether before the Law by the Patriarchs, or in the Law by the lawgiver, or in the New Testament by the Lord and Saviour, or by the Apostles or Apostolic men. And since the observance of those sacrifices has so authentic a tradition, let them say what force these adorations have. If they cannot say this, let them blush that they have produced a useless argument, and let them recognise that they have struggled to join the worship of images to the offering of the holy sacrifices, which is their mother. How, then, can it be believed that images were devised by Catholics for worship, when in fact it is reported that the images of the Gentiles were the first to be made for worship? The use of the image therefore arose when, out of longing for certain brave men, kings, or founders of cities, or inventors of some arts, images or likenesses of them were made for those who had loved them, so that the grief of their descendants or friends might have some remedy in contemplating the images. But gradually, with demons persuading, this error crept into posterity in such a way that those whom the demons had thought should be painted merely for the memory of their names were regarded and worshipped by their successors as gods, and the demons, having enticed them, made wretched people sacrifice to them. By this example we also see the use of images so grow strong that those which were first put together as ornaments of churches and memorials of deeds are now, by the gradual growth of this wicked practice, so exalted by Catholics that they are worshipped, and lamps, incense, first fruits and certain small gifts are offered to them. And, what is worse, as we read was done in parts of Greece, the bishops, who ought to have preached that God alone is to be adored, God alone worshipped, and God alone served, themselves confess that they will serve those images, worship and adore them, and judge those who despise images and are worshippers of God alone to be heretics, and even strive to anathematise them. For, in one and almost the same way, as we have said, the most wicked custom of adoring and worshipping images, or rather demons, grew up among the Gentiles, and among Catholics, which we pursue not without some sorrow of mind, the most foolish custom of adoring images is increasing, and things made for one purpose seem to be used for another. For we do not call the images placed in churches idols, but we refuse to adore and worship them and to offer them service, lest they be called idols. For very often it is not the thing but the cause of the thing that is counted as a crime. Namely, many things which can be used well are turned into a disgrace when they are used badly; and one and the same thing is not the cause of sin for those who use it well, but is the cause of danger for those who use it badly. Therefore we must take care and provide with the utmost diligence that, while some of our people strive to exalt certain things beyond what order demands, the ashes of that most ancient and fleshly error may not revive in them, and that they may not lose within the walls of the city the victory they gained in the field, and that the unsuspected deceit of civil war, which the open attack of a foreign enemy could not subdue, may not overcome them. Since, then, those men chatter that the holy fathers, namely Abel, Noah and Abraham, Moses, Samuel and David, are to be accused, we do not wish to accuse them but to praise them, as Ecclesiasticus says: Let us praise famous men, and our fathers in their generation. The Lord hath wrought great glory by his magnificence from the beginning. Such as did bear rule in their kingdoms, men renowned for their power, giving counsel by their understanding; leaders of the people by their counsels, and by their knowledge of learning wise and eloquent in their instructions; and the rest. Who, then, has so profane a mind as to dare to accuse Abel, who was called just by the Lord himself, whose blood is read to have cried from the earth to the Lord, who is the model and rule of all the just, who was the first to go before the saints who were to suffer persecution, and who was the first to lay the foundations of the city of God, which the rush of the river gladdens? Or who would presume to accuse Noah, a just man, whom the Lord testifies to have found grace before him, who was the second father of the human race after Adam and became the restorer of the world, and who, in a figure of Christ, governed the Church full of diverse peoples amid the empty storms of worldly waves, the ark full of diverse living creatures, and who was the steersman amid the thundering dashing of the waves? He is so adorned with the distinctions of so many merits that he alone, with Daniel and Job, is said to be delivered on the day of judgment, as Ezekiel attests, who says: If I send pestilence upon that land, and pour out my wrath upon it in blood, to cut off from it man and beast; though Noah, Daniel and Job were in the midst of it, as I live, saith the Lord God, they shall deliver neither son nor daughter, but they shall deliver their own souls by their righteousness. In these three saints the whole multitude of saints is signified: by Noah are indicated the governors of the Church, by Daniel virgins and the continent, and by Job the married and penitents. Or who would aim to accuse the patriarch Abraham? He is the first way of believers and the late father of the blessed seed, to whom faith in credulity, not observance of the Law, was reckoned for righteousness; who, seeing the Trinity in a figure and venerating the Unity in a mystery, deserved to hear the secrets of the divine judgment and the astonishing miracle of a son to be received from his wife; who, through the faith of which he held the pattern, perceived figuratively the future distresses near the end of the world, when a great and gloomy terror comes upon him near the end of the day. Or who would presume to accuse Moses the lawgiver? Of him it is written that he was the meekest above all men who were on the earth; who, in a figure of Christ, was set up as mediator between God and men, and, the most wicked enemy being overcome, freed the people from Egyptian servitude by signs and terrible wonders. Or Samuel, who from his very cradle was consecrated to the Lord and served in the Lord's army until decrepit old age. Or David? He is said to have been found a man according to the heart of the Lord, and in him was preferred to others on account of the merits of the saints, so that he prophesied of Christ more openly than all, and through the form of his servant it was made manifest. If we were to present their praises and mysteries one by one, the day would end before the words did. For they did not offer pagan sacrifices to God, but sacrifices full of mysteries. For the Athenians had not yet been called pagans from their villages when sacrifice was already being offered to God by these men; and, so to speak, the city of Athens had not yet been founded, nor had Cecrops handed down to the Gentiles the institutions of offering sacrifices, the erection of altars and the naming of demons, when Abel, Noah and Abraham had already offered sacrifices to God. I say, the saints, whether before the Law or under the Law, offered sacrifices shadowed by typical mysteries, which in the New Testament were completed through the mediator between God and men, the shadowy foreshadowings being removed, and were handed over to the Church, with which it will be content, with his help, until the end. Let the reader, then, recognise from the words of the blessed Augustine why the ancient Fathers offered visibly and sacrificed fleshly sacrifices to God. For he says: There are also spiritual sacred things, whose images the carnal people had to celebrate, so that the foreshadowing of the new people might be made through the servitude of the old. The difference between these two peoples can also be noticed in each of us, since each one of us must, from his mother's womb, live as the old man until he comes to youthful age, where it is no longer necessary to be carnally wise, but he can be turned by his will to spiritual things and be regenerated inwardly. What happens in one man rightly brought up by the order of nature and discipline, this, in due proportion, happens in the whole human race through divine providence, and it is most beautiful to bring it about.

units.la: CAP.XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Contra eos qui dicunt ; Si sanctus Epiphanius imaginum destructor fuit & earum abominator, quomodo ejus discipuli imagines depingebant in Cypriorum insula, in templo quod ejusdem patris nomine titulaverunt : cum videlicet multa pingantur quae non adorantur, & plerumque à bonis magistris mali discipuli oriantur.
units.tr: Against those who say: If holy Epiphanius was a destroyer and abhorrer of images, how did his disciples paint images in the island of Cyprus, in the temple which they named after the same father? For many things are painted which are not adored, and evil disciples often arise from good masters.

units.la: MAGNA sic in hac parte illi de quibus sermo est, ad suum errorem tuendum armorum reperisse gratulantur instrumenta, eo quòd in insula Cypro à cujusdam sancti viri Epiphanii discipulis basilica dicatur fuisse depicta, quasi nulla res possit pingi quae non continuo debeat adorari. Cum ergo imaginum habendarum vel non habendarum usus non praejudicet catholicae fidei puritati, constat eundem Epiphanium sive alium quemlibet sanctum virum, nec imaginum fuisse destructorem, nec earum adoratorem, discipulosque ejus vel quoslibet catholicos viros non ideo basilicas colorum fucis depinxisse, ut picturae adorarentur, sed ut ex eis parietibus pulchritudo inferretur, & rerum gestarum aspicientibus memoria ingereretur. Non enim quia Epiphanii discipuli in insula Cypro basilicam depinxisse perhibentur, idcirco imagines adorabuntur, quoniam non omnia quae pinguntur protinus adorantur. Quae si singula adorari deberent, pauca admodum creaturae quae non adorarentur, remanerent. Cernimus namque in metallis conflatorio sive sculptorio opere, in gemmis insignibusque lapidibus mira sculptoris arte, in marmoribus caeterisque lapidibus latomorum sive sculptorum industria, in lignis caelatoris scalpello, in lithostrotis diversorum colorum per artificem conpaginatis cruslulis, in sericis, laneis necnon & lineis multicoloribus vestibus plumario polymitarioque; opere formatas imagines. Num quid quia praefati viri, sancti scilicet Epiphanii, discipuli in Cypro basilicam depinxerunt, idcirco omnes adorandae sunt? aut quia illi diversis materiis locum exornaverunt divino cultui dedicatum, ideo ad singulas materias quas praemisimus pro imaginibus quae eis in subjecto sunt curvatis poplitibus, flexis cervicibus, crebrescentibus suspiriis, sublevatis reverenter ac plerumque semiclausis luminibus, à fidelibus est currendum? Non igitur consequens est, ut pro eo quòd illi basilicam pinxisse dicuntur, imagines adorentur. Potest etiam huic illorum objectioni aliud rationabiliter opponi, ut illorum adsertio sicut aliis objectionibus nequivit muniri, ita etiam nec hac quoque depicta ab Epiphanii discipulis basilica valeat adstrui: praesertim cum etsi ejusdem sancti viri discipulorum consensus à se inditas parietibus picturas adorare censuisset, nullam ejus vim censura haberet: quoniam plerumque à bonis magistris bene discipuli educati, postmodum neglecta institutione magistrorum efficiuntur perversi. Quod si solerti indagatione quaeratur, factarum literarum exemplis approbabitur. Helisaei igitur viri sancti & duplicis Heliae spiritu ditati discipulo tantus pecuniae amor inrepsit, ut percepto alienigenae munere à magistro spreto exitiabilis etiam aegritudo eum foedarit. Non illum prophetica alloquutio, non magistri eruditio, non signorum terribilium ostensio, non tanti prophetae communis habitatio à tantae peltis, id est, avaritiae labe conpescuit, sed avaritia quae eum invasit, lepram quoque ei cum Syri censu inussit. Judam, etiam, de quo per prophetam scriptum est; Homo pacis meae qui edebat panem meum ampliavit adversum me supplantationem: cui quondam dictum est, Tu vero homo unanimis, dux meus & notus meus, qui simul mecum dulces capiebas cibos, neglecta boni magistri erudi-tione, & revera boni, qui de seipso dixit, An oculus tuus nequam est, quia ego bonus sum? & cui per David dicitur; Bonus es domine, bonitatem tuam doce me: de quo etiam per Hieremiam dicitur; Bonus est dominus speran-tibus in se, animae quaerenti illum: adeo capacis vel maximè rapacis avaritiae furor arripuit, ut magistrum prodere non distulerit, quem non verba caelestia, non vitae fontis inundatio, non signorum exhibitio, non apostolica societas, non apostolici nominis dignitas à tanti sceleris perpetratione cohibuit: qui cognita sui sceleris nequitia indignam vitam digna morte finivit: de quo ait Sedulius,
units.tr: Those of whom we speak thus boast that they have found weapons to defend their error, because in the island of Cyprus a church is said to have been painted by the disciples of a holy man, Epiphanius, as if nothing could be painted that did not at once have to be adored. Since, then, the use or non-use of images does not prejudice the purity of the Catholic faith, it is clear that Epiphanius, or any other holy man, was neither a destroyer of images nor an adorer of them, and that his disciples, or any other Catholic men, did not paint the churches with coloured pigments so that the pictures would be adored, but so that beauty would be added to the walls and the memory of past deeds would be brought to those who look at them. For it does not follow that images will be adored because the disciples of Epiphanius are said to have painted a church in Cyprus, since not everything that is painted is adored at once. If each single thing were to be adored, very few creatures would remain that were not adored. For we see, in metals worked by the furnace or by the chisel, in gems and precious stones by the marvellous skill of the carver, in marble and other stones by the industry of the stonecutters, in wood by the graver's tool, in the mosaic floors of various colours fitted together by the craftsman in little tesserae, and in silk, wool and linen garments of many colours, images formed by the embroiderer and the weaver. Does it follow that, because the disciples of that man, the holy Epiphanius, painted a church in Cyprus, all these things are to be adored? Or, because they adorned a place dedicated to divine worship with various materials, must the faithful therefore bend their knees, bow their necks, sigh repeatedly, raise their eyes reverently and often half close them before each of the materials we have mentioned, for the images that are set in them? It does not follow, then, that images are to be adored because they are said to have painted a church. This objection of theirs may also be reasonably met with another argument: just as their assertion could not be supported against the other objections, so neither can it be established by this objection of the church painted by the disciples of Epiphanius. This is especially so because, even if the disciples of that holy man had agreed to adore the pictures set on the walls, their judgment would carry no weight, since disciples well brought up by good masters often become perverse afterwards, their masters' teaching having been neglected. If this is sought out with careful inquiry, examples from the letters of the past will prove it. The disciple of Elisha, the holy man endowed with the double spirit of Elijah, was overcome by so great a love of money that, after receiving a gift from a foreigner and despising his master, a deadly sickness disfigured him. Neither the prophetic word, nor the teaching of his master, nor the display of terrible signs, nor the common dwelling with so great a prophet, restrained him from the stain of so great a plague, that is, of avarice; but the avarice which seized him also branded him with the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian. Consider also Judas, of whom it is written through the prophet: The man of my peace, who ate my bread, has lifted up his heel against me; and to whom it was once said: But you, a man of one mind, my guide and my familiar, who together with me took sweet food; neglecting the teaching of a good master, and truly good, who said of himself: Is your eye evil because I am good?; and to whom it is said through David: You are good, O Lord; teach me your goodness; of whom also it is said through Jeremiah: The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. Such was the frenzy of avarice, most grasping and most rapacious, that seized him, so that he did not delay in betraying his master; whom neither heavenly words, nor the outpouring of the fountain of life, nor the showing of signs, nor apostolic fellowship, nor the dignity of the apostolic name, restrained from perpetrating so great a crime. He, recognising the wickedness of his own crime, ended his unworthy life by a worthy death. Of him Sedulius says:

units.la: Tunc vir apostolicus, nunc vilis apostata factus.
units.tr: Then an apostolic man, now a base apostate.

units.la: Nicolaus quoq; discipulus Apostolorum & inter septem unà cum beato Stephano in diaconi ministerium consecratus, neglectis postmodum bonorum magistrorum doctrinis, sive bonorum condiaconorum societatibus, haeresiarches est effectus, & qui bonorum operum exercitia exemplis sive verbis, utpote discipulus Apostolorum, instituere debuit, permutatis in contrarium vicibus ipse nefandae haeresis scelus instituit, de qua in Apocalypsi scribitur, Sed hoc habes quod odisti facta Nicolaitarum, quae & ego odi. Si ergo boni prophetae malus discipulus propter avaritiā reprobatur, & boni magistri, domini scilicet & salvatoris nostri, discipulus fuit & proditor effectus abominatur, & sanctorum Apostolorum malus discipulus propter impium dogma à se institutū exsecratur, quid mirum si à bono magistro Epiphanio picturarum adorationem instituendo mali discipuli efficiuntur? & hoc dicentes non cos reprobos judicamus, quippe cùm eorum vitam & conversationem nesciamus, sed propositā conditionali particula, si picturas adorare censuerunt, in eo cos erroneos adseveramus. Aspiciamus ergo Novatum Cypriani episcopi presbyterū Novatianani haeresem condidisse, & suum arbitrium sequutum sancti magistri monita Ipse vi se: Arrium quoq; à catholico magistro eruditum novimus fuisse, & postmodum exitiabilis dogmatis grana seminasse. Quid de singulis referam? pene omnes haeresiarchas catholicorum constat fuisse discipulos, quia nequaquam in suo nomine poterat haeresim quis titulare, nisi illā suo arbitrio repertisset. Quibus exemplis colligitur, nil sancti Epiphanii discipuli magistri sanctitatem profuisse, si ab ecclesiasticis constitutionibus spreta boni magistri eruditione creduntur deviasse.
units.tr: Nicholas also, a disciple of the Apostles and, with the blessed Stephen, consecrated among the seven to the ministry of the deacons, afterwards neglected the teachings of good masters and the fellowship of good fellow deacons, and became the founder of a heresy. He who ought to have taught good works by example and word, as a disciple of the Apostles, reversed the order and himself instituted the wicked crime of an abominable heresy, of which it is written in the Apocalypse: But you have this, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. If, then, the bad disciple of a good prophet is condemned for avarice, and the disciple of the good master, the Lord and our Saviour, is abhorred because he became a traitor, and the bad disciple of the holy Apostles is cursed for the impious doctrine he introduced, why is it surprising if disciples become bad by instituting the adoration of pictures under the good master Epiphanius? In saying this we do not judge them reprobate, since we do not know their life and conduct; but, with the conditional clause proposed, if they have decided to adore pictures, we assert that in this they are in error. Let us look, then, at Novatus, the presbyter of Cyprian the bishop, who founded the heresy of Novatian and followed his own judgment, neglecting the warnings of his holy master. We know that Arius also was taught by a Catholic master and afterwards sowed the seeds of a deadly doctrine. Why should I recount each one? It is almost certain that nearly all the founders of heresies were disciples of Catholics, since no one could give a heresy his own name unless he had devised it by his own judgment. From these examples it is gathered that the disciples of Epiphanius gained nothing from the holiness of their master, if, having spurned the teaching of a good master as set out in ecclesiastical constitutions, they are believed to have strayed.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Quod adulatorie Imperatorem suum sive matrem ejus apostolis coaequare nisi sint dicentes, Sicut olim salutis nostrae rector & persector Jesus proprios suos apostolos sancti spiritus induens virtute emisit, sicut & nunc suos placabiles & apostolorum similes fideles nostros imperatores erexit de eodem spiritu prudentes factos, & idoneos existentes virtute ad perfectionem nostram.
units.tr: That they flatter their Emperor, or his mother, by claiming to make him equal to the apostles, saying: "Just as of old Jesus, the ruler and perfecter of our salvation, sent out his own apostles clothed with the power of the Holy Spirit, so now he has raised up our Emperors, pleasing to him and like the apostles, made wise by the same Spirit and fit, by virtue, for our perfection."

units.la: ESSUROS cum domino Apostolos ad judicandum ejusdem domini veridica voce reperimus, Vos, inquit, qui secuti estis me, in regeneratione cum sederit filius hominis in sede majestatis suae, sedebitis super duodecim thronos, judicantes duodecim tribus Israel: eosque se elegisse de mundo, ut de mundo non essent, sed ut fructum plurimum adferrent, ipse dominus adtestatur, Ego vos, inquies, de mundo elegi, ut de mundo non effetis, & ego elegi vos ut fructum plurimum adferatis, & fructus vester maneat in aeternum: illos esse sal terrae, condimentum videlicet populi, quo insulsa quaeque condiuntur, & insipida saporantur: eos lucem mundi, qui veri lucis, hoc est, Christi, fulgore suae praedicationis verbis mundi tenebras, diffidentiae videlicet caliginem, inradiarunt, manifestum est: illis a domino & in terra per insufflationem datur, & e coelo in igne linguarumque divisione spiritus sanctus ad innuendam dei & proximi dilectionem emittitur: illis solvendi ligandique, peccata remittendi & retinendi, mortuos suscitandi, daemones eiiciendi, infirmos curandi, caeteraque hujusmodi opera faciendi datur potestas, & omnes gentes docendi, & in nomine sanctae trinitatis baptizandi confertur auctoritas: illis gaudere jussum est, quod nomina eorum aeternae vitae coelestis liber insertata teneat: illis dictum est, Beati oculi qui vident quae vos videtis, & aures quae audiunt quae auditis, quia videlicet secundum ejusdem domini & salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi vetacillimum testimonium, multi prophetae & reges voluerunt videre quae illi videbant, & audire quae illi audiebant: quoniam omnium patriarcharum & prophetarum egregius coetus, quamquam redemptorem mundi venturum pro salute mundi prophetiae spiritus eruditione scirent, cumque interioris intuitus oculo quodammodo cernerent, eum tamen quem corporaliter venturum sciebant, corporaliter cernere aestuabant. Quij dum tot meritorum insignibus emineant, totque beatitudinum excellentia polleant, incassum eis illi quorum errores discutimus, imperatores suos adsimilare affectant. Liquido namque patet apostolos prophetis praelatos esse, si apostolis imperatores eorum, ut illi somniant, similes sunt, prophetis praeferuntur, qui Christum quem corporaliter venturum sciebant, corporaliter non viderunt: si prophetis praeferuntur redemptorem mundi corporaliter viderunt. redemptorem autem mundi eos corporaliter non vidisse, evidentissime patet: non igitur prophetis imperatores eorum praeferuntur, nec apostolis, ut illi dicunt, similes sunt. Quomodo ergo apostolis queant adsimilari, cum non solum non sint eis similibus meritis & quiparati, similique sanctitatis nitore praediti, verumetiam eorum sacratissimis praedicationibus in pluribus videantur obniti? aut quomodo poterunt eorum esse similes, quorum neglegunt esse quaeces? Illi sectati sunt caelestia perpetimque mansura, isti sectantur terrestria quaeque & caduca: illi spreto mundo domino adhaerere maluerunt, isti mundi pompis ejusque fumeis gaudiis adhaerentes pletumque domini praecepta spernunt: illi persequutionem propter justitiam patiebantur, isti plectumque propter injustitiam persequuntur: illi tradebantur in concilius, & flagellabantur in synagogis, isti praedicantur in subjectis urbibus, & conlaudantur in populis: illorum epistolae aeternae vitae commercia gerentes ducebantur legendae per provincias & regiones, istorum imagines & effigies gentilicum & obsoletum quendam errorem referentes adorandae circumferuntur per vicos & civitates: illi beati fore a domino dicti sunt, cum eos odissent homines, & persequuti fuissent, & omne malum adversus eos mentientes dixissent, isti in eo se beatos putant, quod se diligi sibique parere, seque conlaudari ab hominibus videntur: illis dicitur; Beati qui nunc fletu quia ridebitis, iitis dicitur; Risus dolore miscetur, & extrema gaudii luctus occupat: illi gaudente mundo contristati sunt, contristato denuo mundo gavisuri sunt, isti gaudente mundo gaudent, contristato mundo contristabuntur: illi euntes in mundum, cujus figuram praeteriturum praedicabant, ejus noxios actus flebant, mittentes aeterni fructus semina, isti in mundo fundari de prosperitate mundi gaudentes, amplexantur praesentis vitae prospera: illi venientes ad judicium venient in exultatione, securi de aeterna remuneratione, portantes manipulos hominum per suam praedicationem conversorum, isti venient cum magno tremore reddituri rationem operum suorum. Sed quid amplius immoramur? quid longius evagamur? quid de ingentibus sylvis modicos flores colligimus, quorum nec millesimam quidem partem colligere valemus? Tanta est distantia inter apostolos & imperatores, quanta inter sanctos & peccatores, & cum apostoli eminean novi testamenti sanctis omnibus, multo amplius eminere creduntur peccatoribus. O adolatio, quur tanta praesumis? O oleum rancoris potius exuberans nidorem, quam lenitatis aut nectaris nitorem! a sacerdotibus venderis, a praesulibus inlectorum quorundam capita inlinis, & quod Propheta sibi adhiberi exhorruit; Oleum, inquiens, peccatoris non impinguet caput meum, id pontificum coetus imperatorum capitibus indit, & quod evangelicae virgines emendum dixerunt a venditoribus, hoc, pro dolor, fideles & maxime populi rectores emunt a praesulibus. Quod ergo ex eodem spiritu, id est, a sancto spiritu eosdem imperatores prudentes & idoneos factos esse virtute ad perfectionem suam fatentur, manifestum est omnes fideles qui veraciter Christiani sunt, sanctum habere spiritum, dicente Apostolo; Quisquis spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est ejus, quod spiritus sancti donum & post baptismum per manus impositionem infundirur, & vitæ munditia secundum meritorum distantiam singulis distribuitur, dicente vase electionis; Unicuique data est gratia secundum mensuram. Quamquam igitur in alio loco scribatur; Non enim ad mensuram dat deus spiritum, ad mensuram tamen fidelibus quibusque impertitur: quod autem ait; Non enim ad mensuram dat deus spiritum, hoc de solo filio qui consubstantialis est patri & spirirui sancto intellegatur, cui non ad mensuram spiritus datur: quoniam juxta Pauli vocem; In ipso habitare corporaliter omnis plenitudo divinitatis creditur. Quod autem ad mensuram dari spiritus & singulis singula distribuere, prout vult, dicitur, hoc de fidelibus quibusque dictum esse absque ambiguitate accipitur. Sed quamvis unumquemque catholicorum constet habere spiritum sanctum, juxta quod superius memoravimus, & exemplis inlustravimus, nullum tamen nostræ ætatis hominem secundum Apostolicæ mensuræ gratiam spiritum sanctum accepisse dicere audemus, aut adfirmare valemus.
units.tr: Hearing the Lord's own word of judgment, we find that the apostles were to sit with him in judgment. "You," he says, "who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you shall also sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." The Lord himself testifies that he chose them out of the world, so that they should not be of the world, but should bear much fruit: "I have chosen you out of the world, that you should not be of the world, and I have chosen you that you should bear much fruit, and that your fruit should remain for ever." It is plain that they are the salt of the earth, the seasoning of the people, by which unsavoury things are seasoned and tasteless things given flavour; that they are the light of the world, who by the brightness of their preaching, by the words of the true Light, that is Christ, lit up the darkness of the world, that is, the mist of unbelief. By the Lord himself, the Holy Spirit was given to them by breathing upon them on earth, and was sent down from heaven in fire and in the division of tongues, to signify the love of God and of neighbour. To them was given the power of binding and loosing, of forgiving and retaining sins, of raising the dead, casting out demons, healing the sick, and doing other works of this kind; and authority was conferred on them to teach all nations and to baptize in the name of the holy Trinity. They were bidden to rejoice because their names were written in the book of eternal heavenly life. To them it was said: "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that hear what you hear", because, as the most true testimony of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ himself has it, "many prophets and kings desired to see what they saw, and to hear what they heard." For the whole illustrious company of all the patriarchs and prophets, although they knew by the teaching of the Spirit of prophecy that the Redeemer of the world would come for the world's salvation, and although they could in some measure discern him with the eye of inward vision, nevertheless longed to see with bodily eyes him whom they knew would come in the body. While these men stand out by the marks of so many merits and excel in so great a height of blessedness, those whose errors we are examining strive in vain to make their emperors like them. For it is clear that the apostles were preferred to the prophets; if their emperors, as those men dream, are like the apostles, they are preferred to the prophets, who knew that Christ would come in the body but did not see him in the body; and if they are preferred to the prophets, they saw the Redeemer of the world in the body. But it is most evident that they did not see the Redeemer of the world in the body. Therefore their emperors are not preferred to the prophets, nor, as those men say, are they like the apostles. How, then, can they be made like the apostles, since they are not only not equal to them in merit and not matched with them, endowed with the same brightness of holiness, but are even seen to strive against the most sacred preaching of the apostles in many respects? Or how can they be like those whose way of life they neglect to follow? The apostles pursued heavenly things, which abide for ever; these men pursue earthly and fading things: the apostles preferred to cling to the Lord, having scorned the world; these men cling to the pomps of the world and its smoky joys, and largely despise the Lord's precepts. The apostles suffered persecution for righteousness' sake; these men persecute with blows for unrighteousness. The apostles were handed over to councils and scourged in synagogues; these men are praised in subject cities and lauded among the peoples. The apostles' letters, carrying on the business of eternal life, were brought to be read through provinces and regions; images and effigies of these men, recalling a certain pagan and obsolete error, are carried about to be adored through villages and cities. The apostles were called blessed by the Lord when men hated them, persecuted them, and said all manner of evil against them falsely; these men think themselves blessed in this, that they are loved, that men obey them, and that they are seen to be praised by men. To the apostles it is said: "Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh"; to these men it is said: "Laughter is mingled with grief, and the end of joy is taken up by sorrow." The apostles were saddened while the world rejoiced, and will rejoice when the world is saddened again; these men rejoice while the world rejoices, and will be saddened when the world is saddened. The apostles, going into the world whose passing figure they proclaimed, wept over its harmful deeds, sowing the seeds of eternal fruit; these men, rejoicing in the world's prosperity and founded in the world, embrace the blessings of the present life. The apostles, coming to judgment, will come with exultation, secure in eternal reward, carrying sheaves of men converted through their preaching; these men will come with great trembling, to render account of their works. But why do we linger longer? Why do we wander further? Why do we gather a few flowers from vast forests, when we cannot gather even the thousandth part? The distance between the apostles and the emperors is as great as that between saints and sinners; and since the apostles stand out above all the saints of the New Testament, they are believed to stand out far more above sinners. O flattery, why do you presume so much? O oil of bitterness, overflowing with a stench rather than the brightness of gentleness or nectar! You are bought from priests, you anoint the heads of certain of the unlearned by prelates; and what the Prophet shuddered to have applied to himself, saying, "Let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head," the company of bishops lays upon the heads of emperors; and what the gospel virgins said was to be bought from the sellers, this, alas, the faithful and especially the rulers of the people buy from the prelates. Therefore, that they confess that the same emperors were made wise and fit by virtue of the same Spirit, that is, by the Holy Spirit, is plainly a claim that all the faithful who are truly Christians have the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: "Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his." It is the gift of the Holy Spirit, poured in after baptism through the laying on of hands, and purity of life is distributed to each according to the measure of their merits, as the chosen vessel says: "To each one grace is given according to the measure." Although it is written in another place, "For God does not give the Spirit by measure," yet it is imparted to each of the faithful by measure. But when it says, "For God does not give the Spirit by measure," this is to be understood of the Son alone, who is of one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to whom the Spirit is not given by measure; for according to the word of Paul, "In him dwells bodily all the fullness of the Godhead." But that the Spirit is given by measure, and that to each one a portion is distributed as he wills, is understood without doubt to be said of each of the faithful. But although it is agreed that every one of the Catholics has the Holy Spirit, according to what we have mentioned above and illustrated with examples, yet we dare not say or affirm that any man of our age has received the Holy Spirit according to the measure of Apostolic grace.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: De eo quod dixerunt, Habet enim prophetia, Ecce virgo in utero accipiet, & pariet filium; hanc autem prophetiam in imaginem nos videntes, videlicet virginem in ulnis ferentem quem genuit, quomodo sustinebimus non adorare & osculari? Quis indisciplinatus mente resistere audebit? in tale osculum dignos enim nosipsos faciamus adorationis, ut non accedentes indigni Ozæ supplicium subeamus.
units.tr: On that which they said, For prophecy has it: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son. But seeing this prophecy in an image, namely a virgin carrying in her arms the one she bore, how shall we not bear to adore and kiss? Who, undisciplined in mind, will dare resist? Let us make ourselves worthy of such a kiss of adoration, so that we, approaching unworthily, do not undergo the punishment of Uzzah.

units.la: PROPHETIA, quæ virginem concepturam & filium parituram intonat, non jam in incertis & ambiguis est quærenda, sed in pectore retinenda, nec ejus archana mysteria sunt in picturis, sed in divinis literis earumque explanatoribus, Apostolis videlicet eorumque successoribus, investiganda, & fide potius quàm oculis intuenda. Non enim idem nobilissimus vates Esaias evangelii nobis potius quàm prophetiæ referens saporem, ait; Nisi pinxeritis & adoraveritis imagines, non permanebitis, sed ait, Si non credideritis, non permanebitis. Manifestum itaque est, eum qui in mandatis divinis fidei integritate vult permanere, & ad æternam remunerationem venire, instrumenta per quæ ad hæc veniat non in parietibus, non in tabulis, non in picturis, non in quibuslibet visibilibus rebus, sed in corde per fidem, in ore per confessionem, in opere per bonorum actuum exhibitionem habere debere, & credere virginem quæ salvatorem protulit mundi, non in mundanorum artificum operibus, sed in æterni & inenarrabilis artificis opere, id est, in cælestibus sedibus esse. Unde necesse est ut quisquis eam adorare desiderat, non in colorum fucis, non in materialibus opificiis, non in quibuslibet officinis, sed illò mentis aciem figat, quò eam cum Christo regnare constat. Nam dum illi dixerint, Hanc autem prophetiam in imaginem nos videntes, videlicet virginem in ulnis ferentem quem genuit, quomodo sustinebimus non adorare & osculari? quis indisciplinatus mente resistere audebit? & nos pene eadem verba sono non sensu, sequuti ingerimus; Hanc aurem picturam in tabula aut pariete cernentes, virginem videlicet depictam puerum in ulnis ferentem, quomodo præsumemus rem insensatam adorare, & opus cujuslibet artificis osculari? quis indisciplinatus tale facinus perpetrare audebit, ut adorationem soli creatori debitam creaturis impendat, & dum vult favere picturis, sacris renitatur scripturis? Esto, imago sanctæ dei genetricis adoranda est, unde scire possumus quæ sit ejus imago, aut quibus indiciis à cæteris imaginibus dirimatur? quippe cùm nulla in omnibus differentia præter artificum experientiam, & eorum quibus operentur opificia, materiarumque qualitatem inveniatur. Cum ergo depictam pulchram quandam fœminâ puerum in ulnis tenere cernimus, si superscriptio necdum facta sit, aut quondam facta casu quodâ demolita, quâ industria discernere valemus, utrum Sara sit Isaac tenês, aut Rebecca Jacob ferens, aut Bethsabee Salomonem jactans, aut Elisabet Johanne bajulans, aut quælibet mulier parvulum suum tenens? & ut ad gentiles fabulas veniamus, quæ plerumq; depictæ inveniantur, unde scire valemus, utrum Venus sit Æneam tenens, an Alcmena Herculem portans, an Andromacha Astyanactagerens? Nam si pro alia alia adoratur, dementia est; si tamen ea quæ adoranda penitus non est, adoratur, vesania est: quod utrumq; cavendum est. Pingitur etiam eadem beata virgo qualiter asellı gestamine vecta, puerum in ulnis ferens Joseph prævio in Ægyptum descenderit, qualiterve ex Ægypto ad terram Israhel redierit (in pluribus namque materiis hæc historia inditur, & non semper in basilicis, sed interdum in vasis escariis sive potatoriis, interdum in sericis indumentis, plerumque tamen in stragulis) rumquidnam hæc omnia adoranda sunt? Cùm ergo in quolibet horum imago sanctæ virginis puerum tenens pecualis animantis rergo suscepta adoratur, numquid non ipsius animantis cum ea imago adoratur? nullo enim pacto in adorando utriusque imaginis, virginis videlicet sive animantis, quædam poterit fieri dirémptio: præsertim cùm unius sint materiæ, unoque artificis ingenio conpaginatæ, aut utriusque adoratio est spernenda, aut utræque sunt adorandæ. Sed dicet fortasse spinosulus aliquis; Hæcadsertio adorandi animantis frustranda est: quoniam cùm quemlibet hominem cathedra sustceptum aut baculo innixum causa salutationis adoramus, non cum eo cathedram neque baculum adorare monstramur, sed homine salutato illa insalutata remanere creduntur. Cujus spinulæ hoc modo quassandæ sunt; Alia est definitio hominis, alia baculi sive cathedræ: quoniam quidem homo definitur ita, Homo est animal rationale, mortale, risibile, & cætera hujuscemodi: cathedra verò vel baculus non eodem modo definiuntur, sed ut res sensu vitaq; carentes, pro artificis experientia vel voluntate ad officia quibus necessaria sunt præparata, & cætera hujuscemodi: ubi liquido patet aliud esse rationalem hominem salutando adorare, aliud cathedram vel baculum, utpote res insensatas, insalutata relinquere. In definitione verò virgineæ sive pecualis animantis imaginii, cum utraq; sint sensu vitaq; carentes, ex una materia factæ, uno eodemq; artifice formatæ, ita sibi mutuo cohærentes, ut sine materiæ, in qua in subjecto sunt, discidio ab invicem nequeant separari, pene nulla est in definiendo distantia. In quibus cum tanta sit paritas, tanta societas, tanta materiæ unitas, aut utriusq; adoratio est suscipienda, aut utriusq; spernenda. Cum ergo altera ab altera dirimi sine discidio nequeat, & utraque, ne forte animantis imago adoretur, adorari non debeant, restat ut utraque adorationis honore careant, & ornamentorum solummodo in basilicis aut in quibuslibet locis teneant, & aspicientibus rerum gestarum memoriam præbeant: quoniam cum tot diverticulis tantos errores imaginum adoratio vergat, nulla eam stare intra sanctam ecclesiam perspicua ratio monstrat. Hortantur ergo illi se mutuo, ut digni efficiantur ad oscula sive adorationes rerum sensu carentium dicentes; In tale osculum dignos enim nosipsos faciamus adorationis, ut non accedentes indigni Oza supercum subeamus. Nos denique dignos nos faciamus ad adorandam divinam majestatem, immo ab omni efficiamur à quo est bene velle & perficere, & ut veri adoratores non secundum eorum vanitatem adoremus dominum in quadam imagine, sed in spiritu & veritate, dicente ipsa veritate; Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu & veritate. Quod verò se ideo ad oscula & adorationes imaginum dignos esse monent, ne forte Ozæ pœnam luant, videant ne illius præsumptionis causa, qua & ille archam domini absque suo adminiculo casuram putavit, & isti nihilominus divini cultus religionem absque imaginum adminiculo frustrandam putant, cujus exiriabilis pœnæ sententiam subeant: quippe cum nec illa nec rueret, cujus sulcimine indiguerit, nec ista ut firmius stet, illarum sulcimine indigeat: & sicut illa nullam deo indigentiam patiente absque aliquo sui casu Ozæ sustentaculo vacante inlapsa ferebatur, ita nimirum ista domino gubernante absque ullo naufragio imaginum opitulatione postposita immerata servatur. Quid ergo est archæ testamenti domini quæ à domino gubernabatur, ne casum pateretur, manum velle subponere, nisi catholicæ religioni quæ à domino utique regitur, ne inter hujus vitæ itinera tituber, imaginum adorationem velle admittere? aut cui adsimilari potest Oza, qui absque sacerdotum & conlevitarum consilio quadam præsumptibili cura novum archæ domini voluit sustentaculum præstare, nisi istis qui absq; sanctorum patrum doctrina & consacerdotum per diversas partes constitutorum consensu arrogantia quadam & superciliosa intentione novam Christianæ religioni imaginum adorationem nisuntur inserere? perdidit igitur vitam qui archam dei tuta sustentare affectavit, quia qui deum qui ubique totus est, ubique mirabilis, re aliqua indigere sit, quod adoretur credit, eumque in rebus visibilibus adorat, cavendum est ne tunc vitam perdat, cum ejus vitalibus monitis procaci mente resistit. Levites ergo isdem recte Oza dicitur qui robustus inter præsumptores quique, nisi audaci mente robustos se crederent, nequaquam synodos in quibus adorandarum imaginum nova constitutio censeretur, agitarent.
units.tr: Prophecy, which proclaims that a virgin will conceive and bear a son, is not to be sought in things uncertain and ambiguous, but kept in the heart. Its hidden mysteries are not in pictures but must be investigated in the divine letters and their expositors, namely the Apostles and their successors, and perceived by faith rather than by the eyes. For the most noble prophet Isaiah, giving us the taste of the gospel rather than of prophecy, does not say: Unless you paint and adore images, you will not remain; he says instead: If you do not believe, you will not remain. It is therefore plain that whoever wishes to remain in the divine commands in integrity of faith, and to come to eternal reward, must have the instruments by which he attains this not on walls, not on boards, not in pictures, not in any visible things, but in the heart through faith, in the mouth through confession, and in work through the display of good deeds. He must believe that the virgin who brought forth the Saviour of the world is not in the works of worldly craftsmen but in the work of the eternal and ineffable Artificer, that is, in the heavenly seats. Hence whoever desires to adore her must fix the gaze of his mind not on the colours of paint, not on material workmanship, not in any workshops, but there where she is known to reign with Christ. For when they have said, But seeing this prophecy in an image, namely a virgin carrying in her arms the one she bore, how shall we not bear to adore and kiss? Who, undisciplined in mind, will dare resist?, we, following almost the same words in sound but not in sense, press on: Seeing this picture on a board or wall, namely a virgin painted carrying a boy in her arms, how shall we presume to adore an insensate thing and kiss the work of any craftsman? Who, undisciplined, will dare to commit such a deed, to bestow on creatures the adoration owed to the sole Creator, and, while wishing to favour pictures, to struggle against the holy Scriptures? Grant that the image of the holy Mother of God is to be adored: how can we know what her image is, or by what signs it is distinguished from other images? For no difference is found among them all except the skill of the artists, the objects on which they work, and the quality of the materials. So when we see a painted, beautiful woman holding a boy in her arms, and no inscription has yet been made, or one was made once but has been destroyed by some chance, by what diligence can we tell whether it is Sarah holding Isaac, or Rebekah carrying Jacob, or Bathsheba dandling Solomon, or Elisabeth bearing John, or any woman holding her little child? And to come to the pagan fables, which are often found painted: how can we know whether it is Venus holding Aeneas, or Alcmena carrying Hercules, or Andromache bearing Astyanax? For if one is adored in place of another, it is madness; if that which ought not to be adored at all is adored, it is frenzy. Both must be avoided. The same blessed virgin is also painted, carried on the back of an ass, bearing the boy in her arms, as she went down into Egypt with Joseph going before, and as she returned from Egypt to the land of Israel. For this story is put on many materials, and not always in churches, but sometimes on food or drinking vessels, sometimes on silk garments, and most often on coverlets. Are all these things then to be adored? When, therefore, in any of these an image of the holy virgin holding the boy is adored, taken on the back of a beast of burden, is not the image of that animal also adored along with her? For in adoring either image, of the virgin or of the animal, no division of one from the other can possibly be made, especially since they are of one material and put together by one artist's ingenuity. Either the adoration of both is to be spurned, or both are to be adored. But perhaps some prickly fellow will say: This assertion about adoring the beast is void, since when we adore any man seated in a chair or leaning on a staff for the sake of greeting, we are not shown to adore the chair or staff along with him; the man is greeted, and the chair and staff are believed to remain unsaluted. The little thorn is to be shaken off in this way. The definition of a man is different from that of a staff or chair. For man is defined thus: Man is a rational, mortal, laughing animal, and so on; but a chair or staff is not defined in the same way, but as a thing lacking sense and life, prepared for the uses for which it is needed according to the craftsman's skill or will, and so on. Here it is clearly plain that to adore a rational man by greeting him is one thing, while to leave a chair or staff, as an insensate thing, unsaluted is another. In the definition, however, of the image of the virgin or of the beast of burden, since both are lacking sense and life, made of one material, formed by one artificer, and so cohering with each other that they cannot be separated without dividing the material in which they subsist, there is almost no distance in definition. Since there is such equality, such fellowship, and such unity of material between them, either the adoration of both must be accepted or both must be spurned. Therefore, since the one cannot be divided from the other without separation, and since both ought not to be adored, lest perhaps the image of the beast be adored, it remains that both should lack the honour of adoration and should hold a place only as ornaments in churches or in any other places, presenting to those who look upon them the memory of things done. For since the adoration of images, with so many byways, tends toward such great errors, no clear reason shows that it can stand within the holy Church. Those men therefore urge one another to make themselves worthy of kisses or adorations of things lacking sense, saying: Let us make ourselves worthy of such a kiss of adoration, so that we, approaching unworthily, do not undergo the punishment of Uzzah. Let us rather make ourselves worthy to adore the divine majesty; nay, let us be made worthy by him from whom comes both the good will and its fulfilment, so that as true worshippers we may adore the Lord not in some image, according to their vanity, but in spirit and truth, the truth itself saying: The true worshippers will adore the Father in spirit and truth. As for their warning that they must make themselves worthy of kisses and adorations of images, lest they pay the penalty of Uzzah, let them see to it that they do not share the presumption of that man, who thought the ark of the Lord would fall without his support. These men, too, think that the religion of divine worship will be frustrated without the support of images, and they undergo the sentence of an inescapable penalty. For neither did that ark, which needed no prop, fall, nor does this one need the prop of those images in order to stand more firmly. Just as that ark was carried on without any fall, the Lord needing no help, and lacking Uzzah's support, so surely this one, with the Lord governing it, is preserved unharmed, without any shipwreck, and with images set aside. What, then, is it to wish to put a hand under the ark of the testament of the Lord, which the Lord governed lest it suffer a fall, except to wish to admit the adoration of images into the Catholic religion, which is certainly ruled by the Lord, lest I stumble along the ways of this life?
