Or to whom can Uzzah be likened, who, without the counsel of the priests and Levites, with a certain presumptuous care, wished to furnish a new support for the ark of the Lord, except to those who, without the teaching of the holy Fathers and with the consent of their fellow priests placed in various parts, strive with a certain arrogance and haughty intention to insert a new adoration of images into the Christian religion? He, therefore, who presumed to support the ark of God safely lost his life. For whoever believes that God, who is wholly everywhere and wondrous everywhere, needs anything to be adored, and adores him in visible things, must beware lest he lose his life when with a bold mind he resists his life-giving admonitions. Uzzah is therefore rightly called a Levite by these men, who, strong among presumers, would by no means have stirred up synods in which a new constitution of adorable images was to be judged, unless they believed themselves strong in a bold mind.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: De eo quod nec sibiipsis parcunt, cum parentibus suis injuriam inserunt dicentes, Pro vero tritico zizania ecclesiasticis agris seminaverunt, vinum miscuerunt aquæ, & proximi potaverunt subversionem turbulentam, & lupi Arabici existentes pellem ovium subsannaverunt indueri, & veritatem prætereuntes mendacium amplexi sunt, sed ova aspidum jactaverunt, & tela aranei secundum prophetam texuerunt, & qui sperat ova eorum comedere, confringens caudam inveniet, & in eo basiliscum venenum & slatum mortiferum repletum.
units.tr: Concerning how they do not spare themselves, while they do injury to their parents, saying: "For true wheat they have sown tares in the fields of the Church, mixed wine with water, and made their neighbours drink a turbulent ruin; and being Arabian wolves, they have mocked at putting on sheep's skins, and, passing over the truth, have embraced a lie. But they have thrown the eggs of asps and woven spiders' webs, as the prophet says; and whoever hopes to eat their eggs, by breaking the shell will find a tail, and in it a basilisk's poison and a deadly breath filled up."

units.la: INTEMPERATA eorum vecordia sicut in cæteris ita & in hoc quoq; deliramento reprehenderunt eo quod majores suos pro tritico zizania sevisse ecclesiasticis agris, vinumque aquæ miscuisse & proximos potasse turbulento potu dixerunt, præsertim cum in hoc negocio pene in omnibus in quibus illi deliquisse creduntur, isti non solum ea non emendasse, verumetiam amplius deliquisse perhibentur: denique secundum poetam qui air, Pro molli viola, pro purpurco narcisso, Carduus & spinis surgat paliurus acutis,
units.tr: Their unbridled folly has rebuked in this respect, as in other things, the same kind of nonsense: they have said that their predecessors sowed tares in the fields of the Church instead of wheat, mixed wine with water, and made their neighbours drink a turbulent draught. This is said especially since, in this matter, in nearly all the points in which those men are believed to have erred, these men are reported not only to have failed to amend them but to have erred even more. Finally, the poet says, "For the soft violet, for the purple narcissus, let thistles and sharp-thorned paliurus rise," and so on.

units.la: istorum majoribus pro tritico surtexerunt zizania, istis verò pro tritico zizaniis nec dum evulsis paliurus surrexit: quia videlicet propheticæ & evangelicæ sive apostolicæ prædicationis neglecto tritico, qua & loca divinis cultibus mancipata exornati celentur, & solius dei cultus & adoratio commendatur, aut in ornamentorum à basilicis abolitione, aut in eorundem ornamentorum adoratione, zizaniorum amentiu & paliuri spinosi perniciosum dogma percepisse monstrantur: & qui debuerant frumento, divini verbi mentes fidelium illius satietatis q sine fastidio est, plenitudine reficere, illo dogmate eas, q ingenti fastidio & amentia nutrit & errorum aculeos ingerit, nituntur insicere. Vino etiã aquã majores suos insicuisse turbulentumq; potū proximis profati sunt propinasse: quib. non absq; ratione obici potest, q majores eores eorum vinum sacri eloquii quo uti debuerant, aquæ permixtione insapidum effecerunt, cum ornamenta à basilicis abolenda sanxerunt: isti vero ejusdem vini potum à prodecessoribus aqua vitiatum veneno acuerunt, cum se imagines adoraturos eisque servitium exhibituros professi, earumque adorationem spernentes anathematibus condemnare conati sunt. Deinde turbulentum potum utrique proximis propinare non erubescunt, cum prædicationem suam, quam sacris eloquiis & bonorum operum exemplis exornare debuerant, vanis & extraordinariis constitutionibus vitiare non differunt, eamque & præsentibus vitâ vel actu monstrare & memoriæ posteritatis scriptis mandare non metuunt. Quòd vero eos sub pellibus ovium lupos cælare, & spreta veritate mendacium amplecti asseverant, idipsum in se ipsis fieri conspicient, si diligenter advertant. Nam dum illi magnam se sanctitatem habere fingentes, cujus quasi zelo accensi imagines ab ecclesiis utpote ne adorentur quæ non ad adorandum ab antiquis positæ fuerant abdicaverunt, & isti eas quasi nimiæ sanctitatis amore accensi adorandas statuunt, nec sibi catholicæ fidei charismata sufficere putant, nisi eis servitium adorationis exhibeant, cum tamen utrique vanæ laudis appetitu id agant, quid aliud faciunt nisi sub pellibus ovium lupos tegunt? quia nimirum dum foris aut zelum aut studium sanctitatis simulant, introrsus lupinam rabiem qua cæteris eminere ambiunt, eosque anathematum dentibus rodunt habere se monstrant: veritatem itaque prætereuntes mendacium utrique amplectuntur, quia dum superbe & arroganter nova quæque constituere anhelant, nec humilitate duce antiquorum patrum exempla sequuntur, ab ea veritate quæ fallere fallique nescit abscedunt, illique mendacio adhærent de quo scriptum est; Ab initio mendax fuit & in veritate non stetit. Quid ergo est veritatem prætere ire, nisi Christi monitis qui auctor humilitatis est per jactantiam contraire? quid est mendacium sequi, nisi ejus qui auctor superbiæ est exempla in novis & in inlicitis constitutionibus inliciendo, & antiquis ac saluti ferris traditionibus obnitendo sectari? Quod quidem utrique tunc faciunt, cum superbiæ vento inflati aut frangendarum aut adorandarum imaginum errorem arripiunt. Porro quod majores suos ova aspidum protulisse, & telam aranearum texuisse asserunt, non mediocres sibi in hac parte contumelias interunt: quippe cum ideo eorum ova sint, quoniam aut ab illis sunt per carnis materiam propagati, aut studiis quibuslibet inbuti, aut certe per manuum inpositionem in ecclesiasticis ordinibus consecrati: & ideo eorum tela sunt, quia ab illis aut ex traduce corporaliter, aut ex doctrina spiritaliter sunt ordinati. Ova ergo aspidum & telam aranearum se non immerito nuncupant, quia & aures suas obdurant, ne scripturarum verba interiore aure audiant, quæ unius & solius dei cultum & adorationem instituunt, & ad capiendas sive inliciendas animas novarum & inutilium constitutionum telam prædicatione ordiri, & opere texere non metuunt, & secundum suam professionem, qui eadem ova esse desiderat, basilisci um introrsus inveniet, quia videlicet quicumque eorum prædicatione uti appetit, mortiferæ ineis traditionis flatum reperit: & dum cupit famem verbi prædicatione solaturus quoddam reperire remedium, vitam perditurus internæ salutis reperit dispendium. Ideo igitur eis in nostra disputatione parcere parvipendimus, quia eos sibimet in sua disputatione pepercisse minime repperimus, sed accepta ab illis reprehendendi materia suis eos spiculis jaculamur. Quæ omnia non sine dilectione facimus, sed hæc agimus, quia eorum ab errore conversionem inimus, si forte aliquando erroris sui portenta sequi contemnaur, & viam quæ ducit ad vitam perpetum tenendam appetant.
units.tr: For their predecessors sowed tares instead of wheat; but these men, with the tares not yet pulled up, have let the paliurus rise instead of wheat. For, having neglected the wheat of prophetic and evangelical or apostolic preaching, by which places devoted to divine worship are adorned and the worship and adoration of God alone is commended, they are shown to have taken up the pernicious doctrine of the tares and the thorny paliurus, either in the removal of ornaments from the churches or in the adoration of those same ornaments. And those who ought to have refreshed the minds of the faithful with wheat, that is with the fullness of the divine word which satisfies without weariness, now strive to sow into them that doctrine which nourishes them with great weariness and folly and thrusts into them the sting of errors. They have also said that their predecessors poured wine mixed with water and gave their neighbours a turbulent drink; it can rightly be objected to them that their predecessors made the wine of holy speech, which they ought to have used, flavourless by mixing it with water, when they decreed that ornaments were to be removed from the churches; but these men have embittered with poison the draught of that same wine, spoiled by the water of their predecessors, when, professing that they would adore images and offer them service, they tried to condemn with anathemas those who scorned their adoration. Then they are not ashamed to pour a turbulent draught on both sides to their neighbours, since they do not hesitate to spoil their preaching, which they ought to have adorned with holy writings and examples of good works, with vain and extraordinary constitutions, and they do not fear to display it to those present by life and deed and to commit it to writing for the memory of posterity. As for their assertion that those men hid wolves under sheep's skins and embraced a lie, having scorned the truth, they will see this happening in themselves if they consider carefully. For while those men, pretending to have great holiness, and as if kindled by zeal for it, removed from the churches the images which had not been set up by the ancients to be adored, and these men, as if kindled by excessive love of holiness, set them up to be adored, and do not think the gifts of the Catholic faith suffice unless they offer them the service of adoration, although both sides do this from a desire for vain praise, what else do they do but cover wolves with sheep's skins? For, while outwardly they feign either zeal or devotion to holiness, they show that inwardly they have the wolfish rage by which they strive to excel the rest and gnaw at them with the teeth of anathemas. Therefore, passing over the truth, both sides embrace a lie, because, while they proudly and arrogantly long to establish every novelty and do not follow the examples of the ancient Fathers with humility as their guide, they turn away from that truth which neither deceives nor can be deceived, and cling to that lie of which it is written: "He was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth." What, then, is it to pass over the truth, except to oppose by arrogance the admonitions of Christ, who is the author of humility? What is it to follow a lie, except to pursue, by introducing novel and unlawful constitutions, the example of him who is the author of pride, and to oppose the ancient traditions, which are fit for salvation? Both sides do this indeed when, puffed up by the wind of pride, they take up the error of either breaking or adoring images. Moreover, in saying that their predecessors brought forth the eggs of asps and wove a spider's web, they do not heap upon themselves small insults in this respect: for these are their eggs, since they were either propagated from those men by the matter of the flesh, or imbued with some studies, or certainly consecrated in the ecclesiastical orders by the laying on of hands; and these are their webs, since they were ordained by those men either bodily, by descent, or spiritually, by teaching. Therefore they do not undeservedly call themselves eggs of asps and a spider's web, because they harden their ears so that they do not hear with the inner ear the words of the Scriptures, which establish the worship and adoration of the one and only God; and they do not fear to weave, in preaching and in deed, the web of new and useless constitutions to catch or entice souls; and according to their own profession, whoever wishes to eat those eggs will find within them a basilisk; that is, whoever desires to be fed by their preaching will find in them the deadly breath of tradition. And while he desires to find some remedy for the hunger of the word through their preaching, he will find, to his loss, the ruin of inner salvation and of life. Therefore we have thought it worthless to spare them in our discussion, because we have found that they did not spare themselves in their own discussion, but, having taken from them the matter for reproach, we hurl our darts at them with their own missiles. We do all this not without love, but we do it because we aim at their conversion from error, if perhaps they may at some time disdain to follow the monstrosities of their error and may desire to hold the way that leads to eternal life.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: Inutilis & inerudita interpretatio eorum qui dum adorare & osculari unum esse adfirmare vellent, dixerunt, Quique sanctorum principium nostræ doctrinæ & eorum successores egregium patrum nostrorum, & has adorari videlicet osculari, idipsum enim utrumque, communem vero Græcæ antiquæ loquutionis osculari & amplecti designatur, & voluntatis extensione aliqua significat amoris, sicuti fero & offero, firmo & confirmo, participo & adoro quod demonstrat osculum & extensionis amicitiæ. quod enim quis diligit & adorat, & quod adorat omnino & diligit.
units.tr: The useless and unlearned interpretation of those who, wishing to maintain that to adore and to kiss are one and the same, said, that the leader of the saints of our doctrine and their successors, the outstanding fathers of ours, and these are to be adored, that is, kissed. For both words mean the same thing, and the common usage of ancient Greek denotes kissing and embracing. By an extension of the will, it signifies some kind of love, just as fero and offero, firmo and confirmo, participo and adoro show a kiss and an extension of friendship. For whoever loves and adores, and whoever adores, certainly also loves.

units.la: IN differentia osculi & adorationis, quæ duo illi unum esse putant, non est plurimum laborandum: quoniam hæc duo nomina tanto inter se distant, quanto & hæ res quarum hæc nomina sunt inter se discrepant: & necessario magnam habent ab alterutro discretionem, cum & ipsæ res plerumque magnam inter se habeant diremptionem: præsertim cum interdum & quæ adoratur non osculetur, & quod osculatur non adoretur. Adoratur enim deus, sed non osculatur: venerantur sancti qui è sæculo cum triumphis meritorum migraverunt, sed nec adorari debent cultu divino, nec osculari possunt. Osculantur è contrario conjuges, liberi, necnon & servi, nec tamen adorantur. Manifestum namque est osculum & adorationem duarum rerum nomina esse. Quomodo ergo erit nominum tanta in sensu unitas, cum rerum in intellectu sit tanta diversitas? aut cur non possint vocabula differri in sensu, cum possint vocabulorum origines differri in actu? non enim res sunt conditæ propter nomina, sed nomina propter res, nec credendum est ut res aptentur nominibus, sed nomina potius aptentur rebus: quoniam & protoplasto animantia adducta à domino fuisse ut videret quid vocaret ea, leguntur. rebus enim à deo conditis idem humani generis pater nomina dedit, non nominibus à se conditis res quibus ipsa nomina inderet ad se adductas perspexit. Plato denique philosophus nomina naturalia esse constituit: & hoc hinc probare contendit, quod quaedam supellex & quodammodo instrumentum sint invicem sensa prodendi, naturalium vero supellectilis sunt naturales, ut oculi instrumenta quidem sunt videndi, qui visus res naturalis est; quare oculos quoque naturales esse necesse est: ita etiam oratio sum naturalium supellex est atque instrumentum, id est, sententiarum, quare ipsa quoque est naturalis. Aristoteles autem dicit non secundum naturam esse orationem, sed secundum placitum, quoniam nec esse orationem supellectilem naturalem. Quod enim dicit non esse instrumentum, non per hoc instrumentum sensa proferri, sed tantum rem esse, orationem secundum positionem, per quam proprias sententias demonstremus. Idem quoque philosophus, cui in hac parte fides potissimum adhibenda est, in libro Perihermeniarum; Nomen dicit esse vocem significativam secundum placitum sine tempore, id est, nomen esse vocem. Sed vocum aliae sunt quae significant, aliae quae nihil significant; nomen autem significat id cujus nomen est: nomen igitur est vox significativa. Vocum significativarum aliae sunt naturaliter, aliae non naturaliter. Naturaliter est vox significativa, ut ea quae dolores aut gaudia, ut sunt interjectiones: non naturaliter vero significativae voces sunt, quas secundum positionem esse dicimus. Secundum positionem vero sunt, quas ipsi sibi homines posuerunt, sicut in superiore exemplo quod de Genesi sumpsimus, monstratum est: quae singula sequi longissimum est. Osculum interea & adorationem, sive osculari & adorare, duas res esse plurimum intelligit inter se distantes manifestum est. Secundum secularium literarum magistros tria sunt quibus omnis conloquutio disputatioque perficitur, res, intellectus, voces. Res sunt quas animi ratione percipimus intellectuque discernimus, ut est adorare, vel osculari, vel aliquid hujusmodi. Intellectus vero est quidam animi vigor quo res ipsas addiscimus, & quid inter se distent discernimus. Voces quibus id quod intellectu capimus significamus, ut pro eo quod est adorare dicimus adoratio, pro eo quod est osculari dicimus osculum. Est aliud quiddam quod significat voces, haec sunt literae. harum enim scriptio, vocum significatio est. Cum igitur haec sunt quatuor, res, intellectus, vox, litera, rem concipimus, intellectum vero voces designant, ipsas vero voces literae significant. unde & praefatus Aristoteles in perihermeniis finis ait; Sunt ergo ea quae sunt in voce earum quae sunt in anima passionum nota; & quae scribuntur, eorum quae sunt in voce. & quemadmodum nec literae omnibus eadem, sic nec eadem voces. quarum autem ha primum nota, eadem omnibus passiones animae sunt: & quarum hae similitudines, res etiam eadem, intellectus videlicet, juxta eruditissimi viri Boetii explanationem, animi quandam passionem designant: quoniam, ut idem Boetius ait, nisi quandam similitudinem rei quam quis intelligit, in anima ratione patiatur, nullus est intellectus. Cum enim video orbem vel quadratum, figuram ejus mente concipio & ejus mihi similitudo in anima ratione formatur, patiturque anima rei intellecta similitudinem. Unde fit ut intellectus & similitudo fit rei & animae passio. Harum autem rursus quatuor, duae sunt naturales, duae secundum hominum positionem. Voces namque & literae secundum positionem sunt: intellectus autem & res naturaliter. hoc illo approbatur, quod apud diversas gentes diversis vocibus utitur & literis, idcirco quoniam ipsi voces quibus uterentur, & literas quibus scriberent, conposuerunt: intellectus autem & res nullus posuit, sed naturaliter sunt. Neque enim quod apud Romanos equus est, apud barbaros cervus, sed apud diversas gentes eadem rerum natura est. Propterea non quod nos intelligimus esse equum, canem barbari putant, sed eadem apud diversissimas gentes substantiarum intellectuumque ratio est constituta. Quare duae harum sunt secundum hominum positionem, id est, voces & literae, duae secundum naturam, res & intellectus, quibus documentis monstratur non ideo adorationem & osculum unum esse, quamvis apud Graecos quandam haec duo nomina habeant consonantiam. Plerumque ergo duo vel plura nomina secundum synonyma unam significationem habent, plerumque etiam nomen secundum homonyma duas vel plures res significat, nec tamen ideo rerum ordo confunditur, aut quodammodo mutilatur, si eis ab hominibus secundum placitum diversissimis nomina dantur. Adjungunt interea his duabus rebus tertiam rem, ut adorare, osculari & amplecti, omnia sint, sed licet illa duo ab alterutro diriminuntur, ita nimirum hoc tertium ab illis duobus diriminatur: quia videlicet quaedam, ut superius memoravimus, adorantur, nec continuo osculantur, quaedam osculantur nec continuo adorantur, pleraque amplectuntur quae nec adorantur, nec osculantur. Amplectitur quilibet quodam eventu lignum aut lapidem aut quamlibet rem, cui osculum ferre super fluum est, nec tamen eam adorat. Osculatur etiam aliquem priorum ad quem reverentia cohibente vix accedere praesumit, nec tamen cum amplectitur. quanto enim haec tria inter se muruo in sensu diuturnum cernuntur, tanto nimirum a ratione eadem exempla quae ab illis ad ea unum esse probanda posita sunt, fiat nosciuntur: quippe cum & illa inter se plurima habeant distantiam, & ista cum ratione nullam habeant consonantiam. Dicunt enim; Quicunque sanctorum principum nostra doctrina, & eorum successores ceregerunt patrum nostrorum & has adorari videlicet osculari, idipsum enim utrumque: communem vero Graeca antiqua loquuntur osculari & amplecti defiguat, & voluntatis extensione aliqua significat amoris, sicut: fero & offero, firmo & confirmo, participo & adoro quod demonstrat osculum & extensionis amicitia. O sensus confundens potius lentem quam ordinans, frangens potius verba quam proferens! O acumen omni piistillo retundens; O machaera plumbea prius aciem retundens quam rem incidat cui incidendae adhibetur! O enim sis mallei potius referens tunionem quam gladii sectionem, frangens potius materias, quam secans! O argumentatio nil adfirmare praeter suos auctores dementes esse valens, nil propositae rei firmitatis exhibens, sed ollummodo latores vecordes esse pandens! Ab eo quod est fero & offero adorare, osculari & amplecti unum esse adstruere nituntur, & praepositionum vires ignorans, quae plerumque alias partes corrumpunt, plerumque ad alia. ab aliis partibus corrumpuntur, plerumq; & corrumpunt & corrumpuntur, interdū nec corrumpunt nec corrūpuntur,eisq; significationes aliquando augent,aliquando minuunt, aliquando permutant, dum vana quædam adstruēda appetit,vanis ea quibusdā assertionibus adprobare cōtendit. Quis ergo ignoret offero,adfero,infero,cōfero,aufero,defero,refero,suffero,differo,profero,praefero,perfero, & cætera, si qua sunt his similia, quanquā ab eo verbo quod est fero veniāt, adhibitis & quadam ex parte corruptis præpositionibus diversissimis effectibus inter se in sensu distare? Aut quis nesciat quod participo & adoro pene nullam sensus concordantiam habeant? firmo namq; & confirmo quanquam in sensu sint communia, ab ea tamen re, cui ab illis adhibentur, prorsus videntur esse extranea. De quibus omnibus si singillatim à nobis disputetur, ita ut in scholis Grammaticorum discitur, hæc soluminodo res vix unius libri textu tenebitur. Sed necillud prætereundum est, quod vanissimam argumentationem suam quadam frivola & inani conclusione, quasi quodam conversibili syllogismo, conficere nisi sint dicentes, Quod enim diligit quis & adorat, & quod adorat omnino & diligit, nescientes ideo hæc duo vicissim minime posse circumverti, quod inæquahia inter se sint, latiusque diligere quàm adorare possit progredi. diligit enim quis uxorem sive prolem, nec tamen adorat eam: diligit servum, ancillam, equum, canem, accipitrem & cætera hujusmodi, nec tamen adorat ea. Sicut ergo verum est cum dicit, Quod adorat quis & diligit, non ita verum esse poterit cum dicit, Quod diligit quis & adorat. non enim hæc circumversio rationabiliter stare potest: quoniam & unum illorum latius, ut diximus, protenditur, & nulla est in his ranta proprietas ut mutuo circumverti credantur. Sicut ergo dici potest converso ordine, Quod hinnibile est equus est, & quod equus est hinnibile est, non sic recte dici potest, Quod diligit quis & adorat, & Quod adorat & diligit: quoniam & in eisdem topicis, ex quibus hæc argumenta procedu.it,in eadem argumentatione quæ à consequentibus nominatur, in qua propositam rem aliquid inevitabiliter consequitur,ut id quod de hinnibili & equo dixinus,pleraq; circumverti possunt, nonnulla vero circumverti nequaquam possunt. Circumverti namq; possunt hæc, ut si quis dicat, Si risibile est, consequens inevitabiliter est ut homo sit, & si homo est necessario risibile est, & cetera his similia. Circumverti autem nequaquam possunt hæc,ut si quis dicat, Si dies est lucet,consequens quippe est, ut si dies est luceat: si satiatus est, consequens est ut comedisse credatur: si ebrius, necessa-rio potasse eum constat: si doctus est,consequens est ut didicisse dicatur: si adorat, consequens est, ut id quod adorat diligat. non enim dici poterit converso ordine, si lucet necessario dies est; si comedit, consequens est ut satiatus sit; cum plura luceant,necramen dies sit,& plerumque comestio, nec dum ad satietatem perveniat: necillud, si bibit ebrius est, si didicit doctus est, si diligit adorat: cum interdum, nec potatio ad ebrietatem, nec disciplina ad magisterium, nec dilectio ad adorationem pertingat. Ponantur ergo singula secundum dialecticorum experientiam, ut facilius adpareat quantum inter se hæc duo distent, vel qualiter hæc circumversio stare non possit. Sunt enim quatuor propositiones inter se quodammodo affectæ, quas philosophi in quadrata formula spectandas scribere consueverunt,ita videlicet ut primæ duæ sint, Omne quod diligit quis adorat,& Nihil quod diligit quis adorat, cæteræ duæ, Quiddam quod diligit quis adorat, Quiddam quod diligit quis non adorat. & primæ duæ dicantur adfirmatio universalis & negatio universalis, cæteræ adfirmatio particularis & negatio particularis: duæ superiores omnino sibi contrariæ sunt, cæteræ verò duæ inferiores subcontrariæ sibi mutuo sunt, & adfirmatio universalis sive particularis subalternæ, & negatio universalis & particularis subalternæ nihilominus dicantur. Ducantur deinde sensus indagationes quasi quædam lineæ angulares duæ, una ab hac adfirmatione universali,Omne quod diligit quis adorat, ad hanc negationé particularem, Quiddam quod diligit quis non adorat: altera ab hac particulari adfirmatione, Quiddam quod diligit quis adorat,ad hanc universalem negationem, Nihil quod diligit quis adorat, & sint inter se contrariæ vel oppositæ: & his ita inter se puguantibus cum utrēque, id est, adfirmatio universalis & negatio particularis, sive adfirmatio particularis & negatio universalis verae esse non possint, una erit falsa, altera vera: sicque vera petinet falsam, & si illa fuerit vera, alia mox à veritate discedet, dicente Apuleio Philosopho Platonico Madaurēsi, qui de hujusmodi syllogistica industria in libro, qui inscribitur, De perihermeneis Apulei, subtilissime disputavit. Universalis, inquit, utravis particularem suam comprobata unq; confirmat, revicta non utiq; infirmat: particularis autem versa vice universalem suam revicta utiq; infirmat, probata utiq; confirmat. Sunt ergo in hac argumentatione duæ superiores universales, id est, Omne quod diligit quis adorat, &, Nihil quod diligit quis adorat, falsæ: quoniam, ut superius dictum est, multa diligit quis quæ non adorat, & alia quæ de his quæ diligit quis adorat: & sunt duæ inferiores particulares, id est, Quiddam quod diligit quis adorat,&, Quiddam quod diligit quis non adorat,utræque verae: quoniam diligit quis Deum juxta illud; Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & adorat eum: ex cujus sanctissima dilectione omnium virtutum nutrimenta procedunt. Diligit quis proximum & salutationis officio adorat eum, & in eo adprobatur vera esse propositio, Quiddam quod diligit quis adorat: adprobatur etiam & hæc vera esse, Quiddam quod diligit quis non adorat, juxta exempla conj.gis,prolis,equi,canis,accipitris, & cætera quæ superius prolata sunt, quæ singula diliguntur, necramen adorantur. Universales & inferiores particulares alternatim positæ opponuntur sibi. Nam si falsa est hæc adfirmatio universalis, Omne quod diligit quis adorat, vera est hæc negatio particularis, Quiddam quod diligit quis non adorat: & si hæc particularis negatio falsa est, adfirmatio universalis vera est. & rursus si hæc negatio universalis, Nihil quod diligit quis adorat, falsa est, hæc adfirmatio particularis, Quiddam quod diligit quis adorat, vera est: & si ista vera non est, neque illa falsa est. Sunt autem duæ inferiores, omnino vera: duæ igitur superiores penitus falsæ esse credendæ sunt. De conversione deniq; talium propositionum,de quibus & nos supe-
units.tr: On the difference between kissing and adoration, which these men think are one and the same, we need not labour much. These two words differ from each other as much as the things they name differ from each other, and they must be quite distinct from one another, since the things themselves are for the most part widely separated. This is especially so because what is adored is sometimes not kissed, and what is kissed is sometimes not adored. God is adored but not kissed. The saints who have departed this age with the triumph of their merits are venerated, but they ought not to be adored with divine worship, nor can they be kissed. On the other hand, spouses, children and even servants are kissed, yet they are not adored. It is plain, then, that kissing and adoration are the names of two different things. How, then, can there be such unity in the meaning of the names when there is such diversity in the things understood? Or why should the words not differ in meaning, when the origins of the words can differ in practice? For things were not made for the sake of names, but names for the sake of things. Nor should we believe that things were fitted to names; rather, names were fitted to things. For we read that the living creatures were brought by the Lord to the first man so that he might see what he would call them. The father of the human race gave names to things created by God; he did not make things to fit names of his own devising. Plato the philosopher held that names are natural, and he tried to prove this from the fact that speech is a kind of tool or instrument for expressing our thoughts, and that natural tools are themselves natural. Thus the eye is an instrument of seeing, and sight is a natural thing; therefore the eyes too must be natural. In the same way speech is the tool and instrument of our natural thoughts, that is, of our opinions, and therefore speech too is natural. Aristotle, however, says that speech is not by nature but by convention, since speech is not a natural tool. For when he says that speech is not an instrument, he does not mean that thoughts are not expressed through it, but only that speech is a thing of convention, a matter of agreement, by which we make our own opinions known. The same philosopher, on whom we should rely above all in this matter, says in his book On Interpretation that a noun is a significant sound by convention, without reference to time; that is, a noun is a word. But some sounds signify and others signify nothing; a noun signifies that of which it is the name; therefore a noun is a significant sound. Of significant sounds, some are significant by nature and others not by nature. A sound is naturally significant, as are those that express pain or joy, such as interjections. Sounds that are significant not by nature we call significant by convention. Those are significant by convention which men themselves have established, as was shown in the example we took above from Genesis; to follow each of these would be very long. Now it is plain that kissing and adoration, or to kiss and to adore, are two things that are very far apart. According to the masters of secular letters, there are three things by which all discourse and disputation is carried on: things, understanding, and words. Things are what we perceive by the reason of the mind and distinguish by the intellect, such as adoring, or kissing, or something of this kind. Understanding is a certain vigour of the mind by which we learn the things themselves and distinguish how they differ from one another. Words are what we use to signify what we grasp by the understanding: for the thing which is to adore we call adoration, and for the thing which is to kiss we call kiss. There is also something else that signifies words, and these are letters; for the writing of letters is the signification of words. Since there are, then, these four things, thing, understanding, word, letter, we conceive the thing, while words designate the understanding, and letters signify the words themselves. Hence the aforesaid Aristotle also says at the end of On Interpretation: "Therefore the things that are in the voice are signs of the affections that are in the soul, and the things that are written are signs of the things that are in the voice. And just as letters are not the same for all, so neither are the voices the same. But the affections of the soul, of which these are primarily signs, are the same for all, and so are the things of which those affections are likenesses." According to the explanation of the very learned Boethius, understanding designates a certain affection of the mind, because, as Boethius also says, unless the mind is affected by reason with some likeness of the thing that someone understands, there is no understanding. For when I see a sphere or a square, I conceive its shape in my mind, and a likeness of it is formed in my soul by reason, and the soul is affected by the likeness of the thing understood. Hence understanding and the likeness are the affection of the soul and of the thing. Of these four, two are natural and two are by human convention. Voices and letters are by convention, but understanding and things are natural. This is shown by the fact that different nations use different voices and letters, because they themselves devised the voices they would use and the letters they would write with; but no one devised understanding and things, which are natural. For what is a horse among the Romans is not a stag among the barbarians; rather, among all the different nations the nature of things is the same. So the barbarians do not call a dog what we understand to be a horse; the reasoning about substances and understandings is established in the same way among the most diverse nations. Therefore two of these four are by human convention, namely voices and letters, and two are by nature, namely things and understanding. By these proofs it is shown that adoration and kissing are not one, even though among the Greeks these two words have some similarity of sound. Often two or more words which are synonyms have one meaning, and often too a single word which is ambiguous signifies two or more things; yet the order of things is not confused or in some way mutilated because the men who gave them names by convention gave them very different names. Moreover, these men add a third thing to these two, namely to adore, to kiss, and to embrace, and all are different things; yet, although those two are distinct from each other, this third is distinct from both of them. For, as we mentioned above, some things are adored but not immediately kissed, some are kissed but not immediately adored, and many are embraced which are neither adored nor kissed. Someone may embrace a piece of wood or a stone, or any object by chance, and it would be absurd to offer it a kiss, yet he does not adore it. Likewise a man may kiss one of the great persons whom, restrained by reverence, he scarcely dares to approach, yet he does not adore him when he kisses him. So the more widely these three are seen to be separated from one another in meaning, the more clearly the examples that they have set forth to prove that these are one are shown to be contrary to reason; for those examples too are very far apart from each other, and these have no agreement with reason. For they say: "Whatever the holy princes of our doctrine and their successors, our fathers, decreed, that these be adored, namely kissed, for both mean the same; but the common usage of ancient Greek speaks of kissing and embracing, and signifies by an extension of the will a certain extension of love, as to bear and to offer, to strengthen and to confirm, to share and to adore, which shows the kiss and the extension of friendship." O sense that confounds rather than orders, that breaks words rather than utters them! O wit that blunts every pestle! O leaden sword that blunts its edge before it cuts the thing it is meant to cut! O argument that resembles the blow of a hammer rather than the cut of a sword, that breaks its material rather than cuts it! O argument that can assert nothing beyond the madness of its own authors, that shows no firmness in the matter proposed, but reveals only frenzied bearers of it! They strive to maintain that to adore, to kiss, and to embrace are one, from to bear and to offer, ignorant of the force of the prepositions, which often corrupt other parts and are often corrupted by other parts, and sometimes both corrupt and are corrupted, and sometimes neither corrupt nor are corrupted; and these prepositions sometimes increase their meanings, sometimes diminish them, and sometimes change them, while they seek to establish certain vain points and try to prove them by vain assertions. Who, then, would not know that offero, adfero, infero, confero, aufero, defero, refero, suffero, differo, profero, praefero, perfero, and the rest, if there are any like these, although they come from the same verb fero, with prepositions added and in some part corrupted, differ among themselves in meaning by very different effects? Or who would not know that participo and adoro have almost no agreement of meaning? For firmo and confirmo, though they are alike in meaning, seem entirely foreign to the thing to which they are applied. If all these matters were discussed by us one by one, as they are taught in the schools of the grammarians, this subject would scarcely be contained in the text of a whole book. But it must also not be passed over that these men construct their most empty argument with a frivolous and vain conclusion, as though by a kind of convertible syllogism, saying: "For whatever someone loves, he also adores; and whatever he adores, he also loves altogether." They do not realise that these two cannot be reversed in turn, because they are unequal, and that loving can extend more widely than adoring. For someone loves his wife or children, yet does not adore them; he loves a servant, a maid, a horse, a dog, a hawk, and other things of this kind, yet does not adore them. So just as it is true when he says, "Whatever someone adores, he also loves," it cannot be true when he says, "Whatever someone loves, he also adores." This reversal cannot reasonably hold, since one of these terms extends more widely, as we have said, and there is no such close property between them that they can be believed to convert one into the other. Just as one may say in reversed order, "What is capable of neighing is a horse, and what is a horse is capable of neighing," but cannot rightly say, "What someone loves he also adores, and what he adores he also loves"; for even in the same topics from which these arguments proceed, in the same kind of argument which is called "from consequents", in which the thing proposed inevitably follows something else, what we have said of the neighing and the horse is that many things can be reversed, but some cannot be reversed at all. Some can be reversed, as when someone says, "If it is capable of laughter, it inevitably follows that it is a man; and if it is a man, it is necessarily capable of laughter," and others like these. But some cannot be reversed at all, as when someone says, "If it is day, it is light; it follows that if it is day it will be light. If he is sated, it follows that he is believed to have eaten; if he is drunk, it is certain that he has drunk; if he is learned, it follows that he is said to have learned; if he adores, it follows that he loves what he adores." For it cannot be said in reversed order: "If it is light, it is necessarily day; if he has eaten, it follows that he is sated," since many things are light and yet it is not day, and eating often does not reach satiety; nor can we say, "If he drinks, he is drunk; if he has learned, he is learned; if he loves, he adores," since sometimes neither drinking reaches drunkenness, nor learning reaches mastery, nor love reaches adoration. Let the individual terms then be set out according to the practice of the logicians, so that it may more easily appear how far these two are apart, and in what way this reversal cannot hold. For there are four propositions which are in some way related to one another, which the philosophers are accustomed to set out in a square formula, namely the first two, "Every thing that someone loves, he adores," and "Nothing that someone loves does he adore"; the other two, "Something that someone loves he adores," and "Something that someone loves he does not adore." The first two are called universal affirmation and universal negation, the others particular affirmation and particular negation. The two upper ones are wholly contrary to each other, while the two lower ones are subcontrary to each other, and the universal or particular affirmation and the universal or particular negation are likewise called subalterns. Then let the lines of inquiry be drawn, as it were, like two angular lines: one from this universal affirmation, "Every thing that someone loves he adores," to this particular negation, "Something that someone loves he does not adore"; the other from this particular affirmation, "Something that someone loves he adores," to this universal negation, "Nothing that someone loves he adores." These are contrary or opposed to each other; and since these are in conflict, when neither can be true, that is, when the universal affirmation and the particular negation, or the particular affirmation and the universal negation, cannot both be true, one will be false and the other true. Thus the true points to the false, and if the one is true, the other immediately departs from truth. So said Apuleius the Platonist philosopher of Madauros, who most subtly disputed about this kind of syllogistic skill in the book entitled On Apuleius's Interpretation. "A universal," he says, "when it is proved, always confirms its particular; when it is refuted, it by no means weakens it. But a particular, in turn, when its universal is refuted, certainly weakens it; when proved, certainly confirms it." In this argument, therefore, the two upper universals, that is, "Every thing that someone loves he adores" and "Nothing that someone loves does he adore," are false; for, as was said above, someone loves many things which he does not adore, and others which he does adore of those things he loves. And the two lower particulars, namely "Something that someone loves he adores" and "Something that someone loves he does not adore," are both true; for someone loves God, according to that saying, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," and adores him, and from this most holy love the nourishment of all virtues proceeds. Someone loves his neighbour and adores him by the duty of greeting, and in this the proposition "Something that someone loves he adores" is shown to be true. The proposition "Something that someone loves he does not adore" is also shown to be true, according to the examples of the wife, child, horse, dog, hawk and the others set forth above, which are each loved and yet are not adored. The universals and the lower particulars, placed alternately, are opposed to each other. For if this universal affirmation, "Every thing that someone loves he adores," is false, then the particular negation, "Something that someone loves he does not adore," is true; and if this particular negation is false, the universal affirmation is true. And again, if this universal negation, "Nothing that someone loves he adores," is false, the particular affirmation, "Something that someone loves he adores," is true; and if that is not true, then the other is not false. But the two lower ones are wholly true; therefore the two upper ones must be believed to be utterly false. Finally, concerning the conversion of such propositions, about which we also disputed somewhat above, the aforesaid philosopher says: "Convertible propositions are called universal negative and its counterpart, that is, the particular affirmative, because their subjects and predicates can always exchange places, the condition of truth or falsity remaining the same; for…

units.la: Levit. 19. superius aliquantulum disputavimus, ita praefatus Philosophus dicit, Convertibiles propositiones dicuntur, universales abdicativa & alterutra ejus, id est, particularis dedicativa, eo quod particulae earum, subjectiva & declarativa, possunt semper inter se servare vices, permanente conditione veritatis aut falsitatis: nam ut est hac vera propositio, Nullus prudens impius, ita si convertis partium vices, verum erit, Nullum impium prudens. item ut falsum est, Nullus homo animal, ita & si convertas falsum erit, Nullum animal homo pari ratione & particularis dedicativa convertitur, Quidam Grammaticus homo est; & contra, Quidam homo Grammaticus est. quod duae caeterae propositiones semper facere non possunt, quanquam interdum convertantur, nec tamen idcirco convertibiles dicuntur. Ergo unaquaeque propositio per omnes figurationes reperienda est, an etiam converca congruat: nec innumerae sunt istae, sed quinque, scilicet. Aut enim proprietas declaratur aliquius, aut genus, aut differentia, aut finis, aut accidens. Ad hanc igitur illorum dictionem frustrandam, & nostram assertionem muniendam multa hujusmodi argumenta adhiberi poterant, & id quod adhibitum est latius potuerat disseri, sed brevitatis causa haec & his similia omittuntur. Ideo namque argumentis ex industria Dialecticae attis venientibus illorum assertionem casfare domino auxiliante patavimus, quia eos nescio qua conversione, quasi quadam syllogistica argumentatione, deliramenta sua roborare voluisse comperimus. CAP. XXIIII. De eo quod superciliose & indocte dixerunt, Similiter & qui ab oriente venerunt conjunximus in eadem Nicaea metropoli, & praesidentibus omnibus nobis caput fecimus Christum. SUPERCILIOSISSIMUM ac potius absurdissimum eorum dictum, qui se sibimet caput fecisse Christum gloriati sunt, dicentes, Praesidentibus omnibus nobis caput fecimus Christum, oppido reprehenditur: quippe cum idem dominus, qui est caput Ecclesiae eandem Ecclesiam ut sibi corpus sibi adsciverit, non ab eadem Ecclesia aut caput esse adscitus sit. Ipse enim Apostolis testatur Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos. Nam si secundum illorum sococdiam Christus ab eis caput factus est, ab eis utique electus est: & si ab eis electus est, praefata ejusdem domini sententia enervatur, non autem praefata domini sententia enervatur: non igitur secundum eorum vanitatem Christus ab eis caput factus est. {a} Joan.1. {b} Symbol. Nicen. {c} Rom.1. Eccl.1. Joan.2. Matth.1. relatum est, quaeri poterit. Factum filii factum patris est, quia utriusque una virtus est, simili modo etiam factum Spiritus sancti factum filii Dei est, propter naturae & voluntatis unitatem. Sive enim pater faciat, sive filius, sive Spiritus sanctus, trinitas est quae operatur, & quicquid tres fecerint, Dei unius est operatio. Potest etiam & Ecclesia domus Christi accipi, quam aedificavit sibi sanguine suo, ornavitque virtutum gemmis & documentorum compectissimis ornamentis: quibus isti non contenti, dum quiddam novum prorogare ejus pulchritudini appetunt, foeditatem ei potius quam pulchritudinem ingerere noscuntur.
units.tr: Levit. 19. As we argued a little earlier, the Philosopher puts it this way: Propositions are called convertible when a universal negative and its converse, that is, a particular affirmative, can always exchange their subject and predicate terms while the condition of truth or falsity stays the same. For example, since this proposition is true, No prudent man is wicked, then if you swap the terms it will be true: No wicked man is prudent. Likewise, since this is false, No man is an animal, its swap will also be false: No animal is a man. By the same reasoning the particular affirmative converts: Some grammarian is a man; and conversely, Some man is a grammarian. The other two propositions cannot always do this, although they sometimes convert, and for that reason they are not called convertible. Each proposition must therefore be tested through all the figures, to see whether its conversion also holds. Nor are these forms countless; there are five: a property of something is declared, or its genus, or its differentia, or its end, or its accident. Many arguments of this kind could be used to defeat their assertion and to fortify ours, and what was used could have been discussed at greater length; but for the sake of brevity these and similar points are omitted. We have deliberately set out to overthrow their assertion with arguments drawn from the art of Dialectic, the Lord helping us, because we have found that they wished to bolster their nonsense by some conversion, as though by a kind of syllogistic argument. CAP. XXIIII. On what they said arrogantly and ignorantly: We also, who came from the East, have met together in the same metropolis of Nicaea, and with all of us presiding we have made Christ the head. The most haughty, or rather most absurd, saying of those who boasted that they had made Christ their head, namely, "With all of us presiding we have made Christ the head," is sharply refuted. Indeed, the same Lord who is the head of the Church, and who has taken that Church to himself as his body, was not himself made head by the Church. For he testifies to the Apostles: You did not choose me, but I chose you. For if, according to their folly, Christ was made head by them, then he was certainly chosen by them; and if he was chosen by them, the aforesaid saying of the Lord is weakened. But the Lord's saying is not weakened; therefore Christ was not made head by them according to their vanity. {a} John 1. {b} Creed of Nicaea. {c} Rom. 1. Eccl. 1. John 2. Matth. 1. It may be asked how this is related. What is done by the Son is done by the Father, since the power of both is one; in the same way, what is done by the Holy Spirit is done by the Son of God, on account of the unity of nature and will. For whether the Father acts, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, it is the Trinity that works, and whatever the three do is the one operation of God. The Church may also be understood as the house of Christ, which he built for himself with his own blood and adorned with the gems of virtues and the most fitting ornaments of teaching. Not content with these, they seek to add some novelty to its beauty, and are known rather to bring deformity than beauty upon it.

units.la: CAP. XXV. Contra eos qui dicunt, quod Epiphanius octoginta capitula digessit de haeresibus, qui tamen, si imagines adorare haeresem sciret, id quoque inter haereses computaret.
units.tr: CHAP. XXV. Against those who say that Epiphanius arranged eighty chapters on heresies, and who, if he had known that adoring images was a heresy, would also have counted it among the heresies.

units.la: IN hoc etiam magnum se munimen adoratores seu cultores imaginum invenisse rati sunt, eo quod Epiphanius quidam, qui haeresum varietates in LXXX capitulis distinxit, si imaginum adorationem haeresem sciret, earumdem imaginum adoratores inter haereticos computaret. His armis nos, qui solius Dei cultu & adoratione contenti sumus, plectere nisi sunt, his jaculis nos confodere moliti sunt, his hastis nos debellare conati sunt, his ensibus nostrae libertatis inruptores se fore crediderunt: ut quasi quodam argumento a genere per quandam reflexionem sumpto dicerent; Si ille, qui generaliter de cunctis haeresibus disputavit, hoc haeresem sciret, hoc quoque inter cateras haereses quae dubitationi intereret: non autem id inter haereses posuit quas digessit, non igitur pro haeresi tenendum est.
units.tr: In this matter too, the worshippers or devotees of images thought they had found a great defence, because a certain Epiphanius, who distinguished the varieties of heresies in eighty chapters, would, if he knew that the adoration of images was a heresy, have counted the adorers of those same images among the heretics. With these weapons they have tried to strike us, who are content with the worship and adoration of the one God alone; with these javelins they have tried to pierce us; with these spears they have tried to overthrow us; with these swords they have believed they would break into our liberty. Their argument, as if drawn from the genus by a kind of reflection, runs: If he who discussed all heresies in general knew this to be a heresy, he would also have counted it among the other heresies that are open to doubt. But he did not place it among the heresies he set out; therefore it must not be held to be a heresy.

units.la: Quibus nos e contrario respondendum putavimus, eosque propriorum armorum instrumentis domino annuente debellare disposuimus, eademque pila, quae ab illis ad nos missa sunt, illis vibrantia detorquentes dirigere non gravabimur, dicentes; Si idem Epiphanius eos, qui imaginum adorationem spernunt, haereticos sciret, in sua generali de haeresibus disputatione eos inter haereticos procul dubio computaret: non autem inter haereticos computavit: non igitur eos haereticos credidisse credendus est.
units.tr: To these we think we should reply in the opposite way. With the Lord's permission we intend to overthrow them with their own weapons, and we will not hesitate to turn back against them the very darts that they sent against us, hurling them back and aiming them at their own side. We say: If this same Epiphanius knew that those who reject the adoration of images were heretics, he would undoubtedly have counted them among the heretics in his general discussion of heresies. But he did not count them among the heretics; therefore it must be believed that he did not think them heretics.

units.la: Quod autem idem Epiphanius non solum imaginum adorationem spreverit, verumetiam eas in Ecclesiis haberi noluerit, his indiciis declaratur. In epistola namque, quae ab illo ad Johannem Episcopum missa est, & a Hieronymo de Graeco in Latinum eloquium translata, ita habetur; Audivi quosdam murmurari contra me, quando simul pergebamus ad locum sanctum, qui vocatur Bethel, ut ibi collectam teci in ecclesiastico facerem, & veniissem ad villam quae dicitur Anablata vidisset, ibi praeterea lucernam ardentem, & interrogassem, quis locus esset, didicissemque esse Ecclesiam, & intrassem ut orarem, invenii ibi velum pendens in foribus ejusdem Ecclesiae tinctum atque depictum, & habens imaginem quasi Christi vel sancti cujusdam: non enim satis mirum est cujus imago fuerit. Cum ergo hoc vidissem in Ecclesia Christi contra auctoritatem Scripturarum, hominis pendere imaginem, scidi illud, & magis dedi consilium custodibus ejusdem loci, ut pauperem mortuum involverent & efferrent: illi, quo contra murmurantes dicerent, Si scindere voluerat, justum erat ut aliud daret velum at mutaret. Quod cum audissem, me daturum esse pollicitus sum, & illico esse missurum. Paululum autem morarum fuit in medio, dum quaero optimum velum pro eo mittere, arbitrabar enim de Cypro mihi esse mittendum. Nunc autem nisi quod potuit reperire, & precor ut jubeas presbytero illius loci suscipere velum a latore, quod a nobis missum est, & deinceps praecipere in ecclesia Christi istiusmodi vela, quae contra religionem nostram veniunt non adpendi. Decet enim hosce latentem hanc imagis habere sollicitudinem & scrupulositatem, quae digna est Ecclesia Christi, & populis qui sibi crediti sunt.
units.tr: That this same Epiphanius not only rejected the adoration of images but also did not want them kept in churches, is shown by the following evidence. In a letter which he sent to John, Bishop, and which Jerome translated from Greek into Latin, we read as follows: "I heard that some were murmuring against me when we were together going to the holy place called Bethel, where I was to make a collection in the church. When I came to the village called Anablatha, I saw there a lamp burning, and I asked what the place was. I learned that it was a church, and I went in to pray. There I found a veil hanging at the doors of that church, dyed and painted, and bearing an image of Christ or of some saint; for I am not sure whose image it was. Since I saw in the church of Christ a human image hanging, contrary to the authority of the Scriptures, I tore it up, and I advised the keepers of that place rather to wrap a dead pauper in it and bury him. They answered murmuring against me that, if I wanted to tear it, it was right that I should give them another veil in its place. When I heard this, I promised that I would give one and would send it at once. There was a brief delay while I looked for the best veil to send in its place, for I thought it should be sent from Cyprus. Now, however, I send what I could find, and I beg you to order the presbyter of that place to receive the veil from the bearer, which has been sent by us, and to command in the church of Christ that such veils, which are contrary to our religion, are not to be hung up. For it becomes these people to have this hidden care and scruple concerning images, which is worthy of the Church of Christ and of the people entrusted to them."

units.la: Hanc enim sententiam de hoc negotio Epiphanii invenimus, quae utrum laudanda an vituperanda sit lectoris arbitrio conceditur. Caeterum veniatur ad beatum Augustinum, interrogetur vir sapientissimus, inquiratur doctor eximius, dicat utrum quaedam haeresis imaginum adorationem utatur. Fecit enim idem vir venerabilis librum de octoginta novem haeresibus, inter quas duae imaginum adorationem censuerunt, Simoniani videlicet & Carpocratiani. Quod ut manifestius fiat, praefati doctoris sententiam eodem libro habentur, singillatim ponantur, ait enim; Simoniani a Simone Mago, qui baptizatus a Philippo diacono, sicut in Actibus Apostolorum legitur, pecuniam voluit a sanctis Apostolis emere, ut etiam per impositionem manuum daretur Spiritus sanctus. Hic magus fallacus decepserat multos. Docebat autem deceptandum turpitudinem, sed ut trahentes (?) ... Deum mundum fecisse docebat: negabat etiam carnis resurrectionem, & adsevebat se Christum: idem qui Jovem se credi volebat, Minervam vero meretricem quandam Selenen, quam sibi socium fecerunt, imagines & suam & eusdem meretricis ...
units.tr: We have found this judgement of Epiphanius on the matter; whether it is to be praised or condemned is left to the judgement of the reader. But let us come to blessed Augustine. Let the most wise man be asked, let the outstanding teacher be consulted, and let him say whether any heresy used the adoration of images. For this venerable man wrote a book on eighty-nine heresies, among which two held the adoration of images, namely the Simonians and the Carpocratians. To make this clearer, the words of that teacher are to be set out one by one from the same book. He says: "The Simonians come from Simon the Magician, who, baptized by Philip the deacon, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, wished to buy from the holy Apostles the power of giving the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands. This false magician had deceived many. He taught that sin was to be disregarded, but ... He taught that God made the world; he also denied the resurrection of the flesh and claimed that he himself was Christ. The same man wished to be believed to be Jupiter, and Minerva, a certain harlot named Selene whom they made their companion, and images of himself and of the same harlot ..."

units.la: Dixerat enim se in monte Sina legem Moysi in patris persona dedisse Judaeis, tempore Tiberii in filii persona putative apparuisse, postea se in linguis igneis Spiritum sanctum super Apostolos venisse: Christum amen nec venisse, nec a Judaeis quicquam pertulisse. Sicut enim haeresis, quae ab eodem Simone exorta est, quae Simoniaca vocatur, omnino a fidelibus spernitur: ita quoque adorandarum imaginum usus penitus spernendus est: Altera quoque haeresis est, quae hunc errore percensetur, quam ita praefatus doctor scripsit. Carpocratite, a Carpocrate caperunt, qui docebat omnem turpem operationem, omnemque adinventionem peccati, nec aliter evadi atque transfiri principatus & potestates quibus haec placent, ut possit ad caelum superius pervenire. Hic etiam Jesum hominem tantummodo & de utroque sexu natum putasse perhibetur: sed accepisse talem animam, quae fuerat in superna esset atque nuntiaret resurrectionem corporis simul cum lege abiciebat. Negabat a Deo factum, sed aliquam virtutibus mundum. Sed a ipsius fuisse traditur socia quaedam Marcellina, quae colebat imagines Jesu & Pauli & Homeri & Pythagorae, adorando in censum q. poscendo.
units.tr: For he had said that on Mount Sinai he gave the law of Moses to the Jews in the person of the Father; that in the time of Tiberius he appeared in the person of the Son, in seeming only; and afterwards that in tongues of fire he came as the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles; but that Christ had neither come nor suffered anything from the Jews. Just as the heresy that arose from this same Simon, and is called Simonian, is wholly rejected by the faithful, so too the practice of worshipping images must be utterly rejected. There is also another heresy that is reckoned as holding this error, which the aforesaid teacher described as follows. The Carpocratians, who took their name from Carpocrates, taught that every shameful act and every invention of sin was lawful, and that one could not otherwise escape, or pass beyond, the rulers and powers who are pleased by these things, so as to reach the higher heaven. He is also said to have held that Jesus was merely a man, born of both sexes, but that he received a soul such as had been in the heavens above; and he rejected together with the law the resurrection of the body. He denied that the world was made by God, but ascribed it to certain powers. It is handed down that a certain companion of his was Marcellina, who worshipped images of Jesus and Paul and Homer and Pythagoras, adoring them and demanding payment for it.

units.la: Nam si forte aliquis hujusce erroris ille veterator dicet, Ideo imagines adorare
units.tr: For if perhaps someone, that old campaigner of this error, should say, "Therefore they worship images,"

units.la: . adorare, inter haereses beatus Augustinus computavit, quia gentilium quorundam, id est, Simonis & Selenae, seu etiam Homeri & Pythagorae adorabant imagines, advertat quod etiam imagines Jesu & Pauli adoratae dicuntur, & id ipsum inter haereses a praefato viro computatum est. Nam si idem vir eximius imagines manufactas Domini sive Apostolorum vel etiam quorumlibet sanctorum adorandas sciret, numquam Jesu & Pauli imaginum adorationem inter haereses computaret.
units.tr: adorare, Blessed Augustine counted among the heresies, because some of the Gentiles, namely Simon and Selene, or even Homer and Pythagoras, worshipped images. Let him note that the images of Jesus and Paul are also said to have been worshipped, and that this very practice has been counted among the heresies by the same aforesaid man. For if that eminent man had known that images of the Lord or of the Apostles, or indeed of any saints made by hands, were to be worshipped, he would never have counted the worship of the images of Jesus and Paul among the heresies.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: Contra eos qui imagines sanctas & sacratas dicunt, easq; in viis sive in plateis, quae plerumq; polluta sunt, poni jubent.
units.tr: Against those who call holy and sacred images, and who order them to be placed in roads or in squares, which are for the most part foul.

units.la: UNGUNT itaq; hi, de quibus sermo est, in hoc negotio duas res, quae sibi utrimq; repugnant: cum videlicet saepissime memoratas imagines sanctas & venerandas nuncupant, easq; in viis sive in plateis, quae plerumq; pollutae sunt, ponendas esse asseverant. Sicut enim non convenit luci & tenebris, calido & frigido, ita nimirum non convenit sanctitati & contaminationi, puritati & impuritati. Unde magna ex parte eos errare constat, cum eas & sanctas esse asserunt, & in locis contaminatis statuendas esse decernunt. Patescit namq; quodammodo in hoc eorum censura, qui eas in viis sive in urbium vicorumq; plateis poni percensent, quod haec sanctitate careant, sicuti & carent cum sculpceret si sanctae esse crederentur, in locis sanctis poni censeretur. Omne sanctum mundum est, nihil munduin inpurum, nihil igitur sanctum impurum: & si haec impurorum locorum sedes secundum illorum censuram quaerunt, inmunditiam, quae sanctitati contraria est, non spernunt: & si inmunditiam non spernunt, nequaquam sanctae dici possunt. Si igitur impurorum locorum sedes quaerunt, sanctae nuncupari nequaquam possunt. nam ut cetera exempla taceamus, quibus doceri potest, unamquamq; rem non inconvenienti, sed convenienti potius rei adhibendam esse debere, ipsorum etiam eloquentiae principium praecepta proferamus, qui in eloquentia hoc observandum pennt censuerunt, utres, locus, tempus, persona consideretur, ne dicantur gravia levibus, ne verecundi verecundis, ne laciva seriis, ne inpudica pudicis, ne incasta castis, ne ridicula tristibus, ne profana religiosis, sed omnia in eloquentiae arte ita essent convenientia, ut nil inconveniens, nil repugnans, singula pro locorum & temporum qualitate moderata manerent. Si ergo in eloquentiae arte hoc ab oratoribus observari jussum est, multo magis nobis in nostrae religionis cultibus observandum est, ut singula quaeque ad religionem pertinentia ita observentur, atque ita habeantur, prout ratio sive ordo exposcit.
units.tr: So these men, of whom we are speaking, anoint two things in this matter which are mutually opposed: namely, while they very often call the aforesaid images holy and venerable, they assert that they are to be placed in roads or in squares, which for the most part are foul. For just as light and darkness, hot and cold, do not agree, so holiness and defilement, purity and impurity, certainly do not agree. Hence it is plain that they err greatly, when they both declare them to be holy and decree that they are to be set up in polluted places. Indeed their judgement, in that they count them as placed in the roads or the squares of cities and villages, shows in some measure that these lack holiness, just as, if they were believed to be holy, they would be thought to be placed in holy places. Everything holy is clean, nothing clean is impure; therefore nothing holy is impure. And if they seek the seats of impure places according to their own judgement, they do not spurn the uncleanness which is contrary to holiness; and if they do not spurn uncleanness, they can by no means be called holy. If, then, they seek the seats of impure places, they can by no means be called holy. For, to pass over other examples by which it can be taught that each thing is to be applied not to an unfitting but rather to a fitting purpose, let us bring forward the precepts of the very principle of their own eloquence, who in rhetoric have judged that this must be observed: that the matter, place, time and person be considered, so that the serious is not joined with the light, the modest with the immodest, the wanton with the serious, the chaste with the unchaste, the pure with the impure, the ridiculous with the sad, the profane with the religious; but that everything in the art of eloquence be so fitting that nothing is unfitting or discordant, and each part remains suited to the quality of places and times. If, then, orators are bidden to observe this in the art of eloquence, much more must we observe it in the worship of our religion, that each thing pertaining to religion be kept and regarded as reason or order demands.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Quod male pictis imaginibus imaginum cultores falli possunt, sive inquirendum ab eis, qui pe- ne omnem fidei Christianae praerogativam in imaginum adoratione sive cultu existimant, quid pauperibus faciendum sit, qui artifices per quos imagines fiunt, omnino curent?
units.tr: That worshippers of images can be deceived by badly painted images; and what is to be asked of those who think almost the whole prerogative of the Christian faith lies in the adoration or worship of images: what must be done for the poor, who wholly neglect the artists by whom images are made?

units.la: OMNIUM artium institutio varia habet exercitia, pictura autem ars est, picturae igitur institutio varia habet exercitia. & hanc exercentes, qui pictores vocantur, alii plus, alii minus eam legunt, alii pulchriora, alii foediora in ea exercent opera: alii formosas, alii deformes componunt imagines. Unde nimirum colligitur, quod illi qui pene omnem fidei suae firmitatem in imaginibus ponunt, earumq; adorationem inter bonorum operum instrumenta adnumerare non erubescunt, & modo pulchras, modo foedas adorant imagines, quodammodo fallantur. Nam si quae imago quanto pulchrior est, tanto amplius habet sanctitatis atq; virtutis, necesse est ut ea quae foedior est, minus habeat sanctitatis atq; virtutis: & si ea quae foedior est minus habet, necesse est ut foediuscula quaeliber, aut nihil, aut modicum habeat: & si ea quae pulchrior est, ideo adrentius adoratur, eo quod causa pulchritudinis amplius habet virtutis, jam non ejus sanctitas ex quadam religione, sed ex artis venit operatione. Et si ea quae minus pulchra est, vel ea quae nihil habet pulchritudinis, adoratur, valde earum adoratores falluntur: cum videlicet res pulchritudine catentes adorate percensent. Si ergo omnes & pulchras & minus pulchras, & nil pulchritudinis habentes aequaliter adorare conclusum est, justitia quae unicuique suum tribuit, de rebus auferatur necesse est. Nam cum pulchras adorant imagines, casu aliquo quo putant se aliquid sanctum adorare, falluntur: cum vero deformes adorant picturas, consulto falluntur: quippe cum res deformes pro sanctis rebus adorant. Sive igitur casu eas, sive consulto adorent, falluntur. Falluntur vero, & merito falluntur, qui cum Deus creator omnium se solum adorari censuerit, res quasdam sensu carentes adorare nituntur: & dum putant se in adorandis imaginibus quandam sanctis exhibere venerationem, soli divinae adorationi quādam prorogant communionem. Quia igitur solus Deus adorandus sit, martyres vero vel quilibet sancti venerandi potius sint quam adorandi, & in hoc opere jam diximus, & egregii doctoris Hieronymi documentis adprobandum est: qui dum contra Vigilantium quendam haereticum, qui martyrum reliquias nequaquam dicebat esse venerandas, scriberet, inter cetera ait; Quis unquam, o insanum caput, martyres adoravit? Si ergo secundum ejusdem sententiam martyres non adorantur, multo minus eorum imagiimagines à fidelibus adorandæ sunt. Quod verò in libro Regnorum Saul legitur Samuhelem suscitatum à Pythonissa adorasse, deprehendi potest, non Samuhelis animam fuisse suscitatam, sed quandam præstigiosa diabolicæ fallaciæ imago Regi Sauli apparuisse, sive in eo quod se adorari permiserit, quod utique vir sanctus facere non permitteret, sive etiam quia pessimo regi dixit, Cras tecum eris: cum videlicet idem in manissimæ nequitiæ rex non cum Propheta moriens, sed cum diabolo futurus erat: qui quos in hoc seculo ad mala opera perpetranda inlicit, secum in futuro ad æternas pœnas trahit. Rex itaque inmanis metiri audiens, in quo habitu esset excitatus, intellexit hunc esse Samuhelem, quid intellexerit retulit, & quia non bene intellexit, contra Scripturam alium adoravit quàm dominum: & putans Samuhelem, adoravit diabolum, ut fructum fallaciæ suæ haberet Satanas. Hoc enim nititur ut adoretur quasi Deus. Si enim verè Samuhel illi apparuisset, non utique vir justus permisisset adorari, qui prædicaverat dominum solum esse adorandum. Et quomodo homo Dei, qui cum Abraham in tefrigerio erat, dicebat ad vitium pestilentiæ dignum ardore gehennæ, Cras tecum eris? His duobus titulis subtilitate fallaciæ suæ prodidit improvidus Satanas, quia & adorari se permisit sub habitu & nomine Samuhelis, quod puto Samuhel non permitteret, & virum peccatis pressum, cum magna distantia peccatorum & justorum sit, cum Samuhele justissimo futurum mentitus est, verum potest videri, si de Samuhelis nomine taceatur, quia Saul cum diabolo futurus erat. ad eum enim transmigravit, quem adoravit. quamquam & à beato Augustino & ab aliis doctoribus diversa de hac re opinentur, & liber Ecclesiasticus ad laudem Samuhelis referat, eo quod mortuus prophetarit. Jam vero illi, qui pene omnem fidei Christianæ prærogativam in imaginum adoratione sive cultu esse existimant, interrogandi sunt, utrum ideo quilibet pauperes fidei suæ patiantur jactuam, eò quòd census indigentia presli non habeant facultatem qua suscipiant pictuam? Si ergo inops quilibet ideo bonorum meritorum erit expers, quia rebus, quibus imagines adipiscatur, caret, locuples ideo auctoritatis meriti prærogativam subiet, eò quòd rebus quibus picturæ emantur abundat. & si iste pro rebus, non pro meritis, aut pœnas, aut præmia suscipiet, & ille pro indigentia non pro operibus judicabitur, imaginum adoratio magnam in Christiana religione arcem conscendet, & justitia quæ merita cujuslibet, non tes explorat, vires magnas ex parte amittet. Quæ omnia dum nulla rerum consequentia adprobari possint, restat ut imaginum cultus nullum in Christiana religione tenere credatur principatum.
units.tr: The training in all the arts has various exercises, and painting is an art, so the training in painting has various exercises too. Those who practise it, called painters, study it to different degrees: some produce finer works, others baser ones; some compose beautiful images, others ugly ones. From this it is clearly gathered that those who place almost the whole firmness of their faith in images, and do not blush to count the adoration of them among the instruments of good works, adore now beautiful and now ugly images, and are in some way deceived. For if an image is more beautiful, it has so much more holiness and virtue; so it must follow that the uglier one has less holiness and virtue, and if it has less, then any quite ugly one has either nothing or very little. And if the more beautiful one is adored more eagerly because, by reason of its beauty, it has more virtue, then its holiness comes not from any religion but from the working of art. And if the less beautiful one, or one having no beauty at all, is adored, its adorers are greatly deceived, since they plainly adore things lacking beauty as holy things. If, then, it has been settled that all images, beautiful, less beautiful and having no beauty, are to be adored alike, justice, which gives each thing its due, must necessarily be removed from things. For when they adore beautiful images, they are deceived by some chance, thinking they adore something holy; when they adore ugly pictures, they are deceived deliberately, since they adore ugly things as holy things. Whether they adore them by chance or deliberately, they are deceived. And they are deceived, and rightly deceived, who, when God the Creator has declared that he alone is to be adored, strive to adore things devoid of sense; and while they think that in adoring images they show a certain veneration to the saints, they in fact grant a certain share of divine adoration to those things. Since God alone is to be adored, and martyrs or any saints are to be venerated rather than adored, as we have already said in this work, and as must be confirmed by the teaching of the excellent doctor Jerome, who, writing against a certain heretic, Vigilantius, who said that the relics of martyrs were in no way to be venerated, said among other things: Who ever, O mad head, adored martyrs? If, then, by his own judgment martyrs are not adored, much less are their images to be adored by the faithful. As for what is read in the book of Kings, that Saul adored Samuel when he was raised by the witch of Endor, it can be grasped that the soul of Samuel was not raised, but some deceptive image of diabolical fraud appeared to King Saul, both in that it permitted itself to be adored, which a holy man would surely never permit, and because it said to that most wicked king, Tomorrow you will be with me: since clearly that monstrously wicked king was to be with the devil, not with the prophet, after his death. The devil lures those whom he entices in this age to perpetrate evil works, and afterwards drags them with him to eternal punishments. So the monstrous king, hearing it, and being told the habit in which he had been raised, understood that this was Samuel; he reported what he had understood, and because he did not understand rightly, he adored, contrary to Scripture, someone other than the Lord; and thinking it was Samuel, he adored the devil, so that Satan might have the fruit of his deceit. For this is what he strives for: to be adored as God. For if Samuel had truly appeared to him, a just man would certainly not have permitted himself to be adored, since he had proclaimed that the Lord alone is to be adored. And how could the man of God, who was with Abraham in the place of refreshment, say to the vile man, worthy of the heat of hell, Tomorrow you will be with me? By these two marks the careless Satan betrayed the cunning of his deceit: first, because he allowed himself to be adored under the guise and name of Samuel, which I think Samuel would not have allowed; and second, because he pretended that a man weighed down by sins would be with the most just Samuel, though there is a great distance between sinners and the just. This could seem true only if nothing is said of the name of Samuel, since Saul was to be with the devil; for he passed over to the one whom he adored. Although blessed Augustine and other teachers hold different views on this matter, and the book of Ecclesiasticus refers it to Samuel's praise, because he prophesied after death. Now those who think that almost the whole prerogative of the Christian faith lies in the adoration or worship of images must be asked whether, for this reason, any poor man suffers loss of his faith, because, lacking means, he has no ability to acquire a painting. If any needy man is to be lacking in good merits because he lacks the means by which he might obtain images, then the wealthy man will undergo a prerogative of authority and merit because he abounds in the means by which paintings are bought. And if the one receives punishments or rewards for his wealth, not for his merits, and the other is judged for his poverty, not for his works, the adoration of images will climb to a great citadel in the Christian religion, and justice, which examines the merits of each person and not their means, will largely lose its great strength. Since none of these consequences can be shown to follow from the nature of things, it remains that the cult of images is not to be believed to hold any principate in the Christian religion.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: Quòd frustra suam synodum universalem nominant, quam tamen constat ab universa- li non fuisse adgregatam Ecclesia.
units.tr: That they vainly call their synod universal, though it is clear that it was not gathered from the whole Church.
