units.la: INTER cætera deliramenta quæ in eadem synodo vel gesta vel scripta dicuntur, hoc quoque non omnibus eorum deliramentis minus est, quod eandem synodum universalem nuncupant, cum neque universalis fidei inconvulsam habeat puritatem, neque per univeTsarum Ecclesiarum gesta constet auctoritatem. Sicut enim Ecclesia universalis est quæ Græco eloquio Catholica dicitur: ita nimirum omne, quicquid ab ejus unitate non discedit, Catholicum nuncupari potest. Omnis enim doctrina Christiana vel quælibet constitutio sive traditio talis esse debet, ut universali conveniat Ecclesiæ. quod nequaquam hæretici observaverunt, qui per diversas mundi partes aliquibus regionum partibus coartati conventicula quædam statuerunt, quibus & se & quam * plures ab ecclesiasticæ unitatis consortio segregaverunt. Cum ergo duarum & trium provinciarum Præsules in unum convenerunt, si antiquorum canonum institutione muniti aliquid prædicationis aut dogmatis * statuunt, quod tamen ab antiquorum patrum dogmatibus non discrepat, Catholicum est quod faciunt, & fortasse dici potest universale: quoniam quamvis non sit ab universo orbis præsulibus actum, tamen ab universorum fide & traditione non discrepat: quod crebro factum in plerisque mundi partibus, quibusdam necessitatibus incumbentibus, scimus. Multa enim concilia gesta sunt, quorum institutionibus sancta munitur & corroboratur Ecclesia. Si vero duarum aut trium provinciarum Præsules in unum convenientes nova quædam statuere cupientes, conventicula quædam faciunt, quia non cum universi orbis Ecclesia sentiunt, sed ab ea quadam ex parte dissentiunt, non est Catholicum quod faciunt, & ideo universale nuncupari non potest. Omne quod Ecclesiasticum est, Catholicum est: & omne quod Catholicum est, universale est: omne autem quod universale est, profanis vocum novitatibus caret: omne igitur quod Ecclesiasticum est, profanis vocum novitatibus caret. * Nam si hæc synodus vocum novitatibus careret, & antiquorum patrum dogmatibus contenta esset, universalis dici poterat. Non autem antiquorum patrum dogmatibus contenta est, non igitur universalis dici potest. Universitas namque ab uno cognominatur, quod uno multoriens verso propagatur. Nam multitudo unitatum vertendo in unum collecta universitas efficitur. Universalem plane eandem synodum non cunctanter profiteri, nisi eam universalis Ecclesiæ dogmatibus sentiremus refragari.
units.tr: AMONG the other nonsense that is said to have been either done or written in that same synod, this is no less absurd than all the rest: that they call it a universal synod, when it has neither the unshaken purity of universal faith nor is it established by the authority of the acts of all the churches. For just as the Church is universal, which in Greek is called Catholic, so whatever does not depart from her unity may rightly be called Catholic. For every Christian doctrine, or any constitution or tradition, ought to be such that it agrees with the universal Church. The heretics did not observe this. Confined to certain parts of the regions across the various parts of the world, they set up little conventicles, by which they cut both themselves and very many others off from fellowship in the ecclesiastical unity. Therefore, when the bishops of two or three provinces meet together, and, fortified by the institution of the ancient canons, decree something concerning teaching or doctrine that nevertheless does not differ from the doctrines of the ancient Fathers, what they do is Catholic, and perhaps may be called universal. For although it has not been done by the bishops of the whole world, it does not differ from the faith and tradition of all. We know this has often been done in many parts of the world when particular necessities pressed. For many councils have been held, by whose institutions the holy Church is protected and strengthened. But if the bishops of two or three provinces, meeting together and wishing to set up some new things, form little conventicles, because they do not agree with the Church of the whole world, but dissent from her in some respect, what they do is not Catholic and therefore cannot be called universal. Whatever is ecclesiastical is Catholic, and whatever is Catholic is universal; but whatever is universal is free from profane novelties of words; therefore whatever is ecclesiastical is free from profane novelties of words. For if this synod were free from novelties of words and content with the doctrines of the ancient Fathers, it could be called universal. But it is not content with the doctrines of the ancient Fathers; therefore it cannot be called universal. For universality takes its name from the one, because it is spread by the one turned many times over. For the multitude of unities gathered by turning into one becomes universality. Clearly we would not hesitate to profess that this same synod is universal, unless we perceived that it runs counter to the doctrines of the universal Church.

units.la: CAP. ULT.
units.tr: Last Chapter

units.la: SCIAT Dominus Apostolicus & Pater noster, & cuncta simul Romanorum Ecclesia, ut secundum quod continet in epistola beatissimi Gregorii, quam ad Serenum Massiliensem Episcopum direxit. Permittimus imagines Sanctorum quicumque eas formare voluerint, tam in Ecclesia, quamquam quamq; extra Ecclesiam, propter amorem Dei & Sanctorum ejus: adorare verò eas nequaquam cogimus; qui noluerint: Frangere vel destruere eas, etiamsi quis voluerit, non permittimus. Et quia sensum sanctissimi Gregorii sequi in hac epistola, universalem Catholicam Ecclesiam Deo placitam, indubitanter liberè profitemur......
units.tr: Let the Lord Apostolic and our Father, and the whole Roman Church together, know that, in accordance with what is contained in the letter of the most blessed Gregory, which he sent to Serenus, Bishop of Marseilles: We permit images of the saints to be made by whoever wish to make them, both in the church and outside the church, out of love for God and his saints. We do not, however, compel anyone to adore them; those who do not wish to, need not. We do not permit them to be broken or destroyed, even if anyone should wish to do so. And because we follow the meaning of the most holy Gregory in this letter, we freely and without doubt profess the universal Catholic Church to be pleasing to God......

units.la: EXPLICIT FELICITER.
units.tr: HERE ENDS HAPPILY.

units.la: CAROLI MAGNI IMP. AUG. RESCRIPTUM ad NICEPHORVM IMP. CONSTANTINOPOLITA- NUM de Pace inter utrumq; Imperium.
units.tr: Rescript of the Emperor Charlemagne Augustus to Nicephorus, Emperor of Constantinople, concerning the peace between the two Empires.

units.la: CUm in omni humanæ actionis initio Domini sit auxilium invocandum, maximè in hoc, quod modo inter nos Deo mediante agitur, negotio, Domini & Salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi omni modo sunt imploranda suffragia, ut qui nomine illius signati sumus, & in dispensatione passionis ejus ab æterno mortis periculo nos redemptos esse confidimus, ea quæ ipso inspirante inchoavimus, ad honestum & utilem perfectionis terminum perducere mereamur, in cujus nomine atque honore Legatum fraternitatis tuæ, quem ad boni recordationis filium nostrum Pipinum Regem militis, Arsatium scilicet gloriosum Spatarium ad nos cum verbis & literis ...... tuæ, benignè atque honorificè suscepimus. Et quamvis ad nos missus non fuisset, veluti ad nos missum, adhibita diligenti cura, & audivimus, & cum eo de his, quæ detulit, quia prudentem animadvertimus, colloquutionem habuimus. Nec immeritò, cum tanta esset non solum in literis, quas attulit, sed etiam in verbis, quæ ore illius nostris auribus insonuerunt, optatæ ac semper optandæ pacis copia, ut valde nobis, & quibuscunque Deum amantibus hujusce modi Legatio placere potuisset; quæ utiq; tanto fuit charitatis ac pacis favo reserata, ut in palato cordis cujusq; fidelis veram possent sapere dulcedinem, possetq; iudicari penitus insipiens, cui talia videntur insipida.
units.tr: Since in every beginning of human action the help of the Lord must be called upon, most of all in this matter which is now being carried on among us by God's mediation, the prayers of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ must by all means be implored, so that we who are marked with his name, and who trust that in the dispensation of his passion we have been redeemed from the eternal danger of death, may deserve to bring to an honourable and useful end those things which we have begun by his inspiration. In his name and honour we have received, kindly and with honour, the envoy of your brotherhood, whom you sent to us with words and letters, namely the glorious Spatharius Arsacius, sent to our son of good memory, King Pepin, the military man. And although he had not been sent to us, yet, as if he had been sent to us, we gave careful attention, we heard him, and, because we perceived him to be a prudent man, we held a conference with him about the things he had brought. And not undeservedly: since there was such abundance of the longed-for and ever-to-be-longed-for peace, not only in the letters he brought but also in the words that sounded in our ears from his mouth, that this embassy could have been very pleasing to us and to all who love God. It was indeed unlocked by such a favour of charity and peace that in the palate of every faithful heart they could taste true sweetness, and he may be judged utterly foolish to whom such things seem insipid.

units.la: 2. Propter quod postquam illum in fines Regni nostri pervenisse comperimus, veluti præ optimæ ac Deo complacita Legatis ejus, temperare nequivimus, opportunè eum ad nostram præsentiam venire fecimus; maximè tamen, quod is, ad quem illum missum constabat, dilectus filius noster Pipinus Rex, divino judicio jam rebus humanis excesserat, neq; nos illum cum infecto negotio tanto, ad quod perficiendum directus erat, vacuum reverti, pari potuimus.
units.tr: 2. Therefore, when we learned that he had arrived within the borders of our kingdom, we could not hold back, as it were from the eagerness of one who brings the best things and things pleasing to God, and we had him brought opportunely into our presence. Chiefly, however, because he to whom he was plainly sent, our beloved son King Pepin, had already passed from human affairs by divine judgment, and we could not let him return empty-handed, with so great a business left undone, for the carrying out of which he had been directed.

units.la: 3. Et non solum propter hoc, sed etiam quod ex tempore, quo primo Imperii tui anno, Michaelem Metropolitanum, & Populum, Asiduum Abbatem, Callistumque gloriosum Candidatum, ad constituendam nobiscum pacem, & fœderanda at q, adunanda hæc duo in Christi charitate Imperia, longæva tua misit dilectio.
units.tr: 3. And not only for this reason, but also because from the time of the first year of your reign your long-lived Affection sent Michael the Metropolitan and Populus, Asiduus the Abbot, and the glorious Candidatus Callistus, to establish peace with us and to join and unite these two Empires in the charity of Christ.

units.la: 4. Veluti in specula positi, longa fuimus expectatione suspensi, præstolantes sive per Legatum, sive per epistolam, quando meritorum scriptis nostris, amabilia fraternitatis tuæ responsa sumeperem. Jamq;, ut se habet humanæ mentis infirmitas, prope desperatio cordi nostro incipiebat oriri; sed fidentes, sperabamus in eo, qui nunquam deserit sperantes in se, quod secundum Apostolum labor noster in ipso vacuus & inanis esse non deberet; ac desiderium nostrum, quod, ut confidimus, ipsius inspiratione concipimus, secundum divitias misericordiæ suæ, complere, & quandocunque ad effectum perducere deberet. Idcirco audito adventu memorati Legati dilectionis tuæ, Arsatii gloriosi Spatarii, magnopere gavisi sumus, confidentes, nos de rebus incertis ad optatam certitudinem perventuros, & de his, quæ prædictis Missis tuis ad te perferenda dedimus, responsum esse receptum. Et revera ita factum est. Sensimus enim ex parte mea, quod desiderabamus, ad completionem votorum nostrorum, divini favorem auxilii, & in verbis ac literis, quæ per Legationem memorati Legati perlata sunt, quamvis ad filium nostrum scripta & directa essent, nō minimam nos desiderare responsionis accepisse portionem.
units.tr: 4. Placed as on a watch-tower, we were held in long expectation, waiting to receive, whether through a messenger or by letter, the kind replies of your brotherhood to our writings. And now, as the weakness of the human mind is, a kind of despair was beginning to arise in our heart; but trusting, we hoped in him who never forsakes those who hope in him, that, according to the Apostle, our labour should not be empty and vain in him, and that he would fulfil, according to the riches of his mercy, the desire which, as we trust, we conceive by his inspiration, and would bring it to effect whenever it ought to be. Therefore, on hearing of the arrival of the aforesaid envoy of your Affection, the glorious Spatharius Arsacius, we rejoiced greatly, trusting that we should come from uncertain matters to the desired certainty, and that a reply had been received concerning those things which we had given to your aforesaid envoys to carry to you. And indeed it was so. For we perceived on my part what we desired, the divine favour of help for the fulfilment of our prayers; and in the words and letters which were brought through the embassy of the aforesaid envoy, although they were written and addressed to our son, we perceived that we had received no small portion of the reply we desired.

units.la: 5. Proinde omnipotenti Deo, non quales debuimus, sed quales potuimus, gratias agimus, quod cordi dilectionis tuæ, quam quæsivimus, ac desiderabilem pacis voluntatem inspirare dignatus est, orantes secundum Apostolum, ut Deus, qui vobis in hac pace velle tribuit, ipse perficere tribuisset. Propter quod nihil morantes, sed omni cunctatione ac dubitatione penitus abjecta, Legatos nostros præparavimus ad tuam amabilem fraternitatem dirigendos.
units.tr: 5. Therefore we give thanks to almighty God, not as we ought, but as we are able, because he has deigned to inspire the heart of your Affection with the desired and longed-for will for peace, which we sought. Praying, according to the Apostle, that God, who has given you the will for this peace, would himself grant to perfect it. Therefore, delaying nothing, but having wholly cast off all hesitation and doubt, we have prepared our envoys to be sent to your kind brotherhood.
1. Thess. 3.

units.la: CAROLI MAGNI IMP- ERATORIS AUGUSTI CONSTITVTIO
units.tr: The Constitution of the Emperor Charles the Great, Augustus

units.la: De pace constituenda & conservanda, & divisione Regni facienda inter fi- lios: edita in Comitiis Theodonis villanis.
units.tr: On establishing and preserving peace, and on making the division of the kingdom among the sons: issued at the assembly at Thionville.

units.la: In nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: IMPERATOR Cæsar CAROLUS, Rex Francorum invictissimus, & Romani Rector Imperii, Pius, Felix, Victor ac Triumphator, semper Augustus, omnibus fidelibus sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ, & cunƈto populo C: t iolico, præsenti & futuro, gentium ac nationum, quæ sub nostro imperio ac regimine constitutæ sunt.
units.tr: Charles, Emperor Augustus, most unconquered king of the Franks and ruler of the Roman Empire, pious, fortunate, victorious and triumphant, ever august, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to the whole Catholic people, present and future, of the peoples and nations which are constituted under our empire and rule.

units.la: 1. Sicut omnibus vobis notum esse, & neminem vestrum latere credimus, quomodo nos divina clementia, cujus nutu ad occasum tendentia sæcula per successiones * generationum reparantur, tres nobis dando filios, magno nos miserationis ac benedictionis suæ ditavit munere, quia per eos secundum vota nostra & spem nostram de Regno confirmavit, & curam oblivioni obnoxiæ posteritatis leviorem fecit. Ita & hoc vobis notum fieri volumus, quod eosdem per Dei gratiam filios nostros Regni à Deo nobisa concessi, donec in corpore sumus, & post nostrum ab hac mortalitate discessum hujus à Deo conservandi Regni vel Imperii nostri hæredes relinquere, si sic divina Majestas annuerit, optamus. Non ut confusè atq; inordinatè, aut sub totius Regni dominatione jurgii controversiam eis relinquamus; sed trina partitione totum Regni corpus dividentes, quam quisquis illorum tueri vel regere debeat, portionem b distribuere & designare voluimus, eo videlicet modo, ut sua quisque portione contentus juxta ordinationem nostram & fines Regni sui, qui ad alienigenas extenduntur, cum Dei adjutorio nitatur defendere, & pacem atque caritatem cum fratre custodire.
units.tr: 1. As you all know, and as we believe no one among you is unaware, the divine mercy, by whose will the ages that are tending towards their setting are renewed through the succession of generations, has enriched us with a great gift of its compassion and blessing, giving us three sons. Through them it has confirmed our kingdom according to our prayers and our hope, and has made lighter the care of a posterity liable to forgetfulness. So we wish this also to be made known to you: that, while we are in the body, and, if the divine Majesty so wills, after our departure from this mortality, we desire to leave as heirs of this kingdom or empire of ours, which by God's grace is to be preserved, those sons whom God has given us. We do not wish to leave them a dispute in confusion and disorder, or a quarrel over the rule of the whole kingdom. Rather, dividing the whole body of the kingdom into three parts, we have wished to assign and distribute to each one a portion which he ought to guard or rule, in such a way that each, content with his own portion, according to our arrangement and the boundaries of his kingdom which extend towards foreign peoples, may strive with God's help to defend it and to keep peace and love with his brother.

units.la: 2. Divisiones verò à Deo conservati & conservandi Imperii vel Regni nostri tales facere placuit, ut Aquitaniam totam c & Vuasconiam (excepto pago Turonico) & quicquid inde ad Occidentem atq; Hispaniam respicit, & de civitate Nivernis, quæ sita est super fluvium Ligerim cum ipso pago Nivernensi, pagum d Avalensem, atque Alsensem, Cabillionensem, Matisconensem, Lugdunensem, e Gabojam, Moriennam, Tarentaliam, Montem Cinisium, Vallem Gegusianam usque ad Clusas, f & inde per terminos Italicorum montium usque ad mare, vel usq; ad Hispanias continetur, hoc est, illam portionem Burgundiæ, & Provinciam ac Septimaniam, vel Gothiam, Ludovico dilecto filio nostro consignavimus.
units.tr: 2. It has pleased us to make the divisions of our empire or kingdom, preserved by God and to be preserved, in this way: we have assigned to our dear son Louis all Aquitaine and Gascony (except the Tours district), and whatever lies from there towards the west and towards Spain; and from the city of Nevers, which is situated on the river Loire, together with the district of Nevers, the districts of Avallon, Auxerre, Chalon, Mâcon and Lyon, Maurienne, Tarentaise, Mont Cenis, the valley of Susa as far as the Clusae, and from there along the borders of the Italian mountains as far as the sea, or as far as Spain. That is, that part of Burgundy, Provence and Septimania, or Gothia, is included.

units.la: 3. Italiam verò, quæ & Longobardia dicitur, & g Bojoariam, sicut Tassilo tenuit, exceptis duabus villis, quarum nomina sunt Ingoldestat, & Lutrahahof, quas h nos quondam Tassiloni beneficiavimus, & pertinet ad pagum, qui dicitur Nortgouue, & de Alamannia partem, quæ in Australi ripa Danubii fluminis est, & de ipso fonte Danubii, currente limite, usq; ad Rhenū fluvium in confinio pagorum Clergouue & Hegouue in locum qui dicitur Auge: & inde per Rhenum fluvium sursum versusq; ad Alpes, quicquid intra hos terminos fuerit, & ad Meridiem vel Orientem respicit, unà cum Ducatu Curiensi & pago Burgouue, Pipino dilecto filio nostro ordinamus.
units.tr: 3. Italy, which is also called Lombardy, and Bavaria, as Tassilo held it, except for two estates, named Ingolstadt and Lutrahahof, which we once granted as a benefice to Tassilo and which belong to the district called Nordgau; and that part of Alemannia which lies on the southern bank of the river Danube, and from the very source of the Danube, along the boundary line, as far as the Rhine, at the point where the districts of Klettgau and Hegau meet, at the place called Au; and from there up along the Rhine towards the Alps, whatever lies within these bounds and faces south or east, together with the duchy of Chur and the district of Burgau, we assign to our dear son Pepin.

units.la: 4. Quicquid autem de Regno nostro extra hos terminos fuerit, id est, Franciam & Burgundiam, excepta illa parte, quam Ludovico dedimus, atque Alemanniam, excepta portione quam Pipino * adscripsimus, Austriam, Neustriam, Thuringiam, Saxoniam, Frisiam, & partem Bajoariæ, quæ dicitur Nortgouue, dilecto filio nostro Carolo cœcessimus, ita ut Carolus & Ludovicus viam habere possint in Italiam ad auxilium * faciendum fratri suo, si ita necessitas exiterit, Carolus per vallem Augustanam, quæ ad Regnum ejus pertinet, & Ludovicus per vallem Segusianam, Pipinus verò & exitum & ingressum per Alpes Noricas atq; Curiam.
units.tr: 4. Whatever of our kingdom lies outside these bounds, that is, France and Burgundy, except that part which we have given to Louis, and Alemannia, except the portion which we have assigned to Pepin, Austria, Neustria, Thuringia, Saxony, Frisia, and that part of Bavaria which is called Nordgau, we have granted to our dear son Charles. Charles and Louis shall have a way into Italy, so that they may give aid to their brother if the need arises: Charles through the Augsburg valley, which belongs to his kingdom, and Louis through the valley of Susa; Pepin, however, shall have both exit and entry through the Noric Alps and Chur.

units.la: 5. Hæc autem tali ordine disposuimus, ut si Carolus, qui major est natu, priusquam ceteri fratres diem obierit, pars Regni quam habebat, dividatur inter Pipinum & Ludovicum, sicut quondam divisum est regnum inter nos & fratrem nostrum Carolomannum, eo modo ut Pipinus illam portionem habeat, quam frater noster Carolomannus habuit, Ludovicus verò illam partem, quam nos in illa partitione suscepimus. Si verò Carolo & Ludovico viventibus, Pipinus debitum humanæ * naturæ compleverit, Carolus & Ludovicus dividant inter se Regnum, quod ille habuit. Et hæc divisio tali modo fiat, ut ab ingressu Italiæ per Augustam civitatem accipiat Carolus Eboreiam, Vercellas, Papiam, & inde per Padum fluvium termino currente usque ad fines Regiensium & ipsum Regium, & Civitatem Novam, atque Murinam usq; ad terminos sancti Petri. Has civitates cum suburbanis & territoriis suis, atque Comitatibus, quæ ad ipsas pertinent, & quicquid inde Romam * pergenti ad lævam respicit de regno quod Pipinus habuit, unà cum Ducatu Spoletano, hanc portionem, sicut prædiximus, accipiat Carolus.
units.tr: 5. We have arranged this in the following order: if Charles, who is the eldest by birth, dies before his other brothers, the part of the kingdom which he held shall be divided between Pepin and Louis, just as the kingdom was once divided between us and our brother Carloman, so that Pepin shall have that portion which our brother Carloman had, and Louis that part which we received in that partition. If, however, while Charles and Louis are living, Pepin shall have paid the debt of human nature, Charles and Louis shall divide between themselves the kingdom which he held. And this division shall be made in such a way that, from the entry into Italy through the city of Augsburg, Charles shall receive Ivrea, Vercelli, Pavia, and from there along the river Po, with the boundary running as far as the borders of Reggio and Reggio itself, and Nuova Città, and Murina as far as the borders of St Peter. These cities, with their suburbs and territories, and the counties which belong to them, and whatever of the kingdom which Pepin held lies to the left of one going from there to Rome, together with the duchy of Spoleto, Charles shall receive as this portion, as we have said before.

units.la: 6. Quicquid autem à prædictis civitatibus vel Comitatibus Romam eunti ad dexteram jacet cet de prædicto regno, id est, portionem quæ remansit de * regione Transpadana, una cum Ducatu Tuscano usq; ad mare Australe, & usq; ad Provinciam * Ludovicus ad augmentum sui regni sortitur. Quod si ceteris superstitibus Ludovicus fuerit defunctus, eam partem Burgundiæ, quam regni ejus adjunximus, cum Provincia & Septimania sive Gothia usq; ad Hispaniam Pipinus accipiat, Carolus vero Aquitaniam atq; Vuasconiam.
units.tr: 6. Whatever lies to the right of one going to Rome from the aforesaid cities or counties, in the aforesaid kingdom, that is, the part which remains of the Transpadane region, together with the duchy of Tuscany as far as the southern sea, and as far as Provence, Louis shall receive for the enlargement of his kingdom. But if Louis shall die while the others survive, Pepin shall take that part of Burgundy which we added to his kingdom, together with Provence and Septimania or Gothia, as far as Spain; and Charles shall take Aquitaine and Gascony.

units.la: 7. Quod si talis filius cujuslibet istorum trium fratrum natus fuerit, quem populus eligere velit, ut patri suo succedat in regni hæreditate, volumus ut in hoc consentiant patrui ipsius puri, & regnare permittant filium fratris sui in portione regni, quam pater ejus eorum fratet habuit.
units.tr: 7. But if a son of any of these three brothers is born whom the people wish to choose to succeed his father in the inheritance of the kingdom, we wish that their uncles consent to this and allow the son of their brother to reign in the portion of the kingdom which his father held among them.

units.la: 8. Post hanc nostræ auctoritatis dispositionem placuit inter prædictos filios nostros statuere atque præcipere propter pacem, quam inter eos perpetuò manere desideramus, ut nullus eorum fratris sui terminos vel regni limites invadere præsumat, neque fraudulenter ingredi ad contubernium regnum ejus, vel marcas minuendas, sed adjuvet unusquisque illorum fratrem suum, & auxilium ei ferat contra inimicos ejus juxta rationem & possibilitatem, sive intra patriam, sive contra exteras nationes.
units.tr: 8. After this disposition of our authority, we have resolved to establish and to command among our aforesaid sons, for the sake of the peace which we desire to remain among them forever, that none of them presume to invade the borders or the limits of his brother's kingdom, nor to enter fraudulently into the territory of his kingdom, nor to diminish its marches; but that each of them shall help his brother and bring him aid against his enemies, as far as reason and ability allow, whether within the fatherland or against foreign nations.

units.la: 9. Neq; aliquis illorum hominem fratris sui pro quibuslibet causis, sive culpis ad se confugientem suscipiat ad intercessionem pro eo faciendam: quia volumus, ut quilibet homo peccans & intercessione indigens intra regnum Domini sui vel ad loca sancta, vel ad honoratos homines consugiat, & inde justam intercessionem mereatur.
units.tr: 9. Nor shall any of them receive the man of his brother who has fled to him for whatever causes or faults, to intercede on his behalf; for we wish that any man who has sinned and needs intercession should flee within the kingdom of his lord, or to holy places, or to honourable men, and there deserve a just intercession.

units.la: 10. Similiter præcipimus, ut quemlibet liberum hominem, qui Dominum suum contra jus voluntatem dimiserit, & de uno regno in aliud profectus fuerit, neque ipse Rex suscipiat, neque hominibus suis consentiat, ut talem hominem recipiant, vel juste retinere præsumant: hoc non solum de liberis, sed etiam de servis fugitivis statuimus ordinandum, ut nulla discordiis relinquatur occasio.
units.tr: 10. Likewise we command that the king himself shall not receive any free man who has left his lord against right and willing, and has gone from one kingdom into another, nor shall he consent that his men receive such a man or presume to retain him justly. We decree that this shall be ordained not only for free men but also for fugitive slaves, so that no occasion of discord may be left.

units.la: 11. Quapropter præcipiendum nobis videtur, ut post nostrum ab hac mortalitate discessum homines uniuscujusque eorum accipiant beneficia unusquisque in regno Domini sui & non in alio, ne forte per hoc, si aliter fecerit, scandalum aliquod accidere possit. Hæreditatem autem suam habeat unusquisque illorum hominum absq; contradictione in unoquoq; regno, quam eum legitime habere contigerit.
units.tr: 11. Therefore it seems to us that it should be commanded that, after our departure from this mortality, the men of each of them shall each receive benefices in the kingdom of his own lord and not in another, lest by chance some scandal should arise if they act otherwise. Let each of these men have his own inheritance, without contradiction, in whichever kingdom it has fallen to him lawfully to hold it.

units.la: 12. Ut unusquisque liber homo post mortem Domini sui licentiam habeat se commendandi inter hæc tria regna ad quodcumque voluerit: similiter & ille, qui nondum alicui est commendatus.
units.tr: 12. That every free man, after the death of his lord, shall have the liberty to commend himself to whichever of these three kingdoms he chooses; likewise also one who has not yet been commended to anyone.

units.la: 13. De traditionibus autem & venditionibus, quæ inter partes fieri solent, præcipimus ut nullus ex his tribus fratribus suscipiat de regno alterius à quolibet homine traditionem, vel vendicionem à quolibet homine, hoc est, terrarum, vineatum, sylvarum, atq; libertatum, servorumq; qui captati sunt, sive cæterorum, quæ hæreditatis nomine censentur, auro, argento, & gemmis, annis, armentibus, necnon & mancipiis non captatis, & his speciebus, quæ proprie ad negotiatores pertinere noscuntur: cæteris vero liberis hominibus hoc minimè interdicendum putamus.
units.tr: 13. Concerning the transfers and sales which are customarily made between parties, we direct that none of these three brothers shall accept from any man a transfer or sale of land in another's kingdom. This means lands, vineyards, forests, and freedoms; slaves who have been captured, and other things which are counted under the name of inheritance; gold, silver and jewels; horses, herds, and likewise unbought slaves; and those kinds of goods which are known to belong properly to merchants. We think, however, that this should not be forbidden to other free men.

units.la: 14. Si quæ autem feminæ, sicut fieri solet, inter partes & regna fuerint ad conjugia postulatæ denegentur juste poscentibus, sed liceat eis vicissim dare & accipere, & affinitatibus populos sociari. Ipsæ vero feminæ potestatem habeant rerum suarum in regno, unde exierant, quando in propter mariti societatem habitant.
units.tr: 14. If any women are sought in marriage between the parties and kingdoms, as is customary, and are refused to those who justly ask, let it nevertheless be permitted for them to give and receive in turn, and for peoples to be joined together by marriage ties. The women themselves shall keep power over their own property in the kingdom from which they came, while they dwell there for the sake of their husband's company.

units.la: 15. De obsidibus autem, qui propter credentias dati sunt, & à nobis per diversa loca ad custodiendum destinati sunt, volumus ut ille Rex, in cujus regno sunt, absque voluntate fratris sui, in cujus regno sublati sunt, in patriam eos redire non permittat, sed potius in futurum in suscipiendis obsidibus alter alteri mutuum ferat auxilium, si frater fratrem hoc facere rationabiliter postulaverit. Idem jubemus & de his, qui pro suis facinoribus in exilium missi vel mittendi sunt.
units.tr: 15. Concerning the hostages who have been given as pledges and sent by us to various places for safekeeping, we wish that the king in whose kingdom they are shall not, without the consent of his brother in whose kingdom they were taken, permit them to return to their homeland. Rather, in future, in receiving hostages, each shall give the other mutual aid, if one brother has reasonably asked the other to do so. We order the same concerning those who have been, or are to be, sent into exile for their crimes.

units.la: 16. Si causa vel intentio controversiæ talis inter partes propter terminos & confinia rerum ortæ fuerint, quæ hominum testimonio declarari vel definiri non possunt: tunc volumus ut declarationem rei dubiæ, judicio crucis, Dei voluntas & rerum veritas * exquiratur, nec aliter quam pro tali causa cujuslibet generis pugna vel campus ad examinationem a judicetur. Si vero quis libet homo de uno regno hominem de altero regno de infidelitate contra b Dominum suum culaverit, mittatur eum Dominus suus ad fratrem suum, ut ibi comprobet, quod de homine dixit.
units.tr: 16. If a cause or matter of dispute has arisen between the parties concerning the boundaries and borders of property, and it cannot be declared or settled by human testimony, then we wish that the decision of the doubtful matter be sought by the judgment of the cross, by God's will and the truth of the matter; and that for such a cause, and for no other, a battle or field of combat of any kind be the test. But if any man from one kingdom has accused a man of the other kingdom of disloyalty towards his lord, let his lord send him to his brother, so that there he may prove what he said about the man.

units.la: 17. Super omnia autem jubemus, ut ipsi tres fratres curam & defensionem Ecclesiæ sancti Petri simul suscipiant, sicut quondam ab avo nostro Carolo & beatæ memoriæ genitore nostro Rege, & à nobis postea suscepta est, ut eam cum Dei adjutorio ab hostibus defendere tantur, & justitiam suam quantum ad ipsos pertinet & ratio postulat, habere faciant. Similiter & de ceteris Ecclesiis, quæ sub illorum fuerint potestate, præcipimus, ut justitiam suam & honorem habeant, & pastores & rectores venerabilium locorum habeant potestatem rerum, quæ ad ipsa pia loca pertinent, in quocumque de his tribus regnis illarum Ecclesiarum possessiones futurint.
units.tr: 17. Above all we order that these three brothers together take up the care and defence of the Church of St Peter, as it was once taken up by our grandfather Charles and by our father of blessed memory, the king, and afterwards by us, so that with God's help they may defend it from enemies, and see that it has its justice as far as pertains to them and reason demands. Likewise, concerning the other churches which shall be under their power, we order that they have their justice and honour, and that the ministers and rulers of those venerable places have power over the property which belongs to those pious places, in whichever of these three kingdoms the possessions of those churches may lie.

units.la: 18. Quod si de his statutis atque convenientiis aliquid casu quolibet vel ignorantia (quod non optamus) fuerit interruptum, præcipimus ut quàm citissimè secundum justitiam emendare studeant, ne forte propter dilationem majus damnum possit accidere.
units.tr: 18. But if anything in these statutes and agreements is interrupted by any chance or ignorance (which we do not wish), we order that they take care to amend it as quickly as possible, according to justice, lest greater loss perhaps arise from the delay.

units.la: 18. De filiabus autem nostris, sororibus scilicet prædictorum filiorum nostrorum, jubemus ut post nostrum ab hoc corpore discessum, licentiam habeat unaquæque eligendi, sub cujus fratris tutela & defensione se conferre velit. Et qualiscumque exillis monasticam vitam elegerit, liceat ei honestè vivere sub defensione fratris sui, in cujus regno degere voluerit. Quæ autem juste & rationabiliter à condigno viro ad conjugium quæsita fuerit, & ei conjugalis vita placuerit, non et denegetur à fratribus suis, si & viri postulantis & feminæ consentientis honesta & rationabilis fuerit voluntas.
units.tr: 18. Concerning our daughters, namely the sisters of the aforesaid sons of ours, we order that after our departure from this body, each of them shall have the liberty to choose under whose brother's guardianship and protection she wishes to place herself. And whichever of them chooses the monastic life, let her be allowed to live honourably under the protection of her brother in whose kingdom she wishes to dwell. But she who has been justly and reasonably sought in marriage by a fitting man, and to whom married life has pleased, shall not be denied by her brothers, if the wish of the man asking and the woman consenting is honourable and reasonable.

units.la: 19. De nepotibus verò nostris, scilicet filiis prædictorum filiorum, qui eis vel jam nati sunt, vel adhuc nascituri sunt, placuit nobis præcipere, ut nullus eorum per quaslibet occasiones quemlibet ex illis apud se accusatum sine justa discussione atque examinatione aut occidere, aut membra mancare, aut excæcare, aut invitum tondere faciat; sed volumus ut honorati sint apud patrem vel patruos suos, & obedientes sint cum omni subjectione, quam decet in tali consanguinitate esse.
units.tr: 19. Concerning our grandsons, namely the sons of the aforesaid sons, who are either already born or are yet to be born, it has pleased us to order that none of them, on any pretext, shall have anyone accused before him put to death, maimed, blinded, or shorn against his will, without just inquiry and examination. Rather we wish that they be honoured by their father or uncles, and that they be obedient with all the submission that befits such kinship.

units.la: 20. Hoc postremò statuendum nobis videtur, ut quicquid adhuc de rebus & constitutionibus, quæ ad profectum & utilitatem eorum pertinent, his nostris decretis atque præceptis addere voluerimus, licà prædictis dilectis filiis nostris observetur atq; custodiatur, sicut ea quæ de his jam statuta & decretipta sunt, custodire & observare præcipimus.
units.tr: 20. Lastly, it seems to us that whatever further matters and constitutions pertaining to their advantage and profit we may wish to add to these our decrees and precepts, shall be observed and kept by the aforesaid beloved sons of ours, just as we order that those things already laid down and decreed concerning these matters be kept and observed.

units.la: 21. Hæc autem omnia ita disposuimus, atque ex ordine firmare decrevimus, ut quàm diu divinæ Majestati placuerit nos hanc corporalem agere vitam, potestas nostra sit super à Deo conservatum regnum atque Imperium istud, sicut hactenus fuit in regimine atq; ordinatione, & omni dominatu Regali atque Imperiali, ut obedientes habeamus prædictos dilectos filios nostros, atque Deo humiliter populum nostrum cum omni subjectione, quæ patri à filiis, & Imperatori ac Regi à suis populis exhibetur. AMEN.
units.tr: 21. We have arranged all these things in this way, and have decided to confirm them in order, so that for as long as it shall please the divine Majesty that we lead this bodily life, our power over this kingdom and empire, preserved by God, shall remain as it has been hitherto in government, ordering, and all royal and imperial lordship; so that we may have the aforesaid beloved sons obedient to us, and our people humbly devoted to God, with all the submission which sons show a father, and subjects show an emperor and king. AMEN.

units.la: CAROLI MAGNI IMP. AUG. LEGES.
units.tr: The Laws of Charles Magnus, Emperor Augustus.

units.la: DISCIPLINAM militarem severius exercuit. Militibus, qui gnaviter fecerant, præmia constituit: negligentes ignominia notavit: ubiq; virtutis spectator extitit.
units.tr: He enforced military discipline with great severity. He set rewards for soldiers who had fought bravely, marked the negligent with disgrace, and everywhere he was a watchful judge of valour.

units.la: 2. In Saxonico bello cum duo gregarii milites, facta testudine munitissimæ urbis aggeres pallent, ac portas effregillent, ambos ad se vocatos pro concione laudavit, & ipsis Præfecturam inter Rhenum Alpesq; dedit.
units.tr: 2. In the Saxon war, when two common soldiers, having formed a testudo, had scaled the ramparts of a very strongly fortified city and broken open its gates, he called both to himself, praised them before the assembly, and gave them command of the district between the Rhine and the Alps.

units.la: 3. In eodem itidem bello duos tyrones, licet vulgo conceptos, fortiter in medio hostium agmine depugnantes, inter cubicularios stipatoresq; suos esse jussit.
units.tr: 3. In the same war he ordered two recruits, though of humble rank, who had fought bravely in the midst of the enemy's column, to be among his chamberlains and bodyguards.

units.la: 4. Item duorum Regulorum filii adolescentes jussi ante portorium noctu excubare, quòd larga vino indulsserant, somno gravi opprimuntur. CAROLUS, ut ejus moserat, evigilar, nocte in paucis clam castra circuit, explorat, num omnia rite fiant, ubi somno præditos offendit, præterque idem, ad tabernaculum redit. Postridie tamen concilio vocato, scicitatur quidnam iscommiserunt, qui Principem & caput Francorum, hostium manibus prodiderit atque exposuerit. Illi veniam rogati suo se ense jugulant: hujusce modi hominem capitali pœna condemnant. CAROLUS illos graviter increpitos, ignominiaque notatos exauthorat, cætera melolumes dimittit.
units.tr: 4. Likewise, two young sons of petty kings were ordered to keep watch at night before the gate. Because they had indulged freely in wine, they were overcome by heavy sleep. Charles, as was his custom, woke, secretly went round the camp at night with a few men to see whether everything was being done properly, and when he found them asleep, he went back to his tent. Next day, however, he called a council and asked what they had done, these men who had betrayed and exposed the prince and head of the Franks to the hands of the enemy. They begged pardon, and then slit their own throats with their swords; the man of this sort they condemned to capital punishment. Charles sharply rebuked the others, marked them with disgrace, dismissed them from their posts, and let them go more mildly in other respects.

units.la: 5. Milites datis nominibus sacramento adacti in ejus verba juraverunt, se illi secundum Deum fore: nec mortem pro ejusdem atq; Reipubl. salute recusaturos.
units.tr: 5. Soldiers, having given their names and bound by oath, swore to his words that they would be faithful to him in accordance with God, and would not refuse death for his safety and that of the commonwealth.

units.la: 6. Vetuit, ne quicquam amicorum, præter herbam, ligna, aquam, à militibus inter proficiscendum adhiberetur.
units.tr: 6. He forbade soldiers to take anything on the march apart from herbs, wood and water.

units.la: 7. Neve alius alium ad bibendum provocaret aut cogeret. ebrium in exercitu de cæteto aquam potare compulit.
units.tr: 7. He forbade anyone to invite or compel another to drink. He made a drunken man in the army drink water from the cask.

units.la: 8. Capitali animadversione eos punivit, qui absque missione castra atque militiam deseruissent.
units.tr: 8. He punished with capital punishment those who deserted camp and military service without discharge.

units.la: 9. Militiam, sacramentumq; detrectantes, prædiis, villis, agris, donis militaribus privavit, ea in alios contulit.
units.tr: 9. Those who refused military service and the oath he deprived of estates, farms, fields and military gifts, and transferred these to others.

units.la: 10. Censum, Chunigosteuram & Vanolehen vocant, quinq; denarios modius frumenti quotannis penitat.
units.tr: 10. They call the census Chunigosteura and Vanolehen; they paid five denarii a year for each modius of grain.

units.la: 11. Is qui militiam detrectabat, morbo aut senectute æs illud multicium militareq; pendebat. Nam munia bellica censumq; quàm accuratissimè exegit, quem Germanicis vocabulis, hereschuldam ipse, & heribannum ab exercitu, vulgus raisogeltum ab expeditione nuncupat.
units.tr: 11. He who refused military service, unless prevented by sickness or old age, paid that military and multiple fine. For he exacted military duties and the levy most strictly, which he called by German names: herisculdam, and heribannum from the army; the common people called it raisogeltum from the expedition.

units.la: 12. Erat salubrem magis, quàm ambitiosum Principem scires, ne templis quidem munia bellica, æs militare, utpote nervos, sine quibus Respubl. nequaquam salva esse posset, condonavit.
units.tr: 12. You would know the prince to be wholesome rather than ambitious: he did not even remit military duties and military money to churches, since these are the sinews without which the commonwealth could by no means be safe.

units.la: Disciplina militaris.
units.tr: Military discipline.

units.la: Contributiones. Ea tempestate Sacerdotes paucis, victu, vestitu levi, parabili ac parco, ad naturæ desideria implenda, contenti fuerunt, decimis victitarunt, de quibus nemini quicquam contribuerunt.
units.tr: Contributions. In that age priests, content with few things, with food, light and plain clothing, ready and sparing, to satisfy the needs of nature, lived on tithes, and contributed nothing from them to anyone.

units.la: 13. CAROLUS, non solùm prædia stipendiaria, agros, prata, vineas, villas, molas, laterarias, calcarias, & hujusmodi redditus, vectigaliaq; : item jumenta, pecudes, mancipia, vetùm & priam supellectilem Præfectorum, Præsidum, Pontificum, Fœminarum sacrarum, & Virorum scriptam habuit. Juxta multitudinem jugerum, agrorum, opum, certus numerus militum, aurti, jumentorum, boum, pecudum, rhedarum, vehiculorum, annonæ, vestimentorum, paludamentorum, armorum, cataphractarum, galearum, gladiorum, scutorum, hastarum, arcuum, sagittarum, pilorum, retrarum : item ferramentorum (quæ sunt palæ, bidentes, ligones, rastra, cophini, dolabræ, securiculæ, serræ) indictus & definitus est.
units.tr: 13. Charles kept a written register not only of stipendiary estates, fields, meadows, vineyards, farms, mills, brickworks, limekilns and such revenues and tolls, but also of draught animals, herds, slaves, and even the household goods of prefects, governors, bishops, and consecrated women and men. In proportion to the number of acres, fields and wealth, a fixed number of soldiers, gold, draught animals, oxen, flocks, carriages, wagons, provisions, clothing, cloaks, arms, mail-coats, helmets, swords, shields, spears, bows, arrows, javelins, and nets was prescribed and defined, as well as iron tools (spades, two-pronged hoes, mattocks, rakes, baskets, axes, hatchets and saws).

units.la: 14. Vetustissimæ Francorum Legi Salicæ capita quædam addidit, quasdam ex integro sanxit: ut de moneta, mensura, ponderibus, quæ per totum Romanum Imperium ad æqualitatem redegit.
units.tr: 14. He added certain chapters to the most ancient Salic Law of the Franks and enacted some provisions afresh, concerning coinage, measures and weights, which he brought to uniformity throughout the whole Roman Empire.

units.la: 15. Galliam in quinos Conventus divisit, Viennensem, Lugdunensem, Senonensem, Rhemensem, Tomagensem, Rhemensem. His cæteris oppida contributa. Unumquodque, jus in finitimo sibi ventu petere jussum. Apud Germanos, quos Cæsar vocat Cisrhenanos, qui in Gallia Belgica caq; habitant, juridici Conventus instituti sunt, Vesoutinus, Mogontinus, Treverensis, Agrippinensis, Cameracensis.
units.tr: 15. He divided Gaul into five judicial assize districts: Vienne, Lyons, Sens, Reims, Tours, and Reims again. To these the other towns were assigned, and each was ordered to seek justice at the court nearest to itself. Among the Germans whom Caesar calls Cisrhenani, who live in Belgic Gaul, judicial assemblies were established at Vesoul, Mainz, Trier, Cologne and Cambrai.

units.la: 16. Sanxit CAROLUS, ut in primaria cujusque regionis urbe, quam Metropolim vocant, Pontifex & Præsor ter quotannis, Aprili, Octobri, Januario, jus dicerent, responderent. & primum pauperes, viduas, pupillos, dato his prudentissimo patrono, diligentissimè audirent, inimicos reconciliarent. Veturinusquè, ne illi lites in diem differrent, neve calumnias facerent. Opulentos quidem ac locupletes, Pontifices, Præfectos, si qui in concordiam redire nolent, ad se haud alio delegarent. Sumptuatium decretum hujuscemodi juri dicundo intentis promulgavit: quotidie Pontifici quadraginta panes, gallinas tres, porcellum unum, ova quindecim, de potu modios tres, de avena cabalhis modios tres: Præsorum panes triginta, modios duos, cæteraque tundem statuit.
units.tr: 16. Charles decreed that in the chief city of each region, which they call the metropolis, the bishop and the prefect should hold court and give judgment three times a year, in April, October and January. They were first to hear the poor, widows and orphans most diligently, a most prudent advocate being assigned to them, and to reconcile enemies. They were not to put off the suits to another day, nor to bring false charges. The rich and powerful bishops and prefects, if they were unwilling to come to agreement, were to be referred to him and to no other. He issued a schedule of allowances for those engaged in dispensing justice: daily to the bishop forty loaves, three hens, one piglet, fifteen eggs, three modii of drink, and three modii of oats for the horses; to the prefects thirty loaves and two modii; and he fixed the rest in the same way.

units.la: 17. Ebrietatem inhibuit, neve alius alii propinaret.
units.tr: 17. He curbed drunkenness and forbade anyone to pour drink for another.

units.la: 18. Sine discrimine universos ad Evangelica oracula, ad placita Christi Domini Dei sectanda coegit.
units.tr: 18. Without distinction he compelled everyone to follow the oracles of the Gospel and to observe the precepts of Christ the Lord God.

units.la: 19. Nundinas diebus festis ademit.
units.tr: 19. He abolished markets on feast days.

units.la: 20. Edixit quoq; prophanum plusquam ter in anno de sacrosancto convivio, quod Eucharistiam nuncupamus, velci non placere.
units.tr: 20. He also decreed that it was profane to absent oneself, more than three times a year, from the holy banquet which we call the Eucharist.

units.la: 21. Festos & solennes sanctosque dies Christo Servatori nostro dicatos, nominum Natalis jus, Calendas Januarias, quando more Judæorum circumsectus est, Epiphaniorum sacrificium octavum diem ejusdem mensis solennè, & Lustrationis quarto Idus Februari: annales vero quibus idem Christus revixit, mortem atque inferos superavit, ac hisce triumphatis cælos ascendit, & deinde in Legatos suos Spiritus sanctorum illapsus est, tantum celebrandas esse scivit. Pra sacros religiosasque dies in æstate, Divo Johannis Baptistæ, Divis Petro & Paulo: in hyeme Divo Martino (cujus sacra secum ferre consuevere Reges Franci) Andreæ, Stephano, Johanni Evangelistæ, & Infantibus ab Herode contrucidatis adjecit.
units.tr: 21. He ordered that only the festal, solemn and holy days dedicated to Christ our Saviour should be celebrated: the day of the Nativity; the Kalends of January, when, after the manner of the Jews, he was circumcised; the sacrifice of the Epiphany, solemnly kept on the eighth day of the same month; and the Purification on the fourth day before the Ides of February. He also prescribed the annual days on which Christ rose again, overcame death and hell, and after his triumph ascended into heaven, and then the Holy Spirit descended upon his apostles. For holy and religious days in summer he added the Divine John the Baptist, and the Divine Peter and Paul; in winter, Divine Martin (whose relics the Frankish kings used to carry with them), Andrew, Stephen, John the Evangelist, and the Infants slaughtered by Herod.

units.la: 22. Præcepit etiam, ut Monachi, Sacerdotes, literis operam sedulò darent, emendatè recte scriberent. In omnibus contubernus Monachorum, Episcoporum ædibus pueros docerent.
units.tr: 22. He also ordered that monks and priests should diligently apply themselves to letters, and write correctly and well. In all monasteries and in the houses of bishops they were to teach boys.

units.la: 23. Mendicis palantibus vetuit quicquam tribui suos quamq; regenem inopes alere: validos, labore victum quærītare, ac desiderio sufficere manus jussit. Idcirco opes Ecclesiasticas in tres divisit partes, duas egenis, tertiam Sacerdotibus attribuit. In singulis gustuonibus donaria æquà lance inter egenos & Sacerdotes bipartitus est.
units.tr: 23. He forbade that anything be given to wandering beggars, or that the poor be supported by their own kin and neighbours. He ordered the able-bodied to seek their food by labour and to supply their needs by their hands. Therefore he divided the ecclesiastical wealth into three parts: two for the needy, the third he assigned to the priests. In each collection of offerings the gifts were divided evenly between the needy and the priests.

units.la: 24. Autor & aliarum Legum fuit, in quibus cavit: Ne temerè & passim sacrificius uteretur: neve cadavera in sanis humarentur: neu Sacerdotes avaritiæ, Veneriqve dediti sent.
units.tr: 24. He was also the author of other laws, in which he provided that sacred things should not be used rashly and everywhere; that bodies should not be buried in holy places; and that priests should not be given over to avarice or to lust.

units.la: 25. Ut Pontifices officio publicè in templo docendi plebem fungerentur.
units.tr: 25. That bishops should discharge the office of publicly teaching the people in the church.

units.la: 26. Ut Sacerdotes avaritiam, gulam, cauponas, negotia prophana, familiaritatem mulierum evitarent, aut Sacerdotio cederent, aut tribu moverentur.
units.tr: 26. That priests should avoid avarice, gluttony, taverns, secular business and familiarity with women; otherwise they were either to give up the priesthood or be removed from their tribe.

units.la: 27. Ut furtes, homicidæ, & hujusmodi crimina committentes, si ad asylum templum vel elapsi forent, tepeterentur, atq; vi eripierentur. Quòd si quis Monachorum, Pontificesve Præfectos illos reddere recusaret, satisfacere damni infecti compensandiq; præstaret, promitteret, si illorum piam aufugisset, id non sua operæ esse factum juraret.
units.tr: 27. That thieves, murderers and those committing such crimes, if they had fled to an asylum or a temple, should be sought out and dragged out by force. But if any monk, bishop or prefect refused to surrender them, he was to promise to make good the damage done, if they had escaped through his carelessness, and to swear that it had not happened through his own fault.

units.la: 28. Jus assiduè summa diligentia dixit, nonnunquam mane, dum inducetur, tanta temporis jactura apud eum erat.
units.tr: 28. He always administered justice with the greatest diligence, sometimes in the morning while the accused was being brought in; so great was the loss of time for him.

units.la: 29. Nulli plures Ducatus, Præfecturasq; aut Sacerdotia concessit, dictitans, sibi & aliis demerendos, beneficiisq; oppignerandos esse.
units.tr: 29. He granted no one more than one duchy, prefecture or bishopric, saying that these were to be earned by himself and by others, and bound to them by benefits.

units.la: 30. In Episcoporum Senatum haud temerè quempiam adlegit: eruditionemque bonitatem in cooptandis illis potissimum spectavit. Neminem nisi antèa sibi probatum & cognitum vit. Nam eum ordinem ad pristinum modum & splendorem à D. Paulo praescriptum reduxit. Curiosè cavit, ne quis avarus, aut ambitiosus, luxuve petditus, unquam Pontificalem apicem adipisceretur.
units.tr: 30. He did not choose anyone rashly into the senate of bishops; in co-opting them he chiefly regarded learning and goodness. He admitted no one unless he had first been tested and known to him. For he restored that order to its former manner and splendour as prescribed by St Paul. He took careful care that no avaricious or ambitious man, or one given to luxury, should ever attain the pontifical dignity.

units.la: 31. Hildegardæ Reginæ petenti pro Sacrificulo suo, idem Proceribus Aulæ rogantibus respondit: Idoneo, etsi pauperi, jam destinavi. Imperatorem mentiri, aut falli non decet, ut obtrudar superis, cujus vitam, mores, ingenium ignoret, & tantòne oneri par sit, compertum non habeat.
units.tr: 31. When Queen Hildegard asked for a priest of her own, and the courtiers likewise made their request, he answered: "I have already destined for it a suitable man, though a poor one. It does not befit an emperor to lie or to be deceived, so as to thrust upon the great men one whose life, morals and character he does not know, and whose fitness for so great a burden he has not ascertained."

units.la: 32. Episcopum Mogontinum, quòd lituum aureum, distinctum gemmis, instar Cæsarei Sceptri usurpasset, severissima coercuit oratione: eidem avariciam, & superbiam pro concione propalam exprobravit, indignabundus & clamitans: En, ait, Pastores nostros, crucem Christi professos, qui spreta cura & pascendarum ovium solicitudine, ostentatione, opibus, luxu, Imperatorem quemvis opulentissimum lacessant.
units.tr: 32. He sharply rebuked the Bishop of Mainz, because he had taken up a golden crozier, set with jewels, in imitation of the imperial sceptre. He also openly reproached him from the pulpit for avarice and pride, speaking indignantly and crying out: "Behold our ministers, who profess the cross of Christ, who, scorning the care and anxious concern for feeding the sheep, vie in display, wealth and luxury with any most opulent emperor."

units.la: 33. Quendam pridie feriarum D. Martini designatum Episcopum, quòd is auctus tanta dignitate, amicis coenam exhibens, & uti fit, mero sese nimium onerans, somno deinde oppressus, nocturnu divinis rebus non interfuisset, rursus Sacerdotio movit: intolerabilem negligentissimumque fore ratus, qui primo die sibi non temperaret, ut sui compos Deum ad iracundiam non provocaret.
units.tr: 33. On the day before the feast of St Martin, a certain man who had been designated bishop, having been raised to such dignity, gave a dinner for his friends and, as usually happens, loaded himself too heavily with wine; then, overcome by sleep, he was absent from the divine services at night. The emperor removed him from the priesthood again, judging him intolerable and too negligent, since he could not control himself on the first day, so that, being not master of himself, he might not provoke God to anger.

units.la: 34. Item alium laetiorem ob Pontificatum donatum, atque gestientem, & ab humo in equum absque scamno sive suppedaneo, uno impetu subsilientem, revocavit: Vales, inquit, ut video viribus, & eques haud malus es: tua opera in bellis, ubi tua virtus enitescat, indigeo. Proinde ignobili & imbecillo oves & gregem pecudum relinque.
units.tr: 34. Likewise, he recalled another man who was overjoyed at being granted the pontificate and was exulting, and who leapt from the ground onto a horse in a single bound, without a stool or footstool: "You are evidently strong," he said, "and you are not a bad horseman. I need your services in wars, where your courage may shine forth. Therefore leave the sheep and the flock of cattle to some lowly and feeble man."

units.la: 35. Pueros, quos Clementi Scoto commiserat, epistolis, versibus, carminibus, orationibus, panegyricis, scriptis, ut periculum de eorum ingenio atque indole faceret, sibi exhiberi jubet. Ubi tenuiores praeter spem profecisse, Nobiles vero gaudiis corporis deditos, cultum animi neglexisse deprehendit, illis ad dextram segregatis: Vos quidem macti virtute, inquit, estote filioli pientissimi, qui nostro Imperio gnaviter defuncti estis. Vestra erunt Sacerdotia locupletissima, & Pontificatus maximi. Ego vos in Aulam adscisco; ex vobis Senatores cooptabo; vos in album Praetorum & Patrum curiam adlegam. Deinde ad Nobilium liberos, quos à laeva collocarat, vultu haud iram dissimulans, ait: At vos comatuli & delicatuli, freti opibus & splendore parentum, nostram Majestatem conspexistis; vitia, otia, luxum, & inertiam bonis literis virtutibusque, contempto decreto nostro praeruliftis. Jubeo, & Deum immortalem testor, nihil penitus commodi, honoris, ne obolum quidem ab Imperatore vestro, cujus jussa aspernati estis, expectate. Faxim, ut omnibus mortalibus ludibrio vivatis: & in vos exempla edam, nisi resipueritis, & negligentiam diligentia expiaveritis.
units.tr: 35. He ordered that the boys whom he had entrusted to Clement the Scot be brought before him, so that he might test their talent and disposition by letters, verses, songs, orations, panegyrics and writings. When he found that the boys of humbler birth had made progress beyond his hopes, but that the nobles, given over to bodily pleasures, had neglected the cultivation of the mind, he set the former apart on his right hand and said: "You, indeed, are made worthy by virtue, dear and most dutiful little sons, who have served our Empire diligently. Yours will be the most richly endowed bishoprics and the highest pontificate. I shall admit you to my court; from among you I shall choose senators; I shall enrol you in the list of prefects and the senate of the Fathers." Then, turning to the sons of the nobles, whom he had placed on his left, he said, his face not concealing his anger: "But you, curled and pampered fellows, relying on the wealth and splendour of your parents, have looked upon our Majesty; yet you have preferred vices, idleness, luxury and sloth to good letters and virtues, disregarding our decree. I command, and I call the immortal God to witness, that you should expect absolutely no advantage, no honour, not even a penny, from your Emperor, whose commands you have spurned. I shall take care that you become a laughing-stock to all mortals; and I shall make an example of you, unless you repent and make amends for your negligence by diligence."

units.la: 36. Universos Veteris ac Novi Instrumenti libros, librariorum imperitia, lectorum oscitantia, interpretum inscitia, & incuria temporum depravatos, ad amussim & veritatem fontis correxit. Extat publicum Decretum; nec sivit in divinis lectionibus templisque inter sacra officia inconditos solecismos barbarismosque inconcinnos obstrepere.
units.tr: 36. He corrected all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which had been corrupted by the ignorance of scribes, the drowsiness of readers, the unskilfulness of translators and the carelessness of the times, restoring them to the exact standard and to the truth of the source. A public decree survives; and he did not allow barbarisms and ungrammatical solecisms to clamour in the divine lessons and churches during the sacred offices.

units.la: LUDOVICI PII IMP. AUG. DECRETA COMITIORUM APUD AQUISGRANENSIUM de anno DCCCXIV.
units.tr: The Decrees of the Assembly at Aachen of the Emperor Louis the Pious, Augustus, in the year 814.

units.la: IMPERATOR Ludovicus Augustus in Conventu Procerum Imperii ad Aquas Graneas, Sacramenta apud se dicere, maximè Praetores, prorsus nihil munerum accepturos, jubet.
units.tr: The Emperor Louis Augustus, at the assembly of the nobles of the Empire at Aachen, orders that the magistrates in particular shall take absolutely no gifts, and that they shall not swear oaths in his presence.

units.la: 2. Ipsis pauperes summopere commendat. Vetat insuper, ne populum extraordinariis tributis, novisve servitutibus expilent.
units.tr: 2. He commends the poor to them very earnestly. He further forbids them to plunder the people with extraordinary taxes or new forms of servitude.

units.la: 3. Nulli delegavit officium, ut non adjiceret: Vide quid agas: non hominis, sed Dei Optimi Maximi minister es, ejusdem Sacramento authoratus es: & agamus, ne quis popularium nos accuset. quodcunque judicabis facturúsve es, in te redundabit. ita tecum agetur, quemadmodum cum alio egeris. Non est enim apud Dominum nostrum iniquitas, aut cupido, acceptióve personarum. Rex Deus omnibus idem, qui nos ad rerum humanarum fastigium provexit, ut inopes plebemque suam ab injuria potentiorum, servitutemque divitum defendamus & adseramus, non ut populi labore atque sudore partis abutamur ditemurque. Cardo & summa religionis Christianae in amandis, promerendis egenis consistit. Hi caelos possident, ab ipsis locupletes & potentissimos quosque mercari oportet. Exiguo conceditur misericordia, potentes potenter tormenta patientur.
units.tr: 3. He has entrusted an office to no one without adding this: "See what you are doing. You are the minister not of man but of God Almighty, and you have been empowered by his sacrament. Let us see to it that none of our subjects can accuse us. Whatever you judge or intend to do will rebound upon you. You will be treated as you have treated another, for with our Lord there is no iniquity, no greed, and no respect of persons." God is the King of all alike, who has raised us to the height of human affairs so that we may defend and maintain the helpless and his people from the injury of the powerful and the servitude imposed by the rich, not that we should abuse and enrich ourselves by the labour and sweat of the people. The heart and sum of the Christian religion consists in loving and assisting the needy. By means of them the powerful and the mightiest must purchase heaven for themselves. Mercy is granted to the humble; the powerful will suffer powerful torments.

units.la: Honoratissimus atque maximus titulus, quem Deus peculiariter sibi vindicat, usurpat, pauperum propugnator, pupillorum tutor, viduarum curator. Huic administrati Imperii sui reddemus rationem.
units.tr: This most honourable and greatest title, which God claims especially for himself, the ruler assumes: the defender of the poor, the guardian of orphans, the protector of widows. To him we shall give an account of our administration of the Empire.

units.la: LUDOVICI PII IMP. AUG. DECRETA COMITIORVM AQVISGRANENSIVM de anno DCCCXVII.
units.tr: The Decrees of the Assembly of Aachen under the Emperor Louis the Pious, Augustus, in the year 817.

units.la: LUDOVICUS Imperator ad Aquas Grancas reversus, Conventum Primorum Regni, more Francorum agit. Interfuere filii ejus, PIPINUS Rex Aquitaniae, LOTHARIUS Rex Bojorum.
units.tr: Louis the Emperor, returning to Aachen (Aquae Grani), held a meeting of the chief men of the kingdom, in the manner of the Franks. Present were his sons: Pepin, King of Aquitaine, and Lothair, King of the Bavarians.

units.la: 1. De Sacerdotum ibi luxu Imperator leges tulit, quibus Pontificibus, Monachorum Patribus, universis deniq; Sacerdotibus, vestimenti preciosi, serici, gemmarum, auri, argenti etiam, in balteis, cultris, vaginis, phaleris, calcaribus, & hujusmodi, usus interdicitur. Dicere solebat Imperator, portentum abominabileq; inferum ludibrium, actis addictum, devotumq; sacris, qui paupertatem Christi amplecti, crucem ejus portare deberet, ad gloriam luxumq; prophanorum aspirare.
units.tr: 1. At this assembly the Emperor passed laws concerning the luxury of the clergy, by which the use of costly garments, silk, jewels, and gold and silver as well, in belts, knives, scabbards, horse-trappings, spurs and the like, is forbidden to bishops, the abbots of monasteries, and all clergy generally. The Emperor used to say that it was a monstrous and abominable mockery of the lower orders, for one given over to sacred things and dedicated to them, who ought to embrace the poverty of Christ and bear his cross, to aspire to the glory and luxury of the profane.

units.la: 2. Eodem Concilio Imperator eum quoque diem, quo Deipara Virgo tertiis relictis in Senatum Coelitum adlecta est, festis addit, celebrariq; praecipit.
units.tr: 2. At the same council the Emperor also added to the festivals the day on which the Virgin Mother of God, having left the tombs behind, was taken up into the heavenly senate, and he ordered that it be celebrated.

units.la: HLUDOVICI PII IMPERA- TORIS AUGUSTI MANDATUM
units.tr: THE MANDATE OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS THE PIOUS AUGUSTUS

units.la: De reformatione abusuum Cleri; ex Concilio Aquisgranensi missum.
units.tr: On the reform of the abuses of the clergy; sent from the Council of Aachen.

units.la: AD ARNONEM SALZBURGENSEM ARCHIEPISCOPUM.
units.tr: TO ARNO, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG.

units.la: IN NOMINE Domini Dei & Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, HLUDOVVICUS divina ordinante providentia Imperator Augustus, venerabili Arnoni Salzpurgensi Archiepiscopo in Domino salutem.
units.tr: In the name of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, Louis, Emperor Augustus by the ordaining providence of God, to the venerable Arno, Archbishop of Salzburg, greeting in the Lord.

units.la: Sacrum & memorabile Concilium divino nutu nostroque studio in Aquisgrani palatio nuper aggregatum, in quo multa ad propagandam Ecclesiasticam dignitatem, praecedente & subsequente gratia Christi, diligenter tractata atq; instituta sunt, tuam nullatenus credimus latere sanctitatem. Sed quia contigit eidem sancto & venerabili Concilio tuam non interfuisse paternitatem, ad tuam destinare decrevimus beatitudinem per praesentem missum nostrum, nomine Nothonem, Quam etiam idcirco penes palarium nostrum diligenter scribi fecimus, ut nihil in se scriptorum vicio depravationis aut detruncationis habens ad te usq; incolumis perveniret.
units.tr: The holy and memorable Council, lately assembled by the will of God and our zeal in the palace at Aachen, in which many matters were carefully treated and established for the advancement of the dignity of the Church, by the preceding and following grace of Christ, we do not believe can have escaped your holiness. But since it happened that your fatherly self was not present at that holy and venerable Council, we have decided to send word to your blessedness through our present envoy, named Nothho. We have also had this copy carefully written out in our palace, so that it might reach you intact, with nothing in it spoiled or cut short by the fault of the scribes.

units.la: Quapropter volumusq; decernimus, ut juxta Metropolitanae sedis tibi canonice collatam dignitatem, nostraq; auctoritatis sanctionem, dioceseos tuae Episcopos & caeteros Ecclesiae Praelatos tempore & loco congruenti ad te arcessere facias, & his coram missó nostro memoratas institutionis formulas perlegi jubeas.
units.tr: Therefore we wish and decree that, in accordance with the dignity of the metropolitan see canonically conferred on you and with the sanction of our authority, you should summon to yourself at a suitable time and place the bishops of your diocese and the other prelates of the Church, and that you should have the aforementioned formulas of instruction read through in the presence of our envoy.

units.la: * Quas habes tom.3.hujus collectionis, sol.164. vires curaverint. quoniam tam diu illum in tua vel conprovincialium tuorum diocesi morati & discurrere unà cum misso tuo jussimus, donec ab omnibus memoratae formulae transcriberetur: ut videlicet cuncta procurans, diligenterque perficiens, cum ad nos illum redire opere expleto tempus permiserit, cuncta, quae acta sunt, vestro utriusque scripto notentur, atque per ipsum tuumque missum nostrae dimiscentiae intimentur, ut sciamus quibus gratiarum actiones referre, quosque etiam dignis correptionibus corrigere debeamus.
units.tr: * Which you have in the third volume of this collection, page 164. We have ordered that he should remain in your diocese, or that of your fellow provincials, and travel about together with your envoy, until the aforementioned formula has been copied by all; so that, by attending to everything and carrying it out diligently, when the time allows him to return to us once the work is completed, everything that has been done may be recorded in a writing from each of you, and be made known to our clemency through him and your envoy, so that we may know to whom we ought to render thanks and whom we ought also to correct with fitting rebukes.

units.la: Si vero aliquis tuae dioceseos eidem Institutioni, vestraeque admonitioni, procaciter reniti voluerit, & eam, quae ab eodem sacro & venerabili Concilio constituta atque decreta est, quantum Dominus ei posse dederit, observare contempserit, praecipimus ut si antea hujusmodi non se correxerit, quicumque ille est, ante praesentiam nostram tua vel missi nostri admonitione venire festinaret, quatenus a nobis juxta quantitatem culpae digne corrigatur. Direximus praeterea tibi pondus & mensuram, secundum quae Clericis & sanctis Monialibus panis & potus aequaliter tribuenda sunt. Quae ut ab omnibus firmissime atque inviolabiliter teneantur, decernimus; & ne quid incrementi aut detrimenti a quoquam patiantur, modis omnibus inhibemus.
units.tr: But if anyone in your diocese should wish to resist insolently this instruction and your admonition, and should disregard the observance of what has been established and decreed by that same sacred and venerable Council, as far as the Lord has given him power, we command that, if he has not previously corrected himself in this way, whoever he may be, he should hasten to come before our presence at the admonition of yourself or our envoy, so that he may be duly corrected by us according to the measure of his fault. Moreover, we have sent you a weight and measure, according to which bread and drink are to be given equally to the clergy and the holy nuns. We decree that these things be held most firmly and inviolably by all, and we forbid in every way that anyone suffer any increase or decrease in them.

units.la: Tuam igitur in calce hujus epistolae admonemus sanctitatem, ut secundum ministerium tibi divino munere collatum, nostrae in hoc negocio saluberrimae admonitioni obedienter & inexcusabiliter pareas, & caeteris in parendo exemplum bonum tribuas. Dignum quippe justumque est, ut quanto sublimius sacerdotii dignitate aliis superemines, & a nobis venerabiliter diligeris, tanto magis ad Dei nostramque voluntatem exequendam, devotiorem te atque promptiorem exhibeas. Vale in Domino, & ora pro nobis.
units.tr: We therefore admonish your holiness, at the close of this letter, that in accordance with the ministry conferred on you by divine gift, you obey and comply without excuse with our most salutary admonition in this matter, and that you give a good example to others in obeying. For it is fitting and just that, the more you excel others in the dignity of the priesthood and are venerably esteemed by us, the more devoted and ready you should show yourself in carrying out the will of God and ours. Farewell in the Lord, and pray for us.

units.la: LUDOVICI PII IMP. AUG. ET ORDINUM IMPERII DECRETUM IN REGEM ROMANORUM ET COMPLICES EIUS, RE- BELLES IMPERIO & LAESAE MAJESTATIS REOS, LATUM IN COMITIIS AQUISGRANENSIBUS, ANNO DCCCXVIII.
units.tr: THE DECREE OF LOUIS THE PIOUS, AUGUSTUS, AND THE ORDERS OF THE EMPIRE, CONCERNING THE KING OF THE ROMANS AND HIS ACCOMPLICES, REBELS AGAINST THE EMPIRE AND GUILTY OF TREASON (LAESA MAIESTAS), PROMULGATED AT THE ASSEMBLY OF AACHEN, IN THE YEAR 818.

units.la: IN Italia Bernardus nepos Imperatoris ex fratre, quorundam pravorum consultorum consiliis obsequens, aditus omnes in Italiam patruo praecludit: univers as urbes in sua verba jurare cogit. Authores hujus conspirationis Episcopi erant, Anshelmus Mediolanensis, Wolfoldus Cremonensis, Theodolphus Aurelianensis: Proceres vero Aulae, Egideus amicorum Regis primus, Reginhartus Cubiculi Praefectus, Reginharius Maginharii filius, cujus avus Hartradus olim in Germaniae Francia cum multis ex ea regione Nobilibus adversus Carolum Magnum conspirarat. Celtae & Itali Bernardo: Belgae & Germani Augusto favebant. Ad hos motus comprimendos Imperator ex omni Germania Galliaque comparato quam celerrime exercitu, in Italiam contendit. Bernardus a suis destitutus, rebus suis diffidens, armis abjectis, apud Cabillonem Heduorum urbem Burgundiae patruo se dedit. Quem caeteri secuti, non solum se tradunt, sed ultro etiam non admoti quaestionibus omnem technam hujus rebellionis detegunt. Augustus omnibus adversariis in suam potestatem redactis, in annum sequentem, qui fuit restituti orbis octingentesimus duodevicesimus, ad Aquas Granenses, cum ibi hyemaret, in Majum mensem, Conventum Imperii indicit. Ubi Procerum sententia juxta leges Romanas Salicamque, Rex cum sociis omnibus & conscriis adfectatae tyrannidis, laesae majestatis reus peragitur, capitalique supplicio condemnatur. Verum Imperator nepotem vita donatum, luminibus duntaxat privari, monasterio concludi jubet: bona publicata confiscataque sunt. Episcopi deposito tribu Sacerdotum moti sunt, in coenobiaque relegati.
units.tr: In Italy Bernard, the emperor's nephew through his brother, yielding to the counsels of certain wicked advisers, blocked all approaches to Italy for his uncle and compelled all the cities to swear allegiance to him. The authors of this conspiracy were the bishops Anselm of Milan, Wolfold of Cremona and Theodulf of Orléans; the leading men of the court were Egidius, the first of the king's friends, Reginhart, the chamberlain, and Reginhar, son of Magenhar, whose grandfather Hartrad had once conspired in the Frankish part of Germany with many nobles of that region against Charlemagne. The Celts and Italians favoured Bernard; the Belgians and Germans favoured Augustus. To put down these disturbances the emperor, having gathered an army as quickly as possible from all of Germany and Gaul, hastened into Italy. Bernard, deserted by his followers, distrusting his own position, laid down his arms and surrendered to his uncle at Chalon, a city of the Aedui in Burgundy. The others followed him, and not only surrendered themselves but, without being questioned, of their own accord revealed every stratagem of this rebellion. Augustus, having brought all his adversaries into his power, summoned an assembly of the Empire for the following year, which was the eight hundred and eighteenth year of the restored world, to Aachen, where he was wintering, for the month of May. There, by the judgment of the leaders, according to Roman law and the Salic law, the king was tried together with all his associates and co-conspirators in the attempted tyranny, as guilty of treason, and was condemned to capital punishment. But the emperor, granting his nephew his life, ordered that he should only be deprived of his eyes and shut up in a monastery; his goods were made public and confiscated. The bishops, deprived of their priestly rank, were removed and relegated to monasteries.

units.la: MICHAELIS BALBI ET THEOPHI- LI IMPP. CONSTANTINOPP. EPISTOLA DE NON ADORANDIS IMAGINIBUS, AD LUDOVICUM PIUM IMPERATOREM ROMANUM, de anno Domini DCCCXXIV.
units.tr: THE LETTER OF THE EMPERORS MICHAEL AND THEOPHILUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE CONCERNING IMAGES NOT TO BE WORSHIPPED, TO LOUIS THE PIOUS, ROMAN EMPEROR, in the year of the Lord 824.

units.la: IN NOMINE PATRIS, ET FILII, ET SPIRITUS SAN- CTI, UNIUS SOLI VERI DEI.
units.tr: IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, OF THE ONE TRUE GOD ALONE.

units.la: MICHAEL & THEOPHILUS fideles in ipso Deo Imperatores Romanorum, dilecto & honorabili fratri HLUDOVVICO glorioso regi Francorum & Langobardorum & vocato corum Imperatori.
units.tr: Michael and Theophilus, emperors of the Romans, faithful in God himself, to our beloved and honourable brother Louis, glorious king of the Franks and Lombards, and so-called emperor of them.
