The duty of our office requires that the goods of the Empire, unlawfully alienated or destroyed, be recalled to the right and property of the same Empire, and to the use and advantage of us, our subjects and the commonwealth. Considering therefore that our forest and that of the aforesaid Empire at Nuremberg, laid waste by fires and clearings to the injury of us and the commonwealth, has for many past times been turned into fields or new-broken land: we therefore, under the pretext of royal favour, and on pain of forfeiting your rights and offices which you hold in that forest, strictly command you that, within a certain day to be fixed before the coming feast of All Saints, you all together and at once present yourselves in person before the Schultheiss and the Councillors at Nuremberg, and, with your hands laid on the holy relics, take a public oath that you will, by royal authority, restore to its former state, that is, to forest and trees, the said forest, which for fifty years past has been destroyed in the aforesaid manner and turned into fields, and will see that it is restored; and that you will not allow any outsiders, who have no right in the forest itself, to take or receive any usufruct of it by sale or any other means; calling upon the counsel and aid of the prudent men, our citizens of Nuremberg, concerning the above matters, if need be. Given at Heimbach, on the fourth day before the Calends of September, in the second year of our reign.

units.la: HENRICI VII. IMPER. AUG. MANDATUM
units.tr: MANDATE OF THE EMPEROR HENRY VII, AUGUSTUS

units.la: SVPER CORONATIONE REGIA REGNI LONGOBARDORVM.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE ROYAL CORONATION IN THE KINGDOM OF THE LOMBARDS.

units.la: HEnricus Dei gratia Romanorum Rex Semper-Augustus, & Rex Fiacorum & Longobardorum, Canonicis Modoezensibus, devotis suis ac dilectis, gratiam suam & omne bonum. Committimus vobis & mandamus, ut Archipresbyter cum tribus aliis senioribus, qui sciunt, quid opus sit ad collationem Coronæ ferreæ, sine ulla dilatione veniant ad nos, portantes omnia privilegia & instrumenta, quæ apud vos Modoetiæ asservantur. Et super his dabitis fidem Alardo de Rolaes, & Clecumpio de Gemule nostris Capitaneis, qui has præsentes vobis apportant. Datum Mediolani, anno secundo nostri Regni.
units.tr: Henry, by the grace of God King of the Romans, ever Augustus, and King of the Franks and Lombards, to the Canons of Monza, his devoted and beloved, greets them with his grace and every good. We commission and command you that the Archpriest, together with three other elders who know what is needed for the conferring of the Iron Crown, come to us without any delay, bringing all the privileges and documents that are kept among you at Monza. And concerning these matters you shall give credence to Alardo de Rolaes and Clecumpio de Gemule, our captains, who bring you these presents. Given at Milan, in the second year of our reign.

units.la: HENRICI VII. IMPER. AUG. EDICTUM
units.tr: EDICT OF THE EMPEROR HENRY VII AUGUSTUS

units.la: DE CORONATIONE ROMANA.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE ROMAN CORONATION.

units.la: HEnricus Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator Semper-Augustus, venerabili Abbati a Waldsassensi, Cistercien-sis Ordinis, devoto suo ac dilecto, gratiam suam & omne bonum.
units.tr: Henry, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, to his devoted and beloved Abbot of Waldsassen, of the Cistercian Order, greeting and all good.

units.la: 1. Magnus Dominus & laudabilis valde, in excelso Divinitatis suæ solio residens, Imperium suum (quod pro meritis ejus inter nationes diversas, quasi cum gentibus à suo Creatore degenerantibus, vacillabat) transfire voluit ad Romanos, ut illic præiret Imperialis excellentiæ thronus, ubi erat Sacerdotalis sedes & Apostolica auctoritas: ita quòd in eodem loco Summi Pontificis & Imperatoris auctoritas reniteret.
units.tr: 1. The great and highly praiseworthy Lord, sitting on the lofty throne of his Divinity, willed to transfer his Empire (which, on account of its merits, was wavering among the diverse nations, as though among peoples who had degenerated from their Creator) to the Romans, so that the throne of imperial excellence might take precedence there, where stood the priestly seat and apostolic authority; so that in the same place the authority of the Supreme Pontiff and of the Emperor might be upheld together.

units.la: 2. Novissimis quippe temporibus, illo translato in Germanos, postquam plures Principes ad ipsum vocatos Imperium, quorum quidam ipsius Imperii assumpsere diadema, quidam non *. divina cooperante clementia, per eos, ad quos spectat, in Romanorum Regem, futurum Imperatorem, rite & concorditer electi, proposuimus ad Urbem pro coronationis nostræ suscipiendis solenniis profectio. Ac sanctissimum in Christo Patrem, Dominum * Clementem Summum Pontificem requisivimus, ut ad Urbem accedens, præfata solennia nobis ibidem tradere dignaretur. Qui cum ex certis causis, juxta nostrum immensum desiderium interesse nequiret: ne dicta coronatio ob sui absentiam impediri valeret, venerabilibus Patribus, Dominis Arnoldo Sanctæ Sedis Apostolicæ Legato, Leonhardo Albanensi, & Nicolao Hostiensi ac Veltrensi Episcopis, ac Francisco Sanctæ Luciæ, necnon Lucæ, Sanctæ Mariæ in via Lata Diaconis Cardinalibus, commisit in hac parte plenariè vices suas, cum clausula, ut si non omnes his exequendis interesse valerent, quatuor, tres, duo, vel unus eorum, dictæ coronationis nostræ negotium expediret.
units.tr: 2. For in the most recent times, the Empire having been transferred to the Germans, after several princes had been called to it, some of whom had assumed the diadem of the Empire itself, and some had not, by the gracious clemency of God, we were duly and harmoniously elected through those to whom it belongs as King of the Romans, the future Emperor, and we resolved to set out for the City to receive the solemnities of our coronation. We asked the most holy Father in Christ, our Lord Clement, the Supreme Pontiff, to come to the City and deign to bestow upon us the aforesaid solemnities there. Since he, for certain reasons, could not be present, in accordance with our immense desire, lest the said coronation be hindered by his absence, he entrusted his office in this matter fully to the venerable Fathers, Lord Arnold, Legate of the Holy Apostolic See, Leonard, Bishop of Albano, and Nicholas, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri, and Francis of Santa Lucia, and Luca, Deacons of Santa Maria in Via Lata, Cardinals, with the proviso that if all of them could not be present to carry these things out, four, three, two, or even one of them might complete the business of our said coronation.

units.la: 3. Verum dictis Leonhardo & Francisco de hac luce subtractis, per dictos Dominos Cardinales superstites, die festo Beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum (quem ad hoc, ut poteramus, virtute dictæ commissionis elegimus) in Ecclesia sancti Joannis Lateranensis, præsente Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum, Abbatum, & aliorum Prælatorum Ecclesiasticorum Ordinum Urbis, Ducum, Comitum, Baronum, Nobilium, ac Romani populi, innumerosa caterva, oleo sacro uncti fuimus, necnon Imperiali diademate coronati, ac aliis debitis ac consuetis solenniis insigniti.
units.tr: 3. But since the said Leonard and Francis had been taken from this light, by the said surviving Lord Cardinals, on the feast day of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul (which day we chose for this purpose, as far as we could, by virtue of the said commission), in the Church of Saint John Lateran, in the presence of Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and other ecclesiastical Prelates of the Orders of the City, of Dukes, Counts, Barons, Nobles, and an innumerable throng of the Roman people, we were anointed with holy oil, and likewise crowned with the Imperial diadem, and adorned with the other due and customary solemnities.

units.la: 4. Hæc autem devotioni tuæ volumus intimare, ut de nostris felicibus successibus valeas exultare. Datum Romæ, quarto Kalendarum Julii, Regni nostri anno quarto, Imperii verò anno primo.
units.tr: 4. Now we wish to make this known to your devotion, so that you may rejoice in our happy successes. Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the fourth year of our reign, but in the first year of our Empire.

units.la: HENRICI VII. IMPER. AUG. SENTENTIA
units.tr: SENTENCE OF HENRY VII, AUGUSTUS EMPEROR

units.la: PROSCRIPTIONIS ET BANNI, LATA IN ROBERTVM SICILIAE & Apulia Regem, Imperio rebellem, Pisis in Comitiis Imperialibus.
units.tr: OF PROSCRIPTION AND BAN, PASSED AT THE IMPERIAL DIET AT PISA AGAINST ROBERT, KING OF SICILY AND APULIA, A REBEL AGAINST THE EMPIRE.

units.la: HENRICUS Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator & Semper-Augustus, ad certitudinem præsentium & memoriam futurorum.
units.tr: HENRY, by the grace of God Roman Emperor and ever-Augustus, to the certainty of the present and the memory of the future.

units.la: 1. Deus judex justus, fortis & longanimus, omnes secundum merita sua judicans, superbientem illum Spiritum, qui ante suum throni um demens se gloria & honore conspiciens, sedem suam ad Aquilonem, ut esset similis Altissimo, ponere cogitavit; de altis cœlorum fastibus ad inferiora terræ in comprobria sempiterna demergens, ipsum omni gratia & spe minimè condignè privando, duxit æternalibus ultionibus exponendum. Sicad præsens justitiam respiciat, & æquitatem videat ipse cœlestium, terrestrium, & infernorum Dominus, qui novit occulta cordium, & apud cujus tribunal omnis cessat calumnia, & veritas nullius nequitiæ tenebris obscuratur. Deponat & nunc de sede potentem, qui tentavit & acerbavit ipsum, & concitavit eum in iram: perdat eum, qui male quærit, & det illi, qui obstinato animo viam innocentiæ refugit & gloriatur in malitia, comprobrium sempiternum: faciat in eum judicium conscriptum, & sic omnibus sanctis ejus.
units.tr: 1. God, the just, strong and long-suffering judge, who judges all according to their deserts, cast down into everlasting shame from the lofty pride of heaven to the lower parts of the earth that proud spirit which, foolishly gazing on itself in glory and honour before his throne, planned to set its seat in the north, to be like the Most High. Rightly depriving it of all grace and hope, which it by no means deserved, he has consigned it to eternal punishments. So may the Lord of heaven, earth and hell, who knows the secrets of hearts, and before whose tribunal all calumny ceases and truth is not darkened by the shadows of any wickedness, now look upon justice and see equity. May he now cast down from his seat the powerful man who tempted and embittered him and provoked him to wrath; may he destroy the one who seeks evil, and give everlasting shame to him who, with an obstinate mind, flees the way of innocence and glories in malice; may he execute upon him the judgment written down, and so upon all his saints.

units.la: 2. Nequitiæ siquidem & proditionis alumnus Robertus, natus claræ memoriæ Caroli Secundi, qui se Siciliæ Regem intitulat, & Imperii Romani adipe impinguatus, incrassatus, & dilatatus contra illud (cui etiam causa feudorum multorum & bonorum ipsius Imperii, quæ hactenus tenuit, & quæ injustè principaliter occupat, humiliter obedire debet) vitiis & iniquitatibus eminens, odia, dolos & fraudes pro fidelitate retribuens, ex detestando ingratitudinis vitio calcaneum rebellionis resumpsit erigere: & contra stimulum indurata nequitia recalcitrare non cessat, nefandaque superbia tumefactus sedem ab Aquilone, hoc est, ab opposito Majestatis Cæsareæ, quam ejus Dominam & Magistram revereri & honorare tenetur, supponere satagens, ipsam convitiis & contumeliis provocavit hactenus, & continuo animo protervo continuè provocare præsumit.
units.tr: 2. Robert, the nursling of wickedness and treachery, son of Charles II of blessed memory, who styles himself King of Sicily, and who has been fattened, thickened and swollen with the fat of the Roman Empire, rises up against it, though he ought humbly to obey it, since it is the cause of the many fiefs and goods of the Empire which he has hitherto held and which he unjustly occupies chiefly for himself. Eminent in vices and iniquities, repaying hatred, deceit and fraud for fidelity, he has taken up from the detestable vice of ingratitude the heel of rebellion, and against the goad he does not cease to kick back in hardened wickedness. Puffed up with abominable pride, eager to set his seat in the north, that is, opposite the Majesty of Caesar, whom he is bound to revere and honour as his Lady and Mistress, he has provoked it with insults and affronts until now, and with a wanton mind he presumes to keep provoking it continually.

units.la: 3. Ipse namque inter ceteros suæ malignitatis conatus, licet antequàm Imperialis coronationis causa proficisceretur ad Urbem, per suas literas speciales pluries culmini nostro scripsisset, quod ipse (sicut ex causa prædicta debebat, & nos, qui nec opere nec verbo gravavimus, nec gravare sed potius gratiosè tractare intendebamus, eundem ex pravitate conscientiæ credebamus) ad exhibendam nobis debitam reverentiam & honorem, jam in dicta coronatione quàm alibi intendebat, & ad id pro viribus se parabat: confederationes tamen, conspirationes, uniones, & ligas in offensam & impedimentum processus Cæsarei, unà cum Florentinis, Lucanis, Senensibus, & aliis nostri Romani Imperii subditis per Lombardiam, & uteos in rebellionis præcipitium excitatos foveat, omne contrarium (sicut expresse dignoscitur) per se suosque procuratores, nuntios & ambaiatores, in nostræ Majestatis injuriam, & offensam & impedimentum processus Cæsarei facere procuravit & fecit. Tractavit etiam, quòd civitas Cremonæ, Parmæ, & Rhegii, quæ sub nostra obedientia consistebant, contra nos & Imperium rebellarent, inducendo tam communia ipsarum civitatum, quàm subditos nostros prædictos ad rebellionem hujusmodi, & eis ad id pollicendo auxilium, consilium, & favorem; & nihilominus dicti Roberti fuit favoribus, suæque nequitiæ consci & ministri civitatis Astensis, & castra Valenuæ, calalis sancti Evasii, & alias nonnullas civitates & castra provinciæ Lombardiæ, quæ mandata nostra juraverant, & nos in eorum Dominum recognoverant, & Officiales nostros receperant & habebant, Officialibus ipsis violenter ejectis, nequiter occupatis, & occupatas & occupata pro Roberto detinent suprascripti. Denique Robertus Johannem fratrem & stipendiarios Romam, videlicet ea intentione transmisit, ut Urbe (si posset) suæ proditioni dolosè subjecta vel saltem turbata, in ejus periculo nefandæ seditionis immissio dictæ coronationis impediret solemnia, prout dicti Johannis & stipendiariorum in ingressu nostro in Urbem prædictam, quamdiu in partibus illis moram traximus, efficaciter operum argumento probantes, unà cum copiosa subditorum dictorum multitudine, quæ per instigationem dicti Roberti submissi sibi subsidii & defensionis fiducia cum armis & equis ad opponendum se nobis & exercendum per excogitatam malitiam simul cum Johanne stipendiarisque prædictis convenit, ibidem contra nos & gentes nostras hostiliter poluerunt insidias, fecerunt insultus, spoliationes, violentias, & homicidia perpetraverunt, viasque publicas & loca, per quæ ad tendendum ad basilicam Principis Apostolorum de Urbe omnibus religionem profitentibus Christianam liber aditus patere debeat, bellicosis apparatibus claudere nobis ac gentibus nostris ad basilicam ipsam, ne ipsa coronatio celebrari valeret, accessum totis viribus prohibere, acaliàs omnimodo quo poterat Majestatem nostram offendere procuraverunt, aliæque prædictus Robertus committebat, & erat in situ contra nos committendi omnia, quæ ad nostri Imperii damnum tenderent, & ad ea modis omnibus quibus poterat nitebatur.
units.tr: 3. Indeed, among his other attempts at malice, although before he set out for the City for the imperial coronation he had written to our height several times through his special letters, saying that he himself (as for the aforesaid cause he ought to do, and as we, who had burdened him neither by deed nor word, nor intended to burden him, but rather to treat him graciously, believed him to do out of a depraved conscience) intended to render us the due reverence and honour, both at the said coronation and elsewhere, and was preparing himself for this with all his strength: nevertheless he fosters confederacies, conspiracies, unions and leagues against the offence and hindrance of the Caesarean proceedings, together with the Florentines, Lucchese, Sienese and other subjects of our Roman Empire throughout Lombardy and Tuscany, incited to the precipice of rebellion. He has caused and done, through himself and his agents, messengers and ambassadors, all the contrary things (as is clearly known), to the injury of our Majesty and to the offence and hindrance of the Caesarean proceedings. He also plotted that the cities of Cremona, Parma and Reggio, which stood under our obedience, should rebel against us and the Empire, by inducing both the commonalties of those cities and our aforesaid subjects to such rebellion, promising them aid, counsel and favour for this. Moreover, the said Robert, being an accomplice and minister of his wickedness and of their favours, holds, as the aforesaid, the city of Asti, the castle of Valenza, the castle of Sant'Evasio, and several other cities and castles of the province of Lombardy, which had sworn to obey our commands, had acknowledged us as their lord, and had received and kept our officials; our officials having been violently expelled and wickedly ousted, these places are occupied and held for Robert. Finally, Robert sent his brother John and mercenaries to Rome, with this intention: that the City, if possible, be deceitfully subjected to his treachery, or at least thrown into confusion, so that by the introduction of nefarious sedition into its danger the solemnities of the said coronation might be hindered. This the said John and the mercenaries proved effectively by their deeds when we entered the aforesaid City, during the time we stayed in those parts; together with a large multitude of the said subjects, who, at the instigation of the said Robert, with the confidence of the aid and defence sent to them, agreed with John and the aforesaid mercenaries to oppose us, with arms and horses, and to exercise their devised malice. There they laid hostile ambushes against us and our forces, made assaults, committed plunders, acts of violence and homicides, and by warlike preparations sought to close the public roads and places through which free access should be open to all professing the Christian religion, to go to the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, and with all their might they sought to prohibit our approach to that basilica, lest the coronation could be celebrated; and they strove by every means to offend our Majesty. And the aforesaid Robert was committing, and was in a position to commit against us, all those things which tend to the damage of our Empire, and he strove for them by every means he could.

units.la: 4. Hæc siquidem crescente clamore notorio, & in pluribus rerum experientia edocente, licet ipsa tam publica & notoria essent, quod nulla possent tergiversatione celari, & nos, qui subjec{ti} non sumus, contra dictum Robertum propter praemissa eo irrequisito potuissemus procedere: tamen ex Augusta clementia (quae libentius emendat in subditis poenas quam puniat; nec exercet serrum in eos, quos sanare potest mulcebris lenitas medicinae) post secessum nostrum ab Urbe praedicta, super dicto notorio & praedictis per ipsum Robertum contra nostram Majestatem commissis ad inquisitionem descendimus, quam ut fidei vel amoris scintilla (si qua forsitan remansit in eo) ipsius viscera tangeret, & ipse interim spatium ad cor redeundi haberet, usque in praesens deliberationibus rationis duximus protrahendam, Robertum praedictum citari legitime fecimus, ut comparere curaret, suam (si posset) innocentiam ostensurus. Verum idem Robertus in sua protervia perseverans, in terminis sibi ad hoc praefixis, vel eorum aliquo vel per se vel per alium comparere contumaciter non curavit. Quare nos super praemissis in ipsius Roberti contumacia fide dignis & sufficientibus receptis testibus, & eorum dictis in scriptis redactis, & per nos solenniter publicatis, & de mandato nostro a Proceribus nostri Palatii cum diligentia recenseritis, & facta nobis de ipsis & per ipsos relatione fideli, per ea, quae probata fuerunt, praedicta omnia & singula publica & notoria esse, in scriptis in verbo pronunciavimus & declaravimus exigente justitia, & postmodum eum requiri & citari sufficienter & peremptorie fecimus, ut certo termino jam elapso coram nobis (ubicunque essemus) ad hanc nostram sententiam audiendam comparere curaret. Quod ipse praescius & diffisus injuriis & offensis in sua obstinatione & contumacia & fraudibus perniciosis induratus, facere praetermisit.
units.tr: 4. These things, with a clamour growing and known to all, and taught by experience in many matters, although they were so public and notorious that they could not be concealed by any evasion, and although we, who are not subject to him, could have proceeded against the said Robert for these reasons without his being asked: nevertheless, out of imperial clemency (which prefers to correct the penalties of subjects rather than punish them, and does not wield the sword against those whom the gentle softness of medicine can heal), after our departure from the aforesaid City we undertook an inquiry into the said notorious matters and the aforesaid crimes committed by the said Robert against our Majesty. We have judged it right to protract this inquiry, by the deliberations of reason, up to the present, so that if any spark of faith or love might perhaps remain in him, it might touch his heart, and he might meanwhile have room to come back to his senses. We had the aforesaid Robert cited lawfully, that he might take care to appear, to show his innocence (if he could). But the same Robert, persisting in his wantonness, within the terms fixed for this purpose, neither in person nor through another, took no care to appear contumaciously. Therefore, concerning the aforesaid matters, in the contumacy of the same Robert, we received trustworthy and sufficient witnesses, and their statements were reduced to writing and solemnly published by us; and by our command these were carefully examined by the nobles of our Palace, and a faithful report of them was made to us. Through what was proved, we declared and pronounced in writing, in the word of justice demanding it, that all the aforesaid matters, both public and notorious, were established; and afterwards we had him sufficiently and peremptorily summoned, so that, the certain term having now elapsed, he might take care to appear before us (wherever we might be) to hear this our sentence. He, however, foreseeing it, and distrustful of his injuries and offences, hardened in his obstinacy and contumacy and pernicious frauds, neglected to do so.

units.la: {ʒ}. Quia igitur dimissis omnibus & singulis (prout apertius in inquisitione continetur) specialiter per dictos testes plenarie nobis constat, nos praedictos & alios praedicti Roberti excessus nefarios & opera detestanda maturo & justo librantes examine, ac illud notissimum nullatenus omittentes, quod ipse Robertus, dum in Urbe praedicta causa praedictae coronationis essemus, dilectissimi nostri Pisani (qui inter ceteros nostros subditos fidelitatis ac opinionis sinceritate, galeas & gentes ad nostrum servitium & honorem Romam mitteret) galeas ipsas in nostrae Majestatis injuriam invadi, spoliari, & gentes praedictas capi & incarcerari, & in carcere detineri mandavit & fecit, & nihilominus in hujusmodi continuationis terminis perseverando, mala malis addendo, & pejora continue committendo, dum contra rebelles nostros direximus signa Caesarea, rebellibus ipsis (sicut publicum & notorium est, & facti evidentia docebat & docet) misit plures armatorum in subsidium, ut eos diutius in eorum rebellionis erroribus confoveret, & attendens quod dum ipse potuit pacem & quietem habere, dum debuit tranquilliratem expectare, a nostra benevolentia & dilectione, quam sibi ex animi sinceritate paraveramus, obtinere noluit, bella quaesivit, iniquitates exercuit, & pro posse curavit, sicut etiam procurare non cessat, in Imperii populos seminare zizanias, suscitare odia, immittere scandala, concitare tumultus, nutrire schismata, & fovere discordias, & sine intermissione in actu committendi continuandique quod potest, contra Imperium nostrum non omisit, non solum in nostri Imperii contemptum Reique publicae detrimentum, sed etiam in perturbationem prosperitatis Ecclesiasticae, quae ad Imperii statum plurimum dignoscitur tendere, & in retardationem negotii Terrae Sanctae, ad quod (teste Deo, qui omnia novit) totis cordibus & affectibus anhelamus, & videntes aperte, quod dictus Robertus irrevocabiliter in signum erroris prolapsus, & obstinatus in dolis, verum veritatis expiavit omnino, & tanquam aspis surda non obtinens auditum, nec mandata nostra, necnon gis poenam, in quam suis culpis [nam omne, quod est ex Deo, vincit mundum; & haec est victoria, qua vincit mundum fides nostra, omni cura custodias cor tuum: nam ab ipso vita procedit, Proverb. cap. 11.] incidisse ac incidere noscitur, nec etiam Imperatoriae plenitudinem potestatis veretur, sed quotidie certivicis durioris efficitur; & quantum ipsum ad poenitudinem expectamus, tanto majorem assumit audaciam malignandi: considerantes etiam, quod ipse Robertus de Imperii crapulatus pingue dine dilatatur, & ex illicitis sibi laxatis habenis furit, & nobis pro obedientia rebellionem, & pro fidelitate debito injurias refert, nosque ac quosque fideles Imperii nobis obedientes pro posse impugnare conatur, ejusque poenas non in aedificationem sed in destructionem, non ad fructum & juvamen ut haberet, sed ad pestem esse dignoscitur: & volentes praemissis injuriis & ipsius fraudibus obviare, & Evangelicam sequi doctrinam, quae nos monet, quod omnis arbor, quae fructum non facit bonum, abscindatur & mittatur in ignem, licet fideles Reges & Principes in suorum dignitatis eminentiam libenter condignis honoribus, & gratiosis favoribus prosequamur, tame ut culpa supplicium timeat, & virtus retributionem expectet, Robertum praedictum, cujus eligimus domare superbiam, & praesumptionem erectam conterere, ipsumque a statu suo quantumcunque sublimi deponere, cum propter praemissa Majestatis criminis reus sit, universis & singulis dignitatibus quocumque titulo comprehensis, quibus se intitulat & decorat, auctoritatibus, honoribus, libertatibus, immunitatibus, & privilegiis, Provinciis, Comitatibus, civitatibus, castris, terris, villis, & aliis feudis, vasallis, bonis, redditibus, juribus, & jurisdictionibus universis tam perpetuis quam temporalibus, quos, quas, & quae habet, tenet, & possidet, vel quasi, seu habuerunt & possiderunt hactenus ejus quomodolibet ipse vel sui praedecessores, privamus: eundem Robertum rebellum, proditorem, & hostem Imperii, dictaque Majestatis crimine reum, de toto praedicto Imperio exbannimus & diffidamus: ipsum li quo tempore in nostram & Imperii fortiam pervenerit, vita per capitis mutilationem privandum in hisce scriptis sententialiter condemnamus.
units.tr: {ʒ}. Since, therefore, with all and each of the charges dismissed (as is set out more openly in the inquiry), it is fully established against this Robert through the said witnesses, we, weighing with mature and just examination the wicked excesses and detestable deeds of the aforesaid Robert and of others, and not omitting that very notorious fact: that while we were in the aforesaid city on account of the aforesaid coronation, Robert ordered and caused our most beloved Pisans (who, above the rest of our subjects, in the sincerity of their loyalty and devotion, had sent galleys and men to Rome for our service and honour) to be attacked and their galleys seized, and the said men to be taken, imprisoned and held in prison, to the injury of our Majesty; and furthermore, persevering in this course of continued offence, adding evils to evils and continually committing worse ones, when we had sent our imperial standards against our rebels, he sent several armed men to those rebels as reinforcements (as is public and notorious, and as the evidence of the deed showed and shows), so that he might keep them longer in the errors of their rebellion; and considering that, while he could have peace and quiet, while he ought to have waited for tranquillity, he was unwilling to obtain our goodwill and affection, which we had prepared for him in all sincerity of mind, but sought wars and practised iniquities, and, so far as he could, took care (as he does not cease to do) to sow tares among the peoples of the Empire, to stir up hatreds, to bring on scandals, to rouse tumults, to nourish schisms and foster discords, and without intermission, in act, he has not ceased to commit and continue whatever he can against our Empire, not only to the contempt of our Empire and the detriment of the commonwealth, but also to the disturbance of the prosperity of the Church, which is well known to tend greatly to the welfare of the Empire, and to the hindrance of the business of the Holy Land, for which (God, who knows all things, is witness) we long with all our hearts and affections; and seeing clearly that the said Robert, having irrevocably fallen into the sign of error and being obstinate in his deceits, has wholly abandoned the truth of truth, and like a deaf asp that does not hear, has neither heeded our commands, nor feared the punishment into which he is known to have fallen and to be falling by his own faults [for everything that is of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory by which our faith overcomes the world: guard your heart with all care, for from it flows life, Proverbs ch. 11], nor does he fear the fullness of imperial power, but every day becomes harder in his stubbornness; and the more we wait for his repentance, the greater the boldness with which he takes up malice: considering also that this Robert is swollen with fat from the grease of the Empire, and rages with the reins of illicit licence loosed upon him, and repays us with rebellion for obedience and with injuries for the loyalty that is owed, and strives to assail us and all the faithful of the Empire who obey us, as far as he can, and is known to make use of his power not for building up but for destruction, not to bear fruit and help, but for ruin: and wishing to meet the aforesaid injuries and his deceits, and to follow the Evangelical doctrine, which warns us that every tree that does not bear good fruit should be cut down and cast into the fire; although we gladly honour faithful kings and princes, in keeping with the eminence of their dignity, with fitting honours and gracious favours, yet so that guilt may fear punishment and virtue may look for reward: we deprive the aforesaid Robert, whose pride we choose to tame and whose raised presumption we choose to crush, and whom we choose to depose from his state, however lofty, since by reason of the aforesaid he is guilty of the crime of majesty, of all and each of the dignities, under whatever title, by which he styles and adorns himself, and of the authorities, honours, liberties, immunities and privileges, provinces, counties, cities, castles, lands, villages and other fiefs, vassals, goods, revenues, rights and jurisdictions, all, both perpetual and temporary, which he, or his predecessors, have in any way had, hold and possess, or as if they have had and possessed hitherto; we declare the same Robert a rebel, traitor and enemy of the Empire, and guilty of the said crime against majesty, and we put him under the ban and outlaw him from the whole aforesaid Empire; and at whatever time he shall come into our power or that of the Empire, we condemn him in these writings by sentence to be deprived of life by beheading.

units.la: 6. Statuentes & mandantes, quod nulla persona cujuscumque nobilitatis, excellentiae, status, vel conditionis existat, nullaque civitas, castrum, villa, vel universitas eidem contra nos & Imperium praebeat publice vel occulte, consilium, auxilium, vel favorem, sub poena centum librarum auri, pro qualibet
units.tr: 6. We decree and command that no person of whatever nobility, eminence, rank or condition, and no city, castle, village or community, shall give to the same man, publicly or secretly, against us and the Empire, counsel, aid or favour, under penalty of one hundred pounds of gold, to be exacted for each

units.la: {y} Inclusa videtur spuria & ab hoc loco aliena. Proverb. 11.
units.tr: {y} The enclosed passage seems spurious and foreign to this place. Proverbs 11.

units.la: Matth. 5. v. 7. Luc. 3. v. 9. libet civitate libras quinquaginta, pro quolibet castro, villa, Marchione, Duce, Comite, Barone, & quolibet Nobili viginti libratum auri, & pro qualibet alia singulari persona, pro vice qualibet qua co‑‑‑‑ti fecerint, committenda: quodque cuilibet liceat impune cives, incolas, habitatores civitatum, castrorum, villarum, & quibuslibet alias singulares personas, cujuscumque status vel conditionis existant, quae contra nostrum honorem obediant ei, vel darent consilium, auxilium, vel favorem, publice vel occulte offendere in persona, rebus, & juribus, & ipsos & ea capere, & arrestare, & retinere: inhibentes etiam & praecipientes expresse, ne aliqui debitores ipsius Roberti de bonis, in quibus ei tenentur in aliquo satisfaciat, vel reddere quomodolibet praesumant, vel alioquin tantundem Camerae nostrae persolvant.
units.tr: Matthew 5:7. Luke 3:9. city fifty pounds, for each castle, village, marquis, duke, count, baron, and each noble twenty pounds of gold, and for each other single person, for each time they shall have done so; and that anyone may freely attack and seize, arrest and hold the citizens, inhabitants, residents of cities, castles, villages, and any other individuals, of whatever rank or condition they may be, who obey him against our honour or give him counsel, aid or favour, publicly or secretly, in their persons, goods and rights: we also expressly forbid and order that none of Robert's debtors presume in any way to pay or hand over to him anything from the goods in which they are bound to him, or otherwise pay the equivalent sum to our Treasury.

units.la: 7. Ad haec sine strepitu & figura judicii compellantur universitates & provincias nostras, civitates, villas, & singulares personas cujuscumque praeminentiae vel excellentiae, etiamsi Regia dignitate, vel cujuscumque alterius dignitatis, conditionis, vel status existant, quae ex aliquo pacto vel promissione seu obligatione dicto Roberto, aut praedecessores sui facto, pacto vel poena, sub qualicumque forma comprehenso, vel comprehensi sint ratione, causa, vel titulo, & specialiter de aliquo servitio faciendo, vel hominum armatorum aliudque subsidium dando, per mare vel per terram, teneretur eidem Roberto, ab ipsis pacto, promissione, obligatione & poena apposita, vasallos quoque & feudatarios, & omnes & singulos, qui eidem fidelitatis vinculo vel alia quacumque ratione vel causa ad aliqua servitia realia vel personalia tenerentur, ab omni articulo fidelitatis, subjectionis, & obedientiae ei vel suis haeredibus faciendis absolvimus penitus & in totum: ita quod nec civitates, castra, villae, universitates, & personae praedictae pacto vel obligatione praedictorum, aut vasalli, aut feudatarii, praefati cives, fidelitatis, subjectionis, & obedientiae ratione, causa vel titulo sibi vel suis haeredibus quomodolibet teneantur. Ipsas etiam contractas, civitates, castra, villas, feudatarios, vasallos, bona, res, jurisdictiones, servitia, & jura, & quaecumque alia sub nostra contenta privatione & absolutione hujusmodi, comilcamus.
units.tr: 7. Moreover, without noise or the form of judicial process, the communities, provinces, cities, villages and individual persons of whatever eminence or excellence, even if they hold royal dignity or any other dignity, condition or status, who by any pact, promise or obligation made with the said Robert or his predecessors, under whatever form, penalty or pact, are or have been bound to the same Robert by reason, cause or title, and especially to perform some service or to give armed men or other aid by sea or by land, we entirely and wholly absolve from that pact, promise, obligation and penalty agreed upon; likewise we absolve from every article of fidelity, subjection and obedience to be rendered to him or his heirs all vassals and feudatories, and all and each of those who were bound to the same by the bond of fidelity or by any other reason or cause to real or personal services: so that neither the cities, castles, villages, communities and persons aforesaid, nor the vassals or feudatories, nor the citizens, are in any way bound to him or to his heirs by reason, cause or title of the aforesaid pact or obligation, or of fidelity, subjection and obedience. We also confiscate the said cities, castles, villages, feudatories, vassals, goods, property, jurisdictions, services and rights, and whatever else is contained under our deprivation and absolution of this kind.

units.la: 8. Demum omnibus & singulis Militibus, Auditoribus, Judicibus, Jureperitis, & Notariis, qui ejusdem Roberti domestici seu familiares existunt, sive aliis, qui in ejus servitio esse noscuntur, & quibusvis aliis, districte praecipiendo mandamus, quod ab ipsius Roberti familiaritate, consiliis, directione, & obsequiis quibuscumque infra duorum mensium spatium ab hodie computandum cum effectu recedant, & nunquam ad ejus servitium vel consilium accedere publice vel occulte praesumant: alioqui ipsos Milites honore ac dignitate militiae, Judices ac Jureperitos judicandi & assidendi omnibus & singulis privilegiis & immunitatibus, ac Notarios notariatus officio: eos videlicet ex dictis Militibus, Auditoribus, Judicibus, Jureperitis, Notariis, qui hujusmodi mandato nostro non paruerint cum effectu, exnunc prout extunc privamus termino suprascripto, & inhabiles & infames reddimus, ita quod elapsis mensibus supradictis ad nullos actus legitimos quocunque tempore postmodum admittatur.
units.tr: 8. Finally, to all and each of the knights, auditors, judges, jurists and notaries who are domestics or familiars of the same Robert, or to others who are known to be in his service, and to all others, we strictly command that within two months from today they withdraw effectively from the familiarity, counsel, direction and all services of the said Robert, and that they never presume to come to his service or counsel, publicly or secretly; otherwise we deprive those knights of the honour and dignity of knighthood, the judges and jurists of the right to judge and sit in judgement, with all privileges and immunities, and the notaries of the office of notary, namely those of the said knights, auditors, judges, jurists and notaries who shall not have effectively obeyed this our command, from now, as from then, at the aforesaid term; and we render them incapable and infamous, so that after the aforesaid two months they are admitted to no lawful acts at any time afterwards.

units.la: 9. Hujusmodi autem privationis, confiscationis, exbannitionis, diffidationis, condemnationis, & absolutionis sententias in his scriptis fecimus, & omnia alia singula facta & incerta facimus existente justitia, & bono Reipubl. requirente, ac ex certa scientia & plenitudine potestatis, supplentes omnem defectum, si quis forsan in inquisitione praedicta, de quibuscumque processibus propterea habitis ob aliquam juris solemnitatem omissam esset habitus, non obstantibus aliquibus legibus, constitutionibus contrariis, vel privilegiis sub quacumque forma verborum concessis: etiamsi de ipsis oporteret de verbo ad verbum in praesentibus fieri mentionem, quae contra praemissa vel praemissorum aliquod posse quomodolibet obiici non opponi, quibus specialiter derogamus:
units.tr: 9. We have made these sentences of deprivation, confiscation, outlawry, diffidation, condemnation and absolution in these writings, and we make all other individual acts and things done, the justice of the matter existing and the good of the commonwealth requiring it, and from certain knowledge and fullness of power, supplying every defect, if perhaps in the aforesaid inquiry, any proceedings held on account of some omitted legal formality should have been held; notwithstanding any contrary laws, constitutions, or privileges granted under any form of words, even if mention of them ought to be made word for word in these presents; whatever may be objected or opposed in any way against the foregoing or any part of them, we specifically derogate from.

units.la: Actum Pilis in praesentia nostrorum Principum & Baronum, ac populi multitudine copiosa, VII. Calend. Maii, regni nostri anno quinto, Imperii vero anno primo, quod fuit MCCCXI.
units.tr: Done at Pilsen in the presence of our princes and barons, and a copious multitude of the people, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth year of our reign and the first year of our empire, which was 1311.

units.la: HENRICI VII. IMPER. AUG. C- ONSTITUTIO DE OFFICIO SCULTETI IN CIVITATE IMPERIALI, ET DE privilegiis Civium.
units.tr: Constitution of Henry VII, Emperor Augustus, concerning the office of the Sculteus in the Imperial city, and concerning the privileges of the citizens.

units.la: HENRICUS Septimus divina favente clementia Romanorum Imperator Semper-Augustus, universis sacri Romani Imperii fidelibus praesentes literas inspecturis, gratiam suam & omne bonum. Dum profectus & commoda fidelium nostrorum debitae solicitudinis studio procuramus, decus & honorem Imperii multipliciter attollimus, & subjectorum obsequia nostris Imperialibus beneplacitis efficimus promptiora. Disponentes igitur affectu benevolo, dilectorum fideliū nostrorum Civium Nurembergensium, quantum digne possumus, votivis supplicationibus benignum praebere consensum, infrascriptos articulos specialiter, quo ad eorum Civium & Civitatis Nurembergensis commoditates agendas, statuimus observandos.
units.tr: Henry VII, by the favour of divine clemency, Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, to all the faithful of the Holy Roman Empire who shall see these present letters, greeting and all good. As we promote the progress and advantage of our faithful subjects with due care, we raise the glory and honour of the Empire in many ways, and make the obedience of our subjects more ready to our Imperial pleasure. Therefore, moved by a kindly disposition, and as far as we rightly can, granting the humble petitions of our beloved faithful citizens of Nuremberg, we decree that the articles set out below be observed, specifically for the advantage of those citizens and of the city of Nuremberg.

units.la: 1. In primis videlicet, quod Sculteus Nurembergensis, qui pro tempore fuerit, stratas communes vel Regias vulgariter appellatas defendere, ac pet eas secure conducere debeat quoslibet transeuntes.
units.tr: 1. First of all, that the Sculteus of Nuremberg, whoever he may be at the time, shall defend the common or royal roads, as they are commonly called, and shall safely escort through them whoever passes.

units.la: 2. Sculteto etiam Nurembergensi & Civibus liceat sub forma juris, in concivem eorum recipere quemlibet requirentem.
units.tr: 2. The Sculteus and the citizens of Nuremberg shall also be permitted, under the form of law, to receive into their fellowship as a citizen anyone who asks.

units.la: 3. Insuper Sculletus Nurembergensis semel quolibet anno coram Consulibus Civitatis eiusdem juramentum praester, de faciendo judicium æquanimiter tam pauperibus quàm divitibus, secundum rationabilem Scabinorum sententiam.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, the Sculteus of Nuremberg shall once a year take an oath before the Consuls of that city, to administer justice evenly to the poor as to the rich, according to the reasoned judgment of the Scabini.

units.la: 4. Item Sculretus Civitatis prædictæ quemlibet civem ipsius detentum debeat excredere sub dejusoria cautione, ac de eo judicare secundum justam & rationabilem sententiam Scabinorum atrocitas facti seu causa detentionis ipsius aliud exigar & requirat.
units.tr: 4. Likewise, the Sculteus of the aforesaid city shall release any citizen of that city who has been detained, under a sworn surety; and he shall judge concerning him according to the just and reasoned judgment of the Scabini, unless the gravity of the deed or the cause of the detention requires otherwise.

units.la: 5. Cæterum quòd omnes utriusque sexus homines dictæ Civitatis Nurmbergensis trahi non possint in causis civilibus ad aliena judicia: sed convenire debeant coram Judice suo, dummodo illo querulantibus justitia non negetur.
units.tr: 5. Furthermore, all men of either sex of the said city of Nuremberg may not be dragged into civil cases before foreign courts; but they shall answer before their own judge, provided that justice is not denied to those who complain there.

units.la: 6. Quicquid etiam Consules & Scabini Civitatis Nurembergensis prædictæ, sub juramento prestito, pro pace ac moderatione rerum venalium intra civitatem eandem statuerint, tam ab civibus quàm à civibus observetur.
units.tr: 6. Whatever the Consuls and Scabini of the aforesaid city of Nuremberg, under oath, shall decide for the peace and regulation of saleable goods within the same city, shall be observed by the citizens and by all others alike.

units.la: 7. Castrum verò & turris in medio ejus sita, à Civitate Nurembergensi in tantum alienari non debent, quin Castellanus & possessor eorum ipsis civibus cautionem faciat, quod decederit tore vel Rege Romano ipsum castrum & turris prædicta, ad gubernandum ea, usque ad creationem, devolvatur ad eos.
units.tr: 7. The castle and the tower situated in the middle of it shall not be alienated from the city of Nuremberg in such a way that the castellan and possessor of them does not give the citizens security that, should the Emperor or the King of the Romans die, the aforesaid castle and tower shall pass to them, to be governed by them until the creation of a new king.

units.la: 8. Quodque Norarius Judicii Provincialis à civitate prædicta non alienetur: sed ibidem reliquam faciat, & Sculteto Norimbergensi obediat pariter & intendat.
units.tr: 8. The notary of the Provincial Court shall not be alienated from the aforesaid city; but he shall remain there and likewise obey and attend to the Sculteus of Nuremberg.

units.la: 9. Nemo etiam sententiam in Judicio Provinciali promulget, nisi Milites vel Honestiati dictæ Civitatis Nurembergensis existant.
units.tr: 9. Nor shall anyone pronounce sentence in the Provincial Court unless he is a knight or one of the honourable men of the said city of Nuremberg.

units.la: 10. Demùm quòd universi & singuli Cives Nurembergenses, & eorum bona, à relocatione pedagiorum solutione eximantur in civitatibus & locis singulis, quorum cives etiam & bona verso apud Civitatem Nurembergensem fuerunt & hactenus exempti pariter & exempta.
units.tr: 10. Lastly, that all and each of the citizens of Nuremberg, and their goods, be exempted from the payment of tolls levied anew in individual cities and places, just as their citizens and goods have hitherto been exempt in the city of Nuremberg, and likewise the places where they are exempt.

units.la: 11. Præmissos autem articulos omnes de speciali gratia & Imperialis plenitudine potestatis, vorem & utilitatem Civium Nurembergensium prædictorum, renore præsentium statuimus, & inviolabiliter ab omnibus observari mandamus; firmirer inhibentes, ne quis ipsos cives in prædicta eorum aliquem, contra præsentis paginæ nostræ renorem, impedire, molestare, vel gravare praesumat. Quod qui secus facere præsumpserit, indigna nostram, & pœnam cœrum librarum aut marcarum medietas Camerae nostræ, reliqua verò passis injuriam persolvarur, se noverit incurrisse. Datum Pisis, III. Idus Junii, Indictione XI. Anno Domini millesimo trecentesimo tertiodecimo: Regni nostri anno quinto, Imperii verò primo.
units.tr: 11. We decree, by special grace and the fullness of Imperial power, that all the aforesaid articles are for the honour and advantage of the aforesaid citizens of Nuremberg, by the tenor of these present letters; and we command that they be inviolably observed by all. We firmly forbid anyone to presume to hinder, molest or burden those citizens in any of the aforesaid matters, contrary to the tenor of this our present document. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall know that he has incurred our displeasure and a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold or silver marks, half to go to our Chamber and the remainder to the injured parties. Given at Pisa, on the third day before the Ides of June, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of our Lord 1313, in the fifth year of our reign and the first of our empire.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMP. AUG. RESCRIPTUM
units.tr: Rescript of Emperor Louis IV, August

units.la: Anno Christi 1315.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1315.

units.la: QVO CIVITATES HELVETICAE AD INSTANTIAM ABBATIS Eremi & Leopoldi Ducis Austriae à Judicio Rotuilensi proscriptae, & ab Episcopo Constantiensi excommunicatae fuerunt, auctoritate Imperiali absolvuntur, & Imperii societati priorum, cœtibus restituuntur.
units.tr: Whereby the Swiss cities, proscribed by the Court of Rottweil at the instance of the Abbot of Einsiedeln and of Leopold, Duke of Austria, and excommunicated by the Bishop of Constance, are absolved by imperial authority and restored to the fellowship and community of the Empire.

units.la: Ludovicus Dei gratia Romanorum Rex Semper Augustus, Prudentibus viris Undervvald, Urach, & in Suitz, fidelibus suis dilectis gratiam suam & omne bonum.
units.tr: Louis, by the grace of God Roman King, ever August, to the prudent men of Unterwalden, Uri, and Schwyz, his faithful and beloved subjects, his grace and every good.

units.la: 1. Majestatem noveritis Regiam adversitatibus vestris ex animo condolere. Verum annuente Altissimo, speramus vestris doloribus brevi in tempore per nos remedia salubria celeberrima. Unde tanquam viri constantissimi adversariorum comminationibus, non finitis animos vestros qualiter demulceri.
units.tr: 1. You should know that Our Majesty sympathises sincerely with your adversities. But, with the Most High granting it, we hope that by Our means salutary and very famous remedies for your sorrows will come in a short time. Wherefore, as men most steadfast, do not let your minds be softened by the threats of your adversaries.

units.la: 2. Præterea, ut ex scriptis vestris collegimus, vos ex parte cujusdam Abbatis, dicti de Einsidlen proscriptionis sententias pervenisse, à quibus vos præsentibus absolvimus, restituentes personas vestras in statum pristinæ libertatis.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, as we have gathered from your writings, you have received sentences of proscription at the instance of a certain Abbot, called of Einsiedeln, from which sentences We now absolve you, restoring your persons to the state of your former liberty.

units.la: 3. Adhæc de sententiis excommunicationum in vos latis Venerabilis Petrus Archiepiscopus Moguntinensis, Princeps noster dilectus, absolutionem committendam Decanis & Rectoribus Ecclesiarum vestrarum vobis veraciter repromisit, & se eisdem velle suas dirigere litteras authorizatas patentes.
units.tr: 3. Furthermore, concerning the sentences of excommunication pronounced against you, the venerable Peter, Archbishop of Mainz, our beloved Prince, has truly promised you that the absolution is to be entrusted to the Deans and Rectors of your churches, and that he himself wishes to send his authorised open letters to them.

units.la: 4. Et securos vos reddimus, quòd omnibus Advocatis & fautoribus nostris, tum Nobilibus, Civitarensibus, vos defensare & coadjuvare præcipimus & monemus, quotiens & quandocunque vos fuerint requisiti. Datum in Nurenberg. VIII. Kal. Junij, Regni nostri anno primo.
units.tr: 4. And we render you secure, since we command and admonish all Our advocates and supporters, both nobles and citizens, to defend and assist you whenever and as often as you shall be called upon. Given at Nuremberg, the 8th day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of Our reign.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. EDICTUM
units.tr: EDICT OF LUDWIG IV, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS

units.la: DE FIDELIBUS IMPERII CONTRA TYRANNIDEM PAPAE RO- MANI & Regis Gallorum tutandis ac defendendis.
units.tr: On protecting and defending the faithful of the Empire against the tyranny of the Roman Pope and the King of the French.

units.la: Ludovicus, quòd sacramento rogatus, religione jurisjurandi adactus esset, se Majestatem Imperii, Reipublicæque nunquam defuturum; inopibus contra fas, præter æquum armis affliget, ad populum. ad populi Germani libertatem confugientibus, quos sine maximo scelere deserere non posset, Italiae Tetrarchas vi Pontificiaque servitute & Philippi Valesii copiis oppressos, Caesareis auspiciis suppetias ferre, vim vi repellere, jure gentium imperat.
units.tr: Ludwig, bound by the sanctity of an oath and by the obligation of his sworn word, declares that he will never fail the majesty of the Empire and the commonwealth. To the people, he declares by the law of nations that he will not, without the greatest wickedness, abandon those who have fled to the liberty of the German people against right and beyond what is fair, and that, under Caesar's auspices, he will bring aid to the Italian tetrarchs who are oppressed by force, by Papal servitude and by the forces of Philip of Valois, and will repel force with force.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. EDICTUM CONTRA INIVSTAM EXCOMMVNICATIONEM PAPAE Joannis XXII.
units.tr: EDICT OF LUDWIG IV, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS, AGAINST THE UNJUST EXCOMMUNICATION BY POPE JOHN XXII

units.la: NOs Ludovicus Romanorum Rex, proponimus adversus Joannem, qui se dicit esse Papam, quòd Christi *testamentum de pace male exequitur, publicam Christianitatis pacem perturbans: nec reminiscitur à sancto Constantino id, quicquid nunc habet, honoris latitanti Silvestro permissum, male gratus Romano Imperio: unde delumpsit omnem, quo nunc abutitur, splendorem, &c.
units.tr: We, Ludwig, King of the Romans, declare against John, who calls himself Pope, that he badly carries out Christ's testament of peace, disturbing the public peace of Christendom. Nor does he remember that whatever honour he now holds, granted by the holy Constantine to the hidden Silvester, was ungratefully repaid to the Roman Empire, and that from it he has drawn all the splendour he now abuses, etc.

units.la: DECRETUM COMITIORUM RATISPONEN- SIUM DE JURIBUS REGNI ET IMPERII CONSERVANDIS ADVERSUS INIQUAS USURPATIONES Papae Romani.
units.tr: DECREE OF THE DIET OF REGENSBURG CONCERNING THE PRESERVATION OF THE RIGHTS OF THE KINGDOM AND EMPIRE AGAINST THE UNJUST USURPATIONS OF THE ROMAN POPE.

units.la: ANno Domini MCCCXXIV. quinto Idus Augusti, Reginoburgii praesentibus Balduino Treverensi, Henrico Agrippinensi, Mathiae Moguntino Archimystis, Joanne Rege Boiemiae, caeterisque Germaniae ac Galliae Episcopis & Proceribus, in conventu per Imperatorem acto factum est Senatusconsultum, ut Caesar operam det, ne Germana libertas in servitutem redigatur, & Majestas Imperii à faucibus Tyranni Romani eripiatur.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1324, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, at Regensburg, in the presence of Baldwin of Trier, Henry of Cologne, Matthias of Mainz, Archbishops, John King of Bohemia, and the other bishops and nobles of Germany and Gaul, at an assembly held by the Emperor, it was enacted by senatorial decree that Caesar should take care that German liberty not be reduced to slavery, and that the majesty of the Empire be snatched from the jaws of the Roman tyrant.

units.la: 2. Ex Consilii itaque decreto vana irritaque esse Joannis XXII. acta declaratum; quicunque ea tuerentur, hostem Reipublicae, bona ejus publica esse, placuit.
units.tr: 2. Accordingly, by decree of the Council, it was declared that the acts of John XXII were vain and void; and it was resolved that whoever defended them should be an enemy of the commonwealth, and his public goods forfeit.

units.la: 3. Otto Charionum Antistes D. Lamperti, & Tolosanus Monachus Dominicanus, sedis Romanae Legati, Germaniâ edicto extrusi sunt.
units.tr: 3. Otto, prior of Charions, and the Dominican monk of Tolosa, legates of the Roman See, were expelled from Germany by edict.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. EDICTUM
units.tr: Edict of Ludwig IV, Emperor Augustus

units.la: PUBLICE CONTRA JOHANNEM XXII. PAPAM ROMANUM IN CO- MITIIS propositum Ratisponae, & oppidatim affixum, concernens jura Regni & Imperii.
units.tr: Published publicly against Pope John XXII, Roman Pope, at the Diet of Regensburg and posted up town by town, concerning the rights of the Kingdom and the Empire.

units.la: CHristus Servator, Dominus atq; Deus noster, ejus legati primarii, Petrus, Paulus, Jacobus, Joannes, tempora periculosa, ubi ad coelum migrarunt, nobis imminere canta-runt, & in primis admonuerunt, ut summopere atque anguium in morem astuti, decreta Pharisaeorum, PseudoChristos, Pseudoprophetas, Pseudoapostolos, à mendacio simulatae religionis ita appellatos, vitarent. Qui se Mystas Christi ferunt, cum sint nuncii Antichristi. Eos inexplebilis honoris, potentiae, pecuniae, atque luxus, avaritia, fastus, quae in proverbium venere, produnt. Non imus inficias, a infor. ingennue. Fatemur, tempora nostra censuram non ferunt. Jampridem corruptus moribus simplicitas Christianorum sptecula coelitus positi tacere non possumus: ne canes muti, juxta Vatem latrare non possunt, simus. Et si lupos pelle ovina tectos abigere ob infelicitatem temporum valemus, resistere tamen, hujuscemodique prodere, munus nostrum est. Quamvis tantundem, ut vellem, non possumus, tamen non assequutus voluisse, abunde pulchrum atque magnificum.
units.tr: Christ our Saviour, Lord and God, and his chief legates, Peter, Paul, James and John, foretold dangerous times, when they had departed to heaven, and above all warned us that we should, like crafty serpents, avoid with the greatest care the decrees of the Pharisees, the false Christs, the false prophets and the false apostles, so called from the lie of a feigned religion. They claim to be initiates of Christ, but they are messengers of Antichrist. Their insatiable greed for honour, power, money and luxury, and their arrogance, which have become proverbial, betray them. We do not deny it; we confess it frankly. Our times do not bear criticism. The simplicity of Christians, long ago corrupted in its morals, cannot be silent, being placed as a watchman from heaven; lest we be like dumb dogs which, as the prophet says, cannot bark. And although we cannot drive off the wolves hidden in sheep's clothing, owing to the unhappiness of the times, it is nonetheless our duty to resist and to expose such men. Although we cannot do as much as we would wish, it is quite a fine and noble thing to have wished to do it.

units.la: 3. Ut rem in pauca conferam, nec diutius ambagibus immorer, circuitioneque utar, remq; aperte dicam. Joannes ille, qui se Papam Vicesimum secundum nuncupat, qualis sit, oviculis Christi beneficio operae pretium est agnoscere, ne deceptae pelle ovina a saevissimo lupo devorentur. Nempe sanguinem Christianorum sitit, discordiae, seditionum mala ubique gentium inter Christianos serit. In Germania & Italia, literis, pollicitationibus, auro, Principes, Tetrarchas, Episcopos, Sacerdotes, Monachos, Cives corrumpere nititur, inducit, sollicitat, ad arma vocat. Adversus divinam providentiam, supremam coeli majestatem, unde omnis potestas exstitit, contra charitatem Christianam fratres in fratres armat, praecipit, ut Christiani mutuum affectum & amorem, quem solum Pater immortalis à nobis exigit, exuant, atma corripiant, atque ut sua viscera vertant, fidem frangant, pacta dissolvant, invicem fraudent, decipiant, imponant, a sacrosancto Imperio deficiant, rebelliones, conspirationem, caedes, incendia, stupra faciant. Nec licet per hunc Antichristum Christianis pacem à Deo datam servare. Tanta est hominis, vel potius Sathanae illius vaecordia, publicè proconscientia scelera sua quasi benefacta praedicat: Cum Christiani, inquit, Principes inter se dissentiant, tum vere Romani
units.tr: 3. To come to the point briefly, and not to linger longer in circumlocutions, I will state the matter openly. That John, who calls himself the twenty-second Pope, is worth knowing about, by the favour of Christ, so that his sheep, deceived by his sheep's clothing, may not be devoured by the most savage wolf. He thirsts indeed for the blood of Christians, and everywhere among the nations he sows the evils of discord and sedition among Christians. In Germany and Italy he tries, leads on and entices, by letters, promises and gold, to corrupt princes, tetrarchs, bishops, priests, monks and citizens, and calls them to arms. Against the divine providence and the supreme majesty of heaven, from whom all power has come, and against Christian charity, he arms brother against brother, and commands Christians to put off the mutual affection and love which the immortal Father alone requires of us, to take up arms, to turn against their own bowels, to break faith, to dissolve treaties, to defraud, deceive and impose upon one another, to fall away from the most holy Empire, and to commit rebellions, conspiracies, murders, arson and rapes. Nor is it lawful for Christians to keep the peace given by God through this Antichrist. Such is the madness of this man, or rather of that Satan, that he publicly proclaims his crimes as if they were good deeds: When Christian princes, he says, disagree among themselves, then truly the Romans are...

units.la: E e manus Sacerdos est. Pontifex Maximus denique regnat, denique dominatur, ubi omnibus discordia, seditione, mutua odio debilitatis formidolosa fit ejus potestas, universi ejus nutui obsequuntur, & vel screatus observant. Seditio atque discordia Germanorum, salus est Romanorum Pontificum. Proinde pro viribus enitendum est Pontifici Maximo, si ita esse velit, ut anguem serpentem, hoc est, Alemannorum Imperium conterat, in cineres atque favillas redigat. Itaque pro-ditat, sua opera effectum esse, ut nullus neque Romae neque in Italia ultra sit, qui Imperii rebus vel faveat, vel studeat. Et profecto ejus fraude duo rebus impositi sumus, quos ut vel una quidem litera (cum tamen undique aurifugae atque vultures sui circumvolitarent, templa, fana, sacras aedes compilarent) in gratiam redigeret, aut ut jure potius, vel apud se, quam armis disceptare hortaretur: tamen abfuit, ut nos ultro ad bellum civile concitaret. Nullam operam dedit, ut inter nos pacem conciliaret, imo magis discordiam aluit, modo mihi, modo Austriaco stndebat: nunc Friderico, nunc Dovico favere se simulabat, ut quisque imbecilliot erat, ita magis huic operam suam polliceba-tur. Ad consecrationem ultro invitabat, per fallaciam utrisque verba dedit, & pronos ad concordiam rursus arma sumere petsuasit. Attu haec omnia egit, ut interea dum domesticis armis, cognatis mutuo sese cocsumerimus, Imperium pessundaret, labefactaret, urbes, castella, populos, Rempublicam in cujus perniciem conspiravit, populumque Christi in servitutem redigit, adversus Sanctos depugnar.
units.tr: The priest is the hand. At last the Supreme Pontiff reigns, at last he rules, where all are weakened by discord, sedition and mutual hatred, and his power becomes formidable; all obey his nod, and even the least of them observe it. The sedition and discord of the Germans is the safety of the Roman Pontiffs. Therefore the Supreme Pontiff must strive with all his might, if he wishes it so, to crush the Alemannic Empire like a crawling serpent, and reduce it to ashes and embers. Let him therefore declare that it is by his work that no one at Rome or in Italy is left who either favours or strives for the affairs of the Empire. And indeed, by his deceit we have been brought into two quarrels. Although the vultures and birds of prey were flying about on every side, plundering temples, shrines and sacred buildings, he did not urge that these disputes be reconciled, or that they be settled by law between ourselves rather than by arms; yet he was far from stirring us up of his own accord to civil war. He made no effort to bring about peace between us; rather, he fed the discord, now favouring me, now the Austrian, now pretending to favour Frederick, now Louis, and the weaker each one was, the more he promised his help to him. He invited both to the consecration, deceived both with words, and persuaded those who were inclined to concord to take up arms again. He did all this so that, while we consumed one another with domestic arms and kinsmen by mutual strife, he might overthrow and weaken the Empire, cities, castles, peoples and the commonwealth, against whose ruin he has conspired, and reduce the people of Christ into slavery, and fight against the saints.

units.la: 3. Sacerdotia maxima, infima, sordidissimisquibusque, modo hostes Reipublicae sint, communi Neminem publici boni studiosum, aut pacis amantem in curiam Sacerdotum allegat. De Phi-rum supercilio nimium sibi assumit, nihil pensi habet, modo animo suo atque libidini per fas nefas morem gerat.
units.tr: 3. He enrolls in the council of priests the greatest, the lowest and the most squalid of men, provided they are enemies of the commonwealth; he enlists no one who is devoted to the public good or loves peace. He takes too much upon himself with the pride of a Pharisee, and has no scruple, so long as he gratifies his own mind and lust by fair means or foul.

units.la: 4. Divina, humana decreta juxta contemnit, atque contumbat. Jus gentium violat, leges prophanat, sacra polluit, indicta causa, necdum reos condemnat. Sibi licere ab sq; niora adjudicat in nos indemnatos sententiam ferre, justitiat. Cum capitalis sit inimicus, publicusque hostis, propria causa auctor, reus & judex est, id quod nec apud Turcas, neque Judaeos, neque Saracenos, neque Sarmatas fieri solet. Eos, qui fidem Caelan servant, & Christo Servatori nostro praecipiunt, nec ullam aliam ob causam haereticos nota inurit. Quicquid libet, licitum judicat; iuribus licentiam. Quid igitur cum illo agam? neque jus, neque bonum, neque aequum exequi, sed det. Nihil videt, nihil facit, nisi quod lubet.
units.tr: 4. He treats divine and human decrees alike with contempt and scorn. He violates the law of nations, profanes laws, pollutes sacred things, and condemns men who have not yet been accused and whose cause has not been heard. He adjudges it lawful for himself to pass sentence against us, unheard and uncondemned. Since he is a capital enemy and a public foe, he is the author, the defendant and the judge in his own cause, which is not done even among the Turks, the Jews, the Saracens or the Sarmatians. He brands as heretics for no other cause those who keep faith and obey Christ our Saviour. Whatever he pleases he judges lawful; he gives licence to rights. What then am I to do with him? He carries out neither law, nor good, nor equity, but only his own will. He sees nothing and does nothing except what pleases him.

units.la: 5. Sathanae spiritum sibi sumit, se similem Altissimo facit, se adorari, (quod Caelis a Joanne fieri prohibuit) pedes sibi osculari, more Diocletiani atque Alexandri, crudelissimorum tyrannorum, perunxit, cum Christus manceps divinitatis, Dominus & Deus noster, pedes eorum suorum piscatorumque laverit, ut a nuncii sui vicissim illis, ad quos missi sunt, faciant. Una atque divina providentia, ipsa suis pollens opibus, nihil indiga nostri, ubique praesens, universa rebus incubat, rebus omnibus per se consulit: nec in manufactis templis habitat. Nos Dei genus in eo vivimus, movemur, & sumus. Ipse coeli & terrae rector est, nisi forsitan artifex, natura effecta, superque terrum parens senio atque labore continuo fatlus, Atlantis ritu, (ut est in fabulis Poetarum culis (qui telpiranti interea loci coelum humeris sustineat) vicaria opera, atque sempiternus auxilio indigeat. Sed nihil fortuito, nihil humana remetitate aut fit, aut regitur. Imperatores terris neque fotte neque casu, neque a mortalibus, neque occulta fatorum potestate dantur, premo numine eliguntur, atque divinitus constituuntur, rebusque humanis a patre indulgent imponuntur.
units.tr: 5. He takes to himself the spirit of Satan and makes himself like the Most High. He has himself adored, which John forbade to be done to himself in heaven; he has his feet kissed, after the manner of Diocletian and Alexander, most cruel tyrants, and he anoints them; whereas Christ, the author of divinity, our Lord and God, washed the feet of his disciples and fishermen, so that they in turn should do the same to those to whom they were sent. The one and divine providence, mighty in its own resources, in need of nothing of ours, everywhere present, broods over all things and takes thought for them all by itself; and it does not dwell in temples made by hand. In it we live, move and have our being. It is the ruler of heaven and earth, unless perhaps, as an artificer made by nature, it is worn out by age and continual labour, and, like Atlas (as in the fables of the poets, who for a while holds up heaven on his shoulders), needs the help of a deputy and an everlasting assistant. But nothing happens by chance, and nothing is done or governed by human rashness. Emperors are given to the lands neither by fortune nor by chance, neither by mortals nor by the hidden power of fates, but are chosen by divine will and appointed by God, and are set over human affairs by the Father's favour.

units.la: 6. Porro Romanus Sacerdos, cujus conversatio in coelis esse debet, urbes, castella, vicos, oppidum, nes, opes, potentiam, tantum splendorem, jus gladii, adventitia non jure suo, sed alieno beneficio cupat, possidet, nempe benevolentia atque liberalitate, ne dicam socordia atque ignavia, Reipublicae Germaniae. At mortalium ingratissimi de optime meritis pessime merentur. Ensem, cujus munificentia tenent, in nostra viscera, quorum beneficiarii sunt, stringere non verentur. Obscuri, versuti, versipelles, Celtarum Occidentalium freti viribus atque amicitia, gerentesque infirmitate, hoc est, levitate atque superstitione confisi, libertati Germaniae plagas tendunt, simplicitati Christianae captiosis aculeis sub magna superficie pietatis imponunt. Darios, Croesos, Epiri aemulantur; pauperiem, ignominiam, contumeliam, famem, sitim, aestum, frigus, mortes, vincula, carcerem, crucem pati (sicut Paulus, & Petrus, & Christus, cui se operam vicariam praesidendo terrae gloriantur, fecerunt & docuerunt) non solum non callent, sed & pejus flagitio timent. Divitias, honorem, solas, Imperia, Regna, honorem spectant: anxius quam ulli hominum ea conquirunt: quae non tantum Christus & ejus legati contempserunt, verum etiam Philosophi, Poetae, Oratores, Historici, alieni a Sacramento verae religionis, aspernanda esse viro sapienti, praecipue sanctinato, constanter praecipiunt, ut quae absque scelere, & aliorum damno, comparari nequeunt, fere malos, nunquam bonos (ut est apud Germanos proverbium) efficiant. Nec sine causa Chiades sentes & spinas: Paulus tete atque laqueos principis Stygii appellavit.
units.tr: 6. Furthermore, the Roman priest, whose citizenship ought to be in heaven, seeks and possesses cities, castles, villages, towns, lands, wealth, power, such splendour and the right of the sword; these things are not his by right, but by another's benefit, namely the goodwill and liberality, not to say the sloth and indolence, of the German commonwealth. Yet the most ungrateful of mortals repay the best of deserts with the worst: they do not hesitate to draw the sword, which they hold by his bounty, against the very vitals of those whose beneficiaries they are. Obscure, crafty, shifty men, relying on the forces and friendship of the Western Celts, and trusting in the weakness of others, that is, in their levity and superstition, spread snares for the liberty of Germany, and impose on Christian simplicity with deceitful barbs under a great show of piety. They emulate Darius, Croesus and Pyrrhus. Poverty, disgrace, insult, hunger, thirst, heat, cold, death, chains, prison and the cross they not only have no skill in enduring (though Paul, Peter and Christ, whom they boast of representing on earth by their vicarious office, both did and taught this), but they fear it worse than any shame. They look to riches, honour, power, kingdoms and empires, and seek them more anxiously than any men; yet Christ and his legates despised these things, and so did philosophers, poets, orators and historians, who are alien to the sacrament of true religion, and who constantly teach that such things are to be spurned by a wise man, and especially by a holy one, since those things which cannot be obtained without crime and the harm of others make men bad, and almost never good (as there is a German proverb). Not without reason did Chilon call them thorns and thistles, and Paul called them the snares of the Stygian prince.

units.la: 7. Et ut est dissociabile Regnum, omnisque potestas impatiens consortis, jam egregii illi Pallas, opibus & splendore a majoribus nostris aucti, ferre parem nequeunt; Caesarem Italia, Romae Christum terris extrusere. a Illi coelum quidem permittunt, b inferos atque terras sibi assumunt Deusque terrarum hominumque non solum dici, sed etiam credi volunt, quasi perinde animae que luguis (quod ne Deus immortalis quidem tentat) imperare possint, atque divisum cum halcyone
units.tr: 7. And since, as the saying goes, a kingdom cannot be shared and all power is impatient of a partner, those outstanding men, the Pallas family, made rich and splendid by our ancestors, cannot bear an equal. They have thrust Caesar out of Italy and Christ out of Rome on earth. They concede heaven to him, but they take hell and earth for themselves. They want to be called and believed gods of earth and men, as if they could rule souls too (which not even the immortal God attempts), and as if they could share their dominion with the halcyon (kingfisher)

units.la: a pro, Apostoli.
units.tr: a That is, of the Apostles.

units.la: a sc. Christo. b intelligit Purgatorium. habeant imperium. Repugnant & maximè diversa sunt, Crucifixus & summa potestas, miles & sacerdos, Imperator & pastor. Regnum & patibulum, corporalia & spiritualia, arma & sacra, bellum & pax, Cæsar & nuncius, Princeps & minister, Dominus & servus. Qui vult esse maximus inter vos, (ait supremus arbiter cœli legatus suus) minimus omnium, atque vester servus sit. Ceteris recumbentibus, quemadmodum ego feci, ad cathedram ministret. Unus magister, & Dominus vester in cœlis; vos autem fratres estis. Bellua multorum capitum, monstrum biceps est, Augustus & Pontifex Maximus. Id quidem fuisse Decium atque Neronem, & hujusmodi Tyrannos, falsorum Deorum cultores, in nomismatis & epigrammatis legimus. Quod de animo & corpore afferunt, nugæ sunt & contortæ conclusiunculæ: sed vero nescimus carnem adversus spiritum pugnare, & animam, nisi e corpore emicuerit, interituram. Lucidbrium naturæ abominabile, ira Dei, stocordia atque ignavia nostra est, Principem Principum servo servire servorum. Si servus servus servorum Dei est, cur non servit? cur non amat? cur non ministrat? cur non pascit? cur non docet? non nunciat? Siquid, quod cupit, esse velit, cur non Christi, Petri & Pauli vestigia in carceribus & periculis variis æmulatur? Cur mentitur, tergiversatur, illegnat, dominatur? Avidltate potentiæ, pecuniâ inna summis miscet, omnia venalia, Deum & hominem habet. Cur vitam Christi parvipendit? qui de hæreditate à fratribus captus etiam arbitret volunt, sed competitores ad Prætorem Cæsaris rejecit, & tribunal relegavit. Cum populus Palæstinæ ultro offerret, aufugit, suum regnum in hoc mundo non esse confitetur. Vicelimus secundus non sine maxima sua atque Reipublicæ pernicie, libidine domini accepsit abit; aliena, quæ nihil ad eum attinent, curat, utitur; sua, hoc est, religionem, spiritum, vitam hominum negligit. Imperium terræ, mortalia, vetante Christo, attripit. Praesides, vanilules, profestis crucem atque pauperiatem, in aliena ditione obtrudit. Ubi res ad inlt terre putin redit, penes se summam potestatem esse comminiscitur. Munus Præfecti Prætorio Rheni Regni Bojorum, intercipere, atque in se transferre conatur. Nec verum est, nulli, qui discordantibus inter se Principibus Reges consalutati fuerint, jus esse potestatis tantæ. Id ignaris Annalium, & quidnam sit mentiri nescient, persuadere conetur. Conradus & Lotharius, Philippus & Otto, Richardus & Alphonsus, Adolphus & Albertus, & nuper Eg o & Fridericus, licet à diversis delecti Principibus, tamen Reges utrque vocabantur & eramus. Nos quidem ceremonia solemni, ex veteri prisca religione instituto, Francofordiæ celebri loco, Comitiis Cæsareis die præscripto habitis, frequenti senatu, non solum à pluribus, sed à duabus classibus sacrorum & prophanorum, superis ritè salutatus atque consultis, creati atque renunciati sumus. Atque inde in urbe, quam Aquas-Granas vocant, in penetralibus ac domicilio sacrosancti Imperii ritè sacra obivimus, diadema, ensem, insignia sulpicato accepimus. Austriacus post Comitia dissoluta, contra decus Imperii, adversus leges, auspicia, contra inter cessionem, & institutum majorum, non statu die, nec tempore constituto, obscuro vico, duobus duntaxat pecunia & affinitate corruptis suffragantibus, demùm irrepsit, utroque se ingessit. Et nostram sane causam immortalis cœli imperator (à quo in summo rerum fastigio constituti sumus, & enim ad inopes, vi oppressos vindicandos, & malos perterritandos accepimus) edocitate, fausisque omnibus, & victoria approbavit. Idcirco rectè, bene ac sapienter, sicuti legibus eram est, ex consilio decreto, more majorum Brandenburgensem Ducatum (quem ille homo, qui vulgo Papa dicitur, Madenburgensem falsò vocat) filio nostro Ludovico in tutelam atque fidem committimus.
units.tr: a That is, of Christ. b He means Purgatory. They have dominion. They are utterly opposed: the Crucified and supreme power, soldier and priest, Emperor and shepherd, kingdom and gallows, bodily and spiritual things, arms and sacred things, war and peace, Caesar and messenger, Prince and minister, Lord and servant. Whoever wishes to be greatest among you, (says the supreme Judge, his legate from heaven) let him be least of all, and your servant. While the others recline, let him serve at table, just as I have done. You have one Teacher and one Lord in heaven; but you are brothers. The beast with many heads, the monster with two heads, is Augustus and Pontifex Maximus. We read in coins and epigrams that Decius and Nero and tyrants of this kind, worshippers of false gods, were indeed such. What they say about soul and body is trifling and twisted little arguments; but in truth we know that the flesh fights against the spirit, and that the soul, unless it has shot out of the body, will perish. The abomination of nature, the wrath of God, our sluggishness and laziness is this: that the Prince of princes serves as a servant of servants. If the servant is the servant of the servants of God, why does he not serve? Why does he not love? Why does he not minister? Why does he not feed? Why does he not teach? Why does he not announce? If he wishes to be what he desires, why does he not imitate the footsteps of Christ, Peter and Paul in prisons and in various dangers? Why does he lie, dodge, deceive, and dominate? Through lust for power, he mixes with money in the highest matters; he has everything for sale, God and man.
