Why does he make light of the life of Christ, who, when he was taken by his brothers from the inheritance, did not wish to be arbiter, but sent the rivals to the praetor of Caesar and sent them away to the tribunal? When the people of Palestine offered him the kingdom of their own accord, he fled, and confessed that his kingdom is not in this world. The twenty-second (Pope), not without his own greatest ruin and that of the commonwealth, has departed in the lust of a lord; he takes care of and uses other people's things, which have nothing to do with him; his own things, that is, religion, spirit, and the lives of men, he neglects. He has usurped the empire of the earth, mortal things, though Christ forbade it. He thrusts presidents, flatterers, and agents, the cross and poverty, into another's dominion. When matters return to the state of earthly things, he devises that supreme power is with himself. He tries to intercept and transfer to himself the office of Praefect of the Praetorium of the Kingdom of the Boii (Bohemia). Nor is it true that no one has such great power, when kings have been acclaimed by princes who disagree among themselves. He tries to persuade those ignorant of the Annals, who do not know how to lie. Conrad and Lothair, Philip and Otto, Richard and Alphonso, Adolf and Albert, and lately I and Frederick, although chosen by different princes, were nevertheless both called and were kings. We indeed, with the solemn ceremony instituted from ancient religion, in the famous place of Frankfurt, at the imperial assembly held on the appointed day, with a full senate, were duly saluted and consulted, not only by most, but by both classes of sacred and profane persons, and were created and proclaimed. And thence, in the city which they call Aachen, in the sanctuary and home of the most sacred Empire, we duly performed the sacred rites and received the diadem, the sword, and the insignia of the Empire. The Austrian, after the assembly was dissolved, against the honour of the Empire, against the laws and auspices, against the agreement and custom of our ancestors, not on a fixed day or at an appointed time, in an obscure village, with only two voters corrupted by money and kinship, at last crept in and forced himself on both. And the immortal Emperor of heaven (by whom we have been placed on the summit of human affairs, and by whom, we have received, to vindicate the poor and oppressed by force, and to terrify the wicked) has indeed approved our cause, with all good fortune and victory, and has taught it. Therefore, rightly, well and wisely, as is lawful, by counsel and decree, after the manner of our ancestors, we commit the Duchy of Brandenburg (which that man whom the common people call Pope falsely calls Madenburg) to our son Ludwig in guardianship and trust.

units.la: Et cum nostri cives, amici, populares, socii pientissimi in Italia à Flaminibus Romanis, quòd nobis hidem servarent, nec ullum aliud propter facinus, armis præter æquum & bonum intercessit, nobis eos deferre non fuit consilium. Quemadmodum sacramento rogati, religiojurandi promiserunt, Regulos Germaniæ clarissimos, de Grayspach, Neyffen, Truhedingen, mum secundum, inde ad Legatum ejus in Italiam, uti pacem componerent, fœdus iccerent, ostro jure jussimus. Nihilominus illis rejectis, adversus Majestatem Imperii, populisque gentium, Legatus ille Joannis, ofor Christianæ charitatis, Mediolanum, Comum, Cremonam, Novariam, Ticinum, Laudem, Mutinam, Veronam, Vicentiam, Felsinam, Placentiam, Brixiam, Alexandriam, Terdonam, Lucam, Pisas, Aretium, Cesenam, Genuæ exulam, Mantuam, Lucernam, Florentiam, Montisferrati, Mauritaniarum et limitum Præfectos, cives, Præsides, Proprætores Imperii, Christianissimos atque nobilissimos viros, hostili animo cum copiis vastat; agros, vicos incendit; stupra, cædes, sacrilegia committit. Illos, quòd bella civilia abhorrerent, à nobis & Imperio deficere nollent, majestatis, scelus perfidiæ admittere recusarent, hæreseos notâ inussit. Romanus Princeps adarcenda hujusce modi flagitia delectus, gladiumque ideò gestans, inopes, insontes cives, Reipublicæ devotissimos (quibus etiam à propinquis opem ferre instituimus) potentia, ignorum oppressos, sine summa infamia, absque summo scelere deserere non potuit, o-fidelissimis atque Christianissimis amicis. Accusetur illius perfidia, qui prior læsit. Vim vi repellere licet.
units.tr: And since our citizens, friends, countrymen, and most pious allies in Italy were held by the Roman Flamens, because they kept faith with us, and no other crime intervened, with arms, beyond what is fair and good, we did not decide to hand them over to him. As they had been asked under oath, and promised by a sworn pledge, we ordered the most illustrious petty kings of Germany, of Grayspach, Neyffen, and Truhedingen, to make peace and form an alliance, first with the second man, then with his legate in Italy, by the imperial law. Nevertheless, when they were rejected, that legate of John, in contempt of the majesty of the Empire and of the peoples of the nations, and of Christian charity, lays waste with hostile mind, with his forces, Milan, Como, Cremona, Novara, Ticino, Lodi, Modena, Verona, Vicenza, Bologna, Piacenza, Brescia, Alessandria, Tortona, Lucca, Pisa, Arezzo, Cesena, Genoa, Mantua, Lucerne, Florence, the prefects, citizens, presidents, and propraetors of the Empire of Montferrat and the Maurine borders, most Christian and most noble men; he sets fire to fields and villages; he commits rapes, murders, and sacrileges. Because they abhorred civil wars, were unwilling to revolt from us and the Empire, and refused to commit the crime of treason and perfidy, he branded them with the mark of heresy. The Roman Prince, chosen to ward off crimes of this kind, and therefore bearing the sword, could not, without great infamy and without great wickedness, abandon the helpless and innocent citizens, most devoted to the commonwealth (whom we also determined to aid through their relatives), oppressed by power and ignored, nor his most faithful and most Christian friends. Let the treachery of him who first injured be accused. It is lawful to repel force by force.

units.la: Pastor bonus Pastor oviculas Christi, & amet, non armis oppugnet, vi opprimat. Argutas calumnias mittit, sed facit; veritatem, sinceritatem Christianam, Christumque, cui verba dare difficile est, simplicitate. Illius conversatio in cœlis; spiritalibus deditus, corporalibus se non contaminat, nostro jure, majorum institutio, sicut jus gentium est, sacra oracula docent, res nostras, incertas, caducas, fluxas, fragiles agentes sinat, & verbum inter nos non commutabimus. Et tan-dem
units.tr: A good shepherd should love the little sheep of Christ, not attack them with arms or crush them by force. He sends subtle calumnies, but he should practise truth, Christian sincerity, and simplicity, toward Christ, to whom it is hard to give words. His conversation is in heaven; devoted to spiritual things, he does not defile himself with bodily things. Let him allow us to manage our own affairs, which are uncertain, fleeting, frail, and fragile, according to our right, the institution of our ancestors, as the law of nations is, and as the sacred oracles teach; and we will not exchange words among ourselves. And at last

units.la: Ec 2 dem desinat tam impudenter mentiri, nisi forsitan omnes Germanos (ut Romanenses autem stultos, caudices, asinos, stipites, plumbeos existimat.
units.tr: let him cease to lie so shamelessly, unless perhaps he thinks all Germans (as he thinks the Romans) are foolish, blockheads, asses, logs, and leaden.

units.la: 10. Me haereticorum (ut ejus verbis utar) fautorem falsò vocat. Christianus sum; atqui ipse Haereticus archa est. Non enim discipulus est Christi, cujus vitam irridet, pauperta-tem floccifacit, pietatem aspernatur, religionem polluit, sacra prophanat, mores spernit, instituta condemnat, dogmata vilipendit. Nam Divum Franciscum, veritatis divinae praeconem, paupertatis Christianae antebiplinum consecraneos ejus universos, Avinione VI. Idus Decembris, anno ab orbe servato MCCCXXIII. pietatis condemnavit. Audite obsecro quam ob causam. Homo pecuniosus, avidusque Impius, angentum Evangelio, (ubi opes scelera vocantur) aurum Christi inopiae praefert; Franciscanos culos ignominioso apud se cognomine, item stolidas pecudes, perniciosas vulpeculas, quae ta religione mundo imponant, populum fallant, nuncupat. Illorum religionem excindere, quod Christum, comites ejus nihil possedisse in terris docent, asserant, praedicent, conantur. Sed contra Franciscanorum Perusiae celebris, universis suffragantibus Theologis, probè ejus facta veritatemque sacris literis, testimonio divino tutati sunt, quamvis magis caecere et vincere disputationibus, hujusmodi genus hominum castigandum foret. Tamen eundem suis coloribus, atque insatiabile avaritiae baratrum et simulachrorum cultorem declararunt. Nam tri pondus ingens, quod ab orbe Christiano, praecipuè Alemannia, Arelatensi Regno, Italia cie expeditionis Aliaticae emunxit; Saracenis, ut Christianis Armeniae, qui ab eo compilant, venire detrectarant, arma inferrent, distribuit. Ut Antichristus non sit, tamen ejus antecursores anteambulonem esse necesse est. A quo ad propugnandum templum Dei, (cujus cura nobis litùs à Deo optimo maximo data est) ad universum totius orbis Senatum Christianum proveniunt &c. Datum Reginoburgi, mense Augusto, Anno Domini MCCCXXIV.
units.tr: 10. He falsely calls me a supporter of heretics (to use his words). I am a Christian; yet he himself is a heretic of the ark. For he is not a disciple of Christ, whose life he mocks, whose poverty he holds cheap, whose piety he scorns, whose religion he defiles, whose sacred things he profanes, whose customs he despises, whose institutions he condemns, whose doctrines he vilifies. For Saint Francis, herald of divine truth, and the whole of his followers, the forerunners of Christian poverty, he condemned as impious at Avignon on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the year of the world's salvation 1323. Hear, I beg you, for what reason. This rich and greedy man, impious, prefers gold to the Gospel (where riches are called crimes) and gold to the poverty of Christ; he calls the Franciscans, with an ignominious nickname applied by him, stupid sheep and harmful little foxes, who by such a religion impose on the world and deceive the people. He attempts, asserts, preaches, and tries to destroy their religion, because they teach that Christ and his companions possessed nothing on earth. But against the Franciscans, the famous at Perugia, all the theologians supporting them, have rightly defended his deeds and the truth by the Holy Scriptures and divine testimony, although such a kind of men ought to be chastised rather by blows and by disputations to be conquered. Nevertheless, they have declared him, in their own colours, an insatiable abyss of avarice and a worshipper of images. For he distributed to those who were to attack the Armenian Christians, who were plundered by him, the enormous weight of money which he extorted from the Christian world, especially from Germany, the Kingdom of Arles, and Italy, for the Asian expedition; they refused to sell arms to the Saracens. Although the Antichrist is not yet here, it is necessary that his forerunners go before him. To defend the temple of God, the care of which was given to us by God most good and greatest, we summon the whole Christian senate of the whole world, etc. Given at Regensburg, in August, in the year of the Lord 1324.

units.la: LVDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. EDICTUM
units.tr: LUDWIG IV, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS: EDICT

units.la: DE EXAVCTORATIONE ET ABDICATIONE JOANNIS XXII. PAPAE, propter tyrannidem, injurias, falsum, & ambitionem Reipublicae perniciosam, veritatis Christianae ac Religioni nostrae exitiosam · publicatum Romae in Synodo generali, ex tertio Concilii decreto, IV. Calendas Maij, Anno Domini MCCCXXVIII.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE DEPOSITION AND ABDICATION OF POPE JOHN XXII, on account of his tyranny, wrongs, falsehood and ambition, ruinous to the Commonwealth, and destructive of Christian truth and of our religion: published at Rome in a general Synod, by decree of the Third Council, on the 28th of April, in the year of the Lord 1328.

units.la: IMPERATOR Ludovicus Quartus, Caesar Augustus, gentis humanae, orbis Christiani custos, à Deo electus, germanis & veris Christianis salutem. Cujus parandae atque constituendae gratiae, relictis focis, aris, patria, genitali solo, pignoribus nondum adultis, in Italiam transvivi, ad caput Urbis Romam, sacrosanctam Imperii domicilium, sedem nostram, pacificè summa omnium quiete favore veni, ibique more majorum, veteri instituto consecrati Imperatoris praenomen, Caesaris Augusti nomen rite suscepimus, atque utrbi & orbi Dei ope & armis, nostra potentia, victrici & invicta dextra praesidemus, excluri nostro jure divinae Majestati resistentes, pacis Christianae violatores, quem ob id à supremo Imperatore acceptum gestamus. Hujusmodi autem tumultus atque discordiarum, perniciosissimaque mala inter Christianos, à malignis Pontificatus Maximi oculis, aliisque fame & inedia morituris, feri & excitari solent. Dum alienis inhiant, alia usurpantem protervam in messem non suam temerè porrigunt, & quod ab altero postulant, in se recipiunt. Equidem hactenus, ut justitia atque aequitate superarem, connivi. Et quemadmodum pientissimum Davida (cum filius ejus Adonias regnum ambiret, adversus Solomonem sapientissimum summâ Deo electum conspiraret) factitasse legimus, scelera patienter tulimus atque dissimulavimus. Verùm ne tenuis & infirmi animi, ignoscendo malis, bonos omnes perditum eamus, lethalem tum, crimina perditissimorum (qui requiescere, donec animi libidinem expleant, non solent) vum ferro, amore Reipublicae, cujus cura nobis à coelesti numine tradita est, relecabimus: lupilem ovinàm jure nostro detrahemus, & ut paucis, missis ambagibus, rem aperiam, aures arrigite, omnium res agitur.
units.tr: LUDWIG the Fourth, Emperor Augustus, guardian of the human race and of the Christian world, chosen by God, greets his German brethren and true Christians. In order to obtain and establish this grace, I left hearth and altar, country, native soil, and children not yet grown, and crossed into Italy. I came to the head of the City, Rome, the sacrosanct home of the Empire, our seat, peacefully and with the favour and quiet of all. There, according to the custom of our ancestors and the ancient institution, I duly received the title of a consecrated Emperor and the name of Caesar Augustus. By God's help, and by our arms and power, with a victorious and unconquered right hand, we preside over the City and the world, resisting by our right those who oppose the divine Majesty, violators of Christian peace, whom for this reason we bear as received from the Supreme Emperor. Now such tumults and discords, and the most destructive evils among Christians, are commonly stirred up and provoked by the malign eyes of the Pontificate, and by others who are about to die of hunger and want. While they gape after what belongs to others, they reach out wantonly into a harvest not their own, and they take upon themselves what they demand from another. Indeed, hitherto, so that I might prevail by justice and equity, I have connived. And just as we read that the most pious David did (when his son Adonijah sought the kingdom and conspired against Solomon the most wise, chosen by God), so we have patiently borne and overlooked the crimes. But lest, by pardoning evils out of a weak and feeble spirit, we allow all good men to perish, we will now, out of love for the Commonwealth, whose care has been entrusted to us by the heavenly power, cut down with the sword the crimes of the most abandoned men, who do not rest until they have satisfied their lust. We will drag the wolf from the flock by our right. And, to speak plainly and without many words, prick up your ears: the matter concerns everyone.

units.la: 2. Universi, vulgus sine authoritate, sine gratia, domi atq; fores venales sumus: majestas & libertas religionis, libertas, Imperiumq; populi Christiani, leges, divina, humana, prodita sunt honorum. Quies in seditionibus, in pace turbae sunt. Homines sceleratissimi, cruentis manibus avaritia nocentissimi, & iidem luxu effeminati, atque ambitione perditi bus fides, decus, pietas, postremò vitia, virtutes, honesta atque inhonesta omnia, quaestui sunt,
units.tr: 2. We are all, the common people, without authority and without grace; at home and at the doors we are for sale. The majesty and liberty of religion, the liberty and Empire of the Christian people, the laws, divine and human, have been handed over to be sold for honours. There is quiet among the seditious, and tumults in peace. The most wicked men, most guilty through avarice with bloody hands, and at the same time effeminate through luxury and ruined by ambition, make everything a matter of gain: faith, honour, piety, and finally vices and virtues, honest and dishonest things alike.

units.la: * qui dicitur Joannes XXII. Papa.
units.tr: * who is called John XXII, Pope.

units.la: Reipublicae Christianae occupant, tumultu ex tumultu, bellum ex bello serunt. Caput factionis cobus ille de Baburco, qui se Papam nominat, ingentem vim pecuniae, quam undique à Christiana fraudulenter corrasit, adversus sanctos Dei, Imperio Christiano devotos, pugnantibus suasu Reguli, boni publici hostis, àque Divo Hainrico Septimo Caesare Augusto proscripti, expedir. Sicut Abiathar Sacerdos, ense Caesareo, nobis à coeli numine commissio, abuntur, talibus hujus saeculi curis contra divinum praeceptum incubat; Regno mundano inhiat; Pastor est personatus, ita mysticus est Antichristus; canis pellicula tectus, in gregem Christi lupus. lupina rabie grassatur; vendit scelera, inferos, superos, beneficia coelestia cauponatur; cum Saracenis Armenios Christianos, quinque annis continenter ejus opem implorantes, infestantibus fredus societatemque init. Borussiorum a primarium Praesidem, ditas inferiasque comminatus, cum Lituanis sanctos Christianos acerrimis, atrocissimis latronibus, inducias facere coegit, hostii regionem prodidit, fenestram invadendi Brandenburgenses Christianos aperuit. Lituani conjurati Baburci, ultro citroque impune per fines Brandenburgensium commearunt: Christianos ferro, caede extinxerunt: ingentes in cunis, in sinu parentum crudelissime contrucidati sunt. Templa, Coenobia, Collegia Sacerdotum, Monachorum compilata, incensa, eversa; Virgines sanctae per vim stuprata; hostia sacra (quod referens horrescens) hasta transfixa, insultante hoste, hoc convicio sublata: En hic est Deus Christianorum. Liberi a complexu parentum, uxores maritorum ad ludibrium hostium abstractae; captivorum greges velut pecudum abstracti sunt. Adhuc Brandenburgensis populus vulnus acceptum luget. Atque haec omnia scelere Vicesimi secundi acta sunt. Quinetiam classem a Franciae Occidentalis Regiae opem Christianis Armeniae incolis adversus Saracenos fetendam, comparatam, astu intercepit. Eadem in Genuenses, qui devotissimi sunt Christiano Imperio, caede abusus est.
units.tr: They seize the Christian Commonwealth, sowing tumult upon tumult and war upon war. The head of the faction is that Jacob of Cahors, who calls himself Pope, and who spends an enormous sum of money, which he has fraudulently scraped together from every side, against the saints of God and those devoted to the Christian Empire. He hires fighters, at the urging of Robert, the enemy of the public good, who was outlawed by the divine Henry VII, Augustus Caesar. Just as Abiathar the priest, though entrusted by the heavenly power with the sword of Caesar, was carried off into such cares of this age against the divine precept, so he (Jacob) devotes himself to worldly kingdoms. He is a minister in disguise, and thus a mystical Antichrist: a wolf in the flock of Christ, wrapped in a sheep's skin, who rages with wolfish fury. He sells crimes, hell and heaven, and trades in heavenly benefits. He enters into a league and treaty with the Saracens against the Christian Armenians, who for five continuous years have implored his aid while they were being attacked. He threatened the chief prince of the Prussians with death and chains, and compelled him to make a truce with the Lithuanians, the fiercest and most atrocious brigands, and betrayed the region to the enemy, opening a window for them to invade the Christians of Brandenburg. The Lithuanians, sworn in league with Jacob, passed back and forth through the territories of Brandenburg with impunity; they slew the Christians with the sword and with slaughter. Vast numbers were most cruelly butchered in their cradles and in the bosoms of their parents. Temples, monasteries, colleges of priests and monks were plundered, burned and overthrown; holy virgins were violated by force; the sacred hosts (a thing horrible to report) were pierced with a spear, and, while the enemy taunted, were raised up with this mockery: Behold the God of the Christians! Children were torn from their parents' embrace, wives from their husbands, to be the mockery of the enemy; flocks of captives were driven off like cattle. To this day the people of Brandenburg mourn the wound they have received. And all these things were done by the crime of the Twenty-second. Moreover, he craftily intercepted a fleet, prepared by the King of Western France to bring aid to the Christian inhabitants of Armenia against the Saracens. The same man has abused the Genoese, who are most devoted to the Christian Empire, with slaughter.

units.la: 4. Imperii Majestatem, authoritatem Reipublicae, temere contra placita Christi usurpando labefactat, polluit. Monstrum biceps, mundanus & spiritualis esse contendit. Christus Servator noster, cui omnis potestas in coelo atque in terra data est, tamen Imperium atque Regnum terrarum, a populo oblatum, suscipere detrectavit. Regnum meum, inquit, non est in hoc mundo. Atque satis constat inter omnes divinae Philosophiae, legum, & Pontificii juris scientissimos, penes Pontificem Romanum neque quamquam esse utramque dignitatem, sacram atque prophanam. Omnis potestas ab immortali Deo atque suprema est Majestate; coeleste beneficium, quod imperamus, non humanum est. Comitiali Conventu delecti, suffragiis Principalibus comprobati, mortalis cujuspiam astipulatione, aliove hominis authoramento nullo pacto indigemus. Sacrosanctum Romanum Imperium, cui Christus, comites ejus, obtemperarunt, & vectigales fuerunt, Sacrificuli saltuosi beneficium esse peinegamus. Caput orbis terrarum a suprema coeli majestate constituti, nulli mortalium, quatenus ad hujus seculi Imperium attinet, tationem reddere debemus.
units.tr: 4. He rashly weakens and defiles the majesty of the Empire and the authority of the Commonwealth by usurping them against the decrees of Christ. He contends that he is a two-headed monster, both worldly and spiritual. Christ our Saviour, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, nevertheless refused to accept the Empire and kingdom of the earth when it was offered to him by the people. My kingdom, he said, is not of this world. And it is quite clear to all the most learned in divine philosophy, in law, and in Papal law, that in the Roman Pontiff there is by no means both dignity, sacred and profane. All power is from the immortal God and the supreme Majesty; the heavenly benefit by which we rule is not of human origin. Chosen by the assembly of the Empire and approved by the votes of the princes, we have no need of any agreement or authorisation from any mortal man. We maintain that the sacrosanct Roman Empire, to which Christ and his companions submitted and paid tribute, is not a benefice of a skulking little priest. The head of the world, established by the supreme majesty of heaven, owes an account to no mortal, so far as concerns the government of this age.

units.la: 4. Alia illius Jacobi pestilentissimi pessima facinora reticeo. Sacrificulos, qui canes muti latrare non audent, poenarum metu, ne veritatem dicant, perterritat. Crimen ambitus, sacrilegium, novumque aucupii, aes receptitii, & quod Avenione habitat, saepius evocatus Roma migrare reculat, quod omnibus bonis cordi non sit, velut levissima, nisi facio; id, quod ad nos spectat, agamus. Jus gladii divinitus nobis traditum ad eradicanda scelera exerceamus, obviam ire factionis potentiae, utilitas Reipublicae, amor religionis atque pietas subigit.
units.tr: 4. I pass over the other most pestilential crimes of that pestilent Jacob. He terrifies the priests, who as mute dogs dare not bark, with the fear of punishment, lest they tell the truth. Simony, sacrilege, and the new trade in hunting for money, the receipt of fees, and he who dwells at Avignon, who, though often summoned, refuses to migrate to Rome, which is not pleasing to all good men, as if it were a most trivial matter, unless I do this: let us do what concerns us. The divinely given right of the sword, to root out crimes, must be exercised; the usefulness of the Commonwealth, the love of religion and piety compel us to meet the power of the faction.

units.la: 5. Jacobum igitur antea a Sacrarum literarum Antistitibus Haeresiarcheu declaratum, ex consilii decreto, more majorum, Pontificatu submotum, atque a Christo repudiatum renunciamus. Habemus bonorum exempla, quibus nobis licere id facere, quod illi fecerunt, putamus. Otto Primus cum Populo Romano, Sacerdotum ejus tribu, Joannem Duodecimum ex albo Pontificum Romanorum ob scelera (quae si ad flagitia Vicesimi secundi comparavetis, ludus est) erasit, alium Pastorem urbi & orbi imposuit. Idem alios complures Imperatores, optimosque Principes fecisse, in Annales & Fastos relatum est. Proinde Jacobum illum crimine verae irreligiositatis, nota haereseos antea a Franciscanis caterisque Theologis inustum, contemptorem paupertatis Christianae, Imperii Antichristi authorem, jure nostro, consilio, sententia, consensu communi Principum, Pontificum, Germaniae, Galliae, Italiae, efflagitantibus Sacerdotibus Populoque Romano, exauguratum, abdicatum, haereticos condemnatum declaramus, proscribimus; acta ejusdem rescindimus; universi Christiani jeunium numero imperiorum atque scelératorum habeant; ab eo omnes decedant; aditum, sermonem velut contagionem, ne quid incommodi accipiant, devitent. Eidem nullus honor committur; & ab his, quorum interest, opera detur, ut deprehensus more majorum puniatur. Quisquis haec fecerit, hostis Reipublicae esto. Nos confestim cum Sacerdotum curia populoque urbi atque orbi pastorem, communi consilio atque veterum instituto, juxta sacrae Historiae leges, rememus.
units.tr: 5. Therefore we declare Jacob, previously pronounced a heresiarch by the bishops of the Holy Scriptures, removed from the Pontificate by decree of the council, according to the custom of our ancestors, and rejected by Christ; and we renounce him. We have examples of good men, by which we think it lawful for us to do what they did. Otto the First, with the Roman People and its priestly tribe, struck John XII from the roll of Roman Pontiffs on account of crimes (which, if you compare them with the outrages of the Twenty-second, are child's play), and set another shepherd over the city and the world. It is recorded in the Annals and Fasti that he and several other emperors and excellent princes did the same. Accordingly, by our right, by counsel, by sentence, by the common consent of the princes, of the Pontiffs, of Germany, France and Italy, and at the urgent request of the priests and the Roman People, we declare that Jacob, branded with the mark of heresy of true irreligion, previously stigmatised by the Franciscans and other theologians, a despiser of Christian poverty, the author of the Antichrist's Empire, is deprived of his office, abdicated, condemned as a heretic, and proscribed; we rescind his acts. Let all Christians count him among the enemies of the Empire and of the wicked; let all withdraw from him; let them avoid access to him and conversation with him as they would contagion, lest they suffer any harm. No honour is to be entrusted to him; and let effort be made by those whom it concerns that, when he is caught, he be punished according to the custom of our ancestors. Whoever does this shall be an enemy of the Commonwealth. We, at once, with the college of priests and the Roman People, will summon a shepherd for the city and the world, by common counsel and the ancient institution, according to the laws of sacred history.

units.la: 6. Hoc edictum ab Imperatore, item Sacerdotum Senatu Populoque Romano signatum est, publicatumque in celeberrimo Myslarum, Populi Romani, Regulorum, Dynastarum, Tetrarcharum, Pontificum Maximorum, Minorum, Antistitum conventu. Datum & factum extra templum augustissimum, Divis Petro atque Paulo legatis Christi dedicatum, octavo decimo die Aprilis, Urbe Romana, cunctis Sacrificis, universo Populo Romano in Regione pro concione publice ejus gratia coacto; Christianae libertatis anno MCCCXXVIII. Invictissimi Imperatoris Ludovici Quarti Caesaris Augusti, Principis optimi, Regni XIV. Imperii vero primo.
units.tr: 6. This edict has been signed by the Emperor, likewise by the senate of priests and the Roman People, and it was published in the most celebrated assembly of the Myslae, the Roman People, the petty kings, dynasts, tetrarchs, the Supreme Pontiffs, the lesser bishops. Given and done outside the most august temple, dedicated to the divine apostles Peter and Paul, the legates of Christ, on the eighteenth day of April, in the City of Rome, all the priests being present, and the whole Roman People gathered publicly for a sermon in the region for this purpose; in the year of Christian liberty 1328. Of the most invincible Emperor Ludwig IV, Augustus Caesar, the best of princes, in the fourteenth year of his reign, but the first of his Empire.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG.
units.tr: LUDWIG IV, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS

units.la: CONSTITUTIO DE OFFICIO COMITIS PALATII LATERANENSIS ROMANI.
units.tr: THE CONSTITUTION CONCERNING THE OFFICE OF COUNT PALATINE OF THE LATERAN PALACE AT ROME.

units.la: Ludovicus Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator Semper-Augustus, Illustri Castrucio Ducilucano, Sacri Lateranensis Palatii Comiti, & Romani Imperii Vexillifero, suo & Imperii fideli dilecto, gratiam suam & omne bonum.
units.tr: Ludwig, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, to the illustrious Castruccio Ducilucano, Count of the Sacred Lateran Palace and Standard-bearer of the Roman Empire, his faithful and beloved servant of the Empire, greeting his grace and every good.

units.la: 1. Dignum est & Majestati Imperiali proprium, ut, sicut quotidie fidelium augetur devotio, ita eius Imperiale culmen augeat dignitatis privilegia & honores. Sane experientia docet, novit Imperialis Majestas maximam fidem, devotionem & constantiam tuam, & quos per ea bis collatos honores, ultra cæteros fideles Imperii de bono in melius quotidie profecisse. Ut igitur præmiorum contemplatione ad ampliores dignitatum apices per Imperiale culmen tua devotio attollatur, de consilio & asensu procerum nostrae Imperialis Aulae, tibi & successoribus tuis & natis, per lineam masculinam in perpetuum, Comitatum sacri Lateranensis Palatii ad fiscum nostrum & sacrum Romanum Imperium iustis & legitimis causis devolutum & appli- catum pronunciamus, & declaramus, & ad omnem dubietatem tollendam devolvimus & applicamus, damus, concedimus, & ex certa scientia, & plenitudine potestatis: & te & praedictos successores tuos ... elligimus, constituimus, praficimus & creamus Comitem & Comitissam sacri Palatii Lateranensis, eosque de Comitatu praedicto investimus & infeudamus, tam veros fideles Imperii ... dantes & concedentes, & tribuentes ubi & eis omnes & singulos honores, & omnia & singula privilegia, & emolumenta, quos & quae Comites praedicti sacri Palatii habent & habuerunt quoque tempore, de consuetudine vel de jure.
units.tr: 1. It is proper to the Imperial Majesty, and worthy of it, that as the devotion of the faithful grows every day, so its Imperial height should increase the privileges and honours of dignity. Indeed experience teaches, and the Imperial Majesty knows, that your very great loyalty, devotion and constancy, and the honours conferred on you on account of these, have each day advanced from good to better, beyond the other faithful of the Empire. Therefore, so that by the consideration of rewards your devotion may be raised by the Imperial height to the higher summits of dignities, with the counsel and assent of the nobles of our Imperial Court, we declare and pronounce that the County of the Sacred Lateran Palace, which for just and lawful causes has devolved and been applied to our fisc and the Sacred Roman Empire, is to you, your successors and your children in the male line forever; and, to remove all doubt, we devolve, apply, give, grant, and from certain knowledge and fullness of power, we choose, appoint, set over and create you and the aforesaid successors of yours as Count and Countess of the Sacred Lateran Palace, and we invest and enfeoff them with the aforesaid County, giving and granting and bestowing upon them, as true faithful men of the Empire, all and each of the honours, and all and each of the privileges and emoluments, which the Counts of the aforesaid Sacred Palace have or have had at any time, by custom or by right.

units.la: 2. Declarantes & nunc per hoc nostrae serenitatis indultum, tibi & praedictis successoribus praedicta Comitatus dignitate competere jus assistendi perpetuo benedictioni, sacrae unctioni & coronationi successorum nostrorum Principum Romanorum, & omnibus & singulis ipsius coronationis solemnitatibus; & praecipue sociandi & deducendi ipsos Romanos Principes, tempore consecrationis fiendae de eis, ad sacram unctionem de ipsis faciendam, & eosdem Romanos Imperatores ... cessores nostros tenendi & juvandi in ipsa sacra unctione & actu ipsius, & eadem unctione perfecta, eos reducendi & sociandi ad altare, & thalamum, prout & quoties principes expedient dire.
units.tr: 2. Declaring also now by this indult of our serenity, that to you and the aforesaid successors, by the dignity of the aforesaid County, belongs the right to be present at the blessing, the sacred anointing and the coronation of our successors, the Roman Princes, and at all and each of the solemnities of that coronation; and especially the right to accompany and escort the Roman Princes themselves, at the time of the consecration to be made concerning them, to the sacred anointing to be performed upon them; and to attend and assist the same Roman Emperors, our predecessors, in the sacred anointing itself and its performance; and, once that anointing is complete, to lead them back and accompany them to the altar and the bridal chamber, as and whenever the princes shall judge it expedient.

units.la: 3. Item jus levandi & tenendi Imperiale diadema, de nostro & successorum nostrorum Romanorum Principum capite, tempore quo Imperialis coronationis solennia celebrantur, & etiam quoque alio tempore, quoties publice ipsum diadema expedient elevare de capite nostro & successorum nostrorum Romanorum Principum reponi.
units.tr: 3. Likewise the right to lift and hold the Imperial diadem from the head of ourselves and of our successors, the Roman Princes, at the time when the solemnities of the Imperial coronation are celebrated, and also at other times, whenever it shall be judged expedient to raise the diadem publicly from our head and that of our successors, the Roman Princes, and to replace it.

units.la: 4. Quae omnia & singula supra scripta valere & tenere volumus, & jubemus ex certa scientia, et plenitudine potestatis, jure aliquo non obstante. Nulli ergo omnino hominum liceat hanc nostram paginam in aliquo violare, vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Si quis vero hoc attentare praesumpserit, gravem indignationem nostram se noverit incurrisse. In cujus rei testimonium praesentes conscribi, & sigilli Majestatis nostrae robore, cum annotatione testium subscriptorum jussimus communiri: Rudolphi Ducis Bavariae Principis & patrui nostri Carissimi, Henrici Ducis Brunsvicensis, Ludovici Ducis de Teck, Hermanni de Linthelberg Cancellarii nostri, Alberti dict: Symiel de Linthelberg Marescalli nostri, Meinhardi Comitis de Hortenburg, Othonis Comitis de Corlamende, Joannis Comitis de Claramonte, Conradi Comitis de Truchendingen, Conradi de Zolulselberg:
units.tr: 4. All and each of the things written above we wish and command to be valid and observed, from certain knowledge and fullness of power, any law to the contrary notwithstanding. Let it therefore be utterly unlawful for any man to violate this our document in any way, or to act against it with rash daring. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he has incurred our grave indignation. In witness of which we have ordered these present letters to be drawn up and strengthened by the seal of our Majesty, with the names of the witnesses subscribed: Rudolf, Duke of Bavaria, Prince and our most dear paternal uncle; Henry, Duke of Brunswick; Ludwig, Duke of Teck; Hermann of Linthelberg, our Chancellor; Albert, called Symiel of Linthelberg, our Marshal; Meinhard, Count of Hortenburg; Otto, Count of Corlamende; John, Count of Claramonte; Conrad, Count of Truchendingen; Conrad of Zolulselberg:

units.la: necnon Nobilium Virorum Jacobi de Columna, Sciarae & Jacobi de Sabellis Senatorum Urbis.
units.tr: and also the noble men Jacob de Columna, Sciara, and Jacob de Sabellis, Senators of the City.

units.la: Datum Romae, 14. die mensis Martii, Indictione 11. Anno Domini 1328. Regni nostri Anno XIV. Imperii vero primo.
units.tr: Given at Rome, on the 14th day of the month of March, in the 11th Indiction, in the year of the Lord 1328, in the 14th year of our reign, and the first of our Empire.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. FORMULA
units.tr: LUDWIG IV, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS, FORMULA

units.la: DE FACULTATE CIVITATIS CONDENDAE ET PRIVILEGIANDAE.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE POWER TO FOUND AND PRIVILEGE A TOWN

units.la: Ludovicus Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator, Semper-Augustus, singulis & universis ad quos praesentes devenerint, gratiam suam & omne bonum. Imperialis requirit & exigit praesentia Celsitudo, ut singulos & universos devote nobis & fideliter famulantes, condignis de beamus praemiorum largitionibus praevenire, ut spe remunerationis ad nostra & Imperii obsequia fidentius & ferventius animentur. Notum igitur volumus universis, tam praesentibus quam futuris, quod nos advertentes devotionem & fidelitatem dilecti fidelis nostri Secretarii Friderici Burggravii de Nurmberg, suisque petitionibus annuentes, eidem authoritatem, facultatem & plenum posse damus & concedimus, dedimus & praesentibus concessimus civitatem munitam in Griedelach construendi, aedificandi & faciendi, ipsamque muris, fossatis & ceteris munimentis quibus muniri ut ceterae sunt solitae civitates, impedimento nullo prorsus aut contradictione, qua obstante firmiter muniendi: ibidemque judicium, cum ad id pertinentibus necessariis habendi Judicis. Judicem ponendi, qui super universis casibus & excessibus, sanguinem, corpus, mutilationem membrorum sive res attingentibus, judicandi plenariam habeat facultatem: ebdomadale forum in eadem civitate, quotiescunque id attemptandum decreverit, proclamandi, & nihilominus celebrandi. Volentes quidem dictam civitatem Grindelach uti & gaudere omni jure, libertate, immunitate & gratia, quibus nostra civitas Nurembergh hactenus usa est, & ex nunc denuò frui poterit & gaudere. In cuius rei testimonium evidens praesentes conscribi, sigilloque nostrae Majestatis jussimus communiri. Datum Coloniae apud Sanctum Petrum, vicesima secunda die mensis Aprilis, Indictione undecima, Anno Domini millesimo trecentesimo vicesimo octavo, Regni nostri anno quarto decimo, Imperii vero primo.
units.tr: Ludwig, by the grace of God Roman Emperor, ever Augustus, to each and all to whom these present letters shall come, his grace and every good. The lofty dignity of the imperial office requires and demands that we anticipate with worthy largesse of rewards all who devotedly and faithfully serve us, so that they may be animated more confidently and ardently to the service of ourselves and of the Empire by the hope of recompense. We therefore wish it to be known to all, both present and future, that we, taking note of the devotion and fidelity of our beloved faithful secretary Frederick, Burgrave of Nuremberg, and granting his petitions, have given, granted and conceded by these presents to him the authority, power and full capacity to build, erect and make a town fortified at Griedelach, and to fortify it with walls, ditches and other defences such as ordinary towns are accustomed to have, with no hindrance or objection whatever standing in the way of its being firmly fortified; and likewise to hold there a court, with the necessary appurtenances, and to appoint a judge who shall have full power to judge all cases and offences touching blood, body, mutilation of limbs or property; and to proclaim and nonetheless hold a weekly market in the same town, whenever he shall decide to attempt it. Wishing indeed that the said town of Grindelach should use and enjoy every right, liberty, immunity and favour which our city of Nuremberg has hitherto enjoyed, and which it may henceforth again enjoy and possess. In witness whereof we have ordered these presents to be drawn up and fortified with the seal of our Majesty. Given at Cologne, at St. Peter's, on the twenty-second day of the month of April, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of our Lord one thousand three hundred and twenty-eight, in the fourteenth year of our reign, and the first of our empire.

units.la: DECRETA COMITIORUM FRANCOFOR- DIANORUM DE ANNO MCCCXXXVIII.
units.tr: Decrees of the Diet of Frankfurt, of the year 1338.

units.la: quorum Edictum infrà Tomo III. sol. 410. publicavimus.
units.tr: Whose edict we published below in Volume III, page 410.

units.la: IMPERATOR LUDOVICUS Augustus & EDUARDUS Rex Anglorum Francofordiam se contulerunt, ubi frequentes Italiae, Germaniae, Galliae, Angliae Purpurati & Pontifices coëunt. Carolus Moravici limitis Praefectus, jussus fide publica cum ducentis equitibus apparere, cum quingentis venit, dum verba LUDOVICI iurat, se in ejus potestate fore dat fidem.
units.tr: Emperor Louis Augustus and Edward, King of the English, betook themselves to Frankfurt, where many cardinals and prelates from Italy, Germany, France and England gathered. Charles, prefect of the Moravian frontier, was ordered to appear under public guarantee with two hundred horsemen. He came with five hundred, and, while he swore the words of Louis, he gave his pledge that he would be in Louis's power.

units.la: 2. Cum praesente Angliae Senatusconsultum perscriptum est, Lex lata est: eum, qui Imperatorem excommunicat, aut sententiam, Bullasque hujusmodi Pontificias absque consilii decreto recipiat, contra Rempublicam facere videri.
units.tr: 2. When the English were present, a decree of the senate was drawn up and a law was passed: that whoever excommunicates the Emperor, or accepts such a sentence or papal bulls without a decision of the council, is seen to act against the commonwealth.

units.la: 3. Eadem quoque, quae Rhenofei à Principibus constituta fuerunt, tutanda esse summa viatque ope juratum ab omnibus.
units.tr: 3. The same measures that were established by the princes on the Rhine are to be defended with the greatest force and effort, as all have sworn.

units.la: 4. Anglius quoque, sententia Procerum, Rex Franciae Procuratorque Imperii per Gallias, consaluratus est. Justi sunt Equites, Milites, Tribuni, Centuriones, Duces, pro viribus eidem auxiliares esse.
units.tr: 4. Edward likewise, by the opinion of the nobles, was sworn in together as King of France and vicar of the Empire throughout Gaul. It is right that knights, soldiers, tribunes, centurions and dukes should be auxiliaries to him according to their strength.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. RESCRIPTUM APOLOGETICUM
units.tr: Apologetic Rescript of Ludwig IV, Emperor Augustus

units.la: CONTRA JOANNIS XXII. PAPAE BULLAM EXCOMMUNI- CATIONIS; concernens jura Regni & Imperii.
units.tr: Against the Bull of Excommunication of Pope John XXII, concerning the rights of the Kingdom and the Empire.

units.la: LUDOVICUS Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator, Semper-Augustus, universis & singulis Regibus Christianorum, ac Patriarchis, Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, Presbyteris, Diaconibus, quocunque honoris culmine praefulgeant, & caeteris Ecclesiarum Praelatis: necnon secularibus Principibus, Marchionibus, Ducibus, Comitibus, Baronibus, Capitaneis, Dominis, Potestatibus, Rectoribus, Judicibus, & Officialibus provinciarum, civitatum, & terrarum Romano Imperio subjectarum, & ipsarum quibuscunque incolis & habitatoribus, ac omnibus & singulis Christi fidelibus, tam Ecclesiasticis quam Secularibus, ad quos praesentes literae pervenerint, gratiam suam & omne bonum.
units.tr: Ludwig, by the grace of God Roman Emperor, ever Augustus, to all and each of the Kings of the Christians, and to Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, Presbyters, Deacons, however exalted their rank of honour, and to the other prelates of the Churches; likewise to the secular Princes, Marquises, Dukes, Counts, Barons, Captains, Lords, Potentates, Rulers, Judges and Officials of the provinces, cities and lands subject to the Roman Empire, and to all their inhabitants and residents, and to all and each of the faithful of Christ, both ecclesiastical and secular, to whom these present letters shall come: his grace and every good.

units.la: Fidem Catholicam, quam sancta mater Ecclesia Catholica, extra quam nullus omninò salvatur, symbolis, Conciliis, & traditionibus ipsius Ecclesiae sacrosanctae, docet & tenet, firmiter credimus, ac fideliter & firmiter confitentes, & ipsius Ecclesiae sanctae doctrinam in sacris Canonibus sequi volentes: quibusdam allegationibus, impugnationibus, & oppositionibus, quae contra electionem ac promotionem de nobis factam ad culmen dignitatis Imperialis, & contra Imperialem auctoritatem, potestatem, & dignitatem opponuntur, ne simplicium corda possint inficere, secundum sacrorum canonum & legum tenorem in his scriptis duximus respondere, & contra ipsos impugnantes & opponentes, & eorum dicta procedimus, prout inferius continetur.
units.tr: The Catholic faith, which the holy Catholic mother Church, outside of which no one at all is saved, teaches and holds by her creeds, councils and traditions, we firmly believe; and, faithfully and steadfastly confessing it, and wishing to follow the teaching of the holy Church itself in the sacred canons, we have judged it right in these writings to answer certain allegations, attacks and objections which are raised against the election and promotion made in our favour to the summit of the imperial dignity, and against the imperial authority, power and dignity, lest they corrupt the hearts of simple people; and we proceed against these attackers and objectors and their statements, as is set out below, in accordance with the tenor of the sacred canons and laws.

units.la: 1. In primis contra Nos & Imperialem authoritatem, & jus Imperii, allegatur & objicitur, quod potestas & authoritas Imperialis est à Papa; & quod electus in Regem Romanorum ex sola electione non est, necdici potest verus Imperator, nec habet potestatem, jurisdictionem, & authoritatem, antequam inunctus, consecretur, & coronetur à Papa, qui (ut dicunt) tam in temporalibus quam in spiritualibus habet plenitudinem potestatis. Ad quae respondemus, hanc opinionem canonibus ac jure & rationi pariter obviare, sicut expressè patet in Decretis, 96. dist. c. cum ad verum, & canon duo sunt, & ca. Imperator. Ubi expressè habetur in haec verba: Duo sunt quippe, quibus principaliter hic mundus regitur, scilicet authoritas sacra Pontificum & Regalis potestas. Habet quippe Imperator privilegium potestatis suae, quam administrandi legibus publicis divinitus consecutus est, nec Imperator jure ratificatus, nec Pontifex jura Imperatoria usurpat. Haec ibi: ubi Glossa Ordinaria dicunt, quòd ista potestates sunt diversae, & quod altera non dependet ab altera, & quòd Imperator non habet potestatem sive imperium a nisi à solo DEO. 93. distinct. c. leginus, ubi in textu dicitur, quòd exercitus facit Imperatorem.
units.tr: 1. First, it is alleged and objected against us and the imperial authority and the right of the Empire, that the power and authority of the Empire is from the Pope; and that one elected King of the Romans by election alone is not, and cannot be called, a true Emperor, nor has power, jurisdiction and authority until he is anointed, consecrated and crowned by the Pope, who (as they say) has the fullness of power both in temporal and in spiritual matters. To which we reply that this opinion conflicts equally with the canons, the law and reason, as is plainly stated in the Decretum, dist. 96, c. Cum ad verum, and c. Duo sunt, and c. Imperator. There it is stated in these words: "There are two things by which this world is principally governed, namely the sacred authority of the Pontiffs and the royal power. The Emperor has the privilege of his power, which he has received from God to administer by public laws; nor does the Emperor ratify the rights of the Pontiff, nor does the Pontiff usurp the imperial rights." Thus far there. Where the Ordinary Gloss says that these powers are distinct, and that the one does not depend on the other, and that the Emperor has power or rule from God alone. Dist. 93, c. Leginus, where the text says that the army makes the Emperor.

units.la: Ec 4 & & Glossa super verbo Imperatorem dicit sic: Ex sola enim electione Principum dico eum verum Imperatorem, sed tamen a Papa confirmetur, ut dixi 73. dist. quamvis. Haec Glossa. Et hoc etiam probatur in Authent. ubi de potestate Imperiali & Pontificali loquitur in haec verba: Quoniam mediator Dei & hominum Christus Iesus sic actibus propriis & dignitatibus distinctis officia potestatis utriusque discernit, ut Imperatores in via vitae Pontificibus indigerent, & Pontifices pro cursu temporalium rerum Imperialibus legibus uterentur spiritualu actio a carnalibus incurbus diflaret, & Deo militans (scilicet Papa) minime se negociis secularibus implicaret, ac vicissim ille (scilicet Imperator) non videretur divinis rebus praesidere, qui esset saecularibus negotiis occupatus. Haec ibi nbi Glossa Ordinaria de utraque potestate loquens, dicit hic: Dum ergo potestas finita fiunt, est hoc argumentum, quod Imperium non habetur a Papa, & quod Papa non habet utrumque gladium. Nam exercitus facit Imperatorem, 93. dist. c. legimus. Et imperium a solo Deo habetur, 23. q. 4. c. quaestum.
units.tr: And the Gloss on the word Imperatorem says this: "For I say that he is a true Emperor by the election of the Princes alone, but nevertheless he is to be confirmed by the Pope, as I said in dist. 73, Quamvis." Thus the Gloss. And this is also proved in the Authentica, which speaks of imperial and pontifical power in these words: "Since Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and men, so distinguishes the offices of each power by their own acts and distinct dignities, that Emperors should need the Pontiffs for the way of life, and the Pontiffs should use the imperial laws for the course of temporal affairs; that spiritual action should be kept apart from carnal cares, and the one who serves God (namely the Pope) should not entangle himself in secular business, and conversely that the other (namely the Emperor) should not seem to preside over divine things, if he were occupied with secular affairs." Thus there. Where the Ordinary Gloss, speaking of both powers, says here: "Therefore, since the powers are made finite, this is the argument that the Empire is not had from the Pope, and that the Pope does not have both swords. For the army makes the Emperor, dist. 93, c. Legimus. And the Empire is had from God alone, 23 q. 4, c. Quaestum."

units.la: si imperium haberet a Papa, posset in temporalibus ad Papam appellari: quod prohibet Alexander III. quod licet temporalia) suam (sc. Papae) jurisdictionem non attingunt, Ext. de Appellat. c. Si duo lis. & Qui filii sunt, c. causam, quae inter, 7. Et ita ego credo istas potestates distinctas esse. Haec Glossa. Et 8. dist. Quod jura humana per Imperatores & Reges saeculi, Deus humano generi distribuit. Et Lex dicit: spirituales & Sacerdotium ab eodem principio processerunt in actum, auth. quomodo oporteat Episcopos & Clericos perduci, in principio, collat. 1. Nec Imperator iurisdictionem Papae, nec Papa iurisdictionem Imperii turbare debet, Ext. de Judic. c. Novit ille. Ex quibus & aliis pluribus, quae brevitatis causa dimitto, clare patet, quod potestas & authoritas Imperialis, est immediate a solo Deo, & non a Papa, electus in Imperatorem ex sola electione est Rex Romanorum, & habet authoritatem, jurisdictionem, & potestatem Imperialem, etiam antequam inungatur, coronetur, & coronetur a Papa. Papa non habet in temporalibus dictam plenitudinem potestatis.
units.tr: If it had the Empire from the Pope, it could be appealed to the Pope in temporal matters; which Alexander III forbids, saying that although temporal matters do not touch his (that is, the Pope's) jurisdiction, Ext. De Appellationibus, c. Si duo lis and Qui filii sunt, c. Causam quae inter, 7. And so I believe that these powers are distinct." Thus the Gloss. And dist. 8: "God distributed human laws to the human race through the Emperors and kings of the world." And the law says: "Spiritual and priestly matters proceeded into act from the same principle," Authentica Quomodo oportet Episcopos, and in the beginning, Collatio 1. Neither should the Emperor disturb the jurisdiction of the Pope, nor the Pope the jurisdiction of the Empire, Ext. De Judiciis, c. Novit ille. From these and many other things, which I omit for brevity, it is clear that the power and authority of the Empire is immediately from God alone, and not from the Pope; one elected Emperor by election alone is King of the Romans, and has imperial authority, jurisdiction and power, even before he is anointed, crowned, and crowned by the Pope. The Pope does not have that fullness of power in temporal matters.

units.la: 3. Sed objicitur, quod ille, qui se Joannem Papam XXII. appellabat, per suos processus calumniavit, sive nullam, callum, & irritam pronunciavit electionem de nobis in Regem Romanorum factam, afferens in suis processibus, nos administrare non posse jura Imperii, & quod adhuc Imperii ad ipsum Joannem pertinebat de jure: & alia plura in ipsis processibus allegens & attentans contra nos & jura Imperii, & contra illos & contra jura & potestates eorum, ad quos Imperio pertinet electio Regis Romanorum, & contra jura & libertates Principum Germaniae & subditorum Imperii, & contra consuetudines antiquitus rationabiliter introductas & observatas, prout in ipsis processibus, imo verius excessibus, continetur. Insuper post dictos processus dam literas sub bulla sua dicitur fecisse, & per mundum publice transmisisse, in quibus Papa, tanquam Dominus universalis, non solum in spiritualibus, sed etiam in temporalibus, de imperio quam de omnibus regnis & dominiis temporalibus totius mundi ad suum libitum disponere et ordinare. Ad quae omnia duximus respondendum, quod dicti omnes processus, alias literae, & omnia & singula, quae per dictum Johannem in praedictis, & contra praedicta, gesta, tentata fuisse dicuntur, fuerunt & sunt nulla, & nullius valoris & momenti, rationibus infra scriptis.
units.tr: 3. But it is objected that he who called himself Pope John XXII, by his proceedings, calumniated, or pronounced null, void and invalid the election made of us as King of the Romans, asserting in his proceedings that we could not administer the rights of the Empire, and that the right of the Empire still belonged to John himself by law; and he alleged and attempted many other things in those same proceedings against us and the rights of the Empire, and against those and their rights and powers to whom the election of the King of the Romans pertains by the Empire, and against the rights and liberties of the Princes of Germany and the subjects of the Empire, and against customs reasonably introduced and observed from of old, as is contained in those proceedings, or rather excesses. Moreover, after the said proceedings he is said to have issued some letters under his seal, and to have publicly sent them through the world, in which the Pope, as universal lord, not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters, claimed to dispose and ordain at his pleasure concerning the Empire as well as all the kingdoms and temporal dominions of the whole world. To all these things we have thought it right to reply that all the said proceedings, the other letters, and all and each of the things which are said to have been done or attempted by the said John in the aforesaid matters and against the aforesaid, were and are null, and of no validity or weight, for the reasons written below.

units.la: 4. Prima ratio est, quoniam Papa quantumcunque Catholicus & legitimus non habet testatem, nec authoritatem aut jurisdictionem in temporalibus, & maxime supra jura Imperii, est immediate a solo Deo, ut evidenter probant Canones & jura superius allegata. Unde, quod praedictus Joannes fecit in praedictis, tanquam a non suo judice factum, nullius fuit momenti: probant aperte canones 11. q. 1. c. pen. & 2. q. 1. c. in primis, juxta sin. & 16. q. 1. c. frater noster, & Ext. de Judic. at si clerici, & Ext. de Consuet. c. ad nostram, & Cod. si non a competenti judice, l. 2. & 3. & nit. cum similibus.
units.tr: 4. The first reason is that the Pope, however Catholic and lawful, has no power, authority or jurisdiction in temporal matters, and especially over the rights of the Empire, which is immediately from God alone, as the canons and laws cited above clearly prove. Hence what the aforesaid John did in these matters, as done by one who was not his judge, was of no weight at all; the canons clearly prove this: 11 q. 1, c. pen., and 2 q. 1, c. In primis, near the end; and 16 q. 1, c. Frater noster; and Ext. De Judiciis, At si clerici; and Ext. De Consuetudine, c. Ad nostram; and Cod. Si non a competenti judice, l. 2 and 3, and others of the same kind.

units.la: 5. Secunda ratio est ex eo, quod dicti processus, imo verius excessus, fuerunt per dictum Johannem contra nos, & in praejudicium enorme nostrum, & illorum qui nos elegerunt in Regem Romanorum, & aliorum Principum Imperii & Alemaniae, ex notorie falsis causis, & nullo foro vocato, nobisque & aliis, quorum interest, absentibus & nullo modo legitime monitis & citatis, dum sacri canones, & jura divina & humana decernant, sententias & processus quoscunque gatos, absentibus iis, quorum causa agitur sive ventilatur, & eis rite & legitime non monitis & citatis, nullius existere firmitatis, 3. q. 4. per totum: & ubi etiam legitur sanctos Pontifices definivisse in haec verba: Omnia, quae adversus absentes in omni negocio aut loco aguntur aut judicantur, irrita erunt, & eracuata omnino, nec aliquam obtinent firmitatem, quia divinae & humanae leges hoc fieri prohibent, ut Ext. de c. in nomine Domini, & in auth. de Testibus, §. haec vero, collat. 7. & ff. Quae sententia sine appellat. rescindunt. l. 1. & edicto, & Cod. Quomodo & quando judex, l. ea quae. Et maxime in causis, quae summi Pontificis judicio reservantur, ordo juris & vigor aequitatis est subtiliter observandus, ut Ext. de Sent. & re judic. c. in causa, quod praedicti processus, imo verius excessus, fuerunt nulli, & nullius valoris penitus & omnino menti.
units.tr: 5. The second reason arises from the fact that the said proceedings, or rather excesses, were brought by the said John against us, and to our very great prejudice, and that of those who elected us King of the Romans, and of the other Princes of the Empire and of Germany, on notoriously false grounds, with no court summoned, and with us and others concerned absent and in no way lawfully warned and cited; whereas the sacred canons, and divine and human law, decree that all judgments and proceedings whatsoever, when those whose cause is being pleaded or debated are absent and have not been duly and lawfully warned and cited, have no firmness at all, 3 q. 4 throughout; and where it is also read that the holy Pontiffs defined in these words: "All things which are done or judged against absent parties in any matter or place shall be void and entirely annulled, and shall have no firmness at all, because divine and human laws forbid this to be done," Ext. De c. In nomine Domini, and Authentica De Testibus, §. Haec vero, Collatio 7; and Digest Quae sententia sine appellatione rescindunt, l. 1; and the Edict, and Cod. Quomodo et quando judex, l. Ea quae. And especially in causes which are reserved to the judgment of the supreme Pontiff, the order of law and the force of equity must be carefully observed; so, as Ext. De Sententia et re judicata, c. In causa, shows, the said proceedings, or rather excesses, were null, and wholly without any validity or weight.

units.la: 6. Nec obviat, si dicatur, quod praedictus Joannes in civitate Avinionis provinciae existens, sua Curia per suas literas, quas dicitur ad fores Ecclesiae majoris Avenionis appendi fecisse, non sententiam citavit: quoniam talis citatio, esto quod appareret, nullatenus fuit nec est dicenda legitima citatio, infra scripta. Prima ratio: quia sunt canones & jura ad hoc, quod censeatur & dicatur citatio firma, necesse est quod habens, qui citandus est, citetur aut personaliter, si inveniri potest, aut, si non poterit inveniri, publice citetur ad domum suam. Aliter, nisi sic citetur, non potest contra procedi, ut aperte probatur, 4. q. 5. c. quisquis, & Ext. De Dolo & contum. c. causam, in textu, & in Glossa, & in 6. venerabilis, in sin. & De Cleric. non residente. c. Ex tua. & Ext. Qui matrimonium accusare possit. c. 1. & De coin possess. causa reiser. c. nlt. & ff. Ex quib. causa majores, l. item aut, §. hoc autem, cum similibus. Et si procedatur, processus nullius est momenti, ut dicitur in superius allegatis juribus, 3. q. 4. c. careant, & ff. Quae sint sine appell. resciind. l. 1. & Cod. Quomodo & quando judex, l. ea qua. Ex quibus juribus clare patet, datur praejudicio quod talis (inquam) citatio per literas in civitate Avioni appensas repertetur factum esse, quod nihilo minus processus per ipsum Johannem factus fuisset irritus & inanis.
units.tr: 6. Nor is it an objection if it is said that the aforesaid John, while he was in the city of Avignon in the province, had his Curia cite us, not in person, but by letters which he is said to have had affixed to the doors of the greater church of Avignon. Such a citation, even if it were to appear, was in no way and is not to be called a lawful citation, for the following reason. First reason: because, according to the canons and laws, for a citation to be considered and called firm, the person who is to be cited must be cited either personally, if he can be found, or, if he cannot be found, publicly at his house. Otherwise, unless he is cited in this way, one cannot proceed against him, as is clearly proved in 4, q. 5, c. quisquis; in Ext. De Dolo et contumacia, c. causam, in the text and the Gloss; in 6, venerabilis, in fine; in De Clericis non residentibus, c. Ex tua; in Ext. Qui matrimonium accusare possit, c. 1; in De cointeressentia possessionis, causa reiser., c. ult.; and in Dig. Ex quibus causis maiores, l. item aut, §. hoc autem, with similar texts. And if proceedings are taken, the process is of no force, as is said in the laws alleged above: 3, q. 4, c. careant; Dig. Quae sint sine appellatione rescindi, l. 1; and Cod. Quomodo et quando iudex, l. ea quae. From these laws it is clear that, granting (I say) that such a citation by letters affixed in the city of Avignon had been found to have been made, the process carried out by the same John would nonetheless have been void and empty.

units.la: 2. Secunda ratio est, quia ad hoc, ut citatio de jure legitima censeatur, & arctet citatum ad veniendum, necessum est quod assignetur illi, qui citandus est, terminus & locus ad comparendum sensus, prout manifeste probant jura, Ext. De Appellat. c. ex parte tua, & 33. q. 2. c. sire de conjug. ubi providentia loci in quo nulla vis formidetur multitudinis, nec fit difficile testes producere vel alteras personas, quae tamen a monibus quam a veniendis Romanis legibus in hujusmodi controversiis requiruntur. Haec ibi: & 3. q. 9. Ext. Ut lit non contestat. c. accedens, & ff. De Judic. l. sed locus. Sed notorium est & indubitatum quod dictus Johannes tam nos quam Imperii nostri fideles & amicos, odio capitali, & etiam exercitu persequebatur de facto, & civitates & jura Imperii sibi usurpare & subjugare, quantum poterat, conabatur. Civitas quoque Avinionis, in qua idem Johannes cum suo consistorio movebat, & ad quam nos per suas literas evocabat, & ille, qui illius civitatis dominium detinebat, nos & omnium Imperium habebat odio notorio & antiquo. Unde patet, quod deciperet, qui dicerent vel sentirent, talem citationem nos ad comparendum modo aliquo coartasse. Quis enim auderet dicere, quod talis consistorii in tali loco periculosum teneremur subire judicium, & in hostium nostrorum sinum, & mortis periculo ultroneo nos offerre? Paret igitur, quod talis citatio, si fiat, de nobis, foret irrita & inanis.
units.tr: 2. The second reason is that, for a citation to be considered lawful and to bind the one cited to appear, a time and a place for appearing must be assigned to the person who is to be cited, as the laws clearly show: Ext. De Appellationibus, c. ex parte tua; 33, q. 2, c. sive de coniugio, where provision is made for a place in which no violence of a crowd is to be feared, nor is it difficult to produce witnesses or other persons, which in matters of this kind are required by the laws of the Romans, rather than by the customs (of the place). Thus far there; and 3, q. 9; Ext. Ut lite non contestata, c. accedens; and Dig. De iudiciis, l. sed locus. But it is notorious and beyond doubt that the said John was in fact persecuting us with mortal hatred, as well as our faithful followers and friends of the Empire, and even with an army, and was trying, as far as he could, to usurp and subjugate to himself the cities and rights of the Empire. The city of Avignon as well, where the same John sat with his consistory, and to which he summoned us by his letters, and he who held the lordship of that city, had a notorious and ancient hatred of us and of the whole Empire. Hence it is plain that those who would say or think that such a citation had bound us to appear in any way would be mistaken. For who would dare to say that we were bound to submit to the judgement of such a consistory in such a place, and to offer ourselves voluntarily into the bosom of our enemies and to the danger of death? It is therefore clear that such a citation, if it were made against us, would be void and empty.

units.la: 3. Tertia ratio sumitur ex eo, quod in sacris canonibus & legibus statuitur, quod nullus in propria causa posset judicare, vel jus sibi dicere, ut probatur 33. q. 4. c. inter querelas, & 23. q. 5. de occidendis, & q. 4. c. 1. & Cod. Ne quis in causa propria judicet, vel jus sibi dicat. Sed manifestum adeo est & notorium, ut nulla possit tergiversatione negari, quod praedictus Johannes de facto contendebat, licet quod in non solum in spiritualibus sed & in temporalibus, & in nos & in totum Imperium, ac jura Imperii usurpare plenitudinem potestatis: & quod super hoc contra nos controversiam & litigium de facto movebat, & jura Imperii etiam hostiliter sibi pro viribus usurpare conabatur; & nos & Imperii nostri fideles, quantum poterat, tanquam adversarios & hostes & inimicos nostros & Imperii, consequi nitebatur. Unde etiam contra eum, tanquam contra adversarium, inimicum, & hostem nostrum & etiam Imperii, pro defensione nostra & etiam fidelium nostrorum, & juris Imperialis ac fidei, appellamus ad futurum generale Concilium, in loco tuto & secuto modo debito & secundum formam sacrorum canonum congregandum. Ex quibus sequitur manifeste, quod dicti processus, immo veriu dicti excessus, per dictum Johannem contra nos & contra fideles nostros & jura Imperii facta fuerunt in propria causa, & temere & perperam attentati: & quod ipse in ipsis processibus se judicem simul & partem effecit, ac per consequens, quod fuerunt irriti & nullius penitus firmitatis.
units.tr: 3. The third reason is drawn from the fact that the sacred canons and laws decree that no one can judge in his own cause, or pronounce law for himself: as is proved in 33, q. 4, c. inter querelas; in 23, q. 5, de occidendis; and q. 4, c. 1; and Cod. Ne quis in causa sua iudicet vel sibi ius dicat. But it is so manifest and notorious that it can be denied by no evasion, that the aforesaid John was in fact claiming for himself not only spiritual but also temporal power, and the fullness of power over us and over the whole Empire, and over the rights of the Empire; and that he was moving, in fact, a controversy and lawsuit against us over this; and he was trying, with all his might, to usurp the rights of the Empire even by hostile means; and he strove to pursue us and our faithful subjects of the Empire, as far as he could, as adversaries, enemies and foes of ours and of the Empire. Hence we also appeal against him, as against an adversary, enemy and foe of ours and of the Empire, for our defence and that of our faithful subjects, and of the imperial law and faith, to a future general Council, to be convened in a safe place and in the due manner and according to the form of the sacred canons. From these things it clearly follows that the said processes, or rather excesses, were carried out by the said John against us, against our faithful subjects and the rights of the Empire, in his own cause, and were rashly and wrongly undertaken; and that in these very proceedings he made himself both judge and party; and consequently that they were null and of no force whatever.

units.la: 4. Tertio objicitur contra nos, quod dictus Johannes tam in nos quam in omnes sequaces ac fideles nostros, habentes & tenentes nos pro Imperatore nomine & honore, & nobis tanquam Imperii obedientes, & reverentiam exhibentes, & in omnibus admittentes nos ad divina, seu nobiles participantes in divinis, aut divina officia celebrantes coram nobis, & praebentes nobis auxilium, consilium, & favorem, de facto excommunicationis sententiam fulminavit: & Ecclesias & civitates, quae contra facerent, Ecclesiastico suppositi judicio. Unde dicitur, Quod sententia pastoris justa sive injusta, servanda est & timenda. Ad quae respondemus & dicimus, quod, secundum sanctiones & jura, hujus sententiae & processus fuerunt & sunt nullae ac nullius firmitatis, nulliusque penitus & momenti: nec sunt aliquo modo timendae nec servandae, nec timendi nec servandi quod evidenter ostenditur & probatur rationibus infra scriptis. Prima ratio sic sumitur. Certum quod cum Praelatus Ecclesiae in suo mandato excedit formam & potestatem a sacris canonibus traditam, & in contra mandatum hujus facientes excommunicationis in singulares personas Ecclesias, & in Universitates, sententias interdicti promulgat, talem sententiam non tenere, nullamque ipso jure fore, nullatenusque observandam, ut probatur per id quod legitur & notatur in Excessibus Praelatorum, c. cum ad quorundam. Temerarium enim est & indignum, aliquem sibi usurpare, quod Romana Catholica Ecclesia non concedit, Ext. De Privileg. c. sane. Sed, probatum est evidenter, sancta Romana Ecclesia Catholica & Apostolica non concedit, ut liber Papae jus Imperii & potestatem in temporalibus usurpare: quia, ut dictum est, ista Papae admittunt, quae solum est in spiritualibus, non contingunt, ut in superius allegato c. Ext. De Apostolis. Et maximum est, quod dictus Johannes per suas antedictas sententias excessit formam potestatem Papae traditam; quia jus Imperii & potestatem in temporalibus sibi usurpare conatus est, sacrorum canonum constituta. Ergo hujus sententiae sunt & fuerunt nullae & nullatenus servandae. Et hic est unus de calibus expressis, in quibus sententia de excommunicatione nullatenus observanda.
units.tr: 4. Thirdly, it is objected against us that the said John, in fact, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against us and against all our followers and faithful subjects, who hold and regard us as Emperor in name and honour, and obey us as the Empire does, and show us reverence, and admit us to divine rites, or who take part in the divine offices with us, or celebrate divine offices in our presence, or give us aid, counsel or favour; and he subjected to ecclesiastical judgement the churches and cities which acted otherwise. Hence it is said: The sentence of a minister, whether just or unjust, is to be observed and feared. To which we answer and say that, according to the sanctions and laws, these sentences and processes were and are null and of no force, and of no validity or weight whatever; nor are they in any way to be feared or observed, nor are those who fear or observe them to be feared; as is evidently shown and proved by the reasons set out below. The first reason is taken thus. It is certain that when a prelate of the Church, in his command, exceeds the form and power handed down by the sacred canons, and promulgates sentences of excommunication against particular persons and churches and communities, and of interdict, against those who act contrary to his command, such a sentence does not hold, and is void by law, and in no way to be observed; as is proved by what is read and noted in Ext. De excessibus praelatorum, c. cum ad quorundam. For it is rash and unworthy for anyone to claim for himself what the Roman Catholic Church does not grant: Ext. De privilegiis, c. sane. But it has been clearly proved that the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church does not grant that the Pope, being free, should usurp the right and power of the Empire in temporal matters; because, as has been said, those things which the Pope admits are those which pertain to spiritual matters only, as in the chapter of Ext. De apostolis alleged above. And the greatest point is that the said John, by his aforesaid sentences, exceeded the form and power handed down to the Pope; because he tried to usurp to himself the right of the Empire and power in temporal matters, which the constitutions of the sacred canons forbid. Therefore the sentences of this kind are and were null, and in no way to be observed. And this is one of the clear cases in which a sentence of excommunication is in no way to be observed.

units.la: 5. Secunda ratio sic sumitur. Certum est de jure, quod ubi est error expressus in sententia vel in mandato praesidentis, puta quia praecipit, quod non obediat suo superiori; vel praecipit aliquid contra Domino, vel statuat contra Deum & Sacram Scripturam, non est audiendus nec timendus.
units.tr: 5. The second reason is taken thus. It is certain by law that where there is an express error in the sentence or command of a superior, for example because he orders someone not to obey his own superior, or orders something against the Lord, or decrees against God and Holy Scripture, that person is neither to be heard nor feared.

units.la: {*} Papalis excommunicatio fulmen brutum. contra Deum, vel contra sacram scripturam, talis sententia ipso jure nullius est momenti, nec etiam ut probatur per illud, quod legitur Ext. De Sententia excommunicationis, c. venerabilibus, juxta sin. in Gloss. & 11. q. 3. c. ii qui praesunt, cum duobus cc. sequentibus. Et idem est, utque sententia est ipso jure nulla, ut probatur aperte per illud quod legitur & notatur Ext. De sententia excommunicationis, c. per tuas. & Ext. De Procurat. c. in nostra praesentia, in fi. & Ext. De Crimine falsi, c. Johannes. Ext. De Sententia & re judicata, c. 1. Sed manifestum est, quod dictus Johannes in dictis suis processibus & sententiis expressit, quod non obediatur nobis, cui omnes Imperio subjecti obedire et reverentiam exhibere secundum divina & humana jura sunt astricti: & quod hoc fecit, volendo sibi jus Imperii potestatem omnimodam in temporalibus contra Dominum & contra justitiam usurpare, ac extenditur, ut dictum est, ejus authoritas & potestas. Ergo ipsae sententiae sunt & fuerunt nullius penitus firmitatis, nec fuerunt nec sunt quomodolibet observandae.
units.tr: {*} A papal excommunication is an empty thunderbolt. If such a sentence is against God or against Holy Scripture, it is void in law of itself and has no force, as is shown by what is read in Ext. De sententia excommunicationis, c. venerabilibus, and in the gloss on it, and in 11 q. 3 c. ii qui praesunt, with the two following chapters. It is likewise null in law, as is clearly shown by what is read and noted in Ext. De sententia excommunicationis, c. per tuas; Ext. De procuratoribus, c. in nostra praesentia, at the end; and Ext. De crimine falsi, c. Johannes; Ext. De sententia et re iudicata, c. 1. But it is plain that the said John, in his processes and sentences, has declared that we, to whom all subjects of the Empire are bound by divine and human law to render obedience and reverence, are not to be obeyed; and that he did this by wishing to usurp for himself, against the Lord and against justice, the full power of the Empire in temporal matters. As has been said, his authority and power extend thus. Therefore those sentences are, and always have been, wholly without firmness, and in no way were or are to be observed.

units.la: 11. Tertia ratio sic sumitur. Manifestum est, quod quando sententia excommunicationis vel interdicti prolata est post appellationem legitimam, nulla est, nec est aliquatenus timenda, ut aperte probatur Ext. De Offic. & potestat. jud. deleg. c. 32. cum olim, in fine, & De Sententia excommunicationis, c. venerabilibus, in fine, & Ext. De Appellat. c. ad hoc, quod & habetur per illud quod legitur Ext. De Sententia excommunicationis, c. per tuas, in Glossa Ordinaria, & per Dominum Hostiensem super c. solet, & in Summa, super quam alios Doctores. Sed manifestum & notorium est, quod dudum contra dictum Johannem & processus, quos ipse de facto fecit contra nos, ac potestatem authoritatem Imperialem, & praejudicium & derogationem fidei Catholicae, quam sancta Ecclesia firmiter hactenus docuit & credidit, & docet & credit & tenet, appellavimus ad generale Concilium, in loco securo & congruo congregandum, & ad sanctam matrem Ecclesiam Catholicam. Quae appellatio fuit ad ipsius Johannis noticiam deducta, prout notorium est & constat etiam per legitima documenta, & quia ipse Johannes, post & contra dictationem promulgavit, & protulit de facto contra nos & fideles nostros, & nos sequentes, & mentes consilium, auxilium, & favorem, dictas excommunicationes & interdicti sententias possunt. Ergo fuerunt & sunt nullae, & nullius valoris & momenti, nec sunt aliquo modo nec observandae.
units.tr: 11. The third reason is put as follows. It is plain that when a sentence of excommunication or interdict is pronounced after a lawful appeal, it is void and in no way to be feared, as is clearly shown in Ext. De officio et potestate iudicis delegati, c. 32, cum olim, at the end; and De sententia excommunicationis, c. venerabilibus, at the end; and Ext. De appellationibus, c. ad hoc. This is also held from what is read in Ext. De sententia excommunicationis, c. per tuas, in the Ordinary Gloss, and from Lord Hostiensis on c. solet, and in his Summa, as well as other doctors.
