But it is plain and notorious that long ago, against the said John and the processes which he himself has carried out against us, against the power and authority of the Empire, and to the prejudice and derogation of the Catholic faith, which holy Church has hitherto firmly taught and believed, and still teaches, believes and holds, we appealed to a general Council, to be convened in a safe and suitable place, and to our holy mother the Catholic Church. This appeal was brought to the notice of John himself, as is notorious and is also established by lawful documents. And since John himself, after and against that appeal, has issued and carried out acts against us, our faithful subjects, and those who follow us, and has given counsel, aid and favour to those [who promulgate] the said sentences of excommunication and interdict, they are and were null, of no value or force, and in no way to be observed.

units.la: 12. Nec obstat, quod dicitur, quod Papa non habet superiorem. Unde, ut aliqui garriunt, rectius est ab ipso quomodolibet appellari. Et vere non obstat, quoniam manifestum est secundum Catholicam & sacrorum canonum, quod Papa, ubi de fide sive de jure divino agitur, habet superiorem in terris, a quo possit judicari: & per consequens, ad ipsum superiorem valet appellari. Probatur etiam notanter per illud, quod legitur & notatur 40. dist. c. Si Papa, ubi expresse dicitur, quod Papa a nemine judicari potest, nisi deviat a fide Catholica. Ergo si Papa deviat a fide, habet superiorem in terris, a quo potest judicari: & per consequens ad ipsum potest appellari. Hoc etiam probat quod dicit Augustinus in epist. ad Glorium & Eleusium & reliquos Donatistas, ubi de Papae & Collegii Cardinalium scribit Dominus sic: Quasi non eis duci possit, & adhuc ut stifirmemus illos Episcopos, qui Romae judicarunt, non bonos fuisse. Refiabat adhuc universalis Ecclesia plenarium, ubi etiam cum ipsis judicibus causa poterit agitari, ut si male judicasse convicti essent, eorum sententia solvere. Augustinus. Ex quibus plurimis authoritatibus, quae brevitatis causa dimittuntur, patet, quod Concilium universale Ecclesiae Catholicae, ubi de jure divino aut de fide agitur, superius est Concilio Papae & Cardinalium, & ipsum solvit & tollit, si ipsi repugnent. Cum defensione juris Imperii, quod est a jure divino, & fidei Catholicae, appellamus ad generale Concilium in loco tuto & securo congregandum, sequitur quod appellatio nostra fuit interposita ad quem legitime potuit appellari.
units.tr: 12. Nor does it stand in the way that it is said the Pope has no superior. Hence, as some chatter, it is more correct to appeal from him in any case. And indeed it does not stand in the way, since it is plain according to the Catholic faith and the sacred canons that when matters of faith or of divine law are at issue, the Pope has a superior on earth by whom he may be judged; and consequently an appeal may lawfully be made to that superior. This is also proved expressly by what is read and noted in D. 40 c. Si Papa, where it is plainly said that the Pope can be judged by no one unless he deviates from the Catholic faith. Therefore, if the Pope deviates from the faith, he has a superior on earth by whom he can be judged, and consequently an appeal may be made to him. This is also proved by what Augustine says in his letter to Glorius, Eleusius and the other Donatists, where he writes, concerning the Pope and the college of Cardinals, as follows: "As if the case could not be brought before them; and, to confirm further that those bishops who judged at Rome were not good men, the universal Church still remained as a plenary council, where the cause could also be argued before the very judges, so that if they were convicted of having judged badly, their sentence might be annulled." Augustine. From these many authorities, which are omitted for brevity, it is clear that a general Council of the Catholic Church, when matters of divine law or faith are at issue, is superior to the Council of the Pope and Cardinals, and annuls and sets it aside if they oppose it. Since we, in defence of the right of the Empire, which is from divine law, and of the Catholic faith, have appealed to a general Council to be convened in a safe and secure place, it follows that our appeal was lodged with the one to whom an appeal could lawfully be made.

units.la: 13. Plures quoque aliae rationes & causae sunt, ex quibus cernitur evidenter, quod praedictae sententiae fuerunt & sunt nullae, ac nullius valoris sive momenti, nec fuerunt nec sunt timendae, quatenus observandae. Quae rationes & causae in appellationibus & provocationibus contra nos, & Nos, & Imperium, & fidem Catholicam, quam Sancta Romana tenet Ecclesia, pugnantes solenniter interjectis, seriatim praesentibus litteris explicantur: quas omnes seriatim praesentibus litteris care, prolixum nimium videretur.
units.tr: 13. There are also many other reasons and causes by which it is clearly seen that the aforesaid sentences were and are null, of no value or force, and were not and are not to be feared or observed. These reasons and causes, set forth solemnly in appeals and provocations lodged against us, against Ourselves, against the Empire and against the Catholic faith, which the holy Roman Church holds, are explained one by one in the present letter. To set them all out one by one here would seem far too lengthy.

units.la: 14. Quamobrem denunciamus & dicimus processus & sententias, de quibus superius dictum fuisse & esse nullas, & nullos, & nullius valoris & momenti, & nullatenus observandas: ac universis & singulis sub nostro Imperio degentibus, cujuscunque status, dignitatis, ac conditionis existentibus, precipimus & mandamus, quatenus nulla persona singularis, aut communitas vel universitas dictas excommunicationis & interdicti sententias praesumat observare, vel facere ac sustinere modo libet observari. Quicunque autem contra hoc nostrum mandatum praesumpserit facere, veniat, eum omnibus feudis, quae ab Imperio tenet, ac omnibus jurisdictionibus, gratiis, & privilegiis, libertatibus & immunitatibus, a nobis vel praedecessoribus nostris et concessis, exnunc privamus.
units.tr: 14. Wherefore we declare and state that the processes and sentences mentioned above are null and void, of no value or force, and in no way to be observed; and to all and each of those living under our Empire, of whatever rank, dignity or condition, we command and order that no single person, community or corporate body presume to observe, or to cause or permit to be observed in any way, the said sentences of excommunication and interdict. And whoever presumes to act against this our command, we deprive him henceforth of all fiefs which he holds from the Empire, and of all jurisdictions, graces and privileges, liberties and immunities granted to him by us or by our predecessors.

units.la: 15. In quorum omnium testimonium & fidem praesentes literas fieri fecimus, & nostrae Majestatis sigillo munivimus.
units.tr: 15. In witness and assurance of all these things we have caused the present letters to be made and have strengthened them with the seal of our Majesty.

units.la: Papa an habeat superiorem judicem. Majestatis bulla justimus & fecimus communiri. Et, ut ipsæ literæ ad communem omnium noticiam deducantur, eas majoris Ecclesiæ de Franckenfurt ostiis appendi sive affigi faciemus, quæ hunc protestum nostrum quasi sonoro præconio publicabunt, ita quòd nullus possit prætendere, vel ignorantiam allegare, quòd ad eum prædicta non pervenerint, sive quòd ea ignoraverit: cùm non sit verisimile occultum & incognitum remanere, quòd tam patenter fuit omnibus publicatum. Datum in oppido nostro de Franckenfurt, die VIII. mensis Augusti, Anno Domini MCCCXXXVIII.
units.tr: Whether the Pope has a superior judge. We have caused it to be secured with the bulla of our Majesty. And so that these letters may be brought to the common notice of all, we shall have them hung or affixed to the doors of the greater church at Frankfurt, which will publish this our protest as with a sounding herald, so that no one can claim or plead ignorance that the aforesaid did not come to him or that he did not know of it, since it is not likely that what has been so openly published to all should remain hidden and unknown. Given in our town of Frankfurt, on the 8th day of August, in the year of our Lord 1338.

units.la: PRINCIPUM ELECTORUM S. ROMANI IMPERII RESCRIPTUM SUPER LUDOVICO IMPERATORE, ET DISCORDIA IMPERII & Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The Rescript of the Electors of the Holy Roman Empire concerning Emperor Louis, and the Discord of Empire and Church.

units.la: EX COMITIIS REINSENSIBUS, Anno Domini M.CCC.XXXVIII.
units.tr: FROM THE DIET AT RHENSE, in the year of the Lord 1338.

units.la: Sanctissimo in Christo Patri ac Domino, Domino Benedicto Papæ, vestri devoti filii, Henricus Dei & Apostolicæ Sedis gratia Archiepiscopus Moguntinensis, Electorum Princeps, Decanus, necnon per Germaniam sacri Imperii Archicancellarius; Balduinus Archiepiscopus Trevirensis, Cancellarius Galliæ; Waleramus Archiepiscopus Coloniensis, Cancellarius Italiæ; Waldemarus Marchio Brandeburgensis, Camerarius; Rudolphus Palatinus, Dapifer; Rudolphus Dux Saxoniæ, Portitor ensis, Romanorum Regis, & coronandi Imperatoris Electores.
units.tr: To the most holy Father in Christ and Lord, Lord Benedict, Pope, your devoted sons: Henry, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See Archbishop of Mainz, Prince Elector, Dean, and also Archchancellor of the Holy Empire throughout Germany; Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier, Chancellor of Gaul; Walram, Archbishop of Cologne, Chancellor of Italy; Waldemar, Margrave of Brandenburg, Chamberlain; Rudolph, Count Palatine, Seneschal; Rudolph, Duke of Saxony, Marshal, Electors of the King of the Romans and of the Emperor to be crowned.

units.la: 1. Gravamur non modicè, & turbamur ex intimis, cùm reverendam sacrosanctam Romanam Ecclesiam, matrem nostram, & ipsius Summos Pontifices, quibus reverentiam & honorem exhibemus promptis & devotis animis omni vice; ac sacrosanctum Imperium, & Imperatores seu Reges ipsius, quorum defensio ad nos ac omnes alios Electores præceteris mundi Principibus specialiter pertinere dinoscitur, sicut temporibus præsentibus videmus, ad invicem discordare. Nam ex hoc non potuerunt sibi & populo Christiano proficere & prodesse, & prout est divinitus institutum, sibi mutuò suffragari. Propter quæ in diversis mundi partibus, provinciis, & terris, ipsis regendas gubernandas commissis, innumera execrabilia pericula animarum, personarum & rerum, & diversa scandala in Dei Ecclesia (quod dolenter referimus) sunt suborta; & majora præsumuntur futuris temporibus, quæ ad planum dici nequeunt vel conscribi, certitudinaliter suboriri. Quæ submoveri non possunt, nisi utraque Potestas contenta sit suis juribus & consuetudinibus hactenus observatis, & reformentur, quæ una contra aliam attemptavit.
units.tr: 1. We are not a little burdened and deeply troubled that the reverend, most holy Roman Church, our mother, and its supreme Pontiffs, whom we honour and revere at all times with ready and devoted hearts, and the most holy Empire and its Emperors or Kings, whose defence is known to belong to us and to all the other Electors above all the princes of the world, are at odds with one another, as we see in the present times. For from this they have been unable to benefit and profit themselves and the Christian people, and to lend mutual support, as has been divinely ordained. On account of this, in various parts, provinces and lands of the world entrusted to their rule and governance, countless dangerous threats to souls, persons and goods, and various scandals (as we sadly report) have arisen in the Church of God; and greater ones, which cannot be described or written down in full, are certainly expected to arise in future times. These cannot be removed unless each power is content with its own rights and customs observed until now, and those things which one has attempted against the other are set right.

units.la: 2. Sanctitati vestræ cum omni devotione & in modum, quem possumus, meliorem & humiliorem referimus bono zelo, quod super premissis & ad consulendum & providendum sacrosanctoRomano Imperio, cujus jura, honores, bona, libertates, & consuetudines, prostrata jacent, & à diversis Ecclesiasticis & Sæcularibus sunt & fuerunt hactenus in grave præjudicium dicti Imperii occupata, & multipliciter conculcata, xv. die mensis Julii, anni xxxviii. in Reinse super alveo Reni Principes Electores super negotiis Imperii tractandis convenire consueverunt ab antiquo, ibidem omnibus Principibus Electoribus Imperii in unum fuimus congregari, & diversis deliberationibus & consiliis præmissis, sicut divinæ gratiæ placuit, omnes unanimes fuimus, & nullo penitus pro defensione & recuperatione jurium, honorum, bonorum, libertatum, consuetudinum Romani Imperii ac totius Christianitatis, ad cujus regimen & defensionem idem Imperium specialiter ordinatum dinoscitur, disposuimus & ordinavimus, pro nobis & successoribus nostris juraverunt jurejurando per sacramenta communiter nobis & omnibus Electoribus nostris quod jura, honores, bona, libertates, & consuetudines dicti Imperii, & nostra, nobis in electione competentia ex consuetudine vel de jure, manuteneamus, defendamus, & illibata cotore posse & viribus nostris, contra omnes homines cujuscumque præeminentiæ, dignitatis, existant; & quòd hoc non obmittamus propter aliqua pericula rerum & personarum, aut prætermissa mandata, processus, per quemcumque aut in quemcumque modum & formam prolati sint, vel proferantur, contra Imperium & nos vel Electores nostros; per quæ dicto Imperio ac nostris Electoribus nostris in prædictis junibus, bonis, hominibus, libertatibus, & consuetudinibus lædi/ictum fit, vel in futurum posset præjudicium generari.
units.tr: 2. With all devotion, and in the best and humblest manner we can, we report to Your Holiness, from a good zeal, concerning the above matters, and for the purpose of consulting and providing for the most holy Roman Empire, whose rights, honours, goods, liberties and customs lie prostrate, and have been and still are seized by various churchmen and laymen to the grave prejudice of the said Empire, and trampled on in many ways: on the fifteenth day of July, in the year 1338, at Rhense on the bank of the Rhine, the Electoral Princes have been accustomed from of old to assemble to deal with the affairs of the Empire. There, all the Electoral Princes of the Empire were gathered together, and after various deliberations and counsels had been held, as it pleased divine grace, we were all of one mind. And we resolved and ordained, for the defence and recovery of the rights, honours, goods, liberties and customs of the Roman Empire and of all Christendom, for whose government and defence the same Empire is known to have been specially ordained, that we and our successors would swear together, by oath upon the sacraments, to ourselves and all our fellow Electors, that we would maintain and defend the rights, honours, goods, liberties and customs of the said Empire, and our own rights which belong to us in the election by custom or by law, and keep them unimpaired with all our strength and power against all men of whatever pre-eminence or dignity they may be; and that we would not neglect this on account of any dangers to goods or persons, or any mandates or processes issued, or to be issued, by anyone and in any manner or form against the Empire and ourselves or our Electors, by which harm is done, or in future could be caused, to the said Empire and to our Electors in the aforesaid rights, goods, men, liberties and customs.

units.la: 3. Et eandem super præmisso lamentabili desiderio, & causis originalibus, ex quibus ortum dinoscitur quod inter sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam, ac sacrum Romanum Imperium & Dominum nostrum Ludovicum Romanorum Imperatorem, jam longis temporibus diligenti & sollicita deliberatione prehabita, nos & alii Electores nostri cognovimus, & nobis constitit evidenter ex processibus Domini Johannis Papæ XXII. prædecessoris vestri, quod ipse primò & postea sententias excommunicationis & interdicti (si sic dici merentur) acalias diversas sententias & processus de facto contra Deum, & justitiam, & juris ordinem fulminavit contra prædictum Dominum nostrum Ludovicum Romanorum Imperatorem, ac fautores & adhærentes sibi; qui à majori parte Principum Electorum fuit rite & rationabiliter in Regem Romanorum electus, in Imperem postea consecrandus; quod fe de administratione Imperii intromisit, non approbata per ipsum praedecessorem vestrum ipsius electione, quam in discordia asserunt celebratam. Per sententias & processus, cum juri & consuetudini Imperii praefato Domino nostro Ludovico & aliis Electoribus Imperii maxime derogetur, cum jure caveatur, & consuetudine, cujus contrarium memoria hominum non exstitit, sit rationabiliter introductum, & sine cujusvis contradictione minime observatum, sicut etiam in praedicto Parlamento per nos & alios Coelectores nostros, praelatos diligenti deliberatione & discussione, ac consilio multorum Principum, Comitum, Baronum, & Nobilium est concorditer declaratum, & sententialiter diffinitum; quod vacante Romano Imperio qui eligitur concorditer, vel a majori parte Principum Electorum, pro Rege Romanorum habendus est; & quod nec nominatione, approbatione, confirmatione, consensu, vel auctoritate Sedis Apostolicae, super administratione bonorum & jurium Imperii indiget, sive titulo Regis mendo; quodque jura & bona Imperii administrare & gubernare poterit, & de jure & consuetudine, nulla Sedis Apostolicae super hoc licentia habita vel obtenta.
units.tr: 3. And concerning the above lamentable desire, and the original causes from which it is known to have arisen, namely that between the holy Roman Church and the sacred Roman Empire and our Lord Louis, Emperor of the Romans, after long and careful and diligent deliberation beforehand, we and our fellow Electors have come to know, and it has been clearly established to us from the processes of Lord John XXII, your predecessor, that he first, and afterwards, fulminated sentences of excommunication and interdict (if such names deserve to be given them) and other various sentences and processes, unlawfully, against God and justice and the order of law, against the said Lord our Louis, Emperor of the Romans, and his supporters and adherents; who, by the greater part of the Electoral Princes, was duly and reasonably elected King of the Romans, to be afterwards consecrated as Emperor; and that he meddled in the administration of the Empire, his election not having been approved by the said your predecessor, although they assert that it was celebrated in discord. Since by these sentences and processes what is owed to the law and custom of the Empire is greatly derogated from, to the said Lord our Louis and the other Electors of the Empire, since the law provides against it, and a custom, of which the contrary is not within human memory, has been reasonably introduced and, without any contradiction, has not been observed; just as it was also solemnly declared and defined in the aforesaid Parliament by us and our other fellow Electors, the prelates, after careful deliberation and discussion, and with the counsel of many princes, counts, barons and nobles: that when the Roman Empire is vacant, he who is elected unanimously, or by the greater part of the Electoral Princes, is to be held as King of the Romans; and that he needs no nomination, approval, confirmation, consent or authority of the Apostolic See for the administration of the goods and rights of the Empire, nor any title of king from it; and that he is able to administer and govern the rights and goods of the Empire, and by law and custom no licence of the Apostolic See for this has been had or obtained.

units.la: 4. Quare cum Sanctitas vestra teneatur prae omnibus Regnis mundi defendere jura Imperii ad defensionem Sedis Apostolicae & totius fidei Christianae est coelitus ordinatum, & sine cujus gubernatione & defensione non potest in opulentia pacis perstare Christianus populus, colere pacis auctorem: clementiae Sanctitatis vestrae supplicamus, cum omni humilitate & reverentia, qua possumus & valemus, quatenus sententias & processus praenotatos, & quidquid *ad nos secutum est, totaliter & penitus revocetis, tanquam in praejudicium Imperii & juris prolatos. Quae jura illibata pro posse servare tenemur ratione a nobis praestiti juramenti, ut in omni obedientia & devotione Ecclesiae Romanae & Sanctitatis vestrae debeamus devotem perpetuo permanere. Et ne, si secus fieret, nos & alii Coelectores nostri, cum aliis Principibus Ecclesiasticis & Saecularibus Alamaniae, cogeremur invenire & quaerere contra eosdem fusus & sententias, quamvis inviti, remedia opportuna. Super praemissis ad Sanctitatem vestram transmittimus, quibus in dicendis & petendis nostro nomine fidem, vestram clementiam adhibere.
units.tr: 4. Wherefore, since Your Holiness is bound, above all the kingdoms of the world, to defend the rights of the Empire, and it has been ordained from heaven for the defence of the Apostolic See and of the whole Christian faith, and without whose government and defence the Christian people cannot remain in the abundance of peace, to cultivate the Author of peace: we beseech the clemency of Your Holiness, with all the humility and reverence we can and are able to show, that you would wholly and entirely revoke the sentences and processes set out above, and whatever has followed from them to us, as having been issued to the prejudice of the Empire and of its law. We are bound to keep these rights unimpaired, as far as we can, by reason of the oath we have taken, so that in all obedience and devotion to the Roman Church and to Your Holiness we ought to remain devoted for ever. And lest, if it were otherwise done, we and our fellow Electors, together with the other ecclesiastical and secular princes of Germany, should be compelled, though unwillingly, to find and seek suitable remedies against the same processes and sentences. We send these matters to Your Holiness, and we ask that you give faith to our clemency in what is to be said and sought in our name.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. CONSTITUTIO DE IMPERII JVRIBVS ET EXCELLENTIA, ET POTESTATE Electi Romanorum Regis; LATA IN COMITIIS COLONIENSIBUS, ANNO DOMINI MCCCXXXVII.
units.tr: THE CONSTITUTION OF LUDWIG IV, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS, CONCERNING THE RIGHTS AND EXCELLENCE OF THE EMPIRE, AND THE POWER OF THE ELECTED KING OF THE ROMANS; ENACTED AT THE DIET OF COLOGNE IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1337.

units.la: ICET jura utriusque Testamenti manifeste declarent, Imperialem dignitatem & potestatem immediate in filio Dei ab antiquo processisse, & Deum per Imperatorem & Reges nunc humano generi aperte tribuisse: & quod Imperator ex sola electione eorum, ad quos pertinet, verus efficitur Imperator, nec alicuius alterius eget confirmatione seu approbatione: quoad temporalia, non habet superiorem, sed eidem gentes subsunt & nationes. Et ipse Dominus noster Jesus Christus mandavit, *quae sunt Dei Deo, & quae sunt Caesaris Caesari reddenda. Quia tamen nulli avaritiae & ambitionis caecitate ducti, & nullius scripturae intelligentiam habentes, tentes a tramite recti sensus in quaedam iniqua & prava commenta, & in assertiones detestabiles, rumpunt, contra potestatem & auctoritatem Imperialem, & jura Imperatorum, Electorum, Principum & Imperii fidelium committentes, fallaciter asserentes, quod Imperialis dignitas est a Papa, & quod Electus in Imperatorem non est verus Imperator nec Rex, nisi prius sive Sedem Apostolicam confirmetur, approbetur, & coronetur: & per hujusmodi prava dogmata hostis antiquus movet lites, jurgia suscitat, contentiones parit, & discordias procurat.
units.tr: Although the laws of both Testaments plainly declare that imperial dignity and power proceeded from the Son of God from the beginning, and that God has openly bestowed them upon the human race through the Emperor and the kings, and that the Emperor, by the sole election of those to whom it belongs, becomes the true Emperor and needs no other confirmation or approval, and that in temporal matters he has no superior, but the peoples and nations are subject to him; and although our Lord Jesus Christ himself commanded that what is God's be rendered to God, and what is Caesar's to Caesar; nevertheless, some men, led by the blindness of greed and ambition and having no understanding of Scripture, wander from the path of right meaning into certain wicked and perverse inventions and detestable assertions. They break out against the power and authority of the Empire and the rights of the Emperors, Electors, Princes and the faithful of the Empire, falsely asserting that imperial dignity comes from the Pope, and that an elected man is not a true Emperor or King unless he is first confirmed, approved and crowned by the Apostolic See. Through such wicked doctrines that ancient enemy stirs up quarrels, provokes strife, breeds contentions and brings about discord.

units.la: 1. Ideo ad tantum malum evitandum, de consilio & consensu Electorum & aliorum Principum Imperii, declaramus, quod Imperialis dignitas et potestas est immediate a solo Deo: & quod re & Imperii consuetudine antiquitus approbata, postquam aliquis eligitur in Imperatorem a Electoribus Imperii concorditer, vel majori parte eorundem, statim ex sola electione verus & Imperator Romanorum censendus & nominandus, & eidem ab omnibus Imperio obediri: & administrandi jura Imperii, & cetera faciendi, quae ad Imperatorem verum pertinent, nariam habet potestatem, nec Papae sive Sedis Apostolicae aut alicujus alterius approbatione, auctoritate indiget vel consensu. Et ea propter hac in perpetuum valitura lege decernimus, ut Electus in Imperatorem concorditer, vel a majori parte Electorum, ex sola electione censeatur, habeatur ab omnibus pro vero & legitimo Imperatore, & eidem ab omnibus subjectis Imperii debeat obediri, & administrationem & jurisdictionem Imperialem, & Imperialis potestatis plenitudinem habeat, & ita habere ac obtinere ab omnibus censeatur & firmiter asseratur.
units.tr: 1. Therefore, in order to avert so great an evil, we declare with the counsel and consent of the Electors and the other Princes of the Empire that imperial dignity and power comes immediately from God alone; and that, as the custom of the Empire has long been approved in practice, once a man has been chosen Emperor by the Electors of the Empire, either unanimously or by the greater part of them, he is at once to be regarded and named true Emperor of the Romans by election alone, and all the Empire is to obey him; and he has full power to administer the rights of the Empire and to do all the other things that belong to a true Emperor, and he needs no approval, authority or consent of the Pope, of the Apostolic See, or of anyone else. For this reason, by a law to remain in force forever, we decree that one elected Emperor, whether unanimously or by the greater part of the Electors, is to be deemed, by election alone, and held by all to be the true and lawful Emperor; that he is to be obeyed by all the subjects of the Empire; that he shall have the administration and jurisdiction of the Empire and the fullness of imperial power; and that he is to be deemed and firmly affirmed to have and hold these things from all.

units.la: 3. Quicumque autem contra haec declarata, decreta, vel definita, aut aliquid eorum asserere, dicere, aut asserentibus seu dicentibus consentire, vel eorum mandatis, vel literis, vel praeceptis dire præsumpserint, eos omnibus scudis, quæ ab Imperio detinent, & omnibus gratiis, jurisdictionibus, privilegiis, & immunitatibus à nobis vel prædecessoribus nostris eis concessis exnunc privamus, & ipso jure & facto decernimus esse privatos. Insuper eos crimen læsæ Majestatis decernimus incurrisse, & pœnis omnibus impositis crimen læsæ Majestatis committentibus subjacere. Datum in Coloniensi civitate Alemaniæ, die, &c. Anno Domini MCCCXXXIX.
units.tr: 3. Whoever, however, presumes to assert, say or consent to those who assert or say anything contrary to these declarations, decrees or definitions, or to dare to act upon their commands, letters or precepts, we now deprive them of all the fiefs they hold from the Empire, and of all the graces, jurisdictions, privileges and immunities granted to them by us or our predecessors; and we decree that by law and in fact they are deprived. Moreover, we decree that they have incurred the crime of high treason, and are liable to all the penalties imposed upon those who commit high treason. Given in the city of Cologne in Germany, on the day, etc., in the year of our Lord 1339.

units.la: LUDOVICI IV. IMPER. AUG. DECLARATIO
units.tr: DECLARATION OF LOUIS IV, EMPEROR AUGUSTUS

units.la: SUPER DIVORTIO MATRIMONII INTER ILLVSTRES VOCA- TOS conjuges, Iohannem vid: licet filium Regis Bohemiæ, & Margaretham Ducissam Karinthiæ celebrato.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE DIVORCE OF THE MARRIAGE CONTRACTED BETWEEN THE ILLUSTRIOUS SPOUSES, JOHN (MARGRAVE OF BRANDENBURG), THE SON OF THE KING OF BOHEMIA, AND MARGARET, DUCHESS OF CARINTHIA

units.la: A Dampliorem evidentiam tam a dictorum, quàm & dicendorum, ad redarguendum quoque voces, & obstruendas fauces malignorum detractorum quorundam, nunc forte dicentium, & dicere volentium in futurum, nos in præsenti negotio sive judicio processisse de facto tantummodo & non de jure; cum judicium de matrimonii divortio faciendo spirituale sit, & propterea ad auctoritatem nostram minimè pertineat, quemadmodum dicunt Episcopi quidam sive Presbyteri cum suis sequacibus, minus verè; idque à paucis retrò temporibus prædicaverunt, & per quasdam verborum fallacias hoc credere fecerunt plurimos simplices Christi fideles. Ad tollendum etiam scrupulum conscientiæ ab hujusmodi fraude deceptorum, atque zizaniam de cordibus hominum per jam dictos ventatis prævaricatores, ac Romanorum Principum persecutores infestos, & Imperialium jurium usurpatores manifestos, undique seminatas præfatorum Doctorum sententias sub breviloquio, quantum possunt, huic rescripto non inutiliter duximus inferendas.
units.tr: For greater clarity, both to refute the voices of certain malicious detractors, who now say or will wish to say in future that in the present matter we proceeded de facto only and not de jure, since the judgment concerning the granting of a divorce is spiritual and therefore does not pertain to our authority, as certain bishops or presbyters and their followers say (less truly), and who have preached this in recent times and by certain verbal fallacies have made many simple faithful of Christ believe it; and also to remove the scruple of conscience from those deceived by such a fraud, and to stop the tares, sown everywhere in the hearts of men by the aforesaid transgressors of the truth, hostile persecutors of the Roman princes, and manifest usurpers of imperial rights, we have thought it not useless to insert into this rescript, in as brief a form as they allow, the opinions of the aforesaid teachers.

units.la: 2. Dicunt ergo & scribunt seriosius in suis tractatibus jam dicti Doctores, quòd Christi fideles reguntur & vivunt sub duplici lege, divina videlicet & humana. Lex autem proprie sumpta præceptum coactivum est de fiendis aut omittendis humanis actibus, sub pœna transgressoribus infligenda. Verum Lex divina est coactivum præceptum à Deo factum immediatè, absque humana deliberatione, propter finem in futuro seculo consequendum, & sub pœna transgressoribus infligenda in eodem tantummodo, non præsenti. Sed Lex humana voluntate seu deliberatione procedens, propter finem immediatè in hoc seculo consequendum, & sub pœna in eodem solummodo transgressoribus infligenda. Juxta quæ oportet attendere, quod secundum utramque jam dictarum legum sunt quædam affirmativè præcepta, de fiendis videlicet: quædam verò negativè, de omittendis scilicer non fiendis, vocata prohibita. Sunt & quædam permissa fieri & non fieri, quæ sub præcepto affirmativè vel negativè non cadunt, & in Lege divina quædam vocata Consilia. Et sunt jam dicta permissa generaliora præceptis, quoniam omne præceptum est permissum fieri, sed econtra non semper. Similiter quoque prohibitum fieri, permissum est non fieri, quamvis non in omnibus econtra. Simile quoque intelligendum secundum legem humanam in affirmativis præceptis, permissis & prohibitis, quamvis differant sub pœnis: quoniam secundum Legem divinam præcepta & prohibita obligant transgressores ad pœnam æternam, secundum humanam verò ad pœnam temporalem.
units.tr: 2. The aforesaid teachers, therefore, say and write more seriously in their treatises that the faithful of Christ are governed and live under a twofold law, namely divine and human. Law, properly taken, is a coercive precept concerning human acts to be done or omitted, with a penalty to be inflicted on transgressors. Divine law, however, is a coercive precept made immediately by God, without human deliberation, for an end to be attained in the future age, with a penalty to be inflicted on transgressors in that age only and not in the present one. Human law, however, proceeds from the will or deliberation of men, for an end to be attained immediately in this age, with a penalty to be inflicted on transgressors in this age only. In accordance with this, one must note that under each of the two laws there are certain things commanded affirmatively, namely to be done, and others commanded negatively, namely to be omitted or not done, called prohibitions. There are also certain things permitted to be done or not done, which do not fall under a precept, affirmative or negative, and which in divine law are called counsels. And these permitted things are more general than precepts, since every precept is permitted to be done, but not conversely. Likewise, what is prohibited is permitted not to be done, although not conversely in all cases. The same must be understood under human law concerning affirmative precepts, permissions and prohibitions, although they differ in their penalties: for under divine law precepts and prohibitions bind transgressors to eternal punishment, but under human law to temporal punishment.

units.la: 3. Est rursum advertendum, quod secundum utramque jam dictarum legum, nomina præcepti & prohibiti duas intentiones sive significationes habere possunt: unam videlicet, quod nomine præcepti sive prohibiti intelligatur actus præcipiendi sive præceptio à præcipiente procedens, quasi activè sumpta. Reliquo verò modo, ut intelligatur per prædicta nomina non actus præcipiendi cujus, qui præcepit vel imperat, sed potius actus aut opus, cui aliquid præcipitur seu imperatur, quasi passivè, quo dicitur ex usu, Servum fecisse præceptum Domini, cum id egit aut agere omisit, quod sibi per dominum præcipiebatur fieri vel omitti; verbi gratia, ut equum parare, vinum propinare, ac reliqua talia. Et isto modo significat sive sonat præceptum sive prohibitum idem quod imperatum, nimirum actum præcipiendi sumptum activè, quoniam hunc non fecit servus, in quantum servus, sed solummodo dominus.
units.tr: 3. It must further be noted that under each of the two laws the terms precept and prohibition can have two meanings or senses. The first is that by the term precept or prohibition is understood the act of commanding, or the command proceeding from the one who commands, taken as it were actively. In the other sense, the aforesaid terms are understood not as the act of commanding by him who orders or enjoins, but rather as the act or work to which something is commanded or enjoined, taken as it were passively. In this sense we say, in common usage, that a servant has carried out his master's precept when he has done or omitted to do what was commanded him by his master to be done or omitted, for example to prepare a horse, to pour out wine, and other such things. In this way the word precept or prohibition signifies or means the same as the thing commanded, namely the act of commanding taken actively, since this act was not performed by the servant as a servant, but only by the master.

units.la: 4. Amplius est etiam attendendum, quod præcepta tam affirmativa quàm negativa, atque permissa vocata consilia, secundum legem divinam spiritualia sunt essentialiter atque dicuntur. Primum quoniam à Spiritu sancto immediatè tradita & instituta sunt, quemadmodum dicit B. Ambrosius super Apostolum posteriori ad Corinth. cap. 9. Spiritualia, inquit, sunt lex Evangelica & verbum Dei. Et sunt etiam fortasse spiritualia, gratiæ sive dona Spiritus sancti, quæ fiunt & perveniunt in animabus Christi fidelium à verbis Evangelicis supradictis. Secundò verò dicuntur etiam divina præcepta spiritualia à vivificando, quoniam ad vivificandum spiritum sive animam humanam data sunt. Sane & propter beatitudinem æternam tradita & statuta fuerunt illa, quæ dicuntur præcepta & prohibita legis divinæ activè sumpta. Alia verò spiritualia quædam non sunt essentialiter, sed à quibusdam spiritualium vocabulum sumpserunt, propterea quod ad prædicta spiritualia exercenda vel ministranda serviunt, & sunt per homines ordinata, quemadmodum persone sive corpora Sacerdotum. Sic quoque domus vocatur Ecclesia, secundum quandam Ecclesiæ significationem. Sic quoque vestes, libri, & instrumenta quædam alia ordinata per homines propter cultum divinum. Sic etiam jeiunia, eleemosynæ, ac reliqui quidam actus & hominum opera de divinis sive spiritualibus, & circa vel propter spiritualia, quibus inexistunt, veluti paramenta, spiritualia dicta sunt. De quibus omnibus, quoniam nota, omittuntur exempla propter abbreviationem sermonis. Proportionaliter quoque secundum Legem humanam sunt praecepta, prohibita, & permissa active sumpta, & alia temporaliter imperata, quae omnia dicuntur temporalia, propterea quod ab homine tradita sunt, & immediate statuta. Et rursus propter vitam huius saeculi temporalem vocatam, quod tempore claudetur & finitur, talia statuta sunt & fuerunt.
units.tr: 4. Further, it must also be noted that precepts, both affirmative and negative, and what are called permissions or counsels, are spiritual in essence and are so called under divine law. First, because they were handed down and instituted immediately by the Holy Spirit, as Blessed Ambrose says on the later Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 9: "The things that are spiritual," he says, "are the Evangelical law and the word of God." And perhaps the spiritual things are also the graces or gifts of the Holy Spirit, which come about and arrive in the souls of the faithful of Christ from the aforesaid Evangelical words. Secondly, the divine precepts are also called spiritual from giving life (vivificare), since they were given to give life to the spirit or human soul. Indeed, those things which are called the precepts and prohibitions of divine law, taken actively, were also handed down and established for the sake of eternal blessedness. Other things, however, are not spiritual in essence, but have taken the name of spiritual from certain spiritual things, because they serve to exercise or minister the aforesaid spiritual things and are ordained by men, as are the persons or bodies of priests. Thus also the house is called the Church, according to a certain sense of the word Church. Likewise garments, books and certain other instruments ordained by men for divine worship. Likewise fasts, almsgivings, and certain other acts and works of men concerning divine or spiritual things, and about or on account of spiritual things, in which they inhere, such as vestments, are called spiritual. Of all these, since they are well known, examples are omitted for the sake of brevity of speech. Proportionally, under human law there are also precepts, prohibitions and permissions taken actively, and other things commanded temporally, all of which are called temporal, because they have been handed down by man and are immediately established by him. And again, such statutes are and were established on account of the temporal life of this age, so called because it is closed and ended in time.

units.la: 4. Insuper attendere convenit, quod quamvis praecepta, & prohibita, & consilia, secundum Legem divinam active sumpta, differant a praeceptis secundum legem humanam, quoniam ab alio legislatore, & ad alium finem, & sub aliis poenis, temporibus & modis eas transgressionibus inferred statuta & ordinata sunt talia, tamen personae cum suis actibus, imperatis & operibus, quibus praecipitur sive imperatur per legem utramque, in omnibus quasi vel saltem in pluribus, eadem esse possunt. Ut ubi gratia, furtum non fieri, vel homicidium, vel rapinam, vel fraudem, aut falsum testimonium, & similia reliqua, quae praecipit tam divina quam humana Lex non esse fienda. Similiter quoque interis praeceptis, ut mutuum restituere, atque depositum. Rursus quod eadem esse possunt personarum consimiles actus, quibus & de quibus tam temporalia, quam circa spiritualia praecepti utraque lex. Nam circa temporalia & de temporalibus tam per Sacerdotes, Episcopos, sive Presbyteros, Diaconos, & alios spirituales ministros, & similiter per non Sacerdotes, vocatos Saeculares aut Laicos, quid fieri vel omitti licitum aut illicitum, secundum praecepta vel contra tam divinae quam humanae legis, & juste corrigenda sive puniendae tam in statu praeteritis saeculi, quam futuri, per poenam transgressores arcendo qualia sunt crimina, quae pridem in exemplis adducta sunt. Sic et de spiritualibus, & circa spiritualia quomodolibet appellata, potest licitum aliquid per praedictas personas & actus ipsatum, & illicitum similiter fieri vel omitti, veluti haereses parere, sive actus illicitos decernere, & bruta quaedam baptisare, daemonibus satisfacere, quemadmodum faciunt quidam sceleratae sortes; alia quoque crimina committere, ut vasa, libros, vestes, & reliqua choralia instrumenta culti divino deservientia rapere vel furari, & reliqua similia hujus, juste in hoc saeculo & futuro punire poenam realem aut personalem, secundum legem utramque, divinam videlicet & humanam, diversis differenter & differentibus poenis, ac judice, loco & tempore, quemadmodum dictum est, & ut ferociose dicetur.
units.tr: 4. Furthermore, it is fitting to note that although precepts, prohibitions and counsels under divine law, taken actively, differ from precepts under human law, since they were so laid down and ordained by another lawgiver, for another end, and under other penalties, times and modes of inflicting them on transgressors, nevertheless the persons with their acts, commands and works, to which something is commanded or enjoined by either law, can be the same in all, or at least in most cases. For example, that theft, murder, robbery, fraud, false witness, and the other similar things which both divine and human law forbid to be done, should not be done. Likewise with precepts such as to restore a loan and a deposit. Again, the same acts of persons can be the same, by which and concerning which both laws command, both in temporal matters and in matters concerning spiritual things. For concerning temporal things and about temporal things, what is lawful or unlawful to be done or omitted, according to the precepts of divine and human law, whether by priests, bishops or presbyters, deacons and other spiritual ministers, or likewise by non-priests called secular or laymen, and what must justly be corrected or punished both in the state of the past age and of the future, by punishment restraining transgressors (such as the crimes which were adduced as examples above). So too concerning spiritual things, and things called spiritual in whatever way, something lawful can be done by the aforesaid persons and their acts, and likewise something unlawful can be done or omitted, such as to produce heresies, or to decree unlawful acts, to baptize brute animals, to satisfy demons, as certain wicked fortune-tellers do; also to commit other crimes, such as to seize or steal the vessels, books, vestments and other choral instruments serving divine worship, and other similar things of this kind, which in this age and the future are justly punished with a real or personal penalty, according to both laws, divine and human, with different penalties differing in kind, and with the judge, place and time differing, as has been said and as will be said more fully below.

units.la: 5. Est adhuc etiam advertendum, quod si praecipit Lex divina fiendum vel omittendum aliquid, quod fieri vel omitti non praecipit Lex humana, sed potius oppositum praecipiat vel permittat, debet servari Legis divinae praeceptum, humana Lege vel ejus oppositio praecepto vel permisso contempro sive dimisso, quoniam praeceptum legis divinae infallibilem continet veritatem, humanae vero legis non sic. Rursum quoniam divinum obligat transgressorem ad poenam aeternam, humanum vero ad temporalem sive finitam, & minus ab homine fugiendam.
units.tr: 5. It must also be noted that if divine law commands something to be done or left undone, which human law does not command to be done or omitted but rather commands or permits the opposite, the precept of divine law must be observed and the opposition of human law, whether a precept or a permission, must be disregarded or set aside. The precept of divine law contains infallible truth, but human law does not. Again, divine law binds the transgressor to eternal punishment, whereas human law binds him to temporal or finite punishment, which is also less to be feared before men.

units.la: 6. Est amplius attendendum, quod utraque jam dictarum legum habet proprium & diversum immediatum Legislatorem & judicem, ut dictum est supra. Et rursus quoniam duplex est judex, unusquisque Doctor solummodo, & fortasse etiam de aliquibus operatur, sicut fidelis est, secundum quod liber disciplinam, quomodo etiam scriptis famosus ille philosophus Aristoteles nominatus, quod quasi est bonus judex eorum quae novit, & hoc bene judicat, veluti medicus de sanu & aegru. Alius vero judex est principans proprie vocatus, cui tradita auctoritas & data coactiva potestas transgressores legum poenas arcendi. Et est hic liquidem judex secundum legem humanam, de quo dixit Apostolus, quod non sine causa gladium portat, id est, coactivam & armatam potestatem habet, quoniam minister Dei est, vindex in iram ei, qui malum agit, esto etiam quod humanarum legum Doctor non existat. Secundum divinam judex est coactivus, de quo Apostolus dicit B. Jacobus in Canonica sua, Unus est legislator & judex, qui potest perdere & liberare.
units.tr: 6. It must further be noted that each of the two laws just mentioned has its own distinct and immediate lawgiver and judge, as has been said above. And since there are two kinds of judge: first, the teacher, who only, and perhaps also in some matters, acts as a faithful judge of what he has learned, as the famous philosopher Aristotle, named in his writings, says that a good judge of the things he knows, and judges them well, just as a physician judges the sick and the healthy. The other judge is properly called the ruler, to whom authority and coercive power have been given to restrain transgressors of the laws by penalties. This is indeed the judge under human law, of whom the Apostle said that he does not bear the sword in vain, that is, he has coercive and armed power, since he is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath upon him who does evil, even though he is not a teacher of human laws. Under divine law the judge is coercive, of whom the blessed Apostle James says in his Canonical Epistle: There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to save.

units.la: 7. His itaque suppositis, tanquam veris & notis, dixerunt & scripserunt in suis tractatibus Doctores, quod secundum legem divinam legislator & judex coactivus secundum ipsam est Christus, sicut per beatum * dictum est supra. Ipse enim tulit legem divinam, seu novum Testamentum, per os tam Apostolorum quam aliorum Sanctorum quorundam. Unde Apostolus: An experimentum ejus quaeritis, qui loquitur in me Christus? Et B. Petrus in sua Canonica dicit: Nonab hominibus prophetia, sed Spiritu S. inspirati locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Hic autem Legislator statuit secundum has legem transgressores judicari & per poenas arceri in futuro saeculo tantum modo, non in isto. Unde Scriptura: Cum venerit filius hominis in sede majestatis suae, sedebitis & vos super sedes duodecim, &c. quod erit in futuro saeculo, sicut manifeste sonat Scriptura, & exponunt omnes Expositores ejusdem. Sunt rursus judices alii secundum legem divinam, quos nihil prohibet esse plures in statu praesentis saeculi, vocati Doctores, & secundum ipsam quorundam actuum sive operum ministrii atque factores, nullam coactivam auctoritatem vel potestatem habentes a Christo seu Lege divina, arcendi quenquam in hoc saeculo, ad aliquid agendum vel omittendum, per poenam aliquam realem. Unde Christus Marci ultimo tales judices vocavit Doctores, dum ipsis in Apostolorum persona dixit: Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos. Et per Malachiam Prophetam: Labia Sacerdotis custodiunt Scripturam, & legem requirent ex ore ejus. Et sunt hi judices, Episcopi sive Sacerdotes, vocati Doctores. Carent autem praedicti judices, & carere debent auctoritate & potestate coactiva, per quamcunque poenam arcendi, sicut dictum est pridem; quoniam tali auctoritate Christus in hoc saeculo carere voluit in persona propria, in quantum homo, dum dixit: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: ecce quantum ad auctoritatem. ratem : si enim esset de hoc mundo, declararent utique ministri mei: ecce quantum ad armatam sive coactivam potestatem. Et rursus idem petenti ab ipso divisionem hæreditatis à fratre, respondit: Homo, quis me constituit judicem aut divisorem super vos, vel inter te & fratrem tuum? Quasi diceret: tale judicium mihi non convenit exercere. Sic etiam tali auctoritate aut coactiva potestate carere voluit Apostolos, & in aliorum persona omnes Episcopos sive Presbyteros, successores ipsius, in quantum fuerat Sacerdos humanus, quoniam in quantum Deus erat, nullus sibi hominum successit vel succedere potuit, dum ipsos inquit: Reges gentium dominantur eorum, vos autem non sic. Planum est, quod Apostolus interdicitur dominari, licut inquit Bernardus. Sic quoque Sacram Scripturam intellexerunt & expositerunt concorditer omnes sancti & approbati Doctores, & idem secundum proprias sententias expresserunt. Quod etiam sciens & de spiritualibus loquens, se non habere potestatem quemquam arcendi, & multominus de temporalibus, unde dicebat Corinthiis: Non dominamur fidei vestrae. Super quo verbo, tam Ambrosius quam Chrysostomus, senserunt concorditer, & expresse dixerunt. Ambrosius quidem: Non dominamur fidei vestrae, id est, non quia dominium aut coactionem patiatur fides vestra, quae voluntatis est, non necessitatis. Chrysostomus autem: In Ecclesia non coactum, sed adquiescentem oportet ad meliora converti. Quod admiratur ille scriens, Apostolus videlicet, dicebat Corinthiis: Non dominamur fidei vestrae. Subjungensque Chrysostomus aut: Non enim a legibus data est nobis, Episcopis sive Presbyteris scilicet, talis potestas, ut anathematizent sententiae cohibeamus homines a delictis: neque si data esset, haberemus ubi exerceremus eiusmodi potestatem, cum Dominus noster, Christus videlicet, non necessitate, id est violentia, aliquos homines traxerit a peccato, sed sua sese ponte subtrahentes remuneratus sit. In quibus etiam verbis supponit Chrysostomus, quod omnis coactiva potestas in hoc saeculo datur a legibus sive Principibus. Quod etiam dicit Hugo de Sancto Victore, de Sacramentis lib. 2. Inquit enim: Quod licet Ecclesia, id est Ecclesiastica personae, Episcopi sive Presbyteri, jurisdictioners coactivas videlicet in personas saeculares exercent, hoc ipsum tamen, quod exercent, a Regia potestate se habent. Non ergo a lege divina, sed ab humana lege, convenit cuiquam in hoc saeculo auctoritas & coactiva potestas, praecipue Episcopo sive Presbytero. Unde Chrysostomus post verba praedicta subinfert: Homo vero si a fide vestra fuerit abductus, multum imminet Sacerdoti patientia, indulgentia exhortatione, ne quod non potest errantem revocare, sed persuadere conabitur, ut ad fidem rectam revertatur, a qua primitus erravit. Idem quoque senserunt omnes sancti Doctores reliqui, atque Expositores juxta sacram Scripturam, quorum sententias hic omissas propter brevitatem copiose videre poterit, cui cura fuerit, in tractatibus novis praefatorum Doctorum.
units.tr: 7. Given these things as true and known, the teachers have said and written in their treatises that under divine law the lawgiver and coercive judge according to it is Christ, as was said above by the blessed [author]. For he delivered the divine law, or the New Testament, through the mouths of the Apostles as well as of certain other saints. Hence the Apostle: Do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ? And the blessed Peter says in his Canonical Epistle: For prophecy came not at any time by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. This Lawgiver has determined that transgressors under this law are judged and restrained by penalties only in the future age, not in this one. Hence Scripture: When the Son of man shall come in his glory, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, etc., which will be in the future age, as Scripture plainly sounds and all its expositors explain. Again, under divine law there are other judges, whom nothing prevents from being several in the present age, called teachers, and who according to the same law are ministers and doers of certain acts or works, having no coercive authority or power from Christ or divine law to restrain anyone in this age, by any temporal penalty, from doing or omitting anything. Hence Christ, in the last chapter of Mark, called such judges teachers, when he said to them in the person of the Apostles: Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them. And through the prophet Malachi: The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth. These judges are the bishops or priests, called teachers. The aforesaid judges, however, lack, and ought to lack, authority and coercive power to restrain anyone by any penalty, as was said before; for Christ himself, as man, chose to lack such authority in his own person in this age. He said: My kingdom is not of this world; see how far this goes as regards authority. For if it were of this world, my ministers would surely fight, see how far this goes as regards armed or coercive power. And again, when a man asked him to divide an inheritance with his brother, he answered: Man, who made me a judge or divider over you, or between you and your brother? As if to say: such judgment is not fitting for me to exercise. So too he willed the Apostles to lack such authority or coercive power, and, in the persons of others, all bishops or elders, his successors, insofar as he was a human priest, for insofar as he was God, no man succeeded him or could succeed him. He said to them: The kings of the nations lord it over them; but you shall not be so. It is plain that the Apostle is forbidden to lord it over others, as Bernard says. All the holy and approved teachers have likewise understood and expounded Holy Scripture in agreement, and have expressed the same according to their own opinions. Paul, knowing this and speaking of spiritual matters, said that he had no power to restrain anyone, and much less in temporal matters, whence he said to the Corinthians: We do not lord it over your faith. Upon this word both Ambrose and Chrysostom agreed and spoke expressly. Ambrose indeed: We do not lord it over your faith, that is, not because your faith suffers dominion or coercion, which belongs to will, not to necessity. Chrysostom: In the Church one must be turned to better things not by compulsion but by consent. The writer admires this, namely the Apostle, who said to the Corinthians: We do not lord it over your faith. And Chrysostom adds: For such power has not been given to us by laws, that is, to the bishops or elders, so that we might pronounce anathema and restrain men from sins; nor, if it had been given, would we have any place to exercise such power, since our Lord, that is Christ, has not drawn any men from sin by necessity, that is by violence, but has rewarded them when they withdraw themselves by their own bridge. In these words Chrysostom also assumes that all coercive power in this age is given by laws or princes. The same is said by Hugh of Saint Victor in his book on the Sacraments, book 2. For he says: Although the Church, that is, the ecclesiastical persons, bishops or elders, exercise coercive jurisdiction over secular persons, they nevertheless have what they exercise from royal power. Therefore authority and coercive power in this age belong to no one by divine law, but by human law, especially to the bishop or elder. Hence, after the words cited, Chrysostom adds: If, however, a man has been led away from your faith, the priest must be very patient, indulgent and exhorting, so that he will try not to recall the one who is straying, which he cannot do, but to persuade him to return to the right faith from which he first strayed. All the other holy teachers and expositors according to Holy Scripture have held the same view; their opinions, omitted here for brevity, may be seen in full by anyone who cares to look in the new treatises of the aforementioned teachers.

units.la: 8. Est etiam similiter secundum legem humanam Legislator, ut civium Universitas, aut ejus pars valentior, vel Romanus Princeps supremus IMPERATOR vocatus. Est & judex coactivus secundum legem eandem, ut Universitas jam dicta, vel Princeps, vel ille vel illi, cui vel quibus Universitas aut Princeps dederit coactivam potestatem, per poenam realem aut personalem in saeculo legis humanae transgressores coercendi. Nequaquam vero legislatores humani sunt Episcopi sive Presbyteri, aut reliqui spirituales Ministri, conjunctim vel divisim, in quantum hujusmodi, sed fortassis in quantum pars aliqua civitatis existunt, secundum quod per humanas rationes citatas & per sacram Scripturam evidenter est monstratum, & per jam dictos Doctores nostros, & ut jam convenienter deductum est. Sunt & alii judices secundum legem humanam, vocati Jurisperiti sive Doctores, nullam coactivam auctoritatem habentes, in quantum hujusmodi, arcendi quemquam in hoc saeculo, per poenam realem aut personalem, ad agendum licitum aliquod, aut illicitum omittendum, sed solummodo docendum, & aliquid secundum legem operandum humanam, quemadmodum Episcopi sive Presbyteri secundum legem divinam.
units.tr: 8. Likewise, under human law the lawgiver is the whole body of citizens, or its stronger part, or the Roman prince called supreme EMPEROR. And under the same law the coercive judge is the aforesaid whole body, or the prince, or he or those to whom the body or the prince has given coercive power to restrain transgressors of human law by a temporal or personal penalty in this age. Bishops or elders, or the other spiritual ministers, either jointly or separately, are by no means human lawgivers, as such; perhaps they are so insofar as they are some part of the state, as has been clearly shown by the human reasons cited and by Holy Scripture, and by the teachers we have mentioned, and as has been conveniently deduced. There are also other judges under human law, called jurists or doctors, who have no coercive authority, as such, to restrain anyone in this age by a temporal or personal penalty from doing something lawful or omitting something unlawful, but only to teach, and to act according to human law, just as bishops or elders act according to divine law.

units.la: 9. Propter quae manifestius intuendum, quod de humanis actibus & operibus circa divina, & de temporalibus, similiter quoque modo circa temporalia, & de temporalibus, poterit dubitatio contingere, dum per consequens interrogatio sive quaestio fieri propter veritatem de dubitatis habendam. Una dubitatio est & quaestio, an videlicet actus illi & opera, de quibus quaeritur, sint fieri vel obligatoria vel prohibita, licita vel illicita, tam secundum legem divinam, quam humanam? Alia dubitatio, quaestio sive interrogatio ex praedictis, utrum videlicet si per quemquam factus aut opera facta vel omissa, pertinent ad judicium Principantis? judicis videlicet coactiva auctoritas est arcere per poenam realem vel personalem, transgressorem legis divinae vel humanae, in praesenti saeculo vel futuro.
units.tr: 9. Hence it may be seen more clearly that doubt may arise concerning human acts and works relating to divine things, and likewise concerning temporal things in the same way, and concerning temporal things; and so, consequently, a question or inquiry may be raised, for the sake of obtaining the truth about what is doubted. One doubt and question is whether those acts and works about which the inquiry is made are obligatory or forbidden, lawful or unlawful, both under divine law and under human law. The other doubt, question or inquiry arising from what has been said is whether, if anyone has done or omitted such acts or works, they belong to the judgment of the ruler, that is, of a judge who has coercive authority to restrain transgressors of divine or human law by a real or personal penalty, in this age or in the age to come.

units.la: 10. De priori quidem quaestione, dubitatione sive interrogatione, respondere ac judicare seu per dictum diffinire pertinet ad Doctores, seu ad judices doctrinales, hujusmodi siquidem auctoritate habentes, quales secundum legem divinam sunt vel esse debet omnes Episcopi, sive Presbyteri, quemodum ostensum est prius, & dixit Apostolus ad Timoth. Oportet Episcopum esse doctorem. Secundum humanam vero legem pertinet haec auctoritas sive judicium ad Jurisperitos sive humanae legis Doctores. Etenim eorum officium est, scire docere si oporteat, praedicare quae sint & qualia praecepta permissa vel prohibita secundum leges praedictas, licita etiam vel illicita fieri vel omitti in actibus humanis; similiter de hujusmodi respondere, cum super his & de iis fuerint requisiti, omni tamen auctoritate & coactiva potestate carentes, quemquam cogendi per poenam in hoc saeculo ad fugiendum vel faciendum aliquid, ut supra sufficienter induximus. Quemadmodum medici de sanitate corporis constituenda vel omissa recuperanda docere habent & operari, secundum artis medicinae praecepta, nec quemquam cogere possunt utilem servare dietam, aut declinare nocivam, per poenam aliquam aut personale facientibus vel omittentibus inferendo. Sic quoque Sacerdotes, qui medici sunt animaanimarum, neminem in hoc mundo per pœnam arcere possunt, secundum Scripturam. Et propterea quamvis Sacerdotibus liceat condere seu facere ordinationes sive exhortationes, circa bonos mores & opera facienda, & malos & crimina fugienda, non tamen nunc dici debent hujusmodi ordinationes Leges, sed potius documenta seu regulæ. Neq; ipsorum judicium per tales regulas circa hominum actus debet appellari judicium sive forum, quia talia nomina proprie sumpta, judicio coactivo convenientia sunt, secundum primam & veram impositionem ipsorum. Potest autem præfatum judicium, quoniam generale est, licet ignoratis personis, de quibus sive de quorum actibus dubitatur & quæritur.
units.tr: 10. As for the former question, doubt or inquiry, to answer it and to judge or define it by pronouncement belongs to the teachers, or to doctrinal judges, who have authority of this kind. Such are, under divine law, all bishops or elders, as has been shown above, and as the Apostle said to Timothy: "A bishop must be a teacher." Under human law, however, this authority or judgment belongs to the jurists, or teachers of human law. For it is their office to know how to teach, if need be, and to declare what the precepts permitted or forbidden by those laws are, and what acts may lawfully be done or omitted among human actions; and likewise to give answers about such matters when they are asked about them and concerning them, yet lacking all authority and coercive power to compel anyone in this age by penalty to shun or do anything, as we have sufficiently shown above. Just as physicians have the duty and the skill to teach and to act for establishing or recovering bodily health, according to the precepts of the medical art, yet cannot compel anyone to keep a useful diet or to avoid a harmful one by inflicting any penalty or personal harm on those who act or fail to act; so too priests, who are physicians of souls, can restrain no one in this world by punishment, according to Scripture. Therefore, although it is lawful for priests to make or issue ordinances or exhortations concerning good morals and the duties to be performed, and concerning evils and crimes to be avoided, such ordinances should not now be called laws, but rather instructions or rules. Nor should their judgment on human acts by such rules be called a judgment or court, because such names, properly taken, belong to coercive judgment, according to their first and true imposition. The aforesaid judgment, however, since it is general, can be exercised even when the persons concerning whose acts doubt and inquiry arise are unknown.

units.la: 11. Secunda vero dubitatio, interrogatio & quæstio potest contingere circa prædictos hominum actus & opera, utrum videlicet si per quempiam sint tales actus aut opera facta vel omissa, pertineant ad judicium principantis judicis vel coactivi, cujus auctoritas est arcere per pœnam realem aut personalem legum transgressores in præsenti sæculo vel futuro. Secundum legem divinam vero est in futuro sæculo tantum modo, non isto. Talis judex est Christus solus, & erunt fortasse secum duodecim Apostoli, de quibus legimus in Scriptura: Cum venerit filius hominis in sede majestatis suæ sedebitis &c. Secundum vero legem humanam talis est principans, auctoritate Legislatorum humanorum, habens potestatem arcendi per pœnam realem aut personalem transgressores legis humanæ, in præsenti tantum modo sæculo, non in illo. Verum ad suum judicium coactivum exercendum non indiget judex secundum legem divinam inquirere veritatem per testimonium, neq; testes arcere dicium pro veritate dicenda, quoniam omnia sunt nuda & aperta oculis ejus. non indiget gladio, armorum ministrorumque potentia coactiva, propter sententiam suam exequendam, pœnam transgressionibus inferendo, quoniam ipse dixit & facta sunt. Sic non autem principans coactivus humanus, quoniam ignorare potest, an quis delatus aut accusatus de illicito actu, illum actum commiserit, vel non. Ideoque tam litigantes, quam testes necesse habet in judicium vocare, ipsosque recusantes per armatam potestatem ad hoc compellere, quoniam per ipsius simplex dictum fortassis non convenient, rei præsertim, & qui pœnam sibi debitam fortasse mutarent infligi.
units.tr: 11. The second doubt, inquiry and question can arise concerning the said acts and works of men, namely whether, if such acts or works have been done or omitted by anyone, they belong to the judgment of a ruling judge with coercive power, whose authority is to restrain transgressors of the laws by real or personal penalty in this age or the age to come. Under divine law, however, this is so only in the age to come, not in this one. Such a judge is Christ alone, and perhaps the twelve Apostles will be with him, of whom we read in Scripture: "When the Son of man shall come in the throne of his majesty, you shall sit," etc. Under human law, however, such a ruler is the one who, by the authority of human lawgivers, has the power to restrain by real or personal penalty the transgressors of human law, only in this age and not in the next. Yet to exercise his coercive judgment, the judge under divine law does not need to inquire into the truth by testimony, nor to compel witnesses to speak the truth, since all things are naked and open to his eyes. He does not need a sword, or the coercive power of arms and armed ministers, to carry out his sentence by inflicting punishment on transgressors, since "he spoke and they were made." It is not so with a human coercive ruler, since he may be unable to know whether the one who has been denounced or accused of an unlawful act committed it or not. Therefore he must summon both litigants and witnesses to judgment, and compel those who refuse by armed power, since by his simple word he will perhaps not come to agreement, especially with the accused, who might perhaps lessen the penalty due to them if it were inflicted.

units.la: 12. Ex hiis igitur jam dictis apparere potest responsio ad principale quæstium, cujus videlicet auctoritas judicandi de divortio matrimonio, vel alterius vel utriusque conjugum facta requisitione. Quoniam si fuerit dubium vel quæstio, utrum propositum matrimonium ex aliqua causa illicitum aut prohibitum sit lege divina, est auctoritas judicandi de eo ac respondendi Episcoporum, sive Presbyterorum, & legis divinæ Doctorum ad hujusmodi statuta, secundum legem honestam, ac consuetudinem regionis, in nullo repugnando coactivæ potestati legis divinæ. Ipsorum cum est scire præcepta, prohibita, & permissa, tam circa matrimonium, quam circa reliquos actus humanos & opera, de quibus & secundum quem modum licitè habet fieri vel omitti, secundum legem prædictam. Ut si dubium sit, & quæratur ab ipsis, an impotentia unius conjugum ad debitum naturale reddendum suo compari conjugi, sit causa efficiens ad divortium matrimonii licitè fiendum inter ipsos, secundum legem divinam, judicare habent & respondere de hoc supradicti sacræ Scripturæ Ministri atque Doctores: quoniam, ut sæpe diximus, hoc officium est ipsorum; quin immo non facientes hoc pœnam rentur per judicem coactivum secundum legem divinam, quamvis in futuro sæculo, non in isto. Unde Apostolus: Væ mihi si non evangelizavero, quod mihi incumbit. Sed si dubium fuerit & quærarur talis defectus, propter quem potest & debet licitè fieri divortium, inexistat alteri conjugum, & alter suo compari sive conjugi inexistere allegat, & propterea conjunx non patiens petat velitque ab impotente sive defectum patiente conjuge de matrimonio separari, est auctoritas sive coactivum judicium de hoc Christi sive Dei, secundum legem divinam, ad arcendum per pœnam conjugem non juvans in futuro tantum sæculo, non in isto, utpote si alium conjugem juste agentem libertatem non permittat, sed violentiam inferens in persona vel rebus ipsum demoliat, impediat vel coarctet. Neque si per hoc eger hic judex informari perierit, ad sciendum utrum talis defectus alteri conjugum inexistat, propter quem de matrimonio debeat separari, quoniam nihil occultum est oculis ejus, quemadmodum dictum est prius. Secundum vero legem humanam, pertinet hoc judicium divortii coactivum, ad pœnam in hoc sæculo transgressoribus inferendam, ad principantem auctoritatem legislatorum humanum. Nam quamvis ad legislatorem humanum, vel ipsius judicem coactivum, non pertineat statuere aut condere spiritualia sive divina præcepta, prohibita, vel permissa, sive cœlestia, tamen de actibus hominum & circa ipsa, quantum circa temporalia, licitè vel illicitè factis vel omissis, tam per Sacerdotes seu per spirituales Ministros, quam per laicos sive sæculares personas, cum spiritualibus non sint effectualiter, judicare coactivo judicio, & arcere per pœnam in hoc sæculo committentes illicita, ad perfactum permittet legislatorem humanum & judicem. Unde Apostolus ad Romanos 13 generaliter neminem excipiendo, malefactores seu legis humanæ non repugnantis legi divinæ transgressores, Presbyterum sive non Presbyterum, inquit: Omnis anima subdita sit potestatibus sublimioribus, Regibus videlicet, Ducibus & Tribunis, secundum Sanctorum expositionem ibidem. Et scribit: Qui enim potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit: & qui ipsis resistunt, damnationem sibi adquirunt, ac eternā videlicet. Et inquit: Minister enim Dei est, vindex in iram ei qui male agit, supple, quicunque sit ille. Non enim sine causa gladium portat, id est, habet armatam & coactivam potestatem. Quod de nullo spirituali ministro dixit Apostolus, sed oppositum magis, cum inquit: Arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia. Et rursus ad Timotheum: Nemo militans Deo implicat se sæcularibus negotiis, id est, litigiosis civilibus. Hiis etiam attestatur B. Petrus in sua Canonica, dum omnes indifferenter, neminem excipiens, inquit: Subditi estote omni humanæ creaturæ propter Dominum, in Principatu videlicet constitutæ, & Regi tanquam præexcellenti, & Ducibus tanquam ab eo missu, ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum, quia est voluntas DEI.
units.tr: 12. From what has now been said, an answer to the principal question can appear, namely who has the authority to judge concerning divorce of a marriage, when a request has been made by one or both spouses. For if there is doubt or question whether a proposed marriage is unlawful or forbidden by divine law for some cause, the authority to judge about it and to answer belongs to the bishops or elders, and to the teachers of divine law, concerning such statutes, according to honest law and the custom of the region, without in any way opposing the coercive power of divine law. It is their task to know the precepts, prohibitions and permissions, both concerning marriage and concerning the other human acts and works, which may lawfully be done or omitted, and in what manner, according to that law. Thus, if there is doubt, and they are asked whether the impotence of one spouse in rendering the natural debt to the other is a efficient cause for a divorce lawfully to be made between them under divine law, the aforesaid ministers and teachers of Holy Scripture have the duty to judge and to answer about this; for, as we have often said, this office is theirs; indeed, those who do not do this are punished by the judge with coercive power under divine law, though in the age to come and not in this one. Hence the Apostle: "Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel, which is laid upon me." But if there is doubt, and such a defect is inquired into, on account of which a divorce may and ought to be lawfully made, namely a defect existing in one spouse, and the other spouse alleges that the defect exists in his or her partner, and therefore the innocent spouse seeks and wishes to be separated from the marriage from the impotent or defective spouse, then the authority and coercive judgment in this matter belongs to Christ or God under divine law, to restrain by punishment the spouse who does not help, in the age to come only and not in this one; for example, if he does not allow the other spouse, acting justly, to have liberty, but by inflicting violence on the person or goods hinders, obstructs or confines him. Nor, if this judge should need to be informed in order to know whether such a defect exists in one of the spouses, on account of which the marriage ought to be dissolved, will he be at a loss, since nothing is hidden from his eyes, as was said before. But under human law, the coercive judgment of divorce belongs to the ruling authority of the human lawgivers, for inflicting punishment in this age on transgressors. For although it does not pertain to a human lawgiver, or to his coercive judge, to establish or enact spiritual or divine precepts, prohibitions or permissions, or heavenly ones, nevertheless, concerning human acts and things done or omitted lawfully or unlawfully in relation to temporal matters, the lawgiver and judge will be permitted to judge by coercive judgment, since they are not effectual in spiritual matters, and to restrain by punishment in this age those who commit unlawful acts, whether by priests or spiritual ministers, or by laymen or secular persons. Hence the Apostle to the Romans, chapter 13, excepting no one in general, speaks of wrongdoers, that is, transgressors of human law not opposed to divine law, whether elder or not an elder: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers," namely to kings, dukes and tribunes, according to the exposition of the Saints there. And he writes: "For whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God; and those who resist will acquire for themselves damnation," namely eternal damnation. And he says: "For he is the minister of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil," that is, whoever he may be. "For he does not bear the sword in vain," that is, he has armed and coercive power. The Apostle did not say this of any spiritual minister, but rather the opposite, when he said: "The weapons of our warfare are not carnal." And again to Timothy: "No one who serves God entangles himself in secular affairs," that is, civil litigious matters. To these things the blessed Peter also bears witness in his Epistle, when he says indifferently to all, excepting no one: "Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake," namely to the one constituted in principality, both to the king as supreme, and to the dukes as sent by him "for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do well, for so is the will of God."

units.la: 13. Hoc igitur modo de matrimonio & reliquis spiritualibus, secundum quod ipsa, vel hominum actus de ipsis, & circa ipsa, in aliquibus conditionibus referuntur ad statuta legis humanæ facta de ipsis; statuta, inquam, in quantum non repugnantia legi divinæ, sed potius sibi consona & decentia, statuere legislatorem; & judicare coactivum judicem sæcularem competens est, quinimmo necessitas requirit. Igitur quantum circa matrimonium contrahendum aut jam contractum, interveniunt plurima, quæ per actus hominum possunt licitè vel illicitè fieri vel omitti: quæ siquidem regulari oportet per legislatorem humanum, aut ejus authoritate judicem coactivum, transgressores arcendo per poenam. Cujus siquidem rei casu in sumendo ponatur, quod alter conjugum post latam sententiam de fiendo divortio matrimonii inter ipsos, ab altero conjuge discedere noluerit, sed secum ipsum per violentiam detinere, aut ipsum etiam personaliter, aut res sive ipsius bona contrectare, quemadmodum durante matrimonio seu ante factum per sententiam divortium contrectabat, puniendus atque cogendus esset per poenam realem aut personalem, in hoc sæculo, & à judice coactivo, ràquam judicatum sive sententiam non observans. Quædam enim viro licebant supra & contra sibi conjugem mulierem, in persona & rebus ipsius exercere ante factum divortium inter ipsos, quæ sibi post divortium non licent: veluti jam dictam sibi conjugem matrimonio separatam arguere, increpare, ac verbis contumeliosis afficere, carnale debitum ab ipsa exigere, aut eandem quomodolibet aliter corporaliter tractare, impudicè tangendo, aut flagellando, aut de bonis suis dotalibus & aliis præter ejus consensum disponere volendo, & similibus reliquis. Ex quibus multa & periculosa scandala post divortium, si fieret, provenirent. Propter quæ omnia tollenda seu prohibenda, & propter communem & evidentem utilitatem, immò necessitatem, competit ac debuit, debet & potest legislator humanus de talibus fiendis vel omittendis statuere, judicare atque compellere, videlicet contendentes in judicium convenire, testes similiter pro veritate dicenda vocare, & transgressores ad comparendum arcere per poenam, reliquum quoque, sententiam diffinitivam super divortio matrimoniali fiendo vel non, profferre. Conformiter tamen in hoc legi divinæ, ipsius videlicet præceptis ac prohibitis nihil per suam sententiam præcipiendo repugnans. Amplius utrumque contendentium sive litigantium in judicio post latam sententiam, ad judicatum per ipsum tenendum & observandum compellere, per poenam in hoc sæculo transgressori sententiæ inferendam.
