For the whole force and substance of their office, and of the oaths they have sworn to it, lies in this: that they attend carefully and understand what is done before them and what they are asked to record, and that they record and publish, sincerely and faithfully, what they have perceived by sight and hearing in the presence of like-minded witnesses, without concealing the truth or mixing in any falsehood, observing the solemnities required by law or by the customs of the places where they draw up instruments, as stated above.

units.la: 18. Notarius autem seu Tabellio, cùm sit Reipublicae serviens, virtute sui officii tenetur de his per his de quibus salrem cum mercedis praestatione rogatur (dummodo aliàs sint licita & non prohibita) facere instrumenta, nisi sit factus Doctor, Decurio, Monachus vel clericus. Veruntamen si se rogari permiserint, tenentur imbreviaturas suas publicare, valentque instrumenta eorum. Poterunt tamen pro his, quibus ultrò se ingerunt, tanquam prohibitioni contrafacientes puniri.
units.tr: 18. A notary or tabellion, since he serves the commonwealth, is bound by virtue of his office to draw up instruments, for payment of his fee, concerning matters about which he is asked (provided they are otherwise lawful and not forbidden), unless he is a doctor, a town councillor, a monk or a cleric. However, if they allow themselves to be asked, they are bound to publish their minutes, and their instruments are valid. Yet they may be punished, as acting against the prohibition, for those matters into which they thrust themselves unasked.

units.la: 19. Sciant etiam Notarii, eorum nullum posse officio suo renunciare, nisi in manus Principis. cujus authoritate est creatus: Vel signetum suum consuetum saltem sine Judicis autoritate, causaque rationabili mutare, aut instrumentum alieno signo signare.
units.tr: 19. Notaries should also know that none of them can renounce his office except into the hands of the prince by whose authority he was created; nor change his customary seal, nor sign an instrument with another's seal, except without the authority of a judge and for a reasonable cause.

units.la: 20. Et quamvis Notarius Protocollum sive abbreviaturam suam extendere, & omnia ponere quae declarant mentem contrahentium vel testatorum citra substantiae mutationem possit: tamen aliter... (text continues)
units.tr: 20. And although a notary may extend his protocol or abbreviation, and put in everything that declares the intention of the contracting parties or testators, without changing the substance; nevertheless otherwise...

units.la: 20. Et quamvis Notarius Protocollum sive abbreviaturam suam extendere, & omnia ponere quæ declarant mentem contrahentium vel testatorum citra substantiæ mutationem possit: tamen alterius sive viventis sive mortui protocollum seu abbreviaturam etiam sibi legatam extendere, seu huic quicquam addere vel detrahere, seu aliter quam de verbo ad verbum in publicam formam redigere sine auctoritate Judicis non potest nec debet cum extenso, & quid sub isto signo &c. vel alius defectuosis, vel abbreviatis verbis forte inibi positis comprehendi intelligatur, ad Judicis, non Notarii aestimationem spectet.
units.tr: 20. And although a notary may extend his protocol or abbreviation, and put in everything that declares the intention of the contracting parties or testators, without changing the substance, nevertheless he cannot and must not, without the authority of a judge, extend another's protocol or abbreviation, whether of a living or dead person, even one bequeathed to him, or add anything to it or remove anything from it, or redact it into public form otherwise than word for word. Whether something is understood to be included under this sign, etc., or under other defective or abbreviated words perhaps placed there, belongs to the judgment of the judge, not of the notary.

units.la: 21. Advertant etiam Notarii, quod quando in extensione & ingrossatione instrumentorum rasuras maximè notabiles & in locis suspectis, in una vel pluribus lipis faciunt vel verba interlinealia, seu ad margines apponunt, à quibus quantum poterit cavendum est, quod extunc in corpore instrumenti, vel saltem subscriptione de his faciant mentionem & approbationem. Et hoc maximè quando talis inter lineaturam est scripta ad marginem facta, non est manus propria ipsius, qui instrumenti renovationem ingrossavit.
units.tr: 21. Notaries should also note that when, in extending and engrossing instruments, they make very noticeable erasures, especially in suspicious places, in one or more lines, or interlinear words, or add things in the margins, which must be avoided as far as possible, they should then make mention of them and approve them in the body of the instrument, or at least in the subscription. This especially applies when such an interlineation or marginal addition is not in the own hand of the person who engrossed the renewed instrument.

units.la: 22. Item Notarii caveant, quia praesenti ordinatione prohibentur scribere instrumenta sua nimis abbreviata vel obscura, vel ambigua verba, quae vitiant instrumenta, nec per ziferas, signa, vel notas, praesertim non communiter omnibus cognitas, cum facile possint mutari & corrumpi, sed scribant per literas integras, communes, legibiles & cognitas, in pergameno, non papyro, in Latina, vel nostra Alemanica lingua.
units.tr: 22. Likewise notaries should take care, since by the present ordinance they are forbidden to write instruments that are too abbreviated or obscure, or that contain ambiguous words, which vitiate instruments; nor to use ciphers, signs or marks, especially those not commonly known to all, since these can easily be altered and corrupted. Instead they should write in full, common, legible and known letters, on parchment, not paper, in Latin or in our German language.

units.la: 23. Si casu amittatur alicujus Notarii protocollum, & de hoc doceatur, poterit Notarius agere contra detinentem instrumenta prius inde extracta, vel si haberi non possunt, examinari facere testes, qui interfuerunt, & inde novum facere protocollum.
units.tr: 23. If by chance a notary's protocol is lost, and this is proved, the notary may sue whoever holds the instruments previously extracted from it; or, if these cannot be had, he may have the witnesses who were present examined and make a new protocol from this.

units.la: 24. Sint etiam Notarii circa instrumentorum editionem & publicationem diligentes & cauti, ne committant errores, cum partes inde ad plures incommoditates, pericula, & expensas saepe deducantur, quas sine dubio ipsi errantes refundere tenebuntur.
units.tr: 24. Notaries should also be diligent and cautious in the issuing and publication of instruments, so that they commit no errors, since parties are often thereby brought into many inconveniences, dangers and expenses, which the erring notaries will without doubt be bound to repay.

units.la: 25. Quod si vero sive probabiliter sive improbabiliter contigerit aliquem incidere errorem, sivem solennitatibus, sive nominibus, locis, temporibus, substantia, sive aliis, tutius est ut talem post editionem, cum Notarii postea videantur functi suo officio ad evitandas ambiguitates disputationes & altercationes varias, non sua, sed Judicis desuper aditi autoritate errores hujusmodi emendentur.
units.tr: 25. But if it happens, whether probably or improbably, that someone falls into an error, whether in solemnities, names, places, times, substance or other matters, it is safer that, after publication, such errors be corrected not by the notaries' own authority, since they are thought to have discharged their office, but by the authority of a judge approached for this purpose, in order to avoid ambiguities, disputes and various quarrels.

units.la: 26. Possunt etiam Notarii actuum coram se gestorum, dum modo tamen ab eo vel his, de cujus vel quorum voluntate dependent actus hujusmodi desuper tempore eorundem actuum rogati fuerint, sine trepidatione alteriusque autoritate, imò tenentur sub poena in Jure expressa edere instrumenta eis qui rogarunt, seu eorum Procuratoribus, haeredibus, successoribus, universalibus vel singularibus talem semel. Sed quando saepius eisdem vel aliis petentibus & petendibus sua interesse, maximè ubi quaestio, seu dubium desuper esset vel rimeretur, aut aliis periculum seu praejudicium ex tali editione verisimiliter imminuert, tutius ac consultius est propter varias in hoc opiniones, ut Notarii faciant se citari coram Judice, cujus autoritate vocatis vocandis vocandi faciant vel denegent.
units.tr: 26. Notaries may also issue copies of acts done before them, provided they are asked to do so, at the time of those acts, by the person, or the persons, on whose will such acts depend, and without hesitation or another's authority. Indeed they are bound, under the penalty laid down in law, to issue an instrument once to those who asked, or to their procurators, heirs or successors, universal or particular. But when they are asked repeatedly by the same or by other persons who have an interest, especially where a question or doubt about the matter exists or arises, or where danger or prejudice is likely to result from such issue to others, it is safer and more prudent, because of the various opinions on this, that the notaries have themselves summoned before a judge, by whose authority they may issue, or refuse to issue, to those who are to be summoned.

units.la: 27. Notarii autem sciant, se non de nocte, nisi ex urgente causa quam exprimant, vel in locis occultis, seu clam rogari, vel instrumentari debere, cum hoc non sine suspicione procederet.
units.tr: 27. Notaries should know that they must not draw up or execute instruments at night, unless for an urgent cause which they state, nor in hidden places or secretly, since this would not proceed without suspicion.

units.la: CAPUT II. De Testamentis.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. On Testaments.

units.la: DEBENT autem Notarii praecipue esse solliciti & diligentes circa Testamentorum & aliarum ultimarum voluntatum confectiones, propter magna ex eis imminentia praejudicia. Sunt enim secundum sacratissimas leges testamentorum genera duo: alterum quod fit in scriptis seu mediante scriptura, clausa seu involuta: alterum vero & communius, quod pet solam nuncupationem sine scriptura, vel aliqua literali solennitate fieri solet, & ideo nuncupativum dicitur, neque scriptura tamen de sua essentia requirit. Item potest & tertium genus adhiberi, quod fit a coeco caeco per nuncupationem, tamen non sine scriptura, utpote tam a Notario quam testibus adhibitus, & rogatis proptiis manibus subscripta singulorumque solitis signetis signata.
units.tr: Notaries ought to be especially careful and diligent in drawing up wills and other last wishes, because of the serious prejudices that arise from them. According to the most sacred laws there are two kinds of testament. One is made in writing, or by means of a writing, either sealed or enclosed. The other, which is the more common, is made by oral declaration alone, without writing or any formal literary solemnity, and is therefore called nuncupative; yet it does not in its essence require writing. A third kind may also be used: a blind man's testament made by oral declaration, though not without writing, since it is written out by the notary and witnesses and signed with the hands of those called and sealed with each one's usual seals.

units.la: 2. Et advertant ipsi Notarii, quod ad singulorum testamentorum praemissorum genera conficiendae requiruntur secundum leges, testes ad minus septem, inclusio ipso Notario. In Codicillis autem, in quibus legata & fideicommissa relinquuntur sine haeredum alicujus institutione, vel in donationibus causa mortis, & in ture, ubi rustici testantur, & plures haberi non possunt testes ad minus quinque. In parentum autem inter liberos, ubi nullum aliud testamentum procedit, quod infirmandum sit, & in militum castris, non autem bellicis expeditionibus existentium testamentis remittitur numerus testium usque ad duos.
units.tr: 2. The notaries themselves should note that for each of the aforesaid kinds of testament, the law requires at least seven witnesses, the notary included. In codicils, in which legacies and trust bequests are left without the appointment of any heir, or in gifts made in view of death, and in a place where country people make their wills and no more than five witnesses can be had, at least five are required. In a parent's will between children, where no other testament is valid that would have to be set aside, and in the wills of soldiers in camp, though not of those on active campaign, the number of witnesses is reduced to two.

units.la: 3. Milites autem in expeditionibus bellicis existentes etiam sine omni solennitate vel teste, quocunque modo velint testari, possunt: non autem existentes in talibus expeditionibus seu castris, Jure communi testantur.
units.tr: 3. Soldiers on active military campaign may make a will in whatever way they wish, even without any solemnity or witness. Those who are not on such campaign, but in camp or garrison, make their wills under the common law.

units.la: 4. Requiritur etiam quod in testamentis non solum rogentur testes, sed specialiter ad actus hujusmodi testandum vocentur, & adhibeantur, vel saltem si casu illine sint, ad hoc praemoneantur. 5. Item requiritur in omni testamento, quòd testator testatrixve verbis intelligentibus loqui aut scribere sciat. Nam neutri eorum sciens mortuo similis in hoc reputatur, & testari non potest.
units.tr: 4. It is also required that in wills the witnesses not only be asked, but be specially summoned and admitted for the purpose of making such a testament, or at least, if they happen to be present by chance, be forewarned of it. 5. It is further required in every testament that the testator, male or female, know how to speak or write in intelligible words. For one who knowingly lacks either of these is counted in this respect like the dead and cannot make a will.

units.la: 6. Præterea etiam requiritur in omni testamento, etiam nuncupativo, ut singula gesta in notam jam recepta relegantur coram testatore, testibusque, antequam ab invicem recederint.
units.tr: 6. Moreover, it is also required in every testament, even a nuncupative one, that each item of the transaction be read back, from a note already taken down, in the presence of the testator and the witnesses, before they separate from one another.

units.la: 7. Caveant ergò Notarii se ab his, qui neque articulatim & intelligibiliter loqui, neque scribere possunt, cùm sint inutestabiles.
units.tr: 7. Notaries must therefore beware of those who can neither speak distinctly and intelligibly nor write, since they are incapable of making a will.

units.la: 8. Videant autem Notarii testamentis adhibiri, & etiam testari volentes, quos adhibeant testes, quia multi prohibentur adhiberi, ut regulariter omnes qui sunt activè vel passivè intestabiles & præterea mulier, hermophroditæ, in quibus muliebria præcellunt, in potestate testantis existens hæres scriptus, & cum eodem in eadem existens potestate. Unde consulitur ut ad requisitum numerum testes alii recipiantur, ne propter aliquorum inhabilitatem testamenta irritentur.
units.tr: 8. Notaries should also see to it, both when wills are being executed and when those wishing to make a will are present, which witnesses they admit, because many are prohibited from being admitted: as a rule, all who are incapable of making a will or of receiving under one, actively or passively, and moreover a woman, and hermaphrodites in whom the female characteristics predominate, and anyone who is written in as heir while under the power of the testator, and anyone who is in the same power as the testator. Hence it is advised that other witnesses be taken to make up the required number, so that the wills are not made void by the incapacity of some.

units.la: 9. Testamenti autem in scriptis (quod magno inusu amplius non est, sed ab eo fit, quin tamen vita neminem suæ ultimæ voluntatis conscium esse vult) talis est forma: Producit testari volens medium coram testibus septem ad id specialiter convocatis seu præmonitis & rogatis viris, liberis, poteribus, omnibus simul præsentibus scripturam consignatam vel ligatam, vel tantùm clausam volutam, sive ipsius testatoris, sive alterius cujuslibet manuscriptam, offertque illam istis testibus singulis eorum subscribendam, & signeris suis solitis signandam: dummodò tamen aperte dixerit esse testamentum quod offertur, ibique coram testibus sua manu propria subscripserit: vel si ipse legere nesciat, vel tunc non posset, alterius octavi testis manu, nomine & jussu suo, in reliqua parte testamenti subscribi faciat. Tunc eodem die & tempore nullo intervallo, vel etiam actu extraneo, nisi tenè necessitatis causa, & modico interrumpente per singulos septem testes propriis suis manibus subscribitur, & sigillis suis seu signis solis signatur.
units.tr: 9. The form of a written testament (which through long disuse is no longer common, and which is made only by one who nonetheless wishes no one to be aware of his last wishes) is as follows. The testator, wishing to make a will, presents to seven witnesses, specially summoned, forewarned and asked for this purpose, men, free persons, and adults, all present together, a document signed or tied up, or merely sealed and enclosed, whether written by the testator himself or by anyone else, and offers it to these witnesses so that each may subscribe it and mark it with his usual seal. Provided, however, that he has openly declared that the document offered is his testament, and has there, in the presence of the witnesses, subscribed it with his own hand. Or, if he cannot read, or then is unable to do so, he shall have the remainder of the testament subscribed by the hand of an eighth witness, in his name and at his command. Then on the same day and at the same time, without any interval or any extraneous act, except perhaps a brief interruption for necessity, each of the seven witnesses subscribes with his own hand and marks it with his own seal or sign alone.

units.la: 10. Testamenti autem nuncupativi forma est: Quia testari volens ejus vel eorum, quos hæredem seu hæredes suos esse velit, legatariorumque nomina, & ea quæ in eo continentur, coram septem testibus ad hoc vocatis & rogatis palam & dilucidè nuncupat & exprimit.
units.tr: 10. The form of a nuncupative testament is this: the testator, wishing to make a will, openly and clearly declares and sets forth, before seven witnesses summoned and asked for this purpose, the name or names of the person or persons whom he wishes to be his heir or heirs, and of the legatees, and the things contained in it.

units.la: 11. In cœci autem testamento requiruntur subscripta, primò quòd tam Notarius quàm testes septem ad hoc vocentur, & cujus causa vocati sint, certificentur: Secundò, quòd testator hæredem seu hæredes à se instituendos, & nedum nomen seu nomina, sed & dignitates seu conditiones alias eorundem pro tanto, quod propter solam nominis seu nominum expressionem non oriri possit ambiguitas, & præterea aliam suam voluntatem tam circa eorundem hæredum institutiones, quàm substitutiones, fideicommissa atque legata coram ipsis Notario & testibus clare exprimat. Tertiò, quòd tabellio, vel si is haberi tunc non posset, octavus testis vocatus vice ejusdem, atque testes singuli pertestatorem ad hoc rogati, uno & eodem tempore, loco, & nullo intervallo seu actu extraneo, nisi forte modico, & necessitate naturæ interveniente, sese in fine utpote in margine instrumenti infrenon subscribant, simulque consignent. Potest autem testari volens vel in ipso actu coram testibus, vel si magis placet, antea per alium quemcunque voluntatem vel testamentum suum dictari & scribi facere, & postea coram testibus & tabellario, prius patefacta, cujus causa vocati sint, chartulam ipsam coram se & testibus recitare: & ubi tenor ejus omnibus notus fuerit, profiteatur testator elogium suum id esse, & ex animi sui, quæ lecta sunt, dispositiones sententia, & in fine sequantur subscriptiones atque signacula, tam testium ut prædicitur singulorum, quàm tabellarii.
units.tr: 11. For a blind man's testament the following are required. First, that the notary and the seven witnesses be summoned for this purpose, and be informed for what purpose they have been called. Second, that the testator clearly declare to the notary and witnesses, not only the name or names of the heir or heirs to be appointed by him, but also their rank or other qualifications, so far that no ambiguity can arise from the expression of their names alone; and moreover that he clearly state his other wish, both regarding the appointment of these heirs and their substitutes, trust bequests and legacies. Third, that the notary, or if he cannot then be had, an eighth witness summoned in his place, and each of the witnesses, asked for this purpose by the testator, at one and the same time and place, without any interval or extraneous act, except perhaps a brief one and one needed by nature, subscribe at the foot, as in the margin of the instrument below, and at the same time mark it with their seals. The testator, wishing to make a will, may either declare his wish or testament in the actual presence of the witnesses, or, if he prefers, have it dictated and written beforehand by anyone else; and afterwards, before the witnesses and the notary, having first disclosed the purpose for which they were called, he may read the paper aloud in their presence. When its tenor is known to all, the testator declares that this is his own statement, and that the dispositions read out are in accordance with his own mind and judgment. At the end follow the subscriptions and seals, of the witnesses individually, as stated above, and of the notary.

units.la: 12. Potest etiam unus vel plures, si propriis signetis carerent, alterius seu aliorum signo vel signis in hoc uti.
units.tr: 12. One or more witnesses, if they lack their own seals, may also use the seal or seals of another or of others for this purpose.

units.la: 13. Istam autem formam non solùm in testamenti cœci, sed codicillorum vel aliarum ultimarum voluntatum confectione observari necesse est.
units.tr: 13. This form must be observed not only in the making of a blind man's testament, but also in the drawing up of codicils and other last wishes.

units.la: 14. Sciturus omnibus Notariis, quòd præfatas testamentorum formas à lege traditas diligenter observare negligentes, præter hoc quòd testamenta aliter facta de Jure civili non subsistunt, etiam Juris pœnas non evitabunt.
units.tr: 14. Let all notaries know that those who negligently fail to observe diligently the aforesaid forms of testaments prescribed by law, besides the fact that wills made otherwise do not stand under civil law, will also not escape the penalties of the law.

units.la: CAPIT. III.
units.tr: CAPUT III.

units.la: De insinuatione literarum Imperialium.
units.tr: On the insinuation of imperial letters.

units.la: Circa Imperialium autem, vel Cameræ nostræ Cæsareæ Judicii literarum citatoriarum, vel quarumcunque aliarum continentium insinuationes, si quis desuper rogatus fuerit, advertat, ut sub præstito in officio suo fidelitatis juramento literas hujusmodi originales illi vel illis quem seu quos diriguntur, retento tamen penes se toto tenore inde descripto, & postea in instrumento insinuationis integrè inserendo, in personam seu personas proprias, vel si commodè haberi non possunt, ad domum seu domos solitæ habitationis earundem, vel per edictum per Judicem decretum præsentent, legant, insinuent, atque illi relinquant quàm fideliter.
units.tr: Concerning the insinuation of imperial letters, whether citatory letters of our Imperial Court of Chamber or any other letters containing notices, if anyone is requested in this matter, let him take heed that, under the oath of fidelity sworn in his office, he present, read, insinuate and faithfully leave the originals of such letters to the person or persons to whom they are addressed, retaining however with himself the full tenor copied from them and afterwards inserting it entire in the instrument of insinuation; he shall do so in the person or persons themselves, or, if they cannot conveniently be found, at the house or houses of their usual residence, or by edict decreed by the judge.

units.la: 2. Quòd si verò ac quotiens contigerit, aliquas tales literas plures personas in diversis residentibus domibus seu locis continere, quibus singulis faciendæ sit præsentatio, seu insinuatio earundem, sciant Notarii hujusmodi præsentationem & insinuationem singulis eorum, de quibus rogatum erint, cum ostensione & lectione originalium esse faciendum, modo & forma præmissis, relicta & tradita cuique eorum copia collationata & concorde, nisi forte in una civitate seu villa, in diversis tamen aedibus habirantes pancioribus copiis fuerint contenti.
units.tr: 2. But if and whenever it happens that some such letters contain several persons residing in different houses or places, to each of whom presentation or insinuation of them must be made, let the notaries know that such presentation and insinuation must be made to each of those persons for whom they have been requested, by showing and reading the originals, in the manner and form set out above, a collated and agreeing copy being left and handed to each of them; unless perhaps, living in one city or village but in different houses, they have agreed to be content with fewer copies.

units.la: 3. Praesentationum autem seu insinuationum suarum huiusmodi & earum dies, menses, annosque & loca singula, & si forte aliquis, cui fit insinuatio, se parere nolit, vel ut Imperatoris vel Judicis Camerae contemptum seu ignominiam irreverenter verba proruperit, instrumentis suis tam his, ad quorum instantiam, quam illis quibus facta fuerit praesentatio sive insinuatio edendis una cum literarum insinuatarum tenoribus integris referant & attestentur sincere & fideliter.
units.tr: 3. As to the presentations or insinuations of this kind, their days, months, years and each place, and if perhaps any person to whom insinuation is made refuses to obey, or irreverently breaks out into words of contempt or disgrace towards the Emperor or the Judge of the Chamber, the notaries shall report and attest sincerely and faithfully, in the instruments to be issued both to those at whose instance and to those to whom the presentation or insinuation was made, together with the full tenors of the letters insinuated.

units.la: CAPIT. IV.
units.tr: CAPUT IV.

units.la: De constitutionibus Actorum & Procuratorum.
units.tr: Concerning the appointment of attorneys and procurators.

units.la: IN constitutionem autem tam actorum, quae a Tutoribus vel Curatoribus minorennium ante lites contestatas, & quidem cum auctoritate & decreti interpositione Judicis fiunt, & fieri debent, quam Procuratorum ad lites, attendant bene Notarii, cum ad Judicium Imperiale veniant quotidie instrumenta procuratoria defectuosa, ut quantum tam ad actus speciales requirentes mandata, quam aliis clausulas apponi solitas & consuetas, de quibus etiam vulgaris habetur forma, bene extendantur instrumenta cum clara specificatione quem vel quos constituunt, sive in solidum, sive divisim Procuratores velit habere, ita, quod non sit melior conditio unius quam alterius seu aliorum. Sed quicquid unus inceperit, alter id continuare possit, mediare, & finire: videlicet ad agendum, defendendum, libellandum, litem contestandum, jurandum de calumnia, & aliud quodcunque licitum juramentum praestandum, ponendum, articulandum, positionibus advertis etiam per juramentum respondendum: Testes & alias probationes producendum, excipiendum, replicandum, duplicandum, triplicandum &c. concludendum, sententias audiendum, ad appellandum & provocandum. Si ad Judicia inferiora dirigantur, Apostolos petendum, recipiendum, appellationis causas prosequendum, alium vel alios loco suo substituendum, istos revocandum, & iterum rotiens quoties substituendum &c. Et generaliter omnia & singula &c. faciendum cum promptissime & cautione solitis de rato & relevando, sub omni constituentis rerum & bonorum obligatione, & haec omnia in extensa communique forma.
units.tr: Notaries should take good care in drawing up the powers of attorney both of acts done by guardians or curators of minors before the joinder of issue, and indeed with the authority and interposition of decree of the judge, which are and ought to be done, and of procurators for suits. For daily there come before the Imperial Court defective powers of attorney. Therefore the instruments should be fully drawn up, with a clear specification of whom they appoint, whether they wish to have their procurators jointly and severally or separately, so that the condition of one is no better than that of another or of the others. But whatever one has begun, another may continue, mediate and finish; namely, to act, to defend, to file a libel, to join issue, to swear the oath of calumny and any other lawful oath to be taken, to propound, to put forward articles, to answer by oath to positions put to him, to produce and object to witnesses and other proofs, to reply, rejoin, triplicate and so on, to conclude, to hear sentences, to appeal and to lodge appeal. If the cause is directed to lower courts, to seek and receive apostles, to pursue causes of appeal, to substitute another or others in his place, to revoke them, and to substitute again as often as may be, and so on. And generally to do all and each thing promptly, with the usual cautions concerning ratification and indemnity, under the obligation of all the goods and property of the principal; and all these things in the extended and common form.

units.la: 2. Et quia multum nunc inolevit practica, ut juretur de calumnia, idemque juramentum plurain se contineat capitula, quae plerunque ista in animas suas juranda mandantes ignorant, necesse est ut de his singulis informentur, & in instrumentis postea inserantur. Sunt enim capitula a jure tradita, & in Judicio Catnetae exprimi solita, ut tam actor quam reus per se, vel suum Procuratorem jurer, quod credat se justam habere causam litigandi, quod protelandi causa, seu fraudulenter dilationes non petat, quotiescunque interrogatur veritatem non occultet, & quod aliis quam quibus jus permittit, nil penitus donet vel promittat, quo pro se sententiam obtinere possit, dolo & fraude omnino remotis.
units.tr: 2. And because it has now become very common in practice that the oath of calumny is taken, and this same oath contains several chapters, which those who give such mandates for their own souls to swear often do not know, it is necessary that they be informed of each of these and that they be afterwards inserted in the instruments. For there are chapters handed down by law and customarily expressed in the court, so that both plaintiff and defendant, in person or through their procurator, swear that they believe they have a just cause for litigating, that they do not seek adjournments for the sake of delay or fraudulently, that whenever they are questioned they do not conceal the truth, and that they give or promise nothing whatever, by fraud or deceit, to anyone other than those to whom the law permits, by which they might obtain sentence in their favour.

units.la: 3. Jurat autem articulos seu positiones suas offerens, si petit & vult quod adversarius per juramentum respondeat sic, quod contenta in eis, quantum factum proprium concernunt, vera sint, & quantum alienum continet factum, quod credat ea esse vera & probabilia.
units.tr: 3. The one offering articles or positions swears, if he asks and wishes that the adversary answer by oath, in such a way that what is contained in them, as far as it concerns his own act, is true, and as far as it contains another's act, he believes it to be true and probable.

units.la: 4. Respondurus autem juret, se responsurum veritatem, utrum credat vel non credat ea quae subjiciuntur esse vera.
units.tr: 4. The one who is to answer swears that he will answer the truth, whether he believes or does not believe that the things put to him are true.

units.la: CAPIT. V.
units.tr: CAPUT V.

units.la: De instrumentis Appellationum.
units.tr: Concerning the instruments of appeal.

units.la: DE Appellatione autem & formalibus suis, in quibus plures & quotidiani occurrunt defectus, Notarii scire debent, quod de Jure civili & ordinatione sacri Romani Imperii omisso medio vel ab interlocutoria seu gravamine, quod postea mediante appellatione a diffinitiva est reparabile, regulariter non appellatur. In casu autem praemisso appellate volens ab interlocutoria, eam in scriptis, & cum causarum gravaminis inscriptione faciat, cum ex causis alias justificari non possit.
units.tr: Notaries ought to know concerning appeal and its formalities, in which many and daily defects occur, that by the civil law and the ordinance of the Holy Roman Empire, an interlocutory decision or a grievance, which afterwards can be repaired by means of an appeal from the final judgment, is as a rule not appealed directly. In the case set out above, one who wishes to appeal from an interlocutory decision must do so in writing, with the grievance stated, since otherwise it cannot be justified by reasons.

units.la: 2. A diffinitiva vero ubi appellari non prohibetur, sine causae seu causarum gravaminis expressione appellari poterit, & quidem verbaliter & sine scriptis, dummodo in continenti post sententiam latam, hoc est, antequam divertatur ad alia, fiat, postea tamen in scriptis redigenda: alioquin autem si ex intervallo appelletur, in scriptis fieri necesse est.
units.tr: 2. From a final judgment, however, where appeal is not forbidden, an appeal may be made without stating the reason or reasons for the grievance; and indeed it may be made orally and without writing, provided it is done immediately after the sentence is pronounced, that is, before one turns to other business, though it must afterwards be put into writing. Otherwise, if the appeal is made after an interval, it must be done in writing.

units.la: 3. Etin summa sciant & advertant omnes Notarii, quod ipsi debent esse Jurisperiti in his saltem, quae Notariatus officium respicunt, hoc est, summam Notariae, ad hoc sciant, partes coram se continentes seu agentes, de solemnitatibus & clausulis ad contractus & actus hujusmodi, earumque validitatem requisitis certificare, & se a contractibus & actibus a Jure reprobatis & prohibitis abstinere, teneantur de imperitia & partibus laesis ad interesse.
units.tr: 3. Finally, let all notaries know and take note that they ought to be lawyers, at least in those matters which concern the office of notary, namely the substance of the notarial office; so that they may know how to certify, for the parties who appear and act before them, the formalities and clauses required for such contracts and acts and for their validity; and that they must refrain from contracts and acts that the law disapproves and forbids; they are liable for their want of skill and for damages to the parties harmed.

units.la: 4. De praemissis igitur tanquam pro generaliorlibus principiis atque cunabulis quibusdam tradi-non stent adeo contenti Notarii, quia indies discant & advertant alia a Jure circa tabellionatus tradita, & quae secundum locorum, in quibus actus hujusmodi geruntur, consuetudines introducta sunt, & circa difficultates seu ambiguitates in actibus coram se gerendis pro casuum varietate & diversitate quandoque occurrentes ad peritiores recurrant, ne imperitia culpaque eorum alios noceat, quia de his tenentur, ut supra monstratum est.
units.tr: 4. Notaries should not rest content with what has been set out above as the more general principles and, as it were, the cradle of the subject; rather, they should learn and take note daily of the other matters laid down by law concerning the notarial office, and of those customs introduced according to the practice of the places where such acts are performed. And when difficulties or ambiguities arise in the acts they conduct, which occur at times because of the variety and diversity of cases, they should have recourse to the more skilled, lest their want of skill and fault harm others, since they are answerable for these things, as has been shown above.

units.la: Datum in civitate nostra Imperiali Coloniensi, octava die mensis Octobris, Anno a Natiuitate Domini millesimo, quingentesimo, duodecimo: Regnorum nostrorum, Romani vicesimo septimo, Hungariae vero vicesimo * tertio.
units.tr: Given in our Imperial city of Cologne, on the eighth day of the month of October, in the year of the Lord's Nativity one thousand five hundred and twelve; in the twenty-seventh year of our reign as Roman king, and the twenty-third of our reign in Hungary.

units.la: Per Regem
units.tr: By the King.

units.la: Ad mandatum Domini Imperatoris proprium
units.tr: By the proper command of the Lord Emperor.

units.la: Sernteiner sst.
units.tr: Sernteiner, secretary.

units.la: MAXIMILIANI I. IMP. AUG. PROPOSITIO DE BELLO TVRCICO
units.tr: Proposition of Emperor Maximilian I, Augustus, concerning the Turkish War

units.la: Ad Principes & Ordines Sacri Rom. Imperii facta in Comitiis Augusta Vindelicorum habitis Anno M D XVIII.
units.tr: Made to the Princes and Estates of the Holy Roman Empire at the Diet held at Augsburg in the year 1518.

units.la: FREQUENTIA vestra, & quae hoc tempore praecipue necessaria est Reipublicae, & mihi pergrata, non obscure indicat voluntatem vestram, & studia erga hanc causam, propter quam domum reviciti estis. Cum enim tam cupide adveneritis, postquam in literis significavi, nos de bello Turco acturos esse, facile intelligo vos ipsos, ut decet sapientes Principes & viros fortissimos, & intelligere, quid a vobis totus orbis terrarum, universa Christi Ecclesia, dignitas huius Imperii requirat: & annos vestros ea virtute ac fortitudine praeditos esse, ut bellum omnium, quae unquam fuerunt, longissimum & gloriosissimum, omnibus votis expectatis.
units.tr: Your numerous attendance, which at this time is especially necessary to the commonwealth and very welcome to me, clearly shows your goodwill and zeal toward this cause, for the sake of which you have returned home. For since you have come so eagerly, after I had announced in my letters that we would deal with the Turkish war, I readily understand that you yourselves, as befits wise princes and most brave men, grasp what the whole world, the entire Church of Christ, and the dignity of this Empire require of you; and that your years are marked by such virtue and courage that you await, with every wish, a war the longest and most glorious of all that have ever been.

units.la: Quare existimo mihi non longa oratione ad vos incitandos opus esse, & expectari a me potius classicum ad inferenda signa, quam hanc in toga & curia adhortationem. Sed tamen belli magnitudo & difficultas primum deliberatione quadam eget, non utrum sit inferendum; siquidem etsi hostes nos bello non lacesserent, neque in finitimis locis ac pene in conspectu nostro grassarentur, tamen oportuit nos liberare orbem terrarum hac crudelissima atque impia barbarie, & ex miserrima servitute tot nationes oppressas eripere: sed illud magis deliberandum esse videtur, cum tantae sint opes ac vires Turcici Regni, cum exercitus in longinquas regiones traducendi, cum fortassis pluribus locis & longo tempore bellum futurum sit, quantis opus sit copiis, an una Germanica natio tantos conficere exercitus, tolerare exercitus; arma, equos, stipendia, commeatus suppeditare possit; qui Reges, qui populi, ad societatem huius pulcherrimae militiae adjungi possint; an ita in Europa pax constituta sit, ne me & vos ex medio cursu revocent homines perfidi, qui, ut saepe ante accidit, vel per occasionem occupare nostra conabuntur, vel turpi aliqua cum hostibus pactione facta metuent, ne fines Imperii proferamus.
units.tr: Therefore I think there is no need for a long speech to rouse you, and that from me you should expect the trumpet call to advance the standards rather than this exhortation in gown and council chamber. Yet the magnitude and difficulty of the war first need some deliberation, not as to whether it should be waged. For even if the enemy did not provoke us with war, nor rage in neighbouring lands and almost within our sight, we ought nonetheless to free the world from this most cruel and impious barbarism, and to snatch so many oppressed nations from miserable servitude. But the question seems to call for more deliberation: given the great wealth and power of the Turkish kingdom, given that armies must be transported into distant regions, given that the war will perhaps be waged in many places and over a long time, how great the forces needed will be; whether the German nation alone can raise such great armies, sustain them, and supply arms, horses, pay and provisions; what kings and peoples can be joined to the alliance of this most glorious campaign; and whether peace in Europe is so firmly established that treacherous men will not recall me and you from the middle of our course, men who, as has often happened before, will either try to seize our lands by opportunity, or, having made some shameful pact with the enemy, will fear that we extend the borders of the Empire.

units.la: De his rebus scio a me requiri orationem prudentibus omnibus. Nam me quidem in hoc Imperii fastigio, non solum in acie Ducem & Imperatorem esse, sed multo magis huius publici consilii ducem atque autorem esse convenit. Quare non de his tantis rebus diu multumque, tot jam exercitatus bellis, & magna fortunae varietate, cogitassem, profecto reprehensione omnium dignus essem.
units.tr: I know that everyone of prudence expects me to speak on these matters. For in this height of the Empire it is fitting that I be not only leader and emperor in the field, but much more the leader and author of this public counsel. Therefore, if I had not, after so many wars and such great changes of fortune, thought long and hard about these great matters, I would certainly deserve the reproach of all.

units.la: Sed mihi credite, cum ab auspiciis meis, recuperata Austria, post mortem Regis Hungariae Matthiae Hunniadae, & ingenti expulso exercitu Turcarum ex Croatia, nihil magis in votis mihi fuerit, quam ut mox exercitus in provincias Turcarum traduceretur, nunquam postea de hoc bello cogitare desii. At nunc quidem occasio percommoda erat hujus suscipiendi. Nam post Mahometi mortem magna de successione inter fratres discordia erat. Sed jam armis invadere Regnum conabatur.
units.tr: But believe me, since from the beginning of my reign, when Austria was recovered after the death of Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary, and a huge Turkish army was driven out of Croatia, nothing has been more in my wishes than that an army be led at once into the Turkish provinces, I have never ceased thinking about this war since then. And indeed the opportunity for undertaking it was very favourable at that time. For after the death of Mahomet there was great discord between the brothers over the succession, yet one of them was already trying to invade the kingdom by arms.

units.la: Verum qui me haec parantem Hu&ctus subito exceperunt? Galli non solum me de possessione Burgundiae per seditionem dejicere conati sunt, sed etiam meo capiti insidias per summum scelus extulerunt. Postea Italia, quae proximis annis singulari consilio patris mei Friderici Imperatoris cata fuerat, iterum Gallicis armis perturbata est. Nam proximo anno post mortem Patris mei, Caroli VIII. cum ingenti exercitu bonam Italiae partem hostiliter pervagatus est.
units.tr: But who suddenly attacked me while I was preparing these things? The French not only tried to drive me from the possession of Burgundy by sedition, but also through the greatest crime plotted against my life. Afterwards Italy, which in recent years had been held in check by the singular policy of my father, Emperor Frederick, was again thrown into turmoil by French arms. For in the year after the death of my father, Charles VIII, with a huge army, overran a good part of Italy as an enemy.

units.la: Quare certam tranquillitatem domi promittere nobis possumus. Hoc caput est negotii. Nam reliqua iqua pars deliberationis multò est facilior. Hæc me cura amplius jam viginti annis exercuit: præcipue quonmodo pacem in Europa firmam constituerem. Hunc mihi finem omnium bellorum semper propositum, non ut latius fines Regni extenderem, sed ut pace petita bellum transferrem in Turcicum. Recum. Hanc ob causam victor multa concessi iis, quos armis domui, ut mea moderatione eos ad pacem invitarem. Hæc præfatus sum aliquanto prolixius, ut quæ mea voluntas in his bellis, quæ gesti sunt, fuerit, plane omnes intelligant, ac sciant, neque antea me iracundia, aut injusta cupiditate unquam arma sumsisse, neque hoc Turcicum bellum alio consilio parare, quam quia necessarium & pium esse judico. Quæ de rebus pauca addidero, postea reliquam deliberationem de copiis, de commeatibus, deque modo belligerendi perexamque domi pace constituta non potest difficilis vobis videri, qui pen ei stis rei militaris, & quibus Germania satis nota est: denique qui arma & opes, & hanc Imperii dignitatem tenere nos scitis, ut vitam & omnes fortunas nostras, ad defensionem & publicam salutem orbis terrarum conferamus.
units.tr: Therefore we can promise ourselves certain tranquillity at home. This is the heart of the matter, for the remaining part of the deliberation is much easier. This care has occupied me for more than twenty years now: above all, how I might establish a firm peace in Europe. This has always been my aim in all wars: not to extend the borders of the realm more widely, but, having sought peace, to turn the war against the Turks. For this reason, as victor, I have granted many concessions to those whom I subdued by arms, so that by my moderation I might invite them to peace. I have said this at some length, so that everyone may plainly understand what my purpose was in these wars that have been waged, and may know that I have never taken up arms out of anger or unjust desire, nor am I preparing this Turkish war for any other purpose than because I judge it necessary and pious. Concerning the other matters I shall add a few things, and afterwards I shall take up the remaining deliberation about forces, provisions, and the manner of waging war. Nor can it seem difficult to you, who are experienced in military affairs and to whom Germany is well known, to establish peace at home first; you who know that we hold arms, resources and this dignity of the Empire, so that we may devote our lives and all our fortunes to the defence and public safety of the world.

units.la: 4. Nec vero quenquam è vobis quidem arbitror esse, qui Turcicum bellum parum necessarium existimet, aut postulet, ut alii potius Reges, aliæ nationes sibi has partes sumant. Nam etiamsi Turcæ, ius finibus jam contenti, non proferrent arma longius, nec nobis periculum denunciarent, nos quidem, quibus Deus præcipue commendavit oibis Christiani defensionem, bellum inferre illis oportebat, ut Græciam & vicinas provincias crudeli servitute liberaremus. Nam si quis putat mitia aut tolerabilia esse Turcarum Imperia, is longè fallitur, nec nobis de Imperii laude cum illis certamen est, sed de religione, de disciplina, de conjugum & liberorum pudicitia. Præcipue autem grassantur in Nobilitatem, nec solum possessiones certæ victis nullæ relinquuntur, sed etiam lixæ & gregarii milites rapiuntur ad supra nobilissimas atque honestissimas matronas, virgines, pueros; ad hæc multis modis extinguunt ac delent Christianam religionem. An non hæc sunt magnæ & justæ causæ, quæ viros fortibus ad tuendam gloriam Dei, & salutem omnium gentium, arma induant?
units.tr: 4. Nor do I think there is any one of you who considers the Turkish war of little necessity, or who asks that other kings and other nations take up these parts for themselves. For even if the Turks, content now with their boundaries, did not carry their arms further, nor declared danger to us, we, to whom God has especially entrusted the defence of the Christian world, ought to make war upon them, so that we might free Greece and the neighbouring provinces from cruel servitude. For if anyone thinks the rule of the Turks is mild or tolerable, he is greatly mistaken; our contest with them is not about the glory of the Empire, but about religion, discipline, and the chastity of wives and children. They rage especially against the nobility: not only are no fixed possessions left to the conquered, but even camp followers and common soldiers are seized, and the most noble and honourable matrons, virgins and boys are carried off; besides, they in many ways extinguish and destroy the Christian religion. Are these not great and just causes which move brave men to take up arms for the defence of the glory of God and the salvation of all peoples?

units.la: 5. Quare ingenti dolore afficior, cum cogito Græciam, quæ non solum doctrinarum parens est, sed etiam omnium laude virtutum excelluit, & diu florentissima pars Ecclesiæ Christianæ fuit, nunc tali servitute oppressam esse, in qua cùm cætera dictu fœda atque horrenda perferenda sunt, tum etiam religio penitus aboletur, & auget meum dolorem, quod res gestæ præcipuè tectantur, Græciam nō sponte, aut sine certamine accepisse hoc jugum. Illa verò multos annos fortissimè dimicans tandem concidit, non virtute superata, sed quia sola tantam hostium multitudinem, & tam longum bellum sustinere non poterat. Audio etiam num tantam esse vim ingeniorum, tantam virtutem Græcæ nationis, ut non alia gens præstantiores duces Turcis suppeditet, quàm Græca, qui (ut audio) quanquam ritibus imbuti Turcicis, tamen memores nostræ nobiscum necessitudinis, invili bellum gerunt in nostris provinciis. Hanc certè nationem, quæ pulcerrimum Ornamentum nominis Christiani, quæque cum majoribus nostris sanguine, fœderibus, & multis officiis conjuncta fuit, cum ob cæteras causas oportuit nos in libertatem vindicare, tum ob hæc merita singularia, quod aliquot sæculis immanem illam barbariem fortissimè repressit, & à nostris cervicibus depulit. Nullum enim justius est officium, quàm servatoribus calamitate aliqua fractis tursus opem ferre, & parem gratiam referre.
units.tr: 5. Therefore I am afflicted with great grief when I think that Greece, which was not only the parent of learning but also excelled in the praise of all virtues, and for a long time was the most flourishing part of the Christian Church, is now oppressed by such servitude, in which, while other shameful and horrible things must be endured, religion too is utterly abolished. My grief is increased by the fact that the records mainly relate that Greece did not accept this yoke willingly or without a struggle. Indeed, after fighting most bravely for many years, she at last fell, not overcome by valour, but because she alone could not sustain so great a multitude of enemies and so long a war. I also hear that there is such great strength of talent and such great virtue in the Greek nation that no other people supplies the Turks with more distinguished commanders than the Greeks, who (as I hear), although steeped in Turkish customs, nevertheless, mindful of our old kinship with them, wage war against their will in our provinces. This nation, surely, which is the most beautiful ornament of the Christian name, and which was joined with our ancestors by blood, treaties and many services, we ought to vindicate to liberty for other reasons, and above all for these singular merits: that for several centuries it bravely held back that monstrous barbarism and drove it from our necks. For there is no more just duty than to bring aid in turn to our saviours, when they have been broken by some calamity, and to repay them with equal kindness.

units.la: 6. Sed quò me dolorabducit? Tanta est enim non solum regnandi cupiditas, sed multo magis humani sanguinis sitis; tantus furor in Turcis, ut non reliquerint nobis deliberationem de inferendo bello liberam, sed de propulsando bello, de defensione religionis Christianæ, quam ubique terrarum delere conantur illa barbaries, consilium capiendum est; retinenda est hujus Imperii majestas, mèdæ conjuges & liberi nostri. Nihil enim occurrimus, paulo post domiis vicinis gentibus in media Germania videbitis excindi urbes, inflammari templa, rapi ad omne flagitii genus conjuges & liberos, divelli infantes à complexu parentum atque interfici, medias secari gravidas mulieres illo acyrnace barbarico, Fanatice religiones, quibus incitari sunt, ne quidem concedunt eis ocium, sed lege coguntur Imperii extendere. Et successus tanti tamque prosperi, annorum fere ducentorum, addunt eis animos, ut quiescere nullo modo possint. Quod si tanta fuit gloriæ atque imperii cupiditas, tanta audacia nunc, cum vires haberet admodum exiguas, nec quicquam nisi littus ad Pontum Euxinum tenerent, ut non mari, non montibus, non magnitudine Græci Imperii deterriti sint, quò minus in Asiam & Europam imperii facerent, cum quidem magnas insuper clades acceperant, an nunc adepti tantam potentiam, tantas vires & hoc remittat fastigium, existimans non delectari Imperii gloria? Atqui verò acerrimus est stiniuius in bellico fissigenius, armorum & Imperii decus, præsertim si aspiret etiam fortuna. Multæ ante nostræ clades intermixtæ postea deinde ut usque q; a proelio, q; Sigismundus Imperator cum Turcis infeliciter comisit, cum interea nullam ipsi insignem cladem acceperint. Itaq; in tanti felici victoriarum cursu, quàm non cessaverunt, videbis. Ut enim omittam res gestas superiorum: Mahometus, qui me puero floruit, summa celeritate, cœ fulmen quoddam, magnam Europæ partem pervagatus est. Cùm in Pannoniis infeliciter dimicasset, victus à Ioanne Hunniade, nequaquam animo fractus est, sed Constantinopolim adortus, diu obsessam, tandem anno ante quam natus sum sexto, vi captam diripuit, crudelissimè interfecto Imperatore Constantino, cognato nostro, & raptis ad stupri eius liberis. Postea capta Thracia, Mysiam invasit, acferè toto illyrico domito, & occupato regno Bosniæ, Græciam adoriuntur, Corinthi vi expugnat, & Peloponnesum dimisit, interfectis Palæologis Demetrio & Thomæ fratribus. Tot regnis ac Provinciis in Europa potitus, adeò non recepit se in otium, ut subinde majora spe aliquid moliretur. Cöstituit provincias in Europa, trajectus in Asia, Trapezuntem expugnat, Rege interfecto. Deinde Mysiæ armis capit; cumq; jam minore Asiam ac Pontum omnem universam tenetur, navat fert bellū in Syriam & Ægyptū. Sed cum Sultanus acie victus pacem peteret, quia majoris gloriæ mæ teriam esse vidit in Europa, fœdus cū Sultano fecit, & rediens in Europā, instructa classe, & contracta copiis trajicit in Italiā, & oppugnavit Hydruntē, ac tantū terroris Italiæ incussit, ut jam Romanus Pontifex fugā pararet: omnia erant in Italia & Gallia bellorū plena. Deinde nō solum Turcarum vires, multo magis Ducis felicitatē, scientiā rei militaris, vigilantiā & celeritatē, omnes gentes formidabant. Memini me puero hunc tanquā Alexandrum alterū prædicari, ejusq; virtuti ac felicitati pionā omnia videri. In tanta tepiditate nostrorū Deus clementer respexit Ecclesiā suā, & illi Tyrannoj mīlitē aditū tenenti manus injecit, eumq; ne funditus Christianū nomen, aras nostras, & sacratissimā Christianam religionē deleret, è medio sustulit atq; extinxit. Quod quidē li agnoscimus, cogitemus non quæ dē cō servatos esse, non ut otiosi ppetuò grassari in Ecclesia Turcas sinamus, sed ut excitati nec quæ cura Ecclesiæ liberandæ & defendēdæ afficiamur, & sciamus Deū rē tā piā suscipientibus auxitūrum. Nā nos quidē, quibus Reipubl. defensio cōmendata est, non alio Deo culiū gratiore plē e pō.
units.tr: 6. But where does my grief carry me? There is not only a lust for ruling but, much more, a thirst for human blood, and such is the fury of the Turks that they have left us no free choice about waging war. We must now decide how to repel the war and defend the Christian religion, which that barbarity is trying to destroy everywhere on earth. We must preserve the majesty of this Empire, our wives and our children. For soon, unless we take care, you will see cities razed in the heart of Germany among our neighbouring peoples, temples set on fire, wives and children dragged off to every kind of outrage, infants torn from their parents' embrace and killed, and pregnant women cut open with that barbarian scimitar. The fanatical religion that drives them does not even allow them rest; by law they are compelled to extend the Empire. And successes so great and so prosperous, lasting nearly two hundred years, give them such courage that they can by no means keep still. If there was such a lust for glory and empire, and such boldness, when they had very small forces and held nothing but the shore of the Black Sea, so that neither the sea, nor the mountains, nor the size of the Greek Empire deterred them from making their empire in Asia and Europe, though they had received great defeats, will they now, having won such power and such forces, relax from this height, as if they took no pleasure in the glory of empire? Yet the spur of the warlike spirit is most keen, the glory of arms and empire, especially when fortune also smiles. Many of our defeats were mixed in afterwards, up to the battle that Emperor Sigismund unluckily fought with the Turks, while they themselves suffered no notable defeat. So in this happy course of victories, you will see how little they have ceased. To pass over the deeds of earlier times: Mehmed, who flourished when I was a boy, with the speed of a thunderbolt roamed over a great part of Europe. When he fought unsuccessfully in Pannonia and was defeated by John Hunyadi, he was in no way broken in spirit, but attacked Constantinople, which he besieged for a long time, and at last, in the sixth year before I was born, took it by force and plundered it, cruelly killing the Emperor Constantine, our kinsman, and carrying off his children to be defiled. Afterwards, having taken Thrace, he invaded Moesia, subdued almost all of Illyricum, and seized the kingdom of Bosnia. Then they turned on Greece, took Corinth by storm and overran the Peloponnese, killing the Palaeologus brothers Demetrius and Thomas. Having gained possession of so many kingdoms and provinces in Europe, he did not retire to rest, but soon attempted greater things with higher hopes. He established provinces in Europe, crossed into Asia, stormed Trebizond and killed its king. Then he took Moesia by arms; and when he already held the whole of Asia Minor and all of Pontus, he carried war into Syria and Egypt. But when the Sultan, defeated in battle, sought peace, he saw that there was more glory to be won in Europe, so he made a treaty with the Sultan. Returning to Europe with a fleet fitted out and troops gathered, he crossed into Italy and attacked Otranto, and struck such terror into Italy that the Roman Pontiff was already preparing to flee; all of Italy and Gaul was full of wars. Then not only the Turkish forces but, far more, the Sultan's good fortune, his skill in military affairs, his vigilance and speed, filled all peoples with dread. I remember that when I was a boy he was proclaimed as another Alexander, and everything seemed to yield to his courage and good fortune. In such lukewarmness of ours, God mercifully looked upon his Church and laid hands on that tyrant as he was pressing on, and removed him from the midst and extinguished him, lest he utterly destroy the Christian name, our altars and the most sacred Christian religion. If we acknowledge this, let us consider that we have been preserved not so that, idle, we should allow the Turks to rage ever more freely against the Church, but that we should be roused and moved by care for freeing and defending the Church, and should know that God will increase His help to those who undertake so pious a task. For we, to whom the defence of the commonwealth has been entrusted, can offer no more pleasing service to God.

units.la: 7. Divinitus & illud accidit, quod nonnihil retardarunt victoriarum Mahometi cursum fortissimi viri, primum Joannes Hunniades, deinde Georgius Scanderbegus, & Rex Hungarii r Machi. Libenter enim commemoro, ut cogitetis salutem Ecclesiæ Deo curæ esse, & ut debitum virtutis monium his ducibus optimē meritis tribuamus. Hos enim Antagonistas, ceu murum, oppositos Deo ruenti Mahomēto, ne subito impetu universam Europam opprimeret. Primum in Pannoniam finis, magno proelio victus est ab Hunniade. Deinde remorata est eum per multos annos Mac. Nam quoad vixit Scanderbegus, repressit Barbarum, & singulari virtute & felicitate patriū R defendit. Hoc mortuo, tandem Macedonia, tam diuturno bello vexata, sine certamine Mahom cessit. Matthias aliquot proeliis deterruit eum ab Hungaria; ad hæc arcem ei Sabaceam, trucidat ercitu Turcico, eripuit.
units.tr: 7. It was also by divine provision that certain most valiant men somewhat slowed the course of Mehmed's victories: first John Hunyadi, then George Scanderbeg, and the King of Hungary, Matthias. I gladly recall these things so that you may consider that the salvation of the Church is God's concern, and that we should render the due praise of virtue to these leaders, who have deserved it so well. For these men, like a wall, were set against Mehmed as he rushed on, so that he might not overwhelm all of Europe with a sudden attack. When he first invaded Pannonia, he was defeated in a great battle by Hunyadi. Then he was held back for many years by Scanderbeg. For as long as Scanderbeg lived, he checked the barbarian and, by singular courage and good fortune, defended his homeland. When he died, Macedonia, long harassed by so protracted a war, passed to Mehmed without a fight. Matthias, in several battles, drove him away from Hungary; and he wrested from him the fortress of Szabács, cutting down the Turkish army.

units.la: 8. Extincto igitur Mahometo, paulisper respitavimus. Nā & domestica dissensio mortē quuta est: sed aliquanto post, sedatis discordiis intestinis, iterū vicinis Regnis bella inferunt. Methonā Venetis ingenti certamine eripuit. Quid nunc Selimū? nonne videtis domita Syria & Ægypto, Hungariæ audacissimē bellū inferre: à qua nisi eū depellimus, quā facile erit Turcis postea pyrltionē irruptiones in Germaniā facere, quoties velint. Ac, mihi credite, non solū formidet, sed etiā magno consilio Turcæ belligerantur, intēti in occasiones omnes; nec omnia simul occupare conātur, sed atque aliqua bello capta, paulatim tentant vicina loca. Ad hoc accedit assiduitas, quā crevisse magnā imperii pīcipuē videmus. Ubi semel pedē posuerunt, inde non facile depelluntur: deinde cōmunitis in locis, q occuparunt, tum demū arma proferunt ulterius. Quare etiāsi Germaniā nondum attingunt, quanquā sæpe jam in Carnos fecerunt irruptiones, tam ubi Hungaria potiti fuerint, erunt intenti in omnes occasiones, ut nos imparatos, aut distractos intestinis discordiis opprimant. Si, ut Bulgaris & Valachis imperarent, nullos labores, nulla defigerunt pericula, quantò magis Germaniā atq; Italiam, ipsas quidem arces Christiani nominis, appetent, quas si tenerent (quod prohibeat Deus) non solum Imperii magnitudine veteres Romanos æquarent, sed etiam totam Christianam religionem delevisse sibi videntur. Habetent accessionem tantarum vitium, ut reliquæ nationes sine ullo certamine cessurae essent. Vos, qui nunc arma geritis, ne Christi nomen aboleatur, quique veram religionem & libertatem vestram defenditis, postea advertus Christum pro nefaria impietate militare, Tyrannō servire, & sultes expectare alicujus Scythæ, cogeremini. Qua immanitate domini in conjuges vestros ac liberos vestros esse? Verecundè dici non possunt ea, quæ non tantum in captivos, sed etiam in suos communes Illud tamen recitabo: capto Byzantio, Imperatoris CONSTANTINI caput cervici abscissum est; a Mahometus fixum gestari per urbem jussit in pilo. Ejus verò conjugem & filias, non ita sanctè, ut Alexander Macedo Darii Regis matrem & conjugem, captivas habuit, sed in convivium adductas irrisit flagitiosè stuprandas suis satellitibus. Eadem in aliis regionibus accidere captivis credibile. Nec quam dicam fortem esse virum, quem talia exempla non movent, qui non summa animi cupiditate desiderat, ut Italiam pugnæ signum proponatur.
units.tr: 8. Therefore, with Mehmed dead, we breathed a little. For domestic dissension also brought about his death. But some time later, the internal discords having been settled, they again made war on neighbouring kingdoms. They snatched Methone from the Venetians after a great struggle. What of Selim now? Do you not see that, with Syria and Egypt subdued, he has most boldly made war on Hungary? If we do not drive him back from there, it will be easy for the Turks afterwards to make raids into Germany whenever they wish. And believe me, the Turks not only fear, but wage war with great deliberation, intent on every opportunity; nor do they try to seize everything at once, but once they have taken some places by war, they gradually attempt the neighbouring places. To this is added the persistence by which we see their empire greatly grown. Once they have set foot somewhere, they are not easily driven out; then, having fortified the places they have seized, only then do they bring their arms further. Therefore, even if they have not yet reached Germany, though they have often already made raids into Carniola, once they have got possession of Hungary they will be intent on every opportunity to crush us unprepared or divided by internal strife. If they ruled over the Bulgarians and Vlachs without labours, without shrinking from dangers, how much more will they seek out Germany and Italy, the very citadels of the Christian name? If they held these (which God forbid), they would not only equal the ancient Romans in the greatness of their empire, but they seem to think they would have wiped out the whole Christian religion. They have such an accession of great forces that the remaining nations would yield without any struggle. You who now bear arms, that the name of Christ may not be abolished, and who defend the true religion and your liberty, will be forced afterwards to fight for an impious wickedness against Christ, to serve a tyrant, and to await the lash of some Scythian. What savagery would there be against your wives and children! Those things cannot be recounted without shame, which they inflict not only on captives but also on their own people. I will nevertheless mention this: when Byzantium was taken, the head of the Emperor Constantine was cut from his neck, and Mehmed ordered it to be carried through the city fixed on a pike. As for his wife and daughters, he did not treat them as chastely as Alexander the Macedonian treated the mother and wife of King Darius when they were captives, but had them brought to a banquet and shamefully mocked, to be ravished by his attendants. It is credible that the same things happen to captives in other regions. Nor can I call a man brave who is not moved by such examples, who does not desire with the greatest eagerness that the signal for battle be given against Italy.

units.la: 9. Itaque cum necesse sit nobis tueri veram religionem, libertatem nostram, conjuges, liberos, leges, ac disciplinā publicā, ad hortor vos ad hujus justissimi ac necessarii belli societatē. Majores nostri quantas res gesserunt, ut in Asia reprimerent Mahometicam barbariem? Illi non dubitabant tantam hostem procul quærere, nunc Turcæ Regnum nobis vicinum invaserunt, nec tam Pannoniæ, quam Germaniæ bellum denunciant. Multos jam annos Hungarorum virtute barbaries illa est à nostris vicibus depulsa: nos vicissim nationi bene meritæ defensionem debemus. Manes etiam fortium virorum, qui in acie propter communem libertatem ceciderunt, flagitant, ut suæ patriæ mutuam referamus, quanquam ipsa non minus periculi nobis, quàm Hungariæ impendet.
units.tr: 9. Therefore, since we must defend the true religion, our liberty, our wives and children, our laws, and our public discipline, I urge you to join this most just and necessary war. What great deeds did our ancestors perform to repel Mahometan barbarism in Asia? They did not hesitate to seek so great an enemy far away. Now the Turks have invaded a kingdom neighboring us, and they declare war not only on Pannonia but on Germany. For many years that barbarism has been driven back from our borders by the valor of the Hungarians, and in turn we owe defense to a nation that has deserved well of us. The shades of brave men who fell in battle for common liberty also demand that we repay what we owe to their fatherland, although that fatherland threatens us with no less danger than it faces from Hungary.

units.la: 10. Reliqua est altera pars deliberationis, quā tis copiis res gerēda sit, quo in loco bellū inferdū, unde cōmeatus subvehendi. Si animi nō abhorret ab hoc bello, hæc deliberatio facilis erit. Nāmus Pōntifex, Rex Hispaniæ, & Veneti, classe instituēt, & civitates in litore Epyri & Peloponesi litas, vadēt. Nostrer exercitus cū Gallicis & Anglicis auxiliis in Pannonias ducēdus erit. Nā ideo properamus ut hoc Regnū Turcico latrocinio liberetur. Inde in Illyricū transferri bellū erit cōmodissim.u. Formulam etiā propono, quantū pecuniæ, quantū equitum ac peditū singulis Principibus Germaniæ morandū esse putē. Commeatus autem ut Danubio convehantur, à me certe providebitur. Quare si ut ipse hoc bellū expectis, deliberationem ita instituetis, ut de formula inter vos convenīat: nam propte h. picipuē hunc cōventus indictus est. Non sumtus, nō labores, nō periculā detrectabimus, si itaucris Deo hoc ob officiū debere, ut hoc bellū summo studio suscipiatis. Christus in extremo judicio rationē à nobis poscet, si, cum Imperii summa dignitas sit penes nos, deserenus cæteras nationes, si non suscipiemus defensionem Christianæ Reipublicæ. Hostium vires non extenuavi. Errant enim, si qui putant, Turcas ignavos aut imbelles esse. Tot victoriæ indicant, eos nec scientiam rei militaris, nec fortitudinem deesse. Polliceor tamen lætum belli exitum, quia Deus favet justis & piis consiliis, ac certum est suam conservaturum ecclesiam. Servat autem non otiosos, sed facientes officium, & serio opem ejus atque auxilium implorantes. Nec multitudinem hostium, nec vires pertimescimus, sed, ut docet nos Psalmus, Illi in curribus, & in equis, nos autem in nomine Dei nostri omnia geremus.
units.tr: 10. There remains the other part of our deliberation: with what forces the war is to be waged, in what place it is to be carried on, and whence supplies are to be brought. If your minds do not shrink from this war, this deliberation will be easy. The Pope, the King of Spain, and the Venetians will equip a fleet and attack the cities on the coasts of Epirus and the Peloponnese. Our army, with French and English auxiliaries, must be led into Pannonia, for we hasten so that this kingdom may be freed from Turkish brigandage. From there the war can most conveniently be transferred into Illyricum. I also propose a schedule of how much money, how many horsemen and foot soldiers each Prince of Germany ought to furnish. As for supplies, I will certainly see to it that they are conveyed by the Danube. Therefore, if you desire this war as I do, conduct your deliberation so that you agree among yourselves on the schedule, for this assembly was summoned chiefly for this purpose. We will not shrink from expense, labors, or dangers, if you believe that you owe this duty to God, that you take up this war with the utmost zeal. Christ at the last judgment will demand an account from us if, since the supreme dignity of the Empire rests with us, we abandon the other nations and fail to undertake the defense of the Christian commonwealth. I have not understated the strength of the enemy. For those are mistaken who think the Turks cowardly or unwarlike; so many victories show that they lack neither skill in military affairs nor courage. Nevertheless I promise a happy outcome to the war, because God favors just and pious counsels, and it is certain that he will preserve his Church. He preserves, however, not those who sit idle, but those who do their duty and earnestly implore his help and aid. We fear neither the multitude of the enemy nor their forces, but, as the Psalm teaches us, "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will do all things in the name of our God."

units.la: S. ROMANI IMPERII PRIN- CIPUM ELECTORUM RESCRIPTUM
units.tr: THE RESCRIPT OF THE ELECTORS, PRINCES OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE

units.la: Datum Cardinali Legato Romæ Pontificis, volentes Leges præscribere Electoribus super electione futuri Imperatoris; in conventu Collegiali Vesaliæ ad Rhenum, Anno MDXIX.
units.tr: Given to the Cardinal Legate of the Roman Pontiff, who wished to prescribe laws to the Electors concerning the election of the future Emperor; at the collegiate assembly at Wesel on the Rhine, in the year 1519.

units.la: LEGATUS, assistentibus sibi Archiepiscopo Regino, &c. nomine Sanctissimi Domini nostri post imprecatam Principibus Electoribus salutem, & oblatam Apostolicam benedictionem, proposuit ut sequitur.
units.tr: The Legate, with Archbishop Regino and others assisting him, in the name of our Most Holy Lord, after wishing the Electoral Princes health and offering the Apostolic blessing, proposed as follows.

units.la: Primò, Principes hortando & animando, ut in statu jam fluctuantis Reipubl. Christianæ de optimo Principe, Rege Romanorum in Imperatorem eligēdo cogitare vellent, qui auctoritate, potentia, rerum gerendarum peritia valeret, & in omnibus optimum Ducem, optimum Senatorem præ se ferat.
units.tr: First, exhorting and encouraging the Princes that, in the present wavering state of the Christian commonwealth, they should consider electing as King of the Romans, to be made Emperor, the best prince, one who is powerful in authority and resources and skilled in conducting affairs, and who shows himself the best leader and the best senator in all things.

units.la: Secundò, ut Regem Neapolitanum, cujus Regni proprietas ad Ecclesiam Romanam spectat, nullo pacto in Romanorum Regem eligant, obstante sibi defectu inhabilitatis & ineligibilitatis ex constitutione Clementis Quarti, id quod plurimis fortissimis argumentis & efficacissimis rationibus, clarissimis exemplis comprobavit, quæ omnia repetere longum esset.
units.tr: Secondly, that they should by no means elect as King of the Romans the King of Naples, whose kingdom belongs by ownership to the Roman Church, since he is disqualified by the defect of ineligibility under the constitution of Clement IV. He proved this with very strong arguments, most effective reasons and very clear examples, all of which it would be long to repeat.

units.la: Tertiò, quia specialiter, immò individualiter sententia sanctissimi Domini nostri Principibus est enodata, petit Legatus, ut similiter, clarè, expressè & individualiter respondsum certum, clarum, nō involucrum aut ambiguum per affirmationem vel denegationem, & per Principes etiam non collegiatos congregatos detur, ut S.D.N. certiorari de eorum voluntate possit.
units.tr: Thirdly, since the judgment of our Most Holy Lord has been set out to the Princes specifically, indeed individually, the Legate asks that a likewise clear, express and individual answer be given, certain and plain, not involved or ambiguous, either by affirmation or denial, and that it be given also by the Princes who are not gathered in college, so that His Holiness may be informed of their will.

units.la: RESPONSVM PRINCIPVM ELECTORVM.
units.tr: THE RESPONSE OF THE ELECTORAL PRINCES

units.la: Reverendissimi & Illustrissimi Principes hic congregati ob causas urgentissimas & hostiles motus repriměndos, qui in territoriis & dominiis post jam vacans Imperium emerserunt, & ut pejora emergant in dies verentes, huc Wesaliam convenerunt: de futuro autem Romanorum Rege eligēdo in nullo sollicit. Quare ad petita Reverendæ Dominationis suæ responsum dare non potuerunt. Sed sibi Reverend. Dominatio sua & omnium proximus sanctissimus Dominus noster Leo Pontifex Maximus persuadeant indubitatissimè, quod ubi ad Romanorum Regis electionē per Reverendissimas & Illustrissimas Dominationes eorum processum fuerit, eos tunc cum in Regem electuros, qui sit gloriæ & honori Sanctæ Sedi Apostolicæ, utilitati & emolumento Reipublicæ Christianæ, incremento sacro Romano Imperio, hostibus Christi nominis formidini, & omni posteritati futurus admirabilis.
units.tr: The most reverend and illustrious Princes gathered here, because of most urgent causes and the need to repress hostile movements which have arisen in territories and dominions while the Empire is now vacant, and fearing that worse things may emerge day by day, have assembled here at Wesel. Concerning the future election of a King of the Romans, however, they are not anxious at all. Therefore they have not been able to give a response to the requests of Your Reverend Lordship. But let Your Reverend Lordship, and our Most Holy Lord Leo, the Supreme Pontiff, be most assuredly persuaded that when the process of electing the King of the Romans has come before their Most Reverend and Illustrious Lordships, they will then choose as King one who will be glorious and honourable to the Holy Apostolic See, useful and profitable to the Christian commonwealth, an increase to the Holy Roman Empire, a terror to the enemies of the name of Christ, and admirable to all posterity.

units.la: Mirantur non minus Principes Electores, sanctissimi Domini nostri institutū, id quod ævo nostro electionum temporibus ab aliquo Romanorum Pontificum auditū est numquam, maximè hoc modo propositum, ut Electoribus legem præscribar, jubeat, vetet. Sperant Beatitudinem suam aliās clementissimam, futuram illam Romanorum Regis electionem boni æquiq; consultuiam.
units.tr: The Electoral Princes marvel no less at the practice of our Most Holy Lord, which in our age has never been heard of at the time of elections from any of the Roman Pontiffs, and especially that it should be proposed in this way, that laws be prescribed to the Electors, that he should command and forbid. They hope that His Beatitude, otherwise most merciful, will take that future election of the King of the Romans in good and equitable part.

units.la: CAROLI V. IMPER. AUG. MANDATUM PROCURATORIUM
units.tr: Mandate of Procuration of Charles V, Emperor Augustus

units.la: Ad Principes Electores super sua electione acceptanda & præstanda.
units.tr: To the Electoral Princes, concerning the acceptance and performance of his election.

units.la: CAROLUS Dei gratia Rex Castellæ, Aragoniæ, Legionis, utriusque Siciliæ, Jherusalem, Navarræ, Granatæ, Toleti, Valenciæ, Gallicæ, Majoricarum, Hispalis, Sardiniæ, Cordubæ, Corsicæ, Murciæ, Giennis, Algarbii, Algeziræ, Gibraltaris, ac Insularum Canariæ, necnō Insularum Indiarum & Terræ Firmæ Maris Oceani; Archidux Austriæ; Dux Burgundiæ, Lotharingiæ, Brabantiæ, Stiriæ, Carinthiæ, Carniolæ, Limburgi, Lucéburgi, Geldriæ, Calabriæ, Athenarum, Neopatriæ; Comes Flandriæ, Habspurgiæ, Tyrolis, Barchenonæ, Artesii, Burgundiæ; Palatinus Hannoniæ, Hollandiæ, Zeelandiæ, Ferretis, Kiburgii, Namurii, Rossilionis, Ceriraniæ, & Zurphaniæ: Landgravius Alsatiæ; Marchio Burgoviæ, Oristani, & Goceani, ac sacri Rom. Imp. Princeps Catholoniæ, Atturiæ, &c. Domin° Frisiæ, Bruc̃, Mohnæ, Salinarū, Mechliniæ, &c. Notū facim° tenore præsentium universis & singulis, ad quos præsentes literæ pervenerint, quod cum nunc post molestissimū obitū C.æf. Majest.
