As the aforesaid matters are set out more fully in the reply mentioned above, the burdens of the German nation, which are too heavy for them, have been arranged briefly, as follows, and handed to the Papal Orator, who had so sincerely and Christianly offered himself in the name of the Most Holy Roman Pontiff; so that the oft-mentioned Orator and Papal Legate may report them to the Holiness that sent him, and may plead on behalf of the German Princes and nobles, and of the orders of the whole Roman Empire, with the same. The grievances mentioned above are these, which now follow chapter by chapter.

units.la: Gravamina Sedis Apostolica, non ferenda Germanis.
units.tr: Grievances of the Apostolic See, not to be borne by the Germans.

units.la: CAP. I. De Dispensationibus are redemptis.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. On Dispensations Bought for Money.

units.la: 1. Inter reliqua onera, vel illud minimè postremo loco est collocandum, quòd constitutionibus humanis multa prohibentur, imperanturque item multa, quæ nullo divino præcepto, vel interdicta sunt, vel imperata. Quod genus sunt: Matrimoniorum tam innumera excogitata obstacula, ex affinitatis, publicæ honestatis cognatione, spirituali, legalique, & consanguinitatis, tam multis gradibus origine trahentia. Ciborum item usus interdictus, quos Deus tamen ad hominis necessitatem creavit, ac cum gratiarum actione promiscuè sumendos Apostolus docuit. Hæc nimirum, atque iis similes complures humanæ constitutiones, eousque ligant homines, donec pecunia sibi harum legum gratiam à statuentibus impetrent: ut ita pecunia faciat divitibus licitum, quod tenuibus gratis sit prohibitum. Illicitisque his legum ac constitutionum humanarum retijaculis, non modo magna nummorum copia à Germanis est expiscata, è Germania & trans Alpes lata: sed & maxima inter æquè Christianos orta iniquitas, plura offendicula, simultates, dum tenues hisce laqueis videntur se illaqueari, non ob aliud, nisi quòd spinas Evangelicas (ita enim Christus divitias non semel appellat) non possideant.
units.tr: 1. Among the other burdens, this must not be placed last: human constitutions forbid many things and likewise command many things that no divine precept forbids or commands. Of this kind are the countless obstacles devised to marriage, arising from affinity, from public propriety, from spiritual and legal kinship, and from blood relationship, which extend through so many degrees. Likewise the use of foods is forbidden, though God created them for human need, and the Apostle taught that they are to be received with thanksgiving by all. These and many similar human constitutions bind men until they obtain relief from these laws from the lawmakers for money. Thus money makes lawful for the rich what is forbidden to the poor without payment. By these unlawful snares of laws and human constitutions, not only has a great quantity of money been drawn from the Germans and carried out of Germany across the Alps, but also the greatest injustice has arisen among fellow Christians, and many stumbling blocks and quarrels, since the poor seem to be ensnared by these traps for no other reason than that they do not possess the Gospel's thorns (for Christ called riches thorns more than once).

units.la: CAP. II. De tempore interdicto.
units.tr: Chapter II. Concerning the forbidden time.

units.la: 2. Pari modo agitur etiam cum celebrandis nuptiarum solennibus, à Dominica Septuagesima, qua cantatur in Ecclesia, Circumdederunt me, &c. sub Quadragesimæ usque inutium, quo tempore ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ primoribus, undique nuptias celebrari interdictum est. Quum tamen interim & ab Ecclesiasticis & à secularibus passim sine discrimine publicè Genialiter vivatur. Sed ita demum interdictum illud procedit, si gratis hoc facere quis intendat. Quòd si nummi spes refulserit, jam quod primum erat prohibitum, impunè ac liberè facere licet. Est enim & hoc grave Germanorum crumenis reiaculum, quo extrahuntur nummi. Nec minus interim gravamen, quòd pauperis divitisque longè diversa, in relaxandis his constitutionibus, sit conditio.
units.tr: 2. In the same way, the celebration of weddings is also dealt with: from Septuagesima Sunday, on which in the Church is sung "The sorrows of death surrounded me" (Circumdederunt me), until the end of Lent, a period in which weddings have been forbidden everywhere by the leaders of the Roman Church. Yet meanwhile, both churchmen and laymen live festive lives openly and without distinction. But that prohibition holds only if someone intends to do this for nothing. If, however, the hope of money shines forth, then what was first forbidden may be done freely and without penalty. For this is also a serious snare for the purses of the Germans, by which money is drawn out. Nor is the burden any less at the same time, that in relaxing these regulations the condition of the poor and of the rich is so very different.

units.la: CAP. III. De oneribus Papalium indulgentiarum.
units.tr: Chapter III. On the burdens of the Papal indulgences.

units.la: 3. Illud importabile jam olim increbuit Romanarum indulgentiarum onus, quando sub persona pietatis, quum aut Basilicas Romanas construere, aut profectionem in Turcas parare polliciti sunt Romani Pontifices, omnem simplicibus, nimiumque credulis Germanis exuxerunt pecuniarum medullam. Et quod longè majoris est faciendum, per has impostu-ras, ac earum conductitios praecones & praedicatores, profligata est Germana Christianorum pietas; dum qui extrudere volebant venales suas Bullas, laudes suis mercibus occinebant, miras & inauditas condonari per emptitias has condonationes, nedum noxas praeteritas, aut futuras viventium; sed & functorum vita existentium in Purgatorio (quod vocant cantores illi indulgentiarum) ignis: modo numeraretur aliquid, modo tiniat dextra. Atque his mercium nundinationibus, simul & spoliata est aere Germania, & Christi pietas extincta; quando quilibet pro precii, quod in has merces expenderat, modo, peccandi impunitatem sibi pollicebatur. Hinc stupra, incestus, adulteria, perjuria, homicidia, furta, rapinae, fœnora, ac tota malorum lerna semel originem sibi traxerunt. Quod enim malorum amplius jam horrebunt mortales, quando ubi peccandi licentiam ac impunitatem, nedum in vita, sed & post obitum, æ-re, licet immodico, comparari posse à nundinatoribus illis indulgentiariis, semel persuasum habent? maximè Germani, quibus per hos veræ pietatis fucos, sub religionis persona, nihil non persuaderi difficile est? ut ingenio plané ad pietatem credulo est Germania.
units.tr: 3. That intolerable burden of Roman indulgences grew up long ago, when the Roman Pontiffs, under the guise of piety, promised either to build the Roman basilicas or to prepare a campaign against the Turks, and stripped the marrow of money from the simple and overly credulous Germans. What is far more to be lamented is that through these impostures, and their hired heralds and preachers, German Christian piety was ruined. Those who wished to push their wares sang the praises of their goods, claiming that these purchased remissions granted wonderful and unheard-of pardons, not only for the past and future sins of the living but also for the fire of those existing in Purgatory (which those singers of indulgences call it). Sometimes the money was counted out, sometimes it jingled in the hand. Through these marketings Germany was both drained of its bronze and Christ's piety was extinguished, since each person, for the price he had spent on these wares, promised himself impunity for sinning. Hence fornication, incest, adultery, perjury, murder, theft, robbery, usury, and the whole Lernaean hydra of evils at once took their origin. For what more of evils will mortals now shudder at, once they have been persuaded that a license and impunity for sinning can be bought from those indulgence-mongers, not only in life but also after death, for money, however excessive? Especially the Germans, to whom nothing is hard to persuade under the name of religion, through these counterfeits of true piety? Germany is indeed so credulous in matters of piety.

units.la: 4. Et licet indulgentiæ hæ non semel in hoc ad Germanos missæ sint, quasi ex venditione pecunia, fideles contra barbaros essent tutandi, ac defendendi: Eventum habent Germani, pecuniam hanc, non in rem fidei, aut alioqui reipublicæ Christianæ, sed in propinquorum luxum, ac sublevandam familiam ipsorum esse versam. quo hæc nata sunt perquam maxima incómoda, quòd & offendicula orta sunt simplicibus; & quod Germani toties sentientes lusam fidem, quum verè jam res postulat, ut contra Turcas instituatur expeditio bellica, nullis rationibus persuaderi se patiuntur, ut credant, quod res ipsa fere notoria est. Ita scilicet instare cervicibus nostris crudeles Turcas: suspicantes semper, prioribus similique agi. Quæ una ratio est, ut tam ægre manus contra Turcas jungant. Quantorum ergo malorum rebus temporalibus, ac Christi fidelium conscientiis, causæ fuerunt Romanæ Indulgentiæ, Apostolica, pro sublimitate captus sui, exigua opera, vel inde, si non ex re ulla alia, conjectura sequi poterit.
units.tr: 4. And although these indulgences were not sent to the Germans only once, on the pretext that the money from their sale would be used to defend the faithful against the barbarians, the Germans have found that this money has been diverted not to the cause of the faith or to the Christian commonwealth, but to the luxury of relatives and the support of their own families. From this the very great inconveniences have arisen: stumbling blocks have been placed before the simple; and because the Germans, perceiving so often that the faith has been mocked, will not be persuaded by any arguments, even when the situation truly demands that a military expedition be undertaken against the Turks, they do not believe what the thing itself makes almost notorious. Namely, that the cruel Turks are bearing down upon our necks; they always suspect that the same things as before are being done. This is the one reason they join hands so reluctantly against the Turks. How great the evils, both temporal and in the consciences of Christ's faithful, that the Roman indulgences have caused, the Apostolic See, for all its lofty understanding, may infer with little effort, if from nothing else, at least from this conjecture.

units.la: 5. Præterea Papalis Sanctitas, cæterique Episcopi, ac Ecclesiæ Romanæ columnæ, quot suæ tantum absolutioni reliquos fecerunt; quorum si unum aut alterum commisceris, numerandum, aut absolutione ibi cadendum est: nempe quòd in hoc reservati sint, ut vel morum aliquid eis accrescat. Quod ex eo conjicere licet, quòd in casibus etiam quantumvis pore honestis, aut necessariis, nunquam tamen, nisi numeretur aliquid, dispensant. At si iuhi numeraverisve, indispensatus perpetuò manere oportet.
units.tr: 5. Moreover, the Papal Holiness and the other bishops, and the pillars of the Roman Church, have reserved to their own absolution as many cases as they have. If you mix in one or another of these, either a sum must be counted out or you must fall short of absolution there. Namely, they are reserved so that some gain may accrue to them from the morals of men. One may conjecture this from the fact that, even in cases however pious or necessary, they never dispense unless something is counted out. But once you have counted it out, you must remain perpetually dispensed.

units.la: 6. Verùm, si quis, unde numeret, habeat, jam nedum præsentes indulgentur harum onum transgressiones; sed & in futurum impune, ut eas ipsas transgredi liceat, indulto per Quo fit, ut ansam inde accipiant ii, cum quibus ira dispensatum est, pejerandi, homicidia, similia flagitia perpetrandi: quando quilibet ex sacerdotum vulgo, absolutionem emptam indulti hi s impartiri poterit. Quæ malorum seges tota ex habendi libidine, aurique sacra fames, nunc Ecclesiasticorum nonnulli miserè excruciantur, originem ducit.
units.tr: 6. But if anyone has the means to pay, then not only are the transgressions of these laws now indulged for those present, but also in future, so that they may transgress them with impunity, by an indulgence through which it comes about that those with whom the dispensation has been granted take occasion to perjure themselves and commit murders and similar crimes. For any one of the common priests will be able to impart to these men an absolution that has been bought. Out of this whole crop of evils, which springs from the lust for having and the accursed hunger for gold, some of the churchmen are now miserably tormented.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: De prædicatoribus indulgentiarum Stationariis.
units.tr: On the preachers of indulgences called Stationarii.

units.la: 7. Est & aliud Indulgentiis vendendis addictum hominum genus, quos Stationarios vulgò vocant. hi rusticorum plerunque abutuntur simplicitate, dum omnes vicos, villas, pagos, angiportus, omniaque peragrant castella & oppidula, prædicantes Sancti cujuspiam, Valentini, Huperti, Cornelii, Anastasiive sanctimoniam, ac quantum ad rem familiarem addat, si quotannis hunc vel illum munusculo aliquo, quod eis Stationariis scilicet in commodum cedat, demulceas: Inscribentesque dehinc simplices, sub Sancti alicujus numen ac tutelam, promittentesque, ut hoc aut alterum morborum genere vacaturus sit, qui eis annuum censum penderit. Quæ omnia in hoc excogitata sunt, ut simplices illi ad vivum usque exugantur. Nam primùm hoc negotium à sancto Antonio coeptum, in innumera morborum genera dehinc svevit diduci: ita ut vix superfuit morbus nunc aliquis, cui Stationarii non & peculiarem Sanctum, tanquam rabernæ vel negotiationi præposuerunt. Procedsitque eò usque ejus mali serpigo, ut pauperum ac simplicium illorum, Quæstuarii ac Stationarii prædicatores, sanguinem vorent & medullam: dumque illi unà cum liberis suis, necessariis spoliantur, in deliciis & luxu plus quàm Sybaritico degunt Stationarii. Quæ res & in primis prælentem sibi Sanctitatis Apostolicæ medicinam postulare videtur, quo interdiceretur Episcopis, cæterisque Ecclesiæ Primatibus, ac eorum Vicariis, ne pro legationis seu functionis hujus admissione quæpiam posthac acciperent precii: néve eas omnino tolerarent amplius, aut quantum per eos fieri paterentur.
units.tr: 7. There is also another class of men given over to selling indulgences, whom they commonly call Stationarii. They mostly take advantage of the simplicity of country folk, going through every village, farm, hamlet, alley and lane, and every fortress and little town, preaching the holiness of some saint, Valentine, Hubert, Cornelius or Anastasius, and how much it will add to a man's household fortunes if he flatters them each year with some small gift that goes to the profit of these Stationarii. Then they enrol the simple folk under the protection and patronage of some saint, promising that whoever pays them an annual sum will be free from this or that kind of disease. All of this has been devised so that those simple folk are drained to the quick. For this business, begun first by Saint Anthony, afterwards spread out into countless kinds of disease, so that hardly any disease remains for which the Stationarii have not appointed a special saint, as if for a shop or a trade. The sore has spread so far that these questing and stationed preachers devour the blood and marrow of the poor and simple, and while those folk are stripped of their necessities along with their children, the Stationarii live in pleasure and luxury more than Sybaritic. This matter seems above all to call for a remedy from the Apostolic See, by which it might be forbidden to bishops and the other primates of the Church, and to their vicars, that they should receive any fee from now on for admitting this legation or function, and that they should altogether stop tolerating it, or at least allow it as little as they can.

units.la: 8. Nec minùs & in hoc à religiosis gravantur prophani, maximè pauperes, quibus res tenuis angusta domi: Nempe quòd mendicitas ordinum Mendicantium nihil in rure, neque in urbe finit non peragratum, dum à terminis, quos pervagantur, Termmarii dicuntur. Quæ quidem pervagationes contra ordinis eorum statuta, neque etiam ad necessitatem, per avaritiam insatiabilem adinvenerunt. Ita enim fit, ut quum in oppidulo, aliquando non admodum ibi, sed perexiguo, duo, tria, aut eo amplius illorum sint conventicula, in quæ omnes eleemosynæ undique disquiri potest, confertur, dum tamen interim morbo aut senio confecti vel incolæ, qui per ætatem ex laboribus & sudoribus suis, una cum uxoribus & liberis honestè vivere, egeant, fame & inedia perecundum necesse habeant. Itaque rogant Sanctitatem Apostolicam Imperii Principes, cæterique Srarus, quatenus Sanctitas sua, paterno animi affectu oppressa & gravamina hæc Indulgentiarum, dispensationum, Stationariorum, Terminariorum quæ e medio tollere, atque ita negotium temperare velit, ne libertas Christiana, servitute humanarum constitutionum penitus extinguatur, illaqueenturque conscientiæ Christi fidelium minutis hominum, quibus nullum est peccatum majus, quàm nummis carere. Non ultrà eum quicquam prohibent, quàm si gratis contravenire quis velit; & dispensant illico quod prohibuerant, numerata scilicet pecunia ampliore. Verùm quòd sincerius cum fidelibus Christi, quam cum suis ovibus agatur, instruanturque potiùs ad pietatem & charitatem mutuam, ex ... Christi. [?]hristi, quàm ad obseruationem cuiusuis traditionis humanæ, formidine pœnæ. Ac si errare eas aliquando labíque contigerit, moneantur, & subleuentur potiùs fraternè; quàm ita seruiliter, ac dure tractentur. Quò omnibus paulo notiùs fiat, pastorem cupere potiùs & quærere salutem ovium, quàm prouata compendia, ac earum lanam.
units.tr: 8. Nor less in this are the laity burdened by the religious, especially the poor, whose household means are slender. For the begging of the Mendicant orders leaves nothing unvisited in the countryside or in the city, and from the districts which they roam they are called Terminarii. These roamings they have invented, contrary to the statutes of their orders and not even out of necessity, through insatiable greed. For it comes about that, when in a little town, sometimes not very large but very small, there are two, three or even more of their convents, into which alms are gathered from everywhere, yet meanwhile the sick, the aged, or the residents who, because of their age, cannot live honourably with their wives and children from their labours and sweat, are obliged to perish by hunger and want. Therefore the Princes of the Empire and the other Estates ask the Apostolic See that its Holiness, moved by fatherly affection, would be pleased to remove these burdens of indulgences, dispensations, Stationarii and Terminarii, and so to manage the matter that Christian liberty is not utterly extinguished by the slavery of human constitutions, and that the consciences of Christ's faithful are not ensnared by petty human regulations, for whom there is no greater sin than lacking money. They forbid nothing further than if someone wishes to do it for nothing; and they at once dispense what they had forbidden, for a larger sum of money. But that Christ's faithful should be dealt with more sincerely than their own sheep, and be instructed rather to piety and mutual charity, ... of Christ, than to the observance of any human tradition through fear of punishment. And if they should ever happen to err or slip, let them be admonished and raised up rather as brothers, not treated so slavishly and harshly. So that it may be made somewhat better known to everyone, that the shepherd desires and seeks the salvation of the sheep rather than their provided gains and their wool.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Quàm iniquè caussæ prophanæ in prima instantia ad Romanum tribunal iudiciarium trahantur.
units.tr: That profane causes are unjustly brought at first instance before the Roman judicial tribunal.

units.la: 9. Quum nedum iuris ratio, sed & rei ipsa series postulet, ut distincti sint iurisdictionum limites, & ut quilibet Ordinarius suis sit finibus contentus, alterumque in exercenda iurisdictione non disturbet: minimè tamen Pontifices Romani pro tempore existentes, æquitatem hanc communem considerarunt, sed neglecta hac, ad petitionem personarum Ecclesiasticarum, laicos non raro in causis ciuilibus, prophanis, puta hæreditatum, aut pignorum, & in prima quidem instantia, coram sede Romana, ac in ius vocari fecerunt. Quæ res nedum ita, ut prædictum est, in ius vocatis, sed & totius Romani Imperii Ordinibus, cedit in iacturam, perniciem, contemptum, ac iurisdictionis dehonestationem, damnumque onemque.
units.tr: 9. Since not only the reason of law but the very nature of the matter requires that the limits of jurisdictions be distinct, and that each ordinary be content with his own boundaries and not disturb another in the exercise of his jurisdiction, the Roman Pontiffs in office have by no means considered this common equity; rather, disregarding it, at the petition of ecclesiastical persons they have not infrequently had laymen summoned to court in civil and profane causes, such as those concerning inheritances or pledges, and in the first instance, before the Roman See. This matter results not only in loss, ruin, contempt and dishonour of jurisdiction, and in damage and burden, for those summoned to court as described, but also for all the Orders of the whole Roman Empire.

units.la: 10. Item cum Romæ quispiam, etiam laicus, interposito iuramento asserit, se non sperare iustitiam apud iudicem competentem in Germania asseque posse; protinus ad tale iuramentum admittitur, & contra partem aduersam decernitur. Sicque processus à iudice Ordinario ex Germania Romano, nec iudice interpellato, nec parte aduersa monita, protrahitur: inde iuramenti prætextu, nec ulla declinatio, nec ulla admittitur probatio, etiamsi plane doceri posset, auctorem illum pejerasse. Quæ res si altius radices ageret, nec principiis resisteretur, omnes tandem causæ ad Romanæ Curiæ tribunal devolverentur, ordinariique universi sua privarentur iurisdictione. Quod non solum contra ordinem iustitiam, sed etiam intolerabile foret. Ea propter sacri Romani Imperii Status Sanctitatem Apostolicam rogitant, ut prædictum onus in Rom. Curia posthac non tolerare velit, sed curare, ut deinde nemo vel Ecclesiasticus, vel Secularis, ob causam prophanam, in prima instantia, Romani in ius vocetur, sed personæ & causæ hæ ordinario iudici, cui immediatè subiacent, relinquantur, ultraque hoc, amplius contra æquitatem non graventur.
units.tr: 10. Likewise, when someone at Rome, even a layman, asserts under oath that he does not hope to obtain justice before a competent judge in Germany, he is at once admitted to such an oath, and a decision is made against the opposing party. Thus the process is drawn away from the ordinary judge in Germany to Rome, neither the judge being summoned nor the opposing party being warned. Then, on the pretext of the oath, neither any declinature nor any proof is admitted, even though it could be plainly shown that that claimant had sworn falsely. If this matter took deeper root, and the beginnings were not resisted, all causes would at last be carried to the tribunal of the Roman Curia, and all ordinaries would be deprived of their jurisdiction. This would be intolerable, and not only contrary to the order of justice. For this reason the States of the Holy Roman Empire beseech the Apostolic Holiness that henceforth it be pleased not to tolerate the aforesaid burden in the Roman Curia, but to take care that hereafter no one, whether ecclesiastic or secular, be summoned to court at Rome in the first instance for a profane cause; rather, that these persons and causes be left to the ordinary judge to whom they are immediately subject, and that they be not burdened beyond this, contrary to equity.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: De conseruatoribus, ac cæteris Papalibus iudicibus.
units.tr: On the conservators, and the other Papal judges.

units.la: 11. Item est & aliud iudicium Papalium, per quos æquè ordinaria attenuatur iurisdictio, genus, quos Conseruatores vulgò vocant: eos Episcopi, cæterique Ecclesiæ Principes, ex Primatibus, vel Abbatibus suæ Diœcesis, à sede Apostolica in hoc impetrare solent, ut coram his, omnes illorum causæ, & lites, quas iam olim instituere cogitant, dirimantur, euocenturque per hos in ius personæ seculares, nobiles & plebei, in causis omnino prophanis; licet actoribus iustitia per ordinarium tribunal nunquam fuerit denegata. Quòd si vocati in ius ire recusauerint, ii contra ius ac phas excommunicatione, licet nulla, feriuntur: cuius rei innumera adduci possint exempla. Ac si, ut cœpit negotium, procedetur, brevi eò rerum veniremus, ut omnes causæ prophanæ, ad Conseruatores hos, cæterosque iudices Ecclesiasticos, laicis nedum suspectos, sed & alioqui incommodos, perttraherentur. Quod ut est intolerabile Germanis Principibus, ita & aperta fronte, cum sacri Romani Imperii pugnat constitutionibus ordinatis, quæ clarè & expressim volunt ac exprimunt, quòd nemo alium ex ordinario ad incompetens tribunal in ius pertrahere debeat. Quapropter Imperii Principes, Proceres, ac Status, Sedi Apostolicæ supplicant, ut gravamina atque onera hæc radicitus, funditusque tollantur & abrogentur.
units.tr: 11. There is also another kind of Papal judges, through whom the ordinary jurisdiction is likewise weakened; they are commonly called Conservators. Bishops and the other princes of the Church commonly obtain these from the Apostolic See, chosen from among the primates or abbots of their own diocese, so that by them all their causes and lawsuits, which they already intend to bring, may be settled, and that by these men secular persons, nobles and commoners alike, are summoned to court in purely secular matters; although justice was never denied to plaintiffs through the ordinary tribunal. If those summoned refuse to appear, they are struck with excommunication, contrary to law and right, though such excommunication is null; of this thing countless examples can be cited. And if matters proceed as they have begun, we would soon reach the point where all secular causes would be drawn before these Conservators and the other ecclesiastical judges, who are not only suspect to laymen but otherwise inconvenient. As this is intolerable to the German Princes, so it also openly conflicts with the established constitutions of the Holy Roman Empire, which clearly and expressly state and provide that no one ought to be summoned to court from the ordinary tribunal before an incompetent tribunal. Therefore the Princes, Nobles and Estates of the Empire beg the Apostolic See that these grievances and burdens be removed and abrogated root and branch.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: De Papalibus delegatis, ac commissariis.
units.tr: Concerning the Papal delegates and commissaries.

units.la: 12. Item Sanctitas Pontificia ad Ecclesiasticarum personarum petitionem, iudices delegatos & commissarios, tanquam Ecclesiasticos iudices, per Germaniam concedere solet, ut impetrantes delinquentes laicos, cuiuscunque etiam dignitatis, vel præeminentiæ, coram ita delegatis, in causis prophanis, iudicio convenire possint. Quod ut de facto sæpenumero præsumunt, ita excommunicationis poena mandatam sibi inter partes iurisdictionem defendere conantur. Quæ omnia & in perniciem populorum secularium, & in iurisdictionis Germanicæ ac ordinariæ iacturam vergunt, & attenuationem.
units.tr: 12. Likewise, at the petition of ecclesiastical persons, the Pontifical Holiness customarily grants throughout Germany delegated judges and commissaries, as if they were ecclesiastical judges, so that those who obtain them may summon lay offenders, of whatever dignity or rank, before such delegates in secular causes. Since they often presume to do this in fact, they also try to defend, by the penalty of excommunication, the jurisdiction entrusted to them between the parties. All these things tend to the ruin of the secular peoples and to the loss and diminution of the German and ordinary jurisdiction.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Quo pacto Ecclesiæ prælati per sedem Apostolicam, ex Episcoporum ordina- ria iurisdictione ac cæterorum suorum defensorum tu- tela eximantur.
units.tr: How the prelates of the Church are exempted by the Apostolic See from the ordinary jurisdiction of the bishops and from the protection of their other defenders.

units.la: 13. Insuper & hoc moliuntur summi Pontifices, monasteria aliquot eximendo, ut ab Episcoporum, porum, eorum scilicet ordinariorum, ac defensorum, protectorumque aliorum jurisdictioni subjecti empti, reddantur immunes, immediateque subjaceant sedi Apostolicæ: quæ res non parum prodest ipsorum ordinariis ac defensoribus, sed & toti Romano Imperio cedit in pacem, tranquillitatem: collatio pecuniaria, pro Imperii necessitate, virtutum Imperii Statibus indicitur. Ita enim ab oneribus publicis exempti, immunitate sua gaudeant. Deinceps etiam auxiliares ad episcopis ac defensoribus suis (quod antehac facere nec illum habebant) non portigant: per quam Rom. Imperii attenuantur nervi, ac decrescunt plus justo vires. Quapropter & hic Imperii Status rogant, præfata onera exemptionum abroganda, tollenda, emendandaque, Episcoporum & defensorum ordinariæ jurisdictioni relinquenda. Ut vel inde Imperium per sedem Apostolicam ita enervatum, vires pristinas eo celerius recuperare queat.
units.tr: 13. Moreover, the supreme Pontiffs also bring about this: by exempting some monasteries, so that they, having been bought and placed under the jurisdiction of the bishops (that is, of their ordinaries) and of their defenders and other protectors, are made immune and lie directly under the Apostolic See. This matter does no small good to the ordinaries and defenders themselves, but also redounds to the whole Roman Empire for peace and tranquillity: a money contribution is imposed on the states of the Empire for the needs of the Empire. For thus, released from public burdens, they enjoy their immunity. Further, they no longer furnish auxiliaries to the bishops and their defenders (which they formerly had been accustomed to do and were bound to do); by this the sinews of the Roman Empire are weakened, and its strength decreases more than is just. Wherefore the states of the Empire also ask that the aforesaid burdens of the exemptions be abrogated, removed and amended, and left to the ordinary jurisdiction of the bishops and defenders, so that the Empire, weakened in this way by the Apostolic See, may recover its former strength the more quickly.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: De attenuatione juris, quod vocant, patronatus.
units.tr: On the diminution of the so-called right of patronage.

units.la: 14. Item, quum per mortes possessorum pro tempore beneficia vacare incipiunt, quorum patronatus ad laicos spectat, seu Ecclesiasticos, tum conantur & Papalis Sanctitas, & ejus legati, juri huic derogare, hoc modo: ut conferant beneficia ita vacantia, Curtisanis, aut cuique libuerit, ita, ut patronis ipsis jus suum præsentandi per hoc adimatur, auferaturque. Hoc prætexitur à sede Apostolica, quasi præventioni hac in re sit locus, ut qui prior beneficium contulerit, quod hæc teneat collatio; licet patroni tempus quoddam habeant, intra cujus beneficia sua liberè, & à nemine præventi, conferre possint. Eam ob rem patronis laicis & Ecclesiasticis ex fictitia hac præventione multa oritur jactura. Quapropter sacri Rom. Imperii Status Apostolicam rogitant, ut talia gravamina atque onera abolcantur, & posthac beneficia cuique patrono relinquantur, nec permittendum Curtisanis, ut dehinc vel per judicium vel suopte ingenio, ad talia beneficia se ingerant: sed statuto irrevocabili sanciendum, quam contra patronos beneficiorum ordinarios, prætextu imaginarii istius juris, præveniri mittitur, fuerit attentatum, quod omne id nullius sit momenti, viribus careat, sitque ipso jure nullum, casum, & invalidum.
units.tr: 14. Likewise, when benefices whose patronage belongs to laymen or to churchmen begin to fall vacant from time to time through the deaths of their holders, the Papal Holiness and his legates attempt to undermine this right in the following way: they confer the benefices thus vacated on their Curtisans, or on whomever they please, so that the patrons themselves are deprived of and stripped of their right to present. The See Apostolic pretends that in this matter there is room for prevention, namely that whoever first confers a benefice holds that conferral valid, although the patrons have a certain period of time within which they may freely confer their own benefices, provided that no one has forestalled them. For this reason a great loss comes to lay and ecclesiastical patrons from this fictitious prevention. Therefore the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire humbly petition the Apostolic See that such grievances and burdens be abolished, that hereafter the benefices be left to each patron, and that the Curtisans not be permitted from now on to thrust themselves into such benefices, either by judicial process or by their own cleverness. Rather, it should be enacted by an irrevocable statute that whatever shall have been attempted against the ordinary patrons of benefices, under the pretext of that imaginary right of prevention, is of no moment, lacks force, and is by law null, void and invalid.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De Ecclesiasticis, qui Romæ, vel inter eundum Romam, mortem opperiuntur.
units.tr: Concerning ecclesiastics who wait for death at Rome, or on the way to Rome.

units.la: 15. Item, & rum Curtisanis, cæterisque, ut prædictum est, inhabilibus personis, per sedem Apostolicam vacantia, collata sunt, officia ac beneficia, cum familiares sunt, suæ, aut qui Curiæ inventi, vel in anno (quod vocant) Jubilæo, inter eundum Romam, aut etiam Romæ agentes, mortui fuerint; tamquam si beneficia hæc sedi Apostolicæ essent commissa, recte atque feudorum committitur. Necconsideratur à Pontificia sanctitate, talia beneficia vel officia de patronatus sint nec ne: per quod Ecclesiastici & laici patroni feudatarii denuo etiam jure suo patronatus ordinario, privati sunt & spoliati.
units.tr: 15. Likewise, offices and benefices which fall vacant through the Apostolic See are also conferred on Curtisans and other persons unfit, as has been said, when they are their household servants, or those found at the Curia, or those who, in the year called the Jubilee, die on the way to Rome or even while staying at Rome; as if these benefices had been committed to the Apostolic See, and were rightly and in the manner of feudal property assigned to it. Nor does the Pontifical holiness consider whether such benefices or offices are of patronage or not; by which means ecclesiastical and lay patrons, as feudatories, are again deprived and despoiled of their ordinary right of patronage.

units.la: 16. Quin etiam aliquando, quum ii qui boni, aut multis prædicti sunt beneficii, Romam veniunt, à Curialibus Cardinalium, tanquam officii gratia ad mensam invitantur Dominorum, inde clam adhibentur testes & notarii, quorum interventu conficiuntur instrumenta, quibus suo tempore probari possit, tales fuisse Curiales Cardinalium, ac ideo beneficia eorum tuum affecta, quam dolo ac fraudis res hæc sit plena, unusquisque bonus facile perpendere possit.
units.tr: 16. Indeed, sometimes when those who are good men, or endowed with many benefices, come to Rome, they are invited to the table of the Lords by the courtiers of the Cardinals, as a mark of favour; then witnesses and notaries are secretly brought in, through whose intervention instruments are drawn up, by which it can be proved at the proper time that such men were Curialists of the Cardinals, and that therefore their benefices are claimed for them; how full this matter is of guile and fraud, any good man can easily perceive.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Quo pacto sub prætextu familiaritatis Papalis curiæ, multorum Beneficiorum per Curti- sanos impugnetur collatio, etiamsi possessores illorum longe antehac talibus fuerint beneficiis investiti.
units.tr: How, under the pretext of familiarity with the Papal court, the conferring of many benefices is assailed by the Curtisans, even where the holders of them have long before been invested with such benefices.

units.la: 17. Neque minus & illud fuerum hucusque fuit, ut ultra prædicta omnia quorundam Beneficiorum, sub nomine officialium vel familiarium Papæ & curiæ Papalis, per idiotas inhabiles personas sit impugnata collatio, ac per illos conatum, tentatumque, si quo modo fieri, ut beneficia hæc in Commendas seu Provisiones (ita enim ipsi vocant) vertere, ac eorum obnoxia reddere queant: hinc prævidentes, regressus, reservationes, pensiones, & plura alia compatibilia, sibi in his competere. Quibus technis ac dolis malis, beneficia illa pene evanuerunt, attenuanturque; cum perpetuo Romanæ curiæ pensionibus annuis serviunt, quasi Germanorum utcunque habilium, nemo unquam ad hæc aspirare possit.
units.tr: 17. Nor has the following been any less common up to now: beyond all the aforesaid, the conferring of certain benefices is assailed, under the name of officials or familiars of the Pope and the Papal court, by unqualified and incompetent persons. They attempt and try, if somehow it can be done, to turn these benefices into commendams or provisions (for so they call them) and to make them liable to themselves; foreseeing this, they claim for themselves in these matters reversions, reservations, pensions, and many other compatible rights. By these wicked tricks and frauds those benefices have almost vanished and are wasted away, while they serve in perpetuity the annual pensions of the Roman court; no one of the Germans, however capable, can ever aspire to them.

units.la: 18. Item, obviam veniunt & tum Germanis non ferenda à Curtisanis onera. Ita enim Germaniam subtili ingenio beneficia venantur, ut concentur viris Presbyteris æque & in vitæ spectabilibus, qui beneficia sua, absque omni controversia, justo titulo, & bona fide nullius. multos jam annos quietè possederant, in longæva possessione negotium facere, possessionem interturbare, ad Romanam curiam, personaliter ut compareant, in jus vocare, ac mille aliis artibus ita eos adigere, ut transactiones quantumvis iniquas, inire necessum habeant, modò supremos hos annos quietè agere velint. Coguntur enim hoc, quo dictum est modo, à Curtisanis ad pensiones annuas, reservata, & id genus alias præstationes. Atque hoc agunt Curtisani nebulones, non propria, ut fertunt, auctoritate; sed Romanorum suorum statutorum, ac regularum, quas vocant, Cancellariæ. Quæ constitutiones omnes quotidie pro libidine Curtisanorum figuntur, ac refiguntur, cùm derogatur prioribus non admodum, ut videbatur, æquis, & feruntur iniquiores. Qua re nedum senio confectis beneficiorum possessoribus, harum decipularum atque fraudum rudibus; sed & beneficiorum collatoribus imponant mille instructi dolis Curtisani. Nam etsi possidens Beneficiorum Presbyter, cum Curtisano litigatore fictitio, non transigat: tamen ita sibi litem facit præstigiator ille Curtisanus, ut si pendente effecta hac controversia, moriatur, beneficii, ut prædictum est, litigiosi possessor, quòd deinde continuò litem faciens, neglecto Collatoris ordinario jure, in possessionem ejus beneficii mittatur. Ea propter denuò atque iterum sacri Rom. Imperii Status justas sanctitati Apostolicæ fundunt preces, velit enumerata omnia Curtisanorum importabilia onera emendare, ac penitus abrogare: Neve illis posthac permittere, ut beneficia Germanorum libera, per machinationes prætatas, oppugnare impune audeant.
units.tr: 18. Likewise, the Curtisans bring upon the Germans burdens that cannot be borne. They hunt benefices in Germany with such cunning that they attack men, priests and persons of respectable life alike, who for many years had quietly possessed their benefices without any controversy, by a just title and in good faith, and who had no claim to them. They stir up trouble over a long possession, disturb the possession, summon them to the Roman court to appear in person before the law, and by a thousand other arts force them so that they must enter into transactions however unjust, provided only they wish to spend their last years in peace. For they are compelled, in the manner already described, by the Curtisans, to pay annual pensions, reserved rights, and other payments of that kind. And the Curtisan rogues do this not by their own authority, as they claim, but by the statutes and rules of their Roman chancery, as they call them. All these constitutions are daily made and remade at the whim of the Curtisans: earlier ones, which seemed not altogether fair, are repealed and still more unfair ones are issued. Thus the Curtisans, equipped with a thousand tricks, bring harm not only to holders of benefices worn out with age, who are unskilled in these snares and frauds, but also to the collators of benefices. For even if a priest holding a benefit does not settle with a fictitious Curtisan litigant, that trickster Curtisan so pursues the suit against him that, if he dies while the controversy is pending, the possessor of the benefice, as has been said, being litigious, is then put into possession of it by the continued pursuit of the suit, the ordinary right of the collator being neglected. For this reason the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire once again pour out their just prayers to the Apostolic Holiness, that it would be pleased to amend and wholly abrogate all the enumerated intolerable burdens of the Curtisans, and not to permit them henceforth to attack with impunity the free benefices of the Germans by the aforesaid machinations.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Quomodo provisiones Ecclesiasticarum dignitatum Romam pertrahantur.
units.tr: How the provisions of ecclesiastical dignities are drawn to Rome.

units.la: 19. Item, quæcunque dignitates, seu beneficia pinguia, utputa, Præposituræ, Decanatus, Canonicatus, ac cætera officia, Canonicatus, Ecclesiæ Curatæ, & beneficia simplicia, quæ sub mensè ordinario, extra Romana mœnia vacare incipiunt, quorum antehac ad jus ordinarium patronatus Ecclesiasticorum & laicorum spectabat collatio, & electio, tum excogitatur à Romana sede, juris patronatus ab ordinariis collatoribus abalienatio: maximè, si possessores pristini beneficiorum aut officiorum dignitatumve talium, familiares vel officiales Papæ aut Cardinalium fuerunt. Ideò rogant Rom. Imper. Status, prædictum etiam onus è medio tollendum, ac patronos collatores ordinarios apud collationem, electionem, præsentationem, & nominationem talium dignitatum ac beneficiorum (jura scilicet ordinaria) defendendos, ac defensos manutenendos. Nec curandum, utrum familiares, vel ossiciales Romanæ curiæ fuerint, qui beneficia hæc possederint, regressum accessumve, aut aliud quoddam jus imaginarium ad ea habuerint: ita quòd tale jus prætentum ordinario patrono ac Collatori, nunc & posthac nullum faciat præjudicium, nullámque generet jacturam, sed per omnia jura ordinaria sinanturillæsa.
units.tr: 19. Likewise, whatever dignities or rich benefices, for example provostships, deaneries, canonries and other offices, canonries, parish churches, and simple benefices, which begin to fall vacant outside the walls of Rome under the ordinary, and whose collation and election formerly belonged to the ordinary right of ecclesiastical and lay patrons, are then devised by the Roman see as an alienation of the right of patronage from the ordinary collators; especially if the former possessors of such benefices, offices or dignities were familiars or officials of the Pope or of the Cardinals. Therefore the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire ask that the aforesaid burden also be removed, and that the patrons and ordinary collators be defended and maintained in their defence in the collation, election, presentation and nomination to such dignities and benefices (that is, in their ordinary rights). Nor is it to be considered whether those who held these benefices were familiars or officials of the Roman curia, or whether they had any right of reversion or succession, or any other imaginary right to them; so that such alleged right shall now and hereafter cause no prejudice to the ordinary patron and collator, produce no loss, but that all ordinary rights be left wholly unharmed.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: De regulis Cancellariæ Papalis, novis technis & reservatis super casibus futuris.
units.tr: On the rules of the Papal Chancery, new devices, and reservations for future cases.

units.la: 20. Adhæc Cancellariæ Romanæ regulæ, quas ad sua compendia subinde excogitare solent Curtisani, ac toties ferre ac revocare; nec non & aliæ subinde novæ artes excogitari cœperunt, quibus beneficia Ecclesiastica ex Germania Romam eò facilius pertraherentur, ad gravarenturque: ita, uti si Germanorum quispiam beneficiorum aliquod ambiat, id quod non aliunde, quàm ex Curtisanorum manu, magna numerata pecunia, aut pensione annua reservata, assequi possit. Neque in hoc Curtisanorum inexplebilis auri litis contenta quiescit, quin novas quotidie artes excogitet, qualis est & illa: cùm super beneficio aliquo vacaturo, duo aut tria millia aureorum ad futuros casus reservantur collatoribus ordinariis, tam Ecclesiasticis quàm secularibus, eorumque juri ordinario, ac ipsis denique Ecclesiasticis beneficiis in prægrande exitium, perniciem, attenuationem & detrimentum. Nam quum casus aliquis futurarum reservationum exstitit, adsequiturque, is beneficium, cui priùs tot reservata etiam super hoc millia, tum ad supremam opem (technas profectò inauditas) confingunt, permutationem, licet reservationem, surrogationem, reservantes sibi ingressum, regressum, accessum, atque alias id genus decipulas, quibus jus ordinariorum collatorum ita exhauritur & attenuatur, ut aut nunquam, aut vix tandem post multorum annorum curricula, patroni ac collatores ordinarii ad jus suum patronatus pervenire possint.
units.tr: 20. Moreover, the rules of the Roman Chancery, which the courtiers are wont from time to time to devise for their own gain, and to bring forth and revoke so often, have been joined by other new arts, devised from time to time, by which ecclesiastical benefices are drawn from Germany to Rome all the more easily and burdened. The result is that if any German seeks some benefice, he can obtain it in no other way than by the hand of the courtiers, with a large sum of money paid down or with an annual pension reserved. Nor does the courtiers' insatiable greed for gold rest content with this; every day they devise new arts, such as this one: when some benefice is about to fall vacant, two or three thousand gold coins are reserved for future cases, to the ordinary collators, both ecclesiastical and secular, and to their ordinary right, and finally to the ecclesiastical benefices themselves, to their great ruin, destruction, weakening and loss. For when some case of future reservations arises and takes effect, the benefice, on which so many thousands have already been reserved for this purpose, they then contrive, as a last resort (surely unheard-of tricks), exchange, even though it is a reservation, substitution, the reserving to themselves of entry, return, access, and other snares of this kind, by which the right of the ordinary collators is so drained and weakened that the patrons and ordinary collators can scarcely ever, or only after the course of many years, recover their right of patronage.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: De Ecclesiasticis beneficiis, Curatis, & non Curatis, in genere.
units.tr: On ecclesiastical benefices, cure of souls and non-cure, in general.

units.la: 21. Nec minùs & illud in Romana curia hucusque observatum est, ut gratiæ & reservationes pectorales, mentales, generales & speciales regressus, accessus, incorporationes, uniones, & concordata, quod suis vocant excogitatis nominibus, ob pecuniæ & privati lucri amorem, super beneficiis præelaturis, præsertim per Germaniam, Curtisanis à sede Romana concederentur. Neque hoc contentus fuit habendi scelleratus amor, quin & ea ipsa beneficia ac Prælaturæ prædictæ, societatibus mercatorum potentum æ re, cum onere census mediocris, sed ita, ut dehinc latiùs venderentur, conteduntur. Qua subtili practica atque techna factum est, quòd plurima, aut certè pinguium beneficiorum, ciorum, magna, si non maxima portio ex Germanorum manu Romam est translata; quae beneficia hinc idiotis inidoneis, ac inhonestis etiam personis, non raro sunt collata: & quidem nec Germanis, sed barbaris, qui Germanam linguam neque loquantur, nec intelligant; ut inauditum dictu hoc inde sit sequitur, quod ovibus Christi praefecti sunt pastores, quorum etsi oves vocem forte audierint, non intelligant. Verum gravius etiam inde oritur Germanis onus, quod quum beneficia haec & Parochiales Ecclesias ipsi propria persona neque possidere, neque gubernare possunt (quod tamen pastoris officium in primis sibi postulabat) nimirum ut subditis parochialibus, & integritate ac innocentia morum, egregium de se praeberent exemplum, ut oves suas, tanquam oves Christi, doctrina solida, syncera, ac ex puris Evangelii fontibus hausta, quantum ad salutem animarum ovium pertineret, ipsi pastores met pascerent. Eorum vero neutrum per pastores illos subditicios curatur. Primum enim ipsi, qui beneficia haec Ecclesiastica a mercatoribus, quo praedictum est, assequuntur modo, quia propria persona possidendum ea sunt minus idonei: Ideo haec eadem aliis aeque, aut longe etiam quam sint, ad onus hoc inhabilioribus, pro annuo censu locant; non secus, atque census ac reddidus annui ex agris locantur & emuntur, ut is demum habeatur emptor idoneus, qui pluris mercem licitaverit. Ita plane pretii quantitate elocantur nunc per Curtisanos Ecclesiastica beneficia. Dehinc quum fere fiat, ut majus pretium annuum offerat, qui ad Ecclesiae munus quam minimum sit idoneus; evenit, ut conducti illi pastores (an praedones recte quis eos dixerit, dubium est) simplici Christi plebeculae po Evangelii limpidissimo fonte, turbidas, protritas, ac ruderibus oppletas, propinent lacunas, dum legendas (quas vocant) Sanctorum, nec ab Ecclesia receptas, & gentilibus fabulis, quam Christianae & Evangelicae doctrinae similioribus, ad populum Christi publice in concione docent. Quid enim aliud docerent indocte docti, ac idiotae illi, qui lautam magis, quam salutem ovium, ut curarent, munus hoc Ecclesiasticum pecunia etiam non modica conduxerunt; ac mercenarii sunt, non (quod Evangelium abominatur) pastores. Ita enim fit, ut Christi simplex plebecula, per suppositios hos pastores, a germana Christi fide, ac in Deum fiducia, in quibus sola requiescit animae salus, ad hominum superstitiosa somnia accommenta, per quae res familiaris mercenariorum conductitiorum, quam Christi gloria augeatur potius, ducatur, trahaturque, ac multiplicibus etiam exactionibus interim gravetur plebs Christi: quando hoc solum curant conductores, ut ultra pensionem locatori pendendam, res ipsa eorum quoque reddatur lautior; expilaturque interea suis nummis ab exteris nationibus, unde nulla nec mutua benevolentia, aut gratiarum actio speranda ei est, Germania: quanquam beneficia haec non ad exteros, sed suos, hoc est Germanos, ut pertinerent, primum fundaverit. Quapropter sacri Romani Imperii Status obnixe quoque rogant, ut praefata onera ac gravamina, per quae tam immenso pecuniarum cumulo spoliatur Germania, quae hinc per Curtisanos male prodigitur, radicitus ac penitus tollantur & auferantur, ita ut beneficia per Germaniam nemini, quam natis Germanis, qui personaliter ea possideant (id quod & aequitas & honestas ipsa sibi postulant) posthac conferantur, ac concedantur.
units.tr: 21. Nor has this been less customary in the Roman court up to now: that graces and reservations, papal and mental, general and special, along with rights of retirement and succession, incorporations, unions and concordats (which they call by their own invented names), were granted from the Apostolic See to courtiers, chiefly for Germany, for the sake of money and private gain, concerning benefices and the aforementioned prelacies. Nor was this wicked love of having content with that alone; they also bundled those very benefices and the said prelacies together and sold them, at a moderate annual rent, to companies of wealthy merchants, but in such a way that they could afterwards be sold more widely. By this subtle practice and trickery it came about that very many, or at least a large, if not the greatest, share of the rich benefits and revenues was transferred from German hands to Rome. From there these benefices have often been conferred on unskilled and dishonourable persons, and indeed not on Germans but on barbarians who neither speak nor understand the German language. So it follows that, shocking to say, shepherds have been set over Christ's sheep, whose sheep, if they happen to hear the voice, do not understand it. But a heavier burden also arises from this for the Germans: since these benefices and parish churches can be neither held nor governed by the holders in person (though this is above all the duty of a pastor), namely that they should set before their parishioners an outstanding example of integrity and innocence of life, and feed their own flock, as Christ's sheep, with sound and pure teaching drawn from the pure fountains of the Gospel, so far as the salvation of the souls of the sheep is concerned. Yet neither of these is done by those substitute pastors. For first, those who obtain these ecclesiastical benefices from the merchants in the manner described are for that very reason less fit to hold them in person; therefore they let them out for an annual rent to others who are equally, or even far more, unfit for this duty, just as the rents and annual income of fields are let out and bought, so that the buyer is finally regarded as suitable if he has bid the highest price for the commodity. In this plain way ecclesiastical benefices are now let out by the courtiers at a price. Then, since it nearly always happens that the one who offers the larger annual sum is the one least fit for the office of the Church, it comes about that these hired pastors (whether one may rightly call them pastors or plunderers is doubtful) pour turbid, trampled and rubbish-filled puddles upon the simple little people of Christ from the most limpid spring of the Gospel. They teach publicly in sermons to Christ's people the so-called legends of the saints, which the Church has not received, and fables more like pagan tales than Christian and evangelical doctrine. For what else would those unlearned learned men and simple folk teach, who have hired this ecclesiastical office for no small sum of money, so as to care for their own luxury rather than the salvation of the sheep? They are hirelings, not (which the Gospel abominates) pastors. Thus it happens that Christ's simple little people, through these substitute pastors, are drawn away from the true faith of Christ and from trust in God, in which alone the salvation of the soul rests, to the superstitious dreams of men; and the household affairs of these hired hirelings are enlarged, rather than the glory of Christ advanced, while meanwhile Christ's people are burdened with manifold exactions. The lessees care only that, beyond the rent to be paid to the lessor, their own estate also be made more lavish; and meanwhile Germany is drained of its money by foreign nations, from whom Germany can hope for no mutual goodwill or thanks, although the founders first intended these benefices to pertain not to foreigners but to their own people, that is, to Germans. Therefore the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire earnestly ask that the aforesaid burdens and grievances, by which Germany is stripped of so immense a heap of money, which is thus wastefully squandered through the courtiers, be torn out and utterly removed by the roots; so that henceforth benefices throughout Germany be conferred and granted to no one except native Germans, who hold them in person (which both equity and honesty themselves demand).

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Quibus nexibus Archiepiscopi ac Episcopi a suis Capitulis ob collationem beneficiorum sint astricti.
units.tr: Concerning the bonds by which archbishops and bishops are bound to their chapters in conferring benefices.

units.la: 11. Nec tantum beneficia ac parochiales Ecclesiae Romae, ob pecuniae favoris, aut familiaris consuetudinis amorem, indoctis, turpibus, ridiculis, ac offendiculorum plenis conferuntur personis: Sed & simile quiddam ab Archiepiscopis & Episcopis committitur, qui per eorum Capitulares congregationes ita obligantur, ut omnia praepinguia beneficia, Curata ac non Curata (quae proculdubio a fundatoribus primum, ut ad doctos ac integros pertinerent viros, sunt fundata) Capitularibus Canonicis, utcunque ad hoc inidoneis, conferre necessum habeant: qui dehinc talia beneficia simplicia ac Curata, indoctis, ac ludicris personis, modo quam maximum pendeant censum annuum, elocant, aeque atque supra de mercatorum societatibus dictum est: ita quod possessores illi conducticii, majorem partem ex illicitis exactionibus vivere, atque ob id subditos eo amplius onerare coguntur. Similiter & cum ceteris Cachedralibus Collegiatisque Ecclesiis, ac earum Capitulis agitur. Item & per Praepositos, reliquosque in dignitate constitutos agitur idem, interim dum sua conferunt beneficia Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: 11. Nor do benefices and parish churches at Rome alone get conferred on unlearned, base, ridiculous persons full of scandals, out of love of money or of familiar acquaintance. Something similar is also done by archbishops and bishops, who are so bound through their chapter assemblies that they must confer all the richly endowed benefices, cure of souls and non-cure alike (which were without doubt first founded by the founders so that they would go to learned and upright men), on the canons of the chapter, however unfit they may be for it. These then let out such simple and cure-of-souls benefices to unlearned and frivolous persons, provided they pay the largest possible yearly rent, just as was said above about the trading companies; so that those tenant possessors are compelled to live mostly on illicit exactions and therefore burden their subjects all the more. The same is done with the other cathedral and collegiate churches and their chapters. Likewise the provosts and the others placed in dignity do the same, while they confer their ecclesiastical benefices.

units.la: 23. Praeterea, qui pinguiora, ita ut praedictum est, habent beneficia, ac Ecclesias Parochiales, utcunque annuas pensiones amplissimas, ex locationis titulo, a conductoribus percipiant, quibus reddititibus a laicis fundatoribus beneficia haec ampliter sunt dotata, tamen committunt locatores, ut domus beneficiarie, praeneglecta aedificiorum cura, penitus collabantur. Nihil enim aliud curant beneficiorum personati isti possessores, aut locatores, quam ut pecuniae aequo majorem summam quotannis a conductoribus recipiant, ac eandem hinc in varios, sed in inhonestos, illicitos, ac offendiculorum, peccatorumque plenos usus convertant: de salute & cura animarum, vel subditorum, vel etiam eorum, quorum ex marsupio vivunt, hoc est fundatorum, prorsus apud hos nulla mentio, respectus (velut Megarensium olim) plane nullus. Ea propter sacri Rom. Imperii Status, ac Principes & Proceres laici, hic quoque, supplicant, Sanctitas Pontificia velit eam offendiculorum sylvam, turbatum rerum otdinem, ac onera hæc justo graviora, tollere, emendareque; ac Archiepiscopos, Episcoposq;, ab obligatione, qua ex promissionis prædictæ nexu tenentur, liberare, solutosque reddere, ac edicto cavere, ne posthac Archiepiscopi & Episcopi, talibus adstringantur vinculis; sed ut deinc nulli beneficium Ecclesiasticum, curam habens animarum, conferatur, qui non sit doctrina, ætareque & moribus ad hoc idoneus, qui & honestam, ac Presbytero dignam vivat vitam, & qui ipse propria illud possideat persona: nec plura quidem, sed unum tantùm beneficium Curatum, seu Parochialem Ecclesiam, Christiane, hoc est fine offendiculis ullis, sed multo, cùm doctrinæ, tum vitæ integritatis fructu administret.
units.tr: 23. Moreover, those who hold richer benefices, and parish churches, in the way described above, receive very large annual pensions from their lessees by way of lease, although the benefices were amply endowed by lay founders with these revenues. Yet the lessors allow the benefice houses, with the care of the buildings neglected, to collapse entirely. For these personal holders or lessors of the benefices care for nothing else than that they receive from the lessees a larger sum of money every year, and then turn the same to various uses, but dishonourable, illicit ones, full of scandals and sins; of the salvation and care of souls, whether of the subjects or even of those from whose purse they live, that is, the founders, there is absolutely no mention or regard among them (as once among the Megarians), none at all. Therefore the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire, and the princes and lay nobles, here too beseech that the Papal Holiness be willing to remove and amend this forest of scandals, this disordered state of affairs, and these burdens heavier than is just; and to free the archbishops and bishops from the obligation by which they are held through the bond of the aforesaid promise, to release and make them free, and to provide by edict that henceforth archbishops and bishops are not bound by such chains; but that thereafter no ecclesiastical benefice carrying cure of souls be conferred on anyone who is not fit for it by learning, age and character, who also lives an honest life worthy of a presbyter, and who holds it in his own person; and not several, but only one cure-of-souls benefice or parish church, which he may administer as a Christian, that is, without any scandals, but with the fruit both of teaching and of integrity of life, and in great abundance.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: De Prælaturarum commendis, ut vocant, & Incorporationibus.
units.tr: On the commendams of prelacies, as they are called, and incorporations.

units.la: 24. Item, & illud hucusque notorie observatum fuit, ut Abbatiæ multæ, Cænobia item plura, ac reliquæ id genus domus, seu Ecclesiasticarum personarum congregationes, fundationes scilicet Imperatoriæ ac Principales, Cardinalibus, Episcopis, ac cæteris Prælatis, in tutelam commendarentur incorporatenturque. Quare factum est, ut per Cardinales, Episcopos ac prælatos illos, quibus ita, ut dictum est, commendatæ erant Abbatiæ ac Monasteria, ita sint attenuata, exhaustaque, quòd cùm antehac in uno illorum monasteriorum quadraginta, quinquaginta, aut ultra hoc etiam personæ satis commodè potuerunt foveri; ut nunc ægre quinque, sex, aut decem necessariis provideri possitalimentis. Quæ res omnis in privata compendia ac commoda Cardinalium est excogitata. Unde nedum plura oriuntur offendicula, sed & gravamina oneraque ardua, ac non ferenda Germanis. Ideoque & hic supplicatur, Abbatias prædictas, Monasteria, ac religiosas cæteras domos, denuo in integrum jus eorum, pristinumque rerum statum restituendas, cavendumque posthac, ne cuiquam tales Commendæ, ut vocant, seu incorporationes concedantur.
units.tr: 24. Likewise, it has been notoriously observed hitherto that many abbeys, also several monasteries, and the other houses of this kind, or congregations of ecclesiastical persons, foundations of the Emperor and the princes, were committed to the protection of cardinals, bishops and other prelates, and incorporated with them. Hence it has come about that, through those cardinals, bishops and prelates to whom the abbeys and monasteries had been so committed, as has been said, they have been so weakened and drained that, whereas formerly forty, fifty or even more persons could fairly comfortably be supported in one of those monasteries, now scarcely five, six or ten can be provided with the necessities of food. This whole arrangement has been devised for the private profit and advantage of the cardinals. From it arise not only more obstacles, but also grievous and heavy burdens, not to be borne by the Germans. Therefore it is also petitioned here that the said abbeys, monasteries and other religious houses be restored to their former right and former condition of property in full, and that it be taken care that henceforth no such commendams, as they are called, or incorporations be granted to anyone.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: De Collegiatis Ecclesiis, quæ super Nobilibus tantum fundatæ sunt.
units.tr: Concerning the Collegiate Churches which were founded for nobles only.

units.la: 25. Insuper, licet quædam sint Collegiatæ Ecclesiæ per Germaniam, quæ à Nobilibus, & in hoc, ut Nobiles tantum summæ atque mediæ sortis ad eas reciperentur, primum sunt fundatæ, in quibus perdiutinæ observatæ ac præscriptæ consuetudinis privilegium est, ut tantum Principes, Comites, Barones, aut alioqui Nobiles acceptari possint, & debeant: Attamen laudabiles hæ consuetudines, jura non scripta, privilegia Papalia, nequaquam curantur, manutenenturve; sed è regione agitur per Curtisanos, ad liberæ electionis Episcoporum, Præpositorum, ac Decanorum, & Canonicorum præpeditionem, ut Coadjutores aliqui, contra Capitularium voluntatem ac consensum, efficiantur. Nec raro Curtisanis, licet indoctis & ignobilibus, parantur ad Canonicatus hujusmodi accessus, non obstantibus statutis & consuetudinibus, & privilegiis præscriptis: ita quòd nobilibus Germanis beneficia subtrahantur, & hæc eadem ignobilibus, vel ob pecuniam, vel familiarem consuetudinem hoc pacto conferuntur: ut, licet impetrantes ignobiles ad ea non admittantur, obstante sibi consuetudine; tamen si quis Principum, Comitum, Baronum, Nobiliumve hæc eadem à Curtisanis impetrare velit, cum colore quodam excogitati oneris, ab eisdem vel emere, vel annuo censu redimere cogatur: quamquam subinde alia huic negotio prætexantur vocabula; quæ res ipsa quoq; Nobilibus Germaniæ, supremæ atq; mediæ conditionis, in magnum cedit onerum ac gravaminum cumulum.
units.tr: 25. Moreover, although there are some collegiate churches throughout Germany which were first founded by nobles, and for this purpose: that only nobles of the highest and middle rank should be received into them, and there is a privilege of long-observed and prescribed custom by which only princes, counts, barons, or otherwise nobles can and must be admitted; nevertheless these praiseworthy customs, unwritten laws and papal privileges are in no way heeded or maintained. Instead, through the Curtisans, the free election of bishops, provosts, deans and canons is obstructed, so that certain coadjutors are appointed against the will and consent of the chapter. Not infrequently, places in such canonries are procured for Curtisans, however unlearned and ignoble they may be, notwithstanding the statutes, customs and prescribed privileges; so that benefices are withdrawn from German nobles, and the same benefices are conferred on ignoble men in this way, either for money or through familiar acquaintance: so that, although ignoble applicants are not admitted because of the custom in force, nevertheless if any prince, count, baron or noble wishes to obtain these same benefices from the Curtisans, he is forced to buy them from them or to redeem them by an annual payment, under some pretext of a devised burden; although other names are sometimes put forward for this business. This very thing also brings a great heap of burdens and grievances upon the nobles of Germany, of the highest and middle condition.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Inveterata Privilegia manutenenda.
units.tr: Long-standing privileges to be maintained.

units.la: 26. Ad hæc, quamvis omnia Ecclesiasticis ac laicis statibus privilegia ac immunitates sint concessæ, Præposituras, aliaq; beneficia & officia per se conferendi atq; eligendi: attamen per Sedem Romanam novæ subinde excogitatæ sunt technæ ac practicæ, per quas privilegiis prædictis derogatur multifariam; imò ea penitus tolluntur, ac turbantur. Ea propter rogant sacri Romani Imperii Status, hoc emendandum, & in posterum cavendum, ac unumquemq; cum suis juribus & privilegiis defendendum, manutenendumq;. Id quod rei æquitas ipsa per se sibi postulat.
units.tr: 26. Moreover, although all the ecclesiastical and lay estates have been granted privileges and immunities, namely the right to confer and elect provostships and other benefices and offices on their own authority, the Roman See has from time to time devised new tricks and practices by which those privileges are derogated in many ways, and indeed are entirely abolished and thrown into confusion. For this reason the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire ask that this be amended, that provision be made against it in future, and that each person be defended and maintained in his rights and privileges. The very equity of the matter itself demands this.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: De Annatis.
units.tr: On Annates.

units.la: 27. Quantum ad Annatas, ut vocant, attinet, quas Ecclesiastici Prælati, Romano Pontifici quotannis pendunt, quasq; ante aliquot annos Germani Principes Sedi Rom. sub certis usq; annorum metis, eo tamen modo, ut persolverentur, consenserunt, quo pecunia hæc ad nihil aliud, quàm contra Turcas parandam defensionem, Romæ tanquam depòsita, fideliter adservaretur. Verùm, cùm anni, in quos præfato modo consensum erat per Germanos, jam olim effluxerint, ac annatas depensas, non contra Turcas, sed aliò experientia Germani Principes didicerint, versas: Ea propter per omnes Imperii ordines illud ipsum pro onere non mediocri hucallegatur, supplicaturq;: id quod in responsione generali oratori Pontificio data, ac in primis ex Cæsareæ Majestatis literis, ad Sanctitatem Pontificiam eam ob rem scriptis, liquidò magis reperitur, quam ob causam laici Status Rom. Imp. vela complicanda censuerunt.
units.tr: 27. As for the annates, as they are called, which the ecclesiastical prelates pay to the Roman Pontiff each year, and which some years ago the German princes agreed to pay to the Roman See at fixed intervals of years, yet in such a way that the money should be faithfully kept at Rome, as if deposited there, for nothing else than the raising of a defence against the Turks: since the years to which the German consent was given in that manner have long since run out, and the German princes have learned from experience that the annates, once spent, were turned not against the Turks but to other purposes, therefore all the orders of the Empire have objected to this very thing as a not inconsiderable burden and have petitioned against it. This is made plainer still in the general reply given to the Papal envoy, and above all from the letters of His Imperial Majesty written to His Papal Holiness on this matter, why the lay estates of the Holy Roman Empire resolved to take up the cause.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: De contributione Ecclesiasticorum, ac religiosarum domuum, contra Turcas; ac pro de- fensione juris & tranquillitatis publicæ.
units.tr: On the contribution of the clergy and of religious houses against the Turks, and for the defence of right and public peace.

units.la: 28. Item, postquam laicorum Imperii Statuum majores Ecclesias, Monasteria, cæterasque religiosas domus per Germaniam, ad laudem omnipotentis, ita ampliter atque hoc pacto dotatas divitiis auxeruntque, quòd jam laici ipsi vix tertiam aut quartam partes in bonis temporalibus possident; atque ob eam causam, necessitati, tam Ecclesiasticorum quàm laicorum sublevandæ, promovandæque, ac manu defendendæ paci ac juri publicis; nec non & in Turcas, cæterosque Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, ac sacri Romani Imperii hostes parandæ expeditioni, præsertim inopia vires minus suppeditant: Ideo negotii ipsius exigit necessitas, æquitasque, quòd sanctitas Pontificia ita æquè ac paterne rem cum ceperet, ut Ecclesiastici etiam, tanquam qui ampliores possidenter divitias, nedum contra Turcas adferendum opem reneantur auxiliares porrigere manus: sed ad tuendum jus publicum, ac tranquillitatem reipub. Christianæ statum, quotannis pecuniæ quippiam contribuendū: ita quòd Archiepiscopi & Episcopi, Ecclesiasticis Prælatis ac personis suæ ditioni subjectis, ipsi soli ad ferendum hanc opem, contributionem prædictam indicere, jus ac potestatem habeant.
units.tr: 28. Likewise, since the greater princes of the lay estates of the Empire have so richly endowed and increased the cathedral churches, monasteries and other religious houses throughout Germany, to the praise of Almighty God, and in such a manner, that the laity themselves now hardly possess a third or a fourth part of the temporal goods; and since for this reason, in order to relieve and advance the need both of the clergy and of the laity, and to defend with force the peace and public right, and also to prepare an expedition against the Turks and the other enemies of the Catholic Church and of the Holy Roman Empire, which our lack of resources especially hinders: the necessity and equity of the matter therefore demand that the Holy See, undertaking the affair as fairly and as fatherly as it can, should see to it that the ecclesiastics also, as those who possess the greater riches, are bound not only to lend aid by stretching out helping hands against the Turks, but also to contribute some money each year for the defence of public right and the safety of the state of the Christian commonwealth; so that the archbishops and bishops alone have the right and power to levy the aforesaid contribution upon the ecclesiastical prelates and persons subject to their jurisdiction, for bringing this aid.

units.la: 29. Atque illud eo moderamine agatur, ut Electores, cæterique Principes & Magistratus Imperii, ab Ecclesiasticis Procerinibus, in eorū Principatibus, Comitatibus, oppidis, ac territoriis, in exercenda jurisdictione non perturbentur, aut præpediantur. Nempe hac ratione, quòd laici inter Ecclesiasticos jus, ac tranquillitatem publicam tueri; & Ecclesiastici sub laicis degentes, co facilius ad communem etiam jus quemq; suum defenderre, ac manutenere poterunt, cùm Ecclesiastici paria onera una cum laicis Magistratibus ac Gubernatoribus provinciarum fe-ne, & contribuere jubebuntur, quæ admodum ad idipsum ex Christiana & Germana charitate, ac ob æquitatem, paritatemq; servandæ, alioqui tenentur; obligatiqué sunt.
units.tr: 29. And let this be done with such moderation that the electors and the other princes and magistrates of the Empire are not disturbed or hindered by the ecclesiastical princes in the exercise of jurisdiction in their principalities, counties, towns and territories. For in this way the laity will be able to protect public right and peace among the ecclesiastics, and the ecclesiastics living under the laity will more easily be able to defend and maintain their own right along with the common right; since the ecclesiastics will be ordered to pay equal burdens together with the lay magistrates and governors of the provinces, and to contribute in the same way, which they are bound and obliged to do for this very purpose by Christian and German charity, and for the sake of equity and parity.

units.la: 30. Et quandoquidem omnes Ecclesiastici, in primis ac præcipuè, merito pro viribus contra Turcas, tanquam hostes Christianæ fidei, ad ferendam opem, parandam defensionem, recuperandumq; manu, quas olim crudelis ille ferro subjugarat Christianorū provincias, teneātur: Eam ob rem, pro licito, bono, ac pariter Christianæ reipub. utili & necessario, visum placitumq; est, ut si quando exigere id necessitas videbitur, quòd mūdus & preciosior supellex Ecclesiarū cathedralium, monasteriorum, cæterarumque Ecclesiarum ac religiosarum domorum, auri, argenti, unionii, aliorumq; preciosorum lapillorum, denique & campanarum pars non necessaria, pro communi Christianæ reip. utilitate in medium conferatur: ne thesaurus ille Ecclesiæ Turcis potius, quàm nobis custodiatur, adservetur. id quod & per Græciæ regnum jam olim usuvenisse experientia ipsa docuit. Quæ res Turcis magno cessit lucro, præsidioque; quando reperto hoc Ecclesiæ mundo, seu thesauro, militibus suis comparare potuerunt uberiorem commeatum; uteò instructiores hinc cæteras Christianorum urbes oppugnarent ac provincias.
units.tr: 30. And since all the ecclesiastics, first and foremost, are rightly bound to bring aid against the Turks, as enemies of the Christian faith, to prepare defence and to recover by force the provinces of the Christians which that cruel man once subjected by the sword, it has therefore been judged and resolved, as lawful, good, and equally useful and necessary for the Christian commonwealth, that if ever necessity should seem to demand it, the superfluous and more precious furnishings of the cathedral churches, monasteries and other churches and religious houses, consisting of gold, silver, pearls and other precious stones, and finally the unnecessary part of the bells, be brought together for the common advantage of the Christian commonwealth; so that the treasure of the Church be kept for us rather than for the Turks. Experience itself has taught that this once happened in the kingdom of Greece as well. That event turned to great gain and advantage for the Turks, since, having found this worldly wealth or treasure of the Church, they were able to procure a more abundant supply for their soldiers, and so, better equipped, they attacked the other cities and provinces of the Christians.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI.

units.la: Ut personæ Ecclesiasticæ ob perpetrata maleficia commeritam nullam luant pœnam.
units.tr: That ecclesiastical persons shall not suffer any punishment they have deserved for the crimes they have committed.

units.la: 31. Item, quicunque Ecclesiasticos recipit ordines, majores seu minores per hoc omnium pœnarum magistratuum secularium, utcunq; magna perpetret maleficia, immunis esse contendit. Nec hoc ita ordinati temerè præsumunt: quòd ab Ecclesiasticis summæ conditionis statibus in peccandi hac licentia manuteneantur. Sæpenumero enim compertum est, ut quum ita consecratis, præsertim Sacerdotibus, per jura canonica legitimæ uxores sint interdictæ; quòd dehinc pudicitiam matronarum, virginum, laicorum scilicet uxorum, filiarum, sororumque attentant, ac noctu interdum que sollicitant. Efficiunt quoque per assiduum ac indefessum laborem, partim muneribus, donisque blanditiis, ut complures honestæ alioqui virgines & matronæ, partim etiam in secretis, quas vocant, Confessionibus (id quod eventu ipso compertum est) diuturna opera labefactentur, ad peccandum offendiculaque commoveantur. Necraro etiam evenit, ut ii, uxores ac filias, maritis patribusque detineant, & remorentur; minantes interim, gladio, aqua, igni ve, ulturos repetitas uxores ... tantorum malorum segetem ex libidine insana contrahunt; mirum quid latrocinis, homicidiis, innocentum delatione, igni, rapina, furto, falso cudendo numismate, ac mille scelerum formis, interim contra divina humanaque jura omnia, non sine magno etiam aliorum offendiculo, libertine ac impuné quotidie committant. Nempe immunitate ac peccandi sua licentia, quam ex privilegiis canonum sibi usurparunt, in hoc freti.
