Cùm enim & semel compertum habent, licere eis impune quidquid libuerit; rum nedum magistratibus civilibus, sed & suis Episcopis ac superioribus medium ostendunt unguem, quodcunque illi vel jubeant, vel vetent. Et tandem ut in peccatis maleficiisque perpetrandis magis adhuc foveantur, præter omnem æquitatis rationem, aliquatenus interdictum Archiepiscopos, & Episcopis, ne malefactores hos publicè criminali judicio reos agere possint, nisi prius degradatos: id quod tantis sumptibus, tanraque pompa celebrari oportet, ut propterea perquam rarissimum uncti illi malefactores merita plectantur pœna. Adhæc adstringuntur, obligantur Episcopi. Episcopi per sua Capitula, ut peri sonas in sacris ordinibus, quod dicitur, constituitas, secundum Canonica etiam jura, poenis utcunq; levibus, punire, affligereque non audeant. Quae res tota eò spectat, ut ex disparitate hac, inter laicos ac Ecclesiasticos simultates, dissidia, atq; odia plus quàm Vatiniana oriantur.
units.tr: 31. Likewise, whoever holds that anyone who receives the major or minor ecclesiastical orders is thereby exempt from all the punishments of the secular magistrates, however great the crimes he commits. Nor do the ordained presume this rashly, but they are upheld in this license to sin by ecclesiastical persons of the highest rank. For it has very often been discovered that, since legitimate wives are forbidden to those so consecrated, especially priests, by the canon law, they then attempt the chastity of matrons, virgins, and the wives and daughters and sisters of laymen, and sometimes solicit them by night. They also bring about, by constant and tireless effort, partly through gifts and flattering presents, and partly in what they call secret confessions (as has been found out in fact), that many women who were otherwise respectable, virgins and matrons alike, are undermined by long labour and drawn into sin and stumbling. It also not rarely happens that these men detain and hold back wives and daughters from their husbands and fathers, threatening meanwhile to take vengeance with the sword, water or fire on the wives they have taken back... From their insane lust they reap a harvest of such great evils: with what freedom and impunity they daily commit robberies, murders, the denunciation of innocent people, arson, rapine, theft, the forging of coin, and a thousand forms of crime, all against divine and human law, and not without great offence to others. Relying, indeed, on their immunity and license to sin, which they have usurped for themselves from the privileges of the canons. For once they have learned that they may do with impunity whatever they please, they show not only the civil magistrates but also their own bishops and superiors not so much as a finger's breadth of yielding, whatever those superiors may command or forbid. And finally, so that they may be fostered all the more in committing sins and crimes, beyond all reason of equity, the archbishops and bishops are in some measure forbidden to bring these malefactors to public criminal trial unless they have first been degraded; and this must be done with such expense and such pomp that those anointed malefactors are very rarely punished as they deserve. Besides this, the bishops are bound and obliged by their own chapters not to dare to punish or afflict, even with however slight penalties, persons who are, as they say, placed in the sacred orders, even according to the canon law. This whole arrangement tends to this end: that from this inequality between laymen and clergy there arise enmities, dissensions, and hatreds greater than Vatinian ones.

units.la: 32. Illud quoque non mediocriter timendum est, ut si personae Ecclesiasticae, jam dicti oneris, aliorumque maleficiorum causa, quae quotidie perpetrare pergunt, non aequa jura, judices aequos, paresque poenas habeant; quod eorum vita offendiculosa apud laicorum vulgus tumultum quempiam, seditionemque pergrandem, nedum contra ipsos, Ecclesiasticos (scilicet, sed & contra magistratus, ac superiores omnes), quòd impunita sinant maleficia tam nororia, commotura, excitaturaque sint.
units.tr: 32. It is also not to be feared to a small degree that if ecclesiastical persons, for the aforesaid burden and for other crimes which they continue to commit daily, do not have equal laws, fair judges and equal penalties, then their offensive way of life will stir up among the common people of the laity some great tumult and sedition, and indeed against the clergy themselves, and also against the magistrates and all superiors, because they allow such notorious crimes to go unpunished.

units.la: 33. Quapropter necessitas, aequitasque ipsa sibi postulant, ut Ecclesiasticarum personarum praedicta praesumpta privilegia abrogentur, aboleantur, e medio tollanturque, ac illarum gratia finaliter stanciatur, caveatur, ac statuatur, quòd ordinati in majoribus vel minoribus constituti, unà cum pedibus laicis, aequa habeant jura, aequos judices, paresque poenas: ita quòd Ecclesiastici nitra laicos, in pagibus delictis, nullam praerendere possint praerogativam, immunitatemve, sed ut quisque delinquentium Ecclesiasticorum, sub quo deliquit judice, ob commissum suum maleficium, secundum debitti qualitatem ac mensuram, non secus atque alii malefactores, poena à jure communi Imperii impositia delicto commensuratàque, plecti, puniri, & affici possit atque debeat. Id quod verè Ecclesiasticis, hoc est probis & eruditis viris, dubio procul, impendio magis arridebit: tantum abest, ut per hoc ledi jus eorum putent. Hacre namque fiet, ut titulo tantum Ecclesiastici, alioqui improbi nebulones, ad obedientiam majoribus debitam, ac ad bene honesteque vivendum compellantur; ad haec retentiones, simultatesque inter eos atque laicos praecaveantur, evitenturque. Denique & hoc ipso ad observandum, colendumque integrae vitae Ecclesiasticos eò magis invitabuntur, promoveanturque.
units.tr: 33. Therefore necessity and equity themselves demand that the aforesaid presumed privileges of ecclesiastical persons be repealed, abolished, and removed from the midst, and that for the sake of these persons it be finally enacted, provided and ordained that those ordained and placed in the major or minor orders, together with lay persons, have equal laws, equal judges and equal penalties; so that the clergy may claim no prerogative or immunity beyond laymen in punishable offences, but that each of the criminal clergy may, before whichever judge he offended, be punished, chastised and afflicted, for the crime he committed, according to the quality and measure of his offence, not otherwise than other malefactors, with a penalty imposed by the common law of the Empire and proportionate to the offence. This will undoubtedly please the clergy, that is, good and learned men, far more, so far is it from their thinking that their right is thereby harmed. For in this way those who are clergy only in name, otherwise wicked scoundrels, will be compelled to the obedience due to their superiors and to living well and honourably; and thereby quarrels and enmities between them and the laity will be forestalled and avoided. Finally, by this very means the clergy will be the more invited and encouraged to observe and cultivate a life of integrity.

units.la: CAP. XXI- I. De onere Banni, seu Excommunicationis.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI. I. On the burden of the Ban, or Excommunication.

units.la: 34. Item, Romae caeterisque in locis per Archiepiscopos ac Episcopos, aut certè eorum Ecclesiasticos judices, multi Christianorum ob causas prophanas, ob pecuniae denique, ac turpis quaestus amorem excommunicantur; multorumque, sed eorum in fide infirmorum, conscientiae per hoc aggravantur, & in desperationem perrahuntur; ac denique ob pecuniae, lucrive tantulum, aut alioqui res minimi precii, ad internecionem usque animae, corporis, honoris, atque rei familiaris, contra divina humanaque jura perducuntur. Quando nemo, nisi ob convictum haereseos crimen, excommunicationis gladio feriendus, aut pro scelusfo à Christiana Catholicaque Ecclesia, sacris literis restantibus, reputandus est. Ea propter facti Romani Imperii Principes, Proceresque ac Status laici rogant, ut Pontificia Sanct. tanquam fidus, Christianus, ac pius pater, velit praefatum onus Banni, seu Excommunicationis, apud sedem Romanam penitus abolere, ac apud caeteros Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, & eorum judices Ecclesiasticos ablegare, tollere, & denique ita lancire, cavereque, ut nemo ullam ob causam, quàm manifestum ac convictum haereseos crimen, & quantum ad Sacrosanctam Christi fidem attinet, excommunicationis fulmine feriatur, aut pro scelusfo à Christiana ac Catholica Ecclesia habeatur. Petiniquum liquidem est, fideles Christi ob temporalium bonorum, lucrive, aut deniq; ullam aliam humanarum constitutionum transgressionem, excepta haeresis perfidia, à Deo Opt. Maximo, suaque Ecclesia Catholica excludi, sejungi, separarique.
units.tr: 34. Likewise, at Rome and in other places, by the Archbishops and Bishops, or at least by their ecclesiastical judges, many Christians are excommunicated for worldly causes, out of love of money in the end and of shameful gain; and the consciences of many, though of those weak in faith, are by this means burdened and dragged into despair; and finally, for the sake of a small sum of money or gain, or for things of very little value otherwise, they are brought, to the utter ruin of soul, body, honour and property, against divine and human law. Since no one ought to be struck with the sword of excommunication, or be regarded by the Christian Catholic Church as a wicked person, except on account of a proven charge of heresy, while the Holy Scriptures stand. Therefore the Princes of the Holy Roman Empire, its Nobles and the lay Estates ask that His Holiness, as a faithful, Christian and pious father, would be pleased to abolish entirely the aforesaid burden of the Ban, or Excommunication, at the Roman See, and to send it away from the other Archbishops, Bishops and their ecclesiastical judges, to remove it, and finally to enact and provide by decree that no one be struck by the thunderbolt of excommunication for any cause other than a manifest and proven charge of heresy, and insofar as it concerns the most holy faith of Christ, nor be regarded as a wicked person by the Christian and Catholic Church. For it is surely unjust that the faithful of Christ be shut out, separated and cut off from God the Best and Greatest, and from His Catholic Church, on account of temporal goods, gain, or finally any other transgression of human constitutions, apart from the treachery of heresy.

units.la: CAP. XXIII. Quo pacto multi cohabitatores oppidorum excommunicati, & ipsi utcunque innocen- tes excommunicantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. In what way many co-inhabitants of towns are excommunicated, and how they are excommunicated although they are in some sense innocent.

units.la: 35. Item & illud in plerisque saepiusculè evenit, quòd vicinorum excommunicati decem, & eo amplius, quos tamen causa nihil omnino contingit, cum ipso principali excommunicationis poena aggravantur. & non ob aliud, quàm ut officiales, Ecclesiastici (scilicet judices, facilius, citiusque pro liberitate sua miseram plebeculam depeculentur, ac pro suo libitu, eorum abutantur simplicitate, i- principales ad quascunque etiam iniquas acceptandas transactiones per hoc compellant, nec. Nam etiamsi excommunicatus ipse, unà cum uxore, liberisque suis, per intolerabilem iniquissimum Banni onus in exilium ire cogatur, quòd hac in re nullus sit Officialibus modus, neque finis, neque ulla facultatum ratio: Tamen nullus est hominibus illis respectus, dufti ia, daraveadhocopera, & percontemptum; an necessitate ita impellente, vel catu povicini cohabitatores, cum excommunicato ipso participarint, commercium ve habuerint; aut haec fuerit concivibus causa, quare excommunicatum merito solum vertere jussisse debeant. Horum pensi habetur nullum. Sed unum curatur hoc per Officiales, ut, quousque principalis excommunicatus, solvendo non est, concives ac vicini sui, uti culpa vacent, ad solutionem tamen quod superesset debiti, cogantur. Quod si aliquando Officialibus in os obtrudatur, contra canonica sua, eos hoc molitur jura, quae pecuniae causa quempiam excommunicari aut interdictum edici vetent: Nihilominus tamen idipsum conantur, causantes interim, nanoh[?] cuniam, sed contumaciam, quae tanto sit major, quanto, unde sibi originem ducit, minores causam, tales excommunicari; atque hac decipula, avaritiam suam Officiales, nugando concedunt.
units.tr: 35. Likewise it happens quite often in many places that ten or more neighbours of an excommunicated man, to whom nothing whatever pertains in the matter, are burdened together with the principal penalty of excommunication. This is done for no other reason than that the officials of the Church (namely the judges) may more easily and quickly plunder the wretched common people for their own freedom, abuse their simplicity at will, and by this means compel the principal parties to accept any transactions whatever, however unjust. For even if the excommunicated man himself, together with his wife and children, is forced into exile by the intolerable and most unjust burden of the ban, there is no limit for the officials in this matter, no end, and no reckoning of their gains. Yet there is no regard at all for those men, whether, under the compulsion of necessity, the neighbours who live with them had shared in intercourse or commerce with the excommunicated man himself, or whether this was the reason the fellow citizens ought rightly to have ordered the excommunicated man to leave. Of this they take no account. The officials attend to one thing only: that, as long as the principal excommunicated man is unable to pay, his fellow citizens and neighbours, though free of fault, are compelled to pay what remains of the debt. If at some time the officials are confronted with the charge that this runs against their canon laws, which forbid anyone to be excommunicated or an interdict to be issued for the sake of money, they nevertheless attempt the same thing, pleading meanwhile not money but contumacy, which is the greater the smaller the cause from which it arises, such that such men are excommunicated. By this snare the officials, with their trifling pretexts, conceal their avarice.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXIV.

units.la: Item & de illicitis interdictis.
units.tr: Likewise, concerning unlawful interdicts.

units.la: 36. Praeterea, cum Sacerdos, aut alioqui Ecclesiastica persona, casu occiditur; tum nedum sifor excommunicatur, sed & totum oppidum, aut totus pagus, iniquissime interdicitur: quod dictum eousque durat, tam diu, interrupta pendent publica Christianorum officia, quoulq; vel tota incolarum ejus loci communitas fecerint homicidii compensationem, homicidium expiarint: non considerato eo, dederitne occasionem, ut se gesserit probe, vel nequirer fuerit occisus sacerdos, vel alias Ecclesiastico ordini adscriptus; licet jura canonica ipsam in quibusdam casibus, modum negotio praescribant. Praegravanturque itaque ex delicto unius, centum alii communiter, nedum contra communem aequitatem, sed & contra omnia divina & humana jura.
units.tr: 36. Moreover, when a priest, or some other ecclesiastical person, is killed by chance, then not only is the guilty man excommunicated, but the whole town or the whole village is most unjustly placed under interdict. This sentence lasts so long, and public Christian services remain suspended for so long, until the whole community of that place has made payment for the homicide or has expiated the killing; without regard to whether the priest gave occasion for it, whether he conducted himself uprightly, or whether he was killed unjustly, or was otherwise enrolled in the ecclesiastical order; although the canon law prescribes the manner of settlement in certain cases. Thus, by the crime of one man, a hundred others are burdened together, not only against common equity but also against all divine and human law.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXV.

units.la: De abrogatione feriarum aliquot dierum.
units.tr: On the abolition of several holy days.

units.la: 37. Insuper & feriarum festorumque dierum tanta copia laicorum vulgus non medio urgetur. Nimirum, cum tot sint religiosi facti dies, ut vix aegre tempus agricolis suppetat quales agri, tot laboribus e terra pellectos, aliquando aqua pluvia, immodicove aestu, non rari grandine, aliave tempestate periclitantes, in horrea conferant: quos tamen fructus, si non festis solennibus praepediti forent, commode, ac citra jacturam ex agro legere, domumque ferre possent. Adde, quod feriatis quoque diebus (qui dubio procul bono consilio, ac in Dei Opt. Max. honorem, primum bene sunt feriati) innumera perpetrantur delicta, peccataque & scelera potius, quae his omnipotens colatur, vencretur. Id quod res ipsa notorium facit: tantum abest, ut tesdem egeat. Eamque ob causam sacri Rom.Imp.Status laici consultius putant, ac reipub. Christianae condubilius, si effrenis feriarum (quae animis, quam externo cultu Christianis, hoc est his, quibus peccatis semper feriandum est, rectius celebrantur) festorumque dierum numerus paulo coerceatur in arctum, minuaturque.
units.tr: 37. Moreover, the common people of the laity are oppressed by no small number of holidays and feast days. Indeed, so many days have been made religious that farmers scarcely have time to gather in the crops from their fields, which were drawn from the earth with so much labour and which are sometimes endangered by rainwater, excessive heat, not infrequently hail or some other storm. Yet they could conveniently and without loss gather that produce from the field and carry it home if they were not hindered by solemn feasts. Add to this that on the holy days too (which were no doubt first well kept with good intent and for the honour of God, most good and most great), countless crimes are committed, sins and rather wickednesses, by which the Almighty is, as it were, served and worshipped. The thing itself makes this notorious; so far is it from needing witnesses. For this reason the sacred Roman Imperial States and the lay estates think it more advisable, and more beneficial to the Christian commonwealth, that the unrestrained number of holidays and feast days (which are more properly kept in the mind than by external worship among Christians, that is, among those for whom there should always be a holiday from sin) be somewhat restrained, and reduced to a narrower limit.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: De Domibus ordinum militarium, ac Balivis, ut vocant, per Apuliam Siciliamq; ordini militari Teutonicorum vi, dolo, Germanorum ditioni ereptis.
units.tr: Concerning the houses of the military orders, and the bailiwicks, as they are called, in Apulia and Sicily, taken from the Teutonic military order by force and fraud and placed under German authority.

units.la: 38. Item licet Dominis ordinis divae Mariae virginis, quos vulgo Fratrum Teutonicorum vocant, ex liberalitate Romanorum Imperatorum celeberrimae memoriae, item & Principum, Comitum & Baronum, in eos collata, caeterorumque Nobilium contributa auctione, certa bona temporalia, ac redditus & census annui, per Apuliam, Siciliam, reliquamque Italiam, empti sint atque adaucti, non ob aliud, quam ut contra hostes Christianae religionis, ad pugnam instructiores forent, habeerentque Germani Nobiles pariter & fidei Catholicae propugnatores, unde commodius & honestius vitam militiae semper paratam vivere possent: ea ex bonorum aliae Praefecturae ejus ordinis quas vulgo Balivias, ac a commeatu ordini parando, Compeaturas vocant, distinctae sunt & distinctae per classes, quas & quiete sine cujuspiam turbatione, per multa secula polluerunt, utinamque: Attamen per praecedentes Romanos Pontifices ordini praedicto bona talia erepta, ac Cardinalibus, Archiepiscopis, Episcopisque; illisque nec Germanis, nec praefati Ordinis militaris exulibus habitatis, lata traditaq; sunt. Quemadmodum & in hunc usque diem militaris Germanorum Ordo hospitaliatus, carere cogitur. Insuper priores Romani Pontifices domus ordinis supradicti locatas, nempe Hieronymo Veneto tradiderunt, ac concesserunt: Eumque ordinis expediti in regno coraverunt; contra Romanorum licet Pontificum ac Imperatorum statuta & Privilegia, totius per eorum praedecessores roborata, quibus ad Germanos tantum Ordinis milites, ut haec omnia nerent, cantum, suncitumque est.
units.tr: 38. Likewise, although the lords of the Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary, whom they commonly call Brothers of the Teutonic Order, were enriched by the generosity of the Roman emperors of most renowned memory, and likewise by princes, counts and barons, and by the contributions of other nobles, and although certain temporal goods, annual revenues and rents were bought and increased for them in Apulia, Sicily and the rest of Italy, for no other purpose than that they might be better equipped for battle against the enemies of the Christian religion, and that German nobles might have defenders of the Catholic faith, from whom they could more conveniently and honourably live a life always ready for military service; nevertheless, those goods were divided among other prefectures of that order, which they commonly call bailiwicks, and commanderies, so called from the provisioning of the order, and were divided into classes, which for many centuries they held in peace without disturbance from anyone. But by the preceding Roman pontiffs those goods were seized from the order and given and granted to cardinals, archbishops and bishops, and not to Germans or exiles of the aforesaid military order who lived there. In the same way, to this day the German military order is forced to go without a hospice. Moreover, the earlier Roman pontiffs leased and granted the houses of the aforesaid order, namely to Girolamo the Venetian, and they set him over the Order's affairs in the kingdom. Yet this is against the statutes and privileges of the Roman pontiffs and emperors, confirmed throughout by their predecessors, by which it was provided and sanctioned that, so that all these things should be of no force, only German knights of the Order should hold them.

units.la: Deinde & Romanenses Curtisani, ordinis supramemorati domos per Italiam, Burgum Papalibus Bullis ac provisionibus attentare conati sunt: quo facto, ordinem ad litteras Romae coegerunt. Id quod non ad mediocrem perniciem & ipsius ordinis, & totius Germaniae vergit nationis. Demum Germanis Stablore quoq;, divi Benedicti Monasterium, contra bullarum quanquam juta, superioribus paucis equidem annis ereptum est, ac in commendam, ut appareat Columnae collatum: quae omnia in perniciem tendunt, ac irrecuperabile Germaniae detrimentum; attentatumq; est, quicquid id est, contra jus & phas, ac aequitatem omnem. Imperii Status hic quoq; rogant, Sanctitas Pontificia velit Militari Teutonicorum ordini, bona ecclesiastica, census & redditus ablatos, abloq; ulteriore mora redhibere, reddere, ac restituere, ipsum, ut quantocyus fiat, mandare, curareve: quemadmodum juris, bonique & aequi ratio hoc sibi postulat.
units.tr: Then the Roman courtiers also tried to seize the houses of the aforesaid order throughout Italy, at Borgo, by papal bulls and provisions; and having done so, they forced the Order to render account at Rome. This tends to no small ruin both of the Order itself and of the whole German nation. Finally, the monastery of St Benedict at Stablo, though contrary to the bulls, was taken from the Germans only a few years ago and granted in commendam, as appears, to the Colonna family. All these things tend to the ruin and irrecoverable loss of Germany; and whatever it is, it has been attempted against law and right and all equity. The Estates of the Empire here also ask that His Papal Holiness be pleased to order and see to it that the ecclesiastical goods, rents and revenues taken from the German military order be returned, restored and given back to it, without further delay and as quickly as possible, as the reason of law, of goodness and of equity itself demands.

units.la: CAP. XXVII. De oneribus sacri Romani Imperii statuum laicorum, contra Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, caeterosque praelatos Ecclesiasticos, eorumque quoq; Capitula, ac suffectos judices, quos vo- cant, Ecclesiasticos.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the burdens of the lay estates of the Holy Roman Empire, against the archbishops, bishops, and other ecclesiastical prelates, and likewise against their chapters, and the so-called ecclesiastical judges appointed as deputies.

units.la: 39. Praeter onera supra memorata, Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum & Praelatorum, quòd hi, ut praedictum est, à sede Romana conservatores delegatos, atq; id genus alios plerosq; Ecclesiasticos impetrant judices, per quos laici non ferendis aggravantur modis; quòd non omnino infrequenter evenit, ut laici in periculum ac perniciem animae, aestimationis, corporis atq; bonorum perducantur, ac quantum per hos stat judices, pertrahantur etiam. Sed hîc nondum finis. Sunt enim complura adhuc alia gravamina, prout ligillatim ea per capita nunc recensebuntur.
units.tr: 39. Besides the burdens mentioned above, there is this further grievance against the archbishops, bishops and prelates: that they obtain from the Roman See, as has been said, conservators and delegated judges, and many other such ecclesiastical judges, through whom the laity are oppressed by intolerable measures. It is not at all rare for laymen to be brought into peril and ruin of soul, reputation, body and goods, and, so far as these judges can manage it, to be dragged down even further. But this is not yet the end. There are many other grievances, which will now be listed one by one, chapter by chapter.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII. Primum, quibus modis laicorum bona immobilia ad Ecclesiasticorum manus; & non contrà, ab Ecclesiasticis ad laicos perveniant.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII. First, by what means the immovable goods of laymen come into the hands of ecclesiastics, and not the reverse, from ecclesiastics to laymen.

units.la: 40. Item, quum à sede Romana constitutionibus sit cautum ac provisum, ne bona Ecclesiastica, praesertim immobilia, regulariter personis laicis, unquam distrahi aut vendi possint; & tamen Ecclesiastici, nulla cogente necessitate, sed tantùm, ut eorum res familiaris reddatur lautior, crescantque census, nunquam non cessant, laicorum praedia emptionibus, innumerisq; aliis modis ad se pellicere, di qua tandem sit possibile via. Quod ipsum quoq; Statibus laicis grave, damnosum, ac intolerabile est. Quamobrem sacri Romani Imperii Status laici, reipub. Germanorum utile, necessariumque putaverunt, ut omnia bona immobilia, soli scil. quae posthac aliquo, quocunq; tandem titulo, à laicis ad Ecclesiasticos pervenirent, possent à laicis superioribus, quorum ditioni praedia haec subjecta forent, tandem ab Ecclesiasticis redimi, lui, atque justo precio vendicari: non consideratò, quicquid contra hoc privilegiorum praetenderent Ecclesiastici.
units.tr: 40. Likewise, although the Roman See has provided by its constitutions and taken care that ecclesiastical goods, especially immovable ones, may as a rule never be alienated or sold to lay persons, nevertheless the ecclesiastics, under no pressing necessity but merely so that their household property may be made more splendid and their revenues may grow, never cease to draw laymen's estates to themselves by purchases and by countless other means, by whatever way it is at last possible. This is also grievous, damaging and intolerable to the lay Estates. For this reason the lay Estates of the Holy Roman Empire judged it useful and necessary for the commonwealth of the Germans that all immovable goods, namely landed estates, which from now on, by whatever title at all, pass from laymen to ecclesiastics, may be redeemed and reclaimed by the lay superiors under whose jurisdiction these estates are subject, from the ecclesiastics, and be claimed at a just price; without regard to whatever privileges the ecclesiastics might put forward against this.

units.la: CAP. XXIX. Quomodo Episcopi bona haereditaria Ecclesiasticorum ad se trahere conentur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX. How bishops try to draw the hereditary goods of churchmen to themselves.

units.la: 41. Necraro & illud facto contigit, quòd quum personae Ecclesiasticae bona haereditario titulo, à majoribus suis, unà cum caeteris cohaeredibus, jure haereditario sibi forte usurparent; ac si dehinc intestati decessissent Ecclesiastici, tum per Episcoporum nonnullos sibiipsis bona illa haereditaria laicorum vendicari coeperunt: non in mediocrem proximorum, venientium ab intestato cognatorum, perniciem ac jacturam. Quae res ipsa quoq; laicis non ferenda, imò, omnimodo onerosa, intolerabilisque est.
units.tr: 41. Nor has it been rare for this to happen as well: when clergy, together with their other coheirs, had by hereditary right seized for themselves goods that came to them by inheritance from their ancestors, and when those clergy then died intestate, some bishops began to claim those hereditary goods for themselves from the laymen. This was no small loss and damage to the nearest relatives, the kinsmen who come to the inheritance on intestacy. This too is something laymen cannot bear: it is in every way burdensome and intolerable.

units.la: CAP. XXX. Quo ingenio, bona quaedam laica, quae Ecclesiis, aut aliis religiosis domibus certis pactio- nibus vendita sunt, vel hypothecata, ditioni Ecclesiasticae subju- gari conentur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX. By what device certain lay goods, which have been sold or pledged to churches or other religious houses under certain agreements, are attempted to be brought under ecclesiastical control.

units.la: 42. Adhaec, si quando casu ita contingit, quòd bona laica temporali jurisdictione subjecta, fructibus, redditibus, censibusve annuis Ecclesiis, ac caeteris religiosis domibus legentur, vendantur, hypothecentur, aut quovis alio titulo tradantur, vel à laicis erga Ecclesias ac monasteria annuo censu tributaria efficiantur; moliuntur Ecclesiastici, talia praedia laica, ex civili potestate ac ditione in Ecclesiasticam transferre, atq; huc utcunq; inquo illicitóve conatui, Episcopi, Ecclesiasticiq; patrocinantur praelati, tuenturq; rem longè iniquissimam; tantum abest, ut in hoc quemquam revereantur Ecclesiastici.
units.tr: 42. Moreover, if it ever happens by chance that lay goods, subject to temporal jurisdiction, are bequeathed to churches and other religious houses by their fruits, rents or annual dues, or are sold, pledged, or handed over by any other title, or are made tributary by laymen to churches and monasteries by an annual census; the clergy attempt to transfer such lay estates from civil power and jurisdiction into the ecclesiastical sphere. And bishops and ecclesiastical prelates support this attempt, whether lawful or unlawful in any way, and they defend a matter most unjust; so far are the clergy from showing any respect in this.

units.la: CAP. XXXI. De collatione beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum jam primùm fundatorum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI. On the conferring of ecclesiastical benefices which were first founded by lay persons.

units.la: 43. Item, quum beneficium aliquod Ecclesiasticum à laicis summae vel mediae conditionis primùm fundatur, dotaturq; , tunc quidam Episcoporum primam ejus beneficii collationem sibi usurpare nituntur; ac beneficii ipsius dotationem, fundationémve priùs confirmare recusant, quàm eorum intentioni acquieverint, qui beneficia ex suis censibus dotarunt, hoc est, fundatores & patroni secundum jura etiam Canonica Collatores ordinarii.
units.tr: 43. Likewise, when some ecclesiastical benefice is first founded and endowed by laymen of high or middling rank, then certain bishops strive to usurp for themselves the first conferral of that benefice, and refuse to confirm the endowment or foundation of the benefice until they have yielded to the wishes of those who endowed the benefice from their own revenues, that is, the founders and patrons, who according to the canon law also are the ordinary conferrers.

units.la: CAP. XXXII. De confirmationibus beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum non necessariis, atque aliis idgenus gravaminibus.
units.tr: CAP. XXXII. Concerning the unnecessary confirmations of ecclesiastical benefices, and other grievances of the same kind.

units.la: 44. Praeterea si quis novam fundationem beneficii Ecclesiastici fraternitatisve erigere, atque eandem confirmari mandam petere velit, quamquam confirmationis hujusce, de jure ac aequitate minimè indigeat: Nihilominus tamen fundatores beneficiorum praeter modum, pecuniarum exactionibus, ad vivum usq; adgravantur, exuguntur q;, ac per Romanorum statuta, technias ac subtiles practicas, eò adiguntur, ut fundationes hæ omnes, quamvis minimi sint precii, necessario confirmentur. Quod ipsum non mediocre Germanorum laicorum est onus.
units.tr: 44. Moreover, if anyone wishes to erect a new foundation of an ecclesiastical benefice or fraternity, and asks that the same be confirmed, although such confirmation is in right and equity scarcely needed at all, nevertheless the founders of benefices are burdened beyond measure with exactions of money, are drained to the quick, and by the statutes of the Romans, by tricks and subtle practices, are driven to the point that all these foundations, however small their value, must of necessity be confirmed. This is no small burden for the German laity.

units.la: CAP. XXX- III.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII.

units.la: De subsidiis, & aliis oneribus, quæ imponuntur Ecclesiasticis, qui collatores habent laicos.
units.tr: On the subsidies and other burdens imposed on ecclesiastics who have lay patrons.

units.la: 45. Deinceps, si quando contingit, Ecclesiasticam personam à laico beneficio aliquo donari, & Episcopo pro investura accipienda præsentari; tum Episcoporum in spiritualibus, ut vocant, Vicarii, pro investura tantum erogant æris, præsentatis illis, quantum collatum beneficium in annuo habet proventu; nonnunquam etiam, quantum bimo. Ita enim altera portio exigitur Episcopo, & reliqua terim Archidiacono, aut Archipresbytero pro investura, vel possessionis traditione.
units.tr: 45. Further, if it happens that an ecclesiastical person is granted some benefice by a layman and is presented to the bishop to receive investiture, then the bishop's vicars in spiritual matters, as they are called, demand money for the investiture alone from those presented, as much as the benefice yields in annual income, and sometimes as much as two years' income. In this way one portion is exacted for the bishop, and the rest for the archdeacon or archpresbyter, for the investiture or the transfer of possession.

units.la: 46. Insuper nimium, pro viribus, illicitis exactionibus gravant Episcopi beneficia, subinde nimirum; nullo licet subsinrurgentes, aut illud sibi admodum postulantes causæ, hoc est, quod jura vocant, manifestæ & rationabiles: ultra etiam modum quem jura communia in calibus evidenter necessariis præscribunt. Illis nempe casibus, quibus solis jura subsidium ab Ecclesiasticis erogari permittunt; fitque ejus rei immodico usu, ut Presbyteris vitæ necessaria, vix aut certè ne illa quidem relinquantur. Denum & in totius populi caput hoc redundat onus, quando ita premuntur Sacerdotes, ut respirare eis non liceat; ni vicissim subditam plebeculam arrodant. Ita ex oneribus lentur omnes, usque; ut nullum gratis, nisi numeretur sempar aliquid, ministrent sacramentum, Ecclesiasticum, Christianum donum, ad quod tamen præcipuum gratis ut facerent, darentque ea gratis, quæ nullo modo reddi possunt, atque ipsi gratis accepissent, sacrosancti Evangelii attestantibus litteris, tenebantur. Ipsa res ipsa fecit notorium.
units.tr: 46. Moreover, bishops burden benefices beyond their strength with illicit exactions, often without any cause arising to justify it, or any cause that itself demands it, that is, one the laws call manifest and reasonable; and beyond the limit which the common laws prescribe in cases that are plainly necessary: namely, those cases alone in which the laws permit aid to be levied from ecclesiastics. By the excessive use of this practice it comes about that scarcely anything, or certainly not even those things, is left to the presbyters for their necessary living. Finally, this burden also falls on the whole body of the people, when the priests are so pressed that they are not allowed to breathe, unless in turn they gnaw at the poor subject folk. Thus all are so weighed down by burdens that they administer no sacrament, no ecclesiastical or Christian gift, gratis unless something is always counted out; yet they were bound, by the clear testimony of the sacred Gospel, to give freely, and above all to give freely those things which can in no way be repaid, and which they themselves had received freely. The thing itself has made this notorious.

units.la: CAP. XXXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIV.

units.la: Quo pacto sapius, & quidem plures una indocti atq; inidonei ordinentur sacerdotes.
units.tr: How it often happens that, and indeed more than one at a time, unlearned and unfit men are ordained priests.

units.la: 47. Item Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, & eorum suffecti, quos Suffraganeos vocant, sæpenumero plures indoctos, idiotas, inhabiles, vilesque ac ludicras personas, ad sacerdotii functionem ordinant: qui cum ex ministerio Ecclesiæ, ad quod minus sunt idonei, vivere non possint, tamen neque aliunde vel ex beneficiis, vel propriis hæreditariis bonis, unde vitam Presbytero dignam ducere queant, habent; sed tantum imaginarios & fictitios, aliquando neq; illos quidem, secum ferunt titulos: hincque dehinc, aut ex innata malitia, morumve levitate, aut qua premuntur egestate (sicut res est malesuada fames) ut inhonesta exerceant commercia, ac munia sacerdotibus obeant indigna. Quæ res ansam subinde ministrat, verè Ecclesiasticos, ac Christo sacros Presbyteros floccipendendi, nihiliq; faciendi; quòd illorum vita coram universo populo offendiculis sit quam refertissima. Interim à quibusdam Episcopis, sex corruptis testibus ad hoc adhibitis, dignus ne sit sacerdotii munere, vel minus, ordinandus, fides adhibetur; qui passim quoq; indignissimos simulatis suis vocibus testantur dignos, adque hoc ministerium aptos ferunt & accommodos: licet non raro nullus personatorum illorum testuum, ordinandum, vel de facie, albus an ater sit, noverit; conanturq; ita Christianis sanctionibus, sub persona, fuco, atq; fictitio tantum prætextu satisfacere.
units.tr: 47. Likewise archbishops, bishops, and their assistants, whom they call suffragans, very often ordain to the priestly office many unlearned, ignorant, unfit, and worthless or frivolous persons. Since these men cannot live from the ministry of the Church, for which they are poorly suited, and they have no other means, either from benefices or from their own inherited property, by which they could lead a life worthy of a priest, but carry with them only imaginary and fictitious titles, and sometimes not even these, they then turn either to their innate malice or frivolous morals, or to the want that presses them (as hunger, the bad counsellor, drives them), so that they engage in dishonourable trades and undertake duties unworthy of priests. This situation gives occasion to despise and think nothing of those who are truly ecclesiastical and priests consecrated to Christ, since the lives of such men are a most abundant stumbling-block before the whole people. Meanwhile, by some bishops, six corrupt witnesses are brought in for this purpose, and credence is given to them as to whether a candidate is worthy of the priestly office, or less worthy, to be ordained. These witnesses, here and there, also testify with their feigned voices that the most unworthy men are worthy and fit and suited to this ministry, although not infrequently none of those masked witnesses knows the candidate to be ordained, even by sight, whether he is white or black. And they try in this way to satisfy the Christian sanctions by a mask, a disguise, and a merely fictitious pretext.

units.la: CAP. XXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXV.

units.la: De impensis immodicis, quæ in Ecclesiarum consecratione insumuntur.
units.tr: On the excessive expenses incurred in the consecration of churches.

units.la: 48. Insuper quum Ecclesias ac templa, prætenuia quidem, Deo dicant, sacrantq; nonnulli Suffraganeorum, subditos utcunq; per se egestate laborantes, superfluis, minimeq; necessariis sumptibus onerant: neq; hoc contenti, quin munera quoque, & illa quidem immodica, à misera plebecula exigant.
units.tr: 48. Moreover, when some suffragans dedicate and consecrate churches and sanctuaries, however modest they are, they burden their subjects, who already labour in poverty, with superfluous and by no means necessary expenses. Not content with this, they also demand gifts from the wretched common people, and those gifts are excessive.

units.la: 49. Item quum laici Ecclesiis altaris donant ornamenta quædam, necnon casulas, & similia, ac in Dei honorem pecunias suas expendunt; nihilominus tamen Suffraganei exigunt, ut talia, priusquam ad altaris convertantur usum, consecrentur, pro qua demum consecratione munera accedonapetuntur innumera. Quapropter æquum est, ut tales abusus deleantur. Et si Suffraganei frustra laborare nolint, ut unicuiq; prælato aut plebano talia faciendi permittatur potestas.
units.tr: 49. Likewise, when laymen give certain ornaments to the churches for the altar, as well as chasubles and the like, and spend their money for the honour of God, the suffragans nevertheless insist that such things be consecrated before they are put to use at the altar, and for this consecration they demand countless fees. Therefore it is right that such abuses be abolished. And if the suffragans are unwilling to labour in vain, let every prelate or parish priest be granted the power to do such things.

units.la: CAP. XXXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVI.

units.la: Quemadmodum cæmiteria nonnunquam superflut, ac minimè necessario consecrentur.
units.tr: How cemeteries are sometimes superfluous, and are consecrated when there is no need.

units.la: 50. Demum, si forte sine armis, pugnis tantùm & capillis in cœmiterio, duo, plures ve manus conferant, aut rixam habeant, ad sanguinis usq; quantumvis modici effusionem; tum ad incredibilem Ecclesiasticorum severitatem recurrunt Ecclesiastici, nec priùs publica Christianorum redintegrant officia, quia civium universitas cœmiterium denuo magna pompa, gravibusq; nec profecto minoribus impensis consecrari curaverit, quàm primum, ut prædictum est, ex prophano redditus sit sepultur æ is locus cel. Quæ omnia in caput tandem redundant laicorum.
units.tr: 50. Finally, if perhaps two or more men come to blows in a cemetery, without weapons, using only fists and hair, or have a brawl, even to the shedding of blood, however small, then the Ecclesiastics resort to an incredible severity. They do not restore the public offices of the Christians until the body of citizens has had the cemetery consecrated again with great ceremony and at no smaller expense than before, since, as has been said, the place was restored from profane to burial use. All these burdens in the end fall back on the heads of the laity.

units.la: 51. Item, Suffraganei excogitaverunt, ut solùm ipsi, & nullus alius Sacerdos, laicis campanas baptisent: credunt deinde simpliciores, ita affirmantibus Suffraganeis, tales campanas baptisatas, dæmones & tempestates pellere. Quapropter innumeri plerunque adhibentur compatres: præcipuè verò, qui fortuna pollent, exorantur, qui baptisationis tempore furem, quo campana religata est, fangunt, ac Suffraganeo præcinente, (quemadmodum in parvulorum baptisatione fieri solet) omnes pariter respondent, ac campanæ nomen ingeminant, vestéque nova, quemadmodum & Christianis fieri solet, campana induitur. Inde ad sumptuosa properatur convivia, quibus præcipuè compatres, ut eò languùs munera offerant, adhibentur; necnon Suffraganei & eorum Capellani, cum multis aliis ministris regaliter pascuntur. Nec hoc satis est, sed & Suffraganeo mercedem persolvere necesse est, quam illi munusculum vocare solent. inde evenit, ut aliquando etiam in parvis villis centum floreni in tali absumantur & expendantur baptisatione: quæ res non solùm superstitiosa, sed etiam Christianæ religioni contraria, ac simpliciorum seductio, & mera est exactio. Veruntamen Episcopi, ut Suffraganeos vel vilissima obærare possint mercede, talia & adhuc absurdiora tolerant. Res igitur tam nephanda & illicita merito aboleri debet. Cæterum si conducere videtur, ut campanæ consecrentur (ita enim Suffraganei baptisationem appellant, quoties à prudentioribus de hac re interpellantur) conveniens erit, ut talis consecratio per unum quenque fiat sacerdotem: quemadmodum cum aqua benedicta, sale, herbis, & similibus fieri solet: idque absque precio & expensis laicorum; ne populus simplex ita educatur, & damno afficiatur, nec non avaritiæ detestandæ præsumptio evitetur.
units.tr: 51. Likewise, the Suffragans have devised that only they, and no other priest, may baptise bells for the laity. The simpler folk then believe, the Suffragans assuring them of it, that bells so baptised drive away demons and storms. For this reason countless godparents are usually summoned, and especially those who are wealthy are begged to attend. At the time of the baptism they touch the rope by which the bell is hung, and while the Suffragan chants in front (as is customary in the baptism of infants), they all respond together and repeat the bell's name. The bell is dressed in a new garment, just as Christians are. Then they hasten to lavish feasts, to which the godparents especially are invited so that they may offer gifts for the occasion; and the Suffragans and their chaplains, together with many other ministers, are feasted like kings. Nor is this enough; they must also pay the Suffragan a fee, which they customarily call a little gift. Hence it happens that sometimes even in small villages a hundred florins are spent and laid out on such a baptism. This practice is not only superstitious and contrary to the Christian religion, but is also a deception of the simpler folk and sheer extortion. Yet the bishops tolerate such things, and even more absurd ones, so that the Suffragans may be kept in debt even at the cheapest rate of pay. Such an unspeakable and unlawful practice ought therefore rightly to be abolished. Moreover, if it seems advisable that bells be consecrated (for so the Suffragans call the baptism whenever the more prudent question them about this matter), it would be fitting for such consecration to be performed by any one priest, as is customary with holy water, salt, herbs and the like, and that without charge and without expense to the laity; so that the simple folk are not led astray and harmed, and the presumption of detestable greed is avoided.

units.la: CAP. XXXVII. Quemadmodum de nova sancti cujuspiam celebritate partem petant oblationis.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVII. How bishops claim a share of the offerings made at the new celebration of some saint.

units.la: 52. Deinceps, si forte per diœcesin Episcopi alicujus nova effertur Sancti celebritas, ad quem passim concursus fit; tum Episcopi aut Prælati eo loci, oblationum omnium tertiam, aut certè quartam partem sibi vendicare præsumunt. Quod tamen domesticae eorum, nempe canonica jura, eis non permittunt; quin oblata illa pecunia, potiùs ac merito, pro totius Christianæ reipub. necessitate, ad contrahendam militum manum, parandumq; expeditioni bellicæ commeatum contra Turcas usurpatetur; aut certè in proximi verteretur necessarios usus.
units.tr: 52. Furthermore, if perhaps a new celebration of some saint is celebrated throughout the diocese of any bishop, to which people flock from everywhere, then the bishops or prelates of that place presume to claim for themselves a third, or at least a fourth, part of all the offerings. Yet their own canon law does not permit them to do so; rather, that money which has been offered ought, more properly and rightly, to be used for the needs of the whole Christian commonwealth: to raise a body of soldiers and to provide supplies for a military expedition against the Turks, or at least to be turned to the necessary uses of the neighbourhood.

units.la: CAP. XXXVIII. Quo pacto illicitam à Præpositis monasteriorum Deo dicatarum virginum petant pecuniam.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVIII. In what way they demand money from the Provosts of the monasteries of virgins dedicated to God, which is unlawful.

units.la: 53. Item, quum monasteria aliqua Deo dicatarum virginum, per Præpositos, seu Præfectos gubernentur, qui tamen ad libitum officio hoc moveri possunt (neq; enim perpetua est hæc Præpositura) attamen Episcopi, acceptatione aut missioni Præpositorum, prius consensum suum adhibere recusant, quàm à monasteriorum Deo devotarum, simpliciumq; puellarum, pecuniæ aliquid numeratum fuerit.
units.tr: 53. Likewise, since some monasteries of virgins dedicated to God are governed by Provosts or Prefects, who may nevertheless be removed from this office at will (for this Provostship is not perpetual), yet the bishops refuse to give their consent to the acceptance or sending of the Provosts until some money has been counted out from the monasteries of women devoted to God and from the simple girls.

units.la: 54. Item, quum Abbas quispiam, aut Abbatissa eligitur, coguntur iterum per Suffraganeos consecrari; licet antea ut monachi & moniales satis superq; sint consecrati; Suffraganeumq; cum suis regie excipere & pascere, ac insuper tanquam muneris loco, magnam persolvere pecuniam. Quæ res non in parvum damnum cedit monasteriorum; sed etiam illorum, quibus monasteria illa sunt subjecta.
units.tr: 54. Likewise, when some abbot or abbess is elected, they are compelled to be consecrated again by the suffragans, although before they had already been consecrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently as monks and nuns; and the suffragan receives and feeds them royally with his people, and moreover pays a large sum of money as though it were a gift. This matter results in no small loss to the monasteries, but also to those to whom those monasteries are subject.

units.la: Insuper Pontifices Summi multa ac varia in curia Romana excogitarunt officia, quæ ipsi immani vendunt precio: quod quidem illi persolvere coguntur, qui (ita jubète pontifice) opera talium indigent officialium, seu scriptorum. Hinc evenit, ut natio Germanica, præcipuè verò Episcopi, quoties Pallium redimunt, aut confirmationem à Romano petunt Pontifice, ac multi alii oppidò aggraventur, ac longe plus, quàm elapsis annis, pecunias suas dilapidare compellantur. Hinc facilè conjicere licer, quot Romæ, quantiq; laquei pro emungendis nummis tendantur. Quapropter talia officia merito deleri debent.
units.tr: Besides, the Supreme Pontiffs have devised many and various offices in the Roman curia, which they sell at an enormous price; and those who need the services of such officials or scribes are indeed compelled to pay this (as the pontiff commands). Hence it happens that the German nation, and especially the bishops, whenever they redeem the pallium or ask for confirmation from the Roman pontiff, and many others, are heavily burdened and are forced to squander far more money than in past years. From this it is easy to conjecture how many and how great the snares are that are set in Rome for squeezing out money. Therefore such offices ought rightly to be abolished.

units.la: CAP. XXXIX. De Archipresbyterorum officialibus, & aliis judicibus Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIX. Concerning the officials of the archpriests, and other ecclesiastical judges.

units.la: 55. Archipresbyterorum quoq; officiales, ut plurimùm, sunt indocti, inhabiles; insuper & scurrilibus moribus, nihil pensi habentes, nihil aventes, quam pecuniam. Et quàm notorie in publicis degant peccatis ac facinoribus, quotidiano discitur usu; per quod laici, quos ob admissa debito modo corripere, ac in pietate Christiana eruditiores & meliores reddere debebant, nedum ad meliorem frugem non perducuntur, sed offendiculis onerantur potiùs. Adhæc per leves ac viles has officialium personas, in quorum conscientiis, nulla Christianæ pietatis viget ratio, sed tantùm sceleratus habendi amor, laici miserè ad vivum usq; in bonis suis spoliantur, ac depræddantur. Id quod Archiepiscopi & Episcopi, si quidem revera, quod dicuntur, essent, hoc est Christi pastores, dubio procul, diutiùs non tolerarent, quovesq; Christi talibus offendiculosis pastoribus curandas, minimè commendarent, pascendasve committerent.
units.tr: 55. The officials of the archpriests too are, for the most part, unlearned and unfit; moreover, with buffoonish morals, they have no regard for anything but money and care for nothing else. How notoriously they live in open sins and crimes is learned from daily experience; through this, the laity, whom they ought to rebuke properly for the faults they have committed and make more learned and better in Christian piety, are not only not brought to better conduct but are rather burdened with stumbling-blocks. Besides, through these slight and worthless officials, in whose consciences there flourishes no principle of Christian piety, but only a wicked love of getting, the laity are wretchedly stripped and plundered of their goods down to the quick. Archbishops and bishops, if they really were what they are called, that is, the shepherds of Christ, undoubtedly would not tolerate this for long, nor would they entrust Christ's flock to be cared for and fed by such stumbling-block shepherds.
Rr

units.la: Cap. XL.
units.tr: Chapter 40.

units.la: Quàm iniquè laici ad vetitum trahantur Ecclesiasticorum tribunal.
units.tr: How unjustly laymen are dragged before the ecclesiastical court, which is forbidden.

units.la: . 56. Ferè & hoc quoq; accidit, ut laici ad Ecclesiasticorum, licet perinique, trahantur judicium. Nam etiamsi actor sit Ecclesiasticus, qui laicum reum judicio convenire intendit; attamen nihilominus ordinariæ jurisdictioni reorum deferunt, quin passim Ecclesiastici tales reos, laicos scilicet quacunq; etiam ob causas civiles ac planè prophanas, ad Ecclesiasticum tribunal, refragantibus omnibus etiam juribus, pertrahere adnituntur: quum tamen maximè conveniat, ac jure non ignoto sit, quem expressim cautum, actorem rei forum sequi debere.
units.tr: 56. It also happens, almost commonly, that laymen are dragged to the judgment of ecclesiastics, however unjustly. For even if the plaintiff is an ecclesiastic who intends to bring a layman accused before a court, nonetheless they defer to the ordinary jurisdiction of the accused; yet everywhere ecclesiastics strive to drag such accused laymen, even in civil and utterly secular matters, before an ecclesiastical tribunal, with all laws resisting. Yet it is most fitting, and is a well-known principle of law, that the plaintiff should follow the forum of the defendant, as is expressly provided.

units.la: Cap. XLI.
units.tr: Chapter 41.

units.la: Quo pacto magistratuum civilium subditi, propter debitam pecuniam, ad judicia Ecclesiastica pertrahantur.
units.tr: How the subjects of civil magistrates are dragged before ecclesiastical courts on account of money owed.

units.la: 57. Præterea Ecclesiastici sæpiusculè laicorum subditos, ob debita pecuniaria, coram Ecclesiastico judice in jus vocant, ac prægravi eorum judiciorum ordine eosdem inibi vexant atq; executionem licet à civili magistratu, adeoq; judice reorum, ordinaria justitia, jurisq; debita executio eis nunquam fuerit vel denegata, vel diutiùs, quàm par sit, procrastinata: fitq; ita per actorem, ut dictum est, petuantiam, quia conventi judicio Ecclesiastico laici, varios ob casus jus suum non ita examussim, vel deducere per imprudentiam, vel non probare per simplicitatem, noverunt, neq; edocti sunt, utin praetentam pronunciantur excommunicationem, ac irreparabile rerum suarum perdu cantur detrimentum, perniciem & jacturam.
units.tr: 57. Furthermore, the ecclesiastical authorities quite often summon the subjects of laymen before an ecclesiastical judge on account of money debts, and harass them there with the very heavy procedure of their courts. Although execution could never have been denied them by the civil magistrate, that is, by the ordinary judge of the accused, nor delayed longer than is proper, and although the debt could be exacted by ordinary justice, it happens in this way, as has been said, through the plaintiff's obstinacy. The laymen who are summoned before an ecclesiastical court, not knowing how to set out their right exactly in various cases, either through imprudence fail to set it out, or through simplicity fail to prove it. Not having been instructed, they are pronounced under the threatened excommunication, and suffer irreparable loss, ruin and damage to their property.

units.la: Cap. XLII.
units.tr: Chapter 42.

units.la: Quàm iniquè laicis judicibus præbeatur occasio, ab Ecclesiasticis subditorum suorum petendi rem sionem.
units.tr: How unjustly an occasion is given to lay judges to be petitioned by their subjects' ecclesiastical judges (for the purpose of remitting cases).

units.la: 58. Insuper & alias ob plures causas illicitas, à judicibus Ecclesiasticis contra personas laicas mittuntur citationes ac monitoria: quanquam tales judices, publica etiam testante fama, indubitanter perspectum habeant, vocatos ita in jus ad ditionis suæ terminos minimè pertinere, illosq; ad ordinarium jus remittendos fore. Quod ipsum quoq; laicorum subjectis, non ferendis modis, graveonerosumq; est. Nam & si causæ, personæq; tales, ad instantiam magistratuum civilium, ac laicorum superiorum petitione, tandem ad jus dicetis laici-ordinarium remittantur tribunal: nihilominus tamen ita immeritò in jus vocati, gravibus onerantur impendiis, damnis, & expensis; eò quòd superiores suos laicos, quos non raro ultra centesimum lapidem peregrè abesse contingit, primùm requirere, deinde literas missionum ab his impetrare, ac tandem eas ipsas judicibus Ecclesiasticis mittere cogantur: interim nuncis ad hoc conducti eroganda est pecunia, cessandum à quotidianis operibus, ferendæ impensæ itinerum atque Advocatorum. Quòd si fortè superiores suos in jus vocati non continuò imploraverint, missionum literas impetrarint, easq; judicibus prædictis transmiserint ac ad monitionem usque processum interea sit: jam Ecclesiastici judices vel requisiti hinc à vocatorum superioribus, quæcunque tandem in jus vocati sit causa, remittere tamen ita vocatos atque admonitos ad ordinarium judicem laicum, recusant.
units.tr: 58. Moreover, for many other unlawful reasons, citations and monitory letters are sent out by ecclesiastical judges against lay persons, although such judges, even by public report, are undoubtedly aware that those summoned into court in this way do not belong within the bounds of their jurisdiction, and that they will have to be sent back to the ordinary court. This too is a burden on lay subjects, and an intolerable one. For even if such cases and persons, at the instance of the civil magistrates and at the petition of superior laymen, are at last remitted to the ordinary lay court for judgment, nevertheless those who have been summoned into court undeservedly are burdened with heavy expenses, losses and costs. This is because they are compelled first to seek out their lay superiors, who are not infrequently absent abroad more than a hundred miles away; then to obtain letters of dismissal from them; and finally to send those letters themselves to the ecclesiastical judges. Meanwhile money must be paid to messengers hired for this purpose, daily work must be given up, and the costs of journeys and of advocates must be borne. But if, perhaps, their superiors have not at once been petitioned by those summoned into court, and have not obtained letters of dismissal and sent them to the said judges, and if in the meantime the proceedings have gone on as far as the monition, the ecclesiastical judges, even when asked by the superiors of those summoned, refuse to remit those summoned and warned, whatever the cause for which they were brought into court, to the ordinary lay judge.

units.la: Cap. XLIII.
units.tr: Chapter 43.

units.la: Quòd judices Ecclesiastici causas aliquot speciales, licet laicas, ita sua afferant ditioni, ut omnino eas remittere nolint.
units.tr: That ecclesiastical judges so claim certain special causes, even though they are lay causes, as their own jurisdiction that they are wholly unwilling to remit them.

units.la: 59. Quùm apud Ecclesiasticum judicem, ob decerptum virginitatis florem: item ob illegitimè natorum, hoc est, naturalium liberorum statum, aut servientium mercedem, viduarumve, quaecunq; etiam judicio ventilantur causæ, contra laicos reos; tum vel interpellati à litigantium laicorum superioribus, judices Ecclesiastici, terminum tamen sistendi jure, nec circumducere, aut ad se in jus vocatos, ordinariæ jurisdictioni ut remittant, precibus induci possunt.
units.tr: 59. When before an ecclesiastical judge, in cases concerning the plucking of a maiden's flower of virginity, likewise concerning the status of illegitimately born children, that is, natural children, or concerning the wages of servants or of widows, whatever causes are debated in court against lay defendants, then the ecclesiastical judges, even when petitioned by the superiors of the lay litigants, cannot be induced by entreaties to withhold the term of appearance in law, nor to delay the matter, nor to remit those summoned before them to the ordinary lay judge.

units.la: Cap. XLIV.
units.tr: Chapter 44.

units.la: De aliis illicitis & inutilibus expensis causarum prophanarum atque ad Ecclesiasticos judices trahuntur, ac denuò remittuntur.
units.tr: Concerning other unlawful and needless expenses of secular suits which are drawn before ecclesiastical judges and then sent back again.

units.la: 60. Adhæc, quum laicus coram judice Ecclesiastico, ut suprà dictum est, iniquè in jus vocatur, demumq; ad petitionem judicis ordinarii remittitur: tunc temere agentis procurator, qui tam malè in jus vocari fecerat laicum reum, mercedem suam, à convento, qui tamen temerè ad vetitum tractus fuit judicium, petit; cogitaque dehinc excommunicationis poena innocens ille ultra expensas, quæ ob malam in jus vocationem in itinera, procuratores, proque impetrandis & redimendis missionum literis, necessariò expenderat. Adde & neglectorum operum æstimationem, jam tandem nulliter & inique emissos judiciarios persolvere, atque ære non immodico, coactus licet, pensare. Namque id si forte recusat, anathematis præstò est gladius: hoc ei minantur judices Ecclesiastici fulmen, ni persolutis vocationum literis, habendi libidinem ipsorum satiaverint. Ita afflictu additurafli tio. Neq; judis ratio, quæ temerè in jus vocato, refundendas dictat expensas, à judicibus his curatur quicquam: imò judiciarius hic eorum ordo, ex diametro, quod ajunt, cum juris boniq; & æqui ordine pugnat. Eum tamen judiciorum ordinem, non ob aliud (quantum conjectura assequi licet) hactenus ita religiosè observarunt, quàm ut plurima actorum turba per hocad eorum alliceretur tribunal. Ita semper iniquum, ex re, quæ merito debebat esse æquissima, studeant facere lucrum.
units.tr: 60. Moreover, when a layman is wrongly summoned before an ecclesiastical judge, as was said above, and is at last remitted at the request of the ordinary judge, the procurator of the rash plaintiff, who had caused the layman defendant to be so wrongly summoned, demands his fee from the party sued, although he was drawn into a case forbidden to him. That innocent man is then threatened with the penalty of excommunication, over and above the expenses which he was necessarily obliged to lay out because of the wrongful summons: the journeys, the procurators, and the cost of obtaining and redeeming the letters of remission. Add to this the estimate of his neglected work, and that he is compelled, though against his will, to pay the judicial fees, issued at last null and unjust, and to settle them with no small sum of money. For if he happens to refuse this, the sword of anathema is at hand: the ecclesiastical judges threaten him with this thunderbolt, unless, once the letters of summons have been paid, he satisfies their greed for having. Thus affliction is added to affliction. Nor do these judges take any account of the principle of justice, which dictates that the expenses be refunded to the man rashly summoned; that judicial order of theirs fights, as the saying goes, diametrically against the order of law, good and equity. Yet they have hitherto observed that order of judicial proceedings so scrupulously for no other reason (as far as conjecture allows us to grasp) than that by this means a great crowd of litigants might be enticed to their tribunal. Thus they always strive to make gain from a thing which ought rightly to be most equitable, and make it unjust.

units.la: CAP. XLV.
units.tr: CAP. XLV.

units.la: Quomodo nova per violentiam instituantur decimarum pres- tationes.
units.tr: How new tithe payments are imposed by violence.

units.la: 61. Item, etsi laici per multa annorum curricula de certis eorum prædiis, neq; majores, neque exiguas, ut vocant, præstiterint decimas: tamen per Ecclesiasticos judices, apud quos iniquis litigant conditionibus, auctoritate judiciaria, ita eis fit negotium, ut aut peritas judicio decimas, sive quidpiam aliud est, quod ab eis exigitur, præstare, persolvere, aut excommunicationis pœnam ferre, necessum habeant. Neq; hoc temerè. Nam etiamsi à sententia, quantumvis iniqua, Romam appellaverint, non eos fugit, quàm onerosus atq; dispar fit & illic litium eventus.
units.tr: 61. Likewise, although for many years laymen have not paid greater or lesser tithes, as they are called, on certain of their lands, the ecclesiastical judges, before whom they litigate on unfair terms, so manage the matter by judicial authority that they are compelled either to pay the tithes, or whatever else is demanded from them, or to bear the penalty of excommunication. And this is not done lightly. For even if they have appealed from the sentence, however unjust, to Rome, they are not unaware how burdensome and unequal the outcome of lawsuits there is too.

units.la: CAP. XLVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVI.

units.la: Quo pacto Ecclesiasticorum officiales ac suffecti, & ipsi laicos ad Ecclesiasticorum tribunal in jus trahere conentur.
units.tr: How the officials and deputies of the clergy, and the clergy's own subordinates, also try to drag laymen before the ecclesiastical court.

units.la: 62. Ad hæc omnia personæ Ecclesiasticæ, nedum ipsæ per se laicos, quibus dictum est, ac similibus casibus, ad Ecclesiasticos trahunt judices; verùm etiam Ecclesiasticorum officiales, suffecti, procuratores, domestici famuli, famulæq;, ac deniq, ipsorum etiam subditi, conantur, adniituntur; idem juris quod eorum habent superiores, sibi ipsis quoq; afferere, usurpareq;.
units.tr: 62. Besides all these cases, ecclesiastical persons drag laymen before ecclesiastical judges not only themselves, in the matters mentioned and in similar cases; but also the officials, deputies, agents, domestic servants, both men and women, and finally even the subjects of the clergy themselves strive and labour to claim and usurp for themselves the same right that their superiors possess.

units.la: CAP. XLVII.
units.tr: CAP. XLVII.

units.la: De causis injuriarum, quæ coram Ecclesiastico ventilantur judicio.
units.tr: On causes of injuries that are brought before an ecclesiastical court.

units.la: 63. Tandem, si quando ex facto evenit, ut Ecclesiasticus contra laicum injuriarum agere, illas forte verbo injurias, intendat: conatur Ecclesiasticus judex eas ipsas quoq; suæ jurisdictioni vendicare causas quo denuo reus judicio conventus, ordinario juri, suæque eripitur atque eximitur jurisdictioni.
units.tr: 63. Finally, if it ever happens in fact that an ecclesiastic brings a suit against a layman for injuries, or perhaps for verbal injuries, the ecclesiastical judge tries to claim these very cases for his own jurisdiction, so that the defendant, once summoned to that court, is snatched away and removed from the ordinary law and from his own jurisdiction.

units.la: CAP. XLVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XLVIII.

units.la: Quemadmodum causæ prophanæ, ob interposita juramenta, Ecclesiastico tribunali afferantur.
units.tr: How secular causes are brought before the ecclesiastical tribunal on account of oaths interposed.

units.la: 64. Insuper & id præsumunt officiales, si quâdo in causis prophanis, acinter personas Ecclesiæ minim è sacratas, dicatásve, sed omnino laicas, data fide, seu præstito juramento, verbo, vel in scriptis, pacta, obligationes, contractus, vel promissiones factæ sint, vel celebratæ: quòd eam ob rem, atq; hujus prætextus ratione, tales prophanæ laicæq; causæ coram ipsis potiùs, quàm ordinario judice agitari debeant: quæ nova Ecclesiasticorum techna usu si increscceret, ac diutius toleraretur, jam actum foret de civili causarum auditorio, quòd omnes prophanæ civilesq; causæ, contractuum atq; transactionum, hac via necessariò ad Ecclesiasticos perraherentur. Quis enim contractus, quæ transactio, quæ denique inter paciscentes conventio, quæ non fit solenni ita stipulatione, aut promissione vallata? Illuc nimirum rerum veniremus, ut in totum civilia eluderentur iudicia. Quod nedum contra æquitatem ipsam, contra omnia iura scripta, sed & civili magistratui intolerabile foret. Nam ut demus hoc interim Ecclesiasticis judicibus, de perjurio commisso, notionem ut habeant: nihilo magis perid causæ ipsius principalis, contractus putà, aut transactionis, quamobrem ille pejeravit, judices competentes erunt; quin perjuros illos ob religionis transgressionem manifestariam tantùm iudicio convenire possent, ac Canonicam huic indicere multam; reservata tamen civili magistratui, qui perjuros pœnali judicio secundùm civiles sanctiones plectere jus habet, commissa sibi ob id pœna.
units.tr: 64. Moreover, the officials also presume this: if, in secular causes, that is, between persons who are not at all consecrated to the Church or dedicated to it, but wholly lay, a pledge has been given or an oath sworn, whether by word or in writing, and pacts, obligations, contracts or promises have been made or concluded, they claim that for this reason, and on the pretext of it, such secular and lay causes ought to be pursued before them rather than before the ordinary judge. If this new trick of the ecclesiastics were to gain ground by use and were tolerated for long, it would soon be all over with the civil hearing of causes, since all secular and civil causes of contracts and transactions would necessarily be drawn by this route before the ecclesiastics. For what contract, what transaction, indeed what agreement between parties is not made with a solemn stipulation or strengthened by a promise? We would come to the point where civil courts were entirely evaded. This would be intolerable not only against equity itself and against all written laws, but also for the civil magistrate. For, granting for the moment that the ecclesiastical judges may have cognizance of perjury committed, they will be no more competent judges of the principal cause itself, of the contract or transaction, for instance, on account of which the man perjured himself. Rather, they could summon those perjurers before their court only for the manifest transgression of religion, and impose on them the canonical fine; yet the penalty committed to the civil magistrate is reserved to him, who has the right to punish perjurers by a penal judgment according to the civil sanctions.

units.la: CAP. XLIX.
units.tr: CAP. XLIX.

units.la: Quonam modo reformationes suorum judiciorum nec observent, neq; manu, hoc est, executione debita tueantur.
units.tr: How they neither observe the reformations of their own courts nor uphold them by hand, that is, by due execution.

units.la: 65. Præterea, nedum rationi consona jura communia, sed & Ecclesiarum aliquot cathedralium propriæ Reformationes notoriæ, in quam plurimis casibus negliguntur, irritaq; fiunt, dum contra nus ex eisdem ducitur sensus. Exequuntur enim hæ contra hos tantùm, quorum potestatem ipsi non tevererentur. At si res potentiores, aut eos, quibus manu pares esse non possumus, contingat, tum ex juris sui rigore remittunt quippiam. Nam etsi maximè Episcopi locorum ordinarii, aut eorum officiarii à vim passis, aut his, quibus contra jus injuriæ illatæ sunt, pro debita justitiæ executione, ac talium gravaminum onerùmve abrogatione interpellentur. Sæpenumero tamen evenit, ut querela hæc, vel Præpositum contingat, vel Decanum, vel certè Capitulum, ac Ecclesiæ canonicos Capitulares, hoc est eos, contra quos loci hujus ordinarius Episcopus utcunque æquitati favens, remorante eum hac via, in electione praestita, ac promissa fide, meritam transgressionis emendationem atq; multam pro-sumere, eisq; infligere non audeat.
units.tr: 65. Moreover, not only the common laws, which are consonant with reason, but also the notorious particular reformations of several cathedral churches are in very many cases neglected and rendered void, while a sense contrary to their plain meaning is drawn from them. For these are enforced only against those whose power they do not fear. But if the matter concerns more powerful persons, or those with whom we cannot be equal in strength, then they relax somewhat of the rigour of their right. For even when the local ordinary bishops, or their officials, are petitioned by those who have suffered violence, or by those to whom injury has been done contrary to law, for the due execution of justice and the abrogation of such grievances or burdens, it nevertheless often happens that this complaint touches the provost, or the dean, or at least the chapter and the canons of the church, that is, those against whom the bishop of the place, however favourable he may be to equity, does not dare to impose the deserved correction of the transgression and fine, being held back by this way of proceeding, namely the oath taken at election and the promised faith.

units.la: 66. Ad haec Episcoporum ac Praelatorum nonnulli, pro tempore Ecclesiasticorum iudicorum Synodorumq;, ad suum libitum, speciales quasdam & praetentas ferunt reformationes, ordinationes, leges atq; statuta, quae ipsa multifariam a iure communi diffident, ac scorsim toti civili magistratui et iurisdictioni, eorumq; subditis derogant, atq; perniciem adferunt. Neq; ullam prae se ferentia aequitatem, quod ad Ecclesiasticorum privata compendia, inq; laicorum necem sint excogitata atq; effecta. Eamque ob rem laici ea acceptare, aut his parere minime tenentur. Nam neque ipsi Ecclesiastici ad mesticas has suas constitutiones secundum rationabilem, synceriorem, ac germanum aequitatis intellectum, observant. Etenim tametsi reformationes huiusmodi, ut plurimum statuant, coram officialibus, eorumq; Ecclesiasticis consistoriis, manifesta ac notoria tantum, minimeq; occulta debere agitari atq; ventilari, considerari; in primis salutem animarum, & honorem Iesu Christo debitum, potius quam pecuniarum lucrum: Attamen ejus rei oppositum, atque ex professo contra negotium ipsum, innumeraq; aliae coniecturae ac circumstantiae plus liquido manifestum reddunt quod partim ex supra enumeratis, partim ex recensendis sequentibus articulis, utcunq; succincte, aestimare facile est.
units.tr: 66. Besides this, some of the bishops and prelates, according to the time, at their own pleasure, issue certain special and so-called reformations, ordinances, laws and statutes for ecclesiastical courts and synods, which in many ways differ from the common law, and which detract from the whole civil magistracy and its jurisdiction, and its subjects, and bring ruin upon them. They show no appearance of equity; rather they have been devised and carried out for the private gain of ecclesiastics and the ruin of laymen. For this reason laymen are in no way bound to accept them or obey them. For the ecclesiastics themselves do not observe these domestic constitutions of theirs according to a reasonable, purer and genuine understanding of equity. Indeed, although reformations of this kind mostly provide that only manifest and notorious matters, and by no means hidden ones, ought to be pursued and examined before the officials and their ecclesiastical consistories, and above all that the salvation of souls and the honour owed to Jesus Christ should be considered rather than gain of money; yet the opposite of this, and openly against the very business itself, and countless other conjectures and circumstances, make it more than plainly evident, which, partly from what has been listed above and partly from the following articles to be recounted, may easily be judged, however briefly.

units.la: CAP. L.
units.tr: CAP. L.

units.la: Quomodo plus pecuniae, quam poenitentiae peccatoribus imponant.
units.tr: How the ecclesiastical judges impose more money than repentance upon sinners.

units.la: 67. Patrum canonibus sancitum est, spiritualibus ac manifestis peccatis, spiritualem poenitentiam seu satisfactionem imponendam esse; ut sic non pecuniae lucrum, sed potius animarum quaeri intelligatur. Id quod supra etiam memoratum est. At Ecclesiastici iudices & officiales, perpetram animadversis canonibus, dictam spiritualem poenitentiam in tantum exasperant, aggravant & augent, ut laici, priusquam eam satisfactionem acceptare velint, pecunia magis sibi ab ipsis unmitatem comparent: qua re laici multum premuntur, Ecclesiastici contra multum ditantur, utpote, qui in suum privatum commodum, & partis agunt munus, & judicis; quod tamen omnibus iunibus dissonum est.
units.tr: 67. It has been enacted by the canons of the Fathers that for spiritual and manifest sins a spiritual repentance or satisfaction is to be imposed, so that it may be understood that the aim is the gain of souls and not the gain of money. This has been mentioned above as well. But the ecclesiastical judges and officials, in plain contravention of the canons, so exaggerate, aggravate and increase the said spiritual repentance that the laymen, before they are willing to accept that satisfaction, buy their release from them with money. By this practice the laity are greatly burdened, while the churchmen are greatly enriched, since they act in their own private advantage and play the part both of party and of judge, which is nevertheless at odds with all laws.

units.la: CAP. LI.
units.tr: CAP. LI.

units.la: Quem in modum honesti viri & mulieres ex falso rumore saepenumero graventur.
units.tr: In what manner honest men and women are often burdened by false rumour.

units.la: 68. Accidit etiam nonnunquam, quod viri & mulieres coram Officiali, seu Ecclesiastico tribunali, ut delictorum ac scelerum fontes, siniistro rumore deferuntur, ac non prius per sententiam innocentes declarantur, quam ubi se iurejurando purgaverint: qua purgatione facta, in pristinum aestimationis statum restituuntur. Et quamvis tam siniistre denuntiatis incommoda, damna, impensas, eam ob rem perpessi, merito refundi deberent: nihilominus tamen innocentes ipsi in dictae restitutionis fidem Officiali, Ecclesiastico ve iudici, duos aureos, cum aurei quarta parte, pro absolutoriis litteris, nequaquam necessariis, numerare coguntur. Et hoc est, cur Officiales, Ecclesiasticique iudices, tam iniquas & illicitas, rumoris falsi, atq; delationis causas, ita adsectentur, ad se evocent, solisq; sibi vendicent. Id tamen ipsum non sine magna singulari, ac gravi iactura mortalium committunt.
