Nam saepius evenit, quod altercantes mulieres, ira, invidia, seu alio quopiam adfectu commotae, invicem se maledictis impetant, conviciis proscindant, in tantumq; demententur, quod altera alteram vel adulterii, vel magicae artis ream insimulet. Quod ubi coram Officiali deducitur, tum illa, quae per secundam alteram probris ac contumeliis adfecerat, iurisjurandi sacramento se excusare, ac purgare cogitur: scilicet, quicquid iniuriarum in alteram profuderit, id omne non ex certo animi proposito, sed ira, invidiaque profectum esse: pariterque modo altera, quae adulterii, necromantiaeve insimulata est, suam innocentiam, quodq; praedictorum nequaquam sibi conscia sit facinorum, iuramento detegere iubetur. Interim vero quilibet apud se facile coniicere poterit, in talibus causis, mulieribus, sive memoratorum scelerum vacuae sint, sive iisdem criminibus obnoxiae, iurandum tamen esse, dummodo famam, honorem, ac vitalem spiritum retinere velint. Qua ex re non solum illicitum pecuniam lucrum quaeritur; sed & deliberatae pejerationes exorquentur, saecularesque iurisdictiones, & iudices in eorum mulctandi officio impediuntur. Et sic contra rationem, impunita remanere delicta necessarium est.
units.tr: 68. It also happens at times that men and women are brought before the Official, or the ecclesiastical court, as sources of crimes and wickedness, on the strength of a sinister rumour, and are not declared innocent by sentence until they have cleared themselves by oath. When that purgation has been made, they are restored to their former standing and reputation. And although they ought rightly to be repaid for the inconveniences, losses and expenses they have suffered on account of so sinister an accusation, nevertheless the innocent are forced to pay the Official, or the ecclesiastical judge, two gold coins and a quarter of a gold coin, for letters of acquittal, which are in no way necessary, as a pledge of that restoration. And this is why the Officials and ecclesiastical judges pursue such unjust and unlawful causes of false rumour and accusation, summon them to themselves, and claim them solely for themselves. Yet they do this not without great and singular loss and harm to mortal men. For it very often happens that women who quarrel, moved by anger, envy, or some other passion, attack one another with curses and tear each other apart with abuse, and go so far in their madness that one accuses the other of adultery or of the art of magic. When this is brought before the Official, then the woman who had heaped insults and reproaches upon the other is compelled to excuse and clear herself by the sacrament of an oath: namely, that whatever injuries she poured out against the other proceeded not from a settled purpose of mind but from anger and envy. Likewise the other, who has been accused of adultery or necromancy, is ordered to disclose her innocence by oath, and that she is in no way conscious of the aforesaid crimes. Meanwhile, anyone may easily conjecture for himself that in such cases women must swear, whether they are free of the said crimes or liable to the same charges, provided only that they wish to keep their reputation, honour and vital breath. From this it results that not only is unlawful money-gain sought, but deliberate perjuries are also extorted, and secular jurisdictions and judges are hindered in their office of punishing them. And so it comes about, contrary to reason, that crimes must remain unpunished.

units.la: CAP. LII.
units.tr: CAP. LII.

units.la: Quomodo Ecclesiastici iudices illicitum ex iactatis matrimoniorum causis petant interesse.
units.tr: How ecclesiastical judges seek an unlawful interest in the disputed causes of marriage.

units.la: 69. Deinceps, quum inter virum atq; foeminam, de pangendis matrimonialibus sacris illis foederibus, negotium, quod inter eos forte agebatur, coeuq; processit, quod ab altera utra partium matrimonii contractus, ex pactionibus illis, ratus, perfectusq; praetendatur; at in ficietur altera: darumque est, ab altera alteri personae vestium, aut alioqui mundi muliebris quidpiam, tanquam arrabonis loco, adservandum ac custodiendum: accidatq; deinde, ut asserti contractus, matrimonii scil. contemplationem, contrahentes, ad Ecclesiasticum perveniant tribunal, ac ibidem per sententiam, in diversum ire iubeantur, separenturque: Tum judex ille Ecclesiasticus iniquè hoc sibi in hac causa praetendit interesse: nimirum, ut omne, quicquid hinc inde arrabonis vice traditum sit, ut hoc sibi cedat tanquam committum. Id quod nedum contra omnia jura, sed & æquitatem atque honestatem ipsam proculdubio est.
units.tr: 69. Next, when a matter arises between a man and a woman concerning the making of those sacred marriage covenants, and it happens to proceed as far as agreement, and one of the parties claims that the marriage contract was made, ratified and completed by those promises, but the other denies it; and something from a woman's dress or other finery is handed by one party to the other as an earnest, to be kept and guarded; and then it happens that the parties, on account of the alleged contract, namely the prospect of marriage, come before the ecclesiastical tribunal, and there by sentence are ordered to go their separate ways and are separated: then that ecclesiastical judge unjustly claims for himself, in this case, an interest, namely that whatever has been handed over on either side as an earnest should pass to him as forfeit. This is undoubtedly contrary not only to all laws, but to equity and decency itself.

units.la: CAP. LIII. Quibus artibus judices Ecclesiastici causas promiscuas, quae coram civili etiam magistratu in judicium deduci possunt, sibi solis vendicare conentur.
units.tr: CAP. LIII. By what arts ecclesiastical judges try to claim for themselves alone those mixed causes which may also be brought to trial before the civil magistrate.

units.la: 70. Item, licet complures sint causæ itα promiscuæ jurisdictionis, ut secundùm jura communia, apud Ecclesiasticos atque civiles judices agitari & puniri possint: sæpiusculè tamen evenit, ut quum civiles judices, concessam sibi hac in re provinciam & jurisdictionem administrare atq; exercere velint; quòd id ipsum ne faciant, per judices Ecclesiasticos, sub excommunicationis pœna eis interdicitur, prohibeturq;. Quod si diutius perstare deberet, brevi Ecclesiastici judices à civili magistratu, ejusq; jurisdictione, quascunq; etiam causas eximerent, suaeq; afferentt ditioni. Id quod Cæsareæ Majest. cæterisq; Imperii Romani membris grave est, & intolerabile. Et quanquam secundùm jura communia, manifesta perjuria atq; adulteria, maleficiorumq; præstigiæ, ac consimiles aliæ causæ, per Ecclesiasticos ac civiles judices, promiscuum, uter occuparit, civiliter pro tempore plecti possint, habeatq; ita præventio hac in re locum: Attamen Ecclesiastici judices contra omnia jura, causas hujuscemodi, solis sibi, suaeq; jurisdictioni usurpare conantur. Quod ipsum jurisdictioni civili non serendum est onus ac gravamen.
units.tr: 70. Likewise, although there are many causes of this mixed jurisdiction, which by the common law may be pursued and punished both before ecclesiastical and before civil judges, it very often happens that when civil judges wish to administer and exercise the jurisdiction and province granted to them in this matter, the ecclesiastical judges forbid and prohibit them, under penalty of excommunication, from doing so. If this were to continue for long, before long the ecclesiastical judges would withdraw from the civil magistrate and its jurisdiction whatever causes they could, and bring them under their own dominion. This is grievous and intolerable to the Imperial Majesty and to the other members of the Roman Empire. And although, according to the common law, manifest perjuries and adulteries, the sorceries of evildoers, and other similar causes may be punished civilly for the time being by either the ecclesiastical or the civil judges, whichever first takes them up, and prevention has its place in this matter, nevertheless the ecclesiastical judges attempt, against all law, to usurp such causes for themselves and their jurisdiction alone. This burden and grievance cannot be tolerated by the civil jurisdiction itself.

units.la: CAP. LIV. Quemadmodum causa prophana, sub prætextu denegatæ executionis, ad Ecclesiastico- rum consistoria trahuntur.
units.tr: CHAPTER LIV. How profane causes are dragged before the consistories of the ecclesiastics under the pretext of denied execution.

units.la: 71. Item, si quando personæ laicæ in causis etiam omnino prophanis, à judicibus Ecclesiasticis citationes impetrare conentur, prætendantque magistratum civilem, debitam sibi juris executionem facere neglexisse; ante quam summariè saltem per evidens aliquod docuerint instrumentum, justitiam, ut queruntur, sibi denegatam: citationes tamen, atque alii judiciarii processus à judicibus Ecclesiasticis, ad solam petentium querelam his decernuntur. Quòd si deinceps ad petitionem, vel civilis judicis, aut partis in jus vocatæ, causæ hujuscemodi ad ordinarium tribunal remittantur, præfigitur civili judici per breve quatuor hebdomadarum, putà tempus fatale; intra quod, actoris intentioni & querimoniæ ex integro, atq; exacte executionis ordine satisfaciat. Ac si in artissimo ita præstituto termino, sententia diffinitiva, aut non fertur, vel executioni lata non mandatur; libertatem dehinc judex Ecclesiasticus dat actori laico, coram suo tribunali, ulteriùs procedendum: fitque non raro, (mirum hoc auditu) ut causa, quæ intra mensis spacium coram civili consistorio agitari, peragiquè debebat, quòd hæc eadem apud Ecclesiasticum judicem triennio, aut eo amplius, pendeat hinc indecisa.
units.tr: 71. Likewise, if lay persons, even in wholly profane causes, try to obtain citations from ecclesiastical judges, alleging that the civil magistrate has failed to carry out the execution of the law owed to them, then, before they have shown, at least summarily, by some clear document, that justice has been denied them as they complain, citations and other judicial proceedings are nevertheless decreed by the ecclesiastical judges on the sole complaint of the petitioners. If afterwards, at the petition either of the civil judge or of the party summoned to court, such causes are remitted to the ordinary tribunal, a fatal period of four weeks is fixed for the civil judge by brief, within which he must satisfy the claimant's intention and complaint anew and carry out the order of execution exactly. And if within this very narrow fixed term a definitive sentence is either not pronounced or not handed down for execution, the ecclesiastical judge then gives the lay claimant liberty to proceed further before his own tribunal. And it often happens (a wonder to hear) that a case which ought to be argued and concluded before the civil court within a month remains undecided before the ecclesiastical judge for three years or longer.

units.la: 72. Ajunt prætetea judices Ecclesiastici, in talibus casibus, prophanas ad se causas pertrahere sibi licere; si magistratus civilis in administranda justitiæ executione negligens inveniatur: è regione tamen ferre minimè possunt, ut in pari casu idem juris cum eis servetur; nimirum ut in causis Ecclesiasticis quispiam, de neglecto cultu justitiæ ab Ecclesiasticis apud laicos, aut civiles magistratus conqueri, ac justitiam sibi per civiles magistratus administrari postulare possit: quanquam jura communia in genere diffiniant, statuantque quo pacto canonica civilibus, & è regione canonicis civilia jura opem suppetiasq; ferre debeant.
units.tr: 72. Furthermore, the ecclesiastical judges claim that in such cases it is lawful for them to draw profane causes to themselves if the civil magistrate is found negligent in administering the execution of justice. Yet on the other side they by no means can bear that the same right be observed toward them in a like case: namely, that in ecclesiastical causes someone may complain to lay persons or civil magistrates of the neglect of justice by the ecclesiastics, and may demand that justice be administered to him by the civil magistrates. Although the common laws in general define and establish how canonical matters ought to bring aid and support to civil ones, and civil matters in turn to canonical ones.

units.la: CAP. LV. Quo pacto Ecclesiastici judices, seculares causas, prætensa præscriptionis prætexтy, in se transferre conentur.
units.tr: CHAPTER LV. In what manner ecclesiastical judges attempt to transfer secular causes to themselves under the pretext of a claimed prescription.

units.la: 73. Neq; hoc pleriisque longa experientia rerum ac eruditione doctis probatur, quòd judices Ecclesiastici quibusdam in locis diuturni usus, quasi possessionis, adimpletæq; præscriptionis prætextu, laicorum controversias coram se dirimendas hactenus præsumpserunt. Nam ea ex re Cæsarea Majest. Romanumq; Imperium haud parum detrimenti patitur: utputa, quòd non minimus Imperii honor, temporalis scilicet jurisdictio, memoratæ præscriptionis velamine minuitur, attenuatur, & penitus ab Imperio ad Ecclesiasticos transfertur. Quod contra recepta, apertaq; jura, nemo est qui nesciat: quibus statuitur & cavetur, ut nulli præscriptioni, quantumvis longæ, adversus præeminentem, tum Papæ, tum Cæsaris potestatem sit locus.
units.tr: 73. Nor is this proved to most men learned through long experience of affairs and erudition: that ecclesiastical judges, in certain places, under the pretext of long-standing use, as of possession, and of completed prescription, have hitherto presumed to settle the disputes of laymen before themselves. For from this matter the Imperial Majesty and the Roman Empire suffer no small harm: for instance, that no small honour of the Empire, namely temporal jurisdiction, is diminished and weakened under the veil of the said prescription, and is wholly transferred from the Empire to the ecclesiastics. Who does not know that this is contrary to the received and open laws, by which it is laid down and provided that no prescription, however long, has place against the pre-eminent power, whether of the Pope or of the Emperor?

units.la: CAP. LVI. Quàm iniquè homicidæ, aliíq; peccatores, ab Ecclesiasticis judicibus duplici afficiantur pœna.
units.tr: CAP. LVI. How unjustly murderers and other sinners are punished twice over by the ecclesiastical judges.

units.la: 74. Quum divina humanaq; jura vetêt, ut nemo duabus cædi debeat virgis: meritò plectiq;, quibus cerebrum est, nonnullarum Cathedralium Ecclesiarum odiosa statuta, perversosque mores, quibus utrumque sexus homicidas, reliquosque majorum, minorumve criminum reos hucusque vexatunt, deterstantur. Nam hactenus servata est consuetudo, quòd homicidii, similiumq; facinorum, quos casus Episcopis reservatos vocant, rei, peractâ in aurem confessione, publicam poenitentiam, in totius populi conspectu, cum magno suorum ipsorum dedecore, ignominia, infamia, subire cogunt. Quare quidem poenitentiae forma non usquequaque improbanda foret; utpote, quae ad primitivae Ecclesiae institutA quàm proximè accederet: si hac contenti, non etiam ampliorem justo, peccantibus graviores, malèque; officiosi Officiales extorquerent pecuniae summam, duplicique delinquentes punirent poena. Quare, mirum quàm multi offendantur. Quòd quàm iniquum, quanìq; longè à Christi intentione alienum, cuiq; sanae mentis conjectura assequendum relinquitur.
units.tr: 74. Since divine and human law forbid that anyone be beaten with two rods, the odious statutes of certain cathedral churches should be struck down, and so should the perverse customs by which murderers of both sexes, and those accused of other major or minor crimes, have been harassed up to now. For the custom so far kept is that those guilty of murder and similar offences, which they call reserved cases for the bishops, after confessing in the ear, are compelled to undergo public penance, in full view of the whole people, to their own great disgrace, ignominy and infamy. Indeed the form of penance should not be condemned in every respect, since it comes very close to the institution of the primitive Church, if they were content with that and did not also extort from the guilty, beyond what is just, a greater sum of money, while the zealous officials punish offenders with a double penalty. So it is a wonder how many are offended. How unjust this is, and how far removed from the intention of Christ, is left for any sound mind to conjecture.

units.la: CAP. LVII. Quomodo funesta pecunia intuitu Ecclesiastici judices & officiales illegitimas cohabitationes & usuras tolerent.
units.tr: CHAP. LVII. How the ecclesiastical judges and officials, for the sake of accursed money, tolerate illegitimate cohabitations and usury.

units.la: 75. Praeterea Officiales, auri sacra pelle&ti fame, usuras ac pecuniae foenus illicitum, nedum interdicunt; sed & passim permittunt, fovent, ac tutantur. Insuper etiam Clericos, Religiosos, & seculares, accepto ab eisdem annuo censu, publicè cum suis concubinis, pellicibus, & aliis id genus meretricibus, illegitimè cohabitare, liberosque procreare sinunt. Quae res ambae quantum scandali, perniciei, detrimenti, fortunis, animabus & corporibus pariant, non est quod recenseatur; quum nemo ... si talpa caecutiat magis, non videat.
units.tr: 75. Moreover the officials, seized by the accursed hunger for gold, not only forbid usury and unlawful money-lending, but also everywhere permit, foster and protect it. Further, for an annual tax received from them, they publicly allow clerics, religious and laymen to live in illegitimate cohabitation with their concubines, mistresses and other women of that kind, and to beget children. How much scandal, ruin, loss to fortunes, souls and bodies these two things bring forth there is no need to recount, since no one ... if a mole grows more blind, does not see.

units.la: 76. Praeterea contingit aliquando, quòd alter conjugum, belli, votorum, seu alia quapiam causa peregrè proficiscatur; qui si aliquanto diutiùs, quàm alterius conferat libidini, abiit: tum Officialis alteri (pacta tamen numeratâ; priùs mercede satis magna) cum alia victitare personâ ac cohabitare indulget, non praehabita priùs diligenti vestigatione, super iterum sit abiens conjunx, an naturaliter cesserit. Et ne hoc eorum factum à quoquam calumniari posset, tolerantiae nomen ei, non sine mortalium offendiculo, sanctique matrimonii contemptu indiderunt.
units.tr: 76. Furthermore it sometimes happens that one spouse sets off abroad because of war, vows or some other cause. If he has gone away for somewhat longer than suits the other's lust, then the official, once a sufficiently large fee has been paid in advance, allows the other to live and cohabit with another person, without first making careful inquiry whether the returning spouse has perhaps died a natural death. And lest anyone could accuse their act, they gave it the name of tolerance, not without stumbling-block to mortals and contempt for holy matrimony.

units.la: CAP. LVIII. Ut officialium delegati, seu Synodales judices, illicitos è domibus census exigant.
units.tr: CHAP. LVIII. That the delegates of the officials, or synodal judges, exact illicit taxes from houses.

units.la: 77. Et hoc Germanis posthac non ferendum onus est, quòd Synodales judices quosdam regionum oppidula & vicos oftiatim peragrant, censusque è domibus annuos exigunt: quos ubi tenuis plebecula persolvere nequit, protinus cum excommunicationis jaculis petitur; ad eorum quoque censuum solutionem cum summa rei familiaris attritione, atque attenuatione compellitur. Quod ut penitus amoveri non potest gravamen, aliquo saltem fine ad aequi bonique regulam coërceatur.
units.tr: 77. And this is a burden the Germans must no longer bear: synodal judges go from door to door through certain small towns and villages of the regions and exact annual taxes from the houses. When the poor common people cannot pay, they are at once assailed with the darts of excommunication, and they are also compelled to pay these taxes with the complete ruin and impoverishment of their household means. Since this grievance cannot be wholly removed, let it at least be restrained by some limit, according to the rule of what is fair and good.

units.la: CAP. LIX. Quo pacto hebdomadaria pecunia à mechanicis exigatur.
units.tr: CHAP. LIX. In what manner weekly money is exacted from craftsmen.

units.la: 78. Pari modo proximè memorati judices, quibusdam in locis à tabularis, pistoribus, lanis, propolis, molitoribus, ejusdemque generis mechanicarum artium professoribus, qualibet septimana pecuniam postulant: quae forte per inopiam non soluta, Ecclesiastico ad id fulmine adiguntur.
units.tr: 78. In the same way the judges just mentioned, in certain places, demand money every week from carpenters, bakers, wool-workers, retailers, millers and practitioners of the same kind of mechanical arts. If, through poverty, it is not paid, they are struck with the ecclesiastical thunderbolt for this purpose.

units.la: CAP. LX. De iniquis Ecclesiasticorum arestis, ut vocant, & impedimentis.
units.tr: CHAP. LX. On the unjust ecclesiastical arrests, as they call them, and impediments.

units.la: 79. Non mediocrem item superioritatis & jurisdictionis temporalis jacturam Caesarea Majest. Romanumque Imperium patitur, ex malè observata hactenus, pluribus in locis, diuturna consuetudine: videlicet, quòd Ecclesiastici judices, ubi inter duos laicos civilis orta est controversia, ad alterius partis petitionem literas inhibitorias emittunt, quibus alteri partium mandant, ne inceptam coram seculari, seu suo judice, litem prosequatur; sed in Ecclesiastico coram se judicio comparent. Cui mandato ubi pars vocata obtemperat, & se suamque causam ad suum ordinarium judicem remittit, in judicio petit: tum primùm libellus, articuli, exceptiones, replicae, duplicae, & caeterae id genus scripturae, utrinque producuntur; quibus, reliquisque actis & agitatis, perlectis, numeratisque, portionibus, quàm ponderatis, tandem interloquuntur, controversiam coram se ventilandam esse. Cui sententiae parere, velint, nolint, parere coguntur: etiamsi maximè ea graventur: quòd appellationem ad Romanam interpositam, ob immensos, tum labores, tum impensas prosequi nequeant. Neque enim cuivis commodum est, adire Romam. An verò talibus, funestisque sententiis se suspectos reddant, necne; cuilibet bono viro conjiciendum relinquitur. Unum hoc certum est, quòd ex jam enumeratis casibus, copiosa civilium causarum sylva, jurisdictioni temporali, ac civili magistratui, indices subtrahitur atque eripitur. Quod non solùm juribus & aequitati, sed etiam rationi contrarium esse dignoscitur.
units.tr: 79. The Imperial Majesty and the Roman Empire likewise suffer no small loss of superiority and temporal jurisdiction, from a long-standing custom, badly observed until now in many places: namely, that when a civil dispute arises between two laymen, the ecclesiastical judges, at the petition of one party, issue letters of prohibition by which they order the other party not to pursue the suit begun before the secular court or its own judge, but to appear before the ecclesiastical court. When the summoned party obeys this command and refers himself and his cause to his ordinary judge, the other asks for a hearing in court. Then at once a libel, articles, exceptions, replies, rejoinders and other such writings are produced on both sides; and when these and the other acts and proceedings have been read, counted and weighed, at last they pronounce that the controversy is to be debated before them. Whether they will or not, the parties are compelled to obey this sentence, even if it weighs very heavily on them, because they cannot pursue an appeal to Rome on account of its immense labours and expenses; for it is not convenient for just anyone to go to Rome. Whether the judges render themselves suspect by such baneful sentences or not is left for any good man to conjecture. This one thing is certain: that from the cases already enumerated, a copious forest of civil causes is withdrawn and snatched away from the judges, from temporal jurisdiction and from the civil magistrate. This is recognised to be contrary not only to rights and equity but also to reason.

units.la: CAP. LXI. Ut plerig; inopia rerum laborantes, judicialium expensarum, variorumq; laborum & expensarum formidine, ad iniquas translationes compellantur.
units.tr: Chapter 61. How many of those who suffer from lack of means are driven, by fear of the costs of litigation and of various labours and expenses, into unjust settlements.

units.la: 80. Neque hoc silentio praeteriri potest, quòd Ecclesiastici judices & officiales, miserosac simplices laicos, multoties ad illicitas, iniquas, sibique penitus nocivas translationes adigunt. Nam si quando eos in jus vocant, magna patronorum, tabularum forensium, scribarum, caeterorumque, quorum opera in judiciario strepitu uri necesse habent, careerva, nullo aere conducta, sed gratuito conquisita, stipati astant, ac pauperibus illis prophanis, egestate pressis, id hominum genus, non nisi magno conducendum est. Quod ubi fortunae, reique familiaris tenuitas denegat, ni penitus causa, etiam justissima, decidere velint; transactionem seu compositionem utcunque iniquam inire coguntur. Quare quantum graventur tenues, nemo est qui non facile id deprehendat.
units.tr: 80. Nor can it pass unmentioned that the ecclesiastical judges and officials often drive simple and wretched laymen into unlawful, unjust, and utterly harmful settlements. For if at any time they summon them to court, the laymen stand surrounded by a great crowd of advocates, clerks of the court, scribes, and others whose services they must have in the noisy business of the courts, a crowd gathered without payment but still very large; and for these poor, unlearned folk, weighed down by want, this class of men cannot be engaged except at great cost. When the narrowness of their fortune and household means forbids this, they are forced, unless they are willing to abandon their cause altogether, even a most just one, to enter into some kind of settlement or compromise, however unjust. Hence no one who is not blind can fail to see easily how heavily the poor are burdened.

units.la: CAP. LXII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXII.

units.la: In multis Ecclesiasticorum consistoriis, externi causarum patroni & procuratores, quam non admittantur.
units.tr: In many consistories of the Church, outside advocates and procurators of causes are not admitted.

units.la: 81. Et hoc hactenus Germanis multum adrulit molestiarum, quod per Ecclesiasticos judices, nullo coram se litigantium partium, aliis uti advocatis & procuratoribus licet, quam iis, quos sibi suis qui tribunalibus, jurisjurandi sacramento obnoxios reddiderunt. Neramen nihilominus externi patroni litigantibus conlulantur; adeo breves praefigunt terminos, ut adiri nequaquam possint. Et ne hoc eorum factum tanquam aequitati contrarium, improbari possit, se id in controversiae commodum tacite affirmant; quo celeriorem per consistorii juratos procuratores sortiatur exitum. Ar interim in clara luce clarius apparet, qua sinceritate, quave dexteritate id agatur. Nempe comperrum habent officiales, se suosque superiores, a consistorii advocatis & procuratoribus timent. Et sic miseri clientes patronorum verecundia, dum quod contra Ecclesiasticum judicem, ejusve superiores, quacunque in parte facere possent, in judicio proponere non audent, ultra quam par sit, negliguntur. Quam tem Ecclesiastici Praelati, iisque quorum in territorio tale exercetur consistorium, quum prohibere, penitusque eradicare deberent, rurantur, ac defendunt. Et id potissimum eam ob causam; ut si quando iplis, subditisve ipsorum in Ecclesiastico judicio experiundum sit, dicti advocati & procuratores contra ipsos, exteris suis clientulis, ea quae causae sibi postulat necessitas, consulere, in judicioque proponere vereantur: ne, si diversum facerent, Praelatos sibi infensos, judicesque sibi male propitios redderent; talemque advocatorum & procuratorum metum ac formidinem, nemo est, cui vel cerebrum sit, cui levam parte mammillae cor saliat, qui inficias ire vel possit, vel audeat; cum id quotidiana experientia adeo eluceat, ut nemini non, nisi forte iis, qui nondum aere lavantur, sit exploratissimum. Quotus enim quisque est advocatorum, vel procuratorum qui non amore, spe, timore, invidia, favore, muneribus, limulibusve adfectibus, animo non aliquando, rectoque consilio dejiciatur: quum nihilominus vacui etiam praedictorum adfectuum, vix tandem precibus, pretioque inducuntur, ut nihil diligentiae, laborum nihil, nihil item clientuli jurium praetermittatur. Enumeratis vero gravaminibus, nulla praesentior adhiberi posset medicina, quam si litigantibus a certo usque limite, & advocatos, & procuratores vel consulere, vel ad consistorium secum adducere liceret.
units.tr: 81. This has hitherto caused the Germans much trouble: the ecclesiastical judges, with no litigating party present before them, allow only those advocates and procurators to be used who are bound to them by the oath of office sworn in their courts. Nor, even so, are outside advocates granted to litigants, since the courts set such short limits that they cannot be approached at all. And lest this practice be condemned as contrary to fairness, they tacitly assert that it serves the interest of the dispute, so that the case may reach a quicker end through the consistory's sworn procurators. Yet in plain light it becomes ever clearer with what sincerity, and with what dexterity, this is done. The officials know full well that they and their superiors fear the consistory's advocates and procurators. And so the wretched clients, out of deference to their patrons, do not dare to put forward in court whatever they could raise against the ecclesiastical judge or his superiors, and so they are neglected beyond what is fair. Although the ecclesiastical prelates, and those in whose territory such a consistory operates, ought to forbid this and root it out completely, they instead tolerate it and defend it. And they do so chiefly for this reason: that if ever they or their subjects have to contend in an ecclesiastical court, the said advocates and procurators would fear to consult, and to put forward in court, what the necessity of the case demands against those very men and their own little clients. Otherwise they would make the prelates hostile to them and the judges ill-disposed towards them. No one who has a brain, or whose heart beats in the left side of his chest, could or would deny such fear of advocates and procurators, since everyday experience makes it so plain that it is well known to everyone, except perhaps to those who have not yet been cleansed with money. For how few advocates or procurators are there who are not at some time turned from their purpose and right counsel by love, hope, fear, envy, favour, gifts, or sordid affections? Yet even those who are free of these emotions are scarcely won over by entreaties and payment, so that no diligence, no labour, and likewise nothing of the rights of their little clients, is passed over. Having listed these grievances, no more immediate remedy could be applied than to allow litigants, from a certain limit on, either to consult advocates and procurators or to bring them along with them to the consistory.

units.la: CAP. LXIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXIII.

units.la: Quam levibus ex causis, pauperibus Sacramenta denegentur.
units.tr: How lightly the sacraments are denied to the poor.

units.la: 82. Et hoc facinus Christi disciplinam profitentibus penitus abominandum est: quod iis, quibus est res angusta domi, ubi parochis & Ecclesiis ad diem solutioni destinatum, per inopiam satisfacere nequeunt, corpus & sanguis Christi, sacrosancta, quae nobis sacramenta in remissionem peccatorum reliquit, denegantur: immo quasi pignus praecluduntur; non attenta ulterioris dilationis, & quidem modicae, peritione. Quanquam tales similesque causae, pro conditione sua, coram secularibus judicibus, merito finem sortiri deberent.
units.tr: 82. This crime is utterly to be abominated by those who profess the discipline of Christ: that the body and blood of Christ, the most holy sacraments which he left us for the remission of sins, are refused to those whose household affairs are straitened, who cannot, through poverty, pay what is owed to the parish priests and churches by the day appointed for payment; they are refused, and even held back as a pledge, without regard to the fact that the delay sought is only a short one. Yet such causes, and causes like them, ought rightly to find an end before the secular judges, according to their own circumstances.

units.la: 83. Item, quum agricolae Aurumni tempore vindemiare cupiunt, quemadmodum unicuique ad suam utilitatem facere licet: nihilominus tamen, si vindemia illa displicet spiritualibus (ut vocant) qui colodecimas possident, miserisinhibent agricolis, sub excommunicationis, necnon pecuniarum poena, ne uvas colligant prius quam ipsi id permittant: unde evenit, ut saepe pauperculi illi non parvo afficiantur damno; cum uvas suas, quas maximis expensis & laboribus per integrum coluerunt annum, vindemiare non audeant. Etiam si illi interim vel frigore pereant, vel etiam marcescere incipiant; tantummodo ob decimarum lucrum iniquum, saepius etiam ob invidiam detestandam. Quae ambo contra jura sunt divina, fas, & omnem pietatem, ac ideo merito aboleri debent.
units.tr: 83. Likewise, when the farmers of Aurum wish to harvest the grapes at the time of the vintage, as each may lawfully do for his own advantage, nevertheless, if that harvest displeases the spiritual men (as they are called) who hold the tithes, they forbid the farmers, under penalty of excommunication and also of fines, to gather the grapes before they themselves have given permission. The result is that these poor folk are often put to no small loss, since they do not dare to harvest the grapes which they have tended with the greatest expense and labour through the whole year. Even if meanwhile the grapes perish from frost, or begin to wither, this is done only for the unjust gain of the tithes, and more often out of hateful envy. Both of these are contrary to the divine laws, to right, and to all piety, and therefore they ought rightly to be abolished.

units.la: CAP. LXIV.
units.tr: CAP. LXIV.

units.la: Ut Ecclesiastici Synodis abutantur.
units.tr: That the ecclesiastics abuse the synods.

units.la: 84. Nec minus molestum, grave, & Germanorum vulgo intolerabile est: quod Synodales judices plurimis in locis quotannis id, quod non nisi post annorum intercapedinem ut fieret, juribus permissum est, obequitant, ac mirum, quid fictitiae jurisdictionis, aut superioritatis exerceant: hoc interim constat, simplici popello hac via, necessaria subtrahi alimenta: neque talis peragratio eo fine & ordinatione, qua summis pontificibus institura est, observatur. Nam pro poenis & correctionibus, quibus facinorosos & criminum fontes a viriis deterrere deberent, pecuniam praesentem & numeratam, & quicquid denique eis in lucellum cedere potest, exigunt. Id quod in superioribus etiam partim memoratum est.
units.tr: 84. No less burdensome, grievous, and generally intolerable to the Germans is this: that the synodal judges, in very many places, make their rounds every year, which by law was permitted only after an interval of several years, and they exercise I know not what fictitious jurisdiction or superiority. Meanwhile it is clear that this practice deprives the simple common people of necessary sustenance, and such a visitation is not carried out for the purpose and under the arrangement for which it was instituted by the supreme pontiffs. For in exacting penalties and corrections, by which they ought to deter wrongdoers and the sources of crimes from vice, they demand ready and counted money, and whatever else can bring them some profit. This has already been mentioned in part above.

units.la: CAP. LXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 65.

units.la: De Canonicis Cathedralium & Collegiatarum Ecclesiarum, parochis, reliquisque religiosis personis: & primùm, Quod iniquis nexibus Episcopi & Prælati à suis adstringantur Capitula.
units.tr: Concerning the canons of cathedral and collegiate churches, parish priests, and other religious persons; and first, that chapters are bound by unjust ties to their bishops and prelates.

units.la: 85. Illicitum est & hoc, planéque iniquum, quod Canonici Ecclesiarumque Cathedralium præeminentiores, quorum in manu potior Ecclesiasticorum judiciorum, Synodorum, ac censurarum pars sita est; reliquique Collegiatarum Ecclesiarum canonici, quibus eligendi superiorem potestas est, nullum in Episcopum, seu Prælatum eligunt: nisi Se prius jurejurando astrinxerit, planéque deverterit; literisque quoque interdum, instrumentisque sigillo probè munitis caverit, ipsis ipsorumque consanguinatis judicibus ac officialibus in nullo, utcunque gravi, vel inhonesto, intolerabilique propositione, le contrarium fore. Ac si quando eos delinquere contigerit, impunè eis per ipsum, ut hoc libi licet.
units.tr: 85. It is also unlawful and plainly unjust that the more eminent canons of the cathedral churches, in whose hands lies the greater part of ecclesiastical judgments, synods and censures, and the other canons of the collegiate churches, who have the power of electing a superior, do not elect any man as bishop or prelate unless he has first bound himself by oath and fully sworn to it, and has also sometimes guaranteed in letters and properly sealed instruments that, whatever the proposal, however grievous, dishonourable or intolerable, he will do nothing contrary to them, to their judges and officials, or to their kinsmen. And if ever they happen to offend, they are dealt with with impunity by him, as he is free to do.

units.la: CAP. LXVI.
units.tr: CAP. LXVI.

units.la: De non ferendis ultra oneribus, quibus miseræ plebs pro Sacramentorum adminis- tratione gravatur.
units.tr: Concerning the burdens, which the wretched common people are weighed down with for the administration of the Sacraments, that must no longer be borne.

units.la: 86. Pleræque item parochiales Ecclesiæ, Monasteriis, Prælatis, aliisque Ecclesiarum Rectoribus, incorporationis, ut vocant, seu alio quopiam jure subditæ sunt: quas & si ipsi juris canonum constitutiones, per se providere tenentur, ubi aliis clocant gubernandas, beneficiorum, ac decimas, plerunque sibi ipsis reservant: & præterea tam enormibus absentiarum pœnis gravant, atque onerant, ut conducti isti Parochi eorumque Vicarii, Vicepleb ani, Sacellani, Custodes, cæterique conductarum Ecclesiarum administratores, competentem sustentationem, ac tiaque alimenta inde habere nequeant. Quo fit, (nam unde conducti isti pastores & mercenarii vivant, habeant oporteat) ut illicitis exactionibus, locatas sibi oviculas, miserè depræment, omnemque substantiam tantum non absumant. Postquam enim altaris, baptismique sacramenta administranda sunt; Primus, Septimus, Tricesimus, Anniversariusque dies peragendus, auriculæ confessio audienda, mortui sepeliendi & quicquid denique reliquum est, quod ad vitæ functorum ceremonias observandas operæ precium arbitrantur, id gratuito faciunt nequaquam, sed tantum exigunt, extorquent, exigunt, quantum miseræ plebecula vel cum summo suo dispendio præstare difficulter potest: talesque exactiones usque ad summum indies augent atque accumulant; nonnunquam quoque excommunicationis fulmine ad solvendum adigunt: plerosque etiam, quibus per inopiam non licet, ad celebranda vita functis obsequia anniversarios, & alias ejus farinæ ceremonias, compellere conantur.
units.tr: 86. Likewise, many parish churches are made subject to monasteries, prelates, and other rectors of churches by incorporation, as they call it, or by some other right. Although the canonical constitutions require these churches' own holders to provide for them personally, they commonly reserve the benefices and tithes to themselves when they hand the churches over to others to be governed. Moreover, they burden and oppress them with such enormous penalties for absence that the hired parsons, their vicars, vice-plebans, chaplains, sextons, and the other administrators of the leased churches cannot get from them a suitable maintenance and food. Hence it happens (for those hired pastors and mercenaries must have some means of living) that they miserably crush the little sheep committed to them by illicit exactions, and all but consume their entire substance. For once the sacraments of the altar and baptism have been administered, they do not think it worth their while to perform gratuitously the first, seventh, thirtieth and anniversary days, to hear private confession, to bury the dead, and whatever else remains that they judge worth observing in the ceremonies for the departed. Rather they demand and extort, they exact as much as the wretched little common folk can scarcely pay even at great cost to themselves; and they increase and pile up such exactions day by day to the maximum. Sometimes they also force payment by the thunderbolt of excommunication, and they try to compel many, who cannot pay because of poverty, to hold anniversary obsequies for the dead and other ceremonies of that sort.

units.la: CAP. LXVII.
units.tr: CAP. LXVII.

units.la: Ut ob missas cantandas & legendas, pecuniam exigant.
units.tr: That they demand money for Masses to be sung and read.

units.la: 87. Neque hoc præterire potest, quum non minimum sit, quo Germani premantur, quòd Sacerdotes, unius diei missas, ad quas aliàs fundationis, seu annuæ recordationis jure, celebrandas obligantur, non semel, sed quater, quinquies, pluriesve venundant: unaque missa, duobus, tribus, aut pluribus Ecclesiasticis beneficiis satis facere præsumunt.
units.tr: 87. Nor can this be passed over, since it is no small burden by which the Germans are oppressed, that priests sell the Masses of a single day, which they are bound to celebrate by the right of foundation or of an annual remembrance, not once but four times, five times, or more; and they presume that one Mass satisfies two, three, or more ecclesiastical benefices.

units.la: CAP. LXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXVIII.

units.la: Quo pacto Parochi, à suis parochialibus subditis, ubi domicilium mutare voluerint, pecunias emulgeant.
units.tr: How the parish priests squeeze money from their parishioners when those wish to change their residence.

units.la: 88. Item, sicubi curatæ Ecclesiæ subditus domicilium matrimonii, seu alterius cujuspiam negotii causa, in aliam transferre parochiam, animo secum volutar; non priùs migrandi licentiam à Parocho impetrat, quàm ubi pro testimonialibus literis aureum numeraverit nummum: quem si vere vel nolit, vel egestate pressus non potest, sacramentorum interdicto, donec satisfecerit, mulctatur. Ex hoc itaque, ac cæteris supra ratio onerib us & gravaminibus facilè deprehenditur, miro modo in modum emicat, quod omnia Rom. Ecclesiæ sacramenta iis, qui opibus abundant, auro venalia sunt: reliquis verò, quibus minimum supperit nummorum, & iniquus est Plurus (ille divitiarum Deus) non impartiuntur, sed pe nitus denegantur.
units.tr: 88. Likewise, wherever a subject of a parish church intends, for the sake of marriage or some other business, to move his household into another parish, he does not obtain from the parish priest permission to migrate until he has paid him a gold coin for the testimonial letters. If he is either unwilling to pay, or is pressed by poverty and cannot, he is punished by an interdict on the sacraments until he has made payment. From this, and from the other burdens and grievances mentioned above, it is easily seen, and in a remarkable way it stands out, that all the sacraments of the Roman Church are sold for gold to those who abound in wealth, while to the rest, who have very little money and for whom Pluto (that god of riches) is unfair, they are not distributed but utterly denied.

units.la: CAP. LXIX.
units.tr: CAP. LXIX.

units.la: Quemadmodum sepultura jus quibusdam mortuorum cadaveribus, magno sit ære redimendum.
units.tr: How burial in consecrated ground must be bought at great cost for certain corpses of the dead.

units.la: 89. Papalibus statutum est canonibus, ut iis dumtaxat publici juris Ecclesiastica denegetur sepultura, quos manifestis & planè notoriis, mortalibus, ut vocant, peccatis, ex communi hac mortalium forte, absque dominici corporis sanguinisve participatione migrasse compertum sit. Verùm Ecclesiastici, non animadversis talibus Pontificum decretis, forte fortuna, aqua suffocatos, gladio, ... na, vel incendio occisos, jugulatos, atque vita casu functos, etiamsi non pateat, peccatis mortalibus obnoxii decesserint, nec ne, in Ecclesiasticam tumulare sepulturam, non permittunt, quousque tam iniquo fato demortuorum uxores, liberi, amicive, ab ipsis cœmeterium non modico ære comparavernt.
units.tr: 89. The Papal canons have laid down that ecclesiastical burial is denied only to those who are known, clearly and plainly, to have departed this common life in manifest and notorious mortal sins, as they call them, and without having partaken of the Lord's body and blood. But the clergy, disregarding such decrees of the Popes, do not permit those who by chance have been drowned in water, slain by the sword, ... or by fire, or killed by a fall, or who have died by some accident, to be buried in ecclesiastical ground, even when it is not clear whether they died guilty of mortal sins or not. They refuse until the wives, children or friends of the dead have bought a burial ground from them for no small sum of money, under such an unjust fate.

units.la: CAP. LXX.
units.tr: CAP. LXX.

units.la: Vt plerique Ecclesiastici, vitam laicam, planeque rixosam agant.
units.tr: That many churchmen lead a secular and thoroughly quarrelsome life.

units.la: 90. Nec minùs etiam Germanis molestum est, quòd potior Parochorum, Sacerdotum, monachorum, aliorumque Ecclesiasticorum pars, in diversoriis, stabulis ac choreis, populorum turbis se admiscent; in plateis item habitu minùs decenti, utputà gladiis, vestibusque ludicris: praeterea rixis, jurgiis, litibus, altercationibus laicos ad iram, & consequenter ad arma provocant, vulnerant, nonnunquam etiam confodiunt. Dein excommunicationis fulmine miseros illos laicos, vel quos laeserunt, eousque divexant, quousque ad libitum suum laici se cum his compositerint.
units.tr: 90. Nor is it less troublesome to the Germans that the greater part of the parish priests, clergy, monks and other churchmen mix with crowds of people in inns, stables and dance-halls; likewise in the streets, dressed in an unseemly manner, for instance with swords and ludicrous garments. Besides, by brawls, quarrels, lawsuits and disputes they provoke the laity to anger and consequently to arms; they wound them and sometimes even stab them. Then, with the thunderbolt of excommunication, they harass those wretched laymen, or those whom they have injured, until the laymen come to terms with them on their own terms.

units.la: 91. Item in locis plerisque Episcopi, & eorum Officiales, non solùm Sacerdotum tolerant concubinatum, dummodo certa persolvatur pecunia: sed & Sacerdotes continentes, & qui absque concubinis degunt, concubinatus censum persolvere cogunt; asserentes, Episcopum pecuniae indigum esse, qua soluta, licere sacerdotibus, ut vel coelibes permaneant, vel concubinas alant. Quàm res haec sine nephanda, nemo non intelligit.
units.tr: 91. Likewise, in many places bishops and their officials not only tolerate the concubinage of priests, provided a certain sum of money is paid, but they also compel celibate priests, and those who live without concubines, to pay a tax for concubinage, asserting that the bishop is in need of money and that, once it is paid, priests may either remain unmarried or keep concubines. No one fails to understand how unspeakable this practice is.

units.la: CAP. LXXI.
units.tr: CAP. LXXI.

units.la: Quo pacto nonnulli Ecclesiastici, publicas exerceant tabernas, & illicita corrodant lucra.
units.tr: How some ecclesiastics run public taverns and gather unlawful gains.

units.la: 92. Ecclesiastici item, potissimùm in his locis, ubi jurisdictionem habent, in templorum dedicationibus, publicas exercent tabernas, suisque Sacellanis & Sacerdotibus, taxillos, chartulas lusorias, & quicquid ad ludum pertinet, convivis administrare, ac omni sepulto pudore, illicitum inde percipere lucrum student: idque superioritatis quodam jure sibi licere asserunt. Quanquam Pontificum canones, Imperatorum leges, omnesque omnium provinciarum magistratus vetent, ne Ecclesiastici utà decoro & honesto devient; utiis se involvant negotiis, circa quae vix laicos occupatos esse decet.
units.tr: 92. Likewise, ecclesiastics, especially in those places where they hold jurisdiction, run public taverns at the dedications of churches, and they supply dice, playing cards and everything connected with gambling to their guests through their chaplains and priests; and, having cast off all shame, they strive to draw unlawful profit from this, claiming that they may do so by a certain right of superiority. Yet the canons of the Popes, the laws of the Emperors, and the magistrates of all the provinces forbid ecclesiastics to depart from what is becoming and honourable, and to entangle themselves in affairs with which laymen scarcely ought to be occupied.

units.la: CAP. LXXII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXII.

units.la: Quomodo Ecclesiastici moribundis, ut suos & legitimos haeredes defrau- dent, persuadeant.
units.tr: How the clergy persuade the dying to defraud their own lawful heirs.

units.la: 93. Inter caetera etiam hoc obticendū est nequaquam, quum non minimum sit onus, quo Germani gravantur; quòd regionum pervagatores, quos vulgò Terminarios ac Stationarios vocant, monachi & sacerdotes, infirmos, animamq; jamjam agentes; ac praesertim eos, quibus aes esse in cista norūt, temporalibúsve bonis abundate compertū habent, blandiloquentia, adulatione, verbisq; venustulis (ut ad pessima quaeque hoc genus hominum semper plus aequo instructum est, atque paratum) adoriuntur, circumveniunt, persuasionibusque fictitiis eò tandem adducunt, quòd sibi potiorem, & pecuniarum & bonorum partem in testamentis legant. Qua re liberi, agnati, ac cognati, reliquiique sui & legitimi haeredes, quibus potiùs tota haereditas illaesa relinquenda erat, contra omnem aequitatem, mirum quàm jactura adficiantur: interdumque ad miseriam usque adigantur.
units.tr: 93. Among other things this must not be passed over: there is no small burden under which the Germans are weighed down, because the wandering collectors of the regions, whom they commonly call Terminarians and Stationaries, monks and priests, approach the sick and those already breathing their last, and especially those whom they know to have money in their chest or to be well supplied with temporal goods. They surround them with flattering speech, adulation and pretty words (as this kind of men is always more than enough equipped and ready for every wickedness), and by sham persuasions they bring them at last to the point of bequeathing in their wills a greater part both of their money and of their goods to themselves. By this means children, agnates and cognates, and their other lawful heirs, to whom the whole inheritance ought rather to have been left unimpaired, are affected by a loss that is wonderful to behold, against all fairness, and are sometimes driven even to misery.

units.la: CAP. LXXIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXIII.

units.la: Quibus medii s innumeram pecuniae summam, Mendicantium ordines Romam import- tent, Virginumq; vestalium monasteria molestent.
units.tr: By what means the Mendicant orders bring an immense sum of money to Rome, and harass the convents of virgins and nuns.

units.la: 94. Quum nemini dubium sit, iis qui jure experiri volunt, pecunia, eaque non modica opus esse; & plerique Mendicantium ordinum regulis addicti, multas causas atque lites in judicialem controversiam, non sine magno ordinariorum, parochorum, atque laicorum detrimento, contra phas, nefasque; immò nulla omnino necessitate exigente, Romam pertrahant: Tribus insuper eorum generalibus, quos vocant, Cardinalitii galeri dignitatem, innumera, ut fertur, pecunia comparaverint. Non parum timendum est, ne non praefati Mendicantium otdinibus subjugati, multa sacrarum virginum; praesertim ea, ubi se solos dominari norunt, monasteria, in quibus Principum, Comitum, Baronum, Nobilium, ac Civium liberi frequenter vitam vivunt, pecuniis expilent, ac depeculentur, & eis dehinc quibuscunque aliis modis, interitus, perniciei, molestiarum, variorumque incommodorum radix atque origo sint: Interimque miserè, captivas moniales, sub perpetui poena carceris adigant, nec cūquam alii, quo secum pacto agant, manifestent: id quod quibusdam in locis plus nimio, proh dolor, comperтum est. Quibus verò pharmacis huic morbo mederi possit, cogitandum relinquitur: Num praestaret, quòd virginum monasteriis, ac Mendicantium ordinibus, in meri ac mixti imperii jurisdictionibus sis, quibus hactenus per jurisdictionum magistratus, ac potestates, nulli praefecti essent curatores, seu dispensatores, duo, aetate, moribus, ac probitate perspicua praestantes viri, unicuique tali moniasterio seorsim praeficerentur, qui omnibus eorum communibus computationibus, acceptorum videlicet & expensorum, interessent; quibusque cuiae esset, ne in posterum praedicta virgmalia coenobia, à Mendicantibus monachis, eorum non necessaria praesentia, vel quocunque alio modo gravarentur. Qua una re procul dubio efficeretur, quòd dictorum monasteriorum annui fructus, census, reddditus, indies augerentur: monialium personae in magnum usque excrescerent numerum: & sic multo meliùs, ubertiùs, utilius, quàm si ipsarum pecunia, vel Romam, vel in alium quempiam locum indecentem, confetatur, sustentari possent.
units.tr: 94. Since no one doubts that those who wish to pursue their rights at law need money, and not a small amount, and since many men bound by the rules of the Mendicant orders drag many cases and lawsuits into judicial dispute, to Rome, contrary to right and law, and with no necessity at all demanding it, to the great loss of the ordinaries, parish priests and laity; moreover, they have bought, as is reported, the dignity of the cardinal's hat for three of their so-called generals with countless money. We have good reason to fear that many convents of holy virgins, subject to the aforesaid Mendicant orders, especially those where they know they alone hold sway, in which the children of princes, counts, barons, nobles and citizens often live, may be stripped and plundered of their money, and that these convents become, by various other means, the root and origin of ruin, destruction, troubles and many kinds of inconvenience. Meanwhile they wretchedly drive captive nuns under the penalty of perpetual imprisonment and reveal to no one else how they deal with them, which, alas, has been discovered in some places to an excessive degree. What remedies could cure this disease is left for consideration. Would it not be better, in the mere and mixed jurisdictions of the empire, where until now no prefects were set over the convents of virgins and the Mendicant orders by the magistrates and officials of the jurisdictions, to appoint two men distinguished by age, character and proven integrity, one for each such convent separately, who would take part in all their common accounts, of receipts and expenses, and whose charge it would be that in future the said convents of virgins be not burdened by the Mendicant monks through their unnecessary presence or in any other way? By this single measure, without doubt, the yearly fruits, census and revenues of the said convents would increase daily, the number of nuns would grow to a great size, and they could be supported far better, more abundantly and more usefully than if their money were carried off either to Rome or to some other unseemly place.

units.la: CAP. LXXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXIV.

units.la: De Romanorum Pontificum legatis & oratoribus nec non Comitibus, quos vocant, Palatinis.
units.tr: Concerning the legates and envoys of the Roman Pontiffs, and also the so-called Palatine Counts.

units.la: 95. Accidit etiam aliquando, quòd legati & oratores Romani, cum Papalibus, ut vocant, facultatibus, in Germaniam mittantur; qui alium facultatum vigore & praetextu, liberos vulgo conceptos, naturales, Bastardos, spurios, damnato ex coitu prognatos, aliôsque, qui contra Christi instituta, legumque sanctiones in mundum editi atque expositi sunt, legitimos efficere, & ad quoscunque status legitimos, idoneos reddere; ad successiones item cum legitimis & naturalibus liberis habiles facere & admittere; omnium denique statuum ac dignitatum capacitatem tribuere conantur. Cuius tamen rei, in Romani Imperii territorio, nullam omnino habent potestatem. Nec parum inde litium, iurgiorum, errorum, controversiarum, offendiculorumque, in sacrosancto Romano Imperio oritur; quòd ex non concesso coitu concepti, cum legitimè editis ad parem admitti debent successionem. Quam rem, ut minimum Germanis molestam, Imperii ordines, tolli, amoveri, penitusque aboleri, summopere petunt.
units.tr: 95. It also sometimes happens that Roman legates and envoys are sent into Germany with what are called Papal faculties. By the force and pretext of these faculties they try to make legitimate those children commonly called conceived out of wedlock, natural children, bastards, and spurious children, born of a condemned union, and others who have been brought into the world and exposed contrary to the institutions of Christ and the sanctions of the laws. They also try to render them fit for any status whatever, to make them capable of succession along with legitimate and natural children, and finally to grant them capacity for all estates and dignities. Yet they have no power at all in this matter within the territory of the Roman Empire. From this there arises no small amount of lawsuits, quarrels, errors, controversies and stumbling blocks in the most holy Roman Empire, because children conceived from a union not permitted must be admitted to an equal succession with those lawfully born. The estates of the Empire, as this matter is at least troublesome to the Germans, most earnestly ask that it be removed, repealed and utterly abolished.

units.la: 96. Pari praeterea modo a Romana sede jam dictis Legatis, Vicecomites Palatini sufficiuntur, simili potestate legitimandi, ad successionem admittendi, & omnia ad instar legatorum, quorum jam antè mentio facta est, efficiendi, neconon notarios creandi. Qui tamen Vicecomites adeò sunt indonei, adeò inhabiles, adeò literarum ignari, adeò deniquerum inexpertes; ut minimum etiam, quod ad notariatus artem pertineat, ignorent. Unde non immeritò subsequitur, quòd multo ineptiores, quàm ipsi sint, credent notarios: ut semper dignum, quod in proverbio est, contingit patellae cooperculum. Quod ipsum Imperii Status, abrogari efflagitim rogitant. Praefati item Apostolicae sedis Nuncii & Legati à jurejurandis, pactis, obligationibus, absolvere: & sic absolutos ad agendum de novo restituere moliuntur. Qua una re aequitati, fideique humanae nihil est adversum magis.
units.tr: 96. In the same way, Palatine Vice-Counts are appointed by the Roman See through the aforesaid legates, with the same power of legitimizing, of admitting to succession, of making everything equal to what the legates, mentioned above, do, and of creating notaries. Yet these Vice-Counts are so unfit, so incompetent, so ignorant of letters and so utterly inexperienced that they do not even know at least what pertains to the art of the notary. Hence it not undeservedly follows that they believe their notaries to be far more inept than they themselves are; as the proverb says, the lid always fits the pan. The estates of the Empire earnestly ask that this very practice be abrogated. The aforesaid Nuncios and Legates of the Apostolic See also undertake to absolve people from oaths, pacts and obligations, and, having so absolved them, they labour to restore them to acting afresh. By this one thing nothing is more opposed to equity and to human faith.

units.la: 97. Conantur insuper beneficia, quae patronatus juri subsunt, conferre: & sic patronis tam Ecclesiasticis, quàm secularibus in juribus suis derogare, penitùsque eos privare: quod etiam merito aboletur.
units.tr: 97. Moreover, they attempt to confer benefices that are subject to the right of patronage, and so to derogate from the rights of patrons, both ecclesiastical and secular, and to deprive them of these entirely; which is also rightly abolished.

units.la: CAP. LXXV.
units.tr: CAP. LXXV.

units.la: Utriusque sexus religiosi, in suorum monasteriorum, clausarum, fundationum, aliorumque conventuum commodum, succeduntsecularibus; quum ipsi vicifim abillis ad hereditates, neque vocentur, neque admittantur.
units.tr: Concerning religious persons of either sex: that they succeed to the goods of their monasteries, cloisters, foundations and other convents, to the advantage of the secular heirs, while they themselves are neither called nor admitted to inheritances from those heirs in turn.

units.la: 98. Neque hoc Germanicorum gravaminum postremum est, quamvis ultimum hic sortiatur locum. Mos non amplius ferendus, hactenus inolevit, pauloque altius, quàm par sit, radices egit: videlicet, quòd Monachi, Moniales, Beguttae, Beghardae, Nolhardi, Conventus, & quicunque tandem sunt, qui se religiosos, & à populariibus segregatos profitentur, parentibus, consanguineis, agnatis, ac ceteris amicis, in hereditariis bonis, aliquando in partem, nonnunquam in totum succeduntʒ At vicifsim eorum cognati, seu necessarii laici, à praetactis religiosis, ad ipsorum hereditates adeundas, non solum non vocantur, sed nec admittuntur quidem. Quod Germanis & grave, & molestum; injustum etiam, ac non diutiùs tolerandum onus est. Ea propter necessariò, ac summa prudentia curandum est, ut deinceps nemo se memoratorum religiosorum votis vel adstringat, vel addicet, nisi priùs ea de re civiles magistratus certiores fecerit: quorum praesentia, auctoritate & consilio religionem ingredi volentibus, à parentibus & amicis, juxta cujusque fortunam ac facultates, mediocriter provideri debet, ut habeant, unde commodè in monasteriis vivere possint. Ea tamen lege, eo pacto & conditione; ut omnibus hereditatibus, omnibusque parentum, fratrum, sororum, cognatorum, coheredum, acquorumcunque aliorum successionibus renuncient: in animumque nequaquam inducant suum, se in posterum hereditario jure quicquam nedum sperare, tantum abest, ut consequi se posse putare queant. Idemque cum his, qui jam olim religiosorum regulis sese subjecerunt, fieri à sacri Rom. Imperii Statibus, & petitur, & censetur.
units.tr: 98. Nor is this the least of the German grievances, although it takes the last place here. A custom that must no longer be endured has taken hold until now and has struck roots somewhat deeper than is fitting. Namely, monks, nuns, Beguttae, Beghards, Nolhards, convents, and whoever at all they are who profess themselves religious and separated from the laity, sometimes succeed their parents, blood relations, agnates and other friends in hereditary goods, in part at times, and sometimes in whole. But in turn their relatives, or lay kinsmen, are not only not called to enter upon their inheritances from the aforesaid religious, but are not even admitted. This is a burden that is grievous and troublesome to the Germans, unjust too, and not to be tolerated any longer. Therefore it must of necessity, and with the greatest prudence, be taken care of that henceforth no one bind or devote himself by vows to the aforesaid religious orders unless he has first informed the civil magistrates of the matter. By their presence, authority and counsel, parents and friends ought to provide moderately, according to each one's fortune and means, for those who wish to enter religion, so that they have something whereby they can live decently in the monasteries. Yet this is on the condition, under this agreement and stipulation: that they renounce all inheritances, and all successions of parents, brothers, sisters, relatives, co-heirs, and any others whatsoever; and that they never bring it into their minds that they may hope for anything at all by hereditary right in future, much less that they may think they can obtain it. The same is both sought and judged to be done by the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire with those who long ago submitted themselves to the rules of the religious.

units.la: CAP. LXXVI.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXVI.

units.la: Quod & in proximè habitâ VVormaciæ comitiis, de hactenus memoratis gravaminibus, tractatum fit.
units.tr: Which was also discussed at the recent Diet of Worms, concerning the grievances mentioned so far.

units.la: 99. Potior item pars, hactenus enumeratorum articulorum, Romanam Sedem, Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, Praelatos, Officiales, Ecclesiastica consistoria, ceterasque Ecclesiasticas personas concernentium, Caesareæ Majestati in proximo Principum ac Proceerum Wormaciæ celebrato conventu, à laicis Imperii columnis & Statibus, in scriptis, non sine supplicibus oblata est precibus: quò praedicta gravamina, aequitate, necessitateq; ita postulantibus, aboleat, atque è medio penitus tollat. Quod ipsum non clam Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, reliquisque Ecclesiasticorum Statibus, in praedictis Comitiis factum est. At hucusque nihil vel immutare, vel emendare coeperunt. Eam ob rem seculares Imperii ordines, necessariò, urgentibúsque ex causis adacti sunt, Papali Sanctitati supra memorata, ac non ampliùs ferenda onera, prout sua Sanctitas, clementi, Christiano, planéque paterno animi adsectu fi- ci pe eri petiit, indicare, atque supplicitèr rogare, quo prædicta gravamina sua Sanctitas emendet, atque è medio tollat.
units.tr: 99. The greater part of the articles enumerated so far, concerning the Roman See, archbishops, bishops, prelates, officials, ecclesiastical consistories and other ecclesiastical persons, was presented in writing, with humble petitions, to His Imperial Majesty at the recent assembly of princes and nobles held at Worms, by the lay pillars and estates of the Empire. They asked, on grounds of equity and necessity, that he abolish the aforesaid grievances and remove them entirely. This was done not secretly from the archbishops, bishops and the other ecclesiastical estates at the said Diet. Yet up to now they have begun to change or amend nothing. For this reason the secular orders of the Empire have been compelled, by necessity and urgent causes, to point out the aforesaid grievances, burdens no longer to be borne, to the Papal Holiness, and humbly to ask that His Holiness, with the merciful, Christian and truly paternal disposition of mind that he himself has sought, amend the aforesaid grievances and remove them.

units.la: CAP. LXXVII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXVII.

units.la: Plura adhuc gravamina ob oculos versantur, indicatu maximè necessaria: quae tamen brevitatis gratia obmittuntur.
units.tr: Several further grievances, most necessary to point out, lie before our eyes; these, however, are passed over for the sake of brevity.

units.la: 100. Quamvis seculares sacrosancti Romani Imperii ordines, longè graviora, multòque plura adhuc haberent onera, quae, æquitate interpellante, indicanda forent: At ne justæ brevitatis modum excedere videantur, jam recensitis hoc tempore, reservatis aliis in magis commodum tempus, contenti esse volunt: Ea spe freti, ea fiducia, nixi, ubi hactenus enumerata abolita fuerint gravamina, quòd & reliqua unà corruitura sint.
units.tr: 100. Although the secular estates of the Holy Roman Empire have far more serious and much more numerous burdens still, which, were justice to demand it, ought to be pointed out, they wish to be content, lest they seem to exceed the measure of a just brevity, with those already recounted at this time, reserving the others for a more convenient time. Relying on this hope and trusting in this confidence, they expect that when the grievances enumerated so far have been abolished, the remaining ones will fall away together with them.

units.la: Peroratio, ac finalis petitio.
units.tr: Peroration and final petition.

units.la: Super hæc omnia, omnium sacri Romani Imperii supremæ atque inferioris conditionis Status um, supplex est adhortatio, humilisque precatio atque petitio, qua Sanctitati Pontificiæ supplicant: quatenus sanctitas sua, omnia prædicta onera ac gravamina, sedis Romanæ, ac sæpedictorum caeterorum Statuum Ecclesiasticorum & personarum Ecclesiasticarum (id quod non semel in præcedentibus quoque justis precibus postulatum est) clementer tollere, emendare, abrogaréque, & è medio auferre dignetur; ac Archiepiscopos & Episcopos, si qua in re per eorum Capitula, gravamina hæc, quò minùs emendare, abrogareque auderent, obligati forent, à promissione, obligationéque tali, mandatis absolutoriis, sevemost veritatem quandam, sed eam quidem necessariam præ se ferentibus, absolvete, liberareque velit: inque omnibus & singulis his, ita paternè ac gratiosè se gerere & exhibere, quòd talia onera atque gravamina in genere, seorsimque, quantocyùs ex radice fundirus, ac penitus tollantur, amoveantur, & emendentur. Quod ipsum, & quidem brevi, futurum, cutatumque iri, Sacri Romani Imperii Status laici, vel ob Opt. Maximi laudem præcipuam, & honorem; hinc rei quoque ipsius necessitatem atque æquitatem maximè, quum, ut prædictum est, Sanctitas Pontificia per oratorem & Legatum suum, ita magnificè, ampliter, ac Christianè se obtulerit, indubiam, certissimámque spem animo conceperunt. E regione, se Sanctitati Pontificiæ, tanquam obsequentes, morigerósque filios, cæteris quoque Statibus Ecclesiasticis, ut in Christo fratres, & commembra capitis unius, nimirum Christi, se devoventes, obligantesque.
units.tr: Over and above all these things, the humble exhortation, lowly prayer and petition of all the estates of the Holy Roman Empire, both supreme and of inferior rank, is addressed to the Papal Holiness, by which they beseech that His Holiness may deign graciously to remove, amend, abrogate and take away from the midst all the aforesaid burdens and grievances of the Roman See and of the other above-mentioned ecclesiastical estates and ecclesiastical persons (a thing which has been asked more than once in earlier just petitions as well); and that he may be pleased to absolve and free the archbishops and bishops from the promise and obligation of such mandates, should they be bound by their chapters, so that they might not dare to amend, abrogate and remove these grievances; and that in all and each of these matters he may conduct and show himself so paternally and graciously that such burdens and grievances, both in general and individually, may be poured out from the root as quickly as possible, and entirely removed, cast out and amended. That this very thing will happen, and indeed soon, and will be brought about, the secular estates of the Holy Roman Empire have conceived an undoubted and most certain hope in their minds, both on account of the chief praise and honour of the Best and Greatest God, and hence especially on account of the necessity and justice of the matter itself, since, as has been said, the Papal Holiness has offered itself through its orator and legate so magnificently, generously and in a Christian manner. On their side, they pledge and bind themselves to the Papal Holiness as obedient and compliant sons, and likewise to the other ecclesiastical estates as brothers in Christ and members of one head, namely Christ.

units.la: Quòd si enumerata onera atque gravamina in præstituto tempore, non etiam ocyùs ex oculis mortalium sublata, atque abolita, & abrogata fuerint (id quod Imperii Romani Status laici futurum minimè suspicantur, augurantúrve) cum Sanctitatem Pontificiam latere nolunt, prædicta urgentissima, atque intolerabilia, penitusque non ferenda onera, diutiùs eos, neque perferre velle, neque tolerare posse: Sed rei ipsius iniquitate & necessitate, huc eos adigi, cogi, atque compelli, pro eorum captu ac industria, de aliis commodioribus forte viis & mediis cogitandi, vestigandi, ac consultandi, quibus tandem modis, qua arte, qua denique solertia, onerum atque gravaminum supra memoratorum, ab Ecclesiasticis exonerati, liberari, ac tandem in pristinam immunitatem & libertatem asseri, atque vendicari possint.
units.tr: But if the enumerated burdens and grievances are not removed and abolished and abrogated within the appointed time, and even more quickly from the eyes of mortals (which the secular estates of the Roman Empire scarcely suspect or expect to happen), since they do not wish to conceal this from the Papal Holiness, they declare that they are unwilling and unable to bear any longer the aforesaid most urgent and intolerable burdens, which cannot be endured at all; but that by the injustice and necessity of the matter itself they are driven, forced and compelled to think, search out and consult, according to their understanding and diligence, on other perhaps more convenient ways and means, by which at last, by what method, what skill, and what cleverness, they may be relieved and freed from the aforesaid burdens and grievances imposed by the ecclesiastics, and at last may claim and vindicate their former immunity and liberty.

units.la: Quemadmodum omnia hæc, priusquam Sanctitatis Pontificiæ orator & Legatus à Norimberga solvisset, eidem per modum responsi hinc legantis Sanctitati referenda, ad longum sunt expositæ, atque enumerata: essentque ita in compendium, & quodammodo per catalogum redacta & recensita, memorato nuncio atque oratori Pontificio ferenda secum Romam tradita; si non præter omnium expectationem, abitionem suam hinc tantopere maturasset, ac inopinatò ita discessisset. Verum ne ob id eò magis Germanorum Principum, Procerum, atque Romani Imperii Statuum consultatio & conclusio Sanctitatem Pontificiam fugere, vel latere possent: tandem placuit, onera ac gravamina, quorum non infrequens tum coram agente adhuc Legato facta fuit mentio, per capita, ac sigillatim ita scripta, Sanctitati Pontificiæ transmittere, eandemque quàm humillimè ac supplicitèr, pro abrogandis hisce oneribus, rogare, obsecrareque; ne deteriora contingant.
units.tr: Since all these things were set out and enumerated at length, before the orator and legate of the Papal Holiness departed from Nuremberg, they were to be reported to His Holiness by way of a reply from here, and handed on to the said nuncio and Papal orator to carry with him to Rome, in summary form and as it were drawn up and recounted in a catalogue; had he not, contrary to everyone's expectation, hastened his departure from here so eagerly and left so suddenly. But lest the deliberation and resolution of the German princes, nobles and estates of the Roman Empire should on that account be able to escape or remain hidden from the Papal Holiness, it was finally agreed to send to the Papal Holiness the burdens and grievances, of which mention was not infrequently made at that time in the presence of the legate still acting here, written out item by item and separately, and to ask and beseech the same Holiness, as humbly and supplicantly as possible, to abrogate these burdens, lest worse things befall.

units.la: CAROLI V. IMPER. AUG. RESCRIPTUM
units.tr: THE RESCRIPT OF THE EMPEROR CHARLES V AUGUSTUS

units.la: AD CLEMENTIS VII. PAPAE CRIMINATIONES, cum Appellatione, & Generalis Concilii indictionis postulatione.
units.tr: IN REPLY TO THE ACCUSATIONS OF POPE CLEMENT VII, with an appeal and a demand for the calling of a General Council.

units.la: Sanctissimo in Christo Patri & Domino, Domino CLEMENTI VII. divina providentia Sacrosanctæ Romanæ ac Universalis Ecclesiæ Summo Pontifici, Domino Reverendissimo,
units.tr: To the most holy Father in Christ and Lord, Lord Clement VII, by divine providence Supreme Pontiff of the Holy Roman and Universal Church, the most reverend Lord,

units.la: KAROLVS divina favente Clementia, Electus Romanorum Imperator semper-Augustus, S. D.
units.tr: CHARLES, by the favour of divine clemency, elected Roman Emperor, ever August, greeting.

units.la: BEATISSIME Pater, Domine reverendissime: Eramus profecto in magna mentis nostræ anxietate, communem totius populi Christiani calamitatem nobiscum tacite deploramus, ob ea quæ à Sanctitate vestra contra nos, statumque nostrum, & sacri Romani Imperii dignitatem
units.tr: MOST blessed Father, most reverend Lord: we were indeed in great anxiety of mind, silently lamenting with ourselves the common calamity of the whole Christian people, because of the things which we heard your Holiness was plotting against us, our state, and the dignity of the Holy Roman Empire

units.la: Anno Christi 1526. dignitatem moliri audiebamus. Verum hanc nostram anxietatem mirum in modum auxerunt literæ Sanctitatis vestræ, quas vigesimo die elapsi mensis Augusti, ejusdem Sanctitatis Nuncius XXIII. Junii expeditas, legendas nobis tradidit: Quum nihil de iis perspicere liceat, quam justiciæ suæ (ut inquit) laudem, nostræ vero ac nostrorum causæ acerrimam damnationem: arma, bella, minas, cædes, pecuniæ, avaritiæ, & ambitionis studium, regnandi, dominandique cupidinem nobis impingi. Quæ profecto nec verum pastorem decent, nec nostræ in Apostolicam Sedem, vestramque Sanctitatem, ac illius dignitatem, devotioni, pietati, ac filiali observantiæ convenire videntur. Quinimo ab eo affectu & studio (quo Christianam Rempubl. ab ipsis ineuntis Principatus nostri annis semper complexi fuimus, quo illius pacem, quietem ac incrementum omni conatu concupivimus, ac pro viribus curavimus) prorsus aliena censeantur, ac nos talibus afficiant spiculis, quod ni honori proprio tacendo detrahere, immaculatamque famam nostram, tacita objectorum approbatione, ladere velimus, cogimur emissa in nos jacula refellere, noistramque innocentiam purgare, ac ab his calumniis immunem ostendere.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1526 we heard that your Holiness was plotting against our dignity. But this anxiety of ours was wonderfully increased by the letter of your Holiness, which the Nuncio of your Holiness handed to us to read, sent on the twentieth day of the past month of August, dispatched on 23 June. Nothing can be made out from it except the praise of your justice (as it says) and the most bitter condemnation of our cause and that of ours; and that arms, wars, threats, slaughters, money, avarice, a zeal for ambition, and a desire for ruling and dominating are being hurled at us. These things certainly do not befit a true shepherd, nor do they seem to agree with our devotion, piety and filial observance towards your Holiness, the Apostolic See and its dignity. Indeed they are thought wholly alien to that disposition and zeal with which we have always embraced the Christian commonwealth from the very beginning of our rule, with which we have desired its peace, quiet and increase with every effort, and have taken care of it to the best of our power. They strike us with such darts that, unless we wish to detract from our own honour by keeping silent, or to injure our spotless reputation by tacitly approving the charges, we are compelled to refute the missiles thrown at us, to clear our innocence and to show ourselves free from these calumnies.

units.la: 2. Nos enim, Patet beatissime, nobis ipsi conscii nostræque etiam conscientiæ arcanis perlustratis, nullam objectorum culpam fateri, nullamque horum nobis calumniam ascribere possumus. Testamur enim Deum, nos nihil antiquius unquam habuisse, quam V.
