Sanctitatem post illius ad lauream Apostolatus apicem felicem assumptionem, velut Christi in terris Vicarium, & innata nobis filiali observantia colere, & venerari. Quem etiam, dum in minoribus ageret, singulari amicitia, & benevolentia continuo complexi sumus, prout & Leonis & Adriani temporibus Sanctitas V. satis experta fuit, universoque orbi notum extitit: nullo modo existimantes gradus ac dignitatis augmentum a Deum, nostrorumque etiam assistentia quæsitum) id posse efficere, ut quicquam ab eadem Sanctitate procederet, quod à pristinis suis moribus atque institutis alienum videretur. Et si multa in nos moliri audiverimus, ut dignitati, æstimationi ac auctoritati nostræ detraheretur: ut felicitas, potestas, & magnitudo regnorum ac Principatuum nobis à Deo Opt. Maxim. collatorum minueretur, & si fasces penitus supprimeretur: hæc tamen nunquam Sanctitati V. ascribenda censuimus: nec etiam contrarium affirmantibus fidem dedimus, nec ideo minus æquo animo pacis vocem semper audivimus, vestramque Sanct. ad illam proponendam & amplectendam, velut rectum Pastorem monuimus, & incitavimus.
units.tr: 2. For we, Most blessed Father, having searched our own consciences and the secrets of our conscience too, can admit no guilt in the charges, nor can we ascribe any of these calumnies to ourselves. We call God to witness that we have never had anything more at heart than to honour and revere your Holiness, after your happy assumption to the summit of the Apostolate, as Christ's Vicar on earth, with the filial devotion innate in us. Even while you were still in lesser office, we embraced you with singular friendship and goodwill, as your Holiness has sufficiently experienced in the times of Leo and Adrian, and as it has become known to the whole world. We never thought that an increase of rank and dignity (sought also with the help of ours) could bring it about that anything should proceed from the same Holiness which seemed alien to its former manners and institutions. And although we have heard that many things were being plotted against us, to diminish our dignity, esteem and authority, that the happiness, power and greatness of the kingdoms and principalities conferred on us by God Most Good and Greatest should be lessened, and even that the fasces should be utterly suppressed, yet we have never thought these things were to be ascribed to your Holiness, nor have we given credence to those affirming the contrary. Nor on that account have we less calmly always heard the voice of peace, and admonished and urged your Holiness, as a right shepherd, to propose and embrace it.

units.la: 3. Semper enim in quacunque fortuna pacis ac quietis cupidi esse studuimus, ad quæ nostra nimus suapte natura inclinatur. Nec unquam inter Christianos (nisi provocati coactive) bellum gessimus, neque tentavimus.
units.tr: 3. For in whatever fortune we have always striven to be desirous of peace and quiet, to which our nature is by its own disposition inclined. Nor have we ever waged or attempted war among Christians, unless provoked and compelled.

units.la: 4. Quum enim classem in hostes dispositam haberemus, Menicè insula ad deditionem coacta: majora pro fide Catholica tentaturi, Gallorum arte, & copiis undique cincti, ad propria tuenda reducimur. Vestræque etiam Sanctitatis opera & ministerio, cum Leone X. fœdus percussimus, ac pro Apostolicæ Sedis, sacrique Imperii juribus, ac dignitatibus tuendis, ipsius Pastoris auctoritate & impulsu, in Insubria ac Liguria arma movimus, nostrumque exercitum Pontificio (cui tunc V. Sanctitas in minoribus agens, munereque legationis fungens, præfectus erat) adjunximus. Quam provinciam profecto, non nisi recta & justa intentione, pro ipsius Christianæ Reipubl. quiete, proque Italiæ liberatione non ex cupiditate, sed suscepimus. Testis est nostrorum operum Deus, verus scrutator cordium, qui intima perspiciens à longe cognoscit, & qui nostram ob id justam causam semper tutatus est: torque insignibus victoriis comprobavit ac justificavit: testis erit Sanctitas Vest. si præteritorum rationem ac memoriam habeat, veraque in lucem promere libeat. Testes sunt ejusdem Sanctitatis V. ministri, sæpius ad pacis ac inducriarum media proponenda transmissi, qui aperte experti sunt, nos semper, rebus etiam nostris secundissimis, qualscunque honestas pacis aut inducriarum conditiones suscipere paratos, quibus & honoris nostri & fœderatorum justa, æqua, ac secura non haberetur. Testantur etiam hæc multiplicia mandata nostra, tum Adriani, tum Sanctitatis vestræ temporibus per nos ad Urbem missa, variæque legationes ad id pro tempore dispositæ ac destinatæ, ut nihil à nobis de his quæ ad pacem attinent, ullo unquam tempore prætermissum arbitremur. Qui non minus æquæ ac honestæ pacis studioli ac zelatores fuimus summufque, quàm injuriarum alacres ac prompti propulsatores, acetiam, ubi ratio suadet, clementissimi remissiores, hilaresque bonorum pro malis, & convicis retributores.
units.tr: 4. When we had a fleet arrayed against the enemy, and the island of Menicè had been forced to surrender, we were about to attempt greater things for the Catholic faith. But we were surrounded on all sides by the craft and forces of the French and were driven back to defend our own. By the work and ministry of your Holiness we struck a league with Leo X, and to defend the rights and dignities of the Apostolic See and the Holy Empire, by the authority and impulse of the same Pastor, we took up arms in Insubria and Liguria, and joined our army to the Papal one, over which your Holiness, then serving in lesser office and discharging the office of legate, was in command. This undertaking we certainly took up not from greed but with a right and just intention, for the quiet of the Christian commonwealth itself and for the liberation of Italy. God, the true searcher of hearts, is witness to our works. He, looking into inner things, knows from afar, has always defended our just cause on that account, and has confirmed and justified it with notable victories. Your Holiness will be a witness too, if you keep the account and memory of past events and are willing to bring the true facts to light. The ministers of this same Holiness are witnesses, having been sent several times to propose means of peace and truce; they clearly found by experience that we were always ready, even in our most fortunate affairs, to accept whatever honourable conditions of peace or truce, provided that they did not treat the just, equal and secure interests of our honour and of our allies as worthless. Our many mandates also bear witness to this, sent by us to the City in the times of Adrian and of your Holiness, and the various embassies arranged and dispatched for this purpose at the time, so that we think nothing concerning matters of peace was ever omitted by us at any time. We have been no less eager and zealous for a peace that is equal and honourable than we have been, above all, ready and prompt to repel injuries, and also, where reason suggests, most merciful when more lenient, and cheerful in repaying good for evil and abuse.

units.la: 5. Ait vestra Sanctitas se conscium nihil prætermisisse, quod, vel ad boni, vel ad honesti Pastoris officium erga universum gregem, vel ad fidelis amicianimum in nos speciatim pertineret. Nolumus in hoc Vest. Sanctit. officium impugnare, nec de illius conscientia & animo contendere: sed operibus credere, reliqua Deo perscrutanda relinquere. Licet autem sic esset, ut ait, id potius divinæ benignitati, cujus gratuito munere id fit, quam humanis viribus aut cujuspiam industriæ tribuendum foret. Esto quod multa nobis secus relata fuerint quæ apertius respondendo detegentur.
units.tr: 5. Your Holiness says that you are conscious of having omitted nothing that pertains either to the office of a good and honourable shepherd towards the whole flock, or to the mind of a faithful friend towards us in particular. We do not wish to assail this duty of your Holiness, nor to contend about your conscience and intention; we trust your works, and leave the rest to be searched out by God. However, even if it were so, as you say, that should be attributed rather to divine kindness, by whose free gift it comes about, than to human powers or anyone's diligence. Granted that many things have been reported to us otherwise, which will be disclosed when we answer more openly.

units.la: 6. Quod autem Vest. Sanctit. subjungit suorum bonorum operum, suique erga nos amoris eum exitum consecutum esse, ut & repulsa totiens à benevolentia & conjunctione nostra, nullum indicium veri amoris apud nos invenerit, sive eorum artibus & dolis, qui eandem Sanctitatem vestram nunquam nobiscum conjunctam esse voluerunt, sive nostra mente oppressionem Italiæ & diminutionem dignitatis Sanctitatis vestræ meditantē. Miramur hæc quidem ab ejusdem Sanctitatis vestræ præcordiis emanasse, adeoque intempestivè, rei veritate prorsus alienam pronunciationem tactam.
units.tr: 6. As for what your Holiness adds, that after your good works and your love towards us, the outcome has been that, though so often repulsed from our goodwill and union, you have found no sign of true love among us, whether through the arts and tricks of those who never wished your Holiness to be united with us, or through our mind meditating the oppression of Italy and the diminution of your Holiness's dignity: we marvel that these things have emanated from the very heart of your Holiness, and that a pronouncement utterly alien to the truth of the matter has been made so unseasonably.

units.la: Papæ non verbis sed operibus credendum. factam. Non enim hi sumus, qui bonorum operum ingrati esse didicerimus, nec qui pro amore odium seu repulsam rependere soleamus. Quinimo reciprocas vices potius reddere, ac etiam pro acceptis beneficiis majora dum licet, impendere; amorisque & benevolentiae vicissitudinem abunde referre solemus. Nec quippe tantae imbecillitatis censendi sumus, ut cujuspiam artibus seu dolis à vera conjunctione & amicitia divelli valeamus: ubi perfectus amicitiae nodus intercesserit, qui contrario opera laqueo, non dissolvatur: minusque nobis oppressio Italiae, imminutioque Sedis Apostolicae, sedis dignitatis ascribi poterit: qui (teste Deo) nihil horum tentavimus nec unquam cogitavimus. Verum omnem conatum, omneque studium adhibuimus, ut Italiam liberam ac quietam redderemus, ut Apostolicam sedem in suo decore, velut illius protector & defensor, stabiliremus ac servaremus: utque pacata Christiana Repub. communia Christianorum arma in perfidos Christianae religionis hostes, communi consilio verterentur. Ubi igitur oppressionis actus non intercessit, nil siniistri de nobis praesumendum fuit. Cum in dubiis meliorem praesumptionem sumendam omnia jura testentur: quae etiam neminem ex praesumptionibus damnant, nisi evidentissimo accedant probationes, aut talis esset praesumptio, adversus quam jura probationem non admitterent. Quod profecto hoc in casu omnino alienum patebit, cum non solum nulla nobis talis obstet praesumptio Juris vel facti, verum omnis suspicionis labes, à recta nostra intentione, nostrisque operibus omnino abesse videatur. Nec quippe hanc nostram synceram mentem, nostramque aestimationem laedere potuit Mediolanensis status, per nostri exercitus duces captus, &c, ut ajunt, occupatus. Hanc enim technam (omnium recte sentientium judicio) repellendam curabimus, dum suo loco de ea re V.S. objectis particularibus respondebimus: omnem rei gestae seriem non palliatam, non obumbratam, sed meram veritate suffultam, aperte ac palam differentes, ab omnibus recti judicii capacibus videndam, inspiciendam, acrecto intellectum oculo judicandam.
units.tr: The Pope is to be believed by deeds, not words. For we are not those who have learned to be ungrateful for good deeds, nor are we accustomed to repay love with hatred or repulse. Rather, we are accustomed to return favours in kind and, as far as we can, to bestow even greater things for benefits received, and to repay abundantly the exchange of love and goodwill. Nor are we to be judged so feeble that we could be torn from true union and friendship by anyone's arts or tricks. Where the perfect knot of friendship has been tied, it is not loosened by the snare of contrary works. Still less can the oppression of Italy or the diminution of the Apostolic See and its dignity be ascribed to us, who (God is witness) have attempted none of these things nor ever thought of them. Rather, we have applied every effort and every zeal to make Italy free and quiet, and to establish and preserve the Apostolic See in its dignity, as its protector and defender; and so that, with the Christian commonwealth pacified, the common arms of Christians might be turned by common counsel against the faithless enemies of the Christian religion. Where, therefore, no act of oppression has intervened, nothing sinister was to be presumed about us. For in doubtful matters all laws testify that the better presumption is to be taken, and these laws condemn no one on presumptions unless clear proofs are added, or unless the presumption were such that the laws would not admit proof against it. That will clearly be wholly foreign to this case, since not only does no such presumption of law or of fact stand in our way, but every stain of suspicion seems wholly absent from our right intention and our works. Nor indeed could the Milanese state, taken by the commanders of our army and, as they say, occupied, harm our sincere mind and our good name. This charge (by the judgement of all right-thinking people) we shall take care to repel when, in its place, we answer the particular charges of your Holiness concerning that matter. We shall set out the whole sequence of events, not disguised, not obscured, but supported by plain truth, openly and publicly, so that all capable of right judgement may see it, examine it, and judge it with a sharpened understanding.

units.la: 7. Si igitur ex his Sanct. Vest. se compulsam, ut ait, praetendat, ad ea consilia à quibus & natura & voluntate semper abhorruisse se asserit, idque; serius actum dicat quam plurimarum rerum indignitas, aut honoris sui, & publici Italiae boni ratio postulabat, arma sallicet capere, quae & justitiae, & Italiae libertati, & sibi ipsi possunt esse praesidio, videat quaeso S.V. quibus fundamentis moveatur: consideret an haec pastorali congruant officio: an hic sit gladius per V. Sanct. evaginandus exercendusque, quem Christus in vaginam potius recondendum censuit, & qui etiam in hostes fidei ab ipso Christiani gregis pastore regulariter exerceri prohibetur. Animadvertat V.S. an ex his honoris sui aut publicae Italiae boni ratio habeatur? an haec justitiae conveniat? an Italiae libertati seu quieti consulatur? an potius ex opposito sugilletur summi Pastoris honor & autoritas, injuste agatur cum ipso Apostolicae sedis protectore ac defensore, turbetur Christiana Respubl. universaque ecclesiae status: Incendatur ignis qui tam facile extingui nequeat: ut tandem Christianorum viribus debilitatis, hostes perfidi, velut lupi rapaces pedetentim Christianum abigant gregem, Novi; errores in dies pullulent, ac demum haereticorum dogmata magis atque magis invalescant, Christianae quoque religioni irreparabile afferant detrimentum.
units.tr: 7. If, therefore, Your Holiness pleads that you were compelled, as you say, to those counsels from which you assert you have always shrunk by both nature and will, and that it was done later than the unworthiness of very many things, or the consideration of your own honour and of the public good of Italy, demanded, namely to take up arms, which can serve as a protection to justice, to Italian liberty, and to yourself, please consider, I ask you, on what foundations you rest. Consider whether these things agree with the pastoral office: whether this is a sword which Your Holiness should draw and wield, when Christ judged it should rather be returned to its scabbard, and which the very Shepherd of the Christian flock forbids to be regularly used even against enemies of the faith. Let Your Holiness observe whether account is taken of your honour or of the public good of Italy by these means; whether they agree with justice; whether consideration is given to Italian liberty or quiet; or rather, on the contrary, whether the honour and authority of the supreme Shepherd is disparaged, whether injustice is done to the very protector and defender of the Apostolic See, whether the Christian commonwealth and the whole state of the Church are thrown into turmoil. A fire is kindled which cannot easily be put out; so that, at last, the strength of the Christians being weakened, the faithless enemies, like rapacious wolves, may gradually drive off the Christian flock; new errors sprout up day by day, and at last the dogmas of the heretics grow ever stronger, bringing irreparable harm also to the Christian religion.

units.la: 8. At protestatur S. Vest. in ipso exordio id non offendendi cujuspiam causa, sed tuendi ac conservandi honoris officiique sui. Sancta quippe haec protestatio, si per contrarium non tolleretur ac inefficax redderetur, si in ipsis defensionis terminis staretur, nec ad ea quae offensionem sapiunt transitus ficeret. Qualiter enim defendendi causa parantur arma ubi nullus est offensor, qui V.Sanct. alius quehonorem aut dignitatem laedat? quam potius, si offensa apparuisset, omni conatu totis; viribus tueri ac protegere studuissemus: nil antiquius in animo habentes quam ea in Apostolicam sedem officia exhibere, quae ad officium Christianissimi Imperatoris pertinent, quaeve Imperiali congruunt dignitati. At ut (ut ipsa S.V. protestatur) defendendi duntaxat erat animus, cur priusquam protestatio illa in lucem prodiret ad manusque nostras scripta vestra pervenirent, tenta est offensio in statu Mediolani, sacri Imperii feudo? Laudensi civitate occupata & a nostrorum (nil tale cogitantium) manibus erepta? Cur Vest. S. ac foederatorum copiis & viribus, nulla etiam praecedente monitione seu diffidatione exercitus nostri apud Mediolanum, non impune tamen, impeditur ac invaditur? Haec si defensionem an potius apertam offensionem sapiant lippis etiam pateret. Verum Vest. S. hanc notam putans evadere, longam exorditur tragoediam narrans quae suo congruunt propositio, his tacitis, quae magis ad veram rei seriem discernendam facere videntur. Unde altius repetendo tota facti series in lucem prodeat: liceatque; unicuique; animi nostri sinceritatem inspicere.
units.tr: 8. But Your Holiness protests at the very outset that this is not done to offend anyone, but to defend and preserve your honour and office. Indeed, this holy protest would be effective, if it were not overturned by the opposite course, if it kept to the very limits of defence, and did not pass over to those things which smack of offence. For why are arms prepared for the sake of defence where there is no offender, who else harms the honour or dignity of Your Holiness? Rather, had an offence appeared, we would have striven with all our effort and strength to protect and shelter you, having nothing more at heart than to render those services to the Apostolic See which pertain to the office of the most Christian Emperor and befit the Imperial dignity. But if, as Your Holiness yourself protests, your intention was only defensive, why, before that protest came to light and your writings reached our hands, was an offence attempted in the state of Milan, a fief of the Holy Empire? Why was the city of Lodi occupied and snatched from the hands of our men, who were thinking of nothing of the kind? Why, without any prior warning or defiance, is our army at Milan hindered and attacked by the forces and troops of Your Holiness and your allies, though not without loss to them? If these things savoured of defence rather than of open offence, they would be plain even to the blear-eyed. But Your Holiness, thinking to escape this charge, begins a long tragedy, narrating those things which suit your purpose and passing over in silence those which seem more relevant to discerning the true sequence of events. Let the whole series of the deed be brought to light by tracing it back from further off, and let each person be permitted to examine the sincerity of our mind.

units.la: 9. Si ea quae S.V. nobis, rebusque nostris, dum in Cardinalatu etiam officia praestitit, animadvertamus, id quippe antecessisse dignoscitur, quod vita functo Maximiliano Caesare, avo nostro paterno felicis recordationis, dum is vivens cum Sacri Imperii Electoribus fundamenta jecisset quibus eidem, in Imperio successor effici possemus cum; cum Gallorum rege, qui filiam suam nobis sponderat, foedere arctissimo junctii esseimus, ut & nos filium nuncuparet, nilque ab eo, quod ab paterno amore alienum seu indignum videretur, prodere putaremus, his taliter ad Imperii assecutionem allectus incitatusque extitit: ut etiam cum taxatione personae propositae inhabilitate ipsius Imperialis dignitatis capellendae, conatus fuerit variis modis Electores inducere, ut illum eligerent, Imperatoremque designarent (quod non ad ipsius Gallorum Regis promotionem tentatum extitit, sed ut per ejusmodi Galli concurrentiam utroque nostrum exclusso, soluto foedere tertius subintraret minoti potentia praeditus cui potius imperaretur quam imperare posset) nihil praetermittendo, ut ab ipsius Imperii adeptione penitus excluderemur. Et cum hujusmodi conatus irriti facti forent, vicissetque sacri Imperii Electorum virtus, qui nec vi, nec metu, nec ullis artibus dimoveri potuerunt, quin Sanct o Spiritu, ab omni præambula promissione prius liberati, unanimi omnium consensu a[illegible, ~4 letters] discrepante, eorum electionis vota uniformiter in nos contulerint nosque Imperatorem [illegible, ~6 letters] designaverint. Quam quidem electionem non tamen voluimus prius acceptare, quam ipsius Leonis Summi Pontificis, V.S. patruelis consensus & auctoritas accederet, cum ea dispensatione, ut eum [illegible, ~4 letters] petio nobis etiam Neapolitanum regnum retinere liceret, lege investituræ minime refragante.
units.tr: 9. If we consider what Your Holiness did for us and our affairs, even while in the Cardinalate, it is clear that this preceded it: when our paternal grandfather, Emperor Maximilian of happy memory, had, while living, laid with the Electors of the Holy Empire the foundations by which we might be made his successor in the Empire, and had joined us in a most close alliance with the King of the French, who had promised us his daughter, and we had thought nothing which seemed alien or unworthy of paternal affection should be betrayed by us, he was thus allured and incited to attain the Empire. Thus, even with a disparagement of the proposed person as unfit to hold that Imperial dignity, he tried in various ways to induce the Electors to elect the King of the French and designate him Emperor (which was attempted not for the advancement of the King of the French himself, but so that, by such a French candidacy, both of us being excluded, the alliance dissolved, a third party might step in endowed with great power, over whom one would rather be commanded than be able to command), leaving nothing untried so that we might be utterly excluded from attaining the Empire. And when attempts of this kind had come to nothing, the virtue of the Electors of the Holy Empire prevailed; they could be moved neither by force, nor fear, nor any arts, so that, freed from every prior promise by the Holy Spirit, with the unanimous consent of all [illegible] dissenting, they conferred their votes of election uniformly upon us and designated us Emperor [illegible]. Yet we did not wish to accept this election before the consent and authority of Leo, the Supreme Pontiff, your cousin, Your Holiness, should also come in, with this dispensation, that by his favour we might also retain the Kingdom of Naples, the law of investiture not opposing.

units.la: 10. Hinc nova cogitantur media, ut ipsius Imperii sacri dignitas illudatur & illius autoritas deprimatur viresque nostræ minuantur. Præterea tamen quod tentatum extitit ex litteris & nuncupatis practicis, ut nostra coronatio apud Aquisgranum differretur impediretur, ac inde Wormatiensi conventus proclaretur, seu potius inutilis inefficaxque redderetur, fuit etiam organo ac medio Alberti Pii Carpen. Comitis, non sine V.San. ministerio & opera (ut fertur) percussum fœdus inter Leonem & Gallum: quo etiam de auferendis a nobis utriusque Siciliæ regnis, deque protectionibus pluriumque tuum ac civitatum Italiæ inter se dividendis, Imperioque Italico penitus usurpando, seu venus evertendo & subvertendo agebatur: prout hæc ex nonnullis interceptis literis, quas originaliter in nostra servamus, liquide constare poterit. At quum Gallus Rex hujus spe fœderis fretus, cupiens suæ ditionis finibrias ampliandi, violato fœdere quod prius nobiscum inierat, per Robertum de Maicha, rebellem subditum nostrum, ad ipsius Gallorum regis stipendii conductum, arma in dominio nostra Galliæ Belgicæ movisset: ipsiusque Galliæ Regis duces & milites, in Italia agentes, etiam apostolicæ sedis dominia tunc possessa, urbem scilicet Rhegium, clanculum occupare conati fuerint, fatemur tunc Sanctit. Vest. opera divum ipsum Leonem, Gallorum amplitudinem magis quam potentiam perhorrescentem, de ipsorumque fide hæsitantem, in partes nostras adductum esse, nobiscumque fœdus iniisse quo suam Sanctitatem, in sua Apostolica dignitate tueri, & Romanæ ecclesiam ante occupatam per Gallos restituere & redintegrare, nec non illustrem Franciscum Sforziam paternum solum & statum a rege Gallo detentum reducere convenimus. Quod quidem animo suscepimus: postergaris oblitis, anterioribus gestis, in statu, honoris, ac dignitatis nostræ præjudicium molitis, ut nil aliud putaremus quam duo orbis luminaria, Vest.Sanct. opera adeo cum pari biliter conjuncta censeri, ut inde mutua horum correspondentia, orbis universus illustrari posset, ad perpetuamque unionem reduci. Hoc itaque fœdere freti cum ipsius divi Leonis copiis nostris adjunctis, & ut antea retulimus sub Vest. Sanctitatis præfectura & legatione per nos actum executumque extitit, ut Parma, Placentia ecclesiæ restitutis, ipsoque illustri Francisco Sforciæ in patrino tolio stabilito, Galli, etiam non sine magna strage ducum nostrorum, virtute illustrium videlicet Prosperi Columnæ Marchionisque Piscariæ aliorum nostri exercitus ducum & militum ab Italia omnino expulsi fuerint. Et hæc sunt quæ Leonis tempore Vest. Sanctitas pro nobis egit. Quæ tamen non ita passim irremunerata fuere. Cum & ipsa Romana ecclesia suum ex his auxerit patrimonium, non solum Parmæ & Placentiæ recuperatione, sed etiam novi census onere regno nostro Neapolitano injuncto, Vestraque, S.(quod non improperandi causa sit dictum) aureorum x. milium pensionem annuam super Metropoli Toletana, nostra quidem liberalitate obtinuit.
units.tr: 10. Hence new means were devised to make a mockery of the dignity of the Holy Empire, to lower its authority, and to diminish our strength. Moreover, besides what was attempted through letters and practices of persons who gave out their designs, so that our coronation at Aachen would be deferred or prevented, and thence the Diet of Worms would be proclaimed, or rather rendered useless and ineffective, the alliance between Leo and the French King was also struck, through the agency and means of Alberto Pio, Count of Carpi, not without the ministry and work of Your Holiness (as is reported). By it, it was also planned to take from us both kingdoms of Sicily, to divide among themselves the protectorates of many of your states and cities of Italy, and to usurp the Italian Empire entirely, or rather to overturn and subvert it. This can be clearly established from some intercepted letters, which we keep in the original. But when the French King, relying on the hope of this alliance and desiring to enlarge the borders of his realm, had broken the treaty he had previously made with us, and through Robert de Maicha, a rebel subject of ours, hired at the French King's own wages, had moved arms in our Belgian dominions in France; and when the commanders and soldiers of the same French King, acting in Italy, also tried secretly to seize the dominions of the Apostolic See then held, namely the city of Reggio, we admit that at that time, through the work of Your Holiness, the divine Leo himself, shrinking more from the greatness than the power of the French, and doubting their good faith, was brought over to our side, and entered into an alliance with us, by which we agreed to protect His Holiness in his Apostolic dignity, to restore and re-establish the Church of Rome, previously occupied by the French, and also to bring back the illustrious Francis Sforza to his paternal soil and state, detained by the French King. This we undertook with a willing mind, setting aside past events and forgetting former deeds, which had been contrived to the prejudice of our state, honour, and dignity; so that we thought of nothing else than that the two lights of the world, through the work of Your Holiness, were so joined in a like bond that by their mutual correspondence the whole world might be illuminated and brought back to a perpetual union. Relying therefore on this alliance, with our forces joined to those of the divine Leo himself, and, as we said before, under the leadership and legation of Your Holiness, it was carried out and accomplished by us, so that Parma and Piacenza were restored to the Church, and the same illustrious Francis Sforza was established in his paternal throne; and the French, not without great slaughter of our commanders, were utterly expelled from Italy, by the valour of the illustrious Prospero Colonna, the Marquis of Pescara, and the other commanders and soldiers of our army. These are the things which Your Holiness did for us in the time of Leo. Yet they were not all left unrewarded: for the Roman Church itself increased its patrimony from them, not only by the recovery of Parma and Piacenza, but also, by our liberality, Your Holiness obtained an annual pension of 10,000 gold ducats on the metropolis of Toledo, the burden of a new tax being imposed on our Kingdom of Naples (which is not said to reproach you).

units.la: 11. Quid autem Adriani tempore gestum fuerit, dissimulemus. Novit S.V. quibus tunc favoribus Adrianus in ejus gratiam suscepisset Cardinalem Volaterranum Vest.S. æmulum acerrimumque adversarium, quot illius artibus & mediis in V.S. caput moliretur, ac qualiter eandem Vest.S. a Florentinæ reipub. administratione excludere conabatur. Novit etiam, nos ita suarum rerum suaque familiæ ac ipsius reipub. Florentinæ protectionem ac patrocinium suscepisse, etiam cum status sui ac suorum nepotum incremento, ut hic Adrianus ipse, nostro favore, nostrique intuitu, non solum Vest.S. in gratiam tunc suscepcerit, verum tanta gratia prosecutus fuerit, ut nihil in rebus status, qui alicuius momenti censentur, Vest.Sanctitate inconsulta, tentaret. Hincque Volaterranus S.V. adversarius cum indignatus nonnulla cum Gallis (suis interceptis literis) moliri videretur. Adriani jussu capitur in vinculaque conjicitur debitas pœnas daturus, ni Adriano morte prævento, autoritate sacri Cardinalium collegii pro novi Pontificis electione liberatus fuisset, & inde electione facta eorundem Cardinalium in gratiam a V.Sanctitate veniam obtinere meruisset: licet paulo post dies suos clauserit extremos. Non dissimulemur tamen, ipso Adriano vivente, postquam in illius gratiam, Sa.V. reducta extitit, illius opera non modice frugi nobis fuisse, in alliciendo eundem Adrianum ad fœdus illud defensivum, quo medio Galli iterum in Italiam redeuntes Mediolanumque obsidenres, fœderatorum præsidia dissolverunt repulsique fuere. Quod & si in Vestræ Sanctitatis Pontificatu fuerit executum, id tamen substitutis & copiis ejusdem Adriani, in vimque præambuli fœderis actum extitit. Quod V.Sanct. opus Sanctum suarum despiciens (novus homo factus novaque dignitate assumpta) nequaquam appropinquandum seu innovandum censuit: licet ipsius fœderis executionem, in qua cæteri fœderati tunc firmiter insistebant, concurrentibus etiam Venetorum copiis, Vestra Sanctitas, prout ratio suadebat, nequaquam impediendum censuerit: quum & si præsidia ecclesiæ eo tempore cessassent non ideo minus nostrorum victoria in manu esse videbatur.
units.tr: 11. Let us pass over what was done in the time of Adrian. Your Holiness knows with what favours Adrian then took into his good graces Cardinal Volterrano, your Holiness's keenest rival and fiercest adversary, how many of his arts and devices he was directing against your Holiness's person, and how he strove to exclude your Holiness from the administration of the Florentine republic. Your Holiness also knows that we took under our protection and patronage the affairs of your Holiness's own state and family and of the Florentine republic itself, even while our own state and our nephews were growing. Through our favour and out of regard for us, this same Adrian not only received your Holiness back into favour but showed such kindness that he would attempt nothing of any weight in matters of state without your Holiness's consent. Hence, when Volterrano, your Holiness's adversary, was indignant and seemed to be plotting something with the French (as his intercepted letters showed), he was seized by Adrian's order and thrown into chains, about to pay the penalty due. Adrian's death prevented this, and by the authority of the sacred college of Cardinals he was freed for the election of a new Pontiff; and after the election he earned pardon from your Holiness through the favour of those same Cardinals, although he ended his days shortly afterwards. Yet let us not pass over in silence that, while Adrian was still alive and after your Holiness had been restored to his favour, your Holiness's work was of no small benefit to us in winning Adrian over to that defensive league, by means of which the French, returning into Italy and besieging Milan, dissolved the garrisons of the allies and were driven back. Although this was carried out in your Holiness's pontificate, it was nevertheless done through the substitutes and forces of that same Adrian, and in virtue of the preliminary league. Your Holiness, disregarding that work of your own (having become a new man and assumed a new dignity), judged that it should in no way be approached or renewed. Yet your Holiness, as reason advised, by no means thought fit to hinder the execution of that league, in which the other allies then firmly persisted, with the Venetian forces also joining in. And although the garrisons of the Church had at that time ceased, our victory nevertheless seemed to be in hand.

units.la: 12. Non tamen ob id S.Vestræ auxilia atque consilia tunc præstita parvipendenda censemus, verum pro his & gratias tunc egimus & adhuc agimus, simulque nos V.Sanctitati debere, & obnoxios esse profitemur: qui etiam vices non solum reciprocas, sed & multiplicatas & longe majora præsidia, si casus se obtulisset Vest.Sanctitati ipsiqueApostolicæ Sedi pro illius tutela & augmento, semper exhibere parati fuimus, & ut filius patri correspondere: a quo etiam proposito quicquid in nos fallo suggestu molitum videatur, nequaquam animum nostrum alienavimus: nec alienaturi sumus, nisi major nos urgeat necessitas in occupandis nostris viribus, ad rerum nostrarum tutelam ac defensionem; quam tamen ita moderatam (un͞ipturi sumus, ut ab offensionis limitibus, quantum fas fuerit, abesse videatur. Hoc enim moderatum temperamentum nos Christo, cujus V.S. vices in terra gerit, debere profitemur.
units.tr: 12. Nevertheless, we do not therefore think that the aid and counsel your Holiness then gave should be held in small regard. Rather, for these we gave thanks then and still give thanks, and at the same time we profess that we owe your Holiness and are bound to you. We have always been ready to offer not only reciprocal services but multiplied and far greater forces, should the occasion arise, for your Holiness's own protection and the increase of the Apostolic See, and as a son to a father we have wished to return the favour. From this purpose we have not turned our minds, whatever may seem to have been plotted against us from the deceitful pulpit, nor shall we turn them, unless some greater necessity presses us to employ our forces in securing and defending our own affairs. Yet we shall use that force with such moderation that it may appear, as far as is right, to keep clear of the boundaries of offence. For we profess that we owe this moderate restraint to Christ, whose place your Holiness holds on earth.

units.la: 13. Reprehendit V.Sanctitas, quod non fideli consilio exercitus nostri duces in Galliam transfuerint, inferens quod ex eo intempestivo (ut ait) transitu, successerit celerior & crassior in Italiam Gallorum irruptio, rege maximi nominis exercitum ducente: ac urbis opulentissimæ Mediolani ab illis receptio. Nos, Beatissime Pater, nec excusamus illius transitus consilium nec impugnamus. Idramen nobis inconsultis actum non extitit, qui id nulla justa ratione negare potuimus. Illustri consanguineo nostro Carolo duci Borbonii, Anglicis etiam præsidiis freto, pro sui status recuperatione, quo, eo quod nostris se addixit obsequiis, privatus extitetat. Durum enim ac prorsus inhumanum visum fuisset, si eo duce, vicesque nostras in Italiam agente, obtenta de communi hoste victoria, ejectisque inde Gallis, victricia arma eidem denegaremus ob rerum suarum nostri causa, ut prætendit, occupandarum consecutionem, ubi potissime ex eo exercitus nostri in Galliam transitu, Italia quietior ac liberior remanere videbatur, a militum quoque gravaminibus & insolentiis, quibus plerunque victores multes uti solent, magis exonerata & exempta reddebatur. Sed cum aliter res tunc successerit, quam putabatur, non quidem nostra, sed ducum culpa, sed belli sorte ita suadente, ut victoria quæ a Deo est, non ita passim pro voto hominum valeat obtineri, valuit saltem ducum prudentia, audacia ac magnanimitas in reducendo opportuno tempore, exercitum illæsum in Italiam, quo ipsorum Gallorum Regis impetus compesci posset, illiusque conatibus obstitit. Qui profecto (ut a fide dignis nobis relatum extitit) a V.S. ejusque ministris ad id fuit persuasus & incitatus (quod tamen pro certo non habemus, nec ita passim credendum putavimus) eam provinciam belli Italici tam acriter impetuosque tentavit, ut favente altissimo justæ nostræ causæ defensore victus, cum maxima suorum clade nobis per Viceregem nostrum Neapolitanum captivus fit redditus: & inde a nobis sub conditionibus V.S. notis, liberatus.
units.tr: 13. Your Holiness reproaches our army's commanders for crossing into France without faithful counsel, claiming that from that untimely (as you say) passage there followed a swifter and fuller French invasion of Italy, led by a king of the greatest renown, and the seizure of the very rich city of Milan by them. We, Most Blessed Father, neither excuse the counsel of that crossing nor attack it. Yet it was not done without our knowledge, and we could not in any just reason deny it: to our illustrious kinsman Charles, Duke of Bourbon, supported also by English forces, for the recovery of his state, from which he had been deprived because he had attached himself to our service. For it would have seemed harsh and utterly inhuman, if, with that duke leading our forces into Italy, and a victory won over our common enemy, and the French driven out, we had denied victorious arms to him, on the pretext, as it was alleged, of our own interest in seizing his property. Indeed, from that crossing of our army into France, Italy seemed likely to remain quieter and freer, and was rendered more relieved and exempt from the burdens and insolence of soldiers, which victors are generally wont to inflict. But since matters then turned out otherwise than was expected, not by our fault but by the fault of the commanders, and by the chance of war, which so decreed (for the victory that is from God cannot be obtained at will by men), yet the prudence, boldness and magnanimity of the commanders at least prevailed, in bringing the army back into Italy at the opportune time, unharmed, where it could check the onset of the French king himself and resist his attempts. He indeed (as we have been told by trustworthy men) was persuaded and incited by your Holiness and your ministers to this (though we do not hold it for certain, nor thought it should be readily believed), and he attacked that province of the Italian war so fiercely and impetuously that, with the Most High favouring the defender of our just cause, he was defeated, and with great slaughter of his own men he was taken captive and handed over to us through our Viceroy of Naples; and from there, on conditions known to your Holiness, he was released by us.

units.la: 14. Excusat V.S. quod cum duces nostri de defensione illarum regionum spem totam posuissent, ac de earum insuper, quæ nostræ erant propriæ periculo commoverentur, eademque V.S. in magno etiam suarum rerum metu esset, ejus conventionibus occurrere coacta fuerit imminenti periculo, quas ait nos optime nosse. Nos tamen earum conventionum veram noticiam habere non possumus: quæ nobis sunt infinis transactæ, quasque nunquam vidimus seu legimus: quæ etiam ministris nunquam oste nsæ fuere in ipsorum Gallorum relatione stare vellemus, qui aliter rem gestam ajunt, quam S. Vest. suis nunciaverit. Volumus nihilominus potius V.S. assertioni confidere. Recolimus enim dum eadem Sanctitas nos de hujusmodi conventionibus (rebus adhuc sub ancipiti Marte laborantibus) suis literis monuisset, afferens nil inde eidem Sanctitati quæsitum quam fidem & securitatem, id exigente, ut a jebat, necessitate, eliciens inde futuræ pacis auspicium. Cum ipsa S. de consueto suo erga nos animo & voluntate nihil omnino remisisse afferaret, cepimus tunc hæc in benigniorem partem V. Sanct. culpam nequaquam arguentes: nec de ejusdem, ut ajebat, erga nos animo & voluntate diffidentes. Id enim potius quorundam suasionibus tribuendum censuimus, qui vires nostras sua detractione deprimendo, hostium potentiam extoliendo V. Sanctitati suaserit res nostras in summo discrimine consistere, hostiumque vero robur, in excelso culmine florere. Sic pristinam V.S. voluntatem in quandam depictam necessitatem transformantes: licet re vera nulla urgens necessitas subesse videretur. Nec tanta erat in ipsis nostris exercitus ducibus desperatio, aut trepidatio, prout S.V. insinuabant illius fœderis autores, qui S.V. terrere studebant, quod ex ipso rei exitu secuta victoria clarius enituit. Ex qua potius quam quod ex eo fœdere pacis auspicium sumendum videbatur in quorundam malignantium artes suis potius passionibus & cupiditatibus, quam saluti reipub. incendentes, sanctum id opus pertur bassent.
units.tr: 14. Your Holiness excuses yourself: since our commanders had placed all their hope in the defence of those regions, and since those regions which were ours were themselves in peril, and your Holiness was also in great fear for your own affairs, you were compelled to meet the imminent danger by those agreements, which you say we know very well. Yet we cannot have a true knowledge of those agreements, which were concluded without our knowledge, and which we never saw or read, and which were never shown to our ministers; nor would we wish to rest on the account of the French themselves, who say the thing was done otherwise than your Holiness reported. We would rather trust your Holiness's assertion. For we recall that when your Holiness informed us by your letters of such agreements (while affairs were still struggling under an uncertain war), you stated that you had sought nothing from them except faith and security, which, as you said, necessity demanded, and that you took from them an omen of future peace. Since you declared that you had in no way departed from your customary feeling and goodwill towards us, we then took these things in the kinder sense, not blaming your Holiness at all, nor distrusting your feeling and goodwill towards us, as you said. We thought rather that this should be attributed to the persuasions of certain men, who, by belittling our strength with their detraction and exalting the power of the enemy, persuaded your Holiness that our affairs were in the greatest danger and that the strength of the enemy flourished at its height; thus they transformed your Holiness's former goodwill into a certain painted necessity, although in truth no pressing necessity seemed to exist. Nor was there such despair or trepidation in our army's commanders, as those authors of the league, who sought to terrify your Holiness, insinuated; as the outcome of the affair, with the victory that followed, shone out more clearly. Those men, inflaming the holy work with their own passions and desires rather than the safety of the commonwealth, disturbed it by the arts of certain malicious persons, rather than taking from that league what seemed to be an omen of peace.

units.la: 15. Commemorat V.S. quæ sibi fuerat cura, quæ cautio rerum nostrarum, asserens tunc rebus nostris nihilominus non minus quam propriis cavisse, Gallorum transitum in regni nostri fines multis rebus temoratum fuisse. Merebatur quidem nostra in S.V. devotio, ut Sanctitas ipsa tali officio fungeretur. Idque exposcebat reipub. salus, ne uberior ignis incenderetur, licet ex ipso affecto potius potuerunt Gallos ipsos tunc aliquandiu in itinere detentos, ut a sacri Imperii civitatibus Lucenli & Senensi pecuniam ac tormenta ad bellum contra nos & regnum nostrum disponendum extorquerent: ut quietum ipsius Senensis civitatis statum tunc perturbarent: Tyrannos intromitterent, ac pro eorum voto civitatis gubernium mutarent: eam civitatem a sacri Imperii devotione omnino divertere satagentes. Novas interim copias in terris ac patrimonio Rom. ecclesiæ ex ipsis pecuniis ab imperialibus civitatibus extortis, congerentes: quibus ad regni nostri invasionem inimicitiores ac potentiores esse possent: nec tanta erat in his urbanitas, ut ab ejusmodi invasione diutius remorari seu retrahi possent, ni Deus Opt. Max. victoria apud Ticinum collata, eorumque rege captivo tantum terrorem incussisset: ut non amplius de invasione, sed potius de eorum salute & fuga cogitare visi fuerint.
units.tr: 15. Your Holiness recalls what care you had for us, and what caution for our affairs, asserting that you then took no less care of our affairs than of your own, and that the passage of the French into the borders of our kingdom was hindered in many ways. Our devotion certainly deserved that your Holiness should discharge such a duty, and the safety of the commonwealth demanded it, lest a wider fire be kindled. Yet from that very disposition the French could rather have been detained for some time on their march, so that they might extort money and artillery from the cities of the Holy Empire, Lucca and Siena, for preparing war against us and our kingdom; so that they might disturb the quiet state of the city of Siena, install tyrants, and change its government to suit their wishes, striving utterly to turn that city away from devotion to the Holy Empire. Meanwhile, they were gathering new forces in the lands and patrimony of the Roman Church, from that money extorted from the imperial cities, so that they might be more hostile and more powerful for the invasion of our kingdom. Nor were they of such courtesy that they could have been delayed or held back for long from such an invasion, had not God, Best and Greatest, by the victory won at Ticino, and by the capture of their king, struck such terror into them that they seemed to think no more of invasion, but rather of their own safety and flight.

units.la: 16. Sed ait V.S. quod si societatem eorum sequi voluisset, maxima eidem præmia non solum non proponebantur, sed etiam parata essent. Arqui quæ ratio, quæ justa causa, quis honestus color Vest. Sanctitatem, directum ejus feudi dominum, movere debuisset ad juvandum invasionem contra propriam feudatarium nil tale merentem, nec tale facinus cogitantem, absentemque, nec monitum, nec impetum, titum, nec de aliqua justa causa subtrahendi feudum convictum. Tenebatur enim Vest. Sanctitas jure feudi tanquam directus illius dominus, potius nos in feudo tueri, quam invasoribus aditum dare, aut se socium invasionis praestare. Eodem enim ordine quo tenetur Vasallus pro feudo domino servire, eodem ordine tenetur dominus vasallum in feudo tueri. Et ex quibus causis vasallus feudum amittit, ex eisdem causis dominus directa proprietate feudi, illiusque directo dominio privatur. Est enim ipsius feudi natura, ut ultro citroque oblationem pariat. Facile quidem fuisset improvisum regnum ac ad defensionem non paratum, nil tale metuens aggredi, & forsan in parte occupare. Sed an id heri licuisset, an haec pastorali officio convenisset: cogitet S. V. Quae enim praemia offerri poterant, quae Christi Vicarium ad tam immane facinus induxissent? Sanctius itaque tunc consultum extitir Vestrae S. ut praemiis illis neglectis non attentaret, quod forsan pro voto non succedisset, nec tentatum coeptum ve consummari potuisset. Sicque merito (ut inquit S.V.) plus apud eam valuisse debuerunt amicitiae nostrae merita, quam praemium ullum. Verum & si meliorem praesumptionem amplecti velimus, nilque de intrinsecis Sanctit. Vest. cordis judicare praesumamus, quod vero Christi Vicario non congrueret: non tamen pro comperto habemus, quid cessante victoria S.V. actura fuisset, quae jam sub accipiti Marte statim Mediolanum colore sequestri, ac depositi a nostrorum ducum manu & protectione eripete: ac in sua potestate, quamdiu de pace tractaretur reponere, & reducere conabatur. Quae etiam, ut ad id nos ac duces ipsos nostros cogeret, illorumque vires minueret, ac necessitatem inducere, asserens antecessoris foedus successorem non ligare. Curavit (ut ajunt) non solum Florentinorum aliorumque potentatuum praesidia, qui ex Adriani foedere ad contributionem defensivam tenebantur subtrahi & denegari. Verum & si nostrorum Venetorum praesidia, ad quae particulari foedere nebantur, sustulisse dicitur, his suadendo ne suas copias, ut tenebantur, nostris jungerent: ut liberi nostri, omni foederatorum auxilio destituti priusquam in campum prodirent, hostesq; adorientur, coacti fuerint, non sine summo labore, & nostris ac Serenissimi Archiducis fratris nostri impensis, novas tum equitum tum peditum copias ex Germania adducere, & cum his exercitum nostrum augere, bellum aggredi speratamq; victoriam nancisci possent.
units.tr: 16. But Your Holiness says that if he had wished to follow their alliance, the greatest rewards would not only have been withheld from him but were even ready to be offered. But what reason, what just cause, what honourable pretext ought to have moved Your Holiness, the direct lord of that fief, to aid an invasion against your own vassal, who deserved nothing of the kind, was not planning such a crime, and was absent, unwarned, unattacked, and not convicted of any just cause for withdrawing the fief? For by the law of the fief Your Holiness, as its direct lord, was bound to protect us in the fief rather than open the way for invaders or make yourself a partner in the invasion. In the same way that a vassal is bound to serve his lord for the fief, the lord is bound to protect the vassal in the fief. And for the same causes by which a vassal loses the fief, the lord is deprived of the direct ownership and direct dominion of the fief. For it is the very nature of a fief that it creates mutual obligation. Certainly the kingdom would have been easily attacked, unprepared and not ready for defence, fearing nothing of the kind, and perhaps partly seized. But whether this would have been lawful, or whether it would have suited the pastoral office, let Your Holiness consider. For what rewards could be offered that would have induced the Vicar of Christ to so monstrous a crime? It would therefore have been wiser for Your Holiness, with those rewards set aside, not to attempt what perhaps would not have turned out as you wished, and what, once attempted, could not have been brought to completion. And so, rightly (as Your Holiness says), the merits of our friendship ought to have weighed more with you than any reward. But even if we wish to embrace a more favourable presumption, and presume nothing to judge of the inner heart of Your Holiness, which would not befit the Vicar of Christ, we nevertheless do not know for certain what Your Holiness would have done had victory been lacking. You, who already, with Mars swooping like a hawk, had immediately tried to snatch Milan from the hand and protection of our commanders under the colour of sequestration and deposit, and to hold it in your own power and restore it while peace was being negotiated. You also, in order to force us and our commanders themselves to this, and to diminish their strength and bring about necessity, asserted that a successor is not bound by the covenant of his predecessor. You took care (as they say) not only to withdraw and deny the garrisons of the Florentines and the other potentates, who under the covenant of Adrian were bound to defensive contribution. It is even said that you removed our Venetian garrisons, to which they were bound by a particular covenant, by persuading them not to join their forces to ours, as they were bound to do; so that our men, deprived of all help from the allies before they could take the field, were forced to attack the enemy, and, not without great labour and at the expense of ourselves and of our most serene brother the Archduke, to bring new companies of horse and foot from Germany, to augment our army with them, and so to begin the war and gain the hoped-for victory.

units.la: 17. Subdit eadem Sanctitas, quod sequuta nostrorum victoria contra Gallos, cum omnis sibi sublata contentio videretur, sine cupiditatis & partium suspicione, nobis etiam foederis vinculo haereto posset: magnumque in nobis Italiae beneficium & Christianitatis totius positum arbitraretur: non solum foedus firmavit, sed quo nostri duces egentes pecuniae exercitum alere ac sustinere possent, centum illis dederit ducatorum millia, conditione appositá, ut si de foedere aliqua nobis dubitatio oriretur, illae Sanctit. Vest. pecuniae restituerentur. Fatemur quidem, Pater Beatissime, Victoriam illam omnem sibi contentionem merito sustulisse: sineque cupiditatis (a qua semper fuimus alieni) partium suspicione, cujus nulla suberat causa nobis haerere potuisse: omnique ratione arbitrandum fuisse, ea in re totius Italiae ac Christianitatis beneficium impositum: ni zizaniae seminator, illius fructum suffocasset. Diffitemur tamen eam in foedere conditionem appositam, quod si dubitatio oriretur, pecuniae nostrae ducibus solutae Vest. Sanct. restituerentur. Quandoquidem ipsius rei gestae seriem longe aliter se habere constet, nec de tali conditione ulla in ipso foedere mentio facta appareat, verum in quodam articulo separato & a capitulis foederis penitus exclusa, enarretur. Quod cum Vestra Sanctitas ad satisfaciendum exercitui nostro, in Italia existenti civitatesque & oppida Sanctae Romanae ecclesiae subjecta, ac oppressionibus, militum sublevanda, salutem & tranquillitatem Italiae custodiendam, summam pecuniae inter Vest. Sanct. nostrosque oratores expressam, suo & exceleast Reipub. dominorum Florentinorum nomine se soluturum promisisset, pie pro tunc ad sexaginta millium ducatorum auri ascensuram. Oratores nostri eidem Vest. S. sub juramento promise- unt quod casu, quo foedus cum ipsis nostris oratoribus pereuslum, & capitula in ipso foedere contenta, non approbaremus non ratificaremus, omnis summa pecuniae, quae per Vestram Sanct. ac per dominos Florentinos soluta fuisset, eidem Sanct. & Florentinis integre restitueretur: cum ea adjectione, quod dorso restitutio integre & plene facta foret, foedus interea, & omnia ipsius foederis capitula, ad unguem observatentur. Quum itaque foedus ipsum, ac singula capitula in eo foedere comprehensa, quampridem ad nos delata fuere rata & grata habuerimus, nostraeque ratificationis literas, cum ipsorum capitulorum foederis insertione in forma debita expeditas Vestrae Sanctitati exhibere fecerimus: quas & vidit & legit, & palpavit, & dando suas reciprocas retinere potuit. Justificare ergo non potest quin purificata fuerit per nos conditio illa, qua deficiente restitutio pecuniarum erat fienda. Quae quidem conditio, & particularis conventio, prout illius verba sonant, nequaquam nos urgebant, ad alia extrinsecus a foedere aut separatim gesta vel tractata. Quinimo potius, & si pecuniarum locus esset restitutioni, cujus tamen contrarium ostenditur, servandum tamen erat foedus. Interim a quo juxta ipsius separati articuli seriem, sine pollicitorum violatione recedi non potuit, necad contraria foedera licite devenire valuit. Sicque satis erroneae, & (salva pace sit dictum) praeter veritatem refertur, quod idem foedus non plene a nobis acceptum, nec probatum fuerit, qui & plane & integre, ut praefertur, omnia in foedere contenta probavimus, rataque habuimus, nil penitus de contentis in eo, nec etiam syllabam aut literam mittentes. Quod si vestra S. hujusce nostrae ratificationis literas recipere, suasque reciprocas (ut par erat) tradere renuit: ni simul traderetur ratificatio duorum articulorum de quibus extra ipsum foedus perscripta particularia, nobis tamen inconsultis separatim & ad partem statum fuerat. Ad quorum approbationem & ex vi foederis (ut praemittitur) astringebamur. Nil est quod culpae nostrae ascribi valeat, si foedus illud minime observatum: sed potius inde violatio exstitit.
units.tr: 17. Your Holiness adds that after our army's victory over the French, when all contention seemed removed, without suspicion of greed or of factions, the alliance could also have been tied to us by the bond of the covenant; and that a great benefit to us in Italy and to all Christendom was thought to have been placed in our hands. Not only did you confirm the covenant, but, so that our commanders, short of money, might be able to maintain and sustain the army, you gave them a hundred thousand ducats, with a condition attached: that if any doubt arose about the covenant on our side, that money should be restored to Your Holiness. We indeed confess, Most Blessed Father, that that victory had rightly removed all contention, and that it was free of any suspicion of greed (from which we have always been alien) or of factions, since no cause for such suspicion could have clung to us; and that by every reckoning it must be judged that a benefit to all Italy and Christendom had been conferred in that matter, had not the sower of tares choked its fruit. Yet we deny that such a condition was attached in the covenant, namely that if doubt arose, the money paid to our commanders would be restored to Your Holiness. For it is clear that the course of the affair itself was quite otherwise, and no mention of any such condition appears in the covenant itself; it is recorded instead in a certain separate article, wholly excluded from the chapters of the covenant. When Your Holiness promised, for the purpose of satisfying our army then in Italy, of relieving the cities and towns subject to the Holy Roman Church from its oppressions and soldiers, and of preserving the safety and tranquillity of Italy, to pay the sum agreed between Your Holiness and our envoys, in your name and in that of the lords of the Florentine republic, which then amounted piously to sixty thousand gold ducats, our envoys promised Your Holiness under oath that, in the event that the covenant concluded with our envoys themselves were not approved or ratified by us, and the chapters contained in the covenant were not accepted, the whole sum of money paid by Your Holiness and by the Florentine lords would be fully restored to Your Holiness and the Florentines, with the addition that the restitution should be made in full before the covenant and all its chapters were observed to the letter. Since, therefore, we have held the covenant itself and each of the chapters contained in it, which were brought to us some time ago, as valid and acceptable, and have caused the letters of our ratification, with the chapters of the covenant inserted in due form, to be delivered to Your Holiness, which you have seen and read and handled, and have been able to keep in exchange for your own reciprocal letters, Your Holiness cannot deny that that condition, by which the restitution of the money was to be made in default, has been fulfilled on our part. That condition, and that particular agreement, as its words sound, did not in any way press upon us with regard to other matters carried out or negotiated outside the covenant or separately. Rather, even if there were room for the restitution of money, which however is shown to be the contrary, the covenant was still to be kept. Meanwhile, according to the sequence of that separate article, we could not withdraw from it without violating our promises, nor could we lawfully enter into contrary covenants. And so it is quite erroneously, and (with respect be it said) contrary to the truth, asserted that the same covenant was not fully accepted and approved by us; for we have approved and held as valid all the things contained in it, fully and entirely, as has been said, sending nothing of what is contained in it, not even a syllable or a letter. But if Your Holiness refuses to receive the letters of this our ratification, and to deliver your reciprocal letters (as was proper), unless at the same time the ratification of the two articles were delivered, which were drawn up separately outside the covenant itself, and were settled on a separate footing without our knowledge: to the approval of which we were bound by force of the covenant (as has been said), there is nothing that can be ascribed to our fault if the covenant was not observed; rather, the violation arose from that.

units.la: Abbas Ab hac enim culpa & labe omnino alieni sumus: & ut id plene liqueat, placet illorum duorum articulorum extrinsecus tractatorum substantiam referre: causasq; differere: quibus non ita passim per nos approbandi viderentur.
units.tr: Far from this fault and stain are we entirely; and so that this may be made fully clear, it pleases us to set out the substance of those two articles, treated outside the covenant, and to explain the reasons why they did not seem to be approvable by us in the ordinary way.

units.la: 18. Ex his enim duobus articulis separatis, alter satis in statu Mediolanen. distribuendum, cum id à nostris oratoribus sua S. expositum esset: ut, juxta fœdus per nos cum Leone percussum, curaremus cum duce Francisco Sforcia, sal eisdem modis & conditionibus à sede & Camera apost. recipi. Nostriq; oratores ad id responderunt: non esse amplius nobis jus utilis dominii ducatus Mediolani, prout ante fuerat cum Leone, data jam per nos eidem duci investitura, sicque rem cum ipso duce necessario dicendum esse. Ipsi autem oratores nostri, non expresso quod id nostro nomine agerent, simpliciter V.S. medio eorum juramento promiserunt quod illustris Vice-rex curaret, ut illustris dux Mediolan. cum Vest. Sanctitate pro hujusmodi sale conveniret. Si igitur haec promissio, quæ non nisi factis tertii pollicetur de ipsoque tertio, nil ultro promittit: quod tertium illum curaturum, ut dux ad concordiam veniret, nil certi decernendo nos urgere videatur: ut hac promissionem præcise ratam habere debeamus. Ita, ut sine ea fœderis per nos approbati & ratificati observantia evanesceat. Judicet id quicunque mentis compos, quandoquidem nostra sententia, & ut peritorum consilio freti, didicimus: nos nequaquam ad ipsius promissionis observantiam astricti causaremur. Respondimus tum in hoc modestius V.S. quod si hujusmodi Sanct. Vest. desiderium nobis prius innotuisset, quod de ipsa salis distributione in statu Mediolani ad opus serenissimi archiducis, fratris nostri, cum ipso Illustri Francisco Sforcia, transactum esset, nostram libenter operam navare studuissemus, ut S.V. hujusce voti compos fieret. Verum & si fratri deesse non possemus, nos tamen cum eo curaturos, ut mediante aliqua honesta recompensa pecuniaria, ipse frater noster, jus hujusmodi distribuendi salis: V.S. ad illius vitam concederet. Id enim æquum & justum videbatur, ne jus illud, quod eidem fratri nostro, pro recompensa præstiti pereum præstitit ad defensionem status Mediolani, deficientibus viribus ac copiis, Vestræ Sanctitatis, aliorumque fœderatorum, eidem infructuosum redderetur.
units.tr: 18. Of these two separate articles, one concerned the distribution of salt in the state of Milan, since Your Holiness had set out that, according to the covenant struck by us with Leo, we should take care, with Duke Francesco Sforza, that salt be received by the See and the Apostolic Chamber on the same terms and conditions. Our envoys replied that we no longer had the right of useful dominion over the Duchy of Milan, as we had before with Leo, the investiture having already been given by us to that same duke, and that the matter therefore had to be settled with the duke himself. Our envoys, however, without stating that they acted in our name, simply promised Your Holiness, under their oath, that the illustrious Viceroy would take care that the illustrious Duke of Milan should come to terms with Your Holiness concerning such salt. If, then, this promise, which promises nothing except the acts of a third party, and promises nothing further on the part of that third party, does not seem to press upon us any definite obligation, since that third party would take care that the duke came to agreement, so that we ought not to be held precisely to this promise, the observance of the covenant approved and ratified by us would vanish without it. Let anyone who is in his right mind judge this, since, as we have learned both from our own opinion and by relying on the counsel of experts, we could in no way be held bound to the observance of that promise. We replied, moreover, in this more modestly to Your Holiness: that if your desire of this kind had been known to us beforehand, we would gladly have endeavoured to assist you, so that Your Holiness might obtain your wish, concerning the very distribution of salt in the state of Milan, which had been arranged for the service of the most serene Archduke, our brother, with the illustrious Francesco Sforza himself. But although we could not fail our brother, we would nevertheless take care with him that, by means of some honourable pecuniary recompense, our brother himself would grant the right of distributing such salt to Your Holiness for his lifetime. For this seemed fair and just, lest that right, which had been granted to our brother as a recompense for his services in defending the state of Milan, should, with the forces and troops of Your Holiness and the other allies failing, become useless to him."

units.la: 19. Alter vero ex his duobus articulis id continebat, quod ad tollendam difficultatem, quæ inter Sanct. V. & nos incidere posset, super controversia Mutinæ & Rhegii, offerebant nostri oratores ut Vestra Sanctitas consequeretur utile ipsarum civitatum dominium superioritatis & directi dominii, jure nobis semper salvo, ita ut S. Vest. extunc recognosceret, & acceptaret hujusmodi directum nostrum dominium ac superioritatem: vestraque S. nobis aut agentibus nostris, centena millia ducatorum aureorum (post recuperatam possessionem eorum quæ illustris dux Ferrariæ à repore obitus Leonis ecclesiæ subtraxerat) persolvere deberet. Huic propositioni & oblationi respondebat Vest. Sanct. pro se & sede Apost. hujusmodi oblata acceptare, prout proponebantur, excepta superioritate & directo dominio nostro: supradictis civitatibus Vestra S. recognoscere renunciavit, ne juribus & superioritati ab Apostolo sede prætensis, præjudicium fieret. Offerente tum Vest. Sanct. se contentam esse, ut ipsius superioritatis controversia videretur & decideretur infra tres menses tunc proximos per V.S. & illius Vice-regem, aut alios qui ab utraque parte simul eligerentur. Et si hujusmodi superioritas nobis adjudicaretur, Apostolica sedes recognosceret prout ab agentibus nostris fuerat propositum. Si vero Apostolicæ sedi adjudicaretur, V.Sanct. ex sua liberalitate & ex eo amore quo nos prosequi profitebatur, nobis condonaret recompensam de qua debemus esse contenti. Hanc Vest. S. responsionem & oblationem ipsi nostri agentes, ita demum acceperunt, ut salva nobis essent omnia jura superioritatis & dominii directi in ipsis civitatibus competentia pertinentia, quibus ob talem acceptationem præjudicium afferre non prætendebant. Consentientes nihilominus, de hujusmodi juribus cognosci, modis & formis per dictam V.S. propositis. Si hæc igitur tam difformiter tam irresolute extra fœderis capitula descripta in ea essent forma, quæ vel ad nos ad ratihabitionem (quam nostri nostro nomine non promiserant) obligaret, vel in nos actionem pararet, qua ad id urgeri possemus, nulla accedente valida stipulatione nec pacto firmiter vestito, ubi etiam tempus decisioni præfixum illum impossibile redderet: consulat in his V.S. peritos & comperiet nos, necad hujusmodi ratihabitione particularem astrictum, nec ex hujus defectu percussi nobiscum fœderis, & per nos indifferenter ac plane approbati, observantiam fuisse defecrendam, nec contrario fœdere frustrandam seu irritandam. Ut tamen modestius cum V.S. pro sua persona qualitate ageremus, ostendimus ea quæ per nostras orationes in hac re tractata fuerant, nequaquam in nostra potestate consistere. Qui nec Imperii juribus præjudicare nec justerni auferre deberemus, nec in nostra esset potestate illum ducem Ferrariæ urgere ad restitutionem petitorum, nisi is armis offensibilibus coerceretur, qui se Imperii vasallum profitebatur, & ea quæ restitui petebantur, de S. Imperii feudo tenere recognoscebat, durumque videretur pro ea re bellum in Italia instaurare. Supplicavimus ergo V.Sanct. ut pro Italiæ quiete, & ne inde novimotus ibidem caurentur, dignaretur eadem Sanctitas Vestra consentire, ut res ipsa, aut per justitiæ tramites, aut per compositionem amicabilem cum ipso duce Ferrariæ fiendam, terminaretur. Et cum hujusmodi oblata Vestræ Sanctitati non placuissent, superveniente postea Reverendissimo Sanctitatis Vestræ Legato, Cardinali de Salviatis, apud nos transegisse, ut Vestræ Sanctitatis mente percepta, non recedentes à recto justitiæ tramite, cupientesque nihilominus quantum fas esset Vest. Sanctitati gratificari, obtulimus eidem nos operam daturos cum effectu, quod sine præjudicio jurium Sacri Romani Imperii, seu alterius cujuslibet, posset Sanctitas Vestra dum sibi expedire videretur, sine cujuspiam resistentia, sineque armorum apparatu sua sponte, per se aut suos ad id deputandos possessionem recuperare, Rhegii & Ruberiæ cum suis pertinentiis tuendam & possidendam, prout antea tenebat & possidebat.
units.tr: 19. The other of these two articles concerned the controversy over Modena and Reggio, which might create a difficulty between Your Holiness and us. Our envoys offered that Your Holiness should obtain the useful dominion of those cities, with the superiority and direct dominion remaining always reserved to us. On this condition Your Holiness would then recognise and accept our direct dominion and superiority, and Your Holiness would pay us, or our agents, one hundred thousand gold ducats after the recovery of the possessions which the illustrious Duke of Ferrara had taken from the Church since the death of Leo. Your Holiness replied to this proposal and offer, on your own behalf and on behalf of the Apostolic See, that you would accept the offers as they were put forward, except for our superiority and direct dominion. Your Holiness renounced recognition of those cities, so that no prejudice would be done to the rights and superiority which the Apostolic See claimed. Your Holiness also offered that the question of that superiority should be examined and decided within the three months next following, by Your Holiness and your Viceroy, or by others chosen jointly by both sides. If the superiority were adjudged to us, the Apostolic See would recognise it, as our agents had proposed. If it were adjudged to the Apostolic See, Your Holiness, out of your generosity and that affection with which you professed to regard us, would grant us the compensation with which we ought to be content. Our agents accepted this response and offer of Your Holiness on the condition that all our rights of superiority and direct dominion in those cities should remain safe, and they did not claim that any prejudice was done to them by such acceptance. Nevertheless they agreed that those rights should be examined in the manner and form proposed by Your Holiness. If, then, these matters were set down outside the chapters of the covenant, so confusedly and so irresolutely, in a form that would bind us to ratify them (which our envoys had not promised in our name), or would furnish an action against us by which we could be urged to it, with no valid stipulation or firmly fixed agreement added, and where even the time fixed for the decision made it impossible: let Your Holiness consult skilled men on this, and you will find that we were neither bound by any particular obligation to such a ratification, nor, through its failure, were we bound to abandon observance of the covenant struck with us, which we had approved plainly and without reservation, nor to frustrate or annul it by a contrary covenant. Yet, in order to deal more moderately with Your Holiness in keeping with your personal dignity, we have shown that the things treated through our envoys in this matter did not in fact lie within our power. We ought neither to prejudice the rights of the Empire nor take them away by force. Nor was it in our power to press the Duke of Ferrara to restore what was demanded, unless he were restrained by offensive arms; he professed himself a vassal of the Empire and acknowledged that the things demanded back were held of the fief of the Holy Empire; and it would seem harsh to renew war in Italy for that reason. We therefore besought Your Holiness, for the sake of the peace of Italy, and so that new disturbances might not be stirred up there, to be pleased to consent that the matter be settled either by the paths of justice or by a friendly agreement to be made with the Duke of Ferrara himself. Since these offers did not please Your Holiness, and afterwards the most Reverend Legate of Your Holiness, Cardinal de Salviati, came to us and carried on negotiations, we, having understood Your Holiness's intention, not departing from the straight path of justice, and yet desiring, so far as right allowed, to oblige Your Holiness, offered that we would effectively work to ensure that Your Holiness might recover possession of Reggio and Ruberia with their appurtenances, to hold and possess as before, without prejudice to the rights of the Holy Roman Empire or of any other party, whenever Your Holiness judged it expedient, by yourself or your deputies appointed for this, without any resistance from anyone and without any display of arms.

units.la: Mutinæ & Rhegii utile dominium Papæ concessum ab Imperatore, salva superioritate. possidebat. Quod tamen Sanctitati vestrae non placuit, licet credere non possemus enim, qui Christi vices in terris gerit, vel unius guttae humani sanguinis jactura, quamcunque secularem ditionem vindicare velle, cum id ab evangelica doctrina prorsus alienum videretur. Quid igitur rebus huiusmodi nobis impingi posset, quum foedus plane à nobis acceptum seu approbatum fuerit. Quo colore nostrae ratificationis literae receptae nō fuerint: Quo jure ipsius Vestrae Sanctitatis reciprocae literae adbis fuerint denegatae: Qua fronte fidei religio, quam V.Sanct. in verbo Romani Pontificis super ipsius foederis observantia personaliter praestitisse dinoscitur, spreta fuerit ac neglecta: cogitet Vest S. ipsa, judicet an sic decceret ab eo foedere discedere, penitusque repugnantia pacisci cum his potius, qui eo tempore pro hostibus habebantur, contra quos potius ponenda erat defensio, ad eorum consuetus repellendos.
units.tr: Modena and Reggio: the useful dominion, granted to the Pope by the Emperor, the superiority being reserved, which he possessed. This, however, did not please Your Holiness. We could not believe that he who holds Christ's place on earth would wish to claim any secular dominion at the cost of the loss of a single drop of human blood, since that seemed entirely alien to the evangelical doctrine. What, then, can be charged against us in such matters, since the covenant was plainly accepted and approved by us? By what pretext were our letters of ratification not received? By what right were the reciprocal letters of Your Holiness itself denied to us? With what effrontery was the faith of religion, which Your Holiness is known to have pledged personally, on the word of the Roman Pontiff, to the observance of that covenant, scorned and neglected? Let Your Holiness herself consider and judge whether it was fitting to withdraw from that covenant, and to make a bargain, totally inconsistent, with those who at that time were regarded as enemies, against whom rather the defence ought to have been directed, in order to repel their usual attacks.

units.la: 20. Quod autem S.V. ad id subjungit, cum propter aemulationem quorundam ex ducibus ingrata caeteris consilia, Pischarię Marchio nonnulla jactare tractareque coepisset, in nostri status detrimentum V.S. illa etiam consilia audivisse ne foedere à nobis rejecto penitus aspernata eidem Sanctitati deesset, ubi nitiac confidere posset. Non possumus profecto non mirari quae in hoc Vestra Sanctitas suis literis profitetur, quae & si nobis saepius, à nostris ducibus aliisque quamplurimis scripta relata fuissent, nusquam tamen à nobis credita sunt, ne adhuc crederemus, nisi V.Sanct. id asseveraret, consessione & assertione in his potissimae, quae proprium factum concernunt, nulla plenior liquido probatio esse posset. Qualia autē fuerint ea, quae Marchio Pischarię in nostri status detrimentum attare & tractare dicebatur, & quae Vest.Sanctitas audivisse faretur, cum in Vest. Sanctitatis literis specifice declarentur, sed sub verborum involucro res iam nephanda tegi videatur, comprobandi acceperit, per ipsius Marchionis literas, quae penes nos servantur, ac per aliorum quorundam, adhuc testimonia, qui hujusce facinoris conscii et participesq; fuerunt. Quibus saris aperte deiegitur, ipsum Pischarię Marchionem non ita proprii honoris ac conscientiae immemorem fuisse quod quicquam in status nostri detrimentum moliri cuperet, sed potius aliter finxisse quam in animo haberet, utrum in nos ac statum nostrum molientium factiones, ac incendia parata, quorum jam fumum iniquo ... raverat, veritatibus indiciis ac argumentis detegeret: hincque facilius nobis praemonitus extinguere potuerit. Sicque finxit se de nobis male contentum, ut inde liberius in molientium partes vocaretur, omnemque rei seriem audire ac funditus intelligere posset.
