Hicque Marchio ipse ad eam tragoediam vocatus simulata fide, in eam conspirationem, cum caeteris illius autoribus convenit, atque consensit: per ustratisque omnibus ad tantum facinus parandum dispositis atque paratis, ac totius negocii serie plane perspecta & intellecta, cum in his V.S. principalis esset autoritas, audivisseque Marchio nuncium ad id per V.S. transmissum, eidem sui parte, ut ait, offerentem sub cujusdam Apostolici Brevis Credentia, regni nostri Neapolitani investituram, & possessionem, si is in ejusdem Sanctitatis & foederatorum cum copiis nostri exercitus, eidem Marchioni magis affectis transiret atque transfugeret: ut inde communibus foederatorum copiis, inter quas & Gallorum copiae, cum ingenti Helvetiorum manu, ad sui regis liberationem Italiae concitatis, uno jactu atque contextu nostrum exercitum prorsus delerent. Nosque non solum à statu Mediolani, sed etiam à regno Neapolitano ac ab omni imperio Italico excluderent: ut inde S.V. nos etiam ab omni Imperiali dignitate deponeret. Finxit Marchio se contentum his annuere, si id cum honore, sine incursu criminis laesae majestatis exequi liceret: & ut super eare perituros consuleret, petiit quindecim dierum dilationem, quibus pendentibus, illi erat in animo nobis rei seriem ascribere, prout & fecit, nec ideo minus se à practicis abstinuit, qui etiam ad hanc fictionem magis colorandam habuit ex urbe consilium peritorum, quo eidem Marchioni persuaderetur, eundem licite posse, ac sine honoris seu fidelitatis praestita laesione, seu praejudicio, sineque ei minus laesae majestatis, in partes Vestrae S. tanquam supremi domini illius regni transfire, feudumque ab eadem sanctitate suscipere, ubi potissime ipsius sanctitatis justus accederet. Si haec igitur pater sancte vera sunt, prout narrat Marchio, qui usque ad ultimum vitae spiritum in ea sententia semper perstitit. Si sunt illa tractata atque jactata consilia, quae V.Sanct. etiam audivisse fatetur: videat ipsa V.Sanctitas, recto sui intellectus oculo, si haec tanto pastore digna censeantur: inspiciat qualis fructus inde colligi possit, quale scandalum, quantusque tumultus ex his in ecclesia Dei ac in universa republ. Christiana nasceretur. Miseranda quippe res esset, ac ab omni fideli catholico deploranda, in quaे itacupatur mentis nostrae judicium, ut quasi somnium illusorium putemus, cui fides tribui non debes ret, cum potissime (ut antea liquide ostendimus) cessæt fundamentum illud satis manifeste erroneum, imo penitus falsum, de foedere à nobis rejecto, quod nunquam rejectum sed plane acceptatum constat.
units.tr: 20. As for what Your Holiness adds, that, because of the jealousy of some of the leaders, which was unwelcome to the others, the Marquis of Pescara had begun to bandy about and discuss certain plans, and that to the detriment of our state Your Holiness had also heard those plans, so that you might not, having wholly rejected the covenant offered by us, be left without support where you could place your trust: we cannot help but wonder at what Your Holiness professes in this in your letters. Although these things were often written and reported to us by our leaders and by very many others, we never believed them, and we would still not believe them, were it not that Your Holiness asserts them. In matters that concern one's own act, no fuller proof can exist than confession and assertion. As to what kind of things those were which the Marquis of Pescara was said to be planning and discussing to the detriment of our state, and which Your Holiness admits to having heard, since they are specifically declared in Your Holiness's letters, yet the matter seems to be covered under a veil of words, though it is in fact an abominable thing, it is to be proved by the Marquis's own letters, which are kept in our possession, and by the testimony of certain others who were privy to and partakers in this crime. From these it is clearly shown that the Marquis of Pescara was not so forgetful of his own honour and conscience as to wish to undertake anything to the detriment of our state; rather, he pretended otherwise than he intended, so that he might by true proofs, indications and arguments uncover the factions and the prepared fires of those plotting against us and our state, whose smoke he had already perceived from afar in its wickedness; and so he might more easily extinguish them, having been forewarned by us. Thus he feigned to be discontented with us, so that he might be more freely called into the party of the plotters, and might be able to hear the whole course of the affair and understand it thoroughly. This Marquis, called to that tragedy under a pretended loyalty, agreed and consented to that conspiracy with its other authors. When all things had been arranged and prepared for so great a crime, and the whole course of the business had been plainly seen and understood, Your Holiness being the principal authority in this, the Marquis heard a messenger sent for this purpose by Your Holiness, who offered him on your part, as he said, under the credence of a certain Apostolic Brief, the investiture and possession of our Kingdom of Naples, if he would pass over and desert, with his troops, from our army to the forces of the said Pope and the confederates, who were more favourable to the Marquis. By this means, with the common forces of the confederates, among whom were the forces of the French, stirred up for the liberation of their king in Italy with a great band of Swiss, they would utterly destroy our army at a single stroke and in one concerted action; and they would exclude us not only from the state of Milan but also from the Kingdom of Naples and from all Italian empire; so that Your Holiness might then deprive us even of all imperial dignity. The Marquis feigned that he agreed to these things, if they could be carried out with honour and without incurring the charge of treason; and, in order to consult on these matters, he asked for a delay of fifteen days. While these were pending, he intended to report the whole course of the affair to us, as indeed he did; nor did he on that account refrain any the less from his dealings. To give more colour to this pretence, he also obtained from the city a council of skilled men, by which the Marquis might be persuaded that he could lawfully pass over to the side of Your Holiness, as the supreme lord of that kingdom, and receive the fief from the same Holiness, without any violation or prejudice to his honour or loyalty, and without any charge of treason, especially where the just cause of Your Holiness would be the more favoured. If these things, most holy Father, are true, as the Marquis, who remained steadfast in this opinion to his last breath, relates; if they are those plans which were discussed and bandied about, which Your Holiness confesses to having heard: let Your Holiness see, with the right eye of your understanding, whether these are thought worthy of so great a shepherd; let her consider what fruit could be gathered from them, what scandal and how great a tumult would arise from these things in the Church of God and in the whole Christian commonwealth. Indeed it would be a miserable thing, to be deplored by every faithful Catholic, if our judgement were so to regard it that we should think it a deceptive dream, in which no faith ought to be placed, especially since (as we have clearly shown above) that foundation, plainly erroneous and indeed wholly false, concerning the covenant rejected by us, has fallen, which it is established was never rejected but plainly accepted.

units.la: 21. Sed ait V.S. se à verbis ad facta nullum aditum tentasse. Utinam sic se res haberet, utinam quae de facto tentatum esset, quia facilius pro verbis verba reddi possent. Facta autem pro infectis habere nequeunt. Ad quod V.Sanct. se de eo officio commendat nos admoneri mandasse, ut duces nostros in Italia quorum in manu res nostrae erant, curaremus de nobis esse contentos, hinc probationem eliciens, eidem esse curae, quietem & stabilitatem rerum nostrarum. Noluimus inficiari id officium à Vest. S. praestitum, eo tamen tempore, quo idem Marchio totius rei seriem nobis aperte disseruerat. Curatem tunc Vestra S. re jam deiecta id nobis nunciandum censuerit, id ejus judicio & conscientiae commendamus. Voluimus tamen & hoc in benigniorem partem suscipere.
units.tr: 21. But Your Holiness says that you made no approach from words to deeds. Would that the matter stood so, and that the attempt concerned words rather than deeds, since words can more easily be answered with words. Deeds, however, cannot be treated as undone. On this point Your Holiness commends yourself for having been ordered to remind us of that duty, namely that our commanders in Italy, into whose hands our affairs were given, should see to it that we were content, and from this you draw the proof that the quiet and stability of our affairs were a concern to you. We have no wish to deny that Your Holiness performed that duty, but it was at the time when the same Marquis had clearly laid out the whole course of events for us. Whether Your Holiness then thought fit to announce this to us, when the matter was already overthrown, we leave to your judgment and conscience. Nevertheless we chose to take this too in the kindlier sense.

units.la: 22. At subjungit V.Sanctitas, quod maximo cum gemitu & dolore suo, atque Italiae totius, cum duces nostri statum nostrum Mediolani occupassent, atque arcem in qua Franciscus Maria residet circumvallare instituissent, postulante à nobis curam & securitatem, adversus dignitatem tantam Italiæ periculo, omnibusque notis atque ignotis flagitantibus paratis qui & auxilia conferrent. Cunctis prope Christianitatis regibus Vestram Sanctitatem animantibus cum non videretur posse resistere monitis, querelis precibusque illorum. Cum vos officii vestri debitum Italiæ calamitas & periculum commune commoveret, tamen adveniente per eos dies ab vestra Sanctitate Commendatore, Herrera Nuncio nostro tractandi causa misso relapsa eadem S. in pristinam spem & cupiditatem benevolentiæ nostræ, sibi quovismodo conciliando dimissis consiliis, conspirationibus, oblationibusque, cunctorum, gravi omnium indignatione & querela, nobis comparare gloriam pacandæ Christianitatis, & moderationis nostræ omnibus declarandæ. Sicque ea conventionum capitula, paucis (ut ait) in locis leviter immutata remisisse ad nos comprobanda, scripsisseque manu sua literas, quibus per Dei misericordiam obsecrando, ut depellere eam suspitionem, quæ de nostra nimia cupiditate omnibus adhærebat, perpetuitatem & fructum amicitiæ suæ nobis pollicebatur, consilium-que fidele dabat, & quæ petendaerant omni cum humanitate & benevolentia à nobis petebat: securitatem videlicet Italiæ duce Mediolani, si quo pacto erraret clementem V.S. amorem. Quæ tot illius opera atque officia erga nos aliaque quamplurima, quæ nobis quotidie postulanti concedebat, ex quibus nobis commodum atque honor accrescebat (ut ait) parvipendimus. His multiplicum querelarum, accusationum, & criminationum fastidium adjungit: quibus tot & tantis (ut inquit) injuriis & causis invita V.S. & gemens de nobis desperare & diffidere & coacta, suamque amicitiam & benevolentiam, quam toties (ut asserit) impudiavimus, multis & magnis regibus adjungere, quorum optimum in Christianitatem publ. & sedem Apostolicam animo. Si Vestra Sanct. aspernata esset, non jam pastoris seu communis patris laudem: sed superbi & insolentis nomen acquisivisset. Hæc, Pater Sancte, horrenda quidem ac penitus abominanda censerentur, ni sicuto veritatis circundari hujusmodi calumnias, convicia, improperia, crimina, facinoraque nobis objecta refellere ac singulatim suo ordine extirpare & enervare studeremus: non quidem Christiano principe digna (si vera forent) sed potius apud inferos recondenda censerentur. Ut igitur hujusmodi calumniarum nobis falso objectarum, fasciculum disrumpamus & colligata spicula in nos conjecta separatim ac gradatim enervemus, cogimur historiam non fabulam recensere, qua rerum gestarum veritas in lucem prodeat. Et cum ab occupatione status Mediolani arcisque obsessione hujusmodi calumniarum principalior sumatur occasio: hincque pendere videantur leges & prophetæ, horum omnium, quæ in nos moliuntur & tentantur. Consequens est, ut pro nostræ villicationis debita ratione reddenda, & nequid occulti remaneat, neve servi nequam nobis nomen ac famam comparemus, sed potius servi fidelis & boni, qui in regnum Domini intrare valeamus, ab ipso stipite initium sumamus, & à capite rationem reddamus oportet, nihil quod ad rem faciat omittentes. Res igitur, ut apertissimis ostenditur documentis, sic se habet.
units.tr: 22. But Your Holiness adds that, to your great groaning and grief and that of all Italy, when our commanders had occupied our state of Milan and had begun to surround the citadel in which Francis Maria resides, we were asked for care and security, against a danger to so great a dignity of Italy, while all men, known and unknown, were demanding and were ready to bring aid as well. Nearly all the kings of Christendom were urging Your Holiness, and since it did not seem possible to resist their admonitions, complaints and prayers, the calamity of Italy and the common danger moved you, as was your duty. Yet in those days, when Commendatore Herrera, our nuncio sent to treat, came from Your Holiness, the same Holiness fell back into her former hope and desire for our goodwill, and, dismissing counsels, conspiracies and offers of everyone, to the grave indignation and complaint of all, sought to win for herself from us the glory of pacifying Christendom and of declaring our moderation to all. And so she sent back to us those articles of agreement, changed slightly (as she says) in a few places, for our approval, and wrote with her own hand a letter in which, begging us through the mercy of God to drive away the suspicion that clung to all men regarding our excessive ambition, she promised the lasting benefit and fruit of her friendship, gave faithful counsel, and asked of us, with all kindness and goodwill, what she had to ask: namely the safety of Italy, with the Duke of Milan, if he should in any way go astray, to be treated with Your Holiness's merciful love. For all these many services and kindnesses toward us, and many others which she granted to our daily requests, from which advantage and honour accrued to us (as she says), we have made little account. To this she adds a tedious heap of complaints, accusations and charges, by which (as she says) Your Holiness, unwilling and groaning, was driven by so many and great injuries and causes to despair of us and distrust us, and to join your friendship and goodwill, which (as she asserts) we have so often spurned, to many great kings, who are most kindly disposed toward Christendom and the Apostolic See. If Your Holiness had rejected them, you would have gained not the praise of a shepherd or common father, but the name of proud and insolent. Father Holy, these things would be thought truly horrible and utterly abominable, did we not strive to refute such calumnies, reproaches, insults, charges, crimes and wicked deeds laid against us, as if they were truth, and to tear them out and weaken them one by one in their proper order. Such things, if they were true, would not be worthy of a Christian prince, but would rather be thought fit to be buried in the depths. So, to break apart the bundle of calumnies falsely laid against us, and to blunt the bound darts thrown at us, one by one and in order, we are compelled to recount not a fable but a history, by which the truth of the events may come to light. And since the occasion for these calumnies is taken chiefly from the occupation of the state of Milan and the siege of the citadel, and since the laws and the prophets seem to depend on this, we must, for the due reckoning of our stewardship, and lest anything remain hidden, and lest we gain for ourselves the name and reputation of wicked servants, but rather of faithful and good servants who may be able to enter the kingdom of the Lord, begin from the very stock and give an account from the head, omitting nothing that bears on the matter. The matter therefore stands thus, as the clearest documents show.

units.la: 23. Postquam Franciscus SForcia hujus nominis primus, & moderni Francisci avus paternus: Ducatum ac statum Mediolani nactus est seu verius occupavit: cum is non intraret per ostium sed per fenestram, necdescenderet à linea vice comitum ducum Mediolani, sed ex persona uxoris ad tale feudum incapacis, jus dicti ducatus prætenderet: Et tanquam strenuus, prudens, ac fortunatus belli dux, non habueritin ipsius ducatus assequtione contradictorem, nunquam tamen is, neque filius ejus primogenitus Galeacius Maria SForcia, nec ex ipso primogenito nepos Joannes Galeacius SForcia ipsius ducatus Mediolani investituram à Sacro Imperio obtinere potuerunt. Successit his Lodovicus SForcia moderni Francisci pater, qui affinitate cum divo Maximiliano Cæsare avo nostro contracta, primus ex SForcianis investituram obtinuit pro se & filiis, ac descendentibus suis ordine successivo, gradu primogenituræ servato. Quo Ludovico primo investito adhuc vivente, insurrexit adversus eum Lodovicus Aurelianensis dux, inde Francorum rex hujus nominis XII. prætendens, quod si ex fœmina linea quispiam in eo ducatu recte succederet, ipse præferendus foret, qui ex descendenti à Valentina Philippi Mariæ Vicecomitis, veri ducis, filiæ legitimæ ortum trahebat. Pacto etiam in contractu matrimonii adjecto, ut deficientibus masculis, ipsa Valentina succederet: quod vacanti Imperio à Sede Apostolica approbatum dicitur, de cujus tamen approbationis viribus nunc disceptandum occasio non offertur. Ipsa autem familia SForciata ab illegitima posteriore genita originem duceret. Ortum est hinc bellum inter ipsum Ludovicum Aurelianensis. Inde Francorum regem, & dictum Ludovicum SForciam, qui Gallorum viribus, & potentia non solum à ducatu & statu ejectus exitcit, sed etiam captivus in Galliam ductus est: ubi tandem dies suos clausit extremos. Hinc Ludovic.rex intelligens se non esse tutum in ducatu Mediolani, nisi à Sacro Imperio investituram obtineret, inito fœdere cum divo Maximiliano Cæsare avo nostro recolendæ memoriæ, actoque de matrimonio seu sponsalibus contrahendis, inter nos & Claudiam ipsius regis Ludov. primogenitam, revocataque per divum Maximilianum investitura, eidem Ludovico SForciæ & liberis antea concessa, investituram dicti ducatus obtinuit, pro se & dicta Claudia ejus filia, casu quo nobiscum nuberet. Ea lege adjecta de expresso ipsius Ludovici suorumque oratorum consensu. Quod si sine culpa nostra dictum matrimonium inter nos & Claudiam quovismodo effectum non haberet, prout non habuit, redderetur ipsa investitura, dicto regi, & Claudiæ filiæ concessa, penitus inefficax nullinsque momenti. Verum omne jus dicti ducatus & status Mediolani, ex ipsa investitura concessum, in nos recta via transiret. Concessa ex tunc illis consentientibus in cum casum nova investitura, in nostri personam præsentem, ad id & nostro nomine stipulante & acceptante, reliquaque ad id requisita solemnia peragente Serenissimo felicis memoriæ Philippo Castellæ rege patre nostro, quam investituram, in solemni forma conceptâ, & & per ipsum divum Maximilianum tunc expeditam, adhuc hodie penes nos habemus. Et licet eo sordere per regem Ludovicum violato, dictaque Claudia ejus filia, matrimonio copulata, cum tunc duci Angolenen. Francif. Moderno Francorum rege, siqueque conditione purificata investitura nobis perfertur, conditionaliter concessa, validum robur & effectum obtineret: ut jus dicti ducatus & status Mediolani in nos translatum censeretur. Ipse tamen divus Cæsar Maximilianus, tum quia publicam potius quam privatam utilitatem curabat, tum quia putabat jus nobis ex investitura prædicta quæsitum salvum esse nullumque præjudicium nobis tunc posse afferri, qui in pupillari ætate constitutus sub illius tutela regebamur. Quo tutelæ officio fretus in illud liquidum, quod nobis competebat necessitate nec expresse remittere poterat. Novam eidem Gallorum regi Ludovico pro se & dictis Claudia filia & Francisco genero investituram concessit, nonnullis etiam conditionibus nequaquam observatis, astrictam ac à nobis, qui jus potissimum prætendere poteramus, nunc approbatam. Qua de re ipse divus Cæsar Maximil. violati fœderis, vindictam prosequens, expulso ab ipso ducatu Mediolani dicto Ludovico Francorum rege, sub colore prioris investituræ, Ludovico S Forciæ cœcessit, & in præmittitur revocatæ, nobis iterum in pupillari ætate, & sub illius tutela degentibus, Maximiliano S Forciam, ejusdem ducis Ludovici filium primogenitum, ad ipsum ducatum & statum Mediolani admisit & induxit. Atis posse fore effectus, immemor beneficii in eum collati, plura cum Gallis hostibus, iniquitate Imperii dedecus & detrimentum molitus est. Indeque inito ac percussio cum his fœdere, prodite eidem arces & statum, ac ad hostes transivit cessitque ducatui. Ex cujus felonia. Si quod jus in eodem ducatu habuisset, ad sacrum imperium devolvebatur. At cum Modernus Francorum rex, tantum extenso jure investiturae Ludovico Regi ejus socero concessit, quam etiam ex jure cesso per dictum Maximilianum S Forciam, ipsius ducatus possessionem, post Ludovici regis mortem nactus esset, per eumdem seu alium ejus nomine nova investitura ab ipso Maximiliano Cæsare: nec à nobis petita, seu obtenta. Sicnos & sacrum imperium contemnendo, pluraque etiam contra decus & honorem ipsius strum, ac ipsius sacri Rom. Imperii moliendo, & in nos ejusdem feudi dominum cervicem elevando, armaque movendo, prout suis propriis literis ac notoriis gestis innotuit, etiamsi validam antea investituram habuisset, prout non habuit, omni illius commodo omnique jure, ipso facto privatus extinctaque totum ad nos & sacrum Romanum Imp. devolutum fuit. Ut si illustris Franciscus S Forcia eodem ducatu Med. Olani, nullum jus posset prætendere, nisi id ex nostra liberalitate & gratia consequatur. Non enim ex investitura prima, jus aliquod habere potest, stante revocatione, ut prius irritum; facta per ipsummet concedentem, eo sc. tempore, quo nondum eidem Francisco duci jus in requisitum dici poterat: sed duntaxat in spe quod facilius tollitur. Ubi potissime plenitudo accedit potestatis, cum cætera ipsius concedentis ac revocantis sententia. Non etiam ex cessione seu tenuatione dicti Maximiliani ejus fratris primogeniti, qui nullam de eo statu habuit investituram, sed simplicem detentionem nullo jure suffultam, cui pariter obstabat paternæ investiturae revocatio. Sicque illius concessio nullius fuit effectus. Nemo enim plus juris in alium transferre potest: quam ipse habeat. Sed demus investituram, eidem Ludovico patri concessam, in suo robore permanere, ipsumque ducem Franciscum juxta illius ordinem ad successionem vocandum, non vocatur ex ea nisi post mortem primogeniti, qui adhuc vivit. Sicque non evenit casus, qui ipsum Franciscum admittat. Non enim primogenitus simpliciter refutavit feudum ante feudi adeptionem: ut Serert locus sequenti in gradu, sed optaro feudo, ubi de fructibus pro libitu ejus, vita comite, disponere poterat etiam invito propinquiore successore cessit & renunciavit. Et cum id egerit, paciscendo cum hostibus in dominum feudi: otum illud jus, quod eidem Maximiliano primogenito competiisset, ad sacrum Imperium devolutum extitit. Sicque nos nullo jure cogebamur, etiam firma stante illa prima investitura hujusmodi ducatum Mediolanensem concedere ipsi illustri Francisco S Forciæ. Saltem vita comite ipsius Maximiliani primogeniti. Quinimo jure merito poteramus ducatum ipsum penes nos retinere eoque interim uti frui. Objicitur nobis fœdus percussum cum divo Leone. Super quo tamen nullum validum fundamentum favoris dicti Francisci S Forciæ adhibari potest. Res est inter alios acta, nihil ibidem cum duce Francisco tractatum est, nec quisquam pro eo ibidem intervenit, nullusque pro eo stipulatus extitit, cui stipulandi jus esset. Et si inter contrahentes res ageretur, emergeret quæstio, an is qui ex eo oriri fundaret, pro parte sua implevisset quod debebat. Sed fatemur omnia solenniter gesta & impleta, ipsumque fœdus percussum, & stipulatum cum ipsomet duce Francisco non datur illi ex eo oriri plus juris quam antea haberet. Sic enim sonant ipsius fœderis verba. Item: Quia illustris Franciscus SForcia dux Barri prætendit ducatum Mediolani sibi deberi ex vi investitura, per felicis memoriæ Max. Maximiliani Cæsarem facta, attentata renunciatione fratris sui primogeniti, per quam se primum successionis iccum afferunt obtinere. Actum extitit & conventum. Quod si idem illustris Franc. Sforcia ducatum ipsum recuperaverit, præfatis contrahentes, eundem in suis juribus conservare curabunt, ac ab omni violentia tueri nitentur. Ecce igitur, quod hic nullum aliud prætendat dux Francisco quam quod supradictum est, abunde tamen enervatum. Ecce quod hic est conventio conditionalis, si ipse dux ducatum recuperaverit, quæ conditio implenda erat in forma specifica æque non impleta, prout ipse implere non poterat, obligatio illa evanescit. Et esto quod soret ipsa conditio firmiter impleta, & purificata. Ecce obligatio illa non disponit nisi de eo conservando in suis juribus. Quæ ut antea ostensum est, nulla sunt nulliusque momenti. Si igitur nos tot titulis, totque juribus fulti, qui ducatum ipsum, fœderatorum nostrorum præsidiis freti, nostra tamen ut plurimum impensa, non sine magna nostrorum jactura, totque præclaris ducibus ac militibus amissis, cum tanta Christiani sanguinis effusione, ex hostium manibus recuperavimus, ab eorumque faucibus eripuimus,& totiens illis redeuntibus,repulsis ac victis servavimus,ac tutati sumus,nulla nos ad id urgete necessitate,sed pro reipub.quiete,ex nostra mera liberalitate ac munificentia, juribus nostris tam claris,tam apertis omnino postpositis ac postergatis, cõsensimus eundem illustrem Franciscum S Forciam,tanto munere dignum facere,eumdemque ad dictum ducatum admittere, ac eidem ipsius ducatus investituram concedere. Quis nam vir sani capitis,nos de cupiditate, de ambitione, de indebita occupatione recte arguere poterit? Quis nam ex his gestis potest elicere sinistram aliquam suspicionem, quod non recto animo intenti videamur ad ea omnia quæ reipubl. Christianæ quietem & tranquillitatem Italiæque libertatem concernere videntur? Adhæc non verbo tantum obtulimus, sed & effectu præstitimus. Fecimus enim ipsum ducem Franciscum totius status possessorem, fecimus in ejus potestate reponi & consignari omnes arces,omnesque civitates,autoritatem & administratione omnimodam eidem permisimus,ut non solum regere & pro libito administrare posset fructus percipiendo,sed etiam alienando,vendendo ac pro ejus voto disponendo. Cujus etiam alienationis,dum ad id requisiti fuimus tanquam à vero duce factas confirmavimus & approbavimus,fecimus in foederibus per nos initis,tum cum Adriano,tum cum Venetis, tum etiam cum cæteris, cum quibus tractavimus eundem, tanquam Mediolani ducem nominari & includi, de ejusque tutela & conservatione transegimus: Concessimusq; tandem investituram dicti ducatus,& pertinentiarum in forma amplissima. Quamad manus equitis Bellæ ipsius ducis Francisci oratoris realiter consignavimus,sub certis conventionibus & obligationibus,per ipsum ducem implendis pro parte impensarum,per nos in ejus beneficium factarum pro adoptione & conservatione dicti status. In quibus tamen ita moderate habuimus,ut nec vix quartam ipsium impensarum partem, per annorum terminos essemus recuperaturi. Hæc profecto scripta patent,nullaque tergiversatione celari potest, cum jam in Notoriotatem transiverint.
units.tr: 23. After Francis Sforza, the first of that name and the paternal grandfather of the present Francis, had got hold of the duchy and state of Milan, or rather seized it, he did not enter by the door but through the window. He did not descend from the line of the Visconti dukes of Milan but claimed the right to that duchy through his wife, who was incapable of holding such a fief. As a vigorous, prudent and lucky war leader, he met with no opponent in acquiring the duchy. Yet neither he nor his firstborn son Galeazzo Maria Sforza, nor Galeazzo's son Giovanni Galeazzo Sforza, could ever obtain the investiture of the duchy of Milan from the Holy Empire. After them came Ludovico Sforza, the father of the present Francis, who, by a marriage alliance with the divine Emperor Maximilian, our grandfather, was the first of the Sforzas to obtain the investiture for himself and his sons and descendants in successive order, the rule of primogeniture being kept. While this Ludovico, already invested, was still alive, Louis, duke of Orléans, afterwards Louis XII, king of the French, rose up against him. He claimed that if the succession in that duchy passed through a female line, he himself should be preferred, since he was descended from Valentina, the legitimate daughter of Filippo Maria Visconti, the true duke. A pact had also been added to the marriage contract that, if males failed, Valentina herself should succeed. It is said that this pact was approved by the Apostolic See while the Empire was vacant, but the force of that approval is not a matter for dispute at present. The Sforza family itself, moreover, was said to descend from a later, illegitimate line. From this a war arose between Louis, duke of Orléans and then king of the French, and the said Ludovico Sforza. Ludovico was not only driven from the duchy and state by the strength and power of the French, but was also led captive into France, where he at last ended his days. Then King Louis, understanding that he could not be safe in the duchy of Milan unless he obtained the investiture from the Holy Empire, made a treaty with our grandfather, the divine Emperor Maximilian, of blessed memory, and an agreement was reached concerning a marriage or betrothal to be contracted between us and Claudia, the firstborn daughter of King Louis. The investiture previously granted by Maximilian to Ludovico Sforza and his heirs was revoked, and King Louis obtained the investiture of the said duchy for himself and for his daughter Claudia, in case she should marry us. This condition was attached with the express consent of Louis himself and of his envoys. If the said marriage between us and Claudia should in any way fail to take effect without fault on our part, as in fact it did not, then the investiture granted to the king and to his daughter Claudia would be wholly ineffective and void, and the whole right to the said duchy and state of Milan, which had been granted by that investiture, would pass directly to us. From then on, with their consent, a new investiture was granted for that eventuality, to our person present, and this was stipulated and accepted in our name, and the other solemnities required for it were carried out by the most serene Philip, king of Castile, of happy memory, our father. We still have that investiture here with us, drawn up in solemn form and dispatched by Maximilian himself. And although the king's condition was violated by Louis, and his daughter Claudia was joined in marriage to Francis, then duke of Angoulême and afterwards king of the French, and although the investiture was conditionally granted, the condition being fulfilled and purified, it would still have had valid force and effect, so that the right to the said duchy and state of Milan would be considered transferred to us. Yet the divine Emperor Maximilian himself, partly because he cared for public rather than private advantage, and partly because he thought the right acquired by us through the aforesaid investiture was safe and that no harm could come to us, since we were then a minor under his guardianship, did not expressly remit what was due to us, which by reason of the guardianship he could not do. He granted a new investiture to the same King Louis of France for himself and for his said daughter Claudia and his son-in-law Francis, with some conditions not observed at all, which was tied to us, who could claim the right above all, and which is now approved. Because of this, the divine Emperor Maximilian, pursuing vengeance for the broken treaty, expelled King Louis of France from the duchy of Milan under colour of the earlier investiture. He granted it to Ludovico Sforza, and, with the aforesaid investiture revoked, he again admitted and installed in the duchy and state of Milan Maximilian Sforza, the firstborn son of that duke Ludovico, while we were again a minor living under the guardianship of Maximilian. As soon as he was able to, Maximilian Sforza, forgetful of the benefit conferred on him, plotted with the French enemies many things to the dishonour and loss of the Empire. Having made a treaty and alliance with them, he handed over the citadels and the state to the enemies, passed over to them and yielded the duchy. If he had had any right in that duchy, it would have devolved to the Holy Empire because of his treachery. But since the present French king, having extended the right of investiture, granted it to King Louis, his father-in-law, and afterwards obtained possession of the duchy after King Louis's death, he obtained a new investiture from Maximilian Caesar himself, through the same man or another in his name, and not sought or obtained from us. Thus, by despising us and the Holy Empire, and by plotting many things against the honour and dignity of us and of the Holy Roman Empire, and by raising his neck against us as lord of that fief and taking up arms, as his own letters and notorious deeds have made known, even if he had had a valid investiture before, as in fact he did not, he was deprived of all its advantages and all its rights by the very fact, and the whole thing passed back to us and to the Holy Roman Empire. So if the illustrious Francis Sforza could claim no right to the duchy of Milan, except what he obtains from our generosity and favour. For he cannot have any right from the first investiture, since, with the revocation made by the grantor himself standing, it is void, at a time when no right to the thing could yet be said to belong to Duke Francis, but only in hope, which is more easily removed. Here, above all, the fullness of power is present, together with the other judgment of the grantor who revokes. Nor does he have a right from the cession or transfer of Maximilian, his elder brother, who had no investiture of that state, but only a simple possession supported by no right, to which the revocation of the paternal investiture was equally an obstacle. So that cession was of no effect. For no one can transfer to another more right than he himself has. But let us grant that the investiture granted to his father Ludovico remains in its force, and that Duke Francis is to be called to the succession according to its order. He is not called by it, unless after the death of the firstborn, who is still alive. So the case that would admit Francis has not arisen. For the firstborn did not simply renounce the fief before he had acquired it, so that the next in rank should take his place. Rather, once the fief was chosen, he could dispose of its revenues as he pleased while he lived, and he ceded and renounced it even against the wish of the nearer heir. And since he did this by bargaining with the enemies against the lord of the fief, all that right which would have belonged to the same firstborn Maximilian devolved to the Holy Empire. Thus we were under no legal obligation to grant the duchy of Milan to the illustrious Francis Sforza, even if the first investiture of this kind stood firm, at least while the firstborn Maximilian was still alive. Indeed, by right we could rightly keep the duchy in our own hands and meanwhile use and enjoy it. It is objected to us that a treaty was made with the divine Leo. But no valid ground for favouring the said Francis Sforza can be drawn from this. The matter was transacted between other parties; nothing was negotiated there with Duke Francis, nor did anyone appear there on his behalf, nor was anyone stipulating for him who had the right to stipulate. And if a matter were being settled between the contracting parties, the question would arise whether he who founded a claim on it had fulfilled on his own side what he owed. But we grant that everything was done and completed solemnly, and that the treaty itself was made and stipulated with Duke Francis himself. Yet it does not give him any more right from it than he had before. For the words of that treaty sound thus: Item: Since the illustrious Francis Sforza, duke of Bari, claims that the duchy of Milan is owed to him by virtue of the investiture made by Maximilian Caesar of happy memory, and since by the attempted renunciation of his firstborn brother they claim to have obtained the first place in the succession, it was agreed and resolved. If the said illustrious Francis Sforza should recover the same duchy, the aforesaid contracting parties will take care to keep him in his rights, and will strive to protect him from all violence. Behold, then, that the duke claims nothing here except what has been said above, and this is abundantly weakened. Behold, that here is a conditional agreement: if the duke should recover the duchy, and this condition was to be fulfilled in a specific form, which was likewise not fulfilled, since he could not fulfil it, that obligation vanishes. And even if the condition had been firmly fulfilled and purified, behold, that obligation provides only for keeping him in his rights. As has been shown before, these rights are null and of no weight. If, then, we, supported by so many titles and so many rights, recovered that duchy from the hands of the enemies, with the help of our allies but mostly at our own expense, not without great loss to our own people, with the loss of so many distinguished dukes and soldiers, with such an effusion of Christian blood, and snatched it from their jaws, and each time they returned, when they were driven back and defeated, we preserved and defended it, with no pressing necessity, but for the peace of the commonwealth and from our pure liberality and munificence, we consented, with our rights so clear and so manifest set wholly aside and disregarded, to make this illustrious Francis Sforza, worthy of so great a gift, and to admit him to the said duchy, and to grant him the investiture of that duchy. What man of sound mind could rightly accuse us of greed, ambition or unjust seizure? What man could draw from these deeds any sinister suspicion that we were not acting with an upright mind toward all those things which seem to concern the peace and tranquillity of the Christian commonwealth and the liberty of Italy? Moreover, we did not offer this only in words, but also performed it in fact. For we made Duke Francis the possessor of the whole state; we had all the citadels and all the cities placed and handed over into his power; we gave him full authority and administration, so that he could not only govern and administer at his pleasure, taking the revenues, but also alienate, sell and dispose of them as he wished. When we were asked to do so, we confirmed and approved these alienations as made by the true duke. In the treaties we made with Hadrian, with the Venetians, and with the others with whom we dealt, we had him named and included as duke of Milan, and we agreed on his protection and preservation. Finally we granted the investiture of the said duchy and its dependencies in the most ample form, which we actually delivered into the hands of Bellaius, the knight and envoy of Duke Francis, under certain conditions and obligations to be fulfilled by the duke, in part for the expenses we had incurred for his benefit in acquiring and preserving the said state. Yet in this we acted so moderately that we would hardly recover a quarter of those expenses within the term of years. These things are plainly written, and no evasion can conceal them, since they have already become notorious.

units.la: 24. Insuper,cum de ipsius illustris Francisci morte dubitaretur,physicique quæ de illius salute desperarent,hincque nova oriretur in nos suspicio Vestræ Sanctit. Venetorum, aliorum Italiæ potentatuum,si statum ipsum Mediolanensem per mortem dicti ducis Francisci ad sacrum Imperium recta via rectoque ordine justitiæ devolvendum,aut in nostra potestate retineremus,aut serenissimo fratri nostro charissimo Ferdinando, Archiduci Austriæ concederemus. Cum & nostram & ipsius fratris nostri potentiam exosam & formidabilem habere viderentur,potius Deo (qui nobis hæc sua clementia & benignitate contulit) ipsiqué fortunæ invidentes,quam aliqua alia justa causa perciti. Placuit Vestræ Sanctitati nos per dictum ejus legatum moneri & hortari, quatenus pro Italiæ quiete, ac ad submovendum cujusvis suspicionis scrupulum in casum mortis, dicti illustris Francisci S Forciæ,ducatum ipsum Mediolani nequaquam in nostra potestate retineremus: Nec pariter ipsi Serenissimo fratri nostro concederemus:sed ipsum ducatum tali personæ traderemus, de qua Italiæ potentatus nullum metum, nulliusque suspicionis objectum habere possent. Ad eumque effectum Vest.Sanct.per dictum legatum alterum duorum nobis ad id proponi fecit, ut ducem Borbonii, aut Georgium de Austria,Cæsaris Maximiliani naturalem filium. Annuimus nihilominus licet ad id nullo jure astringeremur,quod ducatus ipse in casum devolutionis minime penes nos retineretur, nec etiam ipsi Serenissimo fratri nostro concederetur,obtulimusque in eum casum dictum ducatum conferre in personam jure merito gratam & acceptam Vestræ Sanctitati,à qua nihil suspicari posset, quod ad turbandum Italiæ quietem tendere videretur. Licet etiam id à Vest.S.acceptatum non fuerit,nec etiam aliis potentatibus gratum extiterit nisi personam, cui in eum casum ducatum conferre vellemus,·prius nominaremus ut discerni posset an grata & accepta foret.Non fuimus ab hac instantia alieni. Nominavimus in eum casum ipsum illustrem Borbonii ducem,quem Vestra S.primo propositerat, in cum quidem investituram conferre parati,non pro commodo aut augmento nostro, sed pro tollenda suspicionis rubigine qua Vest.S.ac potentatuum animi angebantur, pro submovenda ea umbra nostræ magnitudinis qua intrinsecus premebantur:proque ipsius Italiæ quiete quæ nobis semper cordi fuit, ut potius Christianæ reipub.causam,quam privatam nostram tueremur. Quid igitur cupiditatis nobis ex his ascribi posset:Si ducatum Mediolani & statum tanti momenti tantique valoris(ut præmittitur)per nos recuperatum quem licite retinere poterimus, tot titulis, totq; juribus fulti, semel illustri Franc.S Forciæ concessimus:Iterum si per illius mortem ad nos devolveretur, ad Vest.S.nutum alteri concederet annueremus,ii videlicet,quem V.S.prius nominaverat: Nos tamen justis juribus,tamq; amplo & importanti dominio suffulti(pro quo,si Julius Cæsar revivisceus nostram personam induceret,aut hi qui nobis cupiditatem impingunt,forsan etiam juriurandum violandum cesserent ) nos ipsi non coacti,nulloq; juramenti seu cujusvis obligationis vinculo astricti,nostra sponte pro ipsa repub. jus nostrum tam liquidum abrogare,& à nobis auferre consensimus exclusoetiam proprio fratre,qui jure merito post nos cæteris omnibus anteponendus videbatur. Cum hunc loco filii haberemus in succedendi gradu proximiorem,cui nulla ratione nulloque jure divino , naturali vel civili,extraneus quispiam a interserendus erat fateamur necesse est, non hic cupiditatem, non ambitionem, non avaritiam,non dominandi seu aliena occupandi appetitum inesse.Sed potius amplissimam uberemq; largiatem,munificentiam,ac,si dicere fas est, prodigalitatem dominandiq; contemptum arguere. quod tamen reipub.causa læto hilariq; animo,ultro,nec non sponte præstabamus.
units.tr: 24. Moreover, since there was doubt about the death of the illustrious Francis himself, and the physicians despaired of his recovery, a new suspicion arose against us on the part of Your Holiness, the Venetians and the other powers of Italy: that if the Duchy of Milan fell to the Holy Empire by direct route and proper legal order on the death of the said Duke Francis, we would either keep it in our own power or grant it to our most serene and dearest brother Ferdinand, Archduke of Austria. Since both our power and that of our brother seemed hateful and formidable to them, they were envious of God, who granted us these things by his clemency and kindness, and of fortune itself, rather than moved by any other just cause. Your Holiness was pleased to advise and exhort us, through your said legate, that for the peace of Italy, and to remove every scruple of suspicion in the event of the death of the said illustrious Francis Sforza, we should by no means keep the Duchy of Milan in our power, nor likewise grant it to our said most serene brother, but should hand the duchy over to a person of whom the powers of Italy could have no fear and no object of suspicion. To that end, Your Holiness had the said legate propose to us one of two men: the Duke of Bourbon, or Georg of Austria, the natural son of Emperor Maximilian. We nevertheless agreed, although we were bound by no law to do so, that in the event of the duchy falling vacant it would not be kept by us, nor granted to our said most serene brother, and we offered to confer the duchy in that case upon a person justly pleasing and acceptable to Your Holiness, from whom nothing could be suspected that seemed aimed at disturbing the peace of Italy. Although this was not accepted by Your Holiness, and would not please the other powers unless we first named the person to whom we wished to confer the duchy in that case, so that it could be judged whether he was welcome and acceptable, we did not shrink from this request. In that case we named the illustrious Duke of Bourbon, whom Your Holiness had first proposed, and we were ready to confer the investiture upon him: not for our own convenience or increase, but to remove the rust of suspicion with which the minds of Your Holiness and of the powers were troubled, to dispel that shadow of our greatness by which they were inwardly oppressed, and for the peace of Italy itself, which has always been dear to our heart, so that we might defend the cause of the Christian commonwealth rather than our private cause. What greed, then, could be imputed to us? If we had once granted the Duchy of Milan and a state of such importance and value (as has been said), recovered by us and which we could lawfully have kept, supported by so many titles and so many rights, to the illustrious Francis Sforza; and if, again, on his death it had fallen to us, we agreed to grant it at the nod of Your Holiness to another, namely the one whom Your Holiness had earlier named; yet we, supported by just rights and by so ample and important a dominion (for which, if Julius Caesar came back to life and assumed our person, or those who impute cupidity to us, perhaps would have yielded even to violating an oath), we, not compelled, bound by no oath or any bond of obligation, of our own accord consented to renounce our right, so clear, for the commonwealth and to take it away from ourselves, with even our own brother excluded, who by right seemed to deserve precedence over all others after us. Since we had him in place of a son, the nearest in the order of succession, and no outsider could by any reason, or by any divine, natural or civil law, be interposed before him, we must admit that here there is no greed, no ambition, no avarice, no appetite for ruling or seizing what belongs to others, but rather a most ample and generous largesse, munificence and, if it is lawful to say so, prodigality, and a contempt of dominion. Yet we did this for the sake of the commonwealth, with a glad and cheerful mind, freely and willingly.

units.la: 25. Sed nunc submovenda restat causa illa gemitus & doloris Sanctit.Vest.ac totius Italiæ, qua V. S.tantum affligitur:occupationis sc.ipsius statys Mediolani inde per nostros factæ eam obsessione ar-tu,in qua duxerat.In qua re licet non omni culpa excludere & liberare possemus. Ullam si qua foret in duces belli referendo, quibus dum nos monuissent, de practicis & molitionibus: quæ adversus nos & statum nostrum parabantur. Marchio Pischariæ, ut prætertur, rei conscius, nobis illius scelus citius detexisset, affirmans ipsum ducem Francisco hujusce facinoris reum, ut se statumque illum antistra obedientia subtraheret, ac fœderatorum viribus non habita ratione investituræ, nec fidelitatis per eum prætandæ, nec impensarum, quæ nobis erant resarciendæ in eo statu de facto potius quam de jure tenerentur, atque eo etiam decedente fœderatorum præsidio, nobis exclusis subintraret. In eo statu ejus frater Maximilianus S Forcia, quem jam ipso jure privatum diximus, consentiente etiam Gallorum rege, cui jus dicti Maximiliani, si quod habuisset, cessum erat: ut quoque exercitus noster tumultuantibus populis, ad ipsiusmet ducis Francisci, suorumque agentium, & fœderatorum instantia & solicitudinem deleretur, & in ruinam & præcipitium deduceretur: & si fieri posset, omnes ipsius evicitus duces & milites trucidarentur. Eo etiam signanter adjecto. Quod cum ipse illustris Marchio Pischariæ, habito de eare cum ipso duce Francisco colloquio, ut magis illius intrinsecum animum tentaret, an firmus in ea factionis practica remaneret, ei duci persuadendo dixisset: quod postquam jam a nobis investituram obtinuerat, eratque de ejus statu securus, non oporteret amplius eam practicam prosequi: Idem dux respondisse fertur firmius & commodius esse, quod jam practicatum erat atque conclusum, quam quod ex investitura assequi poterat, concurrente ibidem publica salute Italiæ: quam rei privatæ anteferenda censerentur. Instabant propterea duces ipsi, ut ad has molitiones respicerimus, neve majora scandala inde sequerentur, his licentiam præberemus, ut de ipso Francisco duce & illo Mediolani se nostro nomine asseverarent, pro nostri exercitus tutela, utque exercitum ipsum comminuendum & pene dissolvendum nil tale metuentes: jusseramus, non solum sustineremus, sed etiam geremus, ni penitus ab Italia excludi vellemus. Nos autem qui hæc non facile credebamus, sed partes confictæ simulataque; putabamus: eo quod qui bella tractare solent, potius belli quam pacis negotia cogitant, in hisque libentius animos eorum adoptat. Arbitramur enim, quod sub eo colore putiliter cogere & urgere ad ipsum nostrum exercitum integre servandum sustinendumque: dubitant ne veluti belli cupidi in id præcipites ruerent, ac arma præter nostram voluntatem moverent: Quare etiam nil aliud quam pacem & quietem cuperemus, mandavimus eisdem ne quid novi tentarent in dicto statu Mediolani, nisi in tribus casibus: Si dux Franciscus moreretur: Si Galli cum Helvetiis Italiam intrarent, vel si factionum practicarum executio ex adverso tentaretur, ut hi prius arma contra nos exercitumque nostrum moverent. In quolibet enim horum trium casuum consensimus, quod pro tutela exercitus nostri & rerum nostrarum, se asseverarent in dicto statu Mediolani. Verum cum Hieronymus Moronus, primarius ipsius ducis Francisci Consiliarius, ac ejusdem factionis fertur principalis minister, multiplicatis suis literis monuisset dictum Marchionem Pischariæ, quem putabat factionis participem habere, ut tem suam disponeret, eidem affirmando reliquos factionis socios, jam dispositos paratosque esse, ut in octo vel decem dierum spacio in nostros irruendum esset. Idem Marchio participato cum cæteris ducibus nostris consilio captoque; Moronus, illius habita confessione, totam fere negotii complectente satis conformi in ea quæ Marchio nobis suis literis insinuaverat, collecto exercitu nostro undique sparso, aliquot civitatibus munitis Mediolanum progreditur, ducem Franciscum interpellat, ut pro securitate nostra nostrique exercitus arces & castra dicti status, in nostrorum manus reponeret, idque custodibus illorum exequendum committeret. Annuit dux ipse ut castra nobis traderentur, prout effectu tradita fuere: Duabus duntaxat arcibus principalioribus, quas ipse munierat, Mediolani scilicet in qua ipse recludebatur, & Cremone exceptis: has enim duas in se retinendas censuit, donec de nostra voluntate certus fieret offerens interim, illas nostro nomine tenere, ac obtulit dare, ac per se & per præfectos arcium juramentum præstare, quod ex ipsis arcibus nullum extitit nostro damnum seu præjudicium fieret. Non placuit hæc securitas ducibus nostris, videntque perniciosam in mora. Si arces illæ magis munirentur liberæque permanerent, posse inde exercitus nostri ruinam succedere resque nostras in evidenti periculo remanere. Interpellant denuo, ac iterum atque iterum requirunt sub rebellionis pœna ac læsæ Majestatis criminis confessi atque convicti, quatenus ipsece Mediolani in potestate nostra ac nostrorum posita exiret, suisque copiam faceret, & adversarias, de quibus culpabatur, defensiones ac justificationes, si quas habebat, proponeret, duosque ejus rei conscios, quos penes se habebat in arce reclusos, dimitteret interrogandos, ad amplioris rei gestarum dilucidationem. At cum Dux ipse his non annueret, nisi a nobis mandatum haberet arcem circumvallant: Inrerimque de gestis nos admonent, necessarias causas per quas ad hanc arcem fuerant, enarrant approbationem gestorum a nobis expostulant. Instant, ut eidem duci Francisco rescribamus, mandemusque ut arcem nobis aut nostris tradat. Nos referentes rem hanc præter encentem nostram tentatam, nunquam voluimus nec illorum gesta approbare nec duci (ut petebatur) mandare ut castris dimitteret. Semper enim in animo habuimus, eam accusationem, quæ in ducem terebatur, debito juris ordine tractandam & terminandam. Nunc profecto ejus rei exitu prætentorum veritas elici poterit, cum præparatæ jam diu factionis effectus illuxerit, quo magis ac inceps eidem nostris ducibus credere debeamus, non possumus non laudare & approbare eorum prudentiam & fidem in conservatione dicti status, ipsiusque nostri exercitus illiusque arcis allecuratione ne amplius muniri posset, neve inde majoris mali & incommodi occasio præstaretur. Nec id quidem ita perpetram & injuste gestum videtur prout Sanctit. Vest. sibi suadet, dato enim fundamento quod ipse ex Franciscus læsæ majestatis reus accusaretur. Et si uniusdunraxat testis adesset de polluto, ubi plurimum tamen adest testimonium. Ex quibus etiam si essent socii criminis ac factionis participes, porci ut mem.o merito contra ipsum ducem procedi & ad capturam & ad torturam. Et cogit ut sui copiam faceret, ac in vinculis causam diceret, suasque defensiones & justificationes catceratus adduceret, non autem in arce reclusus audiri debuit. Quinimo contra eum vocatum & non comparentem ac se subtrahentem & resistentem potuit in ejus contumaciam pronunciari, ut pro confesso & convicto haberetur. Sed & priusquam id fiat accusato non comparente, nec sui copiam faciente, licite ad manus curiae redimentur illius bona, quae etiam à die ingressi criminis ipso jure publicata confiscataque censentur. Sicque hinc non tanta causa gemitus & doloris Vest.Sanctitati parata videtur. Si dominus Vasallum ingratum & laesae majestatis reum puniendum censeat, ni forsan quod in mente cadere non potuisset, id gemendum dolendumque putent, quod eidem hanc foveam in quam incidit sub charitatis specie paraverunt, ipsumque ad hujusmodi dilectionem deduxerunt; Sed potius ingemiscere ac dolere deberet non solum V.Sanctitas, sed universa respubl. quod sine justa causa fineque culpa nostra tam ingens excitetur incendium, quo & turbatur universus ecclesiae status & tota scandalizatur Christiana religio.
units.tr: 25. Now there remains to be removed that cause of grief and sorrow which so greatly troubles Your Holiness and all Italy: namely, the seizure of the state of Milan by our men, and the siege by which it was held. In this matter, although we could not wholly free ourselves from blame, if any fault was to be laid on the leaders of the war, who, while warning us about the plots and machinations being prepared against us and our state, were the ones who ... (the sense here is that the commanders reported the schemes to us). The Marquis of Pescara, as is said, being aware of the plot, quickly revealed the crime to us, affirming that Duke Francis himself was guilty of this offence, so that he might withdraw himself and that state from our obedience, and, with the forces of the confederates, enter it and shut us out, without regard to the investiture, to the fidelity to be rendered through him, or to the expenses that were to be repaid to us in that state, which were held to be possessed de facto rather than de jure. Moreover, once the garrison of the confederates had withdrawn, he would do this. In that state his brother Maximilian Sforza, whom we have already said is deprived by law, with the consent also of the King of France, to whom any right of the said Maximilian, if he had one, had been ceded, was to be the instrument: so that our army, with the people in tumult, at the instance and solicitation of Duke Francis himself, his agents and the confederates, would be destroyed and brought to ruin and destruction; and, if it could be done, all its commanders and soldiers would be slaughtered. And this was expressly added: that when the illustrious Marquis of Pescara had held a conference about this with Duke Francis himself, in order to test more closely the duke's inner mind, and whether he remained firm in this plot, and had tried to persuade him that, since he had already obtained the investiture from us and was secure in his state, he ought no longer to pursue that plot, the duke is reported to have replied that what had already been planned and concluded was firmer and more advantageous than what he could obtain from the investiture, the public safety of Italy being at stake, which was to be reckoned more important than private interest. The same dukes therefore urged us to attend to these machinations, lest greater scandals should follow from them, and to grant them leave, on our behalf, to assert their claims against Duke Francis himself and that Milan, for the protection of our army; and that they should not only sustain but also wage the war, unless we wished to be wholly excluded from Italy, we had ordered them, fearing nothing of the kind, to restrain the army and almost dissolve it. We, however, who did not readily believe this and thought the matter feigned and pretended, reasoned that those who are accustomed to conduct wars think more of war than of peace, and that their minds are more readily inclined to such things. For we judged that under that pretext they were trying to press and urge us to keep our army whole and maintained; they feared that, like men eager for war, they would rush headlong into it and take up arms against our will. Therefore, since we desired nothing but peace and quiet, we instructed them not to attempt anything new in the said state of Milan, except in three cases: if Duke Francis should die; if the French with the Swiss should invade Italy; or if the execution of the plotted faction should be attempted by the other side, so that these men first took up arms against us and our army. For in each of these three cases we consented that they might assert themselves in the said state of Milan for the protection of our army and our affairs. But when Jerome Moroni, the chief councillor of Duke Francis and reported to be the principal minister of that faction, by repeated letters had warned the said Marquis of Pescara, whom he thought to be a sharer in the faction, to arrange his affairs, affirming that the remaining associates of the faction were now disposed and ready, so that within a space of eight or ten days we must be attacked, the same Marquis, having shared the matter with our other commanders and taken counsel, and Moroni having been questioned and having confessed, in a account which largely covered the whole business and agreed fairly well with what the Marquis had notified us in his letters, gathered our army, which was scattered everywhere, and, with some cities fortified, advanced to Milan. He called upon Duke Francis to hand over to our men, for our security and that of our army, the citadels and fortresses of that state, and to commit their guarding to our men. The duke himself consented that the fortresses be handed over to us, which was in fact done. Only the two principal citadels, which he had fortified, namely that of Milan, in which he himself was shut up, and that of Cremona, he decided to keep in his own hands until he should be certain of our will, offering meanwhile to hold them in our name, and he offered to give them up, and, both personally and through the commanders of the citadels, to swear an oath that no harm or prejudice to us would come from those citadels. Our commanders were not satisfied with this security, and saw that delay was dangerous: if those citadels were further fortified and remained free, our army might be ruined and our affairs left in evident peril. They again pressed, and again and again demanded, under pain of rebellion and on the charge of treason, since he had been confessed and convicted, that he should come out of the citadel of Milan into our power and that of our men, and give them access, and put forward whatever defences and justifications he had against the accusation brought against him, and release the two accomplices of this matter whom he held shut up in the citadel, so that they might be questioned for a fuller clarification of the facts done. But since the duke himself did not consent to this, unless he had a mandate from us, they besieged the citadel; and meanwhile they reminded us of what had happened, explained the necessary reasons why they had come to this citadel, and demanded from us approval of their acts. They urged us to write back to Duke Francis himself and order him to hand over the citadel to us or to our men. We, reporting that this business was attempted beyond our intention, never wished either to approve their deeds or to order the duke, as was asked, to withdraw from the fortresses. For we always had in mind that the accusation brought against the duke should be handled and concluded in the proper order of law. Now, indeed, from the outcome of this affair the truth of the matters at issue can be brought out, since the effect of the faction long prepared has come to light; and so, from now on, we ought to trust these same commanders of ours all the more. We cannot but praise and approve their prudence and loyalty in preserving the said state and our army, and in preventing that citadel from being fortified any further, lest an occasion of greater evil and inconvenience should be given thereby. Nor indeed does this seem to have been done so rashly or unjustly as Your Holiness supposes. For, granting the foundation that Francis was accused of treason, and even if there were only one witness of the crime, whereas here there is a great deal of testimony, and if they were accomplices and sharers in the crime and faction, it would rightly have been proceeded against the duke himself, both by arrest and by torture. And he was bound to give them access and to plead his case in chains, and bring forward his defences and justifications while in bonds, and not be heard while shut up in a citadel. Indeed, against him, when summoned and not appearing, and withdrawing and resisting, it could have been pronounced in his contumacy that he should be held as confessed and convicted. But even before that is done, with the accused not appearing and not giving access, his goods may lawfully be taken into the hands of the court, which are regarded as published and confiscated by law from the day of the entry of the crime. And so no such great cause of grief and sorrow seems to be prepared for Your Holiness. If a lord judges that an ungrateful vassal guilty of treason should be punished, unless perhaps they think it is to be lamented and grieved over, which could not have come into their minds, that they have prepared this pit, into which he has fallen, under the appearance of charity, and have led him to such affection; but rather it is not only Your Holiness who ought to lament and grieve, but the whole commonwealth, that without just cause and without any fault of ours so great a fire is kindled, by which the whole state of the Church is disturbed and the Christian religion is scandalized throughout.

units.la: 16. Nec sane intelligere possumus quod cuncti prope Christianitatis reges (ut Vest.Sanctit.ait) efflagitarint, agitaverint nec non partiti fuerint in re tanti praejudicii animo & auxilia conferre. Scimus enim & pro certo habemus nec Ungarum nec Polonum nec Portugalensem, nec Danum, hujusce consilii participes seu conscios. Anglus autem & si ejus foederis conservator & protector nominetur, nobis tamen apertis suis literis significavit se nequaquam in id foedus consensisse, nec mandatum dedisse, nec talem protectionem acceptasse nec acceptare velle, licet ad id parte V.S. interpellatus ac instanter requisitus extiterit: se pacis quam semper effl agitavimus mediatorem offerendo. Gallus vero & si cum Sanct. V. ac aliis Italiae potentatibus foedus percusserit, ut eo medio initiores si posset quia jam ex nostro foedere obtinuerit a nobis pacis conditiones exhauriat, liberosque obsides recuperet. Retulit tamen aperto ore quod Vestrae Sanct. impulsu & suasu, etiam priusquam in regnum suum liber remitteretur, de ipso novo foedere ineundo sollicitabatur. Et sunt qui affirmant, ut ex quibusdam literis percepimus: quod V.S. ipso etiam Gallorum tege non petente, eidem juramentum relaxaverit quod nobis praestiterat pro foedere nobiscum prius inito, quod tamen credere nolumus: quandoquidem res talis omnino a pastore Christi Vicario aliena esse deberet, nec ipsius jurisiurandi sine causa spreta religio ad deteriora incentivum praeberet. Merito tamen V.S. his verbis utitur, dimissis consilius & conspirationibus, si verbis addatur effectus. Si vero omnis conspiratio dimittatur cum secundum rectam intelligentiam crimen denotet.
units.tr: 16. We really cannot understand how nearly all the kings of Christendom (as Your Holiness puts it) demanded, discussed, and divided among themselves the matter of so great a prejudice, and resolved to lend their aid. For we know, and hold for certain, that neither the King of Hungary, nor the King of Poland, nor the King of Portugal, nor the King of Denmark took part in or was privy to this plan. The Englishman, although he is named the guarantor and protector of this league, has nevertheless informed us by his own open letter that he has by no means consented to that league, nor given a mandate for it, nor accepted such a protection, nor wishes to accept it, although he was appealed to and urgently requested to do so on Your Holiness's side; he offers himself instead as mediator of the peace which we have always sought. The Frenchman, although he has made a treaty with Your Holiness and the other Italian powers, did so in order that, by this means, he might, if he could, gain the upper hand, since he has already obtained from our treaty the terms of peace and is drawing off his children held as hostages. Yet he has stated openly that, at the urging and persuasion of Your Holiness, even before he was released to return to his kingdom, he was being pressed about entering into this new league. And there are those who affirm, as we have learned from certain letters, that Your Holiness, even though the French king did not ask it, released him from the oath he had sworn to us for the earlier treaty made with us; this we are unwilling to believe, since such a thing ought to be wholly foreign to a minister, the vicar of Christ, and the disregard of an oath sworn without cause would give an incentive to worse things. Yet Your Holiness uses these words rightly, dismissing counsels and conspiracies, if effect is added to the words; for if every conspiracy is dismissed, it denotes a crime according to the correct understanding.

units.la: 27. Quod autem ad ea conventionum capitula, quae attulit Herrera, videamus qualiter S.V. praetendat illa paucis in locis leviter immutata: si enim bene cuncta rimentur, omnes articuli qui cum ipsius legato sic compositi remanserant cum V.S. concludendi: licet ipsam conclusionem V.S. reservandam affecteret, ejus potestate postquam ad nos pervenerat relata atque restricta, mutati penitus ad nos remissi fuere. Ita ut nullus fere remaneret intactus, qui non aliam substantiam aliumque sonum praeferret. Omnes tamen hujusmodi mutationes obmisimus in quatuor duntaxat articulis, hujusmodi conventionum, videlicet 12.13.14.&15. moderationem petentem.
units.tr: 27. As for the articles of agreement which Herrera brought forward, let us see how Your Holiness puts them forward, slightly altered in a few places. For if everything is carefully examined, all the articles which had been settled with his legate, to be concluded with Your Holiness, were sent back to us completely changed, although Your Holiness wished the conclusion itself to be reserved, and after it had come to us in his power it was reported and restricted. So that almost none remained untouched which did not carry another substance and another sound. Yet we have passed over all such alterations in only four articles of these agreements, namely 12, 13, 14 and 15, which ask for moderation.

units.la: 28. In 12. enim ipsorum articulorum qui tem Ducis Ferrariae completebatur, licet omnis substantia, ultra quam tractatum esset, mutari videretur: consensimus tamen nos effecturos cum effectu, quod eadem Sanctitas & intra praefixum tempus, dum sibi expedire videretur, sine cujusque resistentia, sine armorum apparatu recuperare posset, possessionem Rhegii & Rubetiae tenendam & possidendam, prout antea tenebat, ita quod non intelligeretur praejudicatum juribus Imperii aut cujuslibet alterius quam eadem S.V. admittebat. Id solum addidimus quod ad alliciendum ipsum ducem Ferrariae, remittendo eidem quasq; poenas & jus commissum ac absolvendo eum a censuris forsitan incursis, quod prosecto non nisi ad majorem quietem Italiae petebamus, non ignorantes ipsum ducem non aliter sine armis cogi posse: ut Rhegium & Ruberiam dimitteret vel S.V. restituerat, in quibus & jure feudi Imperialis & ratione prioris spolii se potius tuendi censebat. Unde ad providendos novos belli tumultus, & ne remaneret cujusvis incendii scintilla, sed universa Italia in eo foedere sine quovis scrupulo concurreret, id ita agendum necessario censentes, prout nunc agit V.S. nos etiam sub spe defensivi foederis jam percussi, ad ipsius ducis Ferrariae offensionem astringere voluissemus, in quare novos bellorum tumultus timebamus, quos tamen effugere nequivimus, qui du ab offensione nos abstinere curamus, defensioni status, dignitatis & autoritatis nostrae intendere cogimur, & inniti trahimur. Qua de re hujusmodi nostram additionem nequaquam respuendam V.S. putabamus, in hoc enim nec V.S. auctoritati derogatur. Nec a veri pastoris officio declinabatur: sed potius publicae quieti consulebatur.
units.tr: 28. For in the 12th of these articles, which concerned the Duke of Ferrara, although all the substance, beyond what had been treated, seemed to be changed, we nevertheless agreed that we would bring about, with effect, that His Holiness might, within the fixed time, whenever it seemed expedient to him, and without anyone's resistance or any display of arms, recover the possession of Reggio and Rubiera, to be held and possessed as he held them before, so that it would not be understood that anything was prejudiced to the rights of the Empire or of any other party, which Your Holiness admitted. We added only this, that in order to win over the Duke of Ferrara, we would remit to him the penalties and the forfeited right, and absolve him from censures perhaps incurred. This we sought surely only for the greater quiet of Italy, not unaware that the duke could not otherwise be compelled without arms to give up Reggio and Rubiera, which Your Holiness had restored to him, and which he thought he ought rather to defend both by the right of the imperial fief and by reason of his earlier dispossession. Hence, judging it necessary to provide against new tumults of war, and lest any spark of fire should remain, but all Italy should come together in that league without any scruple, just as Your Holiness now acts, we too, already bound by the hope of a defensive league, would have wished to bind ourselves to an offence against the same Duke of Ferrara. Since we feared new tumults of war, which we could not nevertheless escape, we are forced, while we take care to abstain from offence, to attend to the defence of our state, dignity and authority, and are drawn to rely upon it. Wherefore we thought Your Holiness ought by no means to reject this addition of ours, for in this the authority of Your Holiness is not derogated from, nor was the duty of a true minister departed from; rather, care was taken for the public quiet.

units.la: 29. In 13. ipsius foederis seu capitulationis articulo illam salis distributionem in statu Mediolan. continentem, ex quinque correctionibus per V.S. factis eas omnes admisimus, eo duntaxat excepto quod ubi Vest.S. deleri fecerat illa verba ad ejus vitae decursum, satagens illud jus sibi & successoribus perpetuare. Nos qui duntaxat personae S. Vestrae ejus vita comite gratificari volebamus, non autem statum ipsum Mediolani Sacri Imperii feudum perpetuo ecclesiae Rom. astringere, & tali onere semper gravatum remanere sine spe libertatis. Noletes etiam ipsum Serenissimum Archiducem fratrem nostrum juit sibi in ea re concessio perpetuo exclusum remanere. Noluimus illam cancellationem approbare, sed verba illa ad ejus vitae decursus, prout in Capitulatione, quam attulit Herrera, firma manere censumus. Ex ultima vero ipsius articuli correctione admisimus eam partem additionis ibidem per San. V. factam ut esset illa conventio absque praejudicio sedis Apost. Ea autem verba quae his subjungebatur, videlicet de Sale ipso in ducatu Mediolani distribuendo, cum viderentur relativa & subsequentia ad jura sedis Apostolicæ, videremurque fateri jus esse Apostolicæ Sedi illius distributionis, voluimus admittere ne fateremur quod non erat. Sicque in hujus articuli correctione nulla S.Vest.fiebat injuria. Sed potius nos & fratrem nostrum ac sacrum Rom.Imp. ab injuria eximebamus: & non sub verborum involucro disceptationis causam relinquere volebamus: sed clare & aperte dubium omne tollebamus.
units.tr: 29. In the 13th article of that same league or capitulation, which contains that distribution of salt in the state of Milan, we admitted all the five corrections made by Your Holiness, with this one exception: where Your Holiness had caused the words for the course of his life to be deleted, striving to perpetuate that right for himself and his successors. We, who wished only to oblige the person of Your Holiness for the course of his life, did not wish to bind the state of Milan itself, a fief of the Holy Roman Empire, perpetually to the Roman Church, and to remain always burdened with such a burden without hope of liberty. Nor did we wish our most Serene brother, the Archduke, to remain perpetually excluded from that concession. We were unwilling to approve that cancellation, but we judge that those words for the course of his life, as in the capitulation which Herrera brought, should remain firm. From the last correction of that article, however, we admitted that part of the addition made there by Your Holiness, that the agreement should be without prejudice to the Apostolic See. But those words which followed it, namely about distributing the salt itself in the duchy of Milan, since they seemed to be related to and dependent upon the rights of the Apostolic See, and since we saw that we would have to admit that the Apostolic See had the right of that distribution, we chose to admit them, lest we should confess what was not so. Thus in this correction of the article no injury was done to Your Holiness. Rather, we were freeing ourselves, our brother and the Sacred Roman Empire from injury; and we did not want to leave the cause of the dispute wrapped in a veil of words, but we removed every doubt clearly and openly.

units.la: 30. In 14.articulo ipsius capitulationis unde illæ lachrymæ, illæ angustiæ prodierunt, addiderat S.V. in fine ipsius articuli disponen.de statu Mediolani, & duce Franci.SForcia hæc verba formalia: Et quia ipsi Francisco Maria duci nonnulla imputantur contra Cæsarem, aut à Majestate sibi concessum investituram & feudi perpetrata, cupiens eadem Majestas quantum in se est Italiæ fovere quietem, quæ serrari posse non creditur, cum eosdem ducis à statu & ducatu remotione, ideo conventum est quod idem dux in statu ipso permaneat. Et quatenus opus fit in eo per Cæsarem de novo confirmetur, non obstantibus quibuscunque per eum contra majestatem etiam supra dictum est attentatis, etiam si saperent crimen læsæ majestatis. Cæsar namque ducem ipsum pro innocente habere vult, & ex mera liberalitate sua ac totius Italiæ intuitu, totum sibi remittit & indulget si etiam pejus quam dicitur aut creditur erraret. Videat quæsumus, Sanctitas V. quam levis existimanda foret hæc immutatio: quam justa & honesta petitio, quam optimum esset exemplum ad res bene gerendas, ad vasallos & subditos debita fide & obedientia erga dominos continendos: quam egregiam præberet formam augendi & conservandi Sac.Roman.Imp.à Deo institutum, à Propheris prædictum, ab Apostolis prædicatum, & ab ipso Christo nascente, vivente & moriente approbatum. Nos tamen qui nil aliud quam pacem, quam quietem reipublicæ Christianæ cupiebamus, quantum fas Sanctitati Vestræ satisfacere, nullumque rectum nostræ intentionis testimonium intactum, aut dubitationis scrupulum in Vest.Sanctit.mente relinquere putabamus: reformavimus dictum decimum quartum capitulum ipsius capitulationis in hæc verba: Ut autem nihil dubietatu seu suspicionis in hoc fœdere relinqueretur, sed omnis scrupulus de medio tollatur. Cum in priore fœdere potius sub nomine proprio quam appellativo includi videtur illustris Franciscus SForcia dux Mediolani, qui aliquibus jam mensibus gravi vexatus ægritudine, & in summo vitæ discrimine constitutus fuit, etiam de Felonia ac læsæ majestatis crimine accusatus seu inculpatus, & si hunc aut naturali morte aut civili justitia prævia ab ipso ducatu Mediolani excidere contingeret: bene fuisset ac fœdus ipsum ad alium in eodem ducatu ex Cæsaris concessione vel dispositione succedentem protenderetur: ideo ad ampliorem ipsius fœderis declarationem actum extitit. Quod sive ipse Illustris Franciscus SForcia vitam obierit, & ab hoc sæculo migraverit, sive per viam justitiæ dicto ducatu fuerit privatus in eum casum Cæsarea Majestas pro Italia quiete & contemplatione S.D.N. ipsius ducatus Mediolani investituram concedet illustri Carolo Duci Borbonii & Alverinæ. Ita quod S.D.N. & caterí federati qui in hoc fœdere voluerint comprehendi, sint & censeantur astricti ad defensionem ipsius status Mediolani: etiam ad opus dicti illustris ducis Borbonii dum de ipso Ducatu Mediolani fuerit investitus. Quo casu quantum ad omnia in fœdere contenta, tanquam suffectus in locum dicti illustris Francisci SForcia, fungatur omnibus honoribus & oneribus quibus ipse vivens & in tali statu permanens fungi debuisset. Hæc est immutatio quam in hoc articulo fecimus, qui velut justitiæ & æquitati consonam approbandam, & nequaquam respuendam censebamus, minimeque in mentem nostram cadere poterant, Summum pastorem vices Dei gerentem in terris adeo pertinaciter insistere debuisse.
