Quod si Dux Franciscus tanti criminis reus appareret, impune evaderet: cogeremurque inviti illi indulgere, ac in statu illo conservare: sic incentivum majoris ingratitudinis majorisque delicti illi præstando. Arbitramur Vest.Sanct.sat esse debere, si Ducatu illo ad nos & S.Imp.devoluto consentiebamus S.Vest.intuitu, ut nec illum retineremus, nec proprio fratri concederemus. Si personam quam Sanct.Vest. antea ad id gratam habuerat nobisque nominaverat, moriente Duce Francisco providendum non minus gratum esse putaremus, ipso Duce Francisco per justitiam privato: ut quod in naturali morte consenserat, in illius etiam morte civili recusaturus non esset.
units.tr: 30. In the 14th article of that capitulation, whence those tears and those anxieties have come, Your Holiness had added at the end of the article, concerning the arrangement of the state of Milan and Duke Francesco Sforza, these formal words: And because certain things are imputed to the same Duke Francesco Maria against Caesar, or against the investiture and fief granted by His Majesty, His Majesty, desiring as far as in him lies to foster the quiet of Italy, which is not believed to be able to be preserved if the same duke is removed from the state and the duchy, it has therefore been agreed that the same duke shall remain in the state itself. And, so far as it is necessary, he shall be confirmed anew in it by Caesar, notwithstanding whatever has been attempted by him against the majesty, even if it savours of the crime of treason. For Caesar wishes to hold the said duke to be innocent, and from his pure liberality and in regard to all Italy, he remits and pardons him entirely, even if he has erred worse than is said or believed. Let Your Holiness see, we beg, how slight this alteration ought to be judged to be; how just and honourable a request; how excellent an example it would be for carrying on affairs well, for keeping vassals and subjects in due faith and obedience towards their lords; how outstanding a form it would offer for increasing and preserving the Holy Roman Empire, instituted by God, foretold by the prophets, preached by the apostles, and approved by Christ himself, in his birth, life and death. Yet we, who desired nothing but peace and the quiet of the Christian commonwealth, and who thought we should satisfy Your Holiness as far as right allows, and leave no upright testimony of our intention untouched, nor any scruple of doubt in the mind of Your Holiness, have reformed the said fourteenth chapter of that capitulation into these words: So that nothing of doubt or suspicion may be left in this league, but every scruple may be removed from the midst. Since in the earlier league the illustrious Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan, seems to have been included under his proper name rather than under a general title, he who for some months has been troubled by severe sickness and placed in the greatest danger of life, and who has also been accused or charged with felony and the crime of treason, and if it should happen that he is removed from the duchy of Milan, either by natural death or by civil justice first given, it would be well if the league were extended to another succeeding in the same duchy by the concession or disposition of Caesar; therefore, for the fuller declaration of this league, it has been done. Whether the same illustrious Francesco Sforza shall have died and departed from this world, or shall have been deprived of the said duchy by the way of justice, in that case His Caesarean Majesty, for the quiet of Italy and in regard to our Lord the Pope, will grant the investiture of the duchy of Milan to the illustrious Charles, Duke of Bourbon and Auvergne. So that Our Lord the Pope and the other confederates who wish to be included in this league shall be and be deemed bound to the defence of the state of Milan, and also for the work of the said illustrious Duke of Bourbon, once he has been invested with the said duchy of Milan. In that case, as to all things contained in the league, he, as a substitute in the place of the said illustrious Francesco Sforza, shall discharge all the honours and burdens which he himself, living and remaining in such a state, ought to have discharged. This is the alteration which we made in this article; and we judged that it, as agreeing with justice and equity, ought to be approved and by no means rejected, and it could least of all come into our mind that the supreme minister, who holds the place of God on earth, ought to insist so obstinately upon this point. For if Duke Francesco were found guilty of so great a crime, he would escape unpunished, and we should be compelled, though unwilling, to indulge him and keep him in that state, thus giving him an incentive to greater ingratitude and greater wrong. We think Your Holiness should be satisfied, if we consented that the duchy should revert to us and the Holy Empire for the sake of Your Holiness, so that we would neither retain it nor grant it to our own brother. If we thought it no less welcome to provide, on the death of Duke Francesco, for the person whom Your Holiness had previously held as acceptable for this and had named to us, Duke Francesco having been deprived by justice, then he would not refuse, in his civil death, what he had agreed to in his natural death.

units.la: 31. In 15.vero ipsius capitulationis artic. continente prætensas novitates, tentatas contra ecclesiasticam libertatem regno nostro Neapolitano. Cum Vest.Sanctit.fere totum articulum in verbis dispositivis delevisset & cancellasset, his duntaxat verbis. Primo, dispositione dicti articuli addi-tis & commutatis. Quod circa hujusmodi observentur, quæ investitura regni Neapolitani ipsi Cæsari concessa continentur. Nos hanc etiam correctionem & mutationem pro Vest.Sanctita. nutu admisimus, additis duntaxat in fine articuli verbis sequentibus, videlicet bis modo & formis quibus per Ferdinandum regem catholicum ejus antecessorem observata fuere, & juxta ipsius regni privilegia & jura. Quid enim in hoc immutatum quod respuendum videretur? Si antecessoris rectos tramites insequendos putamus, Si jura & privilegia regni nostri servare studeamus, qualiter aut ex his mutationibus tam justis rationibus suffultis.
units.tr: 31. In the fifteenth article of that capitulation, which concerns the alleged novelties attempted in our kingdom of Naples against ecclesiastical liberty, Your Holiness deleted and cancelled almost the whole article, leaving only these operative words: "First, with the disposition of the said article added and changed: What is observed in matters of this kind is what is contained in the investiture of the kingdom of Naples granted to Caesar himself." We too admitted this correction and change at Your Holiness's nod, adding only these words at the end of the article: in the manner and forms by which they were observed by King Ferdinand the Catholic, his predecessor, and according to the privileges and laws of that kingdom. For what was changed in this that ought to seem objectionable? If we think we should follow the straight paths of our predecessor, if we are eager to preserve the privileges and laws of our kingdom, in what way, then, or from these changes, so well supported by just reasons...

units.la: 32. Sumat V.S, illud perspicuum (ut ait) judicium à nobis illudi & pro nihilo haberi. Qualiter inferat in his facultatem primo concessam Herreræ uberiorem fuisse: Et quod facta concordia cū Christianismo restrictiora & jejuniora transmiserimus. Qualiter & quo colore ex his prætendat judicandam eandem Sanctitatem posterem esse, & à nobis contemni, ubi nobis cum aliis amicitia convenisset: quicunque recti sensus & à passione alienus, facile hæc judicare poterit. Nos enim semper recti integriqueque propositi remansimus, prius cum V.S.quam cum quovis alio convenendi. Nos & ante & post cum rege Gallo initum semper in eodem proposito permanentes V.Sanctitatem ejusque ministros pro hujusmodi ineundo sollicitavimusque pulsavimusque, nec quicquam unquã habuimus in ore quod non haberemus in corde. Nos Herreram ad S.V. pro eo fœdere ineundo misimus longe antequam cum ipso rege Gallo concluderemus, citiusque illum aut alium misissemus, ni V. Sanct. legatum veniente, (ut aiebant) cum amplissimo mandato nobiscum concludendi praestolandum censuissemus, ni etiam post illius adventum viso mandato quod à V. S. habebat, & confisi quod illo uti posset, diutius cum eo de ipsius foederis capitulis tractantes, tempus inaniter consumptum cognovissemus. Ubi capitulatione jam formata & cum eo propter concordata dum de conclusione agereiur nobis insinuaverit, quod ex quo post ejus à V. S. recessum mutata essent negocia intenderet conclusione differre, donec V.S. consuluisset. Ob quod sanctius putavimus capitulationem ipsam, prout formata fuerat ad V.S. per Herreram transmittere, putantes ibidem rem celerius posse concludi, licet spe nostra fructrati fuerimus, S. V. ad alios fines tendente, prout exitus demonstravit.
units.tr: 32. Let Your Holiness understand that this "clear judgment," as you call it, is mocked by us and held as nothing. How you infer from these things that the faculty first granted to Herrera was fuller, and that after the agreement with the Christian king we sent terms more restricted and less generous; how and on what pretext you claim from these things that the same Holiness is to be judged to have come second and to be scorned by us, when our friendship had been agreed with others: anyone of sound sense and free from passion can easily judge these things. For we have always remained of upright and sincere purpose, to agree with Your Holiness before any other. Both before and after the agreement with the king of France, remaining always in the same purpose, we have solicited and pressed Your Holiness and your ministers to enter into such an alliance, nor have we ever had in our mouth anything we did not have in our heart. We sent Herrera to Your Holiness to enter into that alliance long before we concluded with the king of France himself, and we would have sent him, or another, sooner, had we not judged that we should await the arrival of the legate (as they said) with the fullest mandate to conclude with us; and even after his arrival, when we had seen the mandate which he had from Your Holiness, and trusting that it could be used, we discovered that we had spent time in vain treating with him at length over the chapters of that alliance. When the capitulation had been drawn up, and while the conclusion was being negotiated with him, he informed us that since his recall from Your Holiness the affairs had changed, and he intended to defer the conclusion until Your Holiness had been consulted. For this reason we thought it more prudent to send the capitulation itself, as it had been drawn up, to Your Holiness through Herrera, believing the matter could be concluded more quickly there. Although our hope was frustrated, since Your Holiness was aiming at other ends, as the outcome showed.

units.la: 33. Nunc ad literas manu V.S. conscriptas de quarum responsione conqueritur deveniendum est, ut etiam inde omnem à nobis repellamus culpam. Ea enim per V. San. eius responsionis culpa nobis in tribus impingitur. Primo quod V.S. ubi clementiam ducis Mediolani petebat, nos rigorem, justitiae obtulimus, ad quod satis diffuse responsum dedimus, dum ipsius ducis negocium ante discussimus, ut sic repetitione non egeat. Id solum hic adjiciendum censemus, non videri in hoc justam S. V. querelam. Si justitiae via amplectendam censuimus: Sine qua vera pax esse non potest. Cum justitia & pax se invicem deosculentur, & ut ad clementia deveniatur prius veritas est habenda. Sunt enim tese Psalmista quatuor sorores concarenatae: Justitia & pax osculatae sunt: Misericordia & veritas obviaverunt sibi. Qui igitur misericordiam expectat, reatum fateatur oportet: Qui pacem vult, justitiam amplectatur. Nec ita passim utendum est clementia, ut delinquendi incitamentum praebeatur. Sed potius ad bonum regimen spectat parcere subiectis & debellare superbos. Non n. indulgendi videtur his qui contumaciter in rebellione perstiterunt, his qui in arcib. munitis se continent, his justitiae executione satagunt evitare. Aeneid.
units.tr: 33. Now we must come to the letters written in Your Holiness's own hand, over whose reply you complain, so that we may also thereby remove all blame from ourselves. For through the fault of that reply Your Holiness charges us with three things. First, that when Your Holiness asked for clemency for the Duke of Milan, we offered the rigour of justice. To this we gave a sufficiently full answer when we first discussed the duke's affair, so it need not be repeated. We think only this should be added here: that Your Holiness's complaint does not seem just in this. If we have thought that the way of justice is to be embraced, without which true peace cannot exist, then justice and peace kiss each other; and to come to clemency, truth must first be had. For, as the Psalmist says, these are four sisters linked together: Justice and peace have kissed; mercy and truth have met each other. Therefore whoever expects mercy must confess his guilt; whoever wants peace must embrace justice. Nor is clemency to be used so indiscriminately that an incitement to wrongdoing is offered. Rather, it belongs to good government to spare the subjects and to subdue the proud. For it does not seem right to indulge those who have obstinately persisted in rebellion, who hold themselves within fortified strongholds, and who strive to escape the execution of justice. Aeneid.

units.la: 34. Secundo redarguitur nostra responsio quod pro culpa quam V.S. in quibusdam esse dicebar, V.S. quodammodo criminaremur, illos immunes criminis fatendo. Sed absit tantus error qui nil ipsa responsione quam propria manu conscripsimus legi poterit, quod criminationem sapere videatur, sed potius venerationem & observantiam Vestrae S. quam semper in verum patrem & pastore praecipuum habuimus. At si id V. S. criminationem putet quod ea afferente: ducem Francisum in aliquo forsan errore, alios quosdam in vera (ut ajebat) ribaldaria iucurrisse ex quibus forsan aliquis jam deo computum reddebat. Nos intelligentes haec à vestra Sanct. referri ad criminandum Marchionem Piscariae tunc vita functum, qui (ut praefertur) antea vivens nobis illius factionis practicam detexerat. Respondimus de mortuis modeste loquendum esse ac in dubio potius bene quam male praesumendum, hominemque mortuum qui per se respondere non poterat, potius laudandum quam vituperandum seu culpandum, Nosque cupere mortuum vivere, ut de seipso rationem redderet. In duce autem non errorem qui in facto proprio cadere non poterat: sed si ea quae illi erant objecta vera apparerent, crimen potius acerrimum ac exemplari punitione dignum censeri. Haec quippe nullam in V.S. criminationem afferunt, ni forsan S. V. seipsam dijudicans fateri vellet (quod non credimus) se ejus factionis conscium aurricemque fuisse, prout Marchio vivens nobis retulerat. Quem forsan ob id de ribaldaria agendum censeret, quod praeter fidem datam illius factionis secreta detexisset, qui tamen ex eo fidelitatis debito, quo nobis prius astringebatur, tacere non poterat, quin seipsum ejusdem criminis reum faceret: ubi propalando tale facinus, veniam praemiumque & laudem jure ita disponente consequebatur.
units.tr: 34. Second, our reply is refuted in that, regarding the fault which Your Holiness was said to have in certain matters, we seemed in some way to accuse Your Holiness by declaring those men innocent of crime. But let there be no such great error: from our reply, which we wrote in our own hand, it can be read that nothing in it savours of accusation, but rather of the veneration and observance which we have always held toward Your Holiness as a true father and chief shepherd. But if Your Holiness thinks that an accusation, because of what was alleged, namely that Duke Francis had perhaps fallen into some error, and certain others into true (as he said) ribaldry, of which some perhaps already render account to God; we, understanding that this was referred by Your Holiness to accusing the Marquis of Pescara, then deceased, who (as stated above) while living had revealed to us the practice of that faction, replied that one should speak modestly of the dead, and in doubt presume well rather than ill; that a dead man who could not answer for himself should be praised rather than reviled or blamed; and that we wished the dead man were alive, so that he might give account of himself. As for the duke, there was no error in him, since he could not fall into error in his own affair; but if the things objected to him appeared true, he should be judged rather a most grievous crime deserving exemplary punishment. These things bring no accusation against Your Holiness, unless perhaps Your Holiness, judging yourself, wished to confess (which we do not believe) that you had been aware of and an accomplice in that faction, as the Marquis, while living, had reported to us. Perhaps he thought the Marquis should be prosecuted for ribaldry on that account, because, beyond the faith given, he had revealed the secrets of that faction; yet from the debt of fidelity by which he was previously bound to us, he could not keep silent without making himself guilty of the same crime. Where, by openly disclosing such a deed, he obtained pardon, reward and praise, as the law itself provides.

units.la: 35. Tertio redarguitur eadem nostra responsio quodque V.S. nobis benigne & large pollicebatur, ea nos tanquam debita & obligata flagitaremus. Sed videamus qualia essent ejusdem Sanctitatis pollicita, qualisque fuerit responsio nostra, ut etiam hanc culpam ruamus: hoc n. V.S. in suis literis sub silentio pertransit, alijs caussam deterius cogitandam relinquens. Ut igitur horum veritas clare pateat, offerebat nobis V.S. si illius votis quo ad ipsum Ducem Franciscum annueremus, se nobis non solum decimas & Cruciatas & pileos & quicquid per spiritualem & temporalem potestatem facultatis haberet praestaturum, sed etiam sanguinem & viram ad nostram exultationem & satisfactionem exhibiturum: Respondemus non convenire reipub. Christianae cruciatam tali conditione perstringi, sed potius libere & sponte offerendam, nec congruum videri ut illa differatur. Poteramus. n. jam in nostris his regnis concedere eo ordine, quo nostri praedecessores illam semper à vestris praedecessoribus obtinuerant, pro promontoriis in Africa. Qui situs adversus fidei hostes tuendis ac propulsandis, quib. ad eum effectu nusquam fuerat denegata, & minus nobis hujusmodi Ecclesiae thesaurum à V.S. denegandi seu differendi censebamus: qui ultra res Africanas prout vestrae S. insinuavimus, cupiebamus etiam cū ea pecunia quae ex ipsa Cruciata colligeretur, rebus Ungaricis adversus Turcas succurrere, ptout & religionis & officii nostri & sanguinis ratio incitabat. Pollicebamurque eam pecuniam nequaquam in alios usus implicandam. Quod si ex ipsius cruciatae denegatione seu dilatione quod ministri Christianitati contingeret, hostesque fidei quicquam molirentur, cum jam tot bellis contra nos & statum nostrum tentatis exhausti essemus, nec sine cruciata occurrere possemus, protestati fuimus id nequaquam nostrae culpae ascribendum, sed potius eidem imputandum qui id denegaret quod tibi non noceret & toti Christianae reipublic. summe prodesse poterat. De pileis autem, diximus unum duntaxat à vestrae felici promotionis exordio à nobis petitum, quem ubi putabamus tam diu differendum, cum esset prima gratia à V. S. manu etiam nostra conscriptis literis petita ac instanter flagitata. Alter vero pileus petitus non fuerat, sed ultro à V. S. oblatus nostroque consensu acceptatus. Sicque alienum censebamus eos nunc pileos tali conditione pertitum, nec de aliqua justa causa subtrahendi feudum convictum. Tenebatur enim Vest. Sanctitas jure feudi tanquam directus illius dominus, potius nos in feudo tueri, quam invasoribus aditum dare, aut se socium invasionis praestare. Eodem enim ordine quo tenetur Vasallus pro feudo domino servire, eodem ordine tenetur dominus vasallum in feudo tueri. Et ex quibus causis vasallus feudum amittit, ex eisdem causis dominus directa proprietate feudi, illiusque directo dominio privatur. Est enim ipsius feudi natura, ut ultro citroque oblationem pariat. Facile quidem fuisset improvisum regnum ac ad defensionem non paratum, nil tale metuens aggredi, & forsan in parte occupare. Sed an id heri licuisset, an haec pastorali officio convenissent: cogitet S. V. Quae enim praemia offerri poterant, quae Christi Vicarium ad tam immane facinus induxissent? Sanctius itaque tunc consultum extitit Vestae S. ut praemiis illis neglectis non attentaret, quod forsan pro voto non succedisset, nec tentatum coeptum vel consummari potuisset. Sicque merito (ut inquit S. V.) plus apud eam valuisse debuerunt amicitiae nostrae merita, quam praemium ullum. Verum & si meliorem praesumptionem ampleéti velimus, nilque de intrinsecis Sanctit. Vest. cordis judicare praesumamus, quod vero Christi Vicario non congruerent: non tamen pro comperto habemus, quid cessante victoria S. V. actura fuisset, quae jam sub anticipiti Marte statim Mediolanum colore sequestri, ac depositi a nostrorum ducum manu & protectione etipere: ac in sua potestate, quamdiu de pace tractaretur reponere, & reducere conabatur. Quae etiam, ut ad id nos ac duces ipsos nostros cogeret, illorumque vires minueret, ac necessitatem induceret, asserens antecessoris foedus successorem non ligare. Curavit (ut ajunt) non solum Florentinorum aliorumque potentatuum praesidia, qui ex Adriani foedere ad contributionem defensivam tenebantur subtrahi & denegari. Verum & si nostrorum Venetorum praesidia, ad quae particulari foedere tenebantur, sustulisse dicitur, his suadendo ne suas copias, ut tenebantur, nostris jungerent: ut sic nostri, omni foederatorum auxilio destituti priusquam in campum prodirent, hostesque adorirentur, coacti fuerint, non sine summo labore, & nostris ac Serenissimi Archiducis fratris nostri impensis, novas tum equitum tum peditum copias ex Germania adducere, & cum his exercitum nostrum augere, quo bellum aggredi sperarentque victoriam nancisci possent.
units.tr: 35. Third, the same reply of ours is refuted, in that Your Holiness kindly and generously promised us things which we demanded as owed and due. But let us see what promises that Holiness made, and what our reply was, so that we may also refute this charge; for Your Holiness passes over this in silence in your letters, leaving others to think the worst of the cause. So that the truth of these things may clearly appear: Your Holiness offered us that, if we would accede to your wishes concerning Duke Francis himself, you would not only grant us tithes, crusade indulgences, caps, and whatever you had by spiritual and temporal power, but would also give your blood and life for our exultation and satisfaction. We replied that it was not fitting for the Christian commonwealth that the crusade be bound by such a condition, but that it should be offered freely and spontaneously, and that it did not seem proper for it to be deferred. For we could already grant it in these our kingdoms, in the same order by which our predecessors had always obtained it from yours, for the promontories in Africa, places for defending and repelling the enemies of the faith, for which purpose it had nowhere been denied. We thought it less proper for us to be refused or kept waiting for this treasure of the Church by Your Holiness. Beyond the African affairs, as we have indicated to Your Holiness, we also wished to use the money collected from the same crusade to aid Hungarian affairs against the Turks, as the reason of religion, of our office and of our blood urged; and we promised that this money would in no way be diverted to other uses. But if from the denial or postponement of the crusade some harm should befall Christendom, and the enemies of the faith should undertake something, since we were already exhausted by so many wars attempted against us and our state, and could not resist without the crusade, we protested that this was in no way to be ascribed to our fault, but rather to him who denied what would not harm Your Holiness and could be most useful to the whole Christian commonwealth. Concerning the caps, we said that only one had been asked of us from the beginning of your happy promotion, and we thought it should be deferred for so long, since it was the first favour asked from Your Holiness, requested also by our own hand in written letters and urgently demanded. The second cap, however, had not been requested, but was offered of its own accord by Your Holiness and accepted with our consent. And so we thought it foreign to demand those caps now on such a condition, nor was there any just cause for withdrawing a fief once conferred. For Your Holiness was bound by the right of a fief, as its direct lord, to protect us in the fief rather than to give entry to invaders or to become a partner in the invasion. For in the same order by which a vassal is bound to serve his lord for the fief, in the same order a lord is bound to protect his vassal in the fief; and for the same causes by which a vassal loses the fief, the lord is deprived of the direct ownership and direct dominion of the fief. For it is the nature of the fief itself to create mutual obligation on both sides. Indeed, it would have been easy to attack the kingdom, unprepared and not ready for defence, fearing nothing of the sort, and perhaps to occupy part of it. But whether this would have been lawful, or whether it would have fitted the pastoral office, let Your Holiness consider. For what rewards could be offered that would have induced the Vicar of Christ to so monstrous a deed? Therefore it was then the more prudent counsel for Your Holiness not to attempt it, neglecting those rewards, lest perhaps it would not have succeeded as desired, and the begun undertaking might have been attempted in vain or not completed. And so, as Your Holiness says, rightly the merits of our friendship ought to have weighed more with you than any reward. But even if we adopt the better presumption, and presume nothing to judge of the inner heart of Your Holiness, namely that such things would not befit the true Vicar of Christ, yet we do not know for certain what Your Holiness would have done had victory been withdrawn. For already under doubtful Mars you tried at once to seize Milan under the colour of sequestration and deposit, from the hand and protection of our commanders, to put it in your own power, and to hold it there as long as peace was being negotiated. You also tried, in order to force us and our commanders to this, and to diminish their forces and induce necessity, asserting that a successor is not bound by the treaty of a predecessor. You took care (as they say) not only that the garrisons of the Florentines and of other powers, who by the Adrian league were bound to defensive contribution, should be withdrawn and denied; but you are also said to have removed the garrisons of our Venetians, to which they were bound by a particular treaty, by persuading them not to join their troops to ours as they were bound to do. Thus our forces, destitute of all help from allies before they went into the field and attacked the enemy, were compelled, not without great labour and at the expense of ourselves and of our most Serene brother the Archduke, to bring new companies of both horse and foot from Germany, and with these to augment our army, so that they might undertake the war and hope to win the victory.

units.la: 17. Subdit eadem Sanctitas, quod sequuta nostrorum victoria contra Gallos, cum omnis sibi
units.tr: 17. The same Holiness adds that, after our men's victory over the French, although every contention seemed to be fabricated,

units.la: fabulata contentio videretur, sine cupiditatis & partium suspicione, nobis etiam foederis vinculo haerere posset: magnumque in nobis Italiae beneficium & Christianitatis totius positum arbitraretur: non solum foedus firmavit, sed quo nostri duces egentes pecuniae exercitum alere ac sustinere possent centum illis dederit ducatorum millia, conditione appositae, ut si de foedere aliqua nobis dubiratio oriretur, illae Sanctit. Vest. pecuniae restituerentur. Fatemur quidem, Pater Beatissime, Victoriam illam omnem sibi contentionem merito sustulisse: sineque cupiditatis (a qua semper fuimus alieni) partium suspicione, cujus nulla suberat causa nobis haerere potuisse: omnique ratione arbitrandum fuisse, ea in re totius Italiae ac Christianitatis beneficium impositum: ni zizaniae seminator, illius fructum suffocasset. Diffitemur tamen eam in foedere conditionem appositam, quod si dubiratio oriretur, pecuniae nostrae ducibus solutae Vest. Sanct. restituerentur. Quandoquidem ipsius rei gestae seriem longe aliter se habere constet, necde tali conditione ulla in ipso foedere mentio facta appareat, verum in quodam articulo separato & a capitulis foederis penitus exclusa, enarretur. Quod cum Vestra Sanctitas ad satisfaciendum exercitui nostro, in Italia existenti civitatesque & oppida Sanctae Romanae ecclesiae subjecta, ac oppressionibus, militum sublevanda, salutem & tranquillitatem Italiae custodiendam, summam pecuniae inter Vest. Sanct. nostrosque oratores expressam, suo & excelsae Reipub. dominorum Florentinorum nomine se soluturum promisisset, pie pro tunc ad sexaginta mille ducatorum auri ascensuram. Oratores nostri eidem Vest. S. sub juramento promiserunt quod casu, quo foedus cum ipsis nostris oratoribus percussum, & capitula in ipso foedere contenta, non approbaremus non ratificaremus, omnis summa pecuniae, quae per Vestram Sanct. ac per dominos Florentinos soluta fuisset, eidem Sanct. & Florentinis integre restitueretur: cum ea adjectione, quod docet restitutio integre & plene facta foret, foedus interea, & omnia ipsius foederis capitula, ad unguem observarentur. Quum itaque foedus ipsum, ac singula capitula in eo foedere comprehensa, quae primum ad nos delata fuere rata & grata habuerimus, nostraeque ratificationis literas, cum ipsorum capitulorum foederis insertione in forma debita expeditas Vestrae Sanctitati exhibere fecerimus: quas & vidit & legit, & palpavit, & dando suas reciprocas retinere potuit. Justificare ergo non potest, quin purificata fuerit per nos conditio illa, qua deficiente restitutio pecuniarum erat fienda. Quae quidem conditio, & particularis conventio, prout illius verba sonant, nequaquam nos urgebant, aut alia extrinsecus a foedere aut separatim gesta vel tractata. Quinimo potius, & si pecuniarum locus esset restitutioni, cujus tamen contrarium ostenditur, servandum tamen erat foedus. Interim quo juxta ipsius separati articuli seriem, sine pollicitorum violatione recedi non potuit, nec ad contraria foedera licite devenire valuit. Sicque satis erroneae, & (salva pace sit dictum) praeter veritatem refertur, quod idem foedus non plene a nobis acceptum, nec probatum fuerit, qui & plane & integre, ut praefertur, omnia in foedere contenta probavimus, rataque habuimus, nil penitus de contentis in eo, nec etiam syllabam aut literam mittentes. Quod si vestra S. hujusce nostrae ratificationis literas recipere, suasque reciprocas (ut parerat) tradere renuit: ni simul traderetur ratificatio duorum articulorum, de quibus extra ipsum foedus perscripta particularia, nobis tamen inconsultis separatim & ad parte tractatum fuerat. Ad quorum approbationem & ex vi foederis (ut praemittitur) astringebamur. Nihil quod culpae nostrae ascribi valeat, si foedus illud minime observatum: sed potius inde violatum exstent.
units.tr: without any suspicion of greed or partisanship, it could still cling to us by the bond of the treaty, and that a great benefit to Italy and to all Christendom was thought to rest in us. He not only confirmed the treaty but also gave our commanders, who lacked money to maintain and support the army, one hundred thousand ducats, on the condition attached that if any doubt arose about the treaty, those sums of Your Holiness would be restored. We admit, Most Blessed Father, that that victory had rightly removed all contention, and that, without any suspicion of partisanship (from which we have always been free) or of greed, which had no basis in our case, it could have clung to us, and by every reckoning it must be judged that a benefit to all Italy and Christendom had been conferred in that matter, unless a sower of tares had choked its fruit. Nevertheless we deny that this condition was attached to the treaty, namely that if doubt arose the money paid to our commanders would be restored to Your Holiness. For it is established that the sequence of the events themselves is quite otherwise, and no mention of such a condition appears in the treaty itself, but it is set out in a certain separate article, wholly excluded from the chapters of the treaty. When Your Holiness promised, to satisfy our army then in Italy, to relieve the cities and towns subject to the Holy Roman Church from the oppressions of soldiers, and to keep Italy safe and tranquil, that you would pay the sum agreed between Your Holiness and our envoys, in your own name and in the name of the lords Florentines of the lofty commonwealth, which then amounted piously to sixty thousand ducats of gold, our envoys promised the same Your Holiness under oath that if we did not approve or ratify the treaty concluded with our envoys and the chapters contained in it, the whole sum paid by Your Holiness and by the lords Florentines would be fully restored to the same Holiness and to the Florentines. They added that, while the restitution was made wholly and fully, the treaty and all its chapters should meanwhile be observed to the letter. Since, therefore, we have held the treaty itself and each chapter contained in it, which were first brought to us, as ratified and acceptable, and have caused our letters of ratification, with the chapters of the treaty inserted, to be dispatched in due form and exhibited to Your Holiness, which you both saw, read and handled, and by giving your reciprocal letters were able to keep, it cannot be justified that the condition on which the money was to be restored in default has not been fulfilled by us. That condition and particular agreement, as its words sound, did not bind us in any way, nor did other matters transacted outside the treaty or separately. Rather, even if there were room for restitution of money, which however is shown to be the contrary, the treaty would nevertheless have had to be kept. Meanwhile, according to the sequence of that separate article, one could not withdraw without violating promises, nor validly come to contrary treaties. And so it is quite erroneously, and (with respect be it said) contrary to the truth, reported that the same treaty was not fully accepted or approved by us, when we have plainly and wholly, as stated, approved all things contained in the treaty and held them ratified, not sending anything at all of what it contains, not even a syllable or a letter. But if Your Holiness refuses to receive the letters of this our ratification and to hand over your reciprocal ones (as you had agreed), unless at the same time the ratification of two articles were handed over, which were drawn up in separate writing outside the treaty, yet without our knowledge and treated apart, for whose approval we were bound by the force of the treaty (as said above), then nothing that can be ascribed to our fault exists. If the treaty was not observed, it has rather been violated by others.

units.la: Abbas Ab hac enim culpa & labe omnino alieni sumus: & ut id plene liqueat, placet illorum duorum articulorum exrinsecus tractatorum substantiam referre: causasq; differere: quibus non ita passim per nos approbandi viderentur.
units.tr: For we are wholly free from this fault and blame. And so that this may be made fully clear, it pleases us to set out the substance of those two articles, which were treated from outside, and to explain the reasons why they should not so readily seem to be approved by us.

units.la: 18. Ex his enim duobus articulis separatis, alter salem in statu Mediolanen. distribuendum, cum id à nostris oratoribus sua S. expositeret: ut, juxta foedus per nos cum Leone percussum, curaremus cum duce Francisco SForcia, sal eisdem modis & conditionibus à sede & Camera apost. recipi. Nostriq; oratores ad id responderent: non esse amplius nobis jus utilis dominii ducatus Mediolani, prout ante fuerat cum Leone, data jam per nos eidem duci investitura, sicque rem cum ipso duce necessario dicendum esse. Ipsi autem oratores nostri, non expresso quod id nostro nomine agerent, simpliciter V.S. medio eorum juramento promiserunt quod illustris Vice-rex curaret, ut illustris dux Mediolan. cum Vest. Sanctitate pro hujusmodi sale conveniret. Si igitur haec promissio, quae non nisi factis tertii pollicetur de ipsoque tertio, nil ultro promittit: quod tertium illum curaturum, ut dux ad concordiam venirer, nil certi decernendo nos urgere videatur: ut hac promissionem praecise ratam habere debeamus. Ita, ut sine ea foederis per nos approbati & ratificati observantia evanesceat. Judicet id quicunque mentis compos, quandoquidem nostra sententia, & ut peritorum consilio freti, didicimus: nos nequaquam ad ipsius promissionis observantiam astricti causaremur. Respondimus tum in hoc modestius V.S. quod si hujusmodi Sanct. Vest. desiderium nobis prius innotuisset, quod de ipsa salis distributione in statu Mediolani ad opus serenissimi archiducis, fratris nostri, cum ipso Illustri Francisco SForcia, transactum esset, nostram libenter operam navare studuissemus, ut S. V. hujusce voti compos fieret. Verum & si fratri deesse non possemus, nos tamen cum eo curaturos, ut mediante aliqua honesta recompensa pecuniaria, ipse frater noster, jus hujusmodi distribuendi salis: V.S. ad illius vitam concederet. Id enim aequum & justum videbatur, ne jus illud, quod eidem fratri nostro, pro recompensa praesidii per eum praestiti ad defensionem status Mediolani, deficientibus viribus ac copiis, Vestrae Sanctitatis, aliorumque foederatorum, eidem infructuosum redderetur.
units.tr: 18. For of these two separate articles, one concerned the distribution of salt in the state of Milan, when Your Holiness put it to our envoys that, according to the covenant we had struck with Leo, we should take care, with Duke Francis Sforza, that salt be received by the See and the Apostolic Chamber on the same terms and conditions. Our envoys replied that we no longer had the right of useful lordship over the Duchy of Milan, as we had had before with Leo, since investiture had already been given by us to that same duke, and so the matter had to be discussed necessarily with the duke himself. Our envoys, however, without stating that they acted in our name, simply promised Your Holiness under oath that the illustrious Viceroy would take care that the illustrious Duke of Milan should come to an agreement with Your Holiness about such salt. If, then, this promise, which concerns only the acts of a third party and pledges nothing of its own accord about that third party, seems to bind us to nothing certain, since it only says that the third party will take care that the duke comes to agreement, then we ought not to be held to a promise of that kind, precisely as ratified. Without it the observance of the covenant approved and ratified by us would vanish. Let anyone who is sane judge this, since, as we have learned from our own opinion and from relying on the counsel of experts, we could not be held to the observance of that promise. We replied then, rather more modestly, to Your Holiness that if your desire of this kind had been made known to us before, and the distribution of salt in the state of Milan, for the use of the most serene Archduke, our brother, had been settled with the illustrious Francis Sforza himself, we would gladly have striven to lend our help, so that Your Holiness might obtain the fulfilment of this wish. But although we could not fail our brother, we would nevertheless take care with him that, in return for some honourable financial compensation, our brother himself would grant to Your Holiness the right of distributing such salt for the duration of his life. For this seemed fair and just, lest that right, which had been granted to our brother as a reward for the protection he had given to defend the state of Milan, should be rendered useless to him, now that the forces and troops of Your Holiness and the other allies were lacking.

units.la: 19. Alter vero ex his duobus articulis id continebat, quod ad tollendam difficultatem, quae inter Sanct. V. & nos incidere posset, super controversia Mutinae & Rhegii, offerebant nostri oratores ut Vestra Sanctitas consequeretur utile ipsarum civitatum dominium superioritatis & directi dominii, jure nobis semper salvo, ita ut S. Vest. extunc recognosceret, & acciperet hujusmodi directum nostrum dominium ac superioritatem: vestraque S. nobis aut agentibus nostris, centena millia ducatorum aureorum (post recuperatam possessionem eorum quae illustris dux Ferrariae a repore obitus Leonis ecclesiae subtraxerat) persolvere deberet. Huic propositioni & oblationi respondebat Vest. Sanct. pro se & sede Apost. hujusmodi oblata acceptare, prout proponebantur, excepta superioritate & directo dominio nostro: supradictis civitatibus Vestra S. recognoscere renunciavit, ne juribus & superioritati ab Apostolo sede praetensis, praejudicium fieret. Offerente tum Vest. Sanct. se contentam esse, ut ipsius superioritatis controversia videretur & decideretur infra tres menses tunc proximos per V.S. & illius Vice-regem, aut alios qui ab utraque parte simul eligerentur. Et si hujusmodi superioritas nobis adjudicaretur, Apostolica sedes recognosceret prout ab agentibus nostris fuerat propositum. Si vero Apostolicae sedi adjudicaretur, V.S. ex sua liberalitate & ex eo amore quo nos prosequi profitebatur, nobis condonaret recompensam de qua deberemus esse contenti. Hanc Vest. S. responsionem & oblationem ipsi nostri agentes, ita demum acceperunt, ut salva nobis essent omnia jura superioritatis & dominii directi in ipsis civitatibus competentia pertinentia, quibus ob talem acceptationem praejudicium afferre non praetendebant. Consentientes nihilominus, de hujusmodi juribus cognosci, modis & formis per dictam V.S. propositis. Si haec igitur tam difformiter tam irresolute extra foederis capitula descripta in ea essent forma, quae vel ad nos ad ratihabitionem (quam nostri nostro nomine non promiserant) obligaret, vel in nos actionem pararet, qua ad id urgeri possemus, nulla accedente valida stipulatione nec pacto firmiter vestito, ubi etiam tempus decisioni praefixum illum impossibile redderet: consulat in his V.S. peritos & comperiet nos, necad hujusmodi ratihabitionem particularem astrictum, nec ex hujus defectu percussi nobiscum foederis, & per nos indifferenter ac plane approbatu, observantiam fuisse deferendam, nec contrario foedere frustrandam seu irritandam. Ut ramen moderatius cum V.S. pro sua persone qualitate ageremus, ostendimus ea quae per nostras orationes in hac 1e tractata fuerant, nequaquam in nostra potestate consistere. Qui nec Imperii juribus praejudicare nec jus tertii auferre deberemus, nec in nostra esset potestate illum ducem Ferrariae urgere ad restitutionem petitorum, nisi is armis offensibilibus coerceretur, qui se Imperii vasallum profitebatur, & ea quae restitui petebantur, de S. Imperii feudo tenere recognoscebat, durumque videretur pro ea re bellum in Italia instaurare. Supplicavimus ergo V.S. ut pro Italiae quiete, & ne inde novimotus ibidem caufarentur, dignaretur eadem Sanctitas Vestra consentire, ut res ipsa, aut per justitiae tramites, aut per compositionem amicabilem cum ipso duce Ferrariae fiendam, terminaretur. Et cum hujusmodi oblata Vestrae Sanctitati non placuissent, supervenientes postea Reverendissimo Sanctitatis Vestrae Legato, Cardinali de Salviatis, apud nos transegisse, ut Vestrae Sanctitatis mente percepta, non recedentes a recto justitiae tramite, cupientesque nihilominus quantum fas esset Vest. Sanctitari gratificari, obtulimus e: idem nos operam daturos cum effectu, quod sine praejudicio jurium Sacri Romani Imperii, seu alterius cujuslibet, posset Sanctitas Vestra dum sibi expedire videretur, sine cujuspiam resistentia, hucque armorum apparatu sua sponte, per se aut suos ad id deputandos possessionem recuperare, Rhegii & Ruberiae cum suis pertinentiis tuendam & possidendam, prout antea tenebat & possidere-
units.tr: 19. The other of these two articles contained the following: to remove the difficulty which might arise between Your Holiness and ourselves over the dispute concerning Modena and Reggio, our envoys offered that Your Holiness should obtain the useful lordship of those cities, of superiority and direct lordship, with our right always preserved, so that Your Holiness would then acknowledge and accept our direct lordship and superiority over them; and that Your Holiness should pay to us, or to our agents, one hundred thousand gold ducats (after recovery of the possessions which the illustrious Duke of Ferrara had taken from the Church since the death of Leo). To this proposal and offer Your Holiness replied that, for yourself and the Apostolic See, you would accept what was offered as it was proposed, except for our superiority and direct lordship: Your Holiness renounced acknowledging those cities, so that no prejudice would be done to the rights and superiority claimed by the Apostolic See. Your Holiness then offered that you were content for the controversy over that superiority to be examined and decided within the three months next following, by Your Holiness and your Viceroy, or by others chosen jointly by both parties. And if that superiority were adjudged to us, the Apostolic See would acknowledge it, as our agents had proposed. But if it were adjudged to the Apostolic See, Your Holiness, out of your generosity and that love with which you professed to cherish us, would remit to us a compensation with which we ought to be content. Our agents finally accepted this reply and offer of Your Holiness on the understanding that all rights of superiority and direct lordship pertaining to us in those cities should remain intact, and they did not claim that they would be prejudiced by such acceptance. Nevertheless they agreed that these rights should be examined in the manner and form proposed by Your Holiness. If, then, these matters, so inconsistently and so irresolutely described outside the chapters of the covenant, were in a form which would bind us to ratification of them (which our envoys had not promised in our name), or would bring an action against us by which we could be pressed to that end, with no valid stipulation or firmly binding pact added, and when the time fixed for the decision made that impossible, let Your Holiness consult experts in these matters, and you will find that we were neither bound to such a particular ratification, nor, through its absence, should the observance of the covenant struck with us and approved by us, without distinction and plainly, have been abandoned, nor frustrated or annulled by a contrary covenant. However, in order to deal more moderately with Your Holiness in consideration of your personal rank, we showed that the matters which had been treated in our negotiations in this regard were in no way within our power; we ought neither to prejudice the rights of the Empire nor to take away the right of a third party, nor was it in our power to press that Duke of Ferrara to restore the things demanded, unless he were restrained by offensive arms, since he professed himself a vassal of the Empire and acknowledged that the things demanded for restoration were held of the fief of the Holy Empire, and it would seem harsh to renew war in Italy for that reason. We therefore begged Your Holiness that, for the peace of Italy, and lest new disturbances arise there on that account, you would deign to agree that the matter should be settled either by the paths of justice or by an amicable composition to be made with the Duke of Ferrara himself. And when these offers did not please Your Holiness, the most Reverend Legate of Your Holiness, Cardinal de Salviati, who came afterwards to us, negotiated with us that, having understood Your Holiness's mind, without departing from the straight path of justice, and yet desiring as far as right allowed to do Your Holiness a favour, we offered that we would bring about, with real effect and without prejudice to the rights of the Holy Roman Empire or of anyone else, that Your Holiness, whenever it seemed expedient to you, could without anyone's resistance, by a display of arms of your own accord, by yourself or by those deputed by you for this, recover possession of Reggio and Rubiera with their dependencies, to be held and possessed as before he had held and possessed them.

units.la: Mutinae & Rhegii utile dominii Papae concessum ab Imperatore, salva superioritate. possidebat. Quod tamen Sanctitati vestræ non placuit, licet credere non possemus eum, qui Clæ vices in terris gerit, vel unius guttæ humani sanguinis jactura, quamcunque secularem ditionem vendicare velle, cum id ab evangelica doctrina prorsus alienum videretur. Quid igitur rebus ni-tibus nobis impingi posset, quum fœdus plane à nobis acceptum seu approbatum fuerit. Quo culenostræ ratificationis literæ receptæ nō fuerint: Quo jure ipsius Vestræ Sanctitatis reciprocæ literæ bis fuerint denegatæ: Qua fronte fidei religio, quam V. Sanct. in verbo Romani Pontificis superfœderis observantia personalitet præstitisse dinoscitur, spreta fuerit ac neglecta: cogitet Vest. S. ipsa, judicet an sic decetet ab eo fœdere discedere, penitusque repugnantia pacisci cum his potui qui eo tempore pro hostibus habebantur, contra quos potius ponenda erat defensio, ad eorum contus repellendos.
units.tr: Your Holiness was not pleased that Modena and Reggio, with the useful lordship granted to the Pope by the Emperor, saving the superiority, were held by him. Yet we could not believe that he who bears Christ's place on earth would wish to claim any secular dominion at the cost of even one drop of human blood, since that seemed utterly foreign to the evangelical doctrine. What then could be charged against us in matters so plain, since the treaty was clearly accepted and approved by us? Our letters of ratification were not received; by what right Your Holiness's reciprocal letters were twice refused; with what face the faith of religion, which Your Holiness is known to have pledged personally in the word of the Roman Pontiff for the observance of the treaty, was scorned and neglected. Let Your Holiness herself consider and judge whether it is fitting to withdraw from that treaty and to make a compact wholly incompatible with those who were then regarded as enemies, against whom rather a defence should have been set up, to repel their attacks.

units.la: 20. Quod autem S.V. ad id subjungit, cum propter æmulationem quorundam ex ducibus grata cæteris consilia, Pischaria Marchio nonnulla jactare tractareque cœpisset, in nostri statumentum V.S. illa etiam consilia audivisse ne fœdere à nobis rejecto penitus aspernata eidem deesset, ubi niti ac confidere posset. Non possumus profecto non mirari quæ in hoc Vestra Sanctitas suis literis profiteretur, quæ & si nobis sæpius, à nostris ducibus aliisque quamplurimis scripta relata fuissent, nusquam tamen à nobis credita sunt, ne adhuc crederemus, ni V.Sanct. id asseveraret, assertione in his potissime, quæ proprium factum concernunt, nulla plenior liquido probatio esse posset. Qualia autem fuerint ea, quæ Marchio Pischaria in nostri status detrimentum praeclare & tractare dicebatur, & quæ Vest. Sanctitas audivisse faretur, cum in Vest. Sanctitatis literis non specifice declarentur, sed sub verborum involucro restant nephanda tegi videantur, comprobanda erit, per ipsius Marchionis literas, quæ penes nos servantur, ac per aliorum quorundam, adhuc viventium testimonia, qui hujusce facinoris conscii participesque fuere. Quibus satis aperte detegitur, Pischaria Marchionem non ita proprii honoris ac conscientiæ immemorem fuisse quod quicquam in status nostri detrimentum moliri cuperet, sed potius aliter finxisse quam in animo haberet, ut vestrum in nos ac statum nostrum molientium factiones, ac incendia parata, quorum jam fumum rat, veioribus indiciis ac argumentis detegeret: hincque facilius nobis præmonitus extingui potuerit. Sicque finxit se de nobis male contentum, ut inde liberius in molientium partes vocaretur, omnemque rei seriem audire ac funditus intelligere posset. Hicque Marchio ipse ad eam tragœdiam vocatus simulata fide, in eam conspirationem, cum cæteris illius autoribus convenit, atque consensit: perstratisque omnibus ad tantum facinus parandum dispositis atque paratis, ac totius negocii serie plane perspecta & intellecta, cum in his V.S. principalis esset autoritas, audivisseque Marchio nuncium ad id per V.S. transmissum, eidem sui parte, ut ait, offerentem sub cujusdam Apostolici Brevis Credentia, regni nostri Neapolitani investituram, & possessionem, si is in ejusdem Sanctitatis & fœderatorum cum copiis nostri exercitus, eidem Marchioni magis affectis transfire atque transfugeret: ut inde communibus fœderatorum copiis, inter quas & Gallorum copiæ, cum ingenti Helvetiorum manu, ad sui regis liberationem Italiæ concitaris, uno jactu atque contextu nostrum exercitum prorsus delerent. Nosque non solum à statu Mediolani, sed etiam à regno Neapolitano ac ab omni imperio Italico excluderent: ut inde S.V. nos etiam ab omni Imperiali dignitate deponeret. Finxit Marchio se contentum his annuere, si id cum honore, sine incursu criminis læsæ majestatis exequi liceret: & ut super ea re peritiores consuleret, petiit quindecim dierum dilationem, quibus pendentibus, illi erat in animo nobis rei seriem aperire, prout & fecit, nec ideo minus se à practicis abstinuit, qui etiam ad hanc fictionem magis colorandam habuit ex urbe consilium peritorum, quo eidem Marchioni persuadebatur, eundem licite posse, ac sine honoris seu fidelitatis præstita læsione, seu præjudicio, sineque criminis læsæ majestatis, in partes Vestræ S. ranquam supremi domini illius regni transfire, feudumque ab eadem sanctitate suscipere, ubi potissime ipsius sanctitatis justus accederet. Si hæc igitur pater sanctus vera sunt, prout narrat Marchio, qui usque ad ultimum vitæ spiritum in ea sententia semper perstitit. Si sunt illa tractata atque jactata consilia, quæ V. Sanct. etiam audivisse fatetur: videat ipsa V. Sanctitas, recto sui intellectus oculo, si hæc tanto pastore digna censeri entur: inspiciat qualis fructus inde colligi possit, quale scandalum, quantusque tumultus ex his in ecclesia Dei ac in universa republ. Christiana nasceretur. Miseranda quippe res esset, ac ab omni fideli catholico deploranda, in quæ ita occupatur mentis nostræ judicium, ut quasi somnium illusorium putemus, cui fides tribui non debet, cum potissime (ut antea liquide ostendimus) cesser fundamentum illud satis manifeste eversum, imo penitus falsum, de fœdere à nobis rejecto, quod nunquam rejectum sed plane acceptatum constat.
units.tr: 20. As for what Your Holiness adds, that when the Marquis of Pescara had begun to put forward and discuss certain plans, out of rivalry among some of the commanders, to the displeasure of the others, Your Holiness also heard those plans to our detriment, lest, the treaty having been rejected by us, she should be left wholly without the support on which she could rely: we cannot but wonder at what Your Holiness professes in this letter. Although reports of this kind were often brought to us by our commanders and by very many others, we never believed them, and we would not believe them even now, had Your Holiness not affirmed it; in matters that concern a man's own deeds, no fuller proof could be had than such an affirmation. But what the plans were that the Marquis of Pescara was said to have distinctly put forward and discussed to the detriment of our state, and which Your Holiness says she heard, since they are not specifically declared in Your Holiness's letter but remain hidden under a veil of words, they seem to be shrouded in wickedness. They must be proved by the Marquis's own letters, which are kept with us, and by the testimony of certain others still living who were privy to and partners in this crime. From these it is plain enough that the Marquis of Pescara was not so forgetful of his honour and conscience as to desire to contrive anything to the detriment of our state; rather, he pretended to be other than he was in his mind, so that he might uncover, by clearer indications and proofs, the factions and the ready fires of those who were plotting against us and our state, whose smoke he already saw; and thus we might be forewarned and more easily extinguish them. So he feigned to be ill-content with us, so that he might be called more freely into the ranks of the plotters, and might hear the whole course of the affair and understand it thoroughly. This Marquis, called to that tragedy under a pretence of loyalty, agreed and consented to that conspiracy with the other authors of it. When all the preparations for so great a crime had been laid out and made ready, and the whole course of the business had been plainly observed and understood, and since Your Holiness held the principal authority in these matters, the Marquis heard that a messenger had been sent to him on Your Holiness's behalf, offering him, on her part, as he says, under the credence of a certain Apostolic Brief, the investiture and possession of our kingdom of Naples, if he would pass over and desert with his troops to Your Holiness and the allies, those in whose army our forces were more attached to the Marquis. Thus, by the combined forces of the allies, among whom were the troops of the French with a great band of Swiss, roused for the liberation of their king in Italy, our army would be utterly destroyed at one blow and in one contrivance; and they would exclude us not only from the state of Milan but also from the kingdom of Naples and from the whole Italian empire, so that Your Holiness might then depose us from all imperial dignity. The Marquis pretended that he would agree to these things if they could be carried out with honour and without incurring the charge of treason; and to consult more skilled men on this matter he asked for a delay of fifteen days. While these were pending, he intended to reveal the whole course of the affair to us, as indeed he did; nor did he on that account refrain from the practices, but he also obtained from the city, to colour this pretence the more, a council of experts, by which the Marquis was persuaded that he could lawfully pass into the party of Your Holiness, as the supreme lord of that kingdom, and receive the fief from that Holiness, without injury to his honour or fidelity, without prejudice and without the charge of treason, especially where the just cause of Your Holiness was clearly on his side. If then these things are true, holy Father, as the Marquis relates, who to his last breath always remained of that mind; and if these are the plans that were discussed and put forward, which Your Holiness confesses she heard, let Your Holiness herself see, with the right eye of her understanding, whether such things can be thought worthy of so great a shepherd; let her consider what fruit could be gathered from them, what scandal, and what great tumult would arise from them in the Church of God and in the whole Christian commonwealth. Indeed it would be a miserable thing, and to be deplored by every faithful Catholic, if the judgement of our mind were so occupied that we should think it a dream of illusion, to which no faith ought to be given; especially since (as we have shown clearly above) that foundation has been plainly overthrown, indeed wholly shown to be false, namely the claim about the treaty rejected by us, which is known never to have been rejected but plainly accepted.

units.la: 21. Sed ait V.S. se à verbis ad facta nullum aditum tentasse. Utinam sic se res haberet, nihilque de facto tentatum esset, quia facilius pro verbis verba reddi possent. Facta autem pro infectis habentur queunt. Ad quod V.Sanct. se de eo officio commendat nos admoneri mandasse, ut duces nostros in Italia quorum in manu res nostræ erant, curaremus de nobis esse contentos, hinc probationem elicitens, eidem esse curæ, quietem & stabilitatem rerum nostrarum. Noluimus inficiari id officium a Vest. S. præstitum, eo tamen tempore, quo idem Marchio totius rei seriem nobis aperte disseruerat. Cur autem tunc Vestra S. re jam detecta id nobis nunciandum censuerit, id ejus judicio & conscientiæ commendamus. Voluimus tamen & hoc in benigniorem partem suscipere.
units.tr: 21. But Your Holiness says that she made no attempt to pass from words to deeds. Would that the matter stood so, and that nothing had been attempted in deed, since words can more easily be answered by words; but deeds cannot be regarded as undone. In this connection Your Holiness commends herself for having charged us, as to her duty, that our commanders in Italy, in whose hands our affairs lay, should take care that we were content, thereby drawing the inference that her concern was the quiet and stability of our affairs. We did not wish to deny that this office was performed by Your Holiness, but at that time, when the same Marquis had openly set out to us the whole course of the affair. Why Your Holiness then, the matter having already been discovered, thought fit to announce this to us, we leave to her judgement and conscience. Nevertheless we chose to take this in the kinder part.

units.la: 22. At subjungit V.Sanctitas, quod maximo cum gemitu & dolore suo, atque Italiæ totius, duces nostri statum nostrum Mediolani occupassent, atque arcem in qua Franciscus Maria residebat circumcircu mvallare instituissent, postulante à nobis cutam & securitatem, adversus dignitatem tantam Italiæ periculo, omnibusque notis atque ignotis flagitantibus paratis qui & auxilia conferent. Cunctis prope Christianitatis regibus Vestram Sanctitatem animantibus cum non videretur posse resistere monitis, querelis precibusque illorum. Cum vos officii vestri debitum Italiæ calamitas & periculum commune commoveret, tamen adveniente per eos dies ab vestra Sanctitate Commendatore, Herrera Nuncio nostro tractandi causa misso relapsa eadem S. in pristinam spem & cupiditatem benevolentiæ nostræ, sibi quovismodo conciliando dimissis consiliis, conspirationibus, oblationibusque cunctorum, gravi omnium indignatione & querela, nobis comparare gloriam pacandæ Christianitatis, & moderationis nostræ omnibus declarandæ. Sicque ea conventionum capitula, paucis (ut ait) in locis leviter immutata remisisse ad nos comprobanda, scripsisseque manu sua literas, quibus per Dei misericordiam obsecrando, ut depellere eam suspitionem, quæ de nostra nimia cupiditate omnibus adhærebat, perpetuitatem & fructum amicitiæ suæ nobis polliceabatur, consiliumque fidele dabat, & quæ petenda erant omni cum humanitate & benevolentia à nobis petebar: securitatem videlicet Italiæ duce Mediolani, si quo pacto erraret clementem V.S. amorem. Quæ tot illius opera atque officia erga nos aliaque quamplurima, quæ nobis quotidie postulanti concedebat, ex quibus nobis commodum atque honor accrescebar (ut ait) parvipendimus. His multiplicum querelarum, accusationum, & criminationum fastidium adjungit: quibus tot & tantis (ut inquit) injuriis & causis invita V.S. & gemens de nobis desperare & diffidere & coacta, suamque amicitiam & benevolentiam, quam totiens (ut asserit) impudiavimus, multis & magnis regibus adjungere, quorum optimum in Christiani reipubl. & sedem Apostolicam animo. Si Vestra Sanct. aspernata esset, non jam pastoris seu communis patris laudem: sed superbi & insolentis nomen acquisivisset. Hæc, Pater Sancte, horrenda quidem ac penitus abominanda censerentur, ni scuto veritatis circundari hujusmodi calumnias, convitia, improperia, crimina, facinoraque nobis objecta refellere ac singulatim suo ordine exturpare & enervare studeremus: non quidem Christiano principe digna (si vera forent) sed potius apud inferos recondita censerentur. Ut igitur hujusmodi calumniarum nobis falso objectarum, facinculum disrumpamus & colligata spicula in nos conjecta separatim ac gradatim enervemus, cogimur historiam non fabulam recensere, qua rerum gestarum veritas in lucem prodeat. Et cum ab occupatione status Mediolani arcisque obsessione hujusmodi calumniarum principalior sumatur occasio: hincque pendere videantur leges & prophetæ, horum omnium, quæ in nos moliuntur & tentantur. Consequens est, ut pro nostræ villicationis debita ratione reddenda, & nequid occulti remaneat, neve servi nequam nobis nomen ac famam comparemus, sed potius servi fidelis & boni, qui in regnum Domini intrare valeamus, ab ipso stipite initium sumamus, & à capite rationem reddamus oporter, nihil quod ad rem faciat omittentes. Res igitur, ut apertissimis ostenditur documentis, sic se habet.
units.tr: 22. But Your Holiness adds that, to her very great grief and that of all Italy, our commanders occupied our state of Milan, and began to surround the citadel in which Francis Maria resided, our Commander Herrera, our nuncio sent for the purpose of negotiating, having come to Your Holiness in those days; and that, when the grievous danger to Italy was urged upon her, and all those known and unknown, who were ready to offer help, were demanding it, nearly all the kings of Christendom were urging Your Holiness, and she could not seem able to resist their warnings, complaints and prayers. Although the calamity of Italy and the common danger moved her to perform the duty of her office, nevertheless, as Your Holiness fell back at that time into her former hope and desire of winning our goodwill, dismissing her counsels, conspiracies and offers of all, to the great indignation and complaint of everyone, she resolved to gain for us the glory of pacifying Christendom and of showing our moderation to all. And so she sent back to us, to be approved, the articles of agreement, changed slightly, as she says, in a few places; and she wrote with her own hand letters in which, begging us through the mercy of God to dispel that suspicion which clung to all of us about our excessive desire, she promised her lasting friendship and its fruit to us, and gave faithful counsel, and asked from us, with all kindness and goodwill, what had to be sought: namely the security of Italy, with the Duke of Milan, if in any way he went astray, relying on Your Holiness's merciful love. These many works and services of hers towards us, and very many others that she granted to us daily as we asked, from which advantage and honour accrued to us (as she says), we have held cheap. To this she adds the weariness of many complaints, accusations and charges, by which, she says, having been driven against her will and with groaning, by so many and such great injuries and causes, Your Holiness despaired of us and distrusted us, and was compelled to join her friendship and goodwill, which (as she asserts) we have so often spurned, to many great kings, whose best intention is towards the Christian commonwealth and the Apostolic See. If Your Holiness had rejected these, she would have acquired not the praise of a shepherd or common father, but the name of proud and insolent. These things, holy Father, would be thought dreadful and utterly abominable, did we not labour to surround these calumnies, reproaches, insults, charges, crimes and misdeeds laid against us with the shield of truth, and to refute them, to expose them one by one in their order and to weaken them; things not worthy of a Christian prince if they were true, but rather to be thought hidden away in hell. Therefore, that we may break the bundle of these calumnies falsely laid upon us, and weaken separately and step by step the bound darts cast against us, we are compelled to recount not a fable but a history, by which the truth of the deeds may come to light. And since the principal occasion for these calumnies is taken from the occupation of the state of Milan and the siege of the citadel, on which all the laws and the prophets seem to hang, of all the things they devise and attempt against us, it follows that, in rendering the due account of our stewardship, and lest anything remain hidden, and lest we gain the name and reputation of wicked servants, but rather of faithful and good servants who may be able to enter into the kingdom of the Lord, we must begin from the very stock and render an account from the head, omitting nothing that bears on the matter. The matter, then, as is shown by the clearest proofs, stands thus.

units.la: 23. Postquam Franciscus SForcia hujus nominis primus, & moderni Francisci avus paternus: Ducatum ac statum Mediolani nactus est seu verius occupavit: cum is non intraret per ostium sed per fenestram, necdescenderet à linea vice comitum ducum Mediolani, sed ex persona uxoris ad tale seudum incapacis, jus dicti ducatus prætenderet: Er tanquam strenuus, prudens, ac fortunatus belli dux, non habuerit in ipsius ducatus allecutione contradictorem, nunquam tamen is, neque filius ejus primogenitus Galeacius Maria SForcia, nec ex ipso primogenito nepos Joannes Galeacius SForcia ipsius ducatus Mediolani investituram à Sacro Imperio obtinere potuerunt. Successit his Lodovicus SForcia moderni Francisci pater, qui affinitate cum divo Maximiliano Cæsare avo nostro contracta, primus ex SForcianis investituram obtinuit pro se & filiis, ac descendentibus suis ordine successivo, gradu primogenituræ servato. Quo Ludovico primo investito adhuc vivente, insurrexit adversus eum Lodovicus Aurelianensis dux, inde Francorum rex hujus nominis XII. prætendens, quod si ex fœmina linea quispiam in eo ducatu recte succederet, ipse præferendus foret, qui ex descendenti à Valentina Philippi Mariæ Vicecomitis, veri ducis, filiæ legitimæ ortum trahebat. Pacto etiam in contractu matrimonii adjecto, ut deficientibus masculis, ipsa Valentina succederet: quod vacanti Imperio à Sede Apostolica approbatum dicitur, de cujus tamen approbationis viribus nunc disceptandum occasio non offertur. Ipsa autem familia SForciata ab illegitima posteriore genita originem duceret. Ortum est hinc bellum inter ipsum Ludovicum Aurelianensem. Inde Francorum regem, & dictum Ludovicum SForciam, qui Gallorum viribus, & potentia non solum à ducatu & statu ejectus extitit, sed etiam captivus in Galliam ductus est: ubi tandem dies suos clausit extremos. Hinc Ludovic. rex intelligens se non esse tutum in ducatu Mediolani, nisi à Sacro Imperio investituram obtineret, inito fœdere cum divo Maximiliano Cæsare avo nostro recolendæ memoriæ, actoque de matrimonio seu sponsalibus contrahendis, inter nos & Claudiam ipsius regis Ludov. primogenitam, revocataque per divum Maximilianum investitura, eidem Ludovico SForciæ & liberis antea concessa, investituram dicti ducatus obtinuit, pro se & dicta Claudia ejus filia, casu quo nobis cum nuberet. Ea lege adjecta de expresso ipsius Ludovici suorumque oratorum consensu. Quod si fine culpa nostra dictum matrimonium inter nos & Claudiam quovismodo effectum non haberet, prout non habuit, redderetur ipsa investitura, dicto regi, & Claudiæ filiæ concessa, penitus inefficax nulliusque momenti. Verum omne jus dicti ducatus & status Mediolani, ex ipsa investitura concessum, in nos recta via transfiret. Concessa ex tunc illis consentientibus in eum calum nova investitura, in nostri personam præsentem, ad id & nostro nomine stipulante & acceptante, reliquaque ad id requisita solemnia peragente Serenissimo felicis memoriæ Philippo Castellæ rege patre nostro, quam investituram, in solemni forma conceptâ, & puimus,& totiens illis redeuntibus,repulsis ac victis servavimus,ac tutati sumus,nulla nos ad id urgete necessitate,sed pro reipub.quiete,ex nostra mera liberalitate ac munificentia, juribus nostris tam claris,ram apertis omnino postpositis ac postergatis, consensimus eundem illustrem Franciscum SForciam,tanto munere dignum facere,eumdemque ad dictum ducatum admittere, ac eidem ipsius ducatus investituram concedere. Quis nam vir sani capitis,nos de cupiditate, de ambitione, de indebita occupatione recte arguere poterit? Quis nam ex his gestis potest elicere sinistram aliquam suspicionem,quod non recto animo intenti videamur ad ea omnia quae reipubl.Christianae quietem & tranquillitatem Italiaeque libertatem concernere videntur? Adhaec non verbo tantum obtulimus,sed & effectu praestitimus. Fecimus enim ipsum ducem Franciscum totius status possessionem, fecimus in ejus potestate reponi & consignari omnes arces,omnesque civitates, autoritatem & administrationem omnimodam eidem permisimus,ut non solum regere & pro libito administrare posset fructus percipiendo,sed etiam alienando,vendendo ac pro ejus voto disponendo. Cujus etiam alienationis,dum ad id requisiti fuimus tanquam a vero duce factas confirmavimus & approbavimus, fecimus in foederibus per nos initis,tum cum Adriano,tum cum Venetis, tum etiam cum caeteris, cum quibus tractavimus eundem, tanquam Mediolani ducem nominari & includi, de ejusque ruina & conservatione transfegimus: Concessimusq; tandem investituram dicti ducatus,& pertinentiarum in forma amplissima. Quam ad manus equitis Bellia ipsius ducis Francisci oratoris realiter consignavimus,sub certis conventionibus & obligationibus,per ipsum ducem implendis pro parte impensarum,per nos in ejus beneficium factarum pro adoptione & conservatione dicti status. In quibus tamen ita moderate habuimus,ut nec vix quartam partem impensarum partem, per annorum terminos esse mus recuperaturi. Haec profecto scripta patent,nullaque tergiversatione caelari potest, cum jam in Notoreitatem transiverint.
units.tr: 23. After Francis Sforza, the first of that name and the paternal grandfather of the present Francis, gained or rather seized the duchy and state of Milan, though he did not enter by the door but through the window, and did not descend from the line of the Visconti dukes of Milan but claimed the right to the duchy through his wife, who was incapable of holding such a fief, he nevertheless, as a vigorous, prudent and fortunate commander in war, faced no opponent in gaining that duchy. Yet neither he, nor his eldest son Galeazzo Maria Sforza, nor the latter's son, the grandson Gian Galeazzo Sforza, could ever obtain the investiture of the duchy of Milan from the Holy Empire. Ludovico Sforza, the father of the present Francis, succeeded them. Having formed a marriage alliance with our grandfather, the divine Emperor Maximilian of happy memory, he was the first of the Sforzas to obtain the investiture for himself and his sons and descendants in successive order, the rule of primogeniture being observed. While this Ludovico was still living after being invested, Louis, duke of Orléans, rose against him. He later became Louis XII, king of the French, and claimed that if any line through a female should succeed in that duchy by right, he himself ought to be preferred, since he was descended from Valentina, the legitimate daughter of Philip Mary Visconti, the true duke. A pact had also been added to the marriage contract that Valentina would succeed if males failed; this is said to have been approved by the Apostolic See while the Empire was vacant, but the force of that approval is not a matter to be debated now. The Sforza family itself, moreover, was said to descend from a later illegitimate child. From this arose a war between Louis of Orléans, then king of the French, and the said Ludovico Sforza. By the power and might of the French, Ludovico was not only driven from the duchy and state but was also led captive into France, where at last he ended his days. Then King Louis, understanding that he could not be safe in the duchy of Milan unless he obtained the investiture from the Holy Empire, made an agreement with our grandfather the divine Maximilian of memorable name, and a betrothal or marriage was arranged between us and Claudia, the king's eldest daughter. The investiture, which Maximilian had revoked from Ludovico Sforza and his children, granted earlier, was then obtained by the king for himself and for his daughter Claudia, in case she married us. This condition was added with the express consent of Ludovico himself and his envoys: that if, through no fault of ours, the said marriage between us and Claudia were in any way not brought about, as in fact it was not, the investiture granted to the king and his daughter Claudia would be rendered wholly ineffective and of no force. But all right to the said duchy and state of Milan, conveyed by that investiture, would pass directly to us. Then, with their consent, a new investiture was granted in the event of that marriage, to be transferred to our person, our father Philip, king of Castile, of most serene and happy memory, stipulating and accepting for us in our name and carrying out the other formalities required for this. We preserved and defended that investiture, drawn up in solemn form, against all who attacked it and sought to recover it, repelling and defeating them each time they returned. No necessity pressed us to do so, but for the peace of the commonwealth, out of our own pure generosity and munificence, we consented to make this illustrious Francis Sforza worthy of so great a gift, setting aside and wholly disregarding our rights, so clear and so manifest, and to admit him to the said duchy and grant him its investiture. What man of sound mind can rightly accuse us of greed, ambition or unjust seizure? Who from these deeds could draw any sinister suspicion that we were not sincerely intent on all those matters which seem to concern the peace and tranquillity of the Christian commonwealth and the liberty of Italy? Moreover, we did not offer these things only in words but also performed them in fact. For we caused Duke Francis to take possession of the whole state, we caused all the citadels and all the cities to be placed and handed over into his power, and we granted him full authority and administration, so that he might not only govern and administer at his pleasure, taking the revenues, but also alienate, sell and dispose of them as he wished. When we were asked to do so, we also confirmed and approved such alienations as having been made by a true duke. In the treaties we made, both with Hadrian and with the Venetians, and also with the others with whom we dealt, we caused him to be named and included as duke of Milan, and we concluded terms regarding his ruin and preservation. At last we granted the investiture of the said duchy and its dependencies in the fullest form. We actually handed it over to the hand of the envoy Francis Bellia, the duke's representative, under certain conditions and obligations to be fulfilled by the duke, in part for the expenses which we had incurred for his benefit in acquiring and preserving the said state. Yet in these matters we dealt so moderately that we did not expect to recover even a quarter of the expenses within the period of years. These things are surely written down and plainly evident, nor can they be concealed by any evasion, since they have now become notorious.

units.la: 24. Insuper,cum de ipsius illustris Francisci morte dubitaretur,physicique quae de illius salute desperarent,hincque nova oriretur in nos suspicio Vestrae Sanctit.
