Venetorum, aliorum Italiae potentatuum,si statum ipsum Mediolanens.per mortem dicti ducis Francisci ad sacrum Imperium recta via rectoque ordine justitiae devolvendum,aut in nostra potestate retineremus,aut serenissimo fratri nostro charissimo Ferdinando,Archiduci Austriae concederemus. Cum & nostram & ipsius fratris nostri potentiam exosam & formidabilem habere viderentur,potius Deo (qui nobis haec sua clementia & benignitate contulit) ipsique fortunae invidentes, quam aliqua alia justa causa perciti. Placuit Vestrae Sanctitati nos per dictum ejus legatum moneri & hortari, quatenus pro Italiae quiete, acad submovenduum cujusvis suspicionis scrupulum in casum mortis, dicti illustris Francisci SForciae, ducatum ipsum Mediolani nequaquam in nostra potestate retineremus: Nec pariter ipsi Serenissimo fratri nostro concederemus:sed ipsum ducatum tali personae traderemus, de qua Italiae potentatus nullum metum,nulliusque suspicionis objectum habere possent. Ad eumque effectum Vest.Sanct.per dictum legatum alterum duorum nobis ad id proponi fecit, ut ducem Borbonii, aut Georgium de Austria,Caesaris Maximiliani naturalem filium. Annuimus nihilominus licet ad id nullo jure astringeremur,quod ducatus ipse in casum devolutionis minime penes nos retineretur, nec etiam ipsi Serenissimo fratri nostro concederetur,obtulimusque in eum casum dictum ducatum conferre in personam jure merito gratam & acceptam Vestrae Sanctitati,a qua nihil suspicari posset, quod ad turbandum Italiae quietem tendere videretur. Licet etiam id a Vest.S.acceptatum non fuerit,nec etiam aliis potentatibus gratum extiterit nisi personam, cui in eum casum ducatum conferre vellemus,·prius nominaremus ut discerni posset an grata & accepta foret.Non fuimus ab hac instantia alieni. Nominavimus in eum casum ipsum illustrem Borbonii ducem,quem Vestra S.primo proposuerat, in eum quidem investituram conferre parati,non pro commodo aut augmento nostro, sed pro tollenda suspicionis rubigine qua Vest.S.ac potentaruum animi augebantur, pro submovenda ea umbra nostrae magnitudinis qua intrinsecus premebantur:proque ipsius Italiae quiete quae nobis semper cordi fuit, ut potius Christianae reipub.causam, quam privatam nostram tueremur. Quid igitur cupiditatis nobis ex his ascribi possit:Si ducatum Mediolani & statum tanti momenti tantique valoris(ut praemittitur) per nos recuperatum quem licite retinere poterimus, tot ritulis, torq; juribus fulti, semel illustri Franc.S Forciae concessimus:Iterum si per illius mortem ad nos devolveretur, ad Vest.S.nutum alteri concederet annueremus,ii videlicet,quem V.S.prius nominaverat: Nos tamen justis juribus,tamq; amplo & importanti dominio suffulti(pro quo,si Julius Caesar revivisceus nostram personam induetet,aut hi qui nobis cupiditatem impingunt,forsan etiam jusiurandum violandum cfferent) nos ipsi non coacti,nulloq; juramenti seu cujusvis obligationis vinculo astricti,nostra sponte pro ipsa repub. jus nostrum tam liquidum abrogare,& a nobis auferre consensimus exclusio etiam proprio fratre,qui jure meritoro post nos caeteris omnibus anteponendus videbatur. Cum hunc loco filii haberemus in succedendi gradu proximiorem,cui nulla ratione nulloque jure divino, naturali vel civili,extraneus quispiam a se referendus erat fateamur necesse est, non hic cupiditatem, non ambitionem,non avaritiam,non dominandi seu aliena occupandi appetitum inesse.Sed potius amplissimam uberemq; largitatem,munificentiam,ac,si dicere fas est, prodigalitatem dominandiq; contemptum arguere. quod tamen reipub.causa laeto hilariq; animo,ultro,nec non sponte praestabamus.
units.tr: 24. Furthermore, when the death of this illustrious Francis was in doubt, and the physicians despaired of his recovery, a new suspicion arose against us, both on the part of Your Holiness, the Venetians and the other potentates of Italy: that we would either keep the state of Milan in our own power or grant it to our most serene and dearest brother Ferdinand, Archduke of Austria, if on the death of the said duke Francis it were to pass to the Holy Empire by the direct and proper order of justice. Since they seemed to regard both our power and that of our brother as hateful and formidable, and envied God, who through his clemency and kindness had bestowed these things upon us, and fortune itself, rather than being moved by any other just cause. Your Holiness saw fit to advise and urge us through your legate, that for the peace of Italy, and to remove every scruple of suspicion, in the event of the death of the said illustrious Francis Sforza we should by no means keep the duchy of Milan in our power, nor likewise grant it to our said most serene brother, but should hand that duchy over to a person of whom the potentates of Italy could have no fear and no cause for suspicion. To that end Your Holiness, through the said legate, had two men proposed to us, the Duke of Bourbon or George of Austria, the natural son of Caesar Maximilian. Nevertheless we agreed, although we were not bound by any right to do so, that in that case of devolution the duchy would not be kept by us, nor granted to our said most serene brother; and we offered to confer it, in that event, upon a person acceptable and welcome to Your Holiness by right and merit, from whom no suspicion could arise that he would tend to disturb the peace of Italy. Although Your Holiness did not accept this, nor was it pleasing to the other potentates, unless we first named the person to whom we wished to confer the duchy in that event, so that it could be discerned whether he would be welcome and acceptable, we did not refuse this request. We named in that event the said illustrious Duke of Bourbon, whom Your Holiness had first proposed, and we were ready to confer the investiture upon him, not for our own advantage or aggrandisement, but to remove the rust of suspicion by which the minds of Your Holiness and of the potentates were troubled, and to remove that shadow of our greatness by which they were oppressed within, and for the peace of Italy itself, which has always been dear to us, so that we might defend the cause of the Christian commonwealth rather than our own private cause. What greed, then, can be ascribed to us from these facts? If we once granted to the illustrious Francis Sforza the duchy and state of Milan, of such weight and value (as has been stated), which we recovered and could lawfully have kept, supported by so many titles and such strong rights, and if, on his death, it were to pass to us, we agreed to give it at the nod of Your Holiness to another, namely the one whom Your Holiness had earlier named. Yet we, supported by just rights and by so ample and important a dominion (for which, if Julius Caesar were to revive and assume our person, or those who attribute greed to us might perhaps even offer us an oath to violate), we ourselves, not compelled, and bound by no bond of oath or of any obligation whatever, of our own accord and for the commonwealth itself, consented to abrogate and remove from ourselves a right so clear, even to the exclusion of our own brother, who by right and merit seemed to be preferred before all others after us. Since we regarded him as a son and the nearest in the order of succession, to whom, by no reasoning and by no divine, natural or civil law, any outsider ought to be preferred, we must admit that there is in this no greed, no ambition, no avarice, no appetite for dominion or for seizing what belongs to others. Rather, these things show the most ample and generous largesse, munificence and, if it is right to say so, prodigality, and contempt of dominion. Yet we did these things for the sake of the commonwealth with a glad and cheerful spirit, willingly and of our own accord.

units.la: 15. Sed nunc submovenda restat causa illa gemitus & doloris Sanctit.Vest.ac totius Italiae, qua V.S.tantum afflligitur:occupationis sc.ipsius status Mediolani inde per nostros factae eum obsessione armatam, in qua duxerat.In qua re licet non omni culpa excludere & liberare possemus. Ullam si qua foret
units.tr: 15. But now there remains to be removed that cause of grief and sorrow to Your Holiness and to all Italy, by which Your Holiness is so greatly afflicted: namely, the occupation of the state of Milan by our men, and the armed siege in which he had led them. In this matter, although we could not wholly clear ourselves of all blame, if there was any such fault

units.la: {i} in duces belli referendo, quibus dum nos monuissent, de practicis & molitionibus: quae adversus nos & statum nostrum parabantur. Marchio Pischariae, ut praefertur, rei conscius, nobis illius scelus radicitus detexisset, affirmans ipsum ducem Francisc. hujusce facinoris reum, ut se statumque illum a nostra obedientia subtraheret, ac foederatorum viribus non habita ratione investiturae, nec fidelitatis per eum praestandae, nec impensarum, quae nobis erant resarciendae in eo statu de facto potius quam de jure tenerentur, atque eo etiam decedente foederatorum praesidio, nobis exclusis subintraret. In eo statu ejus frater Maximilianus S Forcia: quem jam ipso jure privatum diximus, consentiente etiam Gallorum rege, cui jus dicti Maximiliani, si quod habuisset, cessum erat: ut quoque exercitus nostrer tumultuantibus populis, ad ipsiusmet ducis Francisci, suorumque agentium, & foederatorum instantia & solicitudinem deleretur, & in ruinam & praecipitium deduceretur: & si fieri posset, omnes ipsius exercitus duces & milites trucidarentur. Eo etiam lignanter adjecto. Quod cum ipse illustris Marchio Pischariae, habito de eare cum ipso duce Francisco colloquio, ut magis illius intrinsecum animum tentaret, an firmus in ea factionis practica remaneret, ei duci persuadendo dixisset: quod postquam in jam nobis investituram obtinuerat, eratque de ejus statu securus, non oporteret amplius eam practicam prosequi: Idem dux respondisse fertur firmius & commodius esse, quod jam practicatum erat atque concluqsum, quam quod ex investitura assequi poterat, concurrente ibidem publica salute Italiae: quae rei privatae anteferenda censerentur. Instabant propterea duces ipsi, ut ad has molitiones receptaret, neve majora scandala inde sequerentur, his licentiam praeberemus, ut de ipso Francisco duce & Mediolani se nostro nomine asseverarent, pro nostri exercitus tutela, utque exercitum ipsum conservandum & penè dissolvendum nil tale metuentes: jusseramus, non solum sustinerentur, sed ceterum geremus, ni penitus ab Italia excludi vellemus. Nos autem qui haec non facile credebamus, sed pro confictis simulatisque putabamus: eo quod qui bella tractare solent, potius belli quam pacis nec diu agitant, in hisque libentius animos eorum adoptat. Arbitramur enim, quod sub eo colore put... ire cogere & urgere ad ipsum nostrum exercitum integre servandum sustinendumque: dubitantes ne veluti belli cupidi in id praecipites ruerent ac arma praeter nostram voluntatem moverent: Caeteri etiam nil aliud quam pacem & quietem cuperemus, mandavimus eisdem ne quid novi tentarent in dicto statu Mediolani, nisi in tribus casibus: Si dux Franciscus moreretur: Si Galli cum Helvetiis Italiam intrarent, vel si factionum practicarum executio ex adverso tentaretur, ut hi prius arma contra nos exercitumque nostrum moverent. In quolibet enim horum trium casuum consensimus, quod pro tuta exercitus noster & rerum nostrarum, se asseverarent in dicto statu Mediolani. Verum cum Hieronymus Moronus, primarius ipsius ducis Francisci Consiliarius, ac ejusdem factionis fertur principalis minister, multiplicatis suis literis monuisset dictum Marchionem Pischariae, quem putabat factionis participem habere, ut rem suam disponeret, eidem affirmando reliquos factionis socios, jam dispositos paratosque esse, ut in octo vel decem dierum spacio in nostros irruendum esset. Idem Marchio participato cum caeteris ducibus nostris consilio captoque; Morono, illius habita confessione, totam seriem negotii complectentes satis conformi in ea quae Marchio nobis suis literis insinuaverat, collecto exercitu nostro undique sparso, aliquot civitatibus munitis Mediolanum progrediatur, ducem Franciscum interpellat, ut pro securitate nostra nostrique exercitus arces & castra dicti status, in nostrorum manus reponeret, idque custodibus illorum exequendum committeret. Annuit dux ipse ut castra nobis traderentur, prout effectu tradita fuere: Duabus duntaxat arcibus principalioribus, quas ipse munieverat, Mediolani sc. in qua ipse reclusebatur, & Cremone exceptis: has enim duas in se relervandas censuit, donec de nostra voluntate certus fieret offerens interim, illas nostro nomine renuntiare, ac bis dare, ac per se & per praefectos arcium juramentum praestare, quod ex ipsis arcibus nullum exercitum nostro damnum seu praejudicium fieret. Non placuit haec securitas ducibus nostris, videntque in mora. Si arces illae magis munirentur libertaque permanerent, posse inde exercitus nostro numerum succedere resque nostras in evidenti periculo remanere. Interpellant denuo, ac iterum atque requirunt sub rebellionis poena ac laesae Majestatis criminis confessi atque convicti, quatenus ipsice Mediolani in potestate nostra ac nostrorum posita exiret, suisque copiam faceret, & adversarias, de quibus culpabatur, defensiones ac justificationes, si quas habebat, proponeret, ducesque ejus rei conscios, quos penes se habebat in arce reclusos, dimitteret interrogandos, ad amplorem rem gestarum dilucidationem. At cum Dux ipse his non annueret, nisi a nobis mandatum haberet, nostri arcem circumvallant: Interimque de gestis nos admonent, necessarias causas per quas ad hanc vocationem fuerant, enarrant approbationem gestorum a nobis expostulant. Instant, ut eidem duci Francisco rescribamus, mandemusque ut arcem nobis aut nostris tradat. Nos referentes rem hanc praeter nostram tentatam, nunquam voluimus nec illorum gesta approbare nec duci, ut perebatur, mandare aut castris dimitteret. Semper enim in animo habuimus, eam accusationem, quae in ducem trahebatur, debito juris ordine tractandam & terminandam. Nunc profecto ejus rei exitu praetensum veritas elici poterit, cum praeparatae jam diu factionis effectus illuxerit, quo magis ad incepisse eidem nostris ducibus credere debeamus, non possumus non laudare & approbare eorum prudentiam & fidem in conservatione dicti status, ipsiusque nostri exercitus illiusque arcis asseveratione ne amplius muniri posset, neve inde majoris mali & incommodi occasio praestaretur. Nec id quidem itaque nam & injuste gestum videtur prout Sanctit. Vest. sibi suadet, dato enim fundamento quod Franciscus laesae majestatis reus accusaretur. Et si uniusduntaxat testis adesset de politio, ut plures tamen adesset testimonium. Ex quibus etiam si essent loci criminis ac factionis participes, potest... mcito.
units.tr: {i} it should be laid at the door of the commanders of the war. When they had warned us about the plots and schemes that were being prepared against us and our state, the Marquis of Pescara, who was privy to them, as has been said, disclosed the crime to us root and branch. He affirmed that Duke Francis himself was guilty of this outrage: that, in order to withdraw himself and that state from our obedience, and with the forces of the allies, he (without regard to the investiture, or to the fidelity he owed us through it, or to the expenses that were to be repaid to us in that state, which we held by right of fact rather than by right of law) would, on the death of the allied garrison, enter in our absence. In that state his brother Maximilian of Forcia, whom we have already said is by law itself deprived of his rights, was to be installed, with the consent of the king of the French, to whom the right of the said Maximilian, if he had any, had been transferred. Our army was also to be destroyed by the uprising of the people, at the instigation and solicitude of the duke Francis himself, his agents and the allies, and was to be driven to ruin and destruction; and, if it could be managed, all the commanders and soldiers of that army were to be slaughtered. He added this, too, most deceitfully: that when the illustrious Marquis of Pescara had held a conference with Duke Francis himself on this matter, in order to probe more closely his inner mind and see whether he remained firm in this plot, and had urged the duke to persuade himself that, since he had already obtained the investiture from us and was secure in his state, he ought no longer to pursue that plot, the same duke is reported to have replied that what had already been planned and decided was firmer and more advantageous than what he could gain from the investiture, since the public safety of Italy was involved, and that this was to be judged more important than private interest. The dukes therefore pressed the Marquis to accept these schemes, and urged that, unless we gave them leave to proceed against Duke Francis himself and Milan in our name, under the pretext of protecting our army, and to take further measures, greater scandals would follow. We had ordered that they should not only be held back, but should also refrain from any further action, unless they wished to be shut out of Italy altogether. We, however, who did not readily believe this, but thought it feigned and pretended, reasoned as follows: men who are accustomed to conduct wars tend to think more of war than of peace and do not dwell long on peace, and their minds are more readily drawn to war. We suspected that, under that pretext, they were pushing, driving and urging one another in order to keep our army whole and sustained, fearing lest, like men eager for war, they would rush headlong into it and take up arms against our will. We also, wishing nothing but peace and quiet, ordered them not to attempt anything new in the said state of Milan, except in three cases: if Duke Francis should die; if the French, with the Swiss, should enter Italy; or if the execution of the plot should be attempted by the opposing side, so that these men should first take up arms against us and our army. For in each of these three cases we agreed that they might, for the safety of our army and our affairs, assert themselves in the said state of Milan. But when Girolamo Morone, the chief counsellor of Duke Francis himself and reported to be the principal agent of the same faction, had repeatedly written to the said Marquis of Pescara, whom he believed to be a sharer in the plot, urging him to set his affairs in order, assuring him that the remaining partners in the faction were already disposed and ready, so that within eight or ten days they would have to fall upon our men. The same Marquis, having shared the matter with our other commanders and taken their counsel, and having received from Morone a confession of the whole course of the business, which agreed well enough with what the Marquis had reported to us in his letters, gathered our army, which was scattered everywhere, and, with some cities fortified, advanced to Milan. He called upon Duke Francis to hand over, for our security and that of our army, the citadels and forts of the said state into the hands of our men, and to commit their custody to our officers. The duke himself agreed that the forts should be surrendered to us, which was in fact done, except for the two principal citadels which he himself had fortified, namely that of Milan, in which he was shut up, and that of Cremona. He judged that these two should be kept in his own charge until he was certain of our will, offering in the meantime to renounce them in our name, and to give them up, and to swear, both personally and through the prefects of the citadels, that no harm or prejudice should come to our army from those citadels. Our commanders were not satisfied with this security, and, seeing the delay, feared that if those citadels were further fortified and remained free, our army could be cut off from its numbers and our affairs would remain in evident danger. They called on him again and again, under penalty of rebellion and on the charge of treason, the offence being confessed and proved, that he should come out of Milan, which was now in our power and that of our men, and make himself available, and that he should set forth the objections and defences and justifications he might have against the charges, and that he should release for examination the commanders who were privy to the affair, whom he held shut up in the citadel, so that the account of the deeds might be more fully clarified. But when the duke would not agree to this, unless he had our order, our men surrounded the citadel. Meanwhile they reminded us of the deeds, explained the necessary reasons that had led to this summons, and demanded from us approval of their actions. They urged that we should write back to Duke Francis himself, and order him to hand over the citadel to us or to our men. We, judging that this matter had been attempted without our knowledge, never wished either to approve their deeds or to order the duke, as was being demanded, or to dismiss him from the castles. For we always intended that the accusation brought against the duke should be treated and concluded in the due order of law. Now, indeed, by the outcome of this affair the truth of the pretended matter can be drawn out, since the effects of the faction, prepared long ago, have now come to light; so that we ought the more to trust our commanders in what they undertook. We cannot but praise and approve their prudence and fidelity in preserving the said state, and in securing both our army and that citadel so that it could be fortified no further, and so that no occasion of greater evil and inconvenience should arise from it. Nor indeed does it seem to have been done unjustly, as Your Holiness supposes. For, granting the premise that Francis was accused of treason, and even if only one witness were present, and that a suspect one, yet more witnesses were present. Even if those who had been at the place of the crime and were sharers in the faction were present, it could be properly

units.la: Hier. Moronus. merito contra ipsum ducem procedi & ad capturam & ad torturam. Et cogit ut sui copiam faceret, ac in vinculis causam diceret, suasque defensiones & justificationes carceratus adduceret, non autem in arce reclusus audiri debuit. Quinimo contra eum vocatum & non comparentem ac se subtrahentem & resistentem potuit in ejus contumaciam pronunciari, ut pro confesso & convicto haberetur. Sed & priusquam id fiat accusato non comparente, nec sui copiam faciente, licite ad manus curiae redimentur illius bona, quae etiam a die ingressi criminis ipso jure publicata confiscataque censentur. Sicque hinc non tanta causa gemitus & doloris Vest. Sanctitati parata videtur. Si dominus Vasallum ingratum & laesae majestatis reum puniendum censeat, ni forsan quod in mente cadere non potuisset, id gemendum dolendumque putent, quod eidem hanc foveam in quam incidit sub charitatis specie paraverunt, ipsumque ad hujusmodi discrimen deduxerunt: Sed potius ingemiscere ac dolere deberet non solum V. Sanctitas, sed universa respubl. quod sine justa causa sineque culpa nostra tam ingens excitetur incendium, quo & turbatur universus ecclesiae status & tota scandalizatur Christiana religio.
units.tr: Hieronymus Moronus: with good reason proceedings were taken against the duke himself, both for arrest and for torture. The duke was bound to give access to himself and to make his case in chains, and to bring forward his defences and justifications as a prisoner; he ought not to have been heard while shut up in the citadel. Indeed, if he was summoned and did not appear, and withdrew himself and resisted, he could be pronounced in contumacy and held as one who had confessed and been convicted. And even before that is done, when the accused does not appear and does not give access to himself, his goods may lawfully be seized by the hands of the court; and these are regarded as confiscated and made public by law from the day the crime was entered. Thus no such great cause of grief and sorrow seems to be prepared for Your Holiness. If a lord judges that a vassal who is ungrateful and guilty of treason ought to be punished, there is no reason to lament and grieve, unless perhaps they think it must be lamented that they laid this pit, into which he fell, under the appearance of charity, and led him into such peril. Rather, not only Your Holiness but the whole commonwealth ought to lament and grieve that such a huge fire has been kindled without just cause and without any fault of ours, by which the whole state of the Church is disturbed and the Christian religion is thrown into scandal.

units.la: 26. Nec sane intelligere possumus quod cuncti prope Christianitatis reges (ut Vest. Sanctit. ait) effl agitarint, agitaverint nec non partiti fuerint in re tanti praejudicii atima & auxilia conferre. Scimus enim & pro certo habemus nec Ungarum nec Polonum nec Portugalensem, nec Danum, hujusce consilii participes seu conscios. Anglus autem & si ejus foederis conservator & protector nominetur, nobis tamen apertis suis literis significavit se nequaquam in id foedus consensisse, nec mandatum dedisse, nec talem protectionem acceptasse nec acceptare velle, licet ad id parte V.S. interpellatus ac instanter requisitus extiterit: se pacis quam semper effl agitavimus mediatorem offerendo. Gallus vero & si cum Sanct. V. ac aliis Italiae potentatibus foedus percusserit, ut eo medio mitiores si posset quae jam ex nostro foedere obinuerit a nobis pacis conditiones exhauriat, liberosque obsides recuperet. Retulit tamen aperto ore quod Vestrae Sanct. impulsu & suasu, etiam priusquam in regnum suum liber remitteretur, de ipso novo foedere ineundo sollicitabatur. Et sunt qui affirmant, ut ex quibusdam literis percepimus: quod V.S. ipso etiam Gallorum rege non petente, eidem juramentum relaxaverit quod nobis praestiterat pro foedere nobiscum prius inito, quod tamen credere nolumus: quandoquidem res talis omnino a pastore Christi Vicario aliena esse deberet, ne ipsius jurisjurandi sine causa spreta religio ad detectiora incentivum praeberet. Merito tamen V.S. his verbis utitur, dimissis consiliis & conspirationibus, si verbis addatur effectus. Si vero omnis conspiratio dimittatur cum secundum rectam intelligentiam crimen denotet.
units.tr: 26. Indeed we cannot understand how almost all the kings of Christendom, as Your Holiness says, are supposed to have stirred up this business and to have divided among themselves the contribution of money and aid in a matter of such great prejudice. For we know and hold for certain that neither the Hungarian, nor the Pole, nor the Portuguese, nor the Dane is a participant in or party to this plan. The English king, although he is named the conservator and protector of that league, has nevertheless signified to us by his open letter that he has by no means consented to that league, nor given a mandate, nor accepted such protection, nor wishes to accept it, although he was appealed to and urgently requested on Your Holiness's side; he offers himself as mediator of the peace which we have always sought. The French king, indeed, although he struck a league with Your Holiness and the other Italian potentates, did so in order that, through it, he might obtain milder terms of peace from us, if he could, having already obtained from our league what he could, and recover his sons as hostages. He nevertheless reported openly that, at the urging and persuasion of Your Holiness, even before he was released to return to his kingdom, he was being pressed to enter into this new league. And there are those who affirm, as we have learned from certain letters, that Your Holiness, even without the French king asking, relaxed for him the oath which he had given us for the earlier league made with us. We are unwilling to believe this, since such a thing ought to be altogether foreign to the shepherd, Christ's Vicar, lest the religion of an oath sworn in vain provide an incentive to worse deeds. Rightly, however, Your Holiness uses these words, "setting aside counsels and conspiracies", if the effect is added to the words. But if every conspiracy is set aside, since, rightly understood, the word denotes a crime.

units.la: 27. Quod autem ad ea conventionum capitula, quae attulit Herrera, videamus qualiter S.V. praetendat illa paucis in locis leviter immutata: si enim bene cuncta rimentur, omnes articuli qui cum ipsius legato sic compositi remanserant cum V.S. concludendi: licet ipsam conclusionem V.S. reservandam assereret, ejus potestate postquam ad nos pervenerat reserata atque restricta, mutati penitus ad nos remissi fuere. Ita ut nullus fere remaneret intactus, qui non aliam substantiam aliumque sonum praesefferret. Omnes tamen hujusmodi mutationes obmisimus in quatuor duntaxat articulis, hujusmodi conventionum, videlicet 12.13.14.&15. moderationem petentem.
units.tr: 27. As for the articles of agreement which Herrera brought forward, let us see how Your Holiness puts forward those articles, lightly altered in a few places. For if everything is carefully examined, all the articles which had been settled with his legate, to be concluded with Your Holiness, were sent back to us wholly changed, although Your Holiness asserted that the conclusion itself was to be reserved; after the articles came to us, their force was unlocked and restricted by her power. So that hardly any remained untouched which did not present a different substance and a different sound. Yet we passed over all such changes in only four articles of this kind of agreement, namely the 12th, 13th, 14th and 15th, which ask for moderation.

units.la: 28. In 12. enim ipsorum articulorum qui rem Ducis Ferrariae complectebatur, licet omnis substantia, ultra quam tractatum esset, mutari videretur: consensimus tamen nos effecturos cum effectu, quod eadem Sanctitas & intra praefixum tempus, dum sibi expedire videretur, sine cujusque resistentia, sine armorum apparatu recuperare posset, possessionem Rhegii & Ruberiae tenendam & possidendam, prout antea tenebat ita quod non intelligeretur praejudicatum juribus Imperii aut cujuslibet alterius prout eadem S.V. admittebat. Id solum addidimus quod ad alliciendum ipsum ducem Ferrariae, remittendo eidem quasque poenas & jus commissi ac absolvendo eum a censuris forsitan incursis, quod prosecto non nisi ad majorem quietem Italiae petebamus, non ignorantes ipsum ducem non aliter sine armis cogi posse: ut Rhegium & Ruberiam dimitteret vel S.V. restitueret, in quibus & jure feudi Imperialis & ratione prioris spolii se potius tuendi censebat. Unde ad providendos novos belli tumultus, & ne remaneret cujusvis incendii scintilla, sed universa Italia in eo foedere sine quovis scrupulo concurreret, id ita agendum necessario censentes, prout nunc agit V.S. nos etiam sub spe defensivi foederis jam percussi, ad ipsius ducis Ferrariae offensionem astringere voluissemus, in qua re novos bellorum tumultus timebamus, quos tamen effugere nequivimus, qui dum ab offensione nos abstinere curamus, defensioni status, dignitatis & auctoritatis nostrae intendere cogimur, & inniti trahimur. Qua de re hujusmodi nostram additionem nequaquam respuendam V.S. putabamus, in hoc enim nec V.S. auctoritatem derogatur. Nec a veri pastoris officio declinabatur: sed potius publicae quieti consulebatur.
units.tr: 28. In the 12th of those articles, which concerned the business of the Duke of Ferrara, although the whole substance, beyond what had been treated, seemed to be altered, we nevertheless consented that we would bring it about in effect that the same Holiness might, within the fixed time and whenever it seemed expedient to her, without anyone's resistance and without any armed preparation, recover possession of Reggio and Rubiera, to be held and possessed as she held them before, so that it would not be understood as prejudicing the rights of the Empire or of anyone else, as Your Holiness allowed. We added only this: to entice the Duke of Ferrara himself, we remitted to him whatever penalties and forfeiture of rights there were, and absolved him from censures perhaps incurred. We sought this certainly only for the greater quiet of Italy, not being unaware that the duke could not otherwise be compelled, without arms, to give up Reggio and Rubiera or restore them to Your Holiness; he thought he ought rather to defend them, both by the right of the imperial fief and by reason of the earlier spoliation. Hence, to provide against new tumults of war, and lest any spark of fire remain, but all Italy should unite in that league without any scruple, we judged it necessary to act as Your Holiness now does. We too, already bound by a defensive league, had wished to bind ourselves to attack the Duke of Ferrara, though in this matter we feared new tumults of war, which nevertheless we could not escape. For while we take care to abstain from attack, we are compelled to attend to the defence of our state, dignity and authority, and are drawn to rest upon it. For this reason we thought Your Holiness ought not at all to reject this addition of ours, for in this the authority of Your Holiness is not diminished, nor is the office of the true shepherd departed from; rather, public quiet was being consulted.

units.la: 29. In 13. ipsius foederis seu capitulationis articulo illam salis distributionem in statu Mediolan. continentem, ex quinque correctionibus per V.S. factis eas omnes admisimus, eo duntaxat excepto quod ubi Vest. S. deleri fecerat illa verba ad ejus vitae decursum, satagens illud jus sibi & successoribus perpetuare. Nos qui duntaxat personae S. Vestrae ejus vita comite gratificari volebamus, non autem statum ipsum Mediolani Sacri Imperii feudum perpetuo ecclesiae Rom. astringere, & tali onere semper gravatum remanere sine spe libertatis. Nolētes etiam ipsum Serenissimum Archiducem fratrem nostrum juris sibi in ea re concessio perpetuo exclusum remanere. Nolumus illam cancellationem apptobare, sed verba illa ad ejus vitae decursus, prout in Capitulatione, quam attulit Herrera, firma manere censemus. Ex ultima vero ipsius articuli correctione admisimus eam partem additionis ibidem per San. V. factam ut esset illa conventio absque praejudicio sedis Apost. Ea autem verba quae his subjungebatur, videlicet pso rege Gallo concluderemus, cuiusque illum aut alium misissemus, ni V. Sanct. legatum venienté, ut aiebant) cum amplissimo mandato nobiscum concludendi præstolandum censuissemus, ni etiam post illius adventum viso mandato quod à V. S. habebat, & confisi quod illo uti posset, diutius cum eo de ipsius fœderis capitulis tractantes, tempus inaniter consumptum cognovillemus. Vbi capitulationes jam formata & cum eo propter concordata dum de conclusione ageretur nobis insinuaverit, quod ex quo post ejus à V.S. recessum mutata essent negocia intenderet conclusione differre, donec V.S. consuiisset. Ob quod sanctius putavimus capitulationem ipsam, prout formata fuerat ad V.S. per Herreram transmittere, putantes ibidem rem celerius posse concludi, licet spe nostra fructrati fuerimus, S.V. ad alios fines tendente, prout exitus demonstravit.
units.tr: 29. In the 13th article of that same league or capitulation, which contains the distribution of salt in the state of Milan, we admitted all five corrections made by Your Holiness, except only that where Your Holiness had caused the words "for the course of his life" to be deleted, eager to perpetuate that right for herself and her successors. We wished only to favour the person of Your Holiness for the term of her life, but we did not wish to bind the state of Milan, a fief of the Holy Roman Empire, perpetually to the Roman Church, and to leave it always burdened by such a charge without hope of liberty. Nor do we wish our most Serene Archduke, our brother, to remain perpetually excluded from the right conceded to him in that matter. We are unwilling to approve that cancellation, but we judge that those words "for the course of his life" stand firm, as in the Capitulation which Herrera brought. From the last correction of that article, however, we admitted that part of the addition made there by Your Holiness, so that the agreement would be without prejudice to the Apostolic See. But the words which were appended to this, namely that we would conclude with the French king himself, or would send whomever he had sent, we had thought it best to await, unless the legate of Your Holiness came, as they said, with ample mandate to conclude with us. Nor did we stop there: after his arrival, seeing the mandate which he had from Your Holiness, and trusting that he could use it, we dealt with him for a long time on the chapters of that league, and then perceived that time had been wasted in vain. When he informed us that the capitulations, already formed and agreed with him, were to be concluded, he said that since the affairs had changed after his departure from Your Holiness, he intended to defer the conclusion until Your Holiness had been consulted. On account of this we thought it sounder to send that capitulation itself, as it had been drawn up, to Your Holiness through Herrera, believing the matter could be concluded more quickly there. Although we were disappointed in our hope, Your Holiness was aiming at other ends, as the outcome showed.

units.la: 33. Nunc ad literas manu V.S. conscriptas de quarum responsione conquerirur deveniendum est, ut etiam inde omnem à nobis repellamus culpam. Ea enim per V. San. eius responsionis culpa nobis in tribus impingitur. Primo quod V.S. ubi clementiam ducis Mediolani petebat, nos rigorem, justitiæ obtulimus, ad quod satis diffuse responsum dedimus, dum ipsius ducis negociumante discussimus, ut sic repetitione non egeat. Id solum hic adjiciendum censemus, non videri in hoc justam S.V. querelam. Si justitiæ via amplectendam censuimus: Sine qua vera pax esse non potest. Cum justitia & pax se invicem deosculentur, & ut ad clementiā deveniatur prius veritas est habenda. Sunt enim re-ste Psalmista) quatuor sorores concatenatæ: Justitia & pax osculata sunt: Misericordia & veritas obviaverunt sibi. Qui igitur misericordiam expectat, reatum tacerare oportet: Qui pacem vult, justitiam amplectatur. Nec ita passim intendū est clementia, ut delinquendi incentivum præbeatur. Sed potius ad bonū regimen spectat parcere subiectis & debellare superbos. Non. n. indulgendū videtur his qui contumaciter in rebellione perstiunt, his qui in arcib. munitis se continent, his justitiæ executione satagunt evitare.
units.tr: 33. Now we must come to the letters written in Your Holiness's own hand, over whose reply you complain, so that we may also free ourselves of every blame in this matter. By that reply, Your Holiness charges us on three points. First, that when Your Holiness sought the clemency of the Duke of Milan, we offered the rigour of justice. To this we gave a fairly full answer when we discussed the business of that duke, so it need not be repeated here. We think only this should be added: it does not seem that Your Holiness has a just complaint in this. If we resolved to embrace the way of justice, without which true peace cannot exist, it is because justice and peace kiss each other, and to come to clemency, truth must first be had. For, as the Psalmist says, there are four sisters linked together: "Justice and peace have kissed; mercy and truth have met each other." Therefore whoever expects mercy must confess his guilt; whoever wants peace, let him embrace justice. Nor is clemency to be extended so widely that an incentive to wrongdoing is provided. Rather, it belongs to good government to spare subjects and to subdue the proud. For it does not seem right to indulge those who persist obstinately in rebellion, those who hold themselves within fortified citadels, or those who strive to escape by the execution of justice.

units.la: 34. Secundo redarguitur nostra responsio quod pro culpa quam V.S. in quibusdam esse dicebar, V.S. quodammodo criminatur, illos immunes crimiuis fatendo. Sed absit tantus error qui nil ipsa responsione quam propria manu conscripsimus legi poterir, quod criminationem sapere videatur, sed potius venerationem & observantiam Vestræ S. quam semper in verum partem & pastoré præcipuum habuimus. At si id V.S. criminationem putet quod ea afferente: ducem Francisçum in aliquo forsan errore, alios quosdam in vera (ut ajebat) ribaldaria incurrisse ex quibus forsan aliquis jam deo computum reddebat. Nos intelligentes hæc à vestra Sanct. referri ad criminandum Marchionem Pischaria tunc vita functum, qui (ut præfertur) antea vivens nobis illius factionis practicam detexerat. Respondimus de mortuis modeste loquendum esse ac in dubio potius bene quam male præsumendum, hominemque mortuum qui per se respondere non poterat, potius laudandum quam vituperandum seu culpandum, Nosque cupere mortuum vivere, ut de seipso rationem redderet. In duce autem non errorem qui in facto proprio cadere non poterat: sed si ea quæ illi erant objecta vera apparerent, crimen potius acerrimum ac exemplari punitione dignum censeri. Hæc quippe nullam in V.S. criminationem afferunt, ni forsan S.V. seipsam dijudicans fateri vellet (quod non credimus) se ejus factionis conscium autricemque fuisse, prout Marchio vivens nobis retuleterat. Quem forsan ob id de ribaldaria agendum censeret, quod præter fidem datam illius factionis secreta detexisset, qui tamen ex eo fidelitatis debito, quo nobis prius astringebatur, tacere non poterat, quin seipsum ejusdem criminis reum faceret: ubi propalando tale facinus, veniam præmiumque & laudem jure ita disponente consequebatur.
units.tr: 34. Second, our reply is rebuked because, concerning the fault which Your Holiness was said to have in certain matters, Your Holiness is in some way accused, since we admit that those others are free of crime. But far be such great error. Nothing can be read in the reply which we wrote in our own hand that seems to savour of accusation; it rather expresses the reverence and observance we have always shown to Your Holiness, whom we have held as the true and chief shepherd. But if Your Holiness thinks that is an accusation, then by her assertion Duke Francis may perhaps have fallen into some error, and certain others into true ribaldry (as she put it), from which perhaps one of them has already rendered account to God. We understood that these things were brought forward by Your Holiness to accuse the Marquis of Pescara, then deceased, who, living earlier, had disclosed to us the practice of that faction. We replied that one must speak modestly of the dead, and in doubt presume well rather than ill; that a dead man who could not answer for himself ought rather to be praised than reviled or blamed; and that we wished the dead man to be alive, so that he might give an account of himself. As for the duke, he could not fall into error in his own affair; but if the things objected to him appeared true, they were to be judged a most grievous crime, worthy of exemplary punishment. These things bring no accusation against Your Holiness, unless perhaps Your Holiness, judging herself, wished to confess (which we do not believe) that she was a party to and author of that faction, as the living Marquis had reported to us. Perhaps for that reason she thought he should be dealt with as a ribald, since, beyond the faith he had given, he had disclosed the secrets of that faction. Yet from the debt of fidelity by which he was earlier bound to us, he could not keep silent without making himself guilty of the same crime. By declaring such a deed openly, he obtained, by right so ordained, pardon, reward and praise.

units.la: 35. Tertio redarguitur eadem nostra responsio quodque V.S. nobis benigne & large pollicebatur, ea nos tanquam debita & obligata flagitaremus. Sed videamus qualia essent ejusdem Sanctitatis pollicita, qualisque fuerit responsio nostra, ut etiam hanc culpam ruamus: hoc n. V.S. in suis literis sub silentio pertransit, alijs caussam deterius cogitandam relinquens. Ut igitur horum veritas clarepateat, offerebat nobis V.S. si illius votis quo ad ipsum Ducem Francisçum annueremus, se nobis non solū decimas & Cruciatas & pileos & quicquid per spirituālem & temporalem potestatem facultatis haberet præstaturum, sed etiam sanguinem & vitam ad nostram exultationem & satisfactionem exhibiturum: Respondemus non convenire reipub. Christianæ cruciatam tali conditione perstringi, sed potius libere & sponte offerendam, nec congruum videri ut illa differatur. Poteramus. n. jam in nostris his regnis concedere eo ordine, quo nostri prædecessores illam semper à vestris prædecessoribus obtinuerant, pro promontoriis in Africa. Qui situs adversus fidei hostes tuendis ac propulsandis, quib. ad eum effectū nusquam fuerat denegata, & minus nobis hujusmodi Ecclesiæ thesaurum à V.S. denegandū seu differendū censebamus: qui ultra res Africanas prout vestræ S.insinuavimus, cupiebamusetiam cū ea pecunia quæ ex ipsa Cruciata colligeretur, rebus Ungaricis adversus Turcas succutre, prout & religionis & officii nostri & sanguinis ratio incitabat. Pollicebamurque eam pecuniam nequaquam in alios usus implicandam. Quod si ex ipsius cruciatæ denegatione seu dilatione quod linistri Christianitati contingeret, hostelque fidei quicquam molirentur, cum jam tot bellis contra nos & statum nostrum tentatis exhausti essemus, nec sine cruciata occurrere possemus, protestati fuimus id nequaquam nostræ culpæ ascribendum, sed potius eidem imputandum qui id denegaret quod sibi non noceret & toti Christianæ reipublic. summe prodesse poterat. De pileis autem, diximus unum duntaxat à vestræ felici promotionis exordio à nobis petitum, quem ubi putabamus tam diu differendum, cum esset prima gratia à V. S. manu etiam nostra conscriptis literis petita ac iustanter flagitata. Alter vero pileus petitus non fuerat, sed ultro à V.S. oblatus nostroque consensu acceptatus. Sicque alienum censebamus eos nunc pileos tali conditione perstringi, quos tamen V.S. arbitrio tunc relinquendos putavimus, Pollicentes nos de caetero pro his nec pro aliis quibuscunque piis ullam facturos instantiam. Reliquas autem ipsius V.S. oblationes non solum gratas & acceptas habuimus, pro ipsisque gratiis ut decebat retulimus. Sed etiam reciproco, quicquid facultatis haberemus, vitam quoque & sanguinem pro vestrae Sa. honore ac incremento libere obtulimus.
units.tr: 35. Thirdly, our reply is again refuted, and what Your Holiness kindly and generously promised us, you demand from us as if it were owed and due. But let us see what promises that Holiness made and what our reply was, so that we may also avoid this charge. For Your Holiness passes over this in silence in your letter, leaving others to judge the matter more harshly. So that the truth of these points may be made clear: Your Holiness offered us that, if we would consent to your wishes concerning Duke Francis himself, you would grant us not only tithes, crusade indulgences, caps, and whatever faculties you had through spiritual and temporal power, but would also offer your blood and life for our exaltation and satisfaction. We replied that it did not befit the Christian commonwealth that the crusade be bound by such a condition, but that it should be offered freely and willingly, and that it did not seem fitting that it be deferred. For we could already grant it in our kingdoms, in the same manner as our predecessors had always obtained it from yours, for the promontories in Africa, which were established for defending and repelling the enemies of the faith, and to that end had never been refused to them. We thought it less fitting that such a treasure of the Church be refused or deferred by Your Holiness. Beyond the African affairs, as we have made known to Your Holiness, we also wished to use the money collected from the crusade itself to help Hungarian affairs against the Turks, as the cause of religion, of our office, and of our blood urged us. And we promised that this money would in no way be diverted to other uses. But if, through the refusal or delay of the crusade, something harmful should happen to the ministers of Christianity, and the enemies of the faith should attempt anything, since we are already exhausted by so many wars waged against us and our state, and could not resist without the crusade, we protested that this must in no way be ascribed to our fault, but rather to him who refused what could not harm him and could greatly benefit the whole Christian commonwealth. As for the caps, we said that we had asked for only one at the beginning of your happy promotion, and when we thought it would be deferred so long, since it was the first favour, we had asked for it by our own written letter, and insistently demanded it. But the second cap had not been asked for; it was offered by Your Holiness of your own accord and accepted with our consent. So we thought it improper that those caps be now bound to such a condition, though we thought they should be left to Your Holiness's judgment at that time, promising that henceforth we would make no request for these or any other pious things. The remaining offers of Your Holiness we not only held as welcome and accepted, and thanked you for these favours as was fitting, but also, in return, we freely offered whatever resources we had, and even our life and blood, for the honour and increase of Your Holiness.

units.la: 36. Haec sunt, Pater sancte, quae illis literis V.S. manu conscriptis, nostra etiam manu in effectu respondimus, quas in lucem prodire cupimus, ut utriusque nostrum scriptis bene perspectis plane decerni possit, an justa sit culpa quae de his nobis ascribitur, an ne hujusmodi nostra talem redargutionem & criminationem mererentur.
units.tr: 36. These are, Holy Father, the things we have answered in substance, in our own hand, to those letters of Your Holiness written in your own hand. We wish them brought to light, so that from both our writings, carefully weighed, it may be plainly decided whether the blame ascribed to us in these matters is just, or whether our replies deserve such refutation and accusation.

units.la: 37. Ad eam autem accusationem & querelam, quam (ut praefertur) V.S. proponit de nostrorum in Italia agentium iniquitate & contumeliis, ac obloquionibus. Id, teste Deo, affirmandum censemus nil tale a nobis nec nostro jussu prodiisse, nec sub generali nostro mandato comprehendi potuisse quicquam, quod crimen seu delictum saperet. Quod si nobis quid tale legitime constitutum esset, fuissemus de his ut decet edocti vel etiam adhuc edocereamur, non remanerent haec impunita taliterque pro justitiae cultu provideremus, ut nulla horum culpa nobis ascribi posset.
units.tr: 37. As for that accusation and complaint which Your Holiness brings forward (as stated above) concerning the iniquity, insults and slanders of our men acting in Italy, we affirm, God being our witness, that nothing of the kind has come from us or by our command, nor could anything savouring of crime or offence have been included under our general mandate. If anything of the sort had been legitimately established against us, we would have been informed of these matters, as is fitting, or would even now be informed. These things would not remain unpunished, and we would provide for the cultivation of justice in such a way that no fault in them could be ascribed to us.

units.la: 38. De re autem Senensi non recte taxamur, nulla enim justa culpa nobis impingi poterit, quae ad ipsius civitatis quietem stabiliendam ac bene regendam egimus, sed quicquid vero ac justo Principi convenire videretur. Est enim civitas illa antiquissima illius respub. Imperiali ditioni subjecta, & super alias omnes Italiae civitates adeo ab omni avo Sacro Imp. addicta, illiusque devotioni affecta, ut nihil praeditum desiderari queat, habetque propterea ab ipso S. Imp. nostrisque praedecessoribus amplissima privilegia etiam per nos confirmata, quibus ipsa respub. regenda ac gubernanda concediture. Et cum ut ... bus jam annis praeter ipsorum privilegiorum mentem ejusdem reipubl. regimen & gubernium esset tyrannis usurpatum, qui non amore sed timore, non jure potentia ac potius vi illius subditos coercebant. Quorum primus Pandolphus Petrucius: Inde eo mortuo Burgesius ejus filius. Acceo polit auctoritate Leonis Pontificis a regimine expulso, falcem in alienam messem mittendo: Sua S. novam tyrannum instituisset, Cardinalem Petrucium qui eo praetextu quotannis decem aureorum millia eidem Sanctitati persolvere convenerat. Sic eandem remp. Senen. unire satagendo remp. Florentinae ut unde magis Imperii vires in Italia debilitari seu verius enervari possent. Quem Cardin. tyrannum, nos etiam quandiu vixit, ut potius Leoni & ipsi V.S. quam nobis & sacro imp. ac illi reipub. satisfieret, in eodem regimine passi sumus. Eo autem Cardin. mortuo, dum inter nostros esset contentio quid magis illi reipubl. conveniret, an sub solo gubernatore forent regendi, an sub ordine civium ex moribus dictae civitatis erigendo: rem V.S. consilio & ordinationi remittendam censuimus: ut nostrorum contentionem tolleremus. Quorum pars una ad unum illius civitatis regimen deferendum putabat. Altera vero pars civibus & populo committendum satagebat. Electa est tandem inter eos media via, ut necunus solus, necreliqui sine capite gubernarent: ad idque civis nostrorum auctoritate praefectus exstitit. Primo Franciscus Petrucius Borghesius patruus, & cum is V.S. minus idoneus ad id munus esse videretur, Velt. S. cum Fabio Petrucio Burgesii fratre affinitate contracta huncipsius civitatis regimini praeficiendum putavit V.S. Franc. Petrucium illius patruum excludere illamque rempub. ad suae voluntatis libitum in manu habere consenserunt: ni id nostri qui nil aliud quam S.V. in his & aliis omnibus occurrentibus, nostro jussu mote gerere studebant. Admissus est Fabins ipse Petrucius V.S. inruitu, qui intrans ut agnus & cum omni humilitate receptus: tandem adveniente duce Albaniae Gallorum duce, illius praedidis fretus se non agnum sed lupum ostendit: ipsamque rempub. non Imperiali sed Gallicae factioni adjicere conatus est: eam cogendo, ut Gallis & pecuniam & tormenta bellica ad regnum nostrum invadendum Neapolitanum erogaret: ipsique duci Albaniae contra nos, & statum nostrum favorent, & ad illius nutum extorres & seditiosos factionis Gallicae autores in civitatem reducerent. Et cum annuente altissimo de nostrorum victoria certiores effecti Senen. ipsi a jugo servitutis hujusmodi se excutere curarunt. Franciscus & Fabius & eorum adhaerentes, civium, ac populi intentione perspecta, civitatem cum regimine pro derelictis habent: seque ab ipsa civitate abstentarunt. Proceditur contra culpabiles, aliqui (ut ajunt) justitia praevia plectuntur, aliqui certis limitibus proscribuntur & confirmantur. Relique eo deducitur, ut civitas & respublica Senen. per seipsam in libertatem proclamet, reipubl. quae juxta suorum privilegiorum formam intendat: nostraque ditioni, ut par erat, se totaliter devovet. His Vest. Sanct. (ut ajunt) percita, conqueritur suos turbati, maleque tractari, remedium a nobis expetes. Nos qui nil aliud cupiebamus quam Vest. Sanct. in his & longe majoribus satisfacere, nostrorumque in Italia agentium opiniones pro debito justitiae concordare. Commisimus commendatori Herrerae, quem ad Sanctit. Vest. (ut praemittitur) mittebamus, ut is per dictam civitatem Senensem transeundo in accessu & reditu se informaret: de ipsius civitatis gubernio & regimine, tam antiquo quam moderno, tam cum ipsis civibus in civitate manentibus, quam cum extorribus ante expulsis. Quid magis civitati & reipublicae convenire videretur, an uni soli regimen conferendum esset, an pluribus civibus ex decurionum decreto hujusmodi regimen esset concedendum, & hujusmodi informationibus secreto sumptis, ut sub debito sigillo secreti ad nos transmissi oportune provideremus. Interea tamen extorres ad suorum bonorum possessionem & fructus, prout ptius tenebant, restituendos censuimus. Adimplevit Herrera quod ei commissum fuerat, sumpsit informationes ab utrisque, tam civibus quam extorribus: providit extorribus super suorum fructuum perceptione, juribus reipubl. salvis. Misit ad nos informationis omnes clausulas sigillatas. Coperimus mestus reipub. convenire praesens civium gubernium, nium, quam vim tyrannide utentis. Duxim.us igitur nil immutandum donec aliter rebus omnibus perspectis ordinandum censeremus. Interim in lucem prodeunt aliquorum factiones, qui pecunia corrupti & civitatem prodere, & extorres & factiosos in eam inducere, & ipsam rempub. subverrere conabantur: jam per subterraneos cuniculos perque alia media hostibus & rebellibus ad civitatem ingressum praeparantes: inter quas tres apertissimae conspirationes, & (ut ajunt) proditiones detectae sunt. Compertis in factiosorum domibus, montibus, foveis, scalis, armis, munitionibus, & omnibus aliis ad id facinus perpetrandum dispositis, deprehenduntur ut audivimus hi facinorosi in flagranti crimine capiuntur, fatentur delictum, detegunt factionis practicas, damnantur justitia praevia: debito plectuntur supplicio. Si V.Sanct. inter suos amicos & benevolos annumerandos censuerit, si pro his quae in eos gesta sunt querelas praerendat, Si ex his sibi contumelias & opprobria impingi putat, Si cum his omnem nobilitatem exterminaram censuerit: quae potius in ipsa virtute consistit, animadvertat Vest. San.ne gravius pondus humeris suis imponat: neve hujusmodi factionum se conscium tacite fateatur: quod nequaquam illius dignitati & officio convenire videretur. Cum potissimum autore cujus nutu cuncta reguntur, ipsa respub.Senen.suae justae causae apertum praestiterit testimonium, a tot in vasorum congressibus, se suis solum viribus, liberando.
units.tr: 38. As for the affair of Siena, we are not rightly blamed. No just fault can be charged against us for what we have done to establish the peace and good government of that city, but only what seemed fitting for a true and just prince. That city is very ancient, its commonwealth subject to the Imperial dominion, and above all other cities of Italy it has been so devoted to the Holy Empire from of old, and so attached to its loyalty, that nothing more could be desired. For this reason it has received from the Holy Emperor himself and from our predecessors very ample privileges, also confirmed by us, by which the commonwealth itself is granted the right to be ruled and governed. And since some years ago, contrary to the intent of those privileges, the government and rule of that commonwealth had been seized by tyrants, who held its subjects in check not by love but by fear, not by right but rather by force. The first of these was Pandolfo Petrucci; after his death came his son Borghese. Then, with the authority of Pope Leo, they were expelled from power, sending a sickle into another's harvest, and the Cardinal Petrucci set up a new tyranny, on the pretext of which he had agreed to pay ten thousand gold pieces yearly to that Holiness. Thus, eager to join the commonwealth of Siena to that of Florence, so that from there the forces of the Empire in Italy might be weakened, or rather enfeebled. We too, as long as that Cardinal tyrant lived, suffered him to remain in that government, so that he might satisfy Leo and Your Holiness rather than us, the Holy Empire, and that commonwealth. After the Cardinal's death, while there was contention among our men over what would better suit that commonwealth, whether it should be governed by a single ruler alone, or by an order of citizens to be set up according to the customs of that city, we thought the matter should be left to the counsel and decision of Your Holiness, so that we might end the dispute among our men. One party thought that the government of that city should be entrusted to one man; the other party strove to commit it to the citizens and the people. At last a middle way was chosen, so that neither one man alone nor the rest should govern without a head; and to this end a citizen was set over them by the authority of our men. First Francis Petrucci, Borghese's uncle, was chosen; and since he seemed less suitable for this office to Your Holiness, you thought it fitting to set over that city's government Fabio Petrucci, brother of Borghese, with whom you had contracted a kinship by marriage. You agreed to exclude Francis Petrucci, the uncle, and to hold that commonwealth in your hand at your pleasure; had not those of ours, who strove to carry out only Your Holiness's wishes in these and all other matters, by our command, opposed it. Fabio Petrucci himself was admitted at Your Holiness's wish, and, entering like a lamb, was received with all humility. Then, when the Duke of Albany, the French commander, arrived, relying on his support, he showed himself not as a lamb but as a wolf, and tried to bring the commonwealth itself over to the French faction rather than the Imperial one, compelling it to supply the French with money and siege artillery for invading our kingdom of Naples, and to favour the Duke of Albany against us and our state, and, at his nod, to bring back into the city the exiles and rebels who were authors of the French faction. And when, by the will of the Most High, the Sienese were informed of our victory, they took care to shake off such a yoke of servitude. Francis, Fabio, and their adherents, seeing the intention of the citizens and the people, have regarded the city and its government as abandoned, and have withdrawn from the city itself. Proceedings are taken against the guilty; some (as they say) are punished after due trial, others are banished within certain limits and confirmed in that sentence. The rest has been brought to the point that the city and commonwealth of Siena, by its own act, proclaims itself free, to govern the commonwealth according to the form of its privileges, and wholly devotes itself to our dominion, as was right. Your Holiness, (as they say) stirred by these things, complains that your people have been disturbed and ill-treated, and seeks a remedy from us. We, who desired nothing more than to satisfy Your Holiness in these matters and far greater ones, and to bring the opinions of our men in Italy into agreement, as justice requires, committed to Commander Herrera, whom we were sending to Your Holiness (as has been said before), that he should, passing through the city of Siena on his going and returning, inform himself about the government and rule of that city, both ancient and modern, both with the citizens remaining in the city and with the exiles previously expelled: what would seem more fitting for the city and commonwealth, whether the rule should be conferred on one man alone, or whether such government should be granted to several citizens by decree of the councillors; and that, with such information gathered in secret, he should send it to us under the sealed seal of secrecy, so that we might provide in due time. Meanwhile, however, we thought the exiles should be restored to the possession and fruits of their goods, as they had held them before. Herrera carried out what had been committed to him: he gathered information from both sides, from the citizens as well as the exiles, and provided for the exiles concerning the receipt of their revenues, the rights of the commonwealth being preserved. He sent us all the information under sealed clauses. We have judged that the present government of the citizens ought to be left as it is, rather than the violence of a tyrant. We therefore decided that nothing should be changed until, with all matters fully examined, we might judge that otherwise should be ordered. Meanwhile, the factions of certain men have come to light, who, bribed by money, tried to betray the city, and to lead the exiles and seditious men into it, and to subvert the commonwealth itself, already preparing an entry for the enemies and rebels into the city through underground tunnels and other means. Among these, three very open conspiracies and (as they say) betrayals have been detected. Once the houses, mountains, pits, ladders, arms, munitions, and all other things arranged for perpetrating that crime had been discovered in the houses of the conspirators, these criminals, as we heard, were caught in the act of crime, confessed the offence, revealed the practices of the faction, were condemned after due trial, and punished with the penalty they deserved. If Your Holiness counts these men among your friends and well-wishers, if you complain of the things done against them, if you think insults and reproaches are being heaped on you by them, if you judge that all the nobility is to be exterminated with them, which consists rather in virtue itself, let Your Holiness consider whether you are not laying a heavier burden on your own shoulders, and lest you tacitly confess yourself to be a party to such factions: which by no means seems to befit your dignity and office. Especially since the commonwealth of Siena, by its own just cause, has given clear testimony, freeing itself by its own strength from so many attacks of enemies, under the author by whose nod all things are governed.

units.la: 39. Ad illam autem querelam quam Vest.S. profert, quod contra promissum & fidem datam, tot mala per nostros in sanctae Rom.eccle.terris & locis(ut ait)parata fuerunt. Et si nostrorum militum insolentias resque injuste gestas, si quae sunt, nequaquam approbare, nec excusare volumus quin potius ubi fas erit, debita castigatione compescere. Non possumus tamen non mirari, quod S.V. se promissis & fide data juvare velit, quibus antea contradicit, & quae etiam per nos ratificata V.S. respuit ac rejicit: nostram ratificationem impugnans, suamque (ut praedixi mus) denegans, indeq; ad foedus omnino contrarium transitum faciens. In quem casum non tantum exaccebandum videretur, si nostri duces & milites qui sua virtute & viribus Parmam & Placentiam ecclesiae reddidere ac ab hostium faucibus evulsere, totiensque tutari sunt, ut illis victum quaererent, ac de his prout de reliquis ab hostibus recuperatis disponendum censerent, potissimum cum ita haec civitates essent ecclesiae, ex foedere Leonis consignatae, tenendae duntaxat eo jure quo aut per ipsum Leonem tenti fuerunt. Quod jus tamen nullum erat, quandoquidem ad feudum pertinerent Imperii, essentq; per ducatus Mediolani: & de illis nullum eccl.Romana titulum validum nec ab imperio, nec ab eo qui dare posset, obtinuerit.
units.tr: 39. As for the complaint that Your Holiness brings forward, that contrary to promise and to the faith pledged, so many evils (as you put it) have been prepared in the lands and places of the holy Roman Church by our men: we do not wish to approve, nor to excuse, the insolence of our soldiers or any unjust deeds they may have done, but rather, where it is right, to check them with due punishment. Yet we cannot but wonder that Your Holiness wishes to support yourself by promises and the faith pledged, when you yourself contradict them beforehand, and reject and cast off what was also ratified by us. You attack our ratification, deny your own (as I have said), and thereby pass over to a covenant entirely opposed to it. Nor would this seem to call for such great indignation, if our commanders and soldiers, by their own valour and strength, had not restored Parma and Piacenza to the Church and wrested them from the jaws of the enemy, and had defended them so often that they might seek their reward, and might decide about these cities, as about the others recovered from the enemy, as they judged fit. This is especially so since these cities were consigned to the Church by the covenant of Leo, to be held only by that right by which they were held by Leo himself. Yet that right was no right at all, since they belonged as fiefs to the Empire and lay within the Duchy of Milan; and the Roman Church has never obtained a valid title to them, either from the Empire or from anyone who could grant one.

units.la: 40. Quae autem de Legato & Nuncio objiciuntur, quantum illa a veritate distent, etiam ex legati & nuncii assertione parebit. Quam primum enim Legatus in Curiam nostram pervenit, cum jam Nuncius se mandatum habere profiteretur, ut in pace cum Gallo ineunda & tractanda ministris id flagitantibus & sollicitantibus, impeditus fuerit ipsius Viceregis in Italiam transitus. Quinetiam, ut fertur, Si Dom. Hugo illo tempore intra limites ipsius regni Franciae repertus esset, illum pariter detineri curabantur ut ad Vest.Sanct. pervenire nequiret. Sicque magis colorari posset animi vestrae Sanctitatis nobis alienatio, & apertius incusari posset ipsius Dom.Hugonis tardatio, quam etiam vestra Sanctitas sine justa ratione accusare nititur: ubi biduo duntaxat in Cutia Regis Gallorum apud Viceregem se continuit, ad quem missus erat, ad eum duntaxat finem, ut cum Vicerege (si fas esset) ad irer illud Italicum cum dicto Domino Hugone peragendum excitaret. Quod si illum ad id dispositum seu praeparatum non reperiret, reciperet ab ipso Vicerege ulteriorem instructionem, de his quae in regno Neapolitano, post expeditum cum vestra Sanctitate negocium, essent: & inde ipse Dominus Hugo Vicerege dimisso, solus ad exequenda commissa in Italiam transiret: ut sic non recta videatur illatio, quod ibidem se continuerit: ut rerum speculaterur eventum. Minusque incusanda videtur ipsius Domini Hugonis mora in Mediolano facta, quae quintum diem non excessit. Cujus etiam mora potius coacta censetur quam voluntaria. Cum in illius apud Mediolanum primo congressu apparuerint ipsius ducis Suefiae vices nostras in urbe agentis literae, quibus nunciabatur foedus ante per vestram Sanctitatem cum caeteris esse conclusum, eamque non potuisse induci, ut ipsius Domini Hugonis adventum per aliquot dies expectaret. Quinimo resolute respondisse: quod nec per diem nec per horam ipsius foederis conclusionem differret: nunciabat etiam arma jam parata. Exercitum ad iter dispositum, ut nostros adorirentur. Erat quoque rumor publicus & fama, quod clausi essent passus, & aditus ad urbem, quod nostri cursores sive venientes ubique detinebantur: literaeque omnes intercipiebantur: nullusque erat tutus accessus ad vestram Sanctitatem his rationibus coactus fuit Dominus Hugo ibidem supersedere, aciter suum per eos differre, donec a vestrae Sanctitatis ducibus & ministris salvum conductum impetrasset: prout fecit. Qui sicinrerim cum duce Francisco tractare visus est, ut si posset illum induceret nostris ut tenetur, obediret mandatis: utque omni rebellione cessante se nostrae justitiae & gratiae, ut par erat, subjiceret. Nosque & duces nostros de arce in qua continebatur, secuos faceret, ne inde rebus nostris ac exercitui nostro damnum aliquod emergeret, seu incommodum afferri posset: Non est igitur cur de his vestra Sanctitas conqueri deberet, cui nulla ob id fiebat injuria. Quinimo ipso duce nobiscum, vel cum dicto Domino Hugone nostro nomine transfigente, feliciorreddebatur nostra cum vestra Sanctitate conventio, tollebatur que principaliter difficultas illius novi foederis, quod inter nos tractabatur: & quod cum vestra Sanctitate inire putarabamus, ni forsan vestra Sanctitas suis cogitationibus atque conatibus obviam ire putaret, Si Franciscus Sforcia sine Sanct.Vest.autoritate in gratiam reciperetur, illumque sibi obnoxium non haberet.
units.tr: 40. As for the charges made concerning the Legate and the Nuncio, how far they are from the truth will also appear from the assertion of the Legate and the Nuncio themselves. For as soon as the Legate arrived at our court, the Nuncio already declared that he had a commission to treat and conclude peace with the French, at the urging and pressing of ministers, and the passage of the Viceroy himself into Italy was hindered. Moreover, as is reported, if Lord Hugo had at that time been found within the borders of the kingdom of France, care was likewise taken to detain him so that he could not reach Your Holiness. Thus a estrangement of Your Holiness's mind from us might be better colored, and the delay of Lord Hugo might be more openly blamed, which Your Holiness also tries to censure without just cause. For he stayed only two days in the camp of the King of the French with the Viceroy, to whom he had been sent, for the sole purpose of urging the Viceroy (if it were permitted) to go with Lord Hugo to carry out that Italian business. And if he found him not prepared or disposed for this, he was to receive from the Viceroy further instructions about what was to be done in the kingdom of Naples, once the business with Your Holiness had been completed; and then Lord Hugo, having dismissed the Viceroy, was to pass alone into Italy to carry out his commission. Thus the inference that he stayed there in order to watch the outcome of events does not seem correct. Nor does the delay of Lord Hugo made at Milan seem worthy of blame, since it did not exceed five days; and this delay is judged to have been forced rather than voluntary. For at his first meeting at Milan there appeared letters of the Duke of Sessa, who was acting for us in the city, announcing that the covenant had already been concluded by Your Holiness with the others, and that it could not be induced that he should wait for Lord Hugo's arrival for some days. Indeed he replied firmly that he would not put off the conclusion of that covenant by a day or an hour; he also announced that arms were already ready and an army set in motion to attack our men. There was also public rumour and report that the passes and approaches to the city were closed, that our couriers, whether coming or going, were detained everywhere, and that all letters were intercepted, and that there was no safe access to Your Holiness. Lord Hugo was therefore compelled by these circumstances to remain there, and to delay his journey through them until he had obtained a safe conduct from Your Holiness's commanders and ministers, which he did. He seems to have treated with Duke Francesco so that, if he could, he might bring him over to our side, as he was bound to do, to obey our commands, and, with all rebellion ceasing, submit himself, as was fitting, to our justice and grace. And he was to make us and our commanders safe from the citadel in which he was held, lest any loss or inconvenience should arise from it for our affairs or our army. There is therefore no reason why Your Holiness should complain of these things, since no injury was done to you on that account. Indeed, with the Duke himself with us, or with the said Lord Hugo acting in our name, our agreement with Your Holiness would have been made the happier, and the chief difficulty of that new covenant which was being treated between us would have been removed; and that covenant we thought to make with Your Holiness, unless perhaps Your Holiness thought to oppose it by your own designs and efforts, if Francesco Sforza were received back into favour without the authority of Your Holiness, and so were not bound to you.

units.la: 41. Quod autem asseritur nostros interim Parmam occulta proditione etipere tentasse: id e-
units.tr: 41. As for the assertion that our men meanwhile tried to seize Parma by secret treachery: this is

units.la: Papali officio factiones & proditiones non convenient. nim nobis penitus ignotum, sed nos arbitramur duces nostros rem tam arduam nobis incòsultis non ausos fuisse tentare, credimus potius ab aliquo maligno spiritu ad discordiam seminandam adinventum atq; confectum. Quandoquidem ubi nos Parmam simulq; Placentiam recuperare, feudumq; que Imperii, prout fuerat antea, reunire & reintegrare voluissemus, id non occulta prodितione, sed plaam & juste per juris tramites exequendum fuisset: licet nos ita à cupiditate semper alieni fuerimus, ut potius nostra, & Imperii jura negligere, quam publicam quietem turbare maluerimus, & potissimum illam sanctam Apostolicam sedem & catholicam ecclesiam, cui semper (ut par erat) deferte conati sumus. Sicque nostros à praetensa proditione omnino immunes esse censemus, Cum potissime nihil aliud quam de eorum offensione cogitare viderentur, adversus invasionem contra eos praeparatum, prout rei exitus demonstravit.
units.tr: The papal office does not admit factions and treacheries. For it is entirely unknown to us; but we judge that our commanders, without our counsel, did not dare to attempt so grave a matter, and we rather believe that it was devised and contrived by some malignant spirit to sow discord. For if we had wished to recover Parma and Piacenza at the same time, and to restore and reintegrate these fiefs of the Empire as they were before, this would have had to be done not by secret treachery but openly and justly, along the paths of law. Although we have always been so far from greed that we have preferred to neglect our own and the Empire's rights rather than disturb the public peace, and especially that holy Apostolic See and the Catholic Church, to which we have always, as was fitting, endeavoured to show deference. Thus we judge that our men are wholly free from the alleged treachery, since they seem to have thought of nothing but their own defence against an invasion prepared against them, as the outcome of events has shown.

units.la: 42. Unde ex his omnibus criminationibus & querelis in nos adductis, recto semper his judicio sumpto resultare non possent tales injuriae seu causae, quibus vestra Sanct. invita & gemens (ut ait) de nobis desperare aut diffidere debuerit: nec obid (ut asseruit) suam amicitiam & benevolentiam à nobis repudiatam censere, quam potius semper in summo precio habuimus. Nec propterea necesse fuerat Vest. Sanctitati se tot magnis (ut ait) regibus adjungere, nec hos in odium nostrum convertere, Qui non his minorem in Christianam rem & sedem apostol. animum semper habuimus. Et quippe si vestra Sanctitas ab his foederibus & colligationibus contra nos & statum nostrum ac dignitatem tenratus abstinuisset, non propterea, ut inquit, pastoris seu communis patris laudem amisisset: sed potius magis atq; magis confirmasset & auxisset. Sicque merito cum Psalmista dicere possumus: Quare fremuerunt gentes, & populi meditati sunt inania, Astiterunt reges terrae & principes convenerunt in unum, adversus, non inquam dominum & Christum, sed adversus ministrum à domino divinitus institutum ab ipsomet Christo, à quo omnis pendet auctoritas & potestas: qui propterea disrumpet vincula, & linguam eorum, & projiciet à nobis jugum ipsorum, prout in suam divinam benignitatem & clementiam recta nostra intentione, & conscientia freti, plene confidimus.
units.tr: 42. Hence, from all these accusations and complaints brought against us, if a right judgement is always made of them, no such injuries or causes can result as should have led Your Holiness, unwillingly and groaning (as you say), to despair of us or to distrust us; nor, as you assert, should you judge your friendship and goodwill rejected by us, which we have always held in the highest esteem. Nor was it therefore necessary for Your Holiness to join yourself to so many great kings (as you say), nor to turn these against us in hatred; for we have always borne no less a mind toward the Christian cause and the Apostolic See. And indeed, if Your Holiness had refrained from such leagues and alliances against us, our state and dignity, you would not, as you say, have lost the praise of a shepherd or common father, but would rather have confirmed and increased it more and more. And so we may rightly say with the Psalmist: Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?
