The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together, against, I say, not the Lord and Christ, but against the minister instituted by the Lord himself, by Christ, from whom all authority and power depends; who will therefore break their bonds and their tongue, and cast their yoke from us, as we fully trust in his divine goodness and clemency, relying on our upright intention and conscience.

units.la: 43. Subjungit V.S. cum esset res gesta & fides invicem data, eademque sanctitas foedere astricta cum illis regibus, accessit tum demum itineribus lente & tarde confectis dictus Domin. Hugo, eidem Sanctitati conjunctionem & conditiones eas afferens, quas cum vestra Sanctitas tam saepe tamq; vehementer petiisset: totiens (ut ait) repulsa & repudiata fuerit. Quarum tunc excipiendarum occasio, & tempus praeterierunt, Duo haec, Pater Sa. considerada intuendaque videntur: quae profecto non nos tantum, sed omnes recte sentientes in summam admirationem debent inducere, & pro quibus nos in Sanctitatem vestram justiores querelas possumus retorquete. Alterum quod Vest. Sanct. sciens dominum Hugonem praesto venturum, & jamdiu ad iter accinctum cum amplo mandato, & grata resolutione noluerit per aliquot dierum spatium, nostris id summe flagitantibus, ac cum omni instantia requirentibus, illius adventum praestolari. Sed solum illius tarditatem incusando non habito respectu, quod is etiam cursoris more per equos ad id dispositos (quantum illius aetas ac personae qualitas ferre poterat) die noctuq; iter suum festinabat: V. Sanct. adeo voluntarie promperit in hujus damnosiac ad scandalosi foederis participationem. Alterum vero quod eodem Domino Hugone ad Vest. Sanct. provento & (ut V.S. profitetur) optatas eidem conditiones nostro nomine offerente, priusquam aliqua armorum executio tentaretur: eadem San. ita rejicienda censuerit, ut earum accipiendarum occasionem, tempus praeteriisse assereret: non advertens quantum difformiter nobiscum egisset, foedus, quod antea cum nostris oratoribus inierat, jam hinc inde publicatum, & per nos ratificatu ac approbatum, respuendo, fineq; ulla ratione justa ejus literas ratificatorias nostris reciprocas concedere denegando. Nunc e contrario foedus aliud illi repugnans, sub defensionis nomine penitus offensum sub colore universalis pacis disponendo: pacem jam ubiq; contractam disrumpens atque perturbans: & loco pacis bellum ac arma commovens. Adeo inviolabiliter sustinere conatur V.S. ut etiam optatas (ut ait) conditiones, armorum causam submoventes, reciproce recusaverit. Digne damnata quidem haec deformitas in ipso pastore & communi patre: qui omnibus aequalis esse debuisset. Esto enim quod in nobis nostrisq; ministris aliqua mora argui potuisset, prout re veta non poterat, non tamen ipsius morae purgatio jure tanti momenti erat deneganda: ubi potissime nullum erat ad id tempus praefixum, necdies qui interpellaret per horas nullaque poena ad id adjecta, quae moræ excluderet expurgationem, necesse jam aderat contrahentium interesse, ubi armorum motibus nondum executis radix procedebatur, ubi publica quies facilius parabatur. Haec enim, Pater beatiss. non ad propulsandum (ut ait) Italiae servitutis periculum, Christianitatisque perturbationem: sed potius ad effectus penitus contrarios dispositia videntur. Non pro sede apost. armis exercitu munienda. Quae illis non indiget, ubi nullus adest offensor: sed potius pro ipsius apostol. sedis munitionibus profundendis, ecclesiarumque thesauro exhauriendo & effundendo, contra ipsummet Christum, ad Christianae reipublicae detrimentum: inventa sunt non ad justitiae & pacis viam (ut inquit) inter omnes aequis conditionibus parandam: sed potius ad omnem justitiam perturbandam pacemque jam paratam infringendam ac quasi desperandam: non etiam videntur haec consilia seu gesta, quibus S.V. nec coram Deo nec coram hominibus rectam justificationem recipere debeat. Sed potius si fas est dicere, scandalum, ecclesiasticique status gravem perturbationem peperisse videntur.
units.tr: 43. After these things had been done and promises exchanged on both sides, and Your Holiness had bound yourself by the same solemn pact with those kings, Lord Hugo at last arrived, having made his journey slowly and tardily. He brought to Your Holiness the union and those conditions which you had so often and so vehemently sought, though (as he says) they were repeatedly rejected and repudiated. The occasion and the time for accepting them have now passed. Two things, Most Blessed Father, seem worthy of consideration and attention. They ought to throw not only us but all right-thinking people into the greatest astonishment, and on these grounds we can turn back upon Your Holiness more just complaints. The first is this: Your Holiness knew that Lord Hugo was about to come and was already prepared for the journey with ample authority and a welcome resolution. Yet you were unwilling to wait for his arrival for some days, although we urgently asked it and demanded it with every insistence. You paid no regard to his slowness alone, though he hurried on his journey day and night, like a courier, by horses placed ready for the purpose, as far as his age and station could bear. Your Holiness was so readily inclined to join this harmful and scandalous covenant. The second is this: when Lord Hugo had come to Your Holiness and, as you yourself confess, was offering the desired conditions in our name before any use of arms had been attempted, you judged them so wholly to be rejected that you asserted the opportunity of accepting them had passed. You did not notice how unevenly you had dealt with us. You rejected the covenant you had earlier entered into with our envoys, which had been published on both sides and was ratified and approved by us, and you refused, without any just reason, to grant your letters of ratification in return for ours. Now, on the contrary, you are drawing up another covenant opposed to that one, entirely hostile to us under the name of defence and under the colour of universal peace. You are breaking and disturbing the peace already concluded everywhere, and in place of peace you are stirring up war and arms. Your Holiness so stubbornly persists that you have even refused, in return, the conditions you desired (as you say), which would remove the cause of arms. This deformity is truly deserving of condemnation in the very minister and common father, who ought to have been equal to all. For granting that some delay might have been charged against us and our ministers, which in fact could not be the case, still the excuse for such a delay ought not to have been denied on a ground of such weight. Especially so, since no time had been fixed for it, no day had been set to press it by the hours, and no penalty had been added which would exclude the excuse for delay. It was necessary to consider the interest of the contracting parties, since arms had not yet been put in motion and the root of the trouble was still being pursued, and since public quiet could more easily be secured. For these measures, Most Blessed Father, are not arranged to repel (as you say) the danger of servitude for Italy and the disturbance of Christendom, but seem rather to have wholly contrary effects. The apostolic see is not to be fortified with an army of arms, for it has no need of that where there is no attacker. Rather, its own defences are to be poured out, and the treasure of the churches drained and squandered, against Christ himself and to the detriment of the Christian commonwealth. These plans have been devised not to establish the way of justice and peace on equal terms for all (as you say), but rather to disturb all justice, to break the peace already prepared, and to bring it almost to despair. Nor do these counsels or deeds seem such that Your Holiness ought to receive a right justification either before God or before men. Rather, if it is permitted to say so, they seem to have produced scandal and a grave disturbance of the state of the Church.

units.la: 44. At si haec Sanct. V. recto sui intellectus oculo, diligentique circumspectione perlustraverit, comperiet profecto nullum esse regem aut principem nobis recto ordine anteferendum, nullum cui apostolica sedes magis debeat, quemve magis tueri foverequeque deberet. Nullum a que magis filialis obseruantiæ ac devotionis ipsa apost. sedes receperit aut recipere posset. Nullum qui magis Romanam ecclesiam apostolicamque sedem stabilire, conservare, augere cupiat. Nullum ex cuius regnis ac dominiis magis honoris, commodi ac pecuniæ, ad aposto. sedem Romanamque curiam affluat. Si eam ad item recte advertat Vest. Sanctitas, comperiet quod ex Imperio regnisque ac dominiis nostris Hispaniarum, utriusque Siciliæ, Germaniæ, Galliæ, Belgicæ, ac superioris Burgundiæ, plusquam ex cæterorum omnium regnis, ac dominiis simul iunctis, lucri & commodi sedi apostolicæ ac Romanæ curiæ accedit. Non enim patiuntur Reges, alii itaque passim & laute ecclesiarum spolia & annatas ex eorum regnis ad Rom. curiam deferri: qualia autem sint ea lucra, ex centum illis Gravaminibus Nationis Germanicæ colligi poterit: quibus tamen ex ea devotione & observantia, qua semper Vest. Sanctitati ac apostolicæ sedi affecti fuimus: nusquam aures præstare curavimus, nec his animum adiicere. Quod si iusta aliqua ratione vel causa, apostolica sedes his lucris careret, non essent claves aureæ, quæ bellorum Archinia pro libito aperire, & claudere solent, nec Vest. Sanctitas ex regnorum nostrorum pecuniis, atque redditibus exercitum in nos concitaret, nec temporalia arma moveret, quibus potius iustum videretur, ad nostram defensionem uti.
units.tr: 44. But if Your Holiness were to survey these matters with the clear eye of right understanding and careful attention, you would surely find that there is no king or prince who ought to be placed before us in proper order, none to whom the apostolic see ought more to be indebted, or whom it ought more to protect and cherish. Nor has the apostolic see itself received, or could it receive, greater filial observance and devotion from anyone. No one desires more to establish, preserve and increase the Roman Church and the apostolic see. From no kingdoms and dominions does more honour, profit and money flow to the apostolic see and the Roman Curia. If Your Holiness would consider this rightly, you would find that from our Empire and from our kingdoms and dominions of Spain, both Sicilies, Germany, France, Belgium and Upper Burgundy, more profit and advantage comes to the apostolic see and the Roman Curia than from the kingdoms and dominions of all the others taken together. For the kings do not allow church spoils and annates to be carried freely and lavishly from their realms to the Roman Curia everywhere. What gains these are may be gathered from those hundred Grievances of the German Nation. Yet out of that devotion and observance with which we have always been disposed toward Your Holiness and the apostolic see, we have nowhere taken care to lend our ears to these complaints or to give them our attention. But if for some just reason or cause the apostolic see were without these gains, there would be no golden keys, which are wont to open and close the treasuries of wars at will. Nor would Your Holiness stir up an army against us from the money and revenues of our kingdoms, nor move temporal arms, which would seem more just to use for our own defence.

units.la: 45. Quod Vest. Sanctit. testatur se nunc etiam eo animo esse, si ad æquitatem & humanitatem nos referre voluerimus: illius arma non solum nobis non adversa, verumetiam ad res vere gloriosas perpetuo futura: Sin autem in occupanda Italia quotidie magis, & aliis partibus Christianitatis perturbandis, nos non tam naturæ quam cupiditati & consiliis nostrorum obsequi perseveraverimus, Vest. Sanctitatem neque iustitiæ neque libertati Italicæ (qua illius sedis tutela continetur) non defuturam, sed iusta & sancta arma moturam: non tam ad offensionem quam ad defensionem. Sancta quippe est hæc protestatio si verbis facta respondeant. Habet enim V. Sanctitas ex illis iustificationibus quas superius adversus ea, quæ in nos obiecta fuerant retulimus: nostram & æquitatem & humanitatem, simulque admixtam iustitiam, ut si talis ejusdem sanctitatis sit animus, primam ipsius protestationis partem ad effectum deducere valeat. Quod si fecerit, & a nobis gratias, & a Deo præmium reportabit. Habet etiam ex ejusdem iustificationibus late ostensum: nosab occupatione Italiæ, & Christianitatis turbatione, ab omnique cupiditate alienum esse, nilq; unquam iniustum, nil Italicæ libertati contrarium, nil quod Apostolicæ sedi tutela non conveniret per nos tentatum: imo nec cogitatum fuisset. Sicque merito cessabit secunda ipsius protestationis pars, ut nec arma iuste in nos moveri possint, nec offensione nec defensione opus esse videatur. Nos enim ut omnis a nobis absit suspicio. Si V. Sanctitas ejusque fœderati pro illorum parte arma deponere consentiant, erimus pariter ad ipsorum armorum depositionem promptissimi. Verum quippe hanc & rectam viam censen. & V. Sanctit. in his per viscera misericordiæ obsecrat, & per ipsam spem, quam de nobis (ut inquit) concepit, obviam eat immoderatis cupiditatibus, & magis pub. christianitatis bono condonet, quam & nos ad id attrahendos putet: sed rectis V. Sanct. clavibus oleo charitatis delinitis sedabuntur, & ea cura, quam Vest. Sanct. nobis dicit esse communem, cum ambo a Deo (ut recte inquit) in hanc sollicitudinem pro commissis nobis honoribus sumus vocati. Sic agendo facillime expediri quo pariter officio & debito, non minus quam V. Sanctitati non etiam neque defuimus, neque defuturi sumus, quinimo totis viribus atque conatibus anhelamus: ut hæc duo magna luminaria a Deo instituta, ita sibi adinvicem debito ordine correspondeant, & subministrent: ut orbis universus rectam illustrationem recipiat, nec per ipsorum luminarium obiectum Eclipsim in Christiana religione & doctrina causari, & generari, seu diutius sustineri valeat, in maximum Christianæ reipubl. detrimentum.
units.tr: 45. Your Holiness declares that you are now also of such a mind, provided we are willing to refer ourselves to equity and humanity: your arms would then be not only not hostile to us, but would serve truly glorious ends that would last forever. But if we persist in occupying Italy more and more every day and in disturbing other parts of Christendom, obeying not so much our nature as our desires and the counsels of our men, then Your Holiness will not fail justice or Italian liberty (which is kept under the protection of that see), but will move just and holy arms, not so much for offence as for defence. This protestation is indeed holy, if the deeds answer the words. For Your Holiness has, from those justifications which we have set out above against the charges made against us, our equity and humanity, together with justice mixed in. So if such is the mind of that same Holiness, you will be able to carry the first part of your protestation into effect. If you do so, you will receive thanks from us and a reward from God. You also have, from the same justifications, a full account showing that we are alien to the occupation of Italy and to the disturbance of Christendom, and to all cupidity; that nothing unjust, nothing contrary to Italian liberty, nothing that would not befit the protection of the apostolic see, has ever been attempted by us, nor was it even thought of. And so the second part of your protestation will rightly cease, so that arms cannot justly be moved against us, and there seems to be no need either for offence or for defence. For, that all suspicion may be far from us: if Your Holiness and your allies agree to lay down arms on their side, we shall be equally ready to lay down ours. Truly, Your Holiness begs us, by the bowels of mercy, to take this right and direct way, and, by that very hope which you have conceived of us (as you say), to resist immoderate desires. You are to pardon rather for the good of Christendom as a whole than to think we are drawn to them. But with the right keys, softened with the oil of charity, these matters will be calmed. That care which Your Holiness says is common to us, since we have both been called by God (as you rightly say) to this concern for the honours committed to us, will be settled. By acting in this way, the matter can most easily be resolved, with the same duty and obligation. We have neither failed Your Holiness, nor have we failed, nor shall we fail, no less than you; rather, with all our strength and effort we long that these two great lights instituted by God should correspond to and serve each other in due order, so that the whole world may receive right illumination, and that no eclipse may be caused or generated in the Christian religion and doctrine by the interposition of those lights, nor be able to be sustained any longer, to the very great detriment of the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: 46. Ad quod V. Sanctit. in suarum literarum calce subiungit, sub conditione tamen, quasi rem dubiam seu incertam proponens, dum inquit: Quod si, quæ de nostra in pacem generalem voluntate passim ferebantur, veras prudentiæ & pietatis tadices habebant, habemus occasionem declarandi quæ sentiebamus: omnia vere nos ex animo sensisse, atque operibus verba comprobando singularem optimi Principis laudem nobis acquirere: qui si Sanct. vestræ amotem nostrum cupiens, in liberanda Italia, quam suis fœderatis in eorum iustis petitionibus satisfacere instituerimus: erit id nostræ famæ & sapientiæ melius multo accommpodatum, & paci universali securitatique tam retum nostrarum, quam totius Christianitatis magis consentaneum. Putamus, Pater beatissime satis dilucide, & aperte ostensum esse, qualis fuerit nostra in pacem generalem voluntas: ut nec ulla in conditione ponenda necde ea dubitandum videretur: qui nullo unquam figmento, nullave simulatione usi fumus, nil unquam in ore habuimus quod in mente ac voluntate non sederet, omnia vere ex animo sentientes quæ loquebamur operibus verba comprobaturi, si hi quos res tangebat, & sine quibus pax generalis obtineri non poterat, iuste nostræ inclinationi (ut decebat) correspondissent. Sed cum ea sit universalis pacis natura, atque subsistentia, ut in ea omnium consensus universaliter exigatur: omnium voluntas nec cessare debeat concurrere: & econverso ab uno solo ex contendentibus, quicunque fuerit dependeat: & in solius potestate ac voluntate consistar. Ipsam universalem pacem impedire & etiam si facta fortet tutare bellumque movere, & partem alteram etiam invitam, ad ipsum bellum trahere non potuit, ob id aliis reluctantibus, nostraque optima voluntas operibus comprobari. Qui propterea (tanquam omni culpa carentes) non putamus illam optimi principis laudem, a nobis auferendam, seu cujuspiam maledicentia subtrahendam.
units.tr: 46. To this Your Holiness adds at the end of your letter, though under a condition, as if proposing a matter doubtful or uncertain, when you say: "But if the things that were everywhere reported about our willingness towards a general peace had true grounds in prudence and piety, we have an occasion to declare what we felt: that we truly felt everything from our heart, and by confirming words with deeds we might win for ourselves the singular praise of an excellent Prince. If Your Holiness, desiring our friendship, should undertake in the liberation of Italy to satisfy our allies in their just petitions, this will be far better suited to our reputation and wisdom, and more consistent with universal peace and the security of our affairs and of all Christendom." We think, most blessed Father, it has been made clear and plain enough what our will towards a general peace was, so that there seemed to be no need to place any condition on it or to doubt it. We have never used any fiction or pretence, never had on our lips anything that did not sit in our mind and will, truly feeling from our heart everything we said, and ready to confirm our words by deeds, if those whom the matter touches, and without whom general peace could not be obtained, had justly answered our inclination (as was fitting). But since the nature and subsistence of universal peace is such that the consent of all is universally required, the will of all must not cease to concur; and conversely, it depends on one only of the contending parties, whoever he may be, and rests in that one's power and will alone. To hinder universal peace itself, and, even if it were made, to disturb it and stir up war, and to drag the other party into the war even against its will, is a power that he has, while others resist; and our best will can be proved by deeds. Therefore, as if free from all blame, we do not think that this praise of an excellent prince should be taken from us, or subtracted by anyone's slander.

units.la: 47. Sitigitur V.S. prout flagitare videtur, consulere intendat pub. quieti, justæque Italiæ liberati, deponar arma, reponatque gladium Petri in vaginam, idque efficiat, ut etiam sui fœderati arma deponant, quod & nos (ut prædixunus) eodem contextu facturi sumus: ut sic juxta canticum Zacha. sine timore ab inimicis nostris liberati, serviamus illi. Hoc enim facto fundamento, poterit facilius. San st. Ve cam superficiem pacis universalis ædificare & laborare (ut inquit Psalmista) In conveniendo populos innum, & reges ut serviant domino. Et cum ea quæ Dei sunt cunctis rebus sint anteponenda, & inde publica privatis justa ratione præferantur, ne privatorum passio perturbet ea, quæ Dei sunt & quæ ad pub. salutem pertinent, consentaneum videtur: ut prius ab hostibus fidei, à Christianorum cervicibus pop ulsand s, & si fas sit ad ovile Christi adducendis: deque Lutheranorum, aliorumque hæreticorum scns, & erroribus comprimendis, corrigendis atque sedandis, & si licuerit ad ecclesiæ gremium reducen-dis: de aliis quoque omnibus, quæ Rom. ecclesiæ, totiusque Christianæ reipublicæ statum, salutem, conser-vationem, & incrementum concernere possunt, tractetur, & conveniatur.
units.tr: 47. If therefore Your Holiness, as you seem to request, intends to consult public quiet and the just liberty of Italy, let him lay down arms and put the sword of Peter back into its sheath, and bring it about that his allies also lay down their arms, which we too (as we have said) will do in the same agreement; so that, according to the canticle of Zachariah, freed without fear from our enemies, we may serve him. For once this foundation is laid, Your Holiness will more easily be able to build and labour for the outward face of universal peace (as the Psalmist says): When the peoples are gathered together, and the kings, to serve the Lord. And since the things of God are to be placed before all things, and public matters are rightly preferred to private ones, lest the passion of private persons disturb those things which are of God and which pertain to the public welfare, it seems fitting that first there be dealt with and agreed: how the enemies of the faith may be driven from the necks of Christians and, if it is lawful, brought to the fold of Christ; and how the sects and errors of the Lutherans and other heretics may be checked, corrected and calmed, and, if it be permitted, led back to the bosom of the Church; and all the other matters which may concern the state, salvation, preservation and increase of the Roman Church and of the whole Christian commonwealth.

units.la: 48. Demum de justis (ut ait S. vestra) à ratione & æquitate non alienis, privatorum seu fœderatorum querelis, & petitionibus merito ut transigatur conveniri poterit. In quibus tam publicis quam privatis. Si Vest. Sanctit. recto ordine intendere, ac ad ea animum adjicere velit: veri patris ac pastoris officium assumendo, comperiet nos velut devotissimum ac observantissimum filium, illi obtemperantem & obsequentem. Ita in omnibus juri, rationi, æquitati subnixum: ut nihil injustum indebitumve petituri seu desideraturi simus: quin potius justis aliorum petitionibus satisfacturi: ac si expediret, de proprio daturi & dimissuri, pro ipsius Christianæ reipublicæ commodo, proque Christianæ religio-nis augmento. Pro quo etiam imperium, regna, dominia, & quicquid nobis Deus & natura concessit, ac denique vitam ipsam exposituri sumus. Rursus pollicentes nos hæc verba nostra. (Si vestra Sanctitas rem paterno amore complectatur) factis & operibus comprobaturos nihilque omnino pro arte nostra obmissuros, quod ad rem ipsam recte disponendam ac peragendam facere videatur. Quod secus quam putamus evenerit, vestra Sanctitas nostras justas rationes & requisitiones obaudiat. Protestamur coram Deo & hominibus, quod si quid inde ministri Christianæ religioni evenerit, id neque quam nostræ culpæ ascribi possit: à qua omnino nos immunes servare curabimus, nil tamen prætermissuri de his, quæ ad nostram necessariam defensionem videbuntur pertinere quam totis viribus atque conatibus prosequi cogimur, omnibus illis viis ac mediis, quibus & divino & humano jure licebit, & nostra tueri licebit: & quibus honor & dignitas nobis salvi & illæsi permanent: & integre conservententur. Obsecramus igitur Vestram sanctitatem ea reciproca obsecratione, qua erga nos ut ex per viscera videlicet misericordiæ Dei nostri, & per eam spem quam de Vest. Sanct. ad Christianæ nominis salutem conceperamus. Obsecramus etiam per claves illas, quas dominus noster Jesus, ad pascendam Christicolis viam, in regnum cœlorum Petro commisit, quarum etiam administrationem Vestra Sanctitas ut ejusdem Petri successor assumpsit, illis ut decet utendo: Dignetur hæc Christianitatis incommoda & pericula, sua moderatione sedare: ipsamque universalem pacem dirigere, ac perpetuo fundamento stabilire. Habet nunc Vest. Sanctit. veram & apertam actorum & consiliorum nostrorum rationem. Habet ultimas excusationes ac justificationes nostras adversus crimina & opprobria, quæ nobis injuste quidem objiciebantur. Habet nostram sanam, rectamque intentionem, ac voluntarem ad bonum publicum & pacem generalem, quietemque universalem. Habet hilalem nostram devotionem & observantiam. Si Vest. Sanct. paterno amore nos ut filium complectentur, censuerit, si ipsas excusationes ac justificationes nostras, tanquam veras & legitimas, tatalque & gratas habeat: hisque se contentam reddar, ac si de culpis nobis objectis satisfactum putet, nosque ' is culpis carere profiteatur, & sua pronunciatione declaret. Id demum supplicantes ut V.S. non putet: cogi et seu recordetur injuriam seu offensam nobis fuisse illatam, necarbitretur nos præteritorum memoriam habituruin. Sed V.S. eorum omnium oblivisceatur, ut sic recedant vetera novaque sint omnia: cum & nos idem facturi simus. Si V.S. id prout supplicavimus ad miserit.
units.tr: 48. Finally, concerning the just complaints and petitions of private persons or of allies, which (as Your Holiness says) are not alien from reason and equity, it may rightly be agreed that they be settled. In these matters, both public and private, if Your Holiness is willing to proceed in due order and give attention to them, assuming the office of a true father and shepherd, you will find us as a most devoted and dutiful son, obedient and compliant to you. We are so grounded in law, reason and equity in all things that we shall seek or desire nothing unjust or undue; rather we shall satisfy the just petitions of others, and, if it were expedient, give and let go of our own, for the good of the Christian commonwealth and for the increase of the Christian religion. For this we shall also expose our empire, kingdoms, dominions, and whatever God and nature have granted us, and finally life itself. Again, we promise that we will confirm these our words (if Your Holiness embraces the matter with fatherly love) by facts and deeds, and will omit nothing in our power that seems to contribute to arranging and carrying out the matter rightly. If it turns out otherwise than we think, let Your Holiness heed our just reasons and requests. We protest before God and men that if anything of harm to the Christian religion ensues from this, it cannot be ascribed to our fault; from which we will take care to keep ourselves wholly free, yet we shall omit nothing of those things which seem to pertain to our necessary defence, which we are compelled to pursue with all our strength and endeavours, by all those ways and means by which it will be lawful both by divine and human right, and by which our honour and dignity may remain safe and unharmed and be kept entire. We therefore beseech Your Holiness with that mutual entreaty by which we have been moved toward you, namely through the bowels of mercy of our God, and through that hope which we had conceived of Your Holiness for the salvation of the Christian name. We beseech you also by those keys which our Lord Jesus committed to Peter for opening the way of heaven to the faithful, the administration of which Your Holiness has assumed as successor of the same Peter: may it please you to use them as is fitting, to calm by your moderation these discomforts and dangers of Christendom, to direct universal peace itself, and to establish it on a lasting foundation. Your Holiness now has a true and open account of our deeds and counsels. You have our final excuses and justifications against the crimes and reproaches which were unjustly laid against us. You have our sound and upright intention and will towards the public good, general peace and universal quiet. You have our cheerful devotion and observance. If Your Holiness, with fatherly love, shall embrace us as a son, and shall judge, and hold as true, lawful and pleasing, our excuses and justifications, and shall be content with them, and think that satisfaction has been made for the faults laid against us, and shall declare by your own pronouncement that we are free of those faults; this finally we beg, that Your Holiness does not think us compelled, nor remember any injury or offence done to us, nor judge that we will retain the memory of past things. Rather let Your Holiness forget all of these, so that old things pass away and all things become new, since we too shall do the same. If Your Holiness shall send this, as we have asked.

units.la: 49. Verum si Sa.V. nos ab his culpis & objectis immunes non censuerit: nostrasque excusationes & justificationes, pro veris & ultimis non habuerit: si arma contra nos continuarit & illorum depositioni non consenserit: si universalem pacem amplecti nolit cum tunc non patris sed pastoris sed invasoris officium assumeret: si æque recte eorum judex non censeretur: nullo alio tunc superstite superiore, cui nos & nostra objicere debemus, eaqi; omnia quæ nobis objiciuntur aut ut posterum objici possent, vel tentati: sive personam, sive Imperium, regnaque & dominia concernant, vel & ea omnia quæ nobis ex adverso, pro nostra justificatione & innocentia, ad Christianæ reipub. getem prætendimus, & prætendere possumus ad sacri generalis Concilii totius Christianitatis co-lo-nē & judicium remittrenda censuimus. Illique nos & omnia quæ cum S.V. habere possumus, aut inceps habituri sumus, omnino subjicimus. Supplicamus præterea eidem vestræ sanctitati illam, domino hortamur: quatenus pro suo pastorali officio proq; cura & sollicitudine gregis sibi committi dignetur ipsum sacrum generale Concilium indicere, & convocare in loco tuto & congruo, cum debita termini præfixione. Nos enim cum ex his & aliis satis notoriis causis turbari videremus universum ecclesiæ & Christianæ religionis statum, ut nobis ac ipsius reipubl. saluti consulatur, pro his omnibus ad ipsum sacrum universale Concilium, cujus etiam officium per viam querelæ his de causis implorandum censemus: petentes, cum ea qua decet instantia, apostolos & literas dimissorias semel, bis, ter, & plures nobis concedi, & de horum petitione testimoniales literas fieri, ac expeditiones, qua decet forma quibus suis loco & tempore uti valeamus. Et cum ad hæc solenniter peragenda ejusdem solennitatis præsentia minime habere queamus, ut inde forsan futuris gravamin-bus occurramus: has nostras ejus Nuncio Apostolico penes nos agenti & legationis munere nomine Ve. S. fungenti, per actum publicum, coram notario & testibus exhibendas, intimandasque censuimus.
units.tr: 49. But if Your Holiness does not judge us free of these faults and objections, and does not hold our excuses and justifications as true and final; if you continue to wage arms against us and do not consent to their laying down; if you are unwilling to embrace universal peace, then you would assume not the office of a father, nor of a shepherd, but of an invader; if you are not held an equally right judge of them, and no other superior is left over us, to whom we ought to submit ourselves and our affairs, and all those things which are objected to us, or which might be objected in future, or attempted, whether they concern our person, our empire, kingdoms and dominions, or all those things which we put forward, and can put forward, on the other side for our justification and innocence before the body of Christendom: then we have decided to refer these matters to the judgment of the holy general Council of all Christendom. To it we wholly submit ourselves and all that we have, or shall in future have, with Your Holiness. We further beseech and urge that same Your Holiness, by the Lord, that, for your pastoral office and for care and concern for the flock committed to you, you would deign to convoke that holy general Council, and to summon it to a safe and suitable place, with a due fixing of the time. For since we see the state of the whole Church and of the Christian religion being disturbed by these and other sufficiently notorious causes, we decide that for the sake of the salvation of ourselves and of the commonwealth, recourse must be had, for all these things, to that holy universal Council, whose office we also think should be implored by way of complaint for these causes; asking, with due urgency, that letters of dismissal be granted to us once, twice, three times and more, and that testimonial letters be made of this petition, and dispatches drawn up in the proper form, so that we may use them in their proper place and time. And since we cannot be personally present to carry out these things solemnly with the required solemnity, so that perhaps we may thereby meet future burdens, we have decided that these our letters be delivered and intimated to your Apostolic Nuncio, who is with us and performs the office of legate in the name of Your Holiness, by a public act, before a notary and witnesses.

units.la: Datum in Civitate nostra Granatæ, die decimoseptimo mensis Septembris, Anno M.D.XXVI. Regnorum nostrorum Romani VIII. Aliorum vero omnium XI.
units.tr: Given in our city of Granada, on the seventeenth day of September, in the year 1526, in the eighth year of our Roman reign, and the eleventh of all our other kingdoms.

units.la: CAROLVS divina fauente clementia, Electus Romanorum Imperator semper Augustus, Rex Germaniæ, Hispaniarum, &c.
units.tr: CHARLES, by the favouring clemency of God, Elect Roman Emperor, ever Augustus, King of Germany, of Spain, etc.

units.la: EL RET
units.tr: THE KING

units.la: Alphonsus Valdesius.
units.tr: Alphonsus Valdesius.

units.la: CAROLI V. IMPER. AUG. RESCRIPTUM AD CLEMENTEM PAPAM VII.
units.tr: Rescript of Charles V, Emperor Augustus, to Pope Clement VII

units.la: BEATISSIME Pater, Domine Reverendissime; Non mediocri cordis dolore ad literas Sanctitatis Vestræ, quas viccesima tertia Junii ad nos dedit, rescripseramus, quum novissimè ejusdem Sanctitatis Vestræ Nuncius alias literas postridie à priorum data scriptas nobis exhibuit: in quibus licet adhuc videamus Sanctitatem vestram aliam certè opinione de nostra erga universam Respublicam Christianam, & sacrosanctam istam Sedem animo atque voluntate retinere, quàm actiones ipsæ nostræ promererentur, non potuimus tamen non lætati, perspicientes in eisdem literis Sanctitatem vestram propensiori æquiorique animo pacem optare, blandiusque quàm antea nobiscum agere. Atque utinam ita in potestate nostra esset, labantis Christianæ Reipubl. rebus consulere, & pacem universalem denuò componere, prout in aliorum manu bellum movere, & pacatam Christianam Rempub. turbare extitit: Videret profectò Sanctitas vestra ac cæteri ejus Fœderati, quàm sit alienus nostrer ab eorum opinione alienus, licet (ut verum fateamur) nequaquam nobis persuadere possumus nostram Sanctitatem vestram (quæ actiones nostras novit) hæc ex animo & verè dicere, sed potius terroribus quorundam, quibus Christiana tranquillitas minus expedit, perterrefacta ad hæc impulsa videtur. Speramus tamen Deum Opt. Max. cujus gratuita benignitate justa nostra causa hactenus approbata est, Sanctitatis vestræ animum mutaturum, ejusque electi populi saluti potius quàm privatis quorundam affectibus atque dolis consulturum: & Nos, qui & meritis & viribus nostris quodammodo semper divisi, in solius Dei præsidio spem nostram collocavimus, ejusque Clementiæ victorias nobis ab eo concessas acceptas tulimus, nostraque ita protecturum, ut evidentiori etiam testimonio animus noster cunctis patefiat, nosque commodius & liberius ipsius nomen & gloriam, qua nihil nobis charius unquam fuit, promovere valeamus.
units.tr: Most blessed Father, most reverend Lord: We had replied, not without great grief of heart, to the letter of Your Holiness which you sent to us on the twenty-third of June; and then your Holiness's Nuncio presented to us another letter, dated the day after the former. In these letters, although we still see that Your Holiness holds an opinion of our attitude toward the whole Christian Commonwealth and this most holy See that is far different from what our actions deserve, we could not help rejoicing, perceiving in the same letters that Your Holiness desires peace with a more favourable and fairer mind, and deals with us more kindly than before. And would that it were so in our power, to look after the affairs of the tottering Christian Commonwealth and to compose universal peace again, just as it has been in the hands of others to stir up war and disturb the peaceful Christian Commonwealth! Your Holiness and the others of your confederacy would surely see how far our conduct is from their opinion of it, although (to tell the truth) we can by no means persuade ourselves that Your Holiness, who knows our actions, says these things from the heart and truly, but rather that you seem to have been frightened into this by the terrors of certain men, to whom Christian tranquillity is less advantageous. Yet we hope that God, Best and Greatest, by whose free kindness our just cause has hitherto been approved, will change the mind of Your Holiness and will look to the safety of his chosen people rather than to the private passions and deceits of certain men. And we, who have always in some measure relied upon our own merits and strength, but have placed our hope in the protection of God alone, and have accepted with thanks the victories granted us by his Clemency, will so protect our cause that our mind may be made plain to all by even clearer testimony, and that we may be able to promote more conveniently and more freely his name and glory, than which nothing has ever been dearer to us.

units.la: 2. Sanctitatem igitur vestram quanto possumus affectu rogamus, ac per effusum Jesu Christi Redemptoris nostri sanguinem obtestamur, ut Christiani populi calamitatibus profiiciat, nec tot cædes, tot vulnera, totque horrenda mala in Christi corpus, cujus Sanctitatem vestram caput esse profitemur, inferri patiatur.
units.tr: 2. We therefore ask Your Holiness with all the affection we can, and beseech you by the blood of Jesus Christ our Redeemer poured out, that you would be moved by the calamities of the Christian people, and not permit so many slaughters, so many wounds, and so many dreadful evils to be inflicted upon the body of Christ, of which we profess Your Holiness to be the head.

units.la: 3. De peculiari verò nostra erga Sanctitatem vestram voluntate ingenuè fatebimur, nos nihil unquam prætermisisse, quod ad obedientis filii officium pertinere posset.
units.tr: 3. Concerning our particular will toward Your Holiness, we shall frankly confess that we have never omitted anything that could pertain to the duty of an obedient son.

units.la: Datum in civitate nostra Granatæ, die xviii. mensis Septembris, anno Domini M.D.XXVI. Regnorum nostrorum, Romani octavo, aliorum vero omnium undecimo.
units.tr: Given in our city of Granada, on the eighteenth day of September, in the year of the Lord 1526, in the eighth year of our kingdoms of Rome, and the eleventh of all the others.

units.la: CAROLVS divina fauente Clementia, Electus Romanorum Imperator, semper Augustus, ac Germaniæ, Hispaniarum, &c. Rex.
units.tr: CHARLES, by the favour of divine Clemency, Elected Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, and King of Germany, of Spain, etc.

units.tr: TO THE SENATE, OR COLLEGE OF CARDINALS, so that they may themselves announce a general council if the Pope refuses or delays to announce it.

units.la: CAROLUS divina favente Clementia, &c. Reverendissimis in Christo Patribus, Dominis N. Sa. Rom. Ecclesiae Cardinalibus, amicis nostris Charissimis, salutem cum incremento omnis boni.
units.tr: CHARLES, by the favour of divine clemency, etc., to the most reverend Fathers in Christ, our lords N., cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, our most dear friends, greeting, with the increase of every good.

units.la: 1. Reverendissimi in Christo Patres, amici charissimi, tanto profecto animi dolore mens nostra disciruciatur, dum ea, quae Romanum Pontificem suae Pontificiae dignitatis oblitum non contra nos tantum (id enim aequiori animo pateremur) verum in maximum Christiani nominis dedecus, contraque totius Reipub. (quam induxeramus) pacem & tranquillitatem moliri audimus, ut tamen animo certe perturbato, moderatis tamen verbis mentem nostram vobis aperire, actionum nostrarum (quanta pro rei magnitudine licebit brevitate) rationem reddere, & a Reverendissimis Paternitatibus vestris nostro ac totius Christiani populi nomine auxilium implorare cogamur.
units.tr: 1. Most reverend Fathers in Christ, our dearest friends, our mind is indeed tormented with such great grief, while we hear of the plans that the Roman Pontiff, forgetful of his pontifical dignity, is devising, not only against us (for we could bear that with a more even mind) but to the greatest disgrace of the Christian name and against the peace and tranquillity of the whole commonwealth, which we had established. Yet, though our mind is certainly troubled, we are compelled to open our mind to you in moderate words, to give an account of our actions (as briefly as the magnitude of the matter allows), and to implore help from your Reverend Paternities in the name of ourselves and of the whole Christian people.

units.la: 2. Quum enim in ipso Imperii nostri initio a Deo Opt. Max. in tanti Principatus culmine constitutos arbitraremur, non ut Imperii limites cum Christiani sanguinis jactura extendere propagareque studeremus, sed quo Imperialis dignitas autoritate & potentia decorata, & observaretur a multis, & contemneretur a paucis, indeque Christiana Respub. bellorum injuriis in extremum fere discrimen adducta, sempiterna tandem Caesareae dignitatis beneficio pace frueretur. Hoc itaque animo relicta Hispania ad Germaniam venimus, ortas ibidem seditiones inter quosdam Principes, divino favore sedamus, nihilque omittimus, quod (judicio nostro) ab optimo Caesare sperari poterat.
units.tr: 2. For at the very beginning of our empire, we considered ourselves placed by God, the best and greatest, at the summit of so great a principality, not so that we should strive to extend and enlarge the limits of the empire at the cost of Christian blood, but so that the imperial dignity, adorned with authority and power, might be respected by many and scorned by few; and so that the Christian commonwealth, brought almost to the brink of ruin by the injuries of wars, might at last enjoy peace by the everlasting benefit of the imperial dignity. With this intention we left Spain and came to Germany, and there we quelled, by divine favour, the seditions that had arisen among certain princes, and we omit nothing that could (in our judgement) be hoped for from the best of emperors.

units.la: 3. Verum dum nos Christianam tranquillitatem stabilire curamus, ecce Gallorum Rex, quem uti patrem colebamus, nostrae dignitati subinvidens, in statum ac honorem nostrum nihil non moliri conatur, nosque tandem ad arma provocat invitos. Fatetur hoc Summus Pontifex Leo, fatetur Serenissimus Angliae Rex, quos pro pace a Gallo obtinenda saepius sollicitari fecimus, quique iis virtus justae nostrae causae adesse non negarunt. Fatetur & hoc divina justicia, quae ita nobis adfuit, ut post tot partas victorias, omni humano tandem auxilio destituti, victis hostibus, eorumque Rege capto, victores evaserimus. Hinc data opportunitate, qua nostro de Republ. bene merendi studio satisfacere liceret, ab ipsis hostibus victis pacem primi flagitamus, tantumque petimus, ut quae a praedecessorum nostrorum manibus eripuerant, & contra jus fasque occupabant, nobis restituerentur. Aequissima postulata nostra impetramus, pacem inimus, foedus percutimus, & nihil in eo cautum volumus, nisi quae ad Dei gloriam, communem Reipubl. pacem, Christianae religionis decorem & augmentum, & sanctae Sedis Apostolicae veram dignitatem pertinere arbitramur. Percusso foedere, Gallorum Regem captivum nostrum convenimus, omnibus beneficiis, omni humanitate atque benevolentia ejus animum pro Christiana tranquillitate nobis devincire curamus, & mutuo data acceptaque fide, amicitiam firmamus, ac maximo eum honore affectum in Galliam, datis obsidibus, redire permittimus: ad Pontificem caeterosque Christianos Reges scribimus, ut si Christianam Remp. pacatam optarent, eorum patentes literas ad nostrum utrumque mitterent, quibus an hujusmodi foederis beneficio uti vellent, prout conventum fuerat, declararent.
units.tr: 3. But while we were striving to establish Christian tranquillity, behold, the King of the French, whom we had honoured as a father, begrudging our dignity, attempts to contrive everything against our state and honour, and at last provokes us to arms against our will. The Supreme Pontiff Leo confesses this, and the most serene King of England confesses it, whom we often caused to be asked to help obtain peace from the French, and who did not refuse to lend their support to the justice of our cause. Divine justice also confesses it, which so stood by us that, after so many victories had been gained, and we were at last deprived of all human help, the enemies were defeated, their King was taken captive, and we emerged as victors. Hence, with the opportunity given, by which we might satisfy our desire to deserve well of the commonwealth, we first asked the defeated enemies for peace, and we sought only that what had been snatched from the hands of our predecessors and was held against law and right should be restored to us. We obtained our most equitable demands, we made peace, we struck a treaty, and we wished nothing in it to be provided for except what we judged to pertain to the glory of God, the common peace of the commonwealth, the honour and increase of the Christian religion, and the true dignity of the Holy Apostolic See. With the treaty struck, we met the King of the French, our captive, and we took care to bind his mind to us for Christian tranquillity by every kindness, every courtesy and goodwill; and, with faith given and received on both sides, we confirmed friendship, and, having honoured him greatly, we allowed him to return to France, with hostages given. We wrote to the Pontiff and the other Christian kings that, if they wished the Christian commonwealth to be at peace, they should send their open letters to each of us, by which they might declare whether they wished to use the benefit of such a treaty, as had been agreed.

units.la: 4. Nondum tamen sempiternam in Christi populo pacem firmasse gloriari caeperamus, quum novos bellorum tumultus pullulare gravissima animi nostri molestia sentimus. At ubi a Pontifice, de nobis (ut ajebant) non bene contento, id manare audimus, Don Hugonem de Moncada Oratorem nostrum mittimus cum facultate amplissimisque mandatis, ut omnibus mediis, quibus id fieri posset, Pontificem de nobis contentum reddere curaret, ita ut homine audito, nostro animo perspecto, nil aliud a nobis optasse suis ipsemet verbis fateretur. Dumque nil tanto Pastore indignum nobis polllicentes, cujus optimum responsum praestolamur, Pontificis Nuncius literas Sanctitatis suae in forma Brevis proxime elapsi mensis Junii die xxiii, scriptas, xx. Augusti nobis legendas dedit, quibus perlectis, quum non tantum a summo Ecclesiae pastore, a communi omnium patre, Christiqué Vicario, sed etiam a Reverendissimis Paternitatibus vestris sacroque vestro Ordine, quibus Apostolorum autoritas tribuitur, emanatas esse credimus (nec enim rem tanti momenti vobis inconsultis factam putamus) quo simus animi dolore affecti, vos ipsi judicate. Quis enim non miraretur stupuretque, videns a tanto Pontifice, a tot tantisque, tanta religione, pietate, atque prudentia praeditis Patribus tales literas in Christiani Principis, Rom. Caesaris, atq; Apostolicae Sedis protectoris, honorem & dignitatem tam inconsulte prodire? in quibus nihil praeter bella, seditiones, proditiones, perniciosa consilia, temeraria judicia, improperia, injurias, falsas criminationes, aliaque hujusmodi tam a Pontificia dignitate aliena tractantur, idque in Nos optime de Republ. Christiana meritos, & qui nullum unquam nec Caesarem, nec Regem, nec Principem, nec privatum aliquem fuisse fatebimur, qui majori (nec tanta quidem) fide, religione, atque obsequentia sanctam Sedem Apostolicam veneratus sit, qui caeteris posthabitis majori studio ejus ditione & dignitatem tutatus sit.
units.tr: 4. Yet we had not yet begun to boast that we had established everlasting peace among the people of Christ, when we perceive with the greatest distress of our mind that new tumults of war are springing up. But when we hear from the Pontiff, who (as they said) was not well pleased with us, that this was spreading, we send Don Hugo de Moncada as our envoy, with full powers and the most ample instructions, to take care, by every means by which it could be done, to render the Pontiff pleased with us, so that, after hearing the man and perceiving our mind, he himself might confess in his own words that he had wished nothing else from us. And while we, promising nothing unworthy of so great a Pastor, await his best answer, the Pontiff's Nuncio gave us to read a letter of His Holiness, in the form of a Brief, written on the 23rd day of June of the month just past, to be read by us on the 20th of August. When it had been read, we believe that it has issued not only from the supreme pastor of the Church, the common father of all and Vicar of Christ, but also from your Reverend Paternities and your sacred Order, to whom the authority of the Apostles is attributed (for we do not think that a matter of such importance was done without your counsel). With what grief of mind we were affected, you yourselves may judge. For who would not be astonished and amazed to see such letters issue so inconsiderately from so great a Pontiff, and from so many and such great Fathers endowed with such religion, piety and prudence, against the honour and dignity of a Christian prince, the Roman Emperor and protector of the Apostolic See? In them nothing is treated except wars, seditions, treasons, pernicious counsels, rash judgements, reproaches, injuries, false accusations and other things of this kind, altogether foreign to the pontifical dignity; and this is done against us, who have deserved very well of the Christian commonwealth, and of whom we will admit that no emperor, king, prince, nor any private man has ever been, who with greater (or indeed no such) faith, religion and obedience has venerated the Holy Apostolic See, or who, having set aside all others, has with greater zeal defended its dominion and dignity.

units.la: 5. Parmam enim & Placentiam, a Romani Imperii feudo disjunctas, Sedi Romanae, nullo jure cote coacti, possidendas restituimus; importunasq; Germaniæ & universi Romani Imperii preces contra Gravamina & oppressiones, quasi à Sede Romana pati, quum in Wormatiensi Coventu essemus, passim conquerebantur, obturatis auribus pro innata nostra erga Apostolicam Sedem observantia obaudivimus. Subortæ sunt ea de causa varie rerum difficultates & incommoda; pullulat indies magis Lutheranorum insania; Gravamina ubique divulgantur; omnes unanimes remedium implorant, petunt fieri Generale Concilium, in quo & Lutheranæ impietati, & Romanæ Curiæ (ut ajunt) oppressionibus obviam iri possit. In civitate Spirensi Conciliabulum indicunt, ut in seditionibus ortis usque ad Generalis Concilii decisionem ordo aliquis statueretur. Vidimus Germanorum animos in Sedem Romanam graviter commotos, verentesq; ne hujusmodi Conciliabulum Germaniam à Romani Pontificis obedientia averteret, Spirensem congregationem gravissimis poenis prohibemus; eis tamen polliceimur, quanto citius fieri possit, Generalis Concilii indictionem fieri curaturos. De hac re ad Pontificem scribimus, ut Germaniam ab imminenti periculo per hujusmodi Generalis Concilii indictionem liberare dignaretur, instamus. Ipse vero de Conciliabuli prohibitione gratiam habet, Generalis tamen Concilii petitionem in tempus (ut ajebat) magis cōvenies differendam censuit, ita ut pro nostra erga sanctam istam Sedem observantia, maluerimus Pontificis affectibus potius quam Germaniæ precibus annuere.
units.tr: 5. For we restored Parma and Piacenza, which were separated from the fief of the Roman Empire, to be possessed by the Roman See, compelled by no right whatever; and when we were at the Diet of Worms, the importunate prayers of Germany and of the whole Roman Empire, which were everywhere complaining about grievances and oppressions supposedly suffered from the Roman See, we heard with ears closed, out of our innate observance towards the Apostolic See. On this account various difficulties and inconveniences have arisen; the madness of the Lutherans grows daily; grievances are published everywhere; all unanimously implore a remedy, and ask that a General Council be held, in which both the impiety of the Lutherans and the oppressions (as they say) of the Roman Curia might be met. They announced a conventicle in the city of Speyer, so that in the seditions that had arisen some order might be established until the decision of a General Council. Seeing that the minds of the Germans were gravely stirred against the Roman See, and fearing lest such a conventicle should turn Germany away from obedience to the Roman Pontiff, we forbade the Speyer assembly under the most severe penalties; yet we promised them that they would, as soon as possible, see to the announcement of a General Council. We have written to the Pontiff about this matter, urging him to deign to free Germany from the imminent danger by the announcement of such a General Council. But he indeed granted the prohibition of the conventicle as a favour, yet he judged that the petition for a General Council should be deferred to a more convenient time (as he said), so that, out of our observance towards this Holy See, we preferred to yield to the inclinations of the Pontiff rather than to the prayers of Germany.

units.la: 6. Nunc vero Sanctitas sua, vestro etiam (si id credendum est) accedente consilio, tot crimina in nos jactitat, ac si penitus Romanæ Ecclesiæ adversarii hactenus fuissemus. Hinc enim de nostro erga publicam pacem animo (nullo profecto recto judicio) dubitat, nosque à Christianæ Reipubl. perturbatione deterret. Quasi vero noster erga Rempub. animus clarior non sit, quam ut cujuspiam admonitione egeat. Si enim de C. Cæsare judicatum est, quod maluisset non dimicare quam vincere, eoque victoria adepta pacis autores libenter audiverit, cur de nostra voluntate à communi omnium parte per contrarium discernitur? Ille pacis autores audivit, nos vero hostibus victis pacem primi obtulimus, nec tantum hostem captivum Regiæ dignitati restituisse contenti, Lusitaniæ Reginam sororem nostram natu maximam, & in successionis gradu secundam ipsi matrimonio copulavimus, quod profecto ante victoriam minime à nobis impetrare potuisset. Quanto igitur nostra C. Cæsaris Clementiam excedere deberet, vos ipsi judicate.
units.tr: 6. But now His Holiness, with your counsel also (if this is to be believed), hurls so many charges against us as if we had hitherto been utterly enemies of the Roman Church. For thus he doubts (by no sound judgement at all) our mind towards public peace, and he deters us from disturbing the Christian commonwealth. As if our mind towards the commonwealth were not clearer than that it should need anyone's admonition! For if it has been judged of Gaius Caesar that he would rather not have fought than conquered, and that, having gained victory, he willingly listened to the authors of peace, why is our will, by the common voice of all, judged to the contrary? He listened to the authors of peace; but we, when the enemies were conquered, first offered peace, and, not content merely to restore the captive enemy to royal dignity, we also joined in marriage to him our eldest sister, the Queen of Portugal, who stands second in the order of succession; a thing which we could certainly not have obtained from him before the victory. How much, therefore, our clemency ought to exceed that of Gaius Caesar, you yourselves may judge.

units.la: 7. Adhæc etiam Pontifex consilia nostra ad suæ dignitatis & Ecclesiasticæ libertatis oppressionem tendere, videtur asseverare, quum ea, quæ pro Romana Sede præstita commemoravimus, adeò omnibus nota sint, ut inde nonnihil Germanorum animos à nobis alienaverimus.
units.tr: 7. Moreover, the Pontiff seems to assert that our plans are aimed at the oppression of his dignity and of ecclesiastical liberty, since the services we have rendered on behalf of the Roman See are so well known to all that they have somewhat alienated the minds of the Germans from us.

units.la: 8. Perpendite igitur Patres Reverendissimi, an in hoc Pontificis Beatitudo suis, & Apostolicæ Sedis rebus consulat, an sit Pontificiæ dignitatis Christianorum Principum animos adversus Ecclesiæ protectorem ad arma (ut ipsi ajunt) incitare, ac suis stipendiis tot corporibus atq; animabus æternum exitium parare. Causam audite, ut subditum nostrum magni sceleris accusatum, nobis jure prævio punire non liceat, ob id q; armis nobiscum certare contendit. Quod tamen si ex sententia succederet, quid quæso Christi Vicario dignum facturus esset, nisi ut justiciam, quam promovere tenebatur, impediat; Ecclesiæ thesaurum in alios certe usus convertendum exhauriat, ac Romanam Ecclesiam, & universum populum Christianum in extremum discrimen adducat? Hæc ergo atque hujusmodi alia ingenti cordis dolore, perturbato animo pensirantes, publicam Christianam calamitatem nobiscum deplorare cœpimus, atq; non nostro tantum honori, sed Christi gloriæ, ejusq; electi populi saluti consulere ex animo cupientes, ad Pontificis literas rescribimus, justificationem de his, quæ nobis falsò objiciuntur, damus, petimusq; ut Generale Concilium indicat, a alia faciat, quæ ex incluso literarum nostrarum exemplo vobis videre licebit.
units.tr: 8. Consider therefore, Most Reverend Fathers, whether in this matter the Beatitude of the Pontiff is looking after his own affairs and those of the Apostolic See, or whether it befits the dignity of the Pontiff to incite the minds of Christian princes against the protector of the Church to arms (as they themselves say), and by their pay to prepare eternal ruin for so many bodies and souls. Hear the cause: a subject of ours, accused of a great crime, is contending that he may resist us by arms, because it is not permitted for us, under the prior law, to punish him. Yet if this should succeed according to his wish, what, I ask, would the Vicar of Christ have done that was worthy of him, except to impede the justice which he was bound to promote, exhaust the treasury of the Church to be spent certainly on other uses, and bring the Roman Church and the whole Christian people into the greatest peril? Therefore, weighing these and similar matters with great grief of heart and a troubled mind, we have begun to lament with you the public calamity of Christendom, and, desiring from the heart to provide not only for our honour but for the glory of Christ and the salvation of his chosen people, we have written back to the Pontiff's letter, we give a justification of those things which are falsely objected to us, and we ask that he appoint a General Council or do other things, as you will be able to see from the enclosed copy of our letter.

units.la: 9. Quæ omnia, Patres Reverendissimi, vos latere noluimus, ut si ex literis Pontificis, ejusve suasionibus siniistram aliquam suspicionem animi nostri erga sacrosanctam istam Sedem nō bene dispositi concepistis, justificationibus nostris, recto judicio, perspectis, pristinum vestrum erga nos animum induatis, ac omnem prorsus iniquam opinionem abjicientes, labanti Christianitati subveniatis.
units.tr: 9. All these things, Most Reverend Fathers, we did not wish to hide from you, so that if from the Pontiff's letters, or from his persuasions, you have conceived some unfavourable suspicion of our mind towards that most sacred See, then, having perceived our justifications with a right judgment, you may restore your former goodwill towards us, cast aside every unjust opinion, and come to the aid of a tottering Christendom.

units.la: 10. Agite igitur, Patres Reverendissimi, & tanti mali causam cognoscite, Romanum Pontificem tam impio avertite consilio, vestrisq; monitis tantum apud eum efficite, ut meminerit se à Deo Opt. Max. non ad perniciem, sed ad salutem sui populi; non ad arma, sed patientiam & humilitatem in Romani Pontificatus solio constitutum; recordetur q; nos eadem ratione in Romani Principatus apicem evectos, unde peculiari quodam affectu Christianæ Reip. rebus consulere præcæteris tenemur, ni à Principe nostro Christo degenerare velimus. Si vero Beatitudo Pontificis votis nostris tam pro nostra justificatione, quā pro Christianæ religionis salute in Generalis Concilii indictione annuere negaverit, tunc juxta juris ordinem Reverendissimas Paternitates vestras, ac sacrum vestrum Collegium hortamur, requirimus, atq; monemus, ut quæ de indictione Concilii à Pontifice petimus, eo negante, aut plus æquo differente, vos debito ordine procedentes, præstare non differatis. Protestantes apud omnipotentem Deum, si quid inde incommodi ac detrimenti Romanæ Ecclesiæ & Reip. Christianæ accederit, id non nostra, sed eorum culpa futurum, qui suis affectibus potius quam Christi gloriæ, ejusq; populi salutī inservire maluerint: quod de vestro erga Christianam Remp. animo atq; voluntate nobis minime persuadere volumus. Si vero Reverendissimæ Paternitates vestræ æquissima hujusmodi postulata nostra cōcedere negaverint, eorumve executione plusquā decet, ac dignitatis nostræ ratio expostulat, distulerint, nos pro nostra erga Deū gratitudine, proq; dignitate nostra Imperiali, qua ejus gratnita benignitate fungimur, quib. licebit remediis, ita in his pro virili providere curabimus, ut nec Christiglo- riæ nec justiciæ nostræ, nec Christianæ Reip. saluti, paci, & tranquillitati quovis modo defuisse videamur.
units.tr: 10. Come then, Most Reverend Fathers, and learn the cause of so great an evil; turn the Roman Pontiff from so impious a purpose, and by your admonitions bring it about with him that he remembers that he has been placed by God, the Best and Greatest, on the throne of the Roman Pontificate not for the destruction but for the salvation of his people, not for arms but for patience and humility; and let him recall that we too have been raised to the summit of the Roman principate on the same plan, whence we are bound by a peculiar affection to look after the affairs of the Christian commonwealth above all others, unless we wish to degenerate from our Prince Christ. But if the Beatitude of the Pontiff shall refuse to assent to our prayers, both for our justification and for the salvation of the Christian religion, in the summoning of a General Council, then, according to the order of law, we exhort, require and admonish your Most Reverend Paternities and your sacred College that what we ask of the Pontiff concerning the summoning of the Council, if he refuses or delays beyond what is fair, you proceed in due order and do not delay to carry it out. We protest before almighty God that if any harm or detriment shall accrue from this to the Roman Church and the Christian commonwealth, it will be the fault not of us but of those who have preferred to serve their own passions rather than the glory of Christ and the salvation of his people; which we do not wish to believe of your mind and will towards the Christian commonwealth. But if your Most Reverend Paternities shall refuse to grant these most just demands of ours, or have delayed their execution more than is fitting and the reason of our dignity demands, then we, out of our gratitude towards God and out of our Imperial dignity, which we hold by his gratuitous kindness, will take care, to the extent of our strength and by whatever remedies will be permitted us, so to provide in these matters that we may seem in no way to have failed the glory of Christ, our justice, or the safety, peace and tranquillity of the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: Datum in civitate nostra Granatæ, die sexta mensis Octobris, anno Domini M. D. XXVI. Regnorum nostrorum, Romani octavo, aliorum vero omnium undecimo.
units.tr: Given in our city of Granada, on the sixth day of October, in the year of the Lord 1526, in the eighth year of our reign as Roman emperor, and the eleventh of all our other kingdoms.

units.la: YO EL REY
units.tr: YO EL REY

units.la: Alphonsus Valdesius.
units.tr: Alphonsus Valdesius.

units.la: CAROLI V. IMPER. AUG. EDICTUM SVPER CAVSA GALLICA, ET CONVENTIO- NE Madritia.
units.tr: The Edict of Charles V, Emperor Augustus, concerning the French cause and the Convention of Madrid.

units.la: Carolus divina favente Clementia, Electus Romanorum Imperator, Semper Augustus, &c.
units.tr: Charles, by the favour of divine clemency, elected Roman Emperor, ever Augustus, etc.

units.la: Reverendissimis & Illustrissimis Principibus, Sa. Rom. Imperii Electoribus, &c.
units.tr: To the most reverend and illustrious Princes, the Electors of the Holy Roman Empire, etc.

units.la: REVERENDISSIMÆ in Christo Patres, ac Venerabiles, Illustres Principes, amice & consanguinei charissimi. Quæ nostra hactenus de Reipublicæ salute, pace, quiete, & tranquillitate fuerint consilia, adeò omnibus notum arbitramur, ut nullâ hominum malitiâ, fama, honorve nostr ulla ex parte læđi posse videatur. Semper enim ejus animi fuimus, ut non fucatis verbis, & à veritate prorsus alienis (utá plærisque fit) sed reipsa actiones omnes nostras non apud paucos, eosq; omnis recti judicii expertes, sed apud Deum ipsum Opt. Max. qui corda etiam scrutatur, & apud universam Rempub. Christianam comprobaremus.
units.tr: Most reverend fathers in Christ, and venerable, illustrious princes, dear friends and kinsmen. We think it so well known to all what our counsels have been hitherto concerning the safety, peace, quiet and tranquillity of the commonwealth that they seem unable to be harmed in any way by the malice, reputation or honour of men. For we have always been of the mind that our actions should be approved, not by feigned words utterly alien to the truth (as is often the case with most people), but in deed: not before a few who lack all sound judgement, but before God, the best and greatest, who also searches the hearts, and before the whole Christian commonwealth.

units.la: 2. Hinc enim (ne vetustiora repetamus) dum proprii commodi, atq; etiam gloriæ oblii, Reipub. saluti, & præsertim Germaniæ quieti ex animo consulere optamus, Gallorum Regem, quem (ut omnibus notum est) optimo jure captivum penes nos detinebamus, postquam omni benignitate & Clementia in his nostris Hispaniarum regnis excepimus, magnoq; honore à subditis nostris tractatus extitit, tot eum beneficiis affecimus, ut si suæ ipse felicitati non invidisset, in Ticinensi conflictu non modò non cecidisse, sed vicisse ab omnibus videri potuisset. Hostis erat, illi charissimam sororem nostram natu maximam, & in tantorum regnorum successionis gradu secundam matrimonio collocavimus, ut ex hoste sororius fieret. Christianæ Reipub. turbator communi omnium judicio habebatur, communis salutis gloriam illi impartiri voluimus. Multa à prædecessoribus nostris tum Hispaniarum Regibus, tum Burgundionum Ducibus, violenter occupaverat, & præter jus fasq; detinuerat: jura in his nostra illi concessimus, solumq; ab eo petiimus, quæ citra honoris & dignitatis nostræ diminutionem, ac subditorum nostrorum perpetuam indignationem omittere nequivimus, & quæ ipsemet vel non rogatus (si merito Christianissimus nuncupari vellet) nobis restituere debeter. Hisq; beneficiis affectum Regem captivum Regiæ dignitati restituimus, atq; (multis licet dissuadentibus, qui minus ejus fidei credendum asseverabant) illi in Galliam abeundi copiam fecimus, maluimusq; ejus fidem experiri, acilli de jure nostro aliquid potius cedere, quàm ut ulla Christianæ Reipub. mala, si quæ forsan evenirent, quovis modo criminì nostro nostræve culpæ ascribi possent.
units.tr: 2. For here (not to go back to older matters): while we, forgetting our own advantage and even glory, desire from the heart to care for the safety of the commonwealth and especially for the quiet of Germany, we held the King of the French, whom (as is known to all) we rightly held captive in our power. After we received him in our kingdoms of Spain with all kindness and clemency, and he was treated with great honour by our subjects, we bestowed so many benefits upon him that, had he not begrudged his own good fortune, he could have seemed to all to have not only not fallen at the battle of Ticino, but to have conquered there. He was an enemy; we joined to him in marriage our dearest sister, the eldest, and second in the line of succession to such great kingdoms, so that from an enemy he might become a brother-in-law. He was regarded by universal judgement as a disturber of the Christian commonwealth; we wished to share with him the glory of the common safety. He had violently seized many things from our predecessors, both the Kings of Spain and the Dukes of Burgundy, and held them beyond right and law. In these matters we granted him our rights, and asked from him only those things which, without diminution of our honour and dignity and the perpetual indignation of our subjects, we could not omit, and which he himself, even unasked (if he deservedly wished to be called most Christian), ought to have restored to us. With these benefits bestowed, we restored the captive King to his royal dignity, and (though many advised against it, asserting that less trust should be placed in his good faith) we gave him leave to depart into France. We preferred to test his good faith, and to let some of our right go, rather than that any evils befalling the Christian commonwealth, if perhaps they should happen, could in any way be ascribed to our fault or blame.

units.la: 3. Dumq; intestinis seditionibus pacatis, iter nostrum (uti inter nos convenerat) ad Italiam paramus, armaq; nostra in sempiternos religionis nostræ hostes communibus auspiciis convertenda disponimus, quibus & Hungaria defendi, & hostes submoveri potuissent, suam fidem ex nostro metientes animo, ille sævissimum bellum in nos parat, initoq; cum Romano Pontifice, aliisq; nonnullis Italiæ Potentatibus fœdere offensivo, divisoq; inter eos regno nostro Neapolitano; dum aliet varis pollicitationibus omnia, quæ nobis promiserat, se præstiturum asseverat, alter vero ad Hungariæ defensionem nos invitat, ut nos invaderent incautos, nostra ac sacri Romani Imperii domina horstilibus armis aggrediuntur, nullaq; nostri nec amoris nec benevolentiæ, nulla Christianæ Reipub. salutis, nulla religionis nostræ honoris ratio in his habita est.
units.tr: 3. And while, the internal seditions having been quelled, we were preparing our journey to Italy (as we had agreed between us), and were arranging to turn our arms, under common auspices, against the everlasting enemies of our religion, by which both Hungary could be defended and the enemies driven off, he, measuring his faith by our own mind, prepares most savage war against us. Having entered an offensive league with the Roman Pontiff and some other potentates of Italy, with our Neapolitan kingdom divided among them, he, on the one hand, while with various promises he asserts that he will perform everything he had pledged to us, and on the other hand invites us to the defence of Hungary, so that they might attack us while we were unwary, assails our dominions and those of the Holy Roman Empire with hostile arms. No consideration of our love or goodwill, no regard for the safety of the Christian commonwealth, no regard for the honour of our religion was had in these matters.

units.la: 4. Quorum conatus, quam ex eorum sententia justo Dei judicio minimè succedant, Gallus ipse Rex non contentus armis nobiscum congredi, convicia in nos jactat, eaque cum Regio privilegio typis excusa ubiq; circumferri curat, nihil veritus omnino contrariis operibus suamet verba irrita facere. Nos verò (tametsi nobis inscïus ad illam Apologiam seu potius Invectivam, quæ superioribus diebus cum decreto Regio Lutetiæ tum Latinè, tum etiam Gallorum communi idiomate, excusa fuerat, abunde satis responsum extitit) noluimus, immò expresse prohibuimus, ne quid tale in Regnis Dominiisq; nostris imprimeretur, maluimusq; ipsum virtute quàm convictiis vincere, sperantes fore, ut modestia nostra suam petulantiam compesceret.
units.tr: 4. Whose attempts, far from succeeding as they expected, by the just judgement of God, the French King himself, not content to contend with us in arms, hurls insults at us, and has them printed with royal privilege and circulated everywhere, not at all fearing to make his own words void by contrary deeds. We, however (although, unknown to us, a sufficient answer had been abundantly given to that Apology, or rather Invective, which in recent days had been published at Paris with a royal decree, both in Latin and in the common language of the French), did not wish, indeed we expressly forbade, that anything of the kind be printed in our kingdoms and lands. We preferred to conquer him by virtue rather than by reproaches, hoping that our moderation would check his insolence.

units.la: 5. Nunc verò quum exemplum literarum, quas Rex ipse ad vos, cæterosq; sacri Romani Imperii Status scripsit, ex his, quas ad ipsum pro obtinenda libera ad nos veniendi, atque hinc recedendi facultate pro Nuntiis Imperii nomine ad nos destinandis literas dederatis, occasione assumpta, huc allatum sit, non certè manu descriptum, sed Lutetiæ typis excusum, in eoq; ipsum Gallorum Regem suis propriis verbis in nos nostramq; dignitatem atq; honorem citra modestiam invehi videamus, tamen etiam eq etli eo certè animo simus, ut in his turbatis atq; adeò difficilimis temporibus publicam potiùs quàm privatam causam agere cupiamus, ne tamen nostra nimia taciturnitate falsis hujusmodi convitus atq; injuriis fidem quodammodo præstare videamur, velimus nolimus, omnibus veritatem aperire cogimur,atq; actionum nostrarum rationem reddere.
units.tr: 5. But now, since a copy of the letters which the King himself wrote to you and the other Estates of the Holy Roman Empire has been brought here, taken as an occasion from those which you had sent to him requesting the freedom to come to us and to depart hence, and to send envoys to us in the name of the Empire, not copied out by hand but printed at Paris, and in it we see the King of the French inveighing against us and our dignity and honour in his own words without moderation, nevertheless, although we are truly of the mind to pursue, in these troubled and indeed most difficult times, a public rather than a private cause, yet, lest by our excessive silence we seem in some measure to lend credence to such false reproaches and injuries, whether we will or no, we are compelled to lay the truth open to all and to render an account of our actions.

units.la: 6. Ad vos igitur * Apologiam illam, seu verius Invectivam, unà cum ejus Refutatione pro justificatione nostra edita, his annexam mittimus, ut plenius diffusiusq; pernoscatis, quo jure rationeve Gallus suam fidem atque jusjurandum violatum excusare queat: qua ratione se pacis cupidum ostendat, honestaq; pacis media se nobis obtulisse prædicet, dum non modò pactis stare noluerit, sed contra fidem ultrò citroque datam atque acceptam, offensivo fœdere contra nos percussò, cujusmodi exemplum cum his transmittimus, dominia nostra hostilibus armis invasit. Quo affectu Christianam Rempub. nostraq; religionis ornamentum, atq; Christi nominis gloriam prosequatur, qui dum sævissimum Turcarum Tyrannum cum magna militum atq; instrumentorum bellicorum copia Pannoniam invadere audivit, ille in nos bellum movet, viresq; nostras ad Hungariæ defensionem destinandas intra fines nostros pro subditorum nostrorum protectione continere coegit? Quo factum est ut cum maxima Christiani nominis ignominia hostis voto suo potius sit, firmissimo illo religionis propugnaculo suæ impiæ ditioni subjiciendo, florentissimo Rege extincto, Christiq; cultoribus à suis sedibus profligatis, tot templis prophanatis, fusoq; tot innocentium sanguine, quod certè non absque summo cordis dolore referre cogimur. Et quum his cæterisq; Reipub. calamitatibus atq; infortuniis ille causam dederit, nunc se ea molestè tulisse prædicat: quasi suis verbis majorem, quàm illius operibus propriisq; cujusvis oculis fidem habere velit. Hoc tamen animo hæc illum scripsisse arbitramur, ut obstitueret ora his, qui ejus literis interceptis, sua opera suoq; consilio Turcas Hungariam tanto impetu invasisse non cessant aflcverare. Verum aliorum verba omittamus, ad ipsius q; Regis literas tam fido simulatoq; dolore scriptas veniamus.
units.tr: 6. We therefore send you that Apology, or rather Invective, together with its Refutation published for our justification, annexed to this, so that you may learn more fully and at greater length by what right or reason the Frenchman can excuse his violated faith and oath; by what means he shows himself desirous of peace, and declares that he offered us honourable means of peace, when not only did he refuse to abide by the pacts, but, contrary to the faith given and received on both sides, struck an offensive league against us (of which kind of document we send a copy with these) and invaded our dominions with hostile arms. With what disposition he pursues the Christian commonwealth, the ornament of our religion and the glory of the name of Christ, he who, when he heard that the most savage Turkish tyrant was invading Pannonia with a great supply of soldiers and war-machines, moved war against us and forced us to keep within our borders the forces meant for the defence of Hungary and the protection of our subjects?
