As a result it has come about, to the greatest shame of the Christian name, that the enemy has rather achieved his wish of subjecting that most firm bulwark of religion to his impious rule: the most flourishing King has been destroyed, the worshippers of Christ have been driven from their seats, so many temples have been profaned, and so much innocent blood has been shed, which we are compelled to report not without the deepest grief of heart. And since he has given cause for these and the other calamities and misfortunes of the commonwealth, he now proclaims that he took them badly, as if he wished us to put more faith in his words than in his deeds, or in anyone's own eyes. We think, however, that he wrote these things with this intent: to stop the mouths of those who do not cease to assert that, by his intercepted letters and by his counsel and effort, the Turks invaded Hungary with such violence. But let us set aside the words of others, and come to the King's own letters, written with such faithful and feigned grief.

units.la: 7. Si Christianæ Religionis periculum timebat; si Rempub. salvam cupiebat; si ferrum, quod in fidei hostes stringendum erat; si vires, quæ in ipsos vertendæ; si consilia ad eos submovendos exercenda in nosmet ipsos converti, si Christianam manum Christianum sanguinem effundere tantopere execrabatur, cur ipsemet novis bellorum tumultibus excitatis, Rempubl. in discrimen adduxit? cur pacatam turbavit? cur armis dominia nostra invasit, à Christianique sanguinis effusione regni sui initium auspicatus est? cur vires & consilia nostra sæpiùs contra communes Religionis nostræ hostes destinata suis machinationibus suisq; conatibus à communi salute prorsus alienis ad subditorum nostrorum defensionem revocare coegit? quur toties victus, divina justicia justæ nostræ causæ favente, toties adversam mavult experiri fortunam cum Christiani sanguinis effusione, quàm Christi gloriæ, suoque honori ac dignitati consulere?
units.tr: 7. If he feared danger to the Christian religion; if he desired the commonwealth to be safe; if the sword which had to be drawn against the enemies of the faith, if the forces which had to be turned against them, if the counsels to be employed for driving them off, were turned against ourselves; if he so execrated the Christian hand shedding Christian blood, why did he himself, by stirring up new tumults of war, bring the commonwealth into peril? Why did he disturb the peace? Why did he invade our dominions with arms, and begin his reign with the shedding of Christian blood? Why did he force our forces and counsels, which had often been directed against the common enemies of our religion, to be recalled, by his own machinations and efforts utterly alien to the common safety, to the defence of his subjects? Why, so often defeated, with divine justice favouring our just cause, does he prefer again and again to try adverse fortune at the cost of Christian blood, rather than to care for the glory of Christ and for his own honour and dignity?

units.la: 8. Hæc tametsi omnibus omninò nota sint, nihil tamen veritus, an vera an falsa loquatur, omne in nos culpam convertere conatur, dum multo sanguine exiguū terræ spacium nos quærere ait. Exiguo profecto terræ spacio pro tanti Regis redemptione, Burgundiæ videlicet Ducatu, cōtenti fuimus, quæ etiam nunquam petiisemus, ni jus nostrum, quod in eo habemus, prout ex Gallorum Apologiæ Refponsione clarè videre licebit, omnibus notū esset, illiusq; contemptus ignaviæ potiùs, quàm aut Religioni aut liberalitati nobis ascribendus esse videretur. Et licet Rex ipse tum in fœdere, tum etiam extra fœdus, suis propriis verbis ex suo met ore prolatis, sanctoq; jurejurando confirmatis, promiserit se illum nobis restituere velle, deindeq; à captivitate liberatus in suo regno cōstitens, sæpius & verbis & literis propria etiam manu ad nos scriptis, se omnia in fœdere contenta ex integro implere servareque velle profiteretur, ac demum mutata sententia hujusmodi restitutioni intendere noluerit, nunquam tamen violati fœderis injuriam persequi, ejusve dominia invadere, novisve simultatibus publicam tranquillitatem turbare voluimus, verum cum literis tum Nunciis ejus induratum animum sollicitari fecimus, ut promissa observaret: & si non Reipubl. suo tamen honori atq; dignitati consuleret. Ille verò dum mavult Christianam Rempub. in manifesto discrimine adducere, suæq; fidei & jurisjurandi oblivisci, ea, quæ ipse commemorat, mala consequuti sumus: intereaq; quàm falsè apud nos pro Christiana pace amplectenda protestatum fuisse, dicere non vetetur, hisq; met verbis utitur, quibus nos sæpe illum hortati sumus, ne fidem jusjurandumq; violaret.
units.tr: 8. Although all these things are altogether well known, he nevertheless, caring nothing whether he speaks truth or falsehood, tries to turn all the blame upon us, saying that we seek a small patch of land with much bloodshed. We were indeed content with a small patch of land for the ransom of so great a King, namely the Duchy of Burgundy, which we would never even have sought had our right to it not been known to all, as will be clearly seen from the Response to the French Apology, and had its neglect not seemed to be ascribed to cowardice rather than to religion or generosity. And although the King himself, both within the treaty and outside it, in his own words spoken from his own mouth and confirmed by a sacred oath, promised that he would restore it to us, and afterwards, freed from captivity and established in his kingdom, often professed, both in words and in letters written to us in his own hand, that he wished to fulfil and observe completely all that was contained in the treaty; and finally, having changed his mind, he was unwilling to make such a restitution, yet we never wished to pursue the injury of a violated treaty, nor to invade his dominions, nor to disturb the public tranquillity with fresh quarrels. Rather, both by letters and by his envoys, we had his hardened mind urged to keep his promises, and if not for the commonwealth, at least to look to his own honour and dignity. But he, preferring to bring the Christian commonwealth into manifest peril and to forget his faith and his oath, has brought upon us the evils he himself recounts. Meanwhile, I may say, it is not forbidden to say how falsely he protested to us that he embraced Christian peace, and he uses the very words with which we often urged him not to violate his faith and oath.

units.la: 9. Quod igitur variis dilationibus tèpus inane consumitur, qp Christianorū agri vastantur, quod urbes diripiuntur, qp incendia vagantur, quod cædes committuntur, quod hostiū fines propagantur, eorumq; fines in dies accrescunt, debet certè hoc Christiana Respub. Regi Francisco, qui in meditullio Christianitatis constitutus glorians ac jactās se ab hoc Christianitatis incëdio, imminentiq; periculo longè abesse, nihil nō interturbat, nullū in pace vivere permittit, mittēda in Turcas arma in suū caput convertere conatur, Nuncios ad juvandā Remp. destinatos in regno suo detinet, atq; inter suos triumphos Turcarū in sororii nostri regno irruptione annumerat, sibiq; hoc satis esse credit, si à suis Christianisimus nuncupetur, * fororiiq; nostri sorte miserrimam prædicat, qui pro fide, pro religione, pro patria, ac pro Dei gloria Christo Deo Opt. Max. vitam suā devovit, ad felicioremq; vocatus, optimi, strenui, atque magnanimi Principis laudē apud posteros reliquit. Hæc n. fors cuivis sanæ mentis hominī nō miserrima, sed felicissima videri debet: quàm tamē ipsiusmet Franci Regis fors miserior sit, viderit ipse. Nos certè nostrā longè magis cum Hungaro, quàm cum Gallo cōmutare vellemus, licet impudenter adeò toties inculcet, sese omnia tentare velle, quibus Christianæ Reip. tranquillitati consuli posset. Si eam salvā cupit, quis eum ad bellum provocat? quis ejus dominia invadit? quis cum eo contendere vult? quis talem cuperet movere Camarinam? Si suos * liberos, quos nobis obsides dedit, recuperare optat, cur impositas leges non servat? Si, quod potest, impossibile affirmir, cur ipsemet (uti pollicitus est) id captivitatem non reverticur? Invenient profecto nos publicae salutis suaeq; dignitatis quam studiosissimos. Verum si armatilli continuare liber, crimúsne usq; adeò nostri honoris oblivi, ut tantum hostem in gregem nobis commissum debacchari permittamus? Haec igitur admonitio, haec protestatio, quam nobis fieri vult, illi certè longè magis conveniret. Verumtamen pudet profecto nos ad has nugas inanesq; fabulas tot verbis respondere.
units.tr: 9. Therefore the empty time consumed by one delay after another, the fields of Christians laid waste, the cities plundered, fires spreading, slaughters committed, the borders of the enemy extended and their territories growing daily: the Christian commonwealth certainly owes all this to King Francis. He, placed in the very midst of Christendom, boasts and vaunts himself far from this conflagration of Christianity and its imminent danger, throws everything into confusion, allows no one to live in peace, tries to turn upon his own head the arms that should be sent against the Turks, detains in his kingdom the envoys destined to aid the commonwealth, and counts among his triumphs the Turkish invasion of our brother-in-law's kingdom. He thinks it enough for himself to be called "most Christian" by his own people, and he proclaims the lot of our brother-in-law most wretched, who devoted his life for the faith, for religion, for his fatherland and for the glory of God to Christ God Best and Greatest, and who, called to a happier lot, left to posterity the praise of an excellent, vigorous and magnanimous Prince. For this lot ought to seem to any sane man not most wretched but most fortunate. How much more wretched the lot of King Francis himself may be, let him see. For our part, we would far rather exchange our lot with the Hungarian than with the Frenchman, although he so shamelessly keeps repeating that he wishes to attempt everything by which the tranquillity of the Christian commonwealth might be secured. If he wants it secure, who provokes him to war? Who invades his dominions? Who wishes to contend with him? Who would wish to stir up Camarina in this way? If he wishes to recover his sons, whom he gave us as hostages, why does he not keep the laws imposed on him? If, as he can do, he calls the thing impossible, why does he himself not return to captivity, as he promised? Surely they will find us most eager for public safety and for his dignity. But if he continues to rage at liberty, do we seem so forgetful of our honour that we would allow so great an enemy to rage against the flock committed to us? This admonition, this protest, which he wishes to be made to us, would certainly suit him far better. Yet we are truly ashamed to answer these trifles and empty fables with so many words.

units.la: 10. Si procul ab omni periculo distat, si jucunda quiete ac pace intra sui regni fines fruitur, eam certè felicitatem nequaquam invidemus, imò potius ei ex animo gratulamur; magisq; gratulaemur, si dum sua ipse fruitur quiete, suos etiam finitimos in pace vivere permitteret, nec tot bellorum semina ubiq; jactaret, nec tot clandestinis conspirationibus omnia niteretur turbare. Haec licet adeò omnibus nota sint, ut nulla penitus attestatione egere videantur, tamen ad vos scribenda duximus, ne quis existimaret hujusmodi garrulitati fidem aliquam adhibendam esse, néve tot maligna verba ulla ex parte immaculatam famam nostram laedere possent: atq; ut sciatis, per ipsummet Regem Gallum stetisse, quo minus institutum iter, de quo superioribus diebus ad vos scripseramus, perficere quaerimus.
units.tr: 10. If he is far from all danger, if he enjoys pleasant quiet and peace within the bounds of his kingdom, we certainly do not envy him that happiness at all; rather, we congratulate him from our hearts. And we would congratulate him all the more if, while he enjoys his own quiet, he also allowed his neighbours to live in peace, did not scatter the seeds of so many wars everywhere, and did not strive to disturb everything with so many secret conspiracies. Although these matters are so well known to all that they seem to need no testimony whatever, we nevertheless thought fit to write to you, lest anyone should suppose that any credit ought to be given to such chatter, or that so many malicious words could in any way harm our unblemished reputation; and so that you may know that it is owing to the King of France himself that the journey we had begun, about which we wrote to you in recent days, is not being carried through.

units.la: 11. Speramus tamen, favente Deo Opt. Max. nos ita res nostras dispositurós, ut eo etiam relucente, suisq; conatibus irriris ac superatis, nostro de Republ. bene merendi, de religione purganda & propaganda, studio omnino satisfaciamus. Ad id enim die vigesimo proximi mensis Januarii in hoc nostro Castellae Regno, in oppido nostro Valliisoleti, quò nunc tendimus, generalem Conventum celebrabimus, ubi tractabitur de mittendo cum ea, qua decet, celeritate ad Germaniam auxilio, quo non modò ipsam defendere, sed hostium conatus infringere, eosq; à Christianorum cervicibus submovere valeamus. Hispanorum nanq; animi hac injuria commoti & expergefacti, vires, opes, propriumq; sanguinem jam ultrò offerre coeperunt: nosq; ad hanc expeditionem stimulant, pro qua (si expedire videbitur) non regna tantùm ac dominia omnia nostra, sed personam, sanguinem, atq; animam ipsam nostram Christo Deo Opt. Max. nos devovisse profitemur.
units.tr: 11. Yet we hope, with God Best and Greatest favouring us, that we shall so arrange our affairs that, with that also shining forth, and his futile efforts defeated and overcome, we shall fully satisfy our zeal for doing good service to the commonwealth and for purging and propagating religion. For to this end, on the twentieth day of next January, we shall hold a general Assembly in this our kingdom of Castile, in our town of Valladolid, whither we are now making our way. There it will be discussed how aid may be sent to Germany with all due speed, by which we may be able not only to defend it but also to break the enemy's attempts and remove them from the necks of Christians. For the Spaniards, stirred and roused by this injury, have already begun to offer of their own accord their strength, their resources and their own blood; and they urge us on to this expedition, for which (if it seems expedient) we declare that we have devoted to Christ God Best and Greatest not only all our kingdoms and dominions, but our person, our blood and our very soul.

units.la: 12. Si verò interea Gallorum Regi (Deo inspirante) resipiscere contigerit, ad nostramq; amicitiam redire voluerit, nos certè omne illius commodum, honorem, atq; dignitatem ex animo promovere curabimus, illiq; injuriam hanc libenter condonabimus, atq; de jure proprio illi cedere paratae rimus, ut sedatis contentionibus, communibus auspiciis hostes profligare, illosq; à suis sedibus submovere, vel (si Deus concesserit) in ovile Christi redigere facilius valeamus.
units.tr: 12. If meanwhile it happens that the King of the French, God inspiring him, comes to his senses and wishes to return to our friendship, we shall certainly take care to advance all his advantage, honour and dignity from our hearts. We shall gladly pardon him this injury, and we are prepared to cede to him our own right, so that, with the quarrels settled, we may more easily, under common auspices, defeat the enemies, drive them from their seats, or (if God grants it) bring them back into the fold of Christ.

units.la: 13. Latere vos minimè arbitramur, Amice & consanguinei charissimi, perniciosissimas Gallorum artes, qui, quò suum negocium agant, discordias seminare non cessant. Vestrum nunc erit, eam ipsorum verbis fidem praestare, ut intelligant tantorum Principum animos sese frustrà sollicitare.
units.tr: 13. We do not think it escapes you, dearest friend and kinsman, what most pernicious arts the French employ, who never cease sowing discord in order to carry on their own business. It will now be your task to give such faith to their words that they may understand they are trying in vain to stir the minds of such great Princes.

units.la: Datum in civitate nostra Granatae, die penultima Novembris, anno Domini M. D. XXVI. Regni nostri Romani octavo.
units.tr: Given in our city of Granada, on the penultimate day of November, in the year of the Lord 1526, the eighth of our Roman reign.

units.la: CAROLI V. IMPER. AUG. IVRAMENTVM ANTE IMPOSITAM SIBI CORO- NAM Romanam Bononiae praestitum.
units.tr: Oath of Emperor Charles V Augustus, taken at Bologna before the Roman crown was placed upon him

units.la: EGo Carolus Romanorum Rex, & brevi Dei gratia futurus Imperator Caesar, per Deum Divumq; Pettum promitto, polliceor, testificor atq; juro, me in posterum pro viribus, ingenio & facultatibus meis Pontificiae dignitatis & Romanae Ecclesiae perpetuum fore defensorem, nec ullam Ecclesiasticae libertati vim illaturum: sed potestatem, jurisdictionem & dominationem ipsius, quoad ejus fieri potest, conservaturum ac protecturum; cujus rei testem voco Deum ipsum & haec sancta Evangelia.
units.tr: I, Charles, King of the Romans and, by the grace of God, soon to be Emperor and Caesar, promise, pledge, call to witness and swear by God and by the Holy Gospels that, henceforth, with my strength, talent and resources, I will be a perpetual defender of the Pontifical dignity and of the Roman Church; that I will do no violence to ecclesiastical liberty; and that I will preserve and protect, as far as it is possible, the power, jurisdiction and dominion of the same Church. I call God himself and these holy Gospels to witness this.

units.la: CAROLI V. IMPER. AUG. PROPOSITIO
units.tr: THE PROPOSITION OF THE EMPEROR CHARLES V, AUGUSTUS

units.la: In praesentia ejus Majestatis, coram omnibus Electoribus, Principibus & Imperii Ordinibus, in Comitiis Augustanis, die 20. Junii, Anno M DXXX. per Fridericum Pa- latinum de scripto recitata.
units.tr: Read from a written text in the presence of His Majesty, before all the Electors, Princes and Orders of the Empire, at the Diet of Augsburg, on 20 June, in the year 1530, by Frederick the Palatine.

units.la: ROMANA Caesarea Majestas nequaquam dubitat, Majestatis ipsius amicos, agnatos, fratres, patrueles, Electores, Principes, & omnes sacri Romani Imperii ordines, recenti memoria tenere, quod statim post illud tempus, quod Majestas ipsius, Divina providentia & consilio, ad Romani Imperii dignitatem, fastigium & gubernationem, communi Principum Electorum consensu electa, & Aquisgrani inauguratione confirmata fit, conventum ordinum Imperium WormaWormatiæ indixerit, in quo de omnibus sacri Romani Imperii negotiis, summa diligētia, cura & studio clementissime consultarit, & necessarias deliberationes instituerit, & quod Cæsarea Majestas in illis ipsis vigenribus Comitiis adhuc agens, aliorum bellis sit impetita & irritata, ita quidem & adeò, ut licet is planè fuerit ipsius animus, & ea voluntas, in sacri Rom.Imp.finibus diutius permanere & cōmorari: tamen coacta fuerit in Hispanias & paterna sua regna redire, quod tamen fecerit & de ipsorū voluntate, & non prius, quàm Imperii res omnes legitime procurasset, constituto nimirum, ex septemviris, Principibus & aliis Imperii ordinibus, judicio & senatu, & Fratre Ferdinando, velut altero se, Legato sibi delignato per suam absentiam.
units.tr: His Roman Imperial Majesty has no doubt that his friends, kinsmen, brothers and cousins, the Electors, Princes and all the Orders of the Holy Roman Empire, remember well that, immediately after the time when His Majesty, by divine providence and counsel, was chosen by the common consent of the Princely Electors to the dignity, height and government of the Roman Empire, and was confirmed in it by inauguration at Aachen, he summoned a Diet of the Orders of the Empire at Worms. There he most graciously took counsel, with the greatest diligence, care and zeal, on all the affairs of the Holy Roman Empire, and made the necessary deliberations. And while His Imperial Majesty was still engaged in those same Diet sessions, he was attacked and provoked by the wars of others, so that, although it was altogether his purpose and wish to remain and stay longer within the borders of the Holy Roman Empire, he was nevertheless compelled to return to Spain and to his paternal kingdoms. He did so with the consent of the Orders themselves, and not before he had duly provided for all the affairs of the Empire. He appointed, namely, a judicial council and senate drawn from the seven Electors, Princes and other Orders of the Empire, and his brother Ferdinand, as it were another himself, to act as his legate during his absence.

units.la: 2. Qui Legati & Consiliarii, interea dum abesset, plenam habuerint potestatem omnia statuendi, definiendi & agendi, quæ Imperii Romani necessitas, & alia imminentia pericula postulare & requirere viderentur, non secus ac si Majestatis ipsius præsens, & propria persona rebus agendis interesset.
units.tr: 2. These legates and counsellors, while he was away, were to have full power to decide, determine and carry out everything that the necessity of the Roman Empire and other impending dangers seemed to require, just as if His Majesty were present and acting in person.

units.la: 3. Per quam quidem Majest. ipsius absentiam, Frater ejus Ferdinandus, Commissarii & Oratores, in Imperii administratione, omnia, quæ pro conditione rei, post celebrata Wormatiæ Comitia, necessaria, & edicto in illis promulgato non adversari visa fuerint, tali studio, tantaque cura, solicitudine & diligentia fecerint, ut majori facere non potuerint, ita quidem, ut, quod ad conservandam per Imperium communem pacem atq; concordiam, & rectè administrandam justiciam prodesset, nihil in se desiderari passi fuerint. Ob quam etiam causam Cæs. Majest. tranquilliori animo Germaniam deseruit, & in Hispanias ac paterna sua regna est profectus.
units.tr: 3. During His Majesty's absence, his brother Ferdinand and the commissioners and envoys, in the administration of the Empire, did everything that seemed necessary for the situation after the Diet at Worms had been held, and not contrary to the edict promulgated there. They did it with such zeal, such great care, concern and diligence that they could not have done more. Indeed, so that nothing was lacking in what served to preserve the common peace and concord throughout the Empire and to administer justice rightly, they allowed nothing to be left wanting. For this reason too, His Imperial Majesty left Germany with a more tranquil mind and set out for Spain and his paternal kingdoms.

units.la: 4. Interea verò dum in Hispania ageret, Majest. ipsius audivit, non solùm magnas esse per Romanorum Imperium simultates atq; dissidia religionis: verum etiam Turcicum Tyrannum, Christiani nominis ac orthodoxæ fidei infestissimum hostem, magno exercitu collecto, nonnullis Christianis finibus, ac præcipuè regno Ungarico, vim & bellum inferre decrevisse, ejusq; rei jam initium fecisse, ac superatis ibi, & in potestatem suam redactis, aliquot propugnaculis, castellis & arcibus, liberum aditum in Germaniam sibi patefecisse.
units.tr: 4. Meanwhile, however, while he was in Spain, His Majesty heard that not only were there great enmities and dissensions over religion throughout the Roman Empire, but also that the Turkish tyrant, most hostile enemy of the Christian name and of the orthodox faith, had gathered a great army and had resolved to make war on and invade some Christian territories, and especially the kingdom of Hungary. He had already begun this undertaking, and having overcome and brought under his power several bulwarks, fortresses and citadels there, he had opened for himself a free approach into Germany.

units.la: 5. Ob eas etiam impendentes calamitates, Regem Ludovicum Majestatis ipsius fratrem & affinem, ac nationis illius Proceres, insigni legatione ad Majestatis ipsius, per Romanorum Imperii fines designatum legatum, Commissarios & Oratores, tempore Comitiorum Norimbergensium, missum, opem & auxilium Imperii sollicitasse, impendentium periculorum & cladium, à Turca, post superatum Belgradum, & alia nationis Hungaricæ propugnacula, capita, acceptarum, commemoratione addita, eas, quibus nunc ipsi præmerentur calamitatibus & miseriis, omnibus Imperii ordinibus & Christianæ Ecclesiæ membris communes, & ingentia illa pericula brevi omnes oppressura esse, affirmantes, ac nisi continenti & durabili belli apparatu & exercitu Hungari instruerentur, ipsos eliminandis hostibus conaribus nequaquam pares futuros, inferentes.
units.tr: 5. On account of these impending calamities, King Louis, His Majesty's brother and kinsman, and the nobles of that nation, sent an distinguished embassy, with a legate, commissioners and envoys designated through the territories of the Roman Empire, at the time of the Diet of Nuremberg. They sought the aid and assistance of the Empire, recalling the dangers and disasters that were impending, and the losses already suffered at the hands of the Turk after the capture of Belgrade and other bulwarks, cities and strongholds of the Hungarian nation. They added that the calamities and miseries now pressing upon them were common to all the Orders of the Empire and to the members of the Christian Church, and that those great dangers would shortly overwhelm them all. They declared that unless Hungary were equipped with a continuous and lasting military preparation and army, they would by no means be equal to driving out the enemy.

units.la: 6. Si verò in tempore ipsis succurratur, eos, non tantum vim omnem hostilem depellere: verùm etiam sua se posse recuperare, bonam spem concipere, aliorum auxilio si destituantur, ipsos Turcicæ Tyrannidi subjugatum iri, atq; hac ratione futurum, ut & aliis gentibus finitimis, opem ferre non possint, & contra Christianos bellum gerere, ac inimice agere cogantur, ut Legatorum illorum oratio fusius omnia tractavit & commemoravit, de duorum imperiorum, Constantinopolitani & Tragsentini, Dalmatiæ & maximæ partis Croatiæ, aliorumq; multorum regnorum, nationum, urbium, castellorum & arcium, amissione & depopulatione, verba faciens, quod scilicet Turcicus Tyrannus, paucorum annorum spatio, Imperium suum ita extendisset & amplificasset, ut, multis ditionibus non numeratis, duo jam subjugarit Imperia ac viginti possederit Regna, quorum incolæ omnes tristissima servitute premerentur, & Tyrannidi Turcicæ subjecti miserabilem vitam agerent.
units.tr: 6. If, however, they were helped in time, they could not only repel all hostile force but also hope to recover what was theirs. If they were abandoned by others, they would be subjugated to Turkish tyranny, and in this way they would be unable to bring aid to other neighbouring peoples, and would be compelled to wage war against Christians and to act as enemies. The embassy's speech treated and recounted all this at greater length, speaking of the loss and devastation of two empires, Constantinople and Tragsentinum, of Dalmatia and the greater part of Croatia, and of many other kingdoms, nations, cities, castles and citadels. The Turkish tyrant, it said, had in the space of a few years so extended and enlarged his empire that, not counting many dominions, he had already subjugated two empires and possessed twenty kingdoms, whose inhabitants were all oppressed by the most wretched servitude and lived a miserable life under Turkish tyranny.

units.la: 7. Iis verò Legationis Hungaricæ tristissimis querelis, & non longe post, ad multas alias gentes inundaturis calamitatibus, Cæsar. Majest. ita commotam fuisse, ut quo celerius & commodius auxilia mitterentur, totam illam pecuniæ summam, quam ei, inaugurationis causa, Romam proficiscenti, omnes Imperii ordines communi consensu, in Comitiis Wormatiæ celebratis, pendere promisissent, ad sublevandas Hungerorum calamitates, & elidendos hostiles conatus, in bellum illud convertì & erogari clementissime mandarit. Cum verò auxilia illa nec in tempore, nec commode missa & administrata fuerint, Turcicum Tyrannum post superatum Belgradum, alios quoq; portus, urbes, arces, & propugnacula, magna cum clade & calamitate Christianorum, cepisse, ac paulò post Rhodum etiam invasisse, ac difficili obsidione, longoq; bello defatigatam subegisse, quæ hactenus velut altera arx Christianorum fuerit & propugnaculum.
units.tr: 7. Moved by these most sorrowful complaints of the Hungarian embassy, and by the calamities which were soon to flood over many other nations, His Imperial Majesty was so stirred that, so that aid might be sent more quickly and conveniently, he most graciously commanded that the whole sum of money which all the Orders of the Empire had by common consent promised at the Diet of Worms to pay him for his inauguration, when he set out for Rome, should be turned to that war and spent on relieving the calamities of the Hungarians and checking the hostile attempts. But since that aid was neither sent nor administered in time or properly, the Turkish tyrant, after capturing Belgrade, also took other ports, cities, citadels and bulwarks, with great slaughter and calamity to the Christians, and shortly afterwards even invaded Rhodes, and after a difficult siege and a long war, wearied it and subdued it, which until then had been, as it were, the second citadel and bulwark of the Christians.

units.la: 8. Deinde ipsum insatiabili regnandi libidine ardentem, Hungarico regno vicissim bellum intulisse, ac multis arcibus, portubus, oppidis & castellis superatis & captis Ludovici Regis exercitum Turcicæ Tyrannidi & armis violentis resistere volentem profligasse, ac Regem ipsum contrucidasse, ac deinde, victoria parta, longius progressum, omnia propugnacula, oppida & castella inter Savum & Dravum flumina vi cepisse, ac Buda Ungariæ metropoli capta, multisq; aliis locis & urbibus subjugatis & captis, omnia diripuisse ac incendisse, multis Christianis trucidatis, ac reliquis, cum magna auri & argenti vi, in tristissimam servitutem abductis.
units.tr: 8. Then, burning with an insatiable lust for dominion, he turned his arms against the kingdom of Hungary in turn. After overcoming and taking many citadels, ports, towns and fortresses, he routed the army of King Louis, which wished to resist the Turkish tyranny with armed force, and slew the king himself. Then, having won the victory, he advanced further and by force took all the bulwarks, towns and castles between the rivers Sava and Drava. After taking Buda, the metropolis of Hungary, and subjugating and capturing many other places and cities, he plundered and burned everything, slaughtered many Christians, and led the rest away, with great quantities of gold and silver, into most wretched servitude.

units.la: 9. Nec trophæis & spoliis reportatis odii crudelitatem placatam in eo esse: se victoriis tantis auctum, Christianarum nationum populandarum, & pii sanguinis fundendi sitientiorem evasisse, ac truculenti animi conatibus, & cogitationibus in Germanicæ nationis interitum defixis, in Illyricum, cum, Cæs. Majest. Regnum & Principatum, impetum fecisse, accum supra modum omnem ibi graffatus esse, cædibus, incendiis, rapinis, devastationibus agrorum, abduxisse illinc, utriusque generis, treginta hominum millia in miserabilem servitutem, & eos, qui forte per impedimenta sequi non poterant, contrucidasse.
units.tr: 9. Nor was the cruelty of his hatred satisfied with the trophies and spoils he had carried off. Made bolder by such victories, he became more thirsty for plundering Christian nations and shedding innocent blood. With a savage mind fixed on the destruction of the German nation, and with his designs directed to that end, he attacked Illyricum, which is the kingdom and principality of His Imperial Majesty. He raged there beyond all measure with slaughter, fires, robberies and the devastation of fields. From there he carried off thirty thousand people of both sexes into miserable slavery, and those who by chance could not keep up with the baggage he put to death.

units.la: 10. Deinde proxime superiori M. D. XXIX. anno, cum innumerabili exercitu (qualis a tempore Attilæ, qui flagellum Dei dictus sit, non fuerit numeratus) in Ungariam progressum, ea vicissim subjugata, Austriam penetrasse, acejus loci Metropolim obsedisse Viennam, rapinis omnia expilasse, & longe lateque populatum esse agros, prope ad Lyncium & Anisum flumina usque, nec ullum inhumanitatis genus præretermisisse, nulla nec ætatis nec sexus habita ratione, dissectis ac in frustra concisis pueris infantibus, ac honestis matronis ac puellis nefarie stupratis & more pecudum cum ingentibus spoliis, abactis.
units.tr: 10. Then, in the year 1529 just past, with an innumerable army (such as has not been counted since the time of Attila, who was called the scourge of God) he advanced into Hungary, subjugated that in turn, penetrated into Austria, and besieged its metropolis Vienna. He plundered everything with raids and laid waste the fields far and wide, almost as far as the rivers Enns and Ybbs. He left no kind of inhumanity undone, regardless of age or sex. Infants were cut to pieces and hacked into fragments, honourable matrons and maidens were foully ravished, and they were driven off like cattle with huge spoils.

units.la: 11. Itaq; nisi tunc temporis hostis obsidionem solvisset, Cæs. Majest. plane constitutum habuisse, omnibus rebus aliis neglectis & posthabitis, illò proficisci cum copiis, & omne suum robur eò convertere. Datis etiam literis, tùm ad Ferdinandum Regem fratrem, tum ad Proceres atque belli duces Viennæ circumsessos, ut suum adventum profsus expectarent, & fortiter agerent hortatam esse. Cum autem pedem ille referret, mutasse consilium, & multis de causis optimum judicasse, ut rebus per Italiam pacatis Bononiam proficisceretur, & cum Pontifice, de summa Reipublicæ constituenda, deque Religione & fide Christiana, marura consilia caperet. Quæ omnia in literis indictionis fusius tractata sunt & commemorata.
units.tr: 11. Therefore, had the enemy not then lifted the siege, His Imperial Majesty had fully resolved, setting aside and postponing all other business, to set out thither with his forces and turn all his strength in that direction. He also sent letters urging both King Ferdinand his brother and the nobles and commanders besieged in Vienna to await his arrival without fail and to hold firm. When the enemy, however, withdrew, he changed his plan, and for many reasons judged it best, once affairs in Italy were settled, to go to Bologna and there, with the Pope, take counsel on the establishment of the common welfare of the commonwealth, and on religion and the Christian faith. All of this is treated and recounted at greater length in the letters of summons.

units.la: 12. Cum etiam Imperator invictissimus intelligeret, summam necessitatem, & præcipuè hære-ditarii & immanis Turcici hostis rabiem atq; furorem, & Christianæ fidei dissidia requirere & flagitate, ut ejusmodi conventus indiceretur, ac optimum etiam judicaret, ut statim post acceptum Bo-nia diadema (quo sine ullis impedimentis, ut omnibus cóstar, etiam Romæ insigniri potuisset) Neapolim proficisceretur, quod regni illius status & conditio tum inprimis requisiverit: tamen majestate ipsius commodo privato postposito, cogitationem omnem ad communem Christianæ Reipub. utilitatem contulisse, cùm ut animum suum erga Germanicam nationem omnes cognoscerent, cùm ut primo quoq; tempore huic conventui adesset.
units.tr: 12. Since the most invincible Emperor understood that there is the greatest necessity, and especially that the rage and fury of the hereditary and monstrous Turkish enemy, and the dissensions of the Christian faith, demand and urgently require that such an assembly be convened; and since he also judged it best that, immediately after receiving the crown of Hungary (which, as everyone knows, he could have received even at Rome without any hindrance), he should set out for Naples, because the state and condition of that kingdom required his attention above all else: nevertheless, with his own private convenience set aside, he directed all his thought to the common welfare of the Christian commonwealth, so that everyone might recognise his goodwill towards the German nation and that he might attend this assembly at the earliest opportunity.

units.la: 13. Jam verò licet hostis, Divina providentia, forti propugnatorum manu ac veteranorum militum egregia virtute repulsus, Viennam capere non potuerit, tamen ingens damnum esse datum toti provinciæ & aliis finitimis locis, quod vix longo temporis spacio, vicissim sarciri possit.
units.tr: 13. Now, although the enemy, repulsed by Divine providence, by the strong hand of the defenders and the outstanding valour of the veteran soldiers, could not take Vienna, nevertheless great damage was inflicted on the whole province and on other neighbouring places, damage which can hardly be made good again in a long span of time.

units.la: 14. Et licet tum temporis exercitum ille reduxerit, præsidia tamen atq; Duces reliquisse ad fines, qui, ex eo tempore, non modo Ungariam & Croatiam: verumetiam Austriam, Styriam & alia finitima loca assiduis irruptionibus, excursionibus & depopulationibus graviter labefactarint & continenter devastarint. Et quandoquidem fines nunc habeat multis in locis conjunctos nostris finibus, dubium non esse, quin ad proximam occasionem, multo sit major cum manu reversurus, ut sine intermissione, omnes Christiani nominis professores, ad internecionem disperdat ac funditus eradicet, præsertim in Germania. Atq; ante & post expugnatam & capram Constantinopolim, usq; ad has, cum magna Christianarum nationum, urbium, castellorum, & locorum devastatione & excisione, illatas Austriæ clades, quam multa nobis ademerit, quantum Christiani sanguinis hauserit, & quantas in angustias orbem hunc nostrum adegerit, supra est commemoratum, ac cum omnibus notum sit, deploratione potius & querimonia, quàm ulla opus est explicatione prolixiori.
units.tr: 14. And although at that time the enemy led his army back, he left behind garrisons and commanders at the frontiers; from that time on they have grievously weakened and continually devastated not only Hungary and Croatia, but also Austria, Styria and other neighbouring places, by constant incursions, raids and plundering. And since he now holds frontiers in many places joined to our own, there is no doubt that at the next opportunity he will return with a much larger force, so as to destroy without interruption, and utterly root out, all professors of the Christian name, especially in Germany. Moreover, before and after the capture and seizure of Constantinople, down to these recent disasters inflicted on Austria, with great devastation and destruction of Christian nations, cities, castles and places, it has been set out above how many things he has taken from us, how much Christian blood he has drained, and into what straits he has brought this world of ours; and since all know this, it calls for lament and complaint rather than any lengthy explanation.

units.la: 15. Quæ immanissimorum latronum crudelia facta, tanta Christianorum populorum & nationum clade, tantaque sanguinis effusione perpetrata, omnium & singulorum piorum animos vere ac vehementer afficere, & rerum præteritarum exemplis ita commovere debebant, ut certò statuerent, quòd si jam rursus ut antehac, remisse, lentè & cunctanter agetur, neque majoribus quàm huc usque, copiis atque viribus, obviam ibitur illius furori, assiduis irruptionibus & hostilibus conatubus, non esse, quod deinceps ullam salutem sibi polliceantur: sed fore, ut alia, post aliam, provincia amissa, tandem & brevi quidem, in ipsius potestatem redigantur omnes, extirpentur ac funditus deleantur.
units.tr: 15. These cruel deeds of most monstrous robbers, carried out with such a slaughter of Christian peoples and nations and such an effusion of blood, ought truly and vehemently to move the minds of all and each of the godly, and by the examples of past events ought to lead them to resolve firmly that, if once again, as before, action is taken lazily, slowly and hesitantly, and no greater forces and strength than hitherto are brought to meet his fury, then they should promise themselves no safety from his constant incursions and hostile attempts; rather, province after province will be lost, and before long, indeed, all will be brought into his power, rooted out and utterly destroyed.

units.la: 16. Hisquidem de rebus, & aliis Sacri Imperii gravaminibus, & præsertim de assiduis Turcici Tyranni eruptionibus impediendis, & elidendis hostilibus conatibus, per suam absentiam, crebros fuisse coventus ordinum habitos, quibus etiam ipse optaverit coràm interesse: Verùm id sibi per suos adversarios & bella non fuisse integrum, sicut & literis & legationibus, in omnibus Imperii Comitiis, & aliis etiam conventibus demonstrarit, & de absentia se excusarit.
units.tr: 16. Concerning these matters, and other grievances of the Holy Empire, and especially the prevention of the constant sallies of the Turkish tyrant and the checking of hostile attempts, frequent assemblies of the estates have been held during his absence, and he himself had wished to be present in person; but that was not possible for him because of his adversaries and the wars, as he has shown both by letters and by embassies at all the Imperial Diets and at other assemblies, and he has excused his absence.

units.la: 17. Cum quibus quidem adversariis Majest. ipsius, cum propter Imperii & Christianæ Reipub. utilitatem, tùm ut Turcica gravamina commodius levari, averti, componi & tolli possent, nunc transegerit & pactus sit, ac omnibus suis privatis injuriis & offensionibus, ubi primum licuit, Reipublicæ condonatis, pacem cum hoste fecerit, publicæ pacis ae concordiæ causa, ac Turcicis devastationibus & aliis Sacri Imperii gravaminibus exploratis & diligenter pensitatis, suum in Germaniam redirum, longius differre noluisse.
units.tr: 17. With those adversaries, indeed, His Majesty has now come to terms and made a pact, both for the advantage of the Empire and of the Christian commonwealth, and so that the Turkish grievances might more conveniently be relieved, averted, settled and removed; and, having forgiven all his private injuries and offences to the commonwealth as soon as it was possible, he has made peace with the enemy for the sake of public peace and concord. Having carefully explored and weighed the Turkish devastations and the other grievances of the Holy Empire, he was unwilling to delay any longer his return to Germany.

units.la: 18. Igitur relictis Hispaniarum regnis & populis florentissimis, non absque magno discrimine in Italiam trajecisse, & quod ibi reliquum fuerit hostium, atq; adeò totam Italiam pacasse. Quæ quidem res impedimento sibi fuerint, quominus ad constitutum diem hæ adesser, id quod antea quoq; literis consignatum, Electoribus, Principibus & aliis Imperii ordinibus huc cognoscendum misit.
units.tr: 18. Therefore, leaving aside the kingdoms and very flourishing peoples of Spain, he crossed into Italy, not without great danger, and pacified whatever enemies remained there, and indeed all Italy. These matters have hindered him from being present here on the appointed day, which he has also previously notified in writing to the Electors, Princes and other estates of the Empire, to be made known here.

units.la: 19. Cum vero Caes. Majest. intelligat, in multis hactenus celebratis Comiriis, quaedam de durabili & perpetuo belli apparatu contignata, & ad omnes Imperii ordines dimissa esse, ut de iis diligentiores cogitationes susciperent, & cum subditis suis deliberarent, quò, de ejusmodi durabili auxilio, aliquid certè in aliis Comitiis decerni posset: tamen iis nihil actum, sed nonnunquam subitatantum auxilia decreta & missa esse, quae Majest. ipsius sumptibus ac pecunia, ab Imperii ordinibus, ei Romam, inaugurationis gratia, proficiscenti, numeranda militarint, atque haec omnia, propria utilitate posthabita, propter Imperii & Christianae Reipub. utilitatem, in bellum, contra Turcam gerendum, ut supra etiam dictum est, clementissime erogasse & impendisse.
units.tr: 19. Now, since His Caesarean Majesty understands that in the many Diets held so far certain matters concerning a lasting and perpetual state of war-readiness against the Turk have been drafted and sent to all the estates of the Empire, so that they might take more careful thought on them and deliberate with their subjects, in order that something certainly might be decreed at other Diets concerning such lasting aid: nevertheless nothing has been done about them, but only occasional aid has been decreed and sent, which was to be paid to His Majesty, at his own expense and from his own money, by the estates of the Empire, when he set out for Rome for the sake of his inauguration; and all these things, with his own advantage set aside, he has most graciously laid out and spent for the sake of the advantage of the Empire and the Christian commonwealth, for the war to be waged against the Turk, as has also been said above.

units.la: 20. Cum autem hic articulus, de durabili belli contra Turcam apparatu, omnium primus sit ac maximus, & ejusmodi plane, cujus non tantum Imperii, verùm etiam totius Christianae Reipub. interfit, ac dilatae, de hac re, deliberationes in omnium oculis positae sint, ac in posterum etiam magna incommoda & damna praebitutae & daturae videantur, considerando nimirum, quod gravia & impendentia pericula hoc ipsum requirant & flagitent, cum Christiani sanguinis sitientissimus hostis, de furore & rabie in Christianos concepta, nihil remittat, sed indies majora incommoda & detrimenta Christianae Reipub. inferat, adeò ut in suam servitutem omnes redigat, imò ut extra naturae fines exterminet: Caes. Majestatem clementissime inquirere, & mirum in modum rogare Electores, Principes & omnes alios Imperii ordines, ut nulla interposita mora, de perpetuis & durabilibus conra Turcam auxiliis decernendis, diligenter deliberent, & ut vel conditionibus supra propositis, vel alia via, testransfigatur & componatur, summo studio provideat, easque rationes ineant, ne videlicet ullo tempore delit pecunia, apparatus, copiae, vires, atq; hac ratione propositum & consilium immanissimi hostis, de Christianis crudelissimè persequendis & subjugandis, impediatur, ac Christiana Respub. defendi, immanissimo hosti bellum inferri, & amissa regna, ditiones, urbes, castella & arces non solum recuperari, verùm etiam ipsi sua possint eripi atque auferri, atq; ita crudelis. hostis, offensionum & injuriarum tam atrocium & multiplicium justissimam talionem sentiat. Ad quam quidem rem perficiendam, auxilia conferre, Pontificem Max. Caes. Majest. prolixe & liberaliter pollicitum esse, ita ut quantum facultatibus & opibus possit, illud omne, ad avertenda imminentia pericula, sit erogaturus.
units.tr: 20. Since this article concerning a lasting state of war-readiness against the Turk is the first and greatest of all, and is of such a kind that it concerns not only the Empire but the whole Christian commonwealth, and since the deliberations on this matter, long postponed, have been placed before everyone's eyes, and will seem likely to bring and to cause great inconvenience and damage in future also, considering that the grave and impending dangers themselves require and demand this: since the enemy, thirsting most intensely for Christian blood, does not relax the fury and rage he has conceived against Christians, but daily inflicts greater inconvenience and detriment on the Christian commonwealth, to the point that he reduces all to his own slavery, or even drives them beyond the bounds of nature, His Caesarean Majesty most graciously asks, and marvellously begs the Electors, Princes and all the other estates of the Empire, that without any delay they carefully deliberate on decreeing lasting and perpetual aid against the Turk, and that, whether by the conditions proposed above or by some other way, he take the greatest care that the matter be settled and arranged; and that they devise measures so that at no time money, equipment, troops and forces be lacking, and in this way the purpose and plan of the most monstrous enemy to persecute and subjugate Christians most cruelly be hindered, the Christian commonwealth be defended, war be waged against the most monstrous enemy, and the lost kingdoms, dominions, cities, castles and citadels be not only recovered but also be snatched and taken from him, so that the cruel enemy may feel the most just retribution for so many atrocious and manifold offences and injuries. For the carrying out of this, His Majesty has promised, at length and generously, that the Supreme Pontiff will give aid, so that he will expend all that he can with his resources and wealth to avert the impending dangers.

units.la: 21. Adhaec Caesaream Majestatem quoque tametsi pecuniam ei promissam, inaugurationis causa, totum in hunc usum concesserit, licet sumptus in hac solenni coronatione solus omnem fecerit, etli praeterea multam auri, argentiq; vim dependerit: tamen in hoc opere tam sancto ac necessario, cum omnibus suis regnis atque subditis, quod Christiano Caesare dignum, & in ejusmodi casu necessarium sit, facturam esse: ita ut omnes reipsa intelligant, videant & experiantur, Majestatem ipsius, quantum opera, consilio & auxilio poruerit abundè praestitisse. Idem quoque à fratre Ferdinando, Ungariae & Bohemiae Rege, expectandum esse, qui jam orbis Christiani, Germaniae praesertim, velut propugnaculum quoddam objectum furori Turcico, procul dubio, quantum opibus, facultatibus, opera & studio, cum omnibus suis regnis, ditionibus & subditis possit, indefesè sit facturus, & ut antehac fecerit, eaq; omnia felicitet cessisse & bonum eventum sortita esse.
units.tr: 21. Moreover, although His Caesarean Majesty has devoted entirely to this purpose the money promised to him for his inauguration, and although he alone has borne the expense of this solemn coronation, and has further paid out a great quantity of gold and silver, nevertheless in this work so holy and necessary he will act with all his kingdoms and subjects, as befits a Christian Caesar and is necessary in such a case, so that everyone may truly understand, see and experience how abundantly His Majesty has furnished his labour, counsel and aid. The same is to be expected from his brother Ferdinand, King of Hungary and Bohemia, who, already as a kind of bulwark for the whole Christian world, and especially for Germany, set against the Turkish fury, will undoubtedly, with all his kingdoms, dominions and subjects, labour indefatigably with whatever resources, means, labour and zeal he has, as he has done before; and that all these efforts have turned out well and met with a good outcome.

units.la: 22. Insuper Caesar. Majestatem bona spe teneri, omnes alios etiam Christiani nominis Reges, Principes, atq; Dynastas, in hoc pio, Christiano & necessario opere, non esse defuturos auxilio, sed omnia facturos ex officio, quorum nonnullis jam eo nomine scripserit, & alios etiam sit interpellatura.
units.tr: 22. Furthermore, His Caesarean Majesty is confident that all the other kings, princes and dynasts of the Christian name will not be wanting in aid for this pious, Christian and necessary work, but will do everything as their duty requires; some of whom he has already written to on this account, and he will also address others.

units.la: ALTERA PROPOSITIONIS PARS DE CAUSA RE- LIGIONIS AGENS.
units.tr: THE SECOND PART OF THE PROPOSITION, DEALING WITH THE CAUSE OF RELIGION.

units.la: 23. Porrò, ad religionem quod attinet, inde statim à suscepta Imperii administratione, magno sanè cum animi dolore Caesar. Majest. audisse, dissidium illud excitatum & distractiones Ecclesiarum maximas, in nonnullis Germaniae locis ortas esse. Igitur se, ut Romanum Imperatorem, supremum advocatum, & orthodoxae fidei, Christianae religionis, & Ecclesiae Catholicae defensorem vigilem & strenuum, ut medicinam in tempore faceret, pro officii sui ratione omnium Imperii ordinum convenum Wormatiae indixisse, ibiq; de avertendis his malis, sanandis Ecclesiae vulneribus, & tollendis ex ea dissidiis ac schismaribus, ne altius insiderent ea hominum pectoribus, & radices firmiores agerent, deliberationes accuratas ac diligentes instituisse, acre diu multumq; deliberata & benè penitata communi Electorum, Principum, acreliquorum Imperii staruum decretum, componendum ejusmodi distractionibus, & reconciliandis animis, peridoneum fecisse ac promulgasse, cui si obtemperatum esset, non fuisse tot incommodis & malis patefactam viam, neq; tam diversas, & discrepantes sententias in Ecclesiam irrepsisse.
units.tr: 23. Furthermore, as far as religion is concerned, the Emperor's Majesty heard, with great grief of mind, from the very beginning of his administration of the Empire, that this dissension had been stirred up and the greatest disturbances of the Churches had arisen in some parts of Germany. Therefore, as Roman Emperor, supreme advocate and vigilant and vigorous defender of the orthodox faith, the Christian religion and the Catholic Church, in order to apply a remedy in time, he had, in keeping with the duty of his office, summoned an assembly of all the orders of the Empire to Worms, and there had carried out careful and diligent deliberations on how to avert these evils, heal the wounds of the Church, and remove from it the dissensions and schisms, so that they might not sink deeper into men's breasts and take firmer root. After long and much deliberation and due consideration, he had drawn up and promulgated a common decree of the Electors, Princes and remaining estates of the Empire, well suited to settling such disputes and reconciling minds; had this been obeyed, the way would not have been opened to so many inconveniences and evils, nor would such diverse and discordant opinions have crept into the Church.

units.la: 24. Sed paulò post, se reipsa expertum esse, multos posthabitis ac neglectis tam diligentibus deliberationibus & clementibus actionibus, alias rationes & vias priori actioni multis contrarias excogitasse & propositisse, ex quate non tantum existimationis & authoritatis suae sit secuta imminutio & contemptus, verumetiam Dei Opt. Max. voluntatem, legitimum magistratum in verbo ejus, non tantum instituentem, verùm etiam honore afficere jubentem, pertinaciter fuisse rejectam, & contemptam, id quod non tantum in summam omnium Imperii ordinum contumeliam cesserit, eisq; maximo fuerit decornamento: verùm etiam tot rapinis, incendiis, bellis, devastationibus & nulli non calamitatem. lamitatum generi, deinde præbuerit occasionem commodam, & magnam aperuerit fenestram, quæ quidem in numero, popularis illa seditio, & Anabaptistarum secta principem obtinuerint locum, etiamnum ullus earum appareat finis, sed, ut ex multis circumstantiis colligi possit & animadverti, quæ viota instent & paulò post secutura sint mala.
units.tr: 24. But shortly afterwards, he had found from experience that many, having set aside and neglected such diligent deliberations and gentle measures, had devised and proposed other plans and methods, many of them contrary to the earlier action. From this there had followed not only a diminution and contempt of his own esteem and authority, but also that the will of almighty God, who not only institutes lawful magistracy in his Word but also commands that it be honoured, was stubbornly rejected and despised. This had turned not only to the great insult of all the orders of the Empire and to their greatest discredit, but also had given occasion for, and opened a convenient and wide window to, so many robberies, fires, wars, devastations and every kind of calamity. Among these, that popular sedition and the sect of the Anabaptists have taken the leading place; and as yet no end of them appears, but, as can be gathered and observed from many circumstances, evils are at hand and will follow shortly.

units.la: 25. Cum igitur magno sanè cum animi dolore audierit & intellexerit, dissidium hoc crescere & latius propagari, majoresque vires sumere, nec tam diligentibus deliberationibus, mones consiliis & variis actionibus hucusque effectum esse quicquam, se exististimasse, ad legitimam causam componendam tollendum & animos reconciliandos, suam præsentiam multam habuisse commenti. Igitur pro naturæ suæ bonitate & innata mansuetudine, hoc quicquid sit futurum onerosum & molestiæ suscepisse, ac tàm longum & periculosum iter emensum esse, ut juxta literas indictionis quam primum de rei summa cognoscerent, bona spe concepta, hoc suum consilium plurisque proposuit & ad concordiam Ecclesiæ & Reipub. salutem ac utilem pacem omnes pellecturum & invitatum esse, ut hoc facilius res ipsa cognoscI & agenda suscipi possit, animi distracti rursum coalescant, & pestina ubique locorum restituatur pax atque concordia, ac denique Cæs. Majest. juvandæ Religionis propagandæque gloriæ Dei avidissima, in bono necessarioque proposito constanter pergere, & perseverare queat, possintque de aliis etiam rebus, omnibus & singulis profuturis, utiles liberationes.
units.tr: 25. Therefore, having heard and understood with great grief of mind that this dissension grows and spreads more widely and gathers greater strength, and that nothing has yet been achieved by such diligent deliberations, admonitions, counsels and various actions, he had thought that his personal presence would be of great value for settling the lawful cause, removing the disputes and reconciling minds. Accordingly, in keeping with the goodness of his nature and his innate gentleness, he had undertaken this, whatever burden and trouble it might bring, and had made so long and dangerous a journey, so that, in accordance with the letter of the summons, they might as soon as possible learn the substance of the matter. Having conceived good hope, he has proposed this his plan to many, and has resolved to attract and invite all to the concord of the Church and the safety of the Commonwealth and to a useful peace, so that the matter itself may more easily be understood and business undertaken, the divided minds may come together again, and peace and concord may be restored everywhere; and finally, that His Imperial Majesty, most eager to aid religion and to propagate the glory of God, may be able to press on and persevere constantly in this good and necessary purpose, and that useful resolutions may also be reached on other matters, all and each of which will be profitable.

units.la: 26. His rebus omnibus consideratis, Cæs. M. totius negocii seriâ suscipere tractationes & decrevisse, ut non tantum de perniciosis ac crudelibus Turcarum in Christianas regiones incursibus avertendis, frangendis, debilitandis & imminuendis hostis immanissimi viribus, ac impedimentis versutis consiliis: verùm etiam de dirimendis Ecclesiæ contentionibus, ac sopiendis tumultibus dissidiis ageretur. Igitur Cæsar. Majestat. amanter, clementer & seriò petere Electores, Principes ac omnes Imperii status, ut, quid hac de re cujusque animi & sententiæ sit, latino & germanico scripto comprehensum, in medium proponant, quo, juxta literas Indictionis, eò commodius & celerius, res ipsa intelligi definirique possit.
units.tr: 26. With all these things considered, His Imperial Majesty has decided to undertake the whole business in earnest by negotiations, so that there should be discussion not only of averting the pernicious and cruel incursions of the Turks into Christian lands, of breaking, weakening and diminishing the forces of that most savage enemy, and of hindering him by cunning counsels, but also of settling the contentions of the Church and quelling its tumults and dissensions. Accordingly, His Imperial Majesty lovingly, graciously and earnestly asks the Electors, Princes and all the estates of the Empire that each one set forth in writing, in Latin and German, what his mind and opinion is on this matter, so that, in accordance with the letter of the summons, the matter may be understood and settled more conveniently and quickly.

units.la: 27. De abusibus etiam tollendis ineantur rationes, & quales Ecclesiastici erga Politicos, Politici verò Principes vicissim erga Ecclesiasticos se gerere debeant, concludatur, quæq; singulas gravamina, indicetur, ut pristina pax & concordia Ecclesiæ & Reipubl. eò citius & facilius reddi queat.
units.tr: 27. Let plans also be made for removing abuses, and let it be concluded how churchmen ought to conduct themselves towards the civil authorities, and civil princes in turn towards churchmen; and let each of the grievances be pointed out, so that the former peace and concord of the Church and the Commonwealth may be restored all the sooner and more easily.

units.la: REVERENDISSIME Domine: Invictissimus Imperator CAROLUS Semper-Augustus, Serenissimus Ungariæ & Bohemiæ Rex FERDINANDUS; Illustrissimi Electores & Principes præsentes, absentium Legati, & omnes sacri Romani Imperii Ordines, Dignitatis Veltræ orationem gravem, piam, Christianam, & hisce temporibus, si ullis aliis, maximè necessariam, attente audiverunt, & diligenter consideraverunt. Cumq; Invictissimus Imperator sciat, se supremum Ecclesiæ Advocatum, & Reipublicæ Christianæ gubernatorem summum in his terris à Deo constitutum & datum esse, sui quoq; officii esse arbitratur, omnia persequi & tentare, quæ ad tollendas Ecclesiæ discordias, componenda Doctorum dissidia, & pristinam pacem restituendam facere & producere dentur.
units.tr: Most Reverend Lord: The most invincible Emperor Charles, ever Augustus, the most serene Ferdinand, King of Hungary and Bohemia, the illustrious electors and princes present, the legates of those absent, and all the Orders of the Holy Roman Empire, have attentively heard and carefully considered Your Dignity's speech, which was grave, pious, Christian, and, if any speech in these times, most necessary. And since the most invincible Emperor knows that he has been appointed and given by God as the supreme Advocate of the Church and the chief governor of the Christian commonwealth on this earth, he judges it also his duty to pursue and attempt everything that may be done to end the discords of the Church, to settle the disputes of the teachers, and to bring about and restore the former peace.

units.la: 2. Deinde cùm multos nunc annos, Diabolicam rabiem & lupinam immanissimi Turcici sævitiam, maximo cum dolore, sit expertus, extremæ necessitatis rationem habendam esse censens, imposterum omnes suas vires, omnem auri argentiq; vim, in bellum contra Turcas conferre & erogare decrevit, ut pericula Germanicæ Nationi imminentia, & vulnera in Germanicum sanguinem calura, averrat ac prohibeat; & quæ hostis ille efferatissimus Romano Imperio intulerit, vicissim recuperet & subjuget. Cujus Majestati Serenissimus Ungariæ & Bohemiæ Rex FERDINANDUS, aliiq; Romani Imperii Electores, Principes, Comites, Prælati & Ordines, eorum, ita laborum quoque socii, sese fideliter sunt adjuncturi, omnes labores & molestias sumptus, quos debent, facient; omnesq;, si ita postulaverit, Regnorum ac ditionum suarum ipsos pro defendenda actutanda Christiana religione, & ex Imperii finibus hostem truculentissimo abigendo exponent, talesque omninò sese exhibebunt, ut consilia & facta sua in primis Deo, deinde S. Beatissimo Patri nostro Papæ Clementi Septimo, ovium Christi Pastori, & Petri successori pulcherrime, & coram hominibus etiam officio suo satisfacere possint.
units.tr: 2. Then, since for many years now he has experienced, to his great sorrow, the diabolical rage and the wolfish savagery of the most monstrous Turk, and judging that the situation calls for the utmost necessity, he has decided that in future he will devote and expend all his strength and all the means of gold and silver on war against the Turks, so that he may avert and prevent the dangers threatening the German nation and the wounds inflicted on German blood, and in turn recover and subdue what that most savage enemy has inflicted on the Roman Empire. The most serene Ferdinand, King of Hungary and Bohemia, and the other electors, princes, counts, prelates and Orders of the Roman Empire, as companions in these labours, will faithfully join his Majesty; they will bear all the labours, troubles and expenses they owe, and all of them, if he so requests, will expose their kingdoms and dominions to defend the Christian religion now and to drive the most savage enemy from the borders of the Empire. They will conduct themselves in such a way that their counsels and deeds may most fittingly satisfy, first God, then our most blessed Father the Pope Clement VII, Pastor of Christ's sheep and successor of Peter, and also be answerable before men in the discharge of their duty.

units.la: Nos CAROLUS, Dei gratia Imperator Romanorum semper Augustus, &c. Facimus, & declaramus omnibus [illegible, ~12 letters] Principibus, Ecclesiasticis et Secularibus, Electoribus, Cardinalibus, Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, Ducibus, Marchionibus, Comitibus, Baronibus, Civitatibus, et universis Imperii Statibus, quod in conventu Ratisbonensi [illegible, ~40 letters] pacem publicam [illegible, ~25 letters] Imperii sancitam esse, ut [illegible, ~30 letters] eo quod [illegible, ~20 letters] in Germania [?] et Ecclesia [illegible, ~15 letters].
units.tr: We, CHARLES, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, etc., make and declare to all ... princes, ecclesiastical and secular, electors, cardinals, archbishops, bishops, dukes, margraves, counts, barons, cities, and all estates of the Empire, that at the diet of Regensburg ... [illegible] ... the public peace ... [illegible] ... of the Empire has been sanctioned, so that ... [illegible] ... since ... [illegible] ... in Germany [?] and the Church ... [illegible].

units.la: Ita videlicet, quod intra hoc tempus Synodi, vel quo Status Imperii, ut Deum e[?] ... convenient, & alios dei lxxxx [illegible, ~50 letters] ferat, indicat, quamvis ipsius, cuiuscunque, invadat aut cogitet, neve ad hoc homines paratus [illegible, ~60 letters] culpam incurrat, arces, urbes, oppida, castella, pagos, villas vel prædia, [illegible, ~80 letters] neque ullo modo mali [illegible, ~40 letters] verbum, cum omnibus quibus eis fieri possit, et in omnibus tempore completum.
units.tr: Namely, that within this time, until the Synod, or until the estates of the Empire ... [illegible] ... assemble, and ... [illegible] ... bears or indicates, though anyone of whatever rank attacks or contemplates it, nor should men prepared for this ... [illegible] ... incur guilt; fortresses, cities, towns, castles, villages, country estates or farms ... [illegible] ... and in no way ... [illegible] ... word, with all the means by which it can be done, and to be fulfilled at all times.

units.la: Quam pacem publicam [illegible, ~60 letters] Imperator, tam certo et ordinatus [illegible, ~70 letters] benigne [illegible, ~50 letters] quamlibet deinde [illegible, ~90 letters] de [illegible, ~40 letters].
units.tr: This public peace the Emperor ... [illegible] ... so certain and ordered ... [illegible] ... kindly ... [illegible] ... however then ... [illegible] ... of ... [illegible].

units.la: Hæc omnes, ut eo firmius & certius rata publica & communi pax permanere, [illegible, ~120 letters] Statuum imperii, electoris, principum, et aliorum status et ordinum, quæ in [illegible, ~100 letters] iudicium [illegible, ~80 letters] de hac re [illegible, ~60 letters]. atrum tenens, & Commissarii nostri, qui à nobis ad hoc, expressum mandatum habeant, tales processus judiciales inhibere & abrogare, ut suprà dictum est: sicut etiam nos jam ex authoritate & plenitudine Majestatis Cæsareæ, & vera scientia, nunc ut tunc, & tunc ut nunc, eos inhibemus, suspendimus, & abrogamus, vigore & virtute harum literarum.
units.tr: All these things, so that the public and common peace may remain the more firmly and certainly ratified ... [illegible] ... of the estates of the Empire, electors, princes, and other estates and orders, which in ... [illegible] ... judgment ... [illegible] ... concerning this matter ... [illegible] ... holding; and our commissioners, who have from us an express mandate for this, to inhibit and abrogate such judicial proceedings, as stated above. Just as we now, from the authority and fullness of Imperial Majesty and true knowledge, now as then and then as now, inhibit, suspend and abrogate them by the force and virtue of these letters.

units.la: Et si ultra hoc ab ullo judice aut judicio processum, actitatum, aut ulla lata sententia fuerit, id in universum & sigillatim nullum, irritum, & invalidum esse debet, & eum, eosve, contra quos talis processus instituetur, aut sententia feretur, nequaquam obliger aut teneat, ullo modo aut ratione; sine dolo malo, &c. & in signum ac testimonium horum, sigillum &c. Ratisbonæ, M. D. XXXII.
units.tr: And if, beyond this, any process has been carried on or acted upon by any judge or court, or any sentence has been pronounced, this shall be null, void and invalid in general and in particular, and shall in no way or manner bind or hold him or them against whom such process is instituted or such sentence is pronounced; without evil intent, etc. And in sign and testimony of these things, the seal, etc. Regensburg, 1532.

units.la: CAROLI V. IMPER. AUG. FORMULA
