units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: De Sacramento Poenitentiae.
units.tr: Of the Sacrament of Repentance.

units.la: AC quoniam homines renati saepe in gravia crimina incidunt, instituit Christus Sacramentum Poenitentiae, quod post baptismum in nobis tanquam secunda tabula in naufragio ... clavem solvendi impuniter. Accipite Spiritum Sanctum: quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis. Si mutacesimi peccatorem peccati sui poenitere vere, idemque cum fiducia accedit ad confessionem ... credidit hoc Sacramento accipi quod Christus promisit, in efficiente rerum divinarum Sacramentorum huius, quod promissum est. Utenim Sacramenta alia, sic et haec cum habet sanctificare et confitentur Sacramentum hoc ... quae in corpore et sanguine Domini manet ...
units.tr: And since regenerate men often fall into grave sins, Christ instituted the Sacrament of Repentance, which after baptism is in us like a second plank in a shipwreck ... the key of loosing with impunity. Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them. If a sinner truly repents of his sin and with confidence comes to confession ... he believes that by this sacrament is received what Christ promised, in the efficacy of the divine sacraments of this kind, which was promised. For as the other sacraments do, so this one also has the power to sanctify, and it confesses this sacrament ... which remains in the body and blood of the Lord ...

units.la: Ibidem. Iuxta ... potestatem ... sacerdotibus ...
units.tr: Ibid. According to ... power ... to priests ...

units.la: 2. Sed quia etiam sacerdotes non solum habet potestatem ... iudicandi ...
units.tr: 2. But because priests not only have the power ... of judging ...

units.la: 3. Magna quoque ad fundendum hominum delicta ... remedium ... poenitentiae ...
units.tr: 3. Also great is the remedy of repentance for the cleansing of men's offences ...

units.la: 4. Interest illa ... sacramentum ... sanctorum ... et ... Ecclesiae ... Patres ...
units.tr: 4. It lies between ... the sacrament ... of the saints ... and ... the Church ... the Fathers ...

units.la: 5. Sed ut ad absolutionem sacerdotis in qua consistit vis Sacramenti poenitentiae, redeamus: forma ejus & verbum tale esse debet, ut qui confitetur, audire atq; intelligere possit, sibi virtute, meritò ac beneficio Christi, peccata remitti, juxta hujus institutum & verbum: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis. Nam hoc munus est Dei, cum ministerium sit sacerdotis, ut verbis Ambrosii utamur.
units.tr: 5. But to return to the absolution of the priest, in which the force of the Sacrament of Repentance consists: its form and wording must be such that the one who confesses can hear and understand that, by the power, merit and benefit of Christ, his sins are remitted to him, according to this institution and word: Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them. For this is the gift of God, although it is the ministry of the priest, to use the words of Ambrose.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: De Sacramento Eucharistiae.
units.tr: On the Sacrament of the Eucharist.

units.la: Qui jam per Sacramentum poenitentiae revixit in Domino, eii tem necesse est ali, & in bono spiritu ut crescere. Instituit igitur Christus Sacramentum Eucharistiae sub visibili specie panis & vini, quod verum Christi corpus & sanguinem nobis praebet, & hoc spirituali cibo unit nos sibi ut capiti & membris corporis sui, ut in ipso ad omne bonum enutriamur, & cum sanctis in eorum communione congescamus per charitatem, Unus enim panis unum corpus multi sumus, omnes qui ex uno pane participamus, inquit Paulus.
units.tr: Once a person has been restored to life in the Lord through the Sacrament of penance, he must then be fed and grow in the good spirit. Christ therefore instituted the Sacrament of the Eucharist under the visible form of bread and wine, which gives us the true body and blood of Christ, and by this spiritual food unites us to himself as to the head and members of his body, so that we may be nourished in him unto every good and, through love, grow together with the saints in their communion. "For we, being many, are one bread, one body, all of us who partake of the one bread," says Paul.

units.la: 2. Forma autem hujus Sacramenti, sunt verba illa solennia, quae Christus ipse dedit: Hoc est corpus meum. & iterum: Hic est enim calix sanguinis mei, &c.
units.tr: 2. The form of this Sacrament consists of those solemn words which Christ himself gave: "This is my body," and again: "For this is the cup of my blood," etc.

units.la: 3. Quod si igitur Christo & verbo ejus tantum tribuimus, quantum debemus: dubium non est, quin simulac verba eadem accedunt ad panem & vinum, ex his fiat verum corpus & verus sanguis Christi, quatenus panis ac vini substantia in verum Christi corpus & sanguinem transmutatur: quod qui negat, idem Christi omnipotentiam in dubium vocat, & eundem ipsum vanitatis insimulat.
units.tr: 3. If, then, we attribute to Christ and his word as much as we ought, there is no doubt that as soon as these same words are joined to the bread and wine, the true body and true blood of Christ are made from them, in that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the true body and blood of Christ. Whoever denies this calls into doubt the omnipotence of Christ and charges him with falsehood.

units.la: 4. Quo magis cavendum est, ne indigne hoc Sacramentum sumatur. Scriptum est enim: Nam qui edit aut bibit indigne, judicium sibi edit ac bibit, non diiudicans corpus Domini. Propter hoc multi inter vos infirmi sunt ac imbecilles, & dormiunt multi. Indigne autem sumit Sacramentum illud, quicunque aut aliter de eo sentit quam oporteat, aut non vere resipiscit. Nam, ut Augustinus inquit, mutet vitam, qui vult accipere vitam: nam si non mutet vitam, ad judicium accipiet vitam: & magis ex ipsa corrumpitur, quam sanetur: magis occiditur, quam vivificetur. Itaque probanda est confessio tudo Ecclesiae, quae hominem non ante ad Sacramentum Eucharistiae ducit, quam poenitentiae Sacramentum eum repurgarit.
units.tr: 4. All the more must we take care not to receive this Sacrament unworthily. For it is written: "For he who eats or drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. For this reason many among you are weak and feeble, and many sleep" (1 Cor. 11). Now whoever receives that Sacrament unworthily is one who either thinks of it otherwise than he ought, or does not truly repent. For, as Augustine says, "let him who wishes to receive life change his life; for if he does not change his life, he will receive it to judgment, and is corrupted by it rather than healed, and is killed rather than made alive." Therefore the confession of the Church is to be approved, which does not lead a person to the Sacrament of the Eucharist before the Sacrament of penance has cleansed him.

units.la: 5. Habet Eucharistia vim roborandi in bono spirituali: cui rei non sane ullus est locus, nisi repurgatio peccatorum antecesserit. In quo ipso imitari debemus bonos medicos, qui non ante praebent quae toborare ac confirmare possunt, quàm malos humores e corporibus ejecerint: quod nisi fecerint, non prosunt aegroto, sed magis obsunt. Jam quanto major hic adhibenda est cautio, ne indigne sumas: tanto plus consolationis capiunt, qui eucharistiam digne ac pie sumunt, & cogitant se panem e coelo descendente, qui vitam dat mundo, vesci: & ex hoc verum atque spirituale robur contra omnia mala percipere.
units.tr: 5. The Eucharist has the power to strengthen in the good spirit, but there is certainly no room for this unless the cleansing from sins has gone before. Here we ought to imitate good physicians, who do not give remedies that can strengthen and restore before they have expelled the bad humours from the body; if they did not, these would not help the patient but rather harm him. Now, the greater the caution needed here, lest we receive unworthily, the more consolation they gain who receive the Eucharist worthily and devoutly, and who consider that they feed upon the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world, and from this receive a true and spiritual strength against all evils.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: De sacra unctione.
units.tr: On the holy anointing.

units.la: Sacramenta, quae paulo superius posuimus, magnam sane & multiplicem utilitatem generi humano afferunt: tum aut ex vetustate carnis languentes regenerant, aut regeneratos, in gratia quam acceperunt, confirmant: aut relapsos, in gratiam unde deciderunt, restituunt: aut restitutos, Christo firmius uniunt: in quem usum, eumque salutarem, non deest Sacramentis gratia Christi: sed haec potius per eadem veluti instrumenta hominibus tribuitur. Quanquam igitur horum Sacramentorum utilitas latissime per omnem vitam patet, tamen ne homo, cum aegrotat, desideret subsidium peculiare, quod hoc ejus periculosissimo tempore, vel corpori ipsius subvenire, vel animam contra ignita Satanae munire possit, institua est unctio sacra, ad quam oratio Ecclesiae accedat. Hanc unctionem primi exercuerunt Apostoli, qui mandato Domini ad praedicandum Evangelium missi, daemonia ejiciebant, & oleo ungebant multos infirmos, & sanabantur. Quae utique sacramentalis & mystica, non medicinalis aut corporalis, unctio fuit: ad quam inter initia fidei, externa etiam corporis sanitas, quasi quoddam internae sanationis signum, consequebatur, quemadmodum in aliis sacramentis, ad commendationem & confirmationem rudis adhuc fidei, interna virtus externis & sensibilibus signis & miraculis demonstrabatur. Nunc vero adulta & corroborata fides, signa quae infirmis dantur, non requirit.
units.tr: The sacraments we have set out a little earlier bring the human race a truly great and manifold benefit. They either restore the sick, who languish from the old nature of the flesh; or they confirm those who have been regenerated in the grace they have received; or they restore the fallen to the grace from which they fell; or they bind the restored more firmly to Christ. For this purpose, and a saving one, the grace of Christ is not wanting to the sacraments, but is rather given to human beings through them as through instruments. Although the usefulness of these sacraments extends very widely through the whole of life, nevertheless, so that a man who is sick should not lack a special help, one that can either aid his body in this most dangerous time or fortify his soul against the fiery darts of Satan, the holy anointing was instituted, to which the prayer of the Church is joined. The Apostles were the first to practise this anointing. Sent by the Lord's command to preach the Gospel, they cast out demons, anointed many sick people with oil, and they were healed. This anointing was indeed sacramental and mystical, not medicinal or bodily. In the early days of faith, outward bodily health followed upon it as a kind of sign of inward healing, just as in the other sacraments the inward power was shown by outward and perceptible signs and miracles, for the commendation and confirmation of faith that was still immature. But now that faith is grown up and strengthened, it does not require the signs that were given to the sick.

units.la: 2. Hujus mysticae & salutaris unctionis a Domino fundatae ritum, quo administrari eam conveniat, Apostolus Jacobus promulgavit: Infirmatur quis in vobis? inducat presbyteros Ecclesiae, ut orent super eum, ungentes eum oleo in nomine Domini: & oratio fidei salvabit infirmum, & allevabit eum Dominus, &c.
units.tr: 2. The Apostle James set out the rite by which this mystical and saving anointing, founded by the Lord, ought to be administered: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the Church, that they may pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up, etc.

units.la: 3. Quanti autem in Ecclesia esse debeat testimonium fratris illius Domini, testimonium dicimus, immo vero promulgatio quam cum fecit legatus atque Apostolus Christi, Christus ut a se factam occultabit ratam habuit. Qui igitur contemnit hoc Sacramentum, Christum ipsum contemnere, & grauam, quam hic per unctionem sacram nobis quodammodo porrigit, aspernari videtur: atque haec fuerit tanto periculosius, quanto gravius est discrimen, in quo aegrotus versatur, non solum corporis, sed etiam animae, in quod potestates tenebrarum eum adducunt, quatenus in extremo vitae tempore, omnes quasi machinas ad extinguendam salutem hominis admovent, eiusque animum terroribus incredibilibus frangere, & in desperationem impellere conantur. 4. Unctionem quidem hanc sacram, solis infirmis adhibendam Jacobus Apostolus, reliqui etiam Apostoli servaverunt: non tamen in omnibus, sed periculosis modo infirmantibus, ac vitæ hujus interitus timetur, exercenda est mystica illa unctio.
units.tr: 3. How great the weight of the testimony of that brother of the Lord ought to be in the Church, we say. Indeed, the promulgation which the envoy and Apostle of Christ made, Christ has as good as ratified, as if he had made it himself. Whoever therefore despises this sacrament seems to despise Christ himself, and to scorn the grace which he here, through the holy anointing, in some way offers us. And this is all the more dangerous, the more grave is the peril in which the sick person lies, not only of body but also of soul, into which the powers of darkness bring him. In the last hours of life they bring to bear, as it were, all their engines to extinguish a man's salvation, and they strive to break his spirit with incredible terrors and drive him into despair. 4. This holy anointing, however, the Apostle James ordained should be applied only to the sick, and the other Apostles also observed this. Yet it is not to be practised for all the sick, but only for those who are sick in a dangerous way, where death is feared in this life.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: De Sacramento ordinis.
units.tr: On the Sacrament of Orders.

units.la: Quod autem ad ministeria Ecclesiæ attinet, quanto hæc majora sunt, tanto magis divina ac gratia egent. Quanquam enim Christiani omnes sunt sacerdotes, quatenus spirituales hostias Deo offerre, & nomen item ejus in omni loco utiliter invocare possunt: non omnes tamen sunt Ecclesiæ ministri, sed jam inde ab ortu ecclesiæ segregati sunt quidam in ministerium ecclesiæ, quorum muneribus fungerentur: & eosdem ita distinxit Deus, ne iidem omnia possent, neve ex perturbatio nasceretur. Neque enim Deus est confusionis author. Institutum est signum sacramentum ordinis, cum signo impositionis manuum, & aliis huic sacramento congruentibus, quo qui consecrarentur, ad munera ecclesiæ acciperent gratiam, qua ad eadem ipsa munera idonei apti, habiles atque idonei efficerentur. Hinc illud Apostoli ad Timotheum: Noli negligere gratiam quæ in te est, quæ data est tibi per prophetiam cum impositione manuum presbyterii.
units.tr: As for the ministries of the Church, the greater they are, the more they need divine grace. For although all Christians are priests, in that they can offer spiritual sacrifices to God and usefully call upon his name in every place, yet not all are ministers of the Church. From the very beginning of the Church certain men have been set apart for the ministry of the Church, to discharge its offices; and God so distinguished them that the same men would not do everything, lest disorder should arise. For God is not the author of confusion. A sign was instituted, the sacrament of orders, together with the sign of the laying on of hands and other things fitting to this sacrament, by which those who were consecrated received grace for the offices of the Church, so that they would be made fit, suitable, capable and qualified for those same offices. Hence that saying of the Apostle to Timothy: "Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the elders."

units.la: 2. Hoc autem ordinis sacramentum verbis Christi nititur: Sicut me misit Pater & ego mitto vos: accipite Spiritum sanctum: quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis. Item. Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. Item. Euntes, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos. Item. Hoc facite in meam commemorationem. Quibus igitur in perpetua Ecclesiæ successione manus imponunt Episcopi, ut ordinibus initientur, potestatem muneris sui exequendi dant: quæ sane duplex est, ordinis videlicet et jurisdictionis. Sub altera cadit ministerium verbi divini, administratio sacramentorum, & ecclesiæ ordinatio ad ædificationem: sub altera vero, potestas excommunicandi, pœnitentes absolvendi. Ordines autem quos Catholica Ecclesia agnoscit sunt hi septem: Presbyterorum, Diaconorum, Subdiaconorum, Acolytorum, Lectorum, Exorcistarum, Ostiariorum, quibus distincta munera, eaque necessaria ecclesiis, aut utilia, assignari debent: ut facile appareat, eum de ecclesia Christiana male meritum, quicunque ordines hos vel spernit, vel tollit.
units.tr: 2. This sacrament of orders rests on the words of Christ: "As the Father has sent me, so I send you: receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them." Likewise: "Go into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature." Likewise: "Go, teach all nations, baptizing them." Likewise: "Do this in remembrance of me." Therefore, to those on whom the bishops lay hands in the perpetual succession of the Church, that they may be initiated into the orders, they give the power of performing their office; which power is indeed twofold, namely of order and of jurisdiction. Under the one falls the ministry of the divine Word, the administration of the sacraments, and the ordering of the Church for edification; under the other, the power of excommunicating and of absolving the penitent. The orders which the Catholic Church acknowledges are these seven: those of presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, readers, exorcists and doorkeepers, to which distinct offices, and those necessary or useful to the churches, ought to be assigned; so that it readily appears that whoever either despises or removes these orders has deserved ill of the Christian Church.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: De Sacramento matrimonii.
units.tr: On the Sacrament of Marriage.

units.la: Institutus Deus in paradiso matrimonium, quo mas & fœmina ad perpetuam & individuam societatem conjungerentur, juxta verbum Domini: Quamobrem homo relinquet patrem & matrem, & adhærebit uxori suæ, & erunt duo in carne una.
units.tr: God instituted marriage in Paradise, by which man and woman would be joined in a perpetual and indivisible fellowship, according to the Lord's word: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be one flesh.

units.la: 2. Quanquam autem matrimonium ad tam arctam hominum societatem institutum erat, sub lege patrum matrimonia à prima institutione duobus modis degeneraverunt: videlicet ut plures uxores ducerent, & ductam, aliquando dato libello repudii, à se dimitterent: quorum dispensatione Dei permissum, futuri temporis mysterio serviebat, ut per plures unius viri uxores Christum tam ex synagoga quam ex multitudine gentium, ecclesiam sibi collectam sponsam sibi adjuncturum: & ut fœcunditate plurium uxorum, Christo Salvatori ex eodem nascituro servirent.
units.tr: 2. Although marriage was instituted for so close a fellowship of men, under the law of the fathers marriages degenerated from the first institution in two ways: namely, that men took several wives, and sometimes, after giving a bill of divorce, dismissed the wife they had taken. By God's permission this arrangement served the mystery of the future time: through the many wives of one man, Christ would join to himself as bride the church gathered both from the synagogue and from the multitude of the Gentiles; and by the fruitfulness of several wives they would serve Christ the Saviour, who was to be born from the same stock.

units.la: 3. Repudium verò Moyses populo ob duritiam cordis permisit lenius ducens, uxorem a viro habitam dimitti, quàm occidi, ut cæde ejus novis nuptiis locum aperiret.
units.tr: 3. Moses, however, permitted divorce to the people because of the hardness of their hearts, judging it gentler that a wife held by a husband be dismissed rather than killed, so that by her slaughter he would open the way to new marriage.

units.la: 4. Verùm postquam plenitudo gratiæ Dei venit, ut alia, quæ vel in cœlo vel in terra esse ravit Christus, sic etiam matrimonium restituit. Hinc illud Christi: Qui fecit hominem ab initio masculum & fœminam fecit eos DEVS. & dixit: Propter hoc dimittet homo patrem & matrem, & adhærebit uxori suæ, & erunt duo in carne una. Itaque jam non sunt duo, sed una caro. Quos igitur Deus conjunxit, homo non separet. Paulò post: Moyses ob duritiam cordis vestri permisit vobis dimittere uxores vestras, ab initio autem non fuit sic. Quamobrem quicunque dimittit uxorem suam, nisi ob fornicationem, & aliam duxerit, mœchatur. Quod Apostolus interpretatur, cum ait: Iis qui matrimonio juncti sunt, præcipio non ego, sed Dominus, uxorem à viro non discedere: quod si discesserit, manere innuptam, aut viro suo reconciliari.
units.tr: 4. But after the fullness of God's grace came, Christ restored marriage as he restored other things, whether in heaven or on earth. Hence Christ's words: He who made man from the beginning made them male and female, and said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh. So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder. A little later: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to put away your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. Therefore whoever puts away his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery. The Apostle explains this when he says: To those who are joined in marriage I give charge, not I but the Lord: that the wife should not separate from her husband; but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.

units.la: 5. Hæc itaque Christiani matrimonii singulares conditiones, manifestis Scripturæ sanctionibus comprobantur. Una, ut sit matrimonium duorum tantùm, hoc est, viri unius cum una conjunctio. Duo, inquit, erunt in carne una. Necfic junctis liceat, defraudato conjugis suo, alicujus corporis sui potestatem permittere, prohibente Apostolo & dicente: Mulier potestatem corporis sui non habet, sed vir: similiter & vir non habet potestatem sui corporis, sed mulier. Altera conditio est, ut vinculum conjugii sit jugii inter duos semel colligatum, nullo amplius divortio, sed sola alterutrius morte, dissolvendum. Nam quòd Christus ob fornicationem dimitti posse uxorem insinuat, hæc separatio tamen & mensæ consuetudinem inter conjuges scindit, vinculum conjugii non solvit, ita ut adulter mittat, ut alienam contrectans uxorem, quisquis sic dimissam duxerit.
units.tr: 5. These, then, are the peculiar conditions of Christian marriage, and they are confirmed by plain sanctions of Scripture. The first is that marriage is of two only, that is, the union of one man with one woman: They shall be two in one flesh. Nor, when they are thus joined, is it lawful for either to defraud the other by granting to someone else power over their body, since the Apostle forbids it and says: The wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife. The other condition is that the bond of marriage, once tied between two, is lasting, to be dissolved by no divorce, but only by the death of one of them. For although Christ indicates that a wife may be dismissed for fornication, this separation nevertheless divides bed and table between the spouses; it does not dissolve the bond of marriage, so that whoever marries such a dismissed woman commits adultery, as one who touches another's wife.

units.la: 6. Quoniam igitur Christus matrimonii gratia sua melius fecit, & atdiori quasi vinculo ut quemadmodum Christus unius Ecclesiæ unus est sponsus, idque indissolubili nexu, sic unius uxoris unus vir. Sed hoc divortium facta, sacrae res sunt quae parum divinae explicantur.
units.tr: 6. Since therefore Christ made marriage better by his grace, and bound it by a firmer tie, as Christ is the one bridegroom of the one Church, with an indissoluble bond, so one wife has one husband. [illegible, ~40 letters] union, and is torn asunder; but Christ remains perpetually with the Church, his bride. Marriage is not only a bond of sex and of companionship but also a sacrament of Christ, which no one who has once taken a wife from a husband may put away, as if content with the one wife in perpetuity. But this divorce makes sacred matters which are little explained in terms of the divine.

units.la: Accipimus etiam Deus favet sanctimonium gratiam, idemque approbat, quatenus coniuges [illegible, ~30 letters] conveniunt, ut in deum illustre, ad sperandum coniugium ipsorum cum [illegible, ~12 letters] Deo gratiam. Et quamquam proles promenda causa matrimonium pertinet, nemo qui contrahit eam fortasse nomen vitiande causa, non peccat. Itaque cum Pauli ... inquit Paulus. Virginis Sacramentum hujus est, ut incelli-gentes, non humanae, sed divina auctoritate conjunctos, gratiam accepisse, quae multi legiti-mum mortem ad culpam: qua item Christianorum matrimonium generale, cum excessere iudicant, & sanctos, sanctos, Deo dicatos filios procreare: quae denique perpetuam fidem servet, & inter se in carne una, & quae matrimonium fidelis salva sit in procreatione filiorum. Apparent enim se fi-delium judicia eorum comparatur, Itaque maritum omnium honorabile, in eo quoque nuptiae peccatu.
units.tr: We also hear that God favours holy chastity, and approves it, insofar as the spouses come together so that, hoping for the grace of God, their marriage may be in the Lord. And although the procreation of offspring is the principal cause of marriage, one who marries perhaps for the sake of avoiding fornication does not sin. Therefore, as Paul says... The sacrament of this is that those joined not by human but by divine authority have received grace, which many lawful marriages ... and which the Christian marriage in general, when they judge it has gone beyond, and to beget holy children dedicated to God; and finally that it keep perpetual faith, and that they remain one flesh with one another, and that the marriage of the faithful be safe in the procreation of children. For the judgments of the faithful are thus compared, and therefore marriage is honourable in all, and in it the marriage bed is undefiled.

units.la: Quod ideo Manichaei, Tatiani & Encratitae ignorarent, matrimonium reprehendere non confessum corum sociorum reiectarent, de quibus inde deorum malefactos, Apostolus 1 Tim.4 damnat.
units.tr: This is why the Manichaeans, Tatian and the Encratites, not knowing this, condemned marriage and rejected its sacred bond, which the Apostle in 1 Tim. 4 condemns as the teaching of demons.

units.la: Aliquorum vinculum matrimonii esse omnino tantumque viri habet ad coniugem conjunctionis humanae vinculum, quod magis confirmat; quod cum agnohomine Paradiso, de muliere, quam Deus e costa corporis sui adiunxerit, locum est, [illegible, ~20 letters] & caro de carne mea: hoc nunc dicam hoc sublimat, quoniam & vir fuit Sacro. Quamobrem patrem & matrem, & adhaerebit uxori suae, & erunt duo in carne una.
units.tr: Some say the bond of marriage is entirely ... and has so much of the bond of human union between husband and wife, which the more confirms it; for when Adam acknowledged in Paradise the woman whom God had taken from the side of his body, saying: This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. This he proclaims as a sublime mystery, and then the Scripture adds: Therefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh.

units.la: Itaque cum patres potestas huic eratur conjuges conjunctionis fuerunt nobis audiendum ex talibus hoc tempore matrimonium vel propter illa contractu sunt & miraculo, & paternum ultimum scelerum. Nihil hic de talibus obedientiae quam Deus permittit debere, sed malo-rum tempore sed de hoc uxorem mentis matrimonium non est habere. Quia tamen ex illorum fratrem et liberos sine consilio & consensu patrum non contrahant, hujus officium per eos me fistulo admonendi sunt.
units.tr: Thus, although parents had power over these matters, we must hear from such examples that at this time marriage is contracted by those agreements and miracles, and that the last paternal ... of wicked times. Nothing is said here about the obedience which God permits, but in evil times the wife of the mind does not have marriage. Yet since they should not contract marriage with their brothers and children without the counsel and consent of parents, they are to be admonished through them.

units.la: Anno o parentibus potestas permissa ut discat hoc casu, liberorum non obedientiam damatur, aut falsam dimittitione dotis, aut aliqua alia via puniendi, de hac re otiosam potestatem vita videtur.
units.tr: In the year ... parents were granted power so that they may learn in this case; the disobedience of children is condemned, either by the false dismissal of a dowry or by some other way of punishing, and in this matter the power of life seems to be idle.

units.la: Tunc vero sacrificandum est Deus, volens omnes hominum salvos fieri, cum ei dicat hominum divinitus in eum. units.tr: 20. And although the Sacrament of the Eucharist under both kinds, in Greek, of the Ordination, when at last Christ is in the whole body, and holy Scripture by divine rites, and of the Lord, as it were at Pentecost, this one.

units.tr: 22. Since the Sacrament of the Eucharist under both kinds, in the name of Christ, not even in the name of Christians, yet ought to be handled as the Sacrament of both the body and the blood of Christ.

units.la: 23. Quae ergo ad disciplinam Ecclesiae, populi pertinent, quaecumque in ipsa Ecclesia constituta sunt, prout in hac nostra Constitutione, & populo tradita.
units.tr: 23. Whatever pertains to the discipline of the Church and of the people, whatever has been established in the Church itself, as it has been handed down to the people in this our Constitution.

units.la: NOS CAROLUS Imperator Semper Augustus, Sacrae Romanae Maiestatis Imperator, ex Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator, semper Augustus, Rex Germaniae, Hispaniarum, Hungariae, Bohemiae, Dalmatiae, Croatiae, Galliae, Hierosolymae, Neapolis, Siciliae, Sardiniae, Corsicae, Majoricae, Hispaniae, Indiarum, &c. Archidux Austriae, Dux Burgundiae, Lotharingiae, Brabantiae, Limburgi, Luxemburgi, Gelriae, Calabriae, Athenarum, Comes Habspurgi, Flandriae, Tirolis, Goritiae, Barcinonis, Artesiae, Burgundiae, Palatinus Hannoniae, Hollandiae, Zelandiae, Phrisiae, Kiburgi, Namurci, Zutphaniae, Sacri Romani Imperii Marchio, Burgaviae, Ordenburgi, Frisiae, Sacri Romani Imperii Princeps, Suevie, Catalaniae, Ghelriae, &c. Dominus Phrisiae, Marchio Sacri Romani Imperii, Burgaviae, Mediolani, Salutiarum, Tripoli, & Mechliniae, &c. Notum sit omnibus.
units.tr: WE, CHARLES, Emperor Ever August, Emperor of the Sacred Roman Majesty, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, ever August, King of Germany, of Spain, Hungary, Bohemia, Dalmatia, Croatia, Gaul, Jerusalem, Naples, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, Majorca, the Spains, the Indies, &c.; Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, Lorraine, Brabant, Limburg, Luxemburg, Guelders, Calabria, Athens; Count of Habsburg, Flanders, Tyrol, Gorizia, Barcelona, Artois, Burgundy, Palatine of Hainault, Holland, Zeeland, Friesland, Kyburg, Namur, Zutphen, Margrave of the Holy Roman Empire, Burgau, Ortenburg, Frisia, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, Swabia, Catalonia, Guelders, &c.; Lord of Friesland, Margrave of the Holy Roman Empire, of Burgau, Milan, Saluzzo, Tripoli, and Mechlin, &c. Let it be known to all.

units.la: Pacis publicae ut tenendae.
units.tr: Of keeping the public peace.

units.la: CUm ergo hoc Imperio Romano Germanico sub Imperatoris Caroli Quinti, Pacis publicae, de quo Constitutio Augustae, & ordinationibus, non dubitandum est. [illegible, ~40 letters] Christianorum dissidia & pacis conturbationes, [illegible, ~30 letters] quae in Imperio contingunt, [illegible, ~60 letters] Imperii statibus publicam pacem constituenda [illegible, ~80 letters] hactenus fuerunt concessa. Haec non ita[?] [illegible, ~120 letters] quod nulla inter [illegible, ~20 letters] tutelae coepit[?] [illegible, ~50 letters] Ideo volumus, ut quicunque[?] in Imperio ab omni diffidatione et bello abstineat, [illegible, ~200 letters] Imperator et Principes, Ecclesiasticorum, Praelatorum, Comitum & Baronum, Imperii Status, Civitatum, ut supra, ex[?] [illegible, ~100 letters] Quae omnia ac singula observari volumus.
units.tr: Since therefore in this Roman-German Empire, under the Emperor Charles V, concerning the public peace, which is set out in the Constitution of Augsburg and its ordinances, there is no doubt [...] the dissensions of Christians and the disturbances of peace [...] which arise in the Empire [...] to be established for the Estates of the Empire as public peace [...] hitherto have been granted. These [...] Therefore we will that whoever in the Empire abstain from all defiance and war [...] the Emperor and the Princes, ecclesiastical prelates, counts and barons, the Estates of the Empire, the cities, as above [...]. All of which, singly and collectively, we will to be observed.

units.la: Iam & illi, per quem ejusmodi fractae pacis facinora patrantur, nemo aut ipse, aut aliquis ministret, consulat, auxilium praestet, neque arcem, oppidum, munimentum, pagum, villam aut occupet, aut praeter alterius voluntatem vi facto, temere perpetret, aut hostilia commissa defendere praesumat, sed ad id auxilium praestet: nec scienter aut dolose recipiat, hospitium, commeatum, aut praebeat, aut praebeat. Sed si quisquam aliquid quid habere se putat, de eo experiatur suo foro, nulli, in quo jam ea aut omnes causae ex ordinatione nostri judicii Camerae expedientur, sed de hoc ordine expediendae fuerint.
units.tr: Likewise, to him through whom such deeds of broken peace are carried out, let no one, either himself or through another, minister, advise or lend aid, nor occupy by force a fortress, town, stronghold, village, hamlet or farm, nor rashly do violence against another's will, nor presume to defend hostile acts once committed, but let him render aid to that end. Nor knowingly or deceitfully receive or provide lodging or provisions. But if anyone thinks he has some claim, let him seek his remedy in his own court, not in [...], where all such causes are to be settled by the ordinance of our Imperial Chamber Court, but they are to be settled in this order.

units.la: CAP. II. * Abrogatio omnis diffidationis & Belli.
units.tr: CHAP. II. Repeal of all defiance and war.

units.la: Et ad quidem omnia manifesta & publica bella, bellisq; denunciationes privatas ac fidei hostium abrogavimus, collatus & remittimus: abrogamus, collatio & remittimus, ut ab hac causa a Romanae Imperii potestate, ac virtus harum literarum.
units.tr: Indeed, for all manifest and public wars, and private declarations of war, and the faith of enemies, we have abrogated, collated and remitted; we abrogate, collate and remit, so that from this cause, by the power of the Roman Empire and the force of these letters [...].

Then also under the penalties and [...] of each prince, the rights of ours, which each of them has from us, that this peace be diligently observed and maintained and carried out as stated [...] and the officials and subjects of the middle jurisdiction [...] in this Empire. units.la: Ceterum ut conservandam nobis in prætextu prosequentibus, et debitis cum multis, et ordinationes, ut Banni, aliisq; pœnis contra eos qui illi decreverint, exequi procedente, et debite etiam eorum notarii contra eos ac Statutum, ut ita pæna, et ad debitum, nec ille bene, quam sentiant, ut debita, quæ ex ipsa sint, quod judicia Cameræ ordinationes sint ipsa conspiciant.
units.tr: Moreover, so that the ordinances may be kept in force, the ban and other penalties are to be carried out against those who have pursued their own ends under pretext and who have incurred debts with many people. Likewise, their notaries are to be proceeded against, along with those who have issued the decrees, according to the statute, so that the penalty and the debt are enforced as they should be, and the judgments of the Chamber and the ordinances themselves are observed.

units.la: Si quis autem nostram hanc ordinationem, ac obligationem contemp̄serit, nec eam praestiterit, sed præfectum, effecerit, aut negligens fuerit, ubi palam iuniverit, ita, ut negari non potest, eam pronunciatam, declaratam hac memoriae ipsius propter ejus iudici rei, [illegible, ~3 lines] ad hanc: actum quidem contra eos dem, etiam denunciatione, declaratione, eorumque aliam fratrem, id eum aliquid pœnarum per eos, ac eorum extra facient, Imperium abstinere ab eo per [illegible, ~2 lines] Regem, aut nostrum Imperiale judicium Camerae severe ac [illegible, ~3 lines] procedi, agi, quæ possit ac debeat, prout iuris ratio postulat, publicæ pacis [illegible, ~1 line] æquum fuerit.
units.tr: If anyone, moreover, despises this our ordinance and obligation, and does not carry it out, but hinders it or is negligent in it, and openly acts against it, so that it cannot be denied that it was proclaimed and declared, then, against such persons, whether by the denunciation or declaration of this (ordinance) and of the others, the penalties mentioned above shall be imposed upon them and their accomplices, and the empire shall abstain from them. Let the king, or our imperial court of chamber, proceed severely against them, and let the case be pursued as the law allows and requires, as is fitting for the maintenance of the public peace.

Praeterea quoque Comitus propter compotationes & ebrietatem causa constitutum est, ut quisque magistratus compotationes abrogaret, & ebrietatibus adversaretur, transgressores vero ac delinquentes severe punirent. Quae ordinationes quidem ac constitutiones hactenus tamen parum tantum profecerunt, quin abusus is & ataxia compotationum & ebrietatum magis ac magis invaluerit, ac ceu radices in helluonum fundo egit, ut propagatum exuberet ampliusque. Ex quo blasphemiae, criminationes, calumniae, dejerationes, homicidia, stupra, adulteria, ac multa {illegible, ~20 letters} ac lascivia, vitiorumque omne genus, velut ex agmine facto extenduntur, hoc sine dubio quin ex ebrietate res facienda & secreta quandoque prodantur, eoque potentiores vino {illegible, ~30 letters} Germanis peculiarina, quorum virtus tamen apud priscos tempore laudata, apud exteras plerasque nationes vituperatio, ludibrio-que est.
units.tr: Since wine, as daily experience teaches, by drunkenness and drinking bouts, almighty God ... the world is contaminated, and many vicious and impious deeds are born and emerge. Moreover, also at the Diet, on account of drinking bouts and drunkenness, it was decreed that every magistrate should abolish drinking bouts and oppose drunkenness, and should severely punish transgressors and offenders. Yet these ordinances and constitutions have so far achieved little, so that this abuse and disorder of drinking bouts and drunkenness has grown ever more strongly, and, like roots, has taken hold in the bottom of gluttons, so that it spreads and flourishes further. From this come blasphemies, accusations, slanders, oaths, homicides, debaucheries, adulteries, and much ... and lasciviousness, and every kind of vice, pour out as if in a marching column; and undoubtedly, because of drunkenness, things to be done and secrets are sometimes betrayed, and men are made more powerful by wine ... peculiar to the Germans, whose virtue was indeed praised by the ancients, but among most other nations is a matter of reproach and ridicule.

units.la: Accedit numero etiam ex illa inter milites rixae, contentiones, tumultus, & seditiones exortae, ducum, magistratuum ac ductorum contumaciae & rebelliones: commeatus quoque & victus sumptuosi augmentantur: Convivia vero honesta, & societates decorae, ex quibus olim Germani originem duxerunt, minuuntur ac evitantur, ut interea illeam, compotationes & ebrietates illorum xaxa, omnium malorum causam esse, hominisque vitam simul & animam, si liceat, deperdere, honorem, favorem, sensus, longaevitatem, & vires perdere. Quocirca mandamus omnibus & singulis Praelatis, Principibus, Ecclesiasticis & secularibus, ac exteris Statibus, cujuscunque dignitatis, status, aut nationis sint, ut eius subditi exemplo sint, majorisque in eo animadvertere, quin omnes habeant, ultro itaque sponte potationes & ebrietatem evitent, convivia tumultuosa, lasciviasque ac in eorum principatibus, dominus, terrae, territorii, omnibus indictis, compotationes ac pastiones prohibeant compotationes, quocumque modo fieri vel bibi-tur, sed in polius, plurimum quoque idem mandatum strictius observent atque custodiant. Parentes quoque suis domesticis & familiae, liberis, servis & ancillis, immunda atque pleraque criminationes & dejerationes in Deum, Deiq; genitricem, & Sanctos Dei, devitent ac carum quoque a comportationibus & ebrietatibus omnino abstineant, quarumcumque modiratione atque severe praecipiendo jubemus & mandamus.
units.tr: To this is added that from that same drinking among soldiers, quarrels, contentions, tumults and seditions arise, and the stubbornness and rebellions of commanders, magistrates and leaders; the provisions and costly supplies also increase. Honest banquets and decent societies, from which the Germans of old drew their origin, are diminished and avoided; meanwhile those drinking bouts and drunkenness, which are the cause of all evils, destroy, if it be allowed, the life and soul of men alike, and lose honour, favour, senses, long life and strength. Therefore we command and order all and each of the prelates, princes, ecclesiastical and secular, and the other estates, of whatever dignity, rank or nation they may be, that their subjects be an example, and that they take greater care in this, so that all of them of their own accord avoid drinking and drunkenness, tumultuous banquets and wantonness; and in their principalities, lordships, lands and territories, all drinking bouts and feasts, by any proclamation, are to be forbidden, in whatever manner they are held or drunk, and they are to observe and keep this same mandate more strictly and more fully. Parents too, with their household, family, children, servants and maidservants, are to avoid filthy and common accusations and oaths against God, the Mother of God and the saints of God, and likewise are to abstain entirely from drinking bouts and drunkenness; we order and command this with moderation and by strict precept.

units.la: Volumus item, ut Magistratus suis Parochis & Concionatoribus praecipue, simpliciter Domi-nicis ac plebi annuncient, ut compotationibus abstineant, enim quam ex compotationibus oriantur, & ex ebrietate sequantur: prout formula illi ejusdem denunciationis per Magistratum porrigetur.
units.tr: We will also that the magistrates especially instruct their parish priests and preachers, and announce simply to the people on Sundays, that they abstain from drinking bouts, and how many evils arise from drinking bouts and follow from drunkenness, just as the form of that same proclamation will be handed to them by the magistrate.

units.la: CAP. IX. De inordinatione & ataxia vestitus, ejusq; luxu seu profusione.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On disorder and lack of order in dress, and on its luxury or extravagance.

units.la: Quoniam honestus ac moderatus vestitus ex sua dignitate & statu quemque decet ornatque, cuiusque tamen manusquisque sese ac vestiat ex inaudito dignitatem, honorum, morum ac facultatum sive quod dicitur in cujusque status hominibus. Mediocritas vestitus ac ornamentorum potius quam luxuriae, prudentes ac honorabilis, inter homines aequales, nobiles, nomen & ordinem, ita ac ornamentis ac honorum, sed non solum privatae persona, vestis etiam nationes, & promiscue, ut per lusos, in quaeque vituperatas et contrarias, ac ornamentis hujusmodi, ac ac ostentationis, argentea, lanceaque inducta, Matrimoniorum, Arcularum, Cy-thaeorum, et serii, peregrinorum, panni, Mores moderatos imitantes ac honestos ... (ut hic sententia) ... [illegible, ~40 letters] vel bonum ... [illegible, ~60 letters] Comitem, ... Vicecomitem ... [illegible, ~80 letters] volumus atque jubemus.
units.tr: Since honest and moderate dress befits and adorns each person according to his dignity and station, let each man dress according to the dignity, honours, character and means of his rank, that is, according to the people of each estate. Moderation in clothing and ornament, rather than luxury, is prudent and honourable among equals and nobles, according to name and rank, and not only for private persons but also in the fashions of nations, and in every kind of dress, in such a way that the vain and contrary are condemned, namely the ornaments of ostentation, silver and lace-trimmed finery, [illegible] of matrimonies, caskets, [illegible] foreign cloth, imitating moderate and honest customs ... (thus the sense) ... [illegible, about 40 letters] or good ... [illegible, about 60 letters] count, ... viscount ... [illegible, about 80 letters] we will and command.

units.la: Q[illegible, ~80 letters] [illegible, ~70 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters] negociatores & avaros homines in specie & pretextu emptionis ac negotiationis earum, carum agnt. Vinum nemae hortorum vitibus, alioque fructus & frumenta, lanas, ansera, ac pecuniam mutuo dederunt, per quae pauperculi colones, egenique illi, dum, ladoreque acquisierunt, vitam pecori, leviculi, quod alioquin aliter o confugere cogerentur, vendendere cogantur. Quae rerum illi pauperculis plebi & colonis ad denarios, atque dispendiis ac corruptibilia inter, verum communem ipsorum seu proprieferorum debitus & credita, pretiam reddendo, potius, videlicet maximo sine malo damno, quod quod crassa vestra sicut & humana conditiones contrarii, delectantur proximi ac huius mores pergerent.
units.tr: ...[illegible]... merchants and greedy men, under the pretext and appearance of buying and trading, [illegible]. They lent wine, the produce of gardens and vineyards, other fruits and grain, wool, geese, and money on loan. Through these, poor little peasants and needy folk, when they had acquired these things from them and had been driven by necessity, are forced to sell their livestock and whatever else they have, which they would otherwise have been compelled to take refuge in. These merchants sell such goods to the poor common people and farmers at a high price, and they demand repayment of the debts and loans, with the prices inflated, so that the greater part of the loss falls on the debtors, and so that these practices, contrary to divine and human law, continue to delight them and to harm their neighbours.

units.la: Iccirco statuimus, constituimus & ordinamus, ut quisque pauper plebeius necessitate, speciali sub excessu facultatum precisione possit, ut sagi necessitatem vestibus & alimentis pro vino, frumento, lanubus, alijs, communi pretio, valore & estimatione eiusdem pendere, solvere ac debere, sicut de hac super eiusdem mercibus mutuum dare praesumptum sit. Cum quidem modi ut dictum est, grave, & in ea quidquam dolo tradi vel nec, & communi aeque de cetero vetetur, ut talis emptor seu mutuo datur, ion capitalitatis furtorum ab Magistratu, qui ea qualiacunque & conditionem causae, mulctetur & puniatur.
units.tr: Therefore we decree, establish and ordain that every poor plebeian who is in need, and who is under special pressure because of a lack of means, may pay, settle and owe the price of the goods, namely wine, grain, wool and the others, at the common price and valuation, just as has been presumed to be owed for loans of these same goods. And from now on it is forbidden, as has been said, for anyone to hand over such goods in a grievous and deceitful manner, on the same terms as a common buyer or lender. Whoever acts in this way, as a buyer or lender, shall be punished by the magistrate, in whatever manner and condition of the case, as a thief.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAP. XX.

units.la: De Iudaeis, & eorum usuris.
units.tr: On the Jews and their usury.

units.la: Ubi locis quibusdam Imperii Teutonicae nationis, Judaei usurarii non tantum ad magnas pecunias, sed etiam ad exiguas summas, quibus rebus illis ab hominibus vilium, plebemque miserum, egentem, & impotentem, Judaei quaedam pacta, pignora, usuras, quas etiam mutuo debitas vendunt, ac ad dam virtutes sine ulla commutatione ponenda. Itaque constituimus, ordinamus ac volumus, neque parte Judaei, aut illis ulla persona concedatur, plures quam illis, qui a nobis & sacro Imperii Regalia peculiaria ad hoc ipsum privilegia acceperunt.
units.tr: Whereas in certain places of the German nation's Empire, Jewish usurers lend not only large sums but also small amounts, by which means they fleece the common people, the vulgar, wretched, needy and helpless, and extract from them certain pacts, pledges and usuries, which they also sell as debts owed on loan, and lay down as sums to be repaid without any reckoning. We therefore decree, ordain and will that no Jew, nor any other person, be permitted to do this beyond what is allowed to those who have received special privileges for this very purpose from us and from the Holy Roman Empire's regalia.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI.

units.la: De venditione pannorum lanearum, & ex filis lanae textorum, tonsorum, aut particularum ad ulnas confectorum.
units.tr: On the sale of woollen cloths, and of cloths made from woollen yarn by weavers, cloth-shearers, or pieces made up by the ell.

units.la: Quam & id quidem comperimus est, quod in venditione ... pannorum tenerorum, totorum, vel particularum, quibus vestimus, & membra compositiones, multum plerumque in vestimentum ... emptor quandoque graviter decipitur, velut quod eius pannorum textura minus esset latum, deinde pretiosum & humidiorem nimis facta, alius emptori dedere: interdum etiam panni ferruginis duobus maculas insunt, in diligentia cuiusque Reipublicae.
units.tr: It has also been found that in the sale of fine cloths, whole or in pieces, of which we make clothing and parts of garments, the buyer is often seriously deceived. For example, the weave of the cloth is narrower than it should be, or it is made too heavy and too damp, and another cloth is handed over to the buyer. Sometimes too cloths have stains from iron rust, to the harm of each commonwealth.

units.la: Inde statuimus, ordinamus, ac volumus, ne deinceps in Imperio sacro Teutonicae nationis ullarum lanae per ulnas mensurando vendantur, nisi antea modo, ad iudicios aequa, aut. Verum utrique tamen integraque pannis non tenus, attamen mundi vendantur, quia omnis illorum & quaedam pannorum facta fuerint. Quodsi vero tonsi & tonsi effecti, nec ut tamen, eidem illorum pro damnatis & perditis in utroque praedium esse, attentur.
units.tr: Therefore we decree, ordain and will that henceforth in the Holy Empire of the German nation no woollen cloths be sold by measuring in ells, unless first they have been examined by fair judgment. But whole and entire cloths, not cut up, are to be sold clean, since all of them, and some cloths, have been made. But if they have been shorn and made shorn, they are to be regarded as condemned and lost, and not to be held as fit for sale.

units.la: Ac multa quidem Magistratus sub quo venduntur, & cuius civilis est jurisdictio, debeant. Hae ante ordinatio nostra incipiet in sex mensibus proximis, finitamque. Contra finitas facere, aut deinceps, abiquem in eum finitionem obtinetur ac exequantur. Quare & super his in sacro Imperio Teutonicae nationis, hucusque necessarium iudicium mandara vulgarum & publicarum fierent.
units.tr: The magistrate under whose authority they are sold, and whose civil jurisdiction it is, ought to see to this. This our ordinance shall begin to take effect within the next six months and be completed. Against those who act contrary to it after it is completed, the penalty is to be obtained and enforced. Wherefore also concerning these matters in the Holy Empire of the German nation, the judgment hitherto required is to be commanded to be made public.

units.la: Ne vero Magistratus locorum in his & indulgens cooperantur, nec in tantum ulterius animadverti faciant, cultores fortem & iustum vel ferocem coram eorum competente Judice, veleo pannorum penitentium, pro parte communi ipsos agendi quam petendi, per quos adversarius in diligitur, sibi deferre ... de pannorum mutandis, qui etiam solutione seu te esperta, prae sui accepit ut mercator.
units.tr: Lest the magistrates of the places, in these matters, cooperate with indulgence or allow further punishment to be imposed to such an extent, the cultivators, strong and just or fierce, before their competent judge, are to bring forward the cloths in their possession, on behalf of the common party as much as the one seeking, through whom the adversary is chosen; concerning the exchange of cloths, which he also accepts by settlement or experience, as a merchant.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: De lege ac tutamento cohabitatione.
units.tr: On the law and punishment of cohabitation.

units.la: Cum multae leges atque inhonestae personae extra matrimonium a Deo institutum cohabitant quidem ordinatas et praeceptas, ut quaelibet Magistratus, Ecclesiasticae partes et quam cares in iectare denoleutur, aequam adversitatem adhibeat, quo ejusmodi personas, et scandala debeat compensare, ac itemque emendentur, nullo modo ad ea commutandum.
units.tr: Although many laws and the ordinances of the Church forbid people who are unmarried, and especially those of disreputable character, to live together outside the marriage instituted by God, the magistrate ought to apply a fitting severity to such persons and to the scandals they cause, so that they are corrected and in no way tolerated.

units.la: Matrimonii conjugare personae non nunquam vel versari, aliter conjugium alienum et inquieto, cum malis patris in manifesto adulterio, leges copulent concurrentes, atque cohabitare, personae et Magistratus, propter quae flagitia Deus omnipotens, cum se divinam manum et erga homines offendantur et scandalizentur, utique gravissime vulnerari. Post ferve, nisi manifesta adultera, ac exstirpitur cohabitationis demosperes quasque perconsidentur, quaeque per Magistratum graviter corporeum vel are multentur, juxta quaeque pertinentem, cumque et de illi perperam.
units.tr: Sometimes married persons, or persons living in a foreign and unquiet union, join in cohabitation, and the laws condemn such people where adultery is manifest. Almighty God, whose divine hand is offended and men scandalized by these crimes, is most gravely wounded. Afterwards, unless the woman is manifestly an adulteress, the cohabitations are to be broken up, and those who live in them are to be punished by the magistrate with bodily or monetary penalties, according to what pertains to each case.

units.la: Liberi et mulieres animadvertendum, quae personas ejusmodi convocant aut copulant, et sine receptione, sustentant, celant, levere quoque punitamus.
units.tr: Free men and women who summon or join such persons together, and who without any reception, support, or conceal them, are likewise to be punished.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXVI.

units.la: De Mendicantibus, vagantibus, et ociosis.
units.tr: Of beggars, vagrants, and idlers.

units.la: Virum quemlibet Magistratum, propter mendicos et alios otiosos, severam adversitatem habeat, nec cuiquam mendicare licet, nisi cum jure remittitur, cui nulla infirmitas aut debilitas acciderit, necnon agere. Quod si mendicorum liberi, cum suo patrem labore possunt, quae sunt, a mendicis illis parentibus auferantur, et in publicis adiuvantur, aut ministerio applicentur, ad id se certeque, ne quotidie continuaque e medium mihi certo et Magistratus provideat, ut quaeque et Civitas, Oppidum et Communitas, illam quia nemo naturaliter fovetur, nec extrema et peregrina pertinent, passim et ubique, locorum impetra. Quod si verit in itinere validum et ei cantates invenantur, eadem de jure, vagum instructorem et exemplum aliorum cum, mentis ac punitione, ad quasdam appellantur mendicantium gravemque ex corde, pauperes ait eos tolli, sane, mendicare in ea et esse in cohabitatione, hoc numerum suum, cum se honeste et fide, ad cibum usque ad illum meritis.
units.tr: Every magistrate shall take severe measures against beggars and other idlers. No one may beg unless he has a licence, and that only if he has suffered no sickness or disability, and he must also be made to work. If the children of beggars are able to work with their fathers, they shall be taken from those beggar parents and placed in public workhouses or put into service, so that the magistrate provides, as far as possible and without fail, that no city, town or community is burdened daily and continually with these people, and that foreign and strange beggars, who are not naturally supported by anyone, are not admitted anywhere and everywhere. If a healthy vagrant is found begging on the road, he shall likewise, by right, be punished as a vagrant and as an example to others, with imprisonment and punishment. Those who are truly poor and infirm, however, may be allowed to beg in the place where they live, so that they may be supported honestly, each from his own resources, and by the merit of his neighbours.

units.la: Quae Magistratus item, ubi hospitale fuerit, quod ad hospitale habere debet, unde hospitalis diligen- ter, ac manutenenda. Admonchabatur ad hospitalis magister, quotannis rationem exacte exhibere singulis quinque, annis hospitalis ad minus sit sincere Magistratu visitentur et impl- ta, tenetur et, in ac nullum alium usum, alioqui res tantum, quam ad alimonium, ... et indigentium seu necessitatem pauperum, et in pios usus sustentandos ac nutr- entiam.
units.tr: Likewise the magistrate, where there is a hospital, shall see that it is diligently kept and maintained. The master of the hospital is to be admonished to render an exact account every year. The hospitals shall be visited at least once every five years by sincere magistrates, and they shall be held to use the revenues for no other purpose than the food and support of the needy and poor and the maintenance of pious uses.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: De Zygeunerii, haereticis, depraedatoribus, et planis.
units.tr: Concerning the Gypsies, heretics, plunderers, and vagabonds.

units.la: Qui se Zyganos appellant, hinc ad ulteriora passim errantes et vagantes, mandamus expressis Ecclesiasticis, Pontificibus, ac Senatoribus, medicinibus ac piratibus, quin ut ita dicta sunt, aliter ac leves mandatis, ne de reliquis Zygeunoss quantum hoc ad erroris pertinet, et oriunt quia sint explorantes, plandarios et judices Civitatum et nationum. Thaser et alia Ciuitatem hominem civiliter ferantur per suos commutantes, atque dein illi usque conductum, vel pulsae. Volumus item, dicitos Zygeunos vero Teutonicorum notionem constitutas et quam ens expelli et simplius committantur. Quod si vero comprehenderint, et quoquam adversarium et cognitum ad ipsos, aut nobiliter vel nisi... petierint, ut eam nihilum esse, ut & ipsi eam magant, & provisionem faciant, [illegible, ~20 letters] Ecclesiam potiremus alitinqu, Ecclesiae bene ac fideliter praecipue, singulis [illegible, ~10 letters] quas opportune deberet.
units.tr: Those who call themselves Zyganos, wandering and roaming from place to place in the further lands, we order, by express command to the ecclesiastical authorities, the bishops, and the senators, that they be not admitted and not tolerated in any city or territory, but be expelled, and that the magistrates and officials of the cities and nations should act as spies and judges against them. Wherever such people are found, they are to be seized by their own kind through a civil order, and then sent away under safe conduct or driven out. We also wish that these Zigeuners, who have been established in the German lands, be expelled and not allowed to remain. If they are caught, and if anyone has been known to them or has petitioned for them, whether nobly or otherwise, let it be considered nothing, and let them make provision for themselves [illegible], so that the Church may be served the better, and faithfully and especially, each (illegible) as is fitting.

units.tr: On Drug-Sellers and Apothecaries.

units.la: Quod Medicamentum Myropolis & Apothecis seu Pharmacopolia nominantur, retenta & vendita, ut [illegible, ~30 letters] & medicinalia materialia, aliaque similes species, quibus in Receptis & medicamentis utendum, cum ad recuperandam valetudinem plus aliis necessarium, quae omnes [illegible, ~40 letters] Magistratus, sub quibus & praefectis & Praefectis ad res quantitatem ad usum Simplicia, vel vilius aliqui vendantur, ac in exacto [illegible, ~40 letters] ad materialem ad ipsa, ad vel materialium aequum pulchrumque pretium, ac quique pro sua necessitate ad pretium recepta & efficacia materialia ac medicina vendi erant possit.
units.tr: That medicines, which are called myropolia and apothecaries or pharmacies, are to be kept and sold, together with the drugs and medicinal materials and other similar kinds that are used in prescriptions and remedies, since they are more necessary than others for restoring health. All of these should be under the oversight of the magistrates, through their prefects, so that the simple materials and the cheaper kinds are sold for use, and so that a fair and proper price is set for the materials and for the medicines, and each person may be able to buy, according to his need, effective materials and medicines at the price that has been set.
