Et in Capitularibus Ludovici Pii Imperatoris legitur: Sequentia quaedam Capitula, ex Sanctorum Patrum Decretis, & Imperatorum edictis colligere curavimus, atque inter nostra Capitula, lege firmissima tenenda generali consultu, Erchenbaldo Cancellario nostro inferere iussimus. Denique in Constitutione Caroli II, cognomento Calvi Imperatoris, facta in Compendio Carisiacensi, anno DCCCLXI, ita legitur: Praeterea necessarium duximus, ut commendationem nostram ex hoc scribere rogaremus, quae ex more in nostro Palatio apud Cancellarium nostrum retineatur, & inde per Missos (id est, Commissarios nostros) dirigatur. Ut meo animo non inepte Gulielmus Budaeus, vir rerum et peritia, summa eruditione, & amplissima dignitate clarissimus, arbitretur iure quodam te Nomophylacem, id est, legum praesidium & iuris asylum, in Aula & Imperio censeri.
units.tr: That the custody of the laws also belongs to the greatness of your office is sufficiently clear from the ordinance of the Emperor Charlemagne, which Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, cites in his letter to King Carloman, the princes of the Franks, in these words: The Chancellor, who was once called the Secretary, was joined with the envoy; they were subtle, prudent, better and faithful men, who were to write the royal commands without immoderate greed for money, and to keep the secrets faithfully. And in the Capitularies of the Emperor Louis the Pious it is read: We have taken care to gather certain chapters that follow from the decrees of the holy Fathers and the edicts of emperors, and we have ordered them to be inserted among our chapters by Erchenbald, our Chancellor, to be held as the firmest law by a general consultation. Finally, in the constitution of Charles II, surnamed the Bald, Emperor, made at the Compendium of Quierzy in the year 861, it reads thus: Moreover we have thought it necessary to ask that our recommendation be written from this, which is customarily kept in our palace with our Chancellor, and from there sent through the envoys (that is, our commissioners). Thus, in my opinion, Guillaume Budé, a man famous for learning, great scholarship and the highest dignity, judged that by a certain right you are counted in the court and the Empire as Nomophylax, that is, the guardian of the laws and the refuge of justice.

units.la: Postremo dixumus, publicationem quoque Legum & Mandatorum Imperialium esse in tuo pontificio repositam. Quid enim aliud tibi vele subscriptio, quae in Commonitorio Alarici Regis Wisigothorum Gauricum Comitem subnotata est? Anianus vir spectabilis (qui fuit Cancellarius Regis) ex praeceptione D. N. Gloriosissimi Alarici Regis hunc Codicem ac Eius legibus, atque sententiis suis, vel diversis libris eius, &c. consignare iussit. Quo pacto Iustinianum etiam Imperatorem constituit, Gloriosissimi Quaestoris (id est, Cancellarii) publicationes esse necessariam, in Novell. 114, cap. 1, & in auth. gloriosissimo C. de haeredibus.
units.tr: Lastly, I have said that the publication of the imperial laws and mandates also lies within your pontifical office. For what else does the subscription wish you to be, which is written beneath the Commonitory of Alaric, King of the Visigoths, to Count Gauricus? Anianus, a distinguished man (who was Chancellor of the King), by the order of our Lord, the most glorious King Alaric, has commanded this Code and its laws and opinions, or its various books, etc., to be sealed. In the same way the Emperor Justinian also established that the publications of the most glorious Quaestor (that is, the Chancellor) are necessary, in Novel 114, chapter 1, and in the authentic gloriosissimo, C. de haeredibus.

units.la: Ex quibus a me vsq; commemoratis abunde (opinor) lucet, quamobrem vox & custos legum iustitiaeque, armarium legum, & Principis mandatorum appellaris a Cassiodoro, tuo in Imperiali Cancellaria apud Theodoricum Regem, Epistolar. lib. 6 & 8, necnon & Ennodio ... galli parvus, praeses arbiter, legum conditor, ab Aurelio Symmacho Viro Clarissimo Consulis, lib. 1 epist. 17. Tu enim solus es, qui in omni ferme parte administrationis Reipublicae, Principis vicem implere, aut certe obire, vel eodem: qui ve capitis sanctioris & interioris Consilii Cancellariae habens administrationem: qui denique morum legumque prudentiam quaddam regimen recepisse videris. Quod munus primus omnium cognosci.
units.tr: From what I have mentioned, I think it is abundantly clear why you are called the voice and guardian of the laws and of justice, the storehouse of the laws and of the prince's commands, by Cassiodorus in his time in the imperial chancery under King Theodoric (Letters, books 6 and 8), and also by Ennodius ... the little cock of Gaul, president, arbiter, lawgiver, by Aurelius Symmachus, a most distinguished man and consul (book 1, letter 17). For you alone are he who in nearly every part of the administration of the Republic is able to fill the prince's place, or at least to take it up; who holds the management of the chancery of the more sacred and inner council; who, in short, seems to have received a certain governance of wisdom in manners and laws. This office, first of all, was recognised...

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters]Augustus Imperator Romanus, accepisse sibi delatum, non sibi sum[illegible, ~3 letters]e dicitur. Tibi denique id auctoritatis esse oportet, cui omnes Imperii [illegible, ~3 letters]dines, sacri profani, rerum suarum grauissimarum arcana committere [illegible, ~3 letters]n dedignentur.
units.tr: [...] Augustus, the Roman Emperor, is said to have accepted what was offered to him, not for himself [...]. Finally, such authority ought to be yours, to whom all the orders of the Empire, sacred and profane, disdain not to entrust the secrets of their most weighty affairs [...].

units.la: Qui quamuis in tanto dignationis fastigio collocatus sis, tamen vsq; [illegible, ~3 letters]co non extolleris aut fastidis tuo culmine inferiores, vt inaudita ciuili[illegible, ~3 letters]te ac moderatione ianuam & vestibulum omni postulanti, omnibus [illegible, ~3 letters]oris patere patiaris. Et quum te omnibus numeris grauitatis, constantiæ, [illegible, ~3 letters]ueritatis, prudentiæ, temperantiæ, fortitudinis, integritatis, absolutum [illegible, ~3 letters]virum, vndecunque doctum, vndique placentem, non mihi modo, [illegible, ~3 letters]cunctis Imperii Ordinibus, summis, medioximis, minimis constet; ta[ illegible, ~3 letters]en earum rerum seueritatem tantis condimentis humanitatis comita[illegible, ~3 letters]que commitigauisti, vt ex omnibus vnus placuisse videaris, cui sacrum [illegible, ~3 letters]c Capellaniæ & Sacristiæ Imperialis officium à tribus Archicapellanis [illegible, ~3 letters]mmendaretur.
units.tr: Although you have been placed on such a height of dignity, you are not raised up by it nor do you scorn those beneath your summit, but with unheard-of civility and moderation you allow the door and threshold to lie open to every petitioner and to all. And since you are esteemed by all the orders of the Empire, the highest, the middling and the least, as a man complete in every measure of gravity, constancy, truth, prudence, temperance, fortitude and integrity, learned in every way and pleasing on every side, to me and to all; yet you have softened the severity of those matters with such seasonings of humanity and courtesy, that you seem to have pleased all, you to whom the sacred office of Chaplain and Sacristan of the Empire was commended by the three Archchaplains [...].

units.la: Quod ita tibi felix, fortunatum ac proprium esse à Deo Optimo Ma[illegible, ~3 letters]o volo, vt me meaque studia bene præclareque de Republica meren[ illegible, ~3 letters]tibi grata acceptaque, & patrocinio fauoris tui commendata in poste[illegible, ~3 letters]m quoque cupio. Id fiet, vbi votiuum isthoc opus in Capella & Sacristia [illegible, ~3 letters]a æquis oculis, quibus priora mea monumenta solitus es, respexeris, [illegible, ~3 letters] od vti facias, te per genium amoris & affectionis obsecro, quibus il[illegible, ~3 letters]lustre nomen tuum iam pridem olim colo atque obseruo: cui nihil gra[illegible, ~3 letters]ius, nihil iucundius, nihil acceptius contingere vmquam poterit, quam [illegible, ~3 letters]bi officia mea ac studia qualiacumq; præstare simul & comprobare. Dat, [illegible, ~3 letters]rancofordiæ ad Mœnum, pridie Palmarum, A. C. N. M. DC. XIII.
units.tr: I wish this to be as happy, fortunate and proper to you from God Most Good and Greatest, that I and my studies, which have deserved well and excellently of the Republic, may also be pleasing and acceptable to you, and commended to the patronage of your favour in future. This will happen when you look upon this votive work in the chapel and sacristy with the same kindly eyes with which you were accustomed to regard my earlier monuments, and so that you may do this, I beg you by the spirit of your love and goodwill, by which I have long cultivated and observed your illustrious name. Nothing more pleasing, more agreeable or more welcome can ever happen to you than that I should offer and show my services and studies, whatever their quality. Given at Frankfurt on the Main, the day before Palm Sunday, in the year of Christ 1613.

units.la: ELOGIA ET TESTIMONIA DE VSV, AVCTORITATE, ET PRAXI AVTHEN- TICA Legum Capitularium in hac Collectione contentarum. DE LEGE LONGO- BARDORVM.
units.tr: Testimonies and Praises Concerning the Use, Authority and Authentic Practice of the Capitularies Contained in This Collection. CONCERNING THE LAW OF THE LOMBARDS.

units.la: OTHARIVS II. Imperator in Chronico Cassinensi, de compilatore, (vt putatur) harum Legum, sic scribit ad Abbatem Cassinensis Monasterii: Lotharius Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator Augustus; dilectissimo fideli suo Gusbaldo Cassinensi Hierarchae, & Romani Imperij, Cancellario, Capellano ac Principi pacis, gratiam suam & bonam voluntatem. Tuae fidelitati per Imperialia scripta mandamus, vt nostra à Deo conseruande Maiestati Petrum Diaconum, qui à nostra Imperiali Serenitate Logotheta Italicus, Exceptor, Cartularius, & Capellanus Romani Imperij constitutus est, transmittere studeas, recepturum pro fue fidelitatis seruitio digne retributionis premium. Indubitanter enim noueritis, nostram Maiestatem & Collaterales Imperij propter antiquitates & rerum gestarum relationes, eius absentiam ferre non posse. Mitte etiam per eum omnia antecessorum nostrorum priuilegia, quae ei ad Aquaspensiles olim custodienda dedisse meminimus, &c.
units.tr: Lothar II, Emperor, in the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, concerning the compiler (as is thought) of these laws, writes thus to the Abbot of the Monastery of Monte Cassino: Lothar, by the grace of God Augustus Emperor of the Romans, to his most beloved and faithful Gusbald, Bishop of Cassino, Chancellor of the Roman Empire, Chaplain and Prince of Peace, his grace and goodwill. By our imperial writing we command your fidelity that you take care to send to the Majesty of ours, preserved by God, Peter the Deacon, whom our Imperial Serenity has appointed Italian Logothete, Exceptor, Cartularius and Chaplain of the Roman Empire, receiving for the service of your fidelity a worthy reward. For you will know without doubt that our Majesty and the colleagues of the Empire cannot bear his absence on account of the antiquities and the accounts of deeds done. Send also through him all the privileges of our predecessors, which we recall having once given him to keep at Aquaspensiles, etc.

units.la: GVNTHERVS Secretarius Friderici I. Imperatoris, in Ligurino, lib. 2. de Longobardis: Gens astuta, sagax, prudens, industria, sollers, Prouida consilio, legum iurisque perita. Et paulo post: Illa tamen legum prudens, & iuris amori Dedita gens, &c.
units.tr: Gunther, secretary of the Emperor Frederick I, in the Ligurinus, book 2, on the Lombards: A people crafty, shrewd, prudent, industrious, skilful, provident in counsel, and versed in law and right. And a little after: Yet that people, prudent in laws and devoted to love of right, etc.

units.la: Ad quae verba sic commentator IAC. SPIEGELIVS IC. trium Imperatorum, Maximiliani I. Caroli V. & Ferdinandi Secretarius & Consiliarius: Merula Regnum Longobardorum minime crudele fuisse ait, & Legem Longobardam celebrari, cuius praecipue autor Rotaris, & cateri Reges perhibentur. Nec non easdem Italiae Ciuitates, quae in hanc vsque diem iudicia sua ex editis Longobardorum magis, quam ex Decretis Imperatoris exercent. Praeterea Longobardorum Reges eos fuisse, (fremant licet caeterae gentes) qui legibus & armis vniuersam pene Italiam iam a maiorum virtute degeneratam sublevauerint, erexerint, & exornauerint.
units.tr: On these words the commentator Jacob Spiegel, jurist, secretary and counsellor of three emperors, Maximilian I, Charles V and Ferdinand, comments thus: Merula says that the kingdom of the Lombards was by no means cruel, and that the Lombard Law is celebrated, whose chief author is said to be Rothari, and the other kings. Nor do the same cities of Italy, which to this day exercise their judgments more from the published laws of the Lombards than from the decrees of the Emperor. Besides, the kings of the Lombards were those who (let the other peoples rage as they will) by laws and arms raised up, relieved and adorned almost the whole of Italy, already degenerate from the virtue of its ancestors.

units.la: In CONSVETVDINIBVS FEVDORVM, lib. 2. tit. 1. in princ. tradit Obertus de Orto IC. & Consul Mediolanensis: Causarum, quarum cognitio frequenter nobis committitur, alia dirimuntur iure Romano; alia vero legibus Longobardorum; alia autem secundum Regni (id est, Imperij Teutonici in Italia) consuetudinem, &c.
units.tr: In the Consuetudines Feudorum, book 2, title 1, at the beginning, Obertus de Orto, jurist and consul of Milan, teaches: Of the cases whose hearing is frequently committed to us, some are settled by Roman law, others by the laws of the Lombards, and others according to the custom of the kingdom (that is, of the Teutonic Empire in Italy), etc.

units.la: Ad quae verba DIONYS. GOTHOFREDVS IC. in Notis: Longobardi libros authenticos esse hinc colligunt.
units.tr: On these words Dionysius Gothofredus, jurist, in his Notes: From this the Lombards gather that these are authentic books.

units.la: Eodem lib. 2. tit. 12. de Milite vasallo, qui contumax est, in fine princip. Sed si intra annum venerit, restituatur ei possessio: alioquin & beneficium & possessionem amittit, vt in Lombarda de iis qui ad palatium venire contempserint, l. si cuiuscumque. Est l. 3. tit. 43. lib. 2. Legis Longobard.
units.tr: In the same book 2, title 12, on the vassal soldier who is contumacious, at the beginning of the section: But if he comes within a year, possession is to be restored to him; otherwise he loses both the benefice and the possession, as in the Lombard law concerning those who have scorned to come to the palace, the law "si cuiuscumque". This is law 3, title 43, book 2 of the Lombard Law.

units.la: Eodem lib. 2. tit. 58. cap. 1. de Notis feudor. Alioqui adhibeat Dominus quae meliores poterit: liberos tamen, argumentatione legis de ultimis voluntatibus in Lombardia. harda, scilicet illa, quæ dicit; si quis donationem facere voluerit, &c. Est l. 7. tit. 18. lib. 2.
units.tr: In the same book 2, title 58, chapter 1, on the Notes of the fiefs: Otherwise let the lord use whatever better means he can; yet free (persons) by argument from the law on last wills in Lombardy: namely that which says: if anyone wishes to make a donation, etc. This is law 7, title 18, book 2.

units.la: Eod. lib. 2. d tit. 58. cap. 2. de Notis feudor. Quæ omnia supradicta colligi possient per supradictas Leges Longobard. titulo de ultimis voluntatibus, l. si quis, & C: communi dividundo, l. 1, & sin. &c. Est d. l. 7. tit. 18. lib. 2.
units.tr: In the same book 2, title 58, chapter 2, on the Notes of the fiefs: All the foregoing could be gathered from the aforesaid Lombard laws under the title on last wills, the law "si quis", and C., "communi dividundo", laws 1 and the following, etc. This is the same law 7, title 18, book 2.

units.la: Eod. lib. 2. d. tit. 58. cap. 3. Si instrumentum diceretur falsum à domino, daretur defensio vasallo, qui instrumentum ad se deferret, ut in Lombard. Qualiter quis se defend. deb. l. de chartis, &c. Et §. 1. ibid. Notandum est, quod de omni controversia, quæ inter dominum & vasallum oritur, si partes veritatem noverint, omnino cogi debere a domino & paribus dicere veritatem. Qui si dicant, se nescire, cum sciant, & vasallus postulet, dominus eos coget iurare, & veritatem dicere, ut C. de testib. l. si quando, & in Lombard. ut iudex, de off. iud. & in tit. Qualiter quis se defend. deb. l. si qualiscunque causa, & tit. de testibus, l. ut quicunque, & l. vlt. Est l. 31. & l. 34. de chartis, tit. 55. lib. 2: l. 15. ut iudex, tit. 52. lib. 2. l. 13. si qualiscumq; cauf. tit. 55. lib. 2. l. 5. ut quicumque, tit 51. lib. 2.
units.tr: In the same book 2, title 58, chapter 3: If an instrument were said by the lord to be false, the defence would be given to the vassal who brings the instrument forward, as in the Lombard law "How anyone ought to defend himself", the law "de chartis", etc. And §1 there: It must be noted that in every controversy which arises between lord and vassal, if the parties know the truth, they must altogether be compelled by the lord and the peers to tell the truth. If they say they do not know, when they do know, and the vassal asks it, the lord shall compel them to swear and to tell the truth, as in C., "de testibus", the law "si quando", and in the Lombard law "ut iudex", "de officio iudicis", and in the title "How anyone ought to defend himself", the law "si qualiscunque causa", and the title "de testibus", the law "ut quicunque", and the last law. This is law 31 and law 34 "de chartis", title 55, book 2; law 15 "ut iudex", title 52, book 2; law 13 "si qualiscumque causa", title 55, book 2; law 5 "ut quicunque", title 51, book 2.

units.la: Eod lib. 2. tit 58. cap. 4. §. 1. in sin. Sed contrarium reperitur in Lombard. quia licet filius minorem virtutem habeat, quam pater, tamen debet præcise iurare, patrem suum non fuisse debitorem, ut in Lombard. Qualiter quis se def. deb. l. si contigerit. Est l. 7. tit. 55. lib. 2.
units.tr: In the same book 2, title 58, chapter 4, §1 at the end: But the contrary is found in the Lombard law, because although a son has less virtue than his father, nevertheless he must swear outright that his father was not a debtor, as in the Lombard law "How anyone ought to defend himself", the law "si contigerit". This is law 7, title 55, book 2.

units.la: FRAN. CVRTIVS Iunior in tract. Feudor. cap. 6. num. 2. adducit adhuc duos textus, in quibus Leges Longobardorum confirmentur esse authenticæ, ut est text. in c. 1. in sin. Hic potest esse tit. qui suc. teneantur. Est tit. 9. lib.
units.tr: Francis Curtius the Younger, in his tract on the Fiefs, chapter 6, number 2, adduces yet two texts in which the Lombard Laws are confirmed to be authentic, such as the text in chapter 1 at the end: This may be the title "qui succedere teneantur". This is title 9, book

units.la: 1. Feud. vbi innuere videtur Legem Lotharii de precariis, quæ tamen in LegeLongobard. non exstat. Item, text. in c. 1. in princ. Qualiter seu. pro alie. Quem ego titulum in iure Feudor. non reperio.
units.tr: 1 of the Fiefs, where he seems to hint at the law of Lothar concerning precarial grants, which, however, is not found in the Lombard Law. Likewise, the text in chapter 1 at the beginning: How ... pro alie. Which title I do not find in the law of fiefs.

units.la: In CONSVETVDIN. FEVDOR. lib. 2. tit. 39. c. 3. Non est consuetudo Mediolani, ut de felonia aut de infidelitate pugna fiat, licet contrarium sit, quod præcepit Lex Longobardorum, ut de infidelitate pugna fiat. Est l. 30. quibuscumque, tit. 55. lib. 2.
units.tr: In the Consuetudines Feudorum, book 2, title 39, chapter 3: It is not the custom of Milan that a duel be fought over felony or infidelity, although the contrary is what the Law of the Lombards prescribes, namely that a duel be fought over infidelity. This is law 30 "quibuscumque", title 55, book 2.

units.la: HONORIVS II. PAPA, c. 1. de iuram. calumn. in Decretal. Gregorii IX. Papæ, lib. 2. tit. 7.
units.tr: HONORIUS II, Pope, ch. 1, On the Oath of Calumny, in the Decretals of Pope Gregory IX, book 2, title 7.

units.la: Vt ergo dubietas ista auferatur, secundum etiam decisionem filij nostri Henrici quondam Imperatoris, cuius sunt hæc verba, &c. Eius itaque interpretationem corroboramus, & Divi Marciani constitutionem ita interpretari debere decernimus, &c. Est decisio Henrici V. Imp. in l. 11. tit. 47. lib. 2. Legis Longard.
units.tr: So that this doubt may be removed, we also follow the decision of our son Henry, once Emperor, whose words are these, etc. We therefore confirm his interpretation, and we decree that the constitution of Divus Marcian ought to be interpreted in the same way, etc. This is the decision of Emperor Henry V in law 11, title 47, book 2 of the Lombard Law.

units.la: CVRTIVS Iunior d. cap. 6. num. 2. probaturus, Leges Longobardorum in iudicandis litibus auctoritatem habere, profert sententias Glossatorum Iuris vtriusq;, nimirum Accursii, Pilei, Conradi, & Ioannis Teutonici, veterum Iuris interpretum. Verba eius hæc sunt: Quæro, quid sit Liber Longobardorum, & an possit ad decisionem causarum allegari? Circa primum, habetis Gloss. in c. 1. in verbo Scriptum, 33. q. 1. quæ dicit, quendam Carolum fuisse compilatorem Libri Longobardæ. Aliud dixit Odofred. in auth. dos data, C. de donat. ante nupt. quod quidam Reges Apuliæ, qui venerunt de Sardinia in Apuliam, fuerunt compilatores Libri Longobardæ: qui ideo sic appellatus est, quia ipsi habeant longas barbas. Circa secundum vero, nunquid iste liber sit allegabilis ad decisionem causarum, videtur dicendum quod sic, quia Gloss. vbique allegant Legem Longobardam, Ita allegat Gloss. in c. 1. §. hoc autem notandum. in verb. Legibus, qui feud. dar. pof. & in d. c. 1 §. cú vero Corradus, in verb. Dignaretur: quæ dicit, quod Conradus Imp. fecit illam constitutionem & legem, in quâ continebatur, quod non solum filij, sed etiâ nepotes succederent in feudo, vt probatur in d. §. cum vero Corradus; & constituit multa alia, quæ habentur in Longobardia, id est, in Legibus Longobardorum. Ergo sicut § cum vero Corradus, est authenticus: idem erit in aliis legibus ab eo conditis. Sic etiam allegat leges Longobardas Glos. in c. 1. §. qualiter, in verbo, Duellum, de pace tenend. Ad idem text. cum gloss. in c. non est consuetudo, in verbo, licet lex, de alien. feud. pat. & in d. c. 1. §. hoc quoque sciendum, cum gloss. in verb. Gradum. Sic etiam pro decisione feudorum allegat Longobarda iura, vel in c. 1. §. sirusticus, in verb. Voluntate. & in § si miles, in verb. Diuino, de pace ten. Ad idem gloss. in c. 1. in verb. Similibus. An mutus vel alias imperfect. Et non solum in libro Feudorum, sed etiam alibi gloss. allegant legem Longobardam. Ita allegat gloss. in auth. sed nouo iure. C. de feru. fugit. & in l. falsus, §. si iactum. D. de furt. in l. consensu, in princip. verb. Adulterum. C. de repud. in l. sin. in verb. Recuperare. C. de iure domin. impetr.
units.tr: CURTIUS Junior, in the cited chapter 6, number 2, intending to prove that the Lombard Laws have authority in deciding lawsuits, cites the opinions of the Glossators of both laws, namely Accursius, Pileus, Conrad and John the Teuton, the older interpreters of the law. His words are these: I ask, what is the Book of the Lombards, and can it be cited in deciding cases? As to the first point, you have the Gloss on c. 1, under the word Scriptum, 33 q. 1, which says that a certain Charles was the compiler of the Book of the Lombards. Odofred, on the authentic law Dos data, C. de donat. ante nupt., said otherwise: that certain kings of Apulia, who came from Sardinia into Apulia, were the compilers of the Book of the Lombards, which was so called because they had long beards. As to the second point, whether this book may be cited in deciding cases, it seems that it may, because the Gloss everywhere cites the Lombard Law, So the Gloss cites it on c. 1, §. hoc autem notandum, under the word Legibus, qui feud. dar. pos.; and on the same c. 1, §. cum vero, and Conrad, under the word Dignaretur, which says that Emperor Conrad made that constitution and law, in which it was provided that not only sons but also grandsons should succeed to a fief, as is proved in the same §. cum vero Conradus; and he established many other things, which are found in Lombardy, that is, in the Laws of the Lombards. Therefore, just as the §. cum vero Conradus is authentic, so the same will be true of the other laws he enacted. So too the Gloss on c. 1, §. qualiter, under the word Duellum, de pace tenend., cites the Lombard laws. To the same effect, with the gloss on c. non est consuetudo, under the word licet lex, de alien. feud. pat., and on the same c. 1, §. hoc quoque sciendum, with the gloss under the word Gradum. Likewise, for deciding fiefs, it cites the Lombard laws, either in c. 1, §. sirusticus, under the word Voluntate, or in §. si miles, under the word Diuino, de pace ten. To the same effect the gloss on c. 1, under the word Similibus, An mutus vel alias imperfect. And the Gloss cites the Lombard law not only in the Book of Fiefs but also elsewhere. Thus the Gloss on the authentic law sed nouo iure, C. de feru. fugit., cites it, and on l. falsus, §. si iactum, D. de furt.; on l. consensu, in princip., under the word Adulterum, C. de repud.; on l. sin., under the word Recuperare, C. de iure domin. impetr.

units.la: IOANNES SEMECA Glossator Iuris Canonici, ad cauf. 11. q. 1. c. 37. Decreto Gratiani annotat. Non inuenitur in Longobardia, quæ nunc est, sed in Gallia: id est, non exstat in legibus Longobardorum, quæ nunc in vsu habentur, sed in Capitularibus Francorum. est enim cap. 281. lib. 6.
units.tr: JOHN SEMECA, Glossator of Canon Law, annotating on causa 11, q. 1, c. 37 of Gratian's Decretum: It is not found in Lombardy, which is now so called, but in Gaul; that is, it is not found in the laws of the Lombards that are now in use, but in the Capitularies of the Franks. For this is in cap. 281, book 6.

units.la: Allegatur etiam & probatur, vt authentica, hæc lex Longobardorum à GLOSSA Iuris Saxonici prouincialis (Sandtrechts) in Spec Saxon. lib. 1. art. vlt. vbi vocatur, Ius Lombardicum.
units.tr: This Lombard law is also cited and approved, as authentic, by the Gloss of the Saxon provincial law (Sachsenrecht) on the Mirror of the Saxons, book 1, last article, where it is called Lombard Law.

units.la: GLOSSA posterior Speculi Saxon. lib. 3 artic. 82. Huius eius (sc. Caroli Magni) vocabatur Carolus (Martellus) qui fuit etiam Rex Francia & Lombardorum & fecit quasdam Leges in Lombarda per totum: qui etiam postea habuit Imperium.
units.tr: A later Gloss on the Mirror of the Saxons, book 3, article 82: Of this man (namely Charles the Great) was called Charles (Martel), who was also King of France and of the Lombards, and made certain laws throughout Lombardy; he later also held the Empire.

units.la: GAVDENTIVS MERVLA Alexandrinus, lib. 1. Antiquitatis Vicecomitum Mediolanensi circa sin. Lex etiam Longobarda celebratur, cum præcipue auctor Rotaris, & cæteri Reges perhibentur. Quare minime mirandum, si post extinctos Reges, quidam Duces imperauerint; & Longobardi à Ciuitatibus in partem iuris, & libertatis conditionem, quam ipsi erant recepti, sine discrimine ceu indigenæ semper habiti fuerint.
units.tr: GAUDENTIUS MERULA of Alessandria, book 1 of the Antiquities of the Visconti of Milan, near the end: The Lombard law is also celebrated, since its chief author is said to have been Rothari and the other kings. It is therefore by no means surprising that, after the kings had died out, certain dukes ruled, and that the Lombards, received from the cities into a share of the law and the condition of liberty which they themselves had received, were always regarded without distinction as natives.

units.la: BERNARDVS SACCVS Ticinensis, lib. 9. Histor. Ticinen. cap. 5 de Luitprando Rege Longobardorum: Possem alias etiam addere præfationes, quibus ipse Rex humili semper sermone Deo muocato scriptiones Legum suarum instituit. Diuersus penitus à lustiniani iactatione, cuius dicendi vanitatem imperiti admirantur eo loco, Imperatoriam Maiestatem, &c. Et se Gothicum, Alanicum, &c. inscribens, in sui ipsius gloriscatione euanuit: Huiusmodi igitur religione imbutus Lytprandus, tam in ferendis legibus, de suorum Procerum Ducumque cohibendis excessibus, &c.
units.tr: BERNARDUS SACCUS of Pavia, book 9 of the History of Pavia, chapter 5, on Liutprand, King of the Lombards: I could add other prefaces, in which this king, always invoking God in humble speech, set out the writings of his laws. They are wholly unlike the boasting of Justinian, whose vanity of speech the unskilled admire in the place where he writes "Imperial Majesty," etc. And by styling himself Gothic, Alanic, etc., he vanished in self-glorification. Imbued with such piety was Liutprand, both in enacting laws and in restraining the excesses of his nobles and dukes, etc.

units.la: CAROLVS SIGONIVS in Histor. de Regno Italiæ, lib. 8. anno 1007. In quibus illud animadue rsione dignum, cum horum etiam temporum consuetudo ferret, vt omnes ederent, qua quisque lege viuere vellent, Romana, Longobarda, an Salica, Bonifacium (Ducem Tusciæ, Marchionem Ferrariæ, Mantuę & Parmæ, Comitem Canusij, &c.) Longobardam esse professum, Mathildem vero (eius filiam) Salcam, quod ex eorum tabulis, quæ plurimæ in Ecclesia Mutinæ asseruantur, cognoscitur. Quod in patre & filia, non idem in viro & coniuge. Vnde in eodem Tabulario per hæc tempora sic scriptum inuenitur: Maria, quæ professa sum lege viuere Romana, sed nunc pro vito meo lege Longobardorum viuere videor, qui professus est ex natione sua lege viuere Langobardorum.
units.tr: CAROLUS SIGONIUS, in his History of the Kingdom of Italy, book 8, year 1007: In these documents it is worth noting that, since the custom of those times also allowed everyone to declare under which law they wished to live, Bonifacius (Duke of Tuscany, Marquis of Ferrara, of Mantua and Parma, Count of Canossa, etc.) professed to live under Lombard law, while Matilda (his daughter) professed Salic law, as is known from their records, many of which are preserved in the church of Modena. In the father and daughter it was not the same as in the husband and wife. Hence in the same archive, from these times, this is found written: Maria, who professed to live under Roman law, but now, for my husband, I seem to live under Lombard law, since he professed to live under the Lombard law of his nation.

units.la: Iacobus Sirmondus in Catalogo Cæsarum, tit. vlt. Sunt qui Lothari Imperatorem haud minore laude vehendum, quam Diuum Iustinianum eruditum, sedulo Leges Romanorum infinitis voluminibus antea differsas, autoritate Iustiniani in libro Digestorum contractas, Institutionum libros IV. editos, Codicem quoque cura studioque, non multo post Iustinianum, per Iura Langobardorum et Germanicarum gentium, oppressos, in lucem revocarit, quanquam ut statim regione, certa capita Langobardicarum Legum et tamen semper feruentur. Quorum sunt qui volumina Interpretum Iuris Ciuilis versant. Accedunt quæ et hodie sunt Lebentur, clarorum Iureconsultorum Scholiis illustrata Constitutiones Imperatorum Frederici eius, nominis II, qui Bononiense Gymnasium, quia Cives imperata non suspi-ciuntur, Pataum translulit, et quod Imperij maiestatem sartam tectam cupiebat, a Romanis Pontificibus anathematis spiculo districtus est, et candicantes palam, Francis a-stere Legibus ad hanc quoque diem suum stare vigorem in inclyto Siciliæ Regno, quod Neapolitanum vocatur, cuius possessio, si modo tam legibus, quam armis, regnare, ad nullam gentem magis pertineret, quam Alamannicam, &c.
units.tr: JACOBUS SIRMONDUS, in the Catalogue of the Caesars, last title: There are those who would extol the Emperor Lothar no less than the learned Divus Justinian, who by careful study brought back into the light the Laws of the Romans, once scattered through countless volumes, condensed by Justinian's authority into the Book of the Digest, the four books of the Institutes published, and also the Code, which, not long after Justinian, had been oppressed by the laws of the Lombards and the Germanic peoples, though still, as it were, in some regions certain chapters of the Lombard laws are kept in force. Among these are those who handle the volumes of the interpreters of civil law. To these are added the Constitutions of the Emperor Frederick II, which are still in force today, illustrated by the commentaries of famous jurists. He transferred the Bolognese university to Padua, because the citizens did not favour his commands, and because he wished the majesty of the Empire to remain intact, he was struck with the dart of anathema by the Roman Pontiffs, and openly, while the Franks were still in white, his laws maintain their force to this day in the renowned Kingdom of Sicily, which is called Neapolitan, whose possession, if it were to belong to any people more by laws than by arms, would belong to none more than to the Alemannic people, etc.

units.la: Videantur Interpretes Feudorum, quorum sunt dissentientes super autoritate harum Legum Longobardarum opiniones; sed maior & solidior pars est affirmantium, quam negantium. Cui affirmantium parti statuimus rationibus & argumentis accedunt Carolus Siculus I C. in Gl. Bofrius Consiliarius Regius in Notis ad Legem Longobard. Vuolfgangus Barbachius in Annot. ad Capitular. Lotharij Imp. Matthæus de Afflist. sin Comment. ad Constitutiones Neapolitan. Horatius Cauvus in Comment. ad Statuta Mediolanens, & alij in aliis locis propemodum innumerabilibus.
units.tr: The interpreters of the Feudal Law should be consulted; among them there are differing opinions on the authority of these Lombard laws, but the greater and sounder part is of those who affirm them rather than deny them. To the side of those who affirm, we add, with arguments and reasons, Carolus Siculus, I.C., in his Gloss; Bofrius, royal counsellor, in his Notes on the Lombard Law; Wolfgang Barbachius, in his Annotations on the Capitularies of Lothar the Emperor; Matthaeus de Afflictis, in his Commentary on the Neapolitan Constitutions; Horatius Cavus, in his Commentary on the Statutes of Milan; and others in almost countless other places.

units.la: DE CAPITVLARI LOTHARII
units.tr: ON THE CAPITULARY OF LOTHAIR

units.la: Imperatoris.
units.tr: the Emperor.

units.la: Cæsar Baronius Cardinalis Romanus, tom. I. Annal. Ecclesiast. anno 847. num. 12. Quas seruandas præscripserit Lotharius Imperator leges siue subditis regno, constitutio ab eo promulgata ita declarat: Placuit nobis, ut Capitula quæ excerpsimus de Capitulari bonæ memoriæ gloriosissimi aui Domini Caroli, & genitoris nostri Ludouici Imperatoris inuictissimi, fidelibus nostris, & sanctæ Ecclesiæ in Regno Italiæ constituta, perlegem tenentur & seruentur. At quales fuerunt istæ Leges, ipse, qui liber Capitularium docet: nimirum quæ noscuntur magna ex parte acceptæ ex Canonibus et Decretis Romanorum Pontificum, atque ex prædecessoribus Imperatorum, quæ sient optima, seruerentque Ecclesiasticæ immunitatis. Vt non solum sed Ecclesiæ seruanda leges præscribere idem Lotharius dicat, vt potè quod eadem seruanda sint per Romanos Pontifices comprobata. Porro nomine Capitularium appellantur, pro multitudine diuersorum Capitularium collestionum per Carolum Magnum et Ludouicum patrem Lotharium factam hac tempore, quoditam sustinuerunt saeculum, D C C C X L V I. collectio ad celebrandum Mildense Concilium, quæ illo inter alia statuerunt hæc ipsa cap. 8. Vt Capitula Ecclesiastica à domno Karolo Magno Imperatore, necnon a Domno Ludouico Pio Augusto.
units.tr: Caesar Baronius, Roman cardinal, Annales Ecclesiastici, vol. I, anno 847, num. 12: The laws that Emperor Lothar prescribed to be kept by his subjects in the kingdom are declared by the constitution he promulgated as follows: "We have resolved that the chapters which we have excerpted from the Capitulary of the Lord Charles the Great, of happy memory, the most glorious grandfather of our own, and of our father, the most unconquered Emperor Louis, are to be held and observed as law by our faithful subjects and by the holy Church established in the kingdom of Italy." But what kind of laws these were, the book of the Capitularies itself teaches: namely, those which are known to be for the most part taken from the canons and decrees of the Roman Pontiffs and from the earlier emperors, which are the best and which preserve the immunity of the Church. So Lothar prescribes laws not only for the state but for the Church too, since these were approved as observed by the Roman Pontiffs. The name Capitularies is given to the many different collections of chapters made by Charles the Great and by Louis his father, and by Lothar, at this time. This collection, which has lasted to the year 846, was made for the celebration of the Council of Meaux, and among other things that council decreed, in chapter 8, this same matter: that the ecclesiastical chapters promulgated by the Lord Emperor Charles the Great, and also by the Lord Louis the Pious, Augustus,

units.la: Augusto gusto promulgata obnixe seruari precipiantur, sicut & legalia obseruanda esse nosciuntur.
units.tr: promulgated by the Augustus, are to be earnestly observed, just as the secular laws are known to be observed.

units.la: Optime quidem Baronius de promulgatione horum Capitularium sentit: sed non recte de collectione Benedicti Levitae accipit, quae privato studio, non publica auctoritate Imperiali facta fuit. Quare puto, (quod mirandum est in viro tantae lectionis) hoc Capitulare ipsius Lotharii Imperatoris a Card. Baronio non esse visum, quamquam id non ita dudum Moguntiae fuerit cum Epistolis Hincmari Archiepiscopi Rhemensis recusum.
units.tr: Baronius judges rightly about the promulgation of these Capitularies, but he is wrong about the collection of Benedict the Levite, which was made by private zeal and not by public imperial authority. Hence I think (which is remarkable in a man of such wide reading) that this Capitulary of Emperor Lothar himself did not come under the notice of Cardinal Baronius, although not long ago it was reprinted at Mainz together with the Letters of Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims.

units.la: De hoc ipsissimo Capitulari prorsus intelligendum est referri ipsum Lotharii IV. Papae Romani ad hunc ipsum Lotharium Augustum, apud Sanctianum datum anno 10, c. 9, ubi legitur: De Capitulis vel Praeceptis Imperialibus sollicite conservandis, et Pontificum praedecessorum irrefragabiliter custodiendis et confirmandis, quae tum valuimus et valemus, Christo propitio, et nunc in omnium nos conservatione vestra omnibus profitemur. Et si forte aliquis aliter vobis dixerit, vel dicturus fuerit, eum pro certo mendacem.
units.tr: It must certainly be understood that the letter of Pope Lothair IV, dated at Sanctianum in the year 10, c. 9, which refers to this very Capitulary, is addressed to this same Emperor Lothair, where it is read: Concerning the careful preservation of the Capitularies or Imperial precepts, and their irrefragable keeping and confirmation by the predecessors of the Pontiffs, which we have held and hold, Christ being propitious, and now profess to all in your preservation of all things. And if anyone has told you, or shall tell you, otherwise, let him be known for certain to be a liar.

units.la: Vbi Glossa Gregorii XIII. Papae Romani annotat: Omnia haec data a Leone scribuntur, specialiter videntur ad Capitula Caroli et Ludovici, quae Lotharius vniuersa Italia seruari mandauerat.
units.tr: Where the Gloss of Pope Gregory XIII annotates: All these things are written as given by Leo, and they seem especially to refer to the Capitularies of Charles and Louis, which Lothair had ordered to be observed throughout all Italy.

units.la: Videantur Annotationes Viti Amerbachii ad hoc Capitulare, quod ille tamen obseruare non quiuit, esse illud Lotharii Imperatoris auctoritate compilatum pariter atque editum.
units.tr: See the annotations of Vitus Amerbach on this Capitulary, which he nevertheless could not bring himself to observe, to be that compiled and likewise published by the authority of the Emperor Lothair.

units.la: Annon de hoc eodem Capitulari accipiendum est, quod legitur in Synodo Moguntina sub Rhabano Archiepiscopo habita, cap. 16: Regnam pietatem, de oppressione pauperum liberorum, vt non a potentioribus per vniuersum malum ingenium contra iustitiam opprimantur, vel cogantur, vt res suas vendere, sine tradant, ne forte parentes eorum contra iustitiam fiant exheredati, et regalia minuatur, et ipsi propter indigentiam mendici, vel latrones, seu malefactores efficiantur, et vt sepius non fiant manniti ad placita, nisi sicut in Dominico Capitulari praecipitur.
units.tr: Should this not be understood of this same Capitulary, which is read in the Synod of Mainz held under Archbishop Rabanus, chapter 16: Concerning the royal piety and the oppression of poor free men, that they not be oppressed or compelled by the more powerful with every wicked device against justice, to sell or give away their goods, lest perhaps their parents be disinherited against justice, and the royal dues be diminished, and they themselves, through want, become beggars, or robbers, or malefactors; and that they not be summoned to the courts more often than is ordered in the Lord's Capitulary.

units.la: In Concilio Rauennatensi per Ioannem IX. Papam, & Lotharium Imperatorem celebrato, anno Domini DCCCXCVI. cap. 1: Sanctorum Patrum Regulas contempserit, et gloriosissimorum Imperatorum Karoli Magni Imperatoris, et Ludouici, atque Lotharii, necnon et filii eius Ludouici, quae de Ecclesiasticis decretis in eorum Capitularibus statuta atque sancita fuerant, seruauerit; et qui dat, et qui recipit, auctoritate sanctae sedis Apostolicae, et sanctorum Synodi, excommunicationi subiaceat.
units.tr: In the Council of Ravenna, held under Pope John IX and the Emperor Lothair in the year of the Lord 896, chapter 1: Whoever has despised the rules of the holy Fathers, and has not observed what the most glorious Emperors Charles the Great, Louis, and Lothair, and also his son Louis, decreed and sanctioned in their Capitularies concerning ecclesiastical decrees, let him, both giver and receiver, be subject to excommunication by the authority of the holy Apostolic See and of the holy Synod.

units.la: Dewsdedit Cardinalis Romanus in Collectione sua Canonem ex Legibus Romanis ab Imperatore Lothario Augusto promulgatis Cap. 11: vt tellis est Franciscus Pithoeus in praefatione Capitularium per Anseguisum & Benedictum collectorum.
units.tr: Deusdedit, Cardinal of Rome, in his Collection, cites a canon from the Roman laws promulgated by the Emperor Lothair Augustus, chapter 11; as Franciscus Pithoeus testifies in the preface to the Capitularies collected by Ansegisus and Benedict.

units.la: Ioannes Busaeus Iesuita Moguntinus in praefatione ad Hincmari Epistolas, hoc Capitulare appellat, Confirmationem Caroli Magni Epitomes (?) eiusdem constitutum. Et addit: Quia doctrinam communem admonuit, quam et Ioannis, atque omnium consentaneum vs, quae ab Hincmaro traduntur in epistola ad eundem, quae magnam lucem multis Hincmariana dictis conciliare possunt, prout in commentario explicantur.
units.tr: Johannes Busaeus, the Jesuit of Mainz, in the preface to the Letters of Hincmar, calls this Capitulary the confirmation of the Epitome of Charles the Great (?), a constitution of that same. And he adds: Because it recalls the common doctrine, which is in agreement with John and with all, and which are handed down by Hincmar in the letter to the same, which can bring great light to many of Hincmar's sayings, as they are explained in the commentary.

units.la: [Remaining lines of the lower text are heavily damaged and only partly legible.]
units.tr: [Remaining lines of the lower text are heavily damaged and only partly legible.]

units.la: PROLEGOMENVS. DE SPECVLO SA- XONVM.
units.tr: PROLEGOMENA. ON THE MIRROR OF THE SAXONS.

units.la: Mp.Carolus Magnus Aug.in Constitutione de Sede Regia & Iudicio Imperiali Aquisgranensi, tom. 2. Collectionis Constitut.Imperial.sol. 7.Deinde, prout suncti⁊ placuit prudentioribus Regni nostri, Legem Saxonum, Noricorum (id est, Bauarorum) Suevorum (id est, Alamannorum) Francorum, Ribuariorum (id est, Mosellanorum) Salicorum, sicut mos & potestas Imperatorum est, & omnium antecessorum meorum semper fuit, distinctam sub auctoritate Regia & Imperatoria stabilitu, non ex mea adinventione vel corde prolatam, sed uni consilio à me renovatam & auctam in melius, sicut patres & praedecessores mei fecisse perhibentur. Sed intelligit Legem Saxonum illam vetustissimam, quam ab Heroldo edita circumfertur.
units.tr: Emperor Charles the Great, in the constitution on the royal seat and imperial court at Aachen, vol. 2 of the Collection of Imperial Constitutions, p. 7: Then, as it has pleased the wiser men of our kingdom, the Law of the Saxons, of the Noricans (that is, the Bavarians), of the Swabians (that is, the Alamanni), of the Franks, of the Ribuarians (that is, of the Moselle), and of the Salians, as is the custom and power of emperors and has always been that of all my predecessors, should be established in a distinct form under royal and imperial authority. It was not brought forth from my own invention or mind, but renewed and improved by me in one council, as my fathers and predecessors are said to have done. But he means that most ancient Law of the Saxons, which is circulated as edited by Heroldus.

units.la: Wippo Capellanus Cunradi II. cognomento Salici Imperatoris, in eius Vita, cap. 6. in sin. Reuersus Rex de Ribuariis ad Saxoniam, ibi Legem crudelissimam Saxonum, secundum voluntatem eorum, confirmavit roboravit. Sed hic pro Saxonia intelligit Westphaliam, innuitque Legem illam iudicii occulti, de qua alibi tractamus.
units.tr: Wippo, chaplain of Conrad II, surnamed the Salian emperor, in his Life, ch. 6, near the end: The king, returning from the Ribuarians to Saxony, there confirmed and strengthened the most cruel Law of the Saxons, according to their will. But here by Saxony he means Westphalia, and he hints at that law of secret judgment, which we discuss elsewhere.

units.la: Eccard de Repkaw Compilator Speculi huius, lib.3. art.42. scribit: Et etiam cum Leges huius Principum constitutiones gemmis verborum primitus exornabantur, &c.
units.tr: Eckard de Repkaw, compiler of this Mirror, book 3, art. 42, writes: And also when the laws of these princes' constitutions were first adorned with jewels of words, etc.

units.la: Idem lib.3. artic.73. Ipsi etiam ius habebant ministeriales versus ad tempora Wichmanni Archiepiscopi Magdeburgensis. Vixit autem hic Wichmannus tempore Friderici Barbarossae & Henrici VI. Imperatorum.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 73: They themselves also had the right, the ministerial men, down to the times of Wichmann, Archbishop of Magdeburg. This Wichmann lived in the time of the Emperors Frederick Barbarossa and Henry VI.

units.la: Glossa Speculiin prolog Interpretaturus simul & translaturus in Germanicum Eckde de Repkaw Praefatus Saxonibus, cum ad fidem converti sunt Christianam, à Diuis Imperatoribus Constantino & Carolo, pro iure scripto ordinem operis à Deo sumit omnipotenti.
units.tr: Gloss on the Mirror, in the prologue: About to interpret and also to translate into German, Eckde de Repkaw, prefacing for the Saxons, when they were converted to the Christian faith by the divine emperors Constantine and Charles, takes the order of the work as written law from God Almighty.

units.la: Eadem, lib.1. artic.14. Verba sunt Eckde de Repkau auctoris privilegii, &c.
units.tr: The same, book 1, art. 14: These are the words of Eckde de Repkau, author of the privilege, etc.

units.la: Eadem, lib.2. artic.36. Dicere quis posset, auctorem privilegii insufficienter expresse modos defensa contra vendi&c. Respondeo, quod auctor Privilegii Eckde de Repkaw nec plura addere, sed nec minuere potuit, nisi secundum Privilegio, quod ipse ex Latino in Germanicum transtulit, invenerat. Iura enim ampliare vel minuere nemini licet, Imperatori.
units.tr: The same, book 2, art. 36: One could say that the author of the privilege did not sufficiently express the ways of defending against selling, etc. I answer that the author of the Privilege, Eckde de Repkaw, could add nothing more, nor could he diminish anything, except according to the Privilege which he had found and translated from Latin into German. For it is permitted to no one to extend or diminish rights, except the Emperor.

units.la: Eadem, lib. 3. artic. 44. Novae leges coeperunt à Constantino, à quo & ius Saxonibus traditum est, & reliquis, etiamque permixtae & inordinatae. Postea vero Theodosius minor Augustus, ad similitudinem Gregoriani & Hermogeniani Codicem factum Constitutionum, à Constantini temporibus, sub proprio cuiusque Imperatoris titulo, dispo-&c.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 44: New laws began with Constantine, from whom law was also handed down to the Saxons and to the others, and they were mixed together and disordered. Later, however, Theodosius the Younger, Augustus, made a code of constitutions, similar to the Gregorian and Hermogenian codes, from the times of Constantine, under each emperor's own title, arranged, etc.

units.la: Eadem d.lib.3.artic.54. Tractatur hic de electione Regis Romanorum; excerpta, est lex praesens per translatorem Privilegii, ex Constitutionibus Caroli Imperatoris, cum Imperium Theutonicis tradidit. Quicquid enim hic docetur de Imperatoribus Imperioque, non habetur in Legibus, ut Accursius dicit Instit. de iur. nat. gent. & civ. § sed & quod.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 54: This treats of the election of the King of the Romans. This present law is excerpted by the translator of the privilege from the constitutions of Emperor Charles, when he handed the Empire over to the Teutons. For whatever is taught here about emperors and empire is not found in the laws, as Accursius says, Inst. de iur. nat. gent. et civ., § sed et quod.

units.la: Eadem, d.lib.3.artic.65. Super intellectu articuli praesentis, nonnulla fuerunt opiniones & controversiae. Quidam Burchardus Episcopus Magdeburgensis & Comes Otto de Falckenstein, intelligere voluerunt articulum, &c. Alii Radus de Dreuenlehen, & Conradus de Roslaw, intelligere textum voluerunt, &c. Alii vero, ut Henricus de Bethiedrius de Lemwerden, textum intelligere voluerunt, &c. Hi sunt veteres interpretes huius Speculi Saxonici. Vixit autem hic Burchardus Episcopus Magdeburgensis sub tribus Imperatoribus, Primo, Henrico VII. & Ludovico V. Bauaro, promotus in sedem anno 1307, demortuus anno.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 65: Concerning the understanding of the present article, there were various opinions and controversies. Some, Burchard, Bishop of Magdeburg, and Count Otto of Falckenstein, wished to understand the article, etc. Others, Radus of Dreuenlehen and Conrad of Roslaw, wished to understand the text, etc. But others, such as Henry of Bethiedrius of Lemwerden, wished to understand the text, etc. These are the old interpreters of this Saxon Mirror. This Burchard, Bishop of Magdeburg, lived under three emperors: first Henry VII and Louis V of Bavaria. He was promoted to the see in 1307 and died in the year ...

units.la: Eadem, d.lib.3.artic.78. Caute intelligi debet § ille, nec ita grosse, ut infensat, &c. Vasallus contra dominum non invenire non potest; quod tamen toleratius est, quam quod dominum detinere debeat. Ergo ei facere non licet, nec ei licebit id, quod est maius, ut Instit. quib. alien. licet vel non, & ff. de regul. iur. 1. non debet. Etiam habetur Vasallorum, Ex quib. cauff feud amittat. ubi iuratur domino esse auxilio contra vnumquemque: quod non esset, si eum ut hic textus disponit. Habetur etiam 11. q. vlt. de forma. quod vasallus dominum tueri debet ab omni damno; quod esset. Quidam dicunt, quod lex ista corrigit & derogat aliis legibus in contrarium. Respondeo, quod nova lex corrigit: sed Ius Feudale posterius est Saxonico: quare istud non derogat illi. Dicunt etiam quidam, quod Ius Feudale est: quia lex posterius constituta, quae est contraria priori, derogat illi, &c.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 78: The § ille must be understood cautiously, and not so crudely as it is hostile, etc. A vassal cannot fail to find against the lord; which nevertheless is more tolerable than that he should detain the lord. Therefore it is not lawful for him to do so, nor will it be lawful for him to do what is greater, as in Inst. quib. alien. licet vel non, and ff. de regul. iur., l. non debet. It is also held in the Vassals, Ex quib. caus. feud. amittat, where it is sworn to be of help to the lord against everyone, which would not be so if he disposed as this text does. It is also held, 11 q. ult., de forma, that the vassal ought to protect the lord from every harm, which would be... Some say that this law corrects and derogates from other laws to the contrary. I reply that the new law corrects; but the Feudal Law is later than the Saxon, wherefore this does not derogate from that. Some also say that the Feudal Law is later, because a law constituted later, which is contrary to an earlier one, derogates from it, etc.

units.la: Glossa hoc loco respicit ad Carolum Magnum, à quo praesumit hoc Ius Saxonicum provinciale Privilegium Saxonum appellat, esse constitutum; & ideo vetustius esse iure Feudali, quod à Imperatore originem ceperit, ut patet ex sequentibus verbis.
units.tr: This gloss here refers to Charles the Great, by whom it presumes this Saxon provincial law was established. It calls it the privilege of the Saxons, and therefore it is older than feudal law, which took its origin from the Emperor, as is clear from the following words.

units.la: Eadem, lib. 1. artic. 14. Ex quo itaque Provinciale ius antiquius est Feudali, quare & constitutiones Provinciales sequentes iuris Feudalis leges annullari deberent. Carolus enim Magnus, Ius Provinciale Saxonibus statuit: Fre-Imperator Ius Feudale; ut in aliis de vsib. feudor. collat. 10.
units.tr: The same, book 1, art. 14: Since therefore provincial law is older than feudal law, the later provincial constitutions should also annul the laws of feudal law. For Charles the Great established provincial law for the Saxons; the Emperor Frederick established feudal law, as in the others, on the uses of fiefs, collation 10.

units.la: Eadem, lib.3.artic.83. Auctor huius Constitutionis, & duarum sequentium, fuit Otto Primus Magnus Imperatorum.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 83: The author of this constitution, and of the two following, was Otto I, the Great, of the emperors.

units.la: Glossa posteriori in d. lib. 3. art. 82. Privilegium praefens largitum est Saxonibus in Saxenburgo, ab Imperatore anno Domini octingentesimo decimo, anno septimo Imperii sui, die decima Ianuarii: meritoque nomen Dni illius ImpeImperatoris huius operi praponitur. Iura enim & leges id suadent, vt priuilegia omnibus nominatim Imperatorum pu-blicentur, &c.
units.tr: Later gloss on the same book 3, art. 82: The present privilege was granted to the Saxons at Saxenburg by the Emperor in the year of the Lord 810, the seventh year of his reign, on the tenth day of January. And rightly the name of that lord emperor is placed before this work. For laws and rights advise that privileges be published to all by naming the emperors, etc.

units.la: Eadem, d.lib.3 artic.39. Ad renouandum omnem iuris difficultatem, quodque ius complexum habetur, ea-que liquid, quod necessarium fit, omittatur: ancitor priuilegii Eike de Repkaw dei Larare intendit, quod Lacer ... &c. Non tamen opinari quis debet, quod solus ipse Eike, qui auctor priuilegii est, & qui ex Latino in Germanicum priuilegium traduxit, passim ...
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 39: To renew all the difficulty of the law, and what is held as a complex law, and whatever is clear that is necessary be omitted: the author of the privilege, Eike de Repkaw, intends that the Lacer ... etc. Yet no one should think that Eike alone, who is the author of the privilege and who translated the privilege from Latin into German, everywhere ...

units.la: Eadem, d.lib.3. artic. 83. Constitutio praesensis est Ottonis Imperatoris, qua pro confirmatione & renovatione iurium per Carolum Imperatorem Saxonibus sanctiorum lata est.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 83: The present constitution is that of Emperor Otto, by which, for the confirmation and renewal of the rights sanctioned for the Saxons by Emperor Charles, was enacted.

units.la: Eadem, d.l.3. artic. 85. Constitutio praefens est Imperatoris Ottonis Russi, Magni Ottonis filii, anno ... perii sui.
units.tr: The same, book 3, art. 85: The present constitution is that of Emperor Otto the Red, son of Otto the Great, in the year ... of his reign.

units.la: GLOSSA in proœmio ad Wichbildale Constantino Magno Imperatore
units.tr: GLOSS on the Preface to the Wichbild, concerning the Emperor Constantine the Great

units.la: tandem circa annum Domini CCCXI. Constantinus Magnus, primus Christianorum Imperator, qui ... maximam edidit flagem perdomuit, fideique Christiana initiauit, non tamen in toto conuertit, ... eorum arbitrium edidit.
units.tr: At length, around the year of the Lord 311, Constantine the Great, the first Christian Emperor, who ... subdued the greatest ... and initiated into the Christian faith, yet did not convert them entirely, ... he published their judgment.

units.la: Eadem in proœmio ad Wichbild, de Carolo Magno, Saxonum & Sclauorum ... Prouinciale, quod Speculum Saxonum vocatur, apud nos que in vsu habetur, Saxonibus ipsis in xia eorum arbitrium ...
units.tr: The same, in the preface to the Wichbild, concerning Charles the Great, of the Saxons and Slavs ... The Provincial law, which is called the Mirror of the Saxons and is held in use among us, to the Saxons themselves in ... their judgment ...

units.la: Eadem, artic. 7. Wichbildi: Nona autem Leges à Constantino Cesare, a quo & Saxones tum ... runt, &c.
units.tr: The same, article 7 of the Wichbild: But nine laws from Constantine Caesar, from whom also the Saxons then ... they were, etc.

units.la: Ibidem circa finem glossae: Saxones etenim, reliquiae Macedonici exercitus fuerunt, nauibusque in ... Thuringos subiugarunt, regnaque constituerunt; quae & illa sunt per matrisferunt, quae ad tempora ... Imperatoris, qui eosdem subiugando, Christiana fidei initiauit, utraque prouincia flatuit, &c.
units.tr: Likewise near the end of the gloss: The Saxons were indeed the remnants of the Macedonian army, and with ships ... they subdued the Thuringians and established kingdoms; which are also those ... they bore, which to the times of ... the Emperor, who by subduing them initiated them into the Christian faith, established each province, etc.

units.la: Eadem, artic. 10. Wichbildi: Is etiam (Burchardus de Mangelpheldt) ex mandato Imperatoris Russi) in suis prouincialis seu Speculum Saxonum Commentarium fecit, legibusque & canonibus ... in conclatu sedendo facere coactus. Et illico post: Eike vero de Repkau Speculum Saxonum Latinus litteris ... ad instantiamque Comitis Henrici de Phalckenstein in Germanicum traduxit, &c. Atqui Mangelpheldt ... xit non Ottonis II. cognomento Russi, sed Ottonis IV. Imper. temporibus, cui Frider ... succesfsit.
units.tr: The same, article 10 of the Wichbild: He (Burchard of Mangelfeld, by command of the Emperor Russus) made a commentary on the provincial law, or Mirror of the Saxons, in his ..., and was compelled to sit in the conclave to ... laws and canons. And immediately after: Eike of Repgow, however, translated the Mirror of the Saxons from Latin letters into German at the instance and request of Count Henry of Falkenstein, etc. But Mangelfeld ... not in the time of Otto II, surnamed Russus, but of Otto IV the Emperor, to whom Frederick ... succeeded.

units.la: GLOSSA in Ius Feudale Saxonum, cap.19. Iuxtaque iflud Saxonibus datum à Constantino & Carolo Imperatoribus, & in hunc vsque diem observatur.
units.tr: GLOSS on the Saxon Feudal Law, chapter 19: And according to that which was given to the Saxons by the Emperors Constantine and Charles, and has been observed to this day.

units.la: Otto Magnus Imp. in constitutione de locatione & priuilegio Camerae Imperialis Magdeburgensis, quam habes tom.1. Collectionis Constitutionum Imperialium, sol.215. Consequenter fidelibus nostris dilectis atque illorum successoribus, perpetuam in ea ciuitate pacem, gratiam & libertatem, prout a nobilibus & generosis Constantino & Carolo, egregius Saxonibus atque Prouinciae datum est, vt & honorem & emolumentum iustitiae, secundum iuris formam, generaliter & specialiter, &c.
units.tr: Otto the Great, Emperor, in the constitution on the location and privilege of the Imperial Chamber of Magdeburg, which you have in volume 1 of the Collection of Imperial Constitutions, page 215: Consequently to our beloved faithful subjects and their successors, perpetual peace, grace and liberty in that city, as was given to the Saxons and the Province by the noble and distinguished Constantine and Charles, so that both the honour and the profit of justice, according to the form of law, generally and specially, etc.

units.la: De iuribus a Constantino & Carolo Magno latis vide speciales tractatas in libris iuribus prouincialibus & feudalibus, vulgo dictus Keyserrecht Land vnd Lehenrecht/lib.1.cap.3.§.1 pit.5.§.2.cap.9.cap.10.§.1.cap.12.§.1.cap.98.& cap.186.
units.tr: On the rights granted by Constantine and Charles the Great, see the special treatises in the books of provincial and feudal law, commonly called Keyserrecht, Land und Lehenrecht, book 1 chapter 3 §1, tit. 5 §2, chapter 9, chapter 10 §1, chapter 12 §1, chapter 98 and chapter 186.

units.la: Felix Faber Monachus Vlmensis in Hiltoi. Sueuor. lib.1.cap.3. sol.58. Deducitam Caroli tonicis quasdam Leges in suo idiomate, quae adhuc habentur.
units.tr: Felix Faber, monk of Ulm, in the History of the Swabians, book 1 chapter 3, page 58: He brought down from Charles certain laws in his own language, which are still held.

units.la: Georg. Fabricius Rerum memorabilium Saxon. lib.1. anno DCCCXI. Iura Saxonibus Carolo Imperator confirmat.
units.tr: Georg Fabricius, Memorable Things of Saxony, book 1, year 811: The Emperor Charles confirms the laws for the Saxons.

units.la: Iohan. de Lasko Magnus Cancellarius Regni Poloniae, in praefat. in Priuilegium Coronationum Regni Poloniae, &c. Vt sunt Leges Prouinciales vel Terrestres Speculi Saxonum, quod ab ... Magni maleficiat sanctum fuit, &c.
units.tr: Johannes de Lasko, Grand Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland, in the preface to the Privilege of the Coronations of the Kingdom of Poland, etc.: Such as are the Provincial or Territorial Laws of the Mirror of the Saxons, which from ... of Charles the Great was made holy, etc.

units.la: ALEXANDER Rex Poloniae in Confirmatione Priuilegij statutorum Polonia, &c. alios Prouinciali & Feudali iurium libros, qui Diuorum Caroli & Constantini Imperatorum ... bantur, &c.
units.tr: ALEXANDER, King of Poland, in the confirmation of the privilege of the statutes of Poland, etc.: other Provincial and Feudal law books, which were held to be of the divine Emperors Charles and Constantine, etc.

units.la: IASKIER Secretarius Cracouiensis, in praefat. Articulor Speculi Saxonum, ... lienfi reprobatorum: Et quia inter has Speculi Saxonum constitutiones, nonnulla habentur ... Diuorum olim Constantini & Caroli Imperatorum, Saxonibus cum ad fidem conuersi sunt Ch ... tandum, minus maium, & vt in fide perseuerarent suscepta, admissa, & ad eorundem praeceptum ... firmati, &c.
units.tr: JASKIER, Secretary of Kraków, in the preface to the Articles of the Mirror of the Saxons, ... of the Lithuanians reprobated: And because among these constitutions of the Mirror of the Saxons some are held ... of the divine Emperors Constantine and Charles, when the Saxons were converted to the faith of Christ ... at length, to a lesser evil, and that they might persevere in the faith undertaken, admitted, and by their precept ... confirmed, etc.

units.la: BALDVS I C. Consilio 174. cuius initium, Praesupponendum est, lib. 5. Consilior ... dinem habent & statutum Imperiale Caroli Magni, quod nullus possit alienare bona extra iudicium ... riuum fiat, non valeat alienatio, & proximiores possint reuocare alienationem. Quod consuetudo valet, & habitatio ... in Ecclesiam fieret alienatio.
units.tr: BALDUS, I.C., Consilium 174, whose beginning is: It is to be presupposed, book 5 of the Consilia ... have a statute, and the Imperial statute of Charles the Great, that no one may alienate goods outside judgment ... becomes a river, the alienation is not valid, and nearer relatives may revoke the alienation. Because custom holds, and habitation ... into the Church there would be an alienation.

units.la: Adde Dominicum TVSCVM Cardinalem Romanum, Practicar. Conclusio. lib. 7. lit. S. conclus. 49. Hactenus appositumus testimonia, quorum & similium aliqua ... tuntur, qui hoc Speculum Saxonum ad Carolum Magnum Imperatorem refert. Ille qui iuuat doctissimi Canonici Hamburgensis iudicium iubneclere, quod habet in hunc modum ...
units.tr: Add Dominicus Tuscus, Cardinal of Rome, Practicarum Conclusiones, book 7, letter S, conclusion 49. Hitherto we have set down testimonies, some of which and similar ones ... are held, who refer this Mirror of the Saxons to the Emperor Charles the Great. He who helps the judgment of the most learned canon of Hamburg ... to set out, which he has in this manner ...

units.la: Albert. KRANTZIVS in sua Saxonia lib.2. cap.21. In commemoratione Iornandis non debemus, quod gens nostra de illo inflatu prodiit et buccis, dedisse illum Leges Saxonibus, quae ... vocant, extant recollectae, & ad quidem refert Mosfator in annum decimum post ... [illegible, ~40 letters] um vero Imperij eius annum (vt memorat) in arce Saffenborg. Primam commenit suspicionem fecit, quod animo Carolo et Karolini Imperij Gloffator ille perturbat. Dccc1. enim factus est Imperator Karolus: et ideo decimus Christi quoque decimus Imperij. Deinde quod diligentissimi Scriptores illorum temporum, nullam eius rei faciunt mentionem minora multo plurima commemorarent. Nec erat illa in populo barbaro ciuilitas, vt Leges initio requirerent, praesertim quae vniuerso orbi satis erant. Occultum tamen ludicium (quod vocant) facile crediderim eis permissum propter cer- tum durissimam: sed redactas Leges nouas in Codicem, non facile credo, nisi alia mihi documenta referantur. Nam et prodiit esse collectum Codicem de multis obseruantiis gentis: quomodo et Feudorum vsu non ab Imperatore dati, sed liberto descripti, vsum et obseruantiam meruerunt. Quum enim per aetatem crenit ciuilitas, creuit etiam legum obseruantia. Inde factum est, vt quae per tempora sunt vsu approbata, denique sint in codicem redacta: cui ad authoritatem con- tendam falso est nomen Karoli adscriptum. Idque vt credam, facit multorum in textu, plurium autem in glossa, pue- rorum et melior narratio. Nam temporum fuit vterque et Speculator et Gloffator, imperitus. Temerarius calumniator ... lucem clarius vtrumque conuincam. Longum est cunctas percurrere: vnum aliquem de textu passum summamus, ... decernu facile coniecturam facientes: et non modo coniecturam, sed fidem pene oculatam. Originem Regnorum, Saxonum antiquitatem volens ostendere textus lib. 4. artic. 44. ait: In Babylonia coepit Imperium, &c. Haec ... Speculi. Non enim iubet, disponit, interpretatur (vt solet Legislator) sed commemorat, quid obseruetur: quod est Imperatoris, sed Doctoris. Et tamen videamus, quanta sint in paucis verbis friuola commenta, vt liquido cernamus, ... iauiuorajje Karolum, qui et ipse doctus erat, et doctissimus stipabatur. In Babylonia, inquit, coepit Imperium. Iuxta Babylonis loquitur ex sacris literis, tam altius ascendit, quam solent illae hystoriae, vt de Nemroth sumas initium. ... en ex illa Babylone non prouenit Imperium, sed dispersio gentium: quam ostendit Moses, et plenius exequitur Berosus ... nus. Si autem de Regno loquitur Babylonico, non hoc fuit primum, sed Assyriorum in Nino: cuius ciuitatis author et Semiramis continuo primus fuit in omni historia antiquissima. Nam ibi primum constitit Imperium, cui etiam ... in obediunt. Addit, quae toti mundo imperabat. Hoc nulla habent historia, Chaldaeos in Europa vel Africa ... sunt satis et at magnum, si magnam Asiae tenerent partem. Nam neque Romani, quorum latius erat Imperium, toti dominabantur, aliquid in Europa, aliquid in Asia, et totam tenuerunt Africam. Sequitur; Quam Cyrus ex- uauit, et in Persiam transtulit, in qua vsque ad Darium perseueraunt. Quid transtulit? ad quem Darium? Nam Darius erat Cyri nunculus, qui cum magno Cyro res magnas gessit: post Darius Hystaspis filium familiam transtulit Imperium. Sed specificas, quum addat; quem vicit Alexander. Ignorabat illum Arsamidem appellat. Et Imperium, inquit, Graeciae applicauit. Friuolum est: quia nunquam in Graecia ante Constantinum fuit Imperium. Graeci tamen post Alexandrum in Asia imperauerunt, in Syria et Aegypto potissimum. Nam ad Macedonis in Graeciam pari peruenit, et ea non lata. Deinde subnectit nostrer Legislator: Et ibi ilecit vsque dum Romani sibi Imperium assumperunt, et Iulius coepera imperare. Verum est, quod Romani, victo Antiocho Syriae Rege, Regnum ... redegerunt in prouinciam: et superato in Graecia Perse, nouissimo Macedonum Rege, Imperium occupauerunt, relicta ... populis libertate: sed hoc longe ante Iulium. At Aegyptus autem facta est prouincia tempore Caesaris. Deinde quod sequitur de vtraque Romana vrbe potestate, insta tamen ire sinamus: scimus tamen, quot transierunt secula, prius quam spiritualis gladius ... stringeretur. Quod vero ait, quum interim nostri praedecessores ad istam peruenerunt prouinciam: hoc ... contreuerfia Saxo loquitur, non Imperator. Sed quod ait, quum, non apparet, quae tempora figunt. Nam quod Ale- ... et Iulii tempora coniungunt, qui annis pene quingentis distabant, ineptissimum est. Contendit autem Saxones in Asia ... Alexandro. Sed hoc minus pueriliter dixit, vt est inuentum anile et peruum sommum. Quis cum credat gentem ... Asia in nostrum mare peruenisse, quando per aquilonarem regionem, propter mare glaciale, post Hyperboreos mon- tes nauigari? Et Caspium sinum longius distantem quomodo peterent? et inde quo procederent? Quis autem cre- ... esse? In qua terra victores Alexandri Principes sub iugo cuncta tenuerunt, quem timerent victores orbi? Sed hic no- ... bu persuadebat, manere non audebant. Insidia est, vnde ea prodiit narratio. Si legisset, Principes Alexandri ciuilibus bellum se versos, o- ... copias militaris in precio habuisse, non diceret, milites timuisse ab Orientalibus oppressi: qui tanto tam erant sub iugo, ... timerent, non timerentur. Omitto barbarissimos, quos plurimos facit fabulator, vt ea vel maxime reprobat, non esse ... nem Karoli, cuius Scriniarii non ita tituba ssent. Ipse loqueretur in capite, quomodo in Pandectis Imperator, sua fa- ... quibus authoritatem impartitur, quomodo in Codice et Institutionibus, quomodo in nouissimis Authenticis. Sed ca- ... mus. Biremes vult trecentas ex Asia nauigasse. Vnde ea copia nauium fugientibus? Quo nauigauit Classis itine- ... per aquilonarem plagam ostendimus venire non potuisse. Si ex Ponto nauigarent aut ex Syria, longum erat iter ... priusquam ex Babylone peruenirent in mare; et longiore cursu mare tranquillum vsque ad Ga- ... terulis erat ... Quando exibant (vt vis) querendis sedibus, non erat initiore coelo, breuiore itinere, terra, quae susciperet, Pruf- ... sus, vt Rugianique et Albim peterent? non pudet vanitatis? Et quam, oro te, Pruffi, Rugiani, Saxones, eiusdem (vt ... originis et congentiles), vnquam habuerunt aut bello aut pace societatem? Catera videamus. Fugatis Turingo- ... Dominis, &c. Nunquam Turingi nostram tenuere Saxoniam, vt fugarentur: sed inuitati Saxones a Francis in ... ingos, partem Turingiae (quod suo loco ostendimus) pretium militiae acceperunt. Unde nata est fabula de Turingis. Et ne ... videatur omnium literarum, addit de Latino et de Dedititiis, vt ostendat Imperiales se vidisse constitutiones. Ineptissi... aput. Quam, oro te, Latini in Saxonia partem habent? Nolo immorari in re, quam etiam pueri possunt corrigere. ... talia comperies: vt liquido comprobemus, non esse Karoli editionem, quod preferunt Speculum.
units.tr: Albert. KRANTZIVS in his Saxonia, lib. 2, cap. 21: In the commemoration of Jornandes we ought not to pass over that our nation sprang from that windbag and braggart, and that he gave laws to the Saxons, which ... they call, are extant in a collection, and he refers them to the year Mosfator (so he says) ... in the year of his reign, in the castle of Saffenborg. [illegible] The first ground for suspicion is that the author of this Gloss was disturbed by the mind of Charles and the Carolingian empire. For Charles was made emperor in 800, and so it was also the tenth year of Christ and the tenth of his empire. Next, the most diligent writers of those times make no mention of this matter, though they record many much smaller things. Nor was there such civility among that barbarous people that they would at first require laws, especially when those in use were enough for the whole world. I could readily believe that a secret judgement (as they call it) was permitted them on account of a certain harshness; but that the new laws were afterwards gathered into a Code, I do not easily believe unless other evidence is brought to me. For it is known that a Code of many customs of the people was also collected; just as the customs of the Feudal law, not given by an emperor but written down by a freedman, earned their use and observance. For as civility grew with the passing of time, so too did the observance of the laws grow. Hence it came about that what had been approved by use through the ages was at last reduced to a code, and to this code, to win authority for it, the name of Charles was falsely attached. That I believe this is shown by the better narrative of many things in the text and of more in the gloss, for boys. For both the Speculator and the Glossator were inexperienced men of their time. A rash slanderer ... I will convict both more clearly than the light. It would be long to run through them all; let us take up one passage from the text ... deciding easily, making a conjecture, and not only a conjecture but an almost eyewitness faith. Wishing to show the origin of kingdoms and the antiquity of the Saxons, the text of book 4, article 44, says: "The empire began in Babylonia," etc. These ... of the Mirror. For it does not command, arrange or interpret (as a lawgiver usually does) but recounts what is observed; which is the work of a historian, not an emperor. And yet let us see how many frivolous inventions there are in a few words, so that we may plainly perceive ... that Charles, who was himself learned and surrounded by the most learned, was misled. "The empire," he says, "began in Babylonia." If he speaks of Babylon from the sacred letters, he ascends as high as those histories usually do, taking his beginning from Nimrod. ... Yet from that Babylon the empire did not arise, but the dispersion of the nations, which Moses shows and Berosus follows out more fully ... If, however, he speaks of the Babylonian kingdom, this was not the first, but that of the Assyrians under Ninus, whose city's founder, Semiramis, was continually the first in all the most ancient history. For there the empire first stood, to which also ... they obey. He adds that it ruled the whole world. No history has this; the Chaldeans in Europe or Africa ... are enough, and it would be great if they held a great part of Asia. For neither did the Romans, whose empire was wider, rule the whole world: they held something in Europe, something in Asia, and they held the whole of Africa. He follows on: "which Cyrus stripped and transferred into Persia, where they continued until Darius." Transferred what? And to which Darius? For Darius was a kinsman of Cyrus, who accomplished great things with the great Cyrus; afterwards Darius, son of Hystaspes, transferred the empire to his own house. But you are specific, since you add: "whom Alexander conquered." He did not know it, and calls him Arsames. "And he handed the empire," he says, "to Greece." This is frivolous, because there was never an empire in Greece before Constantine. Yet after Alexander the Greeks ruled in Asia, chiefly in Syria and Egypt; for the Macedonians came into Greece in equal measure, and that not widely. Then our lawgiver adds: "And there it remained until the Romans assumed the empire, and Julius began to rule." It is true that the Romans, after defeating Antiochus, king of Syria, reduced the kingdom ... into a province, and after overcoming Perseus, the last king of the Macedonians, in Greece, they seized the empire, leaving the peoples their liberty; but this was long before Julius. Yet Egypt became a province in the time of Caesar. Next, as to what follows about the power of each Roman city, let us allow it to pass for now; we know, however, how many ages passed before the spiritual sword ... was drawn. But as to what he says, "when meanwhile our predecessors came to that province," this ... the Saxon speaks in the controversy, not the emperor. But that he says "when," does not show what times he means. For to join the times of Alexander and Julius, who were nearly five hundred years apart, is most absurd. Moreover, he contends that the Saxons were in Asia ... under Alexander. But he said this less childishly, since it is an invented, old-womanish and most unlikely tale. Who could believe that a people came from Asia into our sea, when one must sail by the northern region, past the Hyperborean mountains because of the icy sea? And how would they make for the Caspian gulf, which lies farther off, and from there where would they go? Who again would believe ... to be? In what land did the victors of Alexander, the princes, hold everything under the yoke, whom would the victors of the world fear? But here ... he was persuading, they did not dare to remain. The trap is whence that narrative came. If he had read that the princes of Alexander turned to civil war, ... valued the military forces, he would not say that the soldiers feared the Orientals, who were oppressed by so great a yoke ... they feared, they were not feared. I omit the barbarous terms which the fabulist makes in great number, which by that very fact he most of all condemns as not ... of Charles, whose secretaries were not so stammering. He would speak in the chapter as the emperor does in the Pandects, whose ... by which he imparts authority, as in the Code and Institutes, as in the most recent Authentics. But let us pass on. He wants three hundred biremes to have sailed from Asia. From where did so great a supply of ships come to these fugitives? Where did the fleet sail? ... we have shown it could not have come by the northern region. If they sailed from Pontus or from Syria, the journey was long ... before they arrived from Babylon at the sea; and by a longer course the sea was calm as far as ... was there ... When they went out (as you wish) to seek homes, was there no earth nearer the sky, by a shorter route, to receive them, that the Prussians ... so that the Rugians and Saxons might make for the Elbe?
